\end{longtable}
}

Water has a disproportionately high heat of vaporisation relative to its
molecular weight --- a direct consequence of its extensive hydrogen
bonding.

\textbf{Thermodynamic decomposition.} The high \(\Delta_{\text{vap}}H\)
is dominated by the enthalpic cost of breaking H-bonds. On vaporisation
each molecule loses about 3.4 H-bonds; if each is worth about 10 kJ/mol
on rupture, the net enthalpy is about 34 kJ/mol from H-bonds alone after
correcting for double-counting of shared bonds, matched by about 7
kJ/mol from the work of expansion (\(P\Delta V\)) and other
contributions. The corresponding entropy gain on vaporisation is
\(\Delta_{\text{vap}}S \approx \Delta_{\text{vap}}H/T_b \approx 109\) J
mol\(^{-1}\) K\(^{-1}\) (Trouton's rule predicts about 85 J mol\(^{-1}\)
K\(^{-1}\) for ``normal'' liquids; water's higher value reflects the
unusually structured liquid state). The enormous
\(\Delta_{\text{vap}}H\) is what makes evaporative cooling so efficient:
each gram of sweat carries away the energy needed to disassemble its
share of the H-bond network.

\subsubsection{High Surface Tension (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma} = 72.8 mN/m at 20 degrees
C)}\label{high-surface-tension-ux3b3-72.8-mnm-at-20-degrees-c}

Surface molecules have fewer neighbours to form H-bonds with, creating a
net inward force. Water's surface tension is among the highest of common
liquids (except mercury). This allows:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Insects (water striders) to walk on water --- their legs distribute
  body weight across about 2 cm\(^2\) of surface area,
  resulting in pressure below the surface tension threshold
\item
  Capillary action: water rises in narrow tubes against gravity,
  critical for tall plants (see
  \cref{sec:unit_VIII_plant_structure_and_water})
\item
  Pulmonary alveolar \hyperref[gl:surfactant]{\textbf{surfactant}}
  (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine, DPPC) reduces surface tension to
  about 25 mN/m to prevent lung collapse during expiration
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome
(NRDS)}

Premature infants often lack sufficient pulmonary surfactant because
type II pneumocytes do not mature until about 35 weeks of
gestation. Without surfactant, alveolar surface tension is too high, and
alveoli collapse during expiration (atelectasis). The infant must expend
enormous energy to re-inflate collapsed alveoli with each breath.
Treatment involves administering exogenous surfactant (e.g., beractant)
directly into the trachea. The development of synthetic surfactant
therapy in the 1980s dramatically reduced neonatal mortality.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Density Anomaly --- Ice
Floats}\label{density-anomaly-ice-floats}

Liquid water is denser than ice because the hexagonal lattice of ice
(perfect tetrahedral H-bond geometry) is less compact than the
fluctuating, partially broken H-bond network of liquid water. This
causes:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Ice floats, so aquatic ecosystems are insulated below, preventing
  freeze-solid
\item
  Maximum density at 4 degrees C, so lakes stratify with cold water at 4
  degrees C at the bottom
\item
  Floating sea ice reflects solar radiation (albedo effect),
  contributing to climate regulation
\end{itemize}

If ice were denser than water, as is the case for nearly most other
substances, lakes and oceans would freeze from the bottom up, making
most aquatic life unsustainable in temperate climates where water bodies
freeze seasonally.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 2:} If ice sank instead of floated, how would this
affect lake ecosystems during winter? Consider both the physical
arrangement and biological consequences.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Water as a Solvent}\label{water-as-a-solvent}

\subsubsection{Hydrophilic Interactions and the Hydration
Shell}\label{hydrophilic-interactions-and-the-hydration-shell}

\textbf{Hydrophilic} (``water-loving'') molecules carry polar groups or
charges that interact favourably with water molecules via hydrogen
bonding or electrostatic attraction. When ionic compounds dissolve in
water, each ion is surrounded by a \textbf{hydration shell} of oriented
water molecules:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Na\(^+\): surrounded by about 6 water molecules (O pointing
  toward Na\(^+\))
\item
  Cl\(^-\): surrounded by about 8 water molecules (H pointing
  toward Cl\(^-\))
\item
  Mg\(^{2+}\): surrounded by about 6 water molecules held very
  tightly (residence time about 1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}s vs.~about 10 ps
  for Na\(^+\))
\end{itemize}

The energy cost of separating the ionic lattice is offset by the energy
released from forming the hydration shell. This balance is captured by
the \textbf{Born equation} for the free energy of ion solvation:

\[\Delta G_{\text{solv}} = -\frac{z^2 e^2 N_A}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 r}\left(1 - \frac{1}{\varepsilon_r}\right) \tag{2.2} \label{eq:unit_I_water_and_life_item_2}\]

where \(z\) is the ion charge, \(r\) is the ionic radius, and
\(\varepsilon_r\) is the dielectric constant of the solvent.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0019_3d0d11815c85.png}
\caption{Sequence diagram for Hydrophilic Interactions and the Hydration Shell showing ordered interaction among Na+ Ion, Water Molecule 1, Water Molecule 2, and Water Molecule 3.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{The Dielectric Constant and Electrostatic
Screening}\label{the-dielectric-constant-and-electrostatic-screening}

Water's high dielectric constant (\(\varepsilon\) = 78.5 at 25 degrees
C) dramatically weakens electrostatic interactions between charges.
Coulomb's law in a medium:

\[F = \frac{q_1 q_2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r r^2} \tag{2.3} \label{eq:unit_I_water_and_life_item_3}\]

In water, the force between two charges is reduced by a factor of 78.5
compared to vacuum. This is why NaCl (lattice energy 787 kJ/mol)
dissolves readily in water but not in hexane (\(\varepsilon\) = 1.9).

\subsubsection{Hydrophobic Effect}\label{hydrophobic-effect}

\textbf{Hydrophobic} (``water-fearing'') molecules carry nonpolar groups
(C--H, C--C) that cannot H-bond with water. When forced into aqueous
solution, surrounding water molecules form a rigid, ordered cage
(\textbf{clathrate structure}) to maintain their H-bonding network. This
\textbf{decreases entropy} (\(\Delta S < 0\)).

The \textbf{hydrophobic effect} is therefore driven by entropy:
aggregating nonpolar molecules together minimises the clathrate-ordered
water, restoring freedom to bulk water molecules (\(\Delta S\)
increases). The free energy change is:

\[\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S \tag{2.4} \label{eq:unit_I_water_and_life_item_4}\]

Because \(\Delta S\) is positive (entropy of the system increases) and
\(\Delta H \approx 0\) (van der Waals interactions in the nonpolar
aggregate are similar to water-water interactions), \(\Delta G < 0\) ---
the aggregation is spontaneous.

\textbf{Quantitative aspects:} The transfer free energy of a hydrocarbon
chain from water to a nonpolar environment is approximately --3.1 kJ/mol
per CH\(_2\) group. For a 16-carbon palmitic acid tail, the hydrophobic
driving force is roughly 50 kJ/mol per chain --- a substantial
thermodynamic force.

The hydrophobic effect explains: - \textbf{Lipid bilayer formation} ---
phospholipid tails aggregate, forming the barrier of cell membranes (see
\cref{sec:unit_II_membrane_transport}) -
\textbf{\hyperref[gl:protein]{Protein} folding} --- hydrophobic side
chains buried in the core; hydrophilic on surface - \textbf{Micelle
formation} --- soap molecules orient with polar heads facing water,
nonpolar tails inside - \textbf{Drug partitioning} --- the octanol-water
partition coefficient (\(\log P\)) predicts drug membrane permeability

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 3:} Why does the hydrophobic effect become
stronger at higher temperatures? Consider the \(T\Delta S\) term in the
Gibbs free energy equation.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Amphipathic Molecules and
Self-Assembly}\label{amphipathic-molecules-and-self-assembly}

Molecules with both hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions are
\textbf{amphipathic} (also called amphiphilic). Their self-assembly
behaviour depends on geometry:

The \textbf{critical micelle concentration (CMC)} is the concentration
above which amphipathic molecules spontaneously form micelles. For SDS,
CMC = 8.2 mM; for bile salts, CMC = 2--12 mM depending on the species.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Osmotic Pressure --- The van 't Hoff
Equation}\label{osmotic-pressure-the-van-t-hoff-equation}

When a selectively permeable membrane separates solutions of different
solute concentrations, \textbf{water moves from low solute (high water
potential) to high solute (low water potential)} by
\hyperref[gl:osmosis]{\textbf{osmosis}}.

\subsubsection{Derivation of the van 't Hoff
Equation}\label{derivation-of-the-van-t-hoff-equation}

The osmotic pressure can be derived from the chemical potential of
water. The chemical potential of water in a solution is:

\[\mu_{\text{water}} = \mu^{\circ}_{\text{water}} + RT\ln a_w \tag{2.5} \label{eq:unit_I_water_and_life_item_5}\]

where \(a_w\) is the water activity. For dilute ideal solutions,
\(a_w \approx 1 - x_s\) where \(x_s\) is the mole fraction of solute.
Using the approximation \(\ln(1-x) \approx -x\) for small \(x\):

\[\mu_{\text{water}} \approx \mu^{\circ}_{\text{water}} - RTx_s \tag{2.6} \label{eq:unit_I_water_and_life_item_6}\]

The osmotic pressure is the external pressure needed to restore the
chemical potential to that of pure water:

\[\pi \bar{V} = RTx_s \tag{2.7} \label{eq:unit_I_water_and_life_item_7}\]

For dilute solutions, \(x_s \approx n_s/n_w\) and
\(n_w\bar{V} \approx V\), giving the \textbf{van 't Hoff equation}:

\[\pi = iCRT \tag{2.8} \label{eq:unit_I_water_and_life_item_8}\]

where: - \textbf{\(i\)} = van 't Hoff factor (number of particles per
formula unit; 2 for NaCl -\textgreater{} Na\(^+\) + Cl\(^-\)) -
\textbf{\(C\)} = molar solute concentration (mol L\(^{-1}\)) -
\textbf{\(R\)} = 8.314 J mol\(^{-1}\) K\(^{-1}\) - \textbf{\(T\)} =
temperature in Kelvin

\subsubsection{Worked Examples}\label{worked-examples-1}

\textbf{Example 1 --- Blood plasma osmotic pressure:} Blood plasma
osmolarity is about 0.3 Osm (made up of NaCl, glucose, proteins, etc.).
Using \(i \cdot C_{\text{total}}\) = 0.3 mol/L, T = 310 K:

\[\pi = 0.3 \times 8.314 \times 310 = 773 \; \text{kPa} \approx 7.6 \; \text{atm} \tag{2.9} \label{eq:unit_I_water_and_life_item_9}\]

This means a 7.6 atm pressure difference would be required to completely
prevent osmotic water movement --- illustrating why
\hyperref[gl:turgor-pressure]{\textbf{turgor pressure}} is critical for
plant cell rigidity (see
\cref{sec:unit_VIII_plant_structure_and_water}).

\textbf{Example 2 --- Sucrose solution:} What osmotic pressure is
generated by a 0.5 M sucrose solution at 25 degrees C? Sucrose does not
dissociate, so \(i = 1\):

\[\pi = 1 \times 0.5 \times 8.314 \times 298 = 1,239 \; \text{kPa} \approx 12.2 \; \text{atm} \tag{2.10} \label{eq:unit_I_water_and_life_item_10}\]

This is why plant cells can generate enormous turgor pressures ---
enough for roots to crack concrete.

\textbf{Example 3 --- Intravenous fluids:} A nurse prepares an isotonic
saline drip using NaCl. What concentration is needed? Plasma osmolarity
= 0.3 Osm; NaCl \(i = 2\):

\[C = \frac{0.3}{2} = 0.15 \; \text{M} = 0.15 \times 58.44 = 8.77 \; \text{g/L} \approx 0.9\% \tag{2.11} \label{eq:unit_I_water_and_life_item_11}\]

This is the basis for ``normal saline'' (0.9\% NaCl), almost universally
used in clinical settings.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome}

When hyponatraemia (low blood sodium, \textless{} 135 mM) is corrected
too rapidly with hypertonic saline, brain cells --- which had adapted to
low osmolarity by losing organic osmolytes --- suddenly find themselves
in a hypertonic environment. Water rushes out of
\hyperref[gl:neuron]{\textbf{neuron}}s and oligodendrocytes, causing
demyelination of pontine neurons. This \textbf{osmotic demyelination
syndrome} (formerly called central pontine myelinolysis) causes
devastating neurological damage including ``locked-in syndrome.'' The
safe correction rate is less than 8 mM/24 h.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Diffusion --- Fick's First
Law}\label{diffusion-ficks-first-law}

Small molecules move passively down their \textbf{concentration
gradients} by Brownian motion --- diffusion. Fick's First Law describes
the net flux \(J\) (mol m\(^{-2}\) s\(^{-1}\)):

\[J = -D \frac{d[C]}{dx} \tag{2.12} \label{eq:unit_I_water_and_life_item_12}\]

where: - \textbf{\(D\)} = diffusion coefficient (m\(^2\) s\(^{-1}\)) ---
depends on molecule size, shape, and temperature - \textbf{\(d[C]/dx\)}
= concentration gradient (mol m\(^{-4}\))

The negative sign indicates flux is in the direction of decreasing
concentration.

\subsubsection{The Stokes-Einstein
Equation}\label{the-stokes-einstein-equation}

The diffusion coefficient is predicted by the Stokes-Einstein equation:

\[D = \frac{k_B T}{6\pi\eta r} \tag{2.13} \label{eq:unit_I_water_and_life_item_13}\]

where \(k_B\) is the Boltzmann constant, \(T\) is temperature, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\eta}}{eta} is
solvent viscosity, and \(r\) is the hydrodynamic radius of the solute.
This equation predicts that:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Larger molecules diffuse more slowly (\(D \propto 1/r\))
\item
  Higher temperature increases diffusion (\(D \propto T\))
\item
  More viscous media slow diffusion (\(D \propto 1/\eta\))
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Reference diffusion coefficients at 37 degrees C:}

\endlastfoot

Glucose & \(6.7 \times 10^{-10}\) & 0.37 \\

\subsubsection{Mean Diffusion Distance and Biological
Design}\label{mean-diffusion-distance-and-biological-design}

\textbf{Mean diffusion distance:} \(\bar{x} = \sqrt{2Dt}\).

For O\(_2\) to diffuse 1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m in water:
\(t = x^2/2D = (10^{-6})^2/(2 \times 2.1 \times 10^{-9}) \approx 0.24 \; \text{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}s}\).
For 1 mm: \(t \approx 238 \; \text{s} \approx 4 \; \text{min}\).

This is why multicellular organisms exceeding about 1 mm
require \textbf{circulatory systems} --- diffusion alone is too slow. It
also explains why:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Mitochondria are typically \textless{} 1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m wide (O\(_2\) diffusion
  time \textless{} 1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}s)
\item
  Capillaries are spaced no more than about 100 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m apart in
  metabolically active tissues
\item
  Alveolar walls are about 0.2 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m thick (gas exchange must be nearly
  instantaneous)
\item
  Neurons require active transport along axons (diffusion over 1 m would
  take about 16 years!)
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Biological Applications of Fick's
Law}\label{biological-applications-of-ficks-law}

\textbf{Application 1 --- Oxygen delivery to muscle fibres:}

During exercise, the O\(_2\) concentration at the capillary wall is
approximately 0.13 mM, and at the centre of a muscle fibre (radius 25
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m) it drops to 0.01 mM. The flux across the fibre radius:

\[J = -D\frac{\Delta C}{\Delta x} = -(2.1 \times 10^{-9})\frac{(0.01 - 0.13) \times 10^3}{25 \times 10^{-6}} = 1.0 \times 10^{-2} \; \text{mol m}^{-2}\text{s}^{-1} \tag{2.14} \label{eq:unit_I_water_and_life_item_14}\]

\textbf{Application 2 --- CO\(_2\) removal from tissues:}

CO\(_2\) produced by \hyperref[gl:aerobic]{\textbf{aerobic}} metabolism
(\(D = 1.9 \times 10^{-9}\) m\(^2\)/s in water) must diffuse from
mitochondria to capillaries. Because CO\(_2\) diffuses about 20 times
faster in air than O\(_2\) in water, gas exchange in the lungs is
limited primarily by O\(_2\) diffusion, not CO\(_2\).

\textbf{Application 3 --- Neurotransmitter diffusion in the synaptic
cleft:}

The synaptic cleft is about 20 nm wide. For acetylcholine
(\(D \approx 5 \times 10^{-10}\) m\(^2\)/s):

\[t = \frac{x^2}{2D} = \frac{(20 \times 10^{-9})^2}{2 \times 5 \times 10^{-10}} = 4 \times 10^{-7} \; \text{s} = 0.4 \; \text{$\mu$s} \tag{2.15} \label{eq:unit_I_water_and_life_item_15}\]

This submicrosecond diffusion time ensures rapid neurotransmission, far
faster than the about 0.5 ms delay of synaptic transmission
(which is dominated by vesicle fusion and receptor activation).

\subsubsection{Solubility Rules and the Thermodynamics of
Dissolution}\label{solubility-rules-and-the-thermodynamics-of-dissolution}

Whether a solute dissolves in water is governed by the Gibbs free energy
of solution:

\begin{equation}
\Delta G_{\text{soln}} = \Delta H_{\text{soln}} - T\Delta S_{\text{soln}}
\label{eq:unit_I_dissolution_dG}
\end{equation}

The enthalpy term has three contributions: breaking solute-solute
interactions (\(\Delta H_1 > 0\)), breaking solvent-solvent interactions
(\(\Delta H_2 > 0\)), and forming solute-solvent interactions
(\(\Delta H_3 < 0\)). The sign and magnitude of
\(\Delta H_{\text{soln}} = \Delta H_1 + \Delta H_2 + \Delta H_3\)
depends on which set of interactions wins.

The textbook rule ``like dissolves like'' is a shorthand for: when
solute-solvent interactions are similar in strength to the bulk
interactions they replace, \(\Delta H_{\text{soln}} \approx 0\) and the
(usually positive) entropy of mixing drives dissolution. When
interactions differ greatly --- as for ionic salts in nonpolar solvents,
or alkanes in water --- \(\Delta H\) and/or \(\Delta S\) oppose
dissolution and the solute remains in its own phase.

\subsubsection{The Hydrophobic Effect
Quantified}\label{the-hydrophobic-effect-quantified}

The \textbf{hydrophobic effect} is the principal driving force for
protein folding, lipid bilayer assembly, and many ligand-binding
reactions. Despite its name, it is \textbf{not} a force; it is a
thermodynamic consequence of the difficulty water has accommodating
nonpolar surfaces.

When a nonpolar molecule is forced into water, the surrounding waters
cannot form their full complement of H-bonds with it. They preserve
their network by reorienting around the solute, sacrificing
translational and rotational entropy. The free energy cost is dominated
not by enthalpy but by \emph{entropy}:

The entropic origin has a striking signature: the hydrophobic effect
\emph{strengthens} with temperature (up to about 70
\(^\circ\)C) because the \(T\Delta S\) term grows. This is why heat
denatures proteins partly by \emph{favouring} hydrophobic exposure (the
cold-denaturation paradox). A 16-carbon palmitate tail, contributing
about 3 kJ/mol per --CH\(_2\)--, generates about 50
kJ/mol of effective driving force into the membrane interior --- enough
to make membrane partitioning essentially irreversible at biological
concentrations.

\subsubsection{Colligative Property: Osmotic Pressure (van 't
Hoff)}\label{colligative-property-osmotic-pressure-van-t-hoff}

The \textbf{osmotic pressure} of a dilute solution is given by the
\textbf{van 't Hoff equation}:

\begin{equation}
\pi = i\,C\,R\,T
\label{eq:unit_I_vant_hoff}
\end{equation}

where \(i\) is the van 't Hoff factor, \(C\) is the molar solute
concentration, \(R\) is the gas constant, and \(T\) is the absolute
temperature. (We re-derive \cref{eq:unit_I_vant_hoff} from chemical
potential below.)

\textbf{Worked example: the osmotic pressure on a red blood cell.}
Plasma osmolarity is 290 mOsm at body temperature (310 K). What pressure
must the cell membrane withstand if placed in pure water? Using
\cref{eq:unit_I_vant_hoff} with \(iC\) = 0.290 osm L\(^{-1}\):

\[\pi = 0.290 \times 8.314\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1} \times 310\,\text{K} = 747\,\text{kPa} \approx 7.4\,\text{atm} \label{eq:unit_I_water_and_life_item_16}\]

This is the pressure of a vehicle tyre. The lipid bilayer cannot resist
such force --- placed in distilled water, a red blood cell swells and
lyses (haemolysis) within seconds. Plant cells, protected by their rigid
cellulose wall, can sustain similar pressures as turgor; this turgor is
what keeps lettuce crisp and what allows plant roots to crack pavement.

\subsubsection{Water Activity and Biological
Processes}\label{water-activity-and-biological-processes}

\textbf{Water activity} (\(a_w\)) is the effective ``thermodynamic
concentration'' of water and is governed by the same chemical potential
expression that gives osmotic pressure:

\begin{equation}
\mu_w = \mu_w^\circ + RT\ln a_w
\label{eq:unit_I_water_activity}
\end{equation}

Adding solutes lowers \(a_w\) below 1 (pure water), which (i) reduces
the rate of water-dependent reactions including hydrolysis, (ii)
inhibits microbial growth, and (iii) suppresses freezing. Most cellular
processes proceed at \(a_w \gtrsim 0.99\). When \(a_w\) falls below 0.6
(e.g., honey, raisins, dried meat), microbial growth halts entirely ---
the basis of most traditional preservation methods. We will quantify
this further in \S 8 below.

\subsubsection{Proton Hopping --- The Grotthuss
Mechanism}\label{proton-hopping-the-grotthuss-mechanism}

Protons (H\(^+\), actually the hydronium ion H\(_3\)O\(^+\)) diffuse
through water roughly 7\(\times\) faster than any other ion of similar
size. The reason is that protons do not move as discrete particles;
instead, the \emph{charge} hops from one water molecule to the next via
a chain of H-bond rearrangements --- the \textbf{Grotthuss mechanism}
(Theodor von Grotthuss, 1806).

Visualise a chain of H-bonded waters linking a proton donor to a proton
acceptor:

\[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+\cdots\text{H--O--H}\cdots\text{H--O--H}\cdots\text{O--H}\cdots\text{A}^- \label{eq:unit_I_water_and_life_item_17}\]

Concerted reorientation of the O--H bonds along the chain (each
requiring about 1 ps) transports a proton across many molecular
diameters in a few picoseconds, \emph{without} any individual water
moving more than fractions of an angstrom. The effective diffusion
coefficient of H\(^+\) in water (9.3 \(\times\) 10\(^{-9}\) m\(^2\)
s\(^{-1}\)) is dominated by Grotthuss hopping rather than vehicular
diffusion.

\textbf{Biological implications:} - \textbf{ATP synthase.} The F\(_o\)
subunit conducts protons across the mitochondrial inner membrane along a
chain of buried waters and protonatable residues (Asp, Glu, Lys);
rotational coupling drives ATP synthesis. The Grotthuss mechanism allows
fast H\(^+\) flux without bulk water flow. - \textbf{Cytochrome c
oxidase} and other proton pumps shuttle protons through ``proton wires''
--- ordered chains of waters and titratable residues. -
\textbf{Aquaporin proton exclusion.} Aquaporins must allow rapid
H\(_2\)O passage but \textbf{block} proton transport (otherwise membrane
potentials would collapse). They achieve this by reorienting a central
water so its O--H bonds break the H-bond chain, defeating the Grotthuss
mechanism while permitting ``vehicular'' water transport. -
\textbf{Photosystem II.} Splits water into O\(_2\) + 4H\(^+\) + 4e\(^-\)
on the lumenal side of the thylakoid; the four protons join the
proton-motive force via H-bond chains in the protein.

\subsubsection{Ice Nucleation and
Cryopreservation}\label{ice-nucleation-and-cryopreservation}

Pure liquid water can be \textbf{supercooled} to about --40 \(^\circ\)C
before homogeneous ice nucleation forces freezing. In real solutions,
\textbf{heterogeneous nucleation} (initiated by surfaces, dust, or
specialised proteins) usually freezes water far above --40 \(^\circ\)C.
Many bacteria (e.g., \emph{Pseudomonas syringae}) express ice-nucleating
proteins that template ice at --2 \(^\circ\)C, weaponising frost on
plant tissues so the bacteria can colonise the resulting wounds.

Cryopreservation of cells (sperm, oocytes, stem cells, organs) exploits
this thermodynamics. Two strategies:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Slow freezing with cryoprotectants.} Glycerol or DMSO at 1--3
  M lowers the freezing point colligatively (\cref{eq:unit_I_vant_hoff})
  and replaces water in hydrogen bonds at membrane surfaces, preventing
  the membrane damage caused by cellular dehydration. Slow cooling
  (0.5--1 \(^\circ\)C/min) lets water leave cells before intracellular
  ice forms.
\item
  \textbf{Vitrification.} Very high cryoprotectant concentrations
  (50\%+) plus rapid cooling (\textgreater10\(^4\) \(^\circ\)C/min)
  glasses water before any ice nucleates. Used for human oocytes and
  embryos with \textgreater90\% post-thaw survival.
\end{enumerate}

The wood frog (\emph{Rana sylvatica}) survives whole-body freezing for
weeks using a natural variant of strategy 1: liver glycogen is rapidly
converted to glucose at about 0 \(^\circ\)C, raising blood
glucose to about 250 mM (10\(\times\) hyperglycaemia by
mammalian standards). Glucose enters cells and lowers the freezing point
intracellularly, while extracellular ice forms harmlessly.

\subsection{Aquaporins --- Molecular Water
Channels}\label{aquaporins-molecular-water-channels}

\subsubsection{Discovery and Structure}\label{discovery-and-structure}

While water can slowly permeate lipid bilayers by diffusion, many cell
types require rapid water transport. In 1992, Peter Agre discovered
\textbf{aquaporins} (AQPs) --- integral membrane proteins that form
selective water channels. Agre received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in
2003 for this discovery.

Aquaporins are homotetramers, with each subunit forming an independent
water pore. Key structural features:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Hourglass shape:} narrow constriction (2.8 angstroms diameter)
  allows primarily single-file water passage
\item
  \textbf{Two NPA motifs} (Asn-Pro-Ala): meet at the centre of the
  channel, creating a positive electrostatic barrier
\item
  \textbf{Aromatic/arginine (ar/R) selectivity filter:} four residues at
  the extracellular constriction determine selectivity
\item
  \textbf{Proton exclusion mechanism:} the NPA motifs reorient water
  molecules mid-channel, breaking the hydrogen-bond ``wire'' that would
  allow proton hopping
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Aquaporin Family and
Functions}\label{aquaporin-family-and-functions}

reabsorption & High water \\
AQP2 & Kidney collecting duct & ADH-regulated water reabsorption &
Regulated \\
AQP3 & Kidney, skin & Water and glycerol transport & Aquaglyceroporin \\
AQP4 & Brain astrocytes & Brain water homeostasis & High water \\
AQP5 & Salivary glands, lacrimal glands & Secretory water flow & High
water \\
AQP7 & Adipocytes & Glycerol release during lipolysis &
Aquaglyceroporin \\
\end{longtable}
}

A single AQP1 channel transports approximately \(3 \times 10^9\) water
molecules per second --- among the fastest known transport rates for any
channel protein.

\subsubsection{Aquaporins in Disease}\label{aquaporins-in-disease}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus}

\hyperref[gl:mutation]{\textbf{Mutation}}s in the AQP2
\hyperref[gl:gene]{\textbf{gene}} cause \textbf{nephrogenic diabetes
insipidus (NDI)}, a condition where the kidneys cannot concentrate urine
despite adequate levels of antidiuretic
\hyperref[gl:hormone]{\textbf{hormone}} (ADH/vasopressin). Patients
produce up to 20 L of dilute urine per day and must drink enormous
quantities of water to avoid dehydration. The most common inherited form
involves autosomal recessive mutations that cause AQP2 to misfold and be
retained in the endoplasmic reticulum. Acquired NDI can result from
lithium therapy (used in bipolar disorder), which downregulates AQP2
expression via mechanisms involving glycogen synthase kinase-3\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Cerebral Oedema and AQP4}

AQP4, the predominant water channel in brain astrocytes, plays a dual
role in cerebral oedema. In cytotoxic oedema (e.g., ischaemic stroke),
AQP4 facilitates water influx into swelling astrocytes, worsening
damage. In vasogenic oedema (e.g., brain tumours), AQP4 helps clear
excess extracellular water. AQP4 is also the target of autoantibodies in
neuromyelitis optica (NMO/Devic's disease), an autoimmune disorder that
mimics multiple sclerosis.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Colligative Properties}\label{colligative-properties}

\textbf{Colligative properties} depend on the number of dissolved
particles, not their identity. They are direct consequences of water
activity reduction by solutes.

\subsubsection{Boiling Point Elevation and Freezing Point
Depression}\label{boiling-point-elevation-and-freezing-point-depression}

\[\Delta T_b = iK_b m \quad \text{and} \quad \Delta T_f = iK_f m \tag{2.16} \label{eq:unit_I_water_and_life_item_18}\]

where \(K_b\) = 0.512 degrees C/m (ebullioscopic constant) and \(K_f\) =
1.86 degrees C/m (cryoscopic constant) for water, \(m\) is molality
(mol/kg solvent), and \(i\) is the van 't Hoff factor.

\textbf{Worked example:} Blood serum has an effective molality of
about 0.3 m (most solutes combined). Freezing point depression:

\[\Delta T_f = 1 \times 1.86 \times 0.3 = 0.558 \; \text{degrees C} \tag{2.17} \label{eq:unit_I_water_and_life_item_19}\]

Clinical osmometers measure this freezing point depression to determine
serum osmolality. Normal serum freezes at --0.56 degrees C,
corresponding to about 290 mOsm/kg.

\subsubsection{Antifreeze Organisms}\label{antifreeze-organisms}

Many organisms survive sub-zero temperatures using biological antifreeze
strategies:

\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Organism
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Strategy
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Mechanism
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Arctic fish (\emph{Dissostichus}) & Antifreeze glycoproteins (AFGPs) &
Bind ice crystal surfaces, inhibit growth \\
Wood frog (\emph{Rana sylvatica}) & Freeze tolerance + glucose
cryoprotectant & Allows extracellular ice; glucose prevents
intracellular freezing \\
Antarctic midge (\emph{Belgica}) & Dehydration + trehalose & Removes
freezable water \\
Spruce bark beetle & Glycerol accumulation & Colligative freezing point
depression to --40 degrees C \\
Winter rye & Antifreeze proteins + supercooling & Survives to --30
degrees C \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Antifreeze proteins (AFPs)} do not work by colligative effects.
Instead, they bind to specific ice crystal faces via a flat, hydrophobic
ice-binding surface, preventing crystal growth. This creates a
difference between the melting point and the freezing point called
\textbf{thermal hysteresis} (typically 1--5 degrees C). Fish AFPs can
depress the freezing point of blood to --2.5 degrees C, matching the
temperature of polar seawater.

estimate the freezing point depression. Why might the observed freezing

\subsection{Water Activity and Microbial
Growth}\label{water-activity-and-microbial-growth}

\subsubsection{Definition of Water
Activity}\label{definition-of-water-activity}

\textbf{Water activity} (\(a_w\)) is the ratio of the vapour pressure of
water in a solution to that of pure water:

\[a_w = \frac{p}{p^{\circ}} \tag{2.18} \label{eq:unit_I_water_and_life_item_20}\]

Pure water has \(a_w = 1.0\). Adding solutes lowers \(a_w\). For an
ideal dilute solution, \(a_w \approx 1 - x_s\) where \(x_s\) is the mole
fraction of solute.

\subsubsection{Water Activity and Food
Preservation}\label{water-activity-and-food-preservation}

Microorganisms require a minimum \(a_w\) for growth:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Organism Type & Minimum \(a_w\) & Example \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Most bacteria & 0.91 & \emph{Salmonella}, \emph{E. coli} \\
Most yeasts & 0.88 & \emph{Saccharomyces} \\
Most moulds & 0.80 & \emph{Aspergillus} \\
Halophilic bacteria & 0.75 & \emph{Halobacterium} \\
Xerophilic moulds & 0.65 & \emph{Xeromyces bisporus} \\
No microbial growth & \textless{} 0.60 & Honey, dried milk powder \\
\end{longtable}
}

Traditional food preservation methods most work by reducing \(a_w\):

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Salting:} NaCl reduces \(a_w\) (salted fish, cured ham)
\item
  \textbf{Sugaring:} sucrose reduces \(a_w\) (jams, candied fruits,
  honey)
\item
  \textbf{Drying:} evaporation removes water (jerky, raisins, dried
  herbs)
\item
  \textbf{Smoking:} combines drying with antimicrobial phenols
\end{itemize}

after 3,000 years. Using the concept of water activity, explain why
honey is essentially immune to microbial spoilage. Why might diluted
honey be more susceptible to
\hyperref[gl:fermentation]{\textbf{fermentation}}?
\end{quote}

\textbf{Concept Check 9:} Aquaporins permit water passage at

\subsection{Water and Adaptation}\label{water-and-adaptation}

Because every biochemical reaction occurs in or at water, organisms in
water-scarce or water-hostile environments have evolved striking
adaptations to defend their hydration state. Three strategies recur
across the tree of life: tolerate water loss, prevent ice formation, and
economise water turnover.

\textbf{Desiccation tolerance (anhydrobiosis).} Tardigrades, the brine
shrimp \emph{Artemia}, many rotifers, and resurrection plants such as
\emph{Selaginella} can lose more than 95\% of their body water and
revive on rewetting. They replace the hydrogen bonds that normally hold
macromolecules in shape with the disaccharide \textbf{trehalose}
(together with late-embryogenesis-abundant, LEA, proteins), which
vitrifies the cytoplasm into a glass that arrests molecular motion and
prevents protein unfolding and membrane fusion. In this state metabolism
is undetectable and survival extends by orders of magnitude.

\textbf{Freeze avoidance and tolerance.} Because dissolved solute
depresses the freezing point primarily colligatively
(\(\Delta T_f = i K_f m\)), small molecules alone cannot protect a fish
in \(-1.9\ ^\circ\)C seawater. Antarctic notothenioid fish instead
secrete \textbf{antifreeze glycoproteins} that adsorb to nascent ice
crystals and arrest their growth, lowering the freezing point
non-colligatively (thermal hysteresis) by roughly \(1\ ^\circ\)C at
millimolar concentrations. Freeze-\emph{tolerant} wood frogs take the
opposite route: they nucleate ice in extracellular spaces and flood
cells with glucose and glycerol so that intracellular water rarely
freezes.

\textbf{Water economy.} A kangaroo rat can survive on metabolic water
alone without drinking: a nasal countercurrent exchanger recovers most
respiratory water vapour, and its kidney concentrates urine roughly
fivefold above plasma osmolarity. Such osmoregulatory extremes --- from
halophilic archaea balancing molar internal K\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} against a near-saturated
brine exterior, to euryhaline fish reversing the direction of their gill
ion pumps between fresh and salt water --- show that controlling water
potential and solute load (\cref{sec:unit_II_membrane_transport}) is as
much a target of natural selection as any catalytic site.

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-4}

For \textbf{Water --- The Molecule of Life}, frontier biology belongs
inside the evidence logic of the chapter. Chemistry-of-life claims now
connect classical bonding and thermodynamics with AI-guided structure
prediction and experimental validation. The core reading question is
this: water's biological effects depend on hydrogen bonding, colligative
context, interfaces, temperature, and solute identity.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

Use AI biomolecular models as hypothesis generators: compare confidence,
conservation, solvent exposure, and assay evidence before turning a
predicted contact into a biological claim
\citep{abramson2024alphafold3}.

\textbf{Source practice:} For structure and interaction claims, cite
experimental structures when available and treat AlphaFold 3 or AFDB
complex predictions as hypotheses to validate with confidence metrics,
conservation, mutagenesis, binding, or cryo-EM/X-ray/NMR evidence
\citep{abramson2024alphafold3,velankar2026alphafolddb2025,emblebi2026alphafoldcomplexes}.

\subsubsection{Extremophiles and Water}\label{extremophiles-and-water}

\textbf{Halophiles} (e.g., \emph{Halobacterium salinarum}) thrive in
salt-saturated brines where water activity \(a_w\) \textless{} 0.75.
Their protective strategy: accumulate compatible solutes (glycine
betaine, ectoine) to maintain osmotic balance without disrupting
\hyperref[gl:enzyme]{\textbf{enzyme}} function. Remarkably, halophilic
enzymes have evolved surfaces rich in acidic residues (Asp, Glu) that
create a hydration shell even in near-saturated salt solutions.

\textbf{Xerophiles} (e.g., \emph{Artemia} brine shrimp) survive complete
desiccation by replacing water with \textbf{trehalose}, which forms a
glassy matrix. Trehalose H-bonds to membrane phospholipid head groups in
place of water, preserving membrane architecture. Tardigrades (water
bears) can survive in a desiccated state (\textbf{tun}) for decades,
reviving upon rehydration.

\textbf{Thermophiles} face the challenge that hydrogen bonds weaken at
high temperatures. \emph{Thermus aquaticus} enzymes compensate with
increased salt bridges, more compact hydrophobic cores, and proline
substitutions that reduce backbone flexibility.

\textbf{Psychrophiles} in Antarctic ice maintain membrane fluidity by
incorporating polyunsaturated fatty acids and short-chain fatty acids.
Their enzymes have increased flexibility (more glycine residues, fewer
prolines) to maintain activity at sub-zero temperatures --- at the cost
of reduced thermal stability.

\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-4}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Water's polarity and H-bonding network underlie its high heat
  capacity, heat of vaporisation, surface tension, and solvent
  properties.
\item
  Hydrophilic/hydrophobic dichotomy drives membrane bilayer formation,
  protein folding, and micelle structure.
\item
  The hydration shell stabilises ions in solution; water's high
  dielectric constant screens electrostatic interactions.
\item
  Osmotic pressure (\(\pi = iCRT\)) governs water movement across
  semipermeable membranes with profound cellular consequences.
\item
  Fick's First Law (\(J = -D \cdot dC/dx\)) quantifies passive
  solute/gas diffusion; slow diffusion over mm distances necessitates
  circulatory systems.
\item
  Aquaporins are selective water channels critical for renal function,
  brain water homeostasis, and lens transparency; mutations cause
  nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
\item
  Colligative properties (freezing point depression, boiling point
  elevation) are exploited by antifreeze organisms.
\item
  Water activity determines microbial growth limits and is the basis of
  traditional food preservation methods.
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See Unit II (membrane transport and aquaporin
  structure), Unit IX (renal concentration gradients and ADH), and Unit
  VIII (transpiration and \hyperref[gl:xylem]{\textbf{xylem}} tension).
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Key Terms}\label{key-terms-4}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Hydrogen bond:} Weak electrostatic attraction between H bonded
  to N/O/F and another electronegative atom
\item
  \textbf{Hydrophilic:} Water-loving; molecules with polar or charged
  groups
\item
  \textbf{Hydrophobic effect:} Entropy-driven aggregation of nonpolar
  molecules in water
\item
  \textbf{Clathrate:} Ordered cage of water molecules around a nonpolar
  solute
\item
  \textbf{Amphipathic:} Molecules with both hydrophilic and hydrophobic
  regions
\item
  \textbf{Osmosis:} Net water movement across a semipermeable membrane
  down its concentration gradient
\item
  \textbf{Osmotic pressure (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\pi}}{pi}):} Pressure required to prevent osmotic
  water flow
\item
  \textbf{Van 't Hoff equation:} \(\pi = iCRT\); relates osmotic
  pressure to solute concentration
\item
  \textbf{Tonicity:} Relative solute concentration affecting cell volume
\item
  \textbf{Diffusion:} Net movement of molecules down a concentration
  gradient
\item
  \textbf{Fick's First Law:} \(J = -D \cdot dC/dx\); relates flux to
  concentration gradient
\item
  \textbf{Diffusion coefficient (\(D\)):} Measure of molecular mobility
  in a medium
\item
  \textbf{Aquaporin:} Integral membrane protein forming a selective
  water channel
\item
  \textbf{Colligative property:} Solution property depending on particle
  number, not identity
\item
  \textbf{Water activity (\(a_w\)):} Effective concentration of water in
  a solution; determines microbial growth
\item
  \textbf{Antifreeze protein:} Protein that inhibits ice crystal growth
  via thermal hysteresis
\item
  \textbf{Dielectric constant (\(\varepsilon\)):} Measure of a medium's
  ability to screen electrostatic interactions
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Review Questions}\label{review-questions-4}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Draw the hydrogen bonding network around a single water molecule. How
  many H-bonds can one water molecule form, and why?
\item
  Explain why water's heat of vaporisation is biologically important.
  Calculate the volume of sweat that must evaporate to remove 500 kJ of
  heat from the body.
\item
  A red blood cell is placed in a solution of 0.45\% NaCl (\(i = 2\), MW
  = 58.44). Calculate the osmolarity of this solution and predict what
  will happen to the cell.
\item
  Using Fick's First Law, explain why alveolar walls are about 0.2 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m
  thick. What would happen to gas exchange efficiency if they were 10 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m
  thick?
\item
  An aquaporin channel transports \(3 \times 10^9\) water molecules per
  second. If a red blood cell contains 200,000 AQP1 channels, how many
  moles of water pass through the cell membrane per second?
\item
  Explain the molecular mechanism by which aquaporins allow water
  passage but exclude protons (H\(^+\) / H\(_3\)O\(^+\)).
\item
  A food scientist wants to reduce the water activity of a fruit jam
  from 0.95 to 0.80 by adding sucrose. Qualitatively, how does this
  protect against microbial spoilage?
\item
  The wood frog (\emph{Rana sylvatica}) survives freezing by
  accumulating glucose in its cells. Explain, using colligative
  properties, how intracellular glucose prevents lethal ice crystal
  formation inside cells even while extracellular ice forms.
\item
  Compare the hydration shells of Na\(^+\) and Mg\(^{2+}\). Which ion
  has a more tightly bound hydration shell, and why? How does this
  affect the biological roles of each ion?
\item
  Derive the relationship between the mean diffusion distance and time
  (\(\bar{x} = \sqrt{2Dt}\)) starting from the concept of a random walk.
  Explain why this relationship makes circulatory systems necessary for
  organisms larger than about 1 mm.
\item
  Using \texttt{osmotic\_pressure}, compare the osmotic pressure (Pa) of
  0.30 M glucose (\(i=1\)) vs.~0.15 M NaCl (\(i=2\)) at 310 K. Which is
  closer to human plasma tonicity?
\item
  A child with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus excretes large volumes of
  dilute urine. Link this \hyperref[gl:phenotype]{\textbf{phenotype}} to
  aquaporin-2 trafficking in collecting ducts and the role of
  vasopressin (ADH) in increasing epithelial water permeability.
\item
  Using \cref{eq:unit_I_dissolution_dG}, predict whether n-octanol (a
  hydrocarbon-like alcohol) is more soluble in water at 25 \(^\circ\)C
  or 60 \(^\circ\)C. Assume \(\Delta H_{\text{soln}} \approx 0\) and the
  dissolution is dominated by the unfavourable entropy of cage
  formation. How does this relate to drug partition coefficients
  (\(\log P\))?
\item
  Explain how the Grotthuss mechanism allows ATP synthase to translocate
  about 10\(^4\) protons per second through its F\(_o\) ring
  without bulk water flow. What would happen if a mutation introduced a
  single Pro residue that broke the proton wire?
\item
  Cryopreservation protocols for human embryos use vitrification (rapid
  cooling with high cryoprotectant concentrations) rather than slow
  freezing. Using your understanding of ice nucleation and water
  activity, explain why vitrification is preferred for delicate cells.
\item
  Use \cref{eq:unit_I_water_activity} to quantify the difference in
  chemical potential of water in pure water (\(a_w = 1\)) versus a 1 M
  sucrose solution (\(a_w \approx 0.98\)) at 310 K. Compare your answer
  to the corresponding osmotic pressure from \cref{eq:unit_I_vant_hoff}.
  Are they consistent?
\end{enumerate}

\item
  Describe the structural levels of
  \hyperref[gl:protein]{\textbf{protein}}s and relate each level to
  function, including modern concepts such as intrinsically disordered
  proteins.
\item
  Explain nucleic acid structure, including A-form, B-form, and Z-form
  DNA, as well as RNA secondary structures.
\item
  Distinguish the structures and roles of carbohydrates and lipids,
  including glycoproteins and sphingolipids.
\item
  Describe ribozymes, their discovery, and their significance for the
  RNA World hypothesis.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Study Blueprint}\label{study-blueprint-5}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Big idea:} Macromolecule structure links monomer chemistry to
  biological function and information storage.
\item
  \textbf{Core concepts:} polymers, dehydration synthesis, protein
  structure, nucleic acids.
\item
  \textbf{Framework alignment:} Vision \& Change: Structure and
  function, Pathways and transformations of energy and matter; AP
  Biology: Energetics, Systems Interactions; NGSS-style topics: Matter
  and Energy in Organisms and Ecosystems, Structure and Function.
\item
  \textbf{Model or quantitative lens:} Polymerization energetics and
  sequence-to-structure reasoning.
\item
  \textbf{Data skill:} Classify molecules from structural evidence
  rather than names alone.
\item
  \textbf{Practice cadence:} Concept Explanation, Statistical Tests and
  Data Analysis, Argumentation.
\item
  \textbf{Common misconception to repair:} Structure is not decoration;
  small chemical changes can redirect function and recognition.
\item

\item

\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Opening Vignette: The Protein That Won Two Nobel Prizes}

In 1955, Frederick Sanger published the complete amino acid sequence of
bovine insulin: 51 amino acids in two chains (A and B) linked by two
disulfide bonds. It had taken him 10 years and was considered one of the
most technically difficult achievements in biochemistry at the time. The
revelation was not just the sequence itself, but what it implied:
proteins are not random polymers --- they are precisely specified
sequences, encoded in \hyperref[gl:gene]{\textbf{gene}}s, determining
unique three-dimensional structures. This work earned Sanger his first
Nobel Prize in Chemistry (1958).

The same molecule --- insulin --- would later become the first human
protein produced by recombinant DNA technology (1982), when the human
insulin gene was inserted into \emph{E. coli} to manufacture
pharmaceutical insulin for diabetics. Before recombinant insulin, most
medical insulin came from pig and cow pancreas, with shortages,
immunological reactions, and ethical concerns. Today, nearly most 500
million diabetics worldwide who require insulin use a product whose
existence depends on understanding the four classes of biological
macromolecules this chapter explores.

\emph{Primary source: Sanger, F. \& Thompson, E. O. P. (1953). The
amino-acid sequence in the glycyl chain of insulin. Biochem. J., 53(3),
353--374.}
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

Biological macromolecules fall into four major classes:
\textbf{carbohydrates}, \textbf{lipids}, \textbf{proteins}, and
\textbf{nucleic acids}. The first three are polymers of small repeating
units (monomers); lipids are an important exception --- they form
assemblies through noncovalent hydrophobic interactions rather than
covalent polymerisation.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0021_9eb74518a708.png}
\caption{The four biological macromolecule families - carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids - with their monomers, characteristic bonds, and cellular roles.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Condensation and
Hydrolysis}\label{condensation-and-hydrolysis}

Most biological polymers are built by \textbf{condensation (dehydration)
reactions}, in which two monomers are joined with the release of one
water molecule per bond:

\[\text{Monomer}_1\text{--OH} + \text{H--Monomer}_2 \rightarrow \text{Monomer}_1\text{--Monomer}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \tag{3.1} \label{eq:unit_I_macromolecules_item_1}\]

The reverse, \textbf{hydrolysis}, uses water to cleave the bond. These
reactions require \hyperref[gl:enzyme]{\textbf{enzyme}} catalysis (see
\cref{sec:unit_I_enzymes_and_kinetics}) and energy input for
condensation.

\textbf{\hyperref[gl:thermodynamics]{Thermodynamics} of bond formation:}

In each case, the monomers must first be ``activated'' by coupling to a
high-energy carrier molecule. This coupling makes the condensation
reaction thermodynamically favourable.

\subsubsection{Worked Example: The Thermodynamics of
Polymerisation}\label{worked-example-the-thermodynamics-of-polymerisation}

\textbf{Problem:} The hydrolysis of a
\hyperref[gl:peptide-bond]{\textbf{peptide bond}} releases approximately
\(\Delta G^{\circ'} = -10 \text{ kJ/mol}\). 1. What is the standard free
energy change (\(\Delta G^{\circ'}\)) for the condensation reaction to
form a single peptide bond? 2. Why does the cell require the hydrolysis
of high-energy bonds (like GTP, where
\(\Delta G^{\circ'} \approx -30 \text{ kJ/mol}\)) to drive this reaction
during protein synthesis in the
\hyperref[gl:ribosome]{\textbf{ribosome}}?

\textbf{Solution:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Calculate the condensation \(\Delta G^{\circ'}\):} Because
  condensation is the exact reverse of hydrolysis, the standard free
  energy change has the same magnitude but the opposite sign:
  \[ \Delta G^{\circ'}_{\text{condensation}} = -(\Delta G^{\circ'}_{\text{hydrolysis}}) = -(-10 \text{ kJ/mol}) = +10 \text{ kJ/mol}  \label{eq:unit_I_macromolecules_item_2}\]

  As \(\Delta G^{\circ'} > 0\), the formation of a peptide bond is
  thermodynamically unfavourable (endergonic) and will not occur
  spontaneously.
\item
  \textbf{Calculate the coupled reaction thermodynamics:} To drive an
  endergonic reaction forward, the cell couples it to a highly exergonic
  reaction. During translation elongation, the ribosome couples the
  formation of a peptide bond to the hydrolysis of GTP down to GDP +
  P\(_i\).

  Summing the free energy changes:
  \[ \Delta G^{\circ'}_{\text{total}} = \Delta G^{\circ'}_{\text{condensation}} + \Delta G^{\circ'}_{\text{GTP\_hydrolysis}}  \label{eq:unit_I_macromolecules_item_3}\]

  \[ \Delta G^{\circ'}_{\text{total}} = (+10 \text{ kJ/mol}) + (-30 \text{ kJ/mol}) = -20 \text{ kJ/mol}  \label{eq:unit_I_macromolecules_item_4}\]
\end{enumerate}

By coupling the unfavourable peptide bond formation (+10 kJ/mol) to the
favourable hydrolysis of GTP (--30 kJ/mol), the overall coupled reaction
becomes highly favourable (--20 kJ/mol), driving protein synthesis
forward with near-perfect unidirectionality.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 1:} Hydrolysis reactions are thermodynamically
spontaneous (\(\Delta G < 0\)), yet polymers are kinetically stable in
cells. What prevents the spontaneous hydrolysis of your DNA, proteins,
and carbohydrates?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Carbohydrates}\label{carbohydrates}

\subsubsection{Monosaccharides}\label{monosaccharides}

The simplest carbohydrates are \textbf{monosaccharides} with the
empirical formula (CH\(_2\)O)\(_n\). They are classified by: -
\textbf{Number of carbons:} trioses (3C), tetroses (4C), pentoses (5C),
hexoses (6C) - \textbf{Functional group:} aldoses (aldehyde) or ketoses
(ketone)

Common examples:

Glucose, galactose, and fructose are \textbf{structural isomers} ---
identical molecular formulas, different atom arrangements. In solution,
glucose exists primarily in the \textbf{ring form} (pyranose,
about 99\%) rather than the open-chain aldehyde form. The two
ring anomers, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-D-glucose and \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-D-glucose, differ primarily in the
orientation of the C1 hydroxyl group, but this distinction has enormous
biochemical significance --- enzymes discriminate exquisitely between
them.

\subsubsection{Disaccharides and
Polysaccharides}\label{disaccharides-and-polysaccharides}

Two monosaccharides join via a \textbf{glycosidic bond} to form a
disaccharide:

\textbf{Polysaccharides} are long chains of monosaccharides serving
structural or storage functions:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Starch (amylose + amylopectin):} \(\alpha(1\to4)\) linkages,
  branching via \(\alpha(1\to6)\) at intervals (about 25
  residues for amylopectin). Storage in plants.
\item
  \textbf{Glycogen:} Like amylopectin but more heavily branched (every
  about 10 residues). Glucose storage in animal liver
  (about 100 g) and muscle (about 400 g).
\item
  \textbf{Cellulose:} \(\beta(1\to4)\) glucose. Structural component of
  plant cell walls. Humans cannot digest it (no beta-glucosidase), but
  gut \hyperref[gl:microbiota]{\textbf{microbiota}} can; cellulose is
  dietary fibre.
\item
  \textbf{Chitin:} \(\beta(1\to4)\) N-acetylglucosamine. Structural
  component of fungal cell walls and arthropod exoskeletons --- the
  second most abundant biopolymer on Earth after cellulose.
\item
  \textbf{Hyaluronic acid:} alternating \(\beta(1\to4)\) glucuronic acid
  and \(\beta(1\to3)\) N-acetylglucosamine. Major component of
  extracellular matrix and synovial fluid.
\end{itemize}

The difference between starch and cellulose --- both glucose polymers
--- lies solely in the glycosidic bond geometry (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha} vs.~\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}). Yet this
single difference makes cellulose rigid and indigestible versus starch
flexible and readily hydrolysed.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0022_817dc0a53fed.png}
\caption{Carbohydrate digestion and absorption. Carbohydrate digestion and absorption pathway. Note the key distinction: alpha-linked polysaccharides (starch) are digested by human enzymes, while beta-linked cellulose passes to the colon where microbial fermentation produces short-chain fatty acids.}
\end{figure}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Lactose Intolerance}

Approximately 65--75\% of the global adult population has reduced
expression of lactase (the brush border enzyme that cleaves lactose)
after weaning --- the ancestral state called \textbf{lactase
non-persistence}. Undigested lactose reaches the colon, where bacterial
fermentation produces H\(_2\), CO\(_2\), and short-chain fatty acids,
causing bloating, flatulence, and diarrhoea. \textbf{Lactase
persistence} (the ability to digest lactose as an adult) evolved
independently in pastoral populations in Europe (about 7,500
years ago) and East Africa (about 3,000 years ago) due to
strong selection pressure from dairy farming. This is one of the
clearest examples of recent human evolution driven by cultural
practices.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 2:} Glycogen is more heavily branched than
amylopectin (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}1-\textgreater6 branch every about 10 residues
vs.~every about 25 residues). How does this increased branching
benefit an animal that needs rapid glucose mobilisation during a ``fight
or flight'' response?
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{The Glycosidic Bond: \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}
vs.~\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}}\label{the-glycosidic-bond-ux3b1-vs.-ux3b2}

The single greatest source of carbohydrate structural diversity is the
\textbf{glycosidic bond} geometry. When a hemiacetal hydroxyl (at the
anomeric carbon, C1 of the cyclic sugar) condenses with a hydroxyl of
another sugar, the resulting linkage can be either \textbf{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}} (the OH/OR
on C1 points down in the standard Haworth projection, \emph{trans} to
the C6 substituent) or \textbf{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}} (OH/OR points up, \emph{cis} to C6).

The biological consequences of this single stereochemical choice are
profound: \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-linked glucose polymers (starch, glycogen) form helices that
pack as soft granules and are readily hydrolysed for energy storage.
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-linked glucose polymers (cellulose) form extended, hydrogen-bonded
sheets that pack into rigid microfibrils with tensile strength rivalling
steel by weight; nature uses them as structural material (plant cell
walls) precisely because they resist enzymatic attack.

\subsubsection{Branching, Linkages, and Polymer
Diversity}\label{branching-linkages-and-polymer-diversity}

Even within the same monosaccharide and same anomeric configuration,
\textbf{branching frequency} dramatically alters function. Glycogen
(animal storage) has \(\alpha(1\to6)\) branches every about 10
residues; amylopectin (plant storage) every about 25 residues.
Heavier branching gives glycogen many more non-reducing ends per
molecule --- and since both glycogen synthase and glycogen phosphorylase
work primarily at non-reducing ends, branching directly accelerates the
rate at which glucose can be added to or removed from the polymer.
During a ``fight or flight'' response, a hepatocyte mobilises glucose
from glycogen at about 10 mM/s; this rate would be unattainable
from a linear polymer with a single non-reducing end.

\subsubsection{Glycoproteins and
Proteoglycans}\label{glycoproteins-and-proteoglycans}

Many proteins are covalently modified with carbohydrate chains
(glycans):

\textbf{Glycoproteins} have relatively short, branched oligosaccharide
chains attached via: - \textbf{N-linked glycosylation:} to asparagine
(Asn) in the consensus sequence Asn-X-Ser/Thr (where X is any amino acid
except Pro). Built up co-translationally on dolichol phosphate in the
ER, then trimmed and modified in the Golgi. - \textbf{O-linked
glycosylation:} to serine (Ser) or threonine (Thr); built up
sequentially in the Golgi. - \textbf{Other linkages:} O-GlcNAc (a single
GlcNAc on Ser/Thr; common cytosolic/nuclear signal), C-mannose (on Trp),
GPI-anchor glycolipids (link some proteins to the membrane outer
leaflet).

Glycoproteins are ubiquitous: antibodies (IgG), blood group antigens
(ABO), mucins (airway protection), and many secreted or surface proteins
carry glycans. Glycosylation affects protein folding, stability,
half-life, and cell-cell recognition. The SARS-CoV-2 spike protein is
heavily N-glycosylated, with at least 22 sites; these glycans shield the
protein from antibody neutralisation, and their removal is a strategy
under exploration for vaccine improvement.

(via osmotic pressure), creating a hydrated gel that resists compression
--- this is why cartilage can support the body's weight.

\subsection{Lipids}\label{lipids}

Lipids are not polymers but are grouped together by their
\textbf{hydrophobicity} --- they do not form regular covalent polymers,
yet their self-assembly into bilayers, vesicles, and membranes is
central to cellular life.

C18:2 \(\Delta^{9,12}\) & 18:2 & 2 & Linoleic acid (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\omega}}{omega}-6 PUFA) &
Vegetable oils \\
C18:3 \(\Delta^{9,12,15}\) & 18:3 & 3 & \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-Linolenic acid (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\omega}}{omega}-3 PUFA) &
Flaxseed, walnuts \\
C20:4 \(\Delta^{5,8,11,14}\) & 20:4 & 4 & Arachidonic acid (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\omega}}{omega}-6) & Meat,
eggs \\
C20:5 \(\Delta^{5,8,11,14,17}\) & 20:5 & 5 & EPA (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\omega}}{omega}-3) & Oily fish \\
C22:6 \(\Delta^{4,7,10,13,16,19}\) & 22:6 & 6 & DHA (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\omega}}{omega}-3) & Fish oil,
brain \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Saturated} fatty acids have no double bonds and pack tightly ---
solid at room temperature (butter, lard). \textbf{Unsaturated} fatty
acids have \emph{cis} double bonds introducing kinks that prevent tight
packing --- liquid at room temperature (olive oil). \textbf{Trans} fats
have \emph{trans} double bonds that pack like saturated fats --- they
are artificial (from industrial hydrogenation) and have adverse
cardiovascular effects.

\textbf{Essential fatty acids:} Linoleic acid (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\omega}}{omega}-6) and \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-linolenic acid
(\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\omega}}{omega}-3) cannot be synthesised by humans (we lack \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Delta}}{Delta}12 and \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Delta}}{Delta}15 desaturases)
and must be obtained from the diet.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0023_c4cbb747f919.png}
\caption{Lipid classes and roles. Classification of lipids. Unlike other macromolecules, lipids are classified by solubility (hydrophobicity) rather than by a common monomer structure. Note the diversity of roles: energy storage, membrane structure, signalling, and waterproofing.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Glycerophospholipids}\label{glycerophospholipids}

Glycerophospholipids (also called phosphoglycerides) are the most
abundant membrane lipids. Their structure: glycerol backbone + 2 fatty
acid chains at positions sn-1 and sn-2 + phosphate group at sn-3 + polar
head group attached to the phosphate.

The \textbf{amphipathic} structure spontaneously forms bilayers in water
--- a thermodynamic consequence of the hydrophobic effect (see
\cref{sec:unit_I_water_and_life}).

\subsubsection{Quantitative Properties of the Lipid
Bilayer}\label{quantitative-properties-of-the-lipid-bilayer}

The ``fluid mosaic'' model of Singer and Nicolson (1972) proposed that
membranes are 2D fluids in which proteins and lipids diffuse laterally.
Quantitative measurements --- especially by fluorescence recovery after
photobleaching (FRAP) and single-particle tracking --- have refined this
picture into a richer, multi-domain landscape.

\textbf{Lipid asymmetry.} The two leaflets of the plasma membrane have
very different compositions: the outer leaflet is enriched in PC,
sphingomyelin, and glycolipids; the inner leaflet in PE, PS, and PI.
This asymmetry is actively maintained by ATP-dependent flippases (move
lipids from outer to inner) and floppases (inner to outer). When PS
appears on the outer leaflet --- the result of activated scramblases
during apoptosis --- it serves as an ``eat-me'' signal for macrophages.
Loss of asymmetry is also a feature of activated platelets (where PS
exposure on the outer leaflet provides a surface for the coagulation
cascade).

\textbf{Lipid rafts.} Cholesterol and sphingolipids self-segregate into
liquid-ordered (\(L_o\)) microdomains within a sea of liquid-disordered
(\(L_d\)) phospholipids. These about 10--200 nm rafts
concentrate specific signalling proteins (GPI-anchored proteins,
Src-family kinases) and are now recognised as functional platforms for
receptor signalling, virus budding, and immune-cell synapse assembly.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 7:} A typical phospholipid diffuses
about 1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m/s laterally in a fluid bilayer but flips between
leaflets primarily once every several hours unaided. Use the structure
of a phospholipid (charged head, hydrocarbon tails) and the energetics
of the hydrophobic effect to explain this 10\(^{12}\)-fold difference.
Why must cells expend ATP on flippases to break this asymmetry?
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Sphingolipids}\label{sphingolipids}

Sphingolipids use \textbf{sphingosine} (rather than glycerol) as the
backbone. Ceramide (sphingosine + fatty acid) is the core structure:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Sphingomyelin:} ceramide + phosphocholine. Major component of
  the myelin sheath that insulates axons; critical for nerve impulse
  conduction velocity.
\item
  \textbf{Cerebrosides:} ceramide + single sugar (glucose or galactose).
  Abundant in brain.
\item
  \textbf{Gangliosides:} ceramide + complex oligosaccharide containing
  sialic acid (Neu5Ac). GM1 is the receptor for cholera toxin.
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Tay-Sachs Disease and Sphingolipid Storage}

Tay-Sachs disease results from deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme
hexosaminidase A, which normally degrades the ganglioside GM2. Without
this enzyme, GM2 accumulates in \hyperref[gl:neuron]{\textbf{neuron}}s,
causing progressive neurodegeneration. Symptoms appear at
about 6 months and include cherry-red macular spots, seizures,
and developmental regression. The disease is invariably fatal by age
3--5. Carrier frequency is about 1/30 in Ashkenazi Jewish
populations due to a \hyperref[gl:founder-effect]{\textbf{founder
effect}}. This is one of about 50 known \textbf{lysosomal
storage diseases}, most caused by deficient hydrolytic enzymes.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Sterols and Steroid
Hormones}\label{sterols-and-steroid-hormones}

\textbf{Cholesterol} has a four-ring steroid nucleus (three 6-carbon
rings + one 5-carbon ring) and a hydroxyl group at C3. In membranes,
cholesterol: - Inserts between phospholipids with its hydroxyl group
near the head groups and its rings among the acyl chains - At high
temperatures: reduces membrane fluidity by restricting phospholipid
movement - At low temperatures: prevents crystallisation by disrupting
ordered packing - Net effect: \textbf{homeoviscous regulation} that
maintains consistent membrane fluidity across a temperature range

Cholesterol is the precursor to most steroid
\hyperref[gl:hormone]{\textbf{hormone}}s: - \textbf{Glucocorticoids}
(\hyperref[gl:cortisol]{\textbf{cortisol}}): stress response,
anti-inflammatory - \textbf{Mineralocorticoids} (aldosterone):
sodium/potassium balance - \textbf{Androgens} (testosterone): male
sexual development - \textbf{Oestrogens} (oestradiol): female sexual
development - \textbf{Progestagens} (progesterone): pregnancy
maintenance - \textbf{Vitamin D\(_3\)} (cholecalciferol): calcium
absorption - \textbf{Bile acids} (cholic acid, chenodeoxycholic acid):
fat emulsification in the duodenum

\subsubsection{Waxes and Other Lipids}\label{waxes-and-other-lipids}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Waxes:} esters of long-chain fatty acids and long-chain
  alcohols; waterproofing (plant cuticle, bee honeycomb, whale head oil,
  ear wax)
\item
  \textbf{Eicosanoids:} signalling lipids derived from arachidonic acid
  (C20:4); include prostaglandins (inflammation, fever, pain),
  thromboxanes (platelet aggregation), and leukotrienes (immune
  response)
\item
  \textbf{Isoprenoids:} built from isoprene units (5C); include
  terpenes, carotenoids, ubiquinone (CoQ), and dolichol
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 3:} Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) irreversibly
inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX), the enzyme that converts arachidonic acid
to prostaglandins and thromboxanes. Explain why aspirin reduces both
pain/inflammation and the risk of heart attacks.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Proteins}\label{proteins}

Proteins are the most structurally and functionally diverse
macromolecules. They serve as: - Structural elements (collagen, keratin,
\hyperref[gl:actin]{\textbf{actin}}, tubulin) - Enzymes (catalysts; see
\cref{sec:unit_I_enzymes_and_kinetics}) - Signalling molecules (growth
factors, receptors, G proteins) - Transport proteins (haemoglobin,
albumin, aquaporins) - Immune molecules (antibodies) - Motor proteins
(myosin, kinesin, dynein)

\subsubsection{Amino Acids}\label{amino-acids}

Most 20 canonical amino acids share a common backbone:

\begin{verbatim}
    NH₂
     |
H — C — COOH
     |
     R (side chain)
\end{verbatim}

The \textbf{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-amino group} (pKa about 9.0) and
\textbf{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-carboxyl group} (pKa about 2.0) flank the \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-carbon,
to which the variable \textbf{R group} is attached. At physiological pH
7.4, the amino group is --NH\(_3^+\) and the carboxyl is --COO\(^-\),
forming a \textbf{zwitterion}.

\textbf{Classification by R group character:}

\textbf{Special amino acids:} - \textbf{Glycine} (R = H) has no
stereogenic centre and maximal conformational flexibility --- often
found in tight turns - \textbf{Proline} has a cyclic side chain bonded
to the backbone nitrogen, restricting rotation and introducing kinks in
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-helices - \textbf{Cysteine} can form \textbf{disulfide bonds}
(--S--S--) with other cysteines under oxidising conditions (ER lumen,
extracellular space) - \textbf{Selenocysteine} (the ``21st amino acid'')
contains selenium instead of sulfur and is encoded by UGA
\hyperref[gl:codon]{\textbf{codon}}s with a special stem-loop (SECIS
element)

\subsubsection{The Peptide Bond}\label{the-peptide-bond}

A peptide bond forms by condensation between the carboxyl of one amino
acid and the amino group of the next:

\[\text{--NH--CHR}_1\text{--CO--NH--CHR}_2\text{--CO--} \ldots \tag{3.2} \label{eq:unit_I_macromolecules_item_5}\]

The peptide bond has \textbf{partial double-bond character}
(about 40\% double bond due to resonance), making it planar and
\textbf{trans} (almost typically; \emph{cis} occurs
about 0.03\% of the time, except before proline where
\emph{cis} occurs about 5\%). This rigidity limits rotation
around the C\(_\alpha\)--C bond to the backbone dihedral angles \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\varphi}}{phi} and \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\psi}}{psi}
(described on a Ramachandran plot), constraining protein conformational
space.

\subsubsection{Ramachandran Plots and Backbone Dihedral
Angles}\label{ramachandran-plots-and-backbone-dihedral-angles}

The polypeptide backbone has three torsional degrees of freedom per
residue:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\omega}}{omega}} (omega): rotation about the peptide C--N bond. Effectively
  fixed at 180\(^\circ\) (\emph{trans}) due to partial double-bond
  character; about 5\% of X-Pro bonds adopt \emph{cis} (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\omega}}{omega} =
  0\(^\circ\)).
\item
  \textbf{\(\varphi\)} (phi): rotation about the N--C\(_\alpha\) bond.
\item
  \textbf{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\psi}}{psi}} (psi): rotation about the C\(_\alpha\)--C bond.
\end{itemize}

Because each peptide unit is rigid and planar, primarily \(\varphi\) and
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\psi}}{psi} can vary. The 1963 paper of G. N. Ramachandran plotted \(\varphi\)
vs.~\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\psi}}{psi} for most amino acids in known protein structures; the plot reveals
dramatic clustering caused by steric clashes (Pauli repulsion between
side chain, carbonyl, and amide atoms when the dihedrals approach
forbidden values).

Two amino acids escape the standard restrictions:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Glycine} has primarily an H atom for its side chain --- no
  steric clash --- and so populates the entire \((\varphi, \psi)\)
  plane, including the disallowed regions used by left-handed helices.
\item
  \textbf{Proline's} side-chain ring fixes
  \(\varphi \approx -65^\circ\), severely restricting backbone
  flexibility. Proline cannot occur in a regular \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-helix beyond position
  4 (no N--H proton available as H-bond donor) and is famous as a
  ``helix breaker.''
\end{itemize}

Real proteins occupy the allowed regions about 98\% of the
time; deviations into ``outlier'' regions are validated indicators of
either (a) genuine functional constraints (e.g., catalytic glycines in a
strained conformation) or (b) modelling errors in low-resolution X-ray
structures. Ramachandran statistics are now a standard quality metric
for crystallographic and AlphaFold-predicted structures.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 6:} Why does Pro almost rarely occur in the middle
of an \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-helix, while Gly is over-represented in tight turns and loops?
Frame your answer in terms of \((\varphi, \psi)\) allowed regions on the
Ramachandran plot.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Levels of Protein
Structure}\label{levels-of-protein-structure}

\textbf{Primary structure:} The amino acid sequence --- the covalent
backbone. Written conventionally from N-terminus to C-terminus. Primary
structure is encoded by genes and determines most higher levels of
structure (Anfinsen's dogma).

\textbf{Secondary structure:} Local regular patterns of backbone
H-bonds: - \textbf{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-Helix:} 3.6 residues/turn, rise 0.15 nm/residue,
H-bond between residue \(i\) and \(i+4\). 100\% right-handed in natural
proteins. Helix dipole (N-terminus \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\delta}}{delta}+; C-terminus \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\delta}}{delta}-) affects function.
Helix-breaking residues: Pro (kinks), Gly (too flexible). -
\textbf{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-Sheet:} extended chains (strands) running parallel or
antiparallel, H-bonded between adjacent strands. Most \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-sheets are
twisted. \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-sheets are the structural basis of silk (fibroin) and amyloid
fibrils. - \textbf{\(3_{10}\)-helix:} tighter than \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-helix (3
residues/turn), H-bond between \(i\) and \(i+3\). Less common; often
found at helix termini. - \textbf{Turns and loops:} allow the
polypeptide chain to reverse direction; typically on protein surface,
often functionally important (e.g., CDR loops in antibodies).

\textbf{Tertiary structure:} The complete 3D fold, stabilised by: -
Hydrophobic core packing (\hyperref[gl:dominant]{\textbf{dominant}}
driving force) - Disulfide bonds (Cys--S--S--Cys; formed in oxidising
compartments like ER lumen) - Salt bridges (Asp/Glu with Lys/Arg) -
H-bonds and van der Waals contacts

\textbf{Common protein folds:}

\textbf{Quaternary structure:} Assembly of two or more polypeptide
chains (subunits). Examples: - \textbf{Haemoglobin:} \(\alpha_2\beta_2\)
tetramer; cooperative O\(_2\) binding - \textbf{Collagen:} triple helix
of three chains with Gly-X-Y repeats (X often Pro, Y often Hyp) -
\textbf{Immunoglobulin G:} two heavy chains + two light chains; Y-shaped
- \textbf{Ribosome:} RNA + \textgreater50 protein subunits

\textbf{Protein denaturation:} Disruption of
secondary/tertiary/quaternary structure by heat, pH extremes,
denaturants (urea, guanidinium), reducing agents (break disulfides).
Primary structure intact; activity lost. Often irreversible (cooked egg
white), but many small proteins refold spontaneously (Anfinsen's
experiment with ribonuclease A).

\subsubsection{Thermodynamics of Protein
Folding}\label{thermodynamics-of-protein-folding}

Protein folding is governed by the same Gibbs equation that governs most
spontaneous processes:

\begin{equation}
\Delta G_{\text{fold}} = \Delta H_{\text{fold}} - T\,\Delta S_{\text{fold}}
\label{eq:unit_I_protein_folding_dG}
\end{equation}

The total \(\Delta G_{\text{fold}}\) for a typical small globular
protein is primarily --20 to --60 kJ/mol --- the difference between two
enormous, partially cancelling terms.

\textbf{Decomposing the folding free energy:}

\toprule\noalign{}

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\midrule\noalign{}
