\subsection{Worked Examples}\label{worked-examples-2}

\textbf{Problem 1:} An enzyme obeys Michaelis-Menten kinetics with
\(K_m\) = 2.0 mM and \(V_{max}\) = 100 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}mol/min. Calculate \(v_0\) at
\hyperref[s]{S} = 0.5 mM, 2.0 mM, 10 mM, and 200 mM.

\emph{Solution:}

\[v_0 = \frac{100 \times [\text{S}]}{2.0 + [\text{S}]} \tag{4.18} \label{eq:unit_I_enzymes_and_kinetics_item_19}\]

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2093}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4651}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3256}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
\hyperref[s]{S} (mM)
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
\(v_0\) (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}mol/min)
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
\% of \(V_{max}\)
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
0.5 & \(100 \times 0.5 / 2.5 = 20.0\) & 20\% \\
2.0 & \(100 \times 2.0 / 4.0 = 50.0\) & 50\% (by definition,
\hyperref[s]{S} = \(K_m\)) \\
10.0 & \(100 \times 10 / 12 = 83.3\) & 83.3\% \\
200.0 & \(100 \times 200 / 202 = 99.0\) & 99.0\% (near saturation) \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Problem 2:} In the presence of a competitive inhibitor at
\hyperref[i]{I} = 5 mM and \(K_i\) = 2.5 mM, what is the new apparent
\(K_m\)? At what \hyperref[s]{S} will \(v_0\) = \(V_{max}/2\)?

\emph{Solution:}
\[\alpha = 1 + \frac{[\text{I}]}{K_i} = 1 + \frac{5.0}{2.5} = 3.0 \tag{4.19} \label{eq:unit_I_enzymes_and_kinetics_item_20}\]

\[K_m^{app} = \alpha K_m = 3.0 \times 2.0 = 6.0 \; \text{mM} \tag{4.20} \label{eq:unit_I_enzymes_and_kinetics_item_21}\]

\(v_0 = V_{max}/2\) when \hyperref[s]{S} = \(K_m^{app}\) = 6.0 mM. The
inhibitor triples the substrate concentration needed for half-maximal
velocity.

\textbf{Problem 3:} The Hill coefficient for haemoglobin is 2.8, and
\(K_{0.5}\) for O\(_2\) is 26 mmHg. Calculate the fractional saturation
at: (a) pO\(_2\) = 40 mmHg (venous blood) (b) pO\(_2\) = 100 mmHg
(arterial blood)

\emph{Solution:}
\[\theta = \frac{[\text{S}]^n}{K_{0.5}^n + [\text{S}]^n} \tag{4.21} \label{eq:unit_I_enzymes_and_kinetics_item_22}\]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  \(\theta = \frac{40^{2.8}}{26^{2.8} + 40^{2.8}} = \frac{40^{2.8}}{26^{2.8} + 40^{2.8}}\)
\end{enumerate}

\(40^{2.8} = e^{2.8 \ln 40} = e^{2.8 \times 3.689} = e^{10.33} = 30{,}600\)

\(26^{2.8} = e^{2.8 \ln 26} = e^{2.8 \times 3.258} = e^{9.12} = 9{,}160\)

\(\theta = \frac{30{,}600}{9{,}160 + 30{,}600} = \frac{30{,}600}{39{,}760} = 0.770\)
(77.0\%)

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  \(100^{2.8} = e^{2.8 \times 4.605} = e^{12.89} = 396{,}000\)
\end{enumerate}

\(\theta = \frac{396{,}000}{9{,}160 + 396{,}000} = 0.977\) (97.7\%)

The difference: haemoglobin loads O\(_2\) to 97.7\% in the lungs and
unloads to 77.0\% in tissues, delivering about 20\% of its
O\(_2\) per circuit. During exercise (venous pO\(_2\) drops to
about 20 mmHg), delivery increases substantially due to the
steep part of the sigmoidal curve.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Computational Bridge}\label{computational-bridge-3}

The Michaelis--Menten hyperbola is implemented directly on
concentrations in \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}M:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ biology.biochemistry }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ michaelis\_menten}

\NormalTok{res }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ michaelis\_menten(}\FloatTok{5.0}\NormalTok{, Vmax}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{120.0}\NormalTok{, Km}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{10.0}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(res.reaction\_rate, res.efficiency)  }\CommentTok{\# v and v/Vmax}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical / systems note:} Many drugs are mechanism-based
inhibitors that shrink effective \(V_\mathrm{max}\) or raise apparent
\(K_m\); statins compete at HMG-CoA reductase's active site,
illustrating competitive themes at a clinically relevant scale.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Bridge to Systems: From Enzyme Kinetics to Metabolic
Flux}\label{bridge-to-systems-from-enzyme-kinetics-to-metabolic-flux}

A single enzyme's \(K_m\), \(V_{\max}\), and Hill coefficient become
inputs to a higher-level question: what is the \textbf{flux} (\(J\), in
mol L\(^{-1}\) s\(^{-1}\)) through a metabolic pathway, and which enzyme
limits it? This question is the bridge from this chapter to Unit III
(bioenergetics and respiration).

\subsubsection{Pathway Flux is Set by Multiple Enzymes, Not
One}\label{pathway-flux-is-set-by-multiple-enzymes-not-one}

The classical idea that a single ``rate-limiting step'' governs a
pathway has been replaced by \textbf{metabolic control analysis} (MCA),
developed in the 1970s by Heinrich, Rapoport, Kacser, and Burns. MCA
assigns each enzyme \(i\) a \textbf{flux control coefficient}:

\begin{equation}
C_i^J = \frac{\partial \ln J}{\partial \ln [E_i]}
\label{eq:unit_I_flux_control_coefficient}
\end{equation}

This is the fractional change in steady-state flux when the activity of
enzyme \(i\) is changed by a small fraction. The \textbf{summation
theorem} states that for any pathway:

\begin{equation}
\sum_i C_i^J = 1
\label{eq:unit_I_summation_theorem}
\end{equation}

Three lessons follow:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Control is distributed.} No single enzyme has \(C_i^J = 1\);
  instead, glycolytic flux in muscle is controlled by hexokinase
  (\(C^J \approx 0.3\)), PFK-1 (\(C^J \approx 0.3\)), pyruvate kinase
  (\(C^J \approx 0.2\)), and others.
\item
  \textbf{Targeting the ``rate-limiting'' enzyme often disappoints.}
  Doubling PFK-1 primarily doubles flux if \(C^J = 1\), which is rarely
  true. This is why metabolic engineering campaigns to improve product
  yields often increase one enzyme tenfold for a 1.5-fold flux gain.
\item
  \textbf{Allosteric regulation tunes the control distribution.} When
  ATP is high, AMP is low, and ATCase or PFK-1 sit in their T-state,
  \(C^J\) for those enzymes rises toward 1; the cell concentrates
  control where it can respond quickly to demand changes.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Enzyme Saturation Modes Determine Pathway
Behaviour}\label{enzyme-saturation-modes-determine-pathway-behaviour}

The local \([\text{S}] / K_m\) ratio for each enzyme determines whether
it operates near saturation or far below. Glycolytic enzymes typically
operate at \([\text{S}] \approx K_m\) (around half-saturation), where
the response to small \([\text{S}]\) changes is approximately linear and
control coefficients are large. Enzymes whose substrates are at
\(\gg K_m\) (saturated) have \(C^J \approx 0\) and exert no flux
control. Designing a pathway thus means choosing \(K_m\) values matched
to physiological metabolite concentrations --- a constraint visible in
the convergent evolution of glycolytic enzymes across most kingdoms of
life.

\subsubsection{Branching Points and
Connectivity}\label{branching-points-and-connectivity}

When a metabolite sits at a branch point (e.g., glucose-6-phosphate, fed
into glycolysis or the pentose phosphate pathway), the control
coefficient for one branch can exceed 1, balanced by a \emph{negative}
control coefficient on the other branch. Allosteric regulation at branch
points (NADPH-mediated inhibition of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase;
citrate inhibition of PFK-1) allows the cell to apportion flux based on
demand.

Unit III revisits these concepts at the level of full pathways
(glycolysis, TCA cycle, electron transport) and shows how
phosphorylation cascades, \hyperref[gl:hormone]{\textbf{hormone}}-driven
changes in enzyme abundance, and substrate cycles allow flux to vary
100-fold between rest and exercise.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 8:} Insulin treatment of a hepatocyte reduces
gluconeogenic flux by about 10\(\times\) within minutes,
primarily by phosphorylating PFK-2/FBPase-2 to raise
{[}fructose-2,6-bisphosphate{]}. Without invoking transcription, explain
how this allosteric activator achieves a 10\(\times\) flux reduction
while individual enzyme abundances remain unchanged. Use the language of
\(C^J\) and \(K_m\).
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-6}

For \textbf{Enzymes and the Kinetics of Catalysis}, frontier biology
belongs inside the evidence logic of the chapter. Chemistry-of-life
claims now connect classical bonding and thermodynamics with AI-guided
structure prediction and experimental validation. The core reading
question is this: enzyme claims should separate binding, catalysis,
regulation, transport limits, and measurement conditions.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

Use AI biomolecular models as hypothesis generators: compare confidence,
conservation, solvent exposure, and assay evidence before turning a
predicted contact into a biological claim
\citep{abramson2024alphafold3}.

\textbf{Source practice:} For structure and interaction claims, cite
experimental structures when available and treat AlphaFold 3 or AFDB
complex predictions as hypotheses to validate with confidence metrics,
conservation, mutagenesis, binding, or cryo-EM/X-ray/NMR evidence
\citep{abramson2024alphafold3,velankar2026alphafolddb2025,emblebi2026alphafoldcomplexes}.

\subsubsection{Current Evidence Map: Enzyme Engineering Evidence
Chain}\label{current-evidence-map-enzyme-engineering-evidence-chain}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0029_16fa34bca390.png}

\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-6}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Enzymes are protein catalysts that lower the activation energy
  \(\Delta G^{\ddagger}\) without altering equilibrium.
\item
  Rate enhancement mechanisms include proximity/orientation, transition
  state stabilisation, acid-base catalysis, covalent catalysis, and
  metal ion catalysis.
\item
  The Michaelis-Menten equation:
  \(v_0 = V_{max}[\text{S}] / (K_m + [\text{S}])\); \(K_m\) approximates
  substrate affinity; \(k_{cat}\) = turnover number; \(k_{cat}/K_m\) =
  catalytic efficiency.
\item
  Enzyme inhibition: competitive (increases apparent \(K_m\)),
  uncompetitive (decreases both \(K_m\) and \(V_{max}\)),
  mixed/noncompetitive (\(V_{max}\) decreases), irreversible (covalent
  inactivation). Each has a characteristic Lineweaver-Burk pattern.
\item
  Allosteric enzymes exhibit sigmoidal kinetics (Hill equation); key for
  metabolic feedback control. ATCase is the paradigm for allosteric
  regulation.
\item
  pH, temperature, and cofactor availability most modulate enzyme
  activity. Vitamin deficiencies impair coenzyme-dependent enzymes.
\item
  Enzymes are classified into seven EC classes (the seventh,
  translocases, added in 2018).
\item
  Modern enzyme applications include CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing,
  industrial biocatalysis, and directed evolution.
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See Unit III (pathway-level flux and regulated
  enzymes), Unit IV (polymerases and repair enzymes), and Unit VII
  (antibiotic targets in bacterial metabolism).
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Key Terms}\label{key-terms-6}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Activation energy (\(\Delta G^{\ddagger}\)):} Energy barrier
  between reactants and transition state
\item
  \textbf{Active site:} Region of enzyme that binds substrate and
  catalyses reaction
\item
  \textbf{Transition state:} Highest-energy intermediate along the
  reaction coordinate
\item
  \textbf{Michaelis constant (\(K_m\)):} Substrate concentration at
  half-maximal velocity
\item
  \textbf{Turnover number (\(k_{cat}\)):} Maximum substrate molecules
  converted per enzyme per second
\item
  \textbf{Catalytic efficiency (\(k_{cat}/K_m\)):} Overall measure of
  enzyme performance
\item
  \textbf{Competitive inhibition:} Inhibitor competes with substrate for
  active site; overcome by high \hyperref[s]{S}
\item
  \textbf{Uncompetitive inhibition:} Inhibitor binds primarily the ES
  complex
\item
  \textbf{Mixed inhibition:} Inhibitor binds both E and ES at an
  allosteric site
\item
  \textbf{Irreversible inhibition:} Covalent modification permanently
  inactivates the enzyme
\item
  \textbf{Allosteric regulation:} Modulation by effector binding at a
  site other than the active site
\item
  \textbf{Hill coefficient (\(n\)):} Measure of cooperativity; \(n > 1\)
  = positive cooperativity
\item
  \textbf{Feedback inhibition:} End product inhibits an early enzyme in
  its biosynthetic pathway
\item
  \textbf{Coenzyme:} Organic cofactor, often derived from a
  water-soluble vitamin
\item
  \textbf{Prosthetic group:} Tightly bound cofactor (e.g., haem, FAD)
\item
  \textbf{Holoenzyme:} Complete enzyme with most cofactors bound
\item
  \textbf{Apoenzyme:} Enzyme protein without its cofactor
\item
  \textbf{EC number:} Four-digit enzyme classification number assigned
  by IUBMB
\item
  \textbf{Transition state analogue:} Inhibitor that mimics the
  transition state geometry
\item
  \textbf{Directed evolution:} Laboratory technique for engineering
  improved enzymes
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Review Questions}\label{review-questions-6}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Explain, using transition state theory, why an enzyme that binds the
  transition state \(10^6\)-fold more tightly than the substrate
  achieves a rate enhancement of approximately \(10^6\)-fold.
\item
  Derive the Michaelis-Menten equation starting from the steady-state
  assumption. State clearly most assumptions made.
\item
  An enzyme has \(K_m\) = 0.2 mM and \(V_{max}\) = 50 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}mol/min. A
  competitive inhibitor (\(K_i\) = 0.1 mM) is added at 0.5 mM. Calculate
  the apparent \(K_m\) and the rate at \hyperref[s]{S} = 0.2 mM with and
  without inhibitor.
\item
  On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, two lines obtained with and without an
  inhibitor are parallel. Identify the type of inhibition and explain
  what molecular event is occurring.
\item
  The Hill coefficient for phosphofructokinase-1 is approximately 3.8.
  What does this tell you about the enzyme's response to changes in
  substrate concentration near \(K_{0.5}\)?
\item
  Explain how aspirin's mechanism of action (irreversible COX
  inhibition) accounts for both its anti-inflammatory properties and its
  use as an antiplatelet drug.
\item
  Why do statins lower blood cholesterol more effectively than simply
  reducing dietary cholesterol intake? Consider the relative
  contributions of endogenous synthesis and dietary absorption.
\item
  A food scientist wants to use an immobilised enzyme in a
  continuous-flow reactor. What are three advantages of enzyme
  immobilisation over using the free enzyme in solution?
\item
  CRISPR-Cas9 requires a PAM sequence (5'-NGG-3') adjacent to its
  target. Explain why this requirement exists and how it affects the
  enzyme's specificity. How does this relate to the concept of substrate
  recognition?
\item
  Pellagra (deficiency of niacin/vitamin B3) causes the ``three Ds'':
  dermatitis, diarrhoea, and dementia. Given that niacin is the
  precursor to NAD\(^+\), explain why this deficiency has such
  widespread systemic effects.
\item
  Using \texttt{michaelis\_menten}, compute \(v\) at \([S] = K_m/2\),
  \(K_m\), and \(2K_m\) for the same \(V_\mathrm{max}\). Verify
  numerically that \(v\) is \textbf{not} linear in \([S]\) even when
  \([S] \ll K_m\) is often approximated as linear.
\item
  Explain why \(k_\mathrm{cat}/K_m\) is a useful upper-bound metric for
  substrate discrimination under cellular subsaturating conditions, and
  give one evolutionary scenario where
  \hyperref[gl:natural-selection]{\textbf{natural selection}} would
  increase this ratio.
\item
  A two-substrate enzyme is studied at varying \hyperref[a]{A} for
  several fixed \hyperref[b]{B}. The Lineweaver-Burk plot reveals
  \textbf{intersecting} lines that meet to the \textbf{left of the
  y-axis}. Use \cref{eq:unit_I_bibi_sequential} and
  \cref{eq:unit_I_bibi_pingpong} to argue whether the mechanism is
  sequential or ping-pong.
\item
  Compare the switching sensitivity (fold-change in \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\theta}}{theta} for a 2\(\times\)
  change in \hyperref[s]{S} near \(K_{0.5}\)) of cooperative enzymes
  with \(n=1, 2, 4, 8\). Why do regulatory (rate-controlling) enzymes
  typically have \(n > 2\) while housekeeping enzymes are usually
  hyperbolic?
\item
  A directed-evolution campaign improves a transaminase's
  \(k_{cat}/K_m\) by 100\(\times\) over six rounds of
  mutation/selection. Discuss two metrics besides \(k_{cat}/K_m\) that
  the campaign should monitor in parallel, and explain why
  \(k_{cat}/K_m\) alone is not sufficient to declare success for an
  industrial process.
\item
  Using \cref{eq:unit_I_summation_theorem}, argue why doubling the
  abundance of a single ``rate-limiting'' glycolytic enzyme rarely
  doubles glycolytic flux. Suggest one cellular scenario where the flux
  control coefficient \(C^J\) for PFK-1 would approach 1.
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Unit II --- The Cell:
Introduction}\label{unit-ii-the-cell-introduction}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Unit II --- The Cell: Introduction}

\subsection*{Why This Unit Matters}\label{why-this-unit-matters-2}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Why This Unit Matters}

In 1665, Robert Hooke pressed a thin sliver of cork against the lens of
a compound microscope he had built himself and saw, for the first time
in human history, the architectural unit of life: the cell. He called
them \emph{cellulae} --- small rooms --- because they reminded him of
monks' chambers in a monastery. What Hooke saw in cork were dead walls.
Antoni van Leeuwenhoek, a decade later, saw living cells: bacteria
darting through pond water, human sperm, red blood cells coursing
through capillaries. The universe had grown smaller in every direction.

Today, three and a half centuries after those first observations, the
cell remains the central unit of biology --- and it turns out to be far
stranger and more sophisticated than Hooke could have imagined. A
typical human liver cell contains about 20,000 different
proteins, about 5 km of DNA, about 5,000 mitochondria,
and about 10 million ribosomes, most coordinated within a
volume of roughly 1,000 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{3}}{3}. Every second, that cell performs thousands
of enzymatic reactions, processes about 20 receptor signals,
divides its mitochondria, degrades misfolded proteins in lysosomes at pH
4.5, and repairs about 10,000 DNA lesions in its nucleus ---
most simultaneously, without a central coordinator.

This unit examines the cell at three levels of resolution: the
\textbf{cellular} (organelle inventory and function), the
\textbf{molecular} (membrane biophysics, signal transduction), and the
\textbf{computational} (mathematical models of cell size constraints,
diffusion, and membrane potential). You will encounter the endosymbiotic
theory --- one of the most elegant and evidence-rich hypotheses in
biology --- and the minimal cell, which asks: what is the irreducible
instruction set for life?

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Opening Vignette: The First Cell You Ever Saw}

In 1665, Robert Hooke pressed a thin sliver of cork against the lens of
a compound microscope he had constructed himself and published his
observations in \emph{Micrographia} --- a book so popular that Samuel
Pepys stayed up until 2 a.m. reading it. Hooke saw a regular array of
empty compartments --- the remnant cell walls of dead plant cells ---
and named them \textbf{cellulae} (from Latin, ``small rooms''). He had
no idea that cells were alive. That insight required a further 174 years
of microscopy, culminating in the cell theory formulations of
\citet{schleiden1838}, Schwann (1839), and \citet{virchow1855}.

Today, a single human body contains approximately 37.2 trillion cells
(Bianconi et al., 2013, \emph{Annals of Human Biology}) --- a number so
large that if laid end-to-end they would circle the Earth 200 times.
Every one of those cells descended, by an unbroken chain of cell
division, from a single fertilised egg roughly nine months before your
birth. And every cell alive on Earth today is the product of 3.7 billion
years of unbroken cell division since the origin of life --- not one
cell has ever been created from scratch by spontaneous generation since
Leuwenhoek looked through his microscope in 1674.

\emph{Primary source: Bianconi, E. et al.~(2013). An estimation of the
number of cells in the human body. Annals of Human Biology, 40(6),
463--471.}
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{The Cell as the Fundamental Unit of
Life}\label{the-cell-as-the-fundamental-unit-of-life}

\subsubsection{Historical Development of Cell
Theory}\label{historical-development-of-cell-theory}

The development of cell theory spans over two centuries and represents
one of the most important unifying principles in biology.

\textbf{Robert \citet{hooke1665}} first observed ``cells'' (actually
dead cell walls) in cork using a compound microscope he built himself.
He published his observations in \emph{Micrographia}, coining the term
``cell'' because the structures reminded him of monks' rooms (cellae) in
a monastery.

\textbf{Antonie van Leeuwenhoek (1674-1683)} constructed single-lens
microscopes achieving about 270x magnification and observed
living cells for the first time --- bacteria (``animalcules''),
protists, sperm cells, and red blood cells in capillary blood flow.

\textbf{Matthias \citet{schleiden1838}}, a botanist, concluded that most
plant tissues are composed of cells and that the cell is the basic unit
of plant structure.

\textbf{Theodor \citet{schwann1839}}, a zoologist and Schleiden's
colleague, extended this principle to animals, proposing that most
animal tissues are also composed of cells. Together, Schleiden and
Schwann formulated the first two tenets of cell theory.

\textbf{Rudolf \citet{virchow1855}} contributed the third tenet with his
famous dictum \emph{omnis cellula e cellula} (``every cell from a
cell''), establishing that cells arise primarily from pre-existing cells
through division. This principle demolished the lingering notion of
spontaneous generation and established the continuity of life.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0031_9e71ef6de137.png}
\caption{Timeline of key milestones in cell theory development, from Hooke's first observations to the modern synthetic minimal cell.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{The Three Original
Postulates}\label{the-three-original-postulates}

The \textbf{cell theory}, formalised by \citet{schleiden1838},
\citet{schwann1839}, and \citet{virchow1855}, rests on three founding
principles:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Most living organisms are composed of one or more cells.}
\item
  \textbf{The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of
  cellular organisms.}
\item
  \textbf{Most cells arise from pre-existing cells} (\emph{omnis cellula
  e cellula} --- Virchow, 1855).
\end{enumerate}

A corollary of the third tenet is that life is a continuous lineage ---
every cell on Earth today descends without interruption from the first
cells, approximately 3.5--3.8 billion years ago. The oldest
microfossils, found in Pilbara (Western Australia) and Barberton (South
Africa), date to about 3.5 Ga and show morphologies consistent
with filamentous prokaryotes.

\subsubsection{Modern Additions to Cell
Theory}\label{modern-additions-to-cell-theory}

Modern cell biology has expanded the original three postulates:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\item
  \textbf{The cell contains heritable information (DNA) that directs its
  activities and is passed to daughter cells.} This was established by
  the work of Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty (1944) and confirmed by
  \citet{hershey1952}.
\item
  \textbf{Most cells have the same basic chemical composition.} Most
  known cells use DNA as genetic material, RNA as intermediary,
  \hyperref[gl:protein]{\textbf{protein}}s as catalysts, and
  \hyperref[gl:phospholipid-bilayer]{\textbf{phospholipid bilayer}}s as
  membranes.
\item
  \textbf{Energy flow (metabolism and biochemistry) occurs within
  cells.} Most metabolic transformations ---
  \hyperref[gl:glycolysis]{\textbf{glycolysis}}, the TCA cycle,
  \hyperref[gl:oxidative-phosphorylation]{\textbf{oxidative
  phosphorylation}} --- take place within or across cell membranes.
\item
  \textbf{Cells contain the information necessary for their own
  reproduction.} The \hyperref[gl:genome]{\textbf{genome}} encodes not
  just structural components but the regulatory logic for cell division,
  differentiation, and programmed cell death.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Virchow and the Origin of Cancer Biology}
Virchow's principle \emph{omnis cellula e cellula} had a profound
clinical implication: if most cells come from pre-existing cells, then
cancer cells must also arise from normal cells through transformation.
Virchow himself applied this reasoning to pathology, founding the field
of cellular pathology. Today, cancer biology rests on the understanding
that \hyperref[gl:mutation]{\textbf{mutation}}s accumulate in somatic
cells, transforming them into malignant clones --- a direct intellectual
descendant of Virchow's third postulate. see
\cref{sec:unit_II_cell_signaling} (Cell Signalling) for oncogenes and
tumour suppressors.
\end{quote}

\textbf{Concept Check 1:} Viruses are not considered ``alive'' by cell
theory standards. List three properties of viruses that exclude them
from cell theory, and one property that challenges the boundary between
living and non-living.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{The Mathematics of Cell
Size}\label{the-mathematics-of-cell-size}

Cells are small --- almost without exception. Why?

The rate of metabolism (nutrient consumption, waste generation) scales
with \textbf{volume} (\(V \propto r^3\)). The rate of exchange with the
environment (nutrient uptake, waste removal) scales with \textbf{surface
area} (\(A \propto r^2\)). The ratio:

\[\frac{A}{V} = \frac{4\pi r^2}{\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3} = \frac{3}{r} \tag{5.1}\]

As \(r\) increases, \(A/V\) decreases. A sphere with \(r = 1\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m has
\(A/V = 3\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m\(^{-1}\). With \(r = 1\) mm (1,000x larger),
\(A/V = 0.003\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m\(^{-1}\). Large cells simply cannot exchange
nutrients fast enough for their metabolic demand.

\subsection{Worked Example: Surface-to-Volume
Calculation}\label{worked-example-surface-to-volume-calculation}

\emph{Problem:} A spherical bacterium has radius \(r = 0.5\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m.
Calculate (a) the surface area, (b) the volume, (c) the \(A/V\) ratio.
Then repeat for a spherical eukaryotic cell with \(r = 10\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m and
compare.

\emph{Solution:}

For the bacterium (\(r = 0.5\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m):

\[A = 4\pi r^2 = 4\pi(0.5)^2 = 3.14 \; \mu\text{m}^2 \tag{5.2}\]

\[V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \frac{4}{3}\pi(0.5)^3 = 0.524 \; \mu\text{m}^3 \tag{5.3}\]

\[\frac{A}{V} = \frac{3.14}{0.524} = 6.0 \; \mu\text{m}^{-1} \tag{5.4}\]

For the eukaryotic cell (\(r = 10\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m):

\[A = 4\pi(10)^2 = 1,257 \; \mu\text{m}^2 \tag{5.5}\]

\[V = \frac{4}{3}\pi(10)^3 = 4,189 \; \mu\text{m}^3 \tag{5.6}\]

\[\frac{A}{V} = \frac{1,257}{4,189} = 0.30 \; \mu\text{m}^{-1} \tag{5.7}\]

The bacterium has a 20-fold higher \(A/V\) ratio, enabling far more
efficient diffusion-based exchange per unit metabolic volume.

\subsubsection{Diffusion Time and Cell
Size}\label{diffusion-time-and-cell-size}

Diffusion time scales with the square of distance:

\[t = \frac{x^2}{2D} \tag{5.8}\]

where \(D\) is the diffusion coefficient. For a small molecule
(\(D \approx 10^{-9}\) m\(^2\)/s) to diffuse across a 1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m cell takes
about 0.5 ms. Across a 1 mm cell, it takes about 500 s
(over 8 minutes). This places an absolute upper limit on cell size for
diffusion-dependent processes.

\subsubsection{Exceptions to Small Cell
Size}\label{exceptions-to-small-cell-size}

\textbf{Exceptions} to small cell size achieve large size by: -
\textbf{Increasing surface area:} intestinal cells have microvilli
(amplify \(A\) by about 600x); root hair cells extend long
projections - \textbf{Reducing metabolically active volume:} plant
vacuoles occupy \textgreater80\% of cell volume but are largely
metabolically inert - \textbf{Reducing effective diffusion distance:}
nerve axons can be \textgreater1 m long but about 1--20 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m in diameter;
active transport supplements diffusion - \textbf{Cytoplasmic streaming:}
in giant plant cells (e.g., \emph{Chara} internodal cells,
\textgreater10 cm), \hyperref[gl:actin]{\textbf{actin}}-myosin-driven
streaming circulates \hyperref[gl:cytoplasm]{\textbf{cytoplasm}} at
about 60 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m/s, overcoming diffusion limitations -
\textbf{Multinucleation:} skeletal muscle fibres (up to 30 cm long)
contain hundreds of nuclei, each governing a local cytoplasmic domain

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 2:} \emph{Thiomargarita namibiensis} is a
bacterium with a diameter of about 750 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m --- visible to the
naked eye. How does it survive despite having an \(A/V\) ratio of about
0.008 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m\(^{-1}\)? (Hint: consider what fills \textgreater95\% of its
volume.)
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{The Cube Law and Why Giant Cells Are
Impossible}\label{the-cube-law-and-why-giant-cells-are-impossible}

The surface-to-volume problem can be sharpened into what physiologists
call the \textbf{cube law of metabolism}. If we model a cell as a sphere
of radius \(r\), mass \(m\), and uniform density \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\rho}}{rho}, then:

\begin{equation}
m = \rho \cdot \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3, \qquad A = 4\pi r^2
\label{eq:unit_II_cube_law_basis}
\end{equation}

Suppose every unit volume of cytoplasm consumes oxygen at a constant
rate \(q\) (mol O\(_2\) s\(^{-1}\) m\(^{-3}\)). The total metabolic
demand \(\dot{M}_\text{demand}\) scales as:

\[\dot{M}_\text{demand} = q \cdot V = q \cdot \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \tag{5.10}\]

Maximum oxygen flux through the membrane is set by Fick's law and is
bounded by surface area:

\[\dot{M}_\text{supply} = P_{O_2} \cdot \Delta[O_2] \cdot A = P_{O_2} \cdot \Delta[O_2] \cdot 4\pi r^2 \tag{5.11}\]

A viable cell requires
\(\dot{M}_\text{supply} \ge \dot{M}_\text{demand}\). Setting these equal
yields a \textbf{maximum admissible radius}:

\begin{equation}
r_\text{max} = \frac{3 \, P_{O_2} \, \Delta[O_2]}{q}
\label{eq:unit_II_rmax}
\end{equation}

For typical mammalian parameters (\(P_{O_2} \approx 1\times10^{-4}\)
m/s, \(\Delta[O_2] \approx 0.2\) mM, \(q \approx 1\) mol O\(_2\)
m\(^{-3}\) s\(^{-1}\)), \(r_\text{max} \approx 60\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m --- close to the
upper bound for actively respiring animal cells. Larger cells must
reduce \(q\) (e.g., plant vacuoles), increase \(A\) (microvilli,
infoldings), or accept partial anoxia in their cores. This is the
\textbf{cube law of metabolism}: demand scales with \(r^3\), supply with
\(r^2\), so any uniform cell hits a hard ceiling on size.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 3a:} Using \cref{eq:unit_II_rmax} with the
parameters above, by what factor would \(q\) have to drop to allow a 1
mm diameter respiring cell to survive without surface amplification?
\end{quote}

vs.~Eukaryote}\label{quantitative-comparison-prokaryote-vs.-eukaryote}

Prokaryotes and eukaryotes occupy fundamentally different scales of
organisation. The differences in linear dimension translate to even
larger gaps in volume, surface area, and information content:

\textbf{Worked Example: Why eukaryotes need internal membranes.} A HeLa
cell with \(r = 10\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m has about 1.25 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m\(^{-1}\) surface-to-volume ---
about 5-fold less than \emph{E. coli}. Yet the eukaryotic cell sustains
roughly 10\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} higher absolute metabolic flux. The arithmetic closes if the
eukaryote \emph{adds internal membrane surface area} equivalent to the
plasma membrane's deficit. Indeed, the inner mitochondrial membrane in a
single hepatocyte provides about \(3 \times 10^4\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m\(^2\)
of additional respiratory surface --- roughly 6\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} the plasma membrane
area. Compartmentalisation is therefore not optional aesthetics: it is
the topological solution to the cube-law constraint on a body plan that
contains 1,000\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} more cytoplasm than a bacterium.

\textbf{Concept Check 3b:} A spherical eukaryotic cell with \(r = 10\)
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m has plasma-membrane area \(A_\text{PM} \approx 1{,}260\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m\(^2\). If
respiratory demand scales with cytoplasmic volume and the cell needs 6\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x}
the plasma-membrane area to support its metabolism, estimate the total
inner membrane area its mitochondria must provide.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Microscopy: Seeing the
Cell}\label{microscopy-seeing-the-cell}

Understanding cells requires seeing them. The history of cell biology is
inseparable from advances in microscopy.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0032_ee5d89460c88.png}
\caption{Overview of microscopy techniques used in cell biology, categorised by resolution capability.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Light Microscopy}\label{light-microscopy}

The \textbf{resolution limit} of light microscopy is governed by the
Abbe diffraction limit:

\[d = \frac{\lambda}{2 \cdot \text{NA}} \tag{5.9}\]

where \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda} is the wavelength of light and NA is the numerical aperture of
the objective. For visible light (\(\lambda \approx 550\) nm) and a
high-quality oil-immersion objective (NA = 1.4): \(d \approx 200\) nm.

\textbf{Bright-field microscopy:} Transmitted light; specimens typically
stained (H\&E, \hyperref[gl:gram-stain]{\textbf{Gram stain}}). Simple
but limited contrast for living cells.

\textbf{Phase-contrast microscopy:} Converts phase differences (from
refractive index variations in transparent specimens) into amplitude
differences visible as contrast. Ideal for observing living, unstained
cells. Invented by Frits Zernike (Nobel Prize in Physics, 1953).

\textbf{Differential interference contrast (DIC/Nomarski):} Uses
polarised light split into two beams that pass through slightly
different optical paths in the specimen. Produces a pseudo-3D relief
image with excellent contrast. Eliminates the ``halo'' artifact of
phase-contrast.

\textbf{Fluorescence microscopy:} Specimens labelled with fluorophores
(antibodies conjugated to FITC, Cy3, Cy5; or genetically encoded GFP and
derivatives). Excitation light of specific wavelength causes fluorophore
emission at a longer wavelength. Enables specific protein localisation,
live-cell imaging, and multiplexing (multiple colours simultaneously).

\textbf{Confocal laser scanning microscopy:} Uses a pinhole to reject
out-of-focus light, producing optical sections about 0.5--1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m
thick. Z-stacks can be reconstructed into 3D images. Essential for thick
specimens and co-localisation studies.

\textbf{Total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF):} Evanescent wave
illuminates about 100 nm of the cell adjacent to the coverslip surface.
Used to study membrane dynamics, vesicle fusion events, and
single-molecule behaviour at the plasma membrane.

\subsubsection{Electron Microscopy}\label{electron-microscopy}

\textbf{Transmission electron microscopy (TEM):} Electrons pass through
ultrathin sections (about 50--70 nm) stained with heavy metals
(uranyl acetate, osmium tetroxide). Resolution about 0.1 nm.
Reveals ultrastructural details of
\hyperref[gl:organelle]{\textbf{organelle}}s, membranes, and
macromolecular complexes.

\textbf{Scanning electron microscopy (SEM):} Electrons scan the surface
of gold- or platinum-coated specimens. Produces stunning 3D topographic
images of cell surfaces, tissue architecture, and microorganisms.
Resolution about 1--5 nm.

\textbf{Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM):} Specimens flash-frozen in
vitreous ice (no staining or fixation) and imaged at liquid nitrogen
temperature. Single-particle analysis reconstructs 3D structures of
proteins and complexes at near-atomic resolution (2--4 angstroms).
Awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2017 (Jacques Dubochet, Joachim
Frank, Richard Henderson). Cryo-EM has revolutionised structural
biology, enabling structures of membrane proteins, ribosomes, and viral
capsids that resist crystallisation.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Cryo-EM and Drug Discovery} Cryo-EM has
become indispensable in pharmaceutical development. The structure of the
SARS-CoV-2 spike protein was solved by cryo-EM within weeks of the
pandemic onset, enabling rapid \hyperref[gl:vaccine]{\textbf{vaccine}}
design (Wrapp et al., 2020, \emph{Science}). Drug binding sites on ion
channels (e.g., TRPV1 pain receptor) and GPCRs have been mapped at
near-atomic resolution, accelerating rational drug design. see
\cref{sec:unit_II_membrane_transport} for membrane protein structures.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Super-Resolution
Microscopy}\label{super-resolution-microscopy}

Super-resolution methods bypass the Abbe diffraction limit, achieving
resolutions of 20--50 nm with light:

\textbf{STED (Stimulated Emission Depletion):} A donut-shaped depletion
beam suppresses fluorescence from the periphery of the excitation spot,
shrinking the effective point spread function. Resolution
about 30--50 nm. Developed by Stefan Hell (Nobel Prize in
Chemistry, 2014).

\textbf{STORM (Stochastic Optical Reconstruction Microscopy):}
Individual fluorophores are stochastically activated, imaged, and
precisely localised over thousands of frames. The composite image
achieves about 20 nm resolution. Co-developed by Xiaowei
Zhuang.

\textbf{PALM (Photoactivated Localisation Microscopy):} Similar to STORM
but uses photoactivatable fluorescent proteins (e.g., mEos, Dendra2).
Particularly suited for live-cell imaging of genetically encoded
constructs. Co-developed by Eric Betzig (Nobel Prize in Chemistry,
2014).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 3:} A researcher wants to study the real-time
dynamics of clathrin-coated pit formation at the plasma membrane of a
living cell. Which microscopy technique would be most appropriate and
why?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Prokaryotic Cells}\label{prokaryotic-cells}

Prokaryotes (\textbf{pro} = before, \textbf{karyon} = nucleus) lack
membrane-bound organelles. They include the domains \textbf{Bacteria}
and \textbf{\hyperref[gl:archaea]{Archaea}}.

\subsubsection{Key Features}\label{key-features}

\subsubsection{Prokaryotic Cell
Structure}\label{prokaryotic-cell-structure}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Plasma membrane:} phospholipid bilayer + integral proteins.
  Site of chemiosmotic ATP synthesis (no mitochondria). In
  photosynthetic bacteria (cyanobacteria, purple bacteria), the membrane
  invaginates to form thylakoid-like structures for the light reactions.
\item
  \textbf{Cell wall:} structurally rigid; resists osmotic lysis.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{Gram-positive} bacteria: thick peptidoglycan layer (20--80
    nm), teichoic acids, no outer membrane. Crystal violet stain
    retained (purple).
  \item
    \textbf{Gram-negative} bacteria: thin peptidoglycan
    (about 2--7 nm) + outer membrane with LPS
    (lipopolysaccharide). Crystal violet not retained (pink after
    safranin counter-stain). The periplasmic space between inner and
    outer membranes contains degradative
    \hyperref[gl:enzyme]{\textbf{enzyme}}s and transport proteins.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Capsule:} polysaccharide layer external to cell wall;
  anti-phagocytic (evades immune system);
  \hyperref[gl:biofilm]{\textbf{biofilm}} formation. \emph{Streptococcus
  pneumoniae} with capsule is virulent; without capsule is avirulent
  (Griffith's transformation experiment, 1928).
\item
  \textbf{Flagellum:} rotating protein filament powered by proton motive
  force (bacteria) or ATP (archaea); each rotation of the bacterial
  flagellar motor about 100 Hz in \emph{E. coli}; composed of
  flagellin protein subunits; the basal body contains a rotary motor
  with stator and rotor components.
\item
  \textbf{Pili (fimbriae):} protein tubes for attachment, conjugation,
  biofilm; Type IV pili can retract to generate motile force
  (``twitching motility''); F-pili mediate DNA transfer during
  conjugation.
\item
  \textbf{Nucleoid:} condensed region containing the circular chromosome
  (typically 1--6 Mbp); not bounded by a membrane; associated with
  nucleoid-associated proteins (NAPs: HU, H-NS, Fis, IHF) that organise
  chromosome topology.
\item
  \textbf{Plasmids:} small circular DNA molecules (1--200 kb) carrying
  accessory \hyperref[gl:gene]{\textbf{gene}}s (antibiotic resistance,
  \hyperref[gl:virulence]{\textbf{virulence}} factors, metabolic
  capabilities); replicate independently; horizontally transferable
  between cells.
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Gram Staining and Antibiotic Selection} The
Gram stain, developed by Hans Christian Gram in 1884, remains the most
important rapid diagnostic test in clinical microbiology. Gram-positive
infections (thick peptidoglycan) respond to beta-lactam antibiotics
(penicillins, cephalosporins) that inhibit peptidoglycan cross-linking
by transpeptidases (PBPs). Gram-negative infections are intrinsically
more resistant because the outer membrane excludes many antibiotics;
treatment often requires aminoglycosides or carbapenems that penetrate
through porins. The rise of multi-drug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria
(e.g., carbapenem-resistant \emph{Klebsiella pneumoniae}) is a major
public health crisis. see \cref{sec:unit_II_cell_structure} for membrane
permeability.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 4:} Why are archaea resistant to antibiotics that
target peptidoglycan synthesis (e.g., penicillin, vancomycin)?
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{The Prokaryotic Cytoskeleton --- A Recent
Revolution}\label{the-prokaryotic-cytoskeleton-a-recent-revolution}

For nearly a century, textbooks asserted that prokaryotes lack a
\hyperref[gl:cytoskeleton]{\textbf{cytoskeleton}}. The discovery of
bacterial cytoskeletal homologues over the past 25 years has overturned
that view: prokaryotes contain dedicated structural and force-generating
filaments that are evolutionary precursors of every major eukaryotic
cytoskeletal class.

\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Eukaryotic homologue
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{FtsZ} & Tubulin (GTPase fold) & Z-ring assembly at midcell;
recruits divisome; constricts during binary fission & 1991 (Bi \&
Lutkenhaus) \\
\textbf{MreB} & Actin (ATP-binding fold) & Helical filaments under inner
membrane; defines rod-shaped cell geometry; coordinates peptidoglycan
synthesis & 2001 (Jones et al.) \\
\textbf{Crescentin (CreS)} & Intermediate filaments (lamins) & Curves
\emph{Caulobacter crescentus} into its vibrioid shape & 2003 (Ausmees et
al.) \\
\textbf{ParM} & Actin & Pushes plasmid copies apart during segregation &
2002 \\
\textbf{Bactofilins (BacA/B)} & None close & Polar localisation;
cell-wall remodelling & 2010 \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{FtsZ and bacterial cytokinesis.} FtsZ polymerises
GTP-dependently into protofilaments that form a contractile
\textbf{Z-ring} at the future division site. The Z-ring recruits the
divisome (FtsA, FtsW, FtsI/PBP3) which synthesises septal peptidoglycan
as the membrane invaginates. FtsZ treadmills around the ring at
about 30 nm/s --- strikingly similar in mechanism to actin
treadmilling, yet evolutionarily a tubulin homologue. The GTP-bound
monomer fold superimposes on alpha/beta-tubulin with RMSD \textless{} 2
Å despite \textless{} 10\% sequence identity, providing direct
structural evidence that the eukaryotic mitotic machinery descends from
a bacterial cell-division protein.

\textbf{MreB and rod-shaped morphology.} MreB filaments rotate around
the bacterial circumference, dragging the \textbf{Rod complex} (RodA,
MreC, MreD, PBP2) that synthesises lateral peptidoglycan. Loss of MreB
converts rod-shaped \emph{E. coli} into spheres (cocci) within minutes;
expression in mutant cocci restores rod shape. MreB is therefore both
structural (filament) and a guidance system (positional cue for
cell-wall synthesis), exactly mirroring eukaryotic actin's dual roles.

\textbf{Crescentin and curvature.} \emph{Caulobacter crescentus} gets
its name from a comma-shaped curve produced by a single helical bundle
of CreS filaments running along the inner curve of the cell. Mutational
loss of \emph{creS} yields straight rods. CreS is biophysically a
coiled-coil of the same family as nuclear lamins and cytokeratins.

These discoveries closed a major textbook gap: \textbf{most three
eukaryotic cytoskeletal classes (microfilaments, microtubules,
intermediate filaments) have prokaryotic ancestors}. The cytoskeleton
predates compartmentalisation by at least 1.5 billion years.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 4b:} A pharmaceutical company is screening for
narrow-spectrum antibiotics that block bacterial cell division without
affecting human cells. Why is FtsZ a more promising target than MreB?
(Consider the structural and functional homology to eukaryotic
counterparts and what happens when each protein is inhibited.)
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Detailed Comparison: Bacteria
vs.~Archaea}\label{detailed-comparison-bacteria-vs.-archaea}

The discovery of Archaea by \citet{woese1977} as a separate domain
transformed our view of life's deep structure. Archaea were initially
described as ``prokaryotes that live in extreme environments,'' but
molecular phylogenetics revealed that Archaea share many features with
eukaryotes that bacteria do not --- a fact now central to debates about
eukaryotic origin (the ``Asgard archaea'' hypothesis). The table below
extends \cref{sec:unit_II_cell_theory} earlier comparison with molecular
detail relevant to drug development, evolution, and astrobiology.

\textbf{Why this matters.} Archaea share information-processing
machinery (transcription, translation, replication) with eukaryotes but
housekeeping/metabolic machinery with bacteria. The leading
``two-domain'' tree (Embley \& Williams; Spang et al.~2015) places
eukaryotes \emph{within} the Asgard archaea, with the mitochondrial
endosymbiont contributing the bacterial-style metabolism. The
bacteria--archaea distinction is not a curiosity --- it is the
structural map for the deepest split in the tree of life.

\textbf{Concept Check 4c:} Why does penicillin kill many bacteria but no

\subsection{Eukaryotic Cells}\label{eukaryotic-cells}

Eukaryotic cells (\textbf{eu} = true; \textbf{karyon} = nucleus) contain
membrane-bound organelles and a true nucleus. They include protists,
fungi, plants, and animals.

\subsubsection{Organelle Inventory}\label{organelle-inventory}

This inventory should not be read as a set of isolated boxes. Eukaryotic
organelles exchange lipids, ions, metabolites, and stress signals
through membrane-contact sites; mitochondria divide and fuse, the ER
wraps around many organelles, lysosomes function as nutrient-sensing
hubs, and biomolecular condensates add non-membrane compartments for
RNA, protein, and signalling control. A modern cell-biological
explanation names the compartment, the traffic route, the time scale,
and the evidence type: microscopy, perturbation, biochemical
fractionation, or single-cell/spatial data.

\subsubsection{Compartmentalisation: The Eukaryotic
Advantage}\label{compartmentalisation-the-eukaryotic-advantage}

The defining feature of eukaryotic cells is
\textbf{compartmentalisation} --- the segregation of biochemical
processes into membrane-bound organelles. This provides several
advantages:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Incompatible reactions can occur simultaneously:} Protein
  synthesis (cytoplasm, pH 7.2) and protein degradation (lysosomes, pH
  4.5) are separated by lysosomal membranes.
\item
  \textbf{Concentration of substrates and enzymes:} Mitochondrial matrix
  concentrates TCA cycle enzymes, increasing reaction rates.
\item
  \textbf{Regulation of gene expression:} The nuclear envelope separates
  transcription (nucleus) from translation (cytoplasm), enabling
  post-transcriptional regulation (splicing, mRNA export, mRNA
  stability).
\item
  \textbf{Expanded membrane surface area:} Internal membranes (ER,
  Golgi, mitochondria) provide enormous surface area for
  membrane-associated reactions.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Endosymbiotic Theory}\label{endosymbiotic-theory}

Lynn Margulis formalised the \textbf{endosymbiotic theory} (1967):
mitochondria and chloroplasts are the descendants of free-living
bacteria engulfed by a proto-eukaryotic host about 1.5--2
billion years ago.

\subsubsection{Evidence for
Endosymbiosis}\label{evidence-for-endosymbiosis}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Double membranes:} Both organelles have inner (bacterial
  plasma membrane) and outer (phagocytic membrane) bilayers.
\item
  \textbf{Circular DNA:} Mitochondrial and chloroplast genomes are
  circular, like bacterial chromosomes.
\item
  \textbf{70S ribosomes:} Organelle ribosomes are structurally
  bacterial-type; sensitive to antibacterials (chloramphenicol,
  erythromycin) that inhibit 70S, not eukaryotic 80S ribosomes.
\item
  \textbf{Binary fission:} Organelles divide by binary fission,
  independently of nuclear cell division, using FtsZ-related proteins.
\item
  \textbf{Phylogenetics:} rRNA sequences of mitochondria are most
  similar to \textbf{alpha-proteobacteria} (e.g., \emph{Rickettsia});
  chloroplasts to \textbf{cyanobacteria}.
\item
  \textbf{Transfer of genes:} about 1,500 mitochondrial-origin
  genes now live in the nuclear genome (gene transfer to nucleus over
  evolutionary time).
\item
  \textbf{Cardiolipin:} The inner mitochondrial membrane contains
  cardiolipin, a lipid characteristic of bacterial membranes.
\item
  \textbf{Formylmethionine:} Mitochondrial protein synthesis initiates
  with N-formylmethionine, as in bacteria, not methionine as in
  eukaryotic cytoplasmic translation.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Primary and Secondary
Endosymbiosis}\label{primary-and-secondary-endosymbiosis}

\textbf{Primary \hyperref[gl:endosymbiosis]{\textbf{endosymbiosis}}}
(mitochondrion; then chloroplast) explains the origin of eukaryotes. The
mitochondrial endosymbiosis is believed to have occurred once in
evolutionary history, as most known eukaryotes either possess
mitochondria or have remnant mitochondria-derived organelles
(hydrogenosomes, mitosomes).

\textbf{Secondary endosymbiosis} (a eukaryote with chloroplast engulfed
by another eukaryote) explains secondary chloroplasts in
dinoflagellates, euglenids, and kelp (evidenced by 3--4 bounding
membranes). \textbf{Tertiary endosymbiosis} has also occurred in some
dinoflagellates.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 5:} If you treated a eukaryotic cell with
chloramphenicol (an antibiotic that inhibits 70S ribosomes), which
organelle's protein synthesis would be specifically affected? Would
cytoplasmic protein synthesis be affected? Explain.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{LUCA: The Last Universal Common
Ancestor}\label{luca-the-last-universal-common-ancestor}

If cell theory is correct that most cells descend from pre-existing
cells \citep{virchow1855}, then the lineages of bacteria, archaea, and
eukaryotes converge backward in time on a single ancestral population:
the \textbf{Last Comprehensive Common Ancestor (LUCA)}. LUCA is not a
fossil --- it is a \emph{reconstruction} assembled from comparative
molecular data. Three classes of evidence let us infer its properties.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Almost universally conserved genes (the LUCA core).} Genes
  shared by Bacteria \emph{and} Archaea --- and absent from horizontally
  transferred outliers --- are candidates for LUCA inheritance. Modern
  reconstructions (Weiss et al.~2016, \emph{Nature Microbiology})
  identify about 355 such ancient gene families. LUCA almost
  certainly possessed: a fully fledged DNA\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}RNA\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}protein machinery (DNA
  polymerase, RNA polymerase, ribosome with rRNA, about 20
  aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases), the
  \hyperref[gl:genetic-code]{\textbf{genetic code}},
  Wood--Ljungdahl-pathway-like CO\(_2\) fixation, {[}Fe--S{]} and
  {[}Ni--Fe{]} metalloenzymes, ATP synthase (rotor/stator architecture),
  and a chemiosmotic membrane.
\item
  \textbf{Geochemistry-constrained habitat.} The metalloenzyme inventory
  (Ni, Fe, Mo, Co, W in unusual valences) suggests LUCA inhabited an
  \textbf{anaerobic, hydrothermal, alkaline environment} --- most
  parsimoniously interpreted as a serpentinising hydrothermal vent
  system on the early ocean floor (about 3.8 Ga). Dependence on
  natural proton gradients across thin inorganic membranes (FeS
  micropores in vent chimneys) preceded the modern membrane-spanning ATP
  synthase, suggesting LUCA was not yet a fully autonomous cell but a
  \emph{pre-cellular} metabolic unit (Lane \& Martin 2012).
\item
  \textbf{The DNA replication anomaly.} Bacterial and archaeal DNA
  polymerases (Family A vs.~Family B) share \emph{no} sequence
  similarity in their catalytic cores, despite both performing the same
  chemistry. The simplest explanation is that LUCA used
  \textbf{RNA-genome replication} and DNA replication evolved twice
  independently \emph{after} the bacterial--archaeal split. This argues
  that LUCA was a late RNA-world organism with a stable genetic code and
  ribosomes but was still transitioning from RNA to DNA storage.
\end{enumerate}

The reconstruction has profound implications. LUCA was not the first
cell --- it was the last common one. Earlier lineages may have existed
but left no descendants. The vast biochemical diversity of modern life
(oxygenic photosynthesis, methanogenesis, eukaryotic
compartmentalisation) most evolved \emph{after} LUCA, layered onto its
conserved core.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 5b:} If LUCA used naturally occurring proton
gradients (from inorganic vent chemistry) rather than self-generated
ones, which modern molecular machinery must have evolved \emph{before}
free-living cells became possible? (Consider what a free-living cell
must do that a vent-bound consortium need not.)
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Viral Replication: Lytic vs.~Lysogenic
Cycles}\label{viral-replication-lytic-vs.-lysogenic-cycles}

Viruses are not cells (no membranes of their own metabolism, no
ribosomes, no autonomous reproduction) and so are excluded from cell
theory by definition. But viruses are cellular \emph{parasites}, and
their replication strategies illuminate what cells must do to maintain
integrity. Bacteriophages --- viruses that infect bacteria --- provide
the textbook example.

\textbf{Lytic cycle (e.g., T4 bacteriophage):} 1. \textbf{Attachment:}
tail fibres bind specific surface receptors (e.g., LPS, OmpC) ---
defines host range. 2. \textbf{Penetration:} the genome is injected into
the \hyperref[gl:cytoplasm]{\textbf{cytoplasm}} through a contractile
tail; capsid remains outside. 3. \textbf{Hijacking:} within
about 2 min, host RNA polymerase transcribes ``early'' phage
genes that degrade the host chromosome (T4 gene 46/47 nucleases) and
reprogramme cell metabolism toward phage production. 4.
\textbf{Replication and assembly:} phage DNA is replicated
(about 100 copies per cell); structural proteins self-assemble
into capsids; DNA is packaged via a portal motor (one of the strongest
molecular machines known: about 57 pN of force, comparable to
muscle myosin). 5. \textbf{Lysis:} about 25 min after
infection, phage lysozyme + holin perforate the cell envelope. The cell
bursts, releasing about 100--200 progeny phages. The host is
dead.

The lytic cycle is the textbook image of viral infection: rapid, fatal,
productive. The single-step \textbf{burst size} (200) and
\textbf{latency time} (25 min) determine the kinetics of phage
epidemics.

\textbf{Lysogenic cycle (e.g., lambda bacteriophage):} 1.
\textbf{Attachment, penetration:} same as lytic. 2.
\textbf{Integration:} the phage genome (linear at injection)
circularises and integrates into the host chromosome at a specific site
(\emph{attB}) via phage integrase. The integrated genome is now a
\textbf{prophage}. 3. \textbf{Quiescence:} the prophage is replicated
passively with the host chromosome at every cell division. Lambda CI
repressor blocks lytic gene expression. The bacterium grows and divides
normally with the prophage as a stowaway. This state can persist for
thousands of generations. 4. \textbf{Induction:} stressors (UV,
mitomycin C, low nutrients) activate the host SOS response \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} RecA
cleaves CI repressor \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} lytic genes are derepressed \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} prophage excises \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
enters lytic cycle.

The lysogenic cycle has profound consequences. \textbf{Specialised
transduction} carries host genes between bacteria when imprecise
excision packages chromosomal DNA. Many bacterial \textbf{virulence
factors are phage-encoded}: diphtheria toxin (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-phage in
\emph{Corynebacterium diphtheriae}), cholera toxin (CTX\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\varphi}}{phi} in \emph{Vibrio
cholerae}), Shiga toxin (Stx phage in EHEC \emph{E. coli} O157:H7),
botulinum toxin types C and D. The lysogen-to-lytic switch ---
controlled by a single repressor --- is the prototype for many
developmental switches and inspired the operon model of
\citet{jacob1961}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Phage Therapy in the Antibiotic-Resistance
Era} Lytic bacteriophages can target antibiotic-resistant bacteria with
exquisite specificity (one phage typically infects one species or even
strain). Compassionate-use phage therapy has cured otherwise-fatal
infections (Steffanie Strathdee, \emph{A. baumannii} sepsis, 2017;
cystic fibrosis \emph{Mycobacterium abscessus}, 2019). Phages are now in
late-stage clinical trials for chronic urinary infections and
prosthetic-joint infections. Phage cocktails --- designed to evade
host-resistance evolution by targeting multiple receptors --- are the
closest realisation of the ``magic bullet'' concept since penicillin.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 5c:} A \emph{V. cholerae} strain loses its CTX\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\varphi}}{phi}
prophage. The resulting strain can colonise the human gut but causes
mild diarrhoea. Why? What does this tell you about the relationship
between cell theory's exclusion of viruses and the practical impact of
viruses on cellular biology?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{The Minimal Cell:
JCVI-syn3.0}\label{the-minimal-cell-jcvi-syn3.0}

In 2016, Craig Venter's team at the J. Craig Venter Institute created
\textbf{JCVI-syn3.0}, a synthetic organism with the smallest genome of
any self-replicating cell: \textbf{473 genes} (531 kb). This was
achieved by systematically deleting genes from \emph{Mycoplasma
mycoides} until primarily essential genes remained.

Key findings: - Of the 473 genes, \textbf{149 (31.5\%) have unknown
function} --- we do not understand why they are essential - The minimal
gene set includes genes for DNA replication, transcription, translation,
membrane synthesis, and central metabolism - No genes for cell wall
synthesis, stress responses, or secondary metabolism were required under
laboratory conditions - JCVI-syn3.0 grows more slowly than its parent
organism, with a doubling time of about 3 hours

This work defines the boundary between chemistry and life and raises
profound questions: What is the minimal instruction set for a living
system? Can we understand life by building it from scratch?

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Synthetic Biology and Minimal Cells} The
minimal cell concept has direct applications in biotechnology.
Engineered minimal cells could serve as ``chassis'' organisms for
producing pharmaceuticals, biofuels, or industrial chemicals with
predictable behaviour and reduced metabolic complexity. Understanding
essential gene sets also identifies new antibiotic targets --- genes
essential for bacterial survival that have no human homologues.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Extremophile Cells}\label{extremophile-cells}

Extremophiles are organisms (primarily archaea, but also some bacteria
and eukaryotes) that thrive in environments previously considered
incompatible with life. They demonstrate the remarkable adaptability of
cellular organisation.

\subsubsection{Implications for
Astrobiology}\label{implications-for-astrobiology}

Extremophiles expand our understanding of habitable environments in the
solar system:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Mars:} Psychrophilic and radiation-resistant organisms suggest
  that microbial life could persist in Martian subsurface brine
  environments
\item
  \textbf{Europa (Jupiter's moon):} Halophilic and barophilic organisms
  thrive under conditions similar to those predicted for Europa's
  subsurface ocean
\item
  \textbf{Enceladus (Saturn's moon):} Hydrothermal vent-associated
  chemolithoautotrophs provide models for life powered by water-rock
  chemistry
\item
  \textbf{Titan:} While no known organisms thrive in liquid methane, the
  existence of extremophiles encourages consideration of exotic
  biochemistries
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 6:} \emph{Ferroplasma acidarmanus} lives at pH 0
(equivalent to battery acid), yet its internal pH is about 5.6.
Calculate the proton concentration gradient across its membrane. How
many orders of magnitude difference is this?
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{By Oxygen Relationship}\label{by-oxygen-relationship}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Obligate aerobe:} requires O\(_2\) (complex animals,
  \emph{Mycobacterium tuberculosis})
\item
  \textbf{Facultative anaerobe:} can grow with or without O\(_2\)
  (yeast, \emph{E. coli})
\item
  \textbf{Obligate anaerobe:} killed by O\(_2\) (\emph{Clostridium
  botulinum}, methanogens)
\item
  \textbf{Aerotolerant anaerobe:} not killed by O\(_2\) but does not use
  it (\emph{Lactobacillus})
\item
  \textbf{Microaerophile:} requires O\(_2\) but at lower concentrations
  than atmospheric (\emph{Campylobacter}, \emph{Helicobacter pylori})
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-7}

For \textbf{Cell Theory and Cell Types}, frontier biology belongs inside
the evidence logic of the chapter. Cell biology is increasingly measured
as live, spatial, single-cell, and perturbational data rather than
static diagrams alone. The core reading question is this: cell-theory
evidence now includes microscopy, lineage tracing, omics, and
synthetic-cell boundary tests.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

Ask what measurement scale is being claimed: nanometre structure,
single-cell transcript abundance, organelle dynamics, tissue context, or
organismal phenotype.

\textbf{Source practice:} For cell-state claims, distinguish microscopy,
live-cell perturbation, single-cell sequencing, spatial transcriptomics,
and biochemical assay evidence before making a causal statement.

\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-7}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Cell theory: most organisms are cells; cells are the basic unit; cells
  come from cells. Modern additions include heritable DNA information
  and shared chemical composition.
\item
  The surface-area-to-volume ratio (\(A/V = 3/r\)) constrains cell size;
  large cells must increase \(A\) or reduce metabolic demand per unit
  volume. Diffusion time scales with \(x^2\), imposing additional size
  limits.
\item
  Microscopy techniques span light (bright-field, phase-contrast, DIC,
  fluorescence, confocal, TIRF), electron (TEM, SEM, cryo-EM), and
  super-resolution (STED, STORM, PALM) methods, with resolutions from
  about 200 nm to sub-nanometre.
\item
  Prokaryotes (Bacteria + Archaea) lack membrane-bound organelles; Gram
  staining discriminates based on cell wall structure. Archaea share
  molecular features with eukaryotes.
\item
  Eukaryotic organelles carry out compartmentalised functions;
  mitochondria and chloroplasts arose by endosymbiosis of bacterial
  ancestors.
\item
  The minimal cell (JCVI-syn3.0, 473 genes) defines the boundary of
  cellular life; extremophiles demonstrate life's adaptability to
  extreme environments.
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See \cref{sec:unit_II_cell_structure} for
  organelle inventory, Unit VII for prokaryotic diversity, and Unit VI
  for common ancestry and LUCA reasoning.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Review Questions}\label{review-questions-7}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  State the three original postulates of cell theory and the three
  modern additions. For each, identify the key experiment or discovery
  that established it.
\item
  A spherical cell has radius 5 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m. Calculate its surface area, volume,
  and \(A/V\) ratio. If the cell doubles its radius, by what factor does
  \(A/V\) change?
\item
  Compare and contrast the cell walls of Gram-positive bacteria,
  Gram-negative bacteria, and archaea. Why are archaea naturally
  resistant to penicillin?
\item
  List six lines of evidence supporting the endosymbiotic origin of
  mitochondria. Which single piece of evidence do you consider most
  compelling, and why?
\item
  Explain why TIRF microscopy would be preferred over confocal
  microscopy for studying single vesicle fusion events at the plasma
  membrane.
\item
  The diffusion coefficient of glucose in water is approximately
  \(6.7 \times 10^{-10}\) m\(^2\)/s. Calculate the time required for
  glucose to diffuse across (a) a 2 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m bacterium and (b) a 100 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m plant
  cell.
\item
  JCVI-syn3.0 has 473 genes, of which 149 have unknown function. Discuss
  the implications of this finding for our understanding of the minimal
  requirements for life.
\item
  Describe how \emph{Deinococcus radiodurans} survives radiation doses
  \textgreater1,000 times the lethal dose for humans. What cellular
  mechanisms enable this extreme resistance?
\item
  Compare the membrane lipids of bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes. How
  do archaeal ether-linked isoprenoid lipids contribute to survival at
  extreme temperatures?
\item
  A pharmaceutical company is developing a new antibiotic. Using your
  knowledge of prokaryotic cell structure, suggest three molecular
  targets that are present in bacteria but absent in human cells.
\item
  Using \breaktt{get\_organelles\_by\_cell\_type}, contrast the organelle
  lists for \texttt{"animal"} and \texttt{"prokaryote"}. Which entries
  best illustrate endosymbiotic theory?
\item
  A spherical bacterium and a spherical eukaryote both rely on
  diffusion. If the eukaryote is 20\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} larger in radius, by what factor
  does the surface-to-volume ratio change relative to the bacterium?
\item
  Using \cref{eq:unit_II_cube_law_basis} and \cref{eq:unit_II_rmax},
  explain why every metabolically active animal cell is \textless{} 100
  \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m in radius unless it has internal membranes, microvilli, or partial
  anoxia. Identify two cell types that violate this rule and explain
  \emph{how} they do so.
\item
  List three bacterial cytoskeletal proteins, their eukaryotic
  homologues, and the function of each. Why was the absence of ``the
  cytoskeleton'' in prokaryotes a textbook error rather than a fact?
\item
  Compare lytic and lysogenic phage cycles in terms of their (a) speed,
  (b) burst size, (c) consequences for the host cell, and (d)
  implications for evolution. Which strategy is more reminiscent of
  ``infectious disease'' and which of ``horizontal gene transfer''?
\item
  Outline the three classes of evidence used to reconstruct LUCA. What
  does the absence of conserved DNA polymerase tell us about LUCA's
  information system?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Discussion Questions}\label{discussion-questions-3}

These questions have no single correct answer --- they are designed to
provoke debate, integrate concepts across sections, and connect cell
biology to broader scientific and ethical questions.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Defining life.} Is JCVI-syn3.0 alive? It self-replicates,
  contains a genome, performs metabolism, and responds to its
  environment --- but every component was designed by humans. If the
  answer is ``yes,'' does that mean we have created life? If ``no,''
  what definition excludes it that does not also exclude obligate
  intracellular pathogens like \emph{Rickettsia} (which depend on host
  metabolism just as syn3.0 depends on enriched media)?
\item
  \textbf{Cell theory under stress.} Cell theory states that most cells
  come from pre-existing cells. But somatic-cell nuclear transfer
  (cloning), induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs from skin
  fibroblasts), and now in-vitro-generated organoids (mini-brains,
  mini-livers) push this principle. Are organoids ``organisms''? Do they
  have moral status if they begin to exhibit coordinated electrical
  activity?
\item
  \textbf{The 149-gene mystery.} JCVI-syn3.0 has 149 essential genes of
  unknown function. Choose one approach (CRISPR screening, AlphaFold
  structural prediction, evolutionary co-occurrence analysis, or
  chemical biology) and argue why it is most likely to crack this set
  first. What ethical or biosafety considerations follow from
  understanding the minimal genome?
\item
  \textbf{Astrobiology and the biosignature problem.} If life on Mars or
  Europa derives from a separate origin, it might lack DNA, ribosomes,
  and ATP --- making it invisible to instruments designed around
  terrestrial biochemistry. How might cell theory be revised if we
  discovered non-cellular life elsewhere? Conversely, what
  \emph{cellular} features might be comprehensive across any
  biochemistry (compartmentalisation? polymer-based information storage?
  membranes?) and why?
\item
  \textbf{Endosymbiosis and modern biotechnology.} Some researchers
  propose engineering new endosymbionts: introducing nitrogen-fixing
  bacteria into plant cells to eliminate fertiliser dependence. What
  lessons from the natural mitochondrial endosymbiosis (gene transfer to
  host nucleus, metabolite exchange, intimate cell-cycle coupling)
  suggest what would be needed for such a designed symbiosis to be
  stable across generations?
\item
  \textbf{The phage-resistance arms race.} Bacteria evolve CRISPR-Cas
  defences; phages evolve anti-CRISPR proteins (Acrs); bacteria evolve
  anti-anti-CRISPR systems. This Red Queen dynamic has continued for
  about 3 billion years. What does it predict about the
  long-term success of phage therapy for antibiotic-resistant infections
  in humans? How might phage-cocktail design exploit or sidestep this
  dynamic?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-8}

\begin{enumerate}

  Describe the structure and function of each major eukaryotic
  \hyperref[gl:organelle]{\textbf{organelle}} in detail.
\item
  Explain the endomembrane system and the secretory/endocytic pathways,
  including coat \hyperref[gl:protein]{\textbf{protein}}s and sorting

\item
  Describe the \hyperref[gl:cytoskeleton]{\textbf{cytoskeleton}}:

  their associated motor proteins.
\item
  Explain how the nucleus controls \hyperref[gl:gene]{\textbf{gene}}
  expression through \hyperref[gl:chromatin]{\textbf{chromatin}}

\item
  Relate organelle dysfunction to specific human diseases.
\item
  Describe mitochondrial dynamics (fusion, fission) and their role in

\item
  Explain the role of peroxisomes, centrosomes, and primary cilia in
  cell biology.
\item
  Describe cell adhesion molecules and their role in tissue
  architecture.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Opening Vignette: The World's Smallest Rotary Motor}

Buried in the envelope of a bacterium is a molecular machine that spins
at 100,000 rotations per minute, driven by a stream of protons flowing
down an electrochemical gradient. The \textbf{bacterial flagellar motor}
--- known since the 1970s from electron microscopy --- is roughly 45 nm
in diameter and converts ion-motive force directly into rotational
movement, propelling the cell at up to 30 body lengths per second. No
human-engineered motor approaches this combination of speed, size, and
efficiency.

The bacterial flagellar motor is assembled from over 40 different
proteins, each with a precise structural role: the MS ring anchors to
the inner membrane; the C ring acts as a cargo dock for proteins to be
secreted; the rod and hook transmit torque; the flagellar filament acts
as a propeller. The motor can switch rotation direction in under a
millisecond, enabling the tumbling runs that allow bacteria to chemotax
toward nutrients (Berg \& Brown, 1972, \emph{Nature}). Cell structure,
as this chapter shows, is not merely a container for biochemistry --- it
is the machinery of life itself.

\emph{Primary source: Berg, H. C. \& Brown, D. A. (1972). Chemotaxis in
Escherichia coli analysed by three-dimensional tracking. Nature,
239(5374), 500--504.}
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}
