Three numerical patterns deserve attention. (1) The internal membrane
area exceeds the plasma membrane area by about 30-fold, so the
plasma membrane is a small fraction of cellular membrane surface. (2)
Mitochondria are the largest membrane reservoir (cristae alone are 20\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x}
the plasma membrane), which is why their dysfunction propagates so
quickly through bioenergetics. (3) NPCs are far rarer than ribosomes
(10\(^3\) vs.~10\(^7\)) yet handle 100\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} more transport events per second
per channel --- they are arguably the most heavily used machinery in the
cell. The chapters that follow refer back to this table so that
quantitative arguments (e.g., ``if mitophagy disposes of 10\% of
mitochondria per day\ldots{}'') have grounded numbers.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{The Nucleus --- The Information
Centre}\label{the-nucleus-the-information-centre}

The \textbf{nucleus} (diameter typically 5--10 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m) is the defining
hallmark of the eukaryotic cell.

\subsubsection{Nuclear Envelope}\label{nuclear-envelope}

The nucleus is bounded by the \textbf{nuclear envelope} --- two
concentric \hyperref[gl:phospholipid-bilayer]{\textbf{phospholipid
bilayer}}s (inner and outer nuclear membrane). The outer nuclear
membrane is continuous with the rough ER. The \textbf{nuclear pore
complex (NPC)} penetrates both membranes at about 3,000 pores
per nucleus. Each NPC is a massive protein assembly (about 120
MDa; 34 distinct nucleoporin proteins, 8-fold rotational symmetry),
gating passage of macromolecules:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Small molecules (\textless40 kDa) diffuse passively through the pore
  channel (diameter about 9 nm)
\item
  Larger molecules require \textbf{nuclear localisation sequences (NLS)}
  or \textbf{nuclear export sequences (NES)} recognised by
  importin/exportin proteins
\item
  The NPC can transport cargo up to about 39 nm in diameter
  (e.g., ribosomal subunits, mRNA-protein complexes)
\item
  Transport is powered by the RanGTP/RanGDP gradient: high RanGTP in the
  nucleus, high RanGDP in the
  \hyperref[gl:cytoplasm]{\textbf{cytoplasm}}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Import mechanism:} Cargo with NLS binds importin-alpha/beta in
the cytoplasm, translocates through the NPC, and RanGTP in the nucleus
causes importin to release its cargo.

\textbf{Export mechanism:} Cargo with NES binds exportin (CRM1) + RanGTP
in the nucleus, translocates out, and RanGAP in the cytoplasm hydrolyses
RanGTP to RanGDP, releasing cargo.

\textbf{NPC architecture in numbers.} Each NPC is built of
about 30 distinct nucleoporin (Nup) species totalling
about 500--1,000 protein subunits arranged with 8-fold
rotational symmetry. The structural scaffold (the ``Y-complex'') forms
two outer rings; cytoplasmic and nuclear filaments project
about 50 nm from each face; FG-repeat nucleoporins (Nup98,
Nup62, Nsp1) line the central channel and form a hydrogel-like phase
that confers selectivity. A single human nucleus contains
about 3,000--5,000 NPCs (density about 10--20 per
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m\(^2\) of nuclear envelope), and each NPC handles roughly
\textbf{1,000 translocation events per second} at peak activity ---
meaning the entire nucleus exchanges about 10\(^7\)
macromolecules per second. The selective barrier is so efficient that
small molecules (\textless40 kDa) cross by simple diffusion in
\textless1 ms while large cargo without NLS/NES are excluded essentially
indefinitely. The energy budget is supplied by the \textbf{RanGTP/GDP
gradient} (10\(^4\):1 nuclear:cytoplasmic ratio for RanGTP), which is
itself maintained by RanGEF (RCC1, chromatin-bound) and RanGAP
(cytoplasmic): the result is a vectorial pump powered by GTP hydrolysis
but requiring no direct translocation ATPase.

\textbf{Pathological NPCs.} The Nup98 gene is fused to dozens of
partners in pediatric leukaemias (Nup98-HOXA9, Nup98-NSD1) --- the
FG-repeat domain provides a phase-separating prion-like domain that
drives oncogenic condensate formation. Nucleoporins also accumulate
damage with age; selective loss of NPC function is a hallmark of
post-mitotic neurons in Alzheimer's and ALS.

\subsubsection{Protein Targeting and
Sorting}\label{protein-targeting-and-sorting}

Every protein synthesised in the cell must reach a specific compartment,
but proteins are made (initially) in primarily two places: free
cytosolic ribosomes and ER-bound ribosomes. \textbf{Sorting signals}
within the polypeptide direct each protein to its destination. Most
signals are short, modular, and additive --- analogous to postal
addresses appended to the same envelope.

\textbf{The SRP pathway in detail.} SRP is a ribonucleoprotein particle
(54 kDa SRP54 GTPase + 6 other proteins + 7SL RNA) that solves a
three-way coordination problem: it must (i) recognise the nascent signal
peptide as it emerges from the ribosome, (ii) pause translation to
prevent premature folding in the cytoplasm, and (iii) deliver the
ribosome--nascent chain to the ER membrane. SRP54 binds the hydrophobic
signal peptide; SRP9/14 contact the ribosome's elongation factor binding
site, halting translation. The complex docks at the SRP receptor (SR,
also a GTPase) on the ER membrane. Reciprocal GTP hydrolysis by SRP54
and SR releases SRP, hands the signal peptide to the \textbf{Sec61
translocon}, and translation resumes --- now co-translationally
threading the polypeptide into the ER lumen. The ``GTPase exchange''
mechanism is deeply conserved: SRP/SR systems occur in bacteria,
archaea, and eukaryotes, with lineage-specific architectural variations.

\textbf{TOM/TIM mitochondrial import.} Mitochondrial matrix proteins
face a unique problem: they must cross \emph{two} membranes while
remaining largely unfolded. The \textbf{TOM complex} (Translocase of
Outer Membrane) --- built around Tom40 (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-barrel channel), Tom20
(presequence receptor), Tom22, and small Tom proteins --- accepts the
presequence on the cytoplasmic side. \textbf{TIM23} (Translocase of
Inner Membrane) then takes over, threaded by the \textbf{PAM motor}
(Presequence translocase-Associated Motor) containing mtHsp70 that uses
ATP hydrolysis to ratchet the polypeptide into the matrix. The inner
membrane potential (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Delta}}{Delta}\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Psi}}{Psi} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}180 mV) provides additional electrostatic
pulling force on the positively charged presequence. Once in the matrix,
MPP (Mitochondrial Processing Peptidase) cleaves the presequence and the
protein folds, often with mtHsp60/Hsp10 chaperonin assistance.

OMM \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-barrel proteins (e.g., porin/VDAC, Tom40 itself) take a different
route: through TOM, into the IMS, then inserted laterally by the
\textbf{SAM complex} (Sorting and Assembly Machinery). Carrier proteins
(e.g., ADP/ATP translocase) of the inner membrane skip TIM23 entirely
and use \textbf{TIM22} for lateral release into the IMM. IMS proteins
use the \textbf{MIA40/Erv1 disulphide relay} for oxidative folding.

\textbf{Why this matters.} Failures of any single targeting pathway
produce specific, severe disease phenotypes --- testimony to how
hard-coded the cellular logistics are. Defects in PEX genes cause
peroxisome biogenesis disorders (Zellweger syndrome). Defects in TIM/TOM
components cause mitochondrial myopathies. ER signal peptide mutations
are now recognised in disorders ranging from preprovasopressin (familial
diabetes insipidus) to coagulation-factor deficiencies. The cell's
postal system has no general delivery option --- every misrouted package
is a disease.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 1b:} A researcher creates a fusion protein with
both an N-terminal mitochondrial presequence \emph{and} a C-terminal SKL
(peroxisomal PTS1). Where is the protein delivered? (Hint: consider
whether targeting is co-translational or post-translational, and which
signal acts first.)
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Chromatin and
Nucleosomes}\label{chromatin-and-nucleosomes}

Human nuclear DNA (2 x 3.2 billion base pairs = 6.4 Gbp total) is
packaged into chromatin. The
\textbf{\hyperref[gl:nucleosome]{nucleosome}} is the basic packaging
unit: 147 bp of DNA wound about 1.75 times around an octamer of
\hyperref[gl:histone]{\textbf{histone}} proteins (2x H2A, H2B, H3, H4)
with linker H1 bridging adjacent nucleosomes.

\textbf{Levels of chromatin compaction:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{10 nm fibre} (beads on a string): nucleosome arrays;
  about 6-fold compaction of naked DNA
\item
  \textbf{30 nm fibre}: solenoid or zigzag arrangement (histone H1
  stabilises); about 40-fold compaction
\item
  \textbf{300 nm loops}: attached to a protein scaffold (condensin,
  cohesin); about 10,000-fold
\item
  \textbf{700 nm condensed chromatin}: mitotic
  \hyperref[gl:chromosome]{\textbf{chromosome}}
\item
  \textbf{1,400 nm} fully condensed: metaphase chromosome;
  about 10,000--20,000-fold compaction total
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{\hyperref[gl:euchromatin]{Euchromatin}} (transcriptionally
active; less compacted)
vs.~\textbf{\hyperref[gl:heterochromatin]{heterochromatin}}
(transcriptionally silent; highly compacted). Histone modifications
(acetylation = active; methylation context-dependent) regulate this
switch --- the \textbf{histone code}.

\subsubsection{Nucleolus}\label{nucleolus}

The \textbf{nucleolus} (1--3 per nucleus) is not membrane-bound. It is
the site of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) transcription by RNA polymerase I and
\hyperref[gl:ribosome]{\textbf{ribosome}} assembly. It disassembles
during \hyperref[gl:mitosis]{\textbf{mitosis}} and re-forms around
\textbf{nucleolus organiser regions (NORs)} on chromosomes 13, 14, 15,
21, and 22 (in humans).

The nucleolus has three ultrastructural regions: - \textbf{Fibrillar
centre (FC):} rDNA gene clusters and RNA Pol I - \textbf{Dense fibrillar
component (DFC):} nascent rRNA processing; fibrillarin -
\textbf{Granular component (GC):} maturing pre-ribosomal particles

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: The Nucleolus in Cancer} Nucleolar size and
number are often increased in cancer cells due to elevated ribosome
biogenesis driven by oncogenes (Myc, mTOR). Pathologists use nucleolar
prominence (AgNOR staining) as a prognostic marker in several cancers.
The RNA Pol I inhibitor CX-5461 is in clinical trials as an anti-cancer
agent that specifically targets ribosome biogenesis.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 1:} A protein has both an NLS and an NES. Would it
be found in the nucleus or cytoplasm? How might the cell regulate its
localisation?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Mitochondria --- Power Plants of the
Cell}\label{mitochondria-power-plants-of-the-cell}

Mitochondria (singular: mitochondrion) are 1--5 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m long, often
branching, highly dynamic organelles. A liver hepatocyte contains
about 1,000--2,000 mitochondria, constituting
about 20\% of cell volume.

\subsubsection{Structural Organisation}\label{structural-organisation}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM):} contains \textbf{porin}
  (VDAC) channels; freely permeable to molecules \textless5 kDa. Also
  contains MAM (mitochondria-associated ER membrane) contact sites for
  Ca\(^{2+}\) and lipid exchange.
\item
  \textbf{Intermembrane space (IMS):} equivalent to cytoplasm in ion
  composition; site of electron carrier cytochrome c; contains
  pro-apoptotic factors (Smac/DIABLO, AIF)
\item
  \textbf{Inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM):} highly folded into
  \textbf{cristae} (10x surface area amplification);
  \textbf{impermeable} to protons --- essential for
  \hyperref[gl:chemiosmosis]{\textbf{chemiosmosis}}; contains electron
  transport chain (ETC) complexes I--IV,
  \hyperref[gl:atp-synthase]{\textbf{ATP synthase}}. The cristae are
  shaped by the MICOS complex (mitochondrial contact site and cristae
  organising system) and OPA1.
\item
  \textbf{Matrix:} aqueous interior; contains mitochondrial DNA,
  ribosomes, TCA cycle enzymes, fatty acid oxidation enzymes, pyruvate
  dehydrogenase complex
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Crista density} correlates with energetic demand: sperm
mitochondria and cardiac muscle mitochondria have densely packed
cristae. Resting cells have fewer, wider cristae.

\subsubsection{Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA)}\label{mitochondrial-dna-mtdna}

Human mtDNA: 16,569 bp, circular, encodes 37 genes: - 13 subunits of
respiratory chain complexes (e.g., ND1-6, COX1-3, ATP6, ATP8) - 22
transfer RNAs - 2 ribosomal RNAs

mtDNA is inherited \textbf{maternally} (sperm mitochondria are typically
ubiquitinated and destroyed in the fertilised egg). This enables
maternal-lineage \textbf{phylogenetic analysis} and forensic
identification. \textbf{Mitochondrial Eve} --- the most recent common
maternal ancestor of living humans --- lived
about 150,000--200,000 years ago in Africa.

\textbf{Mitochondrial diseases} arise from mtDNA
\hyperref[gl:mutation]{\textbf{mutation}}s (point mutations or
deletions): - \textbf{Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON):}
mutations in ND genes leads to retinal ganglion cell degeneration and
blindness - \textbf{MELAS} (Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic
Acidosis, Stroke-like episodes): A3243G mutation in tRNA-Leu -
\textbf{Kearns-Sayre syndrome:} large mtDNA deletions; progressive
external ophthalmoplegia, cardiac conduction defects, retinitis
pigmentosa

\subsubsection{Mitochondrial Dynamics: Fusion and
Fission}\label{mitochondrial-dynamics-fusion-and-fission}

Mitochondria are not static organelles --- they constantly undergo
\textbf{fusion} (joining) and \textbf{fission} (splitting), forming a
dynamic network called the mitochondrial reticulum.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0034_0d2889ec94eb.png}
\caption{Mitochondrial dynamics: the balance between fusion and fission controls mitochondrial morphology, quality control, and biogenesis. Damaged mitochondria are selectively removed by mitophagy via the PINK1/Parkin pathway.}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Fusion proteins:} - \textbf{MFN1/MFN2 (mitofusins):} GTPases on
the OMM; mediate outer membrane tethering and fusion - \textbf{OPA1:}
GTPase on the IMM; mediates inner membrane fusion and cristae
remodelling - Mutations in MFN2 cause \textbf{Charcot-Marie-Tooth type
2A} (peripheral neuropathy) - Mutations in OPA1 cause
\textbf{\hyperref[gl:dominant]{dominant} optic atrophy} (most common
inherited optic neuropathy)

\textbf{Fission proteins:} - \textbf{DRP1 (dynamin-related protein 1):}
cytosolic GTPase recruited to the OMM by adaptors (MFF, MiD49/51, FIS1);
assembles into a ring and constricts the mitochondrion -
\textbf{ER-mitochondria contact sites} mark fission sites; the ER wraps
around the mitochondrion before DRP1 recruitment - Fission is essential
for equal mitochondrial distribution during cell division and for
isolating damaged mitochondria for mitophagy

\textbf{Mitophagy (PINK1/Parkin pathway):} 1. In healthy mitochondria,
PINK1 kinase is imported and degraded by PARL protease 2. In damaged
mitochondria (depolarised), PINK1 accumulates on the OMM 3. PINK1
phosphorylates ubiquitin and recruits \textbf{Parkin} (E3 ubiquitin
ligase) 4. Parkin ubiquitinates OMM proteins, creating autophagy
receptor binding sites 5. Autophagosome engulfs the damaged
mitochondrion for lysosomal degradation

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Mitochondrial Dynamics and Parkinson's
Disease} Mutations in PINK1 and Parkin cause autosomal recessive
early-onset Parkinson's disease (PARK6 and PARK2). The failure of
mitophagy leads to accumulation of damaged mitochondria in dopaminergic
\hyperref[gl:neuron]{\textbf{neuron}}s of the substantia nigra, causing
oxidative stress, energy depletion, and neuronal death. This pathway is
a major therapeutic target. see \cref{sec:unit_II_cell_signaling} for
\hyperref[gl:apoptosis]{\textbf{apoptosis}} pathways.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 2:} Predict the mitochondrial
\hyperref[gl:phenotype]{\textbf{phenotype}} in a cell with a
dominant-negative mutation in DRP1 that prevents GTP hydrolysis. Would
the mitochondria appear fragmented or hyperfused?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{The Endomembrane System and Secretory
Pathway}\label{the-endomembrane-system-and-secretory-pathway}

Several organelles form a functionally integrated \textbf{endomembrane
system}:

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0035_42ef176149c8.png}
\caption{The endomembrane system and secretory/endocytic pathways. COPII vesicles carry cargo anterograde (ER to Golgi); COPI vesicles carry cargo retrograde (Golgi to ER). The trans-Golgi network sorts proteins to lysosomes (via M6P signal), plasma membrane, or secretory granules.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Endoplasmic Reticulum}\label{endoplasmic-reticulum}

\textbf{Rough ER} (RER): studded with ribosomes; site of synthesis,
folding, and initial N-glycosylation of secreted and membrane proteins.
Molecular chaperones (BiP/GRP78, calnexin, calreticulin) ensure proper
folding; misfolded proteins are retrotranslocated for
\textbf{ER-associated degradation (ERAD)} by the proteasome.

The \textbf{signal recognition particle (SRP)} pathway directs secretory
proteins to the ER: 1. Ribosome begins translating mRNA; signal peptide
(about 16--30 hydrophobic amino acids) emerges 2. SRP binds
signal peptide and ribosome, pausing
\hyperref[gl:translation]{\textbf{translation}} 3. SRP-ribosome complex
docks at SRP receptor on ER membrane 4. Signal peptide inserts into the
\textbf{translocon} (Sec61 channel) 5. Translation resumes; polypeptide
is co-translationally threaded into the ER lumen 6. Signal peptidase
cleaves the signal peptide

\textbf{Smooth ER} (SER): lacks ribosomes; functions: - Lipid synthesis
(phospholipids, cholesterol, steroid
\hyperref[gl:hormone]{\textbf{hormone}}s) - Drug/toxin detoxification
(cytochrome P450 enzymes in liver SER) - Ca\(^{2+}\) storage and release
for signalling (sarcoplasmic reticulum in muscle = specialised SER) -
Glycogen metabolism

\textbf{Unfolded protein response (UPR):} Accumulation of misfolded
proteins triggers the UPR --- three ER stress sensor pathways (IRE1,
PERK, ATF6) that expand ER capacity, halt translation, and if
irresolvable, trigger apoptosis. Relevant in diabetes (beta-cells
overwhelmed by insulin demand), neurodegeneration, and cancer.

\textbf{ER quality control and ERAD (in detail).} Newly synthesised
glycoproteins entering the ER lumen are tagged with a
triple-glucosylated N-glycan (Glc\(_3\)Man\(_9\)GlcNAc\(_2\)).
Glucosidases I and II sequentially trim two glucoses, generating a
monoglucosylated form that is recognised by the lectin chaperones
\textbf{calnexin} (membrane-bound) and \textbf{calreticulin} (lumenal).
These chaperones hold the protein in a folding-competent state. If the
protein folds correctly, glucosidase II removes the last glucose and the
protein exits via COPII vesicles. If folding fails, \textbf{UGGT}
(UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase) re-glucosylates it,
sending it back to calnexin/calreticulin --- the
\textbf{calnexin/calreticulin cycle}. Repeated failure marks the protein
for \textbf{ERAD (ER-associated degradation)}:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Recognition:} Mannose trimming by ER mannosidases (EDEM1/2/3)
  creates a ``give up'' signal --- no further folding attempts.
\item
  \textbf{Retrotranslocation:} The misfolded protein is recognised by
  ERAD components (HRD1/SEL1L, gp78, MARCH6) and threaded back to the
  cytoplasm through a retrotranslocation channel (likely Hrd1 itself).
\item
  \textbf{Polyubiquitination:} ER-membrane E3 ligases (Hrd1, gp78)
  attach K48-linked ubiquitin chains.
\item
  \textbf{Extraction:} The AAA+ ATPase \textbf{p97/VCP} (Cdc48 in yeast)
  uses ATP hydrolysis to mechanically extract the ubiquitinated
  polypeptide from the membrane.
\item
  \textbf{Degradation:} The proteasome digests the substrate to small
  peptides.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Three branches of the UPR.} When ERAD cannot keep up with the
load, three transmembrane sensors are activated:

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1935}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2903}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1935}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3226}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\endlastfoot
\textbf{IRE1} & Lumenal domain dimerises on misfolded proteins;
cytoplasmic domain has kinase + endoribonuclease activity & Splices XBP1
mRNA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} active XBP1s transcription factor \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} genes for ER expansion, ERAD,
lipid synthesis & Minutes--hours (chronic adaptation) \\
\textbf{PERK} & Dimerises and trans-phosphorylates eIF2alpha & Global
translation attenuation; selective translation of ATF4 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} CHOP & Minutes
(immediate response) \\
\textbf{ATF6} & Trafficks to Golgi; cleaved by S1P + S2P proteases &
Cytoplasmic fragment is a transcription factor for ER chaperones (BiP,
GRP94) & Hours \\
\end{longtable}
}

If the lesion is repaired, the UPR shuts down and homeostasis resumes.
If the stress is severe or prolonged, \textbf{CHOP} (downstream of
PERK/ATF4) and IRE1's secondary RIDD activity (Regulated IRE1-Dependent
Decay of mRNAs) bias the cell toward apoptosis. The same pathway is
therefore an adaptive thermostat \emph{and} a death timer --- the switch
is set by the integrated stress dose.

\textbf{Worked observation: insulin secretion and ER load.} A pancreatic
beta-cell synthesises about 10\(^6\) insulin molecules per
minute during glucose stimulation. Each must be folded with three
disulphide bonds, processed by PC1/3 and PC2 from proinsulin, and
packaged into secretory granules. ER folding capacity is therefore one
of the rate-limiting steps for insulin secretion. Chronic hyperglycaemia
(in obesity, type 2 diabetes) drives sustained UPR, eventual
CHOP-mediated apoptosis, and progressive beta-cell loss. Pharmacological
chemical chaperones (TUDCA, 4-PBA) and selective IRE1 inhibitors are in
trials to delay this collapse.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: ER Stress and Type 2 Diabetes} Pancreatic
beta-cells produce enormous quantities of insulin (about 1
million molecules per cell per minute during glucose stimulation). This
places extreme demands on the ER folding machinery. Chronic
hyperglycaemia and obesity increase insulin demand beyond ER capacity,
triggering the UPR. Prolonged UPR activation causes beta-cell apoptosis,
contributing to the progressive decline in insulin secretion seen in
type 2 diabetes. Pharmacological chaperones (e.g., TUDCA, 4-PBA) that
reduce ER stress are being investigated as diabetes therapeutics.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Golgi Apparatus}\label{golgi-apparatus}

The Golgi stack (cis-Golgi network, cis, medial, trans, trans-Golgi
network/TGN) receives cargo from the ER in \textbf{COPII-coated
vesicles} and processes proteins by: - O-glycosylation (adding sugars to
Ser/Thr) - Proteolytic processing (e.g., insulin prohormone to insulin)
- Phosphorylation of mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) residues, creating the
lysosomal targeting signal - Sorting to: secretory vesicles, plasma
membrane, lysosomes, or ER (retrograde COPI vesicles)

\textbf{Vesicle coat proteins and their roles:}

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1667}}@{}}

\textbf{Brefeldin A} (BFA) inhibits GBF1 (a GEF for Arf1 GTPase needed
for COPI assembly) and dissolves the Golgi within minutes ---
demonstrating its dynamic membrane flux.

\subsubsection{Lysosomes}\label{lysosomes}

Lysosomes (\hyperref[gl:ph]{\textbf{pH}} 4.5--5.0, maintained by V-type
H\(^+\)-ATPase) contain about 60 acid hydrolases (proteases,
lipases, nucleases, glycosidases) that digest: - \textbf{Autophagy:}
cellular debris and aged organelles (macroautophagy, microautophagy,
chaperone-mediated autophagy) - \textbf{Phagocytosis:} bacteria and
debris (in macrophages, neutrophils) - \textbf{Receptor-mediated
endocytosis:} LDL-cholesterol uptake - \textbf{Extracellular digestion:}
osteoclasts secrete lysosomal contents to resorb bone

\textbf{Types of selective autophagy:} - \textbf{Mitophagy:} selective
removal of damaged mitochondria (PINK1/Parkin pathway) -
\textbf{Pexophagy:} selective removal of excess peroxisomes -
\textbf{Lipophagy:} selective degradation of lipid droplets -
\textbf{Ribophagy:} selective degradation of ribosomes during starvation
- \textbf{ER-phagy/reticulophagy:} selective removal of excess ER

\textbf{Lysosomal storage diseases} result from enzyme deficiencies: -
\textbf{Pompe disease:} alpha-1,4-glucosidase deficiency, glycogen
accumulates, cardiac/muscle failure - \textbf{Gaucher disease:}
glucocerebrosidase deficiency, sphingolipid accumulation in macrophages
- \textbf{Tay-Sachs disease:} hexosaminidase A deficiency, GM2
ganglioside accumulation in neurons, neurodegeneration -
\textbf{Niemann-Pick type C:} NPC1/NPC2 cholesterol transport
deficiency, cholesterol accumulates in lysosomes - Both Pompe and
Gaucher are treatable by \textbf{enzyme replacement therapy (ERT)},
where recombinant enzyme is infused intravenously and targeted to
lysosomes via M6P receptors

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 3:} A patient has I-cell disease (mucolipidosis
II), in which the enzyme that adds M6P to lysosomal enzymes in the
cis-Golgi is defective. Predict the consequences for (a) lysosomal
enzyme targeting, (b) extracellular enzyme levels, and (c) intracellular
digestion.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{The Cytoskeleton}\label{the-cytoskeleton}

The cytoskeleton is a dynamic protein network pervading the cytoplasm,
providing structural support, enabling cell movement, and directing
intracellular traffic.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0036_9b04ee870582.png}
\caption{Cytoskeletal components and their associated motor proteins. Actin filaments are driven by myosin motors, microtubules by kinesin and dynein motors, and intermediate filaments have no associated motors.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Actin Microfilaments}\label{actin-microfilaments}

Actin filaments (F-actin; diameter about 7 nm) are polar,
ATP-driven polymers of globular G-actin monomers. Properties: -
\textbf{Treadmilling:} net polymerisation at the (+) barbed end;
depolymerisation at the (-) pointed end, resulting in net movement of
the filament while maintaining constant length - \textbf{Branching:}
Arp2/3 complex creates about 70-degree branches (lamellipodia,
phagocytic cups); nucleated by WASP/WAVE family activators -
\textbf{Bundling:} Fimbrin (parallel tight bundles in microvilli),
alpha-actinin (looser bundles in stress fibres), villin (intestinal
brush border)

\textbf{Critical concentration and treadmilling --- the quantitative
basis.} A single actin monomer can add to (or dissociate from) either
end of a filament. At each end, the rate constants for assembly
(\(k_+\)) and disassembly (\(k_-\)) define an end-specific
\textbf{critical concentration}:

\begin{equation}
C_c^{\text{end}} = \frac{k_-}{k_+}
\label{eq:unit_II_critical_conc}
\end{equation}

When the free monomer concentration \([G\text{-actin}]\) exceeds
\(C_c\), the end grows; below \(C_c\), the end shrinks. Crucially, the
(+) barbed end and the (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}) pointed end have \emph{different} critical
concentrations because of their different geometries:

\[C_c^{(+)} \approx 0.1 \, \mu\text{M}, \qquad C_c^{(-)} \approx 0.6 \, \mu\text{M} \tag{6.2} \label{eq:unit_II_cell_structure_item_1}\]

In a steady state with \([G\text{-actin}]\) between these two values
(say 0.3 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}M), the (+) end grows continuously while the (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}) end shrinks
continuously --- and the filament \emph{translates} through space at a
steady velocity even though its average length is constant. This is
\textbf{treadmilling}, and the velocity is:

\[v_\text{tread} = \delta \cdot k_+^{(+)} \cdot ([G] - C_c^{(+)}) \tag{6.3} \label{eq:unit_II_cell_structure_item_2}\]

where \(\delta = 2.7\) nm (axial rise per monomer; two monomers per
helical repeat = 5.4 nm). For lamellipodial actin in a migrating
fibroblast, treadmilling proceeds at about 0.1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m/s at 37 °C
--- the molecular speed limit on which crawling cells move.

ATP hydrolysis on the filament shifts the (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-})-end disassembly rate,
increasing the asymmetry between ends; cofilin and ADF
(actin-depolymerising factor) accelerate (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-})-end disassembly; profilin
loads ATP onto G-actin to enrich the (+)-end-favoured pool. The net
result is that \textbf{treadmilling is energetically driven by ATP
hydrolysis} even though the polymerisation reaction itself does not
consume ATP.

\textbf{Microtubule dynamic instability --- the GTP cap.} Microtubules
treadmill very weakly; instead they exhibit \textbf{dynamic instability}
--- alternating phases of growth and rapid shrinkage at a single end.
The (+) end of a growing microtubule carries a ``GTP cap'' (a few
hundred GTP-tubulin subunits added before hydrolysis catches up). When
the cap is intact, polymerisation continues at about 1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m/min.
Stochastic loss of the cap exposes GDP-tubulin, which has a strained
lateral lattice and undergoes rapid catastrophic depolymerisation at
about 10--30 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m/min (``\textbf{catastrophe}''). Catastrophic
shrinkage can be rescued by reformation of a GTP cap
(``\textbf{rescue}''). The four parameters --- growth rate \(v_g\),
shrinkage rate \(v_s\), catastrophe frequency \(f_c\), rescue frequency
\(f_r\) --- completely specify microtubule behaviour and are tuned by a
panoply of plus-end tracking proteins (+TIPs: EB1, CLIP-170) and
depolymerases (kinesin-13/MCAK).

\textbf{Motor proteins on actin:} - \textbf{Myosin II:} generates
contractile force (muscle sarcomere, cytokinesis, cell migration);
bipolar thick filaments; step size about 5--25 nm;
non-processive (releases after each step) - \textbf{Myosin V:}
processive motor for vesicle transport; walks ``hand-over-hand'' with 36
nm steps matching the F-actin helical repeat; transports melanosomes,
ER, secretory vesicles - \textbf{Myosin I:} single-headed; links
membrane to actin cortex; involved in endocytosis and membrane tension

Functions: cell shape, cytokinesis (contractile ring), muscle
contraction, phagocytosis, cell crawling (lamellipodia, filopodia),
intracellular organelle movement.

\subsubsection{Tubulin Microtubules}\label{tubulin-microtubules}

Microtubules (MTs; 25 nm diameter) are hollow tubes of
alpha/beta-tubulin heterodimers forming 13 protofilaments. Properties: -
\textbf{GTP-driven dynamic instability:} rapid switching between growth
(rescue) and catastrophic depolymerisation; GTP cap model --- growing
end has GTP-tubulin; loss of cap triggers depolymerisation -
\textbf{Polarity:} (+) end grows toward cell periphery; (-) end at
\textbf{MTOC/centrosome} - \textbf{Post-translational modifications:}
acetylation (stable MTs), tyrosination/detyrosination, polyglutamylation
--- the ``tubulin code'' directs motor protein binding

\textbf{Motor proteins on microtubules:} - \textbf{Kinesin-1
(conventional kinesin):} anterograde (+ end directed); dimeric,
processive; 8 nm step size matching tubulin repeat; transports vesicles,
mitochondria, mRNA toward cell periphery; speed about 0.8 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m/s
- \textbf{Cytoplasmic dynein:} retrograde (- end directed); large
complex (about 1.2 MDa) with dynactin cofactor; 8 nm steps;
transports ER, Golgi, endosomes, viruses toward cell centre; also drives
mitotic spindle positioning - \textbf{Kinesin-13 (MCAK):} depolymerises
MT ends; critical for spindle dynamics during mitosis

Functions: chromosome segregation (mitotic spindle), flagella/cilia
(axoneme: 9+2 MT arrangement), intracellular vesicle transport (axonal
transport in neurons), cell polarity, cell shape.

\subsubsection{Worked Example: Motor Protein Kinematics and
Energetics}\label{worked-example-motor-protein-kinematics-and-energetics}

\textbf{Problem:} A kinesin-1 motor protein is transporting a
neurotransmitter vesicle down a nerve axon along a microtubule. The
motor moves at a constant velocity of \(v = 0.80 \, \mu\text{m/s}\) and
takes fixed step sizes of \(d = 8 \, \text{nm}\) per step. 1. How many
steps does the kinesin take per second? 2. If kinesin hydrolyses exactly
one ATP molecule per 8 nm step, how many ATP molecules are consumed
during a \(2.4 \, \text{mm}\) transport journey along the axon?

\textbf{Solution:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Calculate the stepping rate:} First, convert velocity to
  nanometres per second to match the step size units:
  \[ v = 0.80 \, \mu\text{m/s} = 800 \, \text{nm/s}  \label{eq:unit_II_cell_structure_item_3}\]

  Calculate the number of steps per second:
  \[ \text{Step rate} = \frac{v}{d} = \frac{800 \, \text{nm/s}}{8 \, \text{nm/step}} = 100 \text{ steps/s}  \label{eq:unit_II_cell_structure_item_4}\]

  The motor takes exactly \textbf{100 steps per second}.
\item
  \textbf{Calculate the energy consumption for the journey:} Convert the
  total distance from millimetres to nanometres:
  \[ D_{\text{total}} = 2.4 \, \text{mm} = 2.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{nm} = 2,400,000 \, \text{nm}  \label{eq:unit_II_cell_structure_item_5}\]

  Calculate the total number of steps:
  \[ \text{Total steps} = \frac{D_{\text{total}}}{d} = \frac{2,400,000 \, \text{nm}}{8 \, \text{nm/step}} = 300,000 \text{ steps}  \label{eq:unit_II_cell_structure_item_6}\]

  Since 1 step = 1 ATP molecule hydrolysed:
  \[ \text{Total ATP consumed} = 300,000 \text{ molecules of ATP}  \label{eq:unit_II_cell_structure_item_7}\]
\end{enumerate}

This calculation highlights the immense energy requirements of axonal
transport; maintaining trillions of synapses across the nervous system
commands a massive proportion of the body's total ATP production.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\item
  \textbf{Calculate the transport time:} The total transport time at
  constant velocity is simply distance divided by velocity:
  \[ t = \frac{D_\text{total}}{v} = \frac{2.4 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{m}}{0.80 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{m/s}} = 3{,}000 \, \text{s} \approx 50 \, \text{min}  \label{eq:unit_II_cell_structure_item_8}\]

  So a kinesin-driven cargo crosses 2.4 mm of axon in just under an
  hour. For a giraffe motor neuron (axon length about 3 m), the
  same calculation yields about 43 days --- consistent with the
  historical observation by Weiss and Hiscoe (1948) that materials
  accumulate above an axonal ligature with a wave-front velocity of a
  few millimetres per day. Compare this with \textbf{passive diffusion}
  of the same vesicle: using \(t = x^2/2D\) with \(D \approx 10^{-12}\)
  m\(^2\)/s for a 100 nm vesicle, \(t \approx 1.4 \times 10^{12}\) s \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~}
  45,000 years. Active transport beats diffusion by \textbf{eight orders
  of magnitude} for cargoes of this size and distance. The cell's choice
  to spend about 10\(^5\) ATPs per vesicle is therefore not
  extravagance --- it is what makes the long axon viable at most.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Worked Example: Comparing kinesin and dynein transport.}

A dendritic spine 50 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m from the cell body needs both anterograde
(kinesin: 0.8 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m/s) and retrograde (dynein: 1.0 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m/s) cargoes. Calculate
the round-trip time and minimum ATP cost for a single cargo cycle.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Anterograde transit:
  \(t_+ = 50 \, \mu\text{m} / 0.8 \, \mu\text{m/s} = 62.5\) s
\item
  Retrograde transit:
  \(t_- = 50 \, \mu\text{m} / 1.0 \, \mu\text{m/s} = 50\) s
\item
  Total transit time: \(\sim 112\) s (cargo handling and motor switching
  add another about 10 s)
\item
  Kinesin steps: \(50{,}000 \, \text{nm} / 8 \, \text{nm} = 6{,}250\)
  steps \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} 6,250 ATP
\item
  Dynein steps (more variable, average about 8 nm): another
  about 6,250 ATP
\item
  Total: about 12,500 ATP per round trip per cargo
\end{itemize}

A single dendrite that supports 100 active spines and turns over 10
cargoes per spine per minute therefore consumes about 10\(^7\)
ATPs/min on motor stepping alone --- roughly 1\% of a neuron's resting
ATP budget devoted to logistics.

\textbf{Taxol} (paclitaxel) stabilises MT and prevents depolymerisation,
arresting mitosis in metaphase. Used in chemotherapy for breast,
ovarian, and lung cancers. It is derived from the bark of the Pacific
yew tree (\emph{Taxus brevifolia}).

\textbf{Colchicine} destabilises MT by binding free tubulin and
preventing polymerisation. Used for gout (inhibits neutrophil migration)
and in cytogenetics (arrests cells in metaphase for karyotyping).

\textbf{Vincristine/vinblastine} (vinca alkaloids from
\emph{Catharanthus roseus}) also destabilise MT. Used in cancer
chemotherapy (lymphomas, leukaemias).

\subsubsection{Intermediate Filaments}\label{intermediate-filaments}

Intermediate filaments (IFs; about 10 nm diameter) are ropelike
cables of coiled-coil proteins. Unlike actin and MT, IFs are not polar
and have no associated motors --- they are \textbf{purely structural}:

\textbf{Lamins} form a meshwork underlying the inner nuclear membrane,
giving the nucleus mechanical rigidity and organising chromatin.
Progerin (mutant lamin A with 50-aa deletion due to a point mutation
activating a cryptic splice site) causes \textbf{Hutchinson-Gilford
progeria syndrome} --- accelerated ageing with death typically by age 13
from cardiovascular disease.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Cytoskeleton Diseases} \textbf{Alexander
disease} (GFAP mutations): Gain-of-function mutations in GFAP cause
Rosenthal fibre accumulation in astrocytes, leading to progressive
leukodystrophy with megalencephaly, seizures, and developmental
regression. \textbf{ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis):} Some familial
ALS cases involve mutations in dynactin (DCTN1) or dynein, disrupting
retrograde axonal transport and causing motor neuron degeneration.
\textbf{Taxol mechanism in cancer therapy:} By hyperstabilising
microtubules, taxol prevents the dynamic instability required for
mitotic spindle function. Chromosomes cannot properly segregate,
activating the spindle assembly checkpoint and ultimately triggering
apoptosis in rapidly dividing tumour cells.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 4:} Kinesin-1 moves toward the (+) end of
microtubules, while dynein moves toward the (-) end. In a neuron, which
direction does each motor move cargo along the axon? Which motor would
transport newly synthesised synaptic vesicle precursors from the cell
body to the synapse?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Centrosomes, Centrioles, and
Cilia}\label{centrosomes-centrioles-and-cilia}

\subsubsection{Centrosome/MTOC}\label{centrosomemtoc}

The \textbf{centrosome} is the primary microtubule organising centre
(MTOC) in animal cells. It consists of two \textbf{centrioles}
(barrel-shaped structures of 9 triplet microtubules arranged in a
pinwheel) surrounded by \textbf{pericentriolar material (PCM)}
containing gamma-tubulin ring complexes (gamma-TuRC) that nucleate new
microtubules.

During mitosis, centrosomes duplicate and migrate to opposite poles of
the cell, organising the mitotic spindle. Centrosome amplification
(\textgreater2 per cell) is common in cancer and contributes to
chromosomal instability.

\subsubsection{Cilia and Flagella}\label{cilia-and-flagella}

\textbf{Motile cilia} (9+2 axoneme: 9 outer doublet MTs + 2 central
singlet MTs, linked by dynein arms and nexin bridges) beat in
coordinated waves. Found on respiratory epithelium (about 200
per cell), fallopian tube epithelium, and ependymal cells lining brain
ventricles.

\textbf{Primary cilia} (9+0 axoneme: no central pair, non-motile) are
mechanosensory/chemosensory antennae present on nearly most mammalian
cells. Function as signalling hubs: - \textbf{Hedgehog signalling:}
Smoothened receptor relocates to the primary cilium upon Hedgehog ligand
binding - \textbf{Polycystin-1/2:} mechanosensitive Ca\(^{2+}\) channels
on kidney primary cilia; sense urine flow

\textbf{Ciliopathies} --- diseases caused by defective cilia: -
\textbf{Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome):} dynein arm
defects; immotile cilia; chronic respiratory infections, situs inversus
(50\%), male infertility - \textbf{Polycystic kidney disease (PKD):}
mutations in PKD1 (polycystin-1) or PKD2 (polycystin-2); defective
primary cilia mechanosensing; uncontrolled tubular cell proliferation
and cyst formation - \textbf{Bardet-Biedl syndrome:} defective ciliary
trafficking; obesity, retinitis pigmentosa, renal anomalies, polydactyly

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 5:} Why does Kartagener syndrome sometimes cause
situs inversus (mirror-reversal of organ asymmetry)? Consider the role
of motile nodal cilia in establishing left-right body asymmetry during
embryonic development.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Peroxisomes}\label{peroxisomes}

Peroxisomes contain oxidases that generate hydrogen peroxide
(H\(_2\)O\(_2\)) as a byproduct of fatty acid beta-oxidation, and
\textbf{catalase} that destroys it:

\[2\text{H}_2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{O}_2 \quad (\text{catalase}) \tag{6.1} \label{eq:unit_II_cell_structure_item_9}\]

\subsubsection{Key Functions}\label{key-functions}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Very-long-chain fatty acid (VLCFA) beta-oxidation:} Shortens
  VLCFAs (\textgreater C22) to medium-chain products that are then
  transferred to mitochondria for complete oxidation
\item
  \textbf{Plasmalogen biosynthesis:} Ether-linked phospholipids
  essential for myelin sheaths; about 50\% of heart
  phospholipids are plasmalogens
\item
  \textbf{Bile acid synthesis:} Side chain oxidation of cholesterol
  intermediates
\item
  \textbf{Amino acid oxidation:} D-amino acid oxidase
\item
  \textbf{Reactive oxygen species management:} Both generation
  (H\(_2\)O\(_2\) from oxidases) and detoxification (catalase,
  peroxidase)
\item
  \textbf{Glyoxylate metabolism:} Alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase
  (AGT) converts glyoxylate to glycine
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Peroxisome Biogenesis}\label{peroxisome-biogenesis}

Peroxisomes form by \textbf{growth and division} of existing peroxisomes
(similar to mitochondria) and also by \textbf{de novo formation} from
ER-derived vesicles. Peroxisomal matrix proteins are imported
post-translationally via \textbf{PTS1} (C-terminal SKL tripeptide) or
\textbf{PTS2} (N-terminal nonapeptide) signals, recognised by PEX5 and
PEX7 receptors.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Peroxisome Biogenesis Disorders}
\textbf{Zellweger syndrome} (the most severe peroxisome biogenesis
disorder) results from mutations in PEX genes (most commonly PEX1).
Absent or non-functional peroxisomes lead to VLCFA accumulation,
plasmalogen deficiency, and bile acid synthesis failure. Affected
infants present with severe hypotonia, seizures, hepatomegaly, and
characteristic facial features, with death typically in the first year.
\textbf{X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (X-ALD):} Mutation in ABCD1 (a
peroxisomal ABC transporter for VLCFA); VLCFA accumulation destroys
adrenal cortex and CNS myelin. Depicted in the film ``Lorenzo's Oil.''
\textbf{Primary hyperoxaluria type 1:} AGT mistargeted from peroxisomes
to mitochondria; oxalate accumulates; kidney stones and renal failure.
see \cref{sec:unit_II_membrane_transport} for ABC transporters.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Cell Adhesion and
Junctions}\label{cell-adhesion-and-junctions}

Multicellular organisms require cells to adhere to each other and to the
extracellular matrix (ECM). Four major families of cell adhesion
molecules (CAMs) and several junction types mediate this:

\subsubsection{Cell Junctions}\label{cell-junctions}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Tight junctions (zonula occludens):} Seal adjacent epithelial
  cells; prevent paracellular diffusion; claudins and occludin form the
  seal; ZO-1/2/3 link to actin cytoskeleton. Create apical-basal
  polarity.
\item
  \textbf{Adherens junctions (zonula adherens):} Cadherin-mediated;
  linked to actin cytoskeleton via catenins (alpha, beta, p120).
  E-cadherin loss is a hallmark of epithelial-mesenchymal transition
  (EMT) in cancer metastasis.
\item
  \textbf{Desmosomes (macula adherens):} Cadherin-mediated (desmogleins,
  desmocollins); linked to intermediate filaments (keratin) via
  plakoglobin and desmoplakin. Provide mechanical strength to skin and
  heart. Autoantibodies against desmoglein-3 cause \textbf{pemphigus
  vulgaris} (life-threatening blistering disease).
\item
  \textbf{Gap junctions:} Connexin hexamers (connexons) form channels
  between adjacent cells; allow passage of ions and small molecules
  (\textless1 kDa); enable electrical coupling (cardiac muscle
  synchrony), metabolic coupling, and intercellular signalling.
  Mutations in connexin-26 (GJB2) are the most common cause of
  hereditary deafness.
\item
  \textbf{Hemidesmosomes:} Integrin alpha6-beta4 links epithelial basal
  surface to basement membrane; connected to keratin intermediate
  filaments. Defects cause epidermolysis bullosa (skin blistering from
  minor trauma).
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 6:} E-cadherin is frequently downregulated in
invasive carcinomas. How would loss of E-cadherin promote cancer
metastasis? Consider both adhesion and signalling functions.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{The Proteasome --- Protein Quality
Control}\label{the-proteasome-protein-quality-control}

While lysosomes degrade proteins within membrane-bound compartments, the
\textbf{ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS)} degrades misfolded, damaged,
or regulatory proteins in the cytoplasm and nucleus.

\subsubsection{The 26S Proteasome}\label{the-26s-proteasome}

The 26S proteasome is a about 2.5 MDa multi-subunit protease
complex consisting of: - \textbf{20S core particle:} barrel-shaped
structure of four stacked heptameric rings (alpha7-beta7-beta7-alpha7);
proteolytic activity (chymotrypsin-like, trypsin-like, and
\hyperref[gl:caspase]{\textbf{caspase}}-like) is sequestered within the
barrel interior - \textbf{19S regulatory particle (cap):} recognises
ubiquitinated substrates, deubiquitinates them, unfolds the polypeptide,
and threads it into the 20S core for degradation

\subsubsection{Ubiquitination --- The Degradation
Signal}\label{ubiquitination-the-degradation-signal}

Ubiquitin (76 amino acids, highly conserved) is conjugated to target
proteins via a three-enzyme cascade:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{E1 (ubiquitin-activating enzyme):} Activates ubiquitin in an
  ATP-dependent reaction (2 E1 enzymes in humans)
\item
  \textbf{E2 (ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme):} Carries activated
  ubiquitin (about 40 E2s in humans)
\item
  \textbf{E3 (ubiquitin ligase):} Confers substrate specificity;
  transfers ubiquitin to the target protein (about 600 E3s in
  humans)
\end{enumerate}

A chain of at least 4 ubiquitin molecules linked via K48 serves as the
proteasomal degradation signal. Other ubiquitin chain types (K63,
M1/linear) serve non-degradative signalling functions (NF-kB activation,
DNA repair, endocytosis).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Proteasome Inhibitors in Cancer}
\textbf{Bortezomib} (Velcade) inhibits the chymotrypsin-like activity of
the 20S proteasome. This causes accumulation of misfolded proteins, ER
stress, and apoptosis. Multiple myeloma cells are particularly sensitive
because they produce enormous quantities of immunoglobulins, generating
high proteasomal load. Bortezomib has transformed multiple myeloma
treatment. Carfilzomib and ixazomib are second-generation proteasome
inhibitors with improved profiles.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{CRISPR Applications in Organelle
Biology}\label{crispr-applications-in-organelle-biology}

The CRISPR-Cas9 system has revolutionised the study of organelle biology
by enabling precise gene editing:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Fluorescent tagging of endogenous proteins:} CRISPR knock-in
  of GFP/mCherry at native loci enables live imaging of organelles at
  endogenous expression levels (avoiding overexpression artifacts)
\item
  \textbf{\hyperref[gl:genome]{Genome}-wide screens:} CRISPR knockout
  libraries have identified new genes required for mitophagy, autophagy,
  ER-phagy, and peroxisome biogenesis
\item
  \textbf{Base editing of mtDNA:} DddA-derived cytosine base editors
  (DdCBEs) can edit mtDNA without double-strand breaks, enabling
  creation of precise mitochondrial disease models
\item
  \textbf{Organelle-targeted degradation:} AID (auxin-inducible degron)
  tagged organelle proteins enable acute, reversible organelle
  disruption
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Computational Bridge}\label{computational-bridge-5}

Membrane-bound organelle counts are explicit in the cell model and can
be queried for teaching comparisons:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ biology.cell }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ get\_organelles\_by\_cell\_type, count\_membrane\_bound\_organelles}

\NormalTok{org }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ get\_organelles\_by\_cell\_type(}\StringTok{"animal"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(count\_membrane\_bound\_organelles(org))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical / systems note:} Mitochondrial disorders and
peroxisomal diseases (e.g.~Zellweger spectrum) show how loss of a single
organelle compartment produces multi-system phenotypes because
compartment-specific metabolites fail to reach the cytosol or nucleus.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsubsection{DddA-Derived Base Editors: Editing the Mitochondrial
Genome Without a Double-Strand
Break}\label{ddda-derived-base-editors-editing-the-mitochondrial-genome-without-a-double-strand-break}

Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) encodes 13 proteins of the electron transport
chain and 22 tRNAs --- mutations here cause a spectrum of
\textbf{mitochondrial diseases} (MELAS, MERRF, Leber's hereditary optic
neuropathy) that affect roughly 1 in 5000 births. CRISPR--Cas9 could not
reach mtDNA because guide RNA import into mitochondria is inefficient,
and any DNA double-strand break in the polyploid (100--10 000 copies per
cell) mitochondrial genome triggers rapid linear-DNA degradation rather
than useful repair.

The breakthrough came from an unusual source: a \textbf{bacterial
interbacterial toxin (DddA)} from \emph{Burkholderia cenocepacia} that
deaminates cytosines in \emph{double-stranded} DNA (most cytidine
deaminases require single-stranded substrates). In 2020, the Liu lab
published \textbf{DddA-derived cytosine base editors (DdCBEs)} --- split
DddA halves fused to programmable TALE arrays that reconstitute
deaminase activity primarily when both halves bind adjacent
mitochondrial sites (\emph{Nature} 2020). Subsequent engineering
produced \textbf{zinc-finger--DdCBEs} (smaller, easier to import),
\textbf{mitoBEs} capable of A-to-G edits, and \textbf{TALED}
(TALE-linked deaminases) for A-to-I conversion. Efficiencies in human
cells now reach 30--50 \% heteroplasmy shift with bystander editing
\textless{} 5 \%.

Worked example: for the MELAS-causing mutation m.3243A\textgreater G in
tRNA\textsuperscript{Leu}, a DdCBE targeting the reverse strand near
position 3244 converts the pathogenic G back to A in about 30
\% of mtDNA copies --- above the threshold needed to cross the
\textbf{heteroplasmy clinical phenotype boundary} (about 80 \%
mutant copies for overt disease). A 2022 report corrected a murine
Ndufa10 mutation \emph{in vivo} via AAV-delivered DdCBE with functional
rescue of respiratory chain complex I. Cautions: off-target
mitochondrial editing rates of about 0.1--1 \% at 30--50
predicted sites; potential nuclear off-targets; the edit is heritable in
the female germline (with the ethical considerations of heritable genome
editing). The technology is a clean example of how \textbf{unusual
biochemistry in obscure organisms} (a bacterial toxin no textbook
mentioned in 2019) can become the keystone of a new therapeutic platform
within 4 years.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-8}

For \textbf{Cell Structure and Organelles}, frontier biology belongs
inside the evidence logic of the chapter. Cell biology is increasingly
measured as live, spatial, single-cell, and perturbational data rather
than static diagrams alone. The core reading question is this: organelle
function is dynamic, contact-mediated, and context-dependent rather than
a fixed list of compartments.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

Ask what measurement scale is being claimed: nanometre structure,
single-cell transcript abundance, organelle dynamics, tissue context, or
organismal phenotype.

\textbf{Source practice:} For cell-state claims, distinguish microscopy,
live-cell perturbation, single-cell sequencing, spatial transcriptomics,
and biochemical assay evidence before making a causal statement.

\subsubsection{Current Evidence Map: Membrane-Bound and Condensate
Organization}\label{current-evidence-map-membrane-bound-and-condensate-organization}

\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-8}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The nucleus houses chromatin (DNA + histones); nuclear pores regulate
  macromolecule traffic via the Ran GTPase system; the nucleolus
  assembles ribosomes and is a cancer prognostic marker.
\item
  Mitochondria have their own circular DNA and ribosomes, consistent
  with endosymbiotic origin; cristae maximise IMM surface area for the
  ETC; fusion/fission dynamics maintain mitochondrial quality via
  PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy.
\item
  The endomembrane system (RER, SER, Golgi, vesicles) coordinates
  protein secretion and glycosylation; COPII (anterograde), COPI
  (retrograde), and clathrin (endocytic) coat proteins direct vesicle
  traffic.
\item
  The cytoskeleton (actin, MTs, IFs) provides structure, enables
  motility, and directs intracellular transport via motor proteins
  (myosin, kinesin, dynein).
\item
  Peroxisomes perform VLCFA oxidation and ROS management;
  centrosomes/cilia function as MTOCs and sensory antennae; cell
  adhesion molecules and junctions maintain tissue architecture.
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See \cref{sec:unit_II_cell_theory} for cell
  theory and \hyperref[gl:endosymbiosis]{\textbf{endosymbiosis}},
  \cref{sec:unit_II_membrane_transport} for membrane traffic, and Unit
  IX for cilia-linked physiology.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Review Questions}\label{review-questions-8}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Describe the mechanism by which a newly synthesised lysosomal enzyme
  is sorted from the trans-Golgi network to the lysosome. What would
  happen if the M6P phosphotransferase were defective?
\item
  Compare and contrast the three types of cytoskeletal filaments (actin,
  microtubules, intermediate filaments) in terms of diameter, polarity,
  \hyperref[gl:nucleotide]{\textbf{nucleotide}} dependence, associated
  motors, and dynamic behaviour.
\item
  Explain the PINK1/Parkin mitophagy pathway. Why do mutations in these
  genes specifically affect dopaminergic neurons in Parkinson's disease?
\item
  A patient presents with recurrent respiratory infections, male
  infertility, and situs inversus. What is the likely diagnosis, and
  what is the molecular basis?
\item
  Describe the unfolded protein response (UPR) and explain its three
  branches (IRE1, PERK, ATF6). Under what circumstances does the UPR
  switch from adaptive to apoptotic?
\item
  Explain how the nuclear pore complex achieves selective transport of
  macromolecules while allowing free diffusion of small molecules.
\item
  Compare the mechanisms by which taxol and colchicine affect
  microtubule dynamics. Both are used clinically --- for what different
  purposes?
\item
  Explain the role of primary cilia as signalling platforms. Why do
  PKD1/PKD2 mutations in primary cilia lead to polycystic kidney
  disease?
\item
  Describe the vesicle coat proteins COPII, COPI, and clathrin. For
  each, specify the transport route, the GTPase involved, and the type
  of cargo carried.
\item
  A cell biologist discovers a new organelle-associated protein.
  Describe a CRISPR-based experimental strategy to determine its
  function and subcellular localisation.
\item
  Using the organelle catalogue, explain why disrupting
  \textbf{mitochondrial} fusion/fission dynamics preferentially affects
  tissues with high ATP turnover.
\item
  Compare one structural difference between COPII-coated vesicles and
  clathrin-coated pits that explains their distinct cargo size ranges.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-9}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}

\item

\item

\item

\item

\item

\item

\item

\item

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Big idea:} Membranes convert gradients, permeability, and
  selective transport into cellular physiology.
\item
  \textbf{Core concepts:} bilayers, diffusion, osmosis, electrochemical
  gradients.
\item

\item

\item

\item
  \textbf{Practice cadence:} Visual Representations, Questions and

\item

  \breaktt{biology.cell.cell\_biology.nernst\_potential}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth]{../figures/ghk_permeability.png}
\caption{Goldman--Hodgkin--Katz permeability sensitivity. Membrane potential is plotted as relative sodium permeability increases while potassium permeability is held fixed and chloride permeability is varied.}
\label{fig:unit_II_ghk_permeability}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Opening Vignette: The Membrane Pump That Makes Cancer Cells
Immortal}

In 1976, July Ling and colleagues at MIT discovered that some tumour
cells were extraordinarily difficult to kill with chemotherapy drugs
because they expressed unusual amounts of a 170 kDa membrane protein ---
later named \textbf{P-glycoprotein} (P-gp) --- that used ATP hydrolysis
to actively export cytotoxic drugs from the cell interior (Juliano \&
Ling, 1976, \emph{Biochimica et Biophysica Acta}). A cancer cell
overexpressing P-gp can reduce the intracellular concentration of
doxorubicin, vincristine, paclitaxel, and dozens of other chemotherapy
agents to sub-lethal levels, rendering the entire drug arsenal
ineffective. This phenomenon --- \textbf{multidrug resistance (MDR)} ---
remains one of the greatest challenges in oncology.

P-gp is an ABC transporter: it has two
\hyperref[gl:nucleotide]{\textbf{nucleotide}}-binding domains (NBDs)
that hydrolyse ATP and two transmembrane domains (TMDs) that form the
drug-export channel. It exemplifies the principle that membranes are not
passive barriers --- they are dynamic, information-processing systems
that control exactly which molecules enter and exit cells, and at what
rate. Understanding that selectivity, and exploiting it therapeutically,
is the central theme of this chapter.

\emph{Primary source: Juliano, R. L. \& Ling, V. (1976). A surface
glycoprotein modulating drug permeability in Chinese hamster ovary cell
mutants. Biochimica et Biophysica Acta, 455(1), 152--162.}
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

In 1972, Singer and Nicolson proposed the \textbf{fluid mosaic model}:
the plasma membrane is a lipid bilayer in which proteins float like
icebergs in a sea of lipids. Both the lipid and protein components can
diffuse laterally within the membrane plane (\textbf{fluid} component),
while the asymmetric distribution of lipids and proteins across the two
leaflets generates \textbf{mosaic} heterogeneity.

\subsubsection{Membrane Lipid
Composition}\label{membrane-lipid-composition}

The plasma membrane is not a homogeneous bilayer but contains distinct
regions of varying composition:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2115}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4231}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3654}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Lipid Class
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
\% of membrane (animal)
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Location preference
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Phosphatidylcholine (PC) & 25--30 & Outer leaflet \\
Phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) & 25 & Inner leaflet \\
Phosphatidylserine (PS) & 10 & Inner leaflet (negatively charged) \\
Sphingomyelin (SM) & 15 & Outer leaflet (rafts) \\
Cholesterol & 20--50 & Both leaflets (condenses rafts) \\
Phosphatidylinositol (PI) & 5 & Inner leaflet (signalling: PIP\(_2\),
PIP\(_3\)) \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Lipid asymmetry} is maintained by \textbf{flippases}
(ATP-dependent; P4-ATPases; move PS and PE to the inner leaflet) and
\textbf{floppases} (ATP-dependent; ABC transporters; move lipids to the
outer leaflet). \textbf{Scramblases} (Ca\(^{2+}\)-activated; TMEM16F)
randomise asymmetry during \hyperref[gl:apoptosis]{\textbf{apoptosis}}
--- externalised phosphatidylserine (PS) is the ``eat me'' signal
recognised by phagocyte receptors (TIM-4, BAI-1, Stabilin-2).

\textbf{Membrane fluidity} depends on lipid composition:
\[\text{Fluidity} \propto \frac{\text{degree of unsaturation} + \text{chain shortness}}{\text{cholesterol content (moderate)}} \tag{7.1} \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_1}\]

Cholesterol has a biphasic effect: at low temperature, it disrupts
crystalline packing (fluidises); at high temperature, it restricts
excessive fluidity (condenses). This \textbf{buffering} effect maintains
membrane fluidity across a physiological temperature range.

\subsubsection{Lipid Rafts and Membrane
Microdomains}\label{lipid-rafts-and-membrane-microdomains}

\textbf{Lipid rafts} are dynamic, cholesterol- and sphingolipid-enriched
microdomains (10--200 nm) in the outer leaflet that preferentially
recruit certain proteins: - \textbf{GPI-anchored proteins} partition
into rafts - \textbf{Signalling receptors} (e.g., T cell receptor, B
cell receptor) cluster in rafts upon ligand binding - \textbf{Caveolins}
(caveolae) represent a specialised, stable form of lipid raft

\textbf{Controversy:} The existence and functional significance of lipid
rafts has been debated. Single-molecule tracking studies reveal that
raft-like domains are transient (about 10--20 ms lifetime),
small (about 10--20 nm), and form/dissolve dynamically. STED
super-resolution microscopy (Eggeling et al., 2009, \emph{Nature})
confirmed that sphingolipids and GPI-anchored proteins are transiently
confined in nanoscale membrane domains, supporting a dynamic raft model.

\subsubsection{Updates to the Fluid Mosaic
Model}\label{updates-to-the-fluid-mosaic-model}

Since 1972, several refinements have been made:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Membrane is more mosaic than fluid:} Up to 50\% of membrane
  area is occupied by proteins; crowding restricts lateral diffusion
\item
  \textbf{Cytoskeletal fences:} The \hyperref[gl:actin]{\textbf{actin}}
  cortex creates corrals (``picket fence'' model, Kusumi et al.) that
  compartmentalise membrane proteins into about 40--300 nm
  domains, restricting free diffusion
\item
  \textbf{Lipid asymmetry} is more extensive than originally appreciated
\item
  \textbf{Membrane curvature} is actively generated by BAR-domain
  proteins, ESCRT complexes, and coat proteins
\item
  \textbf{Transbilayer communication:} Inner and outer leaflet lipids
  can be coupled through interdigitating acyl chains
\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 1:} During apoptosis, phosphatidylserine (PS)
moves from the inner to the outer leaflet. What
\hyperref[gl:enzyme]{\textbf{enzyme}} mediates this, and why is PS
externalisation a critical signal for phagocytic clearance?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Membrane Proteins}\label{membrane-proteins}

\textbf{Integral (transmembrane) proteins} span the bilayer via
alpha-helical segments (of about 20 hydrophobic amino acids
each, sufficient to span the about 3 nm hydrophobic core) or
beta-barrel structures (found primarily in outer membranes of
Gram-negative bacteria, mitochondria, and
\hyperref[gl:chloroplast]{\textbf{chloroplast}}s).

\textbf{Peripheral proteins} associate noncovalently with membrane
surfaces or integral proteins via electrostatic interactions,
\hyperref[gl:hydrogen-bond]{\textbf{hydrogen bond}}s, or hydrophobic
interactions with the lipid headgroup region.

\textbf{Lipid-anchored proteins} are covalently modified with: -
\textbf{GPI-anchors} (outer leaflet): e.g., alkaline phosphatase, CD59
(complement regulator) - \textbf{Myristoyl} groups (inner leaflet,
N-terminal): e.g., Src kinase - \textbf{Palmitoyl} groups (inner
leaflet, Cys residue): e.g., Ras (reversible; regulates membrane
association) - \textbf{Farnesyl/geranylgeranyl} groups (inner leaflet,
C-terminal CAAX): e.g., Ras, Rho GTPases

\subsubsection{Functions of Membrane
Proteins}\label{functions-of-membrane-proteins}
