\subsection{Passive Transport}\label{passive-transport}

Passive transport requires no energy input --- molecules move down their
electrochemical gradient.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0038_993b48293347.png}
\caption{Classification of membrane transport mechanisms, from simple diffusion through channels and carriers to primary and secondary active transport and bulk transport.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Simple Diffusion}\label{simple-diffusion}

For uncharged molecules, flux obeys Fick's First Law:

\[J = -D \frac{d[C]}{dx} = P \cdot \Delta [C] \tag{7.2} \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_2}\]

where \(P\) = permeability coefficient (m/s) =
\(D \cdot K_{\text{oil/water}} / d\) (membrane thickness).

Membrane permeability: - \textbf{High:} small nonpolar molecules
(O\(_2\), CO\(_2\), N\(_2\), ethanol, benzene) - \textbf{Moderate:}
small polar uncharged (water, glycerol, urea) - \textbf{Low:} large
polar (glucose, amino acids) - \textbf{Very low/none:} ions (Na\(^+\),
K\(^+\), Cl\(^-\), Ca\(^{2+}\)) --- require protein channels

The \textbf{partition coefficient} (\(K_{\text{oil/water}}\)) is the
strongest predictor of simple diffusion rate. Overton's rule (1899):
membrane permeability correlates with oil/water partition coefficient.

\subsubsection{Osmosis and the van't Hoff
Equation}\label{osmosis-and-the-vant-hoff-equation}

Although water is technically a small polar molecule, its transport
across cell membranes is fast and quantitative enough to deserve its own
treatment. \textbf{Osmosis} is the net diffusion of water across a
semi-permeable membrane in response to a difference in solute
concentrations. Because water mass is conserved, osmosis amounts to a
redistribution of \emph{volume} --- and uncontrolled osmotic swelling
will lyse a cell.

The thermodynamic driving force is the difference in \textbf{water
chemical potential} \(\mu_w\) between two compartments:

\[\mu_w = \mu_w^0 + RT \ln a_w + \bar{V}_w P \tag{7.24} \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_3}\]

where \(a_w\) is water activity (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} mole fraction in dilute solution) and
\(\bar{V}_w\) is the partial molar volume of water (about 18
mL/mol). Each dissolved solute particle reduces \(a_w\) proportionally
--- this is the molecular origin of colligative properties
(boiling-point elevation, freezing-point depression, vapour-pressure
lowering). Setting \(\mu_w\) equal on both sides of a semi-permeable
membrane and solving for the pressure required to balance a solute
gradient yields \textbf{van't Hoff's law}:

\begin{equation}
\Pi = i M R T
\label{eq:unit_II_vant_hoff}
\end{equation}

where \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Pi}}{Pi} is the \textbf{osmotic pressure} (in atm or Pa), \(M\) is the
solute molar concentration, \(R\) is the gas constant, \(T\) is absolute
temperature, and \(i\) is the \textbf{van't Hoff factor} --- the number
of effective particles produced per formula unit (1 for glucose; 2 for
NaCl; 3 for CaCl\(_2\) at full dissociation).

In SI units with \(R = 0.0821\) L\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.}atm/mol/K and 37 °C (\(T = 310\) K), 1
mM of an ideal solute generates
\(\Pi = 1 \cdot 0.001 \cdot 0.0821 \cdot 310 = 0.0254\) atm \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 25 mmHg.
Plasma is about 290 mOsm/L, generating about 7,500
mmHg of total osmotic pressure --- but cells don't burst because they
are surrounded by isotonic interstitial fluid, and primarily the
\emph{difference} matters.

\textbf{Worked Example: Osmotic swelling of a red blood cell.}

A red blood cell is placed in a hypotonic solution (200 mOsm/L; plasma
is 290 mOsm/L). Calculate (a) the initial osmotic pressure difference
driving water inward, (b) the cell's predicted volume change to reach
equilibrium.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  The osmotic pressure gradient is:
  \[ \Delta \Pi = (290 - 200) \times 10^{-3} \cdot 0.0821 \cdot 310 = 0.0900 \cdot 25.45 = 2.29 \text{ atm} \approx 1{,}740 \text{ mmHg}  \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_4}\]
\end{enumerate}

This drives water into the cell at a flux of
\(J_w = p_f \cdot \Delta C\), where \(p_f \approx 0.02\) cm/s for an
AQP1-rich erythrocyte. For a typical cell
(\(A \approx 140 \, \mu\text{m}^2\), \(V \approx 90 \, \mu\text{m}^3\)),
volume doubling occurs in roughly 200 ms --- fast enough to be visible
in a microscope as the cell swells from biconcave disc to sphere.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  At osmotic equilibrium, water content adjusts to make intracellular
  osmolarity = 200 mOsm/L. If initial intracellular osmolyte content is
  \(V_0 \cdot C_0 = 90 \cdot 290 = 26{,}100\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}mol\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.}\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m\(^3\)/L, the new
  equilibrium volume is:
  \[ V_\text{new} = V_0 \cdot \frac{C_0}{C_\text{new}} = 90 \cdot \frac{290}{200} = 130.5 \, \mu\text{m}^3  \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_5}\]
\end{enumerate}

A 45\% volume increase. RBCs reach a critical volume of
about 150 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m\(^3\) before haemolysis (membrane area cannot
accommodate further sphere expansion), so the cell is on the brink of
lysis.

\textbf{Tonicity terms (clinical):} Hypotonic solutions cause cells to
swell (haemolysis if severe). Isotonic solutions (e.g., 0.9\% NaCl, 5\%
dextrose, lactated Ringer's) preserve volume. Hypertonic solutions cause
cells to shrink (crenation in RBCs). Aquaporin defects cause major fluid
balance disorders: \textbf{AQP2 mutations} cause nephrogenic diabetes
insipidus (water reabsorption fails despite vasopressin); \textbf{AQP4
autoantibodies} cause neuromyelitis optica (astrocyte water-handling
fails, edema and demyelination). The osmotic pressure of plasma proteins
(mostly albumin, about 25 mmHg) is the \textbf{oncotic
pressure} that retains fluid in the vasculature --- its loss in
nephrotic syndrome and liver failure causes generalised oedema.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 1b:} A patient with severe burns receives 4 L of
0.45\% NaCl (``half-normal saline'') rapidly. Calculate the tonicity
relative to plasma (290 mOsm/L) and predict the consequence for red
blood cells.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Facilitated Diffusion via
Channels}\label{facilitated-diffusion-via-channels}

\textbf{Ion channels} are integral membrane proteins forming aqueous
pores. They are: - \textbf{Selective:} ion selectivity filter determines
which ions pass - \textbf{Gated:} open/close in response to specific
stimuli - \textbf{Fast:} ion throughput rates of 10\(^7\)--10\(^8\)
ions/s (near diffusion limit)

\textbf{Gating mechanisms:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Voltage-gated:} opened by membrane-potential change; examples
  include sodium channel Nav1.1--1.9, potassium channel Kv1--12, and
  calcium channel Cav1--3 families.
\item
  \textbf{Ligand-gated, extracellular:} opened by neurotransmitter
  binding; examples include nAChR, GABAA receptor, NMDAR, and AMPAR.
\item
  \textbf{Ligand-gated, intracellular:} opened by second messengers;
  examples include calcium-activated potassium channel BK and retinal
  cGMP-gated channels.
\item
  \textbf{Mechanosensitive:} opened by stretch or pressure; examples
  include Piezo1/2, TREK-1, and bacterial MscL.
\item
  \textbf{Temperature-gated:} opened by heat or cold; examples include
  TRPV1 (\textgreater43 degrees C, capsaicin) and TRPM8 (\textless26
  degrees C, menthol).
\item
  \textbf{Light-gated:} opened by photons; channelrhodopsin ChR2 is the
  standard optogenetic example.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Selectivity filter of K\(^+\) channels} (MacKinnon, Nobel Prize
2003): The selectivity filter contains the signature sequence TVGYG.
Four carbonyl oxygens from each of the four subunits line the pore,
precisely mimicking the hydration shell of K\(^+\) (radius 1.33
angstroms). Na\(^+\) (radius 0.95 angstroms) is too small to be
coordinated effectively --- the energetic cost of dehydrating Na\(^+\)
without compensating coordination makes Na\(^+\) passage unfavourable.
This elegant size-exclusion mechanism achieves 10,000:1 selectivity for
K\(^+\) over Na\(^+\).

\textbf{Aquaporins (AQP):} Facilitate water transport (not solutes).
AQP1 (Peter Agre, Nobel Prize 2003) channels about 3 x 10\(^8\)
water molecules/s while excluding protons (the Grotthuss mechanism is
interrupted by a critical asparagine residue in the channel pore, and
the electrostatic field of the NPA motif reorients water molecules,
preventing H\(_3\)O\(^+\) passage).

\textbf{Aquaporin discovery and selectivity in detail.} Before 1992,
biologists could not explain how erythrocytes and renal tubule cells
achieve water permeability rates 100\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} faster than predicted from the
lipid bilayer alone. Peter Agre's group, while studying Rh-blood-group
proteins, noticed a contaminating 28 kDa membrane protein.
Reconstitution experiments (Preston et al., 1992, \emph{Science})
demonstrated that this protein --- christened \textbf{AQP1}
(aquaporin-1) --- conferred about 10\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} water permeability when
expressed in \emph{Xenopus} oocytes. Agre shared the 2003 Nobel Prize in
Chemistry. Thirteen aquaporin paralogues are now known in humans, with
tissue-specific expression: AQP2 (renal collecting duct,
vasopressin-regulated), AQP4 (astrocyte endfeet, target of NMO
autoantibodies), AQP5 (salivary/lacrimal glands), AQP7 (adipocytes,
glycerol channel).

The structural basis of selectivity is exquisite. Each AQP monomer is a
hexa-helical bundle with two short re-entrant helices (carrying the
conserved \textbf{NPA motifs} --- Asn-Pro-Ala) that meet in the middle
of the membrane to form the narrowest part of the pore
(about 2.8 Å, just wide enough for a single water molecule).
Two mechanisms exclude protons:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Electrostatic barrier:} The two NPA half-helices have positive
  macrodipoles meeting in the middle of the pore --- repelling
  H\(_3\)O\(^+\) but attracting electrically neutral water.
\item
  \textbf{Hydrogen-bond reorientation:} The central asparagines force
  passing water molecules to flip their hydrogen-bond donor/acceptor
  orientation. This breaks the proton-relay (Grotthuss) chain that would
  otherwise allow H\(^+\) to ``hop'' through the channel.
\end{enumerate}

The water permeability coefficient (\(p_f\), the \textbf{osmotic
permeability}) for a single AQP1 channel is
about \(3 \times 10^{-14}\) cm\(^3\)/s, corresponding to
about 3 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 10\(^9\) water molecules/s under typical osmotic
gradients. A red blood cell expressing about 200,000 AQP1
channels can therefore exchange its entire water volume in \textless100
ms --- the basis of erythrocyte swelling/shrinking responses.

\textbf{Clinical aquaporins.} Loss-of-function mutations in AQP2 cause
\textbf{nephrogenic diabetes insipidus} (kidneys cannot concentrate
urine despite normal vasopressin). Autoantibodies against AQP4 cause
\textbf{neuromyelitis optica (Devic's disease)}, a demyelinating
disorder distinct from MS. AQP1 is upregulated in many tumours and is
being explored as a target in glioma therapy.

\textbf{Clinical Connection: Channelopathies.} Ion channel
\hyperref[gl:mutation]{\textbf{mutation}}s cause a wide range of
diseases:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Long QT syndrome:} Mutations in cardiac potassium or sodium
  channels prolong repolarisation and can trigger fatal arrhythmias.
  Drug-development screens therefore test for hERG channel block.
\item
  \textbf{Cystic fibrosis:} Mutations in CFTR disrupt chloride
  transport. The common deltaF508 variant causes misfolding and ER
  retention; modulator combinations such as lumacaftor/ivacaftor and
  elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor partly restore channel function.
\item
  \textbf{Malignant hyperthermia:} RyR1 mutations cause uncontrolled
  Ca\(^{2+}\) release from sarcoplasmic reticulum after exposure to
  volatile anaesthetics. See \cref{sec:unit_II_cell_signaling} for
  calcium signalling.
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 2:} Tetrodotoxin (TTX, from pufferfish) blocks
voltage-gated Na\(^+\) channels by binding the selectivity filter from
the extracellular side. Predict the effects of TTX on (a)
\hyperref[gl:action-potential]{\textbf{action potential}} generation,
(b) nerve conduction, and (c) skeletal muscle contraction.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Ion Channel Gating
Kinetics}\label{ion-channel-gating-kinetics}

A single ion channel in a patch-clamp recording flickers between open
and closed states stochastically. The time-averaged current through a
population of \(N\) channels with single-channel conductance \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma} (in pS =
pico-siemens) and open probability \(P_o\) is:

\begin{equation}
I = N \cdot P_o \cdot \gamma \cdot (V_m - E_\text{rev})
\label{eq:unit_II_macroscopic_current}
\end{equation}

where \(V_m\) is the membrane potential and \(E_\text{rev}\) is the
reversal potential (for a perfectly selective channel,
\(E_\text{rev} = E_\text{ion}\)). This decomposition is one of the most
powerful in biophysics: drugs can change channel function by altering
\(N\) (channel expression/internalisation), \(P_o\) (gating modulators,
allosteric drugs), or \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma} (pore-block, modifications of selectivity
filter), and each can be measured separately.

\textbf{Single-channel conductances of representative channels (in pS):}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{nAChR, muscle endplate:} conductance 30--50 pS; open
  probability about 0.85 with ACh; throughput about 3 x 10\^{}7 ions/s.
\item
  \textbf{BK, large-conductance calcium-activated potassium channel:}
  conductance 200--250 pS; open probability 0.1--0.9 depending on
  calcium; throughput up to 10\^{}8 ions/s.
\item
  \textbf{Kv1.x delayed rectifier:} conductance 10--20 pS; open
  probability about 0.7 at +20 mV; throughput about 10\^{}6 ions/s.
\item
  \textbf{Nav1.x:} conductance 15--20 pS; transient open probability
  below 0.5; throughput about 5 x 10\^{}6 ions/s during an action
  potential.
\item
  \textbf{L-type Cav1.2:} conductance about 25 pS; open probability
  about 0.3; throughput about 10\^{}5 ions/s.
\item
  \textbf{ClC-1 skeletal chloride channel:} conductance about 1 pS with
  gating-coupled pores; open probability about 0.5 at rest.
\item
  \textbf{CFTR chloride channel / ABC transporter:} conductance 8--10
  pS; PKA-dependent open probability 0.3--0.5.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Open probability and gating models.} The open probability
\(P_o\) depends on the gating stimulus (voltage, ligand concentration,
mechanical force). For a voltage-gated channel with effective gating
charge \(z_g\) (typical about 4--6 for Na\(_V\),
about 6--10 for K\(_V\)), the equilibrium open probability
follows a Boltzmann relation:

\[P_o(V) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\left(-\frac{z_g F (V - V_{1/2})}{RT}\right)} \tag{7.19} \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_6}\]

where \(V_{1/2}\) is the half-activation voltage. This sigmoidal curve
is steep (about 5--10 mV per e-fold change) --- small voltage
perturbations cause large changes in \(P_o\), the basis of the action
potential's switch-like behaviour. For ligand-gated channels with \(n\)
binding sites and Hill coefficient \(h\):

\[P_o([L]) = \frac{[L]^h}{[L]^h + K_d^h} \tag{7.20} \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_7}\]

For the muscle nAChR, \(h \approx 1.5\) and \(K_d \approx 30\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}M for
ACh: half-maximal activation at about 30 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}M, full activation by
about 300 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}M. The sub-millisecond opening of nAChRs after ACh
release at the neuromuscular junction (peak {[}ACh{]} about 1
mM at the postsynaptic membrane) ensures essentially complete channel
activation in every action potential.

\subsubsection{Electroneutral vs.~Electrogenic
Transport}\label{electroneutral-vs.-electrogenic-transport}

Whether a transporter contributes net charge to the membrane potential
depends on the \textbf{stoichiometry of the transport cycle}.

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4127}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2063}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Transporter
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Stoichiometry
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Net charge moved per cycle
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Na\(^+\)/K\(^+\)-ATPase & 3 Na\(^+\) out / 2 K\(^+\) in / 1 ATP & +1
outward & Yes \\
Ca\(^{2+}\)-ATPase (SERCA) & 2 Ca\(^{2+}\) in (to ER) / 2 H\(^+\) out /
1 ATP & 0 & No (electroneutral) \\
H\(^+\)/K\(^+\)-ATPase (gastric) & 1 H\(^+\) out / 1 K\(^+\) in / 1 ATP
& 0 & No \\
NCX (Na\(^+\)/Ca\(^{2+}\) exchanger) & 3 Na\(^+\) in / 1 Ca\(^{2+}\) out
& +1 inward & Yes \\
NHE1 (Na\(^+\)/H\(^+\) exchanger) & 1 Na\(^+\) in / 1 H\(^+\) out & 0 &
No \\
SGLT1 (Na\(^+\)/glucose symport) & 2 Na\(^+\) in / 1 glucose & +2 inward
& Yes \\
AE1 (Cl\(^-\)/HCO\(_3^-\) exchanger) & 1 Cl\(^-\) out / 1 HCO\(_3^-\) in
& 0 & No \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Energetic consequences.} Electroneutral transporters move
solutes ``for free'' with respect to the membrane potential --- their
thermodynamic feasibility depends primarily on chemical concentration
gradients. Electrogenic transporters, by contrast, are driven by
\emph{both} concentration and voltage. The Na\(^+\)/K\(^+\)-ATPase, for
example, would still hydrolyse ATP if Na\(^+\) and K\(^+\)
concentrations were equalised, because moving net positive charge
against the membrane potential (interior negative) costs additional
energy: the \textbf{electrochemical gradient} is the relevant
thermodynamic quantity:

\[\Delta G_\text{ion} = RT \ln \frac{[C]_\text{out}}{[C]_\text{in}} + z F V_m \tag{7.21} \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_8}\]

For a 100\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} concentration gradient and 100 mV opposing voltage:
\(\Delta G \approx +12 + 9.6 = 21.6\) kJ/mol. ATP hydrolysis releases
about 50 kJ/mol under cellular conditions, so a single ATP can
drive about 2 ions of net charge against this combined gradient
--- exactly the stoichiometry observed in the Na\(^+\)/K\(^+\)-ATPase (3
Na\(^+\) out -- 2 K\(^+\) in = +1 net per ATP, with margin for
irreversibility).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Channelopathy diagnostics.} When a patient
presents with arrhythmia, episodic weakness, or seizures, modern
diagnostics include \textbf{gene panels} (sequencing known channel
genes) followed by \textbf{functional reconstitution} of variants in
HEK293 or oocyte expression systems. Patch-clamp measurements decompose
the disease-causing change into \(N\), \(P_o\), and \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma} effects: for
example, the cystic fibrosis \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Delta}}{Delta}F508 mutation reduces \(N\) at the
membrane (trafficking defect, fixed by lumacaftor); G551D reduces
\(P_o\) (gating defect, fixed by ivacaftor). The combination drug
Orkambi addresses both --- a triumph of mechanism-guided pharmacology.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Facilitated Diffusion via Carriers
(Uniporters)}\label{facilitated-diffusion-via-carriers-uniporters}

\textbf{GLUT transporters} (SLC2A family; 14 isoforms in humans)
facilitate glucose diffusion:

The \textbf{alternating access mechanism}: the carrier alternates
between outward-facing (substrate binds from extracellular side) and
inward-facing (substrate released to
\hyperref[gl:cytoplasm]{\textbf{cytoplasm}}) conformations. This is
slower than channel transport (about 10\(^2\)--10\(^4\)
molecules/s) but allows specificity and saturability.

\subsection{Worked Example: GLUT Transporter
Kinetics}\label{worked-example-glut-transporter-kinetics}

\emph{Problem:} GLUT1 has \(K_m = 1.5\) mM and \(V_{max} = 200\)
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}mol/min per gram of membrane protein. Blood glucose is about 5
mM. At what fraction of \(V_{max}\) is GLUT1 operating?

\emph{Solution:}

Using the Michaelis-Menten equation:

\[v = \frac{V_{max} \cdot [S]}{K_m + [S]} = \frac{200 \times 5}{1.5 + 5} = \frac{1000}{6.5} = 154 \; \mu\text{mol/min/g} \tag{7.3} \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_9}\]

\[\frac{v}{V_{max}} = \frac{154}{200} = 0.77 = 77\% \tag{7.4} \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_10}\]

GLUT1 operates at 77\% of maximum capacity at normal blood glucose ---
providing a safety margin while ensuring high glucose flux to the brain.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Active Transport}\label{active-transport}

Active transport moves solutes against their electrochemical gradient,
requiring energy (usually ATP hydrolysis or proton motive force).

\subsubsection{Primary Active Transport ---
Pumps}\label{primary-active-transport-pumps}

\textbf{Na\(^+\)/K\(^+\)-ATPase (sodium-potassium pump):} Exports 3
Na\(^+\) and imports 2 K\(^+\) per ATP consumed (overall electrogenic;
net +1 charge out). This pump consumes about 25\% of the body's
ATP (up to 70\% in neurons).

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0039_6d07c3fd2370.png}
\caption{The Post-Albers cycle of the Na\$\textasciicircum{}+\$/K\$\textasciicircum{}+\$-ATPase. The pump alternates between E1 (inward-facing, high Na\$\textasciicircum{}+\$ affinity) and E2 (outward-facing, high K\$\textasciicircum{}+\$ affinity) conformations. Phosphorylation by ATP and subsequent dephosphorylation drive the conformational changes.}
\end{figure}

This maintains: - Resting membrane potential (K\(^+\) gradient) - High
intracellular {[}K\(^+\){]} (about 140 mM) and low
{[}Na\(^+\){]} (about 12 mM) - Low intracellular Na\(^+\) that
drives secondary active transport - Cell volume regulation (preventing
osmotic swelling)

\textbf{Inhibition by ouabain/digitalis:} Cardiac glycosides block the
K\(^+\)-binding E2-P form. This elevates intracellular Na\(^+\), which
reduces Na\(^+\)/Ca\(^{2+}\) exchanger activity (NCX normally uses the
Na\(^+\) gradient to export Ca\(^{2+}\)), so {[}Ca\(^{2+}\){]}\(_i\)
rises, causing stronger cardiac contraction. Used for heart failure;
narrow therapeutic window (toxicity causes arrhythmias).

\textbf{Other primary active transport pumps:} -
\textbf{Ca\(^{2+}\)-ATPase (SERCA):} pumps Ca\(^{2+}\) from cytoplasm
into ER/SR lumen; maintains {[}Ca\(^{2+}\){]}\(_i\) at
about 100 nM (10,000-fold lower than extracellular); critical
for muscle relaxation - \textbf{H\(^+\)/K\(^+\)-ATPase:} gastric
parietal cells; pumps H\(^+\) into stomach lumen
(\hyperref[gl:ph]{\textbf{pH}} about 1); target of proton pump
inhibitors (omeprazole, lansoprazole) for acid reflux/ulcer treatment -
\textbf{V-type H\(^+\)-ATPase:} acidifies lysosomes, endosomes; does not
use a phosphorylated intermediate

\subsubsection{ABC Transporters}\label{abc-transporters}

\textbf{ATP-Binding Cassette (ABC) transporters} are a superfamily of
about 48 members in humans. They use ATP hydrolysis to
transport diverse substrates across membranes:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{MDR1/P-glycoprotein (ABCB1):} Broad-specificity drug efflux
  pump; exports hydrophobic compounds from the cell. Overexpressed in
  many cancers, causing \textbf{multidrug resistance} --- tumour cells
  pump out chemotherapy drugs before they can act. Substrates include
  taxol, doxorubicin, vincristine.
\item
  \textbf{CFTR (ABCC7):} Unique ABC transporter that functions as a
  Cl\(^-\) channel. Mutations cause \textbf{cystic fibrosis} (see
  Clinical Connection above).
\item
  \textbf{ABCA1:} Cholesterol and phospholipid efflux to apoA-I;
  critical for HDL formation. Loss-of-function mutations cause
  \textbf{Tangier disease} (very low HDL, cholesterol deposition in
  tissues).
\item
  \textbf{TAP1/TAP2 (ABCB2/3):} Transport antigenic peptides from
  cytoplasm into ER lumen for MHC class I loading and immune
  presentation.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Secondary Active
Transport}\label{secondary-active-transport}

Uses the Na\(^+\) electrochemical gradient (generated by the primary
pump) to drive uphill transport of other solutes:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Symport (co-transport, same direction):} SGLT1 (intestinal
  glucose): 2 Na\(^+\) + 1 glucose move in together; net uptake even if
  {[}glucose{]}\(_{\text{in}}\) \textgreater{}
  {[}glucose{]}\(_{\text{out}}\). SGLT2 (kidney proximal tubule): 1
  Na\(^+\) + 1 glucose; target of gliflozin drugs for type 2 diabetes.
\item
  \textbf{Antiport (exchange, opposite directions):} NCX
  (Na\(^+\)/Ca\(^{2+}\) exchanger): 3 Na\(^+\) in, 1 Ca\(^{2+}\) out;
  critical for cardiac Ca\(^{2+}\)
  \hyperref[gl:homeostasis]{\textbf{homeostasis}}. NHE (Na\(^+\)/H\(^+\)
  exchanger): Na\(^+\) in, H\(^+\) out; regulates intracellular pH.
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: SGLT2 Inhibitors in Diabetes and Heart
Failure} SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin)
block glucose reabsorption in the kidney proximal tubule, causing
glucosuria (glucose loss in urine) and lowering blood glucose.
Remarkably, these drugs also reduce cardiovascular death and heart
failure hospitalisations, even in non-diabetic patients --- likely
through natriuresis, osmotic diuresis, and favourable metabolic effects.
They represent a rare case where a simple transport mechanism becomes a
blockbuster drug target. see \cref{sec:unit_III_metabolic_integration}
(Metabolic Integration) for insulin signalling.
\end{quote}

bacterial membranes that allows monovalent cations (Na\(^+\), K\(^+\))
to flow freely. Predict how gramicidin would affect (a) the bacterial
membrane potential, (b) the proton motive force, and (c) bacterial ATP
synthesis.
\end{quote}

\subsection{The Nernst Equation and Membrane
Potential}\label{the-nernst-equation-and-membrane-potential}

\subsubsection{Electrochemical
Potential}\label{electrochemical-potential}

The electrochemical potential of an ion is:

\[\tilde{\mu}_i = \mu_i^0 + RT\ln[C_i] + z_i F V \tag{7.5} \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_11}\]

where \(z_i\) = ionic charge, \(F\) = Faraday constant (96,485 C/mol),
\(V\) = membrane potential.

At equilibrium (no net flux), the \textbf{Nernst equation} gives the
equilibrium potential \(E_i\):

\[E_i = \frac{RT}{z_i F} \ln \frac{[C_i]_{\text{out}}}{[C_i]_{\text{in}}} \tag{7.6} \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_12}\]

At 37 degrees C (310 K), \(RT/F\) = 26.7 mV. Converting to log\(_{10}\):

\[E_i = \frac{61.5 \; \text{mV}}{z_i} \log_{10} \frac{[C_i]_{\text{out}}}{[C_i]_{\text{in}}} \tag{7.7} \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_13}\]

\subsubsection{Derivation of the Nernst
Equation}\label{derivation-of-the-nernst-equation}

Starting from the condition of zero net electrochemical driving force at
equilibrium:

\[\Delta \tilde{\mu}_i = 0 \tag{7.8} \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_14}\]

\[RT \ln \frac{[C_i]_{\text{in}}}{[C_i]_{\text{out}}} + z_i F (V_{\text{in}} - V_{\text{out}}) = 0 \tag{7.9} \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_15}\]

\[z_i F \cdot E_i = -RT \ln \frac{[C_i]_{\text{in}}}{[C_i]_{\text{out}}} = RT \ln \frac{[C_i]_{\text{out}}}{[C_i]_{\text{in}}} \tag{7.10} \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_16}\]

\[E_i = \frac{RT}{z_i F} \ln \frac{[C_i]_{\text{out}}}{[C_i]_{\text{in}}} \tag{7.11} \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_17}\]

\subsection{Worked Example: Nernst
Potential}\label{worked-example-nernst-potential}

\emph{Problem:} Calculate the Nernst equilibrium potential for
Ca\(^{2+}\) at 37 degrees C, given {[}Ca\(^{2+}\){]}\(_{\text{out}}\) =
2.5 mM and {[}Ca\(^{2+}\){]}\(_{\text{in}}\) = 0.0001 mM (100 nM).

\emph{Solution:}

\[E_{Ca} = \frac{RT}{z_{Ca}F} \ln \frac{[Ca^{2+}]_{\text{out}}}{[Ca^{2+}]_{\text{in}}} = \frac{26.7 \; \text{mV}}{2} \ln \frac{2.5}{0.0001} \tag{7.12} \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_18}\]

\[E_{Ca} = 13.35 \; \text{mV} \times \ln(25,000) = 13.35 \times 10.13 = +135 \; \text{mV} \tag{7.13} \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_19}\]

The strongly positive \(E_{Ca}\) means that Ca\(^{2+}\) has a massive
driving force to enter cells. Brief Ca\(^{2+}\) channel openings can
therefore cause significant signalling events.

\textbf{Nernst potentials of key ions:}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}llll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Ion & {[}inside{]} (mM) & {[}outside{]} (mM) & \(E_i\) (mV, 37 degrees
C) \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
K\(^+\) & 140 & 5 & -89 \\
Na\(^+\) & 12 & 145 & +63 \\
Ca\(^{2+}\) & 0.0001 & 2.5 & +135 \\
Cl\(^-\) & 4 & 110 & -82 \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Worked Example: Nernst Potentials for K\(^+\), Na\(^+\), and
Cl\(^-\).}

Each row of the table above can be reproduced from
\cref{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_nernst} below by careful
sign-handling. Using the simplified form at 37 °C:
\(E_i = (61.5 \text{ mV} / z_i) \log_{10}([\text{out}]/[\text{in}])\).

\begin{equation}
E_i = \frac{RT}{z_i F} \ln \frac{[C_i]_{\text{out}}}{[C_i]_{\text{in}}}
\label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_nernst}
\end{equation}

\emph{Potassium (z = +1):}
\(E_K = 61.5 \cdot \log_{10}(5/140) = 61.5 \cdot \log_{10}(0.0357) = 61.5 \cdot (-1.447) = -89.0 \text{ mV}\).
K\(^+\) is concentrated inside, so equilibrium drives K\(^+\) outward;
the equilibrium potential is negative (interior must be
about 89 mV more negative to halt K\(^+\) efflux). The resting
membrane potential (\(V_m \approx -70\) mV) is therefore \emph{less
negative} than \(E_K\) --- meaning K\(^+\) continues to leak slowly
outward at rest.

\emph{Sodium (z = +1):}
\(E_{Na} = 61.5 \cdot \log_{10}(145/12) = 61.5 \cdot \log_{10}(12.08) = 61.5 \cdot 1.082 = +66.6 \text{ mV}\).
(Tabulated values vary 63--67 mV depending on the assumed
concentrations.) Na\(^+\) is concentrated outside, so equilibrium drives
Na\(^+\) inward; the equilibrium potential is strongly positive. The
resting membrane potential is \emph{very far} from \(E_{Na}\) ---
meaning Na\(^+\) has a massive electrochemical force driving it inward,
restrained primarily by the low resting Na\(^+\) permeability.

\emph{Chloride (z = \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}1):}
\(E_{Cl} = (61.5 / -1) \cdot \log_{10}(110/4) = -61.5 \cdot \log_{10}(27.5) = -61.5 \cdot 1.439 = -88.5 \text{ mV}\).
(Tabulated values vary 80--90 mV depending on cell type --- neurons have
higher {[}Cl\(^-\){]}\(_i\) than skeletal muscle.) Note the
\emph{negative} sign on \(z_\text{Cl}\) inverts the ratio's effect: a
higher {[}Cl\(^-\){]}\(_o\) than {[}Cl\(^-\){]}\(_i\) yields a
\emph{negative} equilibrium potential, the opposite of K\(^+\). In adult
neurons, \(E_\text{Cl}\) sits near \(V_m\), so Cl\(^-\) is essentially
at equilibrium and small Cl\(^-\) permeability changes (e.g.,
GABA\(_A\)-receptor opening) cause primarily modest hyperpolarisation by
stabilising \(V_m\) near \(E_\text{Cl}\). In neonatal neurons,
{[}Cl\(^-\){]}\(_i\) is higher (about 25 mM) due to immature
KCC2 expression, \(E_\text{Cl}\) becomes about \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}40 mV, and GABA
is \emph{depolarising} --- a fact with major implications for early
brain development and neonatal seizures.

These three numbers --- \(E_K \approx -89\), \(E_{Na} \approx +63\),
\(E_{Cl} \approx -82\) --- together with the relative permeabilities
\(P_K : P_{Na} : P_{Cl}\) generate the entire repertoire of resting and
action potentials in excitable cells.

The resting membrane potential (-70 mV) lies close to \(E_K\) because
the resting cell membrane is about 25x more permeable to
K\(^+\) than Na\(^+\). K\(^+\) ``leaks'' out through K2P (two-pore
domain) leak channels; uncovered negative charges on impermeable
intracellular proteins (Donnan effect) and the electrogenic
Na\(^+\)/K\(^+\) pump (net export of +1 charge per cycle) contribute the
remainder.

\subsubsection{Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz
Equation}\label{goldman-hodgkin-katz-equation}

When multiple ions carry current, the resting membrane potential is
given by the \textbf{Goldman equation}:

\begin{equation}
V_m = \frac{RT}{F} \ln \frac{P_K[K^+]_o + P_{Na}[Na^+]_o + P_{Cl}[Cl^-]_i}{P_K[K^+]_i + P_{Na}[Na^+]_i + P_{Cl}[Cl^-]_o}
\label{eq:unit_II_ghk}
\end{equation}

Note: anions (Cl\(^-\)) appear with reversed subscripts because of their
negative charge.

\textbf{Derivation sketch.} The full Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz (GHK)
derivation begins from the Nernst-Planck equation for ionic flux \(J_i\)
across a membrane of thickness \(d\) in a constant electric field:

\[J_i = -D_i \left( \frac{dC_i}{dx} + z_i C_i \frac{F}{RT} \frac{dV}{dx} \right) \tag{7.22} \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_20}\]

Integrating across the membrane assuming a constant field
(\(dV/dx = -V_m/d\)) and a single permeability \(P_i = D_i \beta_i / d\)
(where \(\beta_i\) is the partition coefficient between water and
membrane) gives the \textbf{GHK current equation}:

\[I_i = z_i F P_i \frac{z_i F V_m / RT}{1 - \exp(-z_i F V_m / RT)} \left( [C_i]_\text{in} - [C_i]_\text{out} \exp(-z_i F V_m / RT) \right) \tag{7.23} \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_21}\]

At the resting membrane potential, the \emph{net} current must be zero:
\(\sum_i I_i = 0\). Solving this for K\(^+\), Na\(^+\), and Cl\(^-\)
(and treating Cl\(^-\) as monovalent anion) algebraically yields the GHK
voltage equation \cref{eq:unit_II_ghk}. The key conceptual takeaways
are: (i) the membrane potential is a \emph{weighted log average} of the
Nernst potentials, with weights set by permeability; (ii) the ion with
the highest permeability dominates; (iii) shifts in permeability ratios
(e.g., during the action potential) produce predictable shifts in
\(V_m\).

\subsection{Worked Example: Goldman
Equation}\label{worked-example-goldman-equation}

\emph{Problem:} Calculate \(V_m\) at 37 degrees C given relative
permeabilities \(P_K : P_{Na} : P_{Cl}\) = 1.0 : 0.04 : 0.45 and the ion
concentrations in the table above.

\emph{Solution:}

\[V_m = 26.7 \; \text{mV} \times \ln \frac{(1.0)(5) + (0.04)(145) + (0.45)(4)}{(1.0)(140) + (0.04)(12) + (0.45)(110)} \tag{7.15} \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_22}\]

\[V_m = 26.7 \times \ln \frac{5.0 + 5.8 + 1.8}{140 + 0.48 + 49.5} = 26.7 \times \ln \frac{12.6}{190.0} \tag{7.16} \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_23}\]

\[V_m = 26.7 \times \ln(0.0663) = 26.7 \times (-2.71) = -72.4 \; \text{mV} \tag{7.17} \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_24}\]

This is close to the experimentally measured
\hyperref[gl:resting-potential]{\textbf{resting potential}} of
about -70 mV.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 4:} During an action potential, the permeability
to Na\(^+\) increases about 500-fold (from \(P_{Na}/P_K\) =
0.04 to about 20). Using the Goldman equation, predict what
happens to \(V_m\). Why does the membrane potential approach but not
quite reach \(E_{Na}\)?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Membrane Potential and the Action
Potential}\label{membrane-potential-and-the-action-potential}

While the Nernst and Goldman equations describe resting membrane
potential, the \textbf{action potential} is the defining electrical
event in excitable cells (neurons, muscle cells, some endocrine cells).

\subsubsection{Phases of the Action
Potential}\label{phases-of-the-action-potential}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Resting state} (\(V_m\) about  -70 mV):
  Voltage-gated Na\(^+\) and K\(^+\) channels are closed. K\(^+\) leak
  channels (K2P family) maintain the resting potential near \(E_K\).
\item
  \textbf{\hyperref[gl:depolarisation]{Depolarisation} to threshold}
  (about -55 mV): Graded potentials (e.g., from synaptic input)
  depolarise the membrane. If threshold is reached, voltage-gated
  Na\(^+\) channels (Na\$\_V\$1.x) open rapidly (activation gate).
\item
  \textbf{Rising phase} (depolarisation): Na\(^+\) influx drives \(V_m\)
  toward \(E_{Na}\) (+63 mV). Positive feedback: depolarisation opens
  more Na\(^+\) channels. This is the Hodgkin-Huxley regenerative cycle.
\item
  \textbf{Overshoot:} \(V_m\) briefly exceeds 0 mV (typically reaches
  +30 to +40 mV but does not reach \(E_{Na}\) because Na\(^+\) channel
  inactivation begins).
\item
  \textbf{Repolarisation:} Na\(^+\) channel inactivation (ball-and-chain
  mechanism, h-gate) closes channels within about 1 ms.
  Voltage-gated K\(^+\) channels (K\(_V\), delayed rectifier) open
  slowly, allowing K\(^+\) efflux, driving \(V_m\) back toward \(E_K\).
\item
  \textbf{Undershoot (afterhyperpolarisation):} K\(^+\) channels remain
  open transiently, overshooting below resting potential
  (about  -80 mV). K\(^+\) channels then close, and \(V_m\)
  returns to rest.
\item
  \textbf{Refractory periods:} Absolute refractory period (Na\(^+\)
  channels inactivated; no action potential possible). Relative
  refractory period (some Na\(^+\) channels recovered; stronger stimulus
  needed).
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Hodgkin-Huxley Model}\label{hodgkin-huxley-model}

Hodgkin and Huxley (Nobel Prize 1963) described the action potential
mathematically using voltage-clamp experiments on the squid giant axon:

\[I_m = C_m \frac{dV}{dt} + g_K n^4 (V - E_K) + g_{Na} m^3 h (V - E_{Na}) + g_L (V - E_L) \tag{7.18} \label{eq:unit_II_membrane_transport_item_25}\]

where \(m\) = Na\(^+\) activation variable, \(h\) = Na\(^+\)
inactivation variable, \(n\) = K\(^+\) activation variable. This model
predicted the ionic basis of the action potential before the molecular
identity of ion channels was known.

\subsubsection{Saltatory Conduction}\label{saltatory-conduction}

In myelinated axons, myelin sheaths (formed by Schwann cells in PNS,
oligodendrocytes in CNS) insulate the axon, reducing membrane
capacitance. Action potentials ``jump'' between \textbf{nodes of
Ranvier} (gaps in myelin where Na\(^+\) channels are concentrated at
about 1,000/um\(^2\)). This increases conduction velocity from
about 1 m/s (unmyelinated C fibres) to about 120 m/s
(large myelinated A-alpha fibres).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Multiple Sclerosis and Demyelination}
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease in which T cells and
antibodies attack CNS myelin. Demyelination exposes K\(^+\) channels
normally under the myelin sheath, causing K\(^+\) leakage and conduction
block. Symptoms include visual disturbances, motor weakness, and sensory
abnormalities. The drug 4-aminopyridine (dalfampridine) blocks exposed
K\(^+\) channels and partially restores conduction, improving walking
ability in MS patients.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 6:} Local anaesthetics (e.g., lidocaine) block
voltage-gated Na\(^+\) channels by entering the channel pore from the
intracellular side in their uncharged form, then becoming protonated and
trapped. Why do local anaesthetics preferentially block small-diameter
pain fibres before large motor fibres?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Bulk Transport: Endocytosis and
Exocytosis}\label{bulk-transport-endocytosis-and-exocytosis}

\subsubsection{Exocytosis and SNARE-Mediated Membrane
Fusion}\label{exocytosis-and-snare-mediated-membrane-fusion}

\textbf{Exocytosis:} secretory vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane,
releasing contents extracellularly.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0040_102315c3d59e.png}
\caption{SNARE-mediated vesicle fusion during regulated exocytosis. The v-SNARE on the vesicle (VAMP/synaptobrevin) and t-SNAREs on the target membrane (syntaxin + SNAP-25) form a tight four-helix bundle that drives membrane fusion. Synaptotagmin acts as the Ca\$\textasciicircum{}\{2+\}\$ sensor that triggers fusion in <1 ms.}
\end{figure}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Synaptic vesicle fusion:} Ca\(^{2+}\) entry through
  voltage-gated Ca\(^{2+}\) channels triggers synaptotagmin, fusion
  occurs in \textless0.2 ms (fastest biological membrane fusion)
\item
  \textbf{Insulin secretion:} glucose metabolism raises ATP/ADP ratio,
  closes K\(_{ATP}\) channels, depolarisation opens Ca\(^{2+}\)
  channels, Ca\(^{2+}\) triggers insulin granule exocytosis
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Botulinum Toxin and Tetanus Toxin} Both
botulinum toxin (Botox) and tetanus toxin are zinc metalloproteases that
cleave SNARE proteins: - \textbf{Botulinum toxin} (7 serotypes A--G)
cleaves VAMP, SNAP-25, or syntaxin at the neuromuscular junction,
preventing acetylcholine release, causing flaccid paralysis. Clinical
uses: dystonia, spasticity, cosmetic wrinkle reduction. -
\textbf{Tetanus toxin} cleaves VAMP in inhibitory interneurons of the
spinal cord, preventing GABA/glycine release, causing unopposed
excitatory activity and spastic paralysis (lockjaw).
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{SNARE Mechanism in
Detail}\label{snare-mechanism-in-detail}

The SNARE hypothesis (Rothman, Schekman, Südhof --- 2013 Nobel Prize in
Physiology or Medicine) explains how vesicles fuse with target membranes
with both spatial and temporal precision. Each fusion event requires a
quartet of helices contributed by a v-SNARE (on the vesicle) and
t-SNAREs (on the target membrane). The four-helix bundle
``\textbf{zippers}'' from the membrane-distal N-terminus toward the
membrane-proximal C-terminus, releasing about 35 \(k_B T\) of
free energy per SNARE complex --- enough to overcome the kinetic barrier
(about 25 \(k_B T\)) for membrane fusion.

\textbf{Compartment-specific SNARE pairs} ensure that each vesicle fuses
primarily with its correct target:

\toprule\noalign{}

Syntaxin-1 + SNAP-25 \\
ER \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} cis-Golgi (COPII) & Sec22 / Bet1 & Syntaxin-5 + Membrin + GS27 \\
Endosome \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} late endosome & VAMP7 / VAMP8 & Syntaxin-7 + Vti1b +
Syntaxin-8 \\
Late endosome \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} lysosome & VAMP7 & Syntaxin-7 + Vti1b + Syntaxin-8 \\

\textbf{The five steps of SNARE-mediated fusion:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Tethering.} Rab GTPases on the vesicle (e.g., Rab3 on synaptic
  vesicles, Rab1 on ER-derived vesicles) bind their effectors on the
  target membrane (long coiled-coil tethers like p115 or large
  multi-subunit complexes like the exocyst). Tethering is reversible and
  provides about 100 nm initial contact.
\item
  \textbf{Docking.} The four SNARE helices begin to pair through their
  N-terminal regions. SM proteins (Sec1/Munc18 family) chaperone the
  syntaxin partner, holding it in an open conformation. At synapses,
  Munc18 + Munc13 prepare syntaxin-1 for SNARE assembly.
\item
  \textbf{Priming.} Partial zippering brings the vesicle within
  about 5 nm of the target membrane. \textbf{Complexin} binds
  the half-zippered SNARE complex, clamping it in a metastable state
  ready to release on demand. Without complexin, vesicles fuse
  spontaneously; with complexin primarily, they cannot fuse --- both
  must be present for regulated fusion.
\item
  \textbf{Triggering.} At the synapse, action-potential-evoked
  Ca\(^{2+}\) entry through voltage-gated Ca\(^{2+}\) channels reaches
  about 10 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}M at the active zone within microseconds.
  Synaptotagmin-1 (Ca\(^{2+}\) sensor with two C2 domains) binds
  Ca\(^{2+}\) and PIP\(_2\), displaces complexin, and releases the
  SNAREs to complete zippering. The whole event takes \textless0.2 ms
  --- the fastest known protein-mediated fusion.
\item
  \textbf{Disassembly.} After fusion, the cis-SNARE complex (the four
  helices now in the same membrane) is dismantled by \textbf{NSF}
  (N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor, an AAA+ ATPase) and its adaptor
  \textbf{alpha-SNAP}. This requires ATP hydrolysis (about 1
  ATP per SNARE complex) and recycles the SNAREs for the next round.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Vesicle Coat Proteins in
Detail}\label{vesicle-coat-proteins-in-detail}

Three major coat systems shape the secretory and endocytic pathways:
\textbf{COPII}, \textbf{COPI}, and \textbf{clathrin}. Each is built
around a small GTPase (Sar1 for COPII, Arf1 for COPI and clathrin) that
anchors to the membrane upon GDP\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}GTP exchange and recruits coat
subunits. Membrane curvature is generated by the geometry of the coat
itself.

nm \\
\textbf{COPI} & Arf1 & \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma}-, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\delta}}{delta}-, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\zeta}}{zeta}-COP (cargo selector via KKXX) & \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-,
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}'-, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}}{epsilon}-COP & Retrograde Golgi\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}ER, intra-Golgi & 60--100 nm \\
\textbf{Clathrin} & Arf1 (TGN) or none (PM) & Adaptor proteins (AP1 at
TGN, AP2 at PM, AP3 at endosome, AP4) & Clathrin triskelions (3 heavy +
3 light chains) & Selective endocytosis; lysosomal sorting & 80--120
nm \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Clathrin triskelions} are 3-legged structures that self-assemble
into open polyhedral lattices (hexagons + pentagons, like a soccer
ball). Each clathrin-coated pit contains about 36 triskelions
arranged into a lattice that gradually curves the membrane into a deep
invagination. The vesicle is then released by \textbf{dynamin}, a GTPase
that wraps as a helical collar around the neck and uses GTP hydrolysis
to constrict and pinch off the bud (about 60--120 nm vesicle,
depending on local geometry). After release, the clathrin coat is
disassembled by Hsc70 + auxilin (J-domain co-chaperone) at the cost of
about 1 ATP per triskelion released.

\textbf{Vesicle traffic in numbers.} A typical mammalian cell sustains
about 10\(^4\) exocytic events and about 10\(^4\)
endocytic events per minute. The plasma membrane area equivalent of one
entire cell is internalised every about 30 minutes --- meaning
the membrane is in dynamic flux, with steady-state composition
maintained by precise SNARE-coupled bidirectional traffic. A typical
secretory neuron at full activity can fuse about 1000 synaptic
vesicles per second.

\subsubsection{Endocytosis}\label{endocytosis}

\textbf{Clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME):} 1. Cargo receptors cluster
in clathrin-coated pits (adaptor AP2 links receptors to clathrin
triskelions) 2. Clathrin assembles into a polyhedral basket, deforming
the membrane into an invagination 3. Dynamin GTPase wraps around the
neck of the invagination and pinches it off (about 60--120 nm
vesicle) 4. Clathrin coat disassembles (uncoated by Hsc70 + auxilin) 5.
Vesicle fuses with early endosome - Examples: LDL receptor, transferrin
receptor, EGF receptor

\textbf{Caveolar endocytosis:} - 50--80 nm flask-shaped invaginations
rich in cholesterol and sphingolipids - Coated with caveolin-1 (integral
membrane protein with hairpin topology) - Functions: transcytosis across
endothelial cells, lipid homeostasis, signalling compartmentalisation

\textbf{Phagocytosis:} - Professional phagocytes (macrophages,
neutrophils, dendritic cells) - Actin-driven pseudopod extension engulfs
large particles (\textgreater0.5 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m): bacteria, dead cells, debris -
Receptors: Fc receptors (opsonised particles), complement receptors,
scavenger receptors, TLRs - Phagosome fuses with lysosomes to form
phagolysosome for degradation

\textbf{Macropinocytosis:} - Non-specific uptake of large volumes of
extracellular fluid - Actin-driven membrane ruffles collapse back onto
the cell surface, trapping fluid in large vesicles (0.2--5 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m) -
Important for antigen sampling by dendritic cells and for nutrient
acquisition by cancer cells (exploited by RAS-mutant tumours)

\subsection{Computational Bridge}\label{computational-bridge-6}

Nernst potentials for tabulated physiological ions are computed in
closed form:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ biology.cell }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ PHYSIOLOGICAL\_IONS, nernst\_potential}

\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ ion }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ PHYSIOLOGICAL\_IONS:}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ ion.charge }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{:}
        \ControlFlowTok{continue}
    \ControlFlowTok{try}\NormalTok{:}
        \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(ion.ion, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(nernst\_potential(ion), }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{), }\StringTok{"mV"}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{except} \PreprocessorTok{ValueError}\NormalTok{:}
        \ControlFlowTok{pass}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical / systems note:} Long QT channelopathies and familial
hyperkalaemic paralysis are reminders that single-ion permeability or
gradient defects reshape the Goldman-style integrative potential you
approximate in silico.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsubsection{AlphaFold-Predicted Transporter Structures: Computational
Biology Meets Membrane
Biophysics}\label{alphafold-predicted-transporter-structures-computational-biology-meets-membrane-biophysics}

Membrane transporter structures have historically been among the hardest
to solve experimentally: hydrophobic surfaces resist crystallisation,
cryo-EM requires stable purified protein, and conformational flexibility
(the very thing that makes transporters work) blurs reconstructions.
\textbf{AlphaFold2} (DeepMind, 2021), \textbf{AlphaFold-Multimer}
(2022), and AlphaFold 3 (2024) changed the workflow by making
high-quality structural hypotheses routine for many folded domains and
complexes, including many membrane proteins
\citep{abramson2024alphafold3,varadi2024alphafolddb}.

By 2024, the \textbf{AlphaFold Protein Structure Database} provided
structure coverage for more than 214 million protein sequences in
UniProt \citep{varadi2024alphafolddb}. This transforms downstream
biology: researchers can inspect predicted transmembrane helices and
cavities in an orphan transporter, nominate binding-site residues,
compare paralogues, and design mutagenesis or cryo-EM experiments before
a solved structure exists. The correct lesson is not that prediction
replaces structure determination; it is that prediction changes what
counts as a good first experiment.

Cautions are important for scientific literacy: AlphaFold predicts
likely static conformations, but transporters function by \emph{cycling}
between conformations (outward-open \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\leftrightarrow}}{<->} occluded \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\leftrightarrow}}{<->} inward-open); a single
model can miss gating, allostery, lipid dependence, and ligand-coupled
state changes. \textbf{Predicted Aligned Error (PAE)} plots flag
low-confidence inter-domain geometries, and \textbf{AlphaFold3}
integrates ligands, ions, nucleic acids, and other biomolecules into
interaction hypotheses \citep{abramson2024alphafold3}. The field now
often generates predicted structures \emph{before} requesting
experimental ones, but strong biological claims still require transport
assays, mutagenesis, binding data, or experimental structures.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-9}

For \textbf{Membrane Structure and Transport}, frontier biology belongs
inside the evidence logic of the chapter. Cell biology is increasingly
measured as live, spatial, single-cell, and perturbational data rather
than static diagrams alone. The core reading question is this: transport
claims require gradients, permeability, electrochemical driving force,
gating, and energy coupling.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

Ask what measurement scale is being claimed: nanometre structure,
single-cell transcript abundance, organelle dynamics, tissue context, or
organismal phenotype.

\textbf{Source practice:} For cell-state claims, distinguish microscopy,
live-cell perturbation, single-cell sequencing, spatial transcriptomics,
and biochemical assay evidence before making a causal statement.

\subsubsection{Current Evidence Map: Transporter Structure to
Function}\label{current-evidence-map-transporter-structure-to-function}

\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-9}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The plasma membrane is a fluid mosaic bilayer with asymmetric lipid
  distribution maintained by flippases. Lipid rafts are dynamic
  cholesterol-sphingolipid microdomains with signalling roles.
\item
  Ion channels achieve selectivity through precise selectivity filters
  (K\(^+\) channel: carbonyl oxygen coordination) and are gated by
  voltage, ligands, mechanical force, or temperature.
\item
  The Na\(^+\)/K\(^+\)-ATPase maintains ionic gradients essential for
  membrane potential, cell volume, and secondary active transport,
  consuming about 25\% of cellular ATP.
\item
  ABC transporters use ATP to transport diverse substrates; clinical
  significance includes multidrug resistance (MDR1) and cystic fibrosis
  (CFTR).
\item
  The Nernst equation gives the equilibrium potential of each ion; the
  Goldman equation gives the actual membrane potential for multiple ions
  simultaneously.
\item
  SNARE proteins mediate membrane fusion in exocytosis; synaptotagmin is
  the Ca\(^{2+}\) sensor for regulated secretion.
\item
  Endocytosis types (clathrin-mediated, caveolar, phagocytosis,
  macropinocytosis) internalise specific cargo or bulk fluid.
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See \cref{sec:unit_I_water_and_life} for water
  and \hyperref[gl:osmosis]{\textbf{osmosis}}, Unit IX for excitable
  tissues, and \cref{sec:unit_II_cell_signaling} for receptor-mediated
  signalling.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Review Questions}\label{review-questions-9}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Derive the Nernst equation from the electrochemical potential
  equation. Calculate \(E_K\) at 20 degrees C (293 K) given
  {[}K\(^+\){]}\(_{\text{in}}\) = 140 mM, {[}K\(^+\){]}\(_{\text{out}}\)
  = 5 mM.
\item
  Explain how the Na\(^+\)/K\(^+\)-ATPase contributes to the resting
  membrane potential both directly (electrogenic pump) and indirectly
  (maintaining K\(^+\) gradient).
\item
  Compare the selectivity mechanisms of K\(^+\) channels and Na\(^+\)
  channels. How does each achieve \textgreater100:1 selectivity for its
  preferred ion?
\item
  A patient is treated with omeprazole for gastric ulcer disease. What
  is the molecular target of this drug, and how does inhibiting it
  reduce gastric acid secretion?
\item
  Explain why MDR1/P-glycoprotein overexpression causes multidrug
  resistance in cancer. Suggest two strategies to overcome this
  resistance.
\item
  Describe the complete SNARE fusion cycle for synaptic vesicle
  exocytosis, from vesicle docking to
  \hyperref[gl:snare-complex]{\textbf{SNARE complex}} disassembly. What
  role does Ca\(^{2+}\) play?
\item
  Using the Goldman equation, predict how the resting membrane potential
  would change if the membrane suddenly became equally permeable to
  Na\(^+\) and K\(^+\).
\item
  Compare clathrin-mediated endocytosis with phagocytosis in terms of
  vesicle size, coat proteins, cytoskeletal involvement, and cell types
  involved.
\item
  Explain the biphasic effect of cholesterol on membrane fluidity. Why
  is this important for cells that experience temperature fluctuations?
\item
  SGLT2 inhibitors cause glucose loss in urine. Calculate the
  approximate caloric loss per day if a diabetic patient loses 70 g of
  glucose per day in urine (glucose: 4 kcal/g).
\item
  Run the Nernst loop in the bridge code and identify which ion's
  equilibrium potential is closest to a typical neuronal resting
  potential; justify using permeability weighting qualitatively.
\item
  Explain why CFTR is called a \textbf{channel} yet sits in the ABC
  transporter superfamily, and how that relates to ATP usage vs.~passive
  flow.
\end{enumerate}

membrane fusion via four-helix bundle zippering \\
\textbf{Clathrin} & Triskelion coat protein forming polyhedral baskets
during receptor-mediated endocytosis \\
\textbf{Channelopathy} & Disease caused by ion channel mutations (e.g.,
Long QT syndrome, cystic fibrosis) \\
\textbf{Macropinocytosis} & Non-specific bulk uptake of extracellular
fluid via actin-driven membrane ruffling \\

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Opening Vignette: When Signals Go Wrong --- HER2 Breast Cancer}

In 1987, Dennis Slamon's team at UCLA reported that about 25\% of breast
cancers showed amplification of the HER2
\hyperref[gl:gene]{\textbf{gene}}, which encodes a receptor tyrosine
kinase embedded in the plasma membrane (Slamon et al., 1987,
\emph{Science}). In normal cells, HER2 is transiently activated when it
binds its ligand --- triggering a cascade of phosphorylation events that
ultimately drive cell proliferation and survival. In tumours with HER2
amplification, the \hyperref[gl:protein]{\textbf{protein}} is expressed
at 40--100 times the normal level; even without ligand, HER2 molecules
are close enough together to activate each other constantly, delivering
an unrelenting ``grow and divide'' signal.

The consequences of understanding this single signalling pathway have
been transformative. In 1998, the FDA approved trastuzumab (Herceptin),
a monoclonal antibody that binds the extracellular domain of HER2 and
blocks its dimerisation and downstream signalling. In HER2-positive
breast cancer, trastuzumab therapy approximately doubled 5-year
survival. Every step in this therapeutic triumph required understanding
how cells receive, transduce, and amplify molecular signals ---
precisely the subject of this chapter.

\emph{Primary source: Slamon, D. J. et al.~(1987). Human breast cancer:
Correlation of relapse and survival with amplification of the HER-2/neu
oncogene. Science, 235(4785), 177--182.}
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

Cells receive and interpret thousands of extracellular signals
simultaneously. Signalling systems share a general architecture:

\textbf{Signal (ligand) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Receptor (detection) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Transduction cascade
(amplification) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Effector \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Response \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Termination}

\subsubsection{Signal Transduction
Logic}\label{signal-transduction-logic}

Signal transduction cascades exhibit four fundamental properties:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Amplification:} One activated receptor activates multiple G
  proteins; each G protein activates multiple adenylyl cyclase
  molecules; each adenylyl cyclase produces many cAMP molecules. A
  single epinephrine molecule can trigger release of
  about 10\(^8\) glucose molecules from glycogen (10\(^6\)-fold
  amplification).
\item
  \textbf{Specificity:} Different cell types express different receptor
  subtypes, G proteins, and effectors. Epinephrine causes glycogen
  breakdown in liver (beta\(_2\)-adrenergic receptor, G\(_s\), cAMP) but
  smooth muscle relaxation in bronchi (same receptor, same second
  messenger, different downstream targets).
\item
  \textbf{Integration:} Multiple signals converge on shared effectors. A
  cell's response reflects the integrated sum of active signalling
  pathways. For example, cell proliferation requires simultaneous growth
  factor (RTK), integrin (adhesion), and survival factor signalling.
\item
  \textbf{Adaptation/desensitisation:} Prolonged stimulation leads to
  reduced response. Mechanisms include receptor phosphorylation (by
  GRKs), arrestin binding, receptor internalisation, and negative
  feedback loops \citep{alon2019}.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Signal Amplification Cascades --- A Quantitative
Treatment}\label{signal-amplification-cascades-a-quantitative-treatment}

Signal amplification is the architectural reason a single hormone
molecule can drive a macroscopic physiological response. Three concepts
make the amplification quantitative: gain per step, overall gain, and
dynamic range.

\textbf{Gain per step.} Each level of a cascade has a gain \(A_i\)
defined as the number of activated downstream molecules per active
upstream molecule (per unit time). For example, a single G\(_s\)\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-GTP
activates about 10 adenylyl cyclase molecules during its
about 1 minute lifetime; each adenylyl cyclase produces
about 1,000 cAMP per second, so over 30 s the gain at this step
is roughly \(10 \times 30{,}000 = 3 \times 10^5\).

\textbf{Overall gain.} For an \(n\)-step cascade, the total
amplification is the product of step gains:

\begin{equation}
G_\text{total} = \prod_{i=1}^{n} A_i
\label{eq:unit_II_signaling_total_gain}
\end{equation}

This product structure means that \emph{removing one step} of a cascade
cuts gain by orders of magnitude, while \emph{adding one step}
multiplies it. The classic epinephrine\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}glycogenolysis cascade has 4
enzymatic amplification steps (receptor \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} G\(_s\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} adenylyl cyclase \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
PKA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} phosphorylase kinase \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} glycogen phosphorylase), each contributing
\(A_i \approx 10^{1.5}\), for \(G_\text{total} \approx 10^{6}\). A
single epinephrine molecule binding a \(\beta_2\) receptor releases
about \(10^8\) glucose molecules from glycogen --- exactly
the gain measured in liver perfusion experiments.

\textbf{Why so many steps?} A simpler cascade with the same gain ---
e.g., one step of \(A = 10^6\) --- would be biologically implausible:
few signalling enzymes have \(k_\text{cat} > 10^4\) s\(^{-1}\) (the
diffusion-limited outliers catalase and carbonic anhydrase are
exceptions), and no cell could sustain enzyme concentrations giving
\(10^6\)-fold amplification in a single reaction. The cascade
architecture solves this by \emph{multiplying} modest gains.

\textbf{Time delay and adaptation.} Each step also adds a time constant
\(\tau_i\) (the lifetime of the activated species). The total response
time is:

\[\tau_\text{total} \approx \sqrt{\sum_i \tau_i^2} \tag{8.0} \label{eq:unit_II_cell_signaling_item_1}\]

For visual transduction (rhodopsin \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} transducin \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PDE6 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} cGMP fall):
individual \(\tau_i\) are about 10 ms, total response
about 50 ms. For epinephrine: hundreds of milliseconds to
seconds. The cascade thus also serves as a \textbf{temporal filter} ---
fast inputs reach the effector quickly, slow inputs are integrated.

\textbf{Cooperativity sharpens the response.} A linear cascade has gain
but not steepness --- the dose--response is hyperbolic (Hill coefficient
1). To make a switch-like response, cells use: - \emph{Multiple binding
sites} (haemoglobin O\(_2\), \(n_H = 2.8\)). - \emph{Multi-site
phosphorylation requiring full occupancy} (ERK requires both Thr and Tyr
phosphorylation; effective \(n_H \approx 5\) in the MAP kinase cascade).
- \emph{Positive feedback loops} (ERK \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} SOS feedback creates
bistability).

The Huang--Ferrell analysis of the MAPK cascade showed mathematically
that \emph{three sequential switches} (each with \(n_H = 1.7\) from its
dual phosphorylation requirement) compose to give an overall Hill
coefficient near 5 --- converting a graded growth-factor input into an
essentially digital ERK output. This is the molecular substrate of the
cell's ``decision making'' between proliferation and quiescence.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 1a:} A six-step cascade has a gain of 10 per step.
What is the total gain? If a single step is removed (now five steps), by
what factor does the total gain change?
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Quantitative Foundations of Signal
Transduction}\label{quantitative-foundations-of-signal-transduction}

\textbf{Receptor--ligand binding equilibrium.} The dissociation constant
\(K_d\) quantifies receptor affinity:

\[K_d = \frac{[\text{R}][\text{L}]}{[\text{RL}]} \tag{8.1} \label{eq:unit_II_cell_signaling_item_2}\]

where \([\text{R}]\) is free receptor concentration, \([\text{L}]\) is
free ligand concentration, and \([\text{RL}]\) is the receptor--ligand
complex. The fraction of receptors occupied at a given ligand
concentration is:

\[\theta = \frac{[\text{L}]}{[\text{L}] + K_d} \tag{8.2} \label{eq:unit_II_cell_signaling_item_3}\]

When \([\text{L}] = K_d\), exactly 50\% of receptors are occupied.
Typical \(K_d\) values: \hyperref[gl:insulin-receptor]{\textbf{insulin
receptor}} about 0.1 nM; epinephrine--beta\(_2\) receptor
about 1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}M.

\textbf{The Hill equation} models cooperative binding and switch-like
signalling responses:

\[\theta = \frac{[\text{L}]^{n_H}}{K_d^{n_H} + [\text{L}]^{n_H}} \tag{8.3} \label{eq:unit_II_cell_signaling_item_4}\]

where \(n_H\) is the Hill coefficient. \(n_H = 1\) gives a hyperbolic
(Michaelis--Menten-like) curve; \(n_H > 1\) produces a sigmoidal
(switch-like) response. The MAPK cascade achieves an effective
\(n_H \approx 5\), creating the ultrasensitive most-or-none ERK
activation observed experimentally (Huang \& Ferrell, 1996,
\emph{PNAS}).

\textbf{Signal amplification cascade.} If each step in a cascade has
amplification factor \(A_i\), the total amplification is:

\[G_{\text{total}} = \prod_{i=1}^{n} A_i = A_1 \times A_2 \times \cdots \times A_n \tag{8.4} \label{eq:unit_II_cell_signaling_item_5}\]

For the epinephrine--glycogen cascade (\(n = 4\) steps,
\(A_i \approx 10^{1.5}\) per step): \(G_{\text{total}} \approx 10^6\),
explaining how one hormone molecule triggers release of \(\sim 10^8\)
glucose molecules.

\subsubsection{Worked Example: Receptor Fractional
Occupancy}\label{worked-example-receptor-fractional-occupancy}

\textbf{Problem:} The epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is an RTK
with a dissociation constant (\(K_d\)) for its ligand, EGF, of
approximately \(2.0 \text{ nM}\) (\(2.0 \times 10^{-9} \text{ M}\)).
Assuming standard non-cooperative binding behaviour (\(n_H = 1\)),
calculate the fractional occupancy (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\theta}}{theta}) of the EGFR population on a cell
surface when the extracellular concentration of EGF is
\(6.0 \text{ nM}\). What concentration of EGF would be required to
achieve 90\% receptor occupancy?

\textbf{Solution:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Calculate occupancy at 6.0 nM:} Using the receptor fractional
  occupancy equation:
  \[ \theta = \frac{[\text{L}]}{[\text{L}] + K_d}  \label{eq:unit_II_cell_signaling_item_6}\]

  Substitute the given values (\([\text{L}] = 6.0 \text{ nM}\),
  \(K_d = 2.0 \text{ nM}\)):
  \[ \theta = \frac{6.0}{6.0 + 2.0} = \frac{6.0}{8.0} = 0.75  \label{eq:unit_II_cell_signaling_item_7}\]

  Thus, \textbf{75\%} of the EGF receptors are bound to ligand.
\item
  \textbf{Calculate the ligand concentration required for 90\%
  occupancy:} Set \(\theta = 0.90\) and solve for \([\text{L}]\):
  \[ 0.90 = \frac{[\text{L}]}{[\text{L}] + 2.0}  \label{eq:unit_II_cell_signaling_item_8}\]

  \[ 0.90([\text{L}] + 2.0) = [\text{L}]  \label{eq:unit_II_cell_signaling_item_9}\]

  \[ 0.90[\text{L}] + 1.80 = [\text{L}]  \label{eq:unit_II_cell_signaling_item_10}\]

  \[ 1.80 = 0.10[\text{L}]  \label{eq:unit_II_cell_signaling_item_11}\]

  \[ [\text{L}] = \frac{1.80}{0.10} = 18.0 \text{ nM}  \label{eq:unit_II_cell_signaling_item_12}\]

  An EGF concentration of \textbf{18.0 nM} is required to saturate 90\%
  of the receptors. Note that achieving \(90\%\) occupancy requires a
  ligand concentration exactly \(9 \times K_d\).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 1:} Epinephrine stimulates both
beta\(_2\)-adrenergic receptors (G\(_s\)-coupled, cAMP elevation) on
bronchial smooth muscle and alpha\(_1\)-adrenergic receptors
(G\(_q\)-coupled, IP\(_3\)/Ca\(^{2+}\)) on vascular smooth muscle. Why
does the same hormone cause bronchodilation in the lungs but
vasoconstriction in skin blood vessels?
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Worked Example: Signal Amplification Through a Kinase
Cascade}\label{worked-example-signal-amplification-through-a-kinase-cascade}

\textbf{Problem:} The MAP kinase module is a three-tier cascade (Raf
\(\rightarrow\) MEK \(\rightarrow\) ERK) in which each activated kinase
phosphorylates and activates roughly \(10\) molecules of the next kinase
(\(A_1 = A_2 = A_3 = 10\)).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Using the cascade gain relation, what is the total amplification of
  the three-tier module?
\item
  If \(50\) growth-factor receptors are activated, how many ERK
  molecules are activated?
\item
  What happens to the total gain if one tier is bypassed (a two-step
  cascade)?
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Solution:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Total gain is the product of the per-step gains:}
  \[ G_{\text{total}} = \prod_{i=1}^{3} A_i = A_1 \times A_2 \times A_3 = 10 \times 10 \times 10 = 10^3  \label{eq:unit_II_cell_signaling_item_13}\]

  The three-tier module amplifies the input \(1{,}000\)-fold.
\item
  \textbf{Scale by the number of activated receptors} (\(N_R = 50\)):
  \[ N_{\text{ERK}} = N_R \times G_{\text{total}} = 50 \times 10^3 = 5.0 \times 10^4  \label{eq:unit_II_cell_signaling_item_14}\]

  So \(50\) activated receptors yield about \(50{,}000\) activated ERK
  molecules.
\item
  \textbf{Drop one tier} (now a two-step cascade,
  \(G = A_1 \times A_2\)):
  \[ G_{\text{2-step}} = 10 \times 10 = 10^2  \label{eq:unit_II_cell_signaling_item_15}\]

  Removing a single tier cuts the gain by a factor of
  \(10^3 / 10^2 = 10\).
\end{enumerate}

Because the cascade gain is a product rather than a sum, each added tier
multiplies the response while a lost tier divides it --- a small number
of detected ligand molecules can therefore drive a large, switch-like
cellular decision, and dropping or inhibiting one kinase tier (a common
drug strategy) sharply attenuates the output.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Cell-Surface Receptors}\label{cell-surface-receptors}

\subsubsection{G Protein-Coupled Receptors
(GPCRs)}\label{g-protein-coupled-receptors-gpcrs}

GPCRs are the largest receptor superfamily (about 800 in
humans; about 34\% of approved drug targets). They have 7
transmembrane alpha-helices, an extracellular N-terminus, and an
intracellular C-terminus. Binding of ligand activates the heterotrimeric
G protein (G-alpha, G-beta-gamma):

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0042_a36ac9dc7103.png}
\caption{The G\$\_s\$-cAMP-PKA signalling cascade and its termination mechanisms. Signal amplification occurs at multiple levels: one receptor activates multiple G proteins, each adenylyl cyclase produces about 1,000 cAMP/s, and PKA phosphorylates multiple substrates.}
\end{figure}

\textbf{G\(_s\) pathway (stimulatory):} Hormone (e.g., epinephrine) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
beta\(_2\)-adrenergic receptor \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} G\(_s\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{adenylyl cyclase}
activated \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} ATP \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{cAMP} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{Protein Kinase A (PKA)} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
phosphorylates multiple downstream targets (glycogen phosphorylase
kinase, CREB \hyperref[gl:transcription]{\textbf{transcription}} factor,
ion channels, etc.)

\textbf{G\(_i\) pathway (inhibitory):} Inhibits adenylyl cyclase,
reducing cAMP. Examples: opioid receptors (mu, delta, kappa), muscarinic
M2 receptors (cardiac parasympathetic), alpha\(_2\)-adrenergic
receptors.

\textbf{G\(_q\) pathway:} Activates \textbf{phospholipase C-beta} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
cleaves PIP\(_2\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{IP\(_3\)} (Ca\(^{2+}\) release from ER via
IP\(_3\) receptors) + \textbf{DAG} (activates Protein Kinase C, PKC).
This dual second messenger system controls smooth muscle contraction,
platelet activation, and secretion.

\textbf{G\(_{12/13}\) pathway:} Activates Rho GEFs \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Rho GTPase \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} ROCK
(Rho-associated kinase) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} cytoskeletal remodelling, cell migration,
smooth muscle contraction.

\textbf{cAMP signalling components:} - \textbf{PDE (phosphodiesterase):}
hydrolyses cAMP to 5'-AMP, terminating the signal. Caffeine and
theophylline inhibit PDE \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} elevated cAMP \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} CNS stimulation,
bronchodilation. Sildenafil (Viagra) inhibits PDE5 (specific for cGMP in
penile smooth muscle). - \textbf{AKAP (A Kinase Anchoring Proteins):}
target PKA to specific subcellular locations, providing spatial
specificity to cAMP signalling. - \textbf{GTPase activity of G-alpha:}
G-alpha is a self-inactivating molecular switch (built-in GTPase;
k\(_{\text{cat}}\) about 1 min\(^{-1}\)). RGS (Regulators of
G-protein Signalling) proteins accelerate GTP hydrolysis, shortening
signal duration.

\subsubsection{The G-Protein Cycle in
Detail}\label{the-g-protein-cycle-in-detail}

Heterotrimeric G proteins (G\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha} + G\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma}) are molecular switches that
integrate three biochemical events: GDP release, GTP binding, and GTP
hydrolysis. The cycle is canonical for most GTPases --- Ras, Rho, Rab,
Ran, and the heterotrimeric G proteins most follow the same logic, with
different specifics.

effector activation \\

closes \\
