}

\textbf{Rate constants and cellular consequences.} For G\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}\(_s\), the
intrinsic GTP hydrolysis rate is about 0.05 s\(^{-1}\) (so the
active state lasts about 20 s without acceleration). RGS
proteins (RGS2, RGS4, RGS9) accelerate this 100--1,000\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x}, shortening the
signal to about 50 ms. Disease example: RGS9 deficiency causes
\textbf{bradyopsia} --- a visual disorder where bright lights produce
after-images that linger because transducin (the rod photoreceptor G\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha})
cannot be turned off rapidly.

\textbf{Why the cycle is reversible.} Each step is in principle
reversible at thermodynamic equilibrium. The cycle is driven
\emph{forward} by: - Receptor activation (provides the catalytic step
for GDP release); - High cellular {[}GTP{]}:{[}GDP{]} ratio
(about 10:1, maintained by metabolism); - Coupling of GTP
hydrolysis to effector dissociation (mass-action irreversibility).

Without metabolic GTP, the cycle would stall. ATP-depleted cells
therefore lose most GPCR-mediated signalling --- one reason why
ischaemic damage propagates so quickly in tissues.

\subsubsection{GPCR Desensitisation and
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-Arrestin}\label{gpcr-desensitisation-and-ux3b2-arrestin}

Continuous stimulation of a GPCR rapidly attenuates its response ---
within seconds to minutes, the system \textbf{desensitises}. This is a
textbook example of a homeostatic negative feedback loop and the
mechanistic basis for clinically important phenomena: tachyphylaxis
(rapid loss of drug effect), tolerance (e.g., to opioids, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-agonists),
and receptor downregulation.

\textbf{Three layers of desensitisation:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Homologous desensitisation (rapid, agonist-specific;
  seconds).}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Active GPCR is phosphorylated by \textbf{GRKs (G-protein-coupled
    receptor kinases)}, especially GRK2 and GRK3. GRK2 specifically
    recognises \emph{active} receptor conformation; ligand-free or
    inactive receptors are not phosphorylated.
  \item
    Phosphorylated GPCR recruits \textbf{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-arrestin} (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-arrestin-1 or
    -2). \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-arrestin binding sterically blocks G-protein coupling --- the
    receptor is now ``uncoupled'' from G\(_s\)/G\(_q\) but still on the
    cell surface.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Heterologous desensitisation (slower, cross-pathway; seconds
  to minutes).}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    PKA and PKC phosphorylate GPCRs at distinct sites, attenuating
    responses to any agonist that activates that receptor (regardless of
    whether it's currently bound). This integrates signalling across
    pathways.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Receptor internalisation (slow, persistent; minutes to
  hours).}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-arrestin recruits clathrin and AP2 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} receptor is internalised in
    clathrin-coated vesicles \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} enters the early endosome.
  \item
    From the endosome: receptors can be \textbf{recycled} back to the
    plasma membrane (rapid, restores response within minutes --- the
    path of \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}\(_2\)-adrenergic receptor) or sorted to \textbf{lysosomes}
    for \textbf{downregulation} (slow, requires hours-to-days for new
    receptor synthesis to restore response --- the path of opioid
    receptors after chronic agonist exposure).
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Beyond G-protein signalling: \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-arrestin as a signalling
scaffold.} Originally thought to ``merely'' terminate G-protein
signalling, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-arrestins are now recognised as scaffolds for their own
kinase cascades --- ERK, JNK, p38 MAPK can be activated by
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-arrestin-bound receptors \emph{after} internalisation, generating a
second wave of signalling distinct from the initial G-protein wave. Some
agonists (called \textbf{biased agonists}) preferentially activate one
pathway: - \textbf{Carvedilol} (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-blocker) inhibits G\(_s\) but
activates \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-arrestin signalling --- this dual action may underlie its
superior efficacy in heart failure compared to other \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-blockers. -
\textbf{TRV130 / oliceridine} (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}-opioid agonist, FDA-approved 2020) is
biased toward G-protein signalling and away from \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-arrestin --- this
reduces respiratory depression and constipation while preserving
analgesia.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 1b:} A patient with asthma uses an inhaled
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}\(_2\)-agonist (albuterol) every 4 hours for several days. The drug
becomes progressively less effective (tachyphylaxis). Explain at the
molecular level --- which mechanism (homologous, heterologous,
internalisation/downregulation) is most likely responsible for each
time-scale of tolerance?
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Second Messenger
Kinetics}\label{second-messenger-kinetics}

Second messengers are diffusible small molecules that connect receptors
to downstream effectors. Their effective signalling depends on three
quantitative parameters: production rate, diffusion (and spatial
spread), and degradation rate.

\textbf{cAMP kinetics.} Adenylyl cyclase produces cAMP at
about 1,000 molecules/s per active enzyme. cAMP degradation by
\textbf{phosphodiesterases (PDEs)} has half-lives ranging from
about 50 ms (cardiac muscle, near-membrane PDE3/PDE4
microdomains) to several seconds (cytoplasmic bulk). Diffusion
coefficient \(D \approx 300\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m\(^2\)/s in cytoplasm; diffusion length
\(\ell = \sqrt{D \tau}\). With \(\tau_{1/2} = 100\) ms,
\(\ell \approx 5\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m --- short enough to create spatial gradients
within a single cell. AKAP scaffolds and PDE microdomains create ``cAMP
nano-domains'' of just about 100 nm where local concentrations
can be 10--100\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} the cell average. This explains how a single cell can
use cAMP to signal \emph{locally} (e.g., individual ion channels)
without flooding the whole cell.

\textbf{The PDE family and pharmacology.} Eleven PDE families exist in
humans, each with tissue-specific expression:

\textbf{The Viagra story (a quintessential mechanism-to-medicine path).}
Pfizer scientists were originally testing sildenafil in 1989 as a
treatment for angina (the rationale: PDE5 inhibition \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} cGMP buildup \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
vasodilation \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} coronary blood flow). Its anti-anginal effects were
modest, but male patients in trials reported a striking side effect.
Pfizer pivoted; sildenafil was approved for erectile dysfunction in 1998
and became a major pharmaceutical product. The mechanism is exquisitely
specific: nitric oxide \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} guanylyl cyclase \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} cGMP \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PKG \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} relaxation of
penile smooth muscle. PDE5 normally degrades cGMP; sildenafil blocks
PDE5; cGMP accumulates \emph{primarily where it is being made} (i.e.,
where NO is released). This ``context-conditional'' pharmacology ---
drug effect primarily where the natural signal is active --- now informs
many other targeted therapies. Tadalafil (Cialis) has a longer half-life
(17.5 h vs.~4 h for sildenafil) due to its different binding kinetics in
the PDE5 active site.

\textbf{IP\(_3\) / Ca\(^{2+}\) kinetics.} IP\(_3\) has a half-life of
about 1 second (rapid dephosphorylation by
IP\(_3\)-5-phosphatase); Ca\(^{2+}\) signals are buffered by
about 99\% by cytoplasmic proteins (calbindin, calretinin) and
re-sequestered by SERCA in \textless1 second. Therefore Ca\(^{2+}\)
``spikes'' and ``waves'' propagate at controllable, intermediate speeds
(about 10--50 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m/s), enabling spatially organised signalling
such as the fertilisation Ca\(^{2+}\) wave that sweeps a sea urchin egg
in about 15 seconds.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Cholera and Pertussis Toxins}
\textbf{Cholera toxin} ADP-ribosylates G\(_s\)-alpha, preventing GTP
hydrolysis. G\(_s\) is constitutively active \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} massive cAMP production
in intestinal epithelial cells \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} CFTR Cl\(^-\) channels open \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Cl\(^-\)
and water secretion \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} severe watery diarrhoea (up to 20 L/day),
potentially fatal from dehydration. \textbf{Pertussis toxin} (whooping
cough) ADP-ribosylates G\(_i\)-alpha, preventing its activation. Without
G\(_i\) inhibition, adenylyl cyclase is overactive \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} elevated cAMP in
respiratory epithelial cells \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} impaired mucociliary clearance \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
persistent cough. see \cref{sec:unit_II_membrane_transport} for CFTR.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Receptor Tyrosine Kinases
(RTKs)}\label{receptor-tyrosine-kinases-rtks}

RTKs are single-pass transmembrane receptors with a cytoplasmic tyrosine
kinase domain. Ligand binding (e.g., EGF, PDGF, insulin, FGF, VEGF) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
receptor \textbf{dimerisation} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{trans-autophosphorylation} of
tyrosines \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} phosphotyrosines recruit adaptor proteins via SH2 and PTB
domains.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0044_a62d4ee8a5da.png}
\caption{The RTK/RAS/MAPK signalling cascade. Each step amplifies the signal: one activated EGFR can activate about 100 RAS molecules, producing about 10,000 activated ERK molecules.}
\end{figure}

Each step amplifies: one activated EGFR \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} about 100 RAS \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
about 10,000 activated ERK molecules.

\subsubsection{Receptor Tyrosine Kinase Activation in
Detail}\label{receptor-tyrosine-kinase-activation-in-detail}

RTKs are activated by \textbf{ligand-induced dimerisation} --- and the
choreography is more elegant than the cartoon suggests. Different RTK
families use different dimerisation strategies:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Bivalent ligand} (e.g., PDGF, VEGF, SCF): the ligand is a
  dimer that bridges two receptor monomers. Binding stoichiometry is 2
  ligands : 2 receptors.
\item
  \textbf{Receptor-mediated dimerisation} (e.g., EGFR, HER2/3/4): the
  ligand is monomeric but binding induces a conformational change that
  exposes a ``dimerisation arm'' on the extracellular domain; two
  ligand-bound receptors then pair through these arms. Stoichiometry: 2
  ligands : 2 receptors.
\item
  \textbf{Pre-formed dimers} (e.g., insulin receptor, IGF-1R): exist as
  covalent (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}\(_2\)\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}\(_2\)) tetramers held together by disulphide bonds.
  Ligand binding does not change quaternary structure but does induce a
  conformational change that brings the two intracellular kinase domains
  into productive juxtaposition.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Trans-autophosphorylation.} Upon dimerisation, the two
intracellular kinase domains phosphorylate each other on multiple
tyrosine residues in trans (kinase A phosphorylates kinase B and vice
versa). This serves three purposes: - Increases kinase activity
about 100-fold by stabilising the active conformation. -
Creates docking sites for downstream adaptor proteins. - Sets a
stoichiometric ``code'' --- different receptors phosphorylate different
tyrosine combinations, recruiting different adaptors.

\textbf{SH2 and PTB domains: phosphotyrosine readers.} Phosphorylated
tyrosines are recognised by two protein-domain types: - \textbf{SH2 (Src
homology 2)} domains, about 100 amino acids, recognise pTyr in
a sequence-specific context (the +1 to +3 residues C-terminal to pTyr
determine specificity). Each SH2 domain has a characteristic preference
(e.g., Grb2 SH2 prefers pYXNX; PI3K-p85 SH2 prefers pYXXM; Src family
SH2 prefers pYEEI). - \textbf{PTB (Phosphotyrosine Binding)} domains
recognise the residues \emph{N-terminal} to pTyr. Examples: Shc, IRS-1.

The combinatorial code of pTyr sites and SH2/PTB readers explains how
the same kinase domain (intrinsically not sequence-specific) can produce
highly specific signalling outputs.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: HER2 and Trastuzumab Reconsidered.}
Trastuzumab binds the membrane-proximal extracellular subdomain IV of
HER2 --- \emph{not} the dimerisation arm. So how does it work? Multiple
mechanisms: (1) it sterically interferes with HER2-HER2
self-dimerisation in amplified cancers; (2) it triggers
\textbf{antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC)} by recruiting
NK cells via Fc receptors; (3) it accelerates HER2 internalisation and
degradation. Trastuzumab-resistant HER2\(^+\) tumours often retain ADCC
sensitivity, which is why \textbf{trastuzumab-emtansine (T-DM1)} --- an
antibody--drug conjugate carrying a microtubule poison --- works after
trastuzumab failure: it exploits residual ADCC and adds direct
cytotoxicity.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{The MAP Kinase Cascade --- Three-Tier
Hierarchy}\label{the-map-kinase-cascade-three-tier-hierarchy}

The MAP kinase (MAPK) cascade is the canonical example of a multi-tier
signalling cascade. Eukaryotes have multiple parallel MAPK cascades; the
best-studied is the \textbf{classical (ERK) MAPK cascade}, but JNK and
p38 stress-activated cascades follow the same architecture:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{MAPKKK (MAP kinase kinase kinase)} --- activated by upstream
  signals (e.g., Ras-GTP for ERK; MEKK1 for JNK; ASK1 for p38).
\item
  \textbf{MAPKK (MAP kinase kinase)} --- phosphorylated and activated by
  MAPKKK on two serines/threonines; in turn, dual-specificity kinase
  (Ser/Thr/Tyr) for the next tier.
\item
  \textbf{MAPK} --- phosphorylated by MAPKK on Thr-X-Tyr motif in the
  activation loop; both phosphorylations required for activity.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Why three tiers?} The architecture provides: -
\textbf{Amplification} --- three sequential gain stages (each
about 10\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x}) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} 1000\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} total amplification. -
\textbf{Ultrasensitivity} --- dual-phosphorylation requirement at the
MAPK tier creates an effective \(n_H \approx 5\) at the output,
converting graded input into switch-like ERK activity (Huang \& Ferrell
1996). - \textbf{Insulation by scaffolds} --- KSR1 binds RAF, MEK1, and
ERK1; this prevents undesired cross-activation between parallel MAPK
cascades that share components. Yeast pheromone-response cascade uses
\textbf{Ste5} scaffold; mammals use KSR1 (ERK), JIP1 (JNK), OSM (p38). -
\textbf{Negative feedback by specific phosphatases} --- DUSP1-6
(dual-specificity phosphatases / MKPs) selectively dephosphorylate
specific MAPKs; their expression is itself induced by ERK, creating a
delayed negative feedback that produces transient ERK activation.

The combination of cascade ultrasensitivity + scaffold insulation + DUSP
feedback is why activation of ``the same RAS-MAPK pathway'' can produce
\emph{opposite} outcomes depending on context: transient activation \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
proliferation (ERK off before cell-cycle arrest); sustained activation \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
differentiation (ERK on long enough to upregulate p21 and exit the
cycle); even higher activation \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} senescence (ERK-driven oncogene-induced
senescence). Cell fate is encoded in the \emph{temporal pattern} of ERK,
not just its peak amplitude.

\subsubsection{Ligand-Gated Ion
Channels}\label{ligand-gated-ion-channels}

Direct coupling of ligand binding to ion flow, bypassing G proteins.
Fastest signalling (about  ms).

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR):} pentameric
  (alpha\(_2\)-beta-gamma-delta); 2 ACh bind \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} conformational change \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  Na\(^+\)/K\(^+\) channel opens \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  \hyperref[gl:depolarisation]{\textbf{depolarisation}} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} muscle
  contraction
\item
  \textbf{GABA\(_A\) receptor:} Cl\(^-\) channel; GABA binding \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  Cl\(^-\) influx \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} hyperpolarisation \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} inhibition. Target of
  benzodiazepines (bind \hyperref[gl:allosteric]{\textbf{allosteric}}
  site \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} enhanced Cl\(^-\) flux \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} sedation/anxiolysis). Also target of
  barbiturates, ethanol, and general anaesthetics.
\item
  \textbf{NMDA glutamate receptor:} requires simultaneous glutamate +
  glycine binding AND membrane depolarisation to remove Mg\(^{2+}\)
  block; Ca\(^{2+}\) entry \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} CaMKII activation \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} LTP (Learning and
  memory). Coincidence detector for Hebbian learning.
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 2:} Curare blocks nAChRs at the neuromuscular
junction. Predict the clinical effects. How does this differ from the
effect of an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (e.g., neostigmine)?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Intracellular Receptors}\label{intracellular-receptors}

Lipophilic signalling molecules (steroid hormones, thyroid hormone,
retinoic acid, vitamin D) diffuse through the membrane and bind
\textbf{cytoplasmic or nuclear receptors} --- ligand-activated
transcription factors. The nuclear receptor superfamily includes 48
members in humans.

\textbf{Classic glucocorticoid pathway:} 1. Cortisol crosses membrane
(lipophilic) 2. Binds glucocorticoid receptor (GR) in
\hyperref[gl:cytoplasm]{\textbf{cytoplasm}} 3. Hsp90 dissociates; GR
dimerises 4. Translocates to nucleus via NLS 5. Binds glucocorticoid
response elements (GREs) in DNA (consensus: AGAACAnnnTGTTCT) 6. Recruits
coactivators (SRC-1, p300/CBP) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} transcriptional activation

Target genes include anti-inflammatory (IkB-alpha, annexin A1),
gluconeogenic (PEPCK, G6Pase), and immunosuppressive genes.
Dexamethasone (synthetic glucocorticoid) is widely used for inflammation
and autoimmune disease.

\textbf{Other nuclear receptors:} - \textbf{Estrogen receptor (ER-alpha,
ER-beta):} breast development, bone density; tamoxifen (antagonist) for
breast cancer - \textbf{PPAR-gamma:} lipid metabolism, adipocyte
differentiation; thiazolidinediones (rosiglitazone) for type 2 diabetes
- \textbf{Thyroid hormone receptor (TR):} metabolic rate; T3 binding
activates genes for thermogenesis and development - \textbf{Vitamin D
receptor (VDR):} calcium
\hyperref[gl:homeostasis]{\textbf{homeostasis}}; calcitriol binding
activates genes for Ca\(^{2+}\) absorption

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Additional Signalling
Pathways}\label{additional-signalling-pathways}

\subsubsection{Wnt/Beta-Catenin Pathway}\label{wntbeta-catenin-pathway}

\textbf{Without Wnt signal:} Beta-catenin is phosphorylated by the
``destruction complex'' (APC + Axin + GSK-3-beta + CK1-alpha) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
ubiquitinated by beta-TrCP \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} proteasomal degradation. Target genes are
off.

\textbf{With Wnt signal:} Wnt binds Frizzled receptor + LRP5/6
co-receptor \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Dishevelled recruited \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} destruction complex inhibited
(Axin sequestered to LRP6) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} beta-catenin accumulates \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} enters nucleus \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
binds TCF/LEF transcription factors \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} activates target genes (c-Myc,
cyclin D1, Axin2).

\textbf{Clinical significance:} APC
\hyperref[gl:mutation]{\textbf{mutation}}s (loss of destruction complex
function) are found in \textgreater80\% of colorectal cancers (familial
adenomatous polyposis, FAP). Beta-catenin is also critical for stem cell
maintenance in the intestinal crypt.

\subsubsection{JAK-STAT Pathway}\label{jak-stat-pathway}

Cytokine receptors (e.g., IL-6R, IFN receptors, erythropoietin receptor)
lack intrinsic kinase activity. Instead, they associate with
\textbf{Janus kinases (JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, TYK2)}:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Cytokine binding \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} receptor dimerisation
\item
  JAKs trans-phosphorylate each other and the receptor
\item
  \textbf{STAT} proteins (Signal Transducers and Activators of
  Transcription) bind phosphotyrosines via SH2 domains
\item
  JAKs phosphorylate STATs
\item
  Phospho-STATs dimerise and translocate to the nucleus
\item
  STAT dimers bind DNA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} activate target genes
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Clinical significance:} - JAK2 V617F mutation: found in
\textgreater95\% of polycythaemia vera (constitutive JAK2 activation \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
excess red blood cell production) - JAK inhibitors (ruxolitinib,
tofacitinib) are used for myeloproliferative disorders and rheumatoid
arthritis - STAT3 is constitutively active in many cancers \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} survival
and proliferation

\subsubsection{Notch Pathway}\label{notch-pathway}

Direct cell-cell signalling (juxtacrine): 1. Delta/Jagged ligand on one
cell binds Notch receptor on adjacent cell 2. Ligand
\hyperref[gl:endocytosis]{\textbf{endocytosis}} generates mechanical
force 3. ADAM protease cleaves Notch extracellular domain 4.
Gamma-secretase cleaves transmembrane domain, releasing \textbf{NICD}
(Notch intracellular domain) 5. NICD translocates to nucleus \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} binds CSL
(RBP-J) transcription factor \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} activates Hes/Hey target genes

\textbf{Clinical significance:} Notch1 activating mutations occur in
about 60\% of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.
Gamma-secretase inhibitors are in clinical trials.

\subsubsection{Signal Termination
Mechanisms}\label{signal-termination-mechanisms}

\subsection{Crosstalk and Signal
Integration}\label{crosstalk-and-signal-integration}

Cells rarely respond to a single signal in isolation. Instead, multiple
pathways interact through \textbf{crosstalk} --- shared components,
convergent effectors, or mutual regulation. Signal integration is what
allows a cell to make complex decisions (proliferate, differentiate, or
die) based on the totality of its signalling environment.

\subsubsection{Convergence and
Divergence}\label{convergence-and-divergence}

\textbf{Convergence:} Multiple upstream signals activate the same
downstream effector. For example, both RTK/RAS/MAPK and Wnt/beta-catenin
pathways converge on cyclin D1 transcription, reinforcing the G1-to-S
transition. Both growth factor (PI3K/Akt) and integrin signalling
converge on mTORC1 to control cell growth.

\textbf{Divergence:} A single activated receptor triggers multiple
downstream cascades simultaneously. EGFR activation simultaneously
engages: - RAS-MAPK (proliferation) - PI3K-Akt (survival) -
PLC-gamma/IP\(_3\)/Ca\(^{2+}\) (immediate responses) - JAK-STAT (gene
expression) - c-Src (cytoskeletal remodelling)

\subsubsection{Scaffold Proteins and Signalling
Specificity}\label{scaffold-proteins-and-signalling-specificity}

Scaffold proteins physically assemble pathway components, ensuring
speed, specificity, and prevention of unwanted crosstalk:

Scaffold proteins explain how the same MAPK cascade can produce
different outcomes in different cell types: the scaffold determines
which substrates are phosphorylated.

\subsubsection{Positive and Negative Feedback
Loops}\label{positive-and-negative-feedback-loops}

\textbf{Positive feedback} creates switch-like (bistable
\citep{tyson2003}) responses: - ERK phosphorylates and activates SOS
(its own upstream GEF), creating an ultrasensitive on/off switch - p53
activates MDM2, which degrades p53 --- but also activates PUMA/NOXA,
creating a ``point of no return'' for apoptosis once the death threshold
is crossed - \hyperref[gl:caspase]{\textbf{Caspase}}-3 cleaves and
activates caspase-9 (amplification loop in apoptosis)

\textbf{Negative feedback} limits signal duration and creates
adaptation: - ERK phosphorylates SOS at inhibitory sites (slow negative
feedback counteracts fast positive feedback) - SOCS proteins induced by
JAK-STAT signalling bind JAKs and target them for degradation - Sprouty
(SPRY) proteins inhibit RAS-MAPK at the level of GRB2-SOS recruitment

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 5:} The MAPK cascade exhibits both positive
feedback (ERK activates SOS) and negative feedback (ERK inhibits SOS at
different sites). How might the relative timing of these feedbacks
create a transient burst of ERK activity followed by adaptation? What
would happen if the negative feedback were eliminated by mutation?
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 6:} A patient with BRAF V600E melanoma is treated
with vemurafenib (BRAF inhibitor) alone. Initial response is dramatic,
but resistance develops in 6--12 months. Sequencing reveals upregulation
of CRAF, NRAS amplification, or MEK1 mutations in different patients.
Explain why each of these ``bypasses'' vemurafenib and why combination
therapy with trametinib (MEK inhibitor) achieves more durable responses.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 7:} A neuron at rest contains
about 10\(^{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}7}\) M cytoplasmic {[}Ca\(^{2+}\){]}. Following an
action potential, {[}Ca\(^{2+}\){]} near a synaptic vesicle rises to
about 10\(^{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}5}\) M for about 1 ms before being
buffered and pumped back. Synaptotagmin has 2 C2 domains, each binding
2--3 Ca\(^{2+}\) ions cooperatively (Hill coefficient about 3).
Explain why this molecular architecture produces an essentially
``most-or-nothing'' exocytotic response to the brief calcium pulse, and
how this differs from the sustained calcium signals used in
CaMKII-mediated long-term potentiation.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 8:} A scaffold protein binds both an upstream
kinase (RAF) and a downstream substrate (ERK) but does not bind the
intermediate kinase (MEK). Predict the qualitative effect on signal
transmission. What does this suggest about why most three components
must be present on the scaffold for productive signalling?
\end{quote}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0045_a48c49019fcd.png}
\caption{Signal integration: multiple pathways converge on key decision nodes. Proliferative signals (RTK, Wnt, cytokines) converge on cyclin D1 transcription. Survival signals (PI3K/Akt) antagonise apoptosis by phosphorylating BAD. The cell's fate (proliferation, growth, or death) depends on the balance of active pathways.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Computational Approaches to Signalling
Networks}\label{computational-approaches-to-signalling-networks}

Modern systems biology uses mathematical modelling to understand
signalling network behaviour:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Boolean networks:} model each node as ON/OFF; useful for large
  networks
\item
  \textbf{Ordinary differential equations (ODEs):} model concentration
  changes over time; quantitative predictions
\item
  \textbf{Stochastic modelling:} accounts for molecular noise in
  low-copy-number signalling (important in stem cell fate decisions)
\end{itemize}

The Huang-Ferrell model of the MAPK cascade demonstrated that the
cascade acts as an ultrasensitive switch: small changes in input (growth
factor concentration) produce most-or-none output (ERK activation). This
switch-like behaviour arises from the dual phosphorylation requirement
for ERK activation.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{The Cell Cycle --- Control Through CDK-Cyclin
Complexes}\label{the-cell-cycle-control-through-cdk-cyclin-complexes}

Cell division is controlled by cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) activated
by their partner cyclins (Nobel Prize 2001: Hartwell, Hunt, Nurse).

\subsubsection{Phases}\label{phases}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}llll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Phase & Event & Duration (typical animal cell) & Key CDK-Cyclin \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
G1 & Growth; protein synthesis & 6--12 h & CDK4/6-Cyclin D \\
S & DNA replication & 6--8 h & CDK2-Cyclin E/A \\
G2 & Growth; mitosis preparation & 3--5 h & CDK1-Cyclin A \\
M & Mitosis + cytokinesis & about 1 h & CDK1-Cyclin B (MPF) \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Checkpoints} ensure cell cycle quality: - \textbf{G1 checkpoint
(restriction point):} cell size adequate? DNA intact? Growth factors
present? CDK4/6-Cyclin D drives pRB phosphorylation \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} E2F release \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
S-phase genes (cyclin E, DNA polymerase, thymidine kinase) -
\textbf{G2/M checkpoint:} DNA repair complete? CDK1-Cyclin B (MPF ---
maturation-promoting factor) triggers mitotic entry. Activated by CDC25
phosphatase; inhibited by Wee1 kinase. - \textbf{Spindle assembly
checkpoint (SAC):} most kinetochores attached to microtubules?
Mad2/BubR1 inhibit \hyperref[gl:anaphase]{\textbf{Anaphase}} Promoting
Complex (APC/C) until satisfied. APC/C then ubiquitinates securin \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
separase released \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} cleaves cohesin \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} sister chromatid separation.

\subsubsection{Tumour Suppressors}\label{tumour-suppressors}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{p53:} ``guardian of the
  \hyperref[gl:genome]{\textbf{genome}}''; activated by DNA damage (via
  ATM/ATR kinases, Chk1/Chk2) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} arrests cell cycle (via p21/WAF1
  inhibiting CDK2) or triggers apoptosis (via PUMA, NOXA); mutated in
  about 50\% of human cancers. MDM2 is the E3 ubiquitin ligase
  that normally keeps p53 levels low; MDM2 inhibitors (nutlins) are in
  clinical trials.
\item
  \textbf{pRB:} binds and represses E2F in G1; CDK4/6 phosphorylation
  releases E2F \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} S phase entry; mutated/deleted in retinoblastoma and
  many cancers. CDK4/6 inhibitors (palbociclib, ribociclib) are used in
  HR\(^+\) breast cancer.
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: CDK4/6 Inhibitors in Cancer} Palbociclib,
ribociclib, and abemaciclib specifically inhibit CDK4/6, preventing pRB
phosphorylation and maintaining E2F repression. This arrests cancer
cells in G1. These drugs have transformed treatment of hormone
receptor-positive, HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer, doubling
progression-free survival when combined with anti-estrogen therapy.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Apoptosis --- Programmed Cell
Death}\label{apoptosis-programmed-cell-death}

Apoptosis eliminates about 80 billion cells per day in the
adult human (equal to approximate cell proliferation). It differs
fundamentally from necrosis:

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Feature
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Apoptosis
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Necrosis
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Initiation & Genetically programmed & Accidental \\
Morphology & Cell shrinkage; DNA laddering; apoptotic bodies & Cell

Inflammation & None (PS ``eat me'' signal) & Severe (DAMPs released) \\
ATP required & Yes & No \\
Caspases & Activated & Not involved \\
\end{longtable}
}

\subsubsection{Intrinsic (Mitochondrial)
Pathway}\label{intrinsic-mitochondrial-pathway}

Triggered by DNA damage, oxidative stress, growth factor withdrawal:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{BH3-primarily proteins} (Bad, Bid, Puma, NOXA) activated by
  cellular stress
\item
  BH3-primarily proteins neutralise anti-apoptotic Bcl-2/Bcl-xL
\item
  \textbf{BAX/BAK} oligomerise in the OMM \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} form pores (MAC channel)
\item
  \textbf{Cytochrome c} released from intermembrane space into cytoplasm
\item
  Cytochrome c + Apaf-1 + ATP/dATP \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{apoptosome} (7-subunit
  wheel, about 1 MDa)
\item
  Apoptosome activates \textbf{caspase-9} (initiator caspase)
\item
  Caspase-9 activates \textbf{caspase-3/-7} (executioner caspases)
\item
  Caspases cleave structural proteins (nuclear lamins, ICAD releasing
  CAD endonuclease \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} DNA fragmentation into about 180 bp
  nucleosomal ladders)
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Bcl-2 family:} anti-apoptotic members (Bcl-2, Bcl-xL, Mcl-1)
bind and inhibit BAX/BAK. Bcl-2 overexpression in follicular lymphoma
(t(14;18) translocation) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} cells cannot die. \textbf{Venetoclax} is a
BH3 mimetic drug that inhibits Bcl-2, restoring apoptosis in chronic
lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL).

\subsubsection{Extrinsic (Death Receptor)
Pathway}\label{extrinsic-death-receptor-pathway}

Triggered by extracellular death ligands (FasL, TNF-alpha, TRAIL):

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Ligand binds death receptor (FAS/CD95, TNFR1, DR4/DR5)
\item
  Death domain oligomers recruit FADD (Fas-associated death domain
  protein)
\item
  Procaspase-8 recruited \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{DISC (Death-Inducing Signalling
  Complex)}
\item
  Caspase-8 auto-activated
\item
  In Type I cells: caspase-8 directly activates caspase-3 (sufficient
  DISC formation)
\item
  In Type II cells: caspase-8 cleaves Bid \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} tBid \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} activates
  mitochondrial pathway (amplification loop)
\end{enumerate}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsubsection{Other Forms of Regulated Cell
Death}\label{other-forms-of-regulated-cell-death}

Beyond classical apoptosis, several other regulated cell death pathways
have been identified:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Necroptosis:} Programmed necrosis triggered by TNF when
  caspase-8 is inhibited. RIPK1 and RIPK3 kinases phosphorylate MLKL,
  which oligomerises and permeabilises the plasma membrane. Important in
  host defence against viruses that express caspase inhibitors.
\item
  \textbf{Pyroptosis:} Inflammatory cell death mediated by gasdermin D
  (GSDMD). Inflammasome activation (NLRP3, NLRC4, AIM2) activates
  caspase-1, which cleaves GSDMD. The N-terminal fragment forms pores in
  the plasma membrane, releasing IL-1-beta and IL-18. Critical in
  \hyperref[gl:innate-immunity]{\textbf{innate immunity}} and sepsis.
\item
  \textbf{Ferroptosis:} Iron-dependent cell death characterised by lipid
  peroxidation. GPX4 (glutathione peroxidase 4) normally prevents lethal
  lipid ROS accumulation. GPX4 inhibition or glutathione depletion
  triggers ferroptosis. Relevant in neurodegeneration, kidney injury,
  and cancer therapy (some drug-resistant tumours are susceptible to
  ferroptosis inducers).
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Ferroptosis in Cancer Therapy}
Drug-resistant cancer cells that have undergone epithelial-mesenchymal
transition (EMT) become highly susceptible to ferroptosis. This
vulnerability arises because EMT upregulates polyunsaturated fatty acid
(PUFA) incorporation into membrane phospholipids, increasing
susceptibility to lipid peroxidation. Ferroptosis-inducing agents
(erastin, RSL3) are being investigated as therapies for
therapy-resistant cancers. Understanding cell death pathway diversity is
critical for developing next-generation anti-cancer strategies.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Cancer as Dysregulated
Signalling}\label{cancer-as-dysregulated-signalling}

Cancer results from accumulated mutations that activate oncogenes
(gain-of-function) and inactivate tumour suppressors (loss-of-function),
disrupting normal signalling control.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Imatinib --- The Paradigm of Targeted
Therapy} Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) is caused by the Philadelphia
chromosome --- a t(9;22) translocation creating the BCR-ABL fusion
protein (constitutively active tyrosine kinase). Before imatinib, 5-year
survival was about 30\%. Imatinib specifically inhibits BCR-ABL
by occupying the ATP-binding site, achieving complete cytogenetic
response in \textgreater80\% of patients and transforming CML into a
manageable chronic disease. This ``bench-to-bedside'' success story
(Brian Druker, Nicholas Lydon) demonstrated that understanding
signalling pathways at the molecular level can lead to revolutionary
therapies.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Clinical Pharmacology of Cell
Signalling}\label{clinical-pharmacology-of-cell-signalling}

Cell signalling is the most pharmacologically tractable layer of
cellular biology --- most major drug classes either activate, inhibit,
or compete with components of a signalling cascade. Understanding the
molecular logic of signalling therefore translates directly into
rational pharmacology. Three case studies illustrate the depth of this
connection.

\textbf{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-Blockers: from signal blockade to chronic-disease treatment.}
Propranolol (1964, James Black, Nobel Prize 1988) was the first
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-adrenergic receptor antagonist. It blocks \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}\(_1\) receptors on
cardiomyocytes (reducing heart rate and contractility, lowering oxygen
demand) and \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}\(_2\) receptors on bronchial smooth muscle (sometimes
causing wheeze in asthmatics). Modern \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-blockers are graded by
selectivity: - \textbf{Non-selective:} propranolol, carvedilol --- block
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}\(_1\), \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}\(_2\), sometimes \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}\(_1\). - \textbf{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}\(_1\)-selective
(``cardioselective''):} metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol --- preferred
when bronchospasm is a concern. - \textbf{Inverse agonists:} carvedilol
--- actively reduces basal G-protein activity, not just blocks ligand
binding. - \textbf{Biased agonists/antagonists:} carvedilol, alprenolol
--- block G\(_s\) but activate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-arrestin signalling, possibly
explaining superior heart failure outcomes.

The mechanistic depth has grown over 60 years: from ``block adrenaline
binding'' \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} ``reduce cAMP'' \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} ``decouple from G-protein'' \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} ``biased
toward \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-arrestin/ERK'' \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} ``remodel chronic gene expression patterns in
failing heart.'' A drug class that began as symptomatic therapy for
angina is now first-line in heart failure precisely \emph{because} it
modulates the chronic-stress signalling fingerprint.

\textbf{Statins: targeting the substrate of a regulatory cascade.}
HMG-CoA reductase catalyses the rate-limiting step of cholesterol
biosynthesis. Statins (lovastatin from \emph{Aspergillus} in 1976;
simvastatin, atorvastatin, rosuvastatin) are competitive inhibitors with
IC\(_{50}\) about 10 nM. Lower hepatic cholesterol synthesis \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
upregulation of LDL receptor (via SREBP-2 transcription factor) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
increased LDL clearance from blood \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} about 30--50\% reduction
in LDL cholesterol. Beyond cholesterol, statins have \textbf{pleiotropic
effects} mediated by reduced isoprenoid (farnesyl, geranylgeranyl)
production: reduced membrane localisation of Rho/Rac GTPases
(anti-inflammatory), reduced platelet aggregation, improved endothelial
function. Many of these effects are arguably more important than
cholesterol lowering for cardiovascular outcomes --- supported by
clinical trials showing benefit even in patients with normal LDL.

\textbf{Imatinib in detail: lessons in resistance.} Imatinib (Gleevec,
2001) binds the inactive (``DFG-out'') conformation of the BCR-ABL
kinase domain at its ATP-binding site. The drug exploits a structural
quirk: the BCR-ABL kinase domain has a hydrophobic pocket that becomes
accessible primarily in the inactive conformation; this pocket is
\emph{not} present in most other kinases, providing remarkable
selectivity. Resistance develops through several mechanisms:

This pattern --- initial dramatic response, eventual development of
resistance via mutation or bypass --- is now the norm in targeted
oncology. Modern strategies use \textbf{combination therapy} designed
against the resistance landscape: BRAF + MEK inhibitors in melanoma,
BCR-ABL + PI3K in CML resistance, EGFR + MEK in lung cancer.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 4b:} A patient with CML on imatinib for 3 years
develops disease progression. Sequencing reveals a T315I mutation in
BCR-ABL. Why does this single amino-acid change confer resistance, and
which next-generation drug would you choose? (Hint: T315 is the
``gatekeeper'' residue lining the imatinib binding pocket.)
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Crosstalk and Signal Integration --- How Cells Process
Multiple
Signals}\label{crosstalk-and-signal-integration-how-cells-process-multiple-signals}

A real cell is not exposed to a single ligand at a time. A hepatocyte
receives glucagon, insulin, growth factors, fatty acids, cytokines, and
adhesion signals \emph{simultaneously}, and must integrate most of them
into a coherent metabolic and proliferative response. Three
architectural features make this integration possible:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Shared second messengers.} Many pathways feed into
  Ca\(^{2+}\), cAMP, or phosphoinositides. The cell's ``state'' is
  encoded in the time-integrated and spatially-resolved levels of these
  second messengers, not in any single signalling event.
\item
  \textbf{Coincidence detection.} Some effectors require \emph{two
  simultaneous} inputs: \textbf{PKC} is fully activated primarily when
  both DAG (membrane targeting) and Ca\(^{2+}\) (cytosolic increase) are
  present; \textbf{NMDA receptor} opens primarily when glutamate binds
  \emph{and} the membrane is sufficiently depolarised. Coincidence
  detection prevents false alarms.
\item
  \textbf{Conditional rules (logic gates).} Cells implement Boolean-like
  decision rules. Cell proliferation in normal epithelia requires growth
  factor (mitogen) AND adhesion (integrin) AND survival (PI3K/Akt). Loss
  of any one input causes anoikis (death by detachment) or quiescence.
  Cancer typically defeats these rules by activating each independently.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Concrete examples of crosstalk:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Insulin--glucagon antagonism in liver.} Both signals reach the
  same hepatocyte. Insulin (via Akt) inhibits gluconeogenic gene
  expression; glucagon (via cAMP/PKA) activates it. The PEPCK and G6Pase
  promoters are bound by both insulin-responsive (FoxO1) and
  cAMP-responsive (CREB) transcription factors with opposing effects ---
  the integrated transcriptional output reflects the
  {[}insulin{]}/{[}glucagon{]} ratio.
\item
  \textbf{Growth factor + integrin convergence on mTORC1.} Growth factor
  \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} RTK \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PI3K \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Akt \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} TSC1/2 inhibition \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Rheb-GTP \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} mTORC1. Integrin \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  FAK \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PI3K \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} same Akt step. Both inputs are required for full mTORC1
  activation; loss of either prevents protein synthesis and cell growth,
  providing a checkpoint against unanchored proliferation.
\item
  \textbf{Stress \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} MAPK pathway crosstalk.} TNF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha} activates IKK \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} NF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}B
  (survival) AND MEKK1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} JNK (apoptosis). The ratio determines outcome:
  brief TNF \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} NF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}B dominates \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} survival; prolonged TNF or with
  cyclohexamide (NF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}B-blocking) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} JNK dominates \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} apoptosis.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Computational modelling of integration.} Modern systems biology
builds these rules into ordinary differential equations (ODEs) or
Boolean networks. A 2009 paper by Janes \& Yaffe (\emph{Nature Reviews
MCB}) showed that 200+ measurements of signalling components in
TNF-treated cells could be reduced to a few \textbf{partial least
squares (PLS)} components that predicted apoptosis vs.~survival
outcomes. The lesson: cells appear to combine many inputs in a
low-dimensional decision space --- a finding that simplifies both basic
understanding and drug design (modulate the dominant principal
components, not 200 individual proteins).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 4:} Why would a combination of a BRAF inhibitor
(vemurafenib) and a MEK inhibitor (trametinib) be more effective than
either alone in BRAF V600E melanoma? Consider pathway reactivation
mechanisms.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Computational Bridge}\label{computational-bridge-7}

Cooperative ligand binding (Hill) captures RTK/RAS-MAPK dosage responses
in reduced form:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ biology.cell }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ hill\_equation}

\NormalTok{theta }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ hill\_equation(}\FloatTok{8.0}\NormalTok{, kd}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{10.0}\NormalTok{, hill\_coefficient}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{2.8}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(theta, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical / systems note:} Dose-response steepness from
cooperativity is one reason combination targeted therapy can widen the
therapeutic window compared with single-agent saturation of one node.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsubsection{Spatial Transcriptomics: Signalling in Tissue
Context}\label{spatial-transcriptomics-signalling-in-tissue-context}

Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) dissociates tissues and so loses
the spatial information that is often the point --- you can measure what
each cell expresses but not \textbf{where it sits relative to its
neighbours}. \textbf{Spatial transcriptomics (ST)} recovers that
geometry by coupling \emph{in situ} RNA capture or detection to
high-throughput sequencing or imaging.

Two commercial platforms dominate. \textbf{10\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} Genomics Visium} prints a
glass slide with about 5000 barcoded spots (55 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m diameter,
about 100 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m spacing); a fresh-frozen tissue section is placed
on the slide, RNA diffuses into the spots, and each spot's transcriptome
is sequenced with its spot barcode. Resolution is sub-cellular to
small-cluster (1--10 cells per spot). \textbf{MERFISH (Multiplexed
Error-Robust FISH)} and \textbf{seqFISH+} instead use combinatorial
error-correcting fluorescent in situ hybridisation to detect thousands
of transcripts at \textbf{diffraction-limited (about 100 nm)
resolution} --- true single-molecule, single-cell spatial mapping.
\textbf{Slide-seq} and \textbf{Stereo-seq} push sequencing-based
approaches toward 10 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m and 500 nm spot sizes respectively.

Why this matters for signalling: paracrine and juxtacrine signalling ---
Notch--Delta, ephrin--Eph, WNT morphogen gradients --- depend on cells
\emph{being close to each other}. Spatial transcriptomics lets
investigators map ligand-expressing cells next to receptor-expressing
cells across a whole tissue section and infer \textbf{ligand-receptor
interaction networks in situ} (tools: CellChat, NicheNet,
SpatialCellChat, 2022-2024). In tumour biology, ST reveals
\hyperref[gl:niche]{\textbf{niches}} of exhausted T cells in
immunologically ``cold'' regions of the same tumour, motivating
spatially-guided immunotherapy combinations. In developmental biology,
ST in mouse embryos (Stereo-seq, \emph{Cell} 2022) produced the first
cell-resolved, tissue-resolved organogenesis atlas. The technology cost
has dropped about 10x every two years; a whole-slide Visium
experiment costs about \$2000 in 2024. For the student, ST is
the bridge between molecular cell biology (``what genes are on?'') and
anatomy (``where?'') --- and it is the platform on which the next decade
of in situ discovery will be built.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-10}

For \textbf{Cell Signalling and Communication}, frontier biology belongs
inside the evidence logic of the chapter. Cell biology is increasingly
measured as live, spatial, single-cell, and perturbational data rather
than static diagrams alone. The core reading question is this:
signalling explanations should include receptor context, dose, timing,
feedback, crosstalk, and cellular state.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

Ask what measurement scale is being claimed: nanometre structure,
single-cell transcript abundance, organelle dynamics, tissue context, or
organismal phenotype.

\textbf{Source practice:} For cell-state claims, distinguish microscopy,
live-cell perturbation, single-cell sequencing, spatial transcriptomics,
and biochemical assay evidence before making a causal statement.

\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-10}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Cell signalling: ligand \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} receptor \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} cascade \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} response. GPCRs use
  cAMP or IP\(_3\)/DAG via heterotrimeric G proteins; RTKs use tyrosine
  phosphorylation and the RAS-MAPK cascade; ion channels open
  immediately upon ligand binding.
\item
  Second messengers (cAMP, cGMP, IP\(_3\), DAG, Ca\(^{2+}\), PIP\(_3\))
  amplify and diversify signals within the cell.
\item
  Signal termination involves GTPase activity, phosphodiesterases,
  protein phosphatases, receptor internalisation, and ubiquitin-mediated
  degradation.
\item
  The Wnt/beta-catenin, JAK-STAT, and Notch pathways control
  development, immune function, and stem cell maintenance.
\item
  The cell cycle is governed by CDK-cyclin complexes; checkpoints (G1,
  G2/M, SAC) ensure fidelity. p53 and pRB are the primary tumour
  suppressors.
\item
  Apoptosis (programmed cell death) proceeds via intrinsic
  (mitochondrial) or extrinsic (death receptor) pathways, both
  converging on executioner caspases.
\item
  Cancer results from dysregulated signalling (oncogenes + tumour
  suppressor loss); targeted therapies exploit specific pathway
  dependencies.
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See Unit IV (growth-factor-driven
  transcription), Unit V (tumour suppressor
  \hyperref[gl:allele]{\textbf{allele}}s), Unit IX (endocrine first
  messengers).
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Review Questions}\label{review-questions-10}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Draw the complete G\(_s\)-cAMP-PKA signalling cascade from epinephrine
  binding to glycogen breakdown. Identify most amplification steps and
  termination mechanisms.
\item
  Compare and contrast GPCRs and RTKs in terms of structure, mechanism
  of activation, downstream signalling, and examples of each.
\item
  Explain the RAS-MAPK pathway. Why is RAS one of the most commonly
  mutated oncogenes in human cancer?
\item
  Describe the Wnt/beta-catenin pathway. Why do APC mutations lead to
  colorectal cancer?
\item
  A patient has a gain-of-function mutation in JAK2 (V617F). Explain the
  molecular mechanism and predict the clinical
  \hyperref[gl:phenotype]{\textbf{phenotype}}.
\item
  Compare the intrinsic and extrinsic apoptosis pathways. Where do they
  converge, and what is the significance of BH3-primarily proteins?
\item
  Explain the mechanism of action of imatinib in CML. Why does
  resistance eventually develop, and how might it be overcome?
\item
  Describe four mechanisms by which cells terminate signalling
  responses. For each, give a specific molecular example.
\item
  Explain how CDK4/6 inhibitors (palbociclib) arrest the cell cycle in
  G1. Why are they used specifically in HR\(^+\) breast cancer?
\item
  Venetoclax is a BH3 mimetic that inhibits Bcl-2. Explain its mechanism
  of action and why it is effective in cancers that overexpress Bcl-2.
\item
  Using \texttt{hill\_equation}, compare fractional occupancy at
  \([L] = K_d\) for \(n = 1\) vs.~\(n = 4\). Which curve better matches
  oxygen binding to haemoglobin, and why?
\item
  Sketch how receptor internalisation provides \textbf{signal
  termination} for RTKs; link to one resistance mechanism in targeted
  cancer therapy.
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Unit III --- Energy and Metabolism:
Introduction}\label{unit-iii-energy-and-metabolism-introduction}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Unit III --- Energy and Metabolism:
Introduction}

\subsection*{Why This Unit Matters}\label{why-this-unit-matters-3}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Why This Unit Matters}

Life is, at its core, an ongoing argument with the second law of
thermodynamics. The second law demands that disorder increases in any
closed system; living organisms are ordered, and they maintain that
order at the price of consuming energy and exporting entropy to their
surroundings. A resting human adult dissipates approximately 80 watts
--- the same as an incandescent light bulb --- in the form of body heat,
CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}, and metabolic waste. Every breath you take, every protein you
synthesise, every ion you pump against its gradient, uses energy
extracted from the oxidation of food.

The molecular currency of this energy economy is ATP (adenosine
triphosphate). At any moment, your cells contain about 50 g of
ATP, yet you consume roughly 40 kg of ATP every day at rest. This means
each ATP molecule is recycled approximately 800 times --- phosphorylated
from ADP in mitochondria, hydrolysed to ADP in the cytoplasm, and
regenerated in an endless chemical cycle. During vigorous exercise, ATP
turnover in muscle can exceed 0.5 kg per minute.

This unit traces energy from its entry point --- sunlight captured by
chlorophyll, or chemical bonds in food --- through the interconnected
pathways of glycolysis, the TCA cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, and
photosynthesis, to its exit as heat and CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}. Each pathway is treated
quantitatively: you will derive ATP yields, calculate free energy
changes, and model the regulatory logic that switches metabolism between
fed and fasted states. The central thread is Peter Mitchell's
chemiosmosis (Nobel Prize 1978): ion gradients across membranes couple
electron flow to ATP synthesis, and the same principle operates in both
mitochondria and chloroplasts.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection*{Current Evidence Thread}\label{current-evidence-thread-3}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Current Evidence Thread}

Read this unit as one regulated network rather than three separate
pathways: respiration, the integrated fasting/fed economy, and
photosynthesis are most constrained by the same currencies of energy
charge, redox poise, and compartmentation, and a claim in one chapter is
primarily as strong as the flux, sensor, and condition it specifies.
Metabolism is now studied as a regulated network constrained by energy,
redox balance, compartmentation, and environment. As you move through
the chapters, keep a two-column note: \textbf{claim} on the left,
\textbf{evidence that would change my confidence} on the right. By the
end of the unit, each major idea should be tied to a measurement, model,
citation, or paper-based lab decision.

\label{sec:unit_III_bioenergetics_and_respiration}

\subsection{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-11}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Define the laws of
  \hyperref[gl:thermodynamics]{\textbf{thermodynamics}} and apply them
  to biological reactions, distinguishing standard
  (\(\Delta G^{\circ\prime}\)) from physiological (\(\Delta G\)) free
  energies.
\item
  Explain the role of ATP as a central phosphoryl-group donor and
  short-term energy carrier, including the molecular basis of its high
  phosphoryl group transfer potential.
\item
  Describe most 10 steps of
  \hyperref[gl:glycolysis]{\textbf{glycolysis}} with
  \hyperref[gl:enzyme]{\textbf{enzyme}}s, intermediates, and regulatory
  mechanisms.
\item
  Explain the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and its regulation.
\item
  Describe most 8 steps of the TCA cycle with carbon tracking, cofactor
  yields, and regulation.
\item
  Describe the electron transport chain complexes I--IV, including
  proton stoichiometry and the Q cycle.
\item
  Explain \hyperref[gl:atp-synthase]{\textbf{ATP synthase}} structure
  and the rotary catalysis mechanism, including the proton-motive force
  equation.
\item
  Calculate net ATP yield from glucose oxidation using modern P/O ratios
  (about 2.5 for NADH, about 1.5 for FADH\(_2\)) and
  explain how the ``30--32 ATP'' number is derived.
\item
  Compare substrate-level and
  \hyperref[gl:oxidative-phosphorylation]{\textbf{oxidative
  phosphorylation}} quantitatively across yield, speed, sustainability,
  and physiological niche.
\item
  Describe \hyperref[gl:fermentation]{\textbf{fermentation}} pathways,
  the Cori cycle, and the glucose-alanine cycle as inter-organ shuttles.
\item
  Explain gluconeogenesis (four bypass enzymes) and its reciprocal
  regulation with glycolysis.
\item
  Quantify reactive oxygen species (ROS) production at the ETC and the
  antioxidant defences that constrain it.
\item
  Distinguish anaplerotic and cataplerotic flux through the TCA cycle in
  the context of inter-organ metabolism.
\item
  Explain physiological (UCP1, brown adipose) and pharmacological (DNP)
  uncoupling at a molecular level.
\item
  Compute the thermodynamic efficiency of glucose oxidation from
  standard free energies of formation.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Opening Vignette: The Heretic Who Was Right About ATP}

In 1961, British biochemist Peter Mitchell proposed something that
nearly the entire biochemistry community considered preposterous: that
the synthesis of ATP was not driven by a hypothetical high-energy
chemical intermediate but by a \textbf{proton gradient across a
membrane} --- a \textbf{proton-motive force} \citep{mitchell1961}.
Mitchell's ``chemiosmotic hypothesis'' met with fierce resistance.
Efraim Racker, one of biochemistry's most respected voices, called it
``an act of faith, not of reason.'' Mitchell spent years defending his
idea from private funds after leaving a university position.

In 1978, the Nobel Committee awarded Peter Mitchell the Nobel Prize in
Chemistry --- alone, without co-recipients --- specifically for the
chemiosmotic hypothesis. It was a stunning vindication. Today we know
that the about 28 molecules of ATP produced per glucose in
oxidative phosphorylation are most driven by the proton gradient that
Mitchell described. The mitochondrion --- and the
\hyperref[gl:chloroplast]{\textbf{chloroplast}} --- are essentially
biological batteries, storing energy as a proton electrochemical
gradient. This chapter explains exactly how they are charged and
discharged.

\emph{Primary source: Mitchell, P. (1961). Coupling of phosphorylation
to electron and hydrogen transfer by a chemi-osmotic type of mechanism.
Nature, 191(4784), 144--148.}
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Thermodynamics of Life}\label{thermodynamics-of-life}

\subsubsection{First and Second Laws}\label{first-and-second-laws}

The \textbf{First Law of Thermodynamics:} Energy cannot be created or
destroyed --- primarily converted. Life obeys this law: every metabolic
reaction converts one form of energy to another, with total energy
conserved.

The \textbf{Second Law of Thermodynamics:} In any spontaneous process,
the total entropy (disorder) of the universe increases. This means no
energy conversion is 100\% efficient --- some energy is typically
dispersed as heat. Living organisms maintain internal order (low
entropy) at the expense of increasing entropy in their surroundings
(heat release, CO\(_2\) production, waste generation).

A useful schematic: a cell is a \textbf{dissipative structure} in the
sense of Prigogine --- its internal order is maintained by a continuous
through-flux of free energy (food, sunlight) and a continuous out-flux
of low-grade heat. Stop the through-flux, and the cell relaxes to
thermal equilibrium --- which is to say, dies.

\subsubsection{Gibbs Free Energy: A Derivation From First
Principles}\label{gibbs-free-energy-a-derivation-from-first-principles}

For a process at constant temperature \(T\) and constant pressure \(P\)
(the conditions inside virtually every cell), the relevant thermodynamic
potential is the \textbf{Gibbs free energy} \(G\). Starting from the
second law, we have for the universe (system + surroundings):

\[\Delta S_{\text{universe}} = \Delta S_{\text{system}} + \Delta S_{\text{surroundings}} \geq 0 \tag{9.0a}\]

Heat released by the system at constant pressure equals
\(-\Delta H_{\text{system}}\), and this heat increases the entropy of
the surroundings by \(-\Delta H_{\text{system}}/T\). Substituting:

\[\Delta S_{\text{universe}} = \Delta S_{\text{system}} - \frac{\Delta H_{\text{system}}}{T} \geq 0 \tag{9.0b}\]

Multiplying both sides by \(-T\) and dropping the ``system'' subscript
yields the \textbf{defining inequality of spontaneity at constant \(T\),
\(P\)}:

\begin{equation}
\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S \leq 0
\label{eq:unit_III_gibbs_free_energy}
\end{equation}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{\(\Delta G < 0\):} reaction is spontaneous (exergonic); energy
  released
\item
  \textbf{\(\Delta G > 0\):} reaction is non-spontaneous (endergonic);
  energy input required
\item
  \textbf{\(\Delta G = 0\):} system is at equilibrium (no net reaction)
\end{itemize}

This is profound: a quantity that depends primarily on the \emph{system}
(not the surroundings) tells us whether the \emph{universe's} entropy
will increase. It is the workhorse of biochemical thermodynamics.

\subsubsection{Standard Free Energy and Actual Free
Energy}\label{standard-free-energy-and-actual-free-energy}

The standard free energy change (\(\Delta G^{\circ\prime}\)) is measured
under biochemical standard conditions (1 M concentrations for reactants
except H\(^+\), \hyperref[gl:ph]{\textbf{pH}} 7.0, 25 degrees C, 1 atm,
and water at unit activity). Under cellular conditions (not standard
state), \(\Delta G\) differs from \(\Delta G^{\circ\prime}\):

\[\Delta G = \Delta G^{\circ\prime} + RT \ln Q \tag{9.2}\]

where \(Q\) = {[}products{]}/{[}reactants{]} (mass action ratio,
reaction quotient).

The relationship between \(\Delta G^{\circ\prime}\) and the equilibrium
constant:

\[\Delta G^{\circ\prime} = -RT \ln K_{eq} \tag{9.3}\]

\textbf{Standard versus physiological \(\Delta G^{\circ\prime}\) for key
hydrolysis reactions} (37 °C, pH 7.0, 1 mM Mg\(^{2+}\)):

\textbf{Key insight:} ATP sits in the \emph{middle} of this spectrum. It
is energetically capable of phosphorylating many low-energy compounds
(glucose, F6P) but can itself be re-synthesised from higher-energy
intermediates such as PEP and 1,3-BPG. This intermediate position is
what makes ATP an effective ``energy currency'' rather than the
highest-potential molecule in the cell.

\textbf{Why cells maintain far-from-equilibrium conditions:} At
equilibrium, \(\Delta G = 0\) and no net work can be done. Cells
maintain metabolite concentrations far from equilibrium
(\(Q \neq K_{eq}\)), keeping \(\Delta G\) strongly negative for
exergonic reactions. This is why cells must continuously consume
nutrients --- to maintain the far-from-equilibrium state that enables
life.

\subsubsection{Worked Example: Free Energy and
Equilibrium}\label{worked-example-free-energy-and-equilibrium}

\emph{Problem:} The \(\Delta G^{\circ\prime}\) for glucose-6-phosphate
isomerase (G6P to F6P) is +1.7 kJ/mol. Calculate \(K_{eq}\) at 37
degrees C. Is this reaction spontaneous under standard conditions?

\emph{Solution:}

\[\Delta G^{\circ\prime} = -RT \ln K_{eq} \tag{9.4}\]

\[1{,}700 = -(8.314)(310) \ln K_{eq} \tag{9.5}\]

\[\ln K_{eq} = \frac{-1{,}700}{2{,}577} = -0.660 \tag{9.6}\]

\[K_{eq} = e^{-0.660} = 0.517 \tag{9.7}\]

Under standard conditions, this reaction is slightly non-spontaneous
(\(\Delta G^{\circ\prime} > 0\)). However, in the cell, the mass action
ratio \(Q\) is kept well below \(K_{eq}\) because F6P is rapidly
consumed by PFK-1, making the actual \(\Delta G\) negative.

\subsubsection{Worked Example: Complete Glucose
Oxidation}\label{worked-example-complete-glucose-oxidation}

\emph{Problem:} Calculate the standard free energy of complete glucose
oxidation (glucose + 6 O\(_2\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} 6 CO\(_2\) + 6 H\(_2\)O) from tabulated
standard free energies of formation, and compare it with the energy
harvested as ATP.

\emph{Solution:} Using \(\Delta G^{\circ}_f\) values (kJ/mol) at 25 °C
--- glucose: \(-910.4\); CO\(_2\) (aq): \(-394.4\); H\(_2\)O (l):
\(-237.1\); O\(_2\): 0:

\[\Delta G^{\circ\prime}_{\text{rxn}} = \sum \Delta G^{\circ}_f(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta G^{\circ}_f(\text{reactants}) \tag{9.7a}\]

\[= [6(-394.4) + 6(-237.1)] - [(-910.4) + 6(0)] = -3{,}789 + 910.4 \approx -2{,}870 \; \text{kJ/mol} \tag{9.7b}\]

If 32 ATP are produced per glucose at a cellular hydrolysis \(\Delta G\)
of \(-50\) kJ/mol, the energy captured as ATP is
\(32 \times 50 = 1{,}600\) kJ/mol. The thermodynamic efficiency of
glucose oxidation in cells is therefore:

\[\eta = \frac{1{,}600}{2{,}870} \approx 56\% \tag{9.7c}\]

The remaining about 44\% is dissipated as heat --- useful for
mammals to maintain body temperature, but ultimately a payment to the
second law. For comparison: a modern combined-cycle gas turbine power
plant achieves about 60\% thermal efficiency at \textgreater800
K, while an automobile engine averages about 25\%. A
56\%-efficient isothermal energy converter operating at 310 K is, by any
engineering standard, remarkable.

\subsubsection{ATP as Energy Currency}\label{atp-as-energy-currency}

ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the cell's central short-term energy
carrier and phosphoryl-group donor for many endergonic reactions. The
phrase ``energy currency'' is useful shorthand, but the cell also uses
ion gradients, redox cofactors such as NADH/NADPH, thioesters such as
acetyl-CoA, and activated carriers such as UDP-glucose.

The high negative \(\Delta G\) of ATP hydrolysis under cellular
conditions (\(-50\) to \(-54\) kJ/mol;
\(\Delta G^{\circ\prime} = -30.5\) kJ/mol) arises from: 1.
\textbf{Electrostatic repulsion} between closely spaced negative charges
on the gamma-phosphate (relieved on hydrolysis) 2. \textbf{Resonance
stabilisation} of inorganic phosphate (P\(_i\)) product --- P\(_i\) has
more resonance forms than the terminal phosphate of ATP 3.
\textbf{Hydration} (solvation enthalpy) of P\(_i\) and ADP --- products
are better hydrated than reactants 4. \textbf{Entropy increase} --- one
molecule becomes two

ATP couples exergonic reactions to endergonic ones via
\textbf{phosphoryl group transfer}. The cell maintains a very high
ATP/ADP ratio (about 10 in most cells; ATP about 3--5
mM, ADP about 0.5 mM), keeping the cellular \(\Delta G\) of
hydrolysis more negative than \(\Delta G^{\circ\prime}\).

\textbf{Daily ATP turnover:} A resting adult uses about 40 kg
of ATP per day (body contains about 50 g at any time, so each ATP
molecule is recycled about 800 times/day). During vigorous
exercise, ATP turnover can reach about 0.5 kg/min --- roughly
the body's mass in ATP equivalents flowing through the adenylate pool
every two hours.

\subsection{Glycolysis}\label{glycolysis}

Glycolysis (Greek: \emph{glykys} = sweet; \emph{lysis} = splitting)
converts one glucose (6C) to two pyruvate (3C), netting 2 ATP and 2
NADH. It occurs in the \textbf{\hyperref[gl:cytoplasm]{cytoplasm}} of
most cells and does not require oxygen.

\end{figure}

\emph{The 10 steps of glycolysis (Mermaid).} The energy investment phase
(steps 1--5) consumes 2 ATP. The energy payoff phase (steps 6--10)
produces 4 ATP and 2 NADH. The three irreversible steps (1, 3, 10) are
the regulatory control points.

\textbf{Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (F2,6BP)} is the most potent activator
of PFK-1 (lowers \(K_m\) for F6P by 50-fold). It is produced by
\textbf{PFK-2} (a bifunctional enzyme with both kinase and phosphatase
domains). Insulin activates PFK-2 kinase activity (producing F2,6BP,
stimulating glycolysis). Glucagon (via PKA) activates PFK-2 phosphatase
activity (destroying F2,6BP, inhibiting glycolysis in liver).

\subsubsection{Energy Accounting}\label{energy-accounting}

Net output from 1 glucose: - 2 ATP (from steps 7 and 10, minus 2 ATP
consumed at steps 1 and 3) - 2 NADH (from step 6; each NADH worth
about 2.5 ATP via oxidative phosphorylation in
\hyperref[gl:aerobic]{\textbf{aerobic}} conditions)

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: The Warburg Effect} Cancer cells often
exhibit the \textbf{Warburg effect} --- high rates of glycolysis even in
the presence of oxygen (``aerobic glycolysis''). Rather than fully
oxidising glucose to CO\(_2\) via the TCA cycle and ETC, cancer cells
convert most glucose to lactate. This seems wasteful (2 ATP vs.~30--32
ATP per glucose), but it provides rapid ATP production and generates
biosynthetic precursors (G6P for pentose phosphate pathway, 3PG for
serine biosynthesis) needed for rapid cell division. PET scanning
exploits this by detecting tumour uptake of
\(^{18}\)F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG). see
\cref{sec:unit_III_metabolic_integration} for metabolic integration.
\end{quote}

reactions proceed in vivo despite being thermodynamically unfavourable
under standard conditions?
\end{quote}

\subsection{Gluconeogenesis: Reverse But Not the
Reverse}\label{gluconeogenesis-reverse-but-not-the-reverse}

Gluconeogenesis is \emph{not} glycolysis run backwards. Three glycolytic
steps (hexokinase, PFK-1, pyruvate kinase) are \textbf{physiologically
irreversible} in the forward direction --- their cellular \(\Delta G\)
values are too negative. Gluconeogenesis bypasses each of these three
steps with dedicated enzymes that use different chemistry, often paying
additional ATP/GTP to make the reverse direction thermodynamically
favourable.

\subsubsection{The Four Bypass
Reactions}\label{the-four-bypass-reactions}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0049_c71600fa6e4f.png}
\caption{Flowchart for The Four Bypass Reactions: Pyruvate (mitochondrion), Oxaloacetate, Malate, and Malate (cytoplasm) form the diagram's primary path or branches.}
\end{figure}

\emph{Gluconeogenesis from pyruvate to glucose (Mermaid).} Four bypass
enzymes (pyruvate carboxylase, PEPCK, FBPase-1, G6Pase) replace the
three irreversible glycolytic steps. The pyruvate-to-PEP conversion
requires two enzymes --- pyruvate carboxylase consumes ATP and PEPCK
consumes GTP --- so the bypass spans two energy-consuming steps.

\subsubsection{The Four Bypass Enzymes in
Detail}\label{the-four-bypass-enzymes-in-detail}

\textbf{1. Pyruvate carboxylase (PC):} A mitochondrial biotin-dependent
carboxylase that converts pyruvate + CO\(_2\) + ATP \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} oxaloacetate + ADP
+ P\(_i\). Two key features: (a) \textbf{allosterically activated by
acetyl-CoA}, providing a feed-forward signal that fat oxidation (which
produces acetyl-CoA) supplies the OAA needed for both gluconeogenesis
and TCA flux; (b) requires biotin as a covalently bound prosthetic group
that carries the activated CO\(_2\) (--N--COO\(^-\)). Biotin deficiency
(rare; most often from chronic raw-egg consumption due to avidin)
disrupts pyruvate carboxylase and three other carboxylases
simultaneously, producing lactic acidosis and ketogenic dysregulation.

\textbf{2. PEPCK (phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase):} A cytosolic (and
partially mitochondrial) GTP-dependent decarboxylase that converts OAA +
GTP \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PEP + CO\(_2\) + GDP. This enzyme is unusual among gluconeogenic
enzymes in that it is regulated almost entirely at the level of
\emph{transcription} --- glucagon (via cAMP\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}PKA\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}CREB) and cortisol (via
the glucocorticoid receptor) potently induce PEPCK mRNA, while insulin
(via FoxO1 phosphorylation and exclusion from the nucleus) potently
represses it. PEPCK transcription has a half-time of about 1
hour, making it a slow but powerful long-term switch.

\textbf{3. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (FBPase-1):} Cytosolic
phosphatase that converts F1,6BP + H\(_2\)O \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} F6P + P\(_i\)
(\(\Delta G^{\circ\prime} = -16.3\) kJ/mol). Critically regulated
\textbf{allosterically} by F2,6BP (strong inhibitor) and AMP (inhibitor)
--- both signals of glycolytic demand or low energy. The same F2,6BP
that \emph{activates} PFK-1 \emph{inhibits} FBPase-1, so a single second
messenger flips the entire futile-cycle node.

\textbf{4. Glucose-6-phosphatase (G6Pase):} A 9-transmembrane-helix
protein whose catalytic site faces the \textbf{lumen of the endoplasmic
reticulum}, accessed by a phosphate transporter (SLC37A4) and a glucose
efflux transporter (GLUT2). Critically, G6Pase is expressed almost
exclusively in \textbf{liver and renal cortex} --- muscle and brain lack
it, which is why these tissues cannot release free glucose to the blood
even though they produce G6P internally. Mutations in G6Pase cause
\textbf{von Gierke disease (GSD I)}: severe fasting hypoglycaemia with
hepatomegaly.

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4167}}

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

Pyruvate kinase & \textbf{Pyruvate carboxylase} + \textbf{PEPCK} & +1

(hydrolysis is exergonic) & Cytoplasm \\

is exergonic) & ER lumen (liver, kidney primarily) \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Net cost:} Synthesising one glucose from two pyruvate consumes
\textbf{6 ATP equivalents} (2 ATP at pyruvate carboxylase \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 2, 2 GTP at
PEPCK \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 2, 2 ATP at PGK \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 2 in the reverse direction). This is why
gluconeogenesis is restricted to tissues with substantial ATP-generating
capacity (liver, renal cortex).

\subsubsection{Reciprocal Regulation}\label{reciprocal-regulation}

The same allosteric and hormonal signals that activate glycolysis
inhibit gluconeogenesis, ensuring the two pathways do not run as a
futile cycle:

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3600}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5200}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Signal
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Glycolysis (PFK-1)
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Gluconeogenesis (FBPase-1)
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate & Strong activator & Strong inhibitor \\
AMP & Activator & Inhibitor \\
Citrate & Inhibitor & Activator \\
Acetyl-CoA & (no direct effect) & Activates pyruvate carboxylase \\
Insulin & \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\uparrow}}{up} PFK-2 kinase \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\uparrow}}{up} F2,6BP \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} glycolysis ON & \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\downarrow}}{down} PEPCK / G6Pase
transcription \\
Glucagon & \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\uparrow}}{up} PFK-2 phosphatase \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\downarrow}}{down} F2,6BP \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} glycolysis OFF & \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\uparrow}}{up} PEPCK /
G6Pase transcription \\
\end{longtable}
}

Glucagon-driven phosphorylation of PFK-2/FBPase-2 simultaneously turns
\emph{off} PFK-1 (glycolysis) and turns \emph{on} FBPase-1
(gluconeogenesis) by destroying F2,6BP. This is a textbook example of
how a single bifunctional enzyme can act as a metabolic switch.

Explain the contribution of renal gluconeogenesis to whole-body glucose
