\subsection{The Cori Cycle and the Glucose-Alanine
Cycle}\label{the-cori-cycle-and-the-glucose-alanine-cycle}

Inter-organ metabolism allows tissues to specialise: muscle generates
ATP rapidly via glycolysis, while liver shoulders the gluconeogenic
burden. Two complementary inter-organ shuttles dominate fasting and
exercise physiology.

\subsubsection{The Cori Cycle (Lactate
Shuttle)}\label{the-cori-cycle-lactate-shuttle}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0050_bd9d9e663fc5.png}
\caption{Flowchart for The Cori Cycle (Lactate Shuttle): Skeletal muscle / RBCs, Glucose, Lactate, and Bloodstream form the diagram's primary path or branches.}
\end{figure}

\emph{Cori cycle: lactate from anaerobic muscle is regenerated to
glucose in the liver (Mermaid).} Each turn nets +2 ATP for muscle but \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}6
ATP for liver, a 4-ATP net loss to the organism --- the metabolic cost
of supporting hypoxic tissue.

\subsubsection{The Glucose-Alanine
Cycle}\label{the-glucose-alanine-cycle}

When muscle proteins are catabolised, branched-chain amino acid carbon
skeletons donate amino groups to pyruvate, forming \textbf{alanine}.
Alanine carries both carbon and nitrogen safely to the liver:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Muscle: Pyruvate + Glutamate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Alanine + \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-Ketoglutarate (alanine
  aminotransferase)
\item
  Alanine travels via blood to liver
\item
  Liver: Alanine + \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-KG \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Pyruvate + Glutamate (alanine
  aminotransferase, reverse)
\item
  Glutamate releases NH\(_4^+\) into the urea cycle; pyruvate enters
  gluconeogenesis
\item
  Glucose returns to muscle via blood
\end{enumerate}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0051_fd7bc334878a.png}
\caption{Flowchart for The Glucose-Alanine Cycle: Skeletal muscle, Branched-chain amino acid catabolism, -NH2 to pyruvate, and Pyruvate form the diagram's primary path or branches.}
\end{figure}

\emph{Glucose-alanine cycle: alanine simultaneously carries
gluconeogenic carbon and waste nitrogen from muscle to liver (Mermaid).}
The liver disposes of NH\(_4^+\) via the urea cycle and exports glucose
back to muscle.

\textbf{Why this is clever:} Alanine simultaneously transports
gluconeogenic carbon and waste nitrogen, replacing the need for two
separate transport systems. It also keeps free ammonia (toxic to the
brain) out of circulation --- nitrogen is delivered directly to the
urea-cycling liver.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 3:} During an acute sprint, muscle lactate output
rises from 1 mM/min to 8 mM/min. Estimate the additional hepatic ATP
demand (in ATP equivalents per minute) required to recycle this lactate
via the Cori cycle, assuming most lactate reaches the liver.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Pyruvate Oxidation and the Citric Acid
Cycle}\label{pyruvate-oxidation-and-the-citric-acid-cycle}

Under aerobic conditions, pyruvate enters the mitochondria (via the MPC,
mitochondrial pyruvate carrier) and is oxidised.

\subsubsection{Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex
(PDC)}\label{pyruvate-dehydrogenase-complex-pdc}

\[\text{Pyruvate (3C)} + \text{CoA} + \text{NAD}^+ \rightarrow \text{Acetyl-CoA (2C)} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{NADH} \tag{9.8}\]

Catalysed by PDC --- a 9.5 MDa multienzyme complex with three catalytic
components (E1: pyruvate dehydrogenase; E2: dihydrolipoyl
transacetylase; E3: dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase) using \textbf{five
cofactors}: TPP (thiamine pyrophosphate, vitamin B\(_1\)), lipoic acid,
FAD (vitamin B\(_2\)), NAD\(^+\) (vitamin B\(_3\)), CoA (vitamin
B\(_5\)).

\textbf{PDC regulation:}

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3000}}@{}}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: PDC Deficiency} Pyruvate dehydrogenase
deficiency is the most common genetic cause of lactic acidosis. Without
PDC, pyruvate cannot enter the TCA cycle and is instead reduced to
lactate. Neurological damage results from the brain's dependence on
glucose oxidation. Treatment: \textbf{ketogenic diet} (high fat, very
low carbohydrate) provides acetyl-CoA directly from fatty acid
beta-oxidation, bypassing the PDC block. Dichloroacetate (DCA) inhibits
PDK, keeping residual PDC active.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{TCA Cycle (Krebs Cycle / Citric Acid
Cycle)}\label{tca-cycle-krebs-cycle-citric-acid-cycle}

The TCA cycle occurs in the mitochondrial matrix. It oxidises acetyl-CoA
to CO\(_2\), generating reduced cofactors (NADH, FADH\(_2\)) that feed
the ETC.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0052_4baeb11d3a60.png}
\caption{Flowchart for TCA Cycle (Krebs Cycle / Citric Acid Cycle): Oxaloacetate (4C), Citrate (6C), Isocitrate (6C), and alpha-Ketoglutarate (5C) form the diagram's primary path or branches.}
\end{figure}

\emph{The eight steps of the TCA cycle (Mermaid).} Each turn oxidises
one acetyl group (2C) to 2 CO\(_2\), producing 3 NADH, 1 FADH\(_2\), and
1 GTP. The cycle turns twice per glucose molecule.

\textbf{Eight steps with details:}

\end{longtable}

\textbf{Carbon tracking:} The two carbons entering as acetyl-CoA are NOT
the same two carbons lost as CO\(_2\) in the first turn --- they are
released in subsequent turns. This can be demonstrated using
\(^{14}\)C-labelled acetyl-CoA.

\textbf{Net per turn:} 3 NADH + 1 FADH\(_2\) + 1 GTP + 2 CO\(_2\)

\textbf{Total from 2 turns (per glucose):} 6 NADH + 2 FADH\(_2\) + 2 GTP
+ 4 CO\(_2\)

\subsubsection{Anaplerotic and Cataplerotic
Reactions}\label{anaplerotic-and-cataplerotic-reactions}

The TCA cycle is not a closed loop in vivo --- intermediates flow in and
out for biosynthesis. \textbf{Anaplerotic} (``filling-up'') reactions
replenish drained intermediates; \textbf{cataplerotic} (``emptying'')
reactions remove intermediates for downstream pathways.

\textbf{Major anaplerotic inputs:}

Pyruvate carboxylase is \textbf{allosterically activated by acetyl-CoA}.
This is biologically elegant: when acetyl-CoA accumulates (high fat
oxidation, fed state) and OAA becomes limiting, the cell senses the
imbalance and replenishes OAA so that citrate synthase can continue.

\textbf{Glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH)} catalyses the reversible
deamination of glutamate to \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-ketoglutarate, releasing NH\(_4^+\). It
uses \emph{either} NAD\(^+\) (catabolic direction) or NADP\(^+\)
(anabolic direction) and is allosterically regulated by ADP (activator)
and GTP (inhibitor) --- making it a sensor of mitochondrial energy
state. In hepatocytes, GDH-driven glutamate catabolism feeds \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-KG into
the TCA cycle and NH\(_4^+\) into the urea cycle, integrating amino-acid
catabolism with both energy production and nitrogen disposal.

\textbf{Major cataplerotic outflows:}

\textbf{Clinical connection --- biotin deficiency:} Because pyruvate
carboxylase, propionyl-CoA carboxylase, and acetyl-CoA carboxylase most
depend on biotin, dietary biotin deficiency (rare; sometimes seen with
chronic raw-egg consumption due to avidin) causes lactic acidosis,
neurological symptoms, and ketogenic dysregulation simultaneously.

\subsection{Oxidative Phosphorylation}\label{oxidative-phosphorylation}

Oxidative phosphorylation (OxPhos) accounts for about 90\% of
ATP production in aerobic organisms. It takes place at the inner
mitochondrial membrane.

\subsubsection{Electron Transport Chain
(ETC)}\label{electron-transport-chain-etc}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0053_648c8b0187e7.png}
\caption{Sequence diagram for Electron Transport Chain (ETC) showing ordered interaction among NADH (matrix), Complex I (NADH:UQ oxidoreductase) 46 subunits, 1 MDa Pumps 4 H+, Ubiquinone (Q) Lipid-soluble mobile carrier, and Complex II (Succinate DH) 4 subunits No H+ pumping.}
\end{figure}

\emph{Electron flow through the ETC complexes I--IV and proton pumping
that generates the proton motive force (Mermaid).} ATP synthase (Complex
V) uses this PMF to synthesise ATP via rotary catalysis.

\textbf{Complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase):} - Largest ETC
complex (about 46 subunits in mammals, about 1 MDa) -
L-shaped structure: hydrophilic arm in matrix (electron transfer),
membrane arm (proton pumping) - Electron path: NADH \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} FMN \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} 7 Fe-S
clusters \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} ubiquinone (Q) - Pumps \textbf{4 H\(^+\)} per NADH oxidised -
Inhibited by \textbf{rotenone} (fish poison, pesticide) and
\textbf{piericidin A}

\textbf{Complex II (succinate:ubiquinone oxidoreductase):} - Also is
step 6 of the TCA cycle (succinate dehydrogenase) - 4 subunits; FAD
covalently bound - Electron path: succinate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} FAD \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Fe-S clusters \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
ubiquinone (Q) - Pumps \textbf{0 H\(^+\)} (insufficient energy from
FADH\(_2\) oxidation to pump protons) - This is why FADH\(_2\) yields
less ATP than NADH

\textbf{Complex III (cytochrome bc\(_1\) complex):} - The \textbf{Q
cycle} mechanism (Mitchell, Nobel Prize 1978) \citep{mitchell1961}: 1.
QH\(_2\) binds Q\(_o\) site; one electron goes to Fe-S cluster \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
cytochrome c\(_1\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} cytochrome c (high potential path) 2. Second
electron goes to cytochrome b\(_L\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} cytochrome b\(_H\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Q at Q\(_i\)
site, forming Q\(^{\bullet-}\) (semiquinone) 3. Second QH\(_2\) repeats;
second electron to Q\(_i\) completes QH\(_2\) formation 4. Net: 2
QH\(_2\) oxidised, 1 Q reduced, 2 cytochrome c reduced, \textbf{4
H\(^+\) pumped per 2e\(^-\)} - Inhibited by \textbf{antimycin A}
(Q\(_i\) site) and \textbf{myxothiazol} (Q\(_o\) site)

\textbf{Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase):} - Contains Cu\(_A\), heme a,
heme a\(_3\)-Cu\(_B\) centres - Transfers 4 electrons to O\(_2\):
\(\text{O}_2 + 4\text{e}^- + 4\text{H}^+_{\text{matrix}} \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\)
- Pumps \textbf{2 H\(^+\) per 2 electrons} (plus 2 H\(^+\) consumed in
water formation) - Inhibited by \textbf{cyanide} (CN\(^-\)),
\textbf{carbon monoxide} (CO), and \textbf{azide} (N\(_3^-\)) --- most
bind heme a\(_3\)-Cu\(_B\)

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Cyanide Poisoning} Cyanide irreversibly
inhibits Complex IV by binding to the Fe\(^{3+}\) of heme a\(_3\). Most
electron flow stops, the proton gradient collapses, and ATP synthesis
ceases. Cells switch to \hyperref[gl:anaerobic]{\textbf{anaerobic}}
glycolysis, producing lactic acid. Death results from inability to
produce sufficient ATP, especially in the brain and heart. Treatment:
hydroxocobalamin (vitamin B\(_{12a}\)) chelates cyanide, or sodium
thiosulphate converts it to less toxic thiocyanate.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Reactive Oxygen Species and Antioxidant
Defence}\label{reactive-oxygen-species-and-antioxidant-defence}

The ETC's job is to deliver four electrons safely onto O\(_2\) to
produce water --- but about 0.1--2\% of electrons ``leak''
prematurely, producing \textbf{reactive oxygen species (ROS)}.

\textbf{Sites of ROS production in the ETC:}

\textbf{The ROS cascade:}

\begin{equation}
\text{O}_2 \xrightarrow{1\text{e}^-} \text{O}_2^{\bullet-} \xrightarrow{\text{SOD}} \text{H}_2\text{O}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Fe}^{2+}} \text{HO}^\bullet + \text{OH}^- + \text{Fe}^{3+}
\label{eq:unit_III_ros_cascade}
\end{equation}

The Fenton reaction (last step) is particularly dangerous: hydroxyl
radicals (HO\(^\bullet\)) are the most reactive biological oxidants and
damage essentially any nearby molecule (DNA, lipids, proteins).

\textbf{Non-enzymatic antioxidants:} Glutathione (GSH; about 5
mM cytosolic), ascorbate (vitamin C), \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-tocopherol (vitamin E,
lipid-soluble), ubiquinone (also acts as antioxidant in its reduced
QH\(_2\) form), and uric acid (about 50\% of plasma antioxidant
capacity in humans).

\textbf{Clinical relevance:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Mitochondrial diseases:} Complex I and III deficiencies often
  present with elevated lactate AND elevated ROS damage markers
  (8-oxoguanine in mtDNA, malondialdehyde in lipids).
\item
  \textbf{Aging (mitochondrial free-radical theory):} Cumulative mtDNA
  damage from ROS may underlie age-related mitochondrial decline. Modern
  data suggests ROS are also signalling molecules, complicating the
  simple ``oxidative damage = aging'' model.
\item
  \textbf{Reperfusion injury:} During ischaemia, ETC carriers become
  highly reduced. Upon reoxygenation, a burst of ROS is released ---
  paradoxically, the \emph{return} of oxygen causes the worst tissue
  damage in stroke and heart attack.
\item
  \textbf{ALS:} Mutations in SOD1 cause about 20\% of familial
  amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The pathology is gain-of-function
  (toxic SOD1 aggregates), not simple loss of antioxidant activity.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{ATP Synthase --- the Rotary
Nanomotor}\label{atp-synthase-the-rotary-nanomotor}

The \textbf{proton-motive force} (PMF) consists of two components ---
the electrical potential (\(\Delta\Psi\)) and the chemical gradient
(\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Delta}}{Delta}pH):

\begin{equation}
\text{PMF} = \Delta\Psi - \frac{2.303RT}{F}\Delta\text{pH} \approx 180 \; \text{mV}
\label{eq:unit_III_proton_motive_force}
\end{equation}

In mitochondria, \(\Delta\Psi \approx 150\) mV contributes
about 80\% of the PMF, while \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Delta}}{Delta}pH about 0.5 units
contributes about 20\%.

The free energy stored per mole of protons translocated against this PMF
is:

\[\Delta G_{\text{H}^+} = F \cdot \text{PMF} \approx 96{,}485 \times 0.180 \approx 17.4 \; \text{kJ/mol} \tag{9.7d}\]

So pumping about 3.67 H\(^+\) to make one ATP requires
about 64 kJ/mol of stored gradient energy --- the budget that
funds an ATP whose cellular hydrolysis \(\Delta G \approx -54\) kJ/mol.
The about 10 kJ/mol surplus is the thermodynamic driving force
that keeps net ATP synthesis flowing forward and sets the response time
of the system to ATP demand.

\textbf{ATP synthase (Complex V)} is a molecular rotary motor:

\textbf{F\(_1\) (catalytic head, matrix-facing):} -
alpha\(_3\)-beta\(_3\)-gamma-delta-epsilon - Three catalytic sites on
beta subunits (binding change mechanism, Boyer) - Each beta subunit
cycles through three states: \textbf{O} (open, empty), \textbf{L}
(loose, binds ADP + P\(_i\)), \textbf{T} (tight, catalyses ATP
synthesis) - 120-degree rotation of gamma converts O\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}L\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}T\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}O

\textbf{F\(_0\) (membrane-spanning proton channel):} - Subunit a (proton
channel) + c-ring (c\(_{10-15}\), varies by species) - Each c-subunit
binds one H\(^+\) from IMS, rotates, releases H\(^+\) to matrix - Full
c-ring rotation (360 degrees) produces 3 ATP

\textbf{Stoichiometry:} If the c-ring has 10 subunits, then 10 H\(^+\)
per revolution, producing 3 ATP, so about 3.3 H\(^+\) per ATP.
With 8 c-subunits (yeast), about 2.7 H\(^+\) per ATP.

Paul Boyer (binding change mechanism) and John Walker (crystal structure
of F\(_1\)) shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 1997. The rotation of
the gamma subunit was directly visualised by Yoshida and colleagues
using fluorescent \hyperref[gl:actin]{\textbf{actin}} filaments attached
to gamma --- one of the most beautiful experiments in biochemistry.

\subsubsection{How the ``30--32 ATP'' Number Is Calculated: P/O
Ratios}\label{how-the-3032-atp-number-is-calculated-po-ratios}

The classical undergraduate value of 38 ATP/glucose came from
\emph{assumed} round-number stoichiometries (3 ATP/NADH, 2
ATP/FADH\(_2\), 1 ATP per substrate-level step). Modern biochemistry
uses \textbf{measured P/O ratios} based on actual c-ring stoichiometry
and proton transport:

\textbf{Proton pumping per substrate:}

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1579}}

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1930}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1754}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3158}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Substrate
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Complex I
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

1 NADH (matrix) & 4 & 4 & 2 & \textbf{10 H\(^+\)} \\
1 FADH\(_2\) (Complex II) & 0 & 4 & 2 & \textbf{6 H\(^+\)} \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Mammalian mitochondrial c-ring:} 8 subunits (recent cryo-EM
data). \textbf{ATP synthase stoichiometry:} 8 H\(^+\) per full
revolution \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} 3 ATP per revolution \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{2.67 H\(^+\)/ATP}.
\textbf{Add P\(_i\) transport:} importing P\(_i\) via the phosphate
carrier costs \textbf{1 additional H\(^+\)} per ATP. So the
\emph{effective} H\(^+\) cost per ATP is approximately \textbf{3.67
H\(^+\)/ATP}.

\begin{equation}
\text{P/O ratio (NADH)} = \frac{10\;\text{H}^+}{3.67\;\text{H}^+/\text{ATP}} \approx 2.5\;\text{ATP per NADH}
\label{eq:unit_III_po_ratio_nadh}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
\text{P/O ratio (FADH}_2\text{)} = \frac{6\;\text{H}^+}{3.67\;\text{H}^+/\text{ATP}} \approx 1.5\;\text{ATP per FADH}_2
\label{eq:unit_III_po_ratio_fadh2}
\end{equation}

\textbf{Total ATP per glucose (aerobic):}

\begin{equation}
\text{ATP}_{\text{glucose}} = \underbrace{2}_{\text{glycolysis SLP}} + \underbrace{2}_{\text{TCA SLP (2 GTP)}} + \underbrace{10 \times 2.5}_{\text{NADH via OxPhos}} + \underbrace{2 \times 1.5}_{\text{FADH}_2\text{ via OxPhos}} \approx 32\;\text{ATP}
\label{eq:unit_III_atp_yield}
\end{equation}

(if cytoplasmic NADH uses the malate-aspartate shuttle;
about 30 ATP if the glycerol-3-P shuttle is used in muscle and
brain).

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}llllll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Stage & NADH & FADH\(_2\) & ATP direct & ATP via OxPhos & Subtotal \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Glycolysis & 2 & 0 & 2 & 2 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 2.5 = 5* & 7 \\
Pyruvate oxidation & 2 & 0 & 0 & 2 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 2.5 = 5 & 5 \\
TCA cycle & 6 & 2 & 2 & 6 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 2.5 + 2 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 1.5 = 18 & 20 \\

\end{longtable}
}

*Glycolytic NADH yields 2.5 ATP (malate-aspartate shuttle) or 1.5 ATP
(glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle), giving 30 or 32 ATP total.

\textbf{The glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle vs.~malate-aspartate shuttle:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Cytoplasmic NADH cannot cross the IMM directly.
\item
  \textbf{Malate-aspartate shuttle} (liver, heart, kidney): NADH
  electrons enter the matrix via OAA\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}malate\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}OAA at full reducing
  potential \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{2.5 ATP each}.
\item
  \textbf{Glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle} (skeletal muscle, brain): NADH
  electrons enter directly into Q via FAD-linked mitochondrial G3PDH \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  \textbf{1.5 ATP each} (skips Complex I).
\end{itemize}

\emph{Solution:}

The thermodynamic efficiency:

\[\eta = \frac{32 \times 30.5}{2{,}870} \times 100\% = 34\% \tag{9.10}\]

Using the more realistic \emph{cellular} \(\Delta G\) of \(-50\) kJ/mol,
efficiency rises to about 56\%, comparable to the best internal
combustion engines and considerably better than most human-engineered
energy converters.

\textbf{Quantitative leverage:} Although substrate-level phosphorylation
contributes roughly 12.5\% of total ATP in this accounting, it is
critical in two scenarios:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Anaerobic conditions:} It is the \emph{primarily} source of
  ATP, so 4 ATP/glucose is everything.
\item
  \textbf{Sprint exercise:} It can produce ATP in milliseconds, before
  mitochondrial respiration ramps up; the phosphocreatine system extends
  this further.
\end{enumerate}

This illustrates why metabolic systems are layered: fast-but-low-yield
substrate-level phosphorylation handles transients while
slow-but-high-yield OxPhos handles steady state.

\textbf{Numerical leverage at the organism level.} A 70 kg adult at rest
uses about 1,400 kcal/day, equivalent to about 250 mol
ATP turned over. If primarily substrate-level phosphorylation operated,
with about 4 ATP/glucose, the body would need to oxidise
about 62 mol glucose/day (= 11 kg). Aerobic OxPhos at
about 32 ATP/glucose reduces the requirement to
about 8 mol = 1.4 kg glucose/day --- a more achievable dietary
intake. The 8-fold yield improvement of OxPhos is precisely what enables
active multicellular life on a planet with bulk-food-supply constraints.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Fermentation}\label{fermentation}

Without O\(_2\) (or in cells that lack mitochondria), pyruvate is not
oxidised aerobically. Instead, \textbf{fermentation} regenerates
NAD\(^+\) so glycolysis can continue:

\textbf{Alcoholic fermentation} (yeast, some bacteria):
\[\text{Pyruvate} \xrightarrow[\text{TPP}]{\text{pyruvate decarboxylase}} \text{Acetaldehyde} + \text{CO}_2 \xrightarrow[\text{NADH} \rightarrow \text{NAD}^+]{\text{alcohol dehydrogenase}} \text{Ethanol} \tag{9.11}\]

\textbf{Lactic acid fermentation} (muscle, erythrocytes,
\emph{Lactobacillus}):
\[\text{Pyruvate} + \text{NADH} \xrightarrow{\text{lactate dehydrogenase}} \text{Lactate} + \text{NAD}^+ \tag{9.12}\]

Both pathways yield primarily \textbf{2 ATP per glucose} (from
glycolysis alone).

\textbf{The Cori Cycle:} In exercising muscle, lactate is exported to
the blood, taken up by the liver, and converted back to glucose via
\textbf{gluconeogenesis} at the cost of 6 ATP. This glucose returns to
the muscle via the blood. The Cori cycle shifts the metabolic burden of
gluconeogenesis from the oxygen-limited muscle to the well-oxygenated
liver.

\textbf{Pasteur Effect:} In the presence of oxygen, yeast switches from
fermentation to aerobic respiration, dramatically reducing glucose
consumption (because 32 ATP/glucose aerobically vs.~2 ATP/glucose by
fermentation --- 16x more efficient).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Lactic Acidosis} Lactic acidosis occurs
when lactate production exceeds clearance. \textbf{Type A} (most
common): tissue hypoxia (shock, cardiac arrest, severe anaemia) forces
reliance on glycolysis. \textbf{Type B}: metabolic causes (liver failure
preventing lactate clearance, metformin in renal impairment, thiamine
deficiency preventing PDC function, mitochondrial diseases). Blood
lactate \textgreater4 mmol/L with pH \textless7.35 indicates lactic
acidosis. Treatment focuses on addressing the underlying cause and
restoring tissue oxygenation.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Mitochondrial Complex Disorders}
\hyperref[gl:mutation]{\textbf{Mutation}}s in nuclear or mitochondrial
\hyperref[gl:gene]{\textbf{gene}}s encoding ETC complex subunits cause a
spectrum of diseases: - \textbf{Complex I deficiency:} Most common ETC
disorder (about 30\% of paediatric mitochondrial disease);
Leigh syndrome (necrotising encephalopathy), optic atrophy,
cardiomyopathy - \textbf{Complex II deficiency:} Rare; associated with
paragangliomas and pheochromocytomas (SDH mutations are tumour
suppressors) - \textbf{Complex III deficiency:} Exercise intolerance,
lactic acidosis - \textbf{Complex IV (COX) deficiency:} Leigh syndrome,
cardiomyopathy; reversible COX deficiency in infants Most are
characterised by lactic acidosis, neurological dysfunction, and exercise
intolerance --- tissues with high energy demands (brain, heart, muscle)
are most affected.
\end{quote}

respiration (via Complex II) to be normal or impaired in this patient?

\end{quote}

\subsection{Uncoupling Proteins and Brown Adipose
Thermogenesis}\label{uncoupling-proteins-and-brown-adipose-thermogenesis}

In most cells, the primary ``exit'' for protons in the IMS back to the
matrix is through ATP synthase. \textbf{Uncoupling proteins (UCPs)}
provide an alternative path that dissipates the proton gradient as heat
--- uncoupling electron transport from ATP synthesis.

\subsubsection{UCP1: The Brown Adipose
Thermogenin}\label{ucp1-the-brown-adipose-thermogenin}

\textbf{Structure:} UCP1 is a 32-kDa, six-transmembrane-helix protein in
the IMM of brown adipocytes. It belongs to the SLC25 mitochondrial
carrier family.

\textbf{Mechanism (proton transport, not pure leak):}

\begin{equation}
\text{H}^+_{\text{IMS}} + \text{FA}^- \xrightarrow{\text{UCP1}} \text{H}^+_{\text{matrix}} + \text{FA}^-
\label{eq:unit_III_ucp1_mechanism}
\end{equation}

Long-chain fatty acid anions (FA\(^-\)) act as cofactors: they bind
H\(^+\) in the IMS, traverse the membrane via UCP1, and release H\(^+\)
in the matrix. UCP1 is \textbf{inhibited by purine nucleotides} (ATP,
ADP, GTP, GDP) and \textbf{activated by fatty acids} released from
intracellular triglyceride stores.

\textbf{Activation cascade in brown adipose tissue (BAT):}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0054_6fd41e09a5eb.png}
\caption{Flowchart for UCP1: The Brown Adipose Thermogenin: Norepinephrine (cold, sympathetic activation), beta3-adrenergic receptor, Adenylyl cyclase, and increased cAMP form the diagram's primary path or branches.}
\end{figure}

\emph{Sympathetic activation of brown adipose thermogenesis (Mermaid).}
Norepinephrine binds \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}\(_3\)-adrenergic receptors \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} cAMP \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PKA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
simultaneous lipolysis (acute fuel) and PGC-1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha} transcription (chronic
mitochondrial biogenesis). UCP1 short-circuits the proton gradient,
releasing energy as heat.

\subsubsection{Physiological Roles}\label{physiological-roles}

\textbf{Hibernating mammals} & Massive BAT depots maintain

\textbf{Cold acclimation} & Chronic cold exposure increases BAT mass and

\textbf{Other UCPs:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{UCP2}: ubiquitously expressed; modest uncoupling activity;
  thought to attenuate ROS and modulate insulin secretion.
\item
  \textbf{UCP3}: skeletal muscle and BAT; possible role in lipid
  handling; debated thermogenic relevance.
\item
  \textbf{Plant UCPs} (PUMPs): present in mitochondria of
  e.g.~\emph{Arum} species, where they generate the heat
  (about 46 °C) that volatilises odours to attract pollinator
  insects.
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: DNP --- A Cautionary Tale}
2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP) is a synthetic chemical uncoupler that
dissipates PMF as heat, mimicking UCP1 across most tissues. In the
1930s, DNP was sold as a weight-loss drug --- patients lost
about 1 kg/week as their basal metabolic rate increased
about 50\%. But the therapeutic window is dangerously narrow:
at slightly higher doses, body temperature rises to \textgreater40 °C
(fatal hyperthermia), and unregulated tissue uncoupling causes
cataracts, neuropathy, and sudden death. DNP was banned in 1938 but
remains a recurrent source of bodybuilding deaths today. The takeaway:
physiological uncoupling is \emph{regulated} (UCP1 activated primarily
in BAT, primarily on demand) --- pharmacological uncoupling is
unregulated and potentially lethal.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Metabolic Poisons and
Inhibitors}\label{metabolic-poisons-and-inhibitors}

Understanding the ETC and oxidative phosphorylation has been greatly
advanced by studying specific inhibitors and metabolic poisons:

\subsubsection{ETC Inhibitors}\label{etc-inhibitors}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4286}}

\subsubsection{Uncouplers}\label{uncouplers}

\textbf{Uncouplers} dissipate the proton gradient without inhibiting
electron transport, allowing respiration to continue at maximum rate
without ATP production:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP):} A lipid-soluble weak acid; carries
  H\(^+\) across the IMM. Was used as a weight-loss drug in the 1930s
  (burns fat by dissipating energy as heat) but was banned due to narrow
  therapeutic window and fatal hyperthermia.
\item
  \textbf{FCCP/CCCP:} Research uncouplers; commonly used in
  mitochondrial stress tests (Seahorse assays)
\item
  \textbf{Thermogenin (UCP1):} The physiological uncoupler in brown
  adipose tissue, developed in the thermogenesis discussion above.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{ATP Synthase Inhibitors}\label{atp-synthase-inhibitors}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Oligomycin:} Blocks the H\(^+\) channel in the c-ring of
  F\(_0\); prevents H\(^+\) flow and ATP synthesis; also halts electron
  transport (because PMF builds up, preventing further H\(^+\) pumping
  by the ETC)
\item
  \textbf{DCCD (dicyclohexylcarbodiimide):} Reacts with a specific
  Asp/Glu residue in the c-subunit, blocking H\(^+\) translocation
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 7:} If oligomycin is added to mitochondria,
electron transport stops. If DNP (an uncoupler) is then added, electron
transport resumes. Explain these observations in terms of the
chemiosmotic model.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 7b:} A researcher exposes isolated mitochondria
sequentially to: (1) succinate, (2) ADP + P\(_i\), (3) rotenone, (4)
DNP. For each addition, predict whether O\(_2\) consumption increases,
decreases, or stays the same, and explain why --- referring to
\cref{eq:unit_III_proton_motive_force} and \cref{eq:unit_III_atp_yield}.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-11}

For \textbf{Bioenergetics and Cellular Respiration}, frontier biology
belongs inside the evidence logic of the chapter. Metabolism is now
studied as a regulated network constrained by energy, redox balance,
compartmentation, and environment. The core reading question is this:
respiration claims should track electrons, protons, redox poise, ATP
yield, and uncoupling.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

A strong metabolic explanation names the flux, the limiting step, the
sensor, and the condition under which the pathway changes direction or
priority.

\textbf{Source practice:} For metabolic claims, keep the organism,
compartment, energetic state, and measurement method visible; a pathway
map is not enough without flux or concentration evidence.

\subsubsection{Current Evidence Map: Respiration Evidence
Accounting}\label{current-evidence-map-respiration-evidence-accounting}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0055_05d0878efc1f.png}
\caption{ATP-yield claims are conditional on shuttle use, proton leak, coupling efficiency, tissue state, and measurement method rather than one fixed number.}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-11}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\)
  (\cref{eq:unit_III_gibbs_free_energy}); cellular reactions are coupled
  to ATP hydrolysis (\(\Delta G \approx -54\) kJ/mol) to drive
  endergonic processes. Cells maintain far-from-equilibrium conditions.
\item
  ATP turnover is about 40 kg/day; the high \(\Delta G\) of
  hydrolysis arises from charge repulsion, resonance stabilisation, and
  hydration of products. ATP sits in the \emph{middle} of the
  phosphoryl-transfer hierarchy, between very high (PEP, 1,3-BPG) and
  very low (glucose-6-P).
\item
  Glucose oxidation has a standard free energy of \(\approx -2{,}870\)
  kJ/mol; cells capture about 56\% of this as ATP, dissipating
  the rest as heat.
\item
  Glycolysis: 10 cytoplasmic steps; net 2 ATP + 2 NADH per glucose;
  regulated by PFK-1 (activated by AMP, F2,6BP; inhibited by ATP,
  citrate).
\item
  Gluconeogenesis: not the reverse of glycolysis --- uses four bypass
  enzymes (pyruvate carboxylase, PEPCK, FBPase-1, G6Pase) at a cost of 6
  ATP equivalents per glucose; reciprocally regulated with glycolysis
  via F2,6BP.
\item
  The Cori cycle and glucose-alanine cycle distribute metabolic burden
  between muscle and liver, supporting hypoxic tissues at a
  4-ATP-per-glucose net cost to the organism.
\item
  PDC links glycolysis to TCA; regulated by
  phosphorylation/dephosphorylation; deficiency causes lactic acidosis.
\item
  TCA cycle: 8 mitochondrial matrix steps; 6 NADH + 2 FADH\(_2\) + 2 GTP
  per glucose; regulated by isocitrate DH and \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-KG DH; anaplerotic
  (pyruvate carboxylase, glutamate dehydrogenase) and cataplerotic flux
  balance the cycle.
\item
  ETC: Complex I (4 H\(^+\)), II (0 H\(^+\)), III (4 H\(^+\) via Q
  cycle), IV (2 H\(^+\)); final electron acceptor = O\(_2\). Modest
  electron leak produces ROS (\cref{eq:unit_III_ros_cascade}); SOD,
  catalase, GPx, and peroxiredoxins constrain damage.
\item
  ATP synthase: F\(_0\)F\(_1\) rotary motor; binding change mechanism;
  about 3.67 H\(^+\) per ATP (including phosphate import).
  Proton-motive force \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 180 mV (\cref{eq:unit_III_proton_motive_force}).
\item
  Modern ATP yield: about 30--32 ATP per glucose aerobically
  (\cref{eq:unit_III_atp_yield}, \cref{eq:unit_III_po_ratio_nadh},
  \cref{eq:unit_III_po_ratio_fadh2}); 2 ATP per glucose anaerobically.
\item
  Uncoupling proteins (UCP1) regulate physiological thermogenesis in
  brown adipose tissue; pharmacological uncouplers (DNP) dissipate the
  same PMF unregulated and are dangerous.
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See \cref{sec:unit_III_photosynthesis} for
  light-driven phosphorylation,
  \cref{sec:unit_III_metabolic_integration} for hormonal integration,
  and Unit X for ecosystem productivity and reduced carbon.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Review Questions}\label{review-questions-11}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Explain why cells must maintain metabolite concentrations far from
  equilibrium. What would happen to ATP synthesis if the cell reached
  thermodynamic equilibrium?
\item
  Describe most 10 steps of glycolysis. Which three steps are
  irreversible and why are these the regulatory control points?
\item
  Compare the four bypass enzymes of gluconeogenesis with the three
  irreversible glycolytic steps they replace. Why is each bypass
  thermodynamically favourable in the gluconeogenic direction?
\item
  Explain the structure and regulation of the pyruvate dehydrogenase
  complex. Why does it require five cofactors?
\item
  Track the fate of both carbon atoms in acetyl-CoA through one turn of
  the TCA cycle. Are these the same carbons released as CO\(_2\)?
\item
  Distinguish between anaplerotic and cataplerotic reactions. Give two
  examples of each, and explain why pyruvate carboxylase is
  allosterically activated by acetyl-CoA.
\item
  Describe the Q cycle in Complex III. Why is this mechanism necessary,
  and how does it contribute to proton pumping?
\item
  Identify the major ETC sites of ROS production and the antioxidant
  enzymes that detoxify each downstream species. Why is the Fenton
  reaction particularly dangerous?
\item
  Explain the binding change mechanism of ATP synthase. How was the
  rotation of the gamma subunit experimentally demonstrated?
\item
  Calculate the ATP yield from complete oxidation of one molecule of
  glucose via glycolysis, PDC, TCA cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation
  (\cref{eq:unit_III_atp_yield}). Explain why the answer is 30 or 32
  depending on the NADH shuttle used, and trace each number back to
  specific P/O ratios.
\item
  Compare alcoholic and lactic acid fermentation. Why is fermentation
  essential even though it produces far less ATP than aerobic
  respiration?
\item
  Compare physiological (UCP1) and pharmacological (DNP) uncoupling. Why
  does the body tolerate UCP1 activity but not DNP, even though both
  dissipate the same PMF as heat?
\item
  A patient presents with exercise intolerance and lactic acidosis.
  Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the ND1 gene (Complex I
  subunit). Explain the biochemical basis of each symptom.
\item
  Explain the Pasteur effect and the Warburg effect. How do they
  represent opposite metabolic strategies?
\item
  Recompute \texttt{atp\_free\_energy} when cytosolic ATP drops to 1 mM
  while ADP rises to 4 mM (Pi fixed). Does hydrolysis become more or
  less exergonic, and why does that matter during exercise?
\item
  Using \breaktt{glycolysis\_summary()} from the same module, state the
  net ATP and NADH from one glucose without writing most ten steps.
\item
  Using \(\Delta G^{\circ\prime}\) values for ATP and PEP hydrolysis,
  compute the standard free energy change of pyruvate kinase (PEP + ADP
  \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} pyruvate + ATP). Compare with the cellular \(\Delta G\) and explain
  the irreversibility.
\item
  Compute the proton motive force from \(\Delta\Psi = -160\) mV and
  \(\Delta\text{pH} = 0.6\) at 37 °C using
  \cref{eq:unit_III_proton_motive_force}. Convert to free energy per
  mole of protons.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Key Terms}\label{key-terms-11}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2857}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.7143}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Term
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Definition
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Gibbs free energy (\(\Delta G\))} & Thermodynamic quantity
predicting reaction spontaneity; \(\Delta G < 0\) = spontaneous \\
\textbf{ATP} & Adenosine triphosphate; central phosphoryl-group donor
and short-term energy carrier; \(\Delta G\) hydrolysis \(\approx -54\)
kJ/mol (cellular) \\
\textbf{Glycolysis} & 10-step cytoplasmic pathway converting glucose to
2 pyruvate + 2 ATP + 2 NADH \\
\textbf{Gluconeogenesis} & Synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate
precursors using four bypass enzymes; 6 ATP equivalents per glucose \\
\textbf{PFK-1} & Phosphofructokinase-1; committed step of glycolysis;
allosterically regulated \\
\textbf{Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex} & Multienzyme complex linking
glycolysis to TCA; 5 cofactors; regulated by phosphorylation \\
\textbf{TCA cycle} & 8-step mitochondrial cycle oxidising acetyl-CoA;
produces 3 NADH + 1 FADH\(_2\) + 1 GTP per turn \\
\textbf{Anaplerotic reaction} & Reaction replenishing TCA cycle
intermediates (e.g., pyruvate carboxylase) \\
\textbf{Cataplerotic reaction} & Reaction removing TCA intermediates for
biosynthesis (e.g., citrate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} acetyl-CoA for FA synthesis) \\
\textbf{Electron transport chain} & Complexes I--IV on IMM; transfers
electrons from NADH/FADH\(_2\) to O\(_2\), pumping H\(^+\) \\
\textbf{Q cycle} & Complex III mechanism doubling H\(^+\) pumping
efficiency per electron pair \\
\textbf{ATP synthase} & F\(_0\)F\(_1\) rotary motor using PMF to
synthesise ATP; about 3.67 H\(^+\)/ATP including P\(_i\)
import \\
\textbf{Proton motive force (PMF)} & Electrochemical gradient of H\(^+\)
across IMM; \(\approx 180\) mV; drives ATP synthesis \\
\textbf{P/O ratio} & ATP molecules produced per oxygen atom reduced;
about 2.5 for NADH, about 1.5 for FADH\(_2\) \\
\textbf{Reactive oxygen species (ROS)} & O\(_2^{\bullet-}\),
H\(_2\)O\(_2\), HO\(^\bullet\) produced by electron leak; constrained by
SOD, catalase, GPx \\
\textbf{Uncoupling protein (UCP1)} & IMM proton channel in brown adipose
tissue; dissipates PMF as heat \\
\textbf{Fermentation} & Anaerobic regeneration of NAD\(^+\); lactic acid
or ethanol pathways; 2 ATP per glucose \\
\textbf{Cori cycle} & Lactate (muscle) to glucose (liver) shuttle;
shifts gluconeogenic cost to liver \\
\textbf{Glucose-alanine cycle} & Inter-organ shuttle carrying both
carbon and waste nitrogen from muscle to liver \\
\textbf{Warburg effect} & Aerobic glycolysis in cancer cells; rapid ATP
+ biosynthetic precursors despite O\(_2\) \\
\textbf{Substrate-level phosphorylation} & Direct transfer of phosphoryl
group from high-energy intermediate to ADP \\
\end{longtable}
}

\subsection{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-12}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Describe \hyperref[gl:chloroplast]{\textbf{chloroplast}} structure and
  the organisation of the photosynthetic membrane.
\item
  Explain the light-harvesting antenna complexes, chlorophyll a/b ratio,
  and energy transfer mechanisms (FRET, exciton transfer).
\item
  Compute the energy of a photon and convert per-molecule values to
  per-mole values for biological calculations.
\item

\item
  Explain the cytochrome b\(_6\)f complex and the Q cycle in
  chloroplasts.
\item
  Describe Photosystem I, linear and cyclic electron flow, and NADPH
  production.
\item
  Explain the Z-scheme of photosynthetic electron transport, including
  standard electrode potentials of each carrier.
\item
  Describe most three phases of the
  \hyperref[gl:calvin-cycle]{\textbf{Calvin cycle}}, including RuBisCO
  biochemistry, structure (L\(_8\)S\(_8\)), catalytic mechanism, and the
  CO\(_2\)/O\(_2\) specificity factor (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\tau}}{tau}).
\item
  Explain the thioredoxin/ferredoxin redox regulation system and the
  activating role of stromal pH and Mg\(^{2+}\).
\item
  Explain photorespiration and its metabolic costs.
\item
  Compare C3, C4, and CAM
  \hyperref[gl:photosynthesis]{\textbf{photosynthesis}} strategies and
  their water-use efficiency, including quantitative trade-offs.
\item
  Evaluate photoprotection (NPQ, xanthophyll cycle) and artificial
  photosynthesis research as responses to excess light and energy
  demand.
\item
  Calculate ATP and NADPH requirements per CO\(_2\) fixed; compare
  biological and artificial photosynthesis efficiencies.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Opening Vignette: Tracing Carbon From Air to Sugar}

In 1950, Melvin Calvin's team at the Lawrence Berkeley National
Laboratory began exposing algae (\emph{Chlorella}) to \texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{4}}{4}CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} --- carbon
dioxide labelled with radioactive carbon-14 --- for very brief intervals
(as short as 5 seconds), then rapidly killing the cells and separating
their compounds by two-dimensional paper chromatography. By tracking
which molecules became radioactively labelled first, then in which
order, Calvin meticulously traced the path of carbon atoms from
atmospheric CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} through a cycle of enzymatic reactions to eventually
emerge as glucose. The complete cycle --- the
\textbf{Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle} --- was published in 1954, and
Calvin received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry alone in 1961.

The cycle's key \hyperref[gl:enzyme]{\textbf{enzyme}}, \textbf{RuBisCO}
(ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase), is arguably the most
important enzyme on Earth: it is responsible for fixing approximately
10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1} tonnes of atmospheric carbon per year, feeding essentially most
non-chemotrophic life. It is also probably the most abundant
\hyperref[gl:protein]{\textbf{protein}} on Earth (approximately 0.7 kg
per person on the planet's surface, an estimated 7 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{8}}{8} tonnes total),
and notably one of the slowest enzymes known, with a kcat of about 3--10
s\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}. Improving RuBisCO efficiency is one of the holy grails of
agricultural biotechnology.

\emph{Primary source: Calvin, M. \& Benson, A. A. (1948). The path of
carbon in photosynthesis. Science, 107(2784), 476--480.}
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Overview of
Photosynthesis}\label{overview-of-photosynthesis}

Photosynthesis is one of Earth's dominant chemical processes: it fixes
approximately \textbf{120 Gt of carbon} from CO\(_2\) per year, sustains
atmospheric oxygen, and supports nearly every heterotrophic food web.

\begin{equation}
6\text{CO}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{light}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\text{O}_2 \quad (\Delta G^{\circ\prime} = +2{,}870 \; \text{kJ/mol})
\label{eq:unit_III_photosynthesis_overall}
\end{equation}

The reaction is highly endergonic --- it requires light energy to drive
it. Photosynthesis occurs in the chloroplast (\textbf{plants and algae})
and at the plasma membrane (\textbf{cyanobacteria}). The process can be
divided into:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Light-dependent reactions} (thylakoid membrane): H\(_2\)O \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  O\(_2\) + NADPH + ATP
\item
  \textbf{Light-independent reactions / Calvin cycle} (stroma): CO\(_2\)
  + ATP + NADPH \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} G3P (sugar)
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Chloroplast Structure}\label{chloroplast-structure}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Outer envelope:} freely permeable (porin-like channels)
\item
  \textbf{Inner envelope:} selective transporters (triose phosphate /
  phosphate antiporter, TPT)
\item
  \textbf{Thylakoid membrane:} site of light reactions; forms stacked
  \textbf{grana} (5--20 thylakoids per granum) + interconnecting
  \textbf{stroma lamellae}
\item
  \textbf{Lumen (thylakoid lumen):} acidified
  (\hyperref[gl:ph]{\textbf{pH}} about 5) by proton pumping;
  about 1,000-fold H\(^+\) gradient
\item
  \textbf{Stroma:} site of Calvin cycle; contains RuBisCO, enzymes,
  chloroplast DNA, 70S \hyperref[gl:ribosome]{\textbf{ribosome}}s
\end{itemize}

Thylakoid membranes are densely packed with protein complexes ---
about 70\% protein by mass, making them one of the most
protein-rich membranes in nature. Each reaction centre is associated
with about 250 antenna
\hyperref[gl:chlorophyll]{\textbf{chlorophyll}} molecules.

\textbf{Chloroplast \hyperref[gl:genome]{\textbf{genome}}:} 120--200 kb
circular DNA; encodes about 120
\hyperref[gl:gene]{\textbf{gene}}s including RuBisCO large subunit,
photosystem subunits, and ribosomal components. Like mitochondria,
chloroplasts originated from
\hyperref[gl:endosymbiosis]{\textbf{endosymbiosis}} (cyanobacteria; see
\cref{sec:unit_II_cell_theory}).

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Light Absorption and Energy
Transfer}\label{light-absorption-and-energy-transfer}

\subsubsection{Photosynthetic Pigments}\label{photosynthetic-pigments}

Chlorophylls absorb light primarily at:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Chlorophyll a:} 430 nm (blue-violet) and 680 nm (red)
\item
  \textbf{Chlorophyll b:} 450 nm and 640 nm (broader absorption;
  accessory pigment)
\item
  \textbf{Carotenoids:} 400--500 nm; \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-carotene, lutein, zeaxanthin;
  also transfer energy to Chl a; function as photoprotectants
\end{itemize}

The \textbf{green wavelengths (about 500--600 nm)} are
reflected --- hence plant colour.

\subsubsection{Photon Energy and Quantum
Efficiency}\label{photon-energy-and-quantum-efficiency}

A \textbf{photon} of red light (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda} = 680 nm) carries:

\begin{equation}
E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{(6.626 \times 10^{-34}\;\text{J\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.}s})(3 \times 10^8\;\text{m/s})}{680 \times 10^{-9}\;\text{m}} = 2.93 \times 10^{-19}\;\text{J} = 1.82\;\text{eV}
\label{eq:unit_III_photon_energy}
\end{equation}

Per mole: \(E = N_A \times E_{\text{photon}} = 176\;\text{kJ/mol}\).

By comparison, blue light (440 nm) photons carry about 272
kJ/mol --- substantially more energy than red. The ``red drop'' in
photosynthetic action spectra reflects the fact that energy in excess of
the redox requirement is dissipated as heat \emph{whichever} photon is
absorbed; longer-wavelength light is therefore proportionally more
efficient on a per-photon basis.

\textbf{Quantum yield of photosynthesis:} The quantum yield (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Phi}}{Phi}) is the
molecules of product per photon absorbed. Two important quantum yields
are defined:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Phi}}{Phi}\(_{\text{O}_2}\)} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 0.10--0.12 mol O\(_2\) per mol photons
  absorbed (under optimal conditions)
\item
  \textbf{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Phi}}{Phi}\(_{\text{CO}_2}\)} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 0.08--0.10 mol CO\(_2\) per mol photons
  (lower because of photorespiration in C3)
\end{itemize}

The \textbf{minimum quantum requirement} (1/\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Phi}}{Phi}) is therefore
about 8--10 photons per O\(_2\) released --- close to the
theoretical minimum of 8 photons (4 photons through PS II + 4 through PS
I per O\(_2\) produced). The remaining inefficiency reflects energy
losses in antenna transfer, NPQ activation, and photorespiration.

\textbf{Quantum efficiency (energy basis):}

\begin{equation}
\eta_{\text{quantum}} = \frac{n_{\text{electrons}} \cdot \Delta E_{\text{redox}}}{n_{\text{photons}} \cdot E_{\text{photon}}}
\label{eq:unit_III_quantum_efficiency}
\end{equation}

For the Z-scheme: 4 electrons span 1.14 V from H\(_2\)O to NADPH,
requiring about 440 kJ/mol of electron flow. With 8 photons of
680 nm light supplying about 1,408 kJ/mol, the redox efficiency
is about 31\% --- the rest is consumed by overpotentials and
dissipated as heat.

\textbf{Comparison with engineered photovoltaics.} A commercial
single-junction silicon solar cell at 22\% efficiency converts solar
irradiance into electricity that must then power \emph{something} ---
and the chain from electricity \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} stored chemical fuel adds losses.
Plants, by contrast, deliver a stored fuel (sugar) directly. The
artificial-photosynthesis discussion returns to this comparison;
\cref{eq:unit_III_quantum_efficiency} sets the upper biological bound.

\subsubsection{Antenna Complexes and Light-Harvesting
Architecture}\label{antenna-complexes-and-light-harvesting-architecture}

Each reaction centre in plants is served by a peripheral antenna of
\textbf{light-harvesting complexes (LHC)}. LHCII alone is the most
abundant membrane protein on Earth (about 50\% of thylakoid
membrane protein).

\textbf{Chlorophyll a/b ratio:}

The Chl a:b ratio of an entire leaf typically ranges from
about 2.5 (sun-adapted) to about 3.5 (shade-adapted
leaves invest more in Chl b--rich LHCII to broaden the absorbed
spectrum). Chl b's broader 450 nm/640 nm absorption is critical for
harvesting green-shifted light filtered through canopy chlorophyll
above.

\textbf{Carotenoid functions:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Light harvesting} in the 450--500 nm range, where Chl absorbs
  poorly (about 30\% of the antenna's spectral coverage)
\item
  \textbf{Triplet quenching:} \(^3\)Chl* (long-lived triplet state,
  formed when singlet excitations are not used quickly) is rapidly
  quenched by carotenoids, preventing \(^1\)O\(_2\) generation
\item
  \textbf{Singlet oxygen scavenging:} any \(^1\)O\(_2\) that does form
  is quenched by carotenoids (the \emph{first} line of antioxidant
  defence)
\item
  \textbf{Structural stabilisation} of LHC protein folds
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Energy Transfer
Mechanisms}\label{energy-transfer-mechanisms}

\textbf{Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET):} Dipole--dipole
coupling between donor (D*) and acceptor (A) chromophores transfers
excitation without electron transfer.

\begin{equation}
k_{\text{FRET}} = \frac{1}{\tau_D} \left( \frac{R_0}{r} \right)^6
\label{eq:unit_III_fret_rate}
\end{equation}

where \(r\) is donor--acceptor separation, \(\tau_D\) is the donor's
excited-state lifetime, and \(R_0\) is the \textbf{Förster radius}
(typically 5--10 nm in Chl networks). The \(r^6\) dependence makes FRET
extremely sensitive to distance --- doubling separation reduces transfer
rate 64-fold. \(R_0\) depends on:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Spectral overlap integral} \(J(\lambda)\): the donor emission
  must overlap the acceptor absorption (red-shifting toward the reaction
  centre)
\item
  \textbf{Orientation factor} \(\kappa^2\): relative orientation of
  donor emission and acceptor absorption transition dipoles (averages to
  2/3 in random orientations, but is precisely tuned in the LHCII
  crystal structure)
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Energy funnel architecture:} Antenna pigments are arranged with
higher-energy absorbing pigments at the periphery and lower-energy
pigments closer to the reaction centre. Excitation cascades ``downhill''
toward the reaction centre with each transfer step, achieving
about 95\% efficiency from initial absorption to charge
separation.

\textbf{Exciton transfer (Dexter mechanism):} When chromophores are
within about 1 nm, electronic wavefunctions overlap and
excitation transfers as a coherent exciton rather than incoherent FRET
hops. Recent 2D electronic spectroscopy (Fleming lab, 2007) revealed
that quantum coherence may persist for picoseconds at room temperature,
possibly contributing to the high transfer efficiency, though the
functional importance remains debated.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 1:} The antenna complex transfers excitation
energy to the reaction centre with about 95\% efficiency. If
100 photons are absorbed by the antenna, how many excitations reach the
reaction centre? What happens to the energy of the about 5
photons that do not reach the reaction centre?
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 1b:} \cref{eq:unit_III_fret_rate} shows that
\(k_{\text{FRET}} \propto 1/r^6\). If two chlorophylls separated by 5 nm
transfer at \(1 \times 10^{10}\) s\(^{-1}\), predict the rate at 7.5 nm
and at 10 nm. What does this mean for the spatial design of LHC
complexes?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Light-Dependent Reactions}\label{light-dependent-reactions}

\subsubsection{Photosystem II (PS II)}\label{photosystem-ii-ps-ii}

PS II is located primarily in appressed grana thylakoids. It is a large
complex (about 350 kDa per monomer; functions as a dimer). Key
components:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Reaction centre (P680):} Special pair of Chl a molecules that
  absorb at 680 nm; the primary electron donor
\item
  \textbf{D1 and D2 proteins:} Core reaction centre proteins (homologous
  to bacterial L and M subunits)
\item
  \textbf{Pheophytin (Pheo):} Primary electron acceptor (chlorophyll
  lacking Mg\(^{2+}\))
\item
  \textbf{Q\(_A\) and Q\(_B\):} Plastoquinone molecules; Q\(_A\) is
  tightly bound (one-electron acceptor), Q\(_B\) is the
  two-electron/two-proton mobile acceptor
\item
  \textbf{Water-splitting complex (OEC, oxygen-evolving complex):}
  Mn\(_4\)CaO\(_5\) cluster; performs the most thermodynamically
  demanding oxidation in biology
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Water oxidation:}

\begin{equation}
2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^+ + 4\text{e}^- \quad (E^{\circ\prime} = +0.82 \text{ V})
\label{eq:unit_III_water_splitting}
\end{equation}

Each molecule of O\(_2\) requires 4 photons (one photon per electron
from water). The OEC's ability to extract electrons one at a time from
water --- accumulating four oxidising equivalents on the
Mn\(_4\)CaO\(_5\) cluster before releasing O\(_2\) in a single concerted
four-electron step --- was unprecedented in biology and is the
inspiration for synthetic water-splitting catalysts.

\textbf{The Kok cycle (S-state cycle):} The OEC cycles through 5
oxidation states (S\(_0\)--S\(_4\)), accumulating 4 oxidising
equivalents before releasing O\(_2\):

\[\text{S}_0 \xrightarrow{h\nu} \text{S}_1 \xrightarrow{h\nu} \text{S}_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} \text{S}_3 \xrightarrow{h\nu} \text{S}_4 \xrightarrow{-\text{O}_2} \text{S}_0 \tag{10.4}\]

Each S-state transition involves one photon absorption and one electron
extraction from the Mn\(_4\)Ca cluster.

\textbf{Primary photochemistry:} P680 absorbs photon \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} excited state
P680* \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} donates electron to pheophytin (charge separation in
about 3 ps) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Q\(_A\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Q\(_B\). After two electrons and two
protons, PQH\(_2\) (plastoquinol) leaves PS II and carries electrons to
Complex III (cytochrome b\(_6\)f).

\textbf{D1 protein damage:} P680\(^+\) is the strongest biological
oxidant (\(E^{\circ\prime} = +1.25\) V). The D1 protein is damaged by
this oxidative stress and must be replaced every 30--60 minutes --- the
most rapid protein turnover in the cell. This
\textbf{photoinhibition/repair cycle} requires a dedicated FtsH protease
and ribosomal machinery in the thylakoid.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Herbicides Targeting PS II} \textbf{DCMU
(diuron)} and \textbf{atrazine} block the Q\(_B\) binding site on D1,
preventing electron flow from PS II. This kills plants by halting
photosynthesis. Atrazine is one of the most widely used herbicides
globally. Resistance has evolved in some weed species through a single
Ser264Gly \hyperref[gl:mutation]{\textbf{mutation}} in D1 that reduces
atrazine binding. Understanding PS II structure is essential for
developing new herbicides and for bioengineering more efficient
photosynthesis.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Cytochrome b\(_6\)f
Complex}{Cytochrome b_6f Complex}}\label{cytochrome-b_6f-complex}

After PS II, PQH\(_2\) is oxidised by the \textbf{cytochrome b\(_6\)f
complex}, which pumps H\(^+\) into the lumen via the \textbf{Q-cycle},
analogous to Complex III in mitochondria:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  PQH\(_2\) binds at the luminal (Q\(_p\)) site
\item
  One electron passes to the Rieske Fe-S protein \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} cytochrome f \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  \textbf{plastocyanin} (PC, soluble Cu-protein in the lumen)
\item
  Second electron passes to cytochrome b\(_6\) (low potential) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  cytochrome b\(_6\) (high potential) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PQ at the stromal (Q\(_n\)) site
\item
  Net: 2 H\(^+\) released to lumen per PQH\(_2\) oxidised, plus 2
  H\(^+\) consumed from stroma per PQ reduced
\end{enumerate}

The b\(_6\)f complex also produces superoxide as a byproduct, which can
trigger signalling cascades for acclimation to changing light
conditions.

\subsubsection{Photosystem I (PS I)}\label{photosystem-i-ps-i}

PS I reaction centre: \textbf{P700} (Chl a pair absorbing at 700 nm). PS
I is located primarily in non-appressed stroma lamellae and at the
margins of grana.

\textbf{Electron flow through PS I:} P700 + photon \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} P700* \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} A\(_0\)
(Chl a) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} A\(_1\) (phylloquinone) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} F\(_X\) (Fe-S) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} F\(_A\)/F\(_B\)
(Fe-S) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{ferredoxin} (Fd, soluble Fe-S protein in stroma) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
\textbf{ferredoxin-NADP\(^+\) reductase (FNR)} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{NADPH}

\subsubsection{The Z-Scheme: Standard Electrode
Potentials}\label{the-z-scheme-standard-electrode-potentials}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0056_eb22b5920e20.png}
\caption{Sequence diagram for The Z-Scheme: Standard Electrode Potentials showing ordered interaction among H2O (E degrees ' = +0.82 V), OEC (Mn4Ca), P680/PS II (E degrees ' = +1.25 V), and Plastoquinone Pool (PQH2).}
\end{figure}

\emph{The Z-scheme of photosynthetic electron transport (Mermaid).} Two
photons (absorbed by PS II and PS I) drive each electron from water
(\(E^{\circ\prime} = +0.82\) V) to NADPH (\(E^{\circ\prime} = -0.32\)
V), spanning a total potential of 1.14 V. The ``Z'' shape arises from
plotting electron carriers against their redox potential.

The two large upward jumps (P680\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}P680\emph{, P700\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}P700}) require
absorption of red-light photons. The intervening downward drops drive
PMF buildup and NADPH formation. This gives the canonical ``Z'' shape.

The Gibbs free energy stored in moving 4 electrons from water to NADPH:

\begin{equation}
\Delta G^{\circ\prime} = -nF\Delta E = -(4)(96{,}485)(1.14) \approx -440\;\text{kJ/mol}_{\text{e}^-}
\label{eq:unit_III_z_scheme_energy}
\end{equation}

(N.B. negative sign indicates the \emph{reverse} reaction is
spontaneous; light energy is required to drive electrons \emph{uphill}
from water to NADPH.)

\textbf{Concept Check 2x:} Plastocyanin (\(E^{\circ\prime} = +0.37\) V)
reduces P700\(^+\) (\(E^{\circ\prime} = +0.45\) V). Calculate
\(\Delta G^{\circ\prime}\) for this electron transfer per mole of
electrons. Does the redox flow proceed downhill in the dark or primarily

\subsubsection{Linear vs.~Cyclic Electron
Flow}\label{linear-vs.-cyclic-electron-flow}

\textbf{Linear electron flow (LEF):} H\(_2\)O \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PS II \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PQ \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} b\(_6\)f \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
PC \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PS I \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Fd \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} NADPH. Produces both ATP and NADPH. ATP:NADPH ratio
about 1.3:1.

\textbf{Cyclic electron flow (CEF):} Ferredoxin returns electrons to the
b\(_6\)f complex (via PQ), generating additional PMF for ATP synthesis
without NADPH production. This adjusts the ATP:NADPH ratio to match
Calvin cycle demands (3:2 per CO\(_2\)).

CEF is mediated by two pathways: - \textbf{PGR5/PGRL1 pathway:} Major
route; ferredoxin \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PQ via PGRL1 - \textbf{NDH-dependent pathway:}
Chloroplast NAD(P)H dehydrogenase complex; minor route

The functional necessity of CEF was first inferred from the gap between
the ATP demand of the Calvin cycle (3 ATP per CO\(_2\)) and what LEF
alone supplies (about 2.6 ATP per CO\(_2\) at 14:3 H\(^+\)/ATP
stoichiometry); CEF closes the gap. Hager's classic experiments on the
xanthophyll cycle \citep{hager1971} and subsequent work showed that the
magnitude of CEF varies dynamically with light and CO\(_2\) --- itself a
regulatory layer.

\subsubsection{Chemiosmotic ATP Synthesis
(Chloroplast)}\label{chemiosmotic-atp-synthesis-chloroplast}

The PMF generated by H\(^+\) accumulation in the lumen (from water
splitting + PQ reduction + b\(_6\)f Q-cycle) drives \textbf{chloroplast
\hyperref[gl:atp-synthase]{\textbf{ATP synthase}} (CF\(_1\)F\(_0\))}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Structure and mechanism analogous to mitochondrial ATP synthase
\item
  c-ring has 14 subunits in spinach chloroplasts (vs.~8--15 in
  mitochondria)
\item
  about 4.67 H\(^+\)/ATP (14 H\(^+\) per revolution / 3 ATP)
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Net output of light reactions (per 2 H\(_2\)O oxidised / 2 NADPH
produced):}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  1 O\(_2\)
\item
  2 NADPH
\item
  about 3 ATP (from linear flow; cyclic flow provides
  additional ATP)
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Worked Example: Energy Requirements for Carbon
Fixation}\label{worked-example-energy-requirements-for-carbon-fixation}

\emph{Problem:} Calculate the ATP and NADPH consumed to synthesise one
molecule of glucose, and determine how many photons must be absorbed
(assuming 8 photons per O\(_2\) for linear electron flow).

\emph{Solution:}

Net Calvin cycle stoichiometry per CO\(_2\) fixed: \textbf{3 ATP + 2
NADPH}, as derived in the Calvin-cycle stoichiometry discussion below.
Per glucose (6 CO\(_2\) fixed): \textbf{18 ATP + 12 NADPH}.

Linear electron flow produces NADPH at a fixed ratio of 2 NADPH per 4
e\(^-\) (4 photons per electron pair), so 12 NADPH require:

\[n_{\text{photons}} = 12 \times 4 = 48\;\text{photons (LEF primarily)} \tag{10.4a}\]

But linear flow produces about 12 ATP from this (12 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 1.0 ATP per NADPH
at about 1:1 stoichiometry --- far short of the 18 ATP
required). The shortfall of 6 ATP must be supplied by \textbf{cyclic
electron flow}, which is estimated to require about 6--9
additional photons. Total: \textbf{about 54--57 photons per
glucose}.

This is why the often-cited ``48 photons per glucose'' is a \emph{lower
bound} assuming perfect Z-scheme efficiency; real plants need somewhat
more to balance the ATP:NADPH ratio.

Stoichiometry}\label{worked-example-calvin-cycle-stoichiometry}

\emph{Problem:} Track the 18 ATP and 12 NADPH demand of the Calvin cycle
through the three phases for 6 CO\(_2\).

This 18:12 = 3:2 ATP:NADPH demand is the \emph{target} the light
reactions must hit. Pure LEF delivers ATP:NADPH about 1.3, so plants
tune the LEF/CEF balance to close the gap; under light limitation, CEF
is upregulated.

\textbf{Concept Check 2:} The Calvin cycle requires 3 ATP and 2 NADPH
per CO\(_2\) fixed. Linear electron flow produces ATP and NADPH in
approximately a 1.3:1 ratio. How does cyclic electron flow help satisfy
the Calvin cycle's ATP:NADPH ratio of 3:2 (= 1.5:1)?
\end{quote}

\subsection{The Calvin Cycle (Light-Independent
Reactions)}\label{the-calvin-cycle-light-independent-reactions}

The Calvin cycle fixes CO\(_2\) into organic compounds in the stroma. It
has three phases:

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0057_4ad799402a8f.png}
\caption{Flowchart for The Calvin Cycle (Light-Independent Reactions): Phase 1: Carboxylation, RuBP (5C), 2 x 3-PGA (3C), and Phase 2: Reduction form the diagram's primary path or branches.}
\end{figure}

\emph{The three phases of the Calvin cycle (Mermaid).} For every 3
CO\(_2\) fixed, 9 ATP and 6 NADPH are consumed, and 1 net G3P (3C) is
produced. Six turns of the cycle produce one glucose molecule.

\subsubsection{RuBisCO: Structure and Catalytic
Mechanism}\label{rubisco-structure-and-catalytic-mechanism}

\textbf{Structure:} Plant RuBisCO is a hexadecamer (L\(_8\)S\(_8\)) ---
eight large subunits (about 55 kDa, plastid-encoded \emph{rbcL}
gene) and eight small subunits (about 15 kDa, nucleus-encoded
\emph{RbcS} gene family). The L subunits contain the catalytic site at
the L-L dimer interface (so 8 active sites per holoenzyme); the S
subunits play structural and modulatory roles, contributing to the cap
of the assembly. Total mass is about 520 kDa, making RuBisCO
one of the largest stromal soluble enzymes.

\textbf{Activation requires CO\(_2\) + Mg\(^{2+}\):} A separate,
\emph{non-substrate} CO\(_2\) molecule first reacts with Lys201 of the
active site to form a \textbf{carbamate}, which then chelates a
Mg\(^{2+}\) ion. Primarily the carbamylated, Mg\(^{2+}\)-bound enzyme
can bind RuBP and proceed with catalysis. The mechanism cleverly
\emph{senses} CO\(_2\) availability twice: once to activate the enzyme
and once during turnover.

\textbf{RuBisCO activase (an AAA+ ATPase)} removes inhibitory sugar
phosphates (CA1P, RuBP) from RuBisCO's active site, allowing
carbamylation. This step is \textbf{light-dependent} (requires ATP) ---
connecting Calvin cycle activation to the energy state of the
chloroplast.

\textbf{Catalytic mechanism (in seven steps):}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  RuBP binds and is deprotonated at C3 to form a 2,3-enediol
  intermediate (the rate-limiting enolisation)
\item
  The enediol attacks CO\(_2\) (or O\(_2\) --- see photorespiration)
\item
  C2-C3 bond cleavage produces a six-carbon \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-keto acid intermediate
\item
  Hydration of the C3 carbon
\item
  C2-C3 cleavage releases the first 3-PGA
\item
  Stereospecific protonation produces the second 3-PGA
\item
  Product release
\end{enumerate}

The slow \(k_{\text{cat}}\) (about 3--10 s\(^{-1}\)) is dominated by the
enolisation step (step 1) and by the stringent steric constraints needed
to \emph{select} CO\(_2\) over O\(_2\) in step 2. Faster RuBisCOs leak
more O\(_2\) into the active site, producing photorespiration.

\textbf{The CO\(_2\)/O\(_2\) specificity factor (S\(_{c/o}\), also \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\tau}}{tau}):}

\begin{equation}
S_{c/o} = \tau = \frac{V_c K_o}{V_o K_c}
\label{eq:unit_III_specificity_factor}
\end{equation}

where \(V_c\), \(V_o\) are maximal carboxylase/oxygenase rates and
\(K_c\), \(K_o\) are Michaelis constants. Higher S\(_{c/o}\) = more
selective for CO\(_2\) over O\(_2\).
