\textbf{The fundamental trade-off:} Across the tree of life, \(S_{c/o}\)
and \(k_{\text{cat}}\) are \emph{negatively correlated}. Faster RuBisCOs
are less selective. This appears to be a thermodynamic constraint on the
enediol intermediate's reactivity --- the same electronic features that
make it react with CO\(_2\) also make it react with O\(_2\).

\subsubsection{Carboxylation (Carbon
Fixation)}\label{carboxylation-carbon-fixation}

\[\text{RuBP (5C)} + \text{CO}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{RuBisCO}} 2 \times \text{3-PGA (3C)} \tag{10.5}\]

\textbf{RuBisCO} is the most abundant protein on Earth
(about 0.7 billion tonnes globally; about 50\% of leaf
protein). Despite its central importance, RuBisCO has remarkable
limitations:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Slow:} \(k_{\text{cat}} = 3\)--\(10\) s\(^{-1}\) (typical
  enzymes: 10\(^2\)--10\(^3\) s\(^{-1}\))
\item
  \textbf{Indiscriminate:} also reacts with O\(_2\) (\textbf{oxygenase
  activity}), leading to \textbf{photorespiration} and wasting
  about 25\% of fixed carbon in C3 plants
\item
  Plants compensate for RuBisCO's slowness by producing enormous
  quantities of it
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Reduction}\label{reduction}

This is the primary reductive step of the Calvin cycle: the ATP and
NADPH generated by the light reactions are spent here to convert 3-PGA
into the triose phosphate G3P. For every 6 CO\(_2\) fixed, 12 G3P are
produced --- 2 leave as the cycle's net carbohydrate yield and 10 are
recycled to regenerate RuBP.

\[\text{3-PGA} + \text{ATP} \rightarrow \text{1,3-BPG} + \text{ADP} \quad (\text{phosphoglycerate kinase}) \tag{10.6}\]

\[\text{1,3-BPG} + \text{NADPH} \rightarrow \text{G3P} + \text{NADP}^+ + \text{P}_i \quad (\text{G3P dehydrogenase}) \tag{10.7}\]

\subsubsection{Regeneration of RuBP}\label{regeneration-of-rubp}

Five G3P molecules (15 carbons) are rearranged through a complex 10-step
pathway (involving transketolase, aldolase,
sedoheptulose-1,7-bisphosphatase, ribulose-5-phosphate epimerase, and
ribulose-5-phosphate isomerase) to regenerate 3 RuBP (15 carbons),
consuming 3 ATP.

\subsubsection{Stoichiometry}\label{stoichiometry}

\textbf{To fix 6 CO\(_2\) (net gain 1 hexose):}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  6 CO\(_2\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} (3 ATP + 2 NADPH per CO\(_2\)) = \textbf{18 ATP + 12
  NADPH}
\item
  Light reactions must supply: 18 ATP and 12 NADPH
\item
  Requires about 48 photons (8 per CO\(_2\); 4 photons for 2
  electrons through PS II + PS I \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 2 electron pairs per NADPH) for
  NADPH; additional photons for cyclic electron flow to meet ATP demand
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Worked Example: Energy Efficiency of
Photosynthesis}\label{worked-example-energy-efficiency-of-photosynthesis}

\emph{Problem:} Calculate the energy efficiency of photosynthesis given
that 48 photons of red light (680 nm, 176 kJ/mol each) are required to
fix 6 CO\(_2\) into 1 glucose (\(\Delta G^{\circ\prime}\) of glucose
combustion = 2,870 kJ/mol).

\emph{Solution:}

Total light energy input: \(48 \times 176 = 8{,}448\) kJ/mol

Energy stored in glucose: \(2{,}870\) kJ/mol

\begin{equation}
\eta = \frac{2{,}870}{8{,}448} \times 100\% = 34\%
\label{eq:unit_III_photosynthesis_efficiency}
\end{equation}

This is remarkably efficient for an energy conversion process.
Whole-canopy photosynthetic efficiency in a real crop is typically
around 1--3\%, because most of the year's incoming photosynthetically
active radiation (PAR) is lost to (i) reflection, (ii) photorespiration,
(iii) leaf shading and saturation, (iv) plant respiration, and (v)
suboptimal water/nutrient supply.

\textbf{Starch vs.~sucrose export:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Starch} (alpha-glucose polymer) stored in chloroplast stroma
  during the day \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} remobilised at night to fuel respiration
\item
  \textbf{Sucrose} (glucose-fructose disaccharide) exported to phloem
  via triose phosphate/phosphate antiporter (TPT) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} transported to
  non-photosynthetic tissues (\emph{source-sink} relationship)
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 3:} RuBisCO is the most abundant enzyme on Earth,
yet it is extremely slow (\(k_{cat}\) = 3--10 s\(^{-1}\)). Why hasn't
evolution produced a faster version? Consider the trade-off between
speed and specificity (CO\(_2\) vs.~O\(_2\) discrimination) in light of
the specificity-factor data above.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 3b:} Spinach RuBisCO has \(\tau \approx 90\).
\emph{Galdieria} (red alga) RuBisCO has \(\tau \approx 240\) but
\(k_{\text{cat}} \approx 2.6\) s\(^{-1}\) (vs.~3.3 for spinach). At
ambient \([\text{CO}_2]/[\text{O}_2]\), which enzyme would maximize
CO\(_2\) flux per unit enzyme? When (in what environment) does the
trade-off favour the \emph{Galdieria} form?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Photorespiration}\label{photorespiration}

RuBisCO's oxygenase activity produces \textbf{2-phosphoglycolate} (2C),
which must be recycled through the photorespiratory pathway (C2 cycle):

\[\text{RuBP} + \text{O}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{RuBisCO oxygenase}} \text{3-PGA (3C)} + \text{2-phosphoglycolate (2C)} \tag{10.9}\]

The photorespiratory pathway spans three
\hyperref[gl:organelle]{\textbf{organelle}}s: 1. \textbf{Chloroplast:}
2-phosphoglycolate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} glycolate (phosphatase) 2. \textbf{Peroxisome:}
glycolate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} glyoxylate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} glycine (generates H\(_2\)O\(_2\), destroyed by
catalase) 3. \textbf{Mitochondrion:} 2 glycine \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} serine + CO\(_2\) +
NH\(_3\) + NADH (glycine decarboxylase) 4. \textbf{Peroxisome:} serine \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
hydroxypyruvate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} glycerate 5. \textbf{Chloroplast:} glycerate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} 3-PGA
(phosphorylation by ATP)

\textbf{Cost of photorespiration:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Loses 1 CO\(_2\) per 2 oxygenation events (25\% of fixed carbon)
\item
  Consumes ATP for recovery
\item
  Releases NH\(_3\) (must be re-assimilated)
\item
  At 25 degrees C and current atmospheric CO\(_2\), photorespiration
  reduces net photosynthesis by about 20--30\% in C3 plants
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Photorespiration and Global Food Security}
Reducing photorespiration in crop plants could increase yields by
20--40\%. Approaches include: - \textbf{Engineering a chloroplastic
glycolate bypass} (South et al., 2019, \emph{Science}): reduced
photorespiratory losses by 40\% and increased tobacco biomass -
\textbf{Introducing CO\(_2\)-concentrating mechanisms} (CCMs) from
cyanobacteria into C3 crops - \textbf{Engineering RuBisCO} with improved
CO\(_2\)/O\(_2\) specificity (challenging due to the speed-specificity
trade-off) These efforts matter because the UN World Population
Prospects 2024 projects roughly 9.7 billion people by 2050, while
climate stress, land limits, food loss, and inequitable access constrain
the food system \citep{un2024population}. Higher photosynthetic
efficiency can raise yield potential, but it is not a stand-alone
solution to nutrition, distribution, soil health, or water scarcity.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{C3, C4, and CAM
Photosynthesis}\label{c3-c4-and-cam-photosynthesis}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Why CO\(_2\)-Concentrating Mechanisms
Evolved}{Why CO_2-Concentrating Mechanisms Evolved}}\label{why-co_2-concentrating-mechanisms-evolved}

The atmospheric CO\(_2\):O\(_2\) ratio (about 0.04\%/21\% \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~}
1:525) is hostile to RuBisCO. The fraction of carboxylation versus
oxygenation reactions is approximately:

\begin{equation}
\frac{v_c}{v_o} = S_{c/o} \cdot \frac{[\text{CO}_2]}{[\text{O}_2]}
\label{eq:unit_III_carb_oxy_ratio}
\end{equation}

For C3 plants at 25 °C, typical leaf-internal CO\(_2\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 7 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}M and
O\(_2\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 250 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}M, so \(v_c/v_o \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 80 \times (7/250) \approx 2.2\) ---
meaning about 30\% of RuBisCO turnovers are oxygenations. C4
and CAM plants have evolved spatial or temporal CO\(_2\)-concentrating
mechanisms (CCMs) that raise the local {[}CO\(_2\){]} around RuBisCO
about 10\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} above ambient, suppressing photorespiration.

\subsubsection{C3 Photosynthesis (First stable product:
3-PGA)}\label{c3-photosynthesis-first-stable-product-3-pga}

Standard Calvin cycle. Used by about 85\% of plant species
(wheat, rice, soybeans, most trees). Problem: \textbf{photorespiration}
is severe at high temperature and low CO\(_2\) (e.g., midday in summer,
when \hyperref[gl:stomata]{\textbf{stomata}} close to conserve water).

\subsubsection{C4 Photosynthesis (First stable product: oxaloacetate,
4C)}\label{c4-photosynthesis-first-stable-product-oxaloacetate-4c}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0058_5c955f9bd359.png}
\caption{Flowchart for C4 Photosynthesis (First stable product: oxaloacetate, 4C): Mesophyll Cell, CO2 (atmospheric), Oxaloacetate (4C), and Malate (4C) form the diagram's primary path or branches.}
\end{figure}

\emph{C4 photosynthesis (Mermaid).} Spatial separation of initial
CO\(_2\) fixation (mesophyll cells, PEP carboxylase) and the Calvin
cycle (bundle sheath cells, RuBisCO). This CO\(_2\)-concentrating
mechanism virtually eliminates photorespiration.

\textbf{CO\(_2\)-concentrating mechanism:} CO\(_2\) is captured in
\textbf{mesophyll cells} by PEP carboxylase (no O\(_2\) reactivity;
\(K_m\) for CO\(_2\) about  2 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}M, vs.~RuBisCO \(K_m\)
about 10 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}M) as oxaloacetate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} malate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} transported to
\textbf{bundle sheath cells} via plasmodesmata \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} decarboxylated \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
CO\(_2\) concentrated (10x above ambient) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} RuBisCO operates at
saturating CO\(_2\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} negligible photorespiration.

C4 plants (maize, sugarcane, sorghum, millet) require \textbf{2
additional ATP per CO\(_2\)} fixed (total: 5 ATP + 2 NADPH per CO\(_2\))
but are more efficient at high temperature and high light. Spatial
separation of carboxylation (mesophyll) and Calvin cycle (bundle sheath)
requires specialised leaf anatomy = \textbf{Kranz anatomy} (German:
``wreath'').

\textbf{C4 subtypes} differ in the decarboxylation enzyme in bundle
sheath cells:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{NADP-ME type:} NADP-malic enzyme (maize, sorghum, sugarcane)
\item
  \textbf{NAD-ME type:} NAD-malic enzyme (millet, Amaranthus)
\item
  \textbf{PEP-CK type:} PEP carboxykinase (guinea grass, Panicum)
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{CAM Photosynthesis (Temporal
separation)}\label{cam-photosynthesis-temporal-separation}

\textbf{Crassulacean Acid Metabolism:} stomata open at \textbf{night}
(cool, high humidity \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} low
\hyperref[gl:transpiration]{\textbf{transpiration}}) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} CO\(_2\) fixed by
PEP carboxylase \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} malate stored in vacuole (vacuolar pH drops from
about 7 to about 4 as malic acid accumulates). Stomata
\textbf{close during the day} (prevent water loss) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} malate
decarboxylated \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} CO\(_2\) concentrated around RuBisCO \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Calvin cycle
proceeds.

CAM plants (cacti, agaves, pineapple, orchids, jade plant) have
extremely high water-use efficiency (WUE: about 3--5x higher
than C3). The tradeoff: slow growth due to nighttime carbon storage
limitation and vacuolar capacity.

\subsubsection{Water-Use Efficiency}\label{water-use-efficiency}

Water-use efficiency (WUE) is defined as carbon gained per unit water
lost:

\begin{equation}
\text{WUE} = \frac{A}{E} = \frac{\text{net CO}_2 \text{ assimilation}}{\text{transpiration rate}}
\label{eq:unit_III_water_use_efficiency}
\end{equation}

The intrinsic WUE depends on the leaf-internal:atmospheric CO\(_2\)
gradient:

\begin{equation}
\text{WUE}_{\text{intrinsic}} = \frac{c_a - c_i}{1.6 \cdot (e_i - e_a)}
\label{eq:unit_III_intrinsic_wue}
\end{equation}

where \(c_a\) and \(c_i\) are atmospheric and intercellular CO\(_2\)
concentrations, \(e_a\) and \(e_i\) are ambient and intercellular water
vapour pressures, and 1.6 is the ratio of water-vapour to CO\(_2\)
diffusivity in air.

\textbf{Typical WUE values (mol CO\(_2\) fixed / mol H\(_2\)O
transpired):}

in deserts but at the cost of slow growth.

\subsection{Regulation of the Calvin
Cycle}\label{regulation-of-the-calvin-cycle}

The Calvin cycle does not run in the dark --- several enzymes are
regulated by light-dependent mechanisms to prevent futile cycling with
\hyperref[gl:glycolysis]{\textbf{glycolysis}} and the oxidative pentose
phosphate pathway.

\subsubsection{The Thioredoxin/Ferredoxin Redox Regulation
System}\label{the-thioredoxinferredoxin-redox-regulation-system}

Light reduces the chloroplast thioredoxin pool through a precisely
engineered cascade:

\begin{equation}
\text{PS I} \to \text{Fd}_{\text{red}} \to \text{FTR} \to \text{Trx}_{\text{red}} \to \text{target enzyme (S–S} \to \text{2 SH)}
\label{eq:unit_III_thioredoxin_cascade}
\end{equation}

In detail:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  PS I reduces ferredoxin (Fd, \(E^{\circ\prime} = -0.42\) V).
\item
  Fd-thioredoxin reductase (FTR) --- a unique {[}4Fe-4S{]} enzyme ---
  transfers two electrons to thioredoxin, converting an internal
  disulfide to two free thiols.
\item
  Reduced thioredoxin (Trx-(SH)\(_2\)) reduces specific regulatory
  disulfides on target enzymes.
\item
  Reduction \emph{activates} the target enzyme (in most cases) by
  relieving an inhibitory conformational lock.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0059_86f89afd405c.png}
\caption{Flowchart for The Thioredoxin/Ferredoxin Redox Regulation System: Light, PS I, Ferredoxin (red), and Fd-Thioredoxin Reductase form the diagram's primary path or branches.}
\end{figure}

\emph{The thioredoxin/ferredoxin system as the master light-dependent
redox switch (Mermaid).} Calvin-cycle enzymes carry regulatory
disulfides that are reduced (activated) in the light and re-oxidised
(inactivated) in the dark. This prevents futile ATP/NADPH consumption
during darkness.

Thioredoxin-controlled Calvin-cycle targets include:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{GAPDH (NADP-linked):} activated directly; catalyses the second
  reduction-phase step.
\item
  \textbf{Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (FBPase):} activated directly;
  supports carbon regeneration.
\item
  \textbf{Sedoheptulose-1,7-bisphosphatase (SBPase):} activated
  directly; a major regeneration-phase flux-control enzyme.
\item
  \textbf{PRK (phosphoribulokinase):} activated directly; regenerates
  RuBP.
\item
  \textbf{RuBisCO activase:} regulated indirectly; maintains RuBisCO in
  an active, carbamylated state.
\item
  \textbf{CP12:} reduction releases the GAPDH/PRK complex, reversing
  dark-state inactivation.
\end{itemize}

In the dark, the target disulfides re-oxidise (catalysed by 2-Cys
peroxiredoxins coupled to H\(_2\)O\(_2\)), inactivating the enzymes.
This prevents the Calvin cycle from consuming ATP and NADPH when they
are not being regenerated by the light reactions.

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{CO\(_2\) Concentration
Effects}{CO_2 Concentration Effects}}\label{co_2-concentration-effects}

The flux through the Calvin cycle is also acutely sensitive to CO\(_2\)
supply:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  At low {[}CO\(_2\){]} (e.g., closed stomata, drought), RuBisCO is the
  rate-limiting step and the cycle is ``carboxylation-limited.''
\item
  At intermediate {[}CO\(_2\){]}, the cycle becomes ``RuBP
  regeneration-limited'' --- flux limited by the supply of RuBP from the
  regeneration phase, which in turn depends on the rate of
  light-dependent ATP/NADPH supply.
\item
  At very high {[}CO\(_2\){]} (e.g., \textgreater{} ambient \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 2), the
  cycle can become ``P\(_i\)-limited'' --- phosphate becomes scarce as
  triose phosphate is exported.
\end{itemize}

This three-zone behaviour underlies the classic Farquhar-von
Caemmerer-Berry (FvCB) photosynthesis model, the workhorse of crop and
ecosystem modelling.

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Stromal pH and Mg\(^{2+}\) in the
Light}{Stromal pH and Mg^(2+) in the Light}}\label{stromal-ph-and-mg2-in-the-light}

In the light, H\(^+\) pumping from stroma to lumen has two activating
effects:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Stromal pH rises from about 7.0 to about 8.0
  (RuBisCO and FBPase pH optimum is about 8.0--8.5)
\item
  Stromal {[}Mg\(^{2+}\){]} rises by about 3 mM as Mg\(^{2+}\)
  exits the lumen with the H\(^+\) flux. Mg\(^{2+}\) is required for
  RuBisCO carbamylation and FBPase activity.
\end{itemize}

This is a beautifully integrated example of physical chemistry: the
\emph{same} H\(^+\) transport that builds the PMF for ATP synthesis
simultaneously activates the carbon-fixation enzymes that consume that
ATP.

\subsubsection{CP12 Regulation}\label{cp12-regulation}

\textbf{CP12} is a small regulatory protein that forms a ternary complex
with GAPDH and PRK in the dark, inactivating both enzymes
simultaneously. Light-dependent reduction of CP12 by thioredoxin
releases GAPDH and PRK, activating the Calvin cycle.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 5:} If a mutation in ferredoxin-thioredoxin
reductase (FTR) prevented thioredoxin from being reduced, what would
happen to Calvin cycle activity in the light? Would the light reactions
be affected?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Photoprotection: Non-Photochemical
Quenching}\label{photoprotection-non-photochemical-quenching}

Excess light energy (when absorbed photons exceed the rate at which
electrons can be productively used) can damage the photosynthetic
apparatus through generation of reactive oxygen species, particularly
singlet oxygen (\(^1\)O\(_2\)) from triplet chlorophyll (\(^3\)Chl*).
Plants must dissipate excess excitation safely.

\subsubsection{The Three Components of
NPQ}\label{the-three-components-of-npq}

NPQ is operationally defined as fluorescence quenching that does not
arise from photochemistry:

\begin{equation}
\text{NPQ} = \frac{F_m - F_m'}{F_m'}
\label{eq:unit_III_npq_definition}
\end{equation}

where \(F_m\) is maximum fluorescence in the dark-adapted state and
\(F_m'\) is the maximum fluorescence in the light-adapted state. NPQ has
three kinetic components:

\textbf{qE (energy quenching)} & seconds & Low lumen pH; PsbS

\subsubsection{qE: The Xanthophyll Cycle in
Detail}\label{qe-the-xanthophyll-cycle-in-detail}

When light is in excess, the lumen pH falls below about 5.5,
triggering two parallel events:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{PsbS protonation:} PsbS is a small (about 22 kDa)
  intrinsic membrane protein with two lumen-exposed glutamate residues
  that protonate at low pH. Protonation triggers a conformational change
  that brings antenna pigments into close contact, promoting energy
  transfer to a quenching site (a zeaxanthin-Chl heterodimer).
\item
  \textbf{Violaxanthin \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} zeaxanthin:} \textbf{Violaxanthin de-epoxidase
  (VDE)}, activated by low pH, catalyses sequential de-epoxidation
  \citep{hager1971}:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{equation}
\text{Violaxanthin (V)} \xrightarrow[+\text{ascorbate}]{\text{VDE, low pH}} \text{Antheraxanthin (A)} \xrightarrow[+\text{ascorbate}]{\text{VDE}} \text{Zeaxanthin (Z)}
\label{eq:unit_III_xanthophyll_cycle}
\end{equation}

Zeaxanthin (without epoxide groups) has a lower-energy first excited
state than chlorophyll, so it can act as an energy sink --- accepting
excitation from \(^1\)Chl* and dissipating it as heat. The reverse
reaction (Z \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} V) is catalysed by zeaxanthin epoxidase (ZE) in the dark
or low-light conditions.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0060_987a5e8fe209.png}
\caption{Sequence diagram for qE: The Xanthophyll Cycle in Detail showing ordered interaction among Excess light, Lumen pH decreased (about 5), PsbS (2 Glu protonated), and Violaxanthin de-epoxidase.}
\end{figure}

\emph{The xanthophyll cycle and qE quenching cascade (Mermaid).} Lumen
acidification (signal of excess light) protonates PsbS and activates
VDE. Zeaxanthin appears at the LHCII quenching site within seconds and
dissipates excess excitation as heat. When light decreases, lumen pH
rises and the whole system reverses over minutes.

\subsubsection{Carotenoid Quenching of Triplet
States}\label{carotenoid-quenching-of-triplet-states}

Carotenoids (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-carotene, zeaxanthin) directly quench triplet chlorophyll
(\(^3\)Chl*) and singlet oxygen (\(^1\)O\(_2\)), converting the energy
to heat. Without carotenoids, photosynthesis is lethal --- mutants
lacking carotenoid biosynthesis (e.g., norflurazon-treated plants)
bleach and die in light.

The carotenoid triplet state (about 80 kJ/mol) is below both
\(^3\)Chl* (about 110 kJ/mol) and \(^1\)O\(_2\)
(about 94 kJ/mol), so energy transfer is downhill in both
cases.

\subsubsection{State Transitions (qT)}\label{state-transitions-qt}

When PS II is over-excited relative to PS I (e.g., under blue light,
which preferentially excites PS II), the plastoquinone pool becomes
reduced. Reduced PQ activates \textbf{STN7 kinase}, which phosphorylates
LHCII. Phosphorylated LHCII detaches from PS II in grana and migrates to
PS I in stroma lamellae, rebalancing excitation pressure. Under far-red
light (preferentially exciting PS I), PQ becomes oxidised, STN7 is
inactive, and a phosphatase (PPH1/TAP38) returns LHCII to PS II.

\subsubsection{Other Photoprotective
Mechanisms}\label{other-photoprotective-mechanisms}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Chloroplast movements:} In high light, chloroplasts align
  parallel to the light direction (low cross-section); in low light,
  they spread perpendicular (high cross-section). Mediated by
  phototropins.
\item
  \textbf{Reactive oxygen scavenging:} Superoxide dismutase (SOD),
  ascorbate peroxidase (APX), and the glutathione-ascorbate
  (Foyer-Halliwell) cycle detoxify ROS generated by PS I (Mehler
  reaction).
\item
  \textbf{Photorespiration as a safety valve:} Counter-intuitively,
  photorespiration consumes ATP and reductant, draining excess electron
  flow when CO\(_2\) is limiting --- a ``release valve'' that reduces
  ROS pressure on the chloroplast.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 6:} Explain why a plant mutant lacking carotenoids
would die in the light but survive in the dark. What specific
photodamage mechanism would cause cell death?
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 6b:} A \emph{psbs} knockout \emph{Arabidopsis}
lacks the PsbS protein and shows almost no qE, although LHCII and the
xanthophyll cycle are intact. Predict the plant's growth phenotype under
(a) constant moderate light and (b) fluctuating light (sun \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} shade \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} sun
every minute). Why is the fluctuating-light phenotype more severe?
\end{quote}

\subsection{Evolutionary Origins of
Photosynthesis}\label{evolutionary-origins-of-photosynthesis}

Photosynthesis has a complex evolutionary history spanning
about 3.5 billion years:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Anoxygenic photosynthesis} (about 3.5 Ga): Early
  photosynthetic bacteria (e.g., purple bacteria, green sulfur bacteria)
  used a single reaction centre (Type I or Type II) and electron donors
  other than water (H\(_2\)S, Fe\(^{2+}\), H\(_2\)). No O\(_2\)
  produced.
\item
  \textbf{Origin of oxygenic photosynthesis} (about 2.7--3.0
  Ga): Cyanobacteria evolved the ability to link two photosystems (PS II
  and PS I) in series (Z-scheme), enabling water as an electron donor.
  This was the most transformative evolutionary innovation on Earth.
\item
  \textbf{Great Oxidation Event} (about 2.4 Ga): Cyanobacterial
  O\(_2\) production overwhelmed geological sinks (reduced iron,
  sulfur), causing atmospheric O\(_2\) to rise from \textless0.001\% to
  about 2\%. This was catastrophic for obligate anaerobes (the
  ``Oxygen Holocaust'') but enabled
  \hyperref[gl:aerobic]{\textbf{aerobic}} respiration
  (about 18x more efficient ATP production than
  \hyperref[gl:fermentation]{\textbf{fermentation}}).
\item
  \textbf{Primary endosymbiosis} (about 1.5 Ga): A
  cyanobacterium was engulfed by a eukaryotic ancestor, becoming the
  chloroplast. Evidence: double membrane, 70S ribosomes, circular DNA,
  sensitivity to chloramphenicol.
\item
  \textbf{Secondary and tertiary endosymbiosis:} Algae engulfed other
  algae, creating organelles with 3--4 membranes (e.g., chloroplasts of
  brown algae, diatoms, euglenoids). This accounts for the remarkable
  diversity of photosynthetic pigments and chloroplast structures across
  algal lineages.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 7:} The reaction centres of PS II (D1/D2 proteins)
and purple bacteria (L/M subunits) share significant structural and
sequence homology, yet PS II can oxidise water and purple bacterial
reaction centres cannot. What structural innovation in PS II enabled
water oxidation?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Artificial Photosynthesis and Solar
Fuels}\label{artificial-photosynthesis-and-solar-fuels}

Inspired by natural photosynthesis, researchers are developing
artificial systems to convert solar energy into fuels. The diversity of
approaches reveals a tension between \emph{efficiency} (where
photovoltaics excel) and \emph{fuel storage} (where chemistry excels).

\subsubsection{Comparison: Natural vs.~Artificial Light
Conversion}\label{comparison-natural-vs.-artificial-light-conversion}

\textbf{Biological systems.}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{C3 photosynthesis (whole plant):} 0.5--1.5\%
  solar-to-stored-carbon efficiency, producing glucose and starch. Its
  advantage is complete self-assembly and repair; its limit is low
  energy efficiency and dependence on water and mineral nutrients.
\item
  \textbf{C4 photosynthesis (for example, sugarcane):} 1.5--3.5\%
  solar-to-stored-carbon efficiency, producing glucose and sucrose. The
  CO\(_2\)-concentrating mechanism improves performance in hot, bright
  environments, but the anatomical and ATP costs restrict its ecological
  range.
\item
  \textbf{Theoretical biological maximum:} about 12\% for reduced carbon
  under idealised constraints. The main losses come from spectral
  mismatch, RuBisCO kinetics, photorespiration, respiration, and the
  ATP/NADPH cost of carbon fixation.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Engineered energy systems.}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Silicon photovoltaic (single-junction):} about 22\% commercial
  electricity conversion. It is mature and inexpensive, but electricity
  is not a fuel and requires downstream storage.
\item
  \textbf{III--V tandem photovoltaics:} about 33\% in high-performance
  laboratory cells. They maximise single-cell photovoltaic efficiency
  but remain costly and materials-intensive.
\item
  \textbf{Photovoltaics plus electrolysis:} about 10--14\%
  solar-to-H\(_2\) efficiency. Hydrogen is a storable fuel, but
  compression, transport, leakage, and end-use infrastructure remain
  major constraints.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Hybrid and chemical fuel systems.}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Photoelectrochemical cells:} about 4--10\% solar-to-H\(_2\)
  efficiency from water. Direct light-to-fuel integration is attractive,
  but catalyst durability and device stability are limiting.
\item
  \textbf{CO\(_2\) photoreduction with copper-family catalysts:} roughly
  1--5\% for mixtures such as CO, formate, and ethanol. The appeal is
  direct carbon capture into fuels; the challenge is selectivity.
\item
  \textbf{Bio-hybrids with engineered cyanobacteria:} about 0.5--4\% for
  products such as H\(_2\), ethanol, or alkanes. They are
  self-replicating and tunable but slow and fragile.
\item
  \textbf{Synthetic Mn\(_4\)Ca-inspired catalysts:} research-stage
  water-oxidation systems producing O\(_2\) from H\(_2\)O. They teach
  design principles from the oxygen-evolving complex but are not yet
  practical devices.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Why Plants Lag PV (and Why It May Not
Matter)}\label{why-plants-lag-pv-and-why-it-may-not-matter}

A silicon solar cell at 22\% beats C3 photosynthesis at 1\% by an order
of magnitude --- but the comparison is misleading. PV converts photons
to electrons; plants convert photons to \emph{covalently stored carbon}.
To match plants, a PV system must add electrolysis, gas storage, and
CO\(_2\) reduction --- each step lossy. End-to-end PV \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} renewable
methanol systems currently achieve about 5--8\% solar-to-fuel
--- comparable to C4 photosynthesis. The biological system also
self-assembles, self-repairs, and runs at \textless1 sun without exotic
materials.

\textbf{Theoretical efficiency limits.} The ultimate biological limit is
set by the sum of (a) photon-to-electron efficiency in the antenna
(about 95\%), (b) thermalisation losses (longer-wavelength
photons supply about 176 kJ/mol; the enthalpy of a pair of e\(^-\)
across the Z-scheme is about 440 kJ --- so the lower bound is
about 1.14 V \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 4 e\(^-\) / 8 photons \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 176 kJ/mol =
about 31\% before downstream losses), and (c) Calvin cycle and
respiration costs (about 40\% loss). The product is a
theoretical about 12\% solar-to-biomass efficiency.

\subsubsection{Key Research Directions}\label{key-research-directions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Artificial water splitting:} Metal oxide catalysts (e.g.,
  IrO\(_2\), Co-Pi) that oxidise water, coupled to photovoltaic cells.
  The goal: electrochemical production of H\(_2\) and O\(_2\) from water
  using sunlight.
\item
  \textbf{CO\(_2\) reduction:} Electrocatalytic or photocatalytic
  reduction of CO\(_2\) to formate, methanol, or hydrocarbons.
  Challenges include selectivity (CO\(_2\) vs.~H\(^+\) reduction) and
  catalyst durability.
\item
  \textbf{Bio-hybrid systems:} Living photosynthetic organisms
  (cyanobacteria, algae) engineered to produce hydrogen, ethanol, or
  alkanes directly from CO\(_2\) and sunlight.
\item
  \textbf{Synthetic minimal photosystem:} Recreating the core PS II
  Mn\(_4\)Ca water-splitting catalyst in synthetic molecules. The
  Mn\(_4\)CaO\(_5\) cluster structure (revealed by Shen et al., 2011,
  \emph{Nature}, at 1.9 Å resolution) guides biomimetic catalyst design.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Photodynamic Therapy (PDT)} Photodynamic
therapy exploits the same photochemistry that plants must protect
against. A photosensitiser (e.g., porphyrin derivative) is administered
to a patient and preferentially accumulates in tumour tissue. Upon
illumination with specific wavelengths, the photosensitiser generates
singlet oxygen (\(^1\)O\(_2\)), which destroys tumour cells.
Understanding the photophysics of chlorophyll-like molecules (energy
transfer, intersystem crossing, ROS generation) underpins PDT drug
design.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsubsection{Engineering Synthetic Photosynthesis: From
Photorespiration Bypass to Directed Evolution of
Rubisco}\label{engineering-synthetic-photosynthesis-from-photorespiration-bypass-to-directed-evolution-of-rubisco}

Rubisco (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase) is the most
abundant protein on Earth, yet it is famously inefficient:
\(k_{\text{cat}}\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 3 s\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1} and an oxygenation side-reaction that drains
20--50 \% of carbon in warm climates through \textbf{photorespiration}.
Engineering around this rate-limiting step is the central problem of
crop productivity. Three complementary strategies have matured between
2019 and 2024.

\textbf{(1) Photorespiration bypass.} The Long lab (\emph{Science} 2019)
introduced a synthetic glycolate-metabolism pathway into tobacco that
shunts glycolate (the toxic product of Rubisco oxygenation) directly to
pyruvate in the chloroplast rather than sending it through the
peroxisome/mitochondrion loop. Field trials demonstrated a
\textbf{about 40 \% biomass yield increase} over 2 years,
without compromising photosynthetic rate. The same bypass is being
translated into cowpea, soybean, and rice via the Realising Increased
Photosynthetic Efficiency (RIPE) consortium. \textbf{(2)
Cyanobacterial-style carbon-concentrating mechanisms.} Cyanobacteria
compartmentalise Rubisco inside \textbf{carboxysomes} that concentrate
CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} locally, suppressing the oxygenation reaction. Expressing the
bacterial \textbf{BicA} HCO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{3}}{3}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-} transporter plus carboxysome shell
proteins in C\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{3}}{3} plants is a about 10-year synthetic-biology
goal; the Price/Long/Hanson labs have cleared the first milestones in
\emph{Nicotiana} and \emph{Chlamydomonas}. \textbf{(3) Directed
evolution of Rubisco itself.} Classical selection inside \emph{E. coli}
is limited because bacterial Rubisco is too different from plant
Rubisco. The 2024 work by the Savage / Kortemme labs used
\textbf{ribosome-display directed evolution} with MS-based screening to
isolate Rubisco variants with about 2\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} improved specificity
factor (Sc/o = 110 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} 220) --- approaching the theoretical maximum set by
the enzyme's two-step mechanism.

Quantitative targets put the stakes in context: improving crop
photosynthetic efficiency by even 10--20 \% in major C3 crops would be
agronomically large, but the realised food-security gain would depend on
canopy architecture, sink strength, water and nitrogen supply, local
climate, post-harvest losses, and access. Molecular agriculture now has
the tools -- CRISPR-Cas9 in plants, synthetic biology standardisation,
and AI-assisted structural hypotheses for Rubisco and its chaperones --
to test ideas that were largely conceptual a decade ago
\citep{abramson2024alphafold3,varadi2024alphafolddb}.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-12}

For \textbf{Photosynthesis}, frontier biology belongs inside the
evidence logic of the chapter. Metabolism is now studied as a regulated
network constrained by energy, redox balance, compartmentation, and
environment. The core reading question is this: photosynthesis claims
should distinguish light capture, carbon fixation, photorespiration,
water stress, and canopy context.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

A strong metabolic explanation names the flux, the limiting step, the
sensor, and the condition under which the pathway changes direction or
priority.

\textbf{Source practice:} For metabolic claims, keep the organism,
compartment, energetic state, and measurement method visible; a pathway
map is not enough without flux or concentration evidence.

\subsubsection{Current Evidence Map: Photosynthesis Under
Stress}\label{current-evidence-map-photosynthesis-under-stress}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0061_d4c7a9a49ee8.png}
\caption{Photosynthesis in a plant is a coupled carbon-water decision: high light cannot raise growth if CO2 entry, water status, or sink demand becomes limiting.}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-12}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Light reactions (thylakoid): light \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} O\(_2\) (water splitting) + NADPH
  + ATP (\cref{eq:unit_III_photosynthesis_overall},
  \cref{eq:unit_III_water_splitting}). PS II drives water oxidation
  (Mn\(_4\)CaO\(_5\) cluster, Kok cycle); cytochrome b\(_6\)f pumps
  protons via Q cycle; PS I drives NADP\(^+\) reduction.
\item
  Photon energy is given by \(E = hc/\lambda\)
  (\cref{eq:unit_III_photon_energy}); a 680 nm photon supplies 176
  kJ/mol. Quantum yield \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Phi}}{Phi}\(_{\text{O}_2}\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 0.10 corresponds to
  about 10 photons per O\(_2\), close to the theoretical
  minimum of 8.
\item
  Antenna complexes (LHCII, LHCI) use FRET
  (\cref{eq:unit_III_fret_rate}) and exciton transfer to funnel
  excitation to reaction centres at about 95\% efficiency. Chl
  a/b ratios and carotenoid composition are tuned to spectral and
  protective demands.
\item
  The Z-scheme spans 1.14 V (\cref{eq:unit_III_z_scheme_energy}) from
  H\(_2\)O (\(+0.82\) V) through P680, P680\emph{, Pheo, PQ, b\(_6\)f,
  PC, P700, P700}, A\(_0\), Fd to NADPH (\(-0.32\) V), driven by two
  photons per electron.
\item
  RuBisCO is hexadecameric (L\(_8\)S\(_8\), 8 active sites), requires
  CO\(_2\) + Mg\(^{2+}\) for active-site carbamylation, and shows a
  fundamental specificity-factor / turnover trade-off
  (\cref{eq:unit_III_specificity_factor}). Plant
  \(S_{c/o} \approx 80\)--100; theoretical maximum about 400.
\item
  Calvin cycle (stroma): 18 ATP + 12 NADPH fix 6 CO\(_2\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} 1 glucose.
  Photorespiration costs C3 plants about 25\% of fixed carbon
  (the carboxylation/oxygenation ratio is set by
  \cref{eq:unit_III_carb_oxy_ratio}).
\item
  C4 uses Kranz anatomy (spatial separation); CAM uses temporal
  separation (night CO\(_2\) fixation). Both have near-zero
  photorespiration but higher ATP costs. Water-use efficiency
  (\cref{eq:unit_III_water_use_efficiency}) ranks CAM \textgreater{} C4
  \textgreater{} C3 by an order of magnitude.
\item
  The thioredoxin/ferredoxin system
  (\cref{eq:unit_III_thioredoxin_cascade}) couples PS I activity to
  Calvin-cycle enzyme activation via reversible disulfide reduction.
  Stromal pH 8.0 and Mg\(^{2+}\) release further activate RuBisCO and
  FBPase.
\item
  NPQ (\cref{eq:unit_III_npq_definition}) protects the photosynthetic
  apparatus through the xanthophyll cycle
  (\cref{eq:unit_III_xanthophyll_cycle}), state transitions, and
  photoinhibition repair. Carotenoids quench triplet Chl and singlet
  O\(_2\) \citep{hager1971}.
\item
  Artificial photosynthesis bridges biology (engineered cyanobacteria)
  and chemistry (PEC cells, Mn\(_4\)Ca biomimetics); silicon PV is more
  efficient but does not produce storable fuel directly.
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See
  \cref{sec:unit_III_bioenergetics_and_respiration} for chemiosmotic
  coupling in mitochondria vs.~chloroplasts, Unit VIII for whole-plant
  carbon and water trade-offs, and Unit X for primary productivity.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Review Questions}\label{review-questions-12}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Describe the structure of a chloroplast and explain how the
  organisation of the thylakoid membrane is adapted for efficient
  photosynthesis.
\item
  Explain the Z-scheme of photosynthetic electron transport. Why are two
  photosystems needed to move electrons from water to NADP\(^+\)? Quote
  at least three intermediate redox potentials in your answer.
\item
  Calculate the energy of a 440 nm blue photon and a 680 nm red photon
  (per mole). Explain why both are equally effective at driving
  photochemistry despite different photon energies.
\item
  Describe the Kok cycle (S-state cycle) of water oxidation. Why must
  four photons be absorbed to produce one O\(_2\)?
\item
  Compare the Q cycle in Complex III of mitochondria with the Q cycle in
  cytochrome b\(_6\)f of chloroplasts. What is the common functional
  principle?
\item
  Describe RuBisCO's structure and catalytic mechanism. Why is the
  specificity factor \(S_{c/o}\) inversely correlated with
  \(k_{\text{cat}}\) across the tree of life?
\item
  Describe the three phases of the Calvin cycle. Calculate the total ATP
  and NADPH cost to fix 6 CO\(_2\) into one glucose molecule, and the
  minimum number of photons required.
\item
  Explain the thioredoxin/ferredoxin redox regulation system. Which
  Calvin cycle enzymes are activated, and what would happen in a
  \emph{trxR} (thioredoxin reductase) knockout in the light?
\item
  Compare C3, C4, and CAM photosynthesis in terms of leaf anatomy,
  biochemistry, water-use efficiency, and ecological
  \hyperref[gl:niche]{\textbf{niche}}. Use
  \cref{eq:unit_III_intrinsic_wue} to explain why CAM achieves the
  highest WUE.
\item
  Explain the xanthophyll cycle and qE non-photochemical quenching. Why
  is this mechanism essential for plant survival in fluctuating light?
\item
  Calculate the energy efficiency of photosynthesis if 48 photons of 680
  nm light are needed to fix 6 CO\(_2\). Compare this with the
  efficiency of a typical silicon solar cell (about 22\%).
\item
  Engineering reduced photorespiration has been proposed to increase
  crop yields. Describe two approaches and discuss potential risks.
\item
  Call \breaktt{photosynthesis\_rate} at 100 vs.~2000 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}mol m\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2} s\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}
  default parameters. At which irradiance are you nearer light
  saturation, and how does that relate to greenhouse shading trials?
\item
  Compare cyclic vs.~linear electron flow around PS I in terms of

\item
  Compute the Förster transfer rate at \(r = 7\) nm given \(R_0 = 5\) nm

\textbf{Photorespiration} & RuBisCO oxygenase activity; wastes

\textbf{C4 photosynthesis} & CO\(_2\) concentrating mechanism using PEP
carboxylase and Kranz anatomy \\
\textbf{CAM} & Crassulacean acid metabolism; temporal separation of
CO\(_2\) fixation (night) and Calvin cycle (day) \\
\textbf{Water-use efficiency (WUE)} & Carbon fixed per water lost; CAM
\textgreater{} C4 \textgreater{} C3 \\
\textbf{Kok cycle} & S-state cycle of the OEC; accumulates 4 oxidising
equivalents before O\(_2\) release \\
\textbf{Antenna complex} & Light-harvesting pigment-protein complex;
funnels energy to reaction centre \\
\textbf{FRET} & Förster Resonance Energy Transfer; dipole-dipole energy
transfer between pigments; rate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\propto}}{propto} 1/r\(^6\) \\
\textbf{Quantum yield} & Molecules of product per photon absorbed;
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Phi}}{Phi}\(_{\text{O}_2}\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 0.10 \\
\textbf{Non-photochemical quenching (NPQ)} & Thermal dissipation of
excess light energy; comprises qE, qT, qI components \\
\textbf{Xanthophyll cycle} & Violaxanthin \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\leftrightarrow}}{<->} zeaxanthin interconversion;
regulates qE \\
\textbf{PsbS} & PS II protein with two lumen-exposed Glu residues;
protonated at low pH; triggers qE \\
\textbf{Plastocyanin} & Soluble copper protein carrying electrons from
b\(_6\)f to PS I in the lumen \\
\textbf{Kranz anatomy} & Wreath-like leaf anatomy of C4 plants; bundle
sheath surrounds vascular tissue \\
\textbf{Cyclic electron flow} & PS I-mediated; Fd \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PQ \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} b\(_6\)f \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PC \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
PS I; produces ATP without NADPH \\

\subsection{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-13}

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Trace how the cell coordinates catabolic and anabolic pathways through
  shared cofactors and \hyperref[gl:allosteric]{\textbf{allosteric}}
  cross-regulation, and predict the metabolic state from cofactor and
  signal-molecule ratios.
\item
  Describe AMPK and mTORC1 as opposing energy-sensing hubs and explain
  how they toggle the metabolic state of the cell, including the
  molecular basis of mTOR's role as a nutrient sensor (Rag GTPases,
  Ragulator).
\item
  Describe the metabolic states of fed, post-absorptive, fasting, and
  starvation, including hormonal control and the timeline of fuel
  switching.
\item
  Explain insulin signalling in detail: the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway,
  \hyperref[gl:glut4]{\textbf{GLUT4}} translocation mechanism, and
  glycogen synthesis.
\item
  Explain glucagon signalling: cAMP/PKA activation of glycogenolysis,
  gluconeogenesis, and the phosphorylase kinase cascade.
\item
  Distinguish allosteric from transcriptional metabolic regulation given
  an \hyperref[gl:enzyme]{\textbf{enzyme}}-activity time-course, using
  gluconeogenesis bypass-enzyme control as the worked case.
\item
  Compare ATP yield and regulation of glucose versus fatty-acid
  oxidation, and calculate the net ATP yield from palmitoyl-CoA.
\item
  Explain ketone body metabolism and its role during starvation.
\item
  Describe AMPK structure (two catalytic + two regulatory subunits) and
  activation mechanisms (LKB1 vs CaMKK\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}).
\item
  Trace flux control through the glucose-fatty-acid (Randle) cycle under
  fed versus fasted conditions, and predict the resulting respiratory
  quotient.
\item
  Define substrate (futile) cycles and explain their control advantages.
\item
  Explain obesity, metabolic syndrome, and insulin resistance at the
  molecular level, including visceral fat as an endocrine organ.
\item
  Apply metabolic control analysis (MCA): flux control coefficients
  \(C_i^J\) and the summation theorem.
\item
  Calculate the adenylate energy charge from concentrations and predict
  the resulting AMPK activation state.
\item
  Describe modern metabolomics: NMR vs mass spectrometry approaches and
  identification challenges.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Opening Vignette: The Brain on Ketones --- Surviving Starvation}

The human brain is extraordinarily metabolically demanding: it consumes
roughly 20\% of the body's resting energy budget despite constituting
about 2\% of body mass. Under normal conditions, it runs almost
exclusively on glucose. But glucose stores --- maintained as liver
glycogen --- last only about 12--24 hours of fasting. So how does the
brain survive during prolonged starvation?

The liver activates a metabolic programme: free fatty acids released
from adipose tissue are not completely oxidised within the liver itself.
Instead, the liver packages their acetyl-CoA units into \textbf{ketone
bodies} (acetoacetate and \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-hydroxybutyrate) and exports them to the
bloodstream. After 1--2 days of fasting, the brain begins importing
ketones; after 3--5 days, it derives up to 75\% of its energy from
ketone bodies. Circulating ketone concentrations rise from
about 0.1 mM (fed state) to 6--8 mM (prolonged starvation).
This elegant metabolic switch --- coordinated by insulin falling and
glucagon rising --- is one of the clearest examples of metabolic
integration studied in this chapter.

\emph{Primary source: Owen, O. E. et al.~(1967). Brain metabolism during
fasting. Journal of Clinical Investigation, 46(10), 1589--1595.}
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Pathways Are Not Isolated}\label{pathways-are-not-isolated}

\hyperref[gl:glycolysis]{\textbf{Glycolysis}}, the TCA cycle,
beta-oxidation, and biosynthetic pathways do not operate independently.
They share intermediates, co-factors (NAD\(^+\)/NADH, NADP\(^+\)/NADPH,
CoA), and are subject to \textbf{allosteric cross-regulation}.
Integration of these pathways defines the \textbf{metabolic state} of
the cell.

The two fundamental modes: - \textbf{Catabolism} --- break down
nutrients \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} ATP + reduced cofactors (NADH, FADH\(_2\)) -
\textbf{Anabolism} --- use ATP + reduced cofactors (chiefly NADPH) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
biosynthesis of macromolecules

These modes are reciprocally regulated because of shared cofactors and
master regulatory kinases. The metabolic state is encoded in:

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\subsubsection{Fasting Physiology: Fuel Switch
Timeline}\label{fasting-physiology-fuel-switch-timeline}

The body switches fuels in a programmed sequence as fasting progresses.
The transitions are coordinated by falling insulin and rising glucagon
(and later cortisol):

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2456}}

\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Time post-meal
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Predominant fuel
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Liver process
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
0--4 h (absorptive) & Dietary glucose & Glycogenesis, lipogenesis &
Glucose & Insulin high, glucagon low \\
4--12 h (post-absorptive) & Liver glycogen & Glycogenolysis & Glucose &
Glucagon rises \\
12--24 h (early fasting) & Liver glycogen \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} muscle FA & Glycogen
depleting; gluconeogenesis ramping & Glucose (mostly from GNG) & Liver
glycogen mostly depleted by about 24 h \\
1--3 days & Muscle FA + early ketones & Gluconeogenesis (lactate,
alanine, glycerol); ketogenesis starting & Glucose 75\%, ketones 25\% &
Cortisol rises; protein catabolism increases \\
3--7 days & Ketones & Maximal ketogenesis & Glucose 25\%, ketones 75\% &
Brain adapts; muscle protein sparing \\
\textgreater{} 1--2 weeks & Ketones (sustained) & Ketogenesis at steady
state & Ketones 65--75\%, glucose 25--35\% & Resting metabolic rate
falls about 20\% \\
\textgreater{} 30+ days (starvation) & Body protein (terminal) &
Gluconeogenesis from muscle protein dominates & Glucose 50\%, ketones
50\% & Death imminent when about 50\% of protein lost \\
\end{longtable}
}

This fuel-switching timeline is one of the most elegant examples of
metabolic integration. It is also clinically relevant: bariatric
surgery, ketogenic diets, and prolonged fasting interventions most
exploit (or perturb) this same switch.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 1:} Why is it essential that glycolysis and
gluconeogenesis are reciprocally regulated and rarely fully active
simultaneously? What would happen if both ran at maximum rate?
\end{quote}

\subsection{Insulin Signalling: The PI3K/Akt/mTOR
Pathway}\label{insulin-signalling-the-pi3kaktmtor-pathway}

Insulin is the master anabolic \hyperref[gl:hormone]{\textbf{hormone}},
secreted by pancreatic beta-cells in response to elevated blood glucose.
Its signalling cascade is one of the most important in metabolic
regulation:

\[\text{Insulin} \to \text{IR (RTK)} \to \text{IRS-1/2} \to \text{PI3K} \to \text{PIP}_3 \to \text{PDK1 + mTORC2} \to \text{Akt (Thr308 + Ser473)} \tag{11.1}\]

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0063_09287921f06e.png}
\caption{Flowchart for Insulin Signalling: The PI3K/Akt/mTOR Pathway: Insulin, Insulin receptor (alpha2beta2 tyrosine kinase), IRS-1/2 (Tyr phosphorylated), and PI3K (p85/p110) form the diagram's primary path or branches.}
\end{figure}

\emph{Insulin signalling cascade from receptor to downstream metabolic
and growth effects (Mermaid).} Akt is the central node, integrating PDK1
(Thr308) and mTORC2 (Ser473) phosphorylations to drive glucose uptake,
glycogen synthesis, lipogenesis, and protein synthesis.

\textbf{Downstream Akt targets:}

\textbf{GLUT4 translocation mechanism (in detail):}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Basal state.} GLUT4 is sequestered in specialised
  intracellular vesicles (GSVs, GLUT4 storage vesicles)
  about 95\% of the time, with about 5\% at the plasma
  membrane. The vesicles are tethered by the inhibitory Rab-GAP
  \textbf{AS160 (TBC1D4)}, which keeps Rab10 in its GDP-bound (inactive)
  state.
\item
  \textbf{Insulin signal.} Akt phosphorylates AS160 on multiple sites
  (Thr642 most important), inhibiting its GAP activity.
\item
  \textbf{Rab10 activation.} With AS160 off, Rab10 accumulates in the
  GTP-bound active state, promoting vesicle docking at the plasma
  membrane.
\item
  \textbf{SNARE-mediated fusion.} Synaptobrevin-2 (VAMP2) on GSVs
  engages plasma-membrane syntaxin-4 + SNAP-23, driving membrane fusion.
\item
  \textbf{GLUT4 exposure.} GLUT4 appears at the cell surface, increasing
  glucose uptake 10--20-fold.
\item
  \textbf{Endocytosis on signal termination.} When insulin signal ends,
  GLUT4 is endocytosed back to GSVs via clathrin-coated pits and a slow
  constitutive recycling pathway.
\end{enumerate}

In type 2 diabetes, this cascade is disrupted at multiple levels (see
clinical box below) so that GLUT4 translocation is impaired even at high
circulating insulin.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Insulin Resistance and Type 2 Diabetes} In
type 2 diabetes, insulin signalling is impaired at multiple levels: 1.
\textbf{IRS-1 serine phosphorylation} (by JNK, PKC-theta, IKK-beta)
prevents tyrosine phosphorylation by the
\hyperref[gl:insulin-receptor]{\textbf{insulin receptor}} 2.
\textbf{Ceramide accumulation} activates PP2A, which dephosphorylates
Akt 3. \textbf{DAG accumulation} activates PKC-epsilon (liver) and
PKC-theta (muscle), which phosphorylate IRS-1 on inhibitory serine
residues 4. \textbf{ER stress} (from lipid overload) activates JNK \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
IRS-1 Ser307 phosphorylation The net result: GLUT4 translocation is
impaired, glycogen synthesis is reduced, and gluconeogenesis is not
suppressed. Metformin (first-line therapy) works partly through AMPK
activation and partly through inhibition of mitochondrial Complex I. see
\cref{sec:unit_II_cell_signaling} for RTK signalling.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 2:} Thiazolidinediones (e.g., rosiglitazone)
activate PPAR-gamma in adipose tissue, increasing adipocyte
differentiation and lipid storage. Explain how increasing fat storage in
adipose tissue could paradoxically improve insulin sensitivity in muscle
and liver.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Glucagon Signalling: cAMP/PKA
Pathway}\label{glucagon-signalling-camppka-pathway}

Glucagon is secreted by pancreatic alpha-cells when blood glucose falls.
It acts primarily on the \textbf{liver} (hepatocytes express glucagon
receptors; muscle does not):

\textbf{Glucagon \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Glucagon receptor (GPCR) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} G\(_s\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Adenylyl cyclase
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} cAMP \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PKA}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0064_27dc0606c7c7.png}
\caption{Flowchart for Glucagon Signalling: cAMP/PKA Pathway: Glucagon (or epinephrine via beta-AR), Glucagon receptor / beta-AR (GPCR), Galphas, and Adenylyl cyclase form the diagram's primary path or branches.}
\end{figure}

\emph{Glucagon (or epinephrine) signalling cascade in the liver
(Mermaid).} The cAMP/PKA cascade simultaneously activates glycogenolysis
(via phosphorylase kinase) and gluconeogenesis (via CREB transcription)
while suppressing glycolysis (via PFK-2/pyruvate kinase
phosphorylation).

\subsubsection{The Phosphorylase Kinase Cascade --- A Signal
Amplifier}\label{the-phosphorylase-kinase-cascade-a-signal-amplifier}

The chain glucagon \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} GPCR \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} cAMP \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PKA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{phosphorylase kinase}
(PhK) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} glycogen phosphorylase is one of biology's most elegant
amplification cascades. Each step amplifies the signal:

A single glucagon binding event releases a burst of
about 10\(^7\) glucose-1-phosphate molecules within seconds.
This is how a signal at femtomolar hormone concentrations produces a
millimolar metabolite response.

\subsection{Gluconeogenesis}\label{gluconeogenesis}

Gluconeogenesis synthesises glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors
(lactate, glycerol, glucogenic amino acids). It occurs primarily in the
\textbf{liver} and to a lesser extent in the \textbf{kidney cortex}.

Gluconeogenesis is NOT simply the reverse of glycolysis. Three
irreversible glycolytic steps require \textbf{bypass enzymes}:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5172}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3448}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1379}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Glycolytic step (irreversible)
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Gluconeogenic bypass
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Location
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Pyruvate kinase (PEP \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Pyruvate) & \textbf{Pyruvate carboxylase}
(Pyruvate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} OAA; biotin, ATP) + \textbf{PEPCK} (OAA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PEP; GTP) &
Mitochondria + cytoplasm \\
PFK-1 (F6P \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} F1,6BP) & \textbf{Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (FBPase-1)} &
Cytoplasm \\

ER membrane (liver, kidney primarily) \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Cost:} 6 ATP equivalents per glucose synthesised (4 ATP + 2
GTP).

\textbf{Regulation of gluconeogenesis:} - \textbf{Allosteric:} Pyruvate
carboxylase activated by acetyl-CoA; FBPase-1 inhibited by AMP and
F2,6BP - \textbf{Hormonal:} Glucagon (via CREB) induces PEPCK and G6Pase
genes; insulin (via FoxO1) represses them - \textbf{Reciprocal with
glycolysis:} F2,6BP activates PFK-1 (glycolysis) and inhibits FBPase-1
(gluconeogenesis), ensuring they do not run simultaneously

\textbf{Concept Check 3:} Ethanol metabolism in the liver generates
excess NADH (from alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase).
Predict the effect of heavy alcohol consumption on gluconeogenesis and
the risk of hypoglycaemia.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Glycogen Metabolism}\label{glycogen-metabolism}

\subsubsection{Glycogen Structure}\label{glycogen-structure}

Glycogen is a branched polymer of glucose units: - \textbf{Alpha-1,4
linkages:} linear chains (about 8--12 glucose units between
branch points) - \textbf{Alpha-1,6 linkages:} branch points
(about  every 8--12 residues) - \textbf{Glycogenin:}
self-glucosylating primer protein at the core

Liver glycogen (about 100 g): blood glucose
\hyperref[gl:buffer]{\textbf{buffer}}. Muscle glycogen
(about 400 g): local fuel for contraction (rarely exported as
glucose because muscle lacks G6Pase).

\subsubsection{Key Enzymes}\label{key-enzymes}

\textbf{Glycogen phosphorylase:} Cleaves alpha-1,4 linkages from
non-reducing ends, releasing glucose-1-phosphate. Regulated by: -
\textbf{Allosteric activation:} AMP (muscle); glucose (liver,
inhibitory) - \textbf{Covalent modification:} Phosphorylase kinase
phosphorylates Ser14 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} active \textbf{a} form - \textbf{Hormonal
cascade:} Glucagon/epinephrine \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} cAMP \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PKA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} phosphorylase kinase \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
phosphorylase a

\textbf{Glycogen synthase:} Adds UDP-glucose to non-reducing ends
(alpha-1,4 linkages). Active when dephosphorylated (GSK3 phosphorylates
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} inactive; insulin inhibits GSK3 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} GS active).

\textbf{Branching enzyme:} Transfers about 7-residue segments
to create alpha-1,6 branches. Increases solubility and number of
non-reducing ends (more rapid mobilisation).

\textbf{Debranching enzyme:} Bifunctional: transferase activity moves 3
residues from branch, then alpha-1,6-glucosidase cleaves the branch
point, releasing free glucose.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Glycogen Storage Diseases} |{} Type
|{} Enzyme deficiency |{} Features |{} |{}
---- |{} ----------------- |{} -------- |{}
|{} I (von Gierke) |{} Glucose-6-phosphatase |{}
Severe hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis |{}
|{} II (Pompe) |{} Lysosomal alpha-glucosidase |{}
Cardiac/skeletal myopathy; treated by ERT |{} |{} V
(McArdle) |{} Muscle glycogen phosphorylase |{} Exercise
intolerance; ``second wind'' phenomenon |{} |{} VII
(Tarui) |{} Muscle PFK |{} Exercise intolerance,
haemolytic anaemia |{}
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Fatty Acid Oxidation
(Beta-Oxidation)}\label{fatty-acid-oxidation-beta-oxidation}

Beta-oxidation occurs in the \textbf{mitochondrial matrix} and degrades
fatty acyl-CoA by removing 2-carbon units (acetyl-CoA) per cycle.

\subsubsection{Activation and Transport}\label{activation-and-transport}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Activation:} Fatty acid + CoA + ATP \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Acyl-CoA + AMP +
  PP\(_i\) (acyl-CoA synthetase; outer mitochondrial membrane; costs 2
  ATP equivalents)
\item
  \textbf{Carnitine shuttle:} Acyl-CoA cannot cross the IMM. Instead:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{CPT-1} (outer face of IMM): acyl-CoA + carnitine \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
    acylcarnitine + CoA
  \item
    \textbf{Translocase (CACT):} acylcarnitine crosses IMM
  \item
    \textbf{CPT-2} (inner face of IMM): acylcarnitine + CoA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} acyl-CoA +
    carnitine
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{CPT-1 is the rate-limiting step} of beta-oxidation.
\textbf{Malonyl-CoA} (the first committed intermediate of fatty acid
synthesis) \textbf{allosterically inhibits CPT-1}, ensuring that fatty
acid synthesis and oxidation do not occur simultaneously.

\subsubsection{Beta-Oxidation Steps (Each
Cycle)}\label{beta-oxidation-steps-each-cycle}

(C16:0)}\label{atp-yield-from-palmitoyl-coa-c160}

Summing the products of complete fatty-acid oxidation makes the ``fat is
energy-dense'' claim quantitative. Palmitoyl-CoA (16 carbons) undergoes
7 cycles of beta-oxidation:

Some textbooks report 108 ATP (using older P/O ratios) or 129 ATP
(including palmitate rather than palmitoyl-CoA, and using maximal P/O
ratios). The exact number depends on assumed H\(^+\)/ATP stoichiometry
and shuttle costs. The key insight: fatty acids are energy-dense
(about 9 kcal/g vs.~4 kcal/g for carbohydrates) because they
are highly reduced.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: MCAD Deficiency} Medium-chain acyl-CoA
dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency is the most common inherited disorder of
fatty acid oxidation (about 1:10,000 births). During fasting,
patients cannot oxidise medium-chain fatty acids, leading to hypoketotic
hypoglycaemia (low ketones because acetyl-CoA production is impaired,
low glucose because gluconeogenesis lacks acetyl-CoA stimulation of
pyruvate carboxylase). Fatal Reye-like episodes can occur. Management:
avoid prolonged fasting; ensure regular carbohydrate intake.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Fatty Acid Synthesis}\label{fatty-acid-synthesis}

Fatty acid synthesis occurs in the \textbf{cytoplasm} and uses
fundamentally different chemistry from beta-oxidation:

\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

Location & Mitochondrial matrix & Cytoplasm \\

\textbf{Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC)} catalyses the committed step:
acetyl-CoA + CO\(_2\) + ATP \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} malonyl-CoA. This is the key regulatory
enzyme: - \textbf{Activated by:} citrate (allosteric), insulin
(dephosphorylation) - \textbf{Inhibited by:} palmitoyl-CoA (product
inhibition), AMPK phosphorylation (energy depletion), glucagon (via PKA)

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Ketone Body Metabolism}\label{ketone-body-metabolism}

During prolonged fasting (\textgreater24--48 h), the liver converts
excess acetyl-CoA from fatty acid oxidation into \textbf{ketone bodies}:
acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate, and acetone.

\textbf{Synthesis (liver mitochondria):} 1. 2 Acetyl-CoA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
Acetoacetyl-CoA (thiolase) 2. Acetoacetyl-CoA + Acetyl-CoA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} HMG-CoA
(HMG-CoA synthase) 3. HMG-CoA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Acetoacetate + Acetyl-CoA (HMG-CoA
lyase) 4. Acetoacetate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} beta-Hydroxybutyrate (beta-hydroxybutyrate DH;
uses NADH) 5. Acetoacetate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Acetone (non-enzymatic decarboxylation;
exhaled)

\textbf{Utilisation (brain, heart, muscle):} Beta-hydroxybutyrate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
acetoacetate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} acetoacetyl-CoA (via succinyl-CoA transferase, also
called thiophorase) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} 2 acetyl-CoA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} TCA cycle.

\textbf{Key points:} - The liver \textbf{cannot use} ketone bodies
(lacks thiophorase) - The brain normally uses primarily glucose but
during starvation adapts to derive \textbf{about 60--70\%} of
its energy from ketone bodies, sparing muscle protein - This
protein-sparing effect is essential for survival during prolonged
fasting - Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): uncontrolled type 1 diabetes \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
absent insulin \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} massive lipolysis \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} excessive ketone body production \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
metabolic acidosis (\hyperref[gl:ph]{\textbf{pH}} \textless7.3),
dehydration, potentially fatal

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 4:} Why can the liver produce ketone bodies but
not use them? What is the physiological advantage of this arrangement?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{AMPK --- The Cellular Energy
Gauge}\label{ampk-the-cellular-energy-gauge}

\textbf{AMPK} (AMP-activated protein kinase) is a heterotrimer with
\textbf{two catalytic \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-subunits} (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}1 and \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}2 isoforms), \textbf{two
regulatory \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-subunits} (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}1, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}2), and the \textbf{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma}-subunit} that binds
adenine nucleotides --- though the assembled holoenzyme is
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}\(_1\)\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}\(_1\)\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma}\(_1\). (The classic textbook description is that AMPK is
``two catalytic + two regulatory subunits'' referring to the assembly's
binary modules: the catalytic \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}/\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} pair and the regulatory \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}/\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma} pair.) The
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma}-subunit contains four CBS (cystathionine \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-synthase) domains, of which
three bind adenine nucleotides --- AMP, ADP, and ATP --- competitively.
This competitive binding lets the \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma}-subunit \emph{integrate} the entire
adenylate pool, not just one ratio.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0065_0f9add5e4b9c.png}
\caption{AMPK as the cellular energy sensor. Low energy activates AMPK, which simultaneously promotes catabolic pathways and inhibits anabolic pathways. High energy inactivates AMPK, allowing mTORC1-driven anabolism.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{AMPK Activation: LKB1 vs
CaMKK\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}}\label{ampk-activation-lkb1-vs-camkkux3b2}

AMPK is activated when its catalytic \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-subunit is phosphorylated at
\textbf{Thr172}. Two upstream kinases phosphorylate this site under
different physiological conditions:

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1111}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3016}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3492}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Upstream kinase
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Trigger
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{LKB1} (STK11) & Energy stress (high AMP); allosterically primed
by AMP binding to AMPK \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma} & Ubiquitous; constitutively active &
Loss-of-function = Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, predisposes to
gastrointestinal cancers \\
\textbf{CaMKK\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}} & Elevated cytosolic Ca\(^{2+}\) (independent of AMP) &
Brain, muscle, T cells, endothelium & Important in T-cell activation,
osmotic stress \\
\textbf{TAK1} & Inflammatory cytokines (TGF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}, TNF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}) & Limited &
Crosstalk between inflammation and metabolism \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{LKB1 is the dominant kinase under classical energy stress}
(exercise, hypoxia, starvation): AMP binding to AMPK \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma} promotes LKB1
docking and Thr172 phosphorylation, while simultaneously protecting
Thr172 from dephosphorylation by PP2A and PP2C. AMP is therefore not
simply an ``activator'' but an \emph{allosteric primer} that shifts the
AMPK steady state from dephosphorylated to phosphorylated.

\textbf{CaMKK\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} provides a Ca\(^{2+}\)-coupled activation route} --- for
example, in muscle contraction (where Ca\(^{2+}\) release accompanies
ATP demand) or in T-cell activation following T-cell receptor
engagement. This route runs \textbf{in parallel} to the AMP/LKB1 pathway
and lets cells anticipate energy demand from Ca\(^{2+}\) signals before
AMP rises.

\subsubsection{Energy Charge}\label{energy-charge}

The \textbf{energy charge (EC)} of the adenylate system was introduced
by Atkinson \citep{atkinson1968} as a single scalar that captures the
fractional saturation of the adenylate pool with high-energy phosphate:

\begin{equation}
\text{E.C.} = \frac{[\text{ATP}] + \tfrac{1}{2}[\text{ADP}]}{[\text{ATP}] + [\text{ADP}] + [\text{AMP}]}
\label{eq:unit_III_energy_charge}
\end{equation}

The numerator counts each phosphoanhydride bond (ATP has two
phosphoanhydrides, ADP has one), while the denominator counts the total
adenylate pool. So E.C. = 1.0 means most adenylates are ATP; E.C. = 0
means most are AMP.

Most cells maintain EC approximately 0.85--0.95 \citep{atkinson1968}.
AMPK is highly sensitive in the range EC = 0.70--0.85 --- precisely the
window where rising AMP signals impending energy crisis.

\subsection{Worked Example: Energy
Charge}\label{worked-example-energy-charge}

\emph{Problem:} A resting skeletal-muscle biopsy gives adenylate pools
of {[}ATP{]} = 5.0 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}mol/g, {[}ADP{]} = 0.6 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}mol/g, and {[}AMP{]} = 0.05
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}mol/g. Calculate the energy charge and predict whether AMPK is active.

\emph{Solution:}

\textbf{Step 1 --- State the relation and why ADP is half-weighted.} The
energy charge measures the fractional saturation of the adenylate pool
with transferable phosphoanhydride bonds:

\[EC = \frac{[\text{ATP}] + \tfrac{1}{2}[\text{ADP}]}{[\text{ATP}] + [\text{ADP}] + [\text{AMP}]}\]

ATP carries two high-energy phosphoanhydride bonds and ADP carries one,
so on a per-adenylate basis ADP holds exactly half the transferable
phosphate of ATP --- hence the \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) weighting. The
denominator is the conserved total adenylate pool
({[}ATP{]}+{[}ADP{]}+{[}AMP{]}), so \(EC = 1\) when every adenylate is
ATP and \(EC = 0\) when every adenylate is AMP.

\textbf{Step 2 --- Substitute the measured \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}mol/g values.}

\[EC = \frac{5.0 + \tfrac{1}{2}(0.6)}{5.0 + 0.6 + 0.05}\]

Numerator: \(5.0 + 0.5 \times 0.6 = 5.0 + 0.30 = 5.30\). Denominator:
\(5.0 + 0.6 + 0.05 = 5.65\). The shared \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}mol/g units cancel, so the
ratio is dimensionless.

\textbf{Step 3 --- Compute and interpret against the AMPK threshold.}

\[EC = \frac{5.30}{5.65} = 0.938 \tag{11.3}\]

At \(EC = 0.938\) the pool sits in the normal resting band of 0.85--0.95
and well above the AMPK-activation window of 0.70--0.85. Predict: AMPK
is largely inactive and the cell is in an energy-replete state favouring
anabolism. A fall toward \(EC \approx 0.80\) (rising AMP) would move the
pool into the AMPK-sensitive window and switch the cell toward
catabolism.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Metformin and AMPK} Metformin, the most
widely prescribed diabetes drug, activates AMPK indirectly by inhibiting
mitochondrial Complex I, which raises the AMP/ATP ratio. AMPK
activation: - Increases glucose uptake in muscle - Inhibits hepatic
gluconeogenesis (via CREB coactivator CRTC2 phosphorylation) - Reduces
lipogenesis - May have anti-cancer effects (mTORC1 inhibition) Metformin
is also being investigated as an anti-ageing compound (TAME trial). see
\cref{sec:unit_III_bioenergetics_and_respiration} for Complex I.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Worked Example: Flux Control
Coefficient}\label{worked-example-flux-control-coefficient}

\emph{Problem:} In an isolated hepatocyte preparation, a small activator
raises PFK-1 activity by 20\% and the measured glycolytic flux rises by
5\%. A separate manipulation raises the pyruvate-transporter activity by
30\% and flux rises by 3\%. Calculate each flux control coefficient and
determine which step exerts more control over glycolytic flux.

\emph{Solution:}

\textbf{Step 1 --- State the operational form of the flux control
coefficient.} For a small fractional change in enzyme activity,
\(C_i^J = \dfrac{\partial \ln J}{\partial \ln e_i}\) is approximated by
the ratio of fractional changes:

\[C_i^J \approx \frac{\Delta J / J}{\Delta e_i / e_i} \tag{11.9}\]

\textbf{Step 2 --- Substitute for PFK-1.} Here \(\Delta e/e = 0.20\) and
\(\Delta J/J = 0.05\):

\[C_{\text{PFK-1}}^{J} = \frac{0.05}{0.20} = 0.25 \tag{11.10}\]

\textbf{Step 3 --- Substitute for the pyruvate transporter.} Here
\(\Delta e/e = 0.30\) and \(\Delta J/J = 0.03\):

\[C_{\text{transporter}}^{J} = \frac{0.03}{0.30} = 0.10\]

\textbf{Step 4 --- Interpret against the summation theorem.} Both
coefficients fall in the \(C_i^J \approx 0.1\)--\(0.3\) band reported
for glycolytic enzymes. PFK-1 (\(C^J = 0.25\)) exerts more than twice
the flux control of the pyruvate transporter (\(C^J = 0.10\)), so PFK-1
is the more rate-controlling step here --- yet because
\cref{eq:unit_III_mca_summation} requires \(\sum_i C_i^J = 1\), these
two steps together account for primarily \(0.25 + 0.10 = 0.35\) of total
control. The remaining \(0.65\) is distributed across other enzymes: no
single enzyme is \emph{the} rate-limiting step, which is why an
activator targeting PFK-1 alone produces primarily a fractional, not
proportional, increase in flux.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}
