\subsubsection{Amino Acid Sensing: The Ragulator Complex and
Lysosome}\label{amino-acid-sensing-the-ragulator-complex-and-lysosome}

mTORC1 primarily senses amino acid sufficiency by being
\textbf{physically positioned} on the lysosomal surface. The structure
responsible is a multi-protein scaffold called the \textbf{Ragulator
complex} (LAMTOR1--5) that anchors mTORC1 to the cytoplasmic face of the
lysosomal membrane. The amino acid sensing cascade works as follows:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Specific amino acid sensors} detect intracellular
  concentrations:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{Sestrin2} binds and is inhibited by \textbf{leucine} ---
    when Leu is high, Sestrin2 is displaced and stops inhibiting GATOR2.
  \item
    \textbf{CASTOR1} binds and is inhibited by \textbf{arginine} ---
    same logic.
  \item
    \textbf{SAMTOR} senses S-adenosylmethionine (a proxy for
    methionine).
  \item
    \textbf{SLC38A9} senses lysosomal arginine and signals from the
    lysosomal membrane.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{GATOR1/2 GAP/GEF complex.} GATOR1 is a GAP for the Rag GTPases
  (turning them off); GATOR2 inhibits GATOR1. When sensors release
  inhibition of GATOR2, GATOR1 is suppressed, allowing the Rag GTPases
  to enter their active conformation.
\item
  \textbf{Active Rag GTPases} (RagA/B-GTP + RagC/D-GDP) bind Raptor (a
  subunit of mTORC1) and recruit mTORC1 to the lysosomal surface.
\item
  \textbf{At the lysosome}, mTORC1 encounters Rheb-GTP --- provided that
  growth factor signalling has activated it via Akt \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} TSC2 inhibition \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  Rheb-GTP accumulation.
\item
  \textbf{Rheb-GTP fully activates mTORC1} kinase activity. Both signals
  (amino acids \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Rag \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} lysosomal positioning \emph{and} growth factors \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  Rheb-GTP) must converge.
\end{enumerate}

This dual-input gating is why mTORC1 is sometimes described as a
\textbf{coincidence detector}: it primarily signals ``build'' when both
raw materials (amino acids) and external commands (insulin/IGF-1) are
present.

\subsubsection{Rapamycin: Mechanism of
Action}\label{rapamycin-mechanism-of-action}

\textbf{Rapamycin} is a macrolide originally isolated from
\emph{Streptomyces hygroscopicus} on Easter Island (Rapa Nui). It binds
to the immunophilin \textbf{FKBP12} in the cytoplasm; the
FKBP12-rapamycin complex then binds to the FRB domain of mTOR within
mTORC1, allosterically inhibiting kinase activity \emph{primarily in the
mTORC1 complex} (mTORC2 is largely unaffected on short timescales). This
inhibition: - Suppresses cap-dependent translation (4E-BP1
phosphorylation) - Suppresses ribosome biogenesis (S6K1 phosphorylation)
- Activates autophagy - Extends lifespan in yeast, worms, flies, and
mice (about 10--15\% extension at low doses)

Rapamycin and analogues (rapalogues: everolimus, temsirolimus) are
clinically approved as immunosuppressants (transplant rejection
prevention) and anticancer agents (renal cell carcinoma, certain breast
cancers). The TAME trial and large-scale rapamycin/metformin studies are
testing rapalogues as longevity interventions in humans.

\textbf{AMPK and mTORC1 reciprocal inhibition} creates a
\textbf{bistable metabolic switch:} energy-rich \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} mTORC1 on, AMPK off \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
anabolism; energy-depleted \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} AMPK on, mTORC1 off \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} catabolism +
autophagy.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{The Randle Cycle (Glucose-Fatty Acid
Cycle)}\label{the-randle-cycle-glucose-fatty-acid-cycle}

Proposed by Randle et al.~(1963, \emph{The Lancet}), the Randle cycle
describes \textbf{reciprocal inhibition} between glucose and fatty acid
oxidation in heart and skeletal muscle:

\textbf{When fatty acids are high \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} glucose utilisation is suppressed:}
1. Beta-oxidation \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} elevated acetyl-CoA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{PDH kinase (PDK)
activated} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PDH phosphorylated/inactivated \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} less pyruvate oxidation 2.
Beta-oxidation \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} elevated citrate (exported to cytoplasm) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
\textbf{PFK-1 allosterically inhibited} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} glycolysis slows 3. Elevated
intracellular acyl-CoA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PKC-theta (in muscle) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} serine phosphorylation
of \textbf{IRS-1} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} impaired insulin signalling \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} reduced GLUT4
translocation

\textbf{When glucose is high \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} fatty acid oxidation is suppressed:} 1.
Insulin \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} ACC activated \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} malonyl-CoA synthesis increases \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
\textbf{CPT-1 inhibited} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} beta-oxidation blocked 2. Elevated NADH from
glycolysis \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} inhibits beta-oxidation dehydrogenases

\subsubsection{Metabolic Flexibility}\label{metabolic-flexibility}

\textbf{Metabolic flexibility} = the ability to switch between glucose
and fat oxidation in response to fuel availability. Assessed by the
respiratory quotient (RQ):

\[RQ = \frac{\text{CO}_2 \text{ produced}}{\text{O}_2 \text{ consumed}} \tag{11.4}\]

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  RQ = 1.0: pure glucose oxidation
\item
  RQ = 0.7: pure fat oxidation
\item
  Healthy individuals: RQ about 0.95 post-meal \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  about 0.75 fasting (rapid switching)
\item
  Obese/T2D individuals: RQ remains about 0.85 in fasting \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  ``metabolic inflexibility''
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Substrate (Futile) Cycles}\label{substrate-futile-cycles}

A \textbf{substrate cycle} involves two opposing metabolic reactions
operating simultaneously:

\[\text{Fructose-6-P} + \text{ATP} \xrightarrow{\text{PFK-1}} \text{Fructose-1,6-BP} + \text{ADP} \tag{11.5}\]

\[\text{Fructose-1,6-BP} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{FBPase-1}} \text{Fructose-6-P} + \text{P}_i \tag{11.6}\]

Net reaction: ATP \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} ADP + P\(_i\) (energy dissipated as heat)

\textbf{Why substrate cycles are useful (Newsholme hypothesis, 1984):}

\[\text{Amplification factor} = \frac{v_{\text{PFK}} + v_{\text{FBPase}}}{v_{\text{PFK}} - v_{\text{FBPase}}} \tag{11.7}\]

When both enzymes run at 50 U/min each and net flux is 1 U/min, a 10\%
change in PFK produces a 500\% change in net flux --- \textbf{metabolic
rheostat} behaviour. Substrate cycles provide ultrasensitive flux
control at the cost of ATP.

\textbf{Thermogenic substrate cycles:} - \textbf{Brown adipose tissue
(BAT):} UCP1 short-circuits the ETC proton gradient \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} heat
(non-shivering thermogenesis) - \textbf{Sarcolipin/SERCA cycle} in
skeletal muscle: sarcolipin uncouples SERCA Ca\(^{2+}\) pumping from
Ca\(^{2+}\) retention, dissipating ATP as heat - \textbf{Insect flight
muscle:} glycolytic futile cycles generate heat rapidly to reach flight
temperature (about 40 degrees C)

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Obesity and Metabolic
Syndrome}\label{obesity-and-metabolic-syndrome}

Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of conditions (central obesity, insulin
resistance, dyslipidaemia, hypertension, hyperglycaemia) that
dramatically increase cardiovascular disease risk.

\subsubsection{Visceral Fat as an Endocrine
Organ}\label{visceral-fat-as-an-endocrine-organ}

The shift in our understanding of adipose tissue --- from ``passive
triglyceride storage depot'' to ``active endocrine organ'' --- is one of
the most consequential paradigm changes in metabolism research of the
last 30 years. \textbf{Visceral adipose tissue (VAT)}, the fat depot
surrounding intra-abdominal organs, behaves very differently from
subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT):

\textbf{Lipid overflow:} Adipose tissue capacity exceeded \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} ectopic

folding capacity \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} UPR \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} JNK \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} IRS-1 serine phosphorylation 6.
\textbf{Mitochondrial dysfunction:} Incomplete fatty acid oxidation \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
ROS \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} oxidative stress \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} insulin resistance

\subsection{Metabolic Control
Analysis}\label{metabolic-control-analysis}

\textbf{Metabolic control analysis (MCA)} provides a quantitative
framework for understanding how control of metabolic flux is distributed
among pathway enzymes \citep{atkinson1968}.

\textbf{Flux control coefficient (\(C_i^J\)):} The fractional change in
pathway flux (\(J\)) caused by a fractional change in enzyme activity
(\(e_i\)), with most other variables held constant:

\[C_i^J = \frac{e_i}{J} \cdot \frac{\partial J}{\partial e_i} = \frac{\partial \ln J}{\partial \ln e_i} \tag{11.8}\]

Each \(C_i^J\) ranges from 0 (this enzyme has no control over flux) to
about 1 (this enzyme has near-total control). Negative values
are possible for enzymes that produce inhibitors of the pathway.

\textbf{Summation theorem:} The combined flux control coefficients in a
pathway sum to 1:

\begin{equation}
\sum_i C_i^J = 1
\label{eq:unit_III_mca_summation}
\end{equation}

This means control is \textbf{shared} among most enzymes, not
concentrated at a single ``rate-limiting step.'' In practice, one or a
few enzymes may have larger \(C_i^J\) values, but the concept of a
single rate-limiting step is an oversimplification.

For example, in glycolysis under physiological conditions, the flux
control coefficients for hexokinase, PFK-1, pyruvate kinase, and the
pyruvate transporter are most in the range
\(C_i^J \approx 0.1\)--\(0.3\) --- no single enzyme dominates, and the
precise distribution shifts with cellular state. This is why drug
therapies that target a single glycolytic enzyme often have surprisingly
modest effects on overall flux: the pathway redistributes control.

\subsubsection{Metabolomics: Measuring the Metabolic
State}\label{metabolomics-measuring-the-metabolic-state}

\textbf{Metabolomics} is the systematic measurement of small-molecule
metabolites --- the experimental complement to MCA, since you cannot
compute flux control coefficients without measuring concentrations and
fluxes.

\textbf{Key challenges:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Identification.} A typical untargeted LC-MS run detects
  5,000--30,000 features but about 10--20\% can be confidently
  identified. The remaining ``dark metabolome'' comprises mass spectra
  with no database match --- a major bottleneck.
\item
  \textbf{Compartmentation.} Metabolomics typically homogenises tissue,
  losing information about which metabolites were in mitochondria vs
  cytoplasm vs lysosome. Subcellular metabolomics (genetically encoded
  sensors, organelle isolation) is an emerging frontier.
\item
  \textbf{Flux \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\neq}}{!=} concentration.} A high concentration of an intermediate
  may reflect either high flux through that step \emph{or} a downstream
  block. Stable-isotope tracing (\(^{13}\)C-glucose,
  \(^{15}\)N-glutamine) is required to measure fluxes, not
  concentrations.
\end{enumerate}

These data feed directly into MCA models: combining flux measurements
(from \(^{13}\)C tracing) with elasticity coefficients (from in vitro
enzyme kinetics) gives an empirical \(C_i^J\) for each enzyme,
validating or revising textbook claims about which step is
``rate-limiting.''

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 6:} A drug increases hexokinase activity by 50\%
in muscle. From fasting biopsies, the flux control coefficient
\(C_{HK}^J\) for hexokinase in glycolysis was estimated at 0.2. Use
\cref{eq:unit_III_mca_summation} to predict the maximum fractional
change in glycolytic flux. Why is the prediction an upper bound, not a
precise value?
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 7:} A patient with chronic alcohol consumption
shows elevated NADH/NAD\(^+\) ratio in cytoplasm and impaired
gluconeogenesis. Using \cref{eq:unit_III_energy_charge}, predict whether
the energy charge is preserved or depressed, and explain why fasting
hypoglycaemia is a clinical risk.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Computational Bridge}\label{computational-bridge-10}

Drug effects on pathway enzymes are often framed like competitive
inhibitors shifting apparent \(K_m\). The biochemistry module exposes
both curves numerically:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ biology.biochemistry }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ michaelis\_menten, competitive\_inhibition}

\NormalTok{base }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ michaelis\_menten(}\FloatTok{4.0}\NormalTok{, Vmax}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{100.0}\NormalTok{, Km}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{5.0}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{blocked }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ competitive\_inhibition(}\FloatTok{4.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{100.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{5.0}\NormalTok{, inhibitor\_conc}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{5.0}\NormalTok{, Ki}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{2.5}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(base.reaction\_rate, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{), }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(blocked.reaction\_rate, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical / systems note:} Metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors, and GLP-1
agonists reshape the same integrative network (hepatic glucose output,
peripheral uptake, renal glucose loss) that insulin and glucagon command
--- illustrating multi-node control rather than a single
``rate-limiting'' hormone.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-13}

For \textbf{Metabolic Integration and Regulation}, frontier biology
belongs inside the evidence logic of the chapter. Metabolism is now
studied as a regulated network constrained by energy, redox balance,
compartmentation, and environment. The core reading question is this:
metabolic integration depends on compartmentation, hormone state,
nutrient availability, and time scale.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

A strong metabolic explanation names the flux, the limiting step, the
sensor, and the condition under which the pathway changes direction or
priority.

\textbf{Source practice:} For metabolic claims, keep the organism,
compartment, energetic state, and measurement method visible; a pathway
map is not enough without flux or concentration evidence.

\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-13}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{AMPK} (heterotrimer of two catalytic \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha} + two regulatory \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}/\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma}
  modules) is activated by elevated AMP/ATP and ADP/ATP through Thr172
  phosphorylation by \textbf{LKB1} (energy stress) or \textbf{CaMKK\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}}
  (Ca\(^{2+}\)); it promotes catabolism (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-oxidation, glycolysis) and
  inhibits mTORC1 and anabolism; activates autophagy (via ULK1) and
  mitochondrial biogenesis (via PGC-1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}).
\item
  \textbf{mTORC1} (activated by insulin + amino acids + oxygen) is
  positioned at the lysosome by Rag GTPases bound to the
  \textbf{Ragulator complex}; full activation requires both amino
  acid--driven lysosomal recruitment \emph{and} growth factor--driven
  Rheb-GTP. \textbf{Rapamycin} (FKBP12 complex) inhibits mTORC1.
\item
  \textbf{Energy charge} \cref{eq:unit_III_energy_charge} captures the
  fractional saturation of the adenylate pool with high-energy
  phosphate; cells maintain E.C. \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 0.85--0.95.
\item
  \textbf{Insulin} (PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway) drives GLUT4 translocation,
  glycogen synthesis, lipogenesis, and suppresses gluconeogenesis. The
  phosphorylase kinase / GLUT4-vesicle / 14-3-3-BAD effectors are
  characteristic Akt outputs.
\item
  \textbf{Glucagon} (cAMP/PKA cascade) drives glycogenolysis (via
  phosphorylase kinase), gluconeogenesis (via CREB transcription), and
  ketogenesis. The hormonal cascade amplifies the signal
  about 10\(^7\)-fold from femtomolar hormone to millimolar
  metabolite.
\item
  \textbf{Gluconeogenesis} uses four bypass enzymes (pyruvate
  carboxylase, PEPCK, FBPase-1, G6Pase) and costs 6 ATP equivalents per
  glucose.
\item
  \textbf{Beta-oxidation} yields about 106 ATP per
  palmitoyl-CoA; CPT-1 is rate-limiting and inhibited by malonyl-CoA.
\item
  \textbf{Ketone bodies} (acetoacetate, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-hydroxybutyrate) sustain the
  brain during starvation; liver produces but cannot use them. Fasting
  fuel switching follows a programmed timeline from glycogen \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} fatty
  acids \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} ketones over hours-to-weeks.
\item
  \textbf{Randle cycle:} fatty acid--glucose reciprocal inhibition;
  disrupted in type 2 diabetes.
\item
  \textbf{Substrate cycles} enable ultrasensitive flux control and
  thermogenesis; amplification factor = (v\(_1\) + v\(_2\))/(v\(_1\) -
  v\(_2\)).
\item
  \textbf{Metabolic flexibility} (RQ switching) is impaired in
  obesity/T2D due to lipid intermediate accumulation and insulin
  resistance.
\item
  \textbf{Metabolic control analysis} (\cref{eq:unit_III_mca_summation})
  shows that flux control is distributed, not concentrated at a single
  rate-limiting step.
\item
  \textbf{Metabolomics} (NMR + LC-MS) provides the empirical basis for
  MCA, with \(^{13}\)C tracing distinguishing flux from concentration.
\item
  \textbf{Visceral adipose} is a metabolically active endocrine organ
  whose portal-vein drainage drives hepatic insulin resistance, NAFLD,
  and chronic systemic inflammation.
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See \cref{sec:unit_II_cell_signaling} for
  \hyperref[gl:signal-transduction]{\textbf{signal transduction}} to
  mTOR, Unit IX for endocrine first messengers, and
  \cref{sec:unit_I_enzymes_and_kinetics} for enzyme-level kinetics.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Review Questions}\label{review-questions-13}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  A patient presents with an inherited loss-of-function
  \hyperref[gl:mutation]{\textbf{mutation}} in LKB1 (the primary AMPK
  upstream kinase). Predict four metabolic consequences in skeletal
  muscle during fasting.
\item
  Derive the energy charge equation (\cref{eq:unit_III_energy_charge}).
  If {[}ATP{]} = 3.5 mM, {[}ADP{]} = 0.8 mM, {[}AMP{]} = 0.2 mM,
  calculate EC. Is AMPK likely to be active?
\item
  Describe the insulin signalling cascade from receptor binding to GLUT4
  translocation, including the role of AS160, Rab10, and the SNARE
  complex. At which steps does insulin resistance develop in type 2
  diabetes?
\item
  Compare gluconeogenesis with glycolysis. Identify the three bypass
  reactions and explain why they are necessary.
\item
  Calculate the ATP yield from complete oxidation of palmitoyl-CoA
  (C16:0) to CO\(_2\) and H\(_2\)O, showing most sources of ATP.
\item
  Explain ketone body synthesis and utilisation. Why can the brain use
  ketone bodies but the liver cannot? Sketch the fuel-switching timeline
  from fed to 30-day fast.
\item
  The Randle cycle operates in heart muscle. In a patient with type 2
  diabetes and chronically elevated plasma FFA: predict changes in
  cardiac PDH activity, cardiac efficiency, and susceptibility to
  ischaemia.
\item
  Compare the amplification advantages of the PFK-1/FBPase-1 substrate
  cycle in liver with UCP1-mediated thermogenesis in brown adipose
  tissue.
\item
  Explain how metformin improves glycaemic control. Describe its effects
  on Complex I, AMPK, and hepatic gluconeogenesis.
\item
  Describe three molecular mechanisms by which obesity causes insulin
  resistance. For each, identify the lipid species involved and the
  downstream kinase that phosphorylates IRS-1.
\item
  Using the \hyperref[gl:competitive-inhibition]{\textbf{competitive
  inhibition}} example in the bridge, explain why simply raising
  substrate concentration can overcome some drug interactions but not
  others (hint: \(K_m^{app}\) vs.~\(V_\mathrm{max}\)).
\item
  Estimate energy charge for {[}ATP{]}=2 mM, {[}ADP{]}=1.5 mM,
  {[}AMP{]}=0.5 mM. Is AMPK more likely active than at EC \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 0.9?
\item
  Describe how mTORC1 is recruited to the lysosomal surface by amino
  acid availability. What is the role of Sestrin2, GATOR1/2, and the Rag
  GTPases? Why is mTORC1 a ``coincidence detector'' rather than a
  single-input sensor?
\item
  Sketch the phosphorylase kinase amplification cascade and estimate the
  end-to-end signal gain from a single glucagon binding event to
  released glucose-1-phosphate. Why is this amplification
  physiologically necessary?
\item
  Compare the contributions of subcutaneous and visceral adipose tissue
  to whole-body insulin resistance in obesity. Why does visceral fat
  have a disproportionate effect on hepatic outcomes?
\item
  Compare NMR and LC-MS as metabolomics platforms. Which is preferable
  for (a) absolute quantification of glucose in serum, (b) discovery of
  unknown lipid species in muscle biopsies, (c) compartment-resolved
  metabolomics in subcellular fractions?
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{AMPK} & AMP-activated protein kinase; principal energy-sensing
kinase; activated by elevated AMP/ATP via LKB1 or by Ca\(^{2+}\) via
CaMKK\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} \\
\textbf{mTORC1} & Mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1;
growth-promoting kinase; activated by insulin, amino acids, and growth
factors at the lysosomal surface \\
\textbf{Ragulator} & Lysosomal scaffold (LAMTOR1--5) that anchors Rag
GTPases and recruits mTORC1 in response to amino acid availability \\
\textbf{Energy charge (EC)} & ({[}ATP{]} + 1/2{[}ADP{]}) /
({[}ATP{]}+{[}ADP{]}+{[}AMP{]}); normal EC approximately 0.85--0.95 \\
\textbf{Insulin} & Anabolic hormone from beta-cells; PI3K/Akt/mTOR
pathway; drives glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis, lipogenesis \\
\textbf{Glucagon} & Catabolic hormone from alpha-cells; cAMP/PKA; drives
glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, ketogenesis \\
\textbf{Gluconeogenesis} & Synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate
precursors; liver and kidney; costs 6 ATP \\
\textbf{CPT-1} & Carnitine palmitoyl transferase-1; rate-limiting for
mitochondrial fatty acid import; inhibited by malonyl-CoA \\
\textbf{Ketone bodies} & Acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetone;
liver-produced; brain fuel during starvation \\
\textbf{Phosphorylase kinase} & Multi-subunit kinase activated by PKA;
phosphorylates glycogen phosphorylase to active ``a'' form \\
\textbf{Randle cycle} & Reciprocal inhibition of glucose and fatty acid
oxidation in heart and muscle \\
\textbf{Substrate cycle} & Two opposing reactions running
simultaneously; amplifies flux control; generates heat \\
\textbf{Metabolic flexibility} & Ability to switch between glucose and
fat oxidation; impaired in obesity and T2D \\
\textbf{SIRT1} & NAD\(^+\)-dependent deacetylase; caloric restriction
sensor; activates PGC-1alpha \\
\textbf{Metabolic syndrome} & Cluster of central obesity, insulin
resistance, dyslipidaemia, hypertension, hyperglycaemia \\
\textbf{Visceral adipose tissue} & Fat depot draining via portal vein to
liver; endocrine organ secreting TNF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}, IL-6, RBP4 \\
\textbf{Adipokines} & Hormones secreted by adipose tissue (leptin,
adiponectin, resistin, RBP4); regulate appetite and insulin
sensitivity \\
\textbf{Warburg effect} & Aerobic glycolysis in cancer cells; rapid ATP
+ biosynthetic precursors \\
\textbf{Metabolic control analysis} & Quantitative framework for flux
control distribution; summation theorem: sum of \(C_i^J\) = 1 \\
\textbf{Metabolomics} & Systematic measurement of small-molecule
metabolites; NMR and LC-MS as principal platforms \\
\end{longtable}

\section*{Unit IV --- Molecular Genetics:
Introduction}\label{unit-iv-molecular-genetics-introduction}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Unit IV --- Molecular Genetics:
Introduction}

\subsection*{Why This Unit Matters}\label{why-this-unit-matters-4}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Why This Unit Matters}

In 1944, Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, and Maclyn McCarty performed one
of the most transformative experiments in the history of science. They
showed that the "transforming principle" that could convert harmless
\emph{Streptococcus pneumoniae} into a lethal strain was not protein ---
as virtually everyone expected --- but deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA). The
announcement was met with scepticism. DNA seemed too simple: primarily
four nucleotide bases, arranged in an apparently monotonous double
helix. How could such a molecule encode the almost infinite variety of
life?

The answer, revealed over the next three decades, is linguistic in
structure: a four-letter alphabet (A, T, G, C) organised into
three-letter codons, read in a linear sequence, encoding twenty amino
acids, assembled by ribosomes into an effectively unlimited number of
proteins. This is the molecular logic of life: \textbf{information flows
from DNA to RNA to protein}, and control is exerted at every step. The
central dogma, articulated by Francis Crick in 1958, has been refined
but rarely overturned.

This unit examines the molecular machinery that reads, copies, and
expresses genetic information. You will study the multiprotein complexes
that replicate DNA with an error rate of fewer than one mistake per 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{9}}{9}
base pairs, the RNA polymerases that transcribe genes in a regulated,
stimulus-responsive manner, and the ribosome --- a 2.5 MDa
ribonucleoprotein machine that interprets the genetic code at
about 15 amino acids per second. You will also examine how
mutations drive evolution and disease, how the genome is structurally
organised, and how CRISPR-Cas9 has made precise genome editing a
clinical reality \citep{doudna2014}.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection*{Current Evidence Thread}\label{current-evidence-thread-4}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Current Evidence Thread}

Read this unit as molecular genetics built from stacked evidence layers:
DNA sequence and replication fidelity, transcription and translation
output, the chromatin and methylation state that gates that output, and
the variant calls and clinical interpretations that follow from most
three. Molecular genetics now spans single-reference sequences,
telomere-to-telomere assemblies, pangenome graphs, long-read sequencing,
CRISPR medicines, and ethical deployment. As you move through the
chapters, keep a two-column note: \textbf{claim} on the left,
\textbf{evidence that would change my confidence} on the right. By the
end of the unit, each major idea should be tied to a measurement, model,
citation, or paper-based lab decision.

\subsection{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-14}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Describe the structure of DNA and explain why it is well-suited to
  information storage and replication.
\item
  Explain semiconservative replication and the key
  \hyperref[gl:enzyme]{\textbf{enzyme}}s at the replication fork.
\item
  Compare the replication machinery of prokaryotes and
  \hyperref[gl:eukaryote]{\textbf{eukaryote}}s.
\item
  Describe origin licensing, the role of MCM helicases, and how
  re-replication is prevented.
\item
  Explain the \hyperref[gl:telomere]{\textbf{telomere}} end-replication
  problem and the role of telomerase.
\item
  Describe the stages of the \hyperref[gl:cell-cycle]{\textbf{cell
  cycle}} and the function of cyclin-CDK complexes at each checkpoint.
\item
  Explain the DNA damage response pathway involving ATM, ATR, and p53.
\item
  Describe the stages of \hyperref[gl:mitosis]{\textbf{mitosis}} at the
  molecular level, including spindle assembly checkpoint mechanisms.
\item
  Explain the mechanism and biological importance of
  \hyperref[gl:meiosis]{\textbf{meiosis}}, including crossing over and
  \hyperref[gl:independent-assortment]{\textbf{independent assortment}}.
\item
  Describe DNA damage types and the key repair pathways, and connect
  repair defects to human disease.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Opening Vignette --- The Double Helix's Debt to a Woman
Scientist}

In 1952, Rosalind Franklin produced the sharpest X-ray diffraction
photograph of DNA ever captured --- ``Photo 51.'' The image was obtained
without her permission by Maurice Wilkins and shown to James Watson.
Recognising in an instant that the helical periodicity and the 3.4 Å
spacing implied a double helix, Watson and Crick used this insight to
complete their landmark 1953 \emph{Nature} paper. Franklin, who died of
ovarian cancer in 1958 at age 37, rarely received the Nobel Prize
awarded to Watson, Crick, and Wilkins in 1962. Yet her replication
studies --- painstakingly mapping how DNA unwinds, is copied
semiconservatively, and repairs itself --- anticipated the entire field
of cell-cycle biology. Every chapter covering DNA replication and the
cell cycle is, in part, her story.
\end{quote}

\subsection{DNA as the Genetic
Material}\label{dna-as-the-genetic-material}

The Avery-MacLeod-McCarty experiment (1944) demonstrated that DNA (not
\hyperref[gl:protein]{\textbf{protein}}) carries genetic information by
showing that purified DNA from virulent \emph{Streptococcus pneumoniae}
could transform non-virulent strains. The Hershey-Chase blender
experiment (1952) confirmed this with radioactively labelled T4 phage:
\(^{32}\)P-labelled DNA (not \(^{35}\)S-labelled protein) entered
bacterial cells during infection.

\subsubsection{DNA Double Helix
Structure}\label{dna-double-helix-structure}

Watson and Crick's 1953 model of the B-form DNA helix, built on Rosalind
Franklin's X-ray diffraction data (Photo 51) and Chargaff's base-pairing
rules:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Antiparallel complementary strands} running 5' to 3' and 3' to
  5'
\item
  \textbf{Base pairing}: A-T (2
  \hyperref[gl:hydrogen-bond]{\textbf{hydrogen bond}}s), G-C (3 hydrogen
  bonds)
\item
  \textbf{Major groove}: wide (about 22 angstroms) and deep --
  the primary site for sequence-specific protein binding
  (\hyperref[gl:transcription]{\textbf{transcription}} factors,
  restriction enzymes). The pattern of hydrogen bond donors and
  acceptors in the major groove is unique for each base pair, allowing
  proteins to ``read'' the sequence without unwinding the helix.
\item
  \textbf{Minor groove}: narrow (about 12 angstroms) -- bound
  by certain drugs (e.g., netropsin, distamycin) and architectural
  proteins (e.g., HMG-box proteins, TBP)
\item
  \textbf{Right-handed helix}, 10.5 bp per turn, rise 0.34 nm/bp, pitch
  \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~}3.6 nm, diameter 2.0 nm
\end{itemize}

The phosphodiester backbone runs 5' to 3' and carries two negative
charges per \hyperref[gl:nucleotide]{\textbf{nucleotide}} at
physiological \hyperref[gl:ph]{\textbf{pH}} (\(pK_a < 1\)). This
negative charge means DNA repels other nucleic acids and requires
cationic counterions (Mg\(^{2+}\),
\hyperref[gl:histone]{\textbf{histone}}s, polyamines) for compaction and
stability.

\textbf{Alternative DNA conformations:}

\textbf{Information capacity:} The human haploid
\hyperref[gl:genome]{\textbf{genome}} contains approximately 3.1 billion
base pairs, equivalent to roughly 725 megabytes of digital data (2 bits
per base). If fully stretched, the DNA in a single cell would extend
approximately 2 meters, yet it is compacted into a nucleus approximately
6 micrometers in diameter. This compaction is achieved through a
hierarchy of packaging: 147 bp of DNA wraps around each histone octamer
to form a \hyperref[gl:nucleosome]{\textbf{nucleosome}} (the ``beads on
a string''), which further compacts into the 30-nm
\hyperref[gl:chromatin]{\textbf{chromatin}} fiber, loop domains
(anchored by CTCF and cohesin), and ultimately the mitotic
\hyperref[gl:chromosome]{\textbf{chromosome}}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Z-DNA and Autoimmunity} Antibodies against
Z-DNA are found in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
Z-DNA forms transiently behind moving RNA polymerase due to negative
supercoiling, and \hyperref[gl:mutation]{\textbf{mutation}}s in the
Z-DNA binding protein ADAR1 cause Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome, a severe
autoinflammatory disorder. Z-DNA-binding proteins such as ZBP1 (DAI)
also function as innate immune sensors, recognizing viral Z-form nucleic
acids.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{DNA Replication}\label{dna-replication}

Replication is \textbf{semiconservative} -- each daughter double helix
retains one parental strand. This was demonstrated by
\citet{meselson1958} using \(^{15}\)N density gradient centrifugation in
\emph{E. coli}. After one generation in \(^{14}\)N medium, most DNA was
intermediate density (ruling out conservative replication). After two
generations, half was intermediate and half was light (ruling out
dispersive replication).

\subsubsection{Origins of Replication and
Licensing}\label{origins-of-replication-and-licensing}

Replication begins at specific genomic sites called \textbf{origins of
replication (ori)}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Prokaryotes}: \emph{E. coli} has a single origin
  (\emph{oriC}), a 245-bp sequence containing five 9-bp DnaA-binding
  sites (DnaA boxes) and three AT-rich 13-mer repeats that melt first
  upon initiation
\item
  \textbf{Eukaryotes}: Human genome contains approximately 30,000-50,000
  origins; yeast origins are called \textbf{autonomously replicating
  sequences (ARS)}, each approximately 150 bp containing an 11-bp ARS
  consensus sequence (ACS)
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Origin licensing} ensures each origin fires primarily once per S
phase:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  In late M/early G1, the \textbf{Origin Recognition Complex (ORC)}
  binds origins constitutively (in yeast) or dynamically (in metazoans)
\item
  \textbf{Cdc6} and \textbf{Cdt1} load the \textbf{MCM2-7 helicase} (a
  hexameric ring) onto DNA as a double hexamer -- this is the
  ``licensed'' pre-replicative complex (pre-RC)
\item
  At the G1/S transition, \textbf{CDK} (S-CDK = cyclin A-CDK2) and
  \textbf{DDK} (Cdc7-Dbf4) phosphorylate MCM, activating the helicase
  and converting pre-RC to pre-initiation complex (pre-IC)
\item
  Re-licensing is prevented by CDK-mediated phosphorylation of Cdc6
  (targeting it for degradation) and by geminin binding to Cdt1
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{MCM licensing --- molecular detail.} The pre-RC formation
involves a precisely choreographed sequence:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{ORC binding (G1):} ORC1--6 heterohexamer binds origins. ORC1
  contains an ATP-binding AAA+ ATPase fold; ATP hydrolysis triggers
  loading. In humans ORC1 levels oscillate (peaks late M/early G1;
  degraded in S/G2) --- ensuring temporal restriction of licensing.
\item
  \textbf{Cdc6 recruitment:} Cdc6 (also AAA+ ATPase) joins ORC, forming
  an ORC--Cdc6 complex that wraps DNA into a left-handed superhelix.
\item
  \textbf{Cdt1--MCM2-7 loading:} Cdt1 (the licensing factor) binds
  MCM2-7 and chaperones it to the ORC--Cdc6--origin complex. ATP
  hydrolysis by ORC and Cdc6 drives the MCM2-7 ring open at the
  MCM2/MCM5 interface, allowing dsDNA to thread through.
\item
  \textbf{Double hexamer assembly:} A second Cdt1--MCM2-7 is loaded in
  the opposite orientation, creating a head-to-head MCM2-7 double
  hexamer encircling dsDNA. The double hexamer is the licensed pre-RC.
\item
  \textbf{CDT1 destruction in S phase:} Once MCM is loaded, S-CDK
  phosphorylates Cdt1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} ubiquitin ligase SCF\textsuperscript{Skp2} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  proteasomal degradation. \textbf{CRL4\textsuperscript{CDT2}} also
  targets Cdt1 for degradation when bound to chromatin (PCNA-coupled
  mechanism).
\item
  \textbf{Geminin sequesters Cdt1:} Geminin is an inhibitor that binds
  Cdt1, preventing it from re-licensing origins during S/G2/M. Geminin
  levels rise from S phase, peaking in M, and are degraded at anaphase
  by APC/C-Cdc20.
\item
  \textbf{Re-replication prevention is therefore three-fold:}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    CDK-dependent Cdc6 export from nucleus and degradation
  \item
    CDK-dependent Cdt1 degradation
  \item
    Geminin-mediated Cdt1 sequestration
  \item
    Loss of any of these (e.g., siRNA against geminin) causes
    catastrophic re-replication, DNA damage, and apoptosis.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Origin firing in S phase:} A subset of licensed origins fires
  (about 10 \% per cell-cycle round in human cells); the
  remainder are dormant backups. Activation requires \textbf{DDK
  (Cdc7-Dbf4)} phosphorylation of MCM2-MCM4-MCM6 + \textbf{S-CDK}
  phosphorylation of Sld2/Sld3 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} recruitment of \textbf{Cdc45} and
  \textbf{GINS} to form the \textbf{CMG helicase} (Cdc45-MCM-GINS) ---
  the active replicative helicase.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Replication timing domains.} Origin firing is not random in
time. Each about 1 Mb region has a characteristic
\textbf{replication timing}: - \textbf{Early-replicating domains} (S
phase first 1--3 hours): gene-rich, euchromatic, transcriptionally
active, A-compartment, marked by H3K27ac, H3K4me3, high accessibility -
\textbf{Mid-S replicating domains} (3--5 h): transition zones -
\textbf{Late-replicating domains} (5--8 h): heterochromatic, gene-poor,
B-compartment, marked by H3K9me3 and lamina-association (LADs)

Replication timing correlates with chromatin state and is reprogrammed
during cell-fate transitions. Late replication is associated with
elevated mutation rate (about 2\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} background) --- because the
late-S nucleotide pool is depleted of dNTPs (which were consumed
earlier), increasing polymerase mis-incorporation. This explains the
spatial mutation-rate variation observed in cancer genomes:
late-replicating regions accumulate about 2-fold more mutations
per Mb than early-replicating regions.

\textbf{Quantitative parameters of replication licensing:} - Number of
origins per genome: about 30,000--50,000 (about  one
per 50--100 kb) - MCM2-7 loaded per origin: 2 (head-to-head double
hexamer) - Total MCM2-7 in nucleus: about 10--20-fold excess
over origins \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} MCM ``paradox'' - Origins fired per cell cycle:
about 15,000 (about 30 \% of licensed origins) - Dormant
origins: provide backup if a fork stalls or fails --- mutation in ATR
(which suppresses dormant-origin firing under stress) causes Seckel
syndrome (microcephaly, growth failure)

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Meier-Gorlin Syndrome} Mutations in ORC1,
ORC4, ORC6, CDT1, or CDC6 cause Meier-Gorlin syndrome, a rare primordial
dwarfism characterized by short stature, absent or small patellae, and
microtia. This underscores the essential role of origin licensing in
normal growth and development.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{mRNA Vaccines: A Modern Application of Nucleic Acid
Technology}\label{mrna-vaccines-a-modern-application-of-nucleic-acid-technology}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0069_4c0d48a0418b.png}
\caption{Mechanism of mRNA vaccines. Synthetic mRNA encoding a viral antigen is delivered to host cells, where it is translated into protein. The protein is processed and presented to both helper T cells (via MHC II) and cytotoxic T cells (via MHC I), generating both antibody and cellular immune responses.}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Molecular design}:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Sequence optimization}: The mRNA sequence is optimized for
  stability and translation efficiency. This includes:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{5' cap}: A modified guanosine (Cap-1: N7-methylated,
    2'-O-methylated) mimics natural eukaryotic mRNA and prevents
    recognition by innate immune sensors (RIG-I, MDA5)
  \item
    \textbf{5' UTR}: Contains Kozak consensus sequence
    (GCCACC{[}A/G{]}CC) for efficient translation initiation
  \item
    \textbf{Open reading frame (ORF)}: Encodes the target antigen (e.g.,
    SARS-CoV-2 spike protein). The sequence is codon-optimized to match
    human tRNA abundance, reducing rare codon clusters that could stall
    translation.
  \item
    \textbf{3' UTR}: Contains stability elements (e.g., from human
    alpha-globin or cytochrome P450 genes) and poly-A tail (100-150 nt)
    to protect from degradation and enhance translation.
  \item
    \textbf{Nucleoside modifications}: Pseudouridine (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Psi}}{Psi}) or
    N1-methylpseudouridine (m1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Psi}}{Psi}) replace uridine to reduce
    immunogenicity and increase translation efficiency.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{In vitro transcription (IVT)}: The optimized DNA template
  (linearized plasmid or PCR product) is transcribed using T7 RNA
  polymerase in a cell-free system. Nucleoside triphosphates (NTPs)
  including modified UTP (e.g., m1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Psi}}{Psi}-TP) are added. The reaction produces
  a 5'-triphosphate-ended mRNA, which is then enzymatically capped.
\item
  \textbf{Purification and formulation}: The crude mRNA is treated with
  DNase to remove template DNA, then purified (often by tangential flow
  filtration or HPLC). The purified mRNA is formulated into
  \textbf{lipid nanoparticles (LNPs)} --- spherical vesicles
  about 80-100 nm in diameter composed of ionizable cationic
  lipids, cholesterol, phospholipids, and PEG-lipids. The ionizable
  lipid is positively charged at low pH (during formulation) but neutral
  at physiological pH, reducing toxicity. LNPs protect mRNA from
  degradation and facilitate cellular uptake.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Cellular uptake and translation}:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Injection}: mRNA-LNP suspension is injected intramuscularly
  (typically deltoid). The injection site contains antigen-presenting
  cells (APCs) like dendritic cells and macrophages, as well as muscle
  cells.
\item
  \textbf{Uptake}: LNPs fuse with cell membranes or are endocytosed. In
  the endosome, the ionizable lipid becomes protonated, causing
  endosomal membrane disruption and release of mRNA into the cytoplasm.
\item
  \textbf{Translation}: Host ribosomes bind to the 5' cap and translate
  the mRNA into the antigen protein. The protein may be secreted (if
  signal peptide included) or remain intracellular.
\item
  \textbf{Processing and presentation}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{MHC class II pathway}: Exogenous antigen taken up by APCs is
    degraded in lysosomes and presented on MHC II to CD4+ helper T
    cells.
  \item
    \textbf{MHC class I pathway}: Endogenous antigen (produced inside
    the cell) is degraded by the proteasome into peptides, transported
    to the ER via TAP, and presented on MHC I to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells.
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Immune activation}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Humoral immunity}: B cells recognizing the antigen receive
  help from CD4+ T cells and differentiate into plasma cells producing
  neutralizing antibodies (IgG, IgM initially, then IgG). These
  antibodies block viral entry by binding to the spike protein
  receptor-binding domain.
\item
  \textbf{Cellular immunity}: CD8+ T cells recognize infected cells
  presenting viral peptides and kill them, preventing viral replication.
\item
  \textbf{Immune memory}: Long-lived plasma cells and memory B/T cells
  provide lasting protection.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Advantages over traditional vaccines}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{No live virus}: Safer for immunocompromised individuals; no
  risk of reversion to virulence.
\item
  \textbf{Rapid design and manufacturing}: Once the viral sequence is
  known, mRNA can be designed in days and manufactured in weeks
  (cell-free synthesis). Traditional vaccines require growing virus in
  eggs or cell culture (months).
\item
  \textbf{Strong immune response}: Both antibody and T-cell responses
  are robust.
\item
  \textbf{Flexible platform}: The same LNP formulation can deliver mRNA
  for different antigens; the platform can be quickly adapted to new
  variants or emerging pathogens.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Computational aspects}:

Modern mRNA vaccine design relies heavily on computational tools:

\textbf{Clinical impact}: The Pfizer-BioNTech BNT162b2 and Moderna
mRNA-1273 vaccines were developed in under a year from viral sequence
release to emergency use authorization, demonstrating the power of this
technology. Beyond COVID-19, mRNA vaccines are in development for
influenza, HIV, Zika, and personalized cancer vaccines.

\subsubsection{Leading and Lagging
Strands}\label{leading-and-lagging-strands}

DNA polymerase primarily adds nucleotides to the 3'-OH of an existing
primer, and can primarily synthesize in the 5' to 3' direction.
Therefore:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Leading strand}: synthesized continuously 5' to 3' in the same
  direction as fork movement. Requires primarily a single priming event.
  In eukaryotes, primarily synthesized by DNA Pol epsilon.
\item
  \textbf{Lagging strand}: synthesized discontinuously as
  \textbf{Okazaki fragments} (1,000-2,000 nt in prokaryotes; 100-200 nt
  in eukaryotes). Each fragment requires a new RNA primer laid down by
  primase. After extension by DNA Pol delta, the primers are removed by
  a multi-step process:

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{RNase H} degrades the RNA portion of the primer
  \item
    \textbf{FEN1} (flap endonuclease 1) removes the remaining 5' flap
    created when the upstream Okazaki fragment displaces the primer of
    the next fragment
  \item
    \textbf{DNA Pol delta} fills the gap
  \item
    \textbf{DNA Ligase I} seals the nick with a phosphodiester bond
    (consuming ATP)
  \end{enumerate}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Replication fork speed}: \emph{E. coli} replicates its 4.6 Mb
genome from a single origin in approximately 40 minutes
(about 1,000 bp/s). Human cells replicate 3.2 Gb from
approximately 30,000 origins over 6-8 hours of S phase
(about 50 bp/s per fork, but thousands of forks operate
simultaneously).

\subsubsection{PCNA Sliding Clamp -- The Processivity
Engine}\label{pcna-sliding-clamp-the-processivity-engine}

PCNA is a homotrimeric ring (three identical subunits) that encircles
double-stranded DNA and slides freely. It acts as a \textbf{molecular
matchmaker}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Face toward template junction}: binds DNA polymerase (Pol
  delta/epsilon), FEN1, and ligase I through a conserved PIP box motif
\item
  \textbf{Monoubiquitination at K164} (by RAD6/RAD18): recruits Y-family
  translesion synthesis (TLS) polymerases (Pol eta, Pol iota, Pol kappa,
  Rev1) when the fork stalls at DNA damage. TLS polymerases have relaxed
  active sites that can bypass lesions but at the cost of lower fidelity
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{DNA Proofreading and
Fidelity}\label{dna-proofreading-and-fidelity}

The error rate of replication is remarkably low: approximately 1 error
per \(10^{9}\)-\(10^{10}\) base pairs copied. This fidelity results from
three layers:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Base selection by polymerase} (about \(10^{-5}\)
  error rate): The polymerase active site preferentially binds correctly
  paired nucleotides based on geometry and hydrogen bonding
\item
  \textbf{3' to 5' exonuclease proofreading}
  (about \(10^{-2}\) improvement): If a mismatch is
  incorporated, the polymerase pauses; the 3' to 5' exonuclease domain
  excises the incorrect nucleotide and the polymerase re-extends
\item
  \textbf{Mismatch repair (MMR)} (about \(10^{-3}\)
  improvement): Post-replicative scanning by MutS (MSH2/MSH6 in humans),
  which detects mismatches and small insertion/deletion loops
\end{enumerate}

\begin{equation}\text{Overall error rate} \approx 10^{-5} \times 10^{-2} \times 10^{-3} = 10^{-10} \text{ per bp per replication} \tag{12.1}\label{eq:error_rate}\end{equation}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Lynch Syndrome (HNPCC)} Germline mutations
in MMR \hyperref[gl:gene]{\textbf{gene}}s (\emph{MLH1}, \emph{MSH2},
\emph{MSH6}, \emph{PMS2}) cause Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis
colorectal cancer). Affected individuals have a 50-80\% lifetime risk of
colorectal cancer and increased risk of endometrial, ovarian, and
gastric cancers. The hallmark is \textbf{microsatellite instability
(MSI)} -- expansion or contraction of short tandem repeats due to
uncorrected replication slippage. MSI-high tumors respond well to immune
checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1), making Lynch syndrome diagnosis
therapeutically important.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Telomeres and Telomerase}\label{telomeres-and-telomerase}

\textbf{The end-replication problem}: Linear eukaryotic chromosomes
cannot replicate the very 5' end of the lagging strand (no upstream
sequence to place a primer). This means 50-200 bp of telomeric DNA are
lost with each cell division.

\textbf{Telomere structure}: Human telomeres consist of 5-15 kb of the
hexameric repeat TTAGGG, ending in a 150-200 nt single-stranded 3'
overhang. This overhang invades the upstream duplex to form a
\textbf{T-loop} (telomere loop), which is stabilized by the
\textbf{shelterin complex} (TRF1, TRF2, RAP1, TIN2, TPP1, POT1). The
T-loop hides the chromosome end from the DNA damage response, which
would otherwise recognize it as a double-strand break.

\textbf{The shelterin complex --- six-protein architecture and
function:}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1842}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.6053}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2105}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Subunit
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
DNA binding specificity
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Function
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{TRF1} (telomeric repeat factor 1) & dsDNA TTAGGG (Myb domain) &
Negatively regulates telomerase access; controls telomere length \\
\textbf{TRF2} & dsDNA TTAGGG (Myb domain) & Stabilises T-loop;
suppresses ATM-mediated DNA damage signalling at telomeres \\
\textbf{TIN2} & TRF1, TRF2 partner (no DNA binding) & Bridge protein,
stabilises whole complex \\
\textbf{RAP1} & TRF2 partner & NF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}B pathway crosstalk; chromatin
contacts \\
\textbf{TPP1} & TIN2 partner; binds POT1 & Recruits telomerase via TEL
patch \\
\textbf{POT1} & ssDNA TTAGGG-overhang (OB-fold domain) & Suppresses ATR;
protects 3\texorpdfstring{'}{'} overhang \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{T-loop formation in detail.} The 3\texorpdfstring{'}{'} G-rich overhang (150--200
nt) folds back and invades the upstream duplex, displacing one strand
and forming a D-loop (displacement loop) within the T-loop. TRF2 wraps
the DNA, inducing the strand exchange. The structure has been visualised
by electron microscopy and STORM super-resolution. Shelterin coats the
entire telomere --- about about 1 shelterin per 100 bp.

\textbf{Shelterin's six functions in protecting chromosome ends:} 1.
\textbf{Suppress ATM kinase} at telomeres (TRF2-dependent) 2.
\textbf{Suppress ATR kinase} at telomeres (POT1-dependent) 3.
\textbf{Inhibit NHEJ} at chromosome ends (preventing fusions; TRF2-RAP1)
4. \textbf{Inhibit HR} between telomeres (TRF2; preventing
telomere-telomere recombination) 5. \textbf{Recruit telomerase} in cells
where it is active (TPP1-TEL patch) 6. \textbf{Mediate semi-conservative
replication} through telomeres (CST complex with shelterin)

\textbf{Telomere replication problem in detail.} Two distinct issues: 1.
\textbf{Lagging-strand end-replication}: The very 5\texorpdfstring{'}{'} end of the lagging
strand cannot be replicated because there is no upstream template for
primer placement. After RNA primer removal, about 50--100 nt
are lost from the 5\texorpdfstring{'}{'} end of the lagging-strand-complement. 2.
\textbf{Leading-strand end-resection}: The leading strand is synthesised
continuously to the chromosome end, but specialised exonucleases then
resect the 5\texorpdfstring{'}{'} end to generate the 3\texorpdfstring{'}{'} overhang necessary for T-loop
formation.

Result: each replication cycle, about 50--200 bp of TTAGGG
repeats are lost from telomeres in the absence of telomerase.

\textbf{G-quadruplex regulation.} The G-rich telomere sequence can fold
into intramolecular G-quadruplexes (four G's stacked via Hoogsteen
bonds). G-quadruplexes are stabilised by K\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} but inhibit telomerase
access. Drugs that stabilise telomeric G-quadruplexes (e.g., RHPS4,
telomestatin, BRACO19) cause progressive telomere shortening and
senescence in cancer cells --- they are anti-cancer leads but limited by
toxicity in normal stem cells.

\textbf{G-quadruplexes}: The G-rich telomeric sequence can fold into
\textbf{G-quadruplex} structures -- stacked tetrads of four guanines
connected by Hoogsteen hydrogen bonds, stabilized by monovalent cations
(K\(^+\)). G-quadruplexes inhibit telomerase and are targets for
anti-cancer drug development.

\textbf{Telomerase RNA template --- TERC mechanism in detail.} TERC is a
451-nt RNA with several functional regions: (i) a \textbf{template
region} (5\texorpdfstring{'}{'}-CUAACCCUAAC-3\texorpdfstring{'}{'}, about 11 nt) that base-pairs with
the telomere 3\texorpdfstring{'}{'} overhang and dictates the TTAGGG sequence added; (ii) a
\textbf{pseudoknot} (essential structural motif); (iii) a
\textbf{CR4/CR5} stem-loop that binds TERT; (iv) an \textbf{H/ACA scaRNA
box} at the 3\texorpdfstring{'}{'} end (essential for stability and dyskerin binding). The
H/ACA box recruits dyskerin (DKC1) --- mutations in DKC1 cause X-linked
dyskeratosis congenita.

\textbf{Telomerase}: A specialized reverse transcriptase that extends
the 3' overhang:

\begin{equation}5'\text{-}(TTAGGG)_n\text{-OH-3'} \xrightarrow{\text{TERC RNA template: 3'-AAUCCC-5'}} 5'\text{-}(TTAGGG)_{n+1}\text{-OH-3'} \tag{12.2}\label{eq:telomerase}\end{equation}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{TERT} (telomerase reverse transcriptase): the catalytic
  protein subunit
\item
  \textbf{TERC} (telomerase RNA component): 451-nt RNA containing the
  template sequence (in humans, 5'-CUAACCCUAAC-3') used to add TTAGGG
  repeats
\item
  After TERT extends the 3' overhang, conventional DNA Pol alpha/primase
  synthesizes the complementary C-rich strand
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Telomeres, aging, and cancer}: Somatic cells lack telomerase
activity and undergo progressive telomere shortening, eventually
reaching a critically short length that triggers replicative senescence
(the Hayflick limit, about 50-70 divisions for human
fibroblasts). This is a tumor-suppressive mechanism. However,
approximately 85\% of cancers reactivate telomerase (often through TERT
\hyperref[gl:promoter]{\textbf{promoter}} mutations, especially C228T
and C250T), and approximately 15\% use \textbf{ALT (alternative
lengthening of telomeres)} via
\hyperref[gl:recombination]{\textbf{recombination}} between telomeres
(associated with ATRX/DAXX mutations, with C-circles as biomarkers).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Telomere Biology Disorders} Mutations in
TERT, TERC, DKC1, or other telomere maintenance genes cause
\textbf{dyskeratosis congenita} (DC), characterized by bone marrow
failure, pulmonary fibrosis, and mucosal leukoplakia. Patients have
critically short telomeres and premature aging features. Related
conditions include idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and aplastic anemia,
forming a spectrum called \textbf{telomere biology disorders (TBDs)}.
\end{quote}

\subsection{The Cell Cycle}\label{the-cell-cycle-1}

The \textbf{cell cycle} is the ordered series of events by which a cell
duplicates its contents and divides. In a typical mammalian cell, the
cycle takes approximately 24 hours.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0070_1ddf35a993ca.png}
\caption{The eukaryotic cell cycle. G1 contains the restriction point (R), after which the cell is committed to division independent of mitogenic signals. Each transition is guarded by checkpoints.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Cell Cycle Phases}\label{cell-cycle-phases}

\subsubsection{Cyclin-CDK Complexes: The Cell Cycle
Engine}\label{cyclin-cdk-complexes-the-cell-cycle-engine}

The cell cycle is driven by the sequential activation and destruction of
\textbf{cyclin-CDK (cyclin-dependent kinase)} complexes:

\textbf{Regulation of CDK activity:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Cyclin binding}: CDKs are inactive monomers without their
  cyclin partner
\item
  \textbf{Activating phosphorylation}: CAK (CDK-activating kinase)
  phosphorylates the T-loop
\item
  \textbf{Inhibitory phosphorylation}: Wee1 kinase phosphorylates CDK1
  at Tyr15 and Thr14 (inactive); Cdc25 phosphatase removes these
  (activates)
\item
  \textbf{CKI (CDK inhibitors)}: p21\(^{CIP1}\) (induced by p53),
  p27\(^{KIP1}\), p16\(^{INK4a}\) bind and inactivate specific
  cyclin-CDK complexes
\item
  \textbf{Cyclin destruction}: APC/C
  (\hyperref[gl:anaphase]{\textbf{anaphase}}-promoting
  complex/cyclosome) ubiquitinates cyclins A and B for proteasomal
  degradation, ending mitosis
\end{itemize}

biosensor measurements have provided a quantitative picture of CDK
activity dynamics:

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Active complexes
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Approximate timing (mammalian, 24-h cycle)
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Early G1 (mitogen-stimulated) & about 5 \% of peak & Cyclin
D-CDK4/6 (low) & 0--4 h post-mitosis \\
Restriction point & about 20 \% & Cyclin D-CDK4/6 + early
Cyclin E-CDK2 & 6--8 h post-mitosis \\
G1/S transition & about 40 \% & Cyclin E-CDK2 high; Cyclin
A-CDK2 rising & 8--10 h \\
Mid-S & about 50 \% & Cyclin A-CDK2 dominant & 10--14 h \\
G2 & about 70 \% & Cyclin A-CDK2 + early Cyclin B-CDK1 & 14--18
h \\
G2/M transition & about 90 \% & Cyclin B-CDK1 (= MPF) rises
sharply & 18--20 h \\
Mitosis (M-phase) & \textbf{100 \% (peak)} & Cyclin B-CDK1 + Aurora A/B
kinases & 20--22 h \\
Anaphase / Telophase & Drops to \textless{} 10 \% & APC/C-Cdc20 destroys
cyclin B & 22--24 h \\
\end{longtable}
}

The peak-to-trough ratio is about 10-fold. This sharp
threshold-like activity profile is encoded by: - \textbf{Bistability} in
CDK1 activation: Wee1 inhibits CDK1; Cdc25 activates CDK1; both have
positive-feedback loops on themselves through CDK1 phosphorylation,
creating a bistable switch. - \textbf{Timing precision} from cyclin
synthesis and destruction: cyclin A, cyclin B, and securin most have
D-box and KEN-box motifs that direct APC/C-mediated ubiquitination at
precise times.

\subsubsection{Specific Checkpoint Failures in
Cancer}\label{specific-checkpoint-failures-in-cancer}

Cancer is essentially a disease of cell-cycle deregulation. Key
checkpoint mutations and their consequences:

\textbf{(1) RB1 loss (G1/S checkpoint failure)} - Normal:
hypophosphorylated RB binds E2F \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} E2F cannot transcribe S-phase genes
(DNA Pol \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}, PCNA, MCM, thymidine kinase) - Cancer: biallelic RB1
mutations or deletions (retinoblastoma; small-cell lung cancer; bladder;
osteosarcoma) - Consequence: constitutive E2F activity; cells enter S
phase regardless of mitogen status - Therapeutic relevance:
\textbf{CDK4/6 inhibitors (palbociclib, ribociclib, abemaciclib) are
ineffective in RB-null tumours} because the entire downstream pathway is
already deregulated.

\textbf{(2) p53 loss (G1/S and G2/M checkpoints failure)} - Normal: p53
senses DNA damage \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} induces p21 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} arrests CDK2 (G1/S) and CDK1 (G2/M);
also induces apoptosis (BAX, PUMA, NOXA) - Cancer: about 50 \%
of cancers carry p53 mutations (most frequent mutated gene); often
dominant-negative (mutant p53 oligomerises with wild-type to inactivate
it) or gain-of-function (p53\textsuperscript{R175H},
p53\textsuperscript{R273H} stabilise oncogenic chromatin states) -
Consequence: cells with damaged DNA continue dividing; aneuploidy;
centrosome amplification; chromosomal instability - Therapeutic
relevance: PRIMA-1, APR-246 (eprenetapopt) re-fold mutant p53
conformations; HDM2 inhibitors (idasanutlin, milademetan) re-stabilise
wild-type p53 in tumours where p53 is wild-type but suppressed by HDM2
amplification.

\textbf{(3) WEE1/CDC25 deregulation (G2/M checkpoint failure)} - Normal:
Wee1 phosphorylates CDK1 (Tyr15) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} inactive; Cdc25 dephosphorylates \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
activates; balance controls mitotic entry timing. - Cancer-relevant
deregulation: - \textbf{CDC25 amplification} in many tumours (breast,
lung, pancreatic) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} premature CDK1 activation \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} DNA-damaged cells enter
mitosis prematurely \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} mitotic catastrophe (paradoxically anti-tumour in
some contexts). - \textbf{WEE1 inhibition (adavosertib/MK-1775)} is
being trialled in p53-mutant tumours: without p53 (the G1/S guard), the
cell relies on Wee1-mediated G2/M arrest; inhibiting Wee1 forces entry
into mitosis with damaged DNA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} mitotic catastrophe. This is
\textbf{synthetic lethality} with p53 loss.

\textbf{(4) APC/C-Cdc20 / SAC failures} - Normal: SAC (mitotic
checkpoint complex MCC: Mad2 + BubR1 + Bub3) prevents anaphase until
kinetochores are properly attached. - Cancer: \textbf{BUB1B (BubR1)}
loss-of-function causes mosaic variegated aneuploidy syndrome (childhood
cancers, microcephaly). - Tumour-targeting drugs: - \textbf{Taxanes
(paclitaxel, docetaxel)} stabilise microtubules \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} triggering SAC arrest
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} mitotic catastrophe + apoptosis - \textbf{Vincristine, vinblastine,
vinorelbine} depolymerise microtubules \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} SAC arrest

\textbf{(5) MCM helicase / replication-stress tolerance} - Normal: ATR
activates Chk1 in response to stalled forks \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} suppresses dormant origin
firing under stress - Cancer: tumours often have constitutively elevated
replication stress (driven by oncogenic \emph{MYC} or \emph{RAS}); this
provides a vulnerability: - \textbf{ATR inhibitors (berzosertib,
ceralasertib)} block the cancer cell's ability to manage replication
stress \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} genome catastrophe - \textbf{CHK1 inhibitors (LY2603618,
prexasertib)} similarly target the replication-stress response

targeting:}

\subsubsection{Cell Cycle Checkpoints}\label{cell-cycle-checkpoints}

Checkpoints are surveillance mechanisms that halt the cell cycle if
conditions are not met:

\textbf{G1/S Checkpoint (Restriction Point)}: - The \textbf{RB-E2F
pathway} is the molecular switch. In early G1, hypophosphorylated RB
binds and inhibits E2F transcription factors. Mitogenic signals activate
cyclin D-CDK4/6, which partially phosphorylates RB. Cyclin E-CDK2
completes RB hyperphosphorylation, releasing E2F to transcribe genes for
DNA replication (DNA Pol alpha, PCNA, MCM, thymidine kinase). - This is
the ``point of no return'': once past R, the cell will complete S phase
even if mitogens are withdrawn.

\textbf{Intra-S Checkpoint}: - Monitors replication fork stalling and
DNA damage during S phase - Stalled forks activate \textbf{ATR kinase}
(via RPA-coated ssDNA), which phosphorylates \textbf{Chk1} kinase - Chk1
inhibits Cdc25A phosphatase, preventing activation of cyclin A-CDK2 and
cyclin E-CDK2 - Slows origin firing to prevent catastrophic fork
collapse

\textbf{G2/M Checkpoint}: - Prevents entry into mitosis with damaged or
incompletely replicated DNA - \textbf{ATM} (activated by DSBs) and
\textbf{ATR} (activated by ssDNA/stalled forks) phosphorylate
\textbf{Chk2} and \textbf{Chk1} respectively - Chk1/Chk2 phosphorylate
Cdc25C, creating a 14-3-3 binding site that sequesters Cdc25C in the
\hyperref[gl:cytoplasm]{\textbf{cytoplasm}}, preventing it from
activating cyclin B-CDK1 (MPF) - Simultaneously, p53 induces p21, which
directly inhibits cyclin B-CDK1

\textbf{Spindle Assembly Checkpoint (SAC)}: - Prevents anaphase until
most kinetochores are properly attached to spindle microtubules -
Unattached kinetochores catalyze formation of the \textbf{mitotic
checkpoint complex (MCC)}: Mad2, BubR1, Bub3, and Cdc20 - MCC binds and
inhibits \textbf{Cdc20}, preventing activation of APC/C - A single
unattached kinetochore is sufficient for complete arrest (Rieder et
al.~1995) - Once most kinetochores achieve bipolar attachment with
tension, SAC is silenced; Cdc20 activates APC/C, which ubiquitinates
securin and cyclin B - Securin degradation releases \textbf{separase},
which cleaves cohesin (Scc1/Rad21 subunit) -- triggering anaphase

\subsubsection{The DNA Damage Response: ATM/ATR and
p53}\label{the-dna-damage-response-atmatr-and-p53}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0071_6d60c17cec8c.png}
\caption{The DNA damage response pathway. ATM responds to double-strand breaks; ATR responds to replication stress and single-stranded DNA. Both converge on p53, which decides between cell cycle arrest (allowing repair), apoptosis, or senescence depending on damage severity.}
\end{figure}

\textbf{p53: Guardian of the Genome}

p53 is the most frequently mutated gene in human cancers (approximately
50\% of cancers carry \emph{TP53} mutations). Normal p53 function:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Normally kept at low levels} by MDM2 (an E3 ubiquitin ligase)
  that targets p53 for proteasomal degradation (half-life approximately
  20 min)
\item
  \textbf{Stabilized by damage signals}: ATM/ATR-mediated
  phosphorylation of p53 at Ser15 and Chk2-mediated phosphorylation at
  Ser20 disrupt the p53-MDM2 interaction
\item
  \textbf{Acts as a transcription factor} (binds DNA as a tetramer) to
  induce:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{p21} (CDKN1A): CDK inhibitor that arrests the cell cycle at
    G1/S and G2/M
  \item
    \textbf{GADD45}: DNA repair and G2 arrest
  \item
    \textbf{14-3-3sigma}: G2 arrest
  \item
    \textbf{BAX, PUMA, NOXA}: pro-apoptotic Bcl-2 family members (if
    damage is irreparable)
  \item
    \textbf{MDM2} itself: negative feedback loop
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Li-Fraumeni Syndrome} Germline
\hyperref[gl:heterozygous]{\textbf{heterozygous}} \emph{TP53} mutations
cause Li-Fraumeni syndrome (LFS). Patients have a greater than 90\%
lifetime cancer risk, developing sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumors,
adrenocortical carcinoma, and leukemia -- often before age 30. The
remaining wild-type \hyperref[gl:allele]{\textbf{allele}} is lost
somatically (loss of heterozygosity, LOH), consistent with Knudson's
two-hit hypothesis. Many \emph{TP53} mutations are
\hyperref[gl:dominant]{\textbf{dominant}}-negative (mutant p53
tetramerizes with wild-type p53 and inactivates it) or gain-of-function.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Cancer and the Cell
Cycle}\label{cancer-and-the-cell-cycle}

Cancer is fundamentally a disease of uncontrolled cell cycle
progression. Key deregulated pathways:

\subsection{Mitosis: Molecular Events at Each
Stage}\label{mitosis-molecular-events-at-each-stage}

Mitosis distributes one copy of each duplicated chromosome to each
daughter cell. In most mammalian cells it takes approximately 1 hour.

\textbf{Stages of mitosis -- molecular detail:}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2059}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2941}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5000}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Phase
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Duration
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Molecular Events
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Prophase} & about 25 min & Condensin I/II complexes
compact chromosomes (about 10,000-fold); centrosomes
(duplicated in S phase) begin migrating to opposite poles; Aurora A
kinase activates centrosome maturation \\
\textbf{Prometaphase} & about 15 min & Nuclear envelope
breakdown (NEB) by CDK1-mediated lamin phosphorylation (lamins A, B, C
depolymerize); kinetochores (CENP-A, CENP-C, KNL1, Ndc80 complex)
capture spindle microtubules; chromosomes undergo rapid
poleward/anti-poleward oscillations \\
\textbf{Metaphase} & about 5 min & Chromosomes aligned at the
metaphase plate (equidistant from both poles); bipolar attachment
generates tension across sister kinetochores; SAC monitors attachment \\
\textbf{Anaphase A} & about 5 min & Separase cleaves cohesin
Scc1 subunit; sister chromatids separate; kinetochore microtubules
shorten (depolymerization at kinetochore end via Pacman mechanism)
pulling chromosomes poleward at about 1 micrometer/min \\
\textbf{Anaphase B} & about 5 min & Interpolar microtubules
slide apart (kinesin-5/Eg5 pushes poles apart); astral microtubules pull
poles via cortical dynein \\
\textbf{Telophase} & about 10 min & Nuclear envelope re-forms
around each chromosome set (nuclear pore complexes reassemble);
chromosomes decondense; nuclear lamina reforms \\
\textbf{Cytokinesis} & about 5 min & \textbf{Animals}:
contractile ring of \hyperref[gl:actin]{\textbf{actin}} + myosin II
constricts at the cleavage furrow (position determined by central
spindle/RhoA); \textbf{Plants}: cell plate forms from vesicle fusion at
the phragmoplast \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Cohesin and separase}: Cohesin (Smc1/Smc3/Scc1/Scc3) holds
sister chromatids together from S phase. During prophase, most arm
cohesin is removed by the ``prophase pathway'' (Wapl + Polo-like kinase
1 phosphorylation of SA2 subunit). Centromeric cohesin is protected by
\textbf{shugoshin (Sgo1)} and protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A). At anaphase
onset, APC/C-Cdc20 ubiquitinates securin, releasing separase, which
cleaves the remaining centromeric Scc1 -- triggering sister chromatid
separation.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Aneuploidy and Cancer Therapeutics} Defects
in the spindle assembly checkpoint cause chromosome instability (CIN), a
hallmark of cancer. Taxol (paclitaxel) and vincristine exploit
microtubule dynamics to kill cancer cells: taxol stabilizes microtubules
and vincristine destabilizes them, both activating the SAC and
triggering mitotic arrest followed by apoptosis. Mosaic variegated
aneuploidy (MVA) syndrome, caused by biallelic BubR1 mutations, leads to
growth retardation, microcephaly, and childhood cancers.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Meiosis: Generating Genetic
Diversity}\label{meiosis-generating-genetic-diversity}

Meiosis produces haploid (n) \hyperref[gl:gamete]{\textbf{gamete}}s from
\hyperref[gl:diploid]{\textbf{diploid (2n)}} precursors via two
sequential divisions without an intervening S phase:

\subsubsection{Meiosis I (Reductive
Division)}\label{meiosis-i-reductive-division}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3889}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.6111}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Stage
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Key Events
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Prophase I} & The longest and most complex stage; subdivided
into: leptotene (chromosomes condense; telomeres attach to nuclear
envelope forming ``bouquet''), zygotene (homologous chromosomes pair by
synapsis via the \textbf{synaptonemal complex}), pachytene (crossing
over occurs; \textbf{Spo11} makes programmed DSBs; \textbf{Dmc1} and
\textbf{Rad51} mediate strand invasion; about 1-3 crossovers
per chromosome), diplotene (synaptonemal complex disassembles; homologs
connected primarily at \textbf{chiasmata}), diakinesis (further
condensation; nuclear envelope breaks down) \\
\textbf{Metaphase I} & Bivalents (tetrads) align at metaphase plate;
homologs orient randomly (independent assortment) \\
\textbf{Anaphase I} & Homologs separate (reductive division); sister
chromatids remain joined at
\hyperref[gl:centromere]{\textbf{centromere}} (centromeric cohesin
protected by shugoshin/Rec8) \\
\textbf{Telophase I + Cytokinesis} & Two haploid cells, each with n
chromosomes (still replicated = sister chromatids joined) \\
\end{longtable}
}

\subsubsection{Meiosis II (Equational
Division)}\label{meiosis-ii-equational-division}

Essentially a mitotic division of each Meiosis I product. Sister
chromatids separate at anaphase II, producing 4 haploid cells total.

\subsubsection{Sources of Genetic
Diversity}\label{sources-of-genetic-diversity}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Independent assortment}: \(2^{23}\) = approximately 8.4
  million possible chromosome combinations for humans
\item
  \textbf{Crossing over}: generates novel recombinant haplotypes;
  average 1-3 crossovers per chromosome pair per meiosis = approximately
  30-50 total crossovers per meiosis
\item
  \textbf{Fertilization}: \(2 \times 8.4 \times 10^6\) combinations,
  further diversified by crossing over
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{DNA Damage and Repair}\label{dna-damage-and-repair}

DNA sustains approximately 10,000-100,000 lesions per cell per day from
endogenous (hydrolysis, oxidation, replication errors) and exogenous
(UV, chemicals, radiation) sources.

\subsubsection{Types of DNA Damage}\label{types-of-dna-damage}
