\subsubsection{Repair Pathways}\label{repair-pathways}

\textbf{Direct reversal}: - \textbf{Photolyase} (not in humans): uses
visible light energy to directly cleave cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers -
\textbf{MGMT} (O\(^6\)-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase): transfers
the methyl group from O\(^6\)-methylguanine to an active site cysteine
(suicide enzyme -- each MGMT molecule works primarily once)

\textbf{Base excision repair (BER)}: 1. \textbf{DNA glycosylase} (11
types in humans, each recognizing specific lesions) cleaves the
N-glycosidic bond, creating an AP site 2. \textbf{APE1} (AP
endonuclease) cuts the phosphodiester backbone 5' to the AP site 3.
\textbf{DNA Pol beta} fills the single-nucleotide gap 4. \textbf{XRCC1 +
DNA Ligase III} seals the nick

\textbf{Nucleotide excision repair (NER)}: - Repairs bulky,
helix-distorting lesions (CPDs, 6-4 photoproducts, cisplatin adducts) -
\textbf{Global genome NER (GG-NER)}: XPC-RAD23B detects helix distortion
genome-wide - \textbf{Transcription-coupled NER (TC-NER)}: CSB detects
stalled RNA Pol II on the transcribed strand - Both pathways converge:
TFIIH (XPB + XPD helicases) unwinds about 30 bp; XPF-ERCC1 cuts
5' and XPG cuts 3'; the about 24-32 nt fragment is removed; DNA
Pol delta/epsilon fills the gap; ligase seals

\textbf{Mismatch repair (MMR)}: - MSH2/MSH6 (MutSalpha) detects single
base mismatches and 1-nt insertion/deletion loops - MSH2/MSH3 (MutSbeta)
detects 2-13 nt insertion/deletion loops - MLH1/PMS2 (MutLalpha) makes
an incision in the newly synthesized strand - Exonuclease 1 degrades the
error-containing strand; DNA Pol delta resynthesizes

\textbf{Double-strand break repair}: - \textbf{NHEJ} (active throughout
cell cycle): Ku70/Ku80 bind broken ends; DNA-PKcs recruited; Artemis
processes overhangs; XRCC4-Ligase IV seals. Fast but error-prone. -
\textbf{Homologous recombination (HR)} (active in S/G2): MRN complex
resects 5' ends; RPA coats 3' ssDNA; BRCA2 loads RAD51; strand invasion
into sister chromatid; error-free repair.

The choice between NHEJ and HR is regulated by \textbf{53BP1} (favors
NHEJ) versus \textbf{BRCA1} (promotes resection for HR). In S/G2, CDK
phosphorylation activates CtIP to promote resection.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: PARP Inhibitors and Synthetic Lethality}
\textbf{PARP inhibitors} (olaparib, niraparib, talazoparib) exploit
\textbf{synthetic lethality}: PARP1 is essential for single-strand break
repair. In BRCA1/2-deficient tumor cells (which cannot perform HR), PARP
inhibition forces reliance on error-prone NHEJ, leading to genomic
catastrophe and cell death. Normal cells with intact BRCA1/2 survive.
PARP inhibitors are standard of care for BRCA-mutant breast, ovarian,
prostate, and pancreatic cancers.
\end{quote}

\textbf{Concept Check 11.4}

\begin{quote}
\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Why is NHEJ considered error-prone while HR is high-fidelity?
\item
  Explain the concept of synthetic lethality as it applies to PARP
  inhibitor therapy.
\item
  A patient with xeroderma pigmentosum develops melanoma at age 12. What
  repair pathway is deficient, and what type of DNA damage accumulates?
\item
  Compare BER and NER in terms of the type of damage repaired and the
  size of DNA removed.
\end{enumerate}
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Worked Example: Telomere Shortening and the Hayflick
Limit}\label{worked-example-telomere-shortening-and-the-hayflick-limit}

\textbf{Problem}: A human fibroblast is born with telomeres of
\(10{,}000 \text{ bp}\) of TTAGGG repeats. In the absence of telomerase
it loses \(100 \text{ bp}\) of telomeric DNA per division (within the
stated \(50\)--\(200 \text{ bp}\) end-replication range). Replicative
senescence is triggered once telomeres reach a critically short length
of \(\approx 4{,}000 \text{ bp}\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  How many divisions can this cell undergo before senescence?
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Solution}: The expendable telomere reserve is the starting
length minus the senescence threshold; the number of divisions is that
reserve divided by the loss per division:

\begin{equation}n = \frac{10{,}000 \text{ bp} - 4{,}000 \text{ bp}}{100 \text{ bp/division}} = \frac{6{,}000 \text{ bp}}{100 \text{ bp/division}} = 60 \text{ divisions} \tag{12.5}\label{eq:telomere_shortening_divisions}\end{equation}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  How much total telomeric DNA is lost over that lifespan?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{equation}\Delta L = 60 \text{ divisions} \times 100 \text{ bp/division} = 6{,}000 \text{ bp} \tag{12.6}\label{eq:telomere_total_loss}\end{equation}

The predicted \(60\) divisions sits squarely within the measured
Hayflick limit of \(\approx 50\)--\(70\) divisions for human
fibroblasts, showing how the end-replication problem imposes a built-in
replicative clock that limits the proliferative capacity of somatic
cells and acts as a tumour-suppressive barrier.

\subsection{Worked Example: Replication Fork
Dynamics}\label{worked-example-replication-fork-dynamics}

\textbf{Problem}: An \emph{E. coli} cell with a 4.6 Mb genome replicates
bidirectionally from a single origin. The replication fork speed is
1,000 bp/s.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  How long does it take to replicate the entire genome?
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Solution}: Bidirectional replication means two forks travel in
opposite directions. Each fork must cover half the genome:

\begin{equation}t = \frac{4.6 \times 10^6 \text{ bp}}{2 \times 1000 \text{ bp/s}} = 2300 \text{ s} \approx 38.3 \text{ min} \tag{12.3}\label{eq:replication_time_bacteria}\end{equation}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{E. coli} can divide every 20 minutes under optimal conditions.
  How is this possible?
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Solution}: \emph{E. coli} uses \textbf{nested replication}
(multi-fork replication). A new round of replication initiates at
\emph{oriC} before the previous round completes. Thus, a cell dividing
every 20 minutes has multiple replication forks active simultaneously.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\tightlist
\item
  The eukaryotic replication fork speed is about 50 bp/s. If
  the human genome (3.2 Gb) had a single origin, how long would S phase
  take?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{equation}t = \frac{3.2 \times 10^9}{2 \times 50} = 3.2 \times 10^7 \text{ s} \approx 370 \text{ days} \tag{12.4}\label{eq:replication_time_euk}\end{equation}

This is why eukaryotes require approximately 30,000-50,000 origins to
complete replication in approximately 8 hours.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-14}

For \textbf{DNA Replication and the Cell Cycle}, frontier biology
belongs inside the evidence logic of the chapter. Molecular genetics now
spans single-reference sequences, telomere-to-telomere assemblies,
pangenome graphs, long-read sequencing, CRISPR medicines, and ethical
deployment. The core reading question is this: replication claims should
connect polymerase accuracy, checkpoint timing, damage response, and
cancer relevance.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

When a genomic claim depends on a reference, ask whether short reads,
structural variants, ancestry representation, phasing, or clinical
validation could change the interpretation
\citep{humanpangenome2023,fda2023casgevy,fda2024casgevythalassemia}.

\textbf{Source practice:} For genomics and editing claims, distinguish
discovery from clinical actionability, and cite reference resources,
regulatory records, or primary editing studies close to the claim
\citep{humanpangenome2023,fda2026casgevy,chalumeau2025primeediting}.

\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-14}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{DNA structure}: B-form double helix with antiparallel strands;
  major groove allows sequence-specific protein binding; negative
  backbone charge requires cationic neutralization.
\item
  \textbf{Replication}: Semiconservative, bidirectional from licensed
  origins; leading strand continuous (Pol epsilon), lagging strand as
  Okazaki fragments (Pol delta); fidelity maintained by polymerase
  selectivity, 3' to 5' proofreading, and MMR (approximately
  \(10^{-10}\) error rate).
\item
  \textbf{Telomeres}: TTAGGG repeats protected by shelterin and T-loops;
  telomerase (TERT + TERC) extends 3' overhang in germ/stem cells;
  reactivated in most cancers; ALT pathway in approximately 15\%.
\item
  \textbf{Cell cycle}: G1-S-G2-M driven by sequential cyclin-CDK
  activation; checkpoints (G1/S restriction point, intra-S, G2/M, SAC)
  ensure fidelity; p53 integrates damage signals to decide between
  arrest, senescence, and apoptosis.
\item
  \textbf{Mitosis}: Prophase through cytokinesis; cohesin holds sister
  chromatids; separase cleaves at anaphase; SAC ensures bipolar
  attachment via MCC-mediated APC/C inhibition.
\item
  \textbf{Meiosis}: Meiosis I (reductive: homolog separation, crossing
  over at chiasmata) + Meiosis II (equational: sister chromatid
  separation) produce 4 haploid gametes; independent assortment and
  crossing over generate diversity.
\item
  \textbf{DNA repair}: BER (damaged bases), NER (bulky adducts), MMR
  (mismatches), NHEJ and HR (DSBs); defects cause cancer predisposition
  syndromes (Lynch, XP, BRCA-mutant cancers, Li-Fraumeni).
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See \cref{sec:unit_IV_gene_expression} for gene
  expression downstream of replicated DNA, Unit V for segregation of
  sister chromatids, and Unit VII for bacterial replication timing.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

  Using the mutation-per-division estimate in Q3, scale to \textbf{1012}
  cells in a renewing epithelium. When does clonal selection become

\subsection{Key Terms}\label{key-terms-14}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Semiconservative replication} -- each daughter helix contains
  one parental and one newly synthesized strand
\item
  \textbf{Origin of replication} -- specific DNA sequence where
  replication initiates
\item
  \textbf{MCM helicase} -- hexameric helicase loaded during licensing;
  unwinds DNA at replication forks as part of the CMG complex
\item
  \textbf{PCNA} -- homotrimeric sliding clamp ring; tethers polymerases
  for processivity; K164-Ub recruits TLS polymerases
\item
  \textbf{Okazaki fragment} -- short DNA segment synthesized on the
  lagging strand (100-200 nt in eukaryotes)
\item
  \textbf{Telomerase} -- reverse transcriptase (TERT + TERC) that
  extends telomeric repeats using an RNA template
\item
  \textbf{Cyclin-CDK complex} -- heterodimer driving cell cycle
  transitions; cyclin provides specificity, CDK provides kinase activity
\item
  \textbf{Restriction point} -- point in late G1 after which the cell is
  committed to divide independent of mitogens
\item
  \textbf{Spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC)} -- monitors
  kinetochore-microtubule attachment; prevents premature anaphase via
  MCC
\item
  \textbf{Separase} -- protease that cleaves cohesin Scc1 subunit to
  trigger sister chromatid separation at anaphase
\item
  \textbf{p53} -- tumor suppressor transcription factor; induces cell
  cycle arrest, senescence, or apoptosis; mutated in about 50\%
  of cancers
\item
  \textbf{APC/C} -- E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets securin and mitotic
  cyclins for proteasomal degradation
\item
  \textbf{Synaptonemal complex} -- protein scaffold mediating homologous
  chromosome synapsis in meiosis I prophase
\item
  \textbf{Chiasma} -- physical connection between homologs at a
  crossover site during meiosis
\item
  \textbf{Mismatch repair (MMR)} -- post-replicative repair of base-base
  mismatches and small loops; defects cause Lynch syndrome
\item
  \textbf{Homologous recombination (HR)} -- error-free DSB repair using
  sister chromatid as template; requires BRCA1/2 and RAD51
\item
  \textbf{Synthetic lethality} -- cell death resulting from simultaneous
  loss of two compensatory pathways (basis for PARP inhibitor therapy)
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-15}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Describe the mechanism of
  \hyperref[gl:transcription]{\textbf{transcription}} in prokaryotes and
  \hyperref[gl:eukaryote]{\textbf{eukaryote}}s, including
  \hyperref[gl:promoter]{\textbf{promoter}} recognition and elongation.
\item
  Compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic RNA polymerases in terms of subunit
  composition, promoter elements, and regulation.
\item
  Explain RNA processing in eukaryotes: 5' capping, splicing
  (spliceosome mechanism), and 3' polyadenylation.
\item
  Describe alternative splicing and its role in proteome diversity,
  including the mechanism of nonsense-mediated decay.
\item
  \textbf{Predict} the polypeptide produced from a given mRNA sequence,
  applying the genetic code and wobble pairing, including the effect of
  a single-base insertion on the reading frame.
\item
  Describe post-translational modifications and the ubiquitin-proteasome
  degradation pathway.
\item
  \textbf{Distinguish} transcriptional from post-transcriptional
  \hyperref[gl:gene]{\textbf{gene}} regulation (miRNA, siRNA, lncRNA,
  circRNA) given Northern-blot versus Western-blot data.
\item
  Describe epigenetic regulation: DNA methylation,
  \hyperref[gl:histone-code]{\textbf{histone code}}, and their roles in
  development and disease.
\item
  \textbf{Predict} lac- and trp-\hyperref[gl:operon]{\textbf{operon}}
  transcriptional output given specified inducer, repressor, and
  corepressor states.
\item
  Describe the role of Hox genes and homeodomain transcription factors
  in development.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Opening Vignette --- Solving the Problem of the Messenger}

In 1961, Francis Crick and colleagues knew that information flowed from
DNA to \hyperref[gl:protein]{\textbf{protein}}, but the molecular
intermediary was a mystery. Working with Sydney Brenner and François
Jacob at Cambridge, Matthew Meselson performed a deceptively simple
experiment: he mixed radioactively labelled
\hyperref[gl:ribosome]{\textbf{ribosome}}s from bacteria infected with
T4 phage with unlabelled ribosomes, then centrifuged the extract through
a density gradient. The new viral proteins appeared on \emph{old}
unlabelled ribosomes --- proving that ribosomes are non-specific
``machines,'' and that the specificity must come from a short-lived
``messenger'' molecule. Brenner named it messenger RNA. Within a decade,
the entire transcription and translation apparatus --- RNA polymerase,
transfer RNA, \hyperref[gl:codon]{\textbf{codon}}s, the genetic code ---
had been decoded. This vignette illustrates how a single elegant
experiment can overturn received wisdom and open an entire research
programme.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Transcription}\label{transcription}

\subsubsection{Overview: The Central
Dogma}\label{overview-the-central-dogma}

Transcription produces RNA from a DNA template. The \textbf{central
dogma} \citep{crick1958} describes the flow of genetic information:

\begin{equation}\text{DNA} \xrightarrow{\text{transcription}} \text{RNA} \xrightarrow{\text{translation}} \text{Protein} \tag{13.1}\label{eq:central_dogma}\end{equation}

Additional information flows include: \textbf{reverse transcription}
(RNA to DNA; retroviruses, telomerase), \textbf{RNA replication}
(RNA-dependent RNA polymerases in RNA viruses), and \textbf{direct
translation regulation} (riboswitches, IREs).

\subsubsection{Prokaryotic
Transcription}\label{prokaryotic-transcription}

\textbf{RNA polymerase (RNAP)} in \emph{E. coli}: core
\hyperref[gl:enzyme]{\textbf{enzyme}} (\(\alpha_2\beta\beta'\omega\)) +
sigma (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\sigma}}{sigma}) factor:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\sigma}}{sigma} factor recognizes the \textbf{promoter} -- specifically two
  conserved hexameric sequences:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{-10 box} (Pribnow box): consensus TATAAT (named after David
    Pribnow)
  \item
    \textbf{-35 box}: consensus TTGACA
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Promoter strength correlates with similarity to consensus; strong
  promoters (e.g., rRNA genes) match closely at both positions
\item
  The \(\sigma^{70}\) factor is the ``housekeeping'' sigma; alternative
  sigma factors direct RNAP to stress-response promoters (e.g.,
  \(\sigma^{32}\) for heat shock, \(\sigma^{54}\) for nitrogen
  starvation)
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Transcription cycle}: 1. \textbf{Closed complex}: RNAP + \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\sigma}}{sigma} binds
promoter DNA (double-stranded) 2. \textbf{Open complex}:
about 15 bp around the -10 region melt (AT-rich, easier to
denature); transcription bubble forms 3. \textbf{Initiation}: RNAP
synthesizes short abortive transcripts (2-12 nt); \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\sigma}}{sigma} factor released
after about 10 nt (``promoter escape'') 4. \textbf{Elongation}:
RNAP moves along template 3' to 5', synthesizing RNA 5' to 3' at
about 40-80 nt/s; transcription bubble is about 12-14
bp; about 8 bp RNA-DNA hybrid within the bubble 5.
\textbf{Termination}: two mechanisms

\textbf{Termination mechanisms}: - \textbf{Rho-independent (intrinsic)}:
GC-rich inverted repeat in nascent RNA forms a stem-loop hairpin
followed by a run of about 6-8 U residues (weak rU-dA base
pairs) -- hairpin destabilizes RNAP-RNA contact, U-tract promotes
dissociation - \textbf{Rho-dependent}: Rho protein (hexameric helicase)
loads onto rut (Rho utilization) sites on the nascent RNA, translocates
5' to 3' along the RNA (powered by ATP hydrolysis), catches up when RNAP
pauses, and unwinds the RNA-DNA hybrid to release the transcript

\subsubsection{Eukaryotic Transcription}\label{eukaryotic-transcription}

\textbf{Three nuclear RNA polymerases:}

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2143}}

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2619}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2857}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Feature
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
RNA Pol I
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
RNA Pol II
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
RNA Pol III
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Products} & 45S pre-rRNA (18S, 5.8S, 28S rRNA) & Most mRNA; most
snRNA, miRNA & tRNA, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL RNA \\
\textbf{Location} & Nucleolus & Nucleoplasm & Nucleoplasm \\
\textbf{Number of subunits} & 14 & 12 & 17 \\
\textbf{Sensitivity to alpha-amanitin} & Resistant & Very sensitive (1
ug/mL) & Moderately sensitive (10 ug/mL) \\

box, Inr, DPE, BRE, \hyperref[gl:cpg-island]{\textbf{CpG island}}s &
Internal (type I, II) or upstream (type III) \\
\end{longtable}
}

The table is primarily the entry point. In eukaryotes, transcriptional
output depends on promoter architecture, enhancer-promoter looping,
chromatin accessibility, Mediator, pause release, and RNA processing.
RNA Pol II is especially regulated because its C-terminal domain is
phosphorylated in different patterns during initiation, elongation,
splicing, 3'-end formation, and termination. A strong gene-expression
claim therefore asks which polymerase is involved, which regulatory DNA
element is active, which chromatin state permits access, and whether
nascent-RNA, chromatin, or perturbation evidence supports the proposed
mechanism.

\subsubsection{Eukaryotic Promoter
Elements}\label{eukaryotic-promoter-elements}

The RNA Pol II \textbf{core promoter} can contain several elements (not
most are present in every promoter):

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{TATA box} (about 25-30 bp upstream of TSS; consensus
  TATAAAA): Bound by TBP (TATA-binding protein), a subunit of TFIID.
  Present in about 10-20\% of human gene promoters; associated
  with tissue-specific, highly regulated genes.
\item
  \textbf{Initiator element (Inr)}: Overlaps the TSS; consensus
  PyPyAN(T/A)PyPy; recognized by TAF1/TAF2 subunits of TFIID
\item
  \textbf{Downstream promoter element (DPE)}: Located
  about +28-33 relative to TSS; works with Inr in TATA-less
  promoters; recognized by TAF6/TAF9
\item
  \textbf{BRE (TFIIB recognition element)}: Immediately upstream or
  downstream of TATA box; directly contacts TFIIB
\item
  \textbf{CpG islands}: Regions of \textgreater200 bp with
  \textgreater50\% GC content and observed/expected CpG ratio
  \textgreater0.6; found at about 70\% of human gene promoters;
  typically unmethylated in active genes
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Transcription-Targeted Cancer Therapy}
Several cancers are ``transcription-addicted'' -- dependent on
super-enhancers driving oncogene expression. CDK7 inhibitors (THZ1) and
CDK9 inhibitors collapse super-enhancer-driven transcription programs.
BET bromodomain inhibitors (JQ1, OTX015) displace BRD4 from acetylated
\hyperref[gl:histone]{\textbf{histone}}s at enhancers, suppressing MYC
and other oncogene transcription. These represent a new class of
epigenetic cancer therapeutics.
\end{quote}

\subsection{RNA Processing in
Eukaryotes}\label{rna-processing-in-eukaryotes}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0073_8d677c52196e.png}
\caption{Eukaryotic mRNA processing pipeline. Pre-mRNA undergoes co-transcriptional capping, splicing, and polyadenylation before export. Transcripts with premature termination codons (PTCs) are eliminated by nonsense-mediated decay (NMD).}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{5' Capping}\label{capping}

The 5' end of pre-mRNA receives a \textbf{7-methylguanosine cap}
(m\(^7\)G) added co-transcriptionally when the transcript is 20-30 nt
long. The capping reaction involves three enzymatic steps:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{RNA triphosphatase} removes the terminal phosphate from the 5'
  end
\item
  \textbf{Guanylyltransferase} adds GMP in a 5'-5' triphosphate
  \hyperref[gl:linkage]{\textbf{linkage}} (unusual reverse orientation)
\item
  \textbf{Methyltransferase} adds a methyl group to the N-7 position of
  guanine (using SAM as donor)
\end{enumerate}

Cap functions: - Protects from 5' to 3' exonuclease degradation (Xrn1) -
Required for ribosome binding: eIF4E (eukaryotic initiation factor 4E)
specifically recognizes the m\(^7\)G cap - Signals nuclear export via
the cap-binding complex (CBC: CBP20/CBP80) - Enhances splicing of the
first \hyperref[gl:intron]{\textbf{intron}}

\subsubsection{3' Polyadenylation}\label{polyadenylation}

The 3' end is processed by cleavage and polyadenylation:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{CPSF} (cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor)
  recognizes the \textbf{AAUAAA} hexamer (the polyadenylation signal,
  present in about 90\% of human mRNAs)
\item
  \textbf{CstF} (cleavage stimulation factor) binds a downstream GU-rich
  or U-rich element
\item
  Cleavage occurs 10-30 nt downstream of AAUAAA
\item
  \textbf{Poly(A) polymerase (PAP)} adds about 200-250 adenine
  residues (not templated)
\end{enumerate}

Poly(A) tail functions: - Protects from 3' to 5' exonuclease degradation
(exosome) - Bound by \textbf{PABP} (poly(A)-binding protein), which
interacts with eIF4G to circularize the mRNA (closed-loop model),
enhancing translation efficiency - Progressive shortening
(\textbf{deadenylation} by CCR4-NOT complex) is the first and
rate-limiting step in most mRNA degradation pathways

\subsubsection{Pre-mRNA Splicing: The
Spliceosome}\label{pre-mrna-splicing-the-spliceosome}

Introns are removed from pre-mRNA by the \textbf{spliceosome}, one of
the cell's most complex molecular machines:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Composition}: 5 snRNPs (U1, U2, U4, U5, U6) +
  about 100-300 protein subunits; total mass 3-5 MDa
\item
  \textbf{snRNPs}: Each contains one snRNA (except U4/U6, which share) +
  about 7 Sm proteins + snRNP-specific proteins
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Consensus splice site sequences}: - 5' splice site (donor): GU
(almost invariant) - 3' splice site (acceptor): AG (almost invariant) -
Branch point: YNYURAY (Y = pyrimidine, R = purine, N = any); the
conserved \textbf{A} (adenosine) is the branch point nucleophile -
Polypyrimidine tract: about 15-20 pyrimidines between branch
point and 3' SS

\textbf{The splicing mechanism (two transesterification reactions)}:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{First transesterification}: The 2'-OH of the branch point
  adenosine attacks the phosphodiester bond at the 5' splice site (GU).
  This produces:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    A free 5' \hyperref[gl:exon]{\textbf{exon}} with a 3'-OH
  \item
    A lariat intermediate: the intron circularized via a 2'-5'
    phosphodiester bond at the branch point A
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Second transesterification}: The 3'-OH of the free 5' exon
  attacks the phosphodiester bond at the 3' splice site (AG). This
  produces:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Ligated exons (5' exon joined to 3' exon)
  \item
    Released lariat intron (debranched and degraded)
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Spliceosome assembly cycle}: 1. \textbf{E complex}: U1 snRNP
base-pairs with 5' SS; U2AF65 binds polypyrimidine tract; U2AF35
contacts 3' SS AG; SF1/BBP binds branch point 2. \textbf{A complex}: U2
snRNP replaces SF1 at branch point (ATP-dependent); branch point A
bulges out 3. \textbf{B complex}: U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP joins; massive
rearrangement 4. \textbf{B* complex}: U1 and U4 released; U6 replaces U1
at 5' SS; U6-U2 interaction positions catalytic metal ions 5. \textbf{C
complex}: First transesterification occurs 6. \textbf{C* complex}:
Second transesterification; exons ligated; lariat released 7.
\textbf{Post-spliceosomal complex}: snRNPs recycled; EJC (exon junction
complex) deposited about 20-24 nt upstream of each exon-exon
junction

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Spinal Muscular Atrophy and
Splice-Modifying Therapy} Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is caused by
loss of the \emph{SMN1} gene. The paralog \emph{SMN2} has a C-to-T
transition in exon 7 that weakens an exonic splicing enhancer, causing
about 90\% exon 7 skipping and production of a truncated,
unstable protein. \textbf{Nusinersen (Spinraza)} is an antisense
oligonucleotide (ASO) that binds an intronic splicing silencer (ISS-N1)
in \emph{SMN2} intron 7, promoting exon 7 inclusion and full-length SMN
protein production. Approved by FDA in 2016, it was one of the first
splice-modifying therapies. \textbf{Risdiplam (Evrysdi)}, an oral small
molecule that stabilizes U1 snRNP binding at the \emph{SMN2} exon 7 5'
SS, was approved in 2020.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Alternative Splicing}\label{alternative-splicing}

Alternative splicing generates multiple protein isoforms from a single
gene. An estimated \textgreater95\% of human multi-exon genes undergo
alternative splicing.

\textbf{Types of alternative splicing}:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2222}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4444}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Type
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Description
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Example
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Cassette exon (exon skipping) & An exon is included or excluded &
Fibronectin: EDA and EDB exons (tissue-specific) \\
Alternative 5' splice site & Two different 5' SS compete & SV40 T/t
antigen \\
Alternative 3' splice site & Two different 3' SS compete & Adenovirus
E1A \\
Intron retention & An intron is retained in the mature mRNA & Common in
plants; increasingly recognized in mammals \\
Mutually exclusive exons & One of two (or more) exons is included,
rarely both & alpha-tropomyosin; DSCAM \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{DSCAM in \emph{Drosophila}}: The Down syndrome cell adhesion
molecule gene contains 4 clusters of alternatively spliced exons: 12
alternatives for exon 4, 48 for exon 6, 33 for exon 9, and 2 for exon
17. Combinatorially: \(12 \times 48 \times 33 \times 2 = 38,016\)
possible mRNA isoforms -- more than twice the total number of genes in
the \emph{Drosophila} \hyperref[gl:genome]{\textbf{genome}}. DSCAM
diversity is essential for neuronal self-recognition and axon guidance.

\textbf{Quantitative scope in humans.} Genome-wide RNA-seq studies show
that \textbf{about 95 \% of human multi-exon genes undergo
alternative splicing}, with 92 \% producing more than one isoform per
gene at detectable levels (Wang et al.~2008; Pan et al.~2008). Average
number of detected isoforms per multi-exon gene: 4--7
(cell-type-dependent). Approximately 60 \% of alternative-splicing
events are tissue-specifically regulated. Estimates of the number of
distinct splicing events: - about 150,000 cassette-exon events
- about 60,000 alternative 5\texorpdfstring{'}{'}/3\texorpdfstring{'}{'} splice sites -
about 25,000 mutually exclusive exon events -
about 30,000 retained-intron events (especially in plants and
brain)

\textbf{Disease-causing splice site mutations --- clinical examples:} -
\textbf{\emph{BRCA1} IVS5+1G\textgreater A:} disrupts the consensus 5\texorpdfstring{'}{'}
splice site (GT \textgreater{} AT), causing exon 5 skipping and
frameshift; pathogenic for hereditary breast/ovarian cancer. -
\textbf{\emph{DMD} exon 51 deletion:} removes a frame-essential exon,
causing Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Antisense oligonucleotide therapies
(eteplirsen, casimersen) restore the reading frame by inducing exon 51
skipping. - \textbf{\emph{MAPT} IVS10+16C\textgreater T:} disrupts the
regulatory cis-element controlling tau exon 10 inclusion, causing
fronto-temporal dementia with parkinsonism (FTDP-17). Different intronic
mutations in \emph{MAPT} alter the 4R/3R tau ratio. -
\textbf{\emph{SMN2} C840T:} weakens an exonic splicing enhancer in
\emph{SMN2} exon 7, causing exon 7 skipping in 90 \% of \emph{SMN2}
transcripts and producing truncated, unstable SMN protein. This is the
basis of spinal muscular atrophy when \emph{SMN1} is also lost;
nusinersen (an antisense oligonucleotide) restores exon 7 inclusion. -
\textbf{\emph{LMNA} c.1824C\textgreater T (Hutchinson--Gilford
progeria):} activates a cryptic splice donor in exon 11, producing the
truncated lamin-A ``progerin'' that accumulates at the nuclear envelope,
driving accelerated ageing.

Approximately \textbf{15--20 \% of disease-causing point mutations}
disrupt splicing --- either at canonical splice sites (5\texorpdfstring{'}{'} GT, 3\texorpdfstring{'}{'} AG,
branch point), in regulatory elements (ESE, ESS, ISE, ISS), or by
creating cryptic splice sites. This is much higher than was estimated in
the 1990s, when primarily canonical splice-site mutations were
recognised.

\textbf{Regulatory elements controlling alternative splicing}: -
\textbf{Exonic splicing enhancers (ESEs)}: bound by SR proteins
(serine/arginine-rich); promote exon inclusion - \textbf{Exonic splicing
silencers (ESSs)}: bound by hnRNP proteins; promote exon skipping -
\textbf{Intronic splicing enhancers (ISEs)} and \textbf{intronic
splicing silencers (ISSs)}: analogous elements in introns

\subsubsection{Nonsense-Mediated Decay
(NMD)}\label{nonsense-mediated-decay-nmd}

NMD is an mRNA surveillance pathway that degrades transcripts containing
\textbf{premature termination codons (PTCs)}. This protects the cell
from producing truncated, potentially
\hyperref[gl:dominant]{\textbf{dominant}}-negative proteins.

\textbf{Mechanism}: During the first (``pioneer'') round of translation,
the ribosome encounters each exon junction complex (EJC). If translation
terminates \textgreater50-55 nt upstream of an EJC, the ribosome cannot
displace the EJC. The interaction of release factors (eRF1/eRF3) with
UPF1, followed by UPF1 interaction with the downstream EJC-bound
UPF2/UPF3, triggers UPF1 phosphorylation, mRNA decapping, deadenylation,
and degradation.

NMD degrades about 5-10\% of the human transcriptome, including
many alternatively spliced isoforms with PTCs (regulated unproductive
splicing and translation, or RUST).

\textbf{Concept Check 12.1}

\begin{quote}
\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Why is the 5' cap structure a 5'-5' triphosphate linkage rather than
  the usual 3'-5'? What advantage does this provide?
\item
  A \hyperref[gl:mutation]{\textbf{mutation}} changes the branch point A
  to G in a critical intron. Predict the consequence for splicing.
\item
  Explain how nusinersen promotes exon 7 inclusion in SMN2 pre-mRNA.
\item
  Why does NMD require translation (and therefore nuclear export)?
\end{enumerate}
\end{quote}

\subsection{Translation}\label{translation}

\subsubsection{The Genetic Code}\label{the-genetic-code}

The genetic code maps 64 codons (\(4^3 = 64\)) to 20 amino acids plus
stop signals:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4348}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5652}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Property
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Description
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Degenerate (redundant)} & Amino acids are encoded by 1-6
synonymous codons; Leu, Ser, Arg each have 6 codons; Met and Trp each
have 1 \\
\textbf{Unambiguous} & Each codon specifies exactly one amino acid (or
stop) \\
\textbf{Commaless and non-overlapping} & Read in consecutive,
non-overlapping triplets from a fixed start point \\
\textbf{Nearly comprehensive} & Exceptions in mitochondria
(\emph{Mycoplasma}: UGA = Trp; \emph{Tetrahymena}: UAA/UAG = Gln;
mammalian mitochondria: AGA/AGG = Stop) \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Start codon}: AUG (methionine) in eukaryotes; AUG
(formylmethionine) in prokaryotes. Rarely, GUG or UUG serve as
alternative start codons in prokaryotes.

\textbf{Stop codons}: UAA (ochre), UAG (amber), UGA (opal/umber).

\textbf{Wobble base pairing} \citep{crick1966}: The third codon position
(``wobble position'') pairs with the first
\hyperref[gl:anticodon]{\textbf{anticodon}} position with relaxed
stringency:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Anticodon first position & Pairs with codon third position \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
U & A, G \\
C & G primarily \\
A & U primarily \\
G & C, U \\
I (inosine) & A, C, U \\
\end{longtable}
}

Wobble explains how 45 tRNAs (in humans) can decode 61 sense codons.
\textbf{Suppressor tRNAs} are mutant tRNAs that can read stop codons as
amino acids, ``suppressing'' nonsense mutations.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0074_1efbf9c5820e.png}
\caption{The ribosomal translation cycle in eukaryotes. Initiation involves cap-dependent scanning to the start codon. Elongation cycles through decoding, peptide bond formation, and translocation. Termination occurs when a stop codon is recognized by eRF1.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Ribosome Structure}\label{ribosome-structure}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1957}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4130}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3913}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Feature
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Prokaryotic (70S)
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Eukaryotic (80S)
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Small subunit & 30S (16S rRNA + about 21 proteins) & 40S (18S
rRNA + about 33 proteins) \\
Large subunit & 50S (23S + 5S rRNA + about 31 proteins) & 60S
(28S + 5.8S + 5S rRNA + about 49 proteins) \\
Sedimentation coefficient & 70S & 80S \\
Peptidyl transferase center & 23S rRNA & 28S rRNA \\
mRNA binding & Shine-Dalgarno sequence & 5' cap scanning \\
\end{longtable}
}

The ribosome has three tRNA-binding sites: - \textbf{A site
(aminoacyl)}: accepts incoming aminoacyl-tRNA - \textbf{P site
(peptidyl)}: holds the tRNA carrying the growing polypeptide chain -
\textbf{E site (exit)}: depleted (deacylated) tRNA exits here

\textbf{Critical insight}: The peptidyl transferase center (PTC) is
composed entirely of rRNA -- no protein comes within 18 A of the active
site. This demonstrates that the ribosome is a \textbf{ribozyme} (Nobel
Prize 2009: Ramakrishnan, Steitz, Yonath). This supports the \textbf{RNA
world hypothesis}: RNA catalyzed protein synthesis before proteins
existed.

\subsubsection{Translation Initiation, Elongation, and
Termination}\label{translation-initiation-elongation-and-termination}

\textbf{Prokaryotic initiation}: The \textbf{Shine-Dalgarno sequence}
(AGGAGG, about 5-10 nt upstream of AUG) base-pairs with the
anti-SD sequence at the 3' end of 16S rRNA, positioning the AUG in the P
site. IF1 blocks the A site; IF2-GTP escorts fMet-tRNA\(_f^{Met}\) to
the P site; IF3 prevents premature 50S joining. After start codon
recognition, IF2 hydrolyzes GTP, most IFs dissociate, and 50S joins.

\textbf{Eukaryotic initiation} (cap-dependent scanning model): 1.
\textbf{eIF4F complex} (eIF4E + eIF4G + eIF4A helicase) binds the
m\(^7\)G cap 2. eIF4G bridges to eIF3 on the 40S subunit and to PABP on
the poly(A) tail (circularization) 3. \textbf{43S pre-initiation
complex} (40S + eIF1 + eIF1A + eIF3 + eIF5 + ternary complex
{[}eIF2-GTP-Met-tRNA\(_i^{Met}\){]}) loads onto the mRNA near the cap 4.
The 43S complex \textbf{scans} 5' to 3' (powered by eIF4A helicase
activity) until it finds the first AUG in a favorable \textbf{Kozak
context} (RCCAUGG, R = purine; -3 and +4 positions most critical) 5.
Start codon recognition: eIF2 hydrolyzes GTP; eIF5B-GTP promotes 60S
joining; most eIFs released 6. \textbf{80S initiation complex} formed
with Met-tRNA\(_i^{Met}\) in P site

\textbf{Elongation cycle} (about 5-10 amino acids/s in
eukaryotes; about 15-20 aa/s in prokaryotes): 1.
\textbf{Decoding}: aminoacyl-tRNA delivered to A site as part of a
ternary complex with eEF1A (EF-Tu in prokaryotes) and GTP. Correct
codon-anticodon match triggers conformational change; GTP hydrolysis
releases eEF1A 2. \textbf{Peptide bond formation}: Peptidyl transferase
(28S rRNA catalytic activity) transfers the growing peptide from the
P-site tRNA to the A-site amino acid. The reaction is spontaneous
(\(\Delta G < 0\)) -- the aminoacyl ester bond is high-energy 3.
\textbf{Translocation}: eEF2-GTP (EF-G in prokaryotes) promotes
translocation; ribosome moves 3 nt (one codon) along mRNA; tRNAs shift:
A to P, P to E; E-site tRNA dissociates

\textbf{Termination}: When a stop codon enters the A site: -
\textbf{eRF1} (class I release factor) recognizes most three stop codons
(in eukaryotes) -- its shape mimics tRNA - \textbf{eRF3-GTP} (class II
release factor) stimulates eRF1 activity - Water molecule attacks the
peptidyl-tRNA ester bond, releasing the completed polypeptide -
\textbf{ABCE1} (ribosome recycling factor) splits the 80S ribosome into
subunits for re-use

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Antibiotics Targeting the Ribosome} The
structural differences between prokaryotic 70S and eukaryotic 80S
ribosomes make the bacterial ribosome an excellent drug target:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Antibiotic & Target & Mechanism \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Tetracycline & 30S A site & Blocks aminoacyl-tRNA binding \\
Streptomycin & 30S decoding center & Causes misreading of mRNA \\
Chloramphenicol & 50S PTC & Inhibits peptide bond formation \\
Erythromycin & 50S exit tunnel & Blocks peptide exit \\
Linezolid & 50S A site & Prevents fMet-tRNA binding \\
\end{longtable}
}

These antibiotics are selectively toxic because they do not bind
eukaryotic ribosomes efficiently. However, mitochondrial ribosomes
resemble prokaryotic ribosomes, explaining side effects like ototoxicity
(aminoglycosides) in patients with mitochondrial rRNA mutations.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{IRES Elements --- Cap-Independent Translation
Initiation}\label{ires-elements-cap-independent-translation-initiation}

While most eukaryotic translation initiates at the 5\texorpdfstring{'}{'} cap
(eIF4F-mediated scanning), some mRNAs can be translated even when
cap-dependent translation is shut down. They use \textbf{internal
ribosome entry sites (IRES)} --- RNA structural elements that directly
recruit the 40S ribosomal subunit without scanning from the cap.

\textbf{IRES classes (4 main types in eukaryotic and viral mRNAs):}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1042}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1458}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5625}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1875}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Class
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Example
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Initiation factors required
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Mechanism
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Type I & Picornaviruses (poliovirus, coxsackievirus) & Most canonical
eIFs except eIF4E & Internal AUG; PCBP2/3 binding \\
Type II & Picornaviruses (encephalomyocarditis virus, EMCV) & eIF1A,
eIF2, eIF3, eIF4A, eIF4G; \textbf{no eIF4E} & Direct 40S placement at
AUG; cleaved eIF4G is sufficient \\
Type III & Hepatitis C virus (HCV) & Primarily eIF2, eIF3 (and 40S) ---
minimal & Direct binding of 40S to a multi-domain RNA structure (domains
II, III, IV); IIIc binds 40S like a TBP-equivalent for ribosomes \\
Type IV & Cricket paralysis virus (CrPV); intergenic IRES & None --- no
initiator Met-tRNA needed & Pseudoknot mimics tRNA in P site;
translation starts at non-AUG codon \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Hepatitis C IRES --- structural mechanism in detail.} HCV IRES
is one of the most structurally characterised. The IRES adopts a defined
three-domain RNA fold: - \textbf{Domain II} binds the 40S subunit at the
head, positioning the mRNA channel - \textbf{Domain III} (with
sub-domains IIIa, IIIb, IIIc, IIId, IIIe, IIIf) directly contacts
ribosomal proteins; IIIabc binds eIF3 - \textbf{Domain IV} contains the
AUG start codon, positioned directly in the P site - This bypass of cap
recognition and scanning means HCV translation continues even when
cellular cap-dependent translation is suppressed.

\textbf{Cellular IRES elements} drive translation of stress-response
mRNAs when cap-dependent translation is inhibited (e.g., during
apoptosis when eIF4G is cleaved by caspase-3, or during heat shock when
eIF2\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha} is phosphorylated). Examples: \textbf{c-Myc, p53, VEGF, BiP/HSPA5,
XIAP, DAP5, BCL2.} Stress-induced translation of pro-apoptotic
\emph{p53} via its IRES is one of the host's defences against viral
infection.

\textbf{Therapeutic relevance:} - \textbf{eIF4A inhibitors} (silvestrol,
zotatifin) preferentially affect cap-dependent translation of mRNAs with
structured 5\texorpdfstring{'}{'} UTRs --- bypassed by some IRESes. In trial for AML and
CTCL. - \textbf{Eltrombopag} (FDA-approved for thrombocytopenia)
destabilises HCV-IRES--40S contacts as an off-target mechanism.

\subsubsection{Ribosome Profiling --- A Window Into Translation
Dynamics}\label{ribosome-profiling-a-window-into-translation-dynamics}

\textbf{Ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq)} is a technique that captures and
sequences the about 28-nt mRNA fragments protected by
translating ribosomes. Each ``ribosome footprint'' identifies (a) which
mRNA is being translated, (b) which codon is in the A-site at the moment
of capture, and (c) the relative density of ribosomes along the message
--- quantifying \textbf{translation efficiency} at codon resolution.

\textbf{Key insights from ribosome profiling:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Translation efficiency varies across mRNAs by \textgreater{}
  100-fold.} Some mRNAs have many more ribosomes loaded per unit of mRNA
  than others. This is regulated by 5\texorpdfstring{'}{'} UTR features (length, structure,
  upstream ORFs), codon usage in the ORF, and 3\texorpdfstring{'}{'} UTR sequences.
\item
  \textbf{Ribosome stalling on rare codons.} Codons recognised by
  low-abundance tRNAs (e.g., CGA-Arg, CGG-Arg in mammals) cause ribosome
  pausing detectable as elevated read density. Stalling can trigger:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{Co-translational protein folding signals} --- programmed
    pauses allow N-terminal protein domains to fold before C-terminal
    segments emerge.
  \item
    \textbf{Programmed -1 frameshifts} (e.g., HIV gag-pol, SARS-CoV-2
    ORF1ab/RDR-RP).
  \item
    \textbf{Ribosome quality control (RQC):} stalled ribosomes are split
    by Pelota--Hbs1L; the nascent peptide is ubiquitinated by NEMF--LTN1
    and degraded.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Upstream open reading frames (uORFs) regulate
  about 50 \% of mammalian mRNAs.} A short ORF in the 5\texorpdfstring{'}{'} UTR is
  translated first; the scanning ribosome must reinitiate downstream.
  uORF translation typically suppresses main-ORF translation.
  Stress-induced phosphorylation of eIF2\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha} (the integrated stress
  response) increases scanning past inhibitory uORFs, paradoxically
  enhancing translation of stress-response mRNAs (e.g., \emph{ATF4,
  CHOP, GADD34}) that have inhibitory uORFs in their 5\texorpdfstring{'}{'} UTRs.
\item
  \textbf{Codon-level translation kinetics.} Each codon's average dwell
  time can be estimated from ribosome density. Codon-optimised mRNAs
  (e.g., synthetic mRNA vaccines, insulin) have shorter average dwell
  times and higher translation efficiency.
\item
  \textbf{Out-of-frame translation.} Ribo-seq has uncovered hidden ORFs
  (smORFs, 10--100 codons) in regions previously annotated as non-coding
  --- many of which encode functional micropeptides (e.g., MOTS-c from
  mitochondrial 12S rRNA; HOXB-AS3 micropeptide).
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Nonsense-Mediated Decay (NMD) --- Mechanism in
Mechanistic
Detail}\label{nonsense-mediated-decay-nmd-mechanism-in-mechanistic-detail}

NMD destroys mRNAs containing premature termination codons (PTCs),
preventing the production of truncated proteins that would often act as
dominant-negative or gain-of-function pathogens. The key recognition
principle is the \textbf{EJC-distal PTC} rule: a stop codon is
``premature'' if the ribosome encounters it more than about 50
nt upstream of the last exon-exon junction.

\textbf{Key molecular components:}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.6923}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3077}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Component
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Role
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{EJC (exon junction complex)} & Deposited 20--24 nt upstream of
every exon-exon junction during splicing; contains EIF4A3, MAGOH,
Y14/RBM8A, MLN51 (CASC3) \\
\textbf{UPF1 (RENT1)} & RNA helicase + ATPase; central NMD effector;
binds the 3\texorpdfstring{'}{'} UTR after stop codon \\
\textbf{UPF2 (RENT2)} & Bridges UPF1 to UPF3 \\
\textbf{UPF3A/UPF3B} & EJC component; bridges EJC to UPF1/2 \\
\textbf{SMG1} & PIKK-family kinase; phosphorylates UPF1 \\
\textbf{SMG5/6/7} & Recruit decapping (SMG7) and endonuclease cleavage
(SMG6) machinery \\
\textbf{eRF1, eRF3} & Translation termination factors; eRF3 interacts
with UPF1 at PTC \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Mechanism, step-by-step:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{mRNA enters first-round translation} (the ``pioneer round''),
  still bound by CBP80/20 cap-binding complex (not yet the cytoplasmic
  eIF4F).
\item
  \textbf{Ribosome translates from cap to first stop codon.} Each EJC
  encountered by the elongating ribosome is dislodged. EJCs deposited
  downstream of the actual stop codon (in the 3\texorpdfstring{'}{'} UTR) are NOT dislodged.
\item
  \textbf{Stop codon recognition.} eRF1 + eRF3-GTP enter the A site;
  eRF3 hydrolyses GTP; nascent peptide is released by hydrolysis of the
  peptidyl-tRNA ester bond.
\item
  \textbf{UPF1 recruitment.} eRF3 (after release-factor function)
  recruits UPF1 to the terminating ribosome.
\item
  \textbf{EJC-distal proximity check.} UPF1 scans the 3\texorpdfstring{'}{'} UTR; if it
  encounters an EJC within about 50 nt downstream, EJC-bound
  UPF2/UPF3B contact UPF1, activating NMD.
\item
  \textbf{SMG1 phosphorylation of UPF1} at numerous Ser/Thr-Q sites ---
  generates the ``phospho-UPF1'' signal.
\item
  \textbf{Decay execution:}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{SMG6 endonuclease} cleaves the mRNA near the PTC, exposing
    both fragments to exonucleases (XRN1 from 5\texorpdfstring{'}{'}; exosome from 3\texorpdfstring{'}{'}).
  \item
    \textbf{SMG5--SMG7} recruits CCR4--NOT (deadenylation) and DCP1/2
    (decapping) for canonical mRNA decay.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Ribosome recycling and UPF1 dephosphorylation} by PP2A
  complete the cycle.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Clinical NMD exploitation --- three therapeutic strategies:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Read-through compounds} (e.g., \textbf{ataluren/Translarna})
  promote ribosomal mis-decoding at PTCs (especially UGA), allowing
  partial production of full-length protein. Approved in EU for
  nonsense-mutation Duchenne muscular dystrophy (cmDMD).
\item
  \textbf{NMD inhibition} (e.g., NMDI-1, SMG1 inhibitors in development)
  prolongs the half-life of PTC-containing mRNAs, increasing the
  substrate pool for read-through compounds.
\item
  \textbf{Antisense oligonucleotides for exon skipping} (e.g.,
  eteplirsen for DMD, nusinersen for SMA): exclude the PTC-containing
  exon, restoring the reading frame.
\end{enumerate}

NMD also has homeostatic functions beyond pathogen detection: it
degrades a large fraction of physiological alternatively-spliced
isoforms that contain PTCs (regulated unproductive splicing and
translation, RUST), particularly in neurons and during development. NMD
perturbation in flies and mice produces brain phenotypes consistent with
this regulatory role.

\subsubsection{Translation Fidelity --- Mechanism and Error
Rate}\label{translation-fidelity-mechanism-and-error-rate}

Translation fidelity is achieved through multiple kinetic checkpoints,
each contributing to the overall error rate of approximately \textbf{1
in 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{4}}{4} to 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{5}}{5} amino acids} misincorporated:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Aminoacyl-tRNA charging fidelity} by aminoacyl-tRNA
  synthetases (aaRS): each aaRS has high specificity for its cognate
  amino acid (10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{3}}{3}--10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{4}}{4} error in pre-transfer step). Many aaRSs (e.g.,
  IleRS, LeuRS, ValRS, AlaRS, PheRS, ProRS, ThrRS, MetRS) have
  \textbf{post-transfer editing domains} that hydrolyse mischarged tRNAs
  (e.g., Val-tRNA\^{}Ile is edited by IleRS's editing domain, achieving
  10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{5}}{5}--10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{6}}{6} overall error). The ``double-sieve'' mechanism: synthetic
  site selects amino acids that fit \emph{or are smaller than} the
  cognate; editing site rejects amino acids smaller than the cognate.
\item
  \textbf{Initial codon-anticodon recognition} (in the 30S/40S A site):
  Watson-Crick pairing at codon positions 1 and 2 (the wobble at
  position 3 is intentionally relaxed); A-form helix geometry sensing by
  16S rRNA (in bacteria: A1492, A1493, G530 --- the ``monitor bases'').
  Initial selection error rate about 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{3}}{3}.
\item
  \textbf{EF-Tu / eEF1A conformational proofreading} (kinetic
  proofreading via GTP hydrolysis): EF-Tu (in bacteria) or eEF1A (in
  eukaryotes) brings aa-tRNA to the A site; correct codon-anticodon
  pairing accelerates GTP hydrolysis. Incorrect pairings have time to
  dissociate before GTP is hydrolysed (an irreversible step). After GTP
  hydrolysis, a second selection step (``accommodation'') allows further
  discrimination. This adds about 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{3}}{3} to about 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{4}}{4}
  improvement.
\item
  \textbf{Peptidyl transferase activity-coupled fidelity}: the rate of
  peptide bond formation depends on whether the tRNA is correctly
  accommodated; incorrect tRNAs have slower peptide-bond chemistry,
  providing another opportunity for dissociation.
\item
  \textbf{Quality control after translation}: misfolded proteins are
  degraded by the proteasome; ribosomes stalling on damaged mRNAs
  trigger ribosome-associated quality control (RQC) via Pelota-Hbs1L
  splitting and NEMF-LTN1-mediated nascent-peptide ubiquitination.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{equation}\text{Overall translation error} \approx 10^{-3} \times 10^{-3} \times \text{(post-transfer editing)} \approx 10^{-4}\text{ to }10^{-5} \tag{13.4}\label{eq:translation_fidelity}\end{equation}

For a typical about 500-amino acid protein, this error rate
predicts about 5 \% of nascent polypeptides contain at least
one misincorporation. Most are tolerated; a few drive cellular
dysfunction in aging or disease (statin-induced muscle damage from
low-fidelity translation; age-related aggregation diseases). Sub-cohort
of mistranslated proteins are degraded by the proteasome before causing
problems.

\textbf{Clinical translation:} Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, paromomycin)
bind 16S rRNA monitor bases, distorting the codon-recognition geometry
and increasing translation error rate (about 100-fold). This
explains both their bactericidal mechanism (catastrophic protein
synthesis errors) and their toxicities (cochlear hair-cell apoptosis
from mitochondrial mistranslation, especially in patients with the
A1555G 12S rRNA variant).

\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{The Ubiquitin-Proteasome
System}\label{the-ubiquitin-proteasome-system}

The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) is the primary mechanism for
targeted protein degradation:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{E1 (ubiquitin-activating enzyme)}: Activates ubiquitin (76-aa
  protein) in an ATP-dependent reaction; forms E1about  Ub
  thioester bond; humans use 2 main E1 enzymes
\item
  \textbf{E2 (ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme)}: Accepts Ub from E1;
  about 40 E2 enzymes provide some specificity
\item
  \textbf{E3 (ubiquitin ligase)}: Provides substrate specificity;
  about 600 E3 ligases in humans. Two major families:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{RING E3s}: Transfer Ub directly from E2 to substrate (e.g.,
    APC/C, SCF complex, MDM2)
  \item
    \textbf{HECT E3s}: Accept Ub from E2, then transfer to substrate
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Poly-ubiquitination (K48-linked chains of at least 4 Ub) marks the
  substrate for degradation by the \textbf{26S proteasome}
\item
  \textbf{26S proteasome} (2.5 MDa): 20S catalytic core (barrel-shaped;
  contains chymotrypsin-like, trypsin-like, and caspase-like proteases)
  capped by 19S regulatory particles (recognize poly-Ub, unfold
  substrate, feed into 20S core)
\item
  Deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs, about 100 in humans) recycle
  ubiquitin before substrate enters the 20S core
\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Proteasome Inhibitors in Cancer}
\textbf{Bortezomib (Velcade)} is a proteasome inhibitor approved for
multiple myeloma and mantle cell lymphoma. By blocking proteasomal
degradation, it causes accumulation of pro-apoptotic proteins and
misfolded proteins (ER stress), triggering cell death preferentially in
cancer cells with high protein synthesis rates.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Gene Regulation}\label{gene-regulation}

\subsubsection{Prokaryotic Gene Regulation: The Lac
Operon}\label{prokaryotic-gene-regulation-the-lac-operon}

The \emph{E. coli} lac operon \citep{jacob1961} (Jacob and Monod, 1961;
Nobel Prize 1965) was the founding model of gene regulation:

\textbf{Components}: \emph{lacZ} (beta-galactosidase), \emph{lacY}
(permease), \emph{lacA} (transacetylase), preceded by the promoter (P),
operator (O), and regulated by \emph{lacI} (repressor gene,
constitutively expressed from its own promoter).

\textbf{Negative control}: Lac repressor protein (tetramer, encoded by
\emph{lacI}) binds the operator sequences (O1 primary, O2 and O3
auxiliary -- DNA looping between O1 and O3 increases repression
50-fold). When lactose is present, its isomer \textbf{allolactose} (the
true inducer) binds the repressor, causing a conformational change that
reduces DNA-binding affinity by about 1000-fold. Repressor
released; RNAP can transcribe.

\textbf{Positive control (catabolite repression)}: CAP (catabolite
activator protein, also called CRP) + cAMP binds the CAP site upstream
of the lac promoter, bending DNA about 90 degrees and directly
contacting the alpha-CTD of RNAP to activate transcription
about 50-fold. When glucose is present, the phosphotransferase
system (PTS) keeps adenylyl cyclase inactive; {[}cAMP{]} is low; CAP
cannot bind; lac operon expression is reduced even if lactose is
present.

\textbf{Operon logic}: The lac operon is fully ON primarily when lactose
is present AND glucose is absent (high cAMP, CAP active, repressor
released). This makes biological sense: the cell uses glucose (more
efficient) before lactose.

\subsubsection{The Trp Operon (Repressible
System)}\label{the-trp-operon-repressible-system}

The \emph{E. coli} trp operon encodes five enzymes for tryptophan
biosynthesis:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Repression}: When tryptophan is abundant, Trp acts as a
  \textbf{co-repressor} -- it binds the TrpR aporepressor, activating it
  to bind the operator and block transcription
\item
  \textbf{Attenuation}: A leader peptide (trpL) containing two
  consecutive Trp codons (UGG UGG) is located upstream of the structural
  genes. When Trp-tRNA is abundant, the ribosome translates the leader
  rapidly, allowing formation of a terminator hairpin (3-4 stem loop) in
  the mRNA, causing premature termination. When Trp-tRNA is scarce, the
  ribosome stalls at the UGG codons, allowing an anti-terminator hairpin
  (2-3 stem loop) to form instead, permitting read-through transcription
\end{itemize}

This provides fine-tuning: repression gives about 70-fold
regulation; attenuation adds another about 8-fold; combined
about 600-fold.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check:} Glucose is absent and lactose is present while a
\emph{lacI}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-} strain also carries a non-functional \emph{crp} gene ---
predict whether the lac operon is transcribed and justify using both the
repressor and CAP--cAMP states.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Eukaryotic Gene Regulation: Multiple
Levels}\label{eukaryotic-gene-regulation-multiple-levels}

\textbf{Chromatin level}: - \textbf{SWI/SNF complexes} (BAF/PBAF in
mammals): ATP-dependent chromatin remodelers that slide, eject, or
restructure \hyperref[gl:nucleosome]{\textbf{nucleosome}}s to expose or
occlude regulatory sequences - \textbf{HATs} (histone
acetyltransferases, e.g., p300/CBP, PCAF): acetylate histone tails
(primarily H3K9, H3K14, H3K27, H4K16), neutralizing positive charge,
weakening histone-DNA interaction, and recruiting bromodomain-containing
factors -- associated with active transcription - \textbf{HDACs}
(histone deacetylases): remove acetyl groups -- associated with gene
silencing; HDAC inhibitors (vorinostat, romidepsin) are approved for
T-cell lymphoma

\textbf{Transcription factor combinatorics}: The human genome encodes
about 1,500-2,000 transcription factors. Gene expression is
controlled by the combinatorial binding of multiple TFs at enhancers,
which together produce richer logic than any single TF in isolation.
Three canonical principles:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Synergy:} Two TFs bound at adjacent sites produce more than
  the sum of their individual effects. Cooperative DNA binding (when one
  TF stabilises the binding of the next via direct protein--protein
  contact or by inducing DNA bending) and synergistic activation (when
  each TF independently recruits a different co-activator) both
  contribute. The interferon-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} enhanceosome shows about 10\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x}
  synergy: each individual TF drives about 5-fold transcription, but
  together they drive \textgreater{} 1000-fold induction.
\item
  \textbf{Quenching:} A repressor TF bound near an activator can inhibit
  the activator without displacing it (e.g., via histone deacetylation
  recruitment, or by sequestering coactivators in a non-productive
  complex). Examples: GAL80 quenches GAL4 in yeast; BCL6 quenches NF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}B
  in germinal-centre B cells.
\item
  \textbf{Enhanceosome:} A specific stereochemical assembly where the TF
  binding sites are positioned such that most eight (or more) factors
  must bind simultaneously and cooperatively to activate transcription.
  Spacing between binding sites is critical (loss of even one base-pair
  spacing destroys cooperative assembly). The IFN-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} enhanceosome (3.7 kb
  upstream): NF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}B (p50/p65), IRF3, IRF7, ATF2/c-Jun, plus the
  architectural protein HMGA1 wraps the entire 55-bp regulatory region
  into a defined 3D conformation that primarily forms during viral
  infection.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Super-enhancers --- the high-output regulatory class.} First
operationally defined by Whyte and Young (2013), super-enhancers are
unusually large regulatory regions (median about 10 kb, often
\textgreater50 kb) characterised by: - \textbf{H3K27ac density:} at
least 10-fold higher than typical enhancers, often spanning multiple
H3K27ac peaks - \textbf{BRD4 occupancy:} the BET-family reader
concentrates here, as do Mediator and lineage-defining TFs -
\textbf{MED1/MED12 enrichment:} super-enhancers are constructed largely
from Mediator-bound elements - \textbf{Transcriptional output:} drives
high-output expression of cell-identity genes (e.g., \emph{MYC} in
cancer cell lines, lineage-defining TFs like \emph{SOX2} in ES cells,
\emph{PU.1} in haematopoietic cells) - \textbf{Phase separation:}
super-enhancer condensates concentrate Pol II, BRD4, Mediator, CDK7/9
--- see \cref{sec:unit_IV_epigenetics_and_gene_regulation} for detailed
mechanism - \textbf{Identification:} ROSE (Rank Ordering of
Super-Enhancers) algorithm --- rank H3K27ac signal across most
enhancers; the inflection point distinguishes super-enhancers (top
about 3 \% of enhancers, accounting for about 30 \% of
H3K27ac signal) from typical enhancers - \textbf{Therapeutic
implication:} BET inhibitors (JQ1, OTX015, molibresib, mivebresib)
preferentially collapse super-enhancer-driven transcription, providing
tumour selectivity. CDK7 (THZ1, SY-5609) and CDK9 (AZD4573) inhibitors
disrupt the condensate phosphorylation machinery.

The combination of synergy + enhanceosome organisation + super-enhancer
condensates explains why a few hundred lineage-defining genes can be
expressed at very high levels in each cell type, while the rest of the
genome is largely inactive.

\subsubsection{RNA-Based Regulation}\label{rna-based-regulation}

\textbf{\hyperref[gl:microrna]{microRNA (miRNA)}}: - about 22
nt single-stranded RNAs; about 2,000 in the human genome;
regulate about 60\% of protein-coding genes - Biogenesis:
pri-miRNA (transcribed by Pol II) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Drosha/DGCR8 cleave in nucleus to
pre-miRNA (hairpin) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Exportin-5 exports \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{Dicer} cleaves to
about 22 nt duplex \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} one strand loaded into \textbf{RISC}
(RNA-induced silencing complex, containing Argonaute protein) -
Mechanism: miRNA guides RISC to complementary sites (typically in the 3'
UTR; seed sequence = positions 2-8); partial complementarity \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
translational repression + mRNA deadenylation and decay; perfect
complementarity \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} mRNA cleavage (rare in animals)

\textbf{The miRNA pathway in mechanistic detail (mammalian):}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{DICER processing:} DICER (PAZ + DUF + RNase IIIa + RNase IIIb
  domains) measures about 22 nt from the pre-miRNA terminus and
  cleaves to produce a about 22-nt duplex with 2-nt 3\texorpdfstring{'}{'}
  overhangs. DICER's PAZ domain binds the 3\texorpdfstring{'}{'} overhang of the pre-miRNA
  hairpin; the dsRBD anchors the substrate; the two RNase III domains
  cleave both strands in a single catalytic event.
\item
  \textbf{RISC loading complex (RLC):} TRBP + DICER + AGO2 form the RLC.
  The thermodynamic asymmetry rule determines which strand becomes the
  \textbf{guide} vs.~the \textbf{passenger}: the strand whose 5\texorpdfstring{'}{'} end is
  in a less-stable base-paired region is preferentially loaded as the
  guide. The passenger strand is degraded.
\item
  \textbf{AGO2 conformational dynamics:} AGO2 has four domains (N, PAZ,
  MID, PIWI). The MID domain anchors the guide's 5\texorpdfstring{'}{'} phosphate via a
  5\texorpdfstring{'}{'}-anchored binding pocket. The PAZ domain holds the 3\texorpdfstring{'}{'} end (when not
  engaged with target). The PIWI domain has the slicer (RNase H-like)
  active site that cleaves perfectly complementary targets.
\item
  \textbf{Target search and seed-pairing:} The guide miRNA's positions
  2--8 (the \textbf{seed sequence}) must base-pair with the mRNA target
  --- this is the primary recognition determinant. AGO2 conformationally
  remodels to ``extrude'' positions 2--8 in an A-form helix-ready
  geometry for rapid scanning.
\item
  \textbf{mRNA repression by deadenylation--decapping--decay:}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{CCR4--NOT complex} is recruited to the targeted mRNA via
    TNRC6/GW182 family proteins bound to AGO2.
  \item
    \textbf{CCR4 (CNOT6/CNOT6L) and POP2 (CNOT7/CNOT8)} deadenylases
    progressively remove the poly-A tail (deadenylation is the
    rate-limiting step).
  \item
    \textbf{DCP2 (decapping)} removes the 5\texorpdfstring{'}{'} cap, exposing the mRNA to
    \textbf{XRN1} 5\texorpdfstring{'}{'}-to-3\texorpdfstring{'}{'} exonuclease degradation.
  \item
    In parallel, the cytoplasmic \textbf{EXOSOME} complex degrades from
    the 3\texorpdfstring{'}{'} end.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Translational repression in parallel:} GW182 also disrupts
  eIF4F--PABP interaction, preventing closed-loop translation
  initiation. eIF4A helicase activity is reduced. Repression and decay
  are coupled but partially separable.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Seed sequence rules --- quantitative target prediction:}

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5870}}@{}}

\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

6-mer & Perfect 6-bp seed (positions 2--7) & Weak (10--20 \%
repression) \\
7-mer-A1 & Seed + 3\texorpdfstring{'}{'} UTR adenosine at position 1 & Moderate
(about 30 \%) \\

(about 30 \%) \\

extra contribution \\

Because each miRNA can have hundreds to thousands of targets
(TargetScan, miRanda, DIANA-microT predictions), miRNAs typically tune
target levels by 20--60 \% rather than completely silencing them ---
they are ``regulatory thermostats'' rather than on/off switches.

\textbf{siRNA (small interfering RNA)}: - 21 nt; derived from long dsRNA
(exogenous: viral, experimental; endogenous: transposons) - Biogenesis:
Dicer cleaves dsRNA; one strand loaded into RISC - Mechanism: perfect
complementarity to target \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Argonaute-2 (Ago2) cleaves mRNA (``slicer''
activity) - \textbf{RNAi therapeutics}: Patisiran (Onpattro) -- first
FDA-approved siRNA drug (2018), targets TTR mRNA for transthyretin
amyloidosis; inclisiran (Leqvio) -- targets PCSK9 mRNA for
hypercholesterolemia (2021)

\textbf{Long non-coding RNA (lncRNA)}: - \textgreater200 nt;
\textgreater16,000 lncRNA genes in the human genome (likely more) -
Functions: \textbf{XIST} (X-inactivation), \textbf{HOTAIR} (recruits
PRC2 to silence HOXD cluster in trans), \textbf{MALAT1} (nuclear speckle
organization, splicing regulation), \textbf{NEAT1} (paraspeckle
formation)

\textbf{Circular RNA (circRNA)}: - Covalently closed RNA circles formed
by ``back-splicing'' (a downstream 5' SS joins to an upstream 3' SS) -
Functions: miRNA sponges (ciRS-7/CDR1as sponges miR-7, containing
\textgreater70 miR-7 binding sites), protein scaffolds, translated into
peptides in some cases

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check:} A circRNA bearing 70 miR-7 binding sites is
over-expressed in a cell --- predict the direction of change in the
protein output of a miR-7 target mRNA and explain the
post-transcriptional mechanism.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Epigenetic Regulation}\label{epigenetic-regulation}

\textbf{DNA methylation}: - Addition of a methyl group to the 5-position
of cytosine (5mC) in CpG dinucleotides - Catalyzed by \textbf{DNA
methyltransferases}: DNMT1 (maintenance methyltransferase; copies
methylation pattern after replication), DNMT3A/3B (de novo
methyltransferases) - \textbf{CpG islands} at gene promoters: usually
unmethylated in active genes; methylation recruits MeCP2 and MBD
proteins, which recruit HDACs and chromatin compactors, leading to
stable gene silencing - Aberrant methylation in cancer: global
hypomethylation (genome instability) + focal hypermethylation of tumor
suppressor promoters (e.g., RB1, p16/CDKN2A, BRCA1, MLH1)

\textbf{The histone code}:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Modification & Location & Effect \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
H3K4me3 & Promoters & Active transcription \\
H3K36me3 & Gene bodies & Active elongation \\
H3K27ac & Enhancers & Active enhancer \\
H3K27me3 & Promoters/enhancers & Polycomb-mediated silencing \\
H3K9me3 & Heterochromatin & Constitutive silencing (HP1 binding) \\
H4K20me3 & Heterochromatin & Repression \\
H3K4me1 & Enhancers & Poised enhancer (primed but not active) \\
\end{longtable}
}

\subsubsection{Gene Regulation in Development: Hox
Genes}\label{gene-regulation-in-development-hox-genes}

\textbf{Hox genes} encode homeodomain transcription factors that specify
positional identity along the anterior-posterior body axis:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Homeodomain}: about 60 amino acid DNA-binding domain
  (helix-turn-helix motif) recognizing AT-rich sequences
\item
  \textbf{Colinearity}: The order of Hox genes on the
  \hyperref[gl:chromosome]{\textbf{chromosome}} corresponds to their
  expression domains along the body axis (spatial colinearity) and the
  timing of their activation (temporal colinearity)
\item
  \textbf{Conservation}: Hox gene clusters are ancient and highly
  conserved from \emph{Drosophila} (2 clusters: ANT-C and BX-C, 8 genes
  total) to mammals (4 clusters: HOXA-HOXD, 39 genes total)
\item
  \textbf{Mutations}: Loss-of-function Hox mutations cause
  \textbf{homeotic transformations} (one body segment takes on the
  identity of another). In \emph{Drosophila}: \emph{Antennapedia}
  gain-of-function transforms antennae into legs; \emph{bithorax}
  loss-of-function transforms halteres into wings (creating a
  four-winged fly)
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check:} A posterior \emph{Hox} gene is ectopically
expressed in an anterior segment --- predict the homeotic transformation
that results and justify it from the spatial-colinearity rule.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Worked Example: Reading Frame and Protein
Prediction}\label{worked-example-reading-frame-and-protein-prediction}

\textbf{Problem}: The following mRNA sequence is expressed in a
eukaryotic cell:

5'-AUGUUCAAGGACUAUUGCCCGUAGACUU-3'

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  Translate this sequence.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Solution}: Reading in triplets from AUG:

\begin{equation}\text{AUG-UUC-AAG-GAC-UAU-UGC-CCG-UAG-ACU-U} \tag{13.2}\label{eq:reading_frame}\end{equation}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Codon & Amino Acid \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
AUG & Met \\
UUC & Phe \\
AAG & Lys \\
GAC & Asp \\
UAU & Tyr \\
UGC & Cys \\
CCG & Pro \\
UAG & Stop (amber) \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Protein}: Met-Phe-Lys-Asp-Tyr-Cys-Pro (7 amino acids)

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  If a single G is inserted after the first codon
  (AUG\textbf{G}UUC\ldots), what happens?
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Solution}: Frameshift mutation. New reading frame:

\begin{equation}\text{AUG-GUU-CAA-GGA-CUA-UUG-CCC-GUA-GAC-UU} \tag{13.3}\label{eq:frameshift}\end{equation}

Met-Val-Gln-Gly-Leu-Leu-Pro-Val-Asp\ldots{} (completely different
protein, no stop codon in this segment)
