\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-15}

For \textbf{Gene Expression --- Transcription and Translation}, frontier
biology belongs inside the evidence logic of the chapter. Molecular
genetics now spans single-reference sequences, telomere-to-telomere
assemblies, pangenome graphs, long-read sequencing, CRISPR medicines,
and ethical deployment. The core reading question is this: expression
claims should separate transcription, RNA processing, translation,
localization, degradation, and feedback.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

When a genomic claim depends on a reference, ask whether short reads,
structural variants, ancestry representation, phasing, or clinical
validation could change the interpretation
\citep{humanpangenome2023,fda2023casgevy,fda2024casgevythalassemia}.

\textbf{Source practice:} For genomics and editing claims, distinguish
discovery from clinical actionability, and cite reference resources,
regulatory records, or primary editing studies close to the claim
\citep{humanpangenome2023,fda2026casgevy,chalumeau2025primeediting}.

\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-15}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Transcription}: RNAP reads the template strand 3' to 5' to
  produce RNA 5' to 3'. Prokaryotes use a single RNAP with sigma
  factors; eukaryotes use three RNA Polymerases plus general
  transcription factors and Mediator.
\item
  \textbf{Promoter elements}: TATA box (TBP binding), Inr, DPE, BRE, CpG
  islands; enhancers act over long distances via DNA looping.
\item
  \textbf{mRNA processing}: 5' m\(^7\)G cap (eIF4E recognition,
  stability), spliceosome-mediated intron removal (two
  transesterification reactions via lariat intermediate), 3' poly(A)
  tail (PABP, stability, translation).
\item
  \textbf{Alternative splicing}: \textgreater95\% of human multi-exon
  genes; generates proteome diversity; regulated by SR proteins and
  hnRNPs; NMD degrades transcripts with premature stop codons.
\item
  \textbf{Translation}: cap-dependent scanning (eukaryotes) or
  Shine-Dalgarno (prokaryotes); A/P/E sites; elongation cycle; genetic
  code (64 codons, wobble pairing, nearly comprehensive); ribosome is a
  ribozyme.
\item
  \textbf{Post-translational modifications}: phosphorylation,
  glycosylation, ubiquitination, acetylation, methylation, SUMOylation;
  ubiquitin-proteasome system for targeted degradation.
\item
  \textbf{Gene regulation}: prokaryotic operons (lac: inducible; trp:
  repressible with attenuation); eukaryotic: chromatin remodeling,
  histone code, DNA methylation, transcription factor combinatorics,
  miRNA/siRNA/lncRNA.
\item
  \textbf{\hyperref[gl:epigenetics]{Epigenetics}}: heritable changes in
  gene expression without DNA sequence change; DNA methylation (CpG
  islands), histone modifications; dysregulated in cancer.
\item
  \textbf{Development}: Hox genes specify positional identity;
  homeodomain TFs; colinearity of gene order and expression domain.
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See
  \cref{sec:unit_IV_epigenetics_and_gene_regulation} for chromatin and
  RNAi, Unit VI for how expression variation fuels evolution, and
  \cref{sec:unit_II_cell_signaling} for signal-driven transcription
  factors.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Review Questions}\label{review-questions-15}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Compare the promoter recognition mechanisms in prokaryotes (sigma
  factor) and eukaryotes (GTF assembly). Why do eukaryotes require so
  many additional factors?
\item
  Describe the three enzymatic steps of 5' capping. Why is the cap
  essential for translation?
\item
  Explain the two transesterification reactions in splicing. What is the
  lariat intermediate and why does it form?
\item
  How does DSCAM alternative splicing generate 38,016 isoforms from a
  single gene? What biological function does this diversity serve?
\item
  Explain the NMD pathway. Why is it important to destroy mRNAs with
  premature stop codons?
\item
  Compare the mechanisms of eukaryotic and prokaryotic translation
  initiation. What is the Kozak sequence?
\item
  Describe the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway (E1/E2/E3 cascade). Why does
  the human genome encode about 600 E3 ligases but 2 main E1
  enzymes?
\item
  Compare the lac operon (inducible) and trp operon (repressible). How
  does attenuation fine-tune trp operon expression?
\item
  Describe three classes of non-coding RNAs and their roles in gene
  regulation.
\item
  What is the histone code? How do writers, readers, and erasers of
  histone marks coordinate gene regulation?
\item
  Insert a single-base frameshift in a toy 30 nt mRNA after the start
  codon and rerun \texttt{translate\_mrna} in Python. At what point do
  stop codons typically appear compared with in-frame controls?
\item
  Compare how a \textbf{uORF} upstream of a main AUG might tune
  translation initiation without changing DNA sequence.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Key Terms}\label{key-terms-15}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Central dogma} -- the flow of genetic information: DNA to RNA
  to protein
\item
  \textbf{Sigma factor} -- prokaryotic RNAP subunit that recognizes
  promoter sequences
\item
  \textbf{General transcription factors (GTFs)} -- proteins (TFIIA-H)
  required for basal Pol II transcription
\item
  \textbf{Mediator complex} -- coactivator bridging enhancer-bound TFs
  to basal machinery
\item
  \textbf{5' cap (m7G)} -- modified guanosine protecting mRNA 5' end;
  recognized by eIF4E
\item
  \textbf{Spliceosome} -- large RNP complex (U1, U2, U4, U5, U6 snRNPs)
  that removes introns
\item
  \textbf{Branch point} -- intronic adenosine whose 2'-OH attacks the 5'
  splice site in the first transesterification
\item
  \textbf{Alternative splicing} -- generation of multiple mRNA isoforms
  from one gene by differential exon inclusion
\item
  \textbf{Nonsense-mediated decay (NMD)} -- mRNA surveillance destroying
  transcripts with premature stop codons
\item
  \textbf{Wobble base pairing} -- relaxed pairing rules at codon
  position 3/anticodon position 1
\item
  \textbf{Kozak sequence} -- consensus context around eukaryotic AUG
  start codon (RCCAUGG)
\item
  \textbf{Peptidyl transferase} -- ribosomal RNA-based catalytic
  activity forming peptide bonds
\item
  \textbf{Ubiquitin-proteasome system} -- pathway for targeted protein
  degradation via polyubiquitination
\item
  \textbf{miRNA} -- about 22 nt non-coding RNA guiding RISC to
  target mRNAs for translational repression
\item
  \textbf{Epigenetics} -- heritable changes in gene expression without
  alterations to DNA sequence
\item
  \textbf{CpG island} -- GC-rich genomic region; methylation status
  controls gene activity
\item
  \textbf{Histone code} -- combinatorial histone modifications that
  regulate chromatin state and gene expression
\item
  \textbf{Homeodomain} -- 60-aa DNA-binding domain in Hox transcription
  factors specifying positional identity
\item
  \textbf{Operon} -- cluster of co-transcribed prokaryotic genes under
  shared regulatory control
\end{enumerate}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsubsection{Study Blueprint}\label{study-blueprint-16}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Big idea:} Genomic variation becomes biological consequence
  through sequence context, repair, and selection.
\item
  \textbf{Core concepts:} mutation classes, DNA repair, CRISPR, genome
  analysis.
\item
  \textbf{Framework alignment:} Vision \& Change: Information flow,
  exchange, and storage, Structure and function; AP Biology: Information
  Storage and Transmission, Systems Interactions; NGSS-style topics:
  Inheritance and Variation of Traits, Structure and Function.
\item
  \textbf{Model or quantitative lens:} Mutation-rate, edit-efficiency,
  and sequence-comparison calculations.
\item
  \textbf{Data skill:} Classify variants and predict likely molecular
  effect from sequence evidence.
\item
  \textbf{Practice cadence:} Concept Explanation, Questions and Methods,
  Argumentation.
\item
  \textbf{Common misconception to repair:} Not every mutation is
  harmful, and not every harmful mutation changes a protein sequence.
\item
  \textbf{Primary lab:} \cref{sec:lab_unit_IV_mutations_and_genomics}.
\item
  \textbf{Question bank:} \cref{sec:q_unit_IV_mutations_and_genomics}.
\item
  \textbf{Transfer task:} Transfer variant reasoning to cancer genomics,
  ancestry, gene therapy, or microbial evolution.
\item
  \textbf{Bridge to computation:}
  \breaktt{biology.genetics.genetics.hamming\_distance}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Opening Vignette --- One Letter Changes Everything}

In 1949, Linus Pauling published a paper in \emph{Science} titled
``Sickle Cell Anemia, a Molecular Disease'' --- the first time a human
illness was attributed to a chemical change in a specific
\hyperref[gl:protein]{\textbf{protein}}. Eight years later, Vernon
Ingram used the newly developed technique of protein fingerprinting to
identify the precise mutation: a single amino acid substitution,
glutamic acid to valine, at position 6 of the \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-globin chain. Just one
\hyperref[gl:nucleotide]{\textbf{nucleotide}} change --- GAG to GTG ---
makes haemoglobin polymerise under low-oxygen conditions, distorting red
blood cells into rigid sickle shapes that clog capillaries. That one
point mutation causes pain crises, organ damage, and shortened lifespan
for millions worldwide. The sickle-cell story remains the most
compelling illustration of how a single mutational event can cascade
through molecular structure, protein function, cell physiology, and
whole-organism health.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Types of Mutations}\label{types-of-mutations}

A \textbf{mutation} is any heritable change in DNA sequence. Mutations
are the ultimate source of most genetic variation and therefore the raw
material for evolution.

\subsubsection{Mutation Rates: A Quantitative
Framework}\label{mutation-rates-a-quantitative-framework}

The \textbf{per-nucleotide per-generation mutation rate} in humans is
approximately \(\mu \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-8}\) per bp per generation
(Kong et al., 2012, \emph{Nature}). For a diploid genome of
\(2N \approx 6.4 \times 10^9\) bp, the expected number of de novo
mutations per offspring is:

\begin{equation}M = 2N \times \mu \approx 6.4 \times 10^9 \times 1.2 \times 10^{-8} \approx 70\text{--}80 \text{ mutations/generation} \tag{14.1}\label{eq:mutations_per_gen}\end{equation}

The probability of observing exactly \(k\) mutations in a region of
length \(L\) follows the \textbf{Poisson distribution}:

\begin{equation}P(k) = \frac{(\mu L)^k \, e^{-\mu L}}{k!} \tag{14.2}\label{eq:poisson_mut}\end{equation}

This is used to assess whether a \hyperref[gl:gene]{\textbf{gene}} or
genomic region has an excess of mutations relative to the background
rate --- a signature of positive selection or a mutational hotspot.

For genome-wide studies, the \textbf{Bonferroni-corrected significance
threshold} for \(m\) independent tests is:

\begin{equation}\alpha_{\text{corrected}} = \frac{\alpha}{m} = \frac{0.05}{10^6} = 5 \times 10^{-8} \tag{14.3}\label{eq:bonferroni_correction}\end{equation}

This is the standard genome-wide significance threshold for GWAS:
primarily associations with \(p < 5 \times 10^{-8}\) are considered
robust.

The \textbf{Ka/Ks ratio} (also called dN/dS or \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\omega}}{omega}) measures the ratio of
nonsynonymous to synonymous substitution rates, revealing the mode of
\hyperref[gl:natural-selection]{\textbf{natural selection}}:

\begin{equation}\omega = \frac{K_a}{K_s} = \frac{d_N}{d_S} \tag{14.4}\label{eq:omega_ratio}\end{equation}

where \(\omega < 1\) indicates purifying selection, \(\omega = 1\)
neutral evolution, and \(\omega > 1\) positive selection.

Mutations}\label{nucleotide-level-point-mutations}

\subsubsection{Insertions, Deletions, and
Frameshifts}\label{insertions-deletions-and-frameshifts}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Insertion}: One or more nucleotides added to the sequence
\item
  \textbf{Deletion}: One or more nucleotides removed from the sequence
\item
  \textbf{Frameshift}: An insertion or deletion that is NOT a multiple
  of 3 bp -- shifts the entire downstream reading frame, producing a
  completely altered amino acid sequence and usually encountering a
  premature stop codon
\item
  \textbf{In-frame insertion/deletion}: A multiple of 3 bp -- adds or
  removes amino acids without disrupting the reading frame (e.g., the
  deltaF508 mutation in CFTR is a 3-bp deletion removing Phe508, causing
  cystic fibrosis)
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Copy Number Variants and Structural
Mutations}\label{copy-number-variants-and-structural-mutations}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Copy number variants (CNVs)}: Duplications or deletions of
  segments from 1 kb to several Mb. The average human genome contains
  about 1,000 CNVs relative to the reference. CNVs contribute
  more base pairs of variation between individuals than SNPs.
\item
  \textbf{Inversions}: A chromosomal segment is reversed end-to-end.
  Pericentric inversions include the
  \hyperref[gl:centromere]{\textbf{centromere}}; paracentric do not.
  Inversions can disrupt genes at breakpoints or alter regulatory
  landscapes.
\item
  \textbf{Translocations}: A segment moves to a different
  \hyperref[gl:chromosome]{\textbf{chromosome}}. \textbf{Reciprocal
  translocations} exchange segments between two chromosomes.
  \textbf{Robertsonian translocations} fuse the long arms of two
  acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, 22).
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: The Philadelphia Chromosome} The t(9;22)
reciprocal translocation creates the \textbf{Philadelphia chromosome} --
a derivative chromosome 22 carrying the \textbf{BCR-ABL1} fusion gene.
This fusion produces a constitutively active tyrosine kinase that drives
chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML). The targeted tyrosine kinase
inhibitor \textbf{imatinib (Gleevec)} revolutionized CML therapy,
converting a fatal disease into a manageable chronic condition (5-year
survival increased from about 30\% to \textgreater90\%). This
is a paradigm for targeted cancer therapy.
\end{quote}

Disorders}\label{trinucleotide-repeat-expansion-disorders}

\textbf{Anticipation}: These diseases show \textbf{genetic anticipation}
-- earlier onset and increased severity in successive generations --
because the unstable repeats tend to expand further during DNA
replication (particularly during germ cell divisions).

\begin{enumerate}

  Classify the sickle cell mutation (GAG to GUG in beta-globin codon 6)
  by type.
\item
  Why are frameshift mutations generally more deleterious than missense
  mutations?
\item
  Explain why trinucleotide repeat diseases show anticipation.
\item
  The deltaF508 CFTR mutation is a 3-bp deletion. Why is this NOT a
  frameshift?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Mutagenic Agents}\label{mutagenic-agents}

\subsubsection{Physical Mutagens}\label{physical-mutagens}

\textbf{UV radiation (UVB, 280-320 nm)}: - Creates \textbf{cyclobutane
pyrimidine dimers (CPDs)}: covalent bonds form between adjacent
pyrimidines (T-T most common) - Creates \textbf{6-4 photoproducts (6-4
PPs)}: covalent bond between positions 6 and 4 of adjacent pyrimidines -
Both distort the helix and block
replication/\hyperref[gl:transcription]{\textbf{transcription}} -
Repaired by nucleotide excision repair (NER); failure causes xeroderma
pigmentosum

\textbf{Ionizing radiation (X-rays, gamma rays)}: - Creates reactive
oxygen species (ROS) that attack bases and the sugar-phosphate backbone
- Causes single-strand breaks (SSBs) and double-strand breaks (DSBs) -
DSBs are the most dangerous lesion -- if unrepaired, lead to chromosomal
translocations, deletions, or cell death - Repaired by NHEJ and HR

\subsubsection{Chemical Mutagens}\label{chemical-mutagens}

\textbf{Reactive oxygen species (ROS)}: Endogenous byproducts of
\hyperref[gl:aerobic]{\textbf{aerobic}} metabolism (superoxide
O\(_2^{-}\), hydroxyl radical OH\(\cdot\), hydrogen peroxide
H\(_2\)O\(_2\)). ROS oxidize guanine to \textbf{8-oxoguanine (8-oxoG)},
which mispairs with adenine, causing G:C to T:A transversions. Repaired
by BER (OGG1 glycosylase).

\subsubsection{The Ames Test}\label{the-ames-test}

The \textbf{Ames test} (Bruce Ames, 1973) is a bacterial mutagenicity
assay that uses \emph{Salmonella typhimurium} strains carrying various
\textbf{his\(^-\)} (histidine-requiring) mutations:

\textbf{Procedure}: 1. His\(^-\) bacteria are plated on minimal medium
(no histidine) 2. Test chemical applied (with and without liver
microsomal extract S9 to simulate mammalian metabolic activation) 3.
Count revertant colonies (his\(^+\)) that can grow without histidine 4.
Compare to spontaneous reversion rate (negative control) and known
mutagen (positive control)

\textbf{Interpretation}: A significant increase in revertant colonies
indicates the chemical is mutagenic. Different tester strains detect
different mutation types (e.g., TA98 detects frameshifts; TA100 detects
base substitutions).

\textbf{Correlation}: about 80-90\% of known carcinogens are
mutagenic in the Ames test. The Ames test is a standard regulatory tool
for chemical safety screening.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{DNA Damage and Repair}\label{dna-damage-and-repair-1}

The human genome sustains about 10,000-100,000 DNA lesions per
cell per day \citep{ward1988}. Multiple repair pathways maintain genomic
integrity.

\subsubsection{DNA Damage --- Quantitative
Background}\label{dna-damage-quantitative-background}

The endogenous and exogenous lesion load is enormous and well
characterised quantitatively:

\textbf{Replication-associated DSBs} (about 100--500 per cell
during S phase) are particularly dangerous because they break a DNA
strand that is also undergoing semi-conservative replication, producing
daughter molecules with persistent breaks. These represent the bulk of
physiologically encountered DSBs and explain why HR, the high-fidelity
DSB-repair pathway, is preferentially active in S/G2 phase.

The cell maintains genomic integrity by directing each lesion to its
appropriate repair pathway. The remarkable per-base error rate of
replication (about 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{0}}{0}) is achieved through a combination of
polymerase fidelity, proofreading, mismatch repair (post-replicative),
and the various lesion-specific pathways below.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: MGMT Methylation and Glioblastoma}
Glioblastoma is the most aggressive brain tumor (median survival
about 15 months). The alkylating agent \textbf{temozolomide} is
a standard chemotherapy. Tumors with \textbf{MGMT promoter methylation}
(silencing MGMT expression) cannot repair temozolomide-induced
O\(^6\)-methylguanine lesions, making them more sensitive to the drug.
MGMT promoter methylation status is therefore a critical predictive
biomarker: methylated tumors have about 21-month median
survival vs about 12 months for unmethylated tumors when
treated with temozolomide (Hegi et al., 2005, \emph{NEJM}).
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Base Excision Repair (BER) --- Mechanism in
Detail}\label{base-excision-repair-ber-mechanism-in-detail}

BER handles oxidised, deaminated, and alkylated single-base lesions. The
pathway has two main subdivisions:

\textbf{Short-patch BER (single-nucleotide replacement,
about 80 \% of events):} 1. \textbf{DNA glycosylase} recognises
the lesion and cleaves the N-glycosidic bond, producing an abasic (AP)
site. There are 11 DNA glycosylases in humans, each with substrate
specificity:

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1515}}@{}}

\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{OGG1} & 8-oxoguanine paired with C & Most clinically important;

\textbf{MUTYH} & Adenine misincorporated opposite 8-oxoG

\textbf{NTH1} & Oxidised pyrimidines (thymine glycol, dihydrouracil) &

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{AP endonuclease (APE1, also called APE)} cuts the DNA backbone
  5\texorpdfstring{'}{'} to the AP site, leaving a 3\texorpdfstring{'}{'}-OH and a 5\texorpdfstring{'}{'}-deoxyribose phosphate
  (dRP) terminus.
\item
  \textbf{DNA polymerase \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} (pol \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta})} has both DNA polymerase activity
  (fills the 1-nt gap with the correct nucleotide) and \textbf{dRP lyase
  activity} (removes the 5\texorpdfstring{'}{'}-dRP).
\item
  \textbf{DNA ligase III + XRCC1} seals the resulting nick
  (ATP-dependent).
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Long-patch BER (2--10 nucleotide replacement, about 20
\% of events):} - Used when the dRP cannot be removed (e.g., oxidised
dRP) or when the lesion creates a strand-displacement intermediate. -
DNA pol \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\delta}}{delta}/\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}}{epsilon} extends, displacing the 5\texorpdfstring{'}{'} flap; \textbf{FEN1} cleaves the
flap; \textbf{DNA ligase I} seals.

\textbf{OGG1 mechanism specifically} (the most studied glycosylase): -
OGG1 scans DNA for 8-oxoguanine. The 8-oxoG flips out of the helix into
OGG1's catalytic pocket. - Active-site lysine (K249) acts as
nucleophile, attacking the C1\texorpdfstring{'}{'} of the deoxyribose; the N-glycosidic bond
breaks via a Schiff-base intermediate. - A second active-site residue
(D268) hydrolyses the intermediate, releasing the 8-oxoG base and
leaving an AP site. - OGG1 is bifunctional: a \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-elimination at the 3\texorpdfstring{'}{'}
phosphate produces a 3\texorpdfstring{'}{'}-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha},\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-unsaturated aldehyde, which APE1 must
process before pol \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} can extend. - 8-oxoG is mutagenic because it pairs
with adenine (Hoogsteen face) instead of cytosine --- leading to G:C \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
T:A transversions if not repaired.

\textbf{Clinical link --- MUTYH-associated polyposis (MAP):} Biallelic
loss-of-function mutations in MUTYH cause autosomal recessive colorectal
polyposis. The mechanism: OGG1 normally removes 8-oxoG, but if 8-oxoG
escapes repair and is replicated, it pairs with A. MUTYH normally
removes that A; without MUTYH, the A becomes fixed as a G:C \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} T:A
transversion. MAP tumours have a characteristic mutational signature
(transversions at GAA contexts).

Table}\label{comparing-ner-and-mmr-a-side-by-side-table}

The pathways have distinct substrates and proteins, often confused. Here
is a direct comparison:

\subsubsection{HR vs NHEJ --- Pathway Choice
Mechanism}\label{hr-vs-nhej-pathway-choice-mechanism}

The choice between homologous recombination (HR) and non-homologous end
joining (NHEJ) is regulated by cell-cycle phase and a competition at the
broken DNA ends.

\textbf{Pathway-determining factors:}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4667}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4000}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Step
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
NHEJ-favouring
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
HR-favouring
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Cell cycle phase & G1, G0 & S, G2 (sister chromatid available as
template) \\
End sensor & \textbf{Ku70/Ku80} binds DSB ends rapidly & Slow
accommodation; replaces Ku \\
End processing & \textbf{DNA-PKcs} recruited; minimal end resection &
\textbf{MRN complex} (MRE11--RAD50--NBN) initiates short-range
resection \\
End-resection regulator & \textbf{53BP1} + \textbf{RIF1} + \textbf{PTIP}
+ \textbf{shieldin} complex (REV7-MAD2L2-SHLD1/2/3) --- protects ends
from resection & \textbf{CtIP} (CDK-phosphorylated in S/G2) +
\textbf{MRN} initiates resection; \textbf{EXO1} + \textbf{DNA2} +
\textbf{BLM} extend resection \\
Fidelity & Error-prone --- small deletions/insertions at junction &
High-fidelity (uses sister chromatid template) \\
Time scale & Fast (minutes) & Slow (hours) \\
Key proteins (after end-recognition) & DNA-PKcs, Artemis (nuclease),
XRCC4, Ligase IV, XLF/Cernunnos, PAXX & RPA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} BRCA2 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} RAD51 (filament) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
strand invasion \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} D-loop \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} resolution \\
Outcome & Direct ligation of ends (often with deletions \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\leq}}{<=} 50 bp) & Use
of sister chromatid as template; restores original sequence \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{The CDK regulatory switch:} During G1, CDK activity is low; CtIP
is unphosphorylated; 53BP1-shieldin protects ends; Ku70/80 dominates \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
NHEJ. During S/G2, CDK1/2 phosphorylates CtIP at Ser327 and Thr847,
activating its end-resection function; CtIP+MRN displaces Ku \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} HR is
initiated.

\textbf{The BRCA1 vs 53BP1 antagonism.} \textbf{BRCA1} promotes
resection (HR); \textbf{53BP1} blocks resection (NHEJ). The two compete
for binding at H4K20me-marked nucleosomes near the DSB. BRCA1's BRCT
domain reads \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma}H2AX-bound MDC1; 53BP1's tandem Tudor domain reads
H4K20me2. Loss of 53BP1 in BRCA1-deficient cells \textbf{rescues HR}
(because resection is no longer blocked) --- a synthetic-lethal escape
mechanism in PARP-inhibitor resistance.

\textbf{The BRCA2 mechanism.} Once ssDNA is generated by resection, RPA
coats it. BRCA2 then loads RAD51 onto the RPA-coated ssDNA, displacing
RPA. This is the rate-limiting step of HR. Loss of BRCA2 prevents RAD51
loading \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} HR fails \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} cells become ``BRCAness''-positive \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} exquisitely
sensitive to PARP inhibitors (synthetic lethality, see
\cref{sec:unit_IV_dna_replication_and_cell_cycle}).

\textbf{Ku70/80 binding.} Ku70/80 forms a ring that threads onto the DSB
end with extreme avidity (Kd \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 1 nM). It positions the DNA-PKcs
catalytic subunit at the end and protects against resection. The Ku70/80
ring must be removed (by ubiquitination + proteasome) before HR can
proceed in S/G2. This explains why NHEJ has an immediate kinetic
advantage and HR requires time and active disassembly.

\subsection{CRISPR-Cas9: Mechanism and
Applications}\label{crispr-cas9-mechanism-and-applications}

\textbf{Background}: CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short
Palindromic Repeats) is the adaptive immune system of bacteria and
\hyperref[gl:archaea]{\textbf{archaea}}. Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle
Charpentier received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for demonstrating
that CRISPR-Cas9 could be programmed with a synthetic guide RNA for
precise genome editing (Jinek et al., 2012, \emph{Science}).

\subsubsection{Natural CRISPR Immunity}\label{natural-crispr-immunity}

In bacteria, CRISPR functions as immunological memory:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Adaptation}: When a bacterium survives phage infection, a
  short sequence from the phage genome (the \textbf{protospacer}) is
  integrated into the CRISPR array as a new \textbf{spacer} between
  repeat sequences
\item
  \textbf{Expression}: The CRISPR array is transcribed into pre-crRNA,
  which is processed (with tracrRNA in Type II systems) into mature
  crRNA
\item
  \textbf{Interference}: The crRNA guides Cas9 to complementary foreign
  DNA; Cas9 cleaves it, preventing subsequent infection
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Engineered CRISPR-Cas9}\label{engineered-crispr-cas9}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0076_2b34ba77d6a1.png}
\caption{The CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing mechanism. The sgRNA guides Cas9 to a PAM-adjacent target sequence where a DSB is created. Repair by NHEJ produces knockouts; HDR with a donor template allows precise editing. Newer variants (base editors, prime editors) avoid DSBs entirely.}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Key molecular details}: - \textbf{sgRNA (single guide RNA)}: A
fusion of crRNA (20-nt spacer complementary to the target) and tracrRNA
(scaffold that binds Cas9). The about 100-nt sgRNA is most that
is needed to redirect Cas9. - \textbf{PAM (protospacer adjacent motif)}:
For \emph{S. pyogenes} Cas9 (SpCas9), the PAM is \textbf{5'-NGG-3'} on
the non-target strand, immediately 3' of the target sequence. PAM
recognition is the first step; without PAM, Cas9 will not unwind or
cleave. - \textbf{Cleavage}: \textbf{HNH domain} cleaves the strand
complementary to the sgRNA (target strand); \textbf{RuvC domain} cleaves
the non-target strand. Both cuts occur about 3 bp upstream of
the PAM, creating a blunt-ended DSB.

\subsubsection{Beyond Cas9: Expanded
Toolkit}\label{beyond-cas9-expanded-toolkit}

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4333}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Tool
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Cas12a (Cpf1)} & Creates staggered DSB; T-rich PAM (TTTN);
self-processes crRNA array & Multiplexed editing; organisms with AT-rich
genomes \\
\textbf{Cas13 (RNA-targeting)} & Cleaves RNA (not DNA); collateral RNA
cleavage in bacteria & RNA knockdown; viral RNA detection (SHERLOCK
diagnostic) \\
\textbf{dCas9 (dead Cas9)} & Catalytically inactive (D10A + H840A
mutations); binds but does not cut & CRISPRi (transcriptional repression
with KRAB domain); CRISPRa (activation with VP64/p65/Rta) \\
\textbf{Base editors} & dCas9 or Cas9-nickase fused to deaminase & CBE
(cytidine base editor): C-to-T conversion; ABE (adenine base editor):
A-to-G conversion; no DSB needed \\
\textbf{Prime editors} & Cas9-H840A nickase fused to M-MLV reverse
transcriptase + pegRNA & ``Search-and-replace'': any point mutation,
small insertion, or small deletion; no DSB, no donor template needed \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{CRISPR diagnostics:} SHERLOCK and DETECTR exploit collateral
nuclease activity after target recognition: Cas13 collateral RNA
cleavage and Cas12a collateral ssDNA cleavage convert a sequence match
into a fluorescent or lateral-flow signal
\citep{gootenberg2017sherlock,chen2018detectr}. That makes CRISPR a
diagnostic logic as well as an editing logic, but it does not remove the
usual validation burdens: sample preparation, contamination control,
limit of detection, clinical sensitivity/specificity, and variant
coverage still determine whether an assay is deployable.

\textbf{Current evidence: prime editing as promoter rewriting.} Prime
editing is especially useful when the desired change is not simply ``cut
here'' but ``install a small regulatory pattern.'' A 2025 \emph{Blood}
study used prime-editing guide RNAs to introduce multiple
hereditary-persistence-of-fetal-haemoglobin-like edits into the
\emph{HBG1/HBG2} gamma-globin promoters, aiming to reactivate fetal
haemoglobin without making a double-strand break
\citep{chalumeau2025primeediting}. Editing efficiency varied among donor
haematopoietic stem/progenitor cells, so this should be treated as early
translational evidence rather than an approved therapy. The concept is
powerful: regulatory DNA can be edited to change \emph{when and where} a
gene is expressed, not only whether its protein-coding sequence is
intact.

\subsubsection{Therapeutic Applications
(2024-2025)}\label{therapeutic-applications-2024-2025}

\textbf{Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel)}: First CRISPR-based therapy
approved by FDA for sickle cell disease (December 2023) and later for
transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia (January 2024), with EMA
authorisation following in 2024. FDA's 2026 product page lists exa-cel
for sickle cell disease and transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia in
patients 12 years of age and older, with updated approval documentation
\citep{fda2023casgevy,fda2024casgevythalassemia,fda2026casgevy}.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Indication}: Sickle cell disease (SCD) and
  transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia
\item
  \textbf{Mechanism}: Ex vivo CRISPR editing of patient hematopoietic
  stem cells (HSCs) to disrupt the \emph{BCL11A} erythroid enhancer.
  BCL11A is a repressor of fetal hemoglobin (HbF, alpha2-gamma2).
  Disrupting its erythroid enhancer reactivates HbF production, which
  does not sickle and compensates for defective HbS.
\item
  \textbf{Results}: In SCD, the regulatory endpoint is freedom from
  severe vaso-occlusive crises after treatment; transfusion independence
  is the endpoint used for transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia.
  Early exa-cel studies also reported sustained fetal-haemoglobin
  induction, so the durable teaching point is endpoint specificity: the
  same edited cell product is judged against different disease-specific
  clinical outcomes
  \citep{fda2023casgevy,fda2024casgevythalassemia,fda2026casgevy}.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{NTLA-2001 (in vivo CRISPR)}: - \textbf{Indication}:
Transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis - \textbf{Mechanism}: Lipid
nanoparticle (LNP)-delivered Cas9 mRNA + sgRNA targeting the \emph{TTR}
gene in hepatocytes -- direct in vivo editing (no cell harvest needed) -
\textbf{Results}: Single infusion achieved 80-95\% serum TTR reduction
(Gillmore et al., 2021, \emph{NEJM})

\textbf{Safety considerations}: - \textbf{Off-target editing}: sgRNA may
bind sites with 1-3 mismatches. Mitigated by high-fidelity Cas9 variants
(SpCas9-HF1, eSpCas9, HiFi Cas9) and careful guide RNA design
(off-target prediction algorithms: Cas-OFFinder, CRISPOR) -
\textbf{Immunogenicity}: about 79\% of humans have pre-existing
antibodies to SpCas9; strategies include using Cas9 from other species
or transient delivery (mRNA/RNP vs.~viral vectors) - \textbf{NHEJ:HDR
ratio}: about 1000:1 in non-dividing cells (most
therapeutically relevant cells); S/G2 phase favors HDR; base editors and
prime editors circumvent this limitation

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Base Editing for Sickle Cell Disease} An
alternative approach uses adenine base editing to directly convert the
sickle mutation (GAG to GTG = Glu to Val) back to the wild-type or a
benign Makassar variant (GAG to GCG = Glu to Ala). This avoids DSBs
entirely and may be safer than Cas9-based approaches. Clinical trials
are underway (Beam Therapeutics, BEAM-101).
\end{quote}

\textbf{Mitochondrial DNA editing boundary:} Standard CRISPR-Cas systems
work poorly for mtDNA because guide RNAs are difficult to import into
mitochondria. DddA-derived cytosine base editors (DdCBEs) solve part of
the problem by using TALE-DddA protein fusions to install targeted
C\(\cdot\)G-to-T\(\cdot\)A edits in mtDNA without guide RNA
\citep{mok2020mitochondrialbaseediting}. This is a major tool advance,
not a general approved therapy: heteroplasmy, off-target editing,
delivery, selectable mutation classes, and tissue specificity remain the
current translational constraints
\citep{barrerapaez2023mitochondrialediting}.

\subsection{Genomics: The Human Genome}\label{genomics-the-human-genome}

The \textbf{Human Genome Project} (1990-2003; Venter et al., 2001 and
International Human Genome Sequencing Consortium, 2001) produced the
first draft reference. The \textbf{T2T Consortium} (Nurk et al., 2022)
completed the first truly gapless reference genome (CHM13), filling
about 8\% of previously unresolvable sequence (centromeres,
\hyperref[gl:telomere]{\textbf{telomere}}s, segmental duplications, rDNA
arrays).

\subsubsection{Human Genome Composition}\label{human-genome-composition}

\subsubsection{Transposable Elements --- Mechanism and Genomic
Impact}\label{transposable-elements-mechanism-and-genomic-impact}

Transposable elements (TEs) make up about 46 \% of the human
genome --- far more than the about 1.5 \% occupied by
protein-coding exons. They are ancient mobile DNA elements that have
shaped genome architecture over evolutionary time. They fall into three
major classes:

\textbf{Class I --- RNA-mediated retrotransposons (copy-and-paste;
majority of human TEs):}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{LINE-1 (Long Interspersed Nuclear Element 1)} ---
  about 21 \% of human genome; about 500,000 copies;
  about 6 kb full-length. Primarily about 80--100 are
  currently transposition-competent.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Encodes ORF1 (RNA-binding chaperone) and ORF2 (with
    reverse-transcriptase + endonuclease activities)
  \item
    \textbf{Retrotransposition mechanism (Target-Primed Reverse
    Transcription, TPRT):}

    \begin{enumerate}
    \def\labelenumii{\arabic{enumii}.}
    \tightlist
    \item
      L1 transcribed by Pol II \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} L1 mRNA (about 6 kb, capped,
      polyadenylated)
    \item
      L1 mRNA exported to cytoplasm, translated to ORF1p and ORF2p
    \item
      Cis-binding of ORF1p/ORF2p to their own mRNA forms a
      ribonucleoprotein (RNP)
    \item
      RNP enters nucleus
    \item
      ORF2p endonuclease nicks genomic DNA at TTAAAA-like sites,
      exposing 3\texorpdfstring{'}{'}-OH
    \item
      The 3\texorpdfstring{'}{'}-OH primes reverse transcription using L1 mRNA as template
    \item
      Second-strand DNA synthesis completes integration
    \item
      Target site duplication (TSD; 7--20 bp) flanks the new insertion,
      plus a poly-A tail at the 3\texorpdfstring{'}{'} end
    \end{enumerate}
  \item
    Most insertions are 5\texorpdfstring{'}{'}-truncated due to incomplete RT
  \item
    L1 endonuclease nicks about 100 sites/cell per day; most
    fail to complete TPRT (silenced by KRAB-ZFP-driven H3K9me3
    repression)
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Alu elements (Short Interspersed Nuclear Element 1, SINE)} ---
  about 13 \% of human genome; about 1.1 million
  copies; about 300 bp.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Derived from 7SL RNA (signal recognition particle component);
    contain RNA Pol III internal promoter
  \item
    \textbf{Mobilisation requires L1 machinery} (parasitic on LINE-1's
    ORF2p RT/endonuclease)
  \item
    Transcription by Pol III; the Alu RNA recruits L1 ORF2p in
    \emph{trans} and inserts via the same TPRT mechanism
  \item
    Alu elements are densest in gene-rich regions; insertions in introns
    can disrupt splicing or create new alternative exons
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{SVA elements (SINE-VNTR-Alu)} --- about 3,000 copies;
  about 2 kb; younger than Alu (about 25 Mya). Hybrid
  composite.
\item
  \textbf{LTR retrotransposons (HERV --- human endogenous retroviruses)}
  --- about 9 \% of genome; relics of ancient retroviral
  insertions. Most are inactivated; some HERV-K elements remain intact
  and may be re-activated in cancer.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Class II --- DNA transposons (cut-and-paste; about 3 \%
of human genome):} - Most inactivated in modern human genome (no active
class II TE in humans) - Mechanism: a transposase enzyme (encoded by the
TE) recognises terminal inverted repeats (TIRs) flanking the element,
excises the element, and re-integrates it elsewhere - Mariner / Tc1,
hAT, P-element families most derive from class II - Hyperactive
synthetic DNA transposons (e.g., \textbf{Sleeping Beauty},
\textbf{PiggyBac}) are now used as gene-delivery tools in research and
CAR-T therapy

\textbf{Genomic and clinical impact of TE insertions:} -
about 100 \emph{de novo} L1 or Alu insertions per generation
(germline) - about 10--15 \% of disease-causing mutations are
TE insertions (e.g., Alu insertion in \emph{NF1} exon 6 causing
neurofibromatosis; L1 insertion in \emph{DMD} causing Duchenne) - TE
insertions in gene regulatory regions can create new enhancers or
promoters (about 25 \% of mammalian enhancers derive from TEs)
- Active L1 retrotransposition in the brain creates somatic mosaicism
(about 80 unique L1 insertions per neuron) potentially
contributing to neuronal diversity - Cancer cells often re-activate TE
expression (LINE-1 demethylation is a hallmark of global cancer
hypomethylation), contributing to chromosomal instability and
inflammation

\textbf{Defence mechanisms against TE activity:} - \textbf{DNA
methylation} of TE promoters (DNMT3A/B targets active TE families during
germline development) - \textbf{KRAB-ZFP transcriptional repression}:
\textgreater{} 350 KRAB-zinc finger proteins recognise specific TE
families and recruit KAP1/TRIM28 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} SETDB1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} H3K9me3 silencing -
\textbf{piRNA pathway} in germline: piRNAs (26--32 nt) bind PIWI clade
Argonautes (PIWIL1/MILI, PIWIL4/MIWI2) and silence TEs via the
``ping-pong amplification'' cycle - \textbf{APOBEC3 deaminases}:
cytidine deaminases that mutate TE-derived ssDNA, restricting
retrotransposition and HIV integration

\subsubsection{Structural Variants --- Inversions, CNVs, and
Disease}\label{structural-variants-inversions-cnvs-and-disease}

\textbf{Inversions} are large segments of DNA flipped end-to-end. Unlike
SNPs, they are difficult to detect by short-read sequencing (the
inversion preserves sequence content, primarily orientation changes).
Long-read sequencing (PacBio HiFi, Oxford Nanopore) and optical mapping
(Bionano Saphyr) have revealed: - about 40,000 polymorphic
inversions per human genome (most \textless{} 50 kb) - \textbf{HbF
inversion regulators}: A rare inversion at the \emph{BCL11A} locus
disrupts the erythroid-specific enhancer of \emph{BCL11A}, derepressing
fetal haemoglobin (HbF) production. This explains the high HbF
persistence in some Sardinian families and provides the rationale for
therapeutic disruption of \emph{BCL11A} (Casgevy approved for sickle
cell disease). - \textbf{Pericentric inversion of chromosome 9}
(inv(9)(p11q12)): a common normal variant (about 1--3 \% of
population), classically considered benign, but recently associated with
subtle effects on fertility.

\textbf{Copy Number Variants (CNVs)} are duplications or deletions of
segments \textgreater{} 1 kb. Two major mechanisms: -
\textbf{Non-allelic homologous recombination (NAHR)} between segmental
duplications (low-copy repeats, LCRs) --- produces recurrent CNVs at
predictable breakpoints (e.g., 22q11.2 microdeletion, 16p11.2 micro-CNV)
- \textbf{Replication-based mechanisms (FoSTeS, MMBIR)} --- produce
non-recurrent CNVs at variable breakpoints

\textbf{CNVs in autism and schizophrenia:}

\textbf{Why CNVs are so impactful:} Each CNV affects 1--5
dosage-sensitive genes simultaneously. The cumulative effect on neural
development is large because brain development depends on stoichiometric
protein interactions. Rare CNVs (occurring in \textless{} 1 \% of
population) collectively explain about 5 \% of schizophrenia
cases and about 10 \% of autism cases --- a substantial
fraction of risk despite each individual CNV being rare.

\subsubsection{Genomic Variation}\label{genomic-variation}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs)}: about 1 per
  300 bp on average; the human genome contains about 4-5
  million SNPs per individual relative to the reference. Most are
  neutral; about 2\% in coding regions; about 0.5\%
  are missense.
\item
  \textbf{Indels}: about 500,000 per genome; usually 1-50 bp
\item
  \textbf{Copy number variants (CNVs)}: about 1,000 per genome;
  collectively encompass about 4 Mb
\item
  \textbf{Structural variants (SVs)}: inversions, translocations, large
  insertions; about 2,500 per genome
\item
  \textbf{Two individuals differ by about 0.1\% of their
  genomes (about 3 million SNPs)}, but most variation is within
  populations rather than between populations (Lewontin, 1972; Fst
  about 0.12).
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{The ENCODE Project}\label{the-encode-project}

The \textbf{ENCODE} (Encyclopedia of DNA Elements) Project
(2003-present) systematically mapped functional elements in the human
genome:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Key finding}: \textgreater80\% of the genome has at least one
  biochemical function (\hyperref[gl:chromatin]{\textbf{chromatin}}
  accessibility, transcription factor binding,
  \hyperref[gl:histone]{\textbf{histone}} modification, RNA
  transcription)
\item
  \textbf{Revised ``junk DNA'' narrative}: Much non-coding DNA has
  regulatory function (enhancers, insulators, lncRNAs); however,
  ``biochemical activity'' does not necessarily mean ``biologically
  important'' (ongoing debate)
\item
  \textbf{about 400,000 enhancers} identified; most
  disease-associated SNPs (from GWAS) fall in non-coding regulatory
  regions, not protein-coding genes
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Next-Generation Sequencing
Technologies}\label{next-generation-sequencing-technologies}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering

\caption{Genomic sequencing approaches. Short-read (Illumina) provides high throughput and accuracy for variant calling; long-read (Nanopore, PacBio HiFi) resolves structural variants, repeats, and enables de novo assembly.}

\subsubsection{Pangenome Graph
Reasoning}\label{pangenome-graph-reasoning}

The old mental model of a genome reference was a single linear string.
That is still useful, but it hides ancestry-specific haplotypes,
structural variants, alternate gene copies, and repeat-resolved sequence
that do not align cleanly to one coordinate path. The Human Pangenome
Reference Consortium's draft reference introduced a graph built from 47
diverse individuals and 94 phased haplotypes \citep{humanpangenome2023}.
In a graph, a variant is not merely ``different from the reference''; it
is a path through an explicitly represented set of alternatives. This
improves reasoning about structural variation and representation, while
adding new validation obligations: graph alignment, annotation transfer,
clinical reporting, and population sampling must become part of the
claim.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0078_74e762424472.png}
\caption{Pangenome graph reasoning. A graph reference turns population variation into explicit alternate paths, improving structural-variant interpretation while making validation and reporting more complex.}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Genome-Wide Association Studies
(GWAS)}\label{genome-wide-association-studies-gwas}

GWAS identify genetic variants (typically SNPs) associated with complex
traits or diseases by comparing allele frequencies between cases and
controls.

\textbf{Methodology}: 1. Genotype hundreds of thousands to millions of
SNPs across the genome in large cohorts (typically \textgreater10,000
individuals) 2. Test each SNP for association with the
\hyperref[gl:phenotype]{\textbf{phenotype}} using logistic regression
(binary traits) or linear regression (quantitative traits) 3. Apply a
stringent significance threshold (\(p < 5 \times 10^{-8}\)) to account
for about 1 million independent tests (Bonferroni-like
correction) 4. Display results on a \textbf{Manhattan plot}: genomic
position (x-axis) vs.~\(-\log_{10}(p)\) (y-axis); significant
associations appear as peaks above the genome-wide significance line

\textbf{Key concepts}: - \textbf{\hyperref[gl:linkage]{Linkage}
disequilibrium (LD)}: Non-random association of alleles at nearby loci.
A significant SNP may not be the causal variant but rather in LD with it
(a ``tag SNP''). - \textbf{Effect sizes}: Most GWAS-identified variants
have small effect sizes (odds ratio 1.1-1.3); complex traits are highly
polygenic - \textbf{Missing heritability}: GWAS variants collectively
explain primarily a fraction of heritability for most traits (e.g.,
about 25\% of height heritability, despite identifying
\textgreater700 loci)

\textbf{Examples of GWAS discoveries}: - Type 2 diabetes:
\textgreater400 loci, including TCF7L2 (strongest effect), PPARG, KCNJ11
- Age-related macular degeneration: CFH (complement factor H) -- led to
complement-targeted therapies - Autoimmune diseases: HLA region as the
strongest risk factor for type 1 diabetes, celiac disease, rheumatoid
arthritis

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Comparative Genomics and Molecular
Evolution}\label{comparative-genomics-and-molecular-evolution}

\textbf{Synteny}: Conservation of gene order between species. Humans and
mice share about 90\% of genes in syntenic blocks, despite
75-80 million years of divergence.

\textbf{Conserved non-coding elements (CNEs)}: about 5\% of the
human genome is under purifying selection (much more than the
about 1.5\% that encodes protein). These conserved regions
likely include enhancers, silencers, and structural elements essential
for gene regulation.

\textbf{Ultraconserved elements (UCEs)}: A particularly remarkable
subset --- about 481 segments of \texorpdfstring{\textgreater{}=}{>=} 200 bp that are perfectly
identical (100 \% sequence identity) across human, mouse, and rat
genomes (Bejerano et al., 2004 \emph{Science}). These elements have
remained unchanged for about 80 million years, implying extreme
purifying selection. UCEs cluster near developmental transcription
factors (e.g., \emph{DACH1}, \emph{POU3F2}) and are enriched in
enhancers controlling early embryonic patterning. Their function remains
incompletely understood --- paradoxically, knocking out individual UCEs
in mice produces primarily subtle phenotypes, raising questions about
why selection is so strong if redundancy is high.

\textbf{Comparative-genomics signatures of selection:}

\textbf{Why the mutation rate is so finely tuned.} The germline mutation
rate of about 1.2 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{8}}{8} produces about 70 \emph{de
novo} mutations per offspring, an upper limit set by cumulative effects
across generations: too high, and ``Muller's ratchet'' accumulates
deleterious mutations faster than selection can purge them; too low, and
there is insufficient variation for adaptation. Different organisms have
evolved different rates: high-fecundity microbes (10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{9}}{9} to 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{0}}{0}),
mammals (10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{8}}{8}), and viruses with their relaxed proofreading (HIV: 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{5}}{5};
influenza: 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{4}}{4}) reflect different optima between fidelity costs and
adaptive flexibility.

\textbf{Gene duplication and divergence} \citep{ohno1970}: Whole-genome
duplications (WGD) and segmental duplications create paralogous genes.
After duplication: - \textbf{Neofunctionalization}: One copy acquires a
new function - \textbf{Subfunctionalization}: Each copy retains a subset
of the original function - \textbf{Pseudogenization}: One copy
accumulates mutations and becomes a pseudogene

\textbf{Ka/Ks ratio} (dN/dS): The ratio of nonsynonymous (amino
acid-changing) to synonymous (silent) substitution rates: - Ka/Ks
\textless{} 1: purifying (negative) selection (most genes) - Ka/Ks = 1:
neutral evolution - Ka/Ks \textgreater{} 1: positive (adaptive)
selection (rare; examples: immune genes, reproductive proteins)

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Personal Genomics and Ethical
Issues}\label{personal-genomics-and-ethical-issues}

\subsubsection{Pharmacogenomics}\label{pharmacogenomics}

Genetic variation affects drug response:

Pharmacogenomics is strongest when it is treated as one evidence layer
in prescribing rather than a deterministic label. A genotype can alter
enzyme activity, transporter expression, immune recognition, or drug
target sensitivity, but clinical interpretation also depends on ancestry
representation in the evidence base, co-medications, age, liver and
kidney function, indication, and whether the variant is actually phased
or captured by the assay. Pangenome and long-read resources improve the
chance of detecting structural or ancestry-associated variants missed by
a single linear reference, but clinical use still requires validated
phenotype links and reporting standards \citep{humanpangenome2023}.

\subsubsection{Ethical Considerations}\label{ethical-considerations}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Genetic privacy}: Genetic information reveals predisposition,
  not certainty. The \textbf{GINA Act} (Genetic Information
  Nondiscrimination Act, 2008, USA) prohibits genetic discrimination in
  employment and health insurance but does NOT cover life insurance,
  disability insurance, or long-term care insurance.
\item
  \textbf{Direct-to-consumer (DTC) testing}: Companies like 23andMe
  provide ancestry and health risk information. Concerns include:
  limited clinical validity for most variants, potential for anxiety,
  and data privacy (law enforcement access to databases).
\item
  \textbf{BRCA1/2 testing decisions}: Positive results require careful
  genetic counseling. Prophylactic mastectomy reduces breast cancer risk
  by \textgreater90\% but is psychologically significant. The 2013
  \emph{Myriad Genetics} Supreme Court decision (Association for
  Molecular Pathology v. Myriad Genetics) ruled that naturally occurring
  genes cannot be patented but \hyperref[gl:cdna]{\textbf{cDNA}} can be.
\item
  \textbf{Germline editing}: Editing human embryos raises profound
  ethical questions. The 2018 He Jiankui case (CCR5-edited babies in
  China) was widely condemned as premature, reckless, and ethically
  unacceptable. International consensus: germline editing for
  reproduction should not proceed until safety and efficacy are
  established and broad societal consensus is reached.
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Pharmacogenomic Testing in Practice} The
Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium (CPIC) publishes
evidence-based guidelines for 23+ gene-drug pairs. Pre-emptive
pharmacogenomic testing (genotyping a panel of pharmacogenes before any
drug is prescribed) is increasingly implemented in health systems. The
PREDICT study (Vanderbilt) and RIGHT study (Mayo Clinic) demonstrated
that pre-emptive testing is feasible and can prevent adverse drug
reactions.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Worked Example: Per-Gene De Novo Mutation
Probability}\label{worked-example-per-gene-de-novo-mutation-probability}

\textbf{Problem}: The human germline point-mutation rate is
\(\mu \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-8}\) per bp per generation. The dystrophin
gene (\emph{DMD}) has the largest coding sequence in the genome,
\(11{,}058 \text{ bp}\) (both alleles together giving a diploid coding
target \(L = 2 \times 11{,}058 \text{ bp}\)).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the expected number of de novo coding mutations in \emph{DMD}
  per offspring?
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Solution}: The Poisson mean is the per-bp rate times the diploid
coding target length:

\begin{equation}\lambda = \mu L = 1.2 \times 10^{-8} \times 22{,}116 \text{ bp} = 2.65 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mutations/generation} \tag{14.5}\label{eq:dmd_cds_lambda}\end{equation}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  Using the Poisson model, what is the probability that a given child
  carries no new coding mutation in \emph{DMD}?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{equation}P(k=0) = \frac{(\lambda)^0 e^{-\lambda}}{0!} = e^{-2.65 \times 10^{-4}} \approx 0.99973 \tag{14.6}\label{eq:dmd_cds_p0}\end{equation}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the probability of at least one new coding mutation in
  \emph{DMD}?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{equation}P(k \geq 1) = 1 - e^{-\lambda} \approx 2.65 \times 10^{-4} \approx \frac{1}{3{,}800} \text{ births} \tag{14.7}\label{eq:dmd_cds_pge1}\end{equation}

Even though any single child is overwhelmingly likely to inherit an
intact \emph{DMD} coding sequence, a rate of roughly \(1\) in
\(3{,}800\) births applied across a large population continually
regenerates new Duchenne muscular dystrophy alleles --- which is why
this X-linked disorder persists despite strong negative selection
against affected males.

\subsection{Worked Example: Mutation
Analysis}\label{worked-example-mutation-analysis}

\textbf{Problem}: A wild-type mRNA sequence reads:

5'-AUG-UUU-GGA-GAA-CUU-UAG-3'

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  Translate the wild-type sequence.
\end{enumerate}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Codon & Amino Acid \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
AUG & Met \\
UUU & Phe \\
GGA & Gly \\
GAA & Glu \\
CUU & Leu \\
UAG & Stop \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Protein}: Met-Phe-Gly-Glu-Leu (5 amino acids)

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  A transition mutation changes the 10th nucleotide (first position of
  codon 4) from G to A: GAA to AAA.
\end{enumerate}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Codon & Wild-type AA & Mutant AA \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
GAA & Glu & AAA = Lys \\
\end{longtable}
}

This is a \textbf{missense mutation} (Glu to Lys: non-conservative,
charge reversal).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\tightlist
\item
  A transition changes the 7th nucleotide (first position of codon 3)
  from G to A: GGA to AGA.
\end{enumerate}

GGA (Gly) to AGA (Arg): \textbf{missense} (non-conservative; small
nonpolar to large positive).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item
  A deletion removes the 4th nucleotide (U): sequence becomes
  AUG-UUG-GAG-AAC-UUU-AG\ldots{}
\end{enumerate}

This is a \textbf{frameshift mutation}. New reading frame:
Met-Leu-Glu-Asn-Phe\ldots{} (completely different protein, no stop codon
in remaining sequence -- read-through into 3' UTR).

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsubsection{Post-Approval CRISPR Therapeutics: Casgevy and the Safety
Frontier}\label{post-approval-crispr-therapeutics-casgevy-and-the-safety-frontier}

The first CRISPR--Cas9 therapy approved by the FDA and EMA
(\textbf{Casgevy / exagamglogene autotemcel}, Vertex/CRISPR
Therapeutics) provides a quantitative benchmark for the entire field
\citep{fda2023casgevy,fda2024casgevythalassemia,fda2026casgevy}. The
therapy edits autologous CD34\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} haematopoietic stem cells \emph{ex vivo}
at the \textbf{BCL11A enhancer} to de-repress fetal haemoglobin (HbF),
then reinfuses them after conditioning chemotherapy. In the pivotal
trials, \textbf{28 of 29 sickle-cell patients became free of
vaso-occlusive crises for \textgreater{} 12 months}, and \textbf{39 of
42 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-thalassemia patients became transfusion-independent} --- outcomes
previously achievable primarily via allogeneic bone-marrow transplant
with its attendant graft-versus-host morbidity.

The safety discussion that accompanies this approval is instructive.
Off-target editing in CD34\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} cells is measured pre-infusion by
\textbf{GUIDE-seq} and \textbf{deep amplicon sequencing} at 100+
predicted sites --- with Casgevy, off-target editing fell below the
detection floor (about 0.1 \%) at most surveyed loci. Residual
concerns include \textbf{large structural variants} (kilobase-scale
deletions, inversions, chromothripsis) that amplicon-seq can miss;
long-read WGS of treated HSC clones is the emerging gold-standard check.
Longitudinal monitoring follows these patients for \textbf{15 years} for
malignancy, driven by the theoretical risk that any DNA double-strand
break event in a stem cell compartment could, over decades, seed a
clonal expansion. This regulatory framework --- efficacy by molecular
endpoint, safety by unbiased structural-variant surveillance,
surveillance by decade-scale cohort --- is now the template every
subsequent \emph{in vivo} CRISPR therapy (e.g., Verve's PCSK9 base
editor for hypercholesterolaemia) must meet.

\subsubsection{The Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) Consortium: A Truly
Complete Human
Genome}\label{the-telomere-to-telomere-t2t-consortium-a-truly-complete-human-genome}

The human reference genome, from the Human Genome Project's 2003 draft
through GRCh38 (2013), contained \textbf{\textgreater{} 200 Mb of
unresolved gaps} --- chiefly heterochromatic satellite arrays at
centromeres, the short arms of acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21,
22), and segmental duplications. The \textbf{T2T-CHM13 assembly} (Nurk
et al., \emph{Science} 2022) closed these gaps using long-read
sequencing (PacBio HiFi, Oxford Nanopore Ultra-long) on a hydatidiform
mole (uniform haplotype, no
\hyperref[gl:heterozygous]{\textbf{heterozygous}} complications),
yielding the first \textbf{gapless 3.055 Gb human genome}.

What newly resolvable sequence revealed: \textbf{centromeric \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-satellite
arrays} span 0.5--5 Mb per chromosome, organised into higher-order
repeat (HOR) units; the \textbf{rDNA arrays} on acrocentric p-arms vary
from 47 to 287 copies per haploid genome; roughly \textbf{2000
additional protein-coding genes and gene paralogs} were annotated (with
duplications in immunity, olfaction, and neurogenesis). Perhaps most
importantly, T2T demonstrated that prior ``dark'' regions harbour real
medical-genetic variation: \textbf{paracentric inversions at 16p11 and
22q11} --- known susceptibility loci for autism and schizophrenia ---
are present in about 10 \% of haplotypes but invisible to
GRCh38 mapping. The pangenome era extends T2T's logic: the reference is
now a graph, not a single string, and clinical genomic pipelines are
migrating cautiously because graph references improve representation
while adding alignment, annotation, and validation complexity
\citep{humanpangenome2023}.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-16}

For \textbf{Mutations, CRISPR, and Genomics}, frontier biology belongs
inside the evidence logic of the chapter. Molecular genetics now spans
single-reference sequences, telomere-to-telomere assemblies, pangenome
graphs, long-read sequencing, CRISPR medicines, and ethical deployment.
The core reading question is this: genomics claims should distinguish
variant discovery, pathogenic interpretation, ancestry representation,
and clinical actionability.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

When a genomic claim depends on a reference, ask whether short reads,
structural variants, ancestry representation, phasing, or clinical
validation could change the interpretation
\citep{humanpangenome2023,fda2023casgevy,fda2024casgevythalassemia}.

\textbf{Source practice:} For genomics and editing claims, distinguish
discovery from clinical actionability, and cite reference resources,
regulatory records, or primary editing studies close to the claim
\citep{humanpangenome2023,fda2026casgevy,chalumeau2025primeediting}.

Follow-Up}\label{current-evidence-map-genome-editing-from-variant-to-follow-up}

\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-16}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Mutations} range from single nucleotide changes (transitions,
  transversions, silent, missense, nonsense) to large chromosomal
  rearrangements (deletions, duplications, inversions, translocations).
  Frameshifts and nonsense mutations are typically most disruptive.
\item
  \textbf{Mutagenic agents} include UV radiation (CPDs), alkylating
  agents (EMS), intercalators (ethidium bromide), and ROS (8-oxoG). The
  Ames test screens chemicals for mutagenicity.
\item
  \textbf{DNA repair}: BER (damaged bases), NER (bulky adducts), MMR
  (mismatches), NHEJ/HR (DSBs), Fanconi pathway (interstrand
  crosslinks). Defects cause cancer predisposition (XP, Lynch syndrome,
  BRCA-associated cancers, Fanconi anemia).
\item
  \textbf{CRISPR-Cas9}: sgRNA + Cas9 creates DSB at PAM-adjacent site;
  NHEJ for knockouts, HDR for precise edits. Base editors (C-to-T,
  A-to-G) and prime editors avoid DSBs. First approved therapy: Casgevy
  (sickle cell disease via BCL11A disruption).
\item
  \textbf{Human genome}: about 3.2 Gb; about 20,000
  protein-coding genes (1.5\%); 46\% transposable elements; ENCODE shows
  \textgreater80\% has biochemical activity. T2T consortium completed
  gapless reference (2022).
\item
  \textbf{NGS technologies}: Illumina (short-read, high throughput),
  PacBio HiFi and Nanopore (long-read, structural variant resolution).
\item
  \textbf{GWAS}: Identify SNP-trait associations at genome-wide
  significance (\(p < 5 \times 10^{-8}\)); most complex trait variants
  have small effect sizes; results displayed on Manhattan plots.
\item
  \textbf{Ethics}: GINA Act protections, pharmacogenomic testing
  (CYP2D6, warfarin dosing), BRCA testing decisions, germline editing
  moratorium.
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See
  \cref{sec:unit_IV_dna_replication_and_cell_cycle} for repair pathways,
  Unit V for inheritance of variants, and Unit VII for CRISPR origins in
  bacterial immunity.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Review Questions}\label{review-questions-16}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Distinguish between transitions and transversions. Which is more
  common and why?
\item
  Explain why frameshift mutations are generally more deleterious than
  missense mutations. Give an exception where a missense mutation is
  highly pathogenic.
\item
  A patient has microsatellite instability in their colorectal tumor.
  What DNA repair pathway is likely defective? Name the genes involved.
\item
  Describe the CRISPR-Cas9 mechanism step by step, from guide design to
  DSB repair.
\item
  Compare base editing and prime editing. When would you choose each
  technology?
\item
  What is the ``end-replication problem'' of the Human Genome Project,
  and how did the T2T consortium solve it?
\item
  Explain GWAS methodology. Why does a Manhattan plot show peaks, and
  what does a significant peak mean?
\item
  What is linkage disequilibrium, and why is it important for
  interpreting GWAS results?
\item
  Describe the pharmacogenomic basis for warfarin dose variation. Which
  genes are involved?
\item
  Discuss the ethical issues raised by the He Jiankui CRISPR babies
  case. What international guidelines exist for germline editing?
\item
  Explain why a SNP in a \textbf{splice donor} can have larger effect
  sizes than a missense change in the same exon, using NMD concepts.
\item
  A GWAS hit lies in intronic sequence with no coding change. Propose
  two mechanistic classes of causal variants compatible with that
  pattern.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Key Terms}\label{key-terms-16}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Transition} -- purine-to-purine or pyrimidine-to-pyrimidine
  point mutation
\item
  \textbf{Transversion} -- purine-to-pyrimidine (or reverse) point
  mutation
\item
  \textbf{Frameshift mutation} -- insertion/deletion not a multiple of 3
  bp, altering reading frame
\item
  \textbf{Nonsense-mediated decay (NMD)} -- mRNA surveillance pathway
  eliminating transcripts with premature stop codons
\item
  \textbf{Trinucleotide repeat expansion} -- unstable repeat growth
  causing anticipation in diseases like Huntington
\item
  \textbf{Ames test} -- bacterial mutagenicity assay using
  histidine-requiring Salmonella revertants
\item
  \textbf{CRISPR-Cas9} -- RNA-guided endonuclease for programmable
  genome editing
\item
  \textbf{PAM (protospacer adjacent motif)} -- short DNA sequence (NGG
  for SpCas9) required for Cas9 binding
\item
  \textbf{Base editor} -- dCas9/nickase fused to deaminase for C-to-T or
  A-to-G conversion without DSB
\item
  \textbf{Prime editor} -- Cas9-nickase + reverse transcriptase + pegRNA
  for search-and-replace editing
\item
  \textbf{GWAS (genome-wide association study)} -- unbiased scan for
  SNP-trait associations across the genome
\item
  \textbf{Linkage disequilibrium} -- non-random association of alleles
  at nearby loci
\item
  \textbf{Manhattan plot} -- genome-wide visualization of association
  p-values
\item
  \textbf{Pharmacogenomics} -- study of genetic variation affecting drug
  response
\item
  \textbf{ENCODE} -- Encyclopedia of DNA Elements; mapped functional
  elements across the human genome
\item
  \textbf{Copy number variant (CNV)} -- duplication or deletion of a
  genomic segment \textgreater1 kb
\item
  \textbf{Synthetic lethality} -- cell death from simultaneous loss of
  two compensatory pathways
\end{enumerate}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-17}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Define \hyperref[gl:epigenetics]{\textbf{epigenetics}} and distinguish
  epigenetic modifications from DNA sequence changes.
\item
  Describe \hyperref[gl:nucleosome]{\textbf{nucleosome}} structure and
  the levels of \hyperref[gl:chromatin]{\textbf{chromatin}} compaction
  from the 11-nm fibre to the metaphase
  \hyperref[gl:chromosome]{\textbf{chromosome}}.
\item
  Explain the major classes of \hyperref[gl:histone]{\textbf{histone}}
  modifications (acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation,
  ubiquitination, sumoylation) and how they are written, erased, and
  read.
\item
  Describe the mechanism and function of DNA methylation, including
  \hyperref[gl:cpg-island]{\textbf{CpG island}}s, the DNMT1/3A/3B
  \hyperref[gl:enzyme]{\textbf{enzyme}}s, TET-mediated demethylation,
  and the role of methylation in \hyperref[gl:gene]{\textbf{gene}}
  silencing.
\item
  Distinguish Polycomb (PRC1/PRC2) and Trithorax (MLL/COMPASS) systems
  and explain how they maintain repressive and activating states.
\item
  Compare ATP-dependent chromatin remodelling families (SWI/SNF, ISWI,
  CHD/NuRD, INO80) and their distinct mechanisms.
\item
  Explain X-chromosome inactivation (Lyonisation) and the role of the
  XIST lncRNA, escape genes, and skewing.
\item
  Describe genomic imprinting using IGF2/H19 and Prader--Willi/Angelman
  as paradigms.
\item
  Explain how 3D genome organisation --- TADs, loops, compartments, and
  biomolecular condensates --- shapes transcription.
\item
  Explain microRNA (miRNA \citep{fire1998}) biogenesis and the mechanism
  of RISC-mediated post-transcriptional silencing.
\item
  Model the maintenance of DNA methylation and Polycomb marks across
  cell divisions quantitatively, and predict the consequences of
  perturbing each layer.
\item
  Evaluate evidence for transgenerational epigenetic inheritance in
  humans, the mechanism of mitotic and meiotic transmission of
  epigenetic marks, and the clinical implications of epigenetic
  dysregulation in cancer and neurodevelopmental disease.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Opening Vignette --- The Landscape That Changed Genetics}

In 1942, the developmental biologist Conrad Waddington drew a diagram
that would define a science. He sketched a marble rolling down a
hillscape of ridges and valleys --- each valley representing a stable
cell fate, each ridge a threshold that once crossed was difficult to
reverse. He called this the \textbf{epigenetic landscape}: the topology
of developmental possibilities. Waddington coined ``epigenetics'' from
the Greek \emph{epi-} (above) to describe the heritable changes in gene
expression that occurred \emph{above} or \emph{beyond} the DNA sequence
--- changes that could not be explained by Mendelian genetics alone. He
had no idea of the molecular mechanisms. That understanding would come
forty years later.

In 1961, Mary Lyon \citep{lyon1961} noticed something peculiar in female
mice \hyperref[gl:heterozygous]{\textbf{heterozygous}} for coat-colour
\hyperref[gl:mutation]{\textbf{mutation}}s: their fur was a mosaic, not
intermediate. She proposed that in every cell of a female mammal, one of
the two X chromosomes is randomly and permanently silenced --- a
hypothesis proven so thoroughly that it was renamed Lyonisation. The
silenced X does not have a different DNA sequence. It has a different
\emph{chemistry}: dense methylation, hypoacetylated histones, and a long
non-coding RNA called XIST that coats the entire chromosome. This was
the first clear demonstration that a whole chromosome could be heritably
silenced without changing a single base pair. Epigenetics had found its
molecular identity.

Three more revolutions followed. In 2000, Strahl and Allis
\citep{strahl2000} proposed that distinct combinations of histone
modifications --- a ``histone code'' --- encode regulatory information
beyond the DNA sequence itself, predicting an entire pharmacology of
writers, erasers, and readers that has now produced FDA-approved drugs.
In the 2000s, chromosome-conformation-capture (Hi-C) revealed that the
genome is folded into stereotyped contact domains (TADs) where enhancers
find their cognate promoters, and that disrupting these domains can
mis-wire developmental control. And in the 2010s, biomolecular
condensates and phase separation reframed the nucleus as a collection of
liquid-like assemblies that concentrate transcriptional machinery at
super-enhancers. These insights together turned epigenetics from a
metaphor into a quantitative, druggable discipline.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Chromatin Structure and Nucleosome
Organisation}\label{chromatin-structure-and-nucleosome-organisation}

\subsubsection{The Nucleosome: Fundamental
Unit}\label{the-nucleosome-fundamental-unit}

Eukaryotic DNA is not naked; it is complexed with
\hyperref[gl:protein]{\textbf{protein}}s to form \textbf{chromatin}. The
fundamental repeating unit is the \textbf{nucleosome}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Histone octamer:} 2 copies each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4 ---
  forming a spool-like protein disk
\item
  \textbf{DNA wrapping:} about 147 bp of DNA wound 1.65 times
  around the histone octamer in a left-handed superhelix
\item
  \textbf{Linker DNA:} 10--80 bp connecting adjacent nucleosomes;
  associated with histone H1
\item
  \textbf{Bead-on-a-string:} nucleosomes connected by linker DNA form an
  11-nm fibre --- the first level of compaction
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Core histone structure:} Each core histone has: - A
\textbf{globular domain} forming the nucleosome disc surface through the
\textbf{histone fold} motif (three \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-helices linked by two short loops;
pairs of histones form four-helix bundles: H3--H4 and H2A--H2B) - An
unstructured \textbf{N-terminal tail} extending beyond the disc (4--35
residues depending on histone) --- this is where most post-translational
modifications occur - A short \textbf{C-terminal tail} (especially
prominent on H2A and H2B) that also accepts modifications including
ubiquitination

\textbf{Histone variants:} In addition to canonical H2A/H2B/H3/H4,
mammalian cells express variant histones that confer specialised
properties on chromatin where they are deposited:
