\subsubsection{Topologically Associating Domains
(TADs)}\label{topologically-associating-domains-tads}

Chromatin organises into DNA loops of 100 kb--1 Mb delineated by
\textbf{CTCF} (insulator protein) binding sites and \textbf{cohesin}
ring complexes. Within TADs, enhancers preferentially contact
\hyperref[gl:promoter]{\textbf{promoter}}s of the same TAD. TAD
boundaries are largely conserved across cell types and species. The
dominant model for TAD formation is \textbf{loop extrusion}: cohesin
loads on chromatin and reels DNA through its ring lumen ATP-dependently
until it stalls at convergently oriented CTCF binding sites, leaving
behind a chromatin loop. Quantitatively, mammalian genomes contain
about 3,000--10,000 TADs (about 1 Mb median), and
knockdown of CTCF or cohesin (RAD21, NIPBL) blurs or abolishes most
boundaries within hours.

\begin{equation}P_{\text{contact}}(s) \propto s^{-\alpha}, \quad \alpha \approx 1.0\text{–}1.2 \text{ for fractal globule (interphase)} \tag{15.1}\label{eq:hic_scaling}\end{equation}

\textbf{Hi-C methodology in detail.} Hi-C is a
chromosome-conformation-capture variant that measures contact frequency
between every pair of genomic loci genome-wide. The protocol:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Cross-link} chromatin with formaldehyde (1 \% for 10 min),
  preserving protein-mediated DNA contacts.
\item
  \textbf{Restriction digest} with a 4-cutter (DpnII, MboI) or 6-cutter
  (HindIII), creating sticky-ended fragments still tethered by
  cross-linked proteins.
\item
  \textbf{Fill-in with biotinylated nucleotides} to mark cleaved ends,
  then \textbf{proximity ligate} at low DNA concentration so that
  intermolecular ligations are improbable --- primarily fragments held
  together by cross-linked proteins (i.e., physically proximal \emph{in
  vivo}) ligate.
\item
  \textbf{Streptavidin pulldown} enriches biotinylated junction reads,
  paired-end Illumina sequencing identifies which genomic loci were
  joined.
\item
  \textbf{Heatmap normalisation} (ICE, KR-balanced) yields a contact
  matrix; diagonal-rich blocks are TADs; off-diagonal stripes identify
  loop anchors at convergent CTCF.
\end{enumerate}

Derivative methods refine the assay: \textbf{Micro-C} uses MNase
digestion to nucleosome resolution; \textbf{Capture-Hi-C} enriches for
promoter-anchored contacts (4DN consortium); \textbf{HiChIP / PLAC-seq}
combines ChIP for an active mark (H3K27ac) with proximity ligation;
\textbf{ChIA-PET} uses paired-end tagging on antibody-immunoprecipitated
chromatin; \textbf{Hi-C 3.0 / Pore-C} uses long-read multi-way contact
mapping.

Disruption of TAD boundaries (e.g., by large deletions, inversions, or
single-nucleotide CTCF site disruptions) can cause misregulation of
developmental genes --- a mechanism termed \textbf{enhancer hijacking}.
Lupiáñez et al.~(2015) showed that microdeletions removing TAD
boundaries near \emph{EPHA4} fuse adjacent regulatory landscapes,
mis-targeting limb enhancers to \emph{PAX3} or \emph{WNT6} and producing
congenital limb malformations (brachydactyly, syndactyly).

\textbf{Loop extrusion --- the dynamic model.} Single-molecule imaging
and live-cell Hi-C now support a kinetic loop-extrusion model with
quantitative parameters: - Cohesin (SMC1/SMC3 + RAD21/SCC1 +
STAG1/STAG2) is loaded onto chromatin by \textbf{NIPBL/MAU2} (the loader
complex). - It extrudes DNA into a growing loop at about 0.5--2
kb/s, consuming ATP at the SMC ATPase head. - \textbf{WAPL} unloads
cohesin (residence time about 20 min unloaded by WAPL,
vs.~\textgreater{} 1 h for the \textbf{cohesin-STAG2} ``stalled'' form
at CTCF anchors). - CTCF binds asymmetrically (a 19-bp consensus with a
defined orientation): convergent CTCF pairs trap extruding cohesin,
generating loops with measured loop sizes about 100 kb to 2 Mb.
- Acute auxin-induced degron depletion of RAD21 dissolves most loops
within about 15 min; restoration takes about 30--60
min --- confirming that TADs and loops are dynamic, not static
structures.

\subsubsection{A/B Compartments}\label{ab-compartments}

At the megabase scale, the genome partitions into two interaction
``compartments'':

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{A compartment} --- gene-rich, active (H3K4me3, H3K27ac,
  accessible chromatin), positioned toward the nuclear interior
\item
  \textbf{B compartment} --- gene-poor, repressed (H3K9me3,
  lamina-associated), positioned at the nuclear periphery
\end{itemize}

Compartment switching during cell-fate transitions correlates with
replication timing changes (early-replicating \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\leftrightarrow}}{<->} late-replicating) and
with large-scale gene expression remodelling. Hi-C (and its derivatives
Micro-C, Capture-Hi-C, ChIA-PET) measures these contacts genome-wide.

breaks a CTCF site at the boundary of a TAD containing the \emph{SHH}
limb enhancer (ZRS, about 1 Mb upstream of \emph{SHH}). Predict
the developmental phenotype if the inversion places ZRS into a TAD
containing an unrelated proto-oncogene. What
chromosome-conformation-capture experiment would confirm enhancer
hijacking?
\end{quote}

\subsection{Histone Modifications --- The Histone
Code}\label{histone-modifications-the-histone-code}

Histone tails are subject to a large number of post-translational
modifications (PTMs). The \textbf{\hyperref[gl:histone-code]{histone
code} hypothesis} \citep{strahl2000} proposes that specific combinations
of marks specify distinct chromatin states and downstream outcomes.

The histone-code reference table below systematically catalogs
\textgreater{} 25 modifications recurrently studied in mammalian
chromatin biology, paired with the \textbf{writer enzyme},
\textbf{eraser enzyme}, \textbf{reader domain} that recognises the mark,
the \textbf{histone position} (nucleosome face, exposed N-terminal tail,
C-terminal tail), the typical \textbf{genomic location}, and the
\textbf{functional effect} (activation, repression, or
context-dependent). This is the chromatin biologist's periodic table ---
the working vocabulary of writers, readers, and erasers that defines
every targeted therapy in clinical epigenetics.

The bottom rows reflect a major recent expansion of the histone code:
short-chain acyl-CoAs derived from intermediary metabolism (lactate,
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-hydroxybutyrate, crotonyl-CoA, succinyl-CoA, butyryl-CoA) are
deposited by the same KAT/HAT enzymes (especially p300) that write
acetyl marks, directly coupling \textbf{metabolic state} to chromatin
state. The lactyl mark, in particular, has become the molecular
signature of the Warburg-effect--polarised tumour-associated macrophage.

\subsubsection{Histone Acetylation}\label{histone-acetylation}

\textbf{Writers:} Histone acetyltransferases (HATs) --- CBP/p300,
GCN5/PCAF, TIP60, MOF. \textbf{Erasers:} Histone deacetylases (HDACs)
--- 18 human HDACs in four classes (Class I/II/III/IV, where Class III =
NAD\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+}-dependent sirtuins SIRT1--7). \textbf{Readers:} Bromodomains (e.g.,
BRD4, TFIID subunit TAF1, BAF180 of PBAF, BPTF). YEATS domains (AF9,
ENL) read both acetyl and longer acyl marks.

\textbf{Mechanism:} Acetylation of lysine \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}}{epsilon}-amino groups by transfer
from acetyl-CoA. Neutralises the positive charge on lysine,
\textbf{weakening histone--DNA electrostatic interactions}, loosening
chromatin and facilitating
\hyperref[gl:transcription]{\textbf{transcription}} factor binding.

\begin{equation}\text{Lys-NH}_3^+ + \text{acetyl-CoA} \xrightarrow{\text{HAT}} \text{Lys-NH-COCH}_3 + \text{CoA-SH} + \text{H}^+ \tag{15.2}\label{eq:hat}\end{equation}

\textbf{Key active marks:} - \textbf{H3K27ac:} Marks active enhancers
(distinguishes active from poised enhancers, which carry H3K27me3) -
\textbf{H3K9ac, H3K14ac, H4K16ac:} Found at active promoters and
transcribed gene bodies

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection --- HDAC inhibitors (full clinical
profile):} Histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi) are FDA-approved
anticancer drugs. - \textbf{Vorinostat (SAHA)} --- FDA approved 2006 for
cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL). Hydroxamate pan-HDACi. Median time to
response about 2 months; objective response about 30
\%. - \textbf{Romidepsin (Istodax)} --- FDA approved 2009 for CTCL and
2011 for peripheral T-cell lymphoma. Cyclic depsipeptide; class-I
selective. Distinct dose-limiting toxicities (GI, fatigue,
thrombocytopenia). - \textbf{Panobinostat (Farydak)} --- FDA approved
2015 for relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma in combination with
bortezomib + dexamethasone. Pan-HDACi; superior CD138+ plasma-cell
apoptosis when combined with proteasome inhibitor. - \textbf{Belinostat
(Beleodaq)} --- FDA 2014 for PTCL. - \textbf{Tucidinostat (Chidamide)}
--- China-approved 2014 for PTCL; first benzamide HDACi.

Mechanism in cancer: re-activation of silenced tumour-suppressor genes
(p21, gelsolin, RhoB, BCL6); accumulation of acetylation on non-histone
targets (HSP90 chaperone client release, p53 stabilisation, NF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}B
inhibition). Combination with \textbf{DNMT inhibitors} is being explored
to reverse layered silencing, a theme developed later in the
cancer-epigenetics discussion.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Histone Methylation}\label{histone-methylation}

\textbf{Writers:} Histone methyltransferases (HMTs) --- most contain SET
domains (except DOT1L, which has a 7\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-strand methyltransferase fold
derived from class V methyltransferases). \textbf{Erasers:} Histone
demethylases --- KDM1/LSD1 (FAD-dependent; works on me1 and me2
primarily; cannot demethylate me3 because it requires a free lysine
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}}{epsilon}-amino lone pair); KDM2--7 (Jumonji-domain, Fe(II)/\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}KG-dependent; can
remove me3 by hydroxymethyl-amine intermediate that decomposes to
formaldehyde and demethylated lysine). \textbf{Readers:} Chromodomains
(HP1 reads H3K9me3; CBX2/4/6/7/8 of PRC1 read H3K27me3); PHD fingers
(TAF3, BPTF, ING proteins read H3K4me3); Tudor domains (53BP1 reads
H4K20me2; SMN reads symmetrical R-methylation); MBT domains; WD40 (EED
reads H3K27me3); PWWP domains (read H3K36me3).

Unlike acetylation (typically activating), \textbf{methylation is
context-dependent}: the same modification on different residues has
opposite effects.

\textbf{Bivalent domains:} In embryonic stem cells, many developmental
gene promoters carry \textbf{both H3K4me3 and H3K27me3} simultaneously
--- a ``bivalent'' state. These genes are poised for either rapid
activation (upon H3K27me3 removal by KDM6A/UTX) or repression (upon
H3K4me3 removal) during differentiation. About 2,500 promoters are
bivalent in human ES cells; most resolve to monovalent during lineage
commitment.

\subsubsection{Phosphorylation and
Ubiquitination}\label{phosphorylation-and-ubiquitination}

\textbf{H3S10ph (H3 Ser10 phosphorylation):} - Writer: Aurora B kinase
(\hyperref[gl:mitosis]{\textbf{mitosis}}), MSK1/2 (mitogenic signalling)
- Function: Chromosome condensation during mitosis; gene activation by
14-3-3 reader binding

\textbf{H2AX-S139ph (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma}H2AX):} - Writer: ATM/ATR kinases at double-strand
breaks - Function: Marks DSB sites; recruits MDC1 and DNA repair
machinery; visible as bright immunofluorescence foci at break sites

\textbf{H2AK119ub (H2A monoubiquitination):} - Writer: RNF2/RING1B (part
of PRC1 complex) - Function: Represses transcription elongation; part of
Polycomb silencing; read by Polycomb-like proteins

\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Polycomb and Trithorax --- Cellular Memory
Systems}\label{polycomb-and-trithorax-cellular-memory-systems}

The \textbf{Polycomb (PcG)} and \textbf{Trithorax (TrxG)} group proteins
were discovered in \emph{Drosophila} as gene families whose
loss-of-function alleles cause homeotic transformations of body
segments. They constitute the cell's principal \textbf{cellular memory
systems}: once a developmental gene is set ON or OFF in a progenitor,
PcG/TrxG complexes propagate that state through most subsequent mitotic
divisions of the lineage.

\subsubsection{Polycomb Repressive Complexes --- Structural
Detail}\label{polycomb-repressive-complexes-structural-detail}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0081_44e01d6a348a.png}
\caption{Polycomb silencing operates as a feedback-amplified two-mark system: PRC2 writes H3K27me3, which recruits more PRC2 (positive feedback) and recruits canonical PRC1 (via CBX) which writes H2AK119ub. Variant PRC1 acts upstream at unmethylated CpG islands and seeds H2AK119ub which itself recruits PRC2. The mutual reinforcement explains how Polycomb domains span hundreds of kilobases and persist through cell divisions.}
\end{figure}

\textbf{PRC1 --- comprehensive subunit inventory:} - Catalytic core:
\textbf{RING1A} (RNF1) or \textbf{RING1B} (RNF2) E3 ubiquitin ligase + a
PCGF partner (PCGF1, PCGF2/MEL18, PCGF3, PCGF4/BMI1, PCGF5, PCGF6). -
\textbf{Canonical PRC1 (cPRC1):} RING1A/B + PCGF2/4 (MEL18/BMI1) + a
\textbf{CBX} (CBX2/4/6/7/8) chromobox subunit + PHC1/2/3 + SCMH1/L2. The
CBX chromodomain reads H3K27me3, anchoring cPRC1 onto Polycomb-marked
chromatin. PHC SAM-domain polymerisation drives \textbf{chromatin
compaction in cis} (head-to-tail oligomerisation creates a
phase-separated Polycomb body). - \textbf{Variant PRC1 (vPRC1):}
RING1A/B + PCGF1/3/5/6 + RYBP (or YAF2) instead of CBX. Recruited to
\textbf{unmethylated CpG islands} via KDM2B (PCGF1 complex,
``ncPRC1.1'') or via E2F6 (PCGF6). Deposits H2AK119ub \emph{upstream} of
H3K27me3 --- a key insight: vPRC1 acts first, then PRC2.2 reads
H2AK119ub via JARID2.

\textbf{PRC2 --- comprehensive subunit inventory:} - Catalytic core:
\textbf{EZH2} (or paralog \textbf{EZH1}; SET-domain methyltransferase).
EZH2 is faster but EZH1 is dominant in non-dividing cells. -
\textbf{EED} binds H3K27me3 product \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} allosteric activation of EZH2 (the
\textbf{read-write feedback} that generates broad Polycomb domains). -
\textbf{SUZ12} scaffold links the SET-domain catalytic core to the
DNA/RNA-recognition modules. - \textbf{RBBP4/7} histone chaperone
presents the H3 tail substrate. - \textbf{Accessory subunits define
context-dependent variants:} - \textbf{PRC2.1:} PCL1/2/3 (PHF1, MTF2,
PHF19) + EPOP or PALI1. The PHF Tudor domains read H3K36me3, restricting
PRC2.1 from active gene bodies. - \textbf{PRC2.2:} AEBP2 + JARID2.
JARID2 reads H2AK119ub deposited by variant PRC1 and stimulates PRC2
activity (closing the recruitment loop). - \textbf{Reaction kinetics:}
H3K27 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} H3K27me1 (k\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 0.05 s\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} H3K27me2 (k\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 0.02 s\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} H3K27me3
(k\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{3}}{3} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 0.005 s\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}), with each step about 3-fold slower;
EED-allosteric stimulation increases k\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{3}}{3} by about 6-fold on
neighbouring nucleosomes carrying me3. - \textbf{Recruitment hierarchy:}
unmethylated CpG islands (via PRC2.2/JARID2 reading H2AK119ub from
variant PRC1, \emph{or} via PRC2.1/PCL with KDM2B); broad gene-body
recognition by EED reading existing me3; lncRNA recruitment (HOTAIR,
XIST repA, KCNQ1OT1, ANRIL).

\textbf{Mechanism of Polycomb--Trithorax antagonism:} PRC2.1 cannot act
on H3K36-methylated chromatin (PCL Tudor reads H3K36me3 antagonistically
--- the CPL paradox). Conversely, \textbf{ASH1L} (the Trithorax-group
H3K36 methyltransferase) deposits H3K36me2 at active gene bodies,
blocking PRC2 spreading. The cell uses this as a positive/negative
selection: H3K36me-active = Polycomb-restricted; H3K36me-absent =
Polycomb-permissive.

\subsubsection{Trithorax Group (TrxG) --- Antagonising
Polycomb}\label{trithorax-group-trxg-antagonising-polycomb}

\textbf{The COMPASS family --- six MLL/SET1 complexes in mammals:} -
\textbf{MLL1/KMT2A} (mixed-lineage leukaemia 1) --- large promoter
H3K4me3 deposition; MLL1-AF4/AF9/ENL fusions cause infant acute
lymphoblastic or acute myeloid leukaemia. - \textbf{MLL2/KMT2B} ---
closely related to MLL1; redundant at most loci; selective at others. -
\textbf{MLL3/KMT2C} and \textbf{MLL4/KMT2D} --- write enhancer H3K4me1
(poised and active enhancers); KMT2D is among the most frequently
mutated chromatin-regulator genes in cancer (about 10 \% of
B-cell lymphoma and bladder cancer). - \textbf{SET1A/KMT2F} and
\textbf{SET1B/KMT2G} --- write the bulk of promoter H3K4me3 in adult
tissues; SET1A loss-of-function in MDS and CHIP.

Most six complexes share a \textbf{WRAD module}
(WDR5--RbBP5--ASH2L--DPY30) that allosterically activates the SET-domain
catalytic subunit by about 600-fold. This makes WRAD a
tractable allosteric drug target --- small-molecule WDR5--MLL interface
inhibitors (OICR-9429) are in early-phase trials for MLL-rearranged
leukaemia.

\textbf{The Polycomb--Trithorax balance} is maintained dynamically.
Differentiation cues that activate gene expression typically deploy
three concurrent steps: (i) UTX/JMJD3 removes H3K27me3, (ii) MLL/COMPASS
deposits H3K4me3, and (iii) BAF complexes evict residual PRC1.
Conversely, lineage repression deposits PRC1/PRC2 marks at the relevant
promoter.

\textbf{Clinical translation --- EZH2 inhibitors:} -
\textbf{Tazemetostat (Tazverik)} is a small-molecule SET-domain
inhibitor of EZH2, FDA-approved (2020) for \textbf{epithelioid sarcoma}
(which loses INI1/SMARCB1 --- a SWI/SNF subunit --- and becomes
hyper-dependent on EZH2 silencing) and \textbf{EZH2-mutant follicular
lymphoma}. Mechanism: SAM-competitive small molecule occupies the EZH2
SET-domain pocket. Approved dose 800 mg BID PO. Median PFS in INI1-loss
epithelioid sarcoma trial: 5.5 months vs 1.9 placebo; ORR 15 \%. -
\textbf{Valemetostat} (EZH1 + EZH2 dual inhibitor) was approved in 2022
in Japan for adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma (ATL); ORR 48 \%. -
\textbf{Ivosidenib + tazemetostat} combinations in IDH-mutant glioma are
in trial, exploiting the IDH-mutant tumour's dependence on
Polycomb-driven differentiation block.

The mechanism is paradigmatic of \textbf{synthetic lethality} in
chromatin: tumours with SWI/SNF loss become dependent on Polycomb
silencing of cell-cycle inhibitors, so EZH2 inhibition selectively
re-activates suppressors primarily in the cancer cells.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Worked Example 1 --- Polycomb Spreading Model with Read-Write
Feedback}

\textbf{Setup:} A naive promoter has 2 nucleosomes carrying H3K27me3
(call this ``seed''), recruiting PRC2 with EED-driven allosteric
activation. PRC2 deposits H3K27me3 on the next nucleosome with rate
constant \emph{k} per generation. Each cell division dilutes existing
H3K27me3 by half (passive demethylation through nucleosome turnover,
since newly deposited histones at the replication fork are
unmethylated). The gene body comprises 50 nucleosomes.

\textbf{Question:} Derive the steady-state H3K27me3 density along the
gene body for \emph{k} = 1, 2, and 5 marks per generation. What is the
minimum \emph{k} needed for the silencing mark to spread fully (\texorpdfstring{\textgreater{}=}{>=} 90 \%
of nucleosomes methylated)?

\textbf{Solution:} Let \(m_n\) be the average number of H3K27me3-marked
nucleosomes at generation \(n\), with \(m_0 = 2\) (seed). Each
generation: - Half of existing marks are passively diluted:
\(m_{\text{post-replication}} = m_n / 2\). - PRC2 deposits \emph{k} new
marks at neighbouring nucleosomes (read-write spreading):
\(m_{n+1} = m_n / 2 + k\).

Steady-state when \(m_{\infty} = m_{\infty} / 2 + k\), so
\(m_{\infty} = 2k\) marked nucleosomes.

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\emph{k} (marks/gen) & Steady-state \(m_\infty\) & Gene-body coverage \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
1 & 2 & 4 \% (silencing fails) \\
2 & 4 & 8 \% \\
5 & 10 & 20 \% \\
25 & 50 & 100 \% (saturated) \\
45 & 90 & 100 \% (rapid saturation) \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Insight:} For full coverage of a 50-nucleosome gene body (\texorpdfstring{\textgreater{}=}{>=} 45
marks at steady state), \emph{k} must exceed about 22 marks per
generation --- i.e., PRC2 must deposit \textgreater{} 11\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} the seed
quantity each cell cycle. This is achievable primarily with the
\textbf{EED--allosteric read-write loop}: each existing H3K27me3
catalytically recruits more PRC2 to neighbouring nucleosomes, creating
positive feedback. Without this loop (e.g., in EED-mutant cells),
Polycomb domains collapse over a few divisions. This is why
\textbf{EED-binding small molecules (EED226, MAK683)} are emerging as
alternative EZH2-pathway inhibitors that disrupt the feedback loop
selectively.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{DNA Methylation}\label{dna-methylation}

\subsubsection{CpG Methylation
Mechanism}\label{cpg-methylation-mechanism}

In mammals, DNA methylation occurs almost exclusively on cytosine in the
context \textbf{5\texorpdfstring{'}{'}-CpG-3\texorpdfstring{'}{'}} dinucleotides (the ``p'' denotes the
phosphodiester bond between C and G). The methylated form is
\hyperref[gl:5-methylcytosine]{\textbf{5-methylcytosine (5mC)}}, often
called the ``fifth base.''

\begin{equation}\text{Cytosine} + \text{S-adenosylmethionine} \xrightarrow{\text{DNMT}} \text{5-methylcytosine} + \text{S-adenosylhomocysteine} \tag{15.3}\label{eq:DNMT}\end{equation}

\subsubsection{The DNA Methylation Machinery --- In
Depth}\label{the-dna-methylation-machinery-in-depth}

\textbf{Maintenance methyltransferase --- DNMT1:} the workhorse enzyme
that ensures heritability of CpG methylation across cell divisions. -
DNMT1 has a two-domain architecture: an N-terminal regulatory domain
(containing CXXC, BAH1/2, and replication-foci targeting RFTS
subdomains) and a C-terminal catalytic domain. - \textbf{Substrate
specificity:} preferentially methylates \textbf{hemi-methylated CpGs}
--- sites where the parental strand carries 5mC but the newly
synthesised daughter strand is unmodified. Affinity for hemi-methylated
CpGs is about 10--40-fold higher than for unmethylated CpGs. -
\textbf{Recruitment --- the UHRF1--DNMT1 axis:} the protein
\textbf{UHRF1} (``ubiquitin-like with PHD and RING finger domains 1'')
is the molecular bridge that targets DNMT1 to replicating
heterochromatin. UHRF1 has \textbf{five domains}: UBL (ubiquitin-like),
TTD (Tudor --- reads H3K9me2/3), PHD (reads unmethylated H3R2), SRA
(reads hemi-methylated CpG via base-flipping), and RING (E3 ubiquitin
ligase). The dual recognition of (a) hemi-methylated CpG (via SRA) AND
(b) H3K9me2/3 (via TTD) ensures that DNMT1 propagates methylation
primarily at chromatin states already marked for repression. -
\textbf{The mechanism cycle (per CpG):} 1. UHRF1 SRA domain flips the
5mC out of the helix, exposing the unmethylated daughter cytosine. 2.
UHRF1 RING ubiquitinates H3K18 (H3 tail) --- creating a docking site for
DNMT1's RFTS domain. 3. DNMT1 RFTS binds H3K18ub; DNMT1 catalytic domain
transfers a methyl group from SAM to the daughter cytosine. 4. SAH
(S-adenosyl-homocysteine) released; UHRF1 dissociates; cycle repeats. -
\textbf{Quantitative parameters:} maintenance efficiency per CpG \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}}{epsilon} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~}
0.95 in healthy cells. Each replication fork carries about 50
CpGs/s of unmethylated daughter DNA into the lumen --- DNMT1 must fix
them within minutes before chromatin reassembly. -
\textbf{Loss-of-function:} mouse Dnmt1-knockout embryos die at E9.5 with
genome-wide demethylation, ectopic gene expression, and replication-fork
instability. Conditional knockouts in tissue-specific contexts produce
lineage-specific failures (haematopoietic stem-cell exhaustion;
intestinal epithelial collapse).

\textbf{De novo methyltransferases --- DNMT3A, DNMT3B:} - Both have an
N-terminal regulatory PWWP domain (reads H3K36me3) and an ADD domain
(reads unmethylated H3K4 = H3K4me0). PWWP recognition couples \emph{de
novo} methylation deposition to gene-body H3K36me3-marked regions; ADD
ensures methylation deposition is excluded from H3K4me3-marked active
promoters (a fundamental safeguard against silencing active genes). -
Establish \emph{new} methylation patterns during germline development,
gametogenesis, and early embryogenesis. - Both require \textbf{DNMT3L}
(catalytically inactive; missing the SET-like motif required for SAM
binding) as a regulatory partner that stimulates activity
about 15-fold and itself reads H3K4me0 --- coupling methylation
deposition to \emph{absence} of active marks. - DNMT3A: predominant in
oocyte, embryonic stem cells, haematopoietic stem cells;
loss-of-function mutations are frequent in \textbf{clonal
haematopoiesis} (about 5 \% of healthy individuals over age 70)
and AML (about 20 \% of cytogenetically normal AML); also
Tatton-Brown--Rahman syndrome (germline DNMT3A loss with overgrowth). -
DNMT3B: predominant in B cells, embryonic stem cells; loss-of-function
causes \textbf{ICF syndrome} (immunodeficiency, centromeric instability,
facial anomalies) due to demethylation of pericentromeric satellites.

\textbf{Demethylation --- TET family enzymes --- the active
demethylation pathway:} - TET1, TET2, TET3 are
Fe(II)/\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases (each about 2,000
amino acids) with conserved C-terminal catalytic domains. They
sequentially oxidise:

\begin{equation}5\text{mC} \xrightarrow{\text{TET}} 5\text{hmC} \xrightarrow{\text{TET}} 5\text{fC} \xrightarrow{\text{TET}} 5\text{caC} \xrightarrow{\text{TDG/BER}} \text{C} \tag{15.4}\label{eq:tet_oxidation}\end{equation}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Reaction details:} TET enzymes consume O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} and \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}KG, producing
  CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} and succinate. Each oxidation step transfers an oxygen atom from
  O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} to the methyl carbon of cytosine.
\item
  \textbf{Active demethylation by base excision repair:}
  5-formylcytosine (5fC) and 5-carboxylcytosine (5caC) are recognised
  and excised by \textbf{thymine DNA glycosylase (TDG)}, which has a
  100-fold preference for 5fC/5caC over 5mC. TDG cleaves the
  N-glycosidic bond, leaving an abasic (AP) site. \textbf{APE1} then
  makes a single-nucleotide cut; \textbf{DNA Pol \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}} fills the gap with
  unmodified cytosine; \textbf{DNA ligase III + XRCC1} seal the nick.
  This is the canonical BER pathway adapted for methyl-cytosine erasure.
\item
  \textbf{5hmC is itself a stable mark with distinct biology, not merely
  an intermediate.} Different cell types have dramatically different
  5hmC/5mC ratios --- embryonic stem cells about 0.1 \%,
  neurons about 0.7 \% (Purkinje cells reach about 40
  \% of modified cytosines as 5hmC), cardiomyocytes about 0.5
  \%, tumour cells often \textless{} 0.05 \% (a \textbf{5hmC depletion
  signature} now used in liquid-biopsy diagnostics on platforms such as
  EpiCheck and GRAIL Galleri).
\item
  \textbf{Tissue-specific TET expression:} TET1 in stem cells (regulates
  pluripotency); TET2 in haematopoietic cells (clonal haematopoiesis);
  TET3 in zygote and neurons (post-fertilisation paternal demethylation;
  neural plasticity).
\item
  \textbf{Clinical relevance:} TET2 is the most frequently mutated
  epigenetic-writer gene in haematopoietic cancers --- loss-of-function
  TET2 mutations are present in about 15 \% of AML, 50 \% of
  CMML, and define \textbf{clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate
  potential (CHIP)} (about 10 \% of people over age 70). The
  oncometabolite \textbf{2-hydroxyglutarate} (produced by mutant IDH1/2)
  competitively inhibits TET (and other \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}KG-dependent dioxygenases),
  causing genome-wide hypermethylation in IDH-mutant gliomas and AML
  (the \textbf{CIMP} phenotype).
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Methodological caveat:} Bisulphite sequencing (the traditional
5mC gold standard) \textbf{cannot distinguish 5mC from 5hmC} because
both resist bisulphite-induced deamination. Modern methods that resolve
oxidation states:

\textbf{Clinical liquid-biopsy translation:} GRAIL's Galleri test
analyses cell-free DNA methylation patterns at \textgreater{} 100,000
CpG sites; multi-cancer early detection (MCED) sensitivity
about 67 \% for stage I--IV combined; tissue-of-origin
localisation accuracy about 93 \%. The technology exploits that
each tissue has a distinct methylation pattern, and tumours shed cfDNA
with their tissue-specific signature.

\subsubsection{CpG Islands and Gene
Regulation}\label{cpg-islands-and-gene-regulation}

\textbf{CpG islands (CGIs):} about 28,000 regions in the human
genome (about 500 bp--2 kb) with: - Observed/expected CpG ratio
\textgreater{} 0.6 - CG content \textgreater{} 55\% - Located near
about 70\% of mammalian gene promoters

\textbf{Normally unmethylated} in somatic cells. Methylation at CGI
promoters is strongly associated with \textbf{stable transcriptional
silencing}; the illustrative methylation heatmap in
\cref{fig:unit_IV_methylation_heatmap} should be read as a beta-value
pattern across loci and samples, not as patient or cell-line evidence.
In empirical data, silencing operates by: 1. Steric blockade of TF
binding (e.g., methylation at Sp1 sites) 2. Recruitment of methyl-CpG
binding proteins (MBD family: MBD1, MBD2, MBD3, MBD4; MeCP2; Kaiso) 3.
MBD-associated \textbf{NuRD complex} (MBD2/3-CHD4-HDAC1/2) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
deacetylation \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} chromatin compaction

\textbf{CpG depletion in the rest of the genome:} Methylated CpGs are
mutation hotspots (5mC \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} T deamination produces a C\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}T transition). Over
evolutionary time, most CpGs outside islands have been lost ---
explaining the genome-wide CpG suppression. CpG islands have escaped
depletion because methylation is normally absent and the deamination \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
mutation pressure is removed.

\subsubsection{Quantitative Maintenance Through
Replication}\label{quantitative-maintenance-through-replication}

Let \(f_n\) be the fraction of CpGs methylated after \(n\) divisions in
the absence of \emph{de novo} methylation:

\begin{equation}f_n = f_0 \times \left(\frac{1-\epsilon}{2}\right)^n + f_0 \times \frac{1+\epsilon}{2} \tag{15.5}\label{eq:methyl_decay}\end{equation}

where \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}}{epsilon} is the maintenance efficiency of DNMT1 (typically
about 0.95 --- i.e.~each hemimethylated CpG is restored 95 \%
of the time at the replication fork). Even high maintenance efficiency
therefore produces measurable \textbf{stochastic demethylation} over
many divisions, which is why constitutively silenced genes also have
backup repressive marks (H3K27me3, H3K9me3, H2AK119ub).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Worked Example 2 --- DNMT1 efficiency and the kinetics of clonal
demethylation}

\textbf{Setup:} A research group treats a cancer cell line with a DNMT1
small-molecule inhibitor that reduces \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}}{epsilon} from 0.95 to 0.50 (50 \%
maintenance per CpG per division). The cells divide every 24 h. The
cancer cell line carries an aberrantly hypermethylated \emph{MLH1}
promoter at \emph{f\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0}} = 0.95 (95 \% CpG methylation).

\textbf{Question:} How many days until methylation drops below the
\emph{f} = 0.30 threshold typically required for re-expression?

\textbf{Solution:} Using \cref{eq:methyl_decay},
\(f_n = f_0 \times \left(\frac{1-\epsilon}{2}\right)^n + f_0 \times \frac{1+\epsilon}{2}\)
--- but at \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}}{epsilon} = 0.5 the steady-state floor is
\(f_0 \cdot (1+0.5)/2 = 0.75 \cdot f_0 = 0.71\) for \emph{f\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0}} = 0.95.
The floor exceeds the 0.30 threshold, so methylation will not drop below
0.30 with \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}}{epsilon} = 0.5 alone. To re-express MLH1, you need either complete
DNMT1 inhibition (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}}{epsilon} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} 0) or active demethylation (TET upregulation).
With \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}}{epsilon} = 0:

\(f_n = f_0 / 2^n\)

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Generation \emph{n} & \(f_n\) \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
0 & 0.95 \\
1 & 0.475 \\
2 & 0.238 \\
3 & 0.119 \\
\end{longtable}
}

Threshold crossed between generation 1 and 2 --- i.e., \textbf{2 cell
divisions \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 48 h} after starting full DNMT1 inhibition. This kinetic is
exactly why clinical responses to azacitidine/decitabine in MDS take
about 4--6 cycles (about 3--4 months) of continuous
suppression to manifest: maintaining \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}}{epsilon} near zero is necessary but
insufficient --- the cell must also divide several times to dilute the
existing mark.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection:} In cancer, two genome-wide patterns are
consistently found: 1. \textbf{Global hypomethylation}: Repetitive
elements (LINE-1, SINE) become unmethylated \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} chromosomal instability,
reactivation of transposons, mis-regulated lineage genes. 2.
\textbf{Focal CGI hypermethylation}: Tumour-suppressor gene promoters
(BRCA1, MLH1, VHL, CDKN2A/p16, MGMT, DAPK) become methylated \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
silencing.

\textbf{DNMT inhibitors} (azacitidine, decitabine) are nucleoside
analogs incorporated into DNA; trapped DNMT1 forms a covalent adduct,
causing passive demethylation. Approved for myelodysplastic syndrome
(MDS) and AML. Combination with \textbf{HDAC inhibitors} is actively
trialled. \textbf{Liquid biopsies} (e.g., GRAIL Galleri, Guardant
Reveal) score hundreds of methylation features in cell-free DNA to
detect early-stage cancer with tissue-of-origin localisation.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 4:} A patient is treated with decitabine for
high-risk MDS. After 4 cycles, the bone-marrow blast count is unchanged.
Bisulphite sequencing of blast DNA shows the targeted \emph{p15/CDKN2B}
CGI is now 30 \% methylated (from 90 \% at baseline), but transcript
levels remain undetectable. Propose three independent mechanisms that
could explain transcriptional silencing despite DNMT1 inhibition, and
design a bench experiment to distinguish them.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Genomic Imprinting --- Mechanisms and Reciprocal
Phenotypes}\label{genomic-imprinting-mechanisms-and-reciprocal-phenotypes}

\textbf{Genomic imprinting} is a form of epigenetic regulation in which
genes are expressed from a single parental
\hyperref[gl:allele]{\textbf{allele}} in a parent-of-origin-specific
manner. about 150 genes are imprinted in humans, organised into
about 30 imprinted clusters each controlled by an
\textbf{imprint control region (ICR)} that is differentially methylated
on the two parental chromosomes.

\subsubsection{Imprint Control Regions (ICRs) --- The Master
Switch}\label{imprint-control-regions-icrs-the-master-switch}

ICRs are \textbf{differentially methylated regions (DMRs)} that are: 1.
Established in the germline in a sex-specific pattern (paternal ICRs in
spermatogenesis; maternal ICRs in oogenesis). 2. Maintained throughout
somatic lineages --- they escape post-fertilisation reprogramming via
specialised protective mechanisms (e.g., \textbf{ZFP445} +
\textbf{TRIM28/KAP1} + \textbf{DPPA3} = the ICR-protection triad in
early embryos). 3. Read by sequence-specific factors (e.g.,
\textbf{CTCF} at unmethylated maternal IGF2/H19 ICR; methyl-binding
proteins at methylated paternal ICRs).

\textbf{The CTCF insulator model --- the canonical mechanism at
IGF2/H19:} CTCF binds CCCTC consensus motifs in the unmethylated ICR.
CTCF blocks the enhancer--promoter looping interaction by recruiting
cohesin to form a chromatin loop ``barrier.'' When the ICR is
methylated, CTCF cannot bind (its zinc fingers fail to recognise
methylated CpGs), so the enhancer is free to loop over and contact the
\emph{IGF2} promoter.

\subsubsection{The IGF2/H19 Locus --- Insulator-based Imprinting
(Detailed
Mechanism)}\label{the-igf2h19-locus-insulator-based-imprinting-detailed-mechanism}

The canonical example is the \textbf{IGF2/H19 locus} on chromosome
11p15:

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0082_dd4913419cc7.png}
\caption{Imprinting at the IGF2/H19 locus. Paternal allele (top): DMR is methylated, CTCF cannot bind; enhancer contacts IGF2 to IGF2 expressed, H19 silent. Maternal allele (bottom): DMR unmethylated, CTCF binds and insulates enhancer from IGF2; enhancer contacts H19 to H19 expressed, IGF2 silent.}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Functional consequences of the locus:} - \textbf{IGF2}
(insulin-like growth factor 2): paternally expressed; potent fetal
growth factor (signals through IGF1R / IGF2R). Drives placental and
fetal growth. - \textbf{H19}: maternally expressed; a 2.3-kb spliced
lncRNA; reservoir of miR-675 (which targets \emph{IGF1R}, creating a
feedback loop). In some tissues H19 itself acts as a tumour suppressor
by inhibiting IGF1R signalling.

\subsubsection{The 15q11--q13 Locus --- Prader--Willi / Angelman
(Comprehensive
Mechanism)}\label{the-15q11q13-locus-praderwilli-angelman-comprehensive-mechanism}

A different mechanism operates at the \textbf{15q11--q13} imprinted
cluster:

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3214}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\emph{SNRPN, NDN, MAGEL2} & Paternally expressed & Maternal copies

\emph{UBE3A} & Maternally expressed (in neurons) & Paternal \emph{UBE3A}

from the paternal allele \\
\end{longtable}

\textbf{Mechanism details:} - The \textbf{SNURF-SNRPN ICR} sits
about 30 kb upstream of \emph{SNRPN} and is methylated on the
maternal allele (silencing maternal \emph{SNRPN, NDN, MAGEL2}) and
unmethylated on the paternal allele (where these genes are expressed). -
The unmethylated paternal ICR drives transcription of a long
polycistronic transcript that extends about 600 kb to produce
\emph{SNRPN, SNORD-cluster snoRNAs} (SNORD115, SNORD116), and
\emph{UBE3A-ATS} (the antisense to \emph{UBE3A}). - \emph{UBE3A-ATS}
transcription on the paternal allele suppresses paternal \emph{UBE3A}
expression --- \emph{primarily in neurons}. This is the most surprising
aspect of the locus: the imprint is \textbf{brain-specific}.

\textbf{Phenotypes --- the parental-conflict reciprocal:} -
\textbf{Prader--Willi syndrome}: Loss of \textbf{paternal} 15q11--q13
expression --- by paternal deletion (about 70\%), maternal
uniparental disomy (about 25\%), or imprinting centre defect
(about 3\%). Phenotype: neonatal hypotonia, hyperphagia and
obesity, intellectual disability, hypogonadism, growth-hormone
deficiency. The hypothalamic phenotype (especially the SNORD116 loss)
drives the food-intake dysregulation. - \textbf{Angelman syndrome}: Loss
of \textbf{maternal} \emph{UBE3A} expression in the same region --- by
maternal deletion (about 70\%), paternal uniparental disomy
(about 5\%), imprinting centre defect (about 5\%), or
\emph{UBE3A} point mutation (about 10\%). Phenotype: severe
intellectual disability, seizures, ataxic gait, ``happy puppet''
demeanour, absence of speech. UBE3A is an E3 ubiquitin ligase critical
for synaptic plasticity; loss in neurons disrupts excitatory/inhibitory
balance.

\textbf{Therapeutic angle --- antisense oligonucleotide reactivation:}
Activation of the silenced paternal \emph{UBE3A} by antisense
oligonucleotides targeting \emph{UBE3A-ATS} is in clinical trials for
Angelman syndrome (Ionis/Biogen ION-582/GTX-102, Phase 1/2 trials
underway 2024). The strategy: deplete the antisense lncRNA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} de-repress
paternal \emph{UBE3A} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} restore neuronal UBE3A protein. Intrathecal
delivery is required because UBE3A imprinting is brain-specific.

\subsubsection{Beckwith--Wiedemann and Silver--Russell --- Reciprocal
Disorders}\label{beckwithwiedemann-and-silverrussell-reciprocal-disorders}

The IGF2/H19 ICR also produces two reciprocal phenotypes --- a textbook
illustration of \textbf{dosage and parental conflict}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Beckwith--Wiedemann syndrome (BWS):} biallelic IGF2 expression
  (loss of maternal imprint, \textbf{hypermethylation} of the maternal
  ICR at H19) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} maternal allele now expresses IGF2 like the paternal \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  fetal overgrowth, macrosomia (birth weight \textgreater{} 4 kg),
  macroglossia, omphalocele, hypoglycaemia, hemihyperplasia, and a 7.5
  \% risk of childhood embryonal tumours (Wilms tumour, hepatoblastoma,
  neuroblastoma, rhabdomyosarcoma). Diagnosis: methylation analysis of
  the H19 DMR shows hypermethylation; some cases also have paternal UPD
  of 11p15 (about 20 \%).
\item
  \textbf{Silver--Russell syndrome (SRS):} biallelic H19 expression / no
  IGF2 (loss of paternal imprint, \textbf{hypomethylation} of the
  paternal ICR) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} paternal allele now silent like the maternal \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} severe
  intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), postnatal short stature, body
  asymmetry, characteristic triangular face, fifth-finger clinodactyly.
  Diagnosis: hypomethylation of the H19 DMR (about 50 \%) or
  maternal UPD of chromosome 7 (about 10 \%).
\end{itemize}

This ``mirror image'' pair illustrates the \textbf{parental-conflict
(kinship)} theory: paternally-expressed growth factors maximise
embryonic growth (paternal genes care less about maternal resources,
since the same father may not father subsequent siblings);
maternally-expressed antagonists restrain growth (the mother distributes
resources across multiple offspring).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 5:} A child is born with severe IUGR,
characteristic facial features, and asymmetric limbs. Methylation
analysis shows that both the paternal and maternal copies of the 11p15.5
ICR are \emph{hypomethylated}. Predict the likely diagnosis. Explain why
hypermethylation versus hypomethylation at the \emph{same} ICR produces
\emph{opposite} phenotypes (BWS vs SRS).
\end{quote}

\subsection{X-Chromosome Inactivation (Lyonisation) --- In
Depth}\label{x-chromosome-inactivation-lyonisation-in-depth}

In female placental mammals, dosage compensation for about 900
X-linked genes is achieved by transcriptionally silencing one of the two
X chromosomes in every somatic cell.

\textbf{Key features:} - \textbf{Random choice:} Either the maternal or
paternal X can be inactivated in each cell (choice is random in each
blastomere nucleus). Imprinted paternal X-inactivation occurs in mouse
extra-embryonic lineages but not in humans. - \textbf{Clonal
maintenance:} Once established (about  day 4.5 in human
embryo), the inactive state is mitotically heritable in most daughter
cells --- the same X is silenced in every descendant. - \textbf{Barr
body:} The inactive X (Xi) forms a dense heterochromatic body (Barr
body) visible by interphase cytology. - \textbf{Incomplete:}
about 15--25\% of X-linked genes \textbf{escape} inactivation.
Most escapees lie in the \textbf{pseudoautosomal regions (PAR1, PAR2)}
that recombine with the Y; others (e.g., \emph{KDM6A}, \emph{KDM5C},
\emph{DDX3X}, \emph{ZFX}) escape across the X. Escape genes contribute
to female-biased autoimmune disease and to Turner syndrome
haploinsufficiency phenotypes.

\textbf{Molecular mechanism --- a hierarchical cascade (timing and
milestones):}

\textbf{XIST regulation by TSIX:} The antisense lncRNA \emph{TSIX}
(transcribed across XIST in the opposite direction) keeps XIST repressed
on the future active X (Xa). The mutual exclusion of XIST/TSIX between
alleles enforces monoallelic XIST expression. \emph{TSIX} itself is
regulated by \emph{XITE} (X-inactivation intergenic transcription
element) and by chromatin-state asymmetries between the two alleles in
early embryogenesis.

\textbf{Reactivation in iPSC reprogramming:} When somatic female cells
are reprogrammed to induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), the inactive
X reactivates --- XIST is silenced, H3K27me3 is lost, DNA methylation is
removed, and both alleles express X-linked genes again. This is a unique
window for studying XCI dynamics. iPSCs derived from female patients
with X-linked disease may have variable X-inactivation patterns after
differentiation, complicating disease modelling.

\textbf{Clinical implications --- X-linked diseases in heterozygous
females:}

\begin{equation}\text{P(affected)} \approx \int_0^1 g(x) \cdot \mathbf{1}[x \le x_{\text{threshold}}] \, dx \tag{15.6}\label{eq:xci_skew}\end{equation}

where \(g(x)\) is the distribution of X-inactivation skewing across
cells. \textbf{Skewed X-inactivation} (where one allele is silenced in
\textgreater75 \% of cells) explains why heterozygous female carriers of
X-linked diseases (Duchenne muscular dystrophy, Rett syndrome, X-linked
agammaglobulinaemia) show variable severity. Skewing arises when: -
Random inactivation by chance produces an extreme distribution -
Cell-autonomous selection eliminates clones with the active mutant
allele (e.g., immunodeficiencies) - A \emph{XIST} or \emph{XIC} mutation
biases choice - Skewing is age-dependent: fraction of women with
\textgreater{} 75 \% skewing rises from about 5 \% at birth to
about 25 \% by age 60 (clonal drift in haematopoiesis).

\textbf{Lyon's evidence} \citep{lyon1961}: Female mice heterozygous for
coat-colour mutations show patchy (mosaic) coat colour --- a direct
consequence of random X-inactivation producing patches of cells
expressing one allele or the other. The same mosaicism is seen in human
female carriers of X-linked albinism, X-linked anhidrotic ectodermal
dysplasia (Christ--Siemens--Touraine, with patchy sweat glands), and
X-linked retinoschisis (patchy retinal involvement).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Worked Example 3 --- Predicting penetrance from XCI skewing}

\textbf{Setup:} A female patient is heterozygous for a Duchenne muscular
dystrophy (DMD) deletion. Muscle weakness is observed in cells where the
wild-type (active) allele is on the inactivated X. Assume that DMD
muscle fibres are syncytial (myofibres pool many nuclei); a fibre is
dystrophic if \textgreater{} 50 \% of its nuclei express the deleted
allele.

\textbf{Question:} If XCI is unbiased (mean skewing = 0.5, standard
deviation \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\sigma}}{sigma}\_skew = 0.05 across mononuclear cells), what fraction of
myofibres will be dystrophic? What if the patient has clonal-skewing
where \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\sigma}}{sigma}\_skew = 0.20?

\textbf{Solution:} A fibre is dystrophic if more than half its nuclei
have the wild-type allele inactivated. With \emph{N} = 20 nuclei per
fibre and a per-nucleus probability \emph{x} of expressing the deleted
allele (= probability wild-type X is inactivated), the fibre is
dystrophic when more than \emph{N}/2 nuclei out of \emph{N} express the
deleted allele.

For unbiased XCI, \emph{x} per nucleus \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 0.5, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\sigma}}{sigma}\_x = 0.05. Per fibre,
the average fraction of mutant-expressing nuclei \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 0.5 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\pm}}{+/-} 0.05/\texorpdfstring{\(\sqrt{\;}\)}{sqrt}20 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 0.5
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\pm}}{+/-} 0.011. Almost no fibres exceed 50 \% (by about \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\sigma}}{sigma}\_fibre \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 1 \%).

For clonal-skewing \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\sigma}}{sigma}\_skew = 0.20 across mononuclear precursors, mean
per-fibre fraction is 0.5 but with much wider variance: \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\sigma}}{sigma}\_fibre \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~}
0.20/\texorpdfstring{\(\sqrt{\;}\)}{sqrt}20 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 0.045. Now about 25 \% of fibres exceed 50 \% mutant
expression and become dystrophic.

\textbf{Insight:} Manifesting Duchenne muscular dystrophy in
heterozygous female carriers (about 10 \% show muscle weakness)
is largely explained by \textbf{age-acquired XCI skewing} in
haematopoietic and myogenic precursors. Treatment strategies:
skewing-modulating ASOs to redirect XCI; or AAV-DMD gene therapy
(rebalancing dystrophin expression).
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 6:} A 4-year-old girl is diagnosed with severe
Rett syndrome. Sequencing reveals a heterozygous loss-of-function
mutation in \emph{MECP2}. XCI analysis shows 95 \% skewing toward
inactivation of the \emph{wild-type} allele. Explain (i) why this
skewing pattern produces severe disease, (ii) why some Rett patients
with the same mutation are mildly affected, and (iii) whether modulating
XCI skewing therapeutically could be a treatment strategy.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Chromatin Remodelling Complexes --- Mechanism in
Detail}\label{chromatin-remodelling-complexes-mechanism-in-detail}

In addition to covalent modifications, chromatin structure is actively
remodelled by ATP-dependent complexes that slide, eject, or restructure
nucleosomes. Most four families share a conserved \textbf{Snf2-family
ATPase} (SF2 helicase superfamily) but couple ATP hydrolysis to distinct
nucleosome operations.

\subsubsection{The Four Major Remodeller
Families}\label{the-four-major-remodeller-families}

\textbf{Mechanism in detail --- the ``wave'' model of DNA
translocation:} Most remodellers translocate DNA through the nucleosome
by alternately gripping minor groove with two RecA-like ATPase lobes.
Each ATP cycle introduces a 1-bp DNA bulge that propagates around the
histone surface, effectively pulling DNA into the nucleosome from one
side and ejecting it from the other. The size of the ATP-driven movement
varies (1--10 bp per cycle) and explains the family-specific outcomes
(single-nucleosome repositioning vs.~processive slides vs.~ejection).
Substrate recognition differs: - \textbf{SWI/SNF} binds at SHL-2
(superhelical location -2 from the dyad), gripping nucleosomal DNA
about 20 bp from the histone--DNA boundary. - \textbf{ISWI}
binds the linker DNA flanking the nucleosome and uses an autoinhibitory
AutoN domain that is released by H4-tail acetylation. -
\textbf{CHD/NuRD} binds via a tandem chromodomain that reads H3K9me3
(CHD3) or H3K4me0 (CHD4), targeting the complex to silenced chromatin. -
\textbf{INO80} binds the H2A.Z-H2B dimer for selective exchange.

\subsubsection{SWI/SNF Specifically --- The Cancer-Most-Mutated
Remodeller}\label{swisnf-specifically-the-cancer-most-mutated-remodeller}

The mammalian BAF complex contains 12--15 subunits, including ATPase
BRG1 or BRM, ARID1A/B (DNA-binding), and SMARCB1/INI1. Its assembly is
highly cell-type-specific (npBAF in neural progenitors \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} nBAF in
post-mitotic neurons, with subunit swap at \emph{MIR9} induction; esBAF
in embryonic stem cells). BAF: - \textbf{Evicts PRC1/PRC2 from enhancers
within minutes} (this is the basis for the synthetic-lethal sensitivity
of SWI/SNF-mutant tumours to EZH2 inhibitors). - Generates
nucleosome-depleted regions (NDRs) at enhancers and promoters - Recruits
transcription factors (e.g., pioneer TFs FOXA1, GATA4) by exposing their
motifs - Specific complexes: - \textbf{canonical BAF (cBAF):} contains
ARID1A or ARID1B and DPF1/2/3 - \textbf{polybromo BAF (PBAF):} contains
BAF180/PBRM1, ARID2, and BRD7 --- required for IFN response and
differentiation - \textbf{non-canonical BAF (ncBAF/GBAF):} contains
BRD9, GLTSCR1/L, and BRG1 --- found in synovial sarcoma (where SS18-SSX
fusions hijack ncBAF)

\subsubsection{Targeted Epigenome Editing with dCas9
Fusions}\label{targeted-epigenome-editing-with-dcas9-fusions}

The CRISPR toolkit has expanded far beyond DNA cutting. A catalytically
dead \textbf{dCas9} (D10A + H840A) retains its ability to be guided to a
specific DNA sequence by a sgRNA but no longer cleaves --- turning it
into a programmable DNA-binding scaffold. Fusing dCas9 to an epigenetic
enzyme creates a targeted ``writer'' or ``eraser'' of chromatin state
\citep{doudna2014}:

\emph{FMR1} silencing; reactivation of tumour suppressors \\
dCas9--p300 & Programmable H3K27 acetylation & Programmable enhancer
activation \\
dCas9--KRAB & Recruits KAP1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} SETDB1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} H3K9me3 & \textbf{CRISPRi} ---
stable repression of any gene \\
dCas9--LSD1 & H3K4me1/2 demethylation & Enhancer decommissioning \\
dCas9--VPR (VP64-p65-Rta) & Transcriptional activation &
\textbf{CRISPRa} --- about 10-to-1000-fold induction \\
dCas9--PRC1 (RING1B--PCGF4) & H2AK119ub deposition & Polycomb-style
silencing \\
\end{longtable}
}

The clinical promise is substantial: a dCas9--DNMT3A targeting the
\emph{HBG1/2} promoter re-activates fetal haemoglobin in adult
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-thalassaemia patients without permanent genome modification.
CRISPRoff-induced silencing of \emph{PCSK9} in liver cells is being
pursued for hypercholesterolaemia. The key limitation is off-target
\hyperref[gl:epigenome]{\textbf{epigenome}} editing --- bystander
methylation at sequence-similar loci --- which the field now addresses
with paired-sgRNA and split-dCas9 designs.

\begin{quote}
{[}!NOTE{]} Unlike Cas9-mediated gene editing, epigenome editing is
\textbf{reversible}: the perturbation fades unless it is
self-reinforcing through mitotic heritability of DNA methylation. This
makes it attractive as a research tool (transient perturbation) and a
therapy (tunable, removable), but means durable clinical effects require
either continuous dCas9 expression or recruitment of self-propagating
chromatin states (e.g., H3K27me3 spreading by PRC2).
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection:} \textbf{SWI/SNF subunits are mutated in
about 20\% of human cancers}, the highest mutation frequency of
any single chromatin regulator. ARID1A (about 10\%),
SMARCA4/BRG1 (about 5\%), SMARCB1/INI1 (childhood rhabdoid
tumours, near-almost universally biallelic loss), PBRM1
(about 40\% of clear-cell renal cell carcinoma). Many
SWI/SNF-mutant tumours become \textbf{synthetically lethal with EZH2}
(PRC2) inhibition because they over-rely on Polycomb repression of
cell-cycle inhibitors when SWI/SNF cannot evict PRC1/2.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

Separation}\label{three-dimensional-genome-organisation-and-phase-separation}

\subsubsection{TADs, Loops, and Compartments --- Spatial
Layers}\label{tads-loops-and-compartments-spatial-layers}

The genome is folded across multiple length scales, and each scale
contributes to gene regulation:

\textbf{LADs (Lamina-Associated Domains):} about 1,300 genomic
regions (median about 1 Mb) attached to the nuclear lamina via
lamin B receptor, marked by H3K9me2/me3, gene-poor and transcriptionally
repressive. Lamina detachment correlates with gene activation during
differentiation.

\subsubsection{Biomolecular Condensates and Phase
Separation}\label{biomolecular-condensates-and-phase-separation}

Chromatin is not a static polymer; many regulatory proteins undergo
\textbf{liquid--liquid phase separation} (LLPS) or form
\textbf{condensates} with elevated local concentration. Intrinsically
disordered regions (IDRs) on transcription factors (e.g., \textbf{BRD4},
\textbf{Mediator} subunits, \textbf{RNA Pol II} CTD-associated factors)
promote clustering at \textbf{super-enhancers} --- unusually large
clusters of enhancers densely occupied by Mediator, co-activators, and
active histone marks (\textbf{H3K27ac}). The resulting
\textbf{transcriptional condensate} concentrates the phosphorylation
machinery that releases promoter-proximal paused Pol II, explaining why
some loci fire at very high rates (oncogenes such as \emph{MYC} in
selected cancers).

\textbf{Quantitative criteria for LLPS in cells:} - IDR-rich proteins
above a saturation concentration \(c_{\text{sat}}\) - Multivalent
interactions (low-affinity, high-valency) between IDRs, with
\(K_d \sim 1\)--\(100\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}M - Round, dynamic droplets that fuse and
undergo FRAP recovery on the seconds-to-minutes timescale - Disassembly
upon 1,6-hexanediol (a hallmark, though imperfect, test)

\textbf{Examples in chromatin biology:}

\textbf{Conceptual link to TADs:} Condensates operate \emph{within} TADs
and at promoter--enhancer loops; disrupting CTCF boundaries can move an
oncogenic enhancer adjacent to a silent proto-oncogene (\textbf{enhancer
hijacking}), a structural-variant mechanism increasingly catalogued in
paediatric tumours.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0084_989de778d28c.png}
\caption{Super-enhancer-associated condensate bridging enhancers to paused Pol II; BET inhibitors weaken acetyl-lysine engagement of BRD4 and dissolve the condensate; CDK8-mediated phosphorylation of Mediator disrupts condensate integrity.}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Clinical angle --- drugging condensates:} - \textbf{BET
bromodomain inhibitors} (e.g., JQ1, OTX015, birabresib, molibresib,
mivebresib) displace BRD4 from acetylated chromatin, collapsing
condensate-associated transcription at \emph{MYC} and other dependency
genes. - \textbf{CDK7 inhibitors} (THZ1, SY-5609) and \textbf{CDK9
inhibitors} target the kinases concentrated in transcription
condensates. - \textbf{EZH2 inhibitors} (tazemetostat) shrink
PRC2-mediated repressive domains. - \textbf{Tumour cells with
super-enhancer-driven oncogenes (MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma,
MLL-rearranged leukaemia, \emph{TAL1}-driven T-cell acute lymphoblastic
leukaemia) can be highly sensitive} to BET inhibition, but response
depends on enhancer wiring, compensatory transcription factors, and
therapeutic window rather than on super-enhancer status alone.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Worked Example 4 --- Polymer Statistics in Hi-C:}

\textbf{Setup:} A human gene at chromosome 7p15 harbours an enhancer 700
kb upstream. We model intra-chromosomal contact probability with the
fractal-globule scaling \cref{eq:hic_scaling},
\(P(s) \propto s^{-\alpha}\), with \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha} = 1.1.

\textbf{Question:} Estimate the probability of physical contact between
enhancer and promoter (s = 700,000 bp). Compare to (a) within-TAD
contact at s = 50 kb and (b) trans-chromosomal contact (genome-wide Hi-C
average \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{6}}{6}).

\textbf{Solution:} Setting \emph{P}(50 kb) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 1 (within-TAD baseline),
the relative \emph{P}(700 kb) = (700/50)\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1} = 14\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 0.063. The
enhancer--promoter contact probability is about 6 \% of the
within-TAD baseline.

Compare to trans-chromosomal: 6 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2} (intra-TAD-distant) versus 1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x}
10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{6}}{6} (trans) = a \textbf{about 60,000-fold preference} for
intra-chromosomal contacts even at long distances.

\textbf{Insight:} CTCF/cohesin loop extrusion concentrates this
60,000-fold enrichment of intra-TAD contacts onto specific
enhancer--promoter pairs, raising effective contact probability another
10--100\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x}. This is why disrupting a single CTCF anchor (about 20
bp deletion) can completely abolish enhancer--promoter looping and
silence the target gene --- even though the enhancer DNA is unchanged.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Non-Coding RNAs in Gene
Regulation}\label{non-coding-rnas-in-gene-regulation}

\subsubsection{MicroRNAs (miRNAs)}\label{micrornas-mirnas}

miRNAs are about 22 nt single-stranded RNAs that direct
post-transcriptional silencing. Over 2,000 annotated human miRNAs
collectively regulate about 60\% of protein-coding genes
\citep{fire1998}.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0085_192a3bb982f8.png}
\caption{miRNA biogenesis and RISC-mediated silencing. Drosha in the nucleus produces pre-miRNA; DICER in the cytoplasm generates the duplex; AGO2 incorporates the guide strand into RISC; partial 3 UTR complementarity leads to translational repression and mRNA decay.}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Key oncogenic miRNA examples:} - \textbf{miR-21} (oncomiR):
Overexpressed in most cancers; targets PTEN, PDCD4, RECK (tumour
suppressors) - \textbf{miR-155} (oncomiR): Overexpressed in B-cell
lymphomas; targets SHIP1 (AKT suppressor) - \textbf{miR-34a} (tumour
suppressor miR): Downstream of p53; targets CDK6, BCL2, SNAIL;
methylated/silenced in many cancers

\subsubsection{Long Non-Coding RNAs
(lncRNAs)}\label{long-non-coding-rnas-lncrnas}

lncRNAs are \textgreater200 nt functional RNA transcripts with no
protein-coding potential. \textgreater100,000 annotated in the human
genome. Mechanisms of action are diverse:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{XIST:} Coats the inactive X chromosome; recruits PRC2 to
  spread H3K27me3, as described in the X-inactivation section.
\item
  \textbf{HOTAIR:} Transcribed from HOXC; binds PRC2 to direct H3K27me3
  deposition at HOXD and other loci
\item
  \textbf{MALAT1:} Nuclear speckle-associated; regulates alternative
  splicing; highly expressed in cancer
\item
  \textbf{H19:} Reservoir for miR-675; tumour suppressor function;
  imprinted, as described in the genomic-imprinting section.
\item
  \textbf{NEAT1:} Paraspeckle scaffold; regulates gene expression by
  nuclear retention of specific mRNAs
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Small Interfering RNAs (siRNAs) and
piRNAs}\label{small-interfering-rnas-sirnas-and-pirnas}

\textbf{siRNAs:} 21--23 nt, perfect complementarity to target; processed
by DICER from long double-stranded RNA (dsRNA). In plants and nematodes,
siRNA pathways mediate transposon silencing and antiviral immunity. In
mammals, dsRNA triggers interferon responses rather than siRNA pathways
in somatic cells; siRNA silencing is more prominent in germ cells and
stem cells.

\textbf{piRNAs (PIWI-interacting RNAs):} 26--31 nt; DICER-independent
(processed by ``ping-pong'' amplification cycle involving PIWI clade
Argonautes: PIWIL1/MILI, PIWIL4/MIWI2). Essential for silencing
transposable elements in the germline. Loss of piRNA pathway in
\emph{Drosophila} or mice causes transposon derepression and
infertility.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Epigenetic Reprogramming and
Inheritance}\label{epigenetic-reprogramming-and-inheritance}

\subsubsection{Mitotic Heritability of Epigenetic Marks --- Detailed
Mechanism}\label{mitotic-heritability-of-epigenetic-marks-detailed-mechanism}

For an epigenetic mark to be ``heritable,'' it must survive DNA
replication and cell division. Different marks have different
mechanisms:

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.0645}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4839}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4516}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Mark
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Mitotic heritability mechanism
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Half-life through divisions
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
5mC at CpGs & DNMT1/UHRF1 maintenance at replication fork & High
(\textgreater10 divisions, about 95\% efficiency) \\
H3K27me3 & Read-write feedback (PRC2 EED reads, EZH2 writes); inherited
on parental nucleosomes which are randomly distributed to both daughter
strands & Medium; restored within 1--2 divisions \\
H3K9me3 & Suv39H1/H2 reads HP1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} recruits more Suv39H; DNMT3A coupling &
High at constitutive heterochromatin \\

H3K27ac & Diluted by half each division; restored by transcription

\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Key conceptual point --- parental nucleosome recycling:} During
DNA replication, parental nucleosomes are split between the two daughter
strands. The histone chaperones \textbf{MCM2} (binds H3-H4 dimers via
its H3-H4 binding domain), \textbf{ASF1} (general H3-H4 chaperone), and
\textbf{FACT} (Spt16-SSRP1, helps recycle H2A-H2B during transcription
and replication) mediate this recycling. The current model:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Parental nucleosome split:} As the replisome opens, parental
  histones are transiently released from DNA.
\item
  \textbf{Asymmetric recycling:} H3-H4 tetramers preferentially deposit
  on the \textbf{leading strand} (via Pol\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}}{epsilon}/MCM2 interaction) or
  \textbf{lagging strand} (via Pol\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}/MCM2-7 helicase-associated MCM2).
  Recent work shows this is biased toward the leading strand in
  proliferating cells (about 60:40), explaining
  strand-asymmetric mark inheritance.
\item
  \textbf{CAF-1 deposits new H3.1-H4:} The chromatin assembly factor
  CAF-1 (CHAF1A/B + RBBP4) is recruited by PCNA at the replication fork.
  CAF-1 deposits \textbf{new} H3.1-H4 tetramers (synthesized from
  S-phase histone gene bursts).
\item
  \textbf{Newly synthesised histones are deposited UNMODIFIED.} Daughter
  chromatin starts at half-density of any given mark.
\item
  \textbf{Restoration to full density depends on the read-write feedback
  loop} --- the existing parental marks recruit the writer enzyme, which
  copies the mark onto neighbouring new histones.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{PRC2 propagation through replication.} EED reads H3K27me3 on a
parental nucleosome \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} allosterically activates EZH2 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} EZH2 deposits
H3K27me3 on a neighbouring (newly assembled) nucleosome. Quantitative
imaging shows that PRC2 activity at recently replicated chromatin is
about 3-fold higher than at established chromatin ---
explaining how the mark ``fills in'' the daughter strand within
about 6 hours of fork passage.

\textbf{DNMT1/UHRF1 mechanism in detail at the fork.} UHRF1 is loaded
onto the replication fork by PCNA. UHRF1 SRA binds hemi-methylated CpG
(the parental strand carries 5mC; the daughter strand has unmodified C).
The UHRF1 RING domain ubiquitinates H3K18 --- creating a docking site
for DNMT1's RFTS domain. DNMT1 transfers a methyl group from SAM to the
daughter cytosine. This coupled mechanism ensures methylation is
restored within seconds of fork passage at active replication.

\subsubsection{Germline Reprogramming}\label{germline-reprogramming}

Somatic epigenetic marks must be erased and re-established in each
generation to prevent transmission of acquired somatic states:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Post-fertilisation reprogramming:} After fertilisation, the
  paternal genome undergoes rapid active demethylation (TET3-mediated
  5mC oxidation) within hours. The maternal genome is demethylated more
  slowly (replication-dependent passive demethylation). Both reach a
  methylation minimum at the blastocyst stage.
\item
  \textbf{Primordial germ cell (PGC) reprogramming:} PGCs migrate to the
  gonads (about  E7.5--E10.5 in mouse; about  weeks
  3--5 in human). They erase CpG methylation genome-wide (including
  imprint control regions) --- the most complete demethylation in the
  mammalian life cycle.
\item
  \textbf{Re-establishment:} DNMT3A/3B with DNMT3L re-methylate the
  genome in a sex-specific pattern during gametogenesis
  (prospermatogonia in males; oocyte growth in females). Imprinted loci
  are methylated in a sex-specific order: paternal imprints in
  spermatogonia (before meiosis); maternal imprints in growing oocytes
  (after meiosis I arrest, prior to ovulation).
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Evidence for Transgenerational Epigenetic Inheritance in
Humans}\label{evidence-for-transgenerational-epigenetic-inheritance-in-humans}

The Dutch Hunger Winter (Hongerwinter, 1944--1945) provides the most
studied human evidence. Dutch civilians subjected to severe famine
(500--1,000 kcal/day) during WWII German occupation showed:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{F1 offspring} (exposed in utero): Increased rates of obesity,
  diabetes, schizophrenia, and CVD in adult life --- consistent with
  developmental programming via altered methylation.
\item
  \textbf{F2 offspring} (children of F1): Increased rates of obesity and
  metabolic syndrome --- suggesting transmission across one germline
  generation.
\item
  \textbf{Mechanism:} Reduced methylation at IGF2 differentially
  methylated regions (DMRs) persists for decades in blood cells of F1
  individuals, detectable compared to unexposed siblings.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Other lines of evidence:} - Överkalix cohort (Sweden): Paternal
grandfather's food supply during slow-growth period correlates with
grandsons' diabetes mortality. - \emph{Agouti} viable yellow
(\(A^{vy}\)) mouse model: Maternal methyl-donor diet (folate, B12,
methionine, choline) during pregnancy shifts coat-colour distribution by
altering methylation of an upstream IAP retrotransposon. -
piRNA-mediated transposon silencing: piRNAs in sperm carry information
about active transposons across generations.

\begin{quote}
{[}!NOTE{]} The evidence for true transgenerational epigenetic
inheritance in humans (affecting F2 and beyond without continued
environmental exposure) is suggestive but not yet definitive.
Confounding by shared post-natal environment and direct exposure of the
F1 germline (the F2 was a primordial germ cell in the F0 grandmother
during the F1 in utero exposure) remains difficult to exclude.
Mechanistically, piRNA-mediated transposon silencing and small-RNA
transmission in sperm provide plausible vehicles, but a clean causal
chain in humans has not been established.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 7:} Imagine a dCas9 fusion protein is targeted to
the \emph{BRCA1} promoter in a breast-cancer cell line, carrying a
DNMT3A catalytic domain. Over several cell divisions, the promoter
becomes hypermethylated and transcription drops. Once dCas9 is
withdrawn, does the methylation persist, relax over mitoses, or become
heritable between cells? Explain in terms of DNMT1 maintenance
methylation, passive demethylation during S-phase, and the absence of
active demethylation by TET enzymes under these conditions.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 8:} A scientist treats cells with the DNMT
inhibitor decitabine for 48 hours, then washes it out. Predicting that
DNMT1 will resume normal activity after washout, will the demethylation
persist, partially recover, or fully recover over the subsequent 10 cell
generations? Sketch a quantitative model assuming \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}}{epsilon} returns to 0.95
instantaneously after washout and starting \emph{f\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0}} = 0.10 (10 \%
methylated post-decitabine).
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Cancer Epigenetics and Clinical Translation ---
Comprehensive}\label{cancer-epigenetics-and-clinical-translation-comprehensive}

Cancer cells display \textbf{systemic epigenetic dysregulation}:
typically global DNA hypomethylation (especially of repetitive
elements), focal hypermethylation of tumour-suppressor CGI promoters,
broad H3K27me3/H3K9me3 redistribution, and aberrant chromatin
remodelling complex composition. The therapeutic implication is that,
unlike genetic mutations, epigenetic states are \textbf{reversible} ---
and several drug classes now target each layer.

\subsubsection{The Cancer Epigenome --- Two Concurrent
Patterns}\label{the-cancer-epigenome-two-concurrent-patterns}

\textbf{Pattern 1: Global hypomethylation.} Repetitive elements (LINE-1,
SINE, IAP, satellite repeats), normally heavily methylated, lose
methylation in nearly most cancers. Consequences: - \textbf{Chromosomal
instability:} demethylation of pericentromeric satellite-2 sequences
disrupts heterochromatin, leading to chromosome bridges, lagging
chromosomes, and aneuploidy. - \textbf{LINE-1 reactivation:}
transposition of L1 elements can disrupt tumour-suppressor genes (e.g.,
L1 insertion in \emph{APC} contributes to colorectal cancer). -
\textbf{Mis-regulated lineage genes:} demethylation of normally
repressed germline genes (e.g., MAGE, NY-ESO-1) creates
\textbf{cancer-testis antigens} that can be exploited for immunotherapy
(e.g., NY-ESO-1 TCR-T cells). - \textbf{Mechanism:} likely loss of DNMT1
maintenance (UHRF1 dysregulation) and/or genome-wide TET2-mediated
demethylation in CHIP-derived clones.

\textbf{Pattern 2: Focal CGI hypermethylation.} Tumour-suppressor gene
promoters become hypermethylated, silencing them. Examples and clinical
relevance:

\emph{DAPK} & Lung, head/neck cancer & Apoptosis loss & Combination with
TRAIL agonists (clinical trials) \\
\end{longtable}
}

The two patterns can coexist --- a single tumour can have global
hypomethylation of repeats AND focal hypermethylation of tumour
suppressors. The mechanism appears to be partial: CGI-targeted DNMT3A/B
activity becomes mis-localised to actively transcribed regions, while
genome-wide DNMT1 maintenance fails at heterochromatin.
