\subsection{X-Inactivation and Dosage
Compensation}\label{x-inactivation-and-dosage-compensation}

\subsubsection{Lyon Hypothesis and
X-Inactivation}\label{lyon-hypothesis-and-x-inactivation}

Mary \citet{lyon1961} proposed that in each female somatic cell, one of
the two X chromosomes is randomly inactivated early in embryonic
development (about  day 5.5 in mouse, about  day 12-16
in human). This inactivation is:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Random}: Either the maternal or paternal X can be inactivated
  in any given cell
\item
  \textbf{Clonal}: Once established, most daughter cells maintain the
  same inactive X
\item
  \textbf{Result}: Adult females are \textbf{genetic mosaics} -- a
  patchwork of cells expressing the maternal X and cells expressing the
  paternal X
\end{itemize}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0095_88ba3c6367df.png}
\caption{The molecular mechanism of X-inactivation. XIST RNA coats the future inactive X chromosome, recruiting Polycomb complexes that establish repressive histone marks and DNA methylation, ultimately condensing the chromosome into a Barr body.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Molecular Mechanism}\label{molecular-mechanism}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{XIST} (X-inactive specific transcript): A 17 kb lncRNA
  transcribed primarily from the X that will be inactivated
\item
  XIST RNA \textbf{coats} the Xi chromosome \emph{in cis} -- spreading
  outward from the X-inactivation center (XIC) at Xq13
\item
  XIST recruits \textbf{PRC2} (Polycomb repressive complex 2), which
  catalyzes histone H3K27 trimethylation
\item
  Additional silencing factors: \textbf{SMCHD1} (structural maintenance
  of chromosomes flexible hinge domain-containing 1) further compacts
  \hyperref[gl:chromatin]{\textbf{chromatin}}
\item
  \textbf{DNA methylation} at \hyperref[gl:cpg-island]{\textbf{CpG
  island}}s provides stable, long-term silencing
\item
  The silenced X is visible as a \textbf{Barr body} at the nuclear
  periphery (sex chromatin test)
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Escape from X-inactivation}: about 15\% of X-linked
genes ``escape'' inactivation and are expressed from both the active and
inactive X. These include genes in the pseudoautosomal regions and some
genes with Y-chromosome homologs. Escape genes explain some phenotypic
features of X-chromosome aneuploidy.

\textbf{Barr body count} = number of X chromosomes minus 1: - 46,XX: 1
Barr body - 47,XXX: 2 Barr bodies - 45,X (Turner): 0 Barr bodies -
47,XXY (Klinefelter): 1 Barr body

\subsubsection{Dosage Compensation Across Species and Beyond Sex
Chromosomes}\label{dosage-compensation-across-species-and-beyond-sex-chromosomes}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3448}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3793}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2759}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Organism
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Mechanism
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Mammals} & X-inactivation (XIST) & One X silenced in XX females;
equal dosage with XY males \\
\textbf{Drosophila} & X upregulation in males (MSL/roX RNA complex) &
Male single X transcribed about 2x; equals female XX \\
\textbf{C. elegans} & X downregulation in XX hermaphrodites (DCC

X \\
\end{longtable}

\textbf{Dosage compensation beyond X-inactivation}: The principle that
gene dosage must be balanced applies far more broadly than the sex
chromosomes. Several other mechanisms address dosage imbalances:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Autosomal dosage sensitivity}: Most genes tolerate small
  dosage changes (1.5x or 2x) without phenotype, but
  \textbf{dosage-sensitive genes} --- typically transcription factors,
  signaling components, and members of multi-protein complexes ---
  produce phenotypes when copy number changes. The \textbf{Williams
  syndrome} deletion (7q11.23) and its reciprocal duplication produce
  opposite cognitive-behavioral phenotypes precisely because of dosage
  sensitivity in the \emph{GTF2I} gene region.
\item
  \textbf{Gene balance hypothesis}: Genes whose products participate in
  stoichiometric complexes (e.g., ribosomal proteins, transcription
  complexes, RNA polymerases) cannot tolerate copy-number changes
  because subunit imbalance disrupts complex assembly. This explains why
  most autosomal monosomies are lethal even when the underlying gene
  mutations would not be.
\item
  \textbf{Compensatory feedback at promoters}: In \emph{Drosophila} and
  yeast, deletion of one allele of a dosage-sensitive gene often
  triggers transcriptional upregulation of the remaining allele,
  partially restoring protein levels (cis-compensation).
\item
  \textbf{microRNA buffering}: Individual miRNAs can buffer the
  expression of dozens of target genes against perturbation. The
  miR-17about 92 cluster, for example, buffers cell-cycle gene
  dosage during proliferation.
\item
  \textbf{Polycomb-mediated maintenance of dosage}: Active and inactive
  states established at gene clusters (Hox genes, the imprinted regions
  of chromosome 15) are maintained through cell division by Polycomb
  (silencing) and Trithorax (activation) complexes, ensuring stable gene
  dosage in each tissue.
\end{itemize}

The core insight is that \textbf{gene dosage is itself a regulated
variable}, defended by multiple parallel mechanisms. X-inactivation is
the most spectacular example because an entire chromosome is silenced,
but it is one strategy among many.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Calico Cats and X-Inactivation} The calico
coat pattern in cats is a visible demonstration of X-inactivation. The
\emph{O} gene (orange) is X-linked: \(X^O\) produces orange pigment;
\(X^o\) produces black pigment.
\hyperref[gl:heterozygous]{\textbf{Heterozygous}} females (\(X^OX^o\))
are mosaics -- patches of orange (cells with \(X^o\) inactivated) and
black (cells with \(X^O\) inactivated). White patches come from a
separate autosomal spotting gene. Nearly most calico cats are female;
rare calico males are usually 47,XXY (Klinefelter).
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{X-Linked Inheritance}\label{x-linked-inheritance}

\subsubsection{X-Linked Recessive
Inheritance}\label{x-linked-recessive-inheritance}

For X-linked recessive traits, males are affected more frequently
because they are hemizygous (a single X):

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Affected males}: \(X^aY\) -- one copy of the recessive allele
  is sufficient
\item
  \textbf{Affected females}: \(X^aX^a\) -- must be homozygous (very
  rare; requires carrier mother AND affected father)
\item
  \textbf{Carrier females}: \(X^AX^a\) -- phenotypically normal
  (usually); can show mosaic expression due to random X-inactivation
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Key X-linked recessive conditions:}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy and
\hyperref[gl:exon]{\textbf{Exon}} Skipping} The \emph{DMD} gene (2.4 Mb,
79 exons) is a frequent target of deletions. Out-of-frame deletions
cause Duchenne (no dystrophin); in-frame deletions cause Becker (partial
dystrophin). \textbf{Exon-skipping therapy} uses antisense
oligonucleotides (ASOs) to mask specific exons during splicing,
converting an out-of-frame deletion to an in-frame deletion (Duchenne to
Becker phenotype). \textbf{Eteplirsen} (FDA-approved 2016) targets exon
51; applicable to about 13\% of DMD patients. Newer ASOs target
other exons.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Linkage and Recombination}\label{linkage-and-recombination}

\subsubsection{Morgan's Experiments}\label{morgans-experiments}

Thomas Hunt Morgan (1910-1915) discovered that some genes do NOT assort
independently -- they are \textbf{linked} on the same chromosome.

In a testcross for body color (b: black recessive) and wing type (vg:
vestigial recessive) in \emph{Drosophila}:

\textbf{Expected (if unlinked)}: 1:1:1:1 ratio of four phenotype classes
\textbf{Observed}: Excess \textbf{parental types} (gray-normal,
black-vestigial) and deficiency of \textbf{recombinant types}
(gray-vestigial, black-normal)

This means b and vg are on the same chromosome, and \textbf{crossing
over} during meiosis generates recombinants at a frequency proportional
to the physical distance between the genes.

\subsubsection{Map Distance and Recombination
Frequency}\label{map-distance-and-recombination-frequency}

\textbf{Recombination frequency (RF)}:

\begin{equation}
RF = \frac{\text{number of recombinant offspring}}{\text{total offspring}} \times 100\%
\label{eq:unit_V_chromosomal_rf_definition}
\end{equation}

\textbf{Map distance} in centimorgans (cM): 1 cM = 1\% recombination
frequency.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  RF \textless{} 50\%: genes are \textbf{linked} (on the same
  chromosome)
\item
  RF = 50\%: genes are \textbf{unlinked} (on different chromosomes OR so
  far apart on the same chromosome that at least one crossover typically
  occurs between them)
\item
  RF can rarely exceed 50\% because a single crossover between two loci
  produces 50\% recombinant and 50\% parental gametes (two chromatids
  involved out of four)
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Three-Point Test Cross}\label{three-point-test-cross}

The three-point test cross determines the order of three linked genes
and the distances between them simultaneously. It is more efficient than
three separate two-point crosses and reveals \textbf{interference}.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Worked Example: 17.2: In \emph{Drosophila},
three linked genes on chromosome
2:}{Worked Example: 17.2: In Drosophila, three linked genes on chromosome 2:}}\label{worked-example-17.2-in-drosophila-three-linked-genes-on-chromosome-2}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  dp (dumpy wings): recessive
\item
  b (black body): recessive
\item
  cn (cinnabar eyes): recessive
\end{itemize}

A triply heterozygous female (dp+ b+ cn+ / dp b cn) is testcrossed to a
triply homozygous recessive male (dp b cn / dp b cn). The offspring are:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Phenotype class & Count & Classification \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
dp+ b+ cn+ & 350 & Parental \\
dp b cn & 345 & Parental \\
dp+ b cn & 62 & Single crossover (region II) \\
dp b+ cn+ & 58 & Single crossover (region II) \\
dp+ b+ cn & 40 & Single crossover (region I) \\
dp b cn+ & 38 & Single crossover (region I) \\
dp+ b cn+ & 5 & Double crossover \\
dp b+ cn & 2 & Double crossover \\
\textbf{Total} & \textbf{900} & \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Step 1: Determine gene order.} Compare the parental classes
(most frequent) to the double crossover classes (least frequent). The
gene that switches position in the double crossover class is the
\textbf{middle gene}.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Parental: dp+ b+ cn+; dp b cn
\item
  Double crossover: dp+ b cn+; dp b+ cn
\end{itemize}

The b gene has switched relative to dp and cn. Therefore, the gene order
is: \textbf{dp -- b -- cn} (b is in the middle).

\textbf{Step 2: Calculate map distances.}

\[\text{Distance dp-b} = \frac{40 + 38 + 5 + 2}{900} \times 100 = \frac{85}{900} \times 100 = 9.4 \text{ cM} \tag{17.1}\]

\[\text{Distance b-cn} = \frac{62 + 58 + 5 + 2}{900} \times 100 = \frac{127}{900} \times 100 = 14.1 \text{ cM} \tag{17.2}\]

\[\text{Total map distance dp-cn} = 9.4 + 14.1 = 23.5 \text{ cM} \tag{17.3}\]

\textbf{Step 3: Calculate interference.}

\[\text{Expected double crossovers} = 0.094 \times 0.141 \times 900 = 11.9 \tag{17.4}\]

\[\text{Observed double crossovers} = 5 + 2 = 7 \tag{17.5}\]

\[\text{Coefficient of coincidence (CoC)} = \frac{\text{observed}}{\text{expected}} = \frac{7}{11.9} = 0.59 \tag{17.6}\]

\[\text{Interference (I)} = 1 - \text{CoC} = 1 - 0.59 = 0.41 \tag{17.7}\]

An interference of 0.41 means that 41\% of expected double crossovers
did not occur -- a crossover in one region partially suppresses
crossovers in the adjacent region (\textbf{positive interference}).

\subsubsection{Mapping Functions}\label{mapping-functions}

Simple RF underestimates true genetic distance because multiple
crossovers between distant loci are undetectable (double crossovers
restore parental configuration).

\textbf{Haldane mapping function} (1919, assumes no chromatid
interference):

\begin{equation}
m = -\frac{1}{2}\ln(1 - 2\theta) \quad \text{(morgans)}
\label{eq:unit_V_chromosomal_haldane}
\end{equation}

where \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\theta}}{theta} = observed RF. As \(\theta \to 0.5\), \(m \to \infty\).

\textbf{Kosambi mapping function} (1944, accounts for positive chromatid
interference):

\begin{equation}
m = \frac{1}{4}\ln\left(\frac{1 + 2\theta}{1 - 2\theta}\right)
\label{eq:unit_V_chromosomal_kosambi}
\end{equation}

Kosambi's function better fits empirical data for moderate distances.

\subsubsection{LOD Score Analysis}\label{lod-score-analysis}

\textbf{LOD (logarithm of odds) score}: Statistical method for testing
linkage in human pedigrees (where controlled crosses are ethically
unfeasible).

\begin{equation}
LOD = \log_{10}\frac{L(\theta)}{L(\theta = 0.5)}
\label{eq:unit_V_chromosomal_lod}
\end{equation}

Where \(L(\theta)\) is the likelihood of the data given recombination
fraction \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\theta}}{theta}, and \(L(0.5)\) is the likelihood under no linkage.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{LOD \textgreater= 3}: Evidence for linkage (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\theta}}{theta} value estimates
  map distance)
\item
  \textbf{LOD \textless= -2}: Evidence against linkage
\item
  \textbf{-2 \textless{} LOD \textless{} 3}: Inconclusive
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Recombination Hotspots and Sex Differences in Map
Length}\label{recombination-hotspots-and-sex-differences-in-map-length}

Recombination is \textbf{not distributed uniformly} across the genome
--- it concentrates in narrow \textbf{hotspots} of about 1--2
kb separated by larger cold regions, and the total map length differs
sharply between male and female meiosis.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{PRDM9 and hotspots}: In humans and mice, the zinc-finger
  histone methyltransferase \textbf{PRDM9} binds specific DNA motifs and
  trimethylates H3K4 and H3K36 at the binding site, recruiting the
  meiotic double-strand break machinery (SPO11). Crossovers
  preferentially form at these PRDM9-marked sites. PRDM9 is itself
  rapidly evolving --- its zinc-finger array changes between populations
  and species, and \emph{Prdm9} knockout mice are sterile due to meiotic
  defects. \textbf{PRDM9 is one of very few genes implicated in
  mammalian speciation through hybrid sterility.}
\item
  \textbf{Hotspot rates}: Within hotspots, recombination rates can reach
  10--100\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} the genome-wide average. The \textbf{HLA region} on
  chromosome 6 contains some of the most active hotspots, contributing
  to the immense allelic diversity of MHC genes.
\item
  \textbf{Cold regions}: Centromeric and pericentric heterochromatin is
  recombination-suppressed, both because of structural constraints and
  because crossovers near centromeres can disrupt segregation.
  Recombination is also reduced near telomeres (in some species) and in
  regions of strong purifying selection.
\item
  \textbf{Sex differences in map length}: The female human genetic map
  is roughly \textbf{1.5--1.8\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} longer} than the male map
  (about 4,400 cM in females vs.~about 2,700 cM in
  males). This reflects more crossovers per meiosis in oogenesis
  (about 70 per cell) than spermatogenesis (about 50
  per cell), and dramatic regional differences --- recombination is
  enriched at telomeres in male meiosis (where obligate crossovers occur
  to ensure disjunction) and more uniformly distributed in female
  meiosis.
\item
  \textbf{Consequences}: Sex-specific maps must be used in linkage
  analysis when transmissions go through one sex predominantly. Large
  family genetic studies routinely report male, female, and sex-averaged
  maps separately.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Why do females have more
crossovers?}\label{why-do-females-have-more-crossovers}

The pronounced sex difference in recombination rate has several proposed
explanations, and most empirical studies suggest more than one is
operating simultaneously:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Oocyte time available}: Female meiosis includes a prolonged
  pachytene during which homolog pairing and crossover designation
  occur. Spermatogenesis is faster and may impose stricter checkpoints
  that limit crossover-pathway entry.
\item
  \textbf{Telomeric vs.~interstitial recombination}: Male meiosis
  enriches crossovers at telomeres because the \textbf{obligate
  crossover} rule (every bivalent must have at least one chiasma to
  segregate properly) is satisfied near chromosome ends, where pairing
  can complete in less time. Female meiosis has the time to distribute
  crossovers more uniformly, including in interstitial regions distant
  from telomeres.
\item
  \textbf{Selection for accuracy in oogenesis}: Because errors during
  the long oocyte arrest are catastrophic, female meiosis may have
  evolved higher recombination rates to ensure \textbf{at least one
  chiasma per bivalent}. Achiasmate bivalents segregate randomly,
  producing aneuploid gametes --- the female reproductive system
  tolerates this poorly because each oocyte represents irreplaceable
  investment.
\item
  \textbf{Sexually antagonistic selection on chromosome conformation}:
  Some authors propose that male and female germlines have different
  optima for genome stability, with selection acting in opposite
  directions on regulators of recombination.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Haldane's rule and
recombination}\label{haldanes-rule-and-recombination}

Haldane's classic 1922 observation extends beyond sex-determination
biology to recombination patterns: in many species the
\textbf{homogametic sex} (XX females in mammals; ZZ males in birds)
shows higher recombination rates than the heterogametic sex. In
\emph{Drosophila}, the asymmetry is extreme --- males have \textbf{no
meiotic recombination at most}, while females have normal
crossover-mediated recombination. In humans, the pattern is muted but
present, with females having about 1.6\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} the male map length.
The \textbf{achiasmate male meiosis} of \emph{Drosophila} and several
other dipterans is supported by alternative bivalent-tethering
mechanisms (the \emph{Mnm} complex) that maintain homolog pairing
without crossovers. The mammalian intermediate pattern reflects partial
achiasmatism --- males still recombine, but with reduced rate and biased
localization to telomeres. Why these sex differences evolved remains an
open question and is one of the most robust empirical generalizations in
the genetics of meiosis.

\begin{figure}[htbp]

\caption{Classification of chromosomal abnormalities. Numerical abnormalities include aneuploidy and polyploidy; structural abnormalities include deletions, duplications, inversions, and translocations.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Aneuploidy: Non-Disjunction in Meiosis I vs.~Meiosis
II}\label{aneuploidy-non-disjunction-in-meiosis-i-vs.-meiosis-ii}

\textbf{Non-disjunction} is the failure of chromosomes to separate
properly during cell division and is the principal source of human
aneuploidy \citep{hassold2001}. It can occur in either meiosis I or
meiosis II, and the two failure modes have \textbf{distinguishable
genetic signatures}.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0097_8b4bc56a0e9b.png}
\caption{Two distinct molecular failure modes of meiotic non-disjunction. MI errors produce trisomic gametes carrying both parental homologs; MII errors produce trisomic gametes carrying two sister copies of a single homolog. Centromere-region marker analysis distinguishes the two - clinically important because they have different mechanisms and risk factors.}
\end{figure}

This MI/MII distinction is clinically important because: -
\textbf{about 75\% of trisomy 21 cases originate in maternal
meiosis I} (the cohesin-decay mechanism described below). - Paternal
trisomy 21 (about 5--10\% of cases) is typically meiosis II in
origin. - Trisomy 18 has a higher proportion of MII errors than trisomy
21, suggesting different mechanistic pressures.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0098_208a090d4b71.png}
\caption{The cohesin-decay model of the maternal age effect. Female oocytes enter MI prophase before birth and remain arrested for decades. Loss of cohesin during this prolonged arrest weakens chromosome cohesion, producing exponentially rising non-disjunction risk with maternal age.}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Quantitative model of the maternal age
curve}\label{quantitative-model-of-the-maternal-age-curve}

The empirical risk of trisomy 21 with maternal age is well fit by an
exponential function:

\begin{equation}
P(\text{T21} \mid \text{age } a) \approx P_0 \, e^{k(a - a_0)}
\label{eq:unit_V_maternal_age_risk}
\end{equation}

with \(P_0 \approx 6.7 \times 10^{-4}\) at age \(a_0 = 20\) and
\(k \approx 0.18\) per year for ages 30--45. This corresponds to a
\textbf{doubling of risk every about 4 years} in the late 30s
and early 40s. Between ages 45 and 49, the curve rises even more steeply
as the oocyte pool nears exhaustion. Because the underlying mechanism
--- cohesin decay during dictyate arrest --- accumulates throughout
reproductive life, the exponential form reflects compounding error rates
per oocyte rather than a sudden threshold. Reproductive endocrinology
uses this curve to set screening recommendations; many countries trigger
non-invasive prenatal testing offers automatically at maternal ages
above 35.

Approximately 90\% of trisomy 21 conceptions and 99\% of trisomy 18
conceptions arise in maternal meiosis; paternal contributions are minor.
The asymmetry reflects the fundamental difference between oogenesis
(limited oocyte pool, decades-long arrest, gradual cohesin decay) and
spermatogenesis (continuous stem-cell division, no arrest, robust
quality control through germ-cell apoptosis).

\subsubsection{Structural Chromosomal Rearrangements: Detailed
Survey}\label{structural-chromosomal-rearrangements-detailed-survey}

Beyond losses and gains of whole chromosomes, \textbf{structural
rearrangements} cause a wide range of human disease. Each rearrangement
type has characteristic mechanisms and clinical signatures.

\paragraph{Translocations}\label{translocations}

A \textbf{translocation} is an exchange of chromosomal material between
non-homologous chromosomes. Two major classes exist.

\textbf{Reciprocal translocations} exchange segments between two
non-homologous chromosomes. Carriers of \emph{balanced} reciprocal
translocations usually retain full genetic dosage --- just rearranged
--- and are typically phenotypically normal. However, their gametes face
severe segregation problems at meiosis I: the four chromosomes involved
must form a quadrivalent at metaphase I, and \textbf{alternate
segregation} produces balanced gametes (about 50\% of meioses).
\textbf{Adjacent-1 and adjacent-2 segregation} produces unbalanced
gametes, leading to recurrent miscarriage (10--25\% per pregnancy) and a
1--10\% risk of an unbalanced live-born child.

\textbf{The Philadelphia Chromosome --- A Cancer Paradigm}:

The \textbf{t(9;22)(q34;q11.2)} reciprocal translocation fuses the
\textbf{BCR} gene (chromosome 22) to the \textbf{ABL1} gene (chromosome
9), creating the \textbf{BCR-ABL1} fusion gene on the derivative
chromosome 22 (the Philadelphia chromosome,
\hyperref[gl:ph]{\textbf{pH}}).

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{BCR-ABL1} encodes a constitutively active tyrosine kinase (210
  kDa in CML; 190 kDa in Philadelphia-positive acute lymphoblastic
  leukaemia)
\item
  Activates RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT, and JAK/STAT signaling -- driving
  uncontrolled proliferation
\item
  \textbf{Imatinib (Gleevec)}: ATP-competitive inhibitor of BCR-ABL1
  tyrosine kinase domain

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    CML 5-year survival: about 30\% (pre-imatinib) to
    \textgreater90\% (post-imatinib)
  \item
    Resistance mutations (e.g., T315I ``gatekeeper'' mutation)
    necessitated second-generation (dasatinib, nilotinib) and
    third-generation (ponatinib) inhibitors
  \item
    \textbf{Asciminib}: First
    \hyperref[gl:allosteric]{\textbf{allosteric}} BCR-ABL1 inhibitor
    (binds myristoyl pocket, not ATP site); approved 2021
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

The Philadelphia chromosome story is one of the great triumphs of
molecular targeted therapy: a structural rearrangement \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} a fusion
oncogene \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} a kinase domain \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} a small-molecule drug \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} a chronic disease
that is no longer fatal for most patients.

\textbf{Robertsonian translocations} fuse two acrocentric chromosomes
(chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21, 22 in humans) at their centromeres,
producing one large derivative chromosome and losing the small short
arms. Carriers have 45 chromosomes but a normal genome content (the lost
short arms contain primarily ribosomal RNA gene clusters, present in
multiple copies elsewhere). The clinical consequence appears in
offspring: a Robertsonian carrier can produce gametes with two copies of
one chromosome, leading to trisomic offspring. \textbf{Robertsonian
translocation t(14;21) is the cause of approximately 4\% of Down
syndrome cases}, with a recurrence risk of 10--15\% (much higher than
the population rate of about 1/700) --- making karyotype
analysis essential for genetic counseling of recurrent Down syndrome
families.

\paragraph{Worked Example 17.3: Robertsonian translocation
segregation}\label{worked-example-17.3-robertsonian-translocation-segregation}

A phenotypically normal woman has a Robertsonian translocation
rob(14;21), giving her a karyotype 45,XX,rob(14;21). At meiosis, the
trivalent formed by chromosome 14, chromosome 21, and the rob(14;21)
derivative can segregate in \textbf{six} different ways, producing six
possible gamete types --- three balanced and three unbalanced:

The empirical recurrence risk of Down syndrome from a maternal
rob(14;21) carrier is \textbf{10--15\%} --- far below the theoretical
1/3 viable expectation because most monosomic and trisomy-14 conceptuses
miscarry early, and because adjacent segregation patterns are not
equally likely. \textbf{For a paternal carrier} the recurrence risk is
much lower (about 1--2\%), because sperm with unbalanced
chromosome content are largely incapable of fertilization (sperm
selection effects). This sex difference in recurrence --- same
translocation, 10\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} different risk depending on the parent of origin ---
is one of the most clinically important consequences of male versus
female meiotic biology and dramatically affects genetic counseling.

\paragraph{Inversions}\label{inversions}

An \textbf{inversion} is a chromosomal segment that has been reversed
end-to-end. Two types exist based on whether the centromere is included.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Pericentric inversions} include the centromere; the inverted
  segment spans both arms.
\item
  \textbf{Paracentric inversions} are confined to one arm; the
  centromere is outside the inverted region.
\end{itemize}

Like balanced reciprocal translocations, inversion carriers are
typically phenotypically normal. The clinical problem arises in meiosis:
to pair correctly with the non-inverted homolog, the inverted segment
must form an \textbf{inversion loop}. Crossovers within the loop produce
unbalanced gametes:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Pericentric inversions}: Crossovers inside the loop generate
  gametes with duplications and deficiencies (and corresponding
  live-born offspring with congenital abnormalities). Recurrence risk
  depends on inversion size and crossover frequency, ranging from 1\% to
  15\%.
\item
  \textbf{Paracentric inversions}: Crossovers inside the loop generate
  dicentric and acentric chromosomes that are typically lost during
  meiosis or early embryonic development; consequently, paracentric
  inversion carriers have higher rates of miscarriage but lower rates of
  liveborn unbalanced offspring than pericentric inversion carriers.
\item
  \textbf{Inversion 9} is a common pericentric inversion
  (about 1\% of Europeans) that is generally considered a
  normal variant --- though some studies suggest mildly elevated risk
  for recurrent pregnancy loss.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Deletion Syndromes}\label{deletion-syndromes}

\textbf{Deletions} remove chromosomal material and produce
\textbf{haploinsufficiency} --- one functional copy is not enough for
normal function. Some classic deletion syndromes:

\textbf{DiGeorge / 22q11.2 deletion syndrome} deserves special attention
as one of the most common microdeletion syndromes and a paradigm for
\textbf{contiguous gene syndromes} --- phenotypes resulting from
haploinsufficiency of multiple adjacent genes simultaneously. The
deletion is typically caused by \textbf{non-allelic homologous
recombination (NAHR)} between low-copy repeats (LCRs) flanking the
region. Within the deleted region, \textbf{TBX1} is the key driver of
cardiac and craniofacial features; other deleted genes contribute to
immune, neurological, and behavioral phenotypes. The 22q11.2 deletion
confers an approximately 25-fold increased risk of schizophrenia, making
it one of the strongest known genetic risk factors for psychotic
illness.

\textbf{Cri-du-chat syndrome} (5p deletion) was first described in 1963
by Jérôme Lejeune (who had identified trisomy 21 four years earlier).
The distinctive cat-like cry in infancy results from laryngeal cartilage
abnormalities. Survival to adulthood is common but with severe
intellectual disability requiring lifelong care.

\paragraph{Duplications}\label{duplications}

Duplications (extra copies of chromosomal segments) typically produce
\textbf{gain-of-function} phenotypes --- opposite to deletions. Many
duplication syndromes are reciprocal to known deletion syndromes:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{22q11.2 duplication syndrome}: Reciprocal to DiGeorge. Highly
  variable, often mild; some carriers are phenotypically normal.
\item
  \textbf{Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A}: Duplication of 17p11.2
  containing \emph{PMP22} causes peripheral neuropathy through PMP22
  overexpression.
\item
  \textbf{MECP2 duplication syndrome} (Xq28): Severe intellectual
  disability and recurrent infections; reciprocal to Rett syndrome
  (caused by \emph{MECP2} loss-of-function mutations in girls).
\end{itemize}

The reciprocal relationship between deletion and duplication phenotypes
confirms gene dosage as the proximate cause and reinforces the
dosage-sensitivity principle developed in the chromosomal-rearrangements
section.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Prenatal Screening for Chromosomal
Abnormalities} \textbf{Cell-free fetal DNA (cfDNA) testing} (NIPT --
non-invasive prenatal testing): Analyzes fetal DNA fragments circulating
in maternal blood (from about 10 weeks gestation). Detects
trisomies 21, 18, 13 and sex chromosome aneuploidies with
\textgreater99\% sensitivity and \textgreater99.5\% specificity for
trisomy 21. Has largely replaced first-trimester combined screening
(nuchal translucency + biochemical markers) as the primary screening
tool. Diagnostic confirmation still requires amniocentesis or chorionic
villus sampling (CVS) for karyotyping or chromosomal microarray.
\textbf{Chromosomal microarray (CMA)} is now the first-line test for
fetal abnormalities or developmental delay, detecting copy-number
changes at sub-megabase resolution.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Genomic Imprinting and Uniparental
Disomy}\label{genomic-imprinting-and-uniparental-disomy}

Mendel's laws assume that the phenotypic effect of an allele is
\textbf{independent of which parent transmitted it}. For most loci this
is true. But about 100--200 human genes show \textbf{genomic
imprinting} --- they are expressed from a single parental allele, with
the other allele silenced by parent-of-origin-specific epigenetic marks
(methylation, chromatin) established during gametogenesis
(\cref{sec:unit_IV_epigenetics_and_gene_regulation}).

\subsubsection{The principle of
imprinting}\label{the-principle-of-imprinting}

For an imprinted gene: - A maternally-imprinted (paternally-expressed)
gene contributes primarily the paternal allele to the offspring's
expression. - A paternally-imprinted (maternally-expressed) gene
contributes primarily the maternal allele. - The ``silent'' allele is
not deleted --- it carries methylation marks acquired during egg or
sperm formation that are preserved through embryogenesis.

This violates Mendel's assumption because the phenotype now depends on
\textbf{which parent contributed which allele}, even at otherwise
equivalent loci.

\subsubsection{Canonical imprinted
regions}\label{canonical-imprinted-regions}

\subsubsection{Mechanisms causing imprinting
disorders}\label{mechanisms-causing-imprinting-disorders}

Imprinting disorders arise through several distinct mechanisms --- and a
key clinical insight is that \textbf{the underlying mutation type is
independent of the disease phenotype}, which depends primarily on
whether the active parental allele is present:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Deletion of the active allele} (about 70--75\% of
  Prader-Willi and Angelman cases). A microdeletion of 15q11-q13 on the
  paternally inherited chromosome causes Prader-Willi; the same
  microdeletion on the maternally inherited chromosome causes Angelman.
  The deletion is identical at the DNA level --- the disease depends on
  which parent transmitted it.
\item
  \textbf{Uniparental disomy (UPD)} (about 25\% of
  Prader-Willi, about 5\% of Angelman cases). Both copies of
  chromosome 15 are inherited from one parent. Maternal UPD15 (no
  paternal contribution) causes Prader-Willi; paternal UPD15 (no
  maternal contribution) causes Angelman. UPD usually arises through
  \textbf{trisomy rescue} --- a trisomic conceptus loses one chromosome
  to revert to disomy; if the lost chromosome was from the parent with a
  single copy, the result is UPD.

  \textbf{Isodisomy vs.~heterodisomy.} UPD comes in two genetically
  distinct flavors that depend on \emph{when} the meiotic error
  occurred:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{Heterodisomy} --- both inherited copies derive from
    \textbf{different homologs} of the parent (the two copies are
    heterozygous for parental polymorphisms). Heterodisomy arises from
    \textbf{meiosis I non-disjunction} followed by trisomy rescue. The
    two homologs of one parent are inherited together, and the offspring
    is heterozygous at centromeric markers from that parent.
  \item
    \textbf{Isodisomy} --- both inherited copies are \textbf{identical}
    sister-chromatid copies of a single parental homolog. Isodisomy
    arises from \textbf{meiosis II non-disjunction} plus trisomy rescue,
    or from a postzygotic mitotic error. The offspring is
    \textbf{homozygous along the entire chromosome} for the
    parent-of-origin's allele.
  \end{itemize}

  Isodisomy is clinically important because it can \textbf{unmask
  recessive alleles}: if the contributing parent is a carrier for a
  recessive disease on the affected chromosome, isodisomy produces
  homozygosity for the recessive allele and the offspring is affected
  --- even though a single parent was a carrier. Documented examples
  include cystic fibrosis from maternal isodisomy 7 and rod monochromacy
  from paternal isodisomy 14. Mixed UPD (heterodisomy at the centromere
  with isodisomic distal regions) reflects a meiosis I error followed by
  a crossover; the relative proportions of iso- and heterodisomic
  regions trace the meiotic crossover that occurred in the parent's
  germline.
\item
  \textbf{Imprinting center mutations} (about 1--2\% of cases).
  Mutations in the imprinting control regions disrupt the establishment
  or maintenance of methylation marks, producing functional UPD without
  sequence changes elsewhere.
\item
  \textbf{\emph{UBE3A} point mutations} (about 10\% of Angelman
  cases). Mutations in the \emph{UBE3A} gene itself, which is expressed
  primarily from the maternal allele in neurons, cause Angelman
  syndrome.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Connection to chromosome
behavior}\label{connection-to-chromosome-behavior}

The imprinting story directly connects molecular biology (DNA
methylation), gametogenesis (where parent-of-origin marks are
established), meiosis (where non-disjunction can produce UPD via trisomy
rescue), and clinical genetics (where the same chromosomal lesion
produces different diseases depending on parental origin). For details
on the establishment and erasure of imprinting marks during germline
development, see \cref{sec:unit_IV_epigenetics_and_gene_regulation}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Why Both Parents Are Needed} Imprinting
explains why mammalian parthenogenesis (development from an unfertilized
egg) and androgenesis (development from sperm primarily) fail. Mouse
experiments combining two pronuclei from one parent --- gynogenetic
embryos with two maternal pronuclei or androgenetic embryos with two
paternal pronuclei --- fail at distinct embryonic stages, demonstrating
that \textbf{maternal and paternal genomes are not interchangeable}.
Imprinted genes have evolved to enforce biparental contribution in
mammalian reproduction.
\end{quote}

\textbf{Concept Check 17.3}

\begin{quote}
\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  A trisomy 21 fetus inherits two centromeric markers from the mother
  --- one identical to grandmother's and one identical to grandfather's
  --- and one paternal centromere. Was the non-disjunction event in
  maternal meiosis I or maternal meiosis II? Explain.
\item
  Using \cref{eq:unit_V_maternal_age_risk} with
  \(P_0 = 6.7 \times 10^{-4}\), \(a_0 = 20\), and \(k = 0.18\), estimate
  the trisomy 21 risk at maternal age 38. How does it compare to age 28?
\item
  A child with cystic fibrosis is born to a mother known to be a CFTR
  carrier and a father whose CFTR sequencing shows two wild-type alleles
  (paternity confirmed). What chromosomal mechanism could explain the
  diagnosis, and what kind of UPD would it require?
\item
  Why does \emph{Drosophila} hyper-transcribe the single male X
  (MOF/MSL) while \emph{C. elegans} halves transcription of both XX
  hermaphrodite chromosomes (DCC), yet mammals silence one X (XIST)?
  What general biological problem do most three solve?
\end{enumerate}
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Recombination Mapping: Physical vs.~Genetic
Distance}\label{recombination-mapping-physical-vs.-genetic-distance}

\textbf{Genetic distance} (cM) does not always correspond linearly to
\textbf{physical distance} (Mb):

\begin{equation}
1 \text{ cM} \approx 1 \text{ Mb (genome-wide average in humans)}
\label{eq:unit_V_chromosomal_cm_to_mb}
\end{equation}

However, this ratio varies dramatically: - \textbf{Hotspots}:
Recombination rates can be 10-100x the average in small regions
(about 1-2 kb); determined by PRDM9 protein (zinc finger domain
recognizes specific DNA motifs) - \textbf{Coldspots}: Centromeric and
heterochromatic regions have very low recombination - \textbf{Sex
differences}: Female genetic maps are about 1.5-1.8x longer
than male maps (more crossovers in female meiosis)

\textbf{Concept Check 17.4}

\begin{quote}

\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  From a three-point testcross of 1\{,\}000 progeny you score 440 + 435
  parentals, 48 + 45 single crossovers in one region, 14 + 12 single
  crossovers in the other, and 4 + 2 double crossovers: use the
  double-crossover class to fix the gene order, then compute both map
  distances and explain why the directly summed parental-to-parental
  distance underestimates the true physical separation.
\end{enumerate}
\end{quote}

\subsection{Inbreeding and the Inbreeding
Coefficient}\label{inbreeding-and-the-inbreeding-coefficient}

\subsubsection{The Inbreeding Coefficient
(F)}\label{the-inbreeding-coefficient-f}

The \textbf{inbreeding coefficient (F)} is the probability that an
individual has two alleles at a locus that are identical by descent
(IBD) -- inherited from the same ancestral allele through both parents.

\textbf{Calculation for offspring of first-cousin mating}:

First cousins share one pair of grandparents. For a specific rare
recessive allele (frequency q) in one grandparent:

\begin{equation}
F = \frac{1}{16} = 0.0625 \quad \text{(for first-cousin offspring)}
\label{eq:unit_V_chromosomal_F_first_cousin}
\end{equation}

\textbf{General formula using path coefficients} \citep{wright1922}:

\begin{equation}
F = \sum\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{n_1 + n_2 + 1}
\label{eq:unit_V_chromosomal_F_path}
\end{equation}

where \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) are the number of links from one parent to the
common ancestor and from the common ancestor to the other parent, summed
over most paths through most common ancestors.

\subsubsection{Consequences of
Inbreeding}\label{consequences-of-inbreeding}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Increased homozygosity}: \(F\) proportion of loci become
  homozygous beyond random expectation
\item
  \textbf{Exposure of recessive alleles}: Rare deleterious recessive
  alleles are more likely to become homozygous
\item
  \textbf{Inbreeding depression}: Reduced fitness (fertility, viability)
  in inbred populations
\item
  \textbf{Examples}: Amish (Ellis-van Creveld syndrome, 1/5,000
  vs.~1/200,000 in general population due to
  \hyperref[gl:founder-effect]{\textbf{founder effect}} +
  consanguinity); Finnish disease heritage (36 rare diseases enriched in
  Finland due to founder effects)
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Consanguinity and Genetic Disease} In
populations where consanguineous marriage is common (parts of Middle
East, South Asia, North Africa: 20-50\% of marriages are
consanguineous), the incidence of autosomal recessive disorders is
significantly elevated. First-cousin offspring have about 6-8\%
risk of congenital abnormality (vs.~about 2-3\% in outbred
populations). Genetic counseling and carrier screening programs are
important in these communities.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Worked Example: Linkage
Analysis}\label{worked-example-linkage-analysis}

\textbf{Problem}: In a testcross, the following offspring are observed
from a female heterozygous for three linked genes (A, B, C) crossed with
a homozygous recessive male:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Class & Phenotype & Count \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
1 & A B C & 412 \\
2 & a b c & 405 \\
3 & A b C & 82 \\
4 & a B c & 78 \\
5 & A B c & 32 \\
6 & a b C & 28 \\
7 & A b c & 3 \\
8 & a B C & 2 \\
Total & & 1,042 \\
\end{longtable}
}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  Determine gene order.
\end{enumerate}

Parental classes: 1 and 2 (most frequent); DCO classes: 7 and 8 (least
frequent).

Compare: Parental = A B C / a b c; DCO = A b c / a B C.

The \textbf{B} gene has switched relative to A and C. Gene order:
\textbf{A -- B -- C}.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  Calculate map distances.
\end{enumerate}

\[d_{A-B} = \frac{82 + 78 + 3 + 2}{1042} \times 100 = \frac{165}{1042} \times 100 = 15.8 \text{ cM} \tag{17.8}\]

\[d_{B-C} = \frac{32 + 28 + 3 + 2}{1042} \times 100 = \frac{65}{1042} \times 100 = 6.2 \text{ cM} \tag{17.9}\]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\tightlist
\item
  Calculate interference.
\end{enumerate}

\[\text{Expected DCO} = 0.158 \times 0.062 \times 1042 = 10.2 \tag{17.10}\]

\[\text{CoC} = \frac{5}{10.2} = 0.49; \quad I = 1 - 0.49 = 0.51 \tag{17.11}\]

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-19}

For \textbf{Chromosomal Inheritance and Linkage}, frontier biology
belongs inside the evidence logic of the chapter. Classical genetics
remains essential, but modern interpretation adds penetrance,
polygenicity, structural variation, ancestry-aware inference, and
uncertainty in risk prediction. The core reading question is this:
chromosome-scale inheritance depends on recombination, segregation,
structural variation, and dosage compensation.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

A good genetics answer separates the Mendelian transmission model from
the evidence needed to use it in a population, family, or clinical
setting.

\textbf{Source practice:} For inheritance and population claims,
separate the model assumptions from sampling, ancestry representation,
penetrance, linkage, and environment.

\subsubsection{Structural Variation, Consent, and Chromosome-Scale
Counseling}\label{structural-variation-consent-and-chromosome-scale-counseling}

Chromosome-scale inheritance is clinically useful because it links a
visible or sequenced rearrangement to a reproductive risk. It is also
easy to overstate. Karyotypes, chromosomal microarrays, short-read
sequencing, long-read sequencing, and graph-reference alignment see
different classes of variation: balanced translocations, copy-number
variants, repeat expansions, inversions, and complex rearrangements can
move between visible cytogenetics and sequence-level evidence. The Human
Pangenome Reference highlights why a single linear reference can miss or
misrepresent variants carried by under-sampled ancestries
\citep{humanpangenome2023}.

For prenatal, carrier, or infertility testing, the counseling note
should name the assay and its blind spots, distinguish screening from
diagnosis, state whether a variant is pathogenic or uncertain, and
explain family implications without treating relatives as automatic
research subjects. Consent and data-retention language matter because
chromosomal findings can expose non-paternity, consanguinity, incidental
adult-onset risks, or information relevant to relatives who did not
choose testing.

\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-19}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Chromosome theory}: \citet{sutton1902} proposed chromosomes
  carry genes; Morgan proved this with X-linked \emph{white} in
  \emph{Drosophila}.
\item
  \textbf{Chromosome architecture}: Centromeres (CENP-A,
  alpha-satellite, kinetochore docking), telomeres (TTAGGG, shelterin,
  telomerase), and the heterochromatin/euchromatin distinction shape
  both mechanics and expression.
\item
  \textbf{Meiosis vs.~mitosis}: A two-division reductional/equational
  program with synapsis, crossing over, and reductional segregation at
  MI is the cellular basis of Mendel's laws.
\item
  \textbf{Sex determination}: XX/XY (mammals, SRY gene), ZW/ZZ (birds),
  XO (grasshoppers), haplodiploidy (hymenoptera), temperature-dependent
  (reptiles).
\item
  \textbf{X-inactivation}: Lyon hypothesis (1961); XIST RNA coats Xi;
  Polycomb-mediated H3K27me3; DNA methylation; Barr body.
  about 15\% of genes escape.
\item
  \textbf{Dosage compensation}: X-inactivation in mammals, MSL
  upregulation in \emph{Drosophila}, DCC downregulation in \emph{C.
  elegans}; broader principles include autosomal dosage sensitivity,
  gene-balance constraints, miRNA buffering, and Polycomb maintenance.
\item
  \textbf{X-linked recessive inheritance}: Males affected
  \textgreater\textgreater{} females; no male-to-male transmission;
  carrier mothers pass to 50\% of sons.
\item
  \textbf{Linkage and recombination}: RF \textless{} 50\% indicates
  linkage; 1 cM \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 1\% recombination; three-point cross determines gene
  order and detects interference; Haldane and Kosambi mapping functions
  correct for undetected double crossovers; PRDM9 directs hotspots;
  female maps are about 1.5--1.8\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} longer than male maps.
\item
  \textbf{Non-disjunction}: MI errors produce trisomies inheriting both
  parental homologs; MII errors produce trisomies inheriting two sister
  copies of one homolog. The cohesin-decay model explains the maternal
  age effect.
\item
  \textbf{Chromosomal abnormalities}: Aneuploidy from non-disjunction
  (trisomies 21, 18, 13; Turner 45,X; Klinefelter 47,XXY); structural
  rearrangements include reciprocal and Robertsonian translocations
  (Philadelphia chromosome \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} BCR-ABL1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} CML), pericentric and
  paracentric inversions, deletion syndromes (DiGeorge 22q11.2,
  Cri-du-chat 5p, Williams 7q11.23, Wolf-Hirschhorn 4p), and reciprocal
  duplication syndromes.
\item
  \textbf{Imprinting and uniparental disomy}: about 100--200
  imprinted human genes; deletion of an expressed allele, UPD via
  trisomy rescue, imprinting-center mutations, or \emph{UBE3A} point
  mutations most cause Prader-Willi or Angelman depending on parental
  origin.
\item
  \textbf{Inbreeding}: F = probability of identity by descent; increases
  homozygosity; exposes recessive alleles; inbreeding depression.
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See
  \cref{sec:unit_IV_dna_replication_and_cell_cycle} for meiosis errors,
  \cref{sec:unit_V_population_genetics} for \(F_{ST}\) and drift, and
  \cref{sec:unit_IV_epigenetics_and_gene_regulation} for imprinting
  disorders.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Key Terms}\label{key-terms-19}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Chromosome theory of heredity} -- genes are located on
  chromosomes; chromosomal behavior in meiosis explains Mendelian laws
\item
  \textbf{Centromere} -- chromosomal region holding sister chromatids;
  site of kinetochore assembly; CENP-A defines identity epigenetically
\item
  \textbf{Telomere} -- terminal TTAGGG repeats bound by shelterin;
  protected by telomerase in stem and germ cells
\item
  \textbf{Heterochromatin} -- densely packed, transcriptionally silenced
  chromatin; constitutive vs.~facultative
\item
  \textbf{SRY} -- sex-determining region Y; master switch for male
  development in mammals
\item
  \textbf{X-inactivation} -- silencing of one X chromosome in female
  somatic cells for dosage compensation
\item
  \textbf{XIST} -- long non-coding RNA that coats and silences the
  inactive X chromosome
\item
  \textbf{Barr body} -- condensed, transcriptionally inactive X
  chromosome visible at nuclear periphery
\item
  \textbf{Hemizygous} -- having a single copy of a gene (e.g., X-linked
  genes in males)
\item
  \textbf{Linkage} -- tendency of genes on the same chromosome to be
  inherited together
\item
  \textbf{Recombination frequency (RF)} -- proportion of recombinant
  offspring; measure of genetic distance
\item
  \textbf{Centimorgan (cM)} -- unit of genetic distance; 1 cM = 1\%
  recombination frequency
\item
  \textbf{Three-point test cross} -- cross using three linked markers to
  determine gene order and distances simultaneously
\item
  \textbf{Interference} -- suppression of nearby crossovers; I = 1 -
  coefficient of coincidence
\item
  \textbf{PRDM9} -- zinc-finger histone methyltransferase that directs
  meiotic recombination hotspots
\item
  \textbf{Non-disjunction} -- failure of chromosomes to separate during
  meiosis, leading to aneuploidy
\item
  \textbf{Aneuploidy} -- abnormal chromosome number (monosomy, trisomy)
\item
  \textbf{Reciprocal translocation} -- exchange of segments between two
  non-homologous chromosomes
\item
  \textbf{Robertsonian translocation} -- centromeric fusion of two
  acrocentric chromosomes
\item
  \textbf{Pericentric inversion} -- inversion that includes the
  centromere
\item
  \textbf{Paracentric inversion} -- inversion confined to one chromosome
  arm
\item
  \textbf{Philadelphia chromosome} -- t(9;22) translocation producing
  BCR-ABL1 fusion; hallmark of CML
\item
  \textbf{Inbreeding coefficient (F)} -- probability that two alleles at
  a locus are identical by descent
\item
  \textbf{LOD score} -- statistical measure of evidence for genetic
  linkage in pedigrees
\item
  \textbf{Pseudoautosomal region} -- segments at X and Y chromosome tips
  that recombine during male meiosis
\item
  \textbf{Dosage compensation} -- mechanism equalizing X-linked gene
  expression between XX and XY individuals
\item
  \textbf{Uniparental disomy (UPD)} -- both copies of a chromosome
  inherited from one parent; cause of imprinting disorders via trisomy
  rescue
\item
  \textbf{Genomic imprinting} -- parent-of-origin-specific expression
  resulting from gametic methylation marks
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-20}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Define \hyperref[gl:allele]{\textbf{allele}} frequency, genotype
  frequency, and \hyperref[gl:gene]{\textbf{gene}} pool.
\item
  State the Hardy-Weinberg \citep{weinberg1908} principle, derive the
  equilibrium equation, and list most five assumptions.
\item
  Apply \hyperref[gl:hardy-weinberg-equilibrium]{\textbf{Hardy-Weinberg
  equilibrium}}
  (Equationabout \eqref{eq:population_genetics_1}) to
  calculate carrier frequencies and estimate disease prevalence.
\item
  Test a population for HWE using the chi-squared test.
\item
  Describe \hyperref[gl:natural-selection]{\textbf{natural selection}}:
  fitness, selection coefficient, dominance coefficient, and types of
  selection.
\item
  Calculate allele frequency change under selection and predict
  equilibrium conditions for balancing selection.
\item
  Explain \hyperref[gl:genetic-drift]{\textbf{genetic drift}}, effective
  population size, bottleneck and
  \hyperref[gl:founder-effect]{\textbf{founder effect}}s.
\item
  Describe gene flow and its effects on population differentiation
  (Fst).
\item
  Apply \hyperref[gl:mutation]{\textbf{mutation}}-selection balance to
  estimate equilibrium frequencies.
\item
  Explain the \hyperref[gl:neutral-theory]{\textbf{neutral theory}} of
  molecular evolution, Ka/Ks ratios, and coalescent theory.
\item
  Use \hyperref[gl:molecular-clock]{\textbf{molecular clock}} methods to
  estimate divergence times.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Opening Vignette --- Algebra, Moths, and the Mathematics of
Populations}

In 1908, a cricket enthusiast named G.H. Hardy --- then England's most
distinguished pure mathematician --- was irritated by a biologist's
claim that \hyperref[gl:dominant]{\textbf{dominant}} alleles
automatically increase in frequency over time. Hardy spent an afternoon
at the cricket match and, in a brief letter to \emph{Science}, produced
the algebraic proof that in the absence of disturbing forces, allele
frequencies remain constant generation after generation. A German
physician, Wilhelm Weinberg, had independently derived the same
principle. The Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium became the null hypothesis of
\hyperref[gl:population-genetics]{\textbf{population genetics}} --- and
its deviations became the heartbeat of evolutionary biology. Nowhere is
this better illustrated than the peppered moth (\emph{Biston betularia})
during England's Industrial Revolution: pollution blackened tree bark,
shifting the population from mostly pale moths to mostly dark (melanic)
ones within decades --- textbook natural selection altering allele
frequencies in real time.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Chapter Roadmap}\label{chapter-roadmap-6}

The chapter is long because it bridges three levels of time and scale
--- read it as a narrowing lens:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{The Hardy-Weinberg null model.} Alleles, genotype frequencies,
  the equilibrium theorem and its assumptions; \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\chi}}{chi}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2} tests of fit.
\item
  \textbf{Four forces that perturb it.} Selection, drift, gene flow, and
  mutation. Each is a named violation of an HWE assumption.
\item
  \textbf{Consequences at the \hyperref[gl:genome]{\textbf{genome}}
  scale.} Neutral theory and molecular evolution, F-statistics and
  population structure, coalescent theory and molecular clocks.
\end{itemize}

If you are reading for the core Mendelian-genetics course, prioritise
the Hardy-Weinberg model and the four evolutionary forces. The
genome-scale extensions connect population genetics to molecular
evolution (Unit VI) and are helpful but optional.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth]{../figures/genetic_drift_trajectories.png}
\caption{Wright--Fisher genetic-drift trajectories for the same starting allele frequency under three effective population sizes. Smaller populations show larger stochastic swings and faster approach to fixation or loss.}
\label{fig:unit_V_genetic_drift_trajectories}
\end{figure}

\subsection{The Gene Pool}\label{the-gene-pool}

A \textbf{population} is a group of individuals of the same species
living in the same area at the same time and that interbreed. The
\textbf{gene pool} is the population's allele set across loci.

\subsubsection{Allele and Genotype
Frequencies}\label{allele-and-genotype-frequencies}

For a biallelic locus with alleles A (frequency \(p\)) and a (frequency
\(q\)):

\begin{equation}
p + q = 1
\label{eq:population_genetics_1}
\end{equation}

\textbf{Calculating allele frequencies from genotype counts:}

Given \(N\) total diploid individuals with \(N_{AA}\) homozygous
dominant, \(N_{Aa}\) \hyperref[gl:heterozygous]{\textbf{heterozygous}},
and \(N_{aa}\) homozygous recessive:

\begin{equation}
p = \frac{2N_{AA} + N_{Aa}}{2N}
\label{eq:population_genetics_2}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
q = \frac{2N_{aa} + N_{Aa}}{2N}
\label{eq:population_genetics_3}
\end{equation}

\textbf{Genotype frequencies:}

\begin{equation}
F_{AA} + F_{Aa} + F_{aa} = 1
\label{eq:population_genetics_4}
\end{equation}

Note that allele frequencies can be calculated from genotype frequencies
but not vice versa (without additional assumptions), because different
combinations of genotype frequencies can yield the same allele
frequencies.

\subsection{Worked Example: 18.1: In a population of 1,000 individuals:
360 AA, 480 Aa, 160
aa.}\label{worked-example-18.1-in-a-population-of-1000-individuals-360-aa-480-aa-160-aa.}

\begin{equation}
p = \frac{2(360) + 480}{2(1000)} = \frac{1200}{2000} = 0.60
\label{eq:population_genetics_5}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
q = \frac{2(160) + 480}{2(1000)} = \frac{800}{2000} = 0.40
\label{eq:population_genetics_6}
\end{equation}

Check: \(p + q = 0.60 + 0.40 = 1.00\) (correct).

\textbf{Concept Check 18.5}

\begin{quote}
\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  A population of 1\{,\}000 has 250 AA, 500 Aa, and 250 aa: show that
  although \(p = q = 0.5\), the genotype counts are not those
  Hardy-Weinberg predicts, and decide from the direction of the
  heterozygote discrepancy whether inbreeding or heterozygote advantage
  is the more likely cause.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Hardy-Weinberg
Equilibrium}\label{hardy-weinberg-equilibrium}

The \textbf{Hardy-Weinberg principle} (G.H. Hardy and Wilhelm Weinberg,
1908) states: in a large, randomly mating population with no
evolutionary forces acting, allele frequencies and genotype frequencies
remain constant from generation to generation.

\subsubsection{Derivation}\label{derivation}

Under random mating, \hyperref[gl:gamete]{\textbf{gamete}}s combine
randomly. The probability of drawing an A allele from the gene pool is
\(p\), and of drawing an a allele is \(q\):

\begin{equation}
P(AA) = p \times p = p^2
\label{eq:population_genetics_7}
\end{equation} \begin{equation}
P(Aa) = p \times q + q \times p = 2pq
\label{eq:population_genetics_8}
\end{equation} \begin{equation}
P(aa) = q \times q = q^2
\label{eq:population_genetics_9}
\end{equation}

Therefore, at equilibrium:

\begin{equation}
\boxed{p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1}
\label{eq:population_genetics_10}
\end{equation}

This can also be written as \((p + q)^2 = 1\), which is simply the
binomial expansion.

\textbf{Key insight}: HW equilibrium is reached in a \textbf{single
generation} of random mating (for autosomal loci), and allele
frequencies do not change across generations.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0099_e2230bd94153.png}
\caption{The five assumptions of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and the evolutionary forces that result from their violation. HWE serves as a null model -- deviations indicate evolutionary forces are acting.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Testing for Hardy-Weinberg
Equilibrium}\label{testing-for-hardy-weinberg-equilibrium}

\textbf{Chi-squared test for HWE:} A real population is tested against
HWE as the null model. Estimate the allele frequencies \(p\) and \(q\)
from the observed genotype counts, compute the genotype counts
\emph{expected} under HWE (\(Np^2\), \(2Npq\), \(Nq^2\) for a sample of
\(N\) individuals), and form \(\chi^2 = \sum (O-E)^2 / E\) over the
genotype classes. The degrees of freedom equal the number of genotype
classes minus the number of alleles --- for a biallelic locus,
\(3 - 2 = 1\) (one degree is spent estimating \(p\) from the same data).
A statistic exceeding the critical value \(\chi^2_{0.05,\,1} = 3.84\)
rejects HWE and indicates that at least one assumption --- random
mating, no selection, no drift, no migration, no mutation --- is
violated.

\paragraph{Worked Example: MN Blood Group
Equilibrium}\label{worked-example-mn-blood-group-equilibrium}

MN blood group data for codominant alleles M and N in a population of
1,000:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Genotype & Observed & Allele Frequency \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
MM & 298 & \\
MN & 489 & \\
NN & 213 & \\
\end{longtable}
}

Step 1: Calculate allele frequencies.

\begin{equation}
p(M) = \frac{2(298) + 489}{2000} = \frac{1085}{2000} = 0.5425
\label{eq:population_genetics_11}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
q(N) = \frac{2(213) + 489}{2000} = \frac{915}{2000} = 0.4575
\label{eq:population_genetics_12}
\end{equation}

Step 2: Calculate expected genotype frequencies under HWE.

\begin{equation}
E(MM) = p^2 \times 1000 = (0.5425)^2 \times 1000 = 294.3
\label{eq:population_genetics_13}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
E(MN) = 2pq \times 1000 = 2(0.5425)(0.4575) \times 1000 = 496.4
\label{eq:population_genetics_14}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
E(NN) = q^2 \times 1000 = (0.4575)^2 \times 1000 = 209.3
\label{eq:population_genetics_15}
\end{equation}

Step 3: Chi-squared test.

\begin{equation}
\chi^2 = \frac{(298-294.3)^2}{294.3} + \frac{(489-496.4)^2}{496.4} + \frac{(213-209.3)^2}{209.3}
\label{eq:population_genetics_16}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
= 0.047 + 0.110 + 0.065 = 0.222
\label{eq:population_genetics_17}
\end{equation}

Degrees of freedom = 3 genotypes - 1 constraint (total N) - 1 estimated
parameter (p) = \textbf{1 df}.

\(\chi^2_{crit}(1 \text{ df}, \alpha = 0.05) = 3.841\)

Since \(0.222 < 3.841\), we \textbf{fail to reject} HWE. This population
is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for the MN locus.

\subsubsection{HWE as a Clinical Tool}\label{hwe-as-a-clinical-tool}

\textbf{Estimating carrier frequencies:}

Hardy-Weinberg estimates are useful clinical first approximations, not
diagnoses. Carrier-frequency calculations assume random mating, correct
disease prevalence, complete ascertainment, and a well-defined
population; those assumptions can fail when founder effects,
consanguinity, population stratification, penetrance, or reference bias
shape the sample. Modern screening therefore combines the HWE null model
with ancestry-aware variant panels, family history, and increasingly
graph-aware or long-read evidence for loci where structural variants
affect interpretation \citep{humanpangenome2023}.

\subsection{Worked Example: Cystic Fibrosis Carrier
Frequency}\label{worked-example-cystic-fibrosis-carrier-frequency}

Cystic fibrosis (CF) prevalence in Northern Europeans has disease (aa)
frequency \(\frac{1}{2,500}\).

\begin{equation}
q^2 = \frac{1}{2500} \implies q = \frac{1}{50} = 0.02
\label{eq:population_genetics_18}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
p = 1 - q = 0.98
\label{eq:population_genetics_19}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
\text{Carrier frequency} = 2pq = 2(0.98)(0.02) = 0.0392 \approx \frac{1}{25}
\label{eq:population_genetics_20}
\end{equation}

Approximately 1 in 25 Northern Europeans is a CF carrier -- critical
information for genetic counseling.

\textbf{ABO blood group HWE analysis} (three alleles: \(I^A\), \(I^B\),
\(i\)):

For a triallelic system: \(p(I^A) + q(I^B) + r(i) = 1\)

Genotype frequencies under HWE:

\begin{equation}
\text{Type A} = p^2 + 2pr, \quad \text{Type B} = q^2 + 2qr, \quad \text{Type AB} = 2pq, \quad \text{Type O} = r^2
\label{eq:population_genetics_21}
\end{equation}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Newborn Screening and Hardy-Weinberg}
Hardy-Weinberg predictions guide newborn screening programs. For PKU (q
approximately 0.01, disease frequency 1/10,000), carrier frequency
approximately 2\%. For sickle cell disease in African Americans (q
approximately 0.05), carrier frequency approximately 9.5\%. For
Tay-Sachs in Ashkenazi Jewish populations (q approximately 0.018),
carrier frequency approximately 1/28. These calculations determine
cost-effectiveness of carrier screening programs.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Natural Selection}\label{natural-selection}

\subsubsection{Fitness and Selection}\label{fitness-and-selection}

\textbf{Absolute \hyperref[gl:fitness]{\textbf{fitness (w)}}}: Expected
number of offspring produced by an individual with a given genotype.

\textbf{Relative fitness (w)}: Fitness of a genotype relative to the
most fit genotype (which is set to 1).

\textbf{\hyperref[gl:selection-coefficient]{Selection coefficient (s)}}:
The reduction in fitness: \(s = 1 - w\).

\textbf{Dominance coefficient (h)}: Describes the fitness of the
heterozygote relative to the two homozygotes:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Genotype & Fitness \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
AA & \(w_{AA} = 1\) \\
Aa & \(w_{Aa} = 1 - hs\) \\
aa & \(w_{aa} = 1 - s\) \\
\end{longtable}
}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(h = 0\): A completely dominant (Aa has same fitness as AA)
\item
  \(h = 0.5\): Additive (codominant fitness effect)
\item
  \(h = 1\): A completely recessive (Aa has same fitness as aa)
\item
  \(h < 0\): Overdominance (heterozygote advantage)
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Change in Allele Frequency Under
Selection}\label{change-in-allele-frequency-under-selection}

For selection against a recessive homozygote (h = 0):

\begin{equation}
\Delta q = \frac{-spq^2}{\bar{w}}
\label{eq:population_genetics_22}
\end{equation}

where \(\bar{w} = 1 - sq^2\) is the mean fitness of the population.

\textbf{Important result}: Selection against a recessive allele becomes
very slow at low frequencies because the allele is ``hidden'' in
heterozygotes. The time to reduce \(q\) from 0.01 to 0.001 is much
longer than from 0.5 to 0.01.

For selection against a dominant allele: much faster because every
carrier is exposed to selection.

\subsection{Worked Example: Recessive Deleterious
Allele}\label{worked-example-recessive-deleterious-allele}

In a population with \(q = 0.3\) (frequency of a recessive deleterious
allele) and \(s = 0.2\) (20\% fitness reduction for aa homozygotes):

\begin{equation}
\bar{w} = 1 - s \cdot q^2 = 1 - 0.2(0.09) = 1 - 0.018 = 0.982
\label{eq:population_genetics_23}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
\Delta q = \frac{-0.2 \times 0.7 \times 0.09}{0.982} = \frac{-0.0126}{0.982} = -0.0128
\label{eq:population_genetics_24}
\end{equation}

After one generation: \(q' = 0.3 - 0.0128 = 0.287\)

\subsubsection{Types of Selection}\label{types-of-selection}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0100_0b2cc58eea47.png}
\caption{Types of natural selection and their effects on allele frequency distributions. Directional selection shifts the mean; stabilizing selection reduces variance; disruptive selection increases variance; balancing selection maintains polymorphism.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Heterozygote Advantage (Balancing
Selection)}\label{heterozygote-advantage-balancing-selection}

When the heterozygote has higher fitness than either homozygote
(\(w_{Aa} > w_{AA}\) and \(w_{Aa} > w_{aa}\)), both alleles are
maintained at a \textbf{stable equilibrium}:

\begin{equation}
\hat{q} = \frac{s_1}{s_1 + s_2}
\label{eq:population_genetics_25}
\end{equation}

where \(s_1\) = selection against AA and \(s_2\) = selection against aa.

\textbf{The sickle cell-malaria paradigm:}

In malaria-endemic regions of sub-Saharan Africa: - \textbf{HbA/HbA}
(normal): susceptible to \emph{Plasmodium falciparum} malaria;
\(w_{AA} = 1 - s_1\), where \(s_1 \approx 0.1-0.15\) - \textbf{HbA/HbS}
(sickle trait): about 10-15x reduced malaria mortality; highest
fitness; \(w_{Aa} = 1\) - \textbf{HbS/HbS} (sickle cell disease): severe
disease; \(w_{aa} = 1 - s_2\), where \(s_2 \approx 0.8-1.0\)

Equilibrium frequency of HbS allele:

\begin{equation}
\hat{q} = \frac{s_1}{s_1 + s_2} = \frac{0.12}{0.12 + 0.90} = 0.118
\label{eq:population_genetics_26}
\end{equation}

This predicts HbS frequency of about 12\%, remarkably close to
the observed about 10-20\% in malaria-endemic West Africa.

\textbf{Other examples of heterozygote advantage:} - \textbf{HbC}
(beta-globin E6K): heterozygotes also resistant to malaria; found in
West Africa - \textbf{G6PD deficiency}: heterozygous females have mosaic
RBCs; malaria resistance - \textbf{CF heterozygotes}: possibly resistant
to cholera or typhoid (debated); explains high carrier frequency
(about 4\% in Europeans) - \textbf{MHC/HLA diversity}:
heterozygotes present more pathogen antigens; frequency-dependent
selection also contributes
