\begin{quote}
\textbf{Opening Vignette --- The Tree That Changed Everything}

In the 1970s, Carl Woese was alone in his University of Illinois
laboratory, painstakingly sequencing ribosomal RNA by subjecting it to
nuclease digestion and then separating fragments on two-dimensional
electrophoresis gels --- an agonisingly laborious technique that took
months per organism. When he sequenced methanogens (thought to be
unusual bacteria), the rRNA pattern was unlike any bacterium. It was
unlike any \hyperref[gl:eukaryote]{\textbf{eukaryote}} too. Woese
concluded they formed a third domain of life --- the Archaea. His 1977
\emph{PNAS} paper was widely dismissed for nearly a decade: a
microbiologist claiming to overturn a century of classification with RNA
fingerprints? Yet the phylogenetic evidence was incontrovertible, and by
the 1990s the three-domain tree had rearranged most of biology. The
lesson: molecular sequence data can reveal evolutionary relationships
invisible to morphology, and great paradigm shifts are often dismissed
before they are accepted.
\end{quote}

\subsection{What Phylogenetics Tells
Us}\label{what-phylogenetics-tells-us}

\textbf{Phylogenetics} is the study of evolutionary relationships among
organisms, inferred from heritable characters (DNA sequences,
\hyperref[gl:protein]{\textbf{protein}} sequences, morphological traits,
behavioral traits). A phylogenetic analysis produces a tree (or network)
that represents the historical pattern of descent from common ancestors.

Phylogenetics addresses four fundamental questions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Evolutionary relationships}: Which organisms are most closely
  related? This is the foundation of modern biological classification --
  taxonomy based on shared ancestry rather than superficial similarity.
\item
  \textbf{Ancestral character states}: What did the ancestors look like?
  By mapping traits onto phylogenies, we can reconstruct the sequence in
  which characters evolved (e.g., when did flight originate in
  insects?).
\item
  \textbf{Timing of diversification}: When did lineages diverge?
  Molecular clocks calibrated with fossil data allow estimation of
  divergence dates even when the fossil record is incomplete.
\item
  \textbf{Biogeographic origins}: Where did lineages originate and how
  did they disperse? Phylogeography combines phylogenetics with
  geographic data to trace the spatial history of lineages.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Applications Beyond
Systematics}\label{applications-beyond-systematics}

Phylogenetics has become indispensable across biology and medicine:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Drug discovery}: Phylogenetic analysis identifies which
  organisms are likely to produce useful bioactive compounds. If a
  species in one clade produces a valuable compound, closely related
  species in the same clade are promising candidates for novel variants.
\item
  \textbf{Epidemiology}: Genomic phylogenetics tracks pathogen spread in
  real time (SARS-CoV-2, HIV, Ebola). Phylogenetic clustering reveals
  transmission chains, identifies superspreader events, and dates
  outbreak origins.
\item
  \textbf{Conservation}: \textbf{Phylogenetic diversity (PD)} metrics
  identify lineages that represent the greatest amount of unique
  evolutionary history. Losing a phylogenetically isolated species
  (e.g., the tuatara, sole survivor of order Rhynchocephalia) eliminates
  more evolutionary history than losing one species from a large,
  diverse clade.
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 1:} Why might a conservation strategy based on
phylogenetic diversity differ from one based simply on species counts?
Give an example of a species with high phylogenetic distinctiveness.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Phylogenetic Diversity and the EDGE
Framework}\label{phylogenetic-diversity-and-the-edge-framework}

\textbf{Phylogenetic diversity (PD)}, formalized by Daniel Faith (1992),
is the \textbf{total branch length} of the phylogeny subtending a given
set of species. A clade of 100 species that diverged 5 Ma has lower PD
than a clade of 30 species spanning 200 Ma, because PD measures
evolutionary history rather than species count alone. The \textbf{EDGE
(Evolutionarily Distinct and Globally Endangered)} initiative of the
Zoological Society of London uses PD-based metrics to prioritize
conservation:

\begin{equation}
\text{EDGE score} = \log(1 + \text{ED}) + \text{GE} \cdot \log(2)
\label{eq:unit_VI_edge_score}
\end{equation}

where \textbf{ED} (evolutionary distinctness) is each species' share of
the phylogeny it sits in, weighted by branch length, and \textbf{GE}
(global endangerment) is the IUCN Red List category as a numerical score
(Least Concern = 0, Critically Endangered = 4). Top EDGE species are
both phylogenetically isolated and at high extinction risk --- their
loss would erase irreplaceable amounts of evolutionary history.

\textbf{EDGE flagship examples}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Tuatara} (\emph{Sphenodon punctatus}) --- sole extant member
  of order Rhynchocephalia, sister group to most squamates (lizards and
  snakes). The tuatara's lineage diverged about 250 Ma, making
  it one of the most phylogenetically distinct vertebrates alive.
  Restricted to about 30 small islands off New Zealand.
\item
  \textbf{Pygmy hippopotamus} (\emph{Choeropsis liberiensis}) --- sole
  survivor of one of two extant hippo lineages, with deep evolutionary
  history.
\item
  \textbf{Aye-aye} (\emph{Daubentonia madagascariensis}) --- sole member
  of the family Daubentoniidae, an evolutionarily distinct lemur lineage
  on Madagascar.
\item
  \textbf{Yangtze giant softshell turtle} (\emph{Rafetus swinhoei}) ---
  fewer than four known living individuals; an entire evolutionary line
  nearly extinct.
\end{itemize}

The EDGE approach contrasts sharply with species-count-based
conservation. A reserve protecting 100 closely related warbler species
preserves much less evolutionary history than a reserve protecting 30
phylogenetically diverse tetrapods --- a counterintuitive but
biologically meaningful prioritization rule.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Tree Terminology and Reading
Phylogenies}\label{tree-terminology-and-reading-phylogenies}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0111_66222deabd2a.png}
\caption{Flowchart for tree terminology and reading phylogenies: root (MRCA of sampled taxa), internal node (divergence event), outgroup, and branch labels define how to read relatedness.}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Key: A and B are sister taxa. The clade (A, B, C) is
monophyletic. The outgroup roots the tree.}

\subsubsection{Fundamental Tree
Components}\label{fundamental-tree-components}

\textbf{Root}: The node representing the most recent common ancestor
(MRCA) of the sampled taxa in the tree. An \textbf{outgroup} -- a taxon
known to be outside the group of interest (the ingroup) -- is used to
determine the position of the root on an unrooted tree.

\textbf{Internal nodes}: Each internal node represents a divergence
event -- a \hyperref[gl:speciation]{\textbf{speciation}} event where an
ancestral lineage split into two daughter lineages. Nodes are
hypothetical ancestors; they are not observed directly but inferred from
the data.

\textbf{Branches}: The lines connecting nodes. In a \textbf{cladogram},
branch lengths have no meaning (primarily topology matters). In a
\textbf{phylogram}, branch lengths represent the amount of evolutionary
change (e.g., substitutions per site). In a \textbf{chronogram}
(ultrametric tree), branch lengths represent time.

\textbf{Tips (leaves)}: The terminal nodes, representing observed taxa
-- either extant species or fossil specimens.

\textbf{Clade (monophyletic group)}: An ancestor and its descendant
lineage. Clades are the preferred units in modern phylogenetic
classification because they preserve common ancestry. The clade Mammalia
includes the descendants of the MRCA of mammals -- bats, whales, humans,
and monotremes alike.

\textbf{Sister groups}: Two clades that share an immediate common
ancestor. In the diagram above, Taxon A and Taxon B are sister taxa;
their clade is sister to Taxon C.

\textbf{Polytomy}: An unresolved node where three or more lineages
diverge simultaneously. A ``hard'' polytomy reflects genuine
simultaneous speciation (rare); a ``soft'' polytomy reflects
insufficient data to resolve the branching order (common).

\subsubsection{Paraphyletic and Polyphyletic
Groups}\label{paraphyletic-and-polyphyletic-groups}

\textbf{Paraphyletic group}: An ancestor and SOME (but not most) of its
descendants. The traditional ``Reptilia'' (turtles, lizards, snakes,
crocodilians) is paraphyletic because it excludes birds, which are
nested within the reptile clade. Modern systematics recognizes that
crocodilians are more closely related to birds than to lizards -- a fact
that the traditional grouping obscures.

\textbf{Polyphyletic group}: A group whose members do NOT share a most
recent common ancestor exclusive to that group. ``Warm-blooded animals''
(birds + mammals) is polyphyletic because endothermy evolved
independently in each lineage. Polyphyletic groups reflect convergent
evolution, not shared ancestry.

\subsubsection{Character Types}\label{character-types}

\textbf{Synapomorphy}: A shared derived character that defines a clade.
The amniotic egg is a synapomorphy of Amniota (reptiles, birds, and
mammals). Synapomorphies are the characters most informative for
identifying clades.

\textbf{Symplesiomorphy}: A shared ancestral character inherited from a
deeper ancestor. The vertebral column is shared by most vertebrates but
does not diagnose any particular clade within vertebrates -- it is a
symplesiomorphy for any subgroup of vertebrates.

\textbf{Autapomorphy}: A unique derived character found in a single
taxon. Feathers are an autapomorphy of Aves (or more precisely, of
Maniraptora within the dinosaur phylogeny, though some non-avian
maniraptorans also had feathers).

\textbf{Homoplasy}: A character state that appears similar in two or
more taxa but was NOT inherited from their common ancestor. Homoplasy
arises through \textbf{convergent evolution} (independent evolution of
similar features -- e.g., wings in bats and birds) or \textbf{reversal}
(return to an ancestral state). Homoplasy confounds phylogenetic
analysis because it falsely suggests shared ancestry.

\subsubsection{Rooting Trees}\label{rooting-trees}

An \textbf{unrooted tree} shows the relationships among taxa but does
not indicate the direction of evolutionary time. To root a tree (and
thereby determine which character states are ancestral versus derived),
one of two approaches is used:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Outgroup rooting}: Include a taxon known to be outside the
  group of interest. The root is placed on the branch connecting the
  outgroup to the ingroup. This is the most common method. For example,
  when constructing a phylogeny of mammals, a reptile (e.g., a
  crocodilian) serves as the outgroup.
\item
  \textbf{Midpoint rooting}: Place the root at the midpoint of the
  longest path between any two taxa. This assumes approximately equal
  rates of evolution across lineages -- an assumption that is often
  violated.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Reading Trees Correctly}\label{reading-trees-correctly}

A critical skill is reading phylogenetic trees by \textbf{topology}
(branching pattern) rather than by the visual arrangement of tips. Trees
can be rotated around any internal node without changing the
evolutionary relationships they depict. The common error of reading
relationships from left to right along the tips (treating one end as
``primitive'' and the other as ``advanced'') is incorrect. Evolution
does not proceed along a ladder from simple to complex; every living
species is equally evolved --- each has been evolving for the same
amount of time since the last comprehensive common ancestor.

\paragraph{Common tree-thinking
misconceptions}\label{common-tree-thinking-misconceptions}

Decades of cognitive-science research on student tree-reading reveal a
recurring set of errors. Recognizing these misconceptions is the
foundation of phylogenetic literacy:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5769}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4231}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Misconception
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Correction
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Ladder thinking}: Trees show a progression from ``primitive''
tips on one side to ``advanced'' tips on the other. & Trees can be
rotated around any node; tip order has no biological meaning. Every tip
is equally distant from the root in time. \\
\textbf{Reading along the tips}: Adjacent tips are necessarily more
closely related than non-adjacent tips. & Adjacency on the page does not
imply evolutionary closeness. Look at the \textbf{branching topology}
--- count the nodes shared on the path back to the MRCA. \\
\textbf{``More evolved''}: Some tips (``higher'' organisms) are more
evolved than others. & Most living species have been evolving for the
same time. There is no ``scala naturae''. A bacterium's lineage is as
long as a human's. \\
\textbf{The root is the oldest extant species}: The root represents an
existing ancestor whose features can be observed today. & The root is a
hypothetical reconstructed ancestor, not a living species. Living
species are at the tips, not the root. \\
\textbf{A polytomy means simultaneous origin}: Three branches emerging
from a single node mean three lineages arose at the same instant. & Most
polytomies are ``soft'' --- they reflect insufficient data to resolve
close branching events, not actual simultaneous origin. Hard polytomies
(true simultaneous divergence) are rare. \\
\textbf{Branch length typically means time}: Most trees show time on a
horizontal axis. & Primarily \textbf{chronograms} (ultrametric trees)
show time. \textbf{Cladograms} show primarily topology.
\textbf{Phylograms} show evolutionary change (substitutions). Typically
check the scale bar. \\
\textbf{Convergent traits = relatedness}: Similar traits (wings in bats
and birds, dorsal fins in dolphins and sharks) imply close relationship.
& Convergent traits are \textbf{homoplasy} --- they reflect similar
selection pressures, not shared ancestry. Use synapomorphies, not
overall similarity, to define clades. \\
\textbf{Cousins versus ancestors}: Living species can be ancestors of
other living species. & Living species are sister taxa to each other,
rarely ancestor--descendant. The MRCA of two living species is a
hypothetical extinct ancestor, even if one species is ``older'' or
``less changed.'' \\
\end{longtable}
}

\paragraph{Tips for reading phylogenetic
trees}\label{tips-for-reading-phylogenetic-trees}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Identify the root} --- it represents the most recent common
  ancestor of the sampled taxa shown. Check the scale bar and any axis
  labels.
\item
  \textbf{Trace lineages back to the MRCA} --- don't read across tips
  horizontally. Find where two taxa share their nearest common ancestor
  by going \textbf{down} to the node where their lineages converge.
\item
  \textbf{Look at the branching pattern, not the layout} --- the same
  topology can be displayed in many visually distinct ways (rectangular,
  slanted, radial, circular).
\item
  \textbf{Distinguish character types} --- mapped traits should be
  inferred from synapomorphies (shared derived characters), not from
  overall similarity.
\item
  \textbf{Note the scale} --- a chronogram with branch lengths in
  millions of years tells a different story from a phylogram with branch
  lengths in substitutions/site.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 2:} Consider the traditional classification
``Reptilia'' that includes turtles, lizards, snakes, and crocodilians
but excludes birds. Is this group monophyletic, paraphyletic, or
polyphyletic? Explain your reasoning based on the phylogenetic position
of birds relative to crocodilians.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Phylogenetic Reconstruction
Methods}\label{phylogenetic-reconstruction-methods}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0112_065c5c6c1e41.png}
\caption{Flowchart for Phylogenetic Reconstruction Methods: Phylogenetic Methods, Distance-Based, Character-Based, and UPGMA form the diagram's primary path or branches.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Distance Methods}\label{distance-methods}

\textbf{UPGMA (Unweighted Pair Group Method with Arithmetic Mean)}: The
simplest clustering algorithm. It assumes a strict molecular clock
(equal rates of evolution across most lineages) and produces an
ultrametric tree where most tips are equidistant from the root. UPGMA
works by iteratively joining the two most similar sequences and
recalculating distances.

\textbf{Limitation}: If the molecular clock assumption is violated (and
it usually is), UPGMA produces incorrect topologies. It is not
recommended for most phylogenetic analyses but remains useful for
constructing guide trees in sequence alignment.

\textbf{Neighbor-Joining (NJ)}: Developed by \citet{saitou1987}, NJ does
NOT assume a molecular clock. It works by star decomposition: starting
with an unresolved star tree, it iteratively identifies the pair of taxa
whose joining minimizes the total branch length. NJ is fast (\(O(n^3)\)
time complexity), produces additive trees with unequal branch lengths,
and provides a good starting tree for more sophisticated analyses. It is
appropriate for large datasets where ML or Bayesian methods would be
computationally prohibitive.

\subsubsection{Worked Example: One UPGMA Clustering Step from a Distance
Matrix}\label{worked-example-one-upgma-clustering-step-from-a-distance-matrix}

\textbf{Problem:} Four taxa (A, B, C, D) have the symmetric pairwise
distance matrix below (substitutions/site). Perform the first UPGMA
clustering step: identify the closest pair, place their common node, and
recompute the reduced distance matrix.

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lllll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
& A & B & C & D \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{A} & --- & 0.10 & 0.40 & 0.42 \\
\textbf{B} & 0.10 & --- & 0.38 & 0.40 \\
\textbf{C} & 0.40 & 0.38 & --- & 0.12 \\
\textbf{D} & 0.42 & 0.40 & 0.12 & --- \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Solution:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Identify the smallest off-diagonal distance.} Scanning the
  matrix, the minimum is \(d_{AB} = 0.10\) substitutions/site. Join A
  and B into cluster \((AB)\).
\item
  \textbf{Place the internal node.} UPGMA builds an ultrametric tree, so
  the node \(U\) joining A and B sits at half the pair distance; the
  branch length from each of A and B up to \(U\) is

  \begin{equation}
  h_U = \frac{d_{AB}}{2} = \frac{0.10}{2} = 0.05 \text{ substitutions/site}
  \label{eq:phylogenetics_8}
  \end{equation}
\item
  \textbf{Recompute distances from the new cluster} as the size-weighted
  arithmetic mean over member pairs (here \(|A| = |B| = 1\)):

  \begin{equation}
  d_{(AB),C} = \frac{d_{AC} + d_{BC}}{2} = \frac{0.40 + 0.38}{2} = 0.39, \qquad
  d_{(AB),D} = \frac{d_{AD} + d_{BD}}{2} = \frac{0.42 + 0.40}{2} = 0.41
  \label{eq:phylogenetics_9}
  \end{equation}

  The distance \(d_{CD} = 0.12\) is unchanged.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Interpretation:} A and B cluster first at node height 0.05
substitutions/site; in the reduced matrix the smallest remaining
distance is \(d_{CD} = 0.12\), so the next step joins C and D, yielding
the tree \(((A,B),(C,D))\) --- exactly what an equal-rate (clock-like)
dataset should produce.

\subsubsection{Maximum Parsimony}\label{maximum-parsimony}

\textbf{Maximum parsimony} selects the tree (or trees) requiring the
fewest total character-state changes. This is an application of Occam's
razor -- the simplest explanation is preferred.

\textbf{Procedure}: For each possible tree topology, map character
changes onto branches to find the minimum number of steps. The tree
requiring the fewest total steps across most characters is the most
parsimonious.

\textbf{Strengths}: Intuitive; does not require an explicit model of
evolution; works well when evolutionary rates are low and homoplasy is
rare.

\textbf{Limitations}: - \textbf{Computationally NP-hard}: The number of
possible tree topologies grows super-exponentially with the number of
taxa. For \(n\) taxa, the number of unrooted bifurcating trees is
\((2n-5)!! = (2n-5)(2n-7)(2n-9)\cdots(3)(1)\). For 10 taxa: 2,027,025
trees. For 20 taxa: \(> 10^{21}\) trees. Heuristic search algorithms are
required. - \textbf{Long-branch attraction (LBA)}: When two distantly
related lineages evolve rapidly, they accumulate homoplasies (convergent
substitutions) that parsimony interprets as synapomorphies, incorrectly
grouping them together. LBA is a systematic error -- adding more data
makes it worse, not better.

\subsubsection{Worked Example: Computing a Parsimony Score for a Small
Character
Matrix}\label{worked-example-computing-a-parsimony-score-for-a-small-character-matrix}

\textbf{Problem:} Four taxa (A, B, C, D) are scored for four binary
morphological characters (state 0 or 1). Using the fixed rooted tree
\(((A,B),(C,D))\), compute the total parsimony score (minimum number of
character-state changes).

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lllll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Taxon & Char 1 & Char 2 & Char 3 & Char 4 \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{A} & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\
\textbf{B} & 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\
\textbf{C} & 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\
\textbf{D} & 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Solution:}

Apply the Fitch bottom-up algorithm to each character independently. At
each internal node take the intersection of its two children's state
sets; if the intersection is empty, take the union and add one step.
Internal nodes: \(X\) = ancestor of \((A,B)\), \(Y\) = ancestor of
\((C,D)\), \(R\) = root.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Char 1} (\(A{=}0, B{=}0, C{=}1, D{=}1\)):
  \(X = \{0\}\cap\{0\}=\{0\}\) (0 steps); \(Y = \{1\}\cap\{1\}=\{1\}\)
  (0 steps); \(R = \{0\}\cap\{1\}=\varnothing \Rightarrow \{0,1\}\)
  (\textbf{1 step}). Subtotal = 1.
\item
  \textbf{Char 2} (\(A{=}0, B{=}1, C{=}1, D{=}1\)):
  \(X = \{0\}\cap\{1\}=\varnothing \Rightarrow \{0,1\}\) (\textbf{1
  step}); \(Y = \{1\}\cap\{1\}=\{1\}\) (0 steps);
  \(R = \{0,1\}\cap\{1\}=\{1\}\) (0 steps). Subtotal = 1.
\item
  \textbf{Char 3} (\(A{=}1, B{=}1, C{=}0, D{=}0\)): \(X=\{1\}\) (0
  steps); \(Y=\{0\}\) (0 steps);
  \(R=\{1\}\cap\{0\}=\varnothing\Rightarrow\{0,1\}\) (\textbf{1 step}).
  Subtotal = 1.
\item
  \textbf{Char 4} (\(A{=}0, B{=}1, C{=}1, D{=}1\)): same pattern as Char
  2 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{1 step}. Subtotal = 1.
\item
  \textbf{Total parsimony score:}

  \begin{equation}
  S = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4 \text{ steps}
  \label{eq:phylogenetics_10}
  \end{equation}
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Interpretation:} The tree \(((A,B),(C,D))\) requires 4 changes;
the two alternative unrooted topologies \(((A,C),(B,D))\) and
\(((A,D),(B,C))\) each require 7, so \(((A,B),(C,D))\) is the
most-parsimonious tree --- Characters 1 and 3 are the
parsimony-informative synapomorphies that group \((A,B)\) apart from
\((C,D)\).

\subsubsection{Maximum Likelihood (ML)}\label{maximum-likelihood-ml}

Maximum likelihood selects the tree that maximizes the probability of
the observed data given the tree topology, branch lengths, and an
explicit model of sequence evolution:

\begin{equation}
L(\text{tree}, \theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{L} P(\text{site}_i \mid \text{tree}, \theta)
\label{eq:phylogenetics_1}
\end{equation}

where \(L\) is the alignment length and \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\theta}}{theta} represents the parameters of
the substitution model.

\textbf{Substitution models} describe the probability of one
\hyperref[gl:nucleotide]{\textbf{nucleotide}} changing to another over a
given evolutionary time:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1923}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4231}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3846}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Model
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Description
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Parameters
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{JC69} (Jukes-Cantor, 1969) & Most substitutions equally likely;
equal base frequencies & 0 free parameters \\
\textbf{K2P} (Kimura 2-parameter, 1980) & Transitions \(\neq\)
transversions; equal base frequencies & 1 (Ti/Tv ratio) \\
\textbf{HKY85} (Hasegawa-Kishino-Yano) & Ti \(\neq\) Tv + unequal base
frequencies & 4 \\
\textbf{GTR} (General Time Reversible) & Most 6 substitution types have
independent rates + unequal base frequencies & 9 \\
\textbf{GTR+\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Gamma}}{Gamma}+I} & GTR + gamma-distributed rate variation across sites +
proportion of invariant sites & 11 \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Model selection} uses information criteria: \textbf{AIC}
\(= 2k - 2\ln L\) (where \(k\) = number of parameters) or \textbf{BIC}
\(= k\ln n - 2\ln L\) (where \(n\) = sample size). The model with the
lowest AIC or BIC provides the best balance of fit and complexity.
Tools: ModelFinder (implemented in IQ-TREE), jModelTest2.

\textbf{Software}: RAxML (Randomized Axelerated Maximum Likelihood),
IQ-TREE (fast ML with ultrafast bootstrap UFBoot2), FastTree
(approximate ML for very large alignments).

\subsubsection{Bayesian Inference}\label{bayesian-inference}

Bayesian phylogenetics uses Bayes' theorem to estimate the posterior
probability of trees:

\begin{equation}
P(\text{tree} \mid \text{data}) = \frac{P(\text{data} \mid \text{tree}) \cdot P(\text{tree})}{P(\text{data})}
\label{eq:phylogenetics_2}
\end{equation}

Since \(P(\text{data})\) -- the marginal likelihood -- is
computationally intractable (it requires summing over most possible
trees), Bayesian inference uses \textbf{Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)}
to sample trees from the posterior distribution. The Metropolis-Hastings
algorithm proposes modifications to the current tree, accepts changes
that improve the likelihood, and occasionally accepts changes that
decrease it (allowing escape from local optima).

\textbf{Output}: A set of posterior trees summarized as a majority-rule
consensus tree. Each node receives a \textbf{posterior probability (PP)}
-- the proportion of sampled trees containing that node. PP
\(\geq 0.95\) is considered statistically significant support.

\textbf{Software}: MrBayes (standard Bayesian phylogenetics),
BEAST/BEAST2 (specialized for time-calibrated chronograms, molecular
clock models, and phylogeography).

\paragraph{Bayesian phylogenetics in
practice}\label{bayesian-phylogenetics-in-practice}

A typical Bayesian phylogenetic workflow consists of the following
steps. \textbf{(1) Specify priors}: a tree prior (often a Yule
pure-birth or birth--death process for species trees, or a coalescent
prior for population-genetic data), a clock-rate prior (e.g., a
lognormal distribution centered at a calibrated rate), and
substitution-model parameter priors. \textbf{(2) Run two or more
independent MCMC chains} for \(10^7\)--\(10^9\) generations, sampling
the tree topology, branch lengths, and model parameters at intervals
(typically every 1,000 generations). \textbf{(3) Diagnose convergence}:
discard the first 10--25\% of samples as ``burn-in'', then verify that
independent chains have reached the same stationary distribution by
inspecting Effective Sample Size (ESS \textgreater{} 200 for most
parameters), Potential Scale Reduction Factor (PSRF \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 1.0), and visual
trace plots in Tracer. \textbf{(4) Summarize}: produce a maximum clade
credibility (MCC) tree, with each node labeled by its posterior
probability and (for chronograms) its 95\% highest posterior density
(HPD) age interval.

\textbf{Comparison with bootstrap support.} A widely cited rule of thumb
is that \textbf{posterior probability \texorpdfstring{\textgreater{}=}{>=} 0.95 is approximately equivalent
to bootstrap support \texorpdfstring{\textgreater{}=}{>=} 70\%}, but the two measures are not
interchangeable. Posterior probabilities tend to be higher than
bootstrap values for the same node --- sometimes considerably so when
the substitution model is misspecified. The interpretation differs as
well: a 95\% posterior probability means ``given the model and data,
there is a 95\% probability that this clade is correct''; a 70\%
bootstrap value means ``70\% of pseudoreplicate datasets recover this
clade''. Modern best practice is to report both measures, and to treat
single nodes with PP \textless{} 0.95 or bootstrap \textless{} 70 as
\textbf{unresolved}.

\paragraph{Strict clock vs.~relaxed clock: when to use
each}\label{strict-clock-vs.-relaxed-clock-when-to-use-each}

Bayesian phylogenetic dating uses one of two molecular-clock frameworks.
A \textbf{strict clock} assumes a single substitution rate across the
entire tree; this is appropriate for \textbf{closely related taxa}
(within-species or recent congeners), where the assumption is testable
and often defensible --- e.g., dating SARS-CoV-2 lineages within a
single pandemic, or dating Native American mtDNA lineages relative to
the Bering Strait crossing. A \textbf{relaxed clock} allows substitution
rates to vary across branches, drawn from a prior distribution
(uncorrelated lognormal, exponential, or autocorrelated random walk).
Relaxed clocks are appropriate for \textbf{divergent taxa with rate
heterogeneity} --- for example, mammalian phylogenies where rodents
evolve 5--10\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} faster than cetaceans, or insect phylogenies where
holometabolous lineages have generation-time-correlated rate shifts. The
choice of clock is \textbf{testable}: a likelihood-ratio test or
Bayes-factor comparison between strict and relaxed clock models,
evaluated under the same data and tree prior, indicates which is
supported. In practice, modern phylogeneticists routinely default to
relaxed clocks and primarily revert to strict clocks when relaxed-clock
parameter estimates indicate near-uniform rates.

\subsubsection{Bootstrap Analysis}\label{bootstrap-analysis}

\textbf{Non-parametric bootstrap} \citep{felsenstein1985} assesses
branch support by resampling:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Create pseudoreplicates by randomly sampling alignment columns with
  replacement (same length as original alignment).
\item
  Reconstruct a tree from each pseudoreplicate (typically 100--1,000
  replicates).
\item
  The \textbf{bootstrap value} for each branch is the percentage of
  pseudoreplicate trees containing that branch.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Interpretation}: Bootstrap \(\geq 70\)\% is generally considered
moderate to strong support. Bootstrap values are conservative estimates
-- a true clade may receive bootstrap support below 70\% if the
supporting signal is concentrated in a few alignment positions that are
not always sampled.

\textbf{Bootstrap vs.~Bayesian PP}: Bayesian posterior probabilities
tend to be higher than bootstrap values for the same node. A common rule
of thumb treats bootstrap support of at least 70\% and posterior
probability of at least 0.95 as broadly comparable thresholds, not
interchangeable measures. However, PP can be inflated by model
misspecification --- when the substitution model fails to capture
features of the data, posterior probabilities become falsely confident.
\textbf{Both metrics should be reported} for each node, and discordance
(high PP, low bootstrap, or vice versa) is itself diagnostic of either
signal heterogeneity or model violation. Modern best practice typically
reports nodes as well-supported primarily when \textbf{both} bootstrap
\(\geq 70\%\) \textbf{and} PP \(\geq 0.95\) are achieved.

\textbf{MCMC convergence diagnostics}: A Bayesian phylogeny depends
strongly on the convergence of the MCMC chains that produced it; high
posterior probabilities are misleading when chains have not mixed across
tree space. Standard diagnostics include:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Effective sample size (ESS)}: For each parameter (tree length,
  individual branch lengths, model parameters), the number of
  independent samples after autocorrelation correction. ESS values
  \(\geq 200\) are typically required for confident inference.
\item
  \textbf{Multiple independent runs}: The same analysis run from
  different random starting points should converge to indistinguishable
  posterior distributions. Discrepancies signal that the chains are
  stuck in local optima.
\item
  \textbf{Trace plots}: Visual inspection of parameter values across
  MCMC iterations should show a stationary ``fuzzy caterpillar''
  pattern, not directional trends or sticking at single values.
\item
  \textbf{Burn-in removal}: The first 10--25\% of MCMC iterations are
  typically discarded as the chain finds the high-posterior region of
  parameter space.
\end{enumerate}

Tools like \textbf{Tracer} (BEAST suite) automate these checks, and
submitting trees without convergence verification is now considered
methodologically inadequate in published phylogenomics.

\subsubsection{Gene Tree versus Species Tree
Discordance}\label{gene-tree-versus-species-tree-discordance}

A central insight of modern phylogenomics is that \textbf{gene trees
frequently disagree with species trees}, even when the underlying
biological process is straightforward speciation. The two main
biological causes:

\paragraph{Incomplete lineage sorting
(ILS)}\label{incomplete-lineage-sorting-ils}

When two speciation events occur in rapid succession, ancestral
polymorphism may not have time to sort completely between the daughter
lineages. Some loci will retain the ancestral relationship while others
will track the species tree --- producing a mosaic of gene trees that
disagree with each other and with the true species history. ILS is most
severe when:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Effective population size of the ancestor is large} (\(4N_e\)
  about  time between speciations)
\item
  \textbf{Speciation events are temporally close} (the ``anomaly zone''
  of phylogenetics)
\item
  \textbf{Recombination is high} so that adjacent loci have independent
  histories
\end{itemize}

The classic case is the human--chimpanzee--gorilla trichotomy:
about 30\% of human nuclear loci show \textbf{gene trees
grouping human with gorilla, or chimp with gorilla}, rather than the
species-tree topology of (human, chimp) sister to gorilla. The
discordance reflects ILS during the rapid succession of
human--chimp--gorilla speciation events about 6--8 Ma.

\textbf{Coalescent-based methods} (ASTRAL, MP-EST, *BEAST) explicitly
model gene-tree discordance under the multi-species coalescent and infer
the \textbf{species tree} as the topology that maximizes likelihood
across many gene trees. Concatenation methods (which simply combine most
loci into one alignment) can be \textbf{statistically inconsistent}
under high ILS --- they sometimes converge to the wrong tree as more
data are added.

\paragraph{Horizontal gene transfer
(HGT)}\label{horizontal-gene-transfer-hgt}

In prokaryotes, gene-tree discordance often reflects \textbf{horizontal
acquisition} rather than incomplete sorting. A gene tree that places a
thermophilic bacterium within the archaea may indicate that the
bacterium acquired the gene from an archaeal source through HGT, rather
than the species tree placing it incorrectly. Detecting HGT requires:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Phylogenetic incongruence}: gene tree topology contradicts the
  consensus species tree.
\item
  \textbf{Atypical sequence features}: GC content, codon usage bias, or
  dinucleotide signature differing from the host genome.
\item
  \textbf{Patchy phylogenetic distribution}: gene present in distantly
  related organisms while absent from close relatives.
\end{enumerate}

Tools like \textbf{DistAL} and reconciliation methods (Notung,
Ranger-DTL) systematically identify HGT events by comparing gene trees
with reference species trees.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Real-World Connection: COVID-19 Phylogenetics}

The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic demonstrated the power of real-time
phylogenetics. Within weeks of the first
\hyperref[gl:genome]{\textbf{genome}} sequence being shared (January
2020), phylogenetic analysis confirmed the virus's origin in the
betacoronavirus clade related to bat coronaviruses. Platforms like
Nextstrain (nextstrain.org) provided continuously updated phylogenetic
trees from millions of viral genomes deposited in GISAID. Bayesian
time-calibrated analyses (BEAST) dated the most recent common ancestor
to approximately November 2019. Phylogenetic tracking identified the
emergence and global spread of Variants of Concern (Alpha, Delta,
Omicron), revealing that each arose from a single geographic origin and
spread globally through human travel. Genomic epidemiology became a
standard public health tool, guiding variant surveillance,
\hyperref[gl:vaccine]{\textbf{vaccine}} updating, and travel policy. The
pandemic validated decades of investment in phylogenetic methodology and
demonstrated that evolutionary biology has direct, immediate public
health applications.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 3:} Why is long-branch attraction a problem
specifically for maximum parsimony but less so for maximum likelihood?
(Hint: consider whether each method uses an explicit model of
substitution rates.)
\end{quote}

\subsection{Molecular Clocks}\label{molecular-clocks-1}

\subsubsection{The Molecular Clock
Hypothesis}\label{the-molecular-clock-hypothesis}

\citet{zuckerkandl1965} observed that the number of amino acid
differences between homologous proteins from different species is
roughly proportional to the time since those species diverged. This
\textbf{molecular clock} hypothesis -- that neutral substitutions
accumulate at an approximately constant rate -- allows divergence times
to be estimated from sequence data.

The theoretical basis comes from Kimura's
\hyperref[gl:neutral-theory]{\textbf{neutral theory}} (1968): the rate
of neutral substitution equals the neutral
\hyperref[gl:mutation]{\textbf{mutation}} rate, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}, regardless of
population size. For strictly neutral mutations:

\begin{equation}
k = \mu
\label{eq:phylogenetics_3}
\end{equation}

where \(k\) is the substitution rate per site per generation.

\subsubsection{Clock Calculations}\label{clock-calculations}

\textbf{Jukes-Cantor correction}: Observed sequence divergence
underestimates true divergence because of multiple substitutions at the
same site (saturation). The JC69 correction accounts for this:

\begin{equation}
d_{JC} = -\frac{3}{4} \ln\left(1 - \frac{4}{3}p\right)
\label{eq:phylogenetics_4}
\end{equation}

where \(p\) is the observed proportion of differing sites.

\textbf{Divergence time estimation}:

\begin{equation}
t = \frac{d_{JC}}{2\mu}
\label{eq:phylogenetics_5}
\end{equation}

The factor of 2 accounts for substitutions accumulating independently in
both lineages since their divergence from a common ancestor.

\subsubsection{Worked Example: Estimating Divergence Time using
Jukes-Cantor}\label{worked-example-estimating-divergence-time-using-jukes-cantor}

\textbf{Problem:} Human and chimpanzee mitochondrial \emph{cytochrome b}
sequences differ by approximately 1.5\% (\(p = 0.015\)). Assume a
mitochondrial substitution rate of \(\mu \approx 2 \times 10^{-8}\)
substitutions per site per year. 1. Calculate the Jukes-Cantor distance
(\(d_{JC}\)). 2. Estimate the divergence time (\(t\)) between the two
lineages.

\textbf{Solution:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Calculate the Jukes-Cantor distance:} Using the Jukes-Cantor
  correction formula to account for multiple substitutions at the same
  site: \begin{equation}
  d_{JC} = -\frac{3}{4} \ln\left(1 - \frac{4}{3}(0.015)\right) \approx 0.01511 \text{ substitutions/site}
  \label{eq:phylogenetics_6}
  \end{equation}
\item
  \textbf{Estimate the divergence time:} Apply the divergence time
  estimation formula, remembering the factor of 2 (since mutations
  accumulate along both lineages branching from the MRCA):
  \begin{equation}
  t = \frac{d_{JC}}{2\mu} = \frac{0.01511}{2 \times 2 \times 10^{-8}} \approx 3.78 \times 10^5 \text{ years}
  \label{eq:phylogenetics_7}
  \end{equation}
\end{enumerate}

\emph{Note:} This estimate of about 378,000 years for mtDNA is much
lower than the accepted species divergence time of about 6--7 Mya. This
occurs because mitochondrial \hyperref[gl:gene]{\textbf{gene}}s evolve
significantly faster than the genome-wide average, and substituting a
long-term nuclear calibration rate yields an artificially recent
divergence for rapidly evolving loci.

\subsubsection{Rate Calibration}\label{rate-calibration}

Molecular clocks must be calibrated against independent time estimates:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Fossil record}: Fossils provide \textbf{minimum age
  constraints} -- a fossil establishes that a lineage existed by that
  time, but the actual divergence must be older. The oldest known fossil
  of a clade provides a minimum bound on the clade's age.
\item
  \textbf{Biogeographic events}: The formation of the Isthmus of Panama
  (about 3 Mya), the separation of Australia from Antarctica (about 45
  Mya), or the formation of volcanic islands (known radiometric ages)
  provide calibration points.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Strict vs.~Relaxed
Clocks}\label{strict-vs.-relaxed-clocks}

\textbf{Strict molecular clock}: Assumes a constant substitution rate
across most lineages. This assumption is often violated because
substitution rates vary with generation time (shorter-generation
organisms evolve faster per unit time), metabolic rate, DNA repair
efficiency, and population size (through the interplay of drift and
selection).

\textbf{Relaxed molecular clock}: Allows the rate to vary among lineages
while still estimating divergence times. Two main approaches: -
\textbf{Autocorrelated rates}: Closely related lineages have similar
rates (rates evolve gradually along the tree). Implemented in BEAST. -
\textbf{Uncorrelated rates}: Each branch draws its rate independently
from a statistical distribution (e.g., lognormal). Implemented in
BEAST2.

\subsubsection{Limitations}\label{limitations}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Rate heterogeneity}: Substitution rates can vary dramatically
  among lineages. Rodents evolve approximately 5--10 times faster than
  cetaceans at synonymous sites.
\item
  \textbf{Generation time effect}: Species with shorter generation times
  accumulate more mutations per unit time because there are more DNA
  replication events per year.
\item
  \textbf{Saturation}: At very large divergence times, multiple
  substitutions at the same site erase the phylogenetic signal. Slowly
  evolving genes (18S rRNA, about 1--2 \(\times 10^{-9}\) substitutions
  per site per year) are needed for deep divergences.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Tip Dating and Bayesian Skyline
Plots}\label{tip-dating-and-bayesian-skyline-plots}

Modern molecular clock analyses go beyond simple point estimates of
divergence times:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Tip dating}: When sequences are sampled at different calendar
  dates (e.g., viral genomes collected over the course of an epidemic),
  the sampling dates themselves provide calibration points. BEAST
  software uses tip dates to estimate substitution rates directly from
  serially sampled data --- no fossil calibration needed. This approach
  was critical for dating the SARS-CoV-2 origin, HIV emergence, and
  influenza evolution.
\item
  \textbf{Bayesian Skyline Plots}: These reconstruct changes in
  effective population size (\(N_e\)) through time from a single
  population sample. By analyzing the distribution of coalescence times
  in a gene genealogy, skyline plots reveal historical population
  expansions, bottlenecks, and declines. Applied to human mtDNA, skyline
  analyses confirm the Out-of-Africa expansion approximately 60--70 kya.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{A timeline of major events in life's
phylogeny}\label{a-timeline-of-major-events-in-lifes-phylogeny}

Phylogenetic methods, when calibrated against the geological record,
reconstruct a deep-time timeline of life on Earth. The major events span
four billion years:

Hadean--Eoarchean & about 4.5--4.0 Ga & Earth forms
(about 4.54 Ga); oceans condense (about 4.4 Ga);
abiogenesis events (debated dates) \\
Eoarchean & about 3.8--3.5 Ga & Earliest evidence of life
(graphite isotope signatures from Greenland; stromatolites in
Australia) \\
LUCA & about 3.8 Ga & Last Comprehensive Common Ancestor ---
root of the tree of life. Inferred from comprehensive molecular
machinery (rRNA, ribosomal proteins, ATP synthase, key tRNAs). LUCA was
likely an anaerobic, hyperthermophilic prokaryote dependent on H\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}/CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}
chemistry near hydrothermal vents. \\

meiotic sexual reproduction. The mitochondrial endosymbiosis is dated to
about 2.0--1.5 Ga. \\

(cyanobacterium \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} primary plastid in archaeplastid ancestor);
diversification of eukaryotic supergroups \\
Neoproterozoic & about 1.0 Ga -- 540 Ma & Snowball Earth
events; first multicellular eukaryotes; \textbf{Ediacaran biota}
(about 575--540 Ma) --- soft-bodied multicellular organisms,
mostly enigmatic in affinity \\
Cambrian & about 540--485 Ma & \textbf{Cambrian explosion}:
most modern animal phyla appear in the fossil record within
about 25 million years. Evolution of mineralized skeletons,
predator-prey ecosystems, complex sensory systems \\
Ordovician & about 485--445 Ma & Diversification of marine
invertebrates; first land plants (bryophytes); \textbf{end-Ordovician
extinction} (about 445 Ma): about 85\% of marine
species lost \\
Silurian--Devonian & about 445--360 Ma & Vascular plants
colonize land; jawed fish (Gnathostomata) diversify; \textbf{first
tetrapods} (about 375 Ma; \emph{Tiktaalik}); \textbf{late
Devonian extinction} \\
Carboniferous & about 360--299 Ma & Coal-forest ecosystems;
first amniotes (reptilian-line ancestors); insects undergo first major
radiation \\
Permian & about 299--252 Ma & Synapsids (mammal ancestors)
dominate; \textbf{end-Permian extinction (Great Dying,
about 252 Ma)}: about 96\% of marine species lost ---
the largest extinction event in life's history \\
Triassic--Jurassic & about 252--145 Ma & Dinosaurs diversify;
first mammals (about 225 Ma) and first birds (Late Jurassic);
\textbf{end-Triassic extinction} (about 201 Ma) \\
Cretaceous & about 145--66 Ma & Flowering plants (angiosperms)
emerge and diversify; mammals remain small but radiate quietly;
\textbf{K-Pg extinction} (about 66 Ma): asteroid impact +
Deccan Traps volcanism eliminate non-avian dinosaurs \\
Cenozoic & about 66 Ma -- present & Mammalian and bird
radiations fill ecological niches; primates evolve; \emph{Homo sapiens}
appears (about 300 ka); \textbf{Holocene/Anthropocene
extinction} ongoing \\
\end{longtable}
}

The central insight from this timeline: life persists across cataclysms
but is reshuffled. The five mass extinctions did not erase the tree of
life but pruned it dramatically --- and \textbf{post-extinction
radiations} repeatedly produce explosive diversification as surviving
lineages occupy emptied ecological space (mammals after the K-Pg, modern
teleost fish after the Permian, etc.).

\subsubsection{Ancestral Sequence Reconstruction
(ASR)}\label{ancestral-sequence-reconstruction-asr}

One of the most striking applications of phylogenetic methods is
\textbf{ancestral sequence reconstruction} --- inferring the DNA or
protein sequences of extinct ancestors from their living descendants.
Given a tree and a substitution model, ASR uses \textbf{maximum
likelihood} or \textbf{Bayesian} methods to estimate the most probable
ancestral state at each internal node and at each site.

\paragraph{How ASR works}\label{how-asr-works}

For each site in a multiple sequence alignment, ASR computes:

\[P(\text{ancestor} = X \mid \text{tip data, tree, model}) \label{eq:unit_VI_phylogenetics_item_1}\]

using the \textbf{Felsenstein pruning algorithm} (which efficiently sums
over most possible ancestral states at internal nodes). Marginal
reconstructions estimate the most probable state at each node
independently; joint reconstructions estimate the most probable combined
ancestral states across the whole tree. Confidence is reported as the
posterior probability for each reconstructed residue --- high-confidence
sites have a single dominant residue (\textgreater95\% probability),
while low-confidence sites have several plausible alternatives.

\paragraph{``Lazarus proteins'': resurrecting extinct
enzymes}\label{lazarus-proteins-resurrecting-extinct-enzymes}

Once an ancestral sequence is reconstructed, it can be
\textbf{synthesized} as a real protein in the laboratory --- a ``Lazarus
protein'' brought back from extinction. This approach has revolutionized
our understanding of how protein function evolves:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Ancestral steroid receptors} (Joe Thornton's lab, since the
  early 2000s): The mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid receptors split
  about 450 Mya. Resurrection of the ancestral receptor showed
  it was a glucocorticoid-like receptor; specificity for cortisol versus
  aldosterone evolved later through a small number of historical
  substitutions. The reconstruction made testable predictions about
  which substitutions enabled the functional shift --- confirmed
  experimentally by mutagenesis on the modern proteins.
\item
  \textbf{Ancestral elongation factors} (Akanuma et al.~2013, Gaucher et
  al.~2008): Ancestral bacterial EF-Tu proteins reconstructed from
  extant sequences proved highly thermostable, with melting temperatures
  of 60--73°C. The thermostability profile across nodes traces planetary
  cooling --- providing \textbf{biological thermometers} that measure
  the temperature history of Earth.
\item
  \textbf{Ancestral \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactamases}: Reconstructed enzymes from before the
  antibiotic era reveal ``promiscuous'' ancestral activity --- the
  ancestral enzymes catalyzed multiple reactions efficiently. Modern
  descendants are more specialized but less catalytically robust. This
  pattern of ancestral promiscuity \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} descendant specialization is
  widespread in enzyme evolution.
\item
  \textbf{Ancestral rhodopsins} illuminate the spectral history of
  vision: by reconstructing visual pigments at deep nodes in the
  vertebrate tree, researchers have inferred the wavelengths of light
  that ancestral fish, amphibians, and reptiles could detect --- and
  found that color vision was repeatedly lost and re-evolved across many
  lineages.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Practical applications of
ASR}\label{practical-applications-of-asr}

ASR is more than a historical exercise --- it is now a
\textbf{protein-engineering platform}. Resurrected ancestral proteins
are routinely \textbf{more thermostable} and \textbf{more catalytically
robust} than their modern descendants --- a pattern repeatedly observed
across ancestral \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactamases, EF-Tu elongation factors, alcohol
dehydrogenases, and rhodopsins. The hypothesised explanation is that
ancestral proteins evolved under broader environmental tolerances (early
Earth was warmer; ancestral metabolisms more flexible), and that
\textbf{modern descendants are specialised but brittle} --- selection
has pruned away robustness in favor of niche-specific performance. The
applied consequence: industrial enzyme engineering increasingly uses ASR
to \textbf{prospect for thermostable scaffolds}, then optimises the
resurrected protein for specific substrate specificity. Ancestral
\emph{Bacillus} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-amylases have been engineered into industrial
laundry-detergent enzymes that retain function at 60--80 °C; ancestral
\emph{Pseudomonas} esterases have been used as starting points for
plastic-degrading enzymes (PETase variants); and pharmaceutical
biotechnology uses ASR to design more thermostable vaccine antigens
(e.g.,

The 16S rRNA gene is ideal for deep phylogenetics because it is present
in all cellular organisms, contains both highly conserved regions (for
universal primer design) and variable regions (for discriminating taxa),
and is long enough (about 1,550 bp) for robust phylogenetic inference.

\subsubsection{Domain Bacteria}\label{domain-bacteria}

Bacteria are the most metabolically diverse domain of life. Major phyla
include:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Proteobacteria}: The largest and most diverse bacterial
  phylum.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Alpha-proteobacteria: includes \emph{Rickettsia} (obligate
    intracellular pathogen) and the SAR11 clade (most abundant organisms
    in the ocean). The ancestor of \textbf{mitochondria} was an
    alpha-proteobacterium.
  \item
    Gamma-proteobacteria: includes \emph{Escherichia coli},
    \emph{Pseudomonas}, \emph{Salmonella}, \emph{Vibrio cholerae}.
  \item
    Epsilon-proteobacteria: includes \emph{Helicobacter pylori} (causes
    gastric ulcers and gastric cancer).
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Firmicutes}: Gram-positive, low-GC content. Includes
  \emph{Bacillus} (anthrax), \emph{Clostridium} (tetanus, botulism),
  \emph{Staphylococcus}, \emph{Lactobacillus} (probiotic fermenters),
  \emph{Streptococcus}.
\item
  \textbf{Bacteroidetes}: \hyperref[gl:dominant]{\textbf{Dominant}} gut
  anaerobes; critical for polysaccharide digestion. \emph{Bacteroides}
  species compose 30--40\% of human fecal bacteria.
\item
  \textbf{Actinobacteria}: Gram-positive, high-GC content.
  \emph{Streptomyces} produces over two-thirds of clinically used
  antibiotics. \emph{Mycobacterium tuberculosis} causes tuberculosis.
\item
  \textbf{Cyanobacteria}: Oxygenic photosynthesizers that produced
  Earth's oxygen atmosphere (Great Oxidation Event, about 2.4 Ga). The
  ancestor of \textbf{\hyperref[gl:chloroplast]{chloroplast}s} was a
  cyanobacterium.
\item
  \textbf{Spirochetes}: Helical morphology. \emph{Treponema pallidum}
  (syphilis), \emph{Borrelia burgdorferi} (Lyme disease).
\item
  \textbf{Chlamydiae}: Obligate intracellular
  \hyperref[gl:parasite]{\textbf{parasite}}s with a unique biphasic
  developmental cycle.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Domain Archaea}\label{domain-archaea}

Archaea were originally found primarily in extreme environments, but
culture-independent methods (metagenomics) have revealed that they are
ubiquitous -- in soils, oceans, and the human gut.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Euryarchaeota}: The most diverse archaeal phylum.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Methanogens (\emph{Methanobacterium}, \emph{Methanosarcina}):
    produce methane as a metabolic byproduct; dominant in
    \hyperref[gl:anaerobic]{\textbf{anaerobic}} environments (wetlands,
    ruminant guts, landfills).
  \item
    Extreme halophiles (\emph{Halobacterium}): thrive in salt-saturated
    environments; use bacteriorhodopsin for light-driven proton pumping.
  \item
    Thermoacidophiles (\emph{Thermoplasma}): grow at
    \hyperref[gl:ph]{\textbf{pH}} 1--2 and temperatures up to 60 degrees
    C.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Crenarchaeota}: Many are hyperthermophiles. \emph{Sulfolobus}
  grows at 80 degrees C and pH 2--3. \emph{Thermoproteus} is an
  anaerobic sulfur-reducing hyperthermophile.
\item
  \textbf{TACK superphylum}: Thaumarchaeota (ammonia-oxidizing archaea
  -- major players in the nitrogen cycle), Aigarchaeota, Crenarchaeota,
  and Korarchaeota.
\item
  \textbf{Asgard archaea}: The most significant discovery in archaeal
  biology in decades. Named after Norse mythology:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{Lokiarchaeota}: Discovered via metagenome-assembled genomes
    from Loki's Castle hydrothermal vent, Arctic Mid-Ocean Ridge.
    Contains \textbf{eukaryotic signature proteins} including homologs
    of \hyperref[gl:actin]{\textbf{actin}}, tubulin-like GTPases, ESCRT
    membrane remodeling complex, and Arp2/3 complex regulators.
  \item
    \textbf{Thorarchaeota}, \textbf{Odinarchaeota},
    \textbf{Heimdallarchaeota}: Additional Asgard lineages with
    progressively more eukaryotic-like features.
  \item
    The Asgard archaea are the \textbf{closest known living relatives of
    eukaryotes}, supporting the ``two-domain'' tree (Eocyte hypothesis)
    in which eukaryotes arose from within Archaea rather than as a
    separate domain.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Domain Eukarya}\label{domain-eukarya}

The \textbf{Last Eukaryotic Common Ancestor (LECA)} already possessed a
nucleus, mitochondria, endomembrane system,
\hyperref[gl:cytoskeleton]{\textbf{cytoskeleton}}, and sexual
reproduction. Modern eukaryotic diversity is organized into several
supergroups:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Amorphea}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{Amoebozoa}: Amoebas, slime molds (\emph{Dictyostelium}),
    \emph{Entamoeba histolytica} (amoebic dysentery).
  \item
    \textbf{Opisthokonta}: Fungi + Metazoa (animals) + choanoflagellates
    (closest unicellular relatives of animals). This grouping -- placing
    fungi as the sister group of animals rather than plants -- was one
    of the great surprises of molecular phylogenetics.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Diaphoretickes}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{SAR clade}: Stramenopiles (diatoms, brown algae, oomycetes)
    + Alveolata (\emph{Plasmodium}, dinoflagellates, ciliates) +
    Rhizaria (foraminifera, radiolarians).
  \item
    \textbf{Archaeplastida}: Glaucophyta + Rhodophyta (red algae) +
    Chloroplastida (green algae + land plants). This clade acquired
    plastids through \textbf{primary
    \hyperref[gl:endosymbiosis]{\textbf{endosymbiosis}}} with a
    cyanobacterium.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Excavata} (debated monophyly): Deep-branching protists
  including \emph{Giardia} (intestinal parasite), \emph{Trichomonas}
  (STI pathogen), \emph{Trypanosoma} (sleeping sickness, Chagas
  disease), and \emph{Euglena}.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Endosymbiotic Theory}\label{endosymbiotic-theory-1}

Lynn Margulis (1967, then writing as Lynn Sagan) proposed that
mitochondria and chloroplasts originated as free-living bacteria
engulfed by ancestral eukaryotic cells. Decades of molecular evidence
have confirmed this theory:

\textbf{Primary endosymbiosis}: - \textbf{Mitochondria}: Descended from
an alpha-proteobacterium. Evidence: mitochondria have their own circular
DNA, replicate by binary fission, have double membranes (inner membrane
= bacterial membrane), use bacterial-type
\hyperref[gl:ribosome]{\textbf{ribosome}}s (70S), and their gene
sequences cluster with alpha-proteobacteria in phylogenetic analyses. -
\textbf{Chloroplasts}: Descended from a cyanobacterium. Evidence:
chloroplasts have circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, double membranes, and
gene sequences grouping with cyanobacteria. Thylakoid membranes resemble
cyanobacterial internal membranes.

\textbf{Secondary endosymbiosis}: A eukaryotic cell engulfs a
photosynthetic eukaryote (which already has a primary plastid). This
explains the three or four membranes surrounding plastids in groups such
as euglenids (two extra membranes from the engulfed cell), diatoms,
dinoflagellates, and cryptophytes. Some secondary plastids even retain a
vestigial nucleus (nucleomorph) from the engulfed alga.

\subsubsection{Horizontal Gene Transfer and the Web of
Life}\label{horizontal-gene-transfer-and-the-web-of-life}

\textbf{Horizontal gene transfer (HGT)} -- the transfer of genetic
material between organisms outside of parent-to-offspring transmission
-- is widespread in prokaryotes and fundamentally challenges the tree
metaphor for representing life's history.

Mechanisms of HGT: - \textbf{Transformation}: Uptake of free
environmental DNA through competence proteins. - \textbf{Transduction}:
Bacteriophage-mediated DNA transfer. - \textbf{Conjugation}: Direct
cell-to-cell transfer via pili; the primary route for antibiotic
resistance \hyperref[gl:plasmid]{\textbf{plasmid}} transfer.

An estimated 20--30\% of genes in a typical prokaryotic genome have been
acquired by HGT. In \emph{E. coli} MG1655, \citet{lawrence1998}
identified approximately 755 genes (about 18\% of the genome) acquired
by HGT, identifiable by atypical GC content,
\hyperref[gl:codon]{\textbf{codon}} usage, and phylogenetic
incongruence.

The prevalence of HGT means that prokaryotic evolution is better
represented by a \textbf{network} or \textbf{web} of life rather than a
strictly bifurcating tree. For eukaryotes, vertical inheritance
dominates the nuclear genome, but organellar genomes and some nuclear
genes (acquired by endosymbiotic gene transfer, EGT) record the history
of endosymbiosis.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0113_dbe0ca0e02a1.png}
\caption{The three domains of life with endosymbiotic organelle origins: mitochondria from alpha-Proteobacteria, chloroplasts from Cyanobacteria, and the Asgard-archaea root of Eukarya.}
\end{figure}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Real-World Connection: Antibiotic Resistance and HGT}

The spread of antibiotic resistance among pathogenic bacteria is
fundamentally a problem of horizontal gene transfer. Resistance genes --
encoding \hyperref[gl:enzyme]{\textbf{enzyme}}s that degrade antibiotics
(beta-lactamases), modify antibiotics (aminoglycoside
acetyltransferases), or pump them out of the cell (efflux pumps) -- are
frequently carried on mobile genetic elements: plasmids, transposons,
and integrons. A single conjugation event can transfer multi-drug
resistance from a harmless gut bacterium to a pathogenic strain. The
NDM-1 (New Delhi metallo-beta-lactamase) gene, first identified in 2008,
has spread globally within years via plasmid-mediated HGT, conferring
resistance to nearly most beta-lactam antibiotics including carbapenems
-- the ``last resort'' drugs. Understanding HGT is essential for
combating the antibiotic resistance crisis.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 5:} Explain why the discovery of Asgard archaea
(particularly Lokiarchaeota) supports a two-domain rather than
three-domain tree of life. What eukaryotic signature proteins were found
in Lokiarchaeota genomes?
\end{quote}

\subsection{Human Phylogeny}\label{human-phylogeny}

\subsubsection{Great Apes and Molecular
Phylogeny}\label{great-apes-and-molecular-phylogeny}

Humans belong to the superfamily \textbf{Hominoidea} (great apes and
lesser apes). Molecular phylogenetics has resolved the relationships
within this group with high confidence:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Gibbons} (family Hylobatidae): lesser apes; diverged from the
  great ape lineage approximately 18--20 Mya.
\item
  \textbf{Orangutans} (\emph{Pongo}): diverged approximately 14 Mya. Two
  species: Bornean (\emph{P. pygmaeus}) and Sumatran (\emph{P. abelii}),
  plus the recently described Tapanuli orangutan (\emph{P.
  tapanuliensis}).
\item
  \textbf{Gorillas} (\emph{Gorilla}): diverged approximately 9--10 Mya.
  Two species: western (\emph{G. gorilla}) and eastern (\emph{G.
  beringei}).
\item
  \textbf{Chimpanzees and bonobos} (\emph{Pan}): Our closest living
  relatives. Humans and chimpanzees share approximately 98.7\% DNA
  sequence identity across alignable regions. Divergence approximately
  6--7 Mya.
\item
  \textbf{Humans} (\emph{Homo sapiens}): The primarily surviving species
  of genus \emph{Homo}.
\end{itemize}

The molecular phylogeny contradicts earlier morphology-based
classifications that grouped orangutans, gorillas, and chimpanzees as
``great apes'' separate from humans. DNA data unambiguously place humans
within the great apes, as the sister taxon of \emph{Pan}.

\subsubsection{Fossil Hominins}\label{fossil-hominins}

The human fossil record is one of the richest and most intensively
studied:

\subsubsection{Out of Africa}\label{out-of-africa}

The \textbf{Out of Africa} hypothesis, supported by both genetic and
fossil evidence, proposes that anatomically modern \emph{Homo sapiens}
evolved in Africa and subsequently dispersed to populate the rest of the
world, largely replacing (but partially admixing with) archaic hominin
populations:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Mitochondrial Eve}: Coalescence analysis of mtDNA places the
  most recent common ancestor of living human mitochondrial lineages in
  Africa approximately 150--200 kya.
\item
  \textbf{Y-chromosomal Adam}: The most recent common ancestor of living
  human Y \hyperref[gl:chromosome]{\textbf{chromosome}}s dates to
  approximately 200--340 kya.
\item
  \textbf{Multiple dispersal events}: Genetic evidence suggests at least
  two major dispersal waves -- an early dispersal to Australia/Oceania
  (about 65 kya) and a later dispersal populating Europe and Asia (about
  45--50 kya).
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Archaic Introgression}\label{archaic-introgression}

One of the most remarkable discoveries of the genomic era is that modern
humans carry DNA from extinct hominin species, acquired through
interbreeding:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Neanderthal admixture}: Non-African modern human populations
  carry approximately 1--4\% Neanderthal-derived DNA. Interbreeding
  occurred approximately 50,000--60,000 years ago in the Middle East.
  Neanderthal \hyperref[gl:allele]{\textbf{allele}}s contribute to
  traits including skin pigmentation, hair texture, immune function, and
  susceptibility to certain diseases.
\item
  \textbf{Denisovan admixture}: Melanesian and Australian Aboriginal
  populations carry approximately 4--6\% Denisovan-derived DNA. The
  Denisovans are known primarily from a few fragmentary fossils from
  Denisova Cave, Siberia, and a mandible from Tibet, but their genomic
  legacy is substantial.
\item
  \textbf{Adaptive introgression}: Some introgressed alleles have been
  maintained by \hyperref[gl:natural-selection]{\textbf{natural
  selection}} because they conferred adaptive advantages:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{EPAS1}: A Denisovan-derived allele of this
    \hyperref[gl:transcription]{\textbf{transcription}} factor helps
    Tibetans adapt to high-altitude hypoxia by blunting the
    erythropoietic response to low oxygen, preventing polycythemia.
  \item
    \textbf{HLA alleles}: Neanderthal and Denisovan-derived HLA variants
    increased immune diversity in modern human populations expanding
    into new pathogen environments.
  \item
    \textbf{BNC2}: A Neanderthal-derived skin pigmentation gene at high
    frequency in European populations.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Ghost lineage introgression}: Analysis of West African genomes
  (Yoruba, Mende) reveals approximately 2--19\% of their ancestry from
  an unknown archaic hominin that diverged from the modern human lineage
  approximately 625 kya -- a ``ghost'' population for which no fossils
  have been identified.
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 6:} Explain why ``Mitochondrial Eve'' does not

coalescence of mitochondrial lineages actually tell us?
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 7:} A phylogenomic analysis of 1,000 mammalian

(sister taxa), B groups mouse with primates, and C groups rat with
primates. Is this pattern consistent with incomplete lineage sorting,

\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 8:} A researcher reconstructs an ancestral steroid
receptor by maximum likelihood from 50 modern sequences. The
reconstructed ancestral residue at one critical position has posterior
probability 0.55 (versus 0.40 for the second-most-likely residue). What
does this low confidence imply about the resurrected protein, and how

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 9:} A SARS-CoV-2 lineage emerges in late 2021 with
a novel constellation of mutations not directly descended from any of
the previously detected variants. The Bayesian time-calibrated tree
dates the most recent common ancestor of this lineage to early 2020.
What scenarios could explain this temporal mismatch --- sustained

zoonotic re-emergence? What additional data would discriminate among
these hypotheses?
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection --- Genomic epidemiology.} Phylogenetic
trees built from pathogen genomes are now routine public-health
infrastructure. For HIV, each new clinical isolate is placed on a
national phylogeny to identify transmission clusters and guide focused
intervention. For hospital-acquired infections (MRSA, \emph{C.
difficile}), whole-genome sequencing plus phylogenetic analysis
distinguishes ward-level outbreaks from sporadic community acquisitions
--- a 2013 Cambridge study traced 15 distinct \emph{C. difficile}
lineages in a single hospital, revealing that about 35 \% of cases were
nosocomial. For SARS-CoV-2, the real-time GISAID phylogeny guided
variant-specific vaccine updates.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection --- Identifying zoonotic spillover sources.}
When Ebola, SARS-CoV, MERS, or H5N1 emerge, the first question is: where
did it come from? Phylogenetic analysis places the human isolate within
the tree of known animal reservoirs, identifying the ancestor branch.
SARS-CoV-2's closest known relatives are horseshoe-bat
(\emph{Rhinolophus}) coronaviruses from Yunnan, China, sharing
about 96 \% sequence identity --- a divergence time estimated
by molecular clock at 40--70 years. These analyses direct surveillance
(which wild populations to screen) and inform policy on wildlife-market
regulation.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Computational Bridge}\label{computational-bridge-20}

Strict-clock time from fractional divergence (per site) is:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ biology.evolution }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ molecular\_clock\_divergence\_time}

\NormalTok{years }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ molecular\_clock\_divergence\_time(}\FloatTok{1e{-}9}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.02}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(years)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical / systems note:} Pathogen phylogenomics during
outbreaks uses the same clock logic with externally calibrated rates
(serial sampling) rather than fossils.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsubsection{Long-Read Sequencing and Deep-Divergence
Phylogenetics}\label{long-read-sequencing-and-deep-divergence-phylogenetics}

The accuracy of any phylogenetic tree is bounded by the fidelity of its
underlying sequence data --- and for billion-year divergences the
short-read Illumina platform (150--300 bp fragments) has been the
bottleneck. Short reads mis-assemble through repetitive regions,
collapse paralogs, and cannot span structural variants.
\textbf{Long-read platforms} --- \textbf{PacBio HiFi} (HIFI: 15--25 kb
reads at 99.9 \% accuracy via circular consensus sequencing) and
\textbf{Oxford Nanopore Ultra-long reads} (100 kb -- 2 Mb reads at
97--99 \% raw accuracy, 99.9 \% after polishing) --- have transformed
the field since 2020.

Three phylogenetic problems that long reads solved: \textbf{(1) The
animal tree of life.} Sponges vs.~ctenophores as the earliest-branching
animal clade --- a 10-year controversy --- was re-adjudicated with 1178
long-read-assembled orthologs (Redmond \& McLysaght, \emph{Nat. Commun.}
2021); the analysis supported \textbf{ctenophores-first}, implying
convergent evolution of the nervous system (or its loss in sponges).
\textbf{(2) Polyploid plant genomes.} The hexaploid wheat genome (5 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x}
the human genome size) was resolvable primarily with HiFi + Hi-C
scaffolding (\emph{Nature} 2023), enabling the first accurate
subgenome-level phylogeny of grass evolution. \textbf{(3) Ancient DNA
phylogenetics.} PacBio HiFi on Pleistocene-age samples now reaches
\textless{} 50 000-year mammoths and permafrost wolves; Nanopore
ultra-long sequencing on sediment-trapped eDNA (eDNA-seq) reconstructs
environments without individual organisms --- extending phylogenetics to
ecosystems rather than single species.

\textbf{Practical workflow for a 2025 phylogenomic study}: HiFi
sequencing to 30\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} coverage (about \$3000 per vertebrate-scale
genome, 2024 prices) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} assembly with hifiasm \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} BUSCO completeness check
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} orthologue identification with OrthoFinder \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} multiple sequence
alignment with MAFFT-einsi \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} species-tree inference with ASTRAL under
the multi-species coalescent \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} dating with MCMCTree against
molecular-clock calibrations from the fossil record. The bottleneck has
shifted from sequence generation to \textbf{taxonomic sampling} --- we
have the tools, we need the specimens.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-23}

For \textbf{Phylogenetics and the Tree of Life}, frontier biology
belongs inside the evidence logic of the chapter. Evolutionary claims
are strongest when they combine mechanism, comparative evidence,
population process, and explicit uncertainty. The core reading question
is this: phylogenetic confidence depends on sampling, model choice,
homology, conflict among loci, and calibration.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

Distinguish adaptation from drift, phylogenetic signal from convergence,
and historical explanation from a testable prediction about present-day
data.

\textbf{Source practice:} For evolutionary claims, prefer evidence that
compares alternatives such as selection, drift, gene flow, constraint,
convergence, and shared ancestry.

\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-23}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Phylogenetics} reconstructs evolutionary relationships from
  molecular and morphological data, enabling classification, divergence
  dating, biogeographic reconstruction, and applications in medicine,
  conservation, and drug discovery.
\item
  \textbf{Tree terminology}: Root (MRCA), nodes (divergence events),
  branches (lineages), tips (observed taxa), clades (monophyletic
  groups). Paraphyletic and polyphyletic groups are invalid in modern
  systematics. Synapomorphies define clades; symplesiomorphies and
  homoplasies do not.
\item
  \textbf{Reconstruction methods}: UPGMA (assumes clock; not
  recommended), Neighbor-Joining (fast, no clock), Maximum Parsimony
  (fewest changes; vulnerable to long-branch attraction), Maximum
  Likelihood (model-based; GTR+\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Gamma}}{Gamma}+I; RAxML, IQ-TREE), Bayesian Inference
  (MCMC sampling; posterior probabilities; MrBayes, BEAST).
\item
  \textbf{Molecular clocks}:
  \(d_{JC} = -\frac{3}{4}\ln(1 - \frac{4}{3}p)\); \(t = d/(2\mu)\);
  calibrated from fossils and biogeographic events; strict vs.~relaxed
  clocks accommodate rate variation.
\item
  \textbf{Three domains}: Bacteria (metabolically diverse; source of
  mitochondria and chloroplasts), Archaea (Asgard archaea closest to
  eukaryotes), Eukarya (Amorphea, Diaphoretickes, Excavata).
  Endosymbiosis produced mitochondria (alpha-proteobacterium) and
  chloroplasts (cyanobacterium).
\item
  \textbf{HGT} is pervasive in prokaryotes (20--30\% of genes); the tree
  of life is more accurately a web for prokaryotes. HGT drives
  antibiotic resistance spread.
\item
  \textbf{Human phylogeny}: Diverged from chimpanzees about 6--7 Mya;
  fossil record spans \emph{Sahelanthropus} to \emph{Homo sapiens};
  Out-of-Africa dispersal; archaic introgression from Neanderthals
  (1--4\% in non-Africans) and Denisovans (4--6\% in Melanesians);
  adaptive introgression (EPAS1, HLA alleles).
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See \cref{sec:unit_VII_bacteria_archaea_viruses}
  for HGT vs.~vertical signal, \cref{sec:unit_IV_mutations_and_genomics}
  for variant interpretation, and
  \cref{sec:unit_X_biomes_and_conservation} for phylogenetic diversity
  in triage.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Key Terms}\label{key-terms-23}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2857}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.7143}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Term
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Definition
