\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Phylogenetics} & The study of evolutionary relationships among
organisms, inferred from heritable characters \\
\textbf{Clade} & A monophyletic group: an ancestor and its complete
descendant lineage \\
\textbf{Synapomorphy} & A shared derived character that defines a
clade \\
\textbf{Symplesiomorphy} & A shared ancestral character inherited from a
more distant ancestor; uninformative for grouping \\
\textbf{Homoplasy} & Similarity not due to shared ancestry; arises from
convergent evolution or reversal \\
\textbf{Outgroup} & A taxon known to fall outside the ingroup; used to
root phylogenetic trees \\
\textbf{Maximum parsimony} & Phylogenetic method selecting the tree
requiring the fewest total character-state changes \\
\textbf{Maximum likelihood} & Method selecting the tree maximizing
\(P(\text{data} \mid \text{tree, model})\) \\
\textbf{Bayesian inference} & Method estimating the posterior
probability of trees using MCMC sampling \\
\textbf{Posterior probability} & \(P(\text{tree} \mid \text{data})\);
Bayesian branch support; \(\geq 0.95\) is significant \\
\textbf{Bootstrap} & Resampling technique for assessing branch support;
\(\geq 70\)\% indicates moderate-strong support \\
\textbf{Molecular clock} & Hypothesis that neutral substitutions
accumulate at approximately constant rate, enabling divergence time
estimation \\
\textbf{Substitution model} & Mathematical description of nucleotide or
amino acid replacement probabilities (e.g., JC69, GTR+\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Gamma}}{Gamma}+I) \\
\textbf{Horizontal gene transfer} & Transfer of genetic material between
organisms outside parent-offspring inheritance \\
\textbf{Endosymbiosis} & Origin of organelles (mitochondria,
chloroplasts) from free-living bacteria engulfed by ancestral
eukaryotes \\
\textbf{Asgard archaea} & Archaeal superphylum (Lokiarchaeota,
Thorarchaeota, etc.) that are the closest known relatives of
eukaryotes \\
\textbf{Phylogenetic diversity (PD)} & Total branch length of a
phylogeny containing a set of species; used in conservation
prioritization \\
\textbf{LECA} & Last Eukaryotic Common Ancestor; possessed nucleus,
mitochondria, endomembrane system \\
\textbf{Introgression} & Incorporation of alleles from one species into
another through hybridization and backcrossing \\
\end{longtable}
}

\subsection{Review Questions}\label{review-questions-23}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Define monophyletic, paraphyletic, and polyphyletic groups. For each,
  provide an example from vertebrate taxonomy and explain why primarily
  monophyletic groups are valid in modern systematics.
\item
  Reconstruct a parsimony analysis for four taxa (A, B, C, D) given the
  following binary characters: Character 1: A=1, B=1, C=0, D=0;
  Character 2: A=1, B=0, C=1, D=0; Character 3: A=1, B=1, C=1, D=0.
  Which tree requires the fewest steps? Is there homoplasy?
\item
  A researcher obtains a 600 bp alignment of the COI gene from two
  beetle species, finding 42 differences. (a) Calculate the observed
  divergence (\(p\)). (b) Apply the Jukes-Cantor correction. (c) Using a
  COI substitution rate of \(2.3 \times 10^{-2}\) per site per million
  years, estimate the divergence time.
\item
  Compare maximum likelihood and Bayesian inference as phylogenetic
  methods. What are the advantages and disadvantages of each? When would
  you choose one over the other?
\item
  Explain why the GTR+\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Gamma}}{Gamma}+I substitution model is preferred over simpler
  models (JC69, K2P) for most real phylogenetic datasets. What
  biological realities does each additional parameter capture?
\item
  Describe the evidence supporting the endosymbiotic origin of
  mitochondria from alpha-proteobacteria. List at least four independent
  lines of evidence.
\item
  Explain how Asgard archaea challenge the three-domain tree of life.
  What specific eukaryotic features have been found in Asgard genomes,
  and what does this imply about the origin of eukaryotes?
\item
  The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic relied heavily on phylogenetic analysis.
  Describe how Bayesian time-calibrated phylogenetics (BEAST) was used
  to (a) date the origin of the pandemic, (b) track the emergence of
  Variants of Concern, and (c) reconstruct transmission chains. How is a
  molecular clock calibrated for a virus with no fossil record?
\item
  Modern non-African humans carry approximately 1--4\% Neanderthal DNA.
  Explain the process by which this DNA was acquired and describe one
  example of adaptive introgression. Why is Neanderthal DNA being
  gradually purged from functionally important genomic regions?
\item
  A conservation biologist must choose between protecting Species X (one
  of 50 species in a diverse, recently radiated clade) and Species Y
  (the sole surviving member of an ancient lineage). Using the concept
  of phylogenetic diversity, argue for which species should receive
  priority and explain the logic behind the EDGE conservation framework.
\item
  Why does uncorrected \(p\)-distance \textbf{underestimate} deep
  divergences, and when is Jukes--Cantor inadequate compared with GTR+\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Gamma}}{Gamma}?
\item
  Name one scenario where a \textbf{network} rather than a bifurcating

\textbf{Phylogenetics and the Tree of Life} should leave a reproducible
trail from a biological claim to the code, figure, diagram, or
paper-based activity that can test it. Use the surfaces below to inspect
the chapter's assumptions, rerun the relevant model, or compare the
manuscript explanation with companion labs and figures.

\section*{Unit VII --- Microbiology:
Introduction}\label{unit-vii-microbiology-introduction}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Unit VII --- Microbiology: Introduction}

\subsection*{Why This Unit Matters}\label{why-this-unit-matters-7}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Why This Unit Matters}

The living world is microbial. In mass, in metabolic diversity, and in
evolutionary history, microorganisms dominate life on Earth. The total
number of prokaryotic cells on Earth (about 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{3}}{3}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{0}}{0}) exceeds the
number of stars in the observable universe by a factor of 100,000. The
deepest branches of the tree of life are most microbial. Photosynthesis
--- the ultimate source of energy for most ecosystems --- was invented
by cyanobacteria more than 2.7 billion years ago. Nitrogen fixation,
without which terrestrial agriculture would collapse, is performed
exclusively by bacteria and archaea. The atmosphere itself was
transformed by microbial metabolism long before any animal breathed it.

Medical microbiology became possible primarily after Robert Koch's
postulates (1877--1884) established the germ theory of disease --- the
revolutionary idea that specific microorganisms cause specific
infections. Alexander Fleming's observation in 1928 that
\emph{Penicillium} mould killed staphylococcal colonies initiated the
antibiotic era, saving an estimated 200 million lives over the following
century. But pathogens evolve. The emergence of multidrug-resistant
organisms (MRSA, XDR-TB, carbapenem-resistant \emph{Enterobacteriaceae})
represents one of the most urgent public health crises of the 21st
century: an estimated 1.27 million deaths were attributable to
antimicrobial resistance in 2019 (Murray et al., 2022, \emph{The
Lancet}).

This unit combines cell biology (structure of bacteria, archaea, and
viruses), quantitative microbiology (growth curves, MIC calculations,
viral replication kinetics), and ecology (the microbiome, biogeochemical
cycles, infectious disease dynamics). You will apply the S-I-R
epidemiological model and calculate R\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0}; model bacterial growth and
antibiotic kill curves; and examine the microbiome as a complex
ecological community whose disruption underlies diseases from \emph{C.
difficile} colitis to metabolic syndrome.

\subsection*{Current Evidence Thread}\label{current-evidence-thread-7}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Current Evidence Thread}

In microbiology, a claim is primarily as strong as the way the organism
was observed: read this unit as an evidence trail in which microbial
life is established through culture, sequencing, and surveillance rather
than as a list of named taxa and diseases. Microbiology and infectious
disease now require One Health reasoning across people, animals,
environments, genomics, and antimicrobial stewardship. As you move
through the chapters, keep a two-column note: \textbf{claim} on the
left, \textbf{evidence that would change my confidence} on the right. By
the end of the unit, each major idea should be tied to a measurement,
model, citation, or paper-based lab decision.

\subsection{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-24}

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Compare the three domains \citep{woese1977} of life and explain how
  rRNA phylogeny established the
  Bacteria-\hyperref[gl:archaea]{\textbf{Archaea}}-Eukarya
  classification.
\item
  Describe bacterial cell structure including peptidoglycan
  architecture, Gram staining outcomes, and the clinical significance of
  LPS.
\item
  Trace the \textbf{peptidoglycan biosynthesis pathway} through
  MurA-MurF, lipid I, and lipid II, identifying the antibiotic targeting
  each step and the resistance mechanism that defeats it.
\item
  Classify bacteria by morphology, arrangement, and metabolic type, and
  identify major pathogenic groups.
\item
  Explain horizontal \hyperref[gl:gene]{\textbf{gene}} transfer
  mechanisms (transformation, transduction, conjugation) and their role
  in bacterial evolution and antibiotic resistance \citep{lawrence1998}.
\item
  Describe \textbf{two-component signal transduction}, \textbf{biofilm}
  formation, and \textbf{quorum sensing} as the molecular basis of
  bacterial sociality, and link them to chronic infections and
  device-associated disease.
\item
  Distinguish Archaea from Bacteria at the molecular level, including
  ether-linked isoprenoid lipids and tetraether monolayers, and describe
  the significance of Asgard archaea for eukaryotic origins.
\item
  Compare the Baltimore classification of viruses, contrast lytic and
  lysogenic cycles, and describe the HIV life cycle and its drug
  targets.
\item
  Explain CRISPR-Cas as a bacterial adaptive immune system, compare
  Types I/II/III, and assess \textbf{phage therapy} as a clinical
  alternative to antibiotics.
\item
  Apply the bacterial growth equation \(N(t) = N_0 \cdot 2^{t/t_d}\) to
  predict cell densities from generation time and infer doubling time
  from optical-density data.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Opening Vignette --- The Rebel Biologist Who Turned Bacteria
into \hyperref[gl:organelle]{\textbf{Organelle}}s}

In 1966, Lynn Margulis --- an unknown 28-year-old junior faculty member
at Boston University --- submitted a paper proposing that mitochondria
and \hyperref[gl:chloroplast]{\textbf{chloroplast}}s were once
free-living bacteria engulfed by a host cell \citep{margulis1967}. The
serial \hyperref[gl:endosymbiosis]{\textbf{endosymbiosis}} hypothesis
was rejected by more than fifteen journals before \emph{Journal of
Theoretical Biology} finally published it. Her evidence: the matching
size and \hyperref[gl:ribosome]{\textbf{ribosome}} type of mitochondria
and bacteria, their independent division by binary fission, and the
circular DNA they share with prokaryotes. When molecular sequencing
arrived in the 1970s, it confirmed everything --- mitochondria are
phylogenetically embedded within the \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-Proteobacteria, and chloroplasts
within the Cyanobacteria. Margulis had been completely right. The
bacterial origin of eukaryotic organelles is now foundational to cell
biology, and stands as one of the most important corrections to the
naive view that bacteria are too simple to matter for complex life.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Bacteria -- Domain Overview and Cell
Structure}\label{bacteria-domain-overview-and-cell-structure}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth]{../figures/bacterial_growth.png}
\caption{Bacterial growth curve: four phases (lag, exponential, stationary, death) plotted as $\log(\text{cell number})$ versus time.}
\label{fig:unit_VII_bacterial_growth}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{The Three Domains of
Life}\label{the-three-domains-of-life}

In 1977, Carl Woese and George Fox revolutionized our understanding of
life's diversity by analyzing ribosomal RNA (rRNA) sequences across
organisms \citep{woese1977}. Their phylogenetic analysis revealed that
life comprises three fundamental domains: \textbf{Bacteria},
\textbf{Archaea}, and \textbf{Eukarya}. This replaced the older
five-kingdom system that had grouped bacteria and archaea together as
``Monera.''

The 16S rRNA gene (in prokaryotes) and 18S rRNA gene (in
\hyperref[gl:eukaryote]{\textbf{eukaryote}}s) serve as molecular
chronometers because they are:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Almost universally present in most cellular life
\item
  Functionally constrained (slow evolutionary rate in conserved regions)
\item
  Sufficiently variable in hypervariable regions (V1-V9) for taxonomic
  resolution
\item
  Rarely subject to horizontal gene transfer
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Prokaryotic Cell
Features}\label{prokaryotic-cell-features}

Bacteria and Archaea share the prokaryotic cell plan, which differs
fundamentally from the eukaryotic organization:

\hyperref[gl:mitosis]{\textbf{Mitosis}} with spindle apparatus \\

The bacterial flagellum is a remarkable molecular machine. Unlike
eukaryotic flagella, which bend in a wave-like motion powered by
ATP-dependent dynein motors, the bacterial flagellum rotates like a
propeller. The basal body contains a rotary motor driven by the proton
motive force (or Na\(^+\) gradient in some marine species), spinning at
up to 1,700 revolutions per second in some species. The flagellar motor
can reverse direction, enabling the ``run and tumble'' chemotaxis
behavior in \emph{E. coli}.

\subsubsection{Bacterial Cell Wall:
Peptidoglycan}\label{bacterial-cell-wall-peptidoglycan}

The bacterial cell wall is composed of \textbf{peptidoglycan} (also
called murein), a mesh-like polymer unique to bacteria. Its structure
consists of:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Glycan strands}: Alternating units of N-acetylglucosamine
  (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM) linked by \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-1,4 glycosidic bonds
\item
  \textbf{Tetrapeptide side chains}: Attached to NAM; typically L-Ala --
  D-Glu -- meso-DAP (or L-Lys) -- D-Ala
\item
  \textbf{Cross-links}: Peptide bridges connecting adjacent glycan
  strands, catalyzed by transpeptidases (penicillin-binding proteins,
  PBPs)
\end{itemize}

The presence of \textbf{D-amino acids} (D-glutamate, D-alanine) is
unusual in biology -- most proteins use exclusively L-amino acids.
D-amino acids confer resistance to host proteases, which evolved to
cleave L-amino acid \hyperref[gl:peptide-bond]{\textbf{peptide bond}}s.

\subsubsection{Peptidoglycan Biosynthesis: A Step-by-Step Antibiotic
Atlas}\label{peptidoglycan-biosynthesis-a-step-by-step-antibiotic-atlas}

Peptidoglycan biosynthesis proceeds in three spatial compartments ---
cytoplasm, inner-membrane interface, and periplasm --- and nearly every
step has a clinically deployed antibiotic that targets it. Understanding
the pathway is therefore equivalent to understanding the chemotherapy of
bacterial infection. The pathway begins with the housekeeping sugar
\textbf{UDP-N-acetylglucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc)} and ends with a covalently
cross-linked sacculus surrounding the entire cell.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0115_ce65da087915.png}
\caption{Cytoplasm-to-periplasm peptidoglycan biosynthesis with five major antibiotic targets - fosfomycin (MurA), D-cycloserine (D-Ala-D-Ala ligase / Alr), bacitracin (C55 carrier recycling), vancomycin (D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of Lipid II), and beta-lactams (PBP transpeptidation).}
\end{figure}

Blocks attachment of pentapeptide to C55 lipid carrier (Lipid I
formation) & Toxic to humans (also blocks N-glycosylation) \\
6 & MurG (UDP-GlcNAc:Lipid I GlcNAc transferase) & (Preclinical) &
Blocks Lipid I \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Lipid II conversion & Investigational \\
7 & C55-PP recycling (BacA/UppP phosphatase) & \textbf{Bacitracin} &
Sequesters undecaprenyl-pyrophosphate, blocking dephosphorylation;
bactoprenol pool exhausted & Topical (Gram-positive) \\
8 & Lipid II flipping (MurJ flippase) & \textbf{Lysobactin} family
(preclinical) & Trap Lipid II in cytoplasm & Investigational \\
9 & Lipid II (D-Ala-D-Ala terminus) & \textbf{Vancomycin, teicoplanin,
dalbavancin, oritavancin} & Glycopeptide H-bonds to D-Ala-D-Ala;
sterically blocks PBP access and transglycosylation & MRSA, \emph{C.
difficile}, VRE-susceptible enterococci \\
10 & Transglycosylation + transpeptidation by PBPs &
\textbf{Penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, monobactams} &
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactam ring acylates PBP active-site serine (suicide substrate; mimics
D-Ala--D-Ala) & Broad \\
11 & Lipid II / membrane & \textbf{Daptomycin} (membrane),
\textbf{lipoglycopeptides}, \textbf{nisin} (lantibiotic) & Bind Lipid II
/ depolarize membrane & MRSA, VRE \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Resistance recapitulates the pathway.} Each drug elicits a
corresponding resistance trick: VanA-type vancomycin resistance in
enterococci (VRE) replaces D-Ala-D-Ala with D-Ala-D-Lac, abolishing one
of the five hydrogen bonds that vancomycin exploits (\texorpdfstring{\textgreater{}=}{>=} 1000-fold MIC
increase; the binding free-energy loss is about 12 kJ/mol per
H-bond); MRSA expresses \textbf{PBP2a} (encoded by \emph{mecA}) with low
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactam affinity (K\(_i\) rises about  1000\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x}); \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactamases
hydrolyse the \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactam ring before it reaches its PBP target, with
extended-spectrum \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactamases (ESBLs) and carbapenemases (KPC, NDM,
OXA-48) progressively defeating each new generation of \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactams. The
pathway thus serves as a unifying framework --- biosynthetic step, drug,
and resistance mechanism are three views of the same chemistry.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Why Vancomycin Stopped Working --- and How
Daptomycin Took Over} Vancomycin was introduced in 1958 and remained
dependable for almost 30 years. The first VRE isolates appeared in
1986--1988 in European and US hospitals, driven by agricultural use of
avoparcin (a glycopeptide growth promoter in livestock); by the early
2000s VRE had spread globally. The molecular trick is elegant: a single
ester linkage (D-Ala-D-Lac instead of the D-Ala-D-Ala amide) costs the
bacterium nothing but eliminates one of the five H-bonds anchoring
vancomycin. Daptomycin (FDA-approved 2003) bypasses the resistance
entirely --- it inserts into the cell membrane in a
Ca\(^{2+}\)-dependent manner, depolarising it without requiring a
peptidoglycan binding site. Daptomycin resistance is now emerging too
(mprF and yycG mutations alter membrane charge), continuing the arms
race.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Gram Staining: The Foundational Diagnostic
Test}\label{gram-staining-the-foundational-diagnostic-test}

The \hyperref[gl:gram-stain]{\textbf{Gram stain}}, developed by Hans
Christian Gram in 1884, remains the single most important initial test
in clinical microbiology. The procedure exploits differences in cell
wall architecture:

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0116_fdf180a01853.png}
\caption{Gram-stain decision tree producing purple (Gram-positive) versus pink (Gram-negative) results from differences in peptidoglycan thickness and outer-membrane architecture.}
\end{figure}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Lipid A}: The toxic moiety; embedded in the outer membrane;
  activates TLR4 on innate immune cells
\item
  \textbf{Core oligosaccharide}: Short sugar chain linking Lipid A to
  the O-antigen
\item
  \textbf{O-antigen}: Variable polysaccharide extending outward;
  serotype-specific; target of antibodies
\end{itemize}

When Gram-negative bacteria lyse during infection, released LPS triggers
massive innate immune activation through the TLR4-MD2 receptor complex.
This can lead to a cytokine cascade (TNF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}, IL-1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}, IL-6), systemic
inflammation, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), and septic
shock -- a life-threatening condition with mortality rates of 30-50\%.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Gram Staining in Diagnosis} The Gram stain
is typically the first test performed on clinical specimens (blood
cultures, cerebrospinal fluid, sputum). Results within 15 minutes guide
empirical antibiotic therapy before culture results are available (24-72
hours). For bacterial meningitis, Gram-positive diplococci suggest
\emph{Streptococcus pneumoniae} (treat with ceftriaxone + vancomycin),
while Gram-negative diplococci suggest \emph{Neisseria meningitidis}
(treat with ceftriaxone alone). This rapid distinction can be
life-saving in an emergency where hours matter.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 1:} A novel bacterium is isolated from a deep-sea
hydrothermal vent. Gram staining produces a pink result. Predict the
cell wall architecture and explain why the alcohol decolorization step
removed the crystal violet-iodine complex from this organism.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 1b:} A clinical microbiology lab tests a bacterial
isolate against six wall-targeted antibiotics. The isolate is resistant
to vancomycin (MIC \textgreater{} 256 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}g/mL) but susceptible to
ampicillin, fosfomycin, and bacitracin. Sequencing reveals a \emph{vanA}
operon. Using the peptidoglycan biosynthesis pathway, explain (a) which
step is altered, (b) why vancomycin fails, and (c) why ampicillin still
works.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 1c:} Fosfomycin is a phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP)
analog that covalently inactivates MurA. \emph{Pseudomonas aeruginosa}
is intrinsically resistant to fosfomycin despite having a functional
MurA. Hypothesise two non-target-based resistance mechanisms (think
about how the drug enters the cell) and propose an experiment using a
\emph{P. aeruginosa} MurA-knockout complemented with the \emph{E. coli}
allele to test whether MurA is responsible.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Morphology and

Bacterial cells exhibit characteristic shapes that aid in
identification:

Cell arrangements reflect division plane and post-division adhesion
patterns:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Diplo-} (pairs): \emph{Diplococcus}, \emph{Neisseria}
\item
  \textbf{Strepto-} (chains): \emph{Streptococcus} -- divides in one
  plane, cells remain attached
\item
  \textbf{Staphylo-} (grape-like clusters): \emph{Staphylococcus} --
  divides in multiple planes
\item
  \textbf{Tetrad} (groups of 4): \emph{Micrococcus} -- divides in two
  perpendicular planes
\item
  \textbf{Sarcina} (cuboidal packets of 8): \emph{Sarcina ventriculi} --
  divides in three planes
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Metabolic Diversity}\label{metabolic-diversity}

Bacteria exhibit unparalleled metabolic diversity -- far exceeding that
of eukaryotes combined. This diversity is classified by energy source
(photo- vs chemo-) and carbon source (auto- vs hetero-):

\textbf{Photoautotrophs} use light energy to fix CO\(_2\):

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{Cyanobacteria} (oxygenic
  \hyperref[gl:photosynthesis]{\textbf{photosynthesis}}): Use water as
  electron donor; produce O\(_2\); responsible for the Great Oxidation
  Event (about 2.4 Ga); ancestors of chloroplasts
\item
  Purple and green sulfur bacteria (anoxygenic): Use H\(_2\)S or S\(^0\)
  as electron donor; no O\(_2\) production; bacteriochlorophyll absorbs
  at longer wavelengths (800-1050 nm)
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Chemoautotrophs (lithotrophs)} derive energy from inorganic
chemical oxidation:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{Nitrosomonas}: NH\(_3\) -\textgreater{} NO\(_2^-\) (ammonia
  oxidation; \hyperref[gl:nitrification]{\textbf{nitrification}} step 1)
\item
  \emph{Nitrobacter}: NO\(_2^-\) -\textgreater{} NO\(_3^-\) (nitrite
  oxidation; nitrification step 2)
\item
  \emph{Thiobacillus}: S\(^0\) -\textgreater{} SO\(_4^{2-}\) (sulfur
  oxidation)
\item
  \emph{Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans}: Fe\(^{2+}\) -\textgreater{}
  Fe\(^{3+}\) (iron oxidation; used industrially in bioleaching of
  copper and gold ores)
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Heterotrophs} (the vast majority) obtain carbon from organic
compounds. They are further classified by oxygen relationship:

\emph{Mycobacterium} species deserve special mention: their cell walls
contain \textbf{mycolic acids} -- long-chain (\(C_{60}\)-\(C_{90}\))
branched fatty acids that form a waxy, hydrophobic barrier. This barrier
makes them resistant to Gram staining (they are classified as
\textbf{acid-fast} bacteria, stained with the Ziehl-Neelsen method using
carbol fuchsin), resistant to many antibiotics, and resistant to
desiccation -- contributing to \emph{M. tuberculosis} survival in
aerosolized droplet nuclei for hours.

\subsection{Bacterial Genetics, Signalling and
Sociality}\label{bacterial-genetics-signalling-and-sociality}

\subsubsection{Binary Fission}\label{binary-fission}

Bacteria reproduce asexually by binary fission: the circular chromosome
is replicated bidirectionally from a single origin of replication
(\emph{oriC}), the cell elongates, a septum forms at mid-cell
(coordinated by the FtsZ ring -- a tubulin homolog), and two daughter
cells separate. Generation times vary enormously:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{Escherichia coli}: about 20 minutes under optimal
  conditions (37 degrees C, rich media)
\item
  \emph{Mycobacterium tuberculosis}: 12-24 hours (contributing to slow
  disease progression and prolonged treatment)
\item
  \emph{Treponema pallidum}: about 33 hours (cannot be cultured
  in vitro)
\end{itemize}

Population growth during exponential phase follows the \textbf{bacterial
growth equation}:

\begin{equation}
N(t) = N_0 \cdot 2^{t/t_d}
\label{eq:unit_VII_bacterial_growth}
\end{equation}

where \(N_0\) is the initial population, \(t\) is time, and \(t_d\) is
the doubling (generation) time. Equivalently, the natural-log form
\(\ln N(t) = \ln N_0 + \mu t\) with \(\mu = (\ln 2)/t_d\) (the
\textbf{specific growth rate}, units of \(\text{time}^{-1}\)) gives a
linear plot of \(\ln N\) versus \(t\) during exponential phase, whose
slope is the experimentally measured \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}.

\emph{(Note: the exponent \(t/t_d\) is often represented as \(n\), the
number of generations).}

\subsubsection{Worked Example: Calculating Bacterial
Growth}\label{worked-example-calculating-bacterial-growth}

\textbf{Problem:} A microbiologist inoculates a broth with \(N_0 = 100\)
cells of \emph{Vibrio natriegens}, which has a generation time of
\(t_d = 15\) minutes under optimal conditions. Assuming the culture
immediately enters the exponential growth phase and maintains it without
nutrient depletion, how many cells will be present after 2 hours?

\textbf{Solution:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Calculate the total time (\(t\)) in consistent units:}
  \[ t = 2 \text{ hours} = 120 \text{ minutes}  \label{eq:unit_VII_bacteria_archaea_viruses_item_1}\]
\item
  \textbf{Calculate the number of generations (\(n\)):}
  \[ n = \frac{t}{t_d} = \frac{120}{15} = 8 \text{ generations}  \label{eq:unit_VII_bacteria_archaea_viruses_item_2}\]
\item
  \textbf{Calculate the final population size \(N(t)\) from
  \cref{eq:unit_VII_bacterial_growth}:}
  \[ N(t) = 100 \cdot 2^8  \label{eq:unit_VII_bacteria_archaea_viruses_item_3}\]

  \[ N(t) = 100 \cdot 256 = 25,600 \text{ cells}  \label{eq:unit_VII_bacteria_archaea_viruses_item_4}\]
\end{enumerate}

After 2 hours, the population will reach \textbf{25,600 cells}. The
rapid doubling of bacteria means that even a small initial inoculum can
quickly reach high densities in favorable environments. After 4 hours
(16 generations), the same culture would reach
\(\approx 6.5 \times 10^6\) cells; after 6 hours (24 generations),
\(\approx 1.7 \times 10^9\) cells --- at which point nutrient limitation
forces the culture into stationary phase.

\subsubsection{Worked Example: Inferring Generation Time from an OD
Growth
Curve}\label{worked-example-inferring-generation-time-from-an-od-growth-curve}

\textbf{Problem:} A microbiology student grows \emph{E. coli} in LB
broth at 37 °C and reads optical density at 600 nm
(\(\mathrm{OD}_{600}\)) every 30 minutes:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lllllll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Time (min) & 0 & 30 & 60 & 90 & 120 & 150 \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\(\mathrm{OD}_{600}\) & 0.05 & 0.10 & 0.20 & 0.40 & 0.80 & 1.60 \\
\end{longtable}
}

Estimate the generation time \(t_d\) during exponential growth.

\textbf{Solution:}

During exponential phase, \(\mathrm{OD}_{600}\) is proportional to cell
density, so \(\mathrm{OD}(t) = \mathrm{OD}_0 \cdot 2^{t/t_d}\). Take the
natural log of both sides:

\[ \ln \mathrm{OD}(t) = \ln \mathrm{OD}_0 + \frac{t}{t_d}\ln 2  \label{eq:unit_VII_bacteria_archaea_viruses_item_5}\]

A plot of \(\ln \mathrm{OD}\) versus \(t\) has slope
\(\mu = (\ln 2)/t_d\). Using the first and last points,

\[ \mu = \frac{\ln(1.60) - \ln(0.05)}{150 - 0} = \frac{0.470 - (-2.996)}{150} = \frac{3.466}{150} \approx 0.0231\ \mathrm{min}^{-1}.  \label{eq:unit_VII_bacteria_archaea_viruses_item_6}\]

Therefore,

\[ t_d = \frac{\ln 2}{\mu} = \frac{0.693}{0.0231} \approx 30\ \mathrm{minutes}.  \label{eq:unit_VII_bacteria_archaea_viruses_item_7}\]

The doubling time is \textbf{about 30 minutes}, consistent with
rich-media growth at 37 °C. Inspection of the table confirms the answer:
\(\mathrm{OD}_{600}\) doubles every 30 min from \(t = 30\) onwards. Real
growth curves deviate at the extremes (lag at the start, stationary
plateau at the end), as the full four-phase curve in
\cref{fig:unit_VII_bacterial_growth} shows; the linear-on-log-plot
region is the main window where \(t_d\) is well defined.

\subsubsection{Horizontal Gene Transfer}\label{horizontal-gene-transfer}

While binary fission produces clonal offspring, \textbf{horizontal gene
transfer (HGT)} is the major driver of bacterial evolution and genetic
diversity \citep{lawrence1998}. Three mechanisms operate:

\textbf{Transformation} involves the uptake of naked DNA from the
environment. Some species are naturally competent -- they express
surface proteins that bind, import, and integrate exogenous DNA.
\emph{Streptococcus pneumoniae} was the organism in Griffith's famous
1928 experiment demonstrating transformation (the ``transforming
principle,'' later identified as DNA by Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty in
1944). In molecular biology, artificial competence is induced by
treating \emph{E. coli} with CaCl\(_2\) and heat shock (42 degrees C for
45 seconds), which transiently increases membrane permeability.

\textbf{Transduction} is phage-mediated DNA transfer between bacteria:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{Generalized transduction}: During lytic replication, bacterial
  DNA fragments are accidentally packaged into phage capsids instead of
  phage DNA. These defective phage particles inject bacterial DNA into
  new host cells, where it can recombine into the chromosome.
\item
  \emph{Specialized transduction}: A lysogenic phage (e.g.,
  bacteriophage \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda}) excises imprecisely from the host chromosome,
  carrying flanking bacterial genes (\emph{gal} or \emph{bio} genes
  flanking the \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda} \emph{attB} site). These hybrid phage particles
  transduce specific genes at high frequency.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Conjugation} requires direct cell-to-cell contact via a sex
pilus encoded by the \textbf{F factor} (fertility
\hyperref[gl:plasmid]{\textbf{plasmid}}). The F\(^+\) donor cell extends
an F pilus that contacts an F\(^-\) recipient, retracting to bring cells
together. A single strand of the F plasmid is transferred and replicated
in the recipient, converting it to F\(^+\). When the F factor integrates
into the chromosome, the cell becomes \textbf{Hfr} (high frequency
\hyperref[gl:recombination]{\textbf{recombination}}), and conjugation
can transfer chromosomal genes to the recipient at high frequency.

\textbf{R-factor plasmids} (resistance plasmids) carry multiple
antibiotic resistance genes and are transferred by conjugation -- this
is the primary mechanism by which antibiotic resistance spreads among
bacterial populations, including between different species.

\subsubsection{Plasmids and Mobile Genetic
Elements}\label{plasmids-and-mobile-genetic-elements}

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2432}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3784}}@{}}

\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\textbf{Transposons} (mobile genetic elements) contribute to
\hyperref[gl:genome]{\textbf{genome}} plasticity. Insertion sequences
(IS elements) are the simplest, encoding primarily transposase flanked
by inverted repeats. Composite transposons (e.g., Tn3 carrying
ampicillin resistance) consist of a resistance gene flanked by IS
elements. Transposons can ``jump'' between chromosome and plasmid,
facilitating the assembly of multi-drug resistance cassettes.

\subsubsection{Two-Component Signal
Transduction}\label{two-component-signal-transduction}

Bacteria sense their environment through ubiquitous
\textbf{two-component systems (TCS)} --- the prokaryotic equivalent of
receptor-tyrosine-kinase + transcription-factor cascades in eukaryotes.
Each system is built from just two proteins:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  A membrane-anchored \textbf{sensor histidine kinase} (HK) with an
  extracellular sensing domain and a cytoplasmic kinase domain. Stimulus
  binding induces ATP-dependent \textbf{autophosphorylation} of a
  conserved histidine residue in the HK dimer (the phosphate is
  transferred from the \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma}-phosphate of ATP to the imidazole nitrogen of
  the histidine sidechain --- a high-energy phospho-amide bond,
  \(\Delta G \approx -50\) kJ/mol on hydrolysis).
\item
  A cytoplasmic \textbf{response regulator} (RR) with a receiver domain
  and an output (usually DNA-binding) domain. The HK transfers its
  phosphate to a conserved aspartate on the RR (a phospho-anhydride;
  faster hydrolysis kinetics, \(t_{1/2} \sim\) seconds to minutes),
  activating it as a transcription factor (or, less commonly, as an
  enzyme or motor regulator).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0117_917b675ef1e3.png}
\caption{Two-component signal transduction. Stimulus to HK autophosphorylation on histidine to phosphotransfer to RR aspartate to DNA binding and gene regulation; intrinsic phosphatase activity resets the system.}
\end{figure}

The two-component circuit is therefore a \textbf{molecular switch} with
three states (off / phosphorylated / phosphatase-reset), tunable by the
relative kinase versus phosphatase activities of the HK. Some HKs
(``classical'' HKs like EnvZ and PhoQ) act as kinase under stimulus and
phosphatase otherwise --- a single protein computing both ON and OFF,
with the stimulus ratio shifting the equilibrium. This bifunctionality
makes the steady-state level of RRabout  P a near-linear
readout of the input --- exactly what is wanted for analog signal
processing inside a cell.

Key features that make TCSs central to bacterial biology: they are
\textbf{modular} (HKs and RRs from one organism often work with
components from another), they are \textbf{fast} (sub-second response),
and there are \textbf{typically 30--80 systems per genome}, allowing
combinatorial integration of many environmental signals. The minimal
\emph{Mycoplasma genitalium} genome has 0 TCSs (it lives in a stable
host environment); free-living soil bacteria like \emph{Myxococcus
xanthus} encode \textgreater{} 100. Several recent antibacterial leads
(e.g., walkmycin against the WalK kinase, an essential cell-wall TCS)
target HKs precisely because they are absent from human cells.

\subsubsection{Biofilms and Quorum
Sensing}\label{biofilms-and-quorum-sensing}

Most bacteria in nature do not live as solitary planktonic cells; they
live in \textbf{biofilms} --- surface-attached, matrix-encased
communities that behave more like a tissue than a free-swimming
population. Biofilm formation proceeds through a stereotyped life cycle,
coordinated by \textbf{quorum sensing (QS)} --- cell-density-dependent
communication via diffusible \textbf{autoinducers} (AHLs in
Gram-negatives, AIPs in Gram-positives, AI-2 across species).

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0118_30f4d049f95f.png}
\caption{Biofilm life cycle from planktonic cell through reversible/irreversible attachment, microcolony, mature biofilm, and quorum-triggered dispersal - coordinated by intracellular c-di-GMP and intercellular autoinducers.}
\end{figure}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Exopolysaccharides} (PIA in \emph{S. aureus}; alginate, Pel,
  Psl in \emph{P. aeruginosa}; cellulose and PNAG in enterics) ---
  provide structural cohesion and protection.
\item
  \textbf{Extracellular DNA (eDNA)} --- released by autolysis; a major
  load-bearing component and a substrate for horizontal gene transfer at
  frequencies up to 1000\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} higher than in planktonic cells.
\item
  \textbf{Matrix proteins} --- amyloid-like curli fibres (\emph{E.
  coli}), Bap proteins, type IV pili.
\item
  \textbf{Lipids and outer-membrane vesicles} --- concentrate hydrolytic
  enzymes and signalling molecules.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Quorum sensing molecules.}

\textbf{Why biofilms matter clinically.} The CDC estimates that
\textbf{about 65--80 \% of chronic and device-associated human
infections involve biofilms}. They are 10--1000\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} more antibiotic
tolerant than planktonic cells because of (1) reduced antibiotic
penetration through EPS --- vancomycin diffusion can be retarded by
100\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x}; (2) \textbf{persister cells} --- metabolically dormant
subpopulations not killed by growth-dependent antibiotics, comprising
0.001--1 \% of biofilm cells; (3) localised enzyme accumulation (e.g.,
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactamase concentrated 100--1000\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} in matrix); and (4) anaerobic
interior microenvironments where aminoglycosides (which require an
electrochemical gradient for uptake) are inactive. Canonical clinical
biofilms include cystic fibrosis lung infections (\emph{P. aeruginosa}
alginate biofilms), prosthetic joint and heart-valve infections
(\emph{S. aureus}, \emph{S. epidermidis}), catheter-associated UTIs
(\emph{E. coli}, \emph{P. mirabilis}), chronic wounds, and dental plaque
(\emph{Streptococcus}, \emph{Porphyromonas}, \emph{Fusobacterium}).

\textbf{Quorum quenching as therapy.} Because most virulence factors are
quorum-regulated, blocking QS \emph{attenuates} virulence without
killing bacteria --- sidestepping the strong selection for resistance
that lytic antibiotics impose. Strategies include: \textbf{(1)}
lactonases (AiiA from \emph{Bacillus}, AhlD) and acylases that hydrolyse
AHLs; \textbf{(2)} synthetic AIP analogs that competitively inhibit
AgrC; \textbf{(3)} halogenated furanones (originally from the seaweed
\emph{Delisea pulchra}) that destabilise LuxR-family receptors;
\textbf{(4)} PqsR antagonists (e.g., M64); \textbf{(5)} c-di-GMP
signalling disruptors. Several are in early clinical trials (notably for
\emph{P. aeruginosa} in cystic fibrosis), though ``anti-virulence''
compounds face the challenge that they do not directly clear infection
--- they must work synergistically with antibiotics or host immunity.

\subsubsection{Endospores}\label{endospores}

Certain Firmicutes -- primarily \emph{Bacillus} (central or subterminal
spores) and \emph{Clostridium} (terminal spores) -- produce
\textbf{endospores} in response to nutrient depletion. The endospore is
the most resistant biological structure known:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Core}: Dehydrated \hyperref[gl:cytoplasm]{\textbf{cytoplasm}};
  calcium-dipicolinic acid complex stabilizes DNA; small acid-soluble
  spore proteins (SASPs) protect DNA from UV and desiccation
\item
  \textbf{Resistance}: Survives boiling (100 degrees C), desiccation, UV
  radiation, and chemical disinfectants
\item
  \textbf{Sterilization}: Requires autoclaving at 121 degrees C, 15 psi
  pressure, for 15-20 minutes
\item
  \textbf{Germination}: Triggered by favorable conditions (nutrients,
  water); rapid return to vegetative growth
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Endospores and Hospital Infection Control}
\emph{Clostridioides difficile} endospores persist on hospital surfaces
for months, resisting alcohol-based hand sanitizers (which are effective
against vegetative bacteria). Healthcare workers must use soap and water
(physical removal) and bleach-based surface disinfectants to prevent
\emph{C. difficile} transmission. \emph{Bacillus anthracis} spores were
used as a bioterrorism agent in the 2001 U.S. anthrax letter attacks,
contaminating postal facilities and requiring years of decontamination.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 2b:} A research lab knocks out the \emph{agrA}
gene (response regulator of the Agr quorum-sensing TCS) in \emph{S.
aureus}. The mutant forms thicker, more persistent biofilms in vitro but
is dramatically less virulent in a mouse skin-abscess model. Reconcile
these two observations using the AgrA on/off switch between biofilm and
toxin production.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 2c:} A patient develops a \emph{Pseudomonas
aeruginosa} bloodstream infection following indwelling-catheter
placement. Blood cultures show vancomycin-susceptible cells with MIC = 1
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}g/mL, yet the patient fails 4 weeks of intravenous vancomycin while the
catheter remains in place. Explain --- using biofilm penetration
kinetics, persister biology, and oxygen gradients --- why the planktonic
MIC is a poor predictor of clinical efficacy in catheter-associated
infection. What therapeutic action almost typically succeeds where
antibiotic monotherapy fails?
\end{quote}

\subsection{Archaea}\label{archaea}

\subsubsection{Distinguishing Features}\label{distinguishing-features}

Archaea are prokaryotes that were long classified with bacteria but
differ fundamentally at the molecular level:

\subsubsection{Archaeal Lipid Biochemistry: Why Hot Vents Don't Melt
Membranes}\label{archaeal-lipid-biochemistry-why-hot-vents-dont-melt-membranes}

The single most diagnostic biochemical feature of Archaea is the
architecture of their membrane lipids. Three differences from
bacterial/eukaryotic phospholipids are simultaneously present, and most
three contribute to extreme stability:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Ether linkages} instead of ester linkages between glycerol and
  the hydrocarbon chains. Ether bonds (C--O--C) are far more chemically
  inert than ester bonds (C--O--C(=O)) --- they resist acid hydrolysis,
  base hydrolysis, oxidation, and high-temperature cleavage.
\item
  \textbf{Isoprenoid (phytanyl) chains} (built from C5 isoprene units,
  with branched methyl groups every 4 carbons) instead of straight-chain
  fatty acids. Methyl branches cause kinks that prevent tight chain
  crystallization at low temperatures (preventing membrane gelling)
  while van-der-Waals interactions between branches stiffen the membrane
  against fluidization at high temperatures.
\item
  \textbf{Glycerol stereochemistry}: archaeal glycerol is
  \emph{sn}-glycerol-1-phosphate (G-1-P); bacterial/eukaryotic glycerol
  is \emph{sn}-glycerol-3-phosphate (G-3-P). The two are enantiomers ---
  a deep, ``lipid divide'' between archaea and the rest of cellular life
  that probably reflects independent invention of phospholipid
  biosynthesis after the LUCA.
\end{enumerate}

Hyperthermophilic archaea (\emph{Sulfolobus}, \emph{Thermococcus},
\emph{Pyrodictium}) take this further by linking two phytanyl chains
end-to-end, forming \textbf{glycerol-dialkyl-glycerol-tetraether (GDGT)}
lipids. Two GDGT molecules then span the entire membrane as a
\textbf{monolayer} (rather than a bilayer), with two glycerol headgroups
(one on each surface) and one continuous hydrocarbon block in the
middle. The covalent backbone makes the membrane behave mechanically
like a single rigid sheet --- it cannot delaminate, leak, or peel apart
even at 113 °C.

Quantitatively: a typical bacterial membrane fluidizes (loses lipid
order) above about 60 °C and disintegrates above
about 100 °C; \emph{Pyrodictium} GDGT monolayers retain
integrity at 113 °C and pH 1, conditions that hydrolyse most
ester-linked lipids in seconds. \textbf{Cyclopentane rings} within the
GDGT chains can be added or removed on the fly to fine-tune membrane
fluidity to growth temperature --- a remarkable example of biochemical
homeoviscous adaptation. Because eukaryotic and bacterial membranes lack
these adaptations, penicillin-class and polymyxin-class antibiotics that
act on bacterial cell envelopes are generally ineffective against
archaea.

\subsubsection{Major Archaeal Groups}\label{major-archaeal-groups}

\textbf{Euryarchaeota} encompasses the broadest metabolic diversity:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Methanogens}: Strict anaerobes that produce methane as a
  metabolic end product. The key reaction is:
  \(\text{CO}_2 + 4\text{H}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\).
  Methanogens inhabit \hyperref[gl:anaerobic]{\textbf{anaerobic}}
  environments including wetlands, rice paddies, landfills, and the
  rumen of cattle. \emph{Methanobrevibacter smithii} is the
  \hyperref[gl:dominant]{\textbf{dominant}} archaeon in the human gut.
  Globally, methanogenesis produces approximately 1 billion tonnes of
  CH\(_4\) annually, contributing approximately 10\% of anthropogenic
  greenhouse gas emissions.
\item
  \textbf{Extreme halophiles}: \emph{Halobacterium salinarum} thrives in
  saturated salt solutions (about 5 M NaCl). It maintains
  osmotic balance by accumulating intracellular KCl to equimolar
  concentrations. Its purple membrane contains
  \textbf{bacteriorhodopsin}, a light-driven proton pump that generates
  ATP via \hyperref[gl:chemiosmosis]{\textbf{chemiosmosis}} -- a form of
  phototrophy independent of
  \hyperref[gl:chlorophyll]{\textbf{chlorophyll}}. The salt flats
  visible from space (pink/red coloration in San Francisco Bay salt
  ponds) owe their color to halophilic archaea.
\item
  \textbf{Thermoacidophiles}: \emph{Thermoplasma acidophilum} grows
  optimally at 59 degrees C and \hyperref[gl:ph]{\textbf{pH}} 2.
  Notably, it lacks a cell wall entirely, surviving in hot acid through
  a reinforced lipid membrane.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Crenarchaeota} includes the most extreme hyperthermophiles:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{Sulfolobus solfataricus}: 80 degrees C, pH 2-3; model organism
  for archaeal molecular biology
\item
  \emph{Pyrodictium occultum}: Grows at 113 degrees C -- among the
  highest known temperatures for life
\item
  \emph{Thermoproteus tenax}: Autotrophic sulfur metabolism at 85
  degrees C
\item
  These organisms possess \textbf{reverse gyrase}, an
  \hyperref[gl:enzyme]{\textbf{enzyme}} that introduces positive
  supercoils into DNA, stabilizing the double helix at extreme
  temperatures
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Asgard Archaea: The Closest Living Relatives of
Eukaryotes}\label{asgard-archaea-the-closest-living-relatives-of-eukaryotes}

\textbf{Asgard Archaea} represent perhaps the most important discovery
in evolutionary biology of the past decade. In 2015, Ettema and
colleagues identified novel archaeal lineages in metagenomic data from
deep-sea sediments near Loki's Castle hydrothermal vent field in the
Arctic Mid-Ocean Ridge. The clade has since expanded into a large
superphylum named for Norse mythology:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Lokiarchaeota} (Loki's Castle, 2015) --- the founding lineage;
  \textgreater{} 100 published MAGs.
\item
  \textbf{Thorarchaeota} (named for Thor) --- abundant in marine
  sediments.
\item
  \textbf{Odinarchaeota}, \textbf{Heimdallarchaeota},
  \textbf{Helarchaeota}, \textbf{Hermodarchaeota},
  \textbf{Wukongarchaeota} --- discovered in successive metagenomic
  surveys 2017--2024.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Eukaryotic signature proteins (ESPs).} What makes Asgard archaea
revolutionary is that they encode an unprecedented cluster of proteins
previously thought to be eukaryote-specific:

\textbf{Phylogenetic placement.} Maximum-likelihood and Bayesian
analyses of conserved markers consistently place Asgard archaea
(especially Heimdallarchaeota) as the \textbf{sister group to most
eukaryotes}, supporting the \textbf{``two-domain tree''} of life
(Bacteria as one domain; Archaea + Eukarya as a single,
rooted-from-within-Archaea clade). This is the \textbf{eocyte
hypothesis} validated at high resolution. The evolutionary inference:
eukaryotes arose by \textbf{endosymbiosis between an Asgard-like
archaeal host} (which contributed the cytoplasm, cytoskeleton, and
information-processing genes) \textbf{and an \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-proteobacterial
endosymbiont} (which became the mitochondrion).

\textbf{Cultivation breakthrough.} In 2020, \emph{Candidatus
Prometheoarchaeum syntrophicum} --- the first cultured Asgard archaeon
--- was reported by Imachi \emph{et al.} (\emph{Nature}) after 12 years
of effort using extremely slow-growth bioreactor cultures fed with
peptides and hydrogen. The organism grows obligately syntrophically with
\emph{Halodesulfovibrio} (sulfate-reducing) and a methanogenic archaeon
(consuming H\(_2\) produced by \emph{Prometheoarchaeum}). Its doubling
time is about  14--25 days; cells are tiny (about 
0.5 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m) and \textbf{extend long branching tentacle-like protrusions}
thought to deliver hydrogen to syntrophic partners. The remarkable
observation is that those tentacles morphologically resemble what one
might predict for an archaeal cell preparing to engulf a bacterial
endosymbiont --- the \textbf{``E\(^3\) model'' of eukaryogenesis}
(Entangle, Engulf, Endogenise) directly suggested by
\emph{Prometheoarchaeum} morphology.

\textbf{Implications.} The discovery of Asgard archaea has narrowed the
``evolutionary gap'' between prokaryotes and eukaryotes from a vast
unbridgeable distance to a graded continuum. Many of the molecular
machines once thought to be uniquely eukaryotic (membrane-trafficking
ESCRTs, actin cytoskeleton, ubiquitin signalling) were already present
in the archaeal common ancestor of eukaryotes. Eukaryogenesis was a
\emph{combinatorial} event: pre-existing archaeal ESPs + acquisition of
a mitochondrion + nucleus + later innovations. Two outstanding questions
remain: (1) how exactly did the first eukaryotic cell engulf the
proto-mitochondrion (phagocytosis-first, syntrophy-first, or
virus-mediated?); (2) which Asgard subgroup is the closest living
relative --- Heimdallarchaeota (current consensus) or a yet-undiscovered
lineage?

\subsubsection{Archaeal Biotechnology}\label{archaeal-biotechnology}

Archaeal enzymes, evolved for extreme conditions, have enormous
biotechnological value:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Taq polymerase} from \emph{Thermus aquaticus} (technically a
  bacterium, but often discussed alongside thermophilic archaea): 70
  degrees C optimum; enabled the
  \hyperref[gl:polymerase-chain-reaction]{\textbf{polymerase chain
  reaction (PCR)}} -- arguably the single most important technique in
  molecular biology; Kary Mullis, Nobel Prize 1993
\item
  \textbf{Pfu polymerase} from \emph{Pyrococcus furiosus}: 3'-to-5'
  proofreading exonuclease activity; higher fidelity than Taq; used when
  accuracy is critical (cloning, mutagenesis)
\item
  \textbf{Vent polymerase} from \emph{Thermococcus litoralis}:
  thermostable with proofreading
\item
  Industrial applications: archaeal proteases, lipases, and amylases for
  high-temperature industrial processes; extremophilic enzymes for
  detergents, food processing, and biofuel production
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 3:} Explain why antibiotics that target
peptidoglycan synthesis (e.g., penicillin, vancomycin) are ineffective
against archaea. What does this tell us about the evolutionary
relationship between bacterial and archaeal cell walls?
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 3b:} Hyperthermophiles use GDGT tetraether
monolayers; mesophilic archaea use diether bilayers. Predict,
qualitatively, how membrane permeability to small molecules (water,
protons, ATP) should differ between the two architectures and what this
implies for chemiosmotic ATP synthesis at 100 °C.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 3c:} Asgard archaea encode actin homologs that
function in vitro indistinguishably from eukaryotic actin. If the
proto-eukaryote inherited actin from an archaeal ancestor, what testable
prediction does this make about the timing of cytoskeletal evolution
relative to the mitochondrial endosymbiosis? Design a
comparative-genomic experiment that could distinguish between the
alternatives.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Viruses}\label{viruses}

\subsubsection{General Features}\label{general-features}

Viruses are obligate intracellular
\hyperref[gl:parasite]{\textbf{parasite}}s that cannot carry out
metabolism independently. They lack ribosomes, cannot generate ATP, and
require host cell machinery for replication. Whether viruses are
``alive'' remains a philosophical and definitional question -- they
exhibit heredity and evolution but not autonomous metabolism or cellular
organization.

A complete virus particle (virion) consists of:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Genome}: DNA or RNA (rarely both); single-stranded or
  double-stranded; linear or circular; segmented or non-segmented
\item
  \textbf{Capsid}: Protein shell assembled from capsomeres; icosahedral
  (20 triangular faces -- \emph{adenovirus}), helical (\emph{tobacco
  mosaic virus}), or complex (\emph{bacteriophage T4})
\item
  \textbf{Envelope} (some viruses): Lipid bilayer derived from host cell
  membrane during budding; contains viral glycoproteins essential for
  host cell attachment and entry
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Baltimore Classification}\label{baltimore-classification}

David Baltimore (Nobel Prize 1975) classified viruses by genome type and
replication strategy into seven classes:

\subsubsection{Bacteriophage Life
Cycles}\label{bacteriophage-life-cycles}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0119_d56546b6ad20.png}
\caption{State diagram of the phage lambda lytic / lysogenic decision and the SOS-induced switch from lysogeny to lytic growth.}
\end{figure}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Adsorption}: Tail fibers (long tail fibers recognize LPS;
  short tail fibers make irreversible contact) bind the surface of
  \emph{E. coli}
\item
  \textbf{DNA injection}: The tail sheath contracts like a syringe,
  driving the tail tube through the outer membrane and injecting
  about 169 kb of linear dsDNA
\item
  \textbf{Early gene expression}: Host RNA polymerase is hijacked;
  phage-encoded anti-sigma factors redirect
  \hyperref[gl:transcription]{\textbf{transcription}}; host DNA is
  degraded by phage nucleases (recycling
  \hyperref[gl:nucleotide]{\textbf{nucleotide}}s)
\item
  \textbf{DNA replication}: Phage DNA replicates using phage-encoded DNA
  polymerase; hydroxymethylcytosine replaces cytosine (protecting phage
  DNA from its own restriction enzymes)
\item
  \textbf{Late gene expression}: Structural proteins (head, tail, tail
  fibers, baseplate) are synthesized
\item
  \textbf{Assembly}: Heads are filled with DNA (headful packaging);
  tails are assembled separately; components join spontaneously
\item
  \textbf{Lysis}: Holin creates pores in the inner membrane; endolysin
  (lysozyme) degrades peptidoglycan; about 100-200 progeny
  phage released per cell; entire cycle takes about 25 minutes
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Bacteriophage lambda (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda}) lysogeny} represents a molecular
decision switch:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  After infection, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda} integrase catalyzes site-specific recombination
  between phage \emph{attP} and bacterial \emph{attB} sites, inserting
  the phage genome into the host chromosome
\item
  The \textbf{CI repressor} (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda} repressor) binds operator sequences,
  repressing lytic genes and maintaining lysogeny -- the prophage
  replicates passively with the host
\item
  Upon DNA damage (UV exposure, mitomycin C), the SOS response activates
  \textbf{RecA}, which stimulates CI repressor autocleavage,
  derepressing lytic genes and initiating the lytic cycle
\item
  Imprecise excision during induction can produce specialized
  transducing phage carrying \emph{gal} or \emph{bio} genes
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Animal Virus Replication}\label{animal-virus-replication}

Animal viruses follow a general replication strategy with virus-specific
variations:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Attachment}: Viral surface protein binds specific host
  receptor (tropism determinant)

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Influenza: hemagglutinin (HA) binds sialic acid residues
  \item
    HIV: gp120 binds CD4 + CCR5 or CXCR4 coreceptor
  \item
    SARS-CoV-2: spike protein binds ACE2 receptor
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Penetration}: Receptor-mediated
  \hyperref[gl:endocytosis]{\textbf{endocytosis}} (most non-enveloped
  viruses) or membrane fusion (enveloped viruses)
\item
  \textbf{Uncoating}: Capsid disassembly releases genome into cytoplasm
  (or nucleus)
\item
  \textbf{Biosynthesis}: Genome replication and protein synthesis
  (location depends on virus type)
\item
  \textbf{Assembly}: New virions assembled in cytoplasm or nucleus
\item
  \textbf{Release}: Budding through host membrane (enveloped viruses --
  acquiring lipid envelope) or cell lysis (non-enveloped viruses)
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{The HIV Life Cycle}\label{the-hiv-life-cycle}

HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) is a Class VI retrovirus with a
complex life cycle and multiple drug targets:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Attachment and fusion}: gp120 binds CD4 on T helper cells,
  then undergoes conformational change to bind coreceptor (CCR5 in early
  infection, CXCR4 in late infection); gp41 mediates membrane fusion
\item
  \textbf{Reverse transcription}: ssRNA genome -\textgreater{} dsDNA via
  reverse transcriptase (RT); RT lacks proofreading (\(\sim 10^{-4}\)
  errors per base per cycle), generating enormous genetic diversity
\item
  \textbf{Nuclear import}: Pre-integration complex enters nucleus
  through nuclear pores
\item
  \textbf{Integration}: Integrase inserts viral dsDNA into host
  chromosome, creating the \textbf{provirus} -- a permanent part of the
  host genome; preferentially integrates into actively transcribed
  regions
\item
  \textbf{Transcription and
  \hyperref[gl:translation]{\textbf{translation}}}: Host RNA Pol II
  transcribes viral mRNA; Tat protein enhances transcription 100-fold;
  Rev protein exports unspliced mRNA from nucleus
\item
  \textbf{Assembly and budding}: Gag and Gag-Pol polyproteins assemble
  at plasma membrane; budding acquires lipid envelope with gp120/gp41
  spikes
\item
  \textbf{Maturation}: Viral protease cleaves Gag-Pol polyprotein into
  functional proteins; immature virion becomes infectious
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Antiretroviral therapy (ART)} targets multiple steps:

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3448}}@{}}

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

NRTIs (nucleoside RT inhibitors) & Reverse transcriptase & Tenofovir,

\subsubsection{Prions}\label{prions}

\textbf{Prions} are infectious agents composed entirely of misfolded
protein -- they contain no nucleic acid. The normal cellular prion
protein (PrP\(^C\), predominantly \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-helical) is converted to the
pathogenic scrapie form (PrP\(^{Sc}\), predominantly \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-sheet) through
templated conformational change. PrP\(^{Sc}\) serves as a seed,
converting neighboring PrP\(^C\) molecules in a chain reaction that
produces amyloid fibrils.

Prion diseases (transmissible spongiform encephalopathies) include:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD)}: Sporadic (most common),
  familial, or iatrogenic
\item
  \textbf{Variant CJD (vCJD)}: Transmitted from bovine spongiform
  encephalopathy (BSE/``mad cow disease'') via contaminated beef
\item
  \textbf{Fatal familial insomnia}: Autosomal dominant; progressive
  insomnia leading to death
\item
  \textbf{Kuru}: Transmitted among the Fore people of Papua New Guinea
  through ritual endocannibalism; studied by Gajdusek (Nobel Prize 1976)
\item
  \textbf{Chronic wasting disease (CWD)}: Affects cervids (deer, elk);
  spreading across North America
\end{itemize}

Stanley Prusiner received the Nobel Prize in 1997 for his prion
hypothesis -- initially controversial because it challenged the central
dogma that most infectious agents require nucleic acid for replication.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Bacteriophage Therapy} With the rise of
antibiotic-resistant infections, bacteriophage therapy is experiencing a
renaissance. The UC San Diego Center for Innovative Phage Applications
and Therapeutics (IPATH) has treated patients with life-threatening
multidrug-resistant infections using personalized phage cocktails. In
2016, Tom Patterson was rescued from a pan-resistant \emph{Acinetobacter
baumannii} infection using phages sourced from sewage. Engineered phages
can be designed to target specific bacterial species while sparing
beneficial \hyperref[gl:microbiota]{\textbf{microbiota}} -- a precision
antimicrobial approach unfeasible with conventional antibiotics.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Phage Therapy: A Pre-Antibiotic Idea Returns to the
Clinic}\label{phage-therapy-a-pre-antibiotic-idea-returns-to-the-clinic}

Phage therapy was discovered by Félix d'Hérelle in 1917, deployed widely
in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe through the 20th century, and
largely abandoned in the West after the introduction of penicillin. The
antibiotic-resistance crisis has driven a global resurgence: as of 2024,
more than 30 phage therapy clinical trials are registered worldwide.

\textbf{Why phages are appealing as therapeutics:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Self-amplification at the site of infection} --- every
  successful infection produces about 50--500 progeny, so dose
  increases where the target bacterium is densest, then declines as the
  infection clears.
\item
  \textbf{Narrow host range} --- most phages target a single species or
  strain, sparing the resident
  \hyperref[gl:microbiota]{\textbf{microbiota}} (a rare property;
  conventional broad-spectrum antibiotics decimate commensals).
\item
  \textbf{Co-evolution with bacteria} --- the same evolutionary force
  that creates antibiotic resistance also creates new phages; phage
  banks can be updated continuously.
\item
  \textbf{Engineerability} --- synthetic biology now enables host-range
  expansion, removal of toxin-encoding genes, addition of CRISPR-Cas
  payloads to specifically target resistance genes, and lytic/lysogenic
  switching.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Clinical milestones (2016--2026):}

\textbf{Phage pharmacokinetics --- why they break the small-molecule
rules.} Conventional antibiotics follow first-order pharmacokinetics:
\(C(t) = C_0 e^{-k_e t}\), with linear AUC/dose relationships. Phages do
the opposite. The phage population grows where bacterial density is high
(auto-dosing) and crashes when the bacteria are gone (auto-clearance).
The simplest model is a Lotka--Volterra-like coupled ODE:

\[ \frac{dB}{dt} = rB - kBP, \qquad \frac{dP}{dt} = bkBP - mP  \label{eq:unit_VII_bacteria_archaea_viruses_item_8}\]

where \(B\) = bacterial density, \(P\) = phage density, \(r\) =
bacterial growth rate, \(k\) = adsorption rate constant (typically
\(10^{-9}\)--\(10^{-7}\) mL min\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}), \(b\) = burst size (50--500), \(m\)
= phage clearance rate. The system has a \textbf{proliferation
threshold} at \(B^* = m / (bk)\): above \(B^*\), phage replicate faster
than they are cleared and amplify; below \(B^*\), they are diluted out.
This means low-dose phage \textbf{will not work} against a sub-threshold
infection --- clinicians must dose above the minimum proliferating
concentration. It also means a single phage dose can clear
orders-of-magnitude more bacteria than its initial titer, making
``dose'' a misleading concept.

\textbf{Pharmacokinetic and regulatory challenges that distinguish
phages from small molecules:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Bacterial resistance is rapid} --- phage receptors mutate at
  \(10^{-6}\)--\(10^{-8}\) per cell per generation. Cocktails of 3--5
  phages targeting non-overlapping receptors slow this; estimated escape
  probability \(\approx \prod_i 10^{-7} = 10^{-21}\) for a 3-phage
  cocktail with independent receptors.
\item
  \textbf{Immune neutralization} --- IgG against phage capsid emerges
  within about 10 days, lowering blood titres and limiting
  repeated systemic dosing.
\item
  \textbf{Pharmacokinetics are non-linear} --- phage concentration
  depends on bacterial density (replication \textgreater{} clearance
  below threshold; opposite above) --- classical AUC/MIC concepts do not
  apply.
\item
  \textbf{Manufacturing \& regulation} --- purified, endotoxin-free
  phage preparations require GMP processes designed for biologicals; the
  FDA has issued personalized/compassionate-use pathways while broad
  regulatory frameworks are still developing.
\item
  \textbf{Lysogenic phages can transduce virulence/resistance genes}
  (Shiga toxin in STEC came from a lambdoid phage); therapeutic phages
  must be obligately lytic and toxin-free.
\end{enumerate}

The pragmatic clinical role emerging by 2026 is \textbf{adjunctive phage
therapy} --- phages combined with antibiotics for biofilm-associated and
multi-drug-resistant infections (prosthetic joints, CF lungs,
complicated UTIs, infective endocarditis), where phage-driven dispersal
of biofilm matrix re-sensitizes persisters to antibiotics and the
antibiotic suppresses phage-resistant escapees. This combination logic
mirrors HIV ART and TB DOTS --- the lesson that single-agent
antimicrobial therapy invites resistance is now being applied to phages
too.

activity, producing approximately one
\hyperref[gl:mutation]{\textbf{mutation}} per genome per replication
cycle. Explain why this high mutation rate is both advantageous for the
virus (immune evasion, drug resistance) and why it also constrains the
maximum genome size of retroviruses compared to DNA viruses like
herpesviruses (about 150 kb genome).
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 4b:} A patient with chronic \emph{Pseudomonas
aeruginosa} lung infection in cystic fibrosis is treated with a phage
cocktail. Within 5 days, the bacterial load drops 100-fold, but by day
14, \emph{P. aeruginosa} has rebounded with mutations in \emph{galU}
(LPS biosynthesis). Explain (a) why galU mutants escape the phage, (b)
why the rebound strain may actually be less fit \emph{in vivo} than the

\subsection{Antibiotic Mechanisms and
Resistance}\label{antibiotic-mechanisms-and-resistance}

\subsubsection{Antibiotic Classes by
Mechanism}\label{antibiotic-classes-by-mechanism}

Antibiotics exploit the structural and biochemical differences between
prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. Each class targets a specific
essential process:

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0120_6f48da85c781.png}
\caption{Antibiotic targets organised by cellular process (cell-wall synthesis, protein synthesis, nucleic-acid synthesis, membrane disruption) alongside the principal resistance mechanisms.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Selective Toxicity}\label{selective-toxicity}

The foundation of antibiotic therapy is \textbf{selective toxicity} --
targeting structures present in bacteria but absent or sufficiently
different in human cells:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Peptidoglycan (absent in human cells) -\textgreater{} beta-lactams,
  vancomycin
\item
  70S ribosomes (vs.~human 80S) -\textgreater{} aminoglycosides,
  tetracyclines, macrolides
\item
  Bacterial DNA gyrase (vs.~human topoisomerase II) -\textgreater{}
  fluoroquinolones
\item
  Bacterial RNA polymerase (structurally distinct from human Pol II)
  -\textgreater{} rifampin
\item
  LPS outer membrane (absent in human cells) -\textgreater{} polymyxins
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Resistance Mechanisms in
Detail}\label{resistance-mechanisms-in-detail}

\textbf{Beta-lactamases} are the most clinically important resistance
mechanism. These enzymes hydrolyze the beta-lactam ring, inactivating
the antibiotic before it reaches its PBP target. Evolution of
beta-lactamases tracks the history of antibiotic development:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Penicillinase (TEM-1, SHV-1) -\textgreater{} resistance to penicillins
\item
  Extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBLs: CTX-M, TEM variants)
  -\textgreater{} resistance to 3rd-generation cephalosporins
\item
  Carbapenemases (KPC, NDM-1, OXA-48) -\textgreater{} resistance to
  carbapenems (last-resort beta-lactams)
\end{itemize}

\textbf{MRSA} (\emph{methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus})
carries the \textbf{mecA} or \textbf{mecC} gene encoding PBP2a/PBP2c,
altered penicillin-binding proteins with low affinity for most
traditional beta-lactam antibiotics. The gene resides on SCC\emph{mec}
(staphylococcal cassette chromosome), acquired by horizontal gene
transfer. Treatment depends on syndrome and susceptibility: vancomycin,
daptomycin, linezolid, or ceftaroline/ceftobiprole in settings where
anti-MRSA cephalosporins are appropriate.

\textbf{Efflux pumps} actively transport antibiotics out of the cell.
The AcrAB-TolC system in \emph{E. coli} and MexAB-OprM in
\emph{Pseudomonas aeruginosa} are tripartite pumps spanning the inner
membrane, periplasm, and outer membrane, conferring resistance to
multiple drug classes simultaneously.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0121_3ff5e572147d.png}
\caption{AMR horizontal-gene-transfer map. Resistance spreads by both clonal expansion and mobile genetic elements, so stewardship must be paired with infection control, wastewater/environmental surveillance, and organism-resistance-pair reporting \textbackslash{}citep\{who2024bppl,cdc2025antibioticuse\}.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{WHO Priority Pathogens
(ESKAPE)}\label{who-priority-pathogens-eskape}

The WHO 2024 Bacterial Priority Pathogens List keeps AMR triage grounded
in public-health burden, resistance trend, transmissibility,
treatability, and pipeline scarcity \citep{who2024bppl}. The
\textbf{ESKAPE} mnemonic remains a useful bedside memory aid, but the
WHO list is broader: it separately prioritises carbapenem-resistant
\emph{Acinetobacter baumannii}, carbapenem- or
third-generation-cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales,
drug-resistant \emph{Mycobacterium tuberculosis}, and other
pathogen-resistance pairs.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: The Antibiotic Resistance Crisis} The WHO
has declared antimicrobial resistance one of the top 10 global public
health threats. An estimated 1.27 million deaths were directly
attributable to bacterial AMR in 2019, with many more associated deaths
\citep{murray2022amr}. The O'Neill review's 10-million-deaths-per-year
scenario remains a warning about unchecked resistance rather than a
forecast that must occur \citep{oneill2016amr}. Major drivers include
unnecessary human antibiotic prescribing, incomplete access to
diagnostics, antibiotic use in food-animal production, and a thin
discovery pipeline in which truly novel antibacterial classes are rare
rather than absent \citep{cdc2025antibioticuse,who2024bppl}.
\end{quote}

\subsection{CRISPR-Cas: Bacterial Adaptive
Immunity}\label{crispr-cas-bacterial-adaptive-immunity}

\textbf{CRISPR} (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic
Repeats) arrays provide bacteria and archaea with an adaptive, heritable
immune system against phages and plasmids. Discovered in 2007 (Barrangou
\emph{et al.}, \emph{Science} 2007), the system has three functional
stages --- \textbf{adaptation, expression (biogenesis), and
interference} --- that map cleanly onto the three steps of any immune
system: memory formation, surveillance, and effector action.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0122_5973a9d90dc7.png}
\caption{The three-stage CRISPR-Cas immune mechanism: adaptation (Cas1-Cas2 captures and integrates new spacers), expression (pre-crRNA processed and loaded onto effector), and interference (target dsDNA cleavage).}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Stage 1 --- Spacer Acquisition
(Adaptation)}\label{stage-1-spacer-acquisition-adaptation}

When a bacterium survives phage infection, the \textbf{Cas1-Cas2
integrase complex} captures a short fragment (about 30 bp) of
phage DNA --- called a \textbf{protospacer} --- adjacent to a
\textbf{PAM} (protospacer adjacent motif). Cas1-Cas2 integrates this as
a new \textbf{spacer} at the leader end of the CRISPR array between two
direct repeats. This constitutes an immunological memory: the spacer
sequence is now permanently encoded in the bacterial chromosome and
inherited by most daughter cells.

\begin{equation}
\text{Cas1-Cas2} + \text{protospacer-PAM} \rightarrow \text{pre-spacer} \xrightarrow{\text{integration}} \text{CRISPR array expanded}
\label{eq:bacteria_archaea_viruses_2}
\end{equation}

\textbf{PAM recognition} ensures self vs non-self discrimination: the
PAM sequence is not present in the CRISPR array itself (repeat sequences
flank spacers, not PAMs), so the bacterium does not attack its own
CRISPR locus. The specific PAM depends on the system: NGG (SpCas9, Type
II), 5'-AAT-3' or 5'-CTT-3' (Type I-E), etc.

\subsubsection{Stage 2 --- crRNA
Biogenesis}\label{stage-2-crrna-biogenesis}

The CRISPR array is transcribed as a long pre-CRISPR RNA (pre-crRNA).
Repeat sequences are cleaved by:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Type I and III}: The \emph{Cas6} endoribonuclease (recognizes
  stem-loop structure in repeats)
\item
  \textbf{Type II}: RNase III + \emph{tracrRNA} (trans-activating crRNA)
  hybridises with the repeat; Cas9 is then loaded with a single-guide
  RNA (sgRNA = crRNA + tracrRNA scaffold)
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Stage 3 --- Interference
(Targeting)}\label{stage-3-interference-targeting}

The crRNA guides the effector complex to matching sequences in foreign
nucleic acid. The CRISPR-Cas systems are now classified into 6 types
(I--VI) and over 30 subtypes; the three most important types are
summarised below:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1750}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2500}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2750}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3000}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Feature
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
\textbf{Type I}
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
\textbf{Type II}
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
\textbf{Type III}
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Effector & Multi-subunit \textbf{Cascade} complex (Cas5--Cas8) + Cas3
helicase-nuclease & Single \textbf{Cas9} nuclease &
\textbf{Cas10}-Csm/Cmr complex \\
Target & dsDNA & dsDNA & ssRNA + transcribed DNA \\
Cleavage mechanism & Cas3 unwinds and \textbf{degrades dsDNA
processively} & Cas9 makes blunt-ended \textbf{double-strand break} 3 bp
upstream of PAM & Co-transcriptional ssRNA cleavage by Csm/Cmr;
signalling output \\
PAM requirement & Yes (recognised by Cas8 of Cascade) & Yes (NGG for
SpCas9; varies by ortholog) & None for RNA target;
protospacer-flanking-sequence (PFS) for DNA \\
Guide RNA & crRNA primarily & crRNA + tracrRNA (or fused sgRNA) & crRNA
primarily \\
Signal molecule & --- & --- & \textbf{cyclic oligoadenylate (cA\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{4}}{4}, cA\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{6}}{6})}
activates non-specific RNase Csm6 \\

& about  5 \% & about  25 \% \\
