AcrIIC families) & Yes (AcrIIIA, anti-cA\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{4}}{4}) \\
Clinical / biotech use & Cas3 large-deletion editing; phage therapy
design (Locus crPhage) & \textbf{Genome editing (Cas9)}; base editors;
prime editors & Biosensing (cA\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{4}}{4} readout); SHERLOCK-style RNA
detection \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Type II (Cas9)} was repurposed for genome editing by Doudna,
Charpentier, and colleagues in 2012 (\emph{Science} 2012), work
recognised with the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. A synthetic sgRNA
directs Cas9 to any genomic target (specified by a 20-nt spacer sequence
+ NGG PAM), where it makes a site-specific DSB. The cell repairs the
break by NHEJ (creating indels --- gene knockout) or HDR (with a
provided template --- precise edit). Variants now include base editors
(cytosine \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} thymine, adenine \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} guanine without DSBs), prime editors
(programmable insertions/deletions guided by an extended pegRNA), and
Cas12/Cas13 systems for DNA/RNA targeting respectively. The same
RNA-guided programmability that powers genome editing also underlies the
\textbf{RNA-interference-like} specificity by which bacteria neutralize
phage genomes --- a striking parallel to eukaryotic small-RNA defense
systems first dissected with C. elegans \citep{fire1998}.

\subsubsection{Anti-CRISPR Proteins}\label{anti-crispr-proteins}

Phages have evolved \textbf{anti-CRISPR (Acr)} proteins that counteract
bacterial CRISPR immunity --- an evolutionary arms race. Over 50 Acr
families have been identified (Pawluk \emph{et al.}, \emph{Nature
Microbiology} 2016; Davidson \emph{et al.}, \emph{Science} 2020 cryo-EM
structures):

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{AcrIF1 (Type I-F inhibitor)}: Binds Cas8f subunit of Cascade;
  blocks crRNA-guided dsDNA binding
\item
  \textbf{AcrIIA2/IIA4 (Type II inhibitors)}: Bind and occlude the
  PAM-recognition domain of Cas9; prevents target engagement
\item
  \textbf{AcrIIIA4}: Degrades the cA\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{4}}{4} second messenger; blocks Csm6
  activation
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: CRISPR-Based Therapies (2023--2026)} The
first CRISPR-based medicines have now been approved. \textbf{Casgevy}
(exagamglogene autotemcel), developed by Vertex and CRISPR Therapeutics,
received FDA approval in December 2023 for sickle cell disease and
January 2024 approval for transfusion-dependent \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-thalassemia; FDA's
2026 product page lists both indications for patients 12 years of age
and older
\citep{fda2023casgevy,fda2024casgevythalassemia,fda2026casgevy}. The ex
vivo approach edits patient HSCs to reactivate fetal haemoglobin (HbF)
by disrupting the BCL11A erythroid enhancer, compensating for defective
adult haemoglobin. Simultaneously, Bluebird Bio's lentiviral gene
therapy Lyfgenia was approved for SCD. By 2026, CRISPR therapies for
transthyretin amyloidosis (intellia NTLA-2001, in vivo hepatic editing)
and \hyperref[gl:heterozygous]{\textbf{heterozygous}} familial
hypercholesterolaemia are in Phase III trials.
\end{quote}

\textbf{Concept Check 6:} \textgreater{} A Type II CRISPR-Cas9 system
fails to cleave a target sequence despite perfect spacer-target
complementarity. List three molecular explanations for this failure,
relating each to a specific step in the CRISPR mechanism (adaptation,
biogenesis, or interference).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 6b:} A bacterial population is challenged with a
phage cocktail. After 5 generations, surviving bacteria are sequenced
--- 70\% have new spacers in their CRISPR array matching the phage; 20\%
have escape mutations in essential phage genes (no new spacer); 10\%
have constitutively expressed Cas9 with broader PAM specificity. Explain
which adaptation strategy is most evolutionary stable, and predict the
population dynamics if a second, immunologically distinct phage is then
introduced.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsubsection{SARS-CoV-2 Variant Evolution: Real-Time Darwin in a
Global
Population}\label{sars-cov-2-variant-evolution-real-time-darwin-in-a-global-population}

The four-year trajectory of SARS-CoV-2 (late 2019 -- present) is the
best-documented example of \textbf{adaptive viral evolution} in
biological history. Public sequencing through GISAID now archives
\textgreater{} 16 million viral genomes, enabling phylogenetic tracking
at daily resolution. The lineage diversification follows a textbook
evolutionary pattern: \textbf{(1) a narrow founder bottleneck}
(Wuhan-Hu-1 reference, December 2019); \textbf{(2) geographic diffusion}
with local \hyperref[gl:founder-effect]{\textbf{founder effect}}s (D614G
rose to global dominance by June 2020, conferring about 20 \%
higher infectivity via an allosteric receptor-binding-domain (RBD)
``open'' state); \textbf{(3) escape-driven positive selection} as
population immunity accumulated, favouring RBD mutations that evade
neutralising antibodies without compromising ACE2 binding.

Five variants of concern (VOCs) illustrate distinct evolutionary forces.
\textbf{Alpha (B.1.1.7, late 2020)} carried N501Y --- a single RBD
mutation increasing ACE2 affinity about 10\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x}. \textbf{Beta
(B.1.351)} and \textbf{Gamma (P.1)} added E484K, which partially escapes
antibodies. \textbf{Delta (B.1.617.2, mid-2021)} carried L452R + T478K
and doubled transmissibility. \textbf{Omicron (B.1.1.529, November
2021)} was the punctuated-evolution event of the pandemic --- \textbf{32
spike mutations at once}, not a gradual lineage from Delta but a sudden
saltation, likely from a long-term infection in an immunocompromised
host (a natural ``mutator'' environment). Omicron escaped most
pre-existing neutralising antibodies but attenuated lung tropism via
reduced TMPRSS2-mediated entry, shifting the disease toward upper
respiratory infection. Subsequent sub-lineages (BA.2, BA.5, XBB, JN.1,
KP.3) follow continuous antigenic drift --- the \textbf{``influenza-like
future''} of SARS-CoV-2 is now the expected trajectory.

Quantitatively: \textbf{Ka/Ks ratios} on the RBD exceed 1.5 across the
pandemic (positive selection), versus about 0.1 for
housekeeping ORFs (purifying selection); \textbf{estimated substitution
rate} is about 2 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{3}}{3} per site per year (2\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} SARS-CoV-1),
consistent with RNA-virus fidelity limits and increased by
population-scale chronic infections. Public-health surveillance now runs
phylogenetic tools (Nextstrain, Pango) in near-real-time;
\hyperref[gl:vaccine]{\textbf{vaccine}} reformulation (WHO TAG-CO-VAC)
follows the influenza-flu-shot paradigm. The pandemic has transformed
biology teaching: evolution is no longer a fossil-record inference but a
live, observable process with weekly GenBank updates.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-24}

For \textbf{Bacteria, Archaea, and Viruses}, frontier biology belongs
inside the evidence logic of the chapter. Microbiology and infectious
disease now require One Health reasoning across people, animals,
environments, genomics, and antimicrobial stewardship. The core reading
question is this: microbial claims should identify taxonomy, genome
architecture, metabolism, resistance mechanism, and environment.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

For AMR and pathogen claims, name the organism-resistance pair, the
selection pressure, the transmission route, and the surveillance
evidence that would change triage
\citep{who2024bppl,cdc2025antibioticuse,murray2022amr}.

\textbf{Source practice:} For pathogen, AMR, and intervention claims,
tie statements to organism-resistance pairs, surveillance evidence,
official guidance, and trial/regulatory status
\citep{who2024bppl,who2025tb,who2025malaria,cdc2025lenacapavirprep,cdc2026candidaauris}.

\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-24}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Three domains of life} (Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya) were
  established by Woese's rRNA phylogeny \citep{woese1977}. Bacteria and
  Archaea share the prokaryotic cell plan but differ fundamentally in
  membrane lipids, cell wall chemistry, and transcriptional machinery.
\item
  \textbf{Bacterial cell walls} contain peptidoglycan, built in an
  11-step pathway (MurA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} MurB \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} MurC--F \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} MraY \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} MurG \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} MurJ flipping \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  transglycosylation \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PBP transpeptidation) that is the target of
  fosfomycin, D-cycloserine, bacitracin, vancomycin, daptomycin, and
  \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactams. Gram-positive bacteria have thick peptidoglycan with
  teichoic acids; Gram-negative bacteria have thin peptidoglycan plus an
  outer membrane with LPS (endotoxin, activates TLR4, causes septic
  shock).
\item
  \textbf{Bacterial growth equation} \(N(t) = N_0 \cdot 2^{t/t_d}\)
  (\cref{eq:unit_VII_bacterial_growth}) describes exponential phase; the
  natural-log form gives a linear plot whose slope is the specific
  growth rate \(\mu = (\ln 2)/t_d\).
\item
  \textbf{Bacterial metabolic diversity} exceeds most eukaryotes:
  photoautotrophs, chemoautotrophs (lithotrophs), and heterotrophs with
  varied oxygen relationships.
\item
  \textbf{Two-component systems} (sensor histidine kinase + response
  regulator, His\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}Asp phosphotransfer) are the dominant prokaryotic
  signal-transduction architecture; \textbf{biofilms} (matrix +
  persisters, c-di-GMP master regulator) and \textbf{quorum sensing}
  (AHL/AIP/AI-2) underpin chronic infections and 65--80 \% of clinical
  infections.
\item
  \textbf{Horizontal gene transfer} (transformation, transduction,
  conjugation) drives bacterial evolution \citep{lawrence1998} and
  antibiotic resistance spread via R-plasmids and transposons.
\item
  \textbf{Archaea} differ from bacteria in ether-linked isoprenoid
  lipids (with G-1-P stereochemistry; tetraether monolayers in
  hyperthermophiles), lack of peptidoglycan, and eukaryote-like
  transcription. \textbf{Asgard archaea} are the closest living
  relatives of eukaryotes and encode actin, ESCRT, and ubiquitin-like
  machinery.
\item
  \textbf{Viruses} (Baltimore classes I-VII) are obligate intracellular
  parasites; bacteriophage lytic/lysogenic cycles and the HIV life cycle
  illustrate replication strategies and drug targets. \textbf{Phage
  therapy} is re-emerging as a clinical adjunct for multi-drug-resistant
  infections, with engineering, cocktail design, and antibiotic
  combination addressing rapid resistance and immune neutralization
  \citep{doub2022phagepseudomonas}. Phage pharmacokinetics are
  non-linear with a proliferation threshold \(B^* = m/(bk)\).
\item
  \textbf{CRISPR-Cas} is a heritable bacterial adaptive immune system
  (adaptation--expression--interference); Types I (Cas3), II (Cas9), and
  III (Cas10) differ in effector architecture, target nucleic acid, and
  PAM requirements. Type II Cas9 has been repurposed as the dominant
  genome-editing technology and now drives FDA-approved therapeutics
  (Casgevy, 2023--2026 FDA records).
\item
  \textbf{Antibiotic resistance} mechanisms (enzymatic inactivation,
  target modification, efflux, reduced permeability) spread via HGT;
  ESKAPE organisms remain a useful mnemonic, but current AMR triage
  should use pathogen-resistance pairs and WHO BPPL priority categories
  rather than a single threat list.
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See \cref{sec:unit_VI_phylogenetics} for
  phylogeny of mobile elements, \cref{sec:unit_VII_infectious_disease}
  for host immunity, and Unit III for metabolic targets of antibiotics.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Key Terms}\label{key-terms-24}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3529}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.6471}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Term
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Definition
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Peptidoglycan} & Bacterial cell wall polymer of NAG-NAM glycan
strands cross-linked by tetrapeptide chains; target of beta-lactam
antibiotics \\
\textbf{Lipid II} & Lipid-anchored peptidoglycan precursor
(undecaprenyl-PP-MurNAc-pentapeptide-GlcNAc); target of vancomycin,
nisin, daptomycin \\
\textbf{Lipopolysaccharide (LPS)} & Gram-negative outer membrane
component (lipid A + core + O-antigen); endotoxin that activates TLR4
and can cause septic shock \\
\textbf{Gram stain} & Differential staining technique distinguishing
thick-walled (Gram-positive, purple) from thin-walled (Gram-negative,
pink) bacteria \\
\textbf{Two-component system (TCS)} & Sensor histidine kinase + response
regulator pair that converts an environmental stimulus into a
transcriptional output via His\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}Asp phosphotransfer \\
\textbf{Biofilm} & Surface-attached, EPS-encased microbial community;
10--1000\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} more antibiotic tolerant than planktonic cells \\
\textbf{c-di-GMP} & Cyclic-di-guanosine-monophosphate; master second
messenger that switches between motile (low) and biofilm (high)
lifestyles \\
\textbf{Quorum sensing} & Cell-density-dependent gene regulation via
secreted autoinducer molecules (AHL, AIP, AI-2) \\
\textbf{Persister cells} & Metabolically dormant subpopulations within a
biofilm that survive antibiotic exposure without genetic resistance \\
\textbf{Binary fission} & Asexual bacterial reproduction; chromosome
replication followed by septum formation and cell division \\
\textbf{Specific growth rate (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu})} & \(\mu = (\ln 2)/t_d\); instantaneous
fractional growth rate in exponential phase, units of
\(\text{time}^{-1}\) \\
\textbf{Horizontal gene transfer} & Transfer of genetic material between
organisms by mechanisms other than vertical (parent-to-offspring)
inheritance \\
\textbf{Transformation} & Uptake of free DNA from the environment by
competent bacteria \\
\textbf{Transduction} & Bacteriophage-mediated transfer of bacterial DNA
between cells \\
\textbf{Conjugation} & Direct cell-to-cell DNA transfer via F pilus;
primary mechanism for R-plasmid spread \\
\textbf{Endospore} & Dormant, highly resistant structure formed by
Bacillus and Clostridium; contains calcium-dipicolinic acid \\
\textbf{Bacteriophage} & Virus that infects bacteria; follows lytic
(cell lysis) or lysogenic (genome integration) cycle \\
\textbf{Lysogeny} & Integration of phage DNA into host chromosome as a
prophage; maintained by CI repressor \\
\textbf{Phage therapy} & Therapeutic use of bacteriophages (often as
cocktails) to treat bacterial infections, especially
multi-drug-resistant ones \\
\textbf{Phage proliferation threshold} & Minimum bacterial density
\(B^* = m/(bk)\) above which a phage population can self-amplify rather
than dilute out \\
\textbf{Baltimore classification} & System classifying viruses into
seven classes based on genome type and replication strategy \\
\textbf{Reverse transcriptase} & RNA-dependent DNA polymerase; used by
retroviruses (HIV) to convert RNA genome to dsDNA \\
\textbf{Prion} & Infectious misfolded protein (PrP\(^{Sc}\)) that
templates conversion of normal PrP\(^C\); no nucleic acid \\
\textbf{MRSA} & Methicillin-resistant \emph{Staphylococcus aureus};
carries mecA gene encoding PBP2a with low beta-lactam affinity \\
\textbf{ESKAPE pathogens} & Six priority antibiotic-resistant organisms:
Enterococcus, S. aureus, Klebsiella, Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas,
Enterobacter \\
\textbf{Asgard archaea} & Deep-branching archaeal lineages (Loki, Thor,
Odin, Heimdall, Hela, Hermod) containing eukaryotic signature proteins;
closest known relatives of eukaryotes \\
\textbf{Eukaryotic signature proteins (ESPs)} & Proteins (actin, ESCRT,
ubiquitin-like, Rab GTPases) encoded by Asgard archaea that were once
thought to be eukaryote-specific \\
\textbf{GDGT lipids} & Glycerol-dialkyl-glycerol-tetraether monolayer
lipids that span the entire archaeal membrane; confer extreme
thermostability \\
\textbf{CRISPR-Cas} & Bacterial/archaeal RNA-guided adaptive immune
system (adaptation--expression--interference); repurposed for genome
editing \\
\textbf{PAM} & Protospacer adjacent motif; short sequence flanking the
target that licenses CRISPR-Cas cleavage and ensures self/non-self
discrimination \\
\end{longtable}
}

\subsection{Review Questions}\label{review-questions-24}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Compare the cell wall structure of Gram-positive and Gram-negative
  bacteria. Explain why Gram-negative sepsis is often more dangerous
  than Gram-positive sepsis, focusing on the role of LPS and TLR4
  signaling.
\item
  A researcher isolates a bacterium from a hot spring (85 degrees C, pH
  3) that has ether-linked lipids, no peptidoglycan, and an RNA
  polymerase with 12 subunits. To which domain does this organism most
  likely belong? Justify your classification using at least three
  molecular features.
\item
  Explain how a single conjugation event involving an R-plasmid carrying
  genes for beta-lactamase (bla), aminoglycoside acetyltransferase
  (aac), and a tetracycline efflux pump (tet) can convert a susceptible
  bacterium into a multidrug-resistant pathogen in a single step. Why is
  this more concerning than resistance arising through chromosomal
  mutation?
\item
  Compare generalized and specialized transduction. For each, describe
  the molecular error that leads to bacterial DNA being packaged in
  phage particles, and explain why specialized transduction transfers
  primarily specific genes while generalized transduction can transfer
  any gene.
\item
  The HIV provirus can remain latent in resting memory CD4\(^+\) T cells
  for decades, even in patients on suppressive ART. Explain why this
  latent reservoir prevents cure and why the ``shock and kill'' strategy
  (reactivating latent virus with latency-reversing agents while the
  patient is on ART) has been proposed.
\item
  Draw the lytic cycle of bacteriophage T4 and calculate the following:
  if a single T4 phage infects an \emph{E. coli} culture containing
  \(10^6\) cells, the burst size is 150, and the lytic cycle takes 25
  minutes, how many phage particles will be present after 3 complete
  lytic cycles (assuming most released phage successfully infect new
  cells)?
\item
  Explain why \emph{Mycobacterium tuberculosis} is neither truly
  Gram-positive nor Gram-negative despite being classified in the
  Gram-positive phylum Actinobacteria. What cell wall component is
  responsible for this anomaly, and what alternative staining method is
  used?
\item
  The discovery of Asgard archaea has strengthened support for the
  ``two-domain tree'' of life over the traditional ``three-domain
  tree.'' Explain the key evidence supporting this model, including the
  eukaryotic signature proteins found in Asgard genomes and what this
  implies about the origin of eukaryotic cells.
\item
  A hospital laboratory reports that a \emph{Klebsiella pneumoniae}
  isolate is resistant to meropenem (a carbapenem) with an MIC of 32
  \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}g/mL. The resistance is mediated by a plasmid-borne KPC-2
  carbapenemase. Describe three infection control measures that should
  be implemented immediately, and explain why carbapenem resistance is
  considered a ``sentinel event'' in infectious disease.
\item
  Compare the replication strategies of influenza virus (Class V,
  segmented (-)ssRNA) and SARS-CoV-2 (Class IV, non-segmented (+)ssRNA).
  Explain why influenza can undergo antigenic shift through reassortment
  while coronaviruses cannot, and discuss the implications for pandemic
  preparedness.
\item
  \textbf{Growth-curve calculation.} Apply
  \cref{eq:unit_VII_bacterial_growth}: a culture of \emph{Streptococcus
  pneumoniae} (\(t_d = 30\) min) starts at \(N_0 = 5 \times 10^3\)
  CFU/mL. (a) After how many minutes will the density reach \(10^9\)
  CFU/mL --- the typical density at which sepsis becomes hemodynamically
  significant? (b) If the patient receives a single dose of ceftriaxone
  that reduces the population by 4 log\(_{10}\) instantly, and if the
  residual bacteria resume growth at the same rate 1 hour later, when
  does the density return to \(10^9\)?
\item
  Estimate phage amplification after three rounds if burst size
  \(B=150\) and every virion infects --- relate to the logistic
  assumptions that break down in real cultures.
\item
  Why are archaeal antibiotics rare compared with bacterial antibiotics,
  given clinical need?
\item
  \textbf{Peptidoglycan pathway integration.} Place fosfomycin,
  D-cycloserine, bacitracin, vancomycin, and ampicillin on the
  peptidoglycan biosynthesis pathway and explain why a single resistance
  mutation generally confers resistance to a single of them --- but
  VanA-type vancomycin resistance and PBP2a (mecA) MRSA evade two by
  altering different parts of the same step.
\item
  \textbf{Two-component systems and antibiotic stewardship.} PhoQ-PhoP
  modifies lipid A in response to host antimicrobial peptides. Explain
  how this TCS contributes to colistin resistance and why a PhoQ
  inhibitor would be expected to ``re-sensitize'' \emph{Salmonella} to
  polymyxins.
\item
  \textbf{Biofilm pharmacology.} A patient with a \emph{S. aureus}
  prosthetic-knee infection fails six weeks of vancomycin. Explain four
  distinct biofilm-related reasons for this failure and design a
  combination strategy targeting at least two of them.
\item
  \textbf{Phage therapy resistance.} A clinical phage cocktail uses

\subsection{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-25}

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Explain the ``great plate count anomaly'' and describe
  culture-independent methods for studying microbial communities,
  including 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and shotgun metagenomics.
\item
  Calculate and interpret alpha and beta diversity metrics for microbial
  communities, including Shannon entropy, Simpson and inverse-Simpson
  indices, and Chao1 richness estimation.
\item
  Distinguish OTU (operational taxonomic unit at 97\% identity) from ASV
  (exact sequence variant) approaches and explain the role of
  rarefaction curves in normalizing diversity comparisons.
\item
  Describe the composition and functional roles of the human
  \hyperref[gl:microbiome]{\textbf{microbiome}} across body sites, with
  emphasis on the gut microbiome and its core/variable components.
\item
  Explain microbiome-host interactions through pattern recognition
  receptors and short-chain fatty acid signalling.
\item
  Explain the relationship between dysbiosis and disease, including
  obesity, inflammatory bowel disease, and colorectal cancer.
\item
  Describe microbial roles in biogeochemical cycles (nitrogen, sulfur,
  carbon), including the gene markers used to track each transformation,
  and explain kill-the-winner dynamics in ocean phage-host systems.
\item
  Describe the roles of microorganisms in
  \hyperref[gl:biofilm]{\textbf{biofilm}} formation, quorum sensing, and
  bioremediation.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Opening Vignette --- You Are Mostly Not You}

For decades, textbooks cited the figure that the human body contains ten
times more bacterial cells than human cells. In 2016, Ron Milo and Ron
Sender published a careful recalculation in \emph{Cell} --- the ratio is
approximately 1:1, with roughly 38 trillion bacteria and 30 trillion
human cells. But the bacteria contribute only about 0.2 kg of body mass,
compared to 70 kg of self. What changed science wasn't the ratio but the
Human Microbiome Project (2007--2016), which used 16S rRNA sequencing to
catalogue about 10,000 microbial species across 18 body sites
in 300 healthy adults. The project revealed that gut microbiome
composition influences immunity, metabolism, neurotransmitter
production, and drug efficacy --- and differs between individuals as
distinctly as a fingerprint. The microbiome is now recognised as an
additional organ, and its disruption (dysbiosis) is linked to
inflammatory bowel disease, obesity, depression, and
antibiotic-associated colitis. We are ecosystems, not individuals.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Microbial Ecology
Approaches}\label{microbial-ecology-approaches}

\subsubsection{The Great Plate Count
Anomaly}\label{the-great-plate-count-anomaly}

In 1985, Staley and Konopka formalized a long-recognized paradox in
microbiology: when environmental samples are examined by direct
microscopic counts or flow cytometry, cell densities of \(10^6\) per
milliliter are typical in aquatic environments. Yet when the same
samples are plated on standard laboratory media, primarily
\(10^2\)-\(10^3\) colony-forming units (CFU) per milliliter grow -- less
than 1\% of the organisms present. This discrepancy, termed the
\textbf{great plate count anomaly}, revealed that the vast majority of
microbial diversity is invisible to traditional culture-based
microbiology.

The reasons for unculturability are diverse:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Unknown nutrient requirements or growth factors
\item
  Obligate syntrophic relationships (organisms that depend on
  metabolites from partner species)
\item
  Extremely slow growth rates (generation times of weeks to months)
\item
  Sensitivity to atmospheric oxygen levels (many are strict anaerobes or
  microaerophiles)
\item
  Dormancy or viable-but-not-culturable (VBNC) states
\item
  Requirement for cell-cell signaling or quorum sensing to initiate
  growth
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Culture-Independent
Methods}\label{culture-independent-methods}

Modern microbial ecology relies on molecular approaches that bypass
cultivation entirely:

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0124_4e149edd74cc.png}
\caption{Multi-omic workflow for culture-independent microbial community profiling: 16S amplicon and shotgun metagenomic DNA approaches answer "who is there" and "what could they do," while metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics, and metabolomics answer "what are they actually doing".}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{The 16S rRNA Amplicon Pipeline: From Sample to ASV
Table}\label{the-16s-rrna-amplicon-pipeline-from-sample-to-asv-table}

\textbf{16S rRNA amplicon sequencing} is the workhorse of microbial
community profiling. Understanding the full pipeline, with its choices
and biases, is essential for interpreting any modern microbiome paper.

\textbf{Why 16S?} The 16S rRNA gene is ideal as a phylogenetic marker
because of three intrinsic properties:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Almost universally present} in most bacteria and
  \hyperref[gl:archaea]{\textbf{archaea}} (about  1500 bp).
\item
  \textbf{Mosaic of conserved and variable regions} --- nine
  hypervariable regions (V1--V9) are sandwiched between highly conserved
  regions that allow universal primer design (e.g., 27F, 515F, 806R,
  1492R).
\item
  \textbf{Slow evolutionary rate} in conserved domains preserves deep
  phylogenetic signal; rapid evolution in V regions enables genus- to
  species-level discrimination.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Region selection.} Different V regions perform differently:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2105}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2105}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2895}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2895}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Region
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Length
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Strengths
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Weaknesses
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
V1--V3 & about  480 bp & Good genus resolution;
\emph{Staphylococcus}-friendly & Misses some Bifidobacterium \\
\textbf{V3--V4} & about  460 bp & \textbf{De facto standard}
for human microbiome (HMP); good Illumina MiSeq fit & Underestimates
Bifidobacterium and some archaea \\
V4 primarily & about  250 bp & Single-end MiSeq; high read
depth & Lower taxonomic resolution \\
V6--V8 & about  440 bp & Better for environmental archaea &
Less reference-database coverage \\
Full-length (1.5 kb) & 1500 bp & Species- to strain-level resolution;
PacBio HiFi or Nanopore & Higher per-base error rate; lower
throughput \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Workflow.}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{DNA extraction} --- bead beating (mechanical lysis of
  Gram-positives, fungi, spores) plus a column-based purification (e.g.,
  DNeasy PowerSoil). Extraction kit choice introduces bias of up to \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\pm}}{+/-} 30
  \% in relative abundances and is now considered a major
  reproducibility issue.
\item
  \textbf{PCR amplification} --- universal primers (515F/806R for V4,
  341F/805R for V3--V4) plus barcoded adapters allow multiplexing.
  \textbf{PCR cycles should be minimised (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\leq}}{<=} 25)} to reduce chimera
  formation; high-fidelity polymerases (Q5, Phusion) reduce error.
\item
  \textbf{Library preparation and sequencing} --- Illumina MiSeq 2 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 300
  bp is standard; about  100 000 reads/sample is typical for
  diversity analyses, with about  10 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} that needed to detect
  rare taxa.
\item
  \textbf{Quality filtering} --- trim adapters and primers; discard
  reads with average Q \textless{} 25 or expected errors \textgreater{}
  1.
\item
  \textbf{OTU clustering vs ASV inference} --- see comparison below.
\item
  \textbf{Taxonomic assignment} --- match representative sequences
  against reference databases (SILVA 138, Greengenes2, RDP) using naive
  Bayes (RDP classifier) or k-mer methods (VSEARCH); confidence
  threshold typically 80 \%.
\item
  \textbf{Diversity analyses and statistics} --- alpha (within-sample)
  and beta (between-sample) diversity, with multiple-comparison
  correction.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{OTU vs ASV: A Decade-Long Methodological
Shift}\label{otu-vs-asv-a-decade-long-methodological-shift}

For about  15 years (2007--2017), microbiome studies
clustered reads into \textbf{operational taxonomic units (OTUs)} at a \texorpdfstring{\textgreater{}=}{>=}
97 \% identity threshold (corresponding roughly to genus-level
groupings). Around 2017, a methodological revolution replaced this with
\textbf{amplicon sequence variants (ASVs)} --- exact, error-corrected
sequences resolved at single-nucleotide precision. The contrast:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1190}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4524}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4286}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Property
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
\textbf{OTUs (de novo, closed-reference)}
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
\textbf{ASVs (DADA2, Deblur, UNOISE3)}
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Clustering & Group reads at 97 \% identity & Statistical denoising; each
unique error-corrected sequence is its own ASV \\
Resolution & Roughly genus-level & Single-nucleotide; potentially
strain-level \\
Reproducibility across studies & \textbf{Poor} (cluster boundaries
depend on dataset) & \textbf{Good} (ASVs are exact sequences) \\
Tolerance to PCR/sequencing errors & High (errors collapsed into
clusters) & Requires explicit error model \\
False-positive rare ASVs & Lower & Higher unless filtered \\
Computational cost & Lower & Higher (DADA2 about  1 hr per
1000 samples) \\
Modern recommendation & Legacy use primarily & \textbf{De facto standard
since about  2018} \\
\end{longtable}
}

The Callahan \emph{et al.} (2017, \emph{ISME Journal}) ``Exact sequence
variants should replace OTUs'' argument has been broadly adopted: ASVs
are reproducible across studies and labs, allow meta-analyses across
datasets, and resolve closely related taxa that 97 \%-clustering would
merge. Closed-reference OTU pipelines (clustering to a fixed reference
database) remain useful for very large meta-analyses but are
increasingly being supplanted.

\textbf{Rarefaction and normalisation.} Different samples are sequenced
to different depths, which artificially inflates richness in deeply
sequenced samples (you see more rare taxa simply because you looked
harder). Two approaches address this:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Rarefaction} --- randomly subsample every sample down to the
  minimum library size before computing diversity. Plotting richness as
  a function of subsample size yields a \textbf{rarefaction curve}: a
  curve that plateaus indicates sufficient sampling depth; one still
  rising indicates undersampling.
\item
  \textbf{Normalisation by total-sum scaling, CSS (cumulative-sum
  scaling), or DESeq2-style geometric means} --- preserves the original
  count data with a statistical correction.
\end{itemize}

Modern best practice: report results from both approaches, confirm
robustness, and rarely compare unrarefied richness across samples of
unequal depth.

\subsubsection{Other Omics Layers}\label{other-omics-layers}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Shotgun metagenomics} sequences most DNA in a sample without
  amplification: no PCR bias; captures most organisms including viruses
  and eukaryotic microbes; enables functional gene profiling; produces
  \textbf{metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs)} --- reconstructed genomes
  of uncultured organisms from metagenomic reads using coverage depth
  and tetranucleotide frequency binning. The Human Microbiome Project
  (HMP, 2008-2014) characterized the microbiomes of 300 healthy adults
  across 18 body sites, generating \textgreater{} 5.2 Tbp of sequence
  data.
\item
  \textbf{Metatranscriptomics} (total mRNA sequencing) reveals which
  genes are actively expressed -- the functional state of the community
  at the time of sampling. This distinguishes between metabolic
  potential (metagenomics) and metabolic activity.
\item
  \textbf{Metaproteomics} identifies the proteins actually translated,
  capturing post-transcriptional regulation.
\item
  \textbf{Metabolomics} profiles the small molecules present in a sample
  using mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) or nuclear magnetic resonance
  (NMR). This captures the chemical outputs and communication molecules
  of the microbial community, including short-chain fatty acids, bile
  acid metabolites, tryptophan derivatives, and quorum sensing signals.
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 1:} A researcher sequences the 16S rRNA gene from
a soil sample and identifies 500 distinct amplicon sequence variants
(ASVs). She then performs shotgun metagenomics on the same sample and
assembles 200 MAGs. Explain why these numbers differ and what types of
organisms might be captured by one method but not the other.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 1b:} A reviewer criticises a 2016 microbiome paper
for using 97 \%-identity OTU clustering instead of ASVs. The authors
respond that re-running with DADA2 gives the same overall conclusions.
Explain (a) what the reviewer's underlying concern is, (b) why the
conclusions might still be the same in this case, and (c) one biological
situation where OTU vs ASV could change a paper's conclusions.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Diversity Metrics}\label{diversity-metrics}

Quantifying microbial community diversity requires mathematical
frameworks borrowed from classical ecology. Diversity has two components
--- \textbf{richness} (how many distinct taxa?) and \textbf{evenness}
(how uniformly are they distributed?) --- and most metrics are weighted
combinations of these.

\textbf{Alpha diversity} (within-sample diversity):

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Observed ASVs/OTUs}: Simple count of distinct taxa; sensitive
  to sequencing depth.
\item
  \textbf{Shannon entropy}: weights both richness and evenness
  logarithmically.
\item
  \textbf{Simpson index} and its \textbf{inverse}: dominance-weighted;
  emphasises common taxa.
\item
  \textbf{Chao1 estimator}: extrapolates from observed
  singletons/doubletons to estimate true richness.
\item
  \textbf{Faith's phylogenetic diversity (PD)}: Sum of branch lengths in
  the phylogenetic tree connecting most observed taxa; incorporates
  evolutionary relationships.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Shannon Diversity Index}\label{shannon-diversity-index}

The Shannon entropy is the single most-used alpha-diversity metric. It
is defined as:

\begin{equation}
H' = -\sum_{i=1}^{S} p_i \ln p_i
\label{eq:unit_VII_shannon}
\end{equation}

where \(S\) is the number of species and \(p_i\) is the relative
abundance (fraction) of species \(i\). Higher \(H'\) means greater
diversity. The maximum \(H'\) for \(S\) species is \(\ln S\), achieved
when most species are perfectly even (\(p_i = 1/S\)); the minimum is 0
(single species). A useful intuition: \(e^{H'}\) is the
\textbf{effective number of equally common species} --- a community with
\(H' = 2.30\) has the same Shannon diversity as 10 perfectly even
species.

\paragraph{Worked Example: Computing Shannon Diversity for Five
Species}\label{worked-example-computing-shannon-diversity-for-five-species}

\textbf{Problem:} A gut microbiome sample contains five dominant species
with the following observed counts: \emph{Bacteroides} (500),
\emph{Faecalibacterium} (300), \emph{Roseburia} (100),
\emph{Akkermansia} (60), \emph{Bifidobacterium} (40). Compute the
Shannon diversity index \(H'\) from \cref{eq:unit_VII_shannon}.

\textbf{Solution:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Total counts:} \(N = 500 + 300 + 100 + 60 + 40 = 1000\).
\item
  \textbf{Relative abundances:}
  \[ p_1 = 0.500,\ p_2 = 0.300,\ p_3 = 0.100,\ p_4 = 0.060,\ p_5 = 0.040.  \label{eq:unit_VII_microbial_ecology_item_1}\]
\item
  \textbf{Compute \(-p_i \ln p_i\) term-by-term:}

  {\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
  \begin{longtable}[]{@{}llll@{}}
  \toprule\noalign{}
  Species & \(p_i\) & \(\ln p_i\) & \(-p_i \ln p_i\) \\
  \midrule\noalign{}
  \endhead
  \bottomrule\noalign{}
  \endlastfoot
  \emph{Bacteroides} & 0.500 & \(-0.693\) & 0.347 \\
  \emph{Faecalibacterium} & 0.300 & \(-1.204\) & 0.361 \\
  \emph{Roseburia} & 0.100 & \(-2.303\) & 0.230 \\
  \emph{Akkermansia} & 0.060 & \(-2.813\) & 0.169 \\
  \emph{Bifidobacterium} & 0.040 & \(-3.219\) & 0.129 \\
  \end{longtable}
  }
\item
  \textbf{Sum:}
  \[ H' = 0.347 + 0.361 + 0.230 + 0.169 + 0.129 \approx 1.236.  \label{eq:unit_VII_microbial_ecology_item_2}\]
\item
  \textbf{Interpretation:} \(e^{H'} = e^{1.236} \approx 3.44\). The
  community has the same Shannon diversity as a perfectly even community
  of about  3.4 species --- capturing the fact that although
  there are 5 species present, the dominance of \emph{Bacteroides} and
  \emph{Faecalibacterium} substantially lowers the effective diversity.
  The maximum possible \(H'\) for 5 species is \(\ln 5 = 1.609\); this
  community has 77 \% of maximum evenness.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Simpson Index and Inverse
Simpson}\label{simpson-index-and-inverse-simpson}

The \textbf{Simpson index} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda} measures dominance --- the probability that
two individuals drawn at random belong to the \emph{same} species:

\[ \lambda = \sum_{i=1}^{S} p_i^2 .  \label{eq:unit_VII_microbial_ecology_item_3}\]

For the example above,
\(\lambda = 0.500^2 + 0.300^2 + 0.100^2 + 0.060^2 + 0.040^2 = 0.250 + 0.090 + 0.010 + 0.0036 + 0.0016 = 0.355\).
Two complementary forms are usually reported:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Gini--Simpson} \(D = 1 - \lambda = 0.645\) --- probability
  that two random individuals are \emph{different} species.
\item
  \textbf{Inverse Simpson} \(1/\lambda = 1/0.355 \approx 2.82\) --- the
  effective number of species under Simpson weighting.
\end{itemize}

Compare with the Shannon effective number (\(e^{H'} = 3.44\)): Simpson
weights are more dominance-sensitive, so its effective number is smaller
because dominant species count more heavily. Reporting both Shannon and
Simpson is now standard because they emphasise different aspects of
community structure: Shannon weights most species roughly
logarithmically; Simpson is dominated by abundant taxa and is less
sensitive to rare taxa or sequencing errors.

\subsubsection{Worked Example: Estimating Species Richness using
Chao1}\label{worked-example-estimating-species-richness-using-chao1}

\textbf{Problem:} A researcher sequences 16S rRNA amplicons from a
deep-sea sediment sample. The initial bioinformatics pipeline identifies
a total of \(S_{obs} = 150\) distinct bacterial species (ASVs).
Examining the abundance tables, the researcher notes that 30 of these
species were observed exactly once (\(f_1 = 30\), singletons), and 10
species were observed exactly twice (\(f_2 = 10\), doubletons). Use the
Chao1 estimator to predict the true species richness of the community.

\textbf{Solution:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Identify the variables:}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Observed species (\(S_{obs}\)) = 150
  \item
    Singletons (\(f_1\)) = 30
  \item
    Doubletons (\(f_2\)) = 10
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Apply the Chao1 formula:}
  \[ \hat{S}_{Chao1} = S_{obs} + \frac{f_1^2}{2f_2}  \label{eq:unit_VII_microbial_ecology_item_4}\]

  \[ \hat{S}_{Chao1} = 150 + \frac{30^2}{2(10)}  \label{eq:unit_VII_microbial_ecology_item_5}\]

  \[ \hat{S}_{Chao1} = 150 + \frac{900}{20}  \label{eq:unit_VII_microbial_ecology_item_6}\]

  \[ \hat{S}_{Chao1} = 150 + 45 = 195  \label{eq:unit_VII_microbial_ecology_item_7}\]
\end{enumerate}

The Chao1 estimator predicts that the true species richness is
\textbf{195 species}. This means that despite sequencing deep enough to
find 150 species, approximately 45 rare species remain undetected in the
sample. The high number of singletons relative to doubletons suggests
that the community has a ``long tail'' of rare taxa and requires deeper
sequencing to capture full diversity.

\textbf{Beta diversity} (between-sample diversity):

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Bray-Curtis dissimilarity}: Abundance-weighted; ranges from 0
  (identical) to 1 (completely different);
  \(BC_{jk} = 1 - \frac{2C_{jk}}{S_j + S_k}\), where \(C_{jk}\) is the
  sum of lesser abundances shared between samples
\item
  \textbf{UniFrac distance}: Incorporates phylogenetic information;
  unweighted UniFrac considers primarily presence/absence of taxa;
  weighted UniFrac also considers abundance
\item
  \textbf{Jaccard index}: Presence/absence primarily;
  \(J = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|}\)
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Rarefaction curves} plot species richness against sampling
effort (number of sequences). A curve that plateaus indicates sufficient
sampling depth; a curve still rising indicates undersampling.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 2:} Two gut microbiome samples have identical
Shannon entropy values (\(H' = 3.5\)) but very different Bray-Curtis
dissimilarity (0.85). Explain how two samples can have the same
within-sample diversity but be highly dissimilar to each other.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 2b:} Compute the Shannon and inverse-Simpson
values for these two communities and explain why the rankings differ:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Community A: 4 species at proportions 0.97, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01
\item
  Community B: 4 species at proportions 0.40, 0.30, 0.20, 0.10
\end{itemize}

Which is more diverse by Shannon? By inverse Simpson? Why?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{The Human Microbiome}\label{the-human-microbiome}

\subsubsection{Overview}\label{overview}

The human body harbors approximately \(3.8 \times 10^{13}\) bacterial
cells -- close to the number of human somatic cells
(\(3.7 \times 10^{13}\)). The microbial gene catalog is far larger:
approximately 3.3 million unique microbial genes compared to
approximately 20,000 human
\hyperref[gl:protein]{\textbf{protein}}-coding genes, a ratio exceeding
150:1. This ``second genome'' provides metabolic capabilities that human
cells lack, effectively extending our biochemical repertoire.

The total mass of the human microbiome is approximately 200 g,
predominantly residing in the colon. Each body site harbors a distinct
microbial community shaped by local environmental conditions
(\hyperref[gl:ph]{\textbf{pH}}, oxygen, moisture, nutrient availability,
immune surveillance).

\subsubsection{Gut Microbiome}\label{gut-microbiome}

The gastrointestinal tract represents the densest microbial habitat on
the human body, with a gradient from relatively sparse colonization in
the stomach (\(10^1\)-\(10^3\) bacteria/mL, limited by gastric acid) to
extraordinary density in the colon (\(10^{11}\) bacteria/mL --
approaching the theoretical packing limit for bacterial cells).

\textbf{\hyperref[gl:dominant]{Dominant} phyla in healthy adults:}

The gut microbiome exhibits considerable inter-individual variation,
influenced by diet (plant-rich diets favor \emph{Prevotella};
animal-rich diets favor \emph{Bacteroides}), geography, age (dramatic
changes in infancy and old age), mode of birth (vaginal delivery
vs.~cesarean section), breastfeeding, and antibiotic exposure.

\subsubsection{Core vs Variable Microbiome and the F/B
Ratio}\label{core-vs-variable-microbiome-and-the-fb-ratio}

Two complementary frameworks describe gut-microbiome composition:

\textbf{Core microbiome} --- taxa present in \texorpdfstring{\textgreater{}=}{>=} 90 \% of healthy
individuals at \texorpdfstring{\textgreater{}=}{>=} 0.1 \% relative abundance. Surprisingly few species
qualify at the species level (5--20 across populations), but at the
\textbf{functional gene} level the core is much larger: \textgreater{}
50 \% of \emph{gene families} are shared across most healthy adults. The
biological inference is that \textbf{functional redundancy is conserved
even when species composition differs} --- the gut requires SCFA
production, bile-acid transformation, and vitamin synthesis, but many
species can supply each function. This is a textbook example of
community-level convergence under functional selection.

\textbf{Variable microbiome} --- the remaining about  80 \%
of taxa, which differ markedly between individuals. Variation is driven
by diet (long-term fiber \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \emph{Prevotella}-dominant; meat-rich Western
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \emph{Bacteroides}-dominant), geography (the Hadza hunter-gatherers
carry \textgreater{} 50 \% of taxa absent from industrialised
populations), age, and antibiotic history.

\textbf{Firmicutes / Bacteroidetes (F/B) ratio.} The two dominant phyla
in the colon historically defined an enterotype-like axis. The Turnbaugh
\emph{et al.} (2006, \emph{Nature}) finding that obese mice have
elevated F/B prompted thousands of follow-up studies; the relationship
in humans is \textbf{considerably more nuanced} than initially reported.
Key caveats: (1) the ratio is method-sensitive (PCR primer choice
affects Bacteroidetes recovery by \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\pm}}{+/-} 30 \%); (2) human F/B in obesity
does not robustly replicate across cohorts (some studies show the
opposite direction); (3) the \emph{functional} signal --- increased
polysaccharide-degradation gene capacity in obese microbiomes --- is
more reproducible than the \emph{taxonomic} F/B ratio. Modern microbiome
research has largely moved away from F/B as a single biomarker and
toward \textbf{functional gene profiles}, \textbf{specific keystone
taxa} (\emph{F. prausnitzii}, \emph{Akkermansia}, \emph{Roseburia}), and
\textbf{microbial metabolites} (SCFAs, secondary bile acids, indole
derivatives).

\textbf{\emph{Akkermansia muciniphila} as a health marker.} \emph{A.
muciniphila} (Verrucomicrobia, 1--4 \% of healthy gut) degrades
intestinal mucin and stimulates host mucin replenishment, paradoxically
\emph{strengthening} the gut barrier. Lower \emph{Akkermansia} abundance
is associated with obesity, type 2 diabetes, IBD, and aging. Pasteurised
\emph{A. muciniphila} (a single non-replicating bacterial supplement,
killed by gentle pasteurisation that preserves the membrane protein
Amuc\_1100 --- which acts on TLR2 to upregulate tight junctions) has
shown improved insulin sensitivity and reduced LDL in early human trials
(Depommier \emph{et al.}, 2019, \emph{Nature Medicine}) --- a striking
case of a defined ``next-generation probiotic'' with a known molecular
mechanism. The European Food Safety Authority approved pasteurised
\emph{A. muciniphila} as a novel food in 2021.

\textbf{Other keystone taxa:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{\emph{Faecalibacterium prausnitzii}} (Firmicutes, 5--15 \% of
  healthy gut) --- major butyrate producer; depleted in IBD; produces a
  15-kDa anti-inflammatory peptide that inhibits NF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}B activation in
  colonocytes.
\item
  \textbf{\emph{Bacteroides fragilis}} --- produces polysaccharide A
  (PSA), a TLR2-Treg-inducing immunomodulator.
\item
  \textbf{\emph{Lactobacillus rhamnosus}} GG --- adheres to epithelium,
  secretes p40/p75 proteins that promote tight-junction integrity; the
  most-studied probiotic strain in clinical use.
\item
  \textbf{\emph{Roseburia intestinalis}} --- secondary butyrate producer
  via the butyrate-CoA-transferase pathway; depleted with fiber-poor
  diets.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Oral Microbiome}\label{oral-microbiome}

The oral cavity harbors over 700 species across distinct habitats
(teeth, gingival crevice, tongue dorsum, buccal mucosa, hard palate).
Key species include:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{Streptococcus mutans}: Primary agent of dental caries;
  metabolizes sucrose to produce lactic acid, lowering local pH below
  the critical threshold (about 5.5) for enamel
  demineralization
\item
  \emph{Porphyromonas gingivalis}: Keystone pathogen in chronic
  periodontitis; produces gingipain proteases that degrade host tissues
  and subvert complement
\item
  \emph{Fusobacterium nucleatum}: Bridge organism in dental plaque
  biofilm formation; recently implicated as enriched in colorectal
  cancer tumors
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Skin Microbiome}\label{skin-microbiome}

The skin (about 1.5 m\(^2\) surface area) harbors \(10^4\)-\(10^6\)
bacteria per cm\(^2\), with community composition varying by
microenvironment:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Sebaceous (oily) sites} (forehead, back): Dominated by
  \emph{Cutibacterium acnes} (formerly \emph{Propionibacterium acnes});
  metabolizes sebum triglycerides; implicated in acne vulgaris
\item
  \textbf{Moist sites} (axillae, groin, toe web): \emph{Staphylococcus},
  \emph{Corynebacterium}; body odor results from bacterial metabolism of
  apocrine sweat components
\item
  \textbf{Dry sites} (forearm, leg): Most diverse; \emph{Cutibacterium},
  \emph{Staphylococcus}, \emph{Micrococcus}
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Vaginal Microbiome}\label{vaginal-microbiome}

In reproductive-age women, the vaginal microbiome is typically dominated
by \emph{Lactobacillus} species (L. crispatus, L. iners, L. gasseri, L.
jensenii), which maintain a protective low pH (about 3.8-4.5)
through lactic acid production. They also produce hydrogen peroxide and
bacteriocins that inhibit pathogen colonization.

Disruption of \emph{Lactobacillus} dominance -- replacement by anaerobes
such as \emph{Gardnerella vaginalis}, \emph{Atopobium vaginae}, and
\emph{Prevotella} -- characterizes \textbf{bacterial vaginosis (BV)},
associated with preterm birth, increased susceptibility to sexually
transmitted infections including HIV, and pelvic inflammatory disease.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Fecal
\hyperref[gl:microbiota]{\textbf{Microbiota}} Transplant (FMT)}
Recurrent \emph{Clostridioides difficile} infection (rCDI) occurs when
antibiotic-disrupted gut microbiota fails to recover, allowing \emph{C.
difficile} spores to germinate and produce toxins A and B. FMT --
transfer of processed stool from a healthy, screened donor -- restores
colonization resistance and achieves cure rates exceeding 90\%, compared
to approximately 30\% for repeated vancomycin courses. The FDA approved
the first standardized FMT products in 2022-2023 (REBYOTA, a
microbiota-based product, and VOWST, purified \emph{Firmicutes} spores
in oral capsules). The mechanism involves restoration of secondary bile
acid production by commensal \emph{Clostridium scindens}, which inhibits
\emph{C. difficile} spore germination, combined with
\hyperref[gl:competitive-exclusion]{\textbf{competitive exclusion}} and
bacteriocin production by restored commensals.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Microbiome Functions and Host
Interactions}\label{microbiome-functions-and-host-interactions}

\subsubsection{Microbiome--Host Molecular
Communication}\label{microbiomehost-molecular-communication}

Host-microbiome interaction is mediated by three classes of molecular
interface: \textbf{(i) pattern-recognition receptors} that surveil
microbe-associated patterns; \textbf{(ii) microbial metabolites} that
act on host receptors; and \textbf{(iii) physical and immune barriers}
that contain the microbiota.

\textbf{Pattern recognition receptors (PRRs).} The intestinal epithelium
and lamina propria express a rich repertoire of PRRs that read the local
microbial milieu in real time:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{TLR2} (with TLR1 or TLR6 heterodimers) --- recognises
  Gram-positive lipoteichoic acid, lipopeptides, and \emph{B. fragilis}
  polysaccharide A (PSA). PSA is a remarkable case: it is a microbial
  ligand that activates \emph{anti-inflammatory} Treg responses via
  TLR2, demonstrating that PRR signalling is not uniformly
  pro-inflammatory but tunable by ligand.
\item
  \textbf{TLR4} --- recognises Gram-negative lipid A; in healthy gut
  TLR4 is low-expressed apically and signals are dampened by negative
  regulators (A20, SIGIRR). Loss of this dampening (e.g., increased TLR4
  in IBD) drives chronic inflammation.
\item
  \textbf{TLR5} --- flagellin sensor; intestinal expression is
  \textbf{basolateral primarily}, so commensal flagellated bacteria in
  the lumen do not trigger inflammation, but invading flagellated
  pathogens that cross the epithelium do. A beautiful example of spatial
  PRR localisation as a discrimination strategy.
\item
  \textbf{TLR9} --- unmethylated CpG DNA; engaged by bacterial DNA in
  endosomes.
\item
  \textbf{NOD1, NOD2} --- cytosolic peptidoglycan fragment sensors; NOD2
  mutations are the strongest single genetic risk for Crohn's disease,
  illustrating how loss of microbial sensing predisposes to dysbiosis.
\item
  \textbf{AhR (aryl hydrocarbon receptor)} --- sensor for
  tryptophan-derived microbial metabolites (indoles, IPA,
  indole-3-aldehyde from \emph{Lactobacillus}); upregulates IL-22,
  mucin, and antimicrobial peptide production by intestinal cells.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) signalling.} SCFAs are not only
fuel but signalling molecules with three identified receptors and one
direct enzymatic mechanism:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2500}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2500}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2500}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2500}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Receptor / target
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Ligand preference
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Cell type
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Effect
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{GPR41 (FFAR3)} & Propionate \textgreater{} butyrate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gg}}{>>} acetate &
Enteroendocrine L-cells; sympathetic neurons & PYY, GLP-1 release;
sympathetic activation \\
\textbf{GPR43 (FFAR2)} & Acetate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} propionate \textgreater{} butyrate &
L-cells; adipocytes; neutrophils & GLP-1; lipogenesis regulation;
neutrophil chemotaxis \\
\textbf{GPR109A (HCAR2)} & Butyrate (also niacin) & Colonocytes;
macrophages; dendritic cells & Treg induction; anti-inflammatory
cascade \\
\textbf{HDAC inhibition} & Butyrate (mM concentrations in the colon) &
Colonocytes; immune cells & Hyperacetylation of histones; epigenetic
anti-inflammatory programmes \\
\end{longtable}
}

Butyrate has been called a ``molecular bridge'' between microbiome and
host because it can engage four mechanisms simultaneously:
G-protein-coupled signalling (GPR41/43/109A), epigenetic regulation
(HDAC inhibition), mitochondrial fuel (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-oxidation provides
about  70 \% of colonocyte ATP), and Treg differentiation
(via GPR109A and HDAC-dependent FoxP3 upregulation). Butyrate
concentrations in the colonic lumen reach 10--20 mM --- 1000\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} higher
than in serum, justifying the local-action interpretation.

\subsubsection{Metabolic Functions}\label{metabolic-functions}

The gut microbiome functions as a metabolic organ, performing
biochemical transformations that human cells cannot:

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0125_21e6e35bf969.png}
\caption{Microbiome metabolic functions: fermentation of fiber to short-chain fatty acids (butyrate, propionate, acetate) with their specific receptor targets and immune outputs; bile-acid deconjugation; vitamin synthesis; and neuroactive metabolite production.}
\end{figure}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Butyrate} (about 20\% of SCFA): Produced primarily by
  \emph{Faecalibacterium prausnitzii}, \emph{Roseburia intestinalis},
  and \emph{Eubacterium rectale}. Serves as the primary energy source
  for colonocytes (providing about 70\% of their energy needs).
  Acts as a \hyperref[gl:histone]{\textbf{histone}} deacetylase (HDAC)
  inhibitor, promoting anti-inflammatory gene expression. Strengthens
  intestinal barrier function by upregulating tight junction proteins
  (claudins, occludin). Induces colonic regulatory T cell (Treg)
  differentiation via GPR109A, promoting immune tolerance.
\item
  \textbf{Propionate} (about 25\% of SCFA): Transported to the liver via
  portal circulation where it regulates gluconeogenesis. Activates GPR41
  and GPR43 receptors on enteroendocrine L-cells, stimulating release of
  GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1, promotes insulin secretion and
  satiety) and PYY (peptide YY, reduces appetite).
\item
  \textbf{Acetate} (about 55\% of SCFA): The most abundant SCFA; enters
  systemic circulation to serve as fuel for peripheral tissues including
  muscle and brain. Activates GPR43 on adipocytes, regulating lipolysis
  and fat storage.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Vitamin synthesis}: Gut bacteria produce essential vitamins
including vitamin K2 (menaquinone, synthesized by \emph{Bacteroides} and
other gut anaerobes), vitamin B12 (cobalamin, by
\emph{Propionibacterium}), folate, biotin, and riboflavin. However, most
microbially produced vitamins are absorbed in the colon, where
absorption efficiency is lower than in the small intestine.

\textbf{Bile acid metabolism}: The liver synthesizes primary bile acids
(cholic acid, chenodeoxycholic acid) conjugated with glycine or taurine.
In the colon, gut bacteria deconjugate these bile acids (bile salt
hydrolases) and perform 7\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-dehydroxylation to produce secondary bile
acids (deoxycholic acid, lithocholic acid). Secondary bile acids are
potent signaling molecules that activate the TGR5 receptor (stimulating
GLP-1 release and energy expenditure) and the farnesoid X receptor (FXR,
regulating lipid and glucose metabolism).

\textbf{Drug metabolism}: The gut microbiome can profoundly affect drug
pharmacokinetics through first-pass microbial biotransformation. The
cardiac glycoside digoxin is inactivated by \emph{Eggerthella lenta};
the anti-cancer prodrug irinotecan is reactivated to its toxic form by
bacterial \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-glucuronidase, causing severe diarrhea; the Parkinson's drug
L-DOPA is decarboxylated by gut bacteria, reducing its bioavailability.

\subsubsection{Immune Development}\label{immune-development}

The microbiome is essential for proper immune system development.
Germ-free mice (raised in sterile isolators) exhibit:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Atrophied Peyer's patches and mesenteric lymph nodes
\item
  Reduced secretory IgA (SIgA) production
\item
  Deficient Th17 cell populations in the lamina propria
\item
  Impaired regulatory T cell function
\item
  Increased susceptibility to infection
\end{itemize}

Colonization of germ-free mice with specific bacteria restores immune
function: segmented filamentous bacteria (SFB) induce Th17 cells in the
small intestine; \emph{Clostridium} clusters IV and XIVa induce colonic
Tregs; \emph{Bacteroides fragilis} polysaccharide A (PSA) activates TLR2
on Tregs, promoting IL-10 production.

In humans, neonatal microbiome composition during a critical
developmental window (first 1-3 years of life) shapes lifelong immune
tone. Disruptions during this window (cesarean delivery, formula
feeding, early antibiotic exposure) are associated with increased risk
of allergic diseases, asthma, and autoimmunity -- consistent with the
``hygiene hypothesis'' and its modern refinement, the ``old friends
hypothesis.''

\subsubsection{Gut-Brain Axis}\label{gut-brain-axis}

The bidirectional communication network between the gut microbiome and
the central nervous system operates through multiple channels:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Vagus nerve}: The tenth cranial nerve provides a direct neural
  pathway from the enteric nervous system (about 100-500
  million \hyperref[gl:neuron]{\textbf{neuron}}s, sometimes called the
  ``second brain'') to the brainstem. Specific bacterial metabolites
  (SCFAs, tryptamine) activate vagal afferents.
\item
  \textbf{Neurotransmitter production}: Approximately 95\% of the body's
  serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, 5-HT) is produced by enterochromaffin
  cells in the gut, stimulated by tryptophan metabolites from gut
  bacteria (especially \emph{Clostridiales}). Gut bacteria also produce
  GABA (\emph{Lactobacillus}, \emph{Bacteroides}), dopamine, and
  norepinephrine.
\item
  \textbf{SCFAs}: Cross the blood-brain barrier; modulate microglial
  maturation and function; influence neuroinflammation
\item
  \textbf{Immune mediators}: Microbial-induced cytokines (IL-6, TNF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha})
  affect brain function via circumventricular organs
\end{itemize}

Experimental evidence includes dramatic behavioral differences in
germ-free mice (increased anxiety-like behavior in some strains,
decreased in others), which can be partially normalized by colonization
with specific probiotic strains (\emph{Lactobacillus rhamnosus} JB-1
reduces anxiety-like behavior via vagal signaling).

\subsubsection{Colonization Resistance}\label{colonization-resistance}

The resident microbiota provides a critical defense against pathogen
colonization through multiple mechanisms:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Competitive exclusion}: Commensals occupy ecological
  \hyperref[gl:niche]{\textbf{niche}}s (nutrient sources, attachment
  sites), preventing pathogen establishment
\item
  \textbf{Bacteriocin production}: Antimicrobial peptides produced by
  commensals directly inhibit pathogen growth
\item
  \textbf{Bile acid-mediated resistance}: Secondary bile acids produced
  by commensals (e.g., \emph{Clostridium scindens} produces deoxycholic
  acid) inhibit \emph{C. difficile} spore germination and vegetative
  growth
\item
  \textbf{Immune priming}: Commensals maintain baseline immune
  surveillance (SIgA, antimicrobial peptide production by Paneth cells)
\end{itemize}

\emph{Salmonella} enterica has evolved strategies to overcome
colonization resistance: it triggers intestinal inflammation (via T3SS
effectors), which disrupts the resident microbiota and generates unique
nutrient sources (tetrathionate, ethanolamine) that \emph{Salmonella}
can metabolize but commensals cannot.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 3:} Explain why broad-spectrum antibiotic
treatment increases the risk of \emph{Clostridioides difficile}
infection, using the concepts of colonization resistance and secondary
bile acid metabolism. Why does FMT work when repeated courses of
vancomycin often fail?
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 3b:} A patient with refractory ulcerative colitis
is treated with butyrate enemas. Symptoms improve over 4 weeks. Explain
the multiple molecular mechanisms by which luminal butyrate can
attenuate colonic inflammation, naming at least three host receptors /
targets engaged. Why might oral butyrate supplements fail where rectal
butyrate succeeds?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Dysbiosis and Disease}\label{dysbiosis-and-disease}

\textbf{Dysbiosis} refers to a compositional and functional imbalance in
the microbiome associated with disease. While causation versus
correlation remains a major challenge in microbiome research, several
disease associations have strong mechanistic evidence:

\textbf{Obesity and Metabolic Syndrome}:

The landmark study by Turnbaugh et al.~(2006, \emph{Nature})
demonstrated that the gut microbiome of obese mice (ob/ob) has an
increased Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes (F/B) ratio compared to lean
littermates. When the obese microbiome was transplanted into germ-free
mice, recipients gained 60\% more body fat than recipients of lean
microbiome -- despite consuming identical diets. The mechanism involves
increased energy harvest from dietary polysaccharides (the obese
microbiome has enhanced capacity to ferment complex carbohydrates) and
altered SCFA profiles affecting host energy regulation.

Metabolic endotoxemia provides an additional mechanism: gut barrier
dysfunction (``leaky gut'') allows LPS translocation into the
bloodstream, triggering chronic low-grade inflammation via TLR4
activation on adipose tissue macrophages, contributing to insulin
resistance.

\textbf{Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)}:

Both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis are associated with:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Reduced overall microbial diversity
\item
  Reduced butyrate-producing bacteria (especially \emph{Faecalibacterium
  prausnitzii}, a potent anti-inflammatory species that produces
  butyrate and secretes anti-inflammatory metabolites)
\item
  Increased Proteobacteria (adherent-invasive \emph{E. coli} in ileal
  Crohn's)
\item
  Reduced secondary bile acid production
\item
  Altered tryptophan metabolism favoring the kynurenine pathway
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Colorectal Cancer (CRC)}:

\emph{Fusobacterium nucleatum} is significantly enriched in CRC tumors
compared to adjacent normal tissue. Mechanistic studies demonstrate that
\emph{F. nucleatum}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Adheres to cancer cells via its FadA adhesin binding to E-cadherin
\item
  Activates the Wnt/\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-catenin signaling pathway, promoting cell
  proliferation
\item
  Recruits tumor-infiltrating myeloid cells that suppress anti-tumor
  immunity
\item
  Correlates with poor prognosis and chemoresistance
\item
  Serves as a potential diagnostic biomarker (detectable in stool
  samples)
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Antibiotic-Induced Dysbiosis}:

Broad-spectrum antibiotics cause profound disruption of the gut
microbiome that can persist for months. Clinical consequences include:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{Clostridioides difficile} infection (CDI): disrupted
  colonization resistance
\item
  Pediatric antibiotic exposure and later obesity, asthma, and allergies
  (multiple epidemiological studies)
\item
  Selection for antibiotic-resistant organisms within the microbiome
  (resistome expansion)
\item
  Loss of bile acid-metabolizing bacteria, altering host metabolic
  signaling
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Microbiome-Based Diagnostics and
Therapeutics} The microbiome is emerging as both a diagnostic tool and
therapeutic target. Stool-based tests for \emph{Fusobacterium nucleatum}
DNA are being developed as non-invasive colorectal cancer screening
supplements. Live biotherapeutic products (LBPs) -- defined microbial
consortia -- are in clinical trials for IBD, metabolic syndrome, and
immune checkpoint inhibitor response enhancement. \emph{Akkermansia
muciniphila} supplementation has shown promise in improving metabolic
parameters in overweight individuals (Depommier et al., 2019,
\emph{Nature Medicine}). The field is moving from correlation to
causation through gnotobiotic mouse models, Mendelian randomization
studies, and interventional trials.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Environmental
Microbiology}\label{environmental-microbiology}

\subsubsection{Soil Microbiology}\label{soil-microbiology}

Soil is among Earth's most microbially diverse habitats, containing
roughly \(10^8\)-\(10^9\) bacterial cells per gram and thousands to tens
of thousands of amplicon sequence variants per gram depending on soil
type, sequencing depth, and the taxonomic cutoff used. The dominant
phyla often include Proteobacteria, Firmicutes, Actinobacteria,
Bacteroidetes, and Acidobacteria, but relative abundances shift strongly
with pH, moisture, carbon input, and land management.

Soil microorganisms drive global carbon decomposition, nitrogen cycling,
phosphorus solubilization, and organic matter turnover. The
\textbf{rhizosphere} (soil zone immediately surrounding plant roots) is
a hotspot of microbial activity, enriched 10-100 fold compared to bulk
soil, driven by root exudates (sugars, amino acids, organic acids) that
feed microbial communities.

\subsubsection{Marine and Environmental Microbiome
Diversity}\label{marine-and-environmental-microbiome-diversity}

Microbial diversity in environmental systems dwarfs that of
multicellular life. The dominant numerical fact about life on Earth is
that there are about  \(10^{30}\) microbial cells globally
--- \textgreater{} 99 \% of Earth's biological cells, and 70--90 \% of
Earth's biomass nitrogen and phosphorus.

\textbf{Ocean.} The ocean contains approximately \(1.2 \times 10^{29}\)
microbial cells in the photic zone alone. Two organisms dominate the
global ocean microbiome:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{SAR11 (\emph{Pelagibacterales})}: The most abundant
  free-living organism on Earth, estimated at
  \(\sim 2.4 \times 10^{28}\) cells globally --- i.e., about 
  25 \% of ocean bacteria. Its genome (about  1.3 Mbp) is
  among the smallest for free-living bacteria, reflecting extreme
  \textbf{genomic streamlining}: the \emph{minimal-cell-cost hypothesis}
  posits that in oligotrophic surface waters where every nitrogen atom
  is precious, selection ruthlessly eliminates non-essential genes.
  SAR11 lacks transcription regulators, sigma factors, sugar-uptake
  systems, and most regulatory pathways --- it lives a high-throughput,
  regulation-free metabolic life.
\item
  \textbf{\emph{Prochlorococcus}} \textbf{and \emph{Synechococcus}}: The
  most abundant photosynthetic organisms on Earth (about 
  \(10^{27}\) cells of \emph{Prochlorococcus} and about 
  \(7 \times 10^{26}\) of \emph{Synechococcus}). \emph{Prochlorococcus}
  was discovered primarily in 1986 (Chisholm), demonstrating how
  recently we have grasped basic ocean ecology. This tiny cyanobacterium
  (\(< 1\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m diameter) accounts for approximately \textbf{20 \% of
  global ocean primary production} --- it makes about 5 \% of the oxygen
  we breathe. Different ecotypes partition the water column by light
  intensity, with high-light ecotypes near the surface and low-light
  ecotypes extending to 200 m depth.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Soil.} Containing about  \(10^8\) bacteria per gram
and often about  \(10^4\)--\(10^5\) ASVs per gram in deep
sequencing studies, soil is one of the largest reservoirs of microbial
diversity. Globally, soil holds about  \(2.6 \times 10^{29}\)
microbial cells. The dominant phyla --- Proteobacteria, Acidobacteria,
Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Verrucomicrobia, Firmicutes --- vary
continuously with pH, moisture, and organic matter. Acidobacteria, in
particular, are abundant in molecular surveys but remain under-cultured
relative to their environmental abundance, which is why metagenomics,
single-cell genomics, and enrichment culture are most needed to connect
sequence diversity to physiology.

\textbf{Deep biosphere.} A relatively recent realisation is that the
\textbf{subsurface biosphere} (rocks, sediments, and aquifers below
about  100 m depth) contains an estimated \(10^{29}\) cells
--- comparable to or exceeding most surface marine biomass. These
extremely slow-growing chemolithotrophs (doubling times of years to
centuries) couple H\(_2\) from rock-water reactions to CO\(_2\)
fixation, sustaining ecosystems that have been functionally isolated
from surface life for about  Ma timescales. The deep
biosphere now constitutes one of the largest reservoirs of unstudied
microbial diversity on the planet.

\textbf{Hydrothermal vents.} Chemolithoautotrophic communities at
hydrothermal vents form the base of food webs completely independent of
sunlight. Sulfur-oxidizing bacteria (\emph{Thiomicrospira},
\emph{Beggiatoa}) and hydrogen-oxidizing archaea (\emph{Methanopyrus})
sustain ecosystems including tube worms (\emph{Riftia pachyptila}, which
lack a digestive system and rely entirely on endosymbiotic
sulfur-oxidizing bacteria housed in a specialized organ called the
trophosome).

\subsubsection{Microbial
Biogeochemistry}\label{microbial-biogeochemistry}

Microbes catalyse virtually every redox transformation of nitrogen,
sulfur, and carbon at the global scale. The key enzymatic steps are now
well-characterised, each linked to a marker gene that ecologists use to
track the corresponding flux in environmental DNA.

\textbf{Nitrogen cycle.} The biogeochemical nitrogen cycle is a
quasi-closed loop of microbially-catalysed redox reactions, every step
of which has a diagnostic gene:

Two transformations deserve special attention. \textbf{Nitrogen
fixation} by nitrogenase (\(N_2 + 8H^+ + 8e^- + 16\)ATP
\(\rightarrow 2\)NH\$\_3 + \(H\)\_2 + 16\$ADP \(+ 16\)P\(_i\)) is
irreversibly inactivated by oxygen, presenting a paradox for
\hyperref[gl:aerobic]{\textbf{aerobic}} diazotrophs. Solutions include
\emph{Rhizobium}-legume symbiosis (root nodules contain
\textbf{leghemoglobin} delivering O\(_2\) to bacteroid respiration while
keeping free O\(_2\) below the threshold for nitrogenase inactivation,
about  10 nM); cyanobacterial \textbf{heterocysts}
(specialised thick-walled cells lacking photosystem II, expressing
nitrogenase, connected to vegetative cells by microplasmodesmata); and
free-living \emph{Azotobacter vinelandii} using respiratory protection
(extremely high respiration rate consumes O\(_2\) before it reaches
nitrogenase) plus conformational protection (FeSII protein binds
nitrogenase in O\(_2\) presence).

\textbf{Anammox} --- anaerobic ammonia oxidation --- was a stunning 1995
discovery (Mulder \emph{et al.}) showing that \emph{Planctomycetes}
couple NH\(_4^+\) oxidation to NO\(_2^-\) reduction, producing N\(_2\)
via the toxic intermediate hydrazine (N\(_2\)H\(_4\), rocket fuel).
Anammox is responsible for about  30--50 \% of marine N\(_2\)
production globally and is now used industrially in wastewater nitrogen
removal (about  90 \% less aeration energy than conventional
nitrification + denitrification).

\textbf{Sulfur cycle.} Parallel redox cycle:
