\textbf{Carbon cycle.} Microbial carbon transformations include CO\(_2\)
fixation (Calvin cycle: \emph{cbbL/cbbM} RuBisCO; reverse TCA,
\emph{aclB}; Wood--Ljungdahl, \emph{fhs/cooS}), methanogenesis
(\emph{mcrA} gene of methyl-CoM reductase --- diagnostic for most
methanogenic archaea), and anaerobic oxidation of methane (AOM, ANME
archaea + sulfate reducers acting via reverse methanogenesis), which
consumes about  80 \% of methane produced in marine sediments
before it reaches the atmosphere --- a globally important methane
filter.

\subsubsection{Phage--Host Dynamics:
Kill-the-Winner}\label{phagehost-dynamics-kill-the-winner}

Viruses (almost entirely phages) outnumber cellular life in the ocean by
about  10 : 1, with \(\sim 10^{30}\) viral particles
globally. Phages are the dominant agents of bacterial mortality, killing
20--40 \% of marine bacteria per day --- comparable to grazing pressure
--- and the dominant agent of horizontal gene transfer.

The \textbf{kill-the-winner (KTW) hypothesis} (Thingstad, 2000) explains
why marine microbial communities can be enormously diverse despite
competitive exclusion:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  When a bacterial species blooms (becomes the ``winner'' --- high cell
  density), its cognate phage finds it efficiently (encounter rate is
  bilinear in \(B \times P\)).
\item
  Phage proliferation crashes the bloom (the proliferation threshold
  \(B^* = m/(bk)\), derived in the previous chapter, is exceeded once
  \(B\) is high enough).
\item
  Other less-abundant species are not at high enough density to sustain
  their own phages, so they are \textbf{not} killed proportionally ---
  they are released from competitive pressure.
\item
  Diversity is \emph{maintained} because phage predation specifically
  punishes dominance, opening niches for rare taxa.
\end{itemize}

The dynamics are analogous to Lotka--Volterra predator--prey cycles but
with one twist: phage population growth is bursty (each successful
infection produces about  50--500 progeny in
about  30 minutes), giving boom-and-bust cycles superimposed
on the long-term equilibrium. \textbf{Cyanophage-cyanobacteria
oscillations} in the ocean have been directly observed via metagenomics,
with measurable phage-mediated turnover of \emph{Prochlorococcus}
populations every few days. KTW is now considered as fundamental as
competitive exclusion for understanding microbial-community structure:
the predator-mediated maintenance of diversity that ecologists
discovered in macroscopic systems (Paine's keystone-predator
experiments) operates equally --- perhaps more strongly --- in microbial
systems.

\subsubsection{Biofilms}\label{biofilms}

Over 80\% of bacteria in natural environments exist in \textbf{biofilms}
-- structured communities enclosed in a self-produced extracellular
polymeric substance (EPS) matrix of polysaccharides, proteins,
extracellular DNA (eDNA), and lipids.

Biofilm formation proceeds through five stages:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Reversible attachment}: Planktonic cells contact a surface via
  \hyperref[gl:van-der-waals-forces]{\textbf{van der Waals forces}} and
  hydrophobic interactions
\item
  \textbf{Irreversible attachment}: Specific adhesin-receptor
  interactions; early EPS production; c-di-GMP (cyclic diguanylate
  monophosphate) levels rise, promoting sessile lifestyle
\item
  \textbf{Microcolony formation}: Cell division and EPS accumulation;
  quorum sensing coordinates gene expression
\item
  \textbf{Mature biofilm}: Complex 3D architecture with water channels;
  metabolic gradients (O\(_2\), pH, nutrients) create distinct
  microniches; HGT frequency increases 1,000-fold
\item
  \textbf{Dispersal}: c-di-GMP degradation; EPS-degrading enzymes
  released; motility genes reactivated; planktonic cells seed new
  surfaces
\end{enumerate}

Biofilms are \textbf{10-1,000-fold more antibiotic-resistant} than
planktonic cells due to:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  EPS barrier limiting antibiotic diffusion
\item
  Metabolically dormant persister cells (not susceptible to
  growth-dependent antibiotics)
\item
  Local accumulation of resistance enzymes (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactamases in the matrix)
\item
  Microenvironment heterogeneity (anaerobic zones where aminoglycosides
  are ineffective)
\end{itemize}

Clinical impact: about 80\% of chronic bacterial infections
involve biofilms (CDC), including cystic fibrosis lung infections
(\emph{Pseudomonas aeruginosa}), dental plaque, prosthetic joint
infections, catheter-associated UTIs, and endocarditis.

\subsubsection{Quorum Sensing}\label{quorum-sensing}

\textbf{Quorum sensing (QS)} is a cell density-dependent communication
system in which bacteria produce and detect small signaling molecules
(\textbf{autoinducers}) that accumulate as the population grows. When
autoinducer concentration exceeds a threshold, coordinate gene
expression is triggered across the population:

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0126_10bf714951fb.png}
\caption{Quorum sensing in Vibrio fischeri: at low cell density LuxI-synthesised AHL diffuses away; once a quorum is reached AHL accumulates, binds LuxR, and triggers the luxCDABE operon producing bioluminescence - used for counterillumination camouflage in the bobtail squid.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Bioremediation}\label{bioremediation}

Microorganisms can be harnessed to degrade environmental pollutants:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{Pseudomonas putida}: Degrades toluene and xylene via the TOL
  \hyperref[gl:plasmid]{\textbf{plasmid}}-encoded pathways; model
  organism for aromatic hydrocarbon bioremediation
\item
  \emph{Geobacter sulfurreducens}: Reduces Fe\(^{3+}\) and U\(^{6+}\);
  used for uranium immobilization at contaminated sites; generates
  electricity in microbial fuel cells via extracellular electron
  transfer
\item
  \emph{Ideonella sakaiensis}: Discovered in 2016 at a PET bottle
  recycling facility in Japan; produces PETase enzyme that degrades
  polyethylene terephthalate (PET) plastic; engineered variants with
  enhanced activity are being developed for plastic waste bioremediation
\item
  Oil spill bioremediation: \emph{Alcanivorax borkumensis} and
  \emph{Marinobacter} species bloom after oil spills, degrading alkanes
  and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons; nutrient addition
  (biostimulation with nitrogen and phosphorus) accelerates degradation
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Microbial Biotechnology}\label{microbial-biotechnology}

\subsubsection{Industrial Fermentation}\label{industrial-fermentation}

Microorganisms have been harnessed for food production for millennia,
and modern biotechnology has expanded their applications enormously:

The current frontier is less about replacing fermentation with a new
idea and more about instrumenting it. Genome-scale metabolic models,
automated strain engineering, continuous bioreactors, metagenomic enzyme
discovery, and precision fermentation now let researchers tune yield,
by-product formation, feedstock use, and contamination risk. Claims
about ``sustainable'' biomanufacturing should therefore report substrate
source, energy input, purification burden, waste stream, and life-cycle
context rather than primarily the engineered microbe.

\subsubsection{Recombinant Protein
Production}\label{recombinant-protein-production}

\emph{E. coli} remains the workhorse for recombinant protein production:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Human insulin (Humulin)}: First recombinant therapeutic
  protein, approved 1982; replaced porcine/bovine insulin
\item
  \textbf{Human growth \hyperref[gl:hormone]{\textbf{hormone}}}:
  Replaced cadaveric pituitary extracts (which transmitted CJD prions)
\item
  \textbf{Erythropoietin (EPO)}: Stimulates red blood cell production;
  produced in CHO (Chinese hamster ovary) cells for proper glycosylation
\item
  \textbf{Hepatitis B \hyperref[gl:vaccine]{\textbf{vaccine}}}:
  Recombinant HBsAg produced in yeast (\emph{Saccharomyces cerevisiae})
  -- the first recombinant vaccine
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Environmental
Biotechnology}\label{environmental-biotechnology}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Biogas production}: Anaerobic digestion by methanogenic
  archaea converts organic waste to methane for energy; widely used in
  wastewater treatment and agricultural waste management
\item
  \textbf{Constructed wetlands}: Engineered ecosystems using microbial
  communities for water purification
\item
  \textbf{Synthetic biology}: Engineered microbial biosensors for
  environmental monitoring (arsenic detection, water quality); metabolic
  engineering for production of biofuels, pharmaceuticals, and commodity
  chemicals from renewable feedstocks
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-25}

For \textbf{Microbial Ecology and the Microbiome}, frontier biology
belongs inside the evidence logic of the chapter. Microbiology and
infectious disease now require One Health reasoning across people,
animals, environments, genomics, and antimicrobial stewardship. The core
reading question is this: microbiome claims should distinguish
correlation, mechanism, host context, perturbation, and causality.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

For AMR and pathogen claims, name the organism-resistance pair, the
selection pressure, the transmission route, and the surveillance
evidence that would change triage
\citep{who2024bppl,cdc2025antibioticuse,murray2022amr}.

\textbf{Source practice:} For pathogen, AMR, and intervention claims,
tie statements to organism-resistance pairs, surveillance evidence,
official guidance, and trial/regulatory status
\citep{who2024bppl,who2025tb,who2025malaria,cdc2025lenacapavirprep,cdc2026candidaauris}.

\subsubsection{Current Evidence Map: Microbiome Causality
Ladder}\label{current-evidence-map-microbiome-causality-ladder}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0127_31af3b622823.png}
\caption{Microbiome claims become stronger as they move from correlation toward perturbation and rescue evidence; many human associations remain context-dependent.}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-25}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The \textbf{great plate count anomaly} reveals that \textless1\% of
  environmental microbes are culturable. Culture-independent methods
  (16S amplicon sequencing, shotgun metagenomics, metatranscriptomics,
  metabolomics) have revolutionized microbial ecology, revealing entire
  new phyla and functional capabilities. \textbf{ASVs (exact sequence
  variants)} have replaced 97 \%-clustered OTUs as the de facto standard
  since about  2018.
\item
  \textbf{Diversity metrics}: Alpha diversity quantifies within-sample
  diversity. Shannon entropy \(H' = -\sum p_i \ln p_i\)
  (\cref{eq:unit_VII_shannon}), Simpson index \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda} and inverse Simpson
  \(1/\lambda\), Chao1 richness, and Faith's PD weight richness and
  evenness differently. Beta diversity (Bray-Curtis, UniFrac, Jaccard)
  quantifies between-sample differences. Rarefaction curves diagnose
  sampling depth.
\item
  The \textbf{human microbiome} (\(3.8 \times 10^{13}\) cells, 3.3
  million genes) varies by body site. The gut microbiome (Firmicutes,
  Bacteroidetes dominant) has a small \textbf{species-level core} but a
  large \textbf{functional core}; \emph{Akkermansia muciniphila},
  \emph{F. prausnitzii}, \emph{B. fragilis}, and \emph{Roseburia} are
  keystone taxa. Microbial SCFAs (butyrate as colonocyte fuel, HDAC
  inhibitor, GPR109A agonist; propionate via GPR41/43; acetate as
  systemic fuel) signal through three GPCRs and HDAC.
  Pattern-recognition receptors (TLR2/4/5, NOD1/2, AhR) read the
  microbial milieu in real time, with PSA from \emph{B. fragilis} a
  striking example of microbial control of Tregs.
\item
  \textbf{Dysbiosis} is associated with obesity (functional
  polysaccharide-degradation gene shift; F/B ratio is method-sensitive
  and not a reliable single biomarker), IBD (reduced \emph{F.
  prausnitzii}, reduced butyrate), colorectal cancer (\emph{F.
  nucleatum} enrichment), and antibiotic-induced \emph{C. difficile}
  infection (FMT achieves \textgreater90\% cure).
\item
  \textbf{Environmental microbiology}: Soil harbors \(10^8\)-\(10^9\)
  bacteria/g; ocean contains \emph{Prochlorococcus} (about 
  \(10^{27}\) cells, 20 \% of global primary production) and SAR11
  (about  \(10^{28}\) cells); deep biosphere holds another
  \(10^{29}\) cells. \textbf{\hyperref[gl:nitrogen-fixation]{Nitrogen
  fixation}} by nitrogenase requires 16 ATP per N\(_2\) and O\(_2\)
  protection. The microbial nitrogen cycle is tracked by \emph{nifH}
  (fixation), \emph{amoA} (nitrification), \emph{nosZ}
  (denitrification), and \emph{hzsA} (anammox); sulfur by \emph{dsrA}
  and \emph{soxB}; carbon by \emph{mcrA} (methanogenesis) and various
  CO\(_2\)-fixation markers. \textbf{Anammox} accounts for 30--50 \% of
  marine N\(_2\) production.
\item
  \textbf{Phage-host kill-the-winner dynamics} maintain ocean diversity:
  phages preferentially predate dominant bacterial species, releasing
  rare species from competitive exclusion. Phages turn over 20--40 \% of
  marine bacteria daily.
\item
  \textbf{Biofilms} (80\% of natural bacteria) are 10-1,000x more
  antibiotic-resistant; \textbf{quorum sensing} coordinates
  population-level behavior via autoinducers (AHL, AIP, AI-2).
\item
  \textbf{Bioremediation} uses microbial metabolism to degrade
  pollutants including hydrocarbons, heavy metals, and plastics
  (PETase).
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See \cref{sec:unit_X_ecosystem_ecology} for
  nutrient cycles, \cref{sec:unit_III_bioenergetics_and_respiration} for
  fermentation products, and \cref{sec:unit_VII_infectious_disease} for
  dysbiosis and infection.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Key Terms}\label{key-terms-25}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3529}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.6471}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Term
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Definition
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Great plate count anomaly} & Observation that \textless1\% of
environmental microorganisms grow on standard laboratory culture
media \\
\textbf{16S rRNA sequencing} & Culture-independent method using the
conserved/variable 16S rRNA gene as a phylogenetic marker for bacterial
identification \\
\textbf{V3--V4 region} & The most common 16S amplicon target
(about  460 bp) used in human microbiome studies; provides
genus-level resolution on Illumina MiSeq \\
\textbf{ASV (amplicon sequence variant)} & Error-corrected exact
sequence inferred by DADA2/Deblur/UNOISE3; replaces 97 \%-identity OTUs
as the modern standard \\
\textbf{OTU (operational taxonomic unit)} & Cluster of 16S sequences at
a fixed identity threshold (typically 97 \%); legacy approach,
reproducibility-limited \\
\textbf{Rarefaction curve} & Plot of richness versus sampling depth used
to assess whether sequencing was deep enough \\
\textbf{Metagenomics} & Shotgun sequencing of total environmental DNA;
reveals community composition and functional gene content without
cultivation \\
\textbf{MAG} & Metagenome-assembled genome; computationally
reconstructed genome of an uncultured organism from metagenomic data \\
\textbf{Alpha diversity} & Within-sample diversity measured by richness
(number of taxa) and evenness (relative abundance distribution) \\
\textbf{Beta diversity} & Between-sample diversity; measures
compositional differences between microbial communities \\
\textbf{Shannon entropy} & Alpha diversity metric:
\(H' = -\sum p_i \ln p_i\); accounts for both richness and evenness;
effective species number is \(e^{H'}\) \\
\textbf{Simpson index} & Probability that two random individuals belong
to the same species: \(\lambda = \sum p_i^2\); complement \(1-\lambda\)
is the Gini-Simpson; reciprocal \(1/\lambda\) is the inverse Simpson
effective number \\
\textbf{Chao1} & Estimator of true richness using singletons and
doubletons: \(\hat{S}_{Chao1} = S_{obs} + f_1^2/(2 f_2)\) \\
\textbf{Microbiome} & The collective community of microorganisms (and
their genomes) inhabiting a defined environment \\
\textbf{Core microbiome} & Taxa or genes present in nearly most healthy
individuals; smaller at species level than at functional-gene level \\
\textbf{Akkermansia muciniphila} & Mucin-degrading Verrucomicrobia
species correlated with metabolic health; pasteurised \emph{A.
muciniphila} approved as novel food (EFSA, 2021) \\
\textbf{Dysbiosis} & Compositional and functional imbalance of the
microbiome associated with disease states \\
\textbf{Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs)} & Bacterial fermentation
products (butyrate, propionate, acetate) with roles in colonocyte
nutrition, immune regulation, and metabolic signaling \\
\textbf{GPR41 / GPR43 / GPR109A} & Three SCFA-sensing GPCRs that
translate microbial fermentation into host hormonal and immune
responses \\
\textbf{Colonization resistance} & Protection against pathogen
establishment provided by resident microbiota through competition,
bacteriocins, and bile acid metabolism \\
\textbf{Fecal microbiota transplant (FMT)} & Transfer of processed donor
stool to restore microbial community in recipients with dysbiosis,
especially recurrent \emph{C. difficile} infection \\
\textbf{Biofilm} & Structured microbial community enclosed in
self-produced EPS matrix; highly antibiotic-resistant \\
\textbf{Quorum sensing} & Cell density-dependent gene regulation via
secreted autoinducer molecules (AHL, AIP, AI-2) \\
\textbf{Nitrogenase} & Enzyme complex (NifH, NifD, NifK) that reduces
N\(_2\) to NH\(_3\); oxygen-sensitive; requires 16 ATP per N\(_2\) \\
\textbf{Anammox} & Anaerobic ammonia oxidation; \emph{Planctomycetes}
couple NH\(_4^+\) + NO\(_2^-\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} N\(_2\) via hydrazine; key gene
\emph{hzsA} \\
\textbf{Comammox} & Complete ammonia oxidation in a single organism
(\emph{Nitrospira inopinata}, 2015 discovery) carrying both \emph{amoA}
and \emph{nxrA} \\
\textbf{Kill-the-winner} & Phage-driven mechanism that maintains
bacterial diversity by preferentially predating dominant taxa \\
\textbf{Bioremediation} & Use of microbial metabolism to degrade or
immobilize environmental pollutants \\
\textbf{Gut-brain axis} & Bidirectional communication between gut
microbiome and CNS via vagus nerve, neurotransmitters, SCFAs, and immune
mediators \\
\end{longtable}
}

\subsection{Review Questions}\label{review-questions-25}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Explain the great plate count anomaly and describe three specific
  reasons why environmental microorganisms may fail to grow on standard
  laboratory media. How has metagenomics addressed this limitation?
\item
  A researcher collects gut microbiome samples from 50 healthy
  individuals and 50 patients with Crohn's disease. Describe which alpha
  and beta diversity metrics you would calculate, what statistical test
  you would use to compare communities (e.g., PERMANOVA on Bray-Curtis
  distances), and predict the expected differences.
\item
  Trace the fate of dietary fiber (resistant starch) from ingestion to
  its effects on host metabolism and immunity. Include the specific
  bacteria involved, the SCFAs produced, the host receptors activated,
  and the downstream physiological effects.
\item
  A patient has experienced four recurrences of \emph{Clostridioides
  difficile} infection despite multiple courses of vancomycin. Explain
  the mechanism by which FMT achieves cure rates exceeding 90\%,
  focusing on colonization resistance and secondary bile acid
  metabolism. Why does vancomycin itself perpetuate the cycle?
\item
  Compare the ecological strategies of SAR11 (genome about 1.3
  Mbp) and \emph{Prochlorococcus} (genome about 1.7 Mbp).
  Explain why both organisms have undergone extreme genome streamlining
  despite occupying different ecological niches, and discuss the
  evolutionary trade-offs of minimal genomes.
\item
  Explain why \emph{Pseudomonas aeruginosa} biofilms in the lungs of
  cystic fibrosis patients are resistant to antibiotic therapy. Describe
  at least four distinct resistance mechanisms that operate within the
  biofilm, and suggest a multi-target therapeutic strategy.
\item
  The Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio is often cited as a biomarker for
  obesity. Critically evaluate this claim by discussing: (a) the
  strength of evidence from gnotobiotic mouse experiments, (b)
  confounding factors in human studies, (c) why this ratio alone is an
  oversimplification of the microbiome-obesity relationship, and (d)
  what functional or species-specific biomarkers have replaced F/B in
  modern research.
\item
  Design an experiment using germ-free mice to determine whether the gut
  microbiome influences anxiety-like behavior through the vagus nerve.
  Include appropriate controls, specify which bacterial species you
  would use for colonization, and describe how you would test vagal
  involvement.
\item
  Nitrogenase is irreversibly inactivated by oxygen, yet
  \emph{Azotobacter vinelandii} is an obligate aerobe that fixes
  nitrogen. Explain the molecular mechanisms by which this organism
  protects its nitrogenase from oxygen damage.
\item
  A biofilm-forming \emph{Staphylococcus aureus} strain causes recurrent
  prosthetic joint infection despite appropriate systemic antibiotic
  therapy. Explain why biofilm removal (surgical debridement) is often
  necessary in addition to antibiotic treatment, and describe how
  persister cells within the biofilm contribute to recurrence.
\item
  \textbf{Shannon diversity practice.} Compute \(H'\) from
  \cref{eq:unit_VII_shannon} for the community
  \(\{200, 100, 50, 20, 10, 10, 5, 5\}\). Then compute the inverse
  Simpson index. Interpret which species drive each metric.
\item
  Using the bridge counts, compute Simpson diversity manually from
  \(p_i\) and compare to \texttt{res.simpson\_index}.
\item
  Contrast \textbf{Faith's PD} with Shannon richness for prioritising
  conservation of microbial lineages.
\item
  \textbf{Marker-gene biogeochemistry.} Describe what biogeochemical
  inference you can draw from a soil metagenome that contains: (a)
  abundant \emph{nifH} but very little \emph{amoA}; (b) abundant
  \emph{amoA} and \emph{nxrA}; (c) \emph{dsrA} and \emph{mcrA} in the
  same sample. What environmental setting could each combination
  represent?
\item
  \textbf{Anammox vs denitrification.} Why has anammox replaced
  conventional denitrification in many modern wastewater plants? Compute
  the stoichiometric advantage in O\(_2\) demand per mole of N removed.
\item
  \textbf{Kill-the-winner test.} Design a 30-day metagenomic time-series

\label{sec:unit_VII_infectious_disease}

\subsection{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-26}

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Apply Koch's postulates and molecular Koch's postulates to evaluate
  evidence for microbial causation of disease, and identify their
  limitations.
\item
  Describe \hyperref[gl:virulence]{\textbf{virulence}} factors
  (adhesins, toxins, invasion machinery, immune evasion strategies) used
  by major bacterial, viral, and eukaryotic pathogens.
\item
  Explain innate immune defenses including physical barriers, pattern
  recognition receptors (TLRs, NLRs, RIG-I, cGAS-STING), the three
  complement pathways and their convergence at C3, and cellular
  effectors (neutrophils with NETosis, macrophages, NK cells with
  missing-self recognition).
\item
  Describe adaptive immunity including V(D)J
  \hyperref[gl:recombination]{\textbf{recombination}}, MHC restriction,
  T helper cell subsets, cytotoxic T cell killing mechanisms, B cell
  activation, affinity maturation, and antibody class switching.
\item
  Compare the eight major \hyperref[gl:vaccine]{\textbf{vaccine}}
  platforms (live attenuated, inactivated, subunit, virus-like-particle,
  toxoid, conjugate, mRNA, viral vector) and apply the
  \hyperref[gl:herd-immunity]{\textbf{herd immunity}} equation
  \(p_c = 1 - 1/R_0\) to compute thresholds for measles, polio, and
  COVID-19 variants.
\item
  Describe antigenic variation in influenza (drift vs shift) and HIV
  (reverse-transcriptase quasi-species clouds), and connect this to
  vaccine reformulation and pandemic risk.
\item
  Catalogue the principal antibiotic-resistance mechanisms (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactamases
  including ESBLs and carbapenemases, efflux pumps, target modification
  including PBP2a in MRSA and 23S rRNA methylation in MLS-resistant
  streptococci, reduced permeability, bypass pathways) and link each to
  specific drug classes.
\item
  Describe the epidemiology and pathogenesis of major infectious
  diseases including tuberculosis, malaria, HIV/AIDS, and influenza, and
  explain the One Health framework.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Opening Vignette --- The Pandemic That Shaped Modern Immunology}

The 1918 influenza pandemic infected an estimated 500 million people ---
one-third of the world's population --- and killed between 50 and 100
million, more than World War I. Most victims were healthy young adults,
a terrifying reversal of the usual mortality pattern, caused by a
cytokine storm in which a vigorous immune response became
catastrophically self-destructive. The pandemic revealed in gruesome
detail the cost of a misdirected immune response and the urgency of
understanding host-pathogen dynamics. From its ashes grew modern
epidemiology, the concept of herd immunity, and the influenza
surveillance networks that today sequence viral
\hyperref[gl:genome]{\textbf{genome}}s in near-real time. When
SARS-CoV-2 emerged in 2019, it was 1918's lessons --- social distancing,
masking, rapid vaccine development --- that shaped the global response.
Infectious disease is not a relic of the past; it is the central
selective pressure on immune system evolution.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Host-Pathogen
Relationships}\label{host-pathogen-relationships}

\subsubsection{Koch's Postulates}\label{kochs-postulates}

In 1884, Robert Koch formalized criteria for establishing that a
specific microorganism causes a specific disease. These four postulates
remain foundational in infectious disease:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The microorganism must be found in most cases of the disease but not
  in healthy individuals
\item
  The microorganism must be isolated from the diseased host and grown in
  pure culture
\item
  The cultured microorganism must cause the same disease when inoculated
  into a healthy, susceptible host
\item
  The same microorganism must be re-isolated from the experimentally
  infected host
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Limitations of Koch's postulates} have become apparent with
advancing knowledge:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Asymptomatic carriers}: \emph{Salmonella typhi} (Typhoid
  Mary), \emph{Neisseria meningitidis} -- healthy carriers exist,
  violating postulate 1
\item
  \textbf{Unculturable organisms}: Viruses (until cell culture),
  \emph{Treponema pallidum}, \emph{Mycobacterium leprae} -- cannot
  fulfill postulate 2
\item
  \textbf{Ethical constraints}: Human experimentation with lethal
  pathogens is prohibited
\item
  \textbf{Polymicrobial disease}: Periodontal disease, bacterial
  vaginosis -- caused by community shifts, not single organisms
\item
  \textbf{Host factors}: \emph{Mycobacterium tuberculosis} causes
  disease in about 5-10\% of infected individuals (the rest maintain
  latent infection)
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Molecular Koch's
Postulates}\label{molecular-kochs-postulates}

In 1988, Stanley Falkow proposed a molecular framework for identifying
virulence determinants:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The virulence \hyperref[gl:gene]{\textbf{gene}} (or its product)
  should be found in pathogenic strains but not in non-pathogenic
  relatives
\item
  Inactivation of the gene (by \hyperref[gl:mutation]{\textbf{mutation}}
  or deletion) should reduce virulence in an appropriate model
\item
  Complementation (restoration of the gene) should restore virulence
\end{enumerate}

This framework has been essential for identifying virulence factors
through targeted gene knockouts and complementation studies in model
organisms.

\subsubsection{The Infection Continuum}\label{the-infection-continuum}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0128_4fb628fe614a.png}
\caption{Decision-tree of pathogen exposure outcomes from initial encounter through clearance, latency, or systemic disease.}
\end{figure}

Not every exposure leads to colonization, not every colonization leads
to infection, and not every infection leads to disease. The outcome
depends on pathogen virulence, inoculum size, route of entry, and host
immune status.

\subsubsection{Virulence Factors}\label{virulence-factors}

Pathogens deploy specific molecular tools to adhere to host tissues,
invade cells, obtain nutrients, and evade immune defenses:

\textbf{Adhesins} mediate initial attachment to host surfaces:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Type IV pili} (\emph{Neisseria gonorrhoeae}, \emph{N.
  meningitidis}): Retractile pili that mediate attachment to epithelial
  surfaces and facilitate twitching motility
\item
  \textbf{FimH} (\emph{E. coli}): Type 1 fimbrial adhesin that binds
  mannose residues on uroepithelial cells, enabling urinary tract
  infection
\item
  \textbf{Fibronectin-binding \hyperref[gl:protein]{\textbf{protein}}s}
  (\emph{Staphylococcus aureus}): Mediate attachment to extracellular
  matrix, enabling wound infections and endocarditis
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Invasion factors}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Type III secretion system (T3SS)}: \emph{Salmonella enterica}
  SPI-1 (Salmonella Pathogenicity Island 1) encodes a molecular syringe
  that injects effector proteins (SopE, SipA) directly into host
  epithelial cells, triggering \hyperref[gl:actin]{\textbf{actin}}
  \hyperref[gl:cytoskeleton]{\textbf{cytoskeleton}} rearrangement and
  bacterial internalization via membrane ruffling
\item
  \textbf{Internalins} (\emph{Listeria monocytogenes}): InlA binds
  E-cadherin, InlB binds Met receptor; trigger receptor-mediated
  \hyperref[gl:endocytosis]{\textbf{endocytosis}}; once internalized,
  Listeria escapes the phagosome (listeriolysin O) and propels itself
  through the \hyperref[gl:cytoplasm]{\textbf{cytoplasm}} using actin
  polymerization (ActA recruits host Arp2/3 complex)
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Capsules}: Polysaccharide capsules (\emph{Streptococcus
pneumoniae}, \emph{Neisseria meningitidis}, \emph{Haemophilus
influenzae} type b) inhibit phagocytosis by preventing complement C3b
deposition and obscuring surface antigens. The pneumococcal capsule has
\textgreater90 serotypes, forming the basis for conjugate vaccine design
(PCV13, PCV20).

\subsubsection{Toxins}\label{toxins}

\textbf{Exotoxins} are secreted proteins with specific mechanisms of
action. Many have the A-B structure: the B (binding) subunit binds a
host cell receptor, and the A (active) subunit enters the cell to exert
its toxic effect:

\textbf{Endotoxin (LPS)}: Unlike exotoxins, endotoxin is not secreted
but released upon bacterial lysis. Lipid A activates TLR4 on
macrophages, triggering release of TNF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}, IL-1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}, and IL-6. At high
concentrations (Gram-negative bacteremia), this causes fever,
hypotension, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), multi-organ
failure, and septic shock.

\textbf{Immune evasion strategies}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Protein A} (\emph{S. aureus}): Binds the Fc region of IgG in
  the ``wrong'' orientation, preventing opsonization and ADCC
\item
  \textbf{IgA protease} (\emph{N. gonorrhoeae}, \emph{H. influenzae}):
  Cleaves secretory IgA at mucosal surfaces
\item
  \textbf{Antigenic variation}: \emph{Trypanosoma brucei} expresses
  variant surface glycoprotein (VSG) from a library of \textgreater1,000
  \emph{vsg} genes, switching expression before the host mounts an
  effective antibody response
\item
  \textbf{Phagosome arrest}: \emph{M. tuberculosis} inhibits
  phagosome-lysosome fusion via LAM (lipoarabinomannan)
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Innate Immunity}\label{innate-immunity}

\subsubsection{Physical and Chemical
Barriers}\label{physical-and-chemical-barriers}

The first line of defense prevents pathogen entry into sterile body
compartments:

A barrier is not just a wall; it is an active ecological and
immunological interface. Skin acidity, mucus flow, antimicrobial
peptides, secretory IgA, iron sequestration, and resident microbiota
most create selection pressures that pathogens must evade. Barrier
failure can therefore come from physical breach, altered chemistry,
disrupted microbial competition, or medical devices that bypass normal
surfaces.

\subsubsection{Pattern Recognition Receptors
(PRRs)}\label{pattern-recognition-receptors-prrs}

The innate immune system detects conserved microbial structures --
\textbf{pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs)} -- through
germline-encoded PRRs. This system provides immediate recognition
without prior exposure:

Key signaling outcomes of PRR activation:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{NF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}B pathway}:
  \hyperref[gl:transcription]{\textbf{Transcription}} of
  pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}, IL-6, TNF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}, IL-8/CXCL8) and
  chemokines
\item
  \textbf{IRF3/7 pathway}: Type I interferons (IFN-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}/\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}) -\textgreater{}
  JAK-STAT signaling -\textgreater{} interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs:
  OAS/RNase L, Mx proteins, PKR) -\textgreater{} antiviral state in
  neighboring cells
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{The Complement System: Three Pathways, One
Cascade}\label{the-complement-system-three-pathways-one-cascade}

The complement system is a cascade of about  30 plasma
proteins that opsonize pathogens, recruit inflammation, and lyse
Gram-negative bacteria. Three pathways converge on a common effector
cascade through the central enzyme \textbf{C3 convertase}, which
hydrolyses C3 into C3a (anaphylatoxin) and C3b (opsonin).

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0129_9049e3a1fb52.png}
\caption{Three pathways of complement activation (classical, lectin, alternative) converge at the C3 convertase, producing C3b (opsonin) and C3a (anaphylatoxin); a second cleavage at C5 generates C5a and the C5b-C9 membrane-attack complex.}
\end{figure}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{C3a} --- a 9-kDa anaphylatoxin: binds C3aR on mast cells
  (degranulation, histamine), endothelial cells (vasodilation, vascular
  permeability), and granulocytes (recruitment).
\item
  \textbf{C3b} --- a 175-kDa opsonin: covalently binds pathogen surface;
  recognized by complement receptor 1 (CR1, CD35) on phagocytes,
  dramatically enhancing phagocytosis.
\end{itemize}

A second cleavage step generates:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{C5a} --- the strongest neutrophil chemoattractant in plasma
  (effective at picomolar concentrations); binds C5aR1.
\item
  \textbf{C5b} --- initiates the \textbf{membrane attack complex (MAC)}:
  C5b + C6 + C7 + C8 + (10--18 copies of) C9 polymerise into a 10-nm
  transmembrane pore that lyses the target cell osmotically. The MAC is
  most effective against Gram-negative bacteria (which lack the thick
  peptidoglycan barrier of Gram-positives); \emph{Neisseria
  meningitidis} and \emph{N. gonorrhoeae} are particularly
  MAC-susceptible --- terminal-complement deficiencies (C5--C9) cause
  recurrent neisserial infections almost exclusively.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Complement regulation.} Self cells avoid complement attack via
membrane-bound and soluble regulators:

\emph{Neisseria meningitidis} and \emph{N. gonorrhoeae} have evolved a
remarkable trick --- they bind host Factor H to their surface using
\textbf{factor H--binding protein (fHbp)}, mimicking self and
inactivating alternative-pathway amplification. fHbp is now a target
antigen in two licensed meningococcal-B vaccines (Bexsero, Trumenba).

\subsubsection{Phagocytosis and Cellular
Effectors}\label{phagocytosis-and-cellular-effectors}

\paragraph{Neutrophil Killing: Oxidative Burst and
NETosis}\label{neutrophil-killing-oxidative-burst-and-netosis}

\textbf{Neutrophils} are the most abundant circulating leukocytes
(50--70 \% of blood leukocytes) and the first cells to arrive at sites
of infection (within minutes of chemokine signal). Their lifespan is
extraordinarily short --- about  6--8 hours in circulation,
about  1--4 days at tissue sites --- reflecting a cell
programmed for rapid microbial killing followed by apoptosis to limit
collateral tissue damage.

\textbf{Oxidative burst (respiratory burst).} Upon phagosome formation,
the \textbf{NADPH oxidase complex (NOX2)} assembles at the phagosome
membrane:

\[ 2\text{O}_2 + \text{NADPH} \xrightarrow{\text{NOX2}} 2\text{O}_2^- + \text{NADP}^+ + \text{H}^+  \label{eq:unit_VII_infectious_disease_item_1}\]

Superoxide (\(O_2^-\)) is rapidly converted to hydrogen peroxide
(\(H_2O_2\)) by superoxide dismutase. \textbf{Myeloperoxidase (MPO)} ---
abundant in neutrophil azurophilic granules --- then catalyses the most
potent step of microbial killing:

\[ \text{H}_2\text{O}_2 + \text{Cl}^- \xrightarrow{\text{MPO}} \text{HOCl} + \text{OH}^-  \label{eq:unit_VII_infectious_disease_item_2}\]

\textbf{HOCl (hypochlorous acid, household-bleach chemistry)} is one of
the most potent oxidants in biology --- it chlorinates microbial
proteins, lipids, and DNA, killing many phagocytosed microbes within
minutes. The phagosome is also acidified (pH about  4.5) and
accumulates antimicrobial peptides (defensins, BPI, lactoferrin).
Survival is uncommon for non-adapted microbes but biologically important
pathogens such as \emph{M. tuberculosis}, \emph{Salmonella}, and
\emph{Leishmania} persist by blocking phagosome maturation, resisting
reactive species, or escaping the vacuole.

\textbf{NETosis.} Discovered in 2004 (Brinkmann \emph{et al.},
\emph{Science}), NETosis is a programmed neutrophil death pathway in
which the cell releases its decondensed
\hyperref[gl:chromatin]{\textbf{chromatin}} --- decorated with
citrullinated \hyperref[gl:histone]{\textbf{histone}}s, neutrophil
elastase, MPO, defensins, and granule contents --- to form
\textbf{neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs)} that physically capture
and chemically kill extracellular bacteria, fungi, and large parasites.
The molecular pathway:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Activation by PAMPs / immune complexes / cytokines triggers ROS
  production by NOX2.
\item
  \textbf{PAD4 (peptidylarginine deiminase 4)} citrullinates histone H3
  (Arg \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} citrulline), neutralizing positive charge and decompacting
  chromatin.
\item
  Nuclear membrane breaks down; chromatin enters cytoplasm; granule
  contents bind to chromatin.
\item
  Plasma membrane lyses, releasing the NET into the extracellular space
  (cell death).
\end{enumerate}

NETs are evolutionarily ancient (zebrafish neutrophils,
\emph{Drosophila} haemocytes, even sea-anemone amoebocytes form similar
traps). Pathological NETosis is now implicated in
\textbf{immunothrombosis} in severe COVID-19 (NETs trap platelets and
trigger coagulation, contributing to microvascular clots), in autoimmune
diseases (citrullinated histones drive ACPA antibodies in rheumatoid
arthritis; anti-NET antibodies in lupus), and in chronic wound failure.

\textbf{Macrophages} are tissue-resident phagocytes with diverse
functions:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Tissue-specific names: Kupffer cells (liver), alveolar macrophages
  (lung), microglia (brain), osteoclasts (bone), Langerhans cells (skin
  -- actually dendritic cells)
\item
  \textbf{M1 polarization} (IFN-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma} + LPS): Pro-inflammatory; produces
  iNOS -\textgreater{} nitric oxide (NO); secretes TNF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}, IL-12;
  activates Th1 responses against intracellular pathogens
\item
  \textbf{M2 polarization} (IL-4, IL-13): Anti-inflammatory; produces
  arginase; secretes IL-10, TGF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}; promotes wound healing, tissue
  repair, and fibrosis
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{NK Cells: Missing-Self and Induced-Self
Recognition}\label{nk-cells-missing-self-and-induced-self-recognition}

\textbf{Natural killer (NK) cells} are innate lymphocytes
(about  5--15 \% of blood lymphocytes) that kill
virus-infected and transformed cells without prior sensitization. They
are the innate immune system's solution to a fundamental problem: how to
detect cells that are \emph{abnormal} from the inside, when no conserved
pathogen pattern is present on the cell surface.

NK-cell killing is governed by an \textbf{integration of inhibitory and
activating receptor signals} --- the ``balance hypothesis.'' A cell is
killed when activating signals exceed inhibitory signals.

\textbf{Missing-self hypothesis (Ljunggren and Karre, 1990).} Healthy
cells display abundant MHC class I on their surface, presenting peptides
for surveillance by CD8\(^+\) T cells. NK cells carry \textbf{inhibitory
KIRs (killer immunoglobulin-like receptors; KIR2DL, KIR3DL)} that
recognise self MHC-I. Engagement delivers an \textbf{inhibitory signal}
through ITIMs (immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibitory motifs),
suppressing the NK-cell killing programme. Many viruses (CMV, HIV, KSHV)
and tumours \textbf{downregulate MHC class I} to avoid CD8\(^+\) T cell
detection --- but this loss removes the inhibitory signal to NK cells,
unmasking the cell for NK-mediated killing. The strategy has trade-offs:
CMV has evolved decoy MHC-I-like proteins (UL18) that bind inhibitory NK
receptors to mimic self.

\textbf{Induced-self via NKG2D.} A complementary mechanism detects
cellular stress. \textbf{NKG2D} is an activating receptor on NK cells
(and on subsets of CD8\(^+\) T cells, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma}\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\delta}}{delta} T cells, NKT cells) that
recognises \textbf{stress-induced ligands}: \textbf{MICA, MICB} (MHC
class I chain-related), \textbf{ULBP1--6} (UL16-binding proteins). These
ligands are \textbf{absent on healthy cells} but induced by:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  DNA damage (ATR/ATM pathway) --- common in transformed cells.
\item
  Viral infection.
\item
  Heat shock response.
\item
  Oxidative stress.
\end{itemize}

NKG2D ligands are MHC-I-like in fold but lack peptide-binding groove and
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}2-microglobulin association. Their induction provides a ``danger
signal'' that bypasses normal MHC-I inhibition. NKG2D engagement signals
through DAP10/DAP12 adaptors to activate cytotoxicity. Many cancers shed
soluble MICA/MICB into circulation as a decoy that downmodulates surface
NKG2D --- an immune escape mechanism now targeted by anti-MICA-shedding
antibodies in cancer immunotherapy.

\textbf{NK-cell killing mechanisms} (shared with CTLs):

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Perforin/granzyme} --- perforin polymerizes in target membrane
  (similar to MAC); granzymes (especially granzyme B) enter and cleave
  caspase-3/7 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \hyperref[gl:apoptosis]{\textbf{apoptosis}}.
\item
  \textbf{Death receptor ligands} --- FasL, TRAIL on NK cell engage Fas,
  DR4/DR5 on target \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} DISC \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} caspase-8 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} apoptosis.
\item
  \textbf{Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC)}: NK cell
  \textbf{CD16 (Fc\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma}RIII)} binds IgG bound to target cell surface \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  directed degranulation. ADCC is the principal mechanism by which
  anti-tumor antibodies (rituximab, trastuzumab) kill cancer cells, and
  a substantial fraction of vaccine-induced antiviral protection.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Inflammation}\label{inflammation}

The cardinal signs of inflammation (rubor, calor, tumor, dolor --
redness, heat, swelling, pain) result from vascular changes triggered by
innate immune activation:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Mast cell degranulation}: Histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes
  -\textgreater{} vasodilation + increased vascular permeability
\item
  \textbf{Cytokine cascade}: IL-1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} (fever, endothelial activation);
  TNF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha} (fever, hypotension, acute-phase response); IL-6 (hepatic
  acute-phase proteins: CRP, fibrinogen, complement, ferritin);
  IL-8/CXCL8 (neutrophil chemotaxis)
\item
  \textbf{Acute-phase response}: Liver produces C-reactive protein
  (CRP), which binds phosphocholine on bacterial surfaces and activates
  complement
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Sepsis and Cytokine Storm} Sepsis is
defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated
host response to infection (Sepsis-3 criteria, 2016). It affects
approximately 49 million people and causes 11 million deaths annually
worldwide (WHO). In sepsis, the normally protective inflammatory
response becomes pathologically amplified: massive cytokine release
(TNF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}, IL-1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}, IL-6) causes widespread endothelial dysfunction,
capillary leak, coagulopathy (DIC), and multi-organ failure. The SOFA
(Sequential Organ Failure Assessment) score quantifies organ
dysfunction. Cytokine storm -- a related phenomenon -- was observed in
severe COVID-19 (IL-6 pathway hyperactivation; treated with tocilizumab,
an IL-6 receptor antagonist) and in cytokine release syndrome (CRS)
following CAR-T cell therapy.
\end{quote}

\textbf{Concept Check 2:} A child with chronic granulomatous disease
(CGD) has a mutation in the gp91phox subunit of NADPH oxidase. Predict
which types of infections this child will be susceptible to, and explain
why catalase-positive bacteria (\emph{S. aureus}, \emph{Aspergillus})
are particularly dangerous in CGD while catalase-negative bacteria
(\emph{Streptococcus}) are not.
\end{quote}

\textbf{Concept Check 2b:} A patient with paroxysmal nocturnal

of GPI-anchored proteins on red blood cells, including CD55 and CD59.
Explain (a) why these red cells are constantly haemolysed by their own
complement system, (b) why the disease is paroxysmal (worse at

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Adaptive Immunity
Overview}\label{adaptive-immunity-overview}

The adaptive immune system provides antigen-specific responses with
immunological memory. Its defining features include:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Specificity}: Each lymphocyte clone bears a unique antigen
  receptor (TCR or BCR) generated by somatic recombination
\item
  \textbf{Diversity}: \(>10^{12}\) possible TCR specificities; \(>10^8\)
  BCR specificities
\item
  \textbf{Clonal selection}: Antigen selects and expands primarily those
  lymphocyte clones with matching receptors
\item
  \textbf{Memory}: Long-lived memory cells mount faster, stronger
  secondary responses upon re-encounter
\item
  \textbf{Self-tolerance}: Autoreactive clones are eliminated (central
  tolerance) or suppressed (peripheral tolerance)
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{MHC Molecules}\label{mhc-molecules}

Major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules present peptide
fragments to T cells, providing the context for antigen recognition:

\textbf{MHC class I} (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C in humans):

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Expressed on \textbf{most nucleated cells}
\item
  Present \textbf{endogenous peptides} (from cytoplasmic proteins):
  proteasome -\textgreater{} peptide fragments -\textgreater{} TAP
  transporter -\textgreater{} ER -\textgreater{} peptide loading onto
  MHC-I -\textgreater{} cell surface
\item
  Recognized by \textbf{CD8\(^+\) T cells} (cytotoxic T lymphocytes)
\item
  Presents viral antigens and tumor antigens from within the cell
\end{itemize}

\textbf{MHC class II} (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ):

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Expressed on \textbf{professional antigen-presenting cells (APCs)}:
  dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells
\item
  Present \textbf{exogenous peptides} (from phagocytosed material):
  endosomal/lysosomal degradation -\textgreater{} CLIP removal by HLA-DM
  -\textgreater{} peptide loading onto MHC-II -\textgreater{} cell
  surface
\item
  Recognized by \textbf{CD4\(^+\) T cells} (helper T cells)
\end{itemize}

MHC genes are the most polymorphic in the human genome
(about 20,000 HLA \hyperref[gl:allele]{\textbf{allele}}s in the
population), ensuring that no pathogen peptide can escape presentation
in most individuals -- a population-level defense strategy.

\subsubsection{T Cell Activation and
Differentiation}\label{t-cell-activation-and-differentiation}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0130_02191e8ef71e.png}
\caption{Three-signal T cell activation by dendritic cells, with cytokine-context-driven differentiation into Th1/Th2/Th17/Treg/Tfh subsets and downstream activation of cytotoxic CD8\$\textasciicircum{}+\$ T cells and antibody-producing B cells.}
\end{figure}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Signal 1}: TCR recognition of peptide:MHC complex (specificity
  signal)
\item
  \textbf{Signal 2}: Co-stimulatory signal -- CD28 on T cell binds B7
  molecules (CD80/CD86) on APC. Without this signal, the T cell becomes
  \textbf{anergic} (functionally unresponsive) -- a mechanism of
  peripheral tolerance
\item
  \textbf{Signal 3}: Cytokine environment determines effector subset
  differentiation
\end{itemize}

\textbf{T helper cell subsets}:

\textbf{Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs, CD8\(^+\))} recognize viral or
tumor antigens on MHC-I and kill target cells through:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Perforin/granzyme pathway}: Perforin polymerizes in the target
  membrane, forming pores; granzyme B enters and activates caspase-3/7
  -\textgreater{} apoptosis
\item
  \textbf{Fas-FasL pathway}: CTL-expressed FasL binds Fas (CD95) on
  target -\textgreater{} DISC formation -\textgreater{} caspase-8
  -\textgreater{} apoptosis
\item
  \textbf{Serial killing}: A single CTL can kill 2-25 target cells
  sequentially via directed degranulation at the immunological synapse
\item
  \textbf{Exhaustion}: In chronic infections (HBV, HCV, HIV), persistent
  antigen exposure leads to upregulation of inhibitory receptors (PD-1,
  TIM-3, LAG-3) and progressive loss of effector function -- the basis
  for PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitor therapy in cancer
\end{itemize}

\subsection{B Cells and Antibodies}\label{b-cells-and-antibodies}

\subsubsection{B Cell Activation}\label{b-cell-activation}

B cell activation pathways differ depending on the nature of the
antigen:

\textbf{T-dependent antigens} (protein antigens): BCR binds and
internalizes antigen -\textgreater{} processes and presents peptides on
MHC-II -\textgreater{} recognized by cognate Tfh cell -\textgreater{}
CD40L-CD40 interaction + IL-21 -\textgreater{} B cell activation,
proliferation, and entry into the germinal center reaction. This pathway
produces high-affinity antibodies, class-switched isotypes, and
long-lived memory.

\textbf{T-independent antigens} (repetitive polysaccharides, LPS):
Cross-link multiple BCRs on the B cell surface -\textgreater{}
activation without T cell help. Produces primarily IgM; limited affinity
maturation; poor memory response. This is why polysaccharide vaccines
(pneumococcal, meningococcal) are poorly immunogenic in children under 2
years (immature T-independent response) and why \textbf{conjugate
vaccines} were developed.

\subsubsection{Germinal Center Reaction}\label{germinal-center-reaction}

The germinal center (GC) in secondary lymphoid organs is the site of
antibody optimization:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Clonal expansion}: Activated B cells (centroblasts)
  proliferate rapidly in the dark zone
\item
  \textbf{Somatic hypermutation (SHM)}: Activation-induced cytidine
  deaminase (AID) introduces point mutations in the variable (V) regions
  of immunoglobulin genes at a rate of about \(10^{-3}\) per
  base pair per division -- one million-fold higher than the normal
  mutation rate. AID deaminates cytidine to uridine in DNA, which is
  then processed by base excision repair or mismatch repair to generate
  diverse mutations.
\item
  \textbf{Affinity maturation}: Mutant B cells (centrocytes) migrate to
  the light zone, where they compete for antigen displayed on follicular
  dendritic cells (FDCs). Primarily B cells with improved BCR affinity
  receive survival signals; the rest undergo apoptosis. This Darwinian
  selection process progressively increases antibody affinity over
  successive rounds.
\item
  \textbf{Class switch recombination (CSR)}: AID also introduces
  double-strand breaks in switch (S) regions upstream of constant region
  genes, enabling recombination that changes the antibody class from IgM
  to IgG, IgA, or IgE while preserving antigen specificity. Cytokine
  signals determine which class is selected: IL-4 -\textgreater{} IgE;
  IFN-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma} -\textgreater{} IgG1; TGF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} -\textgreater{} IgA.
\end{enumerate}

The GC reaction produces two critical outputs: \textbf{long-lived plasma
cells} (migrate to bone marrow; secrete high-affinity antibody for years
to decades) and \textbf{memory B cells} (reside in secondary lymphoid
organs; rapidly reactivate upon antigen re-encounter).

\subsubsection{Antibody Structure and
Function}\label{antibody-structure-and-function}

An antibody molecule consists of two identical heavy (H) chains and two
identical light (L) chains, each containing variable (V) and constant
(C) domains:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Fab region} (fragment antigen-binding): Contains the variable
  domains (VH + VL) that form the antigen-binding site (paratope). The
  three complementarity-determining regions (CDR1, CDR2, CDR3) within
  each variable domain make direct contact with antigen.
\item
  \textbf{Fc region} (fragment crystallizable): The constant domains
  that determine antibody class and mediate effector functions
  (complement activation, Fc receptor binding on phagocytes and NK
  cells, placental transfer).
\item
  \textbf{Hinge region}: Provides flexibility between Fab and Fc,
  allowing bivalent binding to spatially separated epitopes.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Antibody Classes}\label{antibody-classes}

\textbf{Immunological memory} -- the basis of vaccination -- results
from the persistence of long-lived plasma cells and memory B cells. Upon
re-exposure, the secondary response is:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Faster}: Days instead of 1-2 weeks
\item
  \textbf{Stronger}: 10-100 fold higher antibody titers
\item
  \textbf{Higher affinity}: Memory B cells express somatically
  hypermutated, affinity-matured BCRs
\item
  \textbf{Class-switched}: Predominantly IgG (or IgA at mucosal
  surfaces)
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Vaccines and Immunological
Memory}\label{vaccines-and-immunological-memory}

\subsubsection{Vaccine Platforms: Eight Strategies for Inducing
Memory}\label{vaccine-platforms-eight-strategies-for-inducing-memory}

Vaccines exploit the same memory mechanisms that protect us after
natural infection, but without the disease. The eight major platform
classes --- each with distinct strengths, limitations, and clinical
exemplars --- represent a 200-year-progressive enrichment of strategies
for safely tricking the immune system into making memory.

\textbf{mRNA vaccines} are the newest platform and represented a
paradigm shift during the COVID-19 pandemic:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The spike protein sequence of SARS-CoV-2 was published on January 11,
  2020; Moderna had designed its mRNA-1273 vaccine candidate within 48
  hours.
\item
  The mRNA is modified (N1-methylpseudouridine replaces uridine, Karikó
  and Weissman discovery, Nobel Prize 2023) to reduce TLR7/8
  recognition, block 2'-5'-OAS / RNase L degradation, and increase
  translational efficiency 10--100\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x}.
\item
  Lipid nanoparticle (LNP) encapsulation protects the mRNA from
  extracellular nucleases and facilitates cellular uptake; the
  four-component LNP (ionisable lipid, phospholipid, cholesterol,
  PEG-lipid) self-assembles into about  80-nm particles.
\item
  Upon injection, host cells (predominantly muscle and dendritic cells
  at the injection site) translate the mRNA into spike protein, which is
  presented on MHC-I (activating CD8\(^+\) CTLs) and
  secreted/surface-displayed (activating B cells and CD4\(^+\) T cells).
\item
  No integration into host DNA occurs --- mRNA is degraded within hours
  to days.
\item
  Spike is locked in the prefusion conformation by two proline
  substitutions (\textbf{2P mutation}) that preserve neutralising
  epitopes.
\end{itemize}

The platform is now extending to \textbf{influenza} (mRNA-1010),
\textbf{RSV} (mRNA-1345, FDA-approved 2024), \textbf{CMV}, and
\textbf{personalised cancer neoantigen vaccines} (Moderna mRNA-4157 in
Phase III for melanoma).

\subsubsection{Antigenic Variation: How Pathogens Outpace Antibody
Responses}\label{antigenic-variation-how-pathogens-outpace-antibody-responses}

The single greatest challenge for vaccine development against many
viruses is that the immune target itself \textbf{evolves under the
selection pressure of the population's own immune response}. Two
paradigmatic examples illustrate the strategies and the resulting
public-health consequences.

\textbf{Influenza A: drift and shift.} Influenza A is a Class V
segmented (-)ssRNA virus with 8 genome segments. Its surface
glycoproteins \textbf{hemagglutinin (HA, 18 subtypes)} and
\textbf{neuraminidase (NA, 11 subtypes)} are the primary targets of
neutralising antibodies. Influenza A undergoes two distinct mechanisms
of antigenic change:

\textbf{Pandemic history:} - \textbf{1918 H1N1} (``Spanish flu'') ---
50--100 million deaths. - \textbf{1957 H2N2} (``Asian flu'') --- 1--2
million deaths; H2 from avian source reassorted with circulating H1N1. -
\textbf{1968 H3N2} (``Hong Kong flu'') --- 1 million deaths; H3 from
avian source. - \textbf{2009 H1N1} (pandemic) --- about 
284,000 deaths; quadruple reassortant (avian + human + two swine
lineages); milder than predicted because of partial cross-immunity from
related H1N1 strains. - \textbf{H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza
(HPAI)} --- ongoing outbreaks in dairy cattle and poultry (2024--26);
about  60 \% case-fatality rate in the rare human cases;
intense surveillance for adaptation to mammalian transmission.

\textbf{HIV reverse transcriptase: the quasi-species cloud.} HIV uses an
entirely different mechanism --- extreme intra-host evolution. Reverse
transcriptase has an \textbf{error rate of about  3 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{5}}{5}
per base per replication cycle}, and HIV makes about 
\(10^{10}\) virions per day in an untreated patient. With a 9.7-kb
genome, this produces \textbf{every single point mutation in the viral
genome multiple times every day} and a substantial fraction of possible
double mutations. The resulting population --- a cloud of related
sequences around a consensus --- is termed a \textbf{quasi-species}.

Consequences:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Drug resistance is essentially preformed}: any single-target
  monotherapy fails within weeks because resistant variants pre-exist in
  the quasi-species cloud. This is why HIV treatment requires
  \textbf{combination ART} (\texorpdfstring{\textgreater{}=}{>=} 3 drugs from \texorpdfstring{\textgreater{}=}{>=} 2 classes); the
  simultaneous probability of a virion carrying mutations conferring
  resistance to most drugs is astronomically low.
\item
  \textbf{Antibody escape is continuous}: the env gene (gp120/gp41)
  evolves rapidly under neutralising-antibody pressure, with the
  variable loops V1/V2/V3 changing every few weeks within an individual.
\item
  \textbf{Vaccine difficulty}: a vaccine that elicits primarily
  narrowly-specific antibodies will fail. Successful HIV vaccine
  candidates aim for \textbf{broadly neutralising antibodies (bNAbs)}
  that target conserved sites (CD4-binding site, fusion peptide) --- but
  these require unusual germline B cells and prolonged affinity
  maturation, which most vaccinees do not develop.
\end{enumerate}

The HIV quasi-species lesson --- that within-host evolution can generate
resistance faster than therapy can clear the virus --- has now been
applied to influenza, hepatitis C, and SARS-CoV-2 (the 32-spike-mutation
Omicron emergence almost certainly arose from chronic infection of an
immunocompromised host, where prolonged replication permitted
accumulation of escape mutations).

\subsubsection{Herd Immunity}\label{herd-immunity}

When a sufficient proportion of a population is immune, the pathogen's
transmission is interrupted even for non-immune individuals. The
\textbf{herd-immunity threshold} is given by:

\begin{equation}
p_c = 1 - \frac{1}{R_0}
\label{eq:unit_VII_herd_immunity}
\end{equation}

where \(p_c\) is the critical fraction of the population that must be
immune and \(R_0\) is the \textbf{basic reproduction number} (the
expected number of secondary cases from one primary case in a fully
susceptible population). The intuition: each case must produce on
average less than one secondary case for the epidemic to die out;
immunity removes a fraction of the contacts an infectious person makes,
so the \textbf{effective reproduction number} is \(R_e = R_0 (1 - p)\).
Solving for \(R_e = 1\) gives \(p = 1 - 1/R_0\).

(MMR two-dose) & \(0.933 / 0.97 = 0.962\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{96.2 \%} \\
\textbf{Polio} & 5 & \(1 - 1/5 = 0.800\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{80 \%} & 0.99 (IPV
three-dose) & \(0.800 / 0.99 = 0.808\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{80.8 \%} \\
\textbf{COVID-19 (original)} & 2.5 & \(1 - 1/2.5 = 0.600\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{60
\%} & 0.95 (BNT162b2 against original) & \(0.600 / 0.95 = 0.632\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
\textbf{63.2 \%} \\
\textbf{COVID-19 (Omicron)} & 10 & \(1 - 1/10 = 0.900\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{90 \%}
& 0.50 (vs symptomatic infection) & \(0.900 / 0.50 = 1.80\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
\textbf{unattainable} \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Interpretation:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Measles is the textbook case for high-coverage vaccination.}
  Even with the excellent MMR vaccine (\(E \approx 97 \%\)),
  \textgreater{} 96 \% of the population must be vaccinated. A drop from
  96 \% to 92 \% (e.g., due to vaccine hesitancy) reduces immunity below
  threshold and allows outbreaks --- exactly what has happened in the
  2018--2019 US/EU measles resurgences.
\item
  \textbf{Polio's lower \(R_0\)} makes it much more tractable: 80 \%
  coverage with IPV is sufficient. This is why polio is on the verge of
  global eradication while measles is not.
\item
  \textbf{COVID-19 Omicron} illustrates the \textbf{vaccine-coverage
  impossibility} result: when efficacy against transmission is moderate
  (about  50 \%) and \(R_0\) is high (about  10
  due to immune escape and inherent transmissibility), the formula
  \(p_v = p_c / E\) exceeds 100 \%, meaning \textbf{herd immunity by
  vaccination alone is unattainable}. Public-health strategy must rely
  on a combination of vaccination (reducing severity),
  non-pharmaceutical interventions (reducing \(R_0\) below the
  achievable coverage), and accepting endemicity.
\end{enumerate}

The herd-immunity equation also explains why \textbf{small reductions in
vaccine coverage produce disproportionate disease resurgences for
high-\(R_0\) pathogens}: at \(R_0 = 15\), a 1-percentage-point drop in
immune coverage raises the effective reproduction number \(R_e\) by
about \(R_0 \times 0.01 = 0.15\). This non-linearity is why measles
outbreaks dominate vaccine-hesitancy clusters.

\subsubsection{Adjuvants}\label{adjuvants}

Adjuvants amplify the innate immune response to vaccine antigens,
improving adaptive immunity:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Aluminum salts (Alum)}: Oldest adjuvant (since 1926);
  activates NLRP3 inflammasome; depot effect (slow antigen release);
  used in most childhood vaccines
\item
  \textbf{AS04} (Alum + monophosphoryl lipid A): TLR4 agonist; used in
  Cervarix (HPV vaccine)
\item
  \textbf{MF59}: Oil-in-water squalene emulsion; enhances antigen uptake
  by APCs; used in some influenza vaccines
\item
  \textbf{CpG oligodeoxynucleotides}: TLR9 agonist; used in Heplisav-B
  (hepatitis B vaccine)
\item
  \textbf{Matrix-M} (saponin-based): Used in Novavax COVID-19 vaccine;
  potent Th1 and CTL response
\item
  \textbf{AS01} (liposomal MPL + QS-21): Used in Shingrix (zoster) and
  RTS,S (malaria); strong Th1 response
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: SARS-CoV-2 and the COVID-19 Pandemic}
SARS-CoV-2 enters cells via its spike protein binding ACE2, with TMPRSS2
protease facilitating membrane fusion. Variants of concern (Alpha,
Delta, Omicron) accumulated mutations in the spike protein's
receptor-binding domain (RBD) that increased transmissibility and/or
enabled immune evasion. Omicron-lineage viruses substantially escaped
neutralising antibodies from both vaccination and prior infection, while
population immunity and viral evolution shifted severe-disease risk
compared with early pandemic waves. mRNA vaccine development
demonstrated the power of platform technology -- Moderna designed its
vaccine sequence within 48 hours of the viral genome publication, though
regulatory approval required 11 months of clinical trials. Long COVID is
now defined operationally as a chronic condition present at least 3
months after SARS-CoV-2 infection; prevalence estimates vary by cohort,
variant era, vaccination status, and case definition. Mechanistic
studies now emphasise persistent immune activation, T-cell exhaustion
signatures, metabolic dysregulation, possible viral-antigen persistence,
autoimmunity, \hyperref[gl:microbiome]{\textbf{microbiome}} disruption,
dysautonomia, and endothelial dysfunction rather than a single cause
\citep{cdc2026longcovid,longcovid2025immune}.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Antibiotic Resistance: A Comprehensive Mechanism
Catalogue}\label{antibiotic-resistance-a-comprehensive-mechanism-catalogue}

Antibiotic resistance can be classified into five mechanistic
categories. Most clinically important multi-drug-resistant pathogens
combine multiple mechanisms; an isolate may simultaneously hydrolyse
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactams, modify aminoglycosides, methylate ribosomal RNA, and pump out
fluoroquinolones.

\subsubsection{Mechanism 1: Enzymatic
Inactivation}\label{mechanism-1-enzymatic-inactivation}

Direct destruction of the drug by hydrolysis or modification.

\textbf{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactamases} are the most clinically important and most diverse
resistance enzymes. They hydrolyse the \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactam ring (with the
active-site serine --- a tetrahedral covalent intermediate --- or via a
metallo-zinc mechanism) before the drug reaches its PBP target. The
Ambler classification:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1129}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1774}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1613}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3871}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1613}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Class
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Mechanism
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Spectrum
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Inhibitor sensitivity
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Examples
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Class A} (serine) & Active-site serine (Ser70) & Penicillins;
ESBL extends to 3GC & Inhibited by clavulanate, sulbactam, tazobactam,
avibactam & TEM-1, SHV-1 (penicillinases); CTX-M (the dominant ESBL
globally); KPC (carbapenemase) \\
\textbf{Class B} (metallo-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactamase, MBL) & Zn\(^{2+}\) active site;
hydroxide nucleophile & Penicillins, cephalosporins, and carbapenems;
monobactams such as aztreonam are structurally spared by the MBL but can
be hydrolysed by co-produced ESBLs & Inhibited by EDTA in vitro;
\textbf{not inhibited by clinical inhibitors}; aztreonam-avibactam

\textbf{Class C} (AmpC) & Active-site serine & Cephalosporins (including
3GC); poorly inhibited by clavulanate & Cefepime, carbapenems retain
activity & Chromosomal AmpC inducible in \emph{Enterobacter},
\emph{Serratia}, \emph{Citrobacter}, \emph{Pseudomonas}; plasmid-borne
(CMY) \\
\textbf{Class D} (oxacillinase, OXA) & Active-site serine & Variable
(penicillins \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} carbapenems for OXA-48) & Variable inhibitor
susceptibility & OXA-48 (Klebsiella, Mediterranean); OXA-23
(Acinetobacter pan-resistance) \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Other inactivating enzymes:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes (AMEs)} --- three families:
  acetyltransferases (AAC), phosphotransferases (APH),
  nucleotidyltransferases (ANT). Modify amino or hydroxyl groups on the
  drug, abolishing ribosome binding. Plasmid-encoded; \textgreater{} 50
  enzyme variants known.
\item
  \textbf{Chloramphenicol acetyltransferase (CAT)} --- acetylates the
  drug.
\item
  \textbf{Macrolide esterases / phosphotransferases} (Ere, Mph) --- less
  common than ribosomal methylation.
\item
  \textbf{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-glucuronidases} that activate the cancer drug irinotecan
  into its toxic form (gut bacteria; relevant for drug-drug-microbiome
  interactions).
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Mechanism 2: Target
Modification}\label{mechanism-2-target-modification}

Altering the drug target so the antibiotic no longer binds.

\toprule\noalign{}

\emph{dfr} genes encoding drug-resistant DHFR; chromosomal mutations &

\textbf{Sulfonamides} & DHPS (dihydropteroate synthase) & Acquired
\emph{sul} genes; chromosomal mutations & Bypass through alternative
DHPS \\
\textbf{Colistin (polymyxin)} & LPS lipid A & \textbf{mcr-1
phosphoethanolamine transferase} (plasmid-borne, 2015 discovery, China);
chromosomal \emph{pmrAB / phoPQ} mutations & Modifies lipid A phosphates
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} reduced affinity for cationic colistin \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{MRSA mechanism in detail.} \emph{S. aureus} resistant to
methicillin and most earlier \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactams carries the \textbf{mecA gene} on
a mobile genetic element --- \textbf{SCC\emph{mec}} (staphylococcal
cassette chromosome mec). \emph{mecA} encodes \textbf{PBP2a}, an
alternative transpeptidase whose \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactam-binding pocket has rearranged
to drastically lower affinity. The K\(_i\) for ceftriaxone increases
from about  0.05 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}M (PBP2) to about  50 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}M
(PBP2a). When normal PBPs are acylated by \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactam, PBP2a can still
cross-link cell wall, allowing growth. Newer \textbf{5th-generation
cephalosporins} (ceftaroline, ceftobiprole) were specifically engineered
with side chains that bind PBP2a and are now used clinically against
MRSA.

\subsubsection{Mechanism 3: Efflux
Pumps}\label{mechanism-3-efflux-pumps}

Active export of antibiotics out of the cell, often accomplishing
\textbf{multi-drug resistance} through a single pump system.

\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{RND (Resistance-Nodulation-Division)} & Proton motive force &
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactams, fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, chloramphenicol, macrolides
& \textbf{AcrAB-TolC} (\emph{E. coli}); \textbf{MexAB-OprM},
\textbf{MexCD-OprJ}, \textbf{MexEF-OprN}, \textbf{MexXY-OprM} (\emph{P.

(TetA, TetB), macrolides (Mef), fluoroquinolones & TetA, TetB; MdfA \\
\textbf{MATE} & PMF / Na\(^+\) gradient & Fluoroquinolones,

\textbf{SMR (Small Multidrug Resistance)} & PMF & QACs, lipophilic
cations & EmrE \\
\textbf{ABC (ATP-Binding Cassette)} & ATP & Macrolides, ketolides &
LmrA \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{RND tripartite pumps} in Gram-negatives are particularly
devastating because they span the entire cell envelope: an
inner-membrane efflux transporter (e.g., AcrB) coupled via a periplasmic
adaptor (AcrA) to an outer-membrane channel (TolC). The pump exports
drugs straight from the cytoplasm or inner membrane into the
extracellular space, bypassing the periplasm. \emph{P. aeruginosa}
MexAB-OprM is the textbook example: constitutive expression confers
intrinsic resistance to multiple drug classes; mutations in regulators
(e.g., \emph{nfxB}, \emph{mexR}) cause overexpression and clinical
failure.

\subsubsection{Mechanism 4: Reduced
Permeability}\label{mechanism-4-reduced-permeability}

Decreasing drug uptake by altering cell-envelope permeability.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Porin loss} in Gram-negatives: deletions or down-regulation of
  OmpF, OmpC, OprD --- particularly important for hydrophilic \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactams
  and carbapenems. \textbf{OprD loss in \emph{P. aeruginosa}} confers
  imipenem resistance.
\item
  \textbf{LPS modification} in Gram-negatives: reduces hydrophobic-drug
  entry.
\item
  \textbf{Mycobacterial cell wall}: the mycolic-acid layer is
  intrinsically impermeable; \emph{M. tuberculosis} is naturally
  resistant to most antibiotics.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Mechanism 5: Bypass / Target
Overproduction}\label{mechanism-5-bypass-target-overproduction}

Producing more target or alternative target to dilute drug action.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Trimethoprim resistance via} \emph{dfr} genes that encode a
  drug-insensitive DHFR (target replacement).
\item
  \textbf{Sulfonamide resistance via} \emph{sul} genes that encode a
  drug-insensitive DHPS.
\item
  \textbf{Methotrexate resistance} in cancer cells via DHFR
  overexpression --- same principle in eukaryotes.
\end{itemize}

A clinical isolate from a 2019 outbreak in a Greek ICU was reported with
the following resistance profile:

Such isolates may have no reliable standard single-agent option, so
treatment depends on isolate-specific susceptibility testing, source
control, and expert consultation. Options can include cefiderocol,
ceftazidime-avibactam plus aztreonam for some MBL-producing isolates,
aminoglycoside or fosfomycin combinations when active, and
investigational phage therapy. The case illustrates that resistance is
\textbf{modular and additive}: each mechanism arrives independently,
often on plasmids, and accumulates over time. This is why antibiotic
stewardship, infection control, diagnostics, and new drug development
must operate together.

the same combination would fail against an NDM-producer, and (c) how
ESBL-restricted versus carbapenemase-positive resistance is
distinguished by the meropenem-EDTA versus meropenem-boronic-acid

\subsubsection{Key Epidemiological
Metrics}\label{key-epidemiological-metrics}
