\subsubsection{Worked Example: Estimating R0 from an Epidemic
Curve}\label{worked-example-estimating-r0-from-an-epidemic-curve}

\textbf{Problem:} Early in an outbreak, confirmed cases double every
\(T_d = 3.0\) days. The mean serial interval (time between symptom onset
in successive cases) is \(T_s = 5.0\) days. Estimate the basic
reproduction number \(R_0\), then the herd-immunity threshold.

\textbf{Solution:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Exponential growth rate \(r\) from the doubling time.} Early
  case counts grow as \(N(t) = N_0\,2^{t/T_d} = N_0\,e^{rt}\), so
  equating exponents gives \(r = \ln 2 / T_d\):
\end{enumerate}

\[ r = \frac{\ln 2}{T_d} = \frac{0.6931}{3.0} = 0.2310 \text{ day}^{-1} \label{eq:unit_VII_infectious_disease_item_3}\]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Convert growth rate to \(R_0\).} For a fixed
  (delta-distributed) serial interval, the renewal equation gives
  \(R_0 = e^{r T_s}\):
\end{enumerate}

\[ R_0 = e^{r T_s} = e^{0.2310 \times 5.0} = e^{1.155} = 3.17 \label{eq:unit_VII_infectious_disease_item_4}\]

(The simpler linear approximation
\(R_0 \approx 1 + r T_s = 1 + 0.2310 \times 5.0 = 2.16\) is a lower
bound that ignores serial-interval dispersion.)

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Herd-immunity threshold.} Substituting \(R_0 = 3.17\) into the
  herd-immunity relation \(p_c = 1 - 1/R_0\) from
  \cref{eq:unit_VII_herd_immunity}:
\end{enumerate}

\[ p_c = 1 - \frac{1}{3.17} = 0.685 \;\rightarrow\; 68.5\,\% \label{eq:unit_VII_infectious_disease_item_5}\]

\textbf{Interpretation:} A 3-day doubling time with a 5-day serial
interval implies \(R_0 \approx 3.2\), so roughly 69 \% of the population
must be immune to halt sustained transmission --- a value consistent
with an early pandemic-respiratory pathogen, and one that grows sharply
if the doubling time shortens.

\subsubsection{Major Infectious
Diseases}\label{major-infectious-diseases}

\textbf{Tuberculosis} (\emph{Mycobacterium tuberculosis}):

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Global burden: an estimated 10.7 million people fell ill with TB in
  2024 and 1.23 million died, including 150,000 people with HIV
  \citep{who2025tb}. TB remains the leading cause of death from a single
  infectious agent and a major contributor to AMR-associated mortality.
\item
  Transmission: Airborne droplet nuclei (1-5 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m); can remain suspended
  for hours
\item
  Pathogenesis: Inhaled bacilli are phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages
  but arrest phagosome maturation (LAM inhibits PI3K -\textgreater{}
  blocks Ca\(^{2+}\)/calmodulin -\textgreater{} prevents phagolysosomal
  fusion); survive within macrophages at pH 6.4 instead of lethal pH 4.5
\item
  \textbf{Granuloma}: Hallmark of TB pathology -- organized aggregate of
  infected macrophages, epithelioid cells, multinucleated giant cells,
  and T cells; hypoxic caseous necrotic center; both contains and
  protects the bacilli
\item
  Latent TB: 90-95\% of infected individuals contain the infection as
  LTBI (latent TB infection); 5-10\% lifetime risk of reactivation,
  increased by HIV, immunosuppression, malnutrition
\item
  Treatment: standard drug-susceptible pulmonary TB is treated with a
  multi-drug rifamycin-based regimen, classically 6 months of isoniazid
  + rifampicin + pyrazinamide + ethambutol followed by continuation
  therapy; adherence support matters because metabolically slow bacilli
  and granuloma drug penetration make undertreatment risky.
\item
  \textbf{MDR/RR-TB} (multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB),
  \textbf{pre-XDR-TB} (MDR/RR-TB with fluoroquinolone resistance), and
  \textbf{XDR-TB} (MDR/RR-TB plus resistance to a fluoroquinolone and at
  least one additional Group A drug such as bedaquiline or linezolid)
  remain major AMR threats. WHO's consolidated 2025 treatment guidance
  now prioritises shorter most-oral regimens for eligible patients,
  including 6-month BPaLM/BPaL-based options, while reserving longer
  individualized regimens for resistance, toxicity, pregnancy/age
  limits, extrapulmonary disease, or poor early response
  \citep{who2025tb}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0133_d23b238a8412.png}
\caption{TB regimen decision schematic. WHO's shorter BPaLM/BPaL options are eligibility-dependent tools for MDR/RR-TB, not a comprehensive replacement for susceptibility testing, toxicity monitoring, or individualized care \textbackslash{}citep\{who2025tb\}.}
\end{figure}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Global burden: an estimated 282 million cases and 610,000 deaths in
  2024 across 80 countries \citep{who2025malaria}. The WHO African
  Region still accounts for the overwhelming majority of cases and
  deaths, with young children carrying the greatest mortality burden.
\item
  Species: \emph{P. falciparum} (most lethal; 99\% of deaths), \emph{P.
  vivax} (most widespread; hypnozoites cause relapse), \emph{P.
  malariae}, \emph{P. ovale}, \emph{P. knowlesi} (zoonotic, from
  macaques)
\item
  Transmission: Female \emph{Anopheles} mosquito vector; sporozoites
  injected during blood meal
\item
  Life cycle: Sporozoites -\textgreater{} liver (hepatocyte invasion,
  asymptomatic) -\textgreater{} merozoites -\textgreater{} erythrocyte
  invasion (clinical disease: cyclic fever every 48-72 hours
  synchronized with schizogony) -\textgreater{} some become gametocytes
  (taken up by mosquito)
\item
  Immune evasion: \emph{P. falciparum} erythrocyte membrane protein 1
  (PfEMP1) expressed on infected RBC surface mediates cytoadherence
  (sticking to endothelium, avoiding splenic clearance) and rosetting;
  about 60 \emph{var} genes enable antigenic variation
\item
  Vaccine: RTS,S/AS01E (Mosquirix): first approved malaria vaccine
  (2021); targets circumsporozoite protein; protection is partial and
  wanes without booster dosing. R21/Matrix-M is now the second
  WHO-recommended malaria vaccine; both are best understood as additions
  to bed nets, chemoprevention, diagnosis, and vector control rather
  than replacements \citep{who2025malaria}.
\item
  Treatment: Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT); artemisinin
  resistance emerging in Southeast Asia (K13 propeller mutations)
\item
  Vector control frontier: WHO issued a 2025 conditional recommendation
  for indoor \textbf{spatial emanators} (also called spatial repellents)
  as an additional tool in areas with ongoing transmission, used
  alongside insecticide-treated nets rather than replacing them. These
  devices release active ingredients such as transfluthrin into indoor
  air to repel, disorient, or kill mosquitoes, with evidence strongest
  for added indoor protection and remaining gaps for standalone use,
  outdoor protection, humanitarian settings, and resistance management
  \citep{who2025spatialemanators}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0134_2d5aca90a092.png}
\caption{Malaria vector-control comparison. Spatial emanators add an indoor airspace tool to nets and spraying, but local programmes still need entomological surveillance, insecticide-resistance monitoring, and equity-aware deployment.}
\end{figure}

\textbf{HIV/AIDS}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Global burden: an estimated 40.8 million people were living with HIV
  at the end of 2024, with about 1.3 million new infections in 2024 and
  AIDS-related deaths far below their early-2000s peak but still above
  global targets \citep{unaids2025factsheet}.
\item
  Pathogenesis: Progressive depletion of CD4\(^+\) T cells; AIDS defined
  as CD4 count \textless200 cells/\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}L or AIDS-defining illness
\item
  \textbf{ART} (antiretroviral therapy): Combination of 3+ drugs from
  different classes; suppresses viral load to undetectable (\textless50
  copies/mL); near-normal life expectancy if initiated early; does not
  cure (latent proviral reservoir in resting CD4\(^+\) memory T cells
  persists for decades)
\item
  \textbf{PrEP} (pre-exposure prophylaxis): Oral TDF/FTC or TAF/FTC
  remains highly effective when taken as prescribed; long-acting
  injectable cabotegravir and twice-yearly lenacapavir add
  adherence-sparing options. FDA approved lenacapavir PrEP in 2025, and
  CDC guidance reports trial efficacy of 100\% in a cisgender-female
  trial and 96\% in a primarily male trial over 52 weeks
  \citep{cdc2025lenacapavirprep}.
\item
  \textbf{U=U} (Undetectable = Untransmittable): Individuals with
  sustained undetectable viral load on ART cannot sexually transmit HIV
  (PARTNER study, HPTN 052)
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Influenza}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  RNA virus (Orthomyxoviridae); 8 segmented (-)ssRNA genome segments
\item
  Surface glycoproteins: hemagglutinin (HA, 18 subtypes) and
  neuraminidase (NA, 11 subtypes); nomenclature: H1N1, H3N2, etc.
\item
  See ``Antigenic Variation'' section above for full discussion of drift
  and shift.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{One Health and Emerging
Pathogens}\label{one-health-and-emerging-pathogens}

The \textbf{One Health} framework recognizes the interconnection of
human, animal, and environmental health:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Over 70\% of emerging infectious diseases are \textbf{zoonotic}
  (originating from animal reservoirs).
\item
  Drivers of emergence: deforestation and habitat destruction
  (increasing human-wildlife contact), wildlife trade (live animal
  markets), climate change (expanding vector ranges), intensive animal
  agriculture (influenza reassortment, AMR selection).
\item
  Examples: SARS-CoV-2 (probable bat origin via intermediate host),
  Ebola (bat reservoir), avian influenza H5N1 (poultry), Nipah
  (bat-to-pig-to-human), Lyme disease (deer-tick-mouse cycle expanding
  with climate change), mpox (rodent reservoirs in West/Central Africa).
\item
  AMR as a One Health issue: antibiotic exposure in people, food
  animals, aquaculture, and shared environments selects for resistance
  genes that can move through water, soil, food chains, plasmids, and
  mobile genetic elements. Stewardship therefore has to cover
  prescribing, veterinary practice, sanitation, surveillance, and access
  to effective treatment \citep{cdc2025antibioticuse,who2024bppl}.
\item
  Fungal disease also belongs in the AMR frame: the WHO fungal priority
  pathogens list highlights \emph{Candida auris}, \emph{Aspergillus
  fumigatus}, \emph{Cryptococcus neoformans}, and other fungi where
  limited diagnostics, few drug classes, immunocompromised hosts, and
  agricultural azole exposure make resistance a One Health problem
  rather than a hospital-confined issue \citep{who2022fungalpriority}.
  CDC guidance treats \emph{Candida auris} as a healthcare-transmissible
  yeast that is often multidrug-resistant, can colonise patients without
  symptoms, persists on surfaces, requires sequencing or mass
  spectrometry for reliable identification, and should be treated
  primarily when causing clinical infection; echinocandins remain
  typical initial adult therapy, but echinocandin-resistant and
  pan-resistant reports are increasing
  \citep{cdc2026candidaauris,cdc2024candidaauristreatment}.
  Mechanistically, the warning is that AMR phenotypes are assembled from
  enzymes, target changes, efflux, permeability shifts, biofilms,
  tolerance states, and mobile genetic elements; the same resistance
  label can hide different treatment constraints.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Spillover risk factors.} Modern surveillance and modelling have
identified several quantifiable predictors of zoonotic spillover risk:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Phylogenetic distance} --- viruses from primates spill more
  easily than viruses from rodents than from invertebrates.
\item
  \textbf{Receptor compatibility} --- ACE2 in bats, civets, and humans
  is similar enough to permit SARS-CoV-2 cross-species transmission;
  H5N1 sialic-acid receptor preference shifts (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-2,3 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-2,6) signal
  mammalian adaptation.
\item
  \textbf{Population density at the human-animal interface} --- wet
  markets, intensive agriculture, deforestation edges.
\item
  \textbf{Reservoir host species richness} --- Bat species richness
  correlates with the number of zoonotic viruses; rodents are similarly
  important but underrecognised.
\item
  \textbf{Anthropogenic disruption} --- deforestation, climate change,
  urbanisation increase contact rates.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{The PREDICT and Global Virome Project} approaches systematically
sample wildlife to catalog viral diversity and identify high-risk
lineages \textbf{before} spillover. By 2026, sequencing \textgreater{}
200,000 viral genomes from \textgreater{} 30,000 animals across
\textgreater{} 30 countries has identified about  10,000
candidate zoonotic viruses, of which about  1700 share key
receptor-binding features with known human pathogens --- a sobering
reservoir.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection: Antibiotic Stewardship and Real-Time
Resistance Surveillance} The WHO has declared antimicrobial resistance
one of the top 10 global public health threats. An estimated 1.27
million deaths were directly attributable to bacterial AMR in 2019
\citep{murray2022amr}. The O'Neill review's 10-million-deaths-per-year
scenario is a policy warning about uncontrolled resistance, not an
inevitable destiny \citep{oneill2016amr}. Genomic surveillance networks
such as the CDC AR Lab Network and WHO GLASS now track carbapenemases,
\emph{mcr} genes, and emerging plasmids across hospitals and regions.
The lesson from SARS-CoV-2 --- pathogen genomes can be sequenced and
interpreted at population scale --- is being adapted to bacterial AMR,
where slower growth and horizontal gene transfer make the analysis more
complicated.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 7:} Trace a potential pandemic pathway from
deforestation in Southeast Asia. Identify (a) the ecological factors
that elevate spillover risk, (b) the molecular features (receptor
compatibility, reassortment potential) that determine human
transmissibility, (c) the early-warning indicators that PREDICT-style
surveillance would detect, and (d) the One Health interventions that
could reduce future risk.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{mRNA Vaccine Platforms: From Lab Curiosity to Global
Deployment}\label{mrna-vaccine-platforms-from-lab-curiosity-to-global-deployment}

Messenger RNA vaccines --- once a neglected technology because of mRNA's
instability and strong innate-immune activation --- became the
\hyperref[gl:dominant]{\textbf{dominant}} pandemic response platform
between 2020 and 2023. \textbf{BNT162b2 (Pfizer--BioNTech) and mRNA-1273
(Moderna)} demonstrated \texorpdfstring{\textgreater{}=}{>=} 94 \% efficacy against symptomatic COVID-19 in
phase III trials (\textgreater{} 40 000 participants each) within
\textbf{11 months from pathogen identification} --- an unprecedented
pace driven entirely by the modularity of the platform: once a
lipid-nanoparticle delivery system and a nucleoside-modified mRNA
scaffold are validated, swapping the antigen-coding sequence is a matter
of days.

Three molecular innovations make mRNA vaccines work. \textbf{(1)
Nucleoside modification} --- substituting uridines with
\textbf{pseudouridine (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Psi}}{Psi}) or 1-methyl-pseudouridine (m1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Psi}}{Psi})} (Karikó \&
Weissman, Nobel Prize 2023) reduces TLR7/8 activation and blocks
2'-5'-oligoadenylate synthetase / RNase L degradation, so
\hyperref[gl:translation]{\textbf{translation}} is 10--100\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} more
efficient and innate-immune activation is manageable. \textbf{(2) Lipid
nanoparticle (LNP) delivery} --- a four-component formulation (ionisable
lipid ALC-0315 or SM-102, phospholipid DSPC, cholesterol, PEG-lipid)
self-assembles into about 80 nm particles that endocytose into
dendritic cells; at endosomal pH about 5 the ionisable lipid
becomes cationic, fusing with the endosome and releasing mRNA into the
cytoplasm. \textbf{(3) Antigen design} --- the SARS-CoV-2 spike is
locked in the prefusion conformation by two proline substitutions
(\textbf{2P mutation}) that preserve neutralising epitopes.
Manufacturing uses \emph{in vitro} transcription from linear DNA
templates (T7 polymerase), capping with CleanCap analogue, and
microfluidic LNP assembly --- a single about 20 000 L
bioreactor run can produce \textgreater{} 1 billion doses. Remaining
challenges: cold-chain dependence (though ARCT-154 self-amplifying mRNA
vaccines stable at 2--8 °C are in trials), rare myocarditis risk in
young males (about 1--10 per 100 000 doses, typically mild and
self-limiting), and waning antibody titres (6-month boosting needed).
The platform is now extending to influenza (mRNA-1010), RSV (mRNA-1345,
approved 2024), and personalised cancer neoantigen vaccines (mRNA-4157,
phase III for melanoma).

\subsubsection{cGAS--STING: Innate Cytosolic DNA Sensing and Anti-Tumour
Immunity}\label{cgassting-innate-cytosolic-dna-sensing-and-anti-tumour-immunity}

\textbf{Cyclic GMP--AMP synthase (cGAS)} is a cytosolic DNA sensor
identified in 2013 (Chen lab) that binds double-stranded DNA
non-sequence-specifically and, upon DNA engagement, synthesises the
second messenger \textbf{2'3'-cyclic GMP--AMP (2'3'-cGAMP)} from ATP and
GTP. 2'3'-cGAMP binds the ER-resident adaptor \textbf{STING (Stimulator
of Interferon Genes)}, driving TBK1 phosphorylation of IRF3 and thus
\textbf{Type I interferon (IFN-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}/\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta})} transcription. Evolutionarily, the
pathway detects pathogen-derived or mis-localised self-DNA --- cytosolic
DNA is otherwise absent in healthy cells.

Three rapid-fire translational applications: \textbf{(1) Cancer
immunotherapy} --- dying tumour cells release DNA that, once dendritic
cells endocytose it, activates cGAS--STING, priming CD8\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} T-cell
responses. STING agonists (ADU-S100, MK-1454, diABZI) are in
\textgreater{} 30 oncology clinical trials; \textbf{radiation therapy}
is an accidental STING activator (sub-lethal DNA damage \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} micronuclei \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
cytosolic DNA). \textbf{(2) Autoimmunity} --- gain-of-function STING
mutations cause \textbf{SAVI (STING-associated vasculopathy)}, a
paediatric interferonopathy with pulmonary fibrosis and skin
ulcerations; chronic cGAS--STING activation also contributes to
\textbf{age-related inflammation} as mitochondrial and cytosolic DNA
accumulate. \textbf{(3) Anti-viral defence} --- SARS-CoV-2 ORF9b, HSV-1
ICP27, and HIV-1 capsid most suppress cGAS--STING, demonstrating its
evolutionary importance as a front-line sensor. The pathway is now a
canonical example of how fundamental discovery (2013) can translate to
phase III oncology trials in under a decade.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-26}

For \textbf{Infectious Disease and Immunity}, frontier biology belongs
inside the evidence logic of the chapter. Microbiology and infectious
disease now require One Health reasoning across people, animals,
environments, genomics, and antimicrobial stewardship. The core reading
question is this: infectious-disease reasoning should connect pathogen
biology, transmission, immunity, diagnostics, interventions, and equity.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

For AMR and pathogen claims, name the organism-resistance pair, the
selection pressure, the transmission route, and the surveillance
evidence that would change triage
\citep{who2024bppl,cdc2025antibioticuse,murray2022amr}.

\textbf{Source practice:} For pathogen, AMR, and intervention claims,
tie statements to organism-resistance pairs, surveillance evidence,
official guidance, and trial/regulatory status
\citep{who2024bppl,who2025tb,who2025malaria,cdc2025lenacapavirprep,cdc2026candidaauris}.

Pathogens}\label{current-evidence-map-intervention-choice-across-pathogens}

\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-26}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Koch's postulates} remain foundational for establishing
  disease causation but have important limitations (asymptomatic
  carriers, unculturable organisms, polymicrobial disease). Molecular
  Koch's postulates extend the framework to virulence genes.
\item
  \textbf{Virulence factors} include adhesins (pili, FimH), invasion
  machinery (T3SS), toxins (A-B exotoxins: cholera, diphtheria, tetanus,
  botulinum; endotoxin/LPS), capsules, and immune evasion strategies
  (protein A, antigenic variation, phagosome arrest).
\item
  \textbf{\hyperref[gl:innate-immunity]{Innate immunity}} provides
  immediate, non-specific defense: barriers (skin, mucus, acid,
  lysozyme, defensins), PRRs (TLRs, NLRs, RIG-I, cGAS-STING) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} NF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}B +
  IRF3 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} cytokines + type I IFN; \textbf{complement} with three pathways
  (classical via C1q, lectin via MBL/MASPs, alternative via spontaneous
  C3 tickover) converging at C3 convertase, then C5 cleavage and MAC
  formation; cellular effectors (neutrophils with MPO/HOCl oxidative
  burst and NETosis, macrophages M1/M2, NK cells with missing-self via
  inhibitory KIRs and induced-self via NKG2D).
\item
  \textbf{Adaptive immunity}: V(D)J recombination generates diverse TCRs
  and BCRs; MHC-I presents endogenous peptides to CD8\(^+\) CTLs; MHC-II
  presents exogenous peptides to CD4\(^+\) T helpers (Th1, Th2, Th17,
  Treg, Tfh); B cells undergo germinal center reactions (SHM, affinity
  maturation, CSR) producing high-affinity class-switched antibodies and
  long-lived memory.
\item
  \textbf{Vaccines} exploit immunological memory: eight platforms (live
  attenuated, inactivated, subunit, VLP, toxoid, conjugate, mRNA, viral
  vector) span the spectrum from MMR (single-dose lifetime immunity) to
  mRNA (rapid platform with 48-hour design cycle). Herd-immunity
  threshold \(p_c = 1 - 1/R_0\) (\cref{eq:unit_VII_herd_immunity}) ---
  measles requires \textgreater{} 93 \%, polio about  80 \%,
  original COVID-19 about  60 \%, but Omicron-era
  \(R_0 \sim 10\) combined with imperfect vaccine efficacy can exceed
  achievable coverage.
\item
  \textbf{Antigenic variation} in influenza occurs via gradual drift (HA
  point mutations \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} seasonal epidemics) and abrupt shift (segment
  reassortment in animal reservoirs \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} pandemics: 1918, 1957, 1968,
  2009). HIV reverse transcriptase (3 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{5}}{5} errors/bp/cycle) generates
  a quasi-species cloud that defeats monotherapy and complicates vaccine
  development.
\item
  \textbf{Antibiotic resistance} falls into five categories: enzymatic
  inactivation (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactamases --- Class A/B/C/D Ambler; AMEs; CAT; ESBLs
  and carbapenemases KPC/NDM/OXA-48); target modification (PBP2a in
  MRSA; D-Ala-D-Lac in VRE; 23S methylation in MLS; gyrase QRDR
  mutations); efflux (RND tripartite pumps AcrAB-TolC, MexAB-OprM,
  AdeABC); reduced permeability (porin loss); and bypass / target
  overproduction (Dfr, Sul). Pan-resistant ESKAPE isolates combine
  multiple mechanisms simultaneously.
\item
  \textbf{Major infectious diseases}: TB (granuloma, phagosome arrest,
  MDR/XDR crisis), malaria (erythrocyte invasion, PfEMP1 antigenic
  variation, artemisinin resistance), HIV (CD4 depletion, latent
  reservoir, ART, PrEP, U=U), influenza (antigenic drift/shift, pandemic
  potential).
\item
  \textbf{One Health and emerging pathogens}: \textgreater{} 70 \% of
  emerging infections are zoonotic; deforestation, climate change,
  wildlife trade, and agricultural antibiotic use drive emergence and
  AMR. PREDICT-style surveillance now catalogs \textgreater{} 10 000
  candidate zoonotic viruses for early-warning monitoring.
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See \cref{sec:unit_VII_bacteria_archaea_viruses}
  for pathogen biology, \cref{sec:unit_VII_microbial_ecology} for
  microbiome colonisation resistance, and
  \cref{sec:unit_X_population_ecology} for demographic models.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Key Terms}\label{key-terms-26}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3529}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.6471}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Term
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Definition
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Koch's postulates} & Four criteria for establishing that a
specific microorganism causes a specific disease \\
\textbf{Virulence factor} & Microbial product or strategy that
contributes to pathogenicity (adhesins, toxins, capsules, immune
evasion) \\
\textbf{Exotoxin} & Secreted bacterial protein toxin; often A-B
structure (cholera, diphtheria, tetanus, botulinum) \\
\textbf{Endotoxin (LPS)} & Gram-negative outer membrane component
released upon lysis; activates TLR4; causes fever, septic shock \\
\textbf{PAMP} & Pathogen-Associated Molecular Pattern -- conserved
microbial structure detected by host PRRs \\
\textbf{\hyperref[gl:toll-like-receptor]{Toll-like receptor (TLR)}} &
Membrane-bound PRR that recognizes PAMPs and initiates innate immune
signaling \\
\textbf{Inflammasome} & Intracellular multiprotein complex
(NLRP3-ASC-caspase-1) that processes IL-1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} and IL-18 and triggers
pyroptosis \\
\textbf{Complement} & Plasma protein cascade with three pathways
(classical via C1q-antibody, lectin via MBL-carbohydrate, alternative
via spontaneous C3 hydrolysis) converging at the C3 convertase \\
\textbf{C3 convertase} & Central enzyme of complement (C4b2a or C3bBb)
that cleaves C3 into C3a (anaphylatoxin) and C3b (opsonin) \\
\textbf{MAC} & Membrane attack complex (C5b-C9\(_n\)); 10-nm pore that
osmotically lyses Gram-negative bacteria \\
\textbf{Factor H} & Soluble alternative-pathway regulator that binds C3b
on self surfaces; co-opted by \emph{Neisseria} to evade complement \\
\textbf{NETosis} & Programmed neutrophil death pathway in which
decondensed chromatin is extruded as antimicrobial extracellular traps;
PAD4-dependent \\
\textbf{Missing-self hypothesis} & Ljunggren-Karre model: NK cells kill
cells lacking inhibitory MHC-I signals \\
\textbf{NKG2D} & Activating NK-cell receptor recognising stress-induced
ligands (MICA/B, ULBPs); the ``induced-self'' sensor \\
\textbf{MHC class I} & Presents endogenous peptides to CD8\(^+\) CTLs;
expressed on most nucleated cells \\
\textbf{MHC class II} & Presents exogenous peptides to CD4\(^+\) T
helpers; expressed on professional APCs \\
\textbf{Clonal selection} & Antigen selects and expands primarily the
specific lymphocyte clone with matching receptor \\
\textbf{Affinity maturation} & Progressive improvement of antibody
affinity through somatic hypermutation and selection in germinal
centers \\
\textbf{Class switch recombination} & AID-mediated change of antibody
constant region (IgM -\textgreater{} IgG, IgA, or IgE) preserving
antigen specificity \\
\textbf{Herd immunity threshold} & \(p_c = 1 - 1/R_0\); fraction of
population that must be immune to prevent sustained transmission \\
\textbf{\(R_0\)} & Basic reproduction number; mean secondary infections
per primary case in fully susceptible population \\
\textbf{Antigenic drift} & Gradual mutation of surface antigens
(influenza HA/NA) producing seasonal variants \\
\textbf{Antigenic shift} & Reassortment of genome segments between
different influenza strains producing novel pandemic subtypes \\
\textbf{Quasi-species} & The mutant cloud generated by an error-prone
polymerase (HIV reverse transcriptase, RNA-virus RdRp) --- the substrate
of within-host evolution \\
\textbf{VLP (virus-like particle)} & Self-assembled viral capsid lacking
genome; basis of HPV (Gardasil) and HBV vaccines \\
\textbf{mRNA vaccine} & LNP-encapsulated, nucleoside-modified mRNA that
the host translates into antigen; e.g., BNT162b2, mRNA-1273 \\
\textbf{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactamase} & Enzyme that hydrolyses \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactam antibiotics;
Ambler classes A/C/D (serine) and B (metallo); ESBLs, KPC, NDM, OXA \\
\textbf{PBP2a} & Alternative penicillin-binding protein in MRSA, encoded
by \emph{mecA}; low \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactam affinity \\
\textbf{AcrAB-TolC, MexAB-OprM} & Tripartite RND-family efflux pumps
spanning the entire Gram-negative cell envelope; major multi-drug
resistance mechanism \\
\textbf{mcr-1} & Plasmid-borne phosphoethanolamine transferase; first
transferable colistin resistance gene (China, 2015) \\
\textbf{ART} & Antiretroviral therapy; combination drug regimen that
suppresses HIV viral load to undetectable levels \\
\textbf{One Health} & Framework recognizing the interconnection of
human, animal, and environmental health in infectious disease and AMR \\
\end{longtable}
}

\subsection{Review Questions}\label{review-questions-26}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Apply Koch's postulates to \emph{Helicobacter pylori} and peptic ulcer
  disease. Barry Marshall famously fulfilled these postulates by
  self-experimentation in 1984. Identify which postulate was most
  difficult to satisfy and explain why the medical establishment was
  initially skeptical.
\item
  Compare the mechanisms of action of cholera toxin and diphtheria
  toxin. Both use A-B structure and ADP-ribosylation, but they target
  different host proteins. Explain how the same enzymatic mechanism
  (ADP-ribosylation) produces completely different clinical outcomes.
\item
  A patient with terminal complement component deficiency (C5-C9)
  presents with recurrent \emph{Neisseria meningitidis} infections.
  Explain why this specific pathogen is problematic in MAC deficiency
  while most other bacterial infections are handled normally. What does
  this tell you about the relative importance of opsonization versus MAC
  lysis for different pathogens?
\item
  Describe the molecular events of T cell activation, including most
  three signals. Explain why Signal 2 (co-stimulation) is critical for
  preventing autoimmunity, and predict what would happen if a
  pharmaceutical agent blocked B7-CD28 interaction globally.
\item
  A mother's IgG antibodies cross the placenta and protect the newborn
  for the first 3-6 months of life. Explain why this passive immunity
  wanes and why active vaccination is necessary starting at 2 months.
  Which antibody class is most important in breast milk, and how does it
  protect the infant's mucosal surfaces?
\item
  \textbf{Herd immunity calculation.} Calculate from
  \cref{eq:unit_VII_herd_immunity} the herd immunity threshold for a
  novel respiratory pathogen with \(R_0 = 8\). If a vaccine with 90\%
  efficacy is available, what percentage of the population must be
  vaccinated to achieve herd immunity? Show your work using the formula
  \(p_v = p_c / E\).
\item
  Explain why tuberculosis treatment requires 6-9 months of multi-drug
  therapy while most bacterial infections are treated with 7-14 days of
  a single antibiotic. Include the concepts of metabolically dormant
  persisters, granuloma pharmacokinetics, and the rationale for
  combination therapy.
\item
  \textbf{Drift vs shift.} Compare antigenic drift and antigenic shift
  in influenza. Explain why antigenic shift can produce pandemics while
  antigenic drift produces seasonal epidemics. Why is influenza A (but
  not influenza B) capable of antigenic shift, and what role do animal
  reservoirs play? How does the HIV quasi-species cloud differ
  mechanistically from influenza, and why does each strategy defeat
  conventional vaccine design?
\item
  The mRNA COVID-19 vaccines (BNT162b2, mRNA-1273) demonstrated
  about 95\% efficacy in clinical trials but this declined over
  time and with new variants. Explain: (a) the immunological mechanism
  of mRNA vaccines, (b) why booster doses are needed (waning immunity
  vs.~antigenic evolution), and (c) how the N1-methylpseudouridine
  modification improves mRNA vaccine performance.
\item
  Using the One Health framework, explain how deforestation in Southeast
  Asia could lead to a novel pandemic. Trace the pathway from habitat
  destruction to zoonotic spillover, identifying the ecological,
  virological, and epidemiological factors at each step.
\item
  Derive the herd immunity threshold \(p_c = 1 - 1/R_0\) from the
  next-generation intuition and relate to Question 6.
\item
  Explain \textbf{antigenic sin} and how it might bias booster responses
  after sequential variant exposure.
\item
  \textbf{Resistance mechanism integration.} A clinical microbiology lab
  reports a \emph{Klebsiella pneumoniae} isolate with MICs: meropenem \texorpdfstring{\textgreater{}=}{>=}
  16 (R), ceftazidime-avibactam 1 (S), cefepime 8 (R), ciprofloxacin \texorpdfstring{\textgreater{}=}{>=} 4
  (R), gentamicin \texorpdfstring{\textgreater{}=}{>=} 16 (R), tigecycline 0.5 (S), colistin 0.5 (S).
  Sequencing reveals: KPC-2 carbapenemase, AAC(6')-Ib-cr, GyrA Ser83Leu,
  ParC Ser80Ile, RamA overexpression. (a) Which mechanism is responsible
  for each resistance phenotype? (b) Why does ceftazidime-avibactam
  still work? (c) Predict whether this strain would respond to
  imipenem-relebactam and meropenem-vaborbactam, and justify.
\item
  \textbf{Vaccine platform comparison.} A new pathogen emerges with
  seasonal transmission and mild illness in adults, severe in infants,
  no available therapy. Compare the trade-offs for a (a)
  live-attenuated, (b) inactivated, (c) subunit-VLP, (d) mRNA, and (e)
  viral-vector vaccine platform decision, given a 9-month timeline to
  first dose.
\item
  \textbf{Innate immunity integration.} A patient with AIDS (CD4
  \textless{} 50) develops disseminated \emph{Mycobacterium avium
  complex} infection. Explain why both adaptive and innate arms of
  immunity have failed despite intact NK cells, neutrophils, complement,
  and antibodies. What is the role of granuloma formation, and why is
  IFN-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma} critical?
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Unit VIII --- Botany --- Plant Biology:
Introduction}\label{unit-viii-botany-plant-biology-introduction}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Unit VIII --- Botany --- Plant Biology:
Introduction}

\subsection*{Why This Unit Matters}\label{why-this-unit-matters-8}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Why This Unit Matters}

Plants are the foundation of almost every terrestrial food web, the
source of roughly half the oxygen in the atmosphere, and the origin of
many medicines in human pharmacopoeia --- from aspirin (salicylate,
first identified in willow bark) to taxol (from Pacific yew, \emph{Taxus
brevifolia}), morphine, quinine, and artemisinin. More fundamentally,
plants are solar-energy collectors that translate photons into chemical
bonds, feeding the entire biosphere. Each year, land plants and algae
fix approximately 120 billion tonnes of carbon from atmospheric CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} via
photosynthesis --- a flux so large that it modulates global atmospheric
chemistry.

Plant biology is also a discipline of extremes. The tallest trees (coast
redwoods, \emph{Sequoia sempervirens}, 115 m) move water 115 metres
against gravity using primarily cohesion-tension and solar energy,
achieving flow rates in excess of 1 m/hour. Some desert plants survive
total desiccation and revive on rehydration. Others flower in response
to photoperiod cues measured in the phytochrome system with a resolution
of minutes. The \emph{Arabidopsis thaliana} genome was the first plant
genome sequenced (2000), and this small weed has since become the
"\emph{E. coli} of plant biology" --- a model organism for the molecular
dissection of everything from root development to pathogen resistance.

This unit integrates anatomy (vascular organisation, meristems,
root-shoot polarity), physiology (transpiration, water potential, phloem
loading), reproductive biology (alternation of generations, angiosperm
diversity, seed development), and signalling (phytohormones: auxin,
gibberellin, cytokinin, abscisic acid, ethylene). The quantitative spine
is water potential (\(\Psi = \Psi_s + \Psi_p\)) and transpiration
modelled by the van den Honert equation.

\subsection*{Current Evidence Thread}\label{current-evidence-thread-8}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Current Evidence Thread}

In this unit, treat plant biology as a body of evidence: each claim
about structure, water transport, environmental response, or
reproduction should rest on physiological measurement, in vivo imaging,
or a field or engineering trial, not on description alone. Plant biology
links molecular regulation to climate stress, water limitation, crop
resilience, phenology, and ecosystem feedbacks. As you move through the
chapters, keep a two-column note: \textbf{claim} on the left,
\textbf{evidence that would change my confidence} on the right. By the
end of the unit, each major idea should be tied to a measurement, model,
citation, or paper-based lab decision.

\subsection{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-27}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Describe the major organ systems of
  \hyperref[gl:angiosperm]{\textbf{angiosperm}}s: root system (taproot
  vs fibrous), shoot system, and leaf.
\item
  Compare the three plant tissue systems: dermal, ground, and vascular,
  including cell types within each.
\item
  Explain water relations in plants using the four-component water
  potential equation \(\Psi = \Psi_s + \Psi_p + \Psi_m + \Psi_g\).
\item
  Describe \hyperref[gl:transpiration]{\textbf{transpiration}} and the
  cohesion-tension \citep{dixon1894}-adhesion (TACT) mechanism of water
  ascent and critically evaluate its supporting evidence.
\item
  Explain the apoplast vs symplast pathways and the role of the
  Casparian strip and suberin lamella.
\item
  Explain phloem transport and the Münch pressure-flow hypothesis
  \citep{munch1930}, including apoplastic vs symplastic loading.
\item
  Describe stomatal regulation and the role of ABA in drought response
  at the molecular level.
\item
  Explain nutrient uptake strategies including mycorrhizal associations
  and quantitative turgor relations.
\item
  Quantify water-use efficiency at the leaf level and connect it to C3,
  C4, and CAM photosynthetic trade-offs.
\end{enumerate}
