\begin{quote}
\textbf{Opening Vignette --- How a Giant Sequoia Pulls Water 100 Metres
Up}

A mature coast redwood (\emph{Sequoia sempervirens}) can stand 115
metres tall. Getting water from soil to the topmost leaves requires
lifting it against a gravitational pull of roughly 1.1 MPa --- while
simultaneously overcoming resistance to flow through millions of
microscopic \hyperref[gl:xylem]{\textbf{xylem}} conduits. How? The
answer, worked out by Henry Dixon and John Joly in 1894
\citep{dixon1894} and validated with pressure-bomb measurements in the
1960s, is cohesion-tension: water molecules cohere to each other and
adhere to xylem walls so strongly that evaporation from leaf
\hyperref[gl:stomata]{\textbf{stomata}} creates a continuous
negative-pressure column (tension) that pulls water up from the roots.
The column can sustain tensions as low as \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}10 MPa before xylem embolism
shatters it. This entirely passive, thermodynamically driven mechanism
moves trillions of litres of water into Earth's atmosphere annually ---
and is so elegant that engineers studying microfluidics still struggle
to replicate it artificially.
\end{quote}

\subsection{The Plant Body Plan}\label{the-plant-body-plan}

Flowering plants (angiosperms, about 300,000 species) are
organised into two major organ systems that work together to acquire
resources from both soil and atmosphere.

\subsubsection{Root System}\label{root-system}

The root system anchors the plant, absorbs water and minerals, and
stores nutrients. Two major architectural types exist:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Taproot system:} A single
  \hyperref[gl:dominant]{\textbf{dominant}} primary root (derived from
  the embryonic radicle) with smaller lateral roots branching off.
  Common in eudicots (e.g., carrots, dandelions, oaks). Deep taproot
  systems can access water tables several metres below the surface.
\item
  \textbf{Fibrous root system:} A dense mat of similarly sized
  adventitious roots arising from the stem base. The primary root is
  short-lived. Common in monocots (e.g., grasses, wheat, rice).
  Excellent for soil stabilisation and surface nutrient capture.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Root apical meristem (RAM):} Located near the root tip,
protected by the root cap. The RAM contains slowly dividing cells in the
quiescent centre (QC) surrounded by rapidly dividing initial cells that
produce most root tissues. The root tip is organised into distinct
zones:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Root cap} -- protects the meristem; secretes mucilage for
  lubrication; columella cells contain starch-filled amyloplasts
  (statoliths) for gravity sensing
\item
  \textbf{Meristematic zone} -- active cell division
\item
  \textbf{Elongation zone} -- cells expand primarily in length (up to
  10-fold); driven by \hyperref[gl:turgor-pressure]{\textbf{turgor
  pressure}} and cell wall loosening
\item
  \textbf{Maturation zone} -- cells differentiate into specialised
  types; root hairs develop here
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Root hairs} are single elongated epidermal cells that
dramatically amplify surface area (about 600 cm\(^2\) per cm of
root length). Mineral ions are absorbed actively against their
electrochemical gradients by specific transporters (NO\(_3^-\) by
NRT1/NRT2; K\(^+\) by HKT; Fe\(^{2+}\) by IRT1).

\subsubsection{Plant Architecture: Phytomers and
Plastochrons}\label{plant-architecture-phytomers-and-plastochrons}

The shoot is built as a series of repeating modular units called
\textbf{phytomers}. Each phytomer comprises one node, the internode
immediately below it, the leaf attached at the node, and the axillary
bud subtending the leaf. Phytomer iteration generates the entire shoot
--- a tree is, formally, a clonal colony of phytomers expressed by a
single genotype.

The temporal scaffolding is provided by the \textbf{plastochron index
(PI)}, defined as the time interval between successive leaf-primordium
initiations at the SAM (Erickson and Michelini, 1957). At constant
temperature the plastochron is approximately constant for a given
genotype (about 24 h in \emph{Arabidopsis}, about 36 h
in maize), permitting developmental time to be expressed in plastochron
units rather than chronological time. The \textbf{leaf plastochron index
(LPI)} ranks leaves by developmental age --- LPI 0 is the youngest
visible leaf, LPI 1 the next, and so on --- and is the standard
developmental clock for maize and tobacco physiology experiments.

\textbf{Meristematic zones at the SAM} are organised radially and
clonally:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{L1 (tunica outer layer):} Strictly anticlinal divisions; gives
  rise to epidermis
\item
  \textbf{L2 (tunica inner layer):} Mostly anticlinal; produces
  mesophyll, gametes
\item
  \textbf{L3 (corpus):} Anticlinal and periclinal divisions; produces
  vascular and ground tissue
\end{itemize}

Genetic chimeras (e.g., variegated geraniums) reveal these clonal layers
as stable, parallel cell lineages whose interactions specify organ
identity.

\subsubsection{Shoot System}\label{shoot-system}

The shoot system comprises the stem and leaves and is responsible for
\hyperref[gl:photosynthesis]{\textbf{photosynthesis}}, reproduction, and
support.

\textbf{Shoot apical meristem (SAM):} Maintains a pool of pluripotent
stem cells at the shoot tip throughout the plant's life. The SAM is
organised into:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Central zone (CZ):} Slowly dividing stem cells maintained by
  the WUS-CLV3 negative feedback loop
\item
  \textbf{Peripheral zone (PZ):} Faster-dividing cells that form lateral
  organ primordia (leaves, flowers)
\item
  \textbf{Rib zone:} Cells below the CZ that contribute to stem
  internodes
\end{itemize}

Leaves are initiated at the PZ where PIN1-mediated auxin maxima form,
producing the characteristic phyllotaxis pattern (often 137.5 degrees
divergence angle).

\subsubsection{Leaf Anatomy}\label{leaf-anatomy}

Leaf cross-section layers (adaxial to abaxial):

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Upper epidermis + cuticle (waxy layer of cutin; reduces water loss)
\item
  Palisade mesophyll (densely packed columnar cells with abundant
  \hyperref[gl:chloroplast]{\textbf{chloroplast}}s; principal
  photosynthetic layer)
\item
  Spongy mesophyll (loosely packed; CO\(_2\) diffusion through
  intercellular air spaces; about 30-40\% air space)
\item
  Lower epidermis + cuticle
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Stomata:} Pores bounded by two kidney-shaped
\textbf{\hyperref[gl:guard-cell]{guard cell}s}. Stomatal aperture is
controlled by guard cell turgor:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Light activates blue-light phototropins and red-light photosynthesis
  in guard cell chloroplasts. K\(^+\) influx (via K\(^+\)
  inward-rectifying channels) lowers osmotic potential. Water enters by
  \hyperref[gl:osmosis]{\textbf{osmosis}}. Guard cells swell and bow
  apart. Stomata open.
\item
  Drought triggers ABA signalling. ABA activates SnRK2 kinases. SLAC1
  anion channels open, releasing Cl\(^-\). Membrane depolarises. K\(^+\)
  leaves via GORK channels. Water follows osmotically. Guard cells
  deflate. Stomata close.
\end{itemize}

Typical stomatal density: about 200 stomata/mm\(^2\) in many
mesophytes. Each stoma can open or close in minutes. Stomata allow
CO\(_2\) in and O\(_2\) plus water vapour out -- the inevitable tradeoff
between photosynthesis and transpiration.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection:} Understanding stomatal biology is
essential for crop engineering. Overexpression of the SLAC1
\hyperref[gl:gene]{\textbf{gene}} in barley produced plants with more
responsive stomata and 40\% greater water-use efficiency in field
trials, directly relevant to agriculture in drought-prone regions.
\end{quote}

\textbf{Concept Check 1:} Why are most stomata located on the lower
(abaxial) epidermis of leaves rather than the upper surface?

\textbf{Concept Check 2:} A botanist counts an average plastochron of 30
hours in a tomato plant. After 15 days, approximately how many leaf
primordia will have been initiated by the SAM, assuming temperature is
constant?

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Plant Tissue Systems}\label{plant-tissue-systems}

Most plant organs are composed of three tissue systems: dermal, ground,
and vascular.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0137_919e1802461e.png}
\caption{Organisation of the three plant tissue systems showing major cell types within each Dermal tissue forms the outer covering, ground tissue fills the interior, and vascular tissue provides transport.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Dermal Tissue System}\label{dermal-tissue-system}

The dermal tissue system is the outer protective covering of the plant:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Epidermis:} A single layer of tightly packed cells covering
  most surfaces. Secretes the cuticle.
\item
  \textbf{Cuticle:} A waxy layer composed of cutin (a polyester of
  hydroxylated fatty acids) and epicuticular waxes. Minimises water loss
  from non-stomatal surfaces. The cuticle can reduce transpiration by
  95\% compared to an unprotected surface.
\item
  \textbf{Trichomes:} Hair-like epidermal appendages. Diverse functions:
  reduce wind speed at leaf surface (boundary layer), reflect excess
  light, secrete defensive compounds (glandular trichomes of tomato
  produce toxic sesquiterpenes), deter
  \hyperref[gl:herbivory]{\textbf{herbivory}}.
\item
  \textbf{Root hairs:} Tubular extensions of single epidermal cells in
  the root maturation zone. Increase absorptive surface area by
  2-10-fold.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Ground Tissue System}\label{ground-tissue-system}

Ground tissue fills the space between dermal and vascular tissues. Three
cell types:

\textbf{Parenchyma cells:} Living at maturity. Thin primary cell walls.
Functions include photosynthesis (mesophyll), storage (starch in potato
tubers, sugar in sugar beet roots), and wound healing (dedifferentiate
to form callus tissue). Parenchyma cells retain the ability to divide,
making them critical for regeneration.

\textbf{Collenchyma cells:} Living at maturity. Unevenly thickened
primary cell walls (thicker at corners). Provide flexible mechanical
support to growing organs. Found in petioles and young stems. Celery
``strings'' are collenchyma strands.

\textbf{Sclerenchyma cells:} Typically dead at maturity. Thick,
lignified secondary cell walls. Provide rigid support. Two types: fibres
(elongated cells in bundles; flax, hemp) and sclereids (short, irregular
cells; the gritty texture in pears; the hard shell of walnuts).

\subsubsection{Vascular Tissue System -- Xylem in
Detail}\label{vascular-tissue-system-xylem-in-detail}

The vascular tissue system is the plant's long-distance transport
network.

\textbf{Xylem} (water and mineral transport, upward) develops in two
temporally distinct phases that yield mechanically distinct conduits:

\textbf{Protoxylem} matures while the surrounding tissue is still
elongating. Its conduits must therefore stretch with the growing organ,
so secondary-wall lignification is restricted to \textbf{annular}
(ring-shaped) or \textbf{helical} (spiral) thickenings. These
thickenings allow elongation but provide limited collapse-resistance
under tension; protoxylem conduits are typically narrow (5--25 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m) and
frequently obliterated as the tissue matures, leaving an air-filled
lacuna.

\textbf{Metaxylem} differentiates after elongation has ceased. With no
constraint on extensibility, metaxylem develops continuous lignified
walls with \textbf{scalariform} (ladder-like), \textbf{reticulate}
(net-like), or \textbf{pitted} thickenings. Metaxylem conduits are wider
(50--500 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m in some lianas), longer-lived, and bear the bulk of mature
transpiration flux.

A simple mnemonic: \textbf{proto = first} (extensible, ephemeral),
\textbf{meta = mature} (durable, mechanically robust). The transition
can be visualised in any longitudinal section of an elongating maize
root: closer to the tip, narrow protoxylem dominates; further back in
the maturation zone, metaxylem vessels of much greater calibre come
on-line.

The two principal cell types of xylem differ markedly in mechanics:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Tracheids:} Long (1-5 mm), tapered cells with lignified
  secondary walls. Dead at maturity. Water moves between tracheids
  through bordered pit pairs (thin regions in the cell wall where
  secondary wall is absent). The pit membrane consists of the unmodified
  primary walls of the two adjacent cells plus the middle lamella; in
  conifers it bears a thickened central \textbf{torus} suspended by a
  porous \textbf{margo}, allowing the torus to seal the pit aperture if
  the adjacent conduit cavitates (an \textbf{aspirated pit}). Tracheids
  are found in most vascular plants and constitute the primary
  conducting element in most gymnosperms.
\item
  \textbf{Vessel elements:} Shorter (0.2-1 mm) but wider (up to 500 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m
  diameter in some lianas) than tracheids. Stacked end-to-end with
  \textbf{perforation plates} (partial or complete dissolution of end
  walls) forming continuous tubes called vessels. Found primarily in
  angiosperms. More efficient but more vulnerable to cavitation than
  tracheids.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Bordered pit mechanics --- the torus-margo valve:}

The conifer bordered pit is one of the most elegant valve structures in
biology. The pit membrane is differentiated into two regions:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Torus:} A thickened, impermeable central disc
  (about 5 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m diameter) made of cellulose microfibrils embedded
  in a lignified matrix
\item
  \textbf{Margo:} A porous mesh of radial cellulose strands surrounding
  the torus, with pore sizes of 50--200 nm
\end{itemize}

Under normal flow, the torus floats centrally and water moves freely
through the porous margo. When one tracheid embolises, the pressure
differential between the air-filled (atmospheric) and water-filled
(negative pressure) conduits displaces the torus laterally; the torus
seats firmly against the pit aperture, \textbf{aspirating} the pit. The
seal is reinforced by surface tension at the air-water interface inside
the margo pores. Air seeding through this valve requires breaking the
meniscus at the smallest margo pore --- typically requiring tensions of
\(-3\) to \(-10\) MPa, which sets the species' cavitation safety margin.

Angiosperm pit membranes lack a torus; instead they have a homogeneous,
semi-porous structure (typical pore size about 5--20 nm). These
membranes resist air seeding at higher tensions per unit area but lack
the most-or-nothing valving of conifer pits --- once a single membrane
breach opens, the entire vessel cavitates rapidly.

\textbf{Mechanical properties --- the safety-efficiency tradeoff:}

The Hagen-Poiseuille equation predicts that volumetric flow scales as
the \emph{fourth power} of conduit radius:

\begin{equation}
Q = \frac{\pi r^4 \Delta P}{8 \eta L}
\label{eq:unit_VIII_hagen_poiseuille}
\end{equation}

where \(Q\) is volumetric flow (m\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{3}}{3}/s), \(r\) is conduit radius (m),
\(\Delta P\) is pressure drop (Pa), \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\eta}}{eta} is dynamic viscosity (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{3}}{3} Pa\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.}s
for water at 20 °C), and \(L\) is conduit length (m). Doubling the
radius therefore increases conductance 16-fold. Wide vessels (oaks,
ring-porous wood) dominate spring transpiration; narrow tracheids
(conifers, drought-adapted woody species) trade efficiency for
resistance to embolism propagation, since narrower conduits maintain
larger surface-tension forces relative to the column volume.

\textbf{Phloem} (sugar and organic compound transport, bidirectional):

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Sieve tube elements:} Living at maturity but lack nucleus,
  \hyperref[gl:ribosome]{\textbf{ribosome}}s, and tonoplast at maturity.
  Connected end-to-end at sieve plates (modified cell walls perforated
  by sieve pores, 1-15 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m diameter).
  P-\hyperref[gl:protein]{\textbf{protein}} (phloem protein) plugs sieve
  pores when cells are damaged, preventing phloem sap loss.
\item
  \textbf{Companion cells:} Retain full complement of
  \hyperref[gl:organelle]{\textbf{organelle}}s. Connected to sieve tube
  elements by numerous plasmodesmata. Provide metabolic support
  including ATP for active sugar loading. Transfer cells (specialised
  companion cells with wall ingrowths) increase membrane surface area
  for active transport.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Concept Check 3:} Why must xylem conducting cells be dead at
maturity, while phloem sieve tube elements must remain alive?

\textbf{Concept Check 4:} Using the Hagen-Poiseuille relation, calculate
the ratio of volumetric flow between a vessel of radius 100 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m and a
tracheid of radius 25 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m, holding pressure gradient and length constant.
Explain why drought-prone species may nevertheless favour the narrower
conduit.

\textbf{Concept Check 5:} A botanist examines a longitudinal section of
an emerging shoot from a deciduous tree. She notes spirally banded
conduits near the apex but reticulate-pitted conduits 5 cm behind.
Identify each conduit type and explain the developmental logic of the
difference.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Water Relations -- Water
Potential}\label{water-relations-water-potential}

Plants control water movement using \textbf{water potential} (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Psi}}{Psi}, units:
MPa). The complete four-component formulation captures every
thermodynamically relevant contribution to water's free energy:

\begin{equation}
\Psi = \Psi_s + \Psi_p + \Psi_m + \Psi_g
\label{eq:unit_VIII_water_potential}
\end{equation}

where:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{\(\Psi_s\)} = osmotic (solute) potential = \(-iCRT\)
  (typically \(\leq 0\); solutes decrease water potential). \(i\) is the
  van 't Hoff dissociation factor, \(C\) is molar concentration, \(R\)
  is the gas constant, \(T\) is temperature in Kelvin.
\item
  \textbf{\(\Psi_p\)} = pressure (turgor) potential. Positive in turgid
  cells (turgor pressure against cell wall). Negative in xylem under
  tension. Can range from +2 MPa in highly turgid cells to \(-10\) MPa
  or lower in xylem of tall trees.
\item
  \textbf{\(\Psi_m\)} = matric potential. Reflects water binding to
  colloidal surfaces (cell walls, soil clay particles, dry seeds).
  Typically \(\leq 0\). Typically negligible in well-hydrated cells but
  dominates in dry seeds (where \(\Psi_m\) can reach \(-100\) MPa) and
  in dry soils.
\item
  \textbf{\(\Psi_g\)} = gravitational potential = \(\rho g h\).
  Significant primarily in tall trees. At 10 m height, \(\Psi_g = -0.1\)
  MPa. At 100 m (coast redwood), \(\Psi_g = -1.0\) MPa.
\end{itemize}

In well-hydrated, free-flowing systems (most active leaf and root cells)
\(\Psi_m\) is folded into \(\Psi_p\) and the simplified three-component
form \(\Psi = \Psi_s + \Psi_p + \Psi_g\) is used. In dry seeds, lichens,
and very dry soils, \(\Psi_m\) must be retained explicitly. See
\cref{eq:unit_VIII_water_potential}.

\subsubsection{Worked Example: Calculating Water
Potential}\label{worked-example-calculating-water-potential}

\textbf{Problem:} A plant cell has a solute concentration of
\(C = 0.3 \text{ mol L}^{-1}\) sucrose (\(i=1\)) at
\(T = 293 \text{ K}\) (20 °C) and a turgor pressure (\(\Psi_p\)) of
\(0.5 \text{ MPa}\). Assuming normal height where \(\Psi_g = 0\) and the
cell is well hydrated so \(\Psi_m \approx 0\), what is the cell's total
\hyperref[gl:water-potential]{\textbf{water potential (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Psi}}{Psi})}}? If this
cell is placed in an open beaker of pure water (\(\Psi = 0\)), will
water flow into or out of the cell?

\textbf{Solution:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Calculate the osmotic potential (\(\Psi_s\)):} Using the van
  't Hoff equation \(\Psi_s = -iCRT\), where
  \(R = 0.00831 \text{ L MPa mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}\):
  \[ \Psi_s = -(1) \cdot (0.3 \text{ mol L}^{-1}) \cdot (0.00831 \text{ L MPa mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}) \cdot (293 \text{ K})  \label{eq:unit_VIII_plant_structure_and_water_item_1}\]

  \[ \Psi_s \approx -0.73 \text{ MPa}  \label{eq:unit_VIII_plant_structure_and_water_item_2}\]
\item
  \textbf{Calculate the total water potential (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Psi}}{Psi}):}
  \[ \Psi = \Psi_s + \Psi_p + \Psi_m + \Psi_g  \label{eq:unit_VIII_plant_structure_and_water_item_3}\]

  \[ \Psi = -0.73 \text{ MPa} + 0.5 \text{ MPa} + 0 + 0  \label{eq:unit_VIII_plant_structure_and_water_item_4}\]

  \[ \Psi = -0.23 \text{ MPa}  \label{eq:unit_VIII_plant_structure_and_water_item_5}\]
\item
  \textbf{Determine the direction of water flow:} Water typically moves
  from higher water potential to lower water potential. Since the beaker
  of pure water is at \(\Psi = 0\) and the cell is at
  \(\Psi = -0.23 \text{ MPa}\), water will flow \textbf{into the cell}
  until the cell's turgor pressure rises sufficiently to reach
  equilibrium (\(\Psi = 0\)).
\end{enumerate}

Water typically moves from \textbf{higher to lower water potential}
(down the \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Psi}}{Psi} gradient).

\subsubsection{Worked Example: A Leaf Cell at Dawn vs
Midday}\label{worked-example-a-leaf-cell-at-dawn-vs-midday}

\textbf{Problem:} A mesophyll cell at dawn (cool, humid, stomata closed)
has \(\Psi_s = -1.1\) MPa, \(\Psi_p = +0.9\) MPa, \(\Psi_m \approx 0\),
\(\Psi_g \approx 0\). By midday (hot, dry, stomata open and
transpiring), the cell loses water: \(\Psi_s = -1.4\) MPa (solutes
concentrated by about 27\% volume loss), \(\Psi_p = +0.2\) MPa.
Compute \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Psi}}{Psi} in both states and identify which component drives the change.

\textbf{Solution:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Dawn: \(\Psi = -1.1 + 0.9 = -0.2\) MPa
\item
  Midday: \(\Psi = -1.4 + 0.2 = -1.2\) MPa
\end{itemize}

Total \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Psi}}{Psi} has fallen by 1.0 MPa. Decomposing the change:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(\Delta\Psi_s = -0.3\) MPa (small contribution from solute
  concentration)
\item
  \(\Delta\Psi_p = -0.7\) MPa (dominant contribution)
\end{itemize}

The midday plunge is driven primarily by \textbf{loss of turgor}. The
cell remains alive and below the wilting threshold, but it is
approaching the limit at which growth (which requires \(\Psi_p > Y\) in
the Lockhart equation) ceases. This is the molecular basis of midday
``growth pause'' almost universally observed in field crops.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0138_d1e54f8471f6.png}
\caption{Components of water potential and the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum (SPAC) Water moves passively down the water potential gradient from soil to atmosphere. The enormous gradient between leaf and atmosphere drives transpiration.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Quantitative Turgor Relations and
Plasmolysis}\label{quantitative-turgor-relations-and-plasmolysis}

\textbf{Turgor pressure} (\(\Psi_p\)) is generated when a cell with low
internal \(\Psi_s\) takes up water until the cell wall resists further
expansion. The cell-wall yield curve is described by the
\textbf{Lockhart equation} for irreversible expansion:

\begin{equation}
\frac{1}{V}\frac{dV}{dt} = \phi (\Psi_p - Y)
\label{eq:unit_VIII_lockhart}
\end{equation}

where \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\varphi}}{phi} is wall extensibility (a measure of how readily the wall
yields), \(\Psi_p\) is current turgor, and \(Y\) is the yield threshold
below which the wall behaves elastically (no growth). Cells grow
primarily when \(\Psi_p > Y\). In the elongation zone, expansin-mediated
wall loosening reduces \(Y\), allowing growth even at modest turgor.

\textbf{Plasmolysis} is the separation of the protoplast from the cell
wall when the cell is placed in a hypertonic solution (external
\(\Psi_s\) more negative than internal). Three phases:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Incipient plasmolysis:} Turgor reaches zero (\(\Psi_p = 0\));
  at this point \(\Psi = \Psi_s\). The protoplast is just losing contact
  with the wall.
\item
  \textbf{Concave plasmolysis:} Protoplast withdraws inward; plasma
  membrane appears scalloped at the corners.
\item
  \textbf{Convex plasmolysis:} Protoplast becomes a small spherical body
  in the centre of the cell; reversible if rehydrated within minutes,
  but prolonged plasmolysis kills the cell.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Worked Example --- Quantitative Plasmolysis:} A cell at
\(\Psi_p = 0.5\) MPa, \(\Psi_s = -0.73\) MPa is placed in a sucrose
solution at \(\Psi_s = -1.0\) MPa. Water leaves the cell. As water
exits, \(\Psi_s\) becomes more negative (solutes concentrate; assume
volume change of 20\% from full turgor to incipient plasmolysis). At
incipient plasmolysis, \(\Psi_p = 0\) and \(\Psi_{cell} = \Psi_s\) must
equal \(\Psi_{external} = -1.0\) MPa. Since \(\Psi_s\) scales inversely
with cell volume (\(\Psi_s \cdot V\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} constant for ideal solutes), we
calculate the relative volume at incipient plasmolysis as
\(V_p / V_0 = \Psi_{s,0} / \Psi_{s,p} = -0.73 / -1.0 = 0.73\), i.e., the
cell loses about 27\% of its initial volume before
plasmolysing.

At full turgor: \(\Psi_p = -\Psi_s\), so \(\Psi = 0\) (cell is in
equilibrium with pure water).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection:} Agricultural irrigation management relies
on measuring soil water potential with tensiometers. When soil \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Psi}}{Psi} falls
below \(-1.5\) MPa (the permanent wilting point), most crop plants
cannot extract water. Precision irrigation triggered at species-specific
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Psi}}{Psi} thresholds saves 20-40\% of water compared to schedule-based
irrigation.
\end{quote}

\textbf{Concept Check 6:} A seed at storage moisture has
\(\Psi_m \approx -100\) MPa, \(\Psi_s \approx -2\) MPa, and
\(\Psi_p = 0\). When placed on moist filter paper at \(\Psi = -0.05\)
MPa, water is rapidly imbibed. Explain which component dominates the
imbibition gradient and why imbibition is a one-way process.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Water Transport Pathways}\label{water-transport-pathways}

\subsubsection{Apoplast vs Symplast
Pathways}\label{apoplast-vs-symplast-pathways}

Water and dissolved minerals travel from the root surface to the xylem
via two parallel routes:

\textbf{Apoplast pathway:} Water moves through the continuum of cell
walls and intercellular spaces without crossing any membranes. Fast and
non-selective. Driven by mass flow along pressure gradients.

\textbf{Symplast pathway:} Water moves through the continuum of
\hyperref[gl:cytoplasm]{\textbf{cytoplasm}} connected by plasmodesmata
(channels through cell walls, 40-60 nm diameter, lined by ER). Requires
crossing the plasma membrane at entry. Slower but allows selective
transport.

\textbf{Transmembrane pathway:} Water crosses plasma membranes via
aquaporins (water channel proteins, PIP and TIP families;
about 35 aquaporin genes in \emph{Arabidopsis}). Aquaporin
activity is regulated by phosphorylation, \hyperref[gl:ph]{\textbf{pH}},
and Ca\(^{2+}\).

\subsubsection{Root Anatomy in Depth --- The Endodermis as
Filter}\label{root-anatomy-in-depth-the-endodermis-as-filter}

Radial anatomy of a young dicot root (from outside inward):

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Epidermis} with root hairs --- initial absorption surface
\item
  \textbf{Cortex} --- multiple layers of parenchyma; storage and
  apoplastic transport corridor; rich in plasmodesmata
\item
  \textbf{Endodermis} --- single layer; the critical apoplastic
  checkpoint
\item
  \textbf{Pericycle} --- cell layer giving rise to lateral roots
\item
  \textbf{Vascular cylinder (stele)} --- central xylem and phloem
  strands
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{The Casparian strip --- chemistry and synthesis:}

The Casparian strip is a band of \textbf{lignin and suberin} deposited
in the radial and transverse walls of endodermal cells. The two polymers
play distinct, sequential roles:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Lignin} (a phenylpropanoid polymer of monolignol units
  p-coumaryl, coniferyl, and sinapyl alcohol cross-linked by oxidative
  coupling) is deposited first, forming the \textbf{Casparian strip
  proper} --- a discontinuous belt that fuses cell wall to plasma
  membrane. CASP1--CASP5 transmembrane proteins assemble into a
  hexagonal scaffold that recruits ESB1 (a dirigent protein) and PER64
  (a peroxidase), localising lignification to a precise sub-micron belt.
  \emph{casp1 casp3} double mutants have discontinuous strips and leak
  ions into the stele.
\item
  \textbf{Suberin} (an aliphatic-aromatic polyester of long-chain
  \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\omega}}{omega}-hydroxy fatty acids and ferulate esters) is deposited later as the
  \textbf{suberin lamella} on the inner face of the cell wall, after the
  Casparian strip is mature. Suberisation is regulated by SGN3-CIF1/CIF2
  receptor-peptide signalling, which monitors the integrity of the
  Casparian strip via leakage of CIF peptides from stele to cortex.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Why both polymers?} Lignin is hydrophobic and rigid but porous
to small molecules; suberin is even more hydrophobic and seals against
water and ion flow. The two-stage system gives a fast-acting initial
seal (lignin Casparian strip) followed by a slow-developing
reinforcement (suberin lamella) that further restricts symplastic
transport across the inner endodermal face.

\textbf{Bypass routes --- apoplastic leakage at lateral root junctions:}

Where lateral roots emerge from the pericycle, they must rupture the
endodermis and overlying cortex. During the brief window before the
lateral root re-establishes its own endodermis, an \textbf{apoplastic
bypass} allows ions (and pathogens) to enter the stele without crossing
a plasma membrane. This window can be hours to days long.
Quantitatively, about 70\% of soil-borne Na\(^+\) entering the
stele of rice and wheat does so via these junctional leaks rather than
through the proper symplast. The bypass may explain seasonal salt
accumulation in glycophytes (salt-sensitive species) under saline
irrigation.

\textbf{Symplastic vs transmembrane pathways:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Pure symplastic transport} uses plasmodesmata to bypass plasma
  membranes entirely. Plasmodesmal aperture is regulated by callose
  deposition at the neck region; under stress, callose deposition closes
  plasmodesmata, isolating cells.
\item
  \textbf{Transmembrane pathway} crosses plasma membranes twice per cell
  (entry + exit) via aquaporins for water and selective transporters for
  ions. Slowest but most selective.
\end{itemize}

In practice, most three pathways operate simultaneously; the relative
contribution shifts with developmental stage, salinity, and mycorrhizal
colonisation.

\textbf{Passage cells:} In older roots, most endodermal cells deposit a
continuous suberin lamella covering the entire inner surface of the cell
wall. \textbf{Passage cells} --- endodermal cells that retain a thin
wall and lack the suberin lamella, located opposite protoxylem poles ---
provide selective transport routes through the otherwise sealed older
endodermis.

In rice, the endodermis is supplemented by an inner \textbf{exodermis}
(a Casparian-strip-bearing layer just inside the epidermis), giving a
double filter. Rice ranks among the most salt-tolerant cereals partly
because the exodermis blocks Na\(^+\) at the root surface itself.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0139_f70eb6406088.png}
\caption{Apoplast vs symplast routes through a young root and the Casparian-strip checkpoint at the endodermis Most water and ions reaching the xylem must traverse at least one plasma membrane.}
\end{figure}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Transpiration and the Cohesion-Tension
Mechanism}\label{transpiration-and-the-cohesion-tension-mechanism}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Historical Context: The Birth of
Cohesion-Tension Theory
\citep{dixon1894}}{Historical Context: The Birth of Cohesion-Tension Theory}}\label{historical-context-the-birth-of-cohesion-tension-theory}

The question of how water reaches the canopy of a tall tree exercised
plant physiologists throughout the 19th century. Early proposals invoked
\textbf{root pressure} (positive xylem pressure generated by active
mineral secretion overnight; can be measured by exudation from cut
stumps at 0.05--0.5 MPa), but this manifestly cannot lift water more
than about 5 m and is absent during the day in most species.
\textbf{Capillarity} in xylem conduits could lift water about 1 m given
typical conduit radii. \textbf{Atmospheric pressure} can support a
column of about 10.3 m. None of these mechanisms could account for water
rising to 100 m in \emph{Sequoia}.

In 1894, Henry Dixon (Trinity College Dublin) and John Joly proposed a
radical alternative: water in the xylem is under \textbf{tension}
(negative pressure), pulled from above by evaporation rather than pushed
from below \citep{dixon1894}. The idea was counter-intuitive --- bulk
water at \(-1\) MPa is metastable; a single nucleation event should
cause spontaneous boiling --- but the cohesive forces of water (hydrogen
bonds, theoretical tensile strength \(-140\) MPa) and the small radii of
xylem conduits (which suppress nucleation) make the metastable state
biologically sustainable.

\subsubsection{Detailed TACT Mechanism}\label{detailed-tact-mechanism}

Water ascent in tall trees is explained by the
\textbf{cohesion-tension-adhesion (TACT) mechanism}, refined by Renner
(1911), and validated with pressure probes and MRI:

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0140_36d2b095fc82.png}
\caption{The transpiration-cohesion-tension mechanism of water ascent Evaporation at the leaf surface generates tension (negative pressure) that is transmitted through the continuous water column in the xylem, pulling water upward from the roots. Cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to xylem walls maintain the column.}
\end{figure}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Transpiration} from leaves drives evaporation at the mesophyll
  cell wall surface. Water evaporates from the thin film coating the
  cell wall into the substomatal air space, then diffuses out through
  open stomata.
\item
  As water evaporates, the air-water interface retreats into the
  nanoscale pores of the cell wall. Surface tension at this curved
  meniscus generates a large negative pressure (tension), following the
  Young-Laplace equation:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{equation}
\Delta P = \frac{2\gamma \cos\theta}{r}
\label{eq:unit_VIII_young_laplace}
\end{equation}

where \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma} is surface tension of water (0.0728 N/m), \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\theta}}{theta} is contact angle,
and \(r\) is pore radius. For cell wall pores (\(r \approx\) 5-10 nm),
this generates tensions of \(-10\) to \(-30\) MPa.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\item
  This tension propagates through the continuous water columns in xylem
  conduits (tracheids and vessels) because of water's strong
  \textbf{cohesion} (\hyperref[gl:hydrogen-bond]{\textbf{hydrogen
  bond}}s). The theoretical tensile strength of water is approximately
  \(-140\) MPa; in practice, xylem water columns sustain tensions of
  \(-1\) to \(-10\) MPa, with some trees reaching \(-15\) MPa.
\item
  \textbf{Adhesion} of water to the hydrophilic, lignified xylem walls
  prevents the water column from pulling away from the conduit walls.
\item
  The tension at the top of the column draws water from the roots, which
  in turn absorbs water from the soil down the water potential gradient.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Critical Evaluation of the Cohesion-Tension Theory:
Embolism Debate and Synchrotron
Resolution}\label{critical-evaluation-of-the-cohesion-tension-theory-embolism-debate-and-synchrotron-resolution}

The cohesion-tension model is not without controversy, and its mature
form represents a triumph of integrating ecological, physical, and
microscopic evidence --- together with rebuttals to specific objections.

\textbf{Lines of supporting evidence:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Pressure-bomb measurements} (Scholander \emph{et al.}, 1965)
  directly demonstrate that excised stems of transpiring trees release
  water primarily when external pressure is applied, consistent with
  negative xylem pressure prior to excision. Pressure required matches
  predictions of the tension hypothesis (typically \(-1\) to \(-3\) MPa
  for well-watered crops; \(-6\) to \(-10\) MPa under drought).
\item
  \textbf{Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)} in vivo (Holbrook \emph{et
  al.}, 2001) visualises continuous water columns in mature angiosperm
  trunks, with abrupt transitions to embolised conduits matching
  predictions of tension-induced cavitation.
\item
  \textbf{Pressure probes} (Steudle, 1995) in living root cortex cells
  confirm steep tension gradients between epidermis and stele consistent
  with bulk-flow-driven uptake.
\item
  \textbf{Acoustic emission} of xylem during drought (Tyree and Sperry,
  1989) records sharp clicks corresponding to individual cavitation
  events, the count of which scales with drought severity.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{The embolism debate:}

Critics (most prominently U. Zimmermann and colleagues, 1990s--2000s)
argued that water columns under tensions of \(-1\) MPa or more should be
metastable and would cavitate continuously, making sustained negative
pressures of \(-10\) MPa physiologically implausible. The Zimmermann
school proposed alternative ``tissue tension'' models in which water
moved by mechanisms other than bulk flow.

This challenge has been progressively resolved by direct visualisation:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Improved pressure probes} (Wei \emph{et al.}, 1999) confirmed
  predicted tensions in living conduits without artefact.
\item
  \textbf{Synthetic-tree experiments} (Wheeler and Stroock,
  \emph{Nature} 2008) constructed transparent microfluidic devices
  replicating the geometry of a leaf's evaporative surface; these
  ``synthetic trees'' sustained water under tension to \(-22\) MPa,
  mirroring biological systems and proving that cell wall pore geometry
  alone is sufficient to support the predicted tensions.
\item
  \textbf{Synchrotron X-ray micro-CT} (Brodersen \emph{et al.},
  \emph{Plant Physiol.} 2010; Choat \emph{et al.}, \emph{Nature} 2012)
  imaged living xylem in real time and showed that under moderate
  drought, embolisms are confined to a small fraction of conduits ---
  settling the long-running argument over how prevalent embolism is in
  actively transpiring plants. Synchrotron imaging also visualised
  \textbf{embolism repair} under daily root pressure: embolised conduits
  refill overnight in \emph{Vitis} and \emph{Laurus}.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Mechanism of embolism repair:} Two complementary mechanisms are
now well-attested:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Root pressure refilling:} Active mineral secretion into xylem
  at night generates positive xylem pressure (0.05--0.5 MPa) sufficient
  to push water back into embolised conduits. Common in herbaceous
  species and in many trees overnight.
\item
  \textbf{Phloem-driven refilling:} Phloem-derived sugars osmotically
  draw water into embolised conduits via parenchyma cells lining the
  xylem (Salleo \emph{et al.}, 2004; Nardini \emph{et al.}, 2011). This
  mechanism operates against negative bulk xylem pressure and is
  observed during the day.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Net assessment:} The TACT mechanism is correct in its
essentials. Water in xylem is genuinely under tension; the column is
stabilised by cohesion and adhesion at scales where pore geometry
sustains negative pressures far beyond what bulk water could endure. The
system is metastable but biologically sufficient --- and the cost of
occasional cavitation is mitigated by redundant pathways and active
repair.

\subsubsection{Xylem Transport
Parameters}\label{xylem-transport-parameters}

\textbf{Xylem sap velocity} measured by MRI and heat pulse methods: 3-45
m/h in trees; 15-50 m/h in herbaceous plants. Ring-porous trees (oak,
elm) can reach velocities of 40+ m/h in their large early-wood vessels.

\textbf{Transpiration flux} (Fick's first law for water vapour):

\begin{equation}
E = g_s \cdot \Delta w
\label{eq:unit_VIII_transpiration_flux}
\end{equation}

where \(g_s\) = stomatal conductance (mmol m\(^{-2}\) s\(^{-1}\)) and
\(\Delta w\) = vapour pressure difference between leaf interior and
ambient air (mol mol\(^{-1}\)).

A well-watered broadleaf tree can transpire 200-400 litres of water per
day. A large oak may transpire over 150,000 litres during a growing
season.

\subsubsection{Cavitation and Embolism}\label{cavitation-and-embolism}

When xylem tension exceeds the capacity of the water column, dissolved
gas comes out of solution forming a bubble -- \textbf{cavitation}. The
gas bubble expands to fill the conduit, creating an \textbf{embolism}
(air lock) that blocks water flow.

Plants have evolved multiple strategies to manage cavitation:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Vessel element size:} Smaller conduits are more resistant to
  cavitation (higher surface-tension forces maintain the column) but
  less efficient for transport. This creates a safety-efficiency
  tradeoff.
\item
  \textbf{Pit membranes:} In tracheids, bordered pits have a torus-margo
  structure. When one tracheid cavitates, the torus seals against the
  pit aperture, preventing air from spreading to adjacent conduits.
\item
  \textbf{Embolism repair:} Some plants can refill embolisms overnight
  when transpiration ceases and root pressure (positive xylem pressure
  generated by active mineral secretion into xylem) pushes water back
  into embolised conduits.
\item
  \textbf{Redundant pathways:} Multiple parallel conduits ensure that
  loss of some to embolism does not stop water transport entirely.
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection:} The vulnerability of xylem to cavitation
explains why drought-adapted species (e.g., desert shrubs) have narrow
xylem vessels while tropical rainforest trees have wide ones. Climate
change-driven drought is causing widespread forest die-off globally as
tree xylem systems experience unprecedented cavitation stress, termed
``hydraulic failure.'' The 2011 Texas drought killed an estimated 300
million trees.
\end{quote}

\textbf{Concept Check 8:} Modern synchrotron imaging shows that conifer
xylem can withstand tensions of \(-6\) MPa with little embolism, while
many ring-porous angiosperms cavitate at \(-2\) MPa. Explain this
difference in terms of pit membrane structure (torus-margo vs
homogeneous) and conduit dimensions.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Stomatal Regulation}\label{stomatal-regulation}

Stomata represent the critical control point where plants balance carbon
gain (CO\(_2\) uptake for photosynthesis) against water loss
(transpiration).

\subsubsection{Stomatal Opening --- Guard Cell Ion
Fluxes}\label{stomatal-opening-guard-cell-ion-fluxes}

The mechanism of stomatal opening involves a coordinated cascade of ion
fluxes that generate the osmotic gradient driving water entry. The
molecular logic is one of the best-characterised electrophysiological
systems in plants:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Blue light (peak 450 nm)} activates phototropin receptors
  (PHOT1/PHOT2) on guard cells via FMN photoreduction
\item
  \textbf{PHOTs activate plasma membrane H\(^+\)-ATPases} (AHA1, AHA2)
  via 14-3-3-mediated phosphorylation of the C-terminal autoinhibitory
  domain
\item
  \textbf{H\(^+\) extrusion hyperpolarises} the membrane (interior
  becomes more negative, \(V_m\) shifts from \(-100\) to \(-180\) mV)
  and acidifies the apoplast (pH 6 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} 5)
\item
  \textbf{K\(^+\) inward-rectifying channels} (KAT1 in
  \emph{Arabidopsis}; voltage-gated, six-transmembrane Shaker family)
  open at hyperpolarised potentials. K\(^+\) flows down its
  electrochemical gradient into the guard cell, accumulating at
  concentrations of 400--800 mM. KAT1 is the rate-limiting K\(^+\) entry
  channel for stomatal opening; \emph{kat1} knockouts have severely
  reduced light-induced opening.
\item
  \textbf{Cl\(^-\) accumulates} as a charge-balancing
  \textbf{counterion} through SLAH3 and CLC channels operating in
  reverse mode under hyperpolarisation
\item
  \textbf{Malate\(^{2-}\)} is synthesised from chloroplast-derived
  starch via PEP carboxylase and converted by NADP-malate dehydrogenase,
  providing additional charge-balancing osmoticum
\item
  \textbf{Sucrose} accumulates in late-afternoon stomata, supplementing
  K\(^+\)/malate as an osmoticum (afternoon stomata may be 50\%
  sucrose-driven)
\item
  \textbf{Decreased osmotic potential} (\(\Psi_s\) more negative, by
  1.5--2 MPa) drives water influx through aquaporins (PIP1, PIP2)
\item
  \textbf{Guard cells swell.} Their differentially thickened walls
  (thicker on the inner pore-facing wall, thinner on the outer wall)
  cause the cells to bow apart asymmetrically
\item
  \textbf{Stomatal aperture} opens by 5--25 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m depending on species
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Stomatal Closure -- ABA Signalling Cascade in
Detail}\label{stomatal-closure-aba-signalling-cascade-in-detail}

Under drought stress, abscisic acid (ABA) triggers rapid stomatal
closure through a molecular relay that has become a textbook example of
plant signal transduction. The pathway can be summarised in five steps:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{ABA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PYR1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PP2C \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} SnRK2 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} SLAC1}
\end{quote}

Each step in this cascade has been crystallographically resolved
(PYR1-ABA-PP2C ternary complex, Melcher \emph{et al.}, \emph{Nature}
2009; SnRK2-PP2C complex, Soon \emph{et al.}, \emph{Science} 2012) and
is now textbook signalling.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{ABA synthesis:} Soil drying activates NCED3
  (9-\emph{cis}-epoxycarotenoid dioxygenase) in roots, cleaving
  9'-\emph{cis}-violaxanthin/neoxanthin to xanthoxin (ABA precursor).
  Local ABA biosynthesis also occurs in leaf vasculature and guard cells
  themselves.
\item
  \textbf{ABA distribution:} ABA travels via xylem to guard cells and is
  concentrated by the AIT1/NPF4 family of ABA importers and the ABCG25
  exporter.
\item
  \textbf{Receptor binding:} ABA binds \textbf{PYR/PYL/RCAR} receptors
  (14 paralogs in \emph{Arabidopsis}) at a START-domain pocket. This
  binding ``closes'' the receptor's gate loop over the binding pocket.
\item
  \textbf{PP2C inhibition:} The closed ABA-PYR complex docks onto and
  \textbf{inhibits Type-2C protein phosphatases} (ABI1, ABI2, HAB1).
  PP2Cs normally dephosphorylate (and thereby inactivate) downstream
  kinases.
\item
  \textbf{SnRK2 activation:} Released from PP2C inhibition,
  \textbf{SnRK2 kinases} (especially OST1/SnRK2.6) autophosphorylate and
  become active. OST1 phosphorylates downstream targets including:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{SLAC1} anion channel: phosphorylation at Ser120 opens the
    channel; massive Cl\(^-\) and malate\(^{2-}\) efflux
    \textbf{depolarises} the membrane (V\(_m\) shifts to \(-30\) to
    \(-50\) mV)
  \item
    \textbf{GORK} outward-rectifying K\(^+\) channel: opens at
    depolarised potentials; K\(^+\) leaves the cell down its
    electrochemical gradient
  \item
    \textbf{AKT1/KAT1}: inward-rectifying K\(^+\) channels are inhibited
    (preventing K\(^+\) re-entry)
  \item
    \textbf{NADPH oxidase RBOHF}: produces reactive oxygen species (ROS)
    that activate Ca\(^{2+}\)-permeable channels, raising cytosolic
    Ca\(^{2+}\) and amplifying SLAC1/GORK responses
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Osmotic deflation:} Loss of K\(^+\), Cl\(^-\), and malate
  raises \(\Psi_s\) by 1.5 MPa; water exits via aquaporins; turgor drops
\item
  \textbf{Aperture closure:} Stomata close within 5-15 minutes
\end{enumerate}

The ABA cascade integrates with a parallel \textbf{CO\(_2\)-sensing
pathway} (HT1 kinase, MPK4/12) and an \textbf{immune pathway} (FLS2
receptor activated by bacterial flagellin) at the level of SLAC1, which
serves as a hub for diverse closure stimuli.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0141_4b0dcf4ea02b.png}
\caption{The ABA signalling cascade in guard cells ABA binding releases SnRK2 kinases from PP2C inhibition; SnRK2 then drives the ion-flux changes that osmotically deflate the guard cell.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Other Factors Affecting
Stomata}\label{other-factors-affecting-stomata}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{CO\(_2\) concentration:} Elevated internal CO\(_2\) promotes
  closure (reduces need for gas exchange). This is significant under
  rising atmospheric CO\(_2\), where plants partially close stomata,
  reducing transpiration but potentially increasing leaf temperature.
\item
  \textbf{Humidity:} Low humidity (high vapour pressure deficit, VPD)
  promotes closure as a protective response against excessive water loss
\item
  \textbf{Photosynthetically active radiation (PAR):} Drives opening via
  both blue-light specific and photosynthesis-dependent pathways
\item
  \textbf{Circadian clock:} Stomata show anticipatory opening before
  dawn, controlled by the plant circadian clock
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Water-Use Efficiency}\label{water-use-efficiency-1}

Stomatal opening trades CO\(_2\) acquisition against water loss. The
intrinsic water-use efficiency captures this trade-off at the leaf
level:

\begin{equation}
iWUE = \frac{A_n}{g_s}
\label{eq:unit_VIII_iwue}
\end{equation}

where \(A_n\) is net CO\(_2\) assimilation rate (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}mol CO\(_2\)
m\(^{-2}\) s\(^{-1}\)) and \(g_s\) is stomatal conductance to water
vapour (mol H\(_2\)O m\(^{-2}\) s\(^{-1}\)). Higher iWUE means more
carbon fixed per unit water transpired.

\textbf{C3, C4, and CAM trade-offs:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{C3 plants} (most temperate species; rice, wheat, soybean) have
  iWUE about 50--100 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}mol CO\(_2\) mol\(^{-1}\) H\(_2\)O. Their
  primary CO\(_2\)-fixing enzyme RuBisCO operates at near-atmospheric
  {[}CO\(_2\){]} inside the leaf, limiting iWUE.
\item
  \textbf{C4 plants} (maize, sorghum, sugarcane, many tropical grasses)
  concentrate CO\(_2\) in bundle-sheath cells via the C4 pump. Mesophyll
  {[}CO\(_2\){]} is amplified about 10-fold relative to
  ambient, allowing stomata to be partially closed without limiting
  photosynthesis. iWUE about 150--250 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}mol mol\(^{-1}\).
\item
  \textbf{CAM plants} (succulents, cacti, agaves, pineapple) open
  stomata primarily at night, when VPD is low. CO\(_2\) is fixed as
  malate and stored in vacuoles; during the day, decarboxylation
  releases CO\(_2\) inside closed leaves for photosynthesis. iWUE can
  exceed 500 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}mol mol\(^{-1}\) --- an order of magnitude above C3.
\end{itemize}

The progression C3 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} C4 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} CAM represents progressive specialisation for
water-limited environments, with CAM as the most extreme adaptation. The
iWUE differential explains why C4 maize outperforms C3 wheat in hot,
semi-arid climates and why CAM cacti dominate true deserts.

\subsection{Phloem Transport -- The Münch Pressure-Flow
Model}\label{phloem-transport-the-muxfcnch-pressure-flow-model}

Unlike xylem (upward, driven by transpiration tension), \textbf{phloem}
transports photosynthate (sucrose at 0.3-0.9 M plus amino acids,
\hyperref[gl:hormone]{\textbf{hormone}}s, mRNAs, and small proteins)
\textbf{bidirectionally} from sources to sinks.

\subsubsection{Phloem Loading --- Apoplastic vs Symplastic
Pathways}\label{phloem-loading-apoplastic-vs-symplastic-pathways}

How sugars enter sieve tubes from photosynthetic mesophyll determines
key physiological properties: loading rate, concentration limits, and
the species-specific tradeoffs between transport efficiency and
protection from herbivores. The choice of loading strategy is one of the
most striking ecophysiological dichotomies in plants.

\textbf{Apoplastic loading} (Type 2; most herbaceous crops, including
most major cereals, \emph{Arabidopsis}, sugar beet, soybean, tomato):

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Sucrose is exported from mesophyll cells to the apoplast (cell-wall
  space) via \textbf{SWEET11/SWEET12} sucrose efflux carriers
  (uniporters, facilitated diffusion)
\item
  The H\(^+\)-ATPase on the companion-cell plasma membrane creates a
  steep proton gradient (apoplast pH about 5.5; cytoplasm pH
  about 7.5) and a hyperpolarised membrane potential
\item
  \textbf{SUT1} (Sucrose-H\(^+\) symporter; also known as SUC2 in
  \emph{Arabidopsis}) uses the proton gradient to import sucrose against
  its concentration gradient (10--50\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} concentration step). The full
  family of \textbf{sucrose transporters (SUTs)} comprises three clades
  with distinct cellular localisations and kinetic properties: SUT1/SUC2
  is the workhorse loader on companion cells (low \(K_m\)
  about 1 mM); SUT4 localises to tonoplasts and mediates
  vacuolar sucrose mobilisation; SUT2 has been proposed as a sucrose
  sensor with high \(K_m\). Knockout of \emph{SUT1} in maize
  (\emph{sut1} mutants) causes sugar accumulation in source leaves and
  starvation in sinks, confirming its role as the rate-limiting loader.
\item
  Imported sucrose moves through plasmodesmata between companion cell
  and sieve element to enter the conducting stream
\item
  Loading rate: 5--15 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}mol sucrose per cm\(^2\) of leaf per hour
\end{enumerate}

Apoplastic loading is energetically costly (one ATP per sucrose) but
allows very high sieve-tube concentrations (up to 1 M sucrose) by
``uphill'' transport against the concentration gradient.

\textbf{Symplastic loading} (Type 1; many trees, especially temperate
broadleaves like willow, poplar; also many tropical species):

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Sucrose moves from mesophyll to companion cells \textbf{entirely
  through plasmodesmata} without crossing any membrane. Plasmodesmal
  density at the mesophyll--companion cell interface is 10--100 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} higher
  in symplastic loaders than in apoplastic loaders. This is the
  diagnostic anatomical feature of symplastic loading --- first
  established by Gamalei (1989) in his comparative survey of
  \textgreater300 species.
\item
  In specialised ``intermediary cells'' (companion-cell variant),
  sucrose is converted to larger oligosaccharides (raffinose, stachyose)
  by \textbf{galactinol synthase + raffinose synthase}. These larger
  oligosaccharides cannot diffuse back through the narrow plasmodesmal
  aperture (about 3 nm size limit at the desmotubule).
\item
  The accumulated raffinose-family oligosaccharides (RFOs) form a
  one-way \textbf{polymer trap} (Turgeon, 1991), lowering \(\Psi_s\) and
  drawing water into the sieve tube.
\end{enumerate}

Symplastic loading is energetically cheap (no membrane transport) but
limited in concentration. Some temperate trees (apple, \emph{Malus}) use
a third hybrid strategy --- passive symplastic loading without polymer
trapping, where the source-sink concentration gradient alone drives
unloading.

\textbf{Plasmodesmatal conductance and regulation:}

Plasmodesmata are dynamic; their aperture is set by the deposition of
callose (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-1,3-glucan) at the neck. Callose synthases (CalS1/3/7/8) and
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-1,3-glucanases (BG\_pap, BG\_ppap) act antagonistically. Under stress
(wounding, pathogen attack), callose deposition closes plasmodesmata
within minutes, isolating affected cells. SUT1-dependent (apoplastic)
loading is unaffected by plasmodesmal closure; symplastic loaders are
critically dependent on open plasmodesmata and are more vulnerable to
wounding-induced flow disruption.

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{The Münch Pressure-Flow Hypothesis
\citep{munch1930}}{The Münch Pressure-Flow Hypothesis}}\label{the-muxfcnch-pressure-flow-hypothesis}

Ernst Münch's 1930 model remains the consensus explanation for
bidirectional phloem flow, supplemented by about 95 years of
experimental refinement.

\textbf{Mechanism:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Sugar loading at source} (mature leaves) raises sucrose
  concentration in sieve tubes to 0.5--1 M, lowering \(\Psi_s\) to
  \(-2\) to \(-3\) MPa
\item
  Water enters by osmosis from adjacent xylem (where \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Psi}}{Psi} is more
  positive). Turgor pressure (\(\Psi_p\)) rises to +1 to +2 MPa at the
  source
\item
  \textbf{Sugar unloading at sink} (roots, developing fruit, growing
  tips, storage organs) removes sucrose. Sucrose may be cleaved by
  invertase (to glucose + fructose) or sucrose synthase. As sucrose is
  removed, \(\Psi_s\) rises, water exits to surrounding tissues, and
  turgor pressure falls to +0.3 to +0.6 MPa
\item
  The \textbf{pressure gradient} between source (high turgor) and sink
  (low turgor) drives bulk flow through the sieve-tube network along the
  path of least resistance
\item
  The unloaded water re-enters the xylem and is recycled to the source
  (closing the loop)
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Unloading mechanisms} are sink-specific:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Symplastic unloading} (most growing sinks, e.g., root tips,
  developing leaves): sucrose moves through plasmodesmata into
  surrounding cells; intracellular sucrose synthase or invertase cleaves
  it for use.
\item
  \textbf{Apoplastic unloading} (storage sinks isolated by suberin,
  e.g., developing seeds and grains): sucrose is exported by SWEETs into
  the apoplast, then cleaved by cell-wall invertase to glucose +
  fructose, which are imported via hexose transporters. The
  maternal-filial boundary in seeds is typically apoplastic, ensuring
  genetic isolation between mother plant and developing offspring.
\end{itemize}

Flow rates: 0.5-1.5 m/h; rates up to 3 m/h have been measured.

\textbf{Supporting evidence for Münch flow:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Aphid-stylet sap collection} (Mittler, 1953): aphids cleanly
  tap individual sieve tubes; collected sap shows sucrose concentrations
  of 10--25\% w/v, consistent with osmotically active loading
\item
  \textbf{Pressure probes} on individual sieve elements directly measure
  positive turgor of +1--2 MPa near the source and lower turgor near
  sinks
\item
  \textbf{Cessation of flow on cooling} the petiole (which inhibits
  H\(^+\)-ATPase but does not block plasmodesmata) confirms active
  loading is required
\item
  \textbf{Source--sink reversal:} Removing the lower leaves of a soybean
  plant reverses flow direction in the stem (downward to upward) within
  hours, consistent with passive bulk flow following the pressure
  gradient
\item
  \textbf{Mathematical modelling} with realistic sieve-tube geometry
  (Thompson and Holbrook, 2003) shows Münch flow can readily account for
  observed transport rates in trees up to about 100 m, provided
  sieve tubes are wide enough
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Evidence against (and modifications to) Münch flow:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The \textbf{giant-vine objection} (T.W. Mason, 1922): flow rates in
  long vines were measured to exceed Münch's predictions for narrow
  conduits. This was resolved when measurements showed sieve-tube radii
  in such species are actually larger than initially supposed.
\item
  \textbf{Pressure-driven model alone cannot account for observations of
  sieve plate occlusion} (P-protein, callose) in healthy phloem,
  suggesting flow regulation through dynamic plate gating
\item
  \textbf{High-velocity, short-distance flow} in some tropical lianas
  (\textgreater3 m/h) approaches the upper bound of Münch flow and may
  require a supplementary ``relay'' mechanism
\end{enumerate}

The current consensus: Münch pressure-flow is the \textbf{dominant}
mechanism, supplemented by molecular regulators (sieve-plate occlusion,
P-protein gating) that fine-tune flow without overturning the basic
pressure-driven principle.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection:} Girdling (removal of a ring of bark
including phloem) causes sugar accumulation above the girdle and
starvation below, eventually killing the tree. This principle explains
why bark-stripping by elephants, deer, or porcupines can be lethal.
Conversely, targeted phloem disruption is used as a management tool to
kill invasive tree species.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Nitrogen Fixation
Symbiosis}\label{nitrogen-fixation-symbiosis}

Atmospheric N\(_2\) is inaccessible to plants directly. Some plants form
symbiotic associations with nitrogen-fixing bacteria:

\textbf{Rhizobium-legume symbiosis:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Legume roots secrete flavonoids into the rhizosphere
\item
  Flavonoids activate \emph{nod} genes in \emph{Rhizobium}, producing
  Nod factors (lipochitooligosaccharides)
\item
  Nod factors bind NFR1/NFR5 receptors on root hair cells, triggering
  root hair curling and infection thread formation
\item
  Bacteria enter root cortex via infection thread, released into host
  cells, and differentiate into bacteroids within specialised structures
  called nodules
\item
  Bacteroids express \textbf{nitrogenase} (enzyme complex: Fe-protein +
  MoFe-protein) which catalyses:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{equation}
N_2 + 8H^+ + 8e^- + 16\text{ATP} \rightarrow 2NH_3 + H_2 + 16\text{ADP} + 16P_i
\label{eq:unit_VIII_nitrogenase}
\end{equation}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{5}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Leghemoglobin} (produced by host, gives nodules pink colour)
  maintains low O\(_2\) concentration (nitrogenase is irreversibly
  inhibited by O\(_2\)) while supplying O\(_2\) for bacteroid
  respiration
\end{enumerate}

The plant provides photosynthate (sucrose, then metabolised to
malate/succinate) to the bacteroid; the bacteroid provides fixed
nitrogen as NH\(_4^+\) or amino acids (alanine, aspartate).

Other nitrogen-fixing associations: \emph{Frankia} (actinobacterium)
with alder, bayberry; \emph{Anabaena} with water fern \emph{Azolla}
(used as green manure in rice paddies for millennia).

\subsubsection{Mycorrhizal Associations}\label{mycorrhizal-associations}

\textbf{Mycorrhizae} (``fungus-root'') are mutualistic associations
between plant roots and soil fungi. Approximately \textbf{80\% of land
plant species} form mycorrhizal associations. Two major types:

\textbf{Arbuscular mycorrhizae (AM, Glomeromycota):} - Obligate plant
symbionts; cannot grow without host - Fungal hyphae penetrate root
cortical cells and form branched structures called \textbf{arbuscules}
(sites of nutrient exchange, turn over every 4-10 days) - Extraradical
hyphae extend several centimetres into soil, accessing a far greater
soil volume than roots alone - Primary benefit: phosphorus delivery
(hyphae secrete phosphatases and organic acids to solubilise bound P) -
Plant provides up to 20-30\% of photosynthate to fungus - Found in
about 80\% of land plant species; ancestral association dating
to \textgreater400 million years ago

\textbf{Ectomycorrhizae (EM, Basidiomycota + Ascomycota):} - Hyphae form
a dense sheath (mantle) around root tips - \textbf{Hartig net:} Hyphae
penetrate between cortical cells but do not enter cells - Provide
nitrogen (via proteolytic enzymes that break down soil organic matter)
and phosphorus - Dominant in temperate and boreal forest trees
(\emph{Pinus}, \emph{Betula}, \emph{Fagus}, \emph{Quercus}) - Many EM
fungi produce mushrooms (e.g., chanterelles, truffles, \emph{Amanita})

\textbf{Common mycorrhizal networks (CMNs):} Mycorrhizal fungi can
connect multiple plants, forming underground networks. Carbon, water,
and nutrient signals have been documented moving between plants via
these networks, though the ecological significance of active plant-plant
signalling through CMNs remains debated.

\subsection{Adaptations for Water and Nutrient
Acquisition}\label{adaptations-for-water-and-nutrient-acquisition}

\subsubsection{Xerophyte Adaptations}\label{xerophyte-adaptations}

Plants in arid environments have evolved numerous strategies to minimise
water loss and maximise water uptake:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Thick cuticle and epicuticular waxes} (reduce cuticular
  transpiration)
\item
  \textbf{Sunken stomata} in pits or grooves (create humid
  microenvironment; \emph{Nerium oleander})
\item
  \textbf{Reduced leaf surface area} (needles, spines) or deciduousness
  during dry season
\item
  \textbf{CAM photosynthesis} (stomata open at night, close during day;
  CO\(_2\) stored as malate)
\item
  \textbf{Succulence} (water storage in stems or leaves; \emph{Opuntia},
  \emph{Aloe})
\item
  \textbf{Deep or extensive root systems} (mesquite roots can reach 50+
  m depth)
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Hydrophyte Adaptations}\label{hydrophyte-adaptations}

Aquatic and wetland plants face the opposite challenge -- too much water
and often \hyperref[gl:anaerobic]{\textbf{anaerobic}} substrates:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Aerenchyma} (large air-filled cortical spaces for gas
  transport to submerged roots)
\item
  \textbf{Thin or absent cuticle} (CO\(_2\) and O\(_2\) diffuse directly
  from water)
\item
  \textbf{Dissected or thin leaves} (maximise surface area for gas
  exchange in water)
\item
  \textbf{Adventitious roots} from stem nodes
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Carnivorous Plants}\label{carnivorous-plants}

In nutrient-poor environments (bogs, sandy soils), some plants
supplement mineral nutrition by capturing and digesting insects and
other small animals:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Pitcher plants} (\emph{Nepenthes}, \emph{Sarracenia}):
  modified leaves form pitfall traps with slippery surfaces and
  digestive enzymes
\item
  \textbf{Sundews} (\emph{Drosera}): sticky mucilage on tentacle-like
  trichomes; leaf slowly curls around prey
\item
  \textbf{Venus flytrap} (\emph{Dionaea muscipula}): snap trap triggered
  by touch-sensitive trigger hairs; requires two stimulations within 20
  seconds (counting mechanism involves Ca\(^{2+}\) signalling)
\end{itemize}

Most carnivorous plants derive primarily nitrogen and phosphorus from
prey.

\subsection{Computational Bridge}\label{computational-bridge-24}

Whole-cell water potential sums osmotic and pressure components in MPa:

\begin{Shaded}

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-27}

For \textbf{Plant Structure, Water Relations, and Transport}, frontier
biology belongs inside the evidence logic of the chapter. Plant biology
links molecular regulation to climate stress, water limitation, crop
resilience, phenology, and ecosystem feedbacks. The core reading
question is this: plant-water claims require water potential, hydraulic
pathway, stomatal control, tissue anatomy, and stress context.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

A strong plant explanation names the tissue, signal, environmental
driver, measurable trait, and tradeoff between growth, reproduction,
defence, and water use.

\textbf{Source practice:} For plant-stress and crop claims, name the
tissue, environmental driver, field context, and growth-reproduction
tradeoff; separate laboratory potential from agronomic adoption.

\subsubsection{Current Evidence Map: Hydraulic Safety
Tradeoff}\label{current-evidence-map-hydraulic-safety-tradeoff}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0142_2ce273db44e8.png}
\caption{Drought responses should be read as tradeoffs among carbon gain, water loss, hydraulic safety, and growth rather than as simple stress resistance.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Field Translation: Hydraulic Safety
Margins}\label{field-translation-hydraulic-safety-margins}

Water-potential models move from classroom equations to field prediction
when they name the operating range. A hydraulic safety margin compares
the water potential a plant actually reaches during drought with the
water potential that causes damaging loss of xylem conductivity. Choat
and colleagues found that 70\% of 226 sampled forest species from 81
sites operated with margins narrower than 1 MPa against injurious
hydraulic stress \citep{choat2012hydraulicmargins}. That result is a
warning signal, not a one-number forecast: mortality risk also depends
on rooting depth, stored water, non-structural carbohydrate reserves,
stomatal regulation, recovery after embolism, heat load, pests, and
repeated drought history.

When evaluating a drought-tolerant crop or forest-management claim, ask
for the species, tissue, growth stage, vapor-pressure deficit, soil
depth, measured \(\Psi_{\mathrm{min}}\), embolism threshold, and yield
or survival endpoint. A greenhouse water-potential treatment can
demonstrate mechanism, but field adoption requires replicated seasons
and soils because stomatal closure that protects xylem can reduce carbon
gain and reproduction.

\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-27}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Plant body plan:} Root system (taproot or fibrous) + shoot
  system (stem + leaves). Phytomers (node + internode + leaf + axillary
  bud) are the modular building units; plastochron index sets
  developmental time.
\item
  \textbf{Three tissue systems:} Dermal (protection, cuticle, stomata,
  trichomes), ground (parenchyma for photosynthesis/storage, collenchyma
  for flexible support, sclerenchyma for rigid support), vascular
  (xylem: tracheids/vessels for water; phloem: sieve tubes/companion
  cells for sugars).
\item
  \textbf{Xylem development:} Protoxylem (annular/helical, extensible)
  precedes metaxylem (scalariform/pitted, mechanically robust). Vessels
  are wider and more efficient than tracheids but more cavitation-prone
  (Hagen-Poiseuille r\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{4}}{4} scaling). Conifer pits with torus-margo valves
  provide most-or-nothing cavitation isolation; angiosperm homogeneous
  pit membranes are more vulnerable.
\item
  \textbf{Water potential:} Full four-component form
  \(\Psi = \Psi_s + \Psi_p + \Psi_m + \Psi_g\)
  (\cref{eq:unit_VIII_water_potential}) governs direction of water flow;
  matric potential dominates in dry seeds and soils. The SPAC has a
  steep gradient driving water from soil (\(-0.01\) to \(-1.5\) MPa) to
  atmosphere (\(-100\) MPa).
\item
  \textbf{Transport pathways:} Apoplast (cell walls, fast,
  non-selective) vs symplast (cytoplasm via plasmodesmata, selective) vs
  transmembrane (aquaporins + transporters, selective). Casparian strip
  (lignin) + suberin lamella in endodermis force water into symplast for
  quality control; passage cells provide selective bypasses; lateral
  root emergence creates transient apoplastic bypass.
\item
  \textbf{TACT mechanism \citep{dixon1894}:} Transpiration creates
  tension in xylem; water's cohesive H-bonds maintain continuous column;
  adhesion to xylem walls supports the column; water rises passively.
  Critical evaluation: pressure probes, MRI, synthetic-tree experiments,
  and synchrotron X-ray micro-CT confirm tensions of \(-1\) to \(-22\)
  MPa; embolism repair via overnight root pressure and phloem-driven
  refilling mitigates cavitation losses.
\item
  \textbf{Stomatal regulation:} Opening via H\(^+\)-ATPase, KAT1, malate
  accumulation (blue light, phototropins); closure via
  ABA-PYR-PP2C-SnRK2-SLAC1/GORK cascade. Balances CO\(_2\) gain vs water
  loss; iWUE = \(A_n/g_s\) (\cref{eq:unit_VIII_iwue}). C4 and CAM plants
  achieve iWUE 2--10\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} C3 by concentrating CO\(_2\) behind
  partially-closed stomata.
\item
  \textbf{Phloem:} Münch pressure-flow \citep{munch1930} with apoplastic
  loading (SUT1 cotransporter; herbaceous crops; high sieve-tube
  concentration) or symplastic loading via polymer trap (raffinose; many
  trees; many plasmodesmata; lower concentration) at source.
  Bidirectional flow follows turgor gradient; symplastic vs apoplastic
  unloading varies by sink type.
\item
  \textbf{Nutrient uptake:} 17 essential elements (6 macro, 8 micro,
  plus C/H/O). \hyperref[gl:nitrogen-fixation]{\textbf{Nitrogen
  fixation}} by rhizobia in legume nodules. Mycorrhizae (AM and EM)
  enhance P and N uptake in 80\% of plant species.
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See \cref{sec:unit_VIII_plant_reproduction} and
  \cref{sec:unit_VIII_plant_responses} for reproduction and signalling,
  \cref{sec:unit_I_water_and_life} for water
  \hyperref[gl:thermodynamics]{\textbf{thermodynamics}}, and
  \cref{sec:unit_X_biomes_and_conservation} for primary production.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Key Terms}\label{key-terms-27}

Definition

\endlastfoot
\textbf{Water potential (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Psi}}{Psi})} & Free energy of water per unit volume;
determines direction of water movement; units MPa \\
\textbf{Osmotic potential (\(\Psi_s\))} & Component of water potential
due to solute concentration; typically negative \\
\textbf{Turgor pressure (\(\Psi_p\))} & Positive pressure exerted by
cell contents against the cell wall \\
\textbf{Matric potential (\(\Psi_m\))} & Component due to water binding
on colloidal surfaces; dominant in dry seeds and soils \\
\textbf{Casparian strip} & Lignin (then suberin) band in endodermal cell
walls; forces water through symplast \\
\textbf{Suberin lamella} & Continuous suberin layer in mature endodermal
cells; further restricts apoplast \\
\textbf{Passage cell} & Endodermal cell lacking suberin lamella;
provides selective transport bypass \\
\textbf{Cohesion-tension mechanism} & Transpiration-driven water ascent
relying on hydrogen bond cohesion \\
\textbf{Cavitation} & Formation of gas bubble in xylem under excessive
tension \\
\textbf{Stomata} & Pores bounded by guard cells; regulate gas exchange
and transpiration \\
\textbf{Apoplast} & Continuum of cell walls and intercellular spaces \\
\textbf{Symplast} & Continuum of cytoplasm connected by plasmodesmata \\
\textbf{Tracheids} & Elongated, tapered xylem cells with bordered pits;
found in most vascular plants \\
\textbf{Vessel elements} & Wide xylem cells with perforation plates;
primarily in angiosperms \\
\textbf{Bordered pit (torus-margo)} & Conifer pit with thickened central
torus suspended in porous margo; valves on cavitation \\
\textbf{Protoxylem} & Early xylem with annular/helical thickenings;
extensible during organ growth \\
\textbf{Metaxylem} & Late xylem with scalariform/pitted thickenings;
mechanically robust \\
\textbf{Sieve tube elements} & Enucleate phloem cells connected by sieve
plates; conduct sugars \\
\textbf{Companion cells} & Nucleate cells that metabolically support
sieve tube elements \\
\textbf{SUT1 (SUC2)} & Sucrose-H\(^+\) symporter on companion cells;
rate-limiting loader in apoplastic species \\
\textbf{SWEET11/12} & Sucrose efflux carriers; export sucrose from
mesophyll to apoplast \\
\textbf{Polymer trap} & Symplastic loading mechanism using
raffinose-family oligosaccharides \\
\textbf{Plasmodesmatal conductance} & Bulk transfer rate through
plasmodesmata; regulated by callose deposition \\
\textbf{Münch pressure-flow} & Model of phloem transport driven by
turgor pressure gradient from source to sink \\
\textbf{Phytomer} & Modular shoot unit: node + internode + leaf +
axillary bud \\
\textbf{Plastochron index} & Time interval between successive
leaf-primordium initiations \\
\textbf{Mycorrhizae} & Mutualistic root-fungus associations; enhance
nutrient uptake \\
\textbf{Arbuscular mycorrhizae} & AM fungi that form arbuscules inside
root cortical cells; deliver P \\
\textbf{Ectomycorrhizae} & EM fungi that form external mantle and Hartig
net; deliver N and P \\
\textbf{Nitrogenase} & Enzyme complex in nitrogen-fixing bacteria;
converts N\(_2\) to NH\(_3\) \\
\textbf{Aquaporins} & Water channel proteins (PIP, TIP families) in
plant cell membranes \\
\textbf{OST1/SnRK2.6} & Master kinase of guard-cell ABA response;
phosphorylates SLAC1 \\
\textbf{iWUE (intrinsic WUE)} & \(A_n/g_s\); net CO\(_2\) assimilated
per unit stomatal conductance \\
\end{longtable}
}
