\subsection{Review Questions}\label{review-questions-27}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  A plant cell has a solute concentration of 0.4 M, turgor pressure of
  0.3 MPa, and is at ground level. Using \(\Psi_s = -iCRT\) with
  \(i = 1\), \(R = 0.00831\) L MPa mol\(^{-1}\) K\(^{-1}\), and
  \(T = 298\) K, calculate the total water potential. If this cell is
  adjacent to another cell with \(\Psi = -0.5\) MPa, which direction
  will water flow?
\item
  Explain why xylem vessels are more efficient than tracheids for water
  transport but also more vulnerable to cavitation. What structural
  features of tracheids (torus-margo pits) help prevent the spread of
  embolisms? Contrast with angiosperm pit membranes.
\item
  Describe the complete pathway of a water molecule from the soil
  solution to the atmosphere, naming each structure it passes through.
  At which points must the molecule cross a cell membrane?
\item
  Compare apoplastic and symplastic phloem loading. Which is more common
  in herbaceous crop plants? What is the energetic cost of each, and why
  might symplastic loading be advantageous in some environments? Cite
  SUT1 and the polymer-trap mechanism in your answer.
\item
  A farmer observes that phosphorus-deficient plants show improved
  growth when inoculated with arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi but not when
  given additional phosphorus fertiliser alone. Explain this observation
  in terms of the spatial distribution of phosphorus in soil and the
  relative surface area of roots vs mycorrhizal hyphae.
\item
  Explain how the Casparian strip (lignin) and suberin lamella of the
  endodermis act as a quality control checkpoint. What would happen to
  plant ion \hyperref[gl:homeostasis]{\textbf{homeostasis}} if the
  Casparian strip were absent? What is the role of passage cells in
  older roots? Account for apoplastic bypasses at lateral root emergence
  sites.
\item
  During a heat wave, a crop plant simultaneously experiences high
  temperatures (stomatal opening signal from photosynthesis demand) and
  soil drying (ABA-mediated stomatal closure signal). Trace the
  molecular competition between these signals at the level of OST1/SLAC1
  in guard cells and predict which typically dominates.
\item
  Compare and contrast water movement in xylem and phloem in terms of:
  driving force, direction, conducting cell viability, and substances
  transported.
\item
  Describe the nitrogen fixation symbiosis between \emph{Rhizobium} and
  legumes. Why must nitrogenase be protected from oxygen, and how does
  the nodule accomplish this?
\item
  A coast redwood (\emph{Sequoia sempervirens}) is 100 m tall. Calculate
  the gravitational component of water potential at the top of the tree.
  Given that atmospheric \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Psi}}{Psi} can reach \(-100\) MPa at 50\% humidity,
  explain why the tree can still pull water to the canopy.
\item
  Critically evaluate the cohesion-tension theory \citep{dixon1894}.
  Identify two lines of evidence supporting it (including synchrotron
  imaging) and one historical objection that has been resolved. What is
  the air-seeding hypothesis, and how does it apply to torus-margo pits?
\item
  Using \breaktt{transpiration\_flux}, predict whether doubling stomatal
  conductance doubles water loss if the leaf-to-air vapour gradient is
  held fixed. Then compute the iWUE consequence assuming \(A_n\)
  saturates at 80\% of the doubled \(g_s\).
\item
  Contrast \textbf{hydraulic redistribution} via roots with capillary
  rise in soil --- when does each dominate overnight water status?
\item
  Use the Hagen-Poiseuille equation \cref{eq:unit_VIII_hagen_poiseuille}
  to estimate the relative volumetric flow capacity of a 200-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m vessel
  versus a 30-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m tracheid (same length and pressure gradient). How does
  this calculation explain the prevalence of vessels in fast-transpiring
  angiosperms?
\item
  A C3 wheat plant achieves iWUE of 80 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}mol CO\(_2\) mol\(^{-1}\)
  H\(_2\)O; an adjacent C4 maize plant achieves iWUE of 200. Both have
  nearly identical \(A_n\) when measured at noon. Calculate the relative
  \(g_s\) of the two species and explain why C4 plants outcompete C3 in
  semi-arid regions.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-28}

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Describe the alternation of generations and explain the evolutionary
  trend from gametophyte-\hyperref[gl:dominant]{\textbf{dominant}} to
  sporophyte-dominant life cycles across the plant kingdom.
\item
  Compare reproduction in non-vascular plants, seedless vascular plants,
  gymnosperms, and \hyperref[gl:angiosperm]{\textbf{angiosperm}}s.
\item
  Describe angiosperm flower structure and explain the ABCDE model of
  floral organ identity \citep{coen1991}, including the molecular

\item
  Describe pollen grain and embryo sac architecture at cellular

  \citep{nawaschin1898}, including pollen tube chemotropism, synergid
  degeneration, and sperm cell delivery.
\item
  Explain microsporogenesis, megasporogenesis, and endosperm development
  (free-nuclear, cellular, PEG-pathway) including the 2m:1p genome
  dosage.
\item
  Compare seed dormancy types (physical, physiological, morphological,
  morphophysiological, combinatorial) and the molecular basis of
  germination triggers (stratification, scarification, light via
  phytochrome).
\item
  Describe self-incompatibility (SSI vs GSI), apomixis (sporophytic vs
  gametophytic), polyploidy, and vegetative propagation strategies.
\item
  Explain embryogenesis and meristem organisation (SAM/RAM) including
  the WUS-CLV3 feedback loop, fruit development, and parthenocarpy.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Opening Vignette --- The Seeds That Fed a Billion People}

In the 1950s, famines threatened South Asia and Latin America as human
population growth outpaced food production. Norman Borlaug, an American
agronomist working in Mexico with the Rockefeller Foundation, spent a
decade cross-breeding wheat varieties --- shuttling seeds between winter
and summer growing seasons to double selection speed --- until he
produced semi-dwarf, disease-resistant wheat varieties that yielded
three to four times as much grain as traditional tall-stem wheats.
Unlike traditional wheats, the short stems didn't fall over when
supporting heavy grain heads. He introduced these seeds to Pakistan and
India in 1965. By 1970, wheat production had doubled in both countries,
and famine had been averted. Borlaug received the 1970 Nobel Peace
Prize. The same innovations, later extended to rice by the International
Rice Research Institute, constitute the Green Revolution --- a triumph
of applied plant reproductive biology that is estimated to have saved
over a billion lives.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Alternation of
Generations}\label{alternation-of-generations}

Plants have a \textbf{diphasic life cycle} -- alternating between a
diploid \textbf{sporophyte} (spore-producing) generation and a haploid
\textbf{gametophyte} (\hyperref[gl:gamete]{\textbf{gamete}}-producing)
generation. This alternation is unique to plants and some algae; animals
have primarily a brief haploid gametic phase.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0143_b2c05fc6accc.png}
\caption{Alternation of generations showing the two phases of the plant life cycle The sporophyte (2n) produces haploid spores by meiosis. Spores develop into the gametophyte (n), which produces gametes by mitosis. Fertilisation restores the diploid sporophyte.}
\end{figure}

Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts) & \textbf{Haploid gametophyte} (the
leafy ``plant'') & Free-living; nutritionally independent & Water
required (flagellated sperm swim) \\
Pteridophytes (ferns, horsetails) & \textbf{Diploid sporophyte} & Small,
free-living prothallus (about 1 cm\(^2\)); needs moisture &
Water required \\
Gymnosperms (\emph{Pinus}, \emph{Ginkgo}, cycads) & Diploid sporophyte &
Reduced; pollen = 4-celled male gametophyte; archegonia in ovule =
female gametophyte & Wind pollination; no water needed \\
Angiosperms (flowering plants) & Diploid sporophyte & Microscopic,
dependent: pollen = 3-celled; embryo sac = 7-celled, 8-nuclei & Wind or
animal pollination \\
\end{longtable}

\textbf{Why does dominance shift to the sporophyte?} Diploid cells can
mask deleterious recessive \hyperref[gl:mutation]{\textbf{mutation}}s
(\hyperref[gl:heterozygous]{\textbf{heterozygous}} advantage). A diploid
sporophyte can accumulate more genetic material enabling structural
complexity -- leaves, stems, vascular tissue, seeds -- allowing
colonisation of increasingly dry terrestrial habitats. The seed is the
key innovation: it encases the embryo and gametophyte within maternal
tissue, eliminating dependence on external water for fertilisation.

\subsubsection{Worked Example: Tracking Ploidy Through the Angiosperm
Life
Cycle}\label{worked-example-tracking-ploidy-through-the-angiosperm-life-cycle}

\textbf{Problem:} Maize (\emph{Zea mays}) has a sporophyte chromosome
number of \(2n = 20\). Track the chromosome number at each stage of
alternation of generations, then determine the ploidy of the zygote and
the primary endosperm nucleus produced by double fertilisation.

\textbf{Solution:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Establish the haploid number.} The gametophyte (haploid)
  number is half the sporophyte number:
  \[ n = \frac{2n}{2} = \frac{20}{2} = 10 \text{ chromosomes} \label{eq:unit_VIII_plant_reproduction_item_7}\]
\item
  \textbf{Meiosis in the sporophyte.} The diploid megaspore mother cell
  (\(2n = 20\)) undergoes meiosis, producing haploid megaspores with
  \(n = 10\). The surviving megaspore divides \textbf{mitotically} to
  build the embryo sac, so the egg cell and each of the two polar nuclei
  most carry \(n = 10\). The pollen (microgametophyte) likewise delivers
  sperm cells with \(n = 10\).
\item
  \textbf{First fusion --- the zygote.} One sperm fuses with the egg:
  \[ \text{zygote} = n_{\text{egg}} + n_{\text{sperm}} = 10 + 10 = 20 \;\; (2n,\ \text{diploid embryo}) \label{eq:unit_VIII_plant_reproduction_item_8}\]
\item
  \textbf{Second fusion --- the endosperm.} The second sperm fuses with
  the two polar nuclei of the central cell:
  \[ \text{primary endosperm nucleus} = n + n + n = 10 + 10 + 10 = 30 \;\; (3n,\ \text{triploid}) \label{eq:unit_VIII_plant_reproduction_item_9}\]
\item
  \textbf{Genome dosage of the endosperm.} Two of the three genomes are
  maternal (the polar nuclei) and one is paternal (the sperm):
  \[ \frac{\text{maternal}}{\text{paternal}} = \frac{2n}{1n} = \frac{20}{10} = \frac{2}{1} \label{eq:unit_VIII_plant_reproduction_item_10}\]
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Interpretation:} Meiosis halves \(2n = 20\) to \(n = 10\) for
the gametophyte generation; the two sperm-mediated fusions of double
fertilisation then restore a \(2n = 20\) embryo and create a distinctive
\(3n = 30\) endosperm with a fixed 2:1 maternal:paternal dosage --- the
genetic substrate for the parent-of-origin conflict conserved across
flowering plants.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Plant Group Reproductive
Strategies}\label{plant-group-reproductive-strategies}

\subsubsection{Non-Vascular Plants
(Bryophytes)}\label{non-vascular-plants-bryophytes}

\textbf{Mosses} (Bryophyta, about 12,000 species),
\textbf{liverworts} (Marchantiophyta), and \textbf{hornworts}
(Anthocerotophyta) represent the ancestral condition:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The \textbf{gametophyte} is the dominant, photosynthetic plant body
\item
  The sporophyte is small, attached to, and nutritionally dependent on
  the gametophyte
\item
  Flagellated sperm must swim through water films to reach the
  archegonium (female reproductive structure)
\item
  Spores dispersed from capsule (sporangium) at tip of sporophyte seta
\item
  Ecological importance: pioneer colonisers of bare rock, form peat
  (carbon reservoir), retain moisture
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Concept Check 1:} Why are mosses restricted to moist habitats?
What aspect of their reproduction limits their distribution?

\subsubsection{Seedless Vascular Plants (Ferns and
Allies)}\label{seedless-vascular-plants-ferns-and-allies}

\textbf{Ferns} (Polypodiopsida, about 10,500 species) represent
the first major shift to sporophyte dominance:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The \textbf{sporophyte} is the dominant plant (the familiar fern
  \hyperref[gl:frond]{\textbf{frond}})
\item
  Sporangia are clustered in \textbf{sori} (singular: sorus) on the
  underside of fronds, often protected by an indusium
\item
  Meiosis in sporangia produces haploid spores
\item
  Spores germinate into a small, heart-shaped \textbf{prothallus} (the
  independent gametophyte, about 1 cm)
\item
  The prothallus bears both antheridia (produce flagellated sperm) and
  archegonia (produce eggs)
\item
  Sperm must swim through water to the archegonium -- the limiting step
\item
  After fertilisation, the new sporophyte grows from the prothallus,
  which eventually withers
\end{itemize}

Horsetails (\emph{Equisetum}) and club mosses (\emph{Lycopodium},
\emph{Selaginella}) are also seedless vascular plants.
\emph{Selaginella} shows early heterospory (different-sized spores for
male and female gametophytes), a precursor to the seed habit.

\subsubsection{Gymnosperms}\label{gymnosperms}

Gymnosperms (``naked seed'') include conifers (about 630
species), cycads (about 350), \emph{Ginkgo biloba} (1 species),
and gnetophytes (about 70). Key reproductive features:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Heterospory:} Microsporangia (in pollen cones/microstrobili)
  produce microspores that develop into pollen grains (male
  gametophyte). Megasporangia (in ovulate cones) produce megaspores that
  develop into the female gametophyte (with archegonia).
\item
  \textbf{Pollen eliminates the need for water} for fertilisation.
  Wind-dispersed pollen lands on the ovule (pollination drop mechanism
  in many gymnosperms).
\item
  \textbf{Slow fertilisation:} In pines, 12-18 months elapse between
  pollination and fertilisation. The pollen tube grows slowly through
  the nucellus to reach the archegonium.
\item
  \textbf{Seeds:} The fertilised ovule develops into a seed containing
  the embryo, stored food (female gametophyte tissue), and a protective
  seed coat derived from the integuments. Seeds are ``naked'' (not
  enclosed in a fruit).
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Angiosperms (Flowering
Plants)}\label{angiosperms-flowering-plants}

Angiosperms (about 300,000 species) are the most diverse plant
group, with several key innovations:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Flowers:} Specialised reproductive structures that facilitate
  pollination (including animal pollination)
\item
  \textbf{Double fertilisation:} Unique to angiosperms, producing both
  embryo and endosperm
\item
  \textbf{Fruits:} Mature ovary wall enclosing seeds; facilitate
  dispersal
\item
  \textbf{Reduced gametophytes:} Male gametophyte = 3-celled pollen
  grain; female gametophyte = 7-celled, 8-nucleate embryo sac
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Angiosperm Flower Structure and the ABCDE
Model}\label{angiosperm-flower-structure-and-the-abcde-model}

\subsubsection{Flower Architecture}\label{flower-architecture}

Angiosperm flowers are \textbf{modified shoots} (shoot lateral organs
with determinate growth). A \textbf{complete flower} contains four
whorls (from outside inward):

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3636}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Whorl
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Name
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Organ
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\midrule\noalign{}

\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
1 (outermost) & Calyx & Sepals & Protect flower bud; photosynthetic;
sometimes petaloid \\
2 & Corolla & Petals & Attract pollinators via colour (UV patterns
visible to bees), scent (monoterpenes), oil rewards \\
3 & Androecium & Stamens (filament + anther) & Pollen production (male
gametophyte) \\
4 (innermost) & Gynoecium & Carpels (pistil) = stigma + style + ovary &
Pollen reception; pollen tube guidance; ovule enclosure \\
\end{longtable}

\textbf{Floral symmetry:} - \textbf{Actinomorphic (radially symmetric):}
\emph{Rosa}, \emph{Ranunculus}, most basal angiosperms -- generalised
pollinators - \textbf{Zygomorphic (bilaterally symmetric):} Orchidaceae,
Fabaceae, Scrophulariaceae -- specialised pollinators

\textbf{Incomplete flowers} lack one or more whorls. \textbf{Imperfect
flowers} lack either stamens (pistillate/female flowers) or carpels
(staminate/male flowers). Monoecious plants bear both on the same
individual (maize); dioecious plants bear them on separate individuals
(holly, willow).

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{The ABCDE Model and MADS-Box Floral
Quartets
\citep{coen1991}}{The ABCDE Model and MADS-Box Floral Quartets}}\label{the-abcde-model-and-mads-box-floral-quartets}

The combinatorial control of floral organ identity by \textbf{MADS-box
transcription factors} is the foundational discovery of plant evo-devo,
and it provides a quantitative framework for understanding floral
diversity. The classical ABC model (Coen and Meyerowitz, 1991) was
extended by the discovery of D and E classes:

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1111}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3111}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4667}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Whorl
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Organ
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
\hyperref[gl:gene]{\textbf{Gene}}s (\emph{Arabidopsis})
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
1 & Sepal & A + E & AP1, AP2, SEP1-4 \\
2 & Petal & A + B + E & AP1, AP2, AP3, PI, SEP1-4 \\
3 & Stamen & B + C + E & AP3, PI, AG, SEP1-4 \\
4 & Carpel & C + E & AG, SEP1-4 \\
Inside whorl 4 & Ovule & D + E & SHP1, SHP2, STK, SEP1-4 \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Molecular identities of the ABC classes:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{A class (AP1, AP2):} AP1 is itself a MADS-box gene; AP2
  belongs to the unrelated AP2/ERF family --- an ``ABC anomaly''
  reflecting the fact that the canonical model was assembled before most
  molecular identities were known. AP1 specifies sepal identity in whorl
  1 and contributes to petal identity in whorl 2.
\item
  \textbf{B class (AP3 and PI):} Both are MADS-box genes; AP3 and PI
  form an obligate heterodimer (AP3-PI). This heterodimer is required
  for petal (with A) and stamen (with C) specification. \emph{ap3} or
  \emph{pi} single mutants lose petals and stamens.
\item
  \textbf{C class (AG = AGAMOUS):} A MADS-box gene that specifies stamen
  identity (with B) and carpel identity (alone, with E). AG also
  enforces floral meristem determinacy: in \emph{ag} mutants, the floral
  meristem proliferates indefinitely, generating extra petals in place
  of stamens and a new flower in place of a carpel --- the genetic basis
  of ``double flowers'' in cultivated roses, carnations, and
  chrysanthemums.
\item
  \textbf{D class (STK, SHP1, SHP2):} MADS-box genes specifying ovule
  identity within whorl 4. Loss of D-class function converts ovules to
  leaf-like structures.
\item
  \textbf{E class (SEP1, SEP2, SEP3, SEP4):} SEPALLATA MADS-box genes;
  required for combinatorial action of A, B, C, D. \emph{sep1 sep2 sep3
  sep4} quadruple mutants produce primarily sepal-like organs in most
  whorls.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The MADS-box and the floral quartet model:}

The \textbf{MADS-box} is a 56-amino-acid DNA-binding domain (named for
MCM1, AGAMOUS, DEFICIENS, SRF --- the founding members). MADS-box
proteins bind CArG-box DNA motifs (CC{[}A/T{]}\(_6\)GG) and form
\textbf{floral quartets} (Theissen and Saedler, 2001): tetrameric
complexes that combinatorially specify each whorl's identity by binding
two CArG boxes simultaneously, looping the intervening DNA. The
four-protein composition determines target gene specificity:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  AP1-AP1-SEP3-SEP3 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} sepal
\item
  AP3-PI-AP1-SEP3 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} petal
\item
  AP3-PI-AG-SEP3 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} stamen
\item
  AG-AG-SEP3-SEP3 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} carpel
\end{itemize}

\begin{equation}
\text{A} + \text{B} + \text{C} + \text{D} + \text{E} \xrightarrow{\text{combinatorial CArG binding}} \text{floral quartet}
\label{eq:unit_VIII_floral_quartet}
\end{equation}

\textbf{Key predictions and experimental validation:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Removing A class (\emph{ap1}/\emph{ap2} mutants) results in carpels in
  whorls 1 and 2 (C class spreads to fill most whorls)
\item
  Removing B class (\emph{ap3}/\emph{pi} mutants): sepals in whorls 1
  and 2; carpels in whorls 3 and 4
\item
  Removing C class (\emph{ag} mutant): petals instead of stamens (whorl
  3) and further petals indefinitely instead of carpel (whorl 4);
  produces double-petalled ``full'' flowers --- the classic phenotype of
  cultivated double roses, carnations, and chrysanthemums
\item
  Removing E class (\emph{sep1 sep2 sep3 sep4} quadruple mutant): most
  whorls produce sepal-like organs, demonstrating SEP genes are required
  for B, C, and D function
\item
  \textbf{Quintuple ABCDE mutant:} Most whorls produce leaf-like organs
  --- confirming the molecular interpretation of Goethe's 1790
  metamorphosis hypothesis that most floral organs are modified leaves
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection:} Understanding the ABCDE model has
practical applications in crop breeding. Manipulating floral organ
identity genes can create male-sterile lines (essential for hybrid seed
production in rice and wheat) by silencing the B class to convert
stamens to petals. Conversely, increasing petal number in ornamental
varieties relies on partial loss-of-function \emph{ag} alleles. The
multi-billion dollar cut flower industry relies directly on MADS-box
gene variants for double-flowered roses, carnations, and chrysanthemums.
\end{quote}

See \cref{eq:unit_VIII_floral_quartet} for the combinatorial logic; the
empirical demonstration in \emph{Antirrhinum} and \emph{Arabidopsis} is
the foundational work of \citet{coen1991}.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Gametophyte Generation -- Cellular
Architecture}\label{gametophyte-generation-cellular-architecture}

\subsubsection{Male Gametophyte: Microsporogenesis and Pollen Grain
Architecture}\label{male-gametophyte-microsporogenesis-and-pollen-grain-architecture}

The mature pollen grain is the most reduced male gametophyte known ---
three cells encased in a desiccation-resistant wall. Its development is
a textbook case of asymmetric cell division.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0144_c19e702b611c.png}
\caption{Architecture of an angiosperm pollen grain at maturity The tube cell envelops the generative cell, which divides to yield two sperm cells either before pollen release (tricellular pollen) or during tube growth (bicellular pollen at release).}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Pollen wall layers:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Intine (inner):} Cellulose + pectin; uniform thickness;
  secreted by the gametophyte itself
\item
  \textbf{Exine (outer):} Sporopollenin (oxidatively polymerised
  phenylpropanoids and fatty acids); deposited by the surrounding
  sporophytic tapetum. Sporopollenin is among the most chemically inert
  biopolymers known --- it is essentially indestructible by acid, base,
  or enzymatic attack, allowing pollen to survive millions of years in
  sediment. Exine sculpturing patterns (colpi, pores, reticulations) are
  diagnostic for plant families and form the basis of
  \textbf{palynology} (fossil pollen analysis).
\item
  \textbf{Tryphine and pollenkitt:} Lipid-rich material in exine
  cavities; contains species-specific recognition factors (S-locus
  proteins, lipidic adhesins) and is essential for hydration on the
  stigma surface
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pollen cell architecture and microsporogenesis:}

The mature pollen grain is a 3-celled structure: one large
\textbf{vegetative (tube) cell} with a single decondensed nucleus,
enclosing two small \textbf{sperm cells} (the germline). Its development
proceeds through five steps:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Archesporial cells} within the anther microsporangium
  differentiate into diploid \textbf{microspore mother cells (MMCs)} ---
  also called pollen mother cells
\item
  Each MMC undergoes \textbf{meiosis I + II} to produce \textbf{4
  haploid microspores}, initially held as a tetrad surrounded by a
  \textbf{callose} wall (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-1,3-glucan). The tapetum (a sporophytic
  somatic cell layer surrounding the developing microspores) secretes
  \textbf{callase} (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-1,3-glucanase) at a precisely timed point to
  dissolve callose and release individual microspores.
\item
  \textbf{Microspore mitosis I} is \textbf{asymmetric}: the microspore
  nucleus migrates to one side, and an asymmetric division produces a
  small \textbf{generative cell} and a large \textbf{vegetative cell}.
  The generative cell is engulfed by the vegetative cell cytoplasm --- a
  ``cell within a cell'' architecture unique to plant gametogenesis.
  Asymmetric division depends on the GAMETOPHYTE-DEFECTIVE 1 / DUO1
  transcriptional network.
\item
  \textbf{Microspore mitosis II} divides the generative cell to produce
  \textbf{2 sperm cells}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    In \textbf{tricellular pollen} (about 30\% of species;
    \emph{Arabidopsis}, \emph{Brassicaceae}, grasses) mitosis II
    completes before pollen is released from the anther
  \item
    In \textbf{bicellular pollen} (about 70\% of species; most
    flowering plants) mitosis II occurs in the growing pollen tube after
    pollination
  \end{itemize}
\item
  The mature pollen grain = 1 vegetative cell + 2 sperm cells = the
  complete \textbf{male gametophyte}
\end{enumerate}

The two sperm cells are not equivalent: one is ``leading'' and tends to
fuse with the egg, the other ``trailing'' with the central cell. The
recognition mechanism uses cell-surface markers --- though preferred
matching is statistical rather than absolute.

\subsubsection{Female Gametophyte: Megasporogenesis and the
Polygonum-Type Embryo
Sac}\label{female-gametophyte-megasporogenesis-and-the-polygonum-type-embryo-sac}

The angiosperm female gametophyte is also drastically reduced --- a
7-celled, 8-nucleate structure embedded in the ovule. The
\textbf{Polygonum-type} embryo sac (about 70\% of angiosperms)
is the canonical form.

\textbf{Cell types and their functions:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Egg cell} (1, micropylar): Haploid; becomes the zygote upon
  fertilisation. Polarised: nucleus near the chalazal end, large vacuole
  at the micropylar end. Specifies the apical--basal axis of the future
  embryo.
\item
  \textbf{Synergids} (2, micropylar; flank the egg): Haploid. Critical
  functions:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Secrete \textbf{LURE peptides} (CRP810 family; species-specific)
    through the \textbf{filiform apparatus} (an elaborate cell-wall
    labyrinth at the micropylar pole that increases secretory surface
    area), guiding the pollen tube to the ovule
  \item
    One synergid degenerates (programmed cell death) upon pollen tube
    arrival, providing the entry channel
  \item
    Express the \textbf{FERONIA-LORELEI receptor complex} required for
    pollen tube reception and rupture
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Central cell} (1, large, central): Contains \textbf{2 polar
  nuclei} (which fuse before or during fertilisation to form a diploid
  secondary nucleus). Becomes the \textbf{triploid endosperm} upon
  fertilisation with one sperm. The canonical 2:1 maternal:paternal
  genome dosage is widespread across angiosperms and is the substrate
  for genomic imprinting and parental conflict, as discussed in the
  genomic-imprinting section.
\item
  \textbf{Antipodal cells} (3, chalazal): Function in nutritive/transfer
  roles. Highly polyploid (up to 32 n via endoreduplication) in grasses,
  where they are long-lived; in \emph{Arabidopsis} and most dicots,
  antipodals degenerate before fertilisation.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Megasporogenesis and Embryo Sac Development:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  A single \textbf{megaspore mother cell (MMC)} (also called
  megasporocyte) within the ovule's nucellus undergoes meiosis,
  producing 4 haploid megaspores in a linear tetrad along the
  chalazal-micropylar axis
\item
  \textbf{Three megaspores degenerate} via programmed cell death; the
  surviving (typically chalazal) \textbf{functional megaspore} alone
  gives rise to the female gametophyte. The selectivity of which
  megaspore survives is partly genetic (auxin gradients, AGO9-dependent
  siRNA silencing of competing megaspores) and partly stochastic.
\item
  The functional megaspore undergoes \textbf{3 rounds of free nuclear
  mitosis} (without cytokinesis) producing an 8-nucleate coenocyte. The
  8 nuclei migrate to specific positions: 4 nuclei toward each pole.
\item
  \textbf{Cellularisation:} Cell walls form around the 8 nuclei to
  establish the 7 cells: 1 egg + 2 synergids + 1 central cell (with 2
  polar nuclei, one from each pole) + 3 antipodals = the \textbf{mature
  embryo sac}
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Concept Check 2:} A mutation eliminates the synergids during
embryo sac development (synergid-less \emph{gametophyte mutant1}).
Predict which steps of fertilisation will fail and why double
fertilisation cannot proceed.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Pollination, Pollen-Pistil Interactions, and Double
Fertilisation}\label{pollination-pollen-pistil-interactions-and-double-fertilisation}

\subsubsection{Pollination Systems}\label{pollination-systems}

\textbf{Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma} occurs by various
vectors, each associated with characteristic floral traits (pollination
syndromes):

\textbf{80\% of flowering plants} are insect-pollinated (entomophilous).
Global pollination services estimated at about \$577
billion/year (IPBES 2016).

\textbf{Concept Check 3:} A plant species has small, green, scentless
flowers that produce copious dry pollen. What is its likely pollination
vector? What other structural features would you expect?

\subsubsection{Pollen-Pistil Interactions: Self-Incompatibility (SI)
Systems}\label{pollen-pistil-interactions-self-incompatibility-si-systems}

Self-incompatibility (SI) is a widespread genetic mechanism preventing
self-pollination and inbreeding depression. Approximately \textbf{40\%
of angiosperm species} have functional SI. The molecular logic divides
into two paradigms based on whether the pollen's incompatibility
phenotype is determined by its own (haploid) genotype or by the
(diploid) genotype of the pollen-producing parent.

\textbf{Sporophytic SI (SSI)} --- \emph{Brassica} (cabbage, mustard),
\emph{Ipomoea}, Asteraceae

The pollen rejection phenotype is determined by the \textbf{diploid}
sporophytic tissue of the anther (specifically, the tapetum that
deposits proteins onto the pollen wall) --- \emph{not} by the pollen
grain's own haploid genotype.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{S-locus genes:}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{SRK} (S-receptor kinase): Stigma-expressed; receptor on the
    stigma papilla membrane
  \item
    \textbf{SCR/SP11} (S-locus cysteine-rich protein 11; pollen coat
    protein): Deposited on pollen exine by the diploid tapetum during
    pollen maturation
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Mechanism:} When SRK on the stigma encounters its matching SCR
  on the incoming pollen (i.e., self-pollen sharing the same S-haplotype
  as the stigma), SRK autophosphorylates and recruits \textbf{ARC1} (E3
  ubiquitin ligase). ARC1 ubiquitinates \textbf{Exo70A1}, a key
  component of the secretion exocyst required for pollen hydration. The
  pollen fails to hydrate and is rejected at the stigma surface ---
  before pollen tube germination.
\item
  \textbf{Genetic consequence:} Because pollen carries the diploid
  parental S-genotype, most pollen from a heterozygous \emph{S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}} plant
  is rejected by \emph{S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}}, \emph{S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{3}}{3}}, and \emph{S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{3}}{3}} stigmas.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Gametophytic SI (GSI)} --- Solanaceae (\emph{Petunia},
\emph{Nicotiana}, tomato), Rosaceae (apple, pear, almond), Papaveraceae

The pollen rejection phenotype is determined by the pollen grain's own
\textbf{haploid} S-genotype.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{S-locus genes (S-RNase / SLF system):}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{S-RNase}: Pistil-expressed; ribonuclease secreted into the
    style transmitting tract
  \item
    \textbf{SLF (S-locus F-box protein)}: Pollen-expressed; multiple
    SLFs per haplotype, acting collectively
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Mechanism (collaborative non-self recognition):} S-RNase
  enters the growing pollen tube non-specifically. Each SLF can ``tag''
  non-self S-RNases (those whose haplotype does not match the pollen
  tube's own) for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation by the
  SCF\textsuperscript{SLF} complex. \textbf{Self S-RNase escapes
  degradation} because the pollen tube's SLFs cannot recognise the
  matching S-RNase. Surviving S-RNase enters the cytoplasm and degrades
  pollen tube ribosomal RNA, halting tube growth before fertilisation.
\item
  \textbf{Genetic consequence:} A cross between \emph{S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}} and
  \emph{S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{3}}{3}} plants: \emph{S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}} pollen is rejected by both stigmas;
  \emph{S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}} pollen succeeds on the \emph{S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{3}}{3}} stigma; \emph{S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{3}}{3}} pollen
  succeeds on the \emph{S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}} stigma. Half the pollen is accepted;
  offspring genotypes are \emph{S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}}, \emph{S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{3}}{3}}, \emph{S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{3}}{3}} (no
  homozygotes possible).
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Comparative summary:}

\textbf{Evolutionary significance of SI:} Self-incompatibility maintains
heterozygosity and avoids inbreeding depression in obligate outbreeders.
Its breakdown (typically by loss of S-RNase or SLF function) gives rise
to self-compatible lineages, which often go extinct because of genetic
load --- but occasionally undergo spectacular adaptive radiations (e.g.,
self-compatible \emph{Arabidopsis thaliana} descended from
self-incompatible \emph{A. lyrata}; the loss of SI may have facilitated
\emph{A. thaliana}'s colonisation of new habitats by enabling
single-individual founder events).

\subsubsection{Polyploidy and Speciation in
Plants}\label{polyploidy-and-speciation-in-plants}

Plants exhibit far higher rates of polyploidy than animals;
\textbf{about 70\% of angiosperm species} retain evidence of
one or more whole-genome duplications in their evolutionary history.

\textbf{Modes of polyploid origin:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Autopolyploidy:} Whole-genome duplication within a single
  species; chromosomes form quadrivalents at meiosis, often causing
  reduced fertility initially
\item
  \textbf{Allopolyploidy:} Hybridisation between two species followed by
  chromosome doubling; chromosomes from each parental genome pair
  separately as bivalents, restoring fertility. Most cultivated
  polyploids are allopolyploids.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pathways:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Unreduced gamete fusion:} Two 2n gametes fuse to form a 4n
  zygote (one in 1000 gametes is unreduced)
\item
  \textbf{Somatic doubling:} Spontaneous chromosome doubling in a
  meristematic cell during somatic growth
\item
  \textbf{Triploid bridge:} Triploids (3n) produce a wide variety of
  unbalanced gametes; some 4n offspring arise from these
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Polyploid crops:} Wheat (hexaploid: AABBDD genomes from three
ancestral diploids), cotton (tetraploid), strawberry (octoploid), banana
(often triploid, sterile), oats (hexaploid).

\textbf{Polyploidy promotes speciation} because new polyploids are
reproductively isolated from their parental species (triploid offspring
of a 2n \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 4n cross are sterile), creating an instant reproductive
barrier. Polyploids often exhibit \textbf{heterosis} (hybrid vigour),
enlarged organs (the basis of many crop polyploids), and increased
ecological tolerance.

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Double Fertilisation
\citep{nawaschin1898}}{Double Fertilisation}}\label{double-fertilisation}

Sergei Nawaschin's 1898 discovery of double fertilisation in
\emph{Lilium martagon} and \emph{Fritillaria tenella} --- observing two
simultaneous nuclear fusions in a single ovule --- was transformative
for plant biology and remains the defining synapomorphy of angiosperms.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0145_712477dd19ef.png}
\caption{Double fertilisation in angiosperms One sperm fuses with the egg to form the diploid zygote (which develops into the embryo). The second sperm fuses with the central cell's two polar nuclei to form the triploid primary endosperm nucleus (which develops into the nutritive endosperm). This process is unique to angiosperms.}
\end{figure}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Pollen tube germination on the stigma:} Compatible pollen
  hydrates within minutes on the stigma surface; the \textbf{vegetative
  (tube) cell} extends a callose-walled tube. Tip growth is driven by:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    A \textbf{tip-focused {[}Ca\(^{2+}\){]} gradient}
    (about 1.5--10 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}M at the apex; about 150 nM in the
    shank)
  \item
    Vesicle-mediated wall deposition (callose for tube wall, pectin for
    the inner wall)
  \item
    Cytoplasmic streaming carrying the generative/sperm cells to the tip
  \item
    Growth rates: 1--10 mm/h in \emph{Lilium}, 1 cm/h in maize
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Spermatogenesis during tube elongation (in bicellular
  species):} The generative cell, carried in the tube cell cytoplasm,
  undergoes mitosis II during pollen tube growth, producing the two
  sperm cells. In tricellular species (\emph{Arabidopsis}, grasses),
  this division has already occurred before pollen release.
\item
  \textbf{Pollen tube guidance --- chemotropism:} The pollen tube
  navigates through the style and ovary toward a single receptive ovule
  via a cascade of guidance cues:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{Style cues:} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma}-aminobutyric acid (GABA) gradient in the
    transmitting tract; cysteine-rich peptides
  \item
    \textbf{Funicular guidance:} Short-range cues from ovary tissue
  \item
    \textbf{Micropylar guidance:} \textbf{LURE peptides} (defensin-like,
    cysteine-rich; CRP810 family) released from the synergid filiform
    apparatus; species-specific. \emph{Torenia} LURE1/LURE2 attract
    pollen tubes specifically of the same species --- the molecular
    basis of inter-species pollination barriers. LURE peptides bind PRK6
    receptor kinases on the pollen tube tip, biasing tip growth toward
    the source.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Synergid degeneration:} As the pollen tube approaches the
  ovule, \textbf{one of the two synergids undergoes programmed cell
  death} (within minutes; the receptive synergid). Loss of synergid
  integrity:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Creates the entry channel into the embryo sac
  \item
    Releases pre-stored signalling molecules
  \item
    Exposes the \textbf{FERONIA (FER)} receptor kinase / \textbf{LORELEI
    (LRE)} GPI-anchored co-receptor complex on the persisting synergid
    surface
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Pollen tube reception and rupture:} FER-LRE signalling, via
  reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated by RBOH NADPH oxidases and
  elevated cytosolic {[}Ca\(^{2+}\){]}, triggers explosive rupture of
  the pollen tube tip, releasing the two sperm cells into the embryo
  sac. The signalling depends on RALF peptides binding FER. In
  \emph{fer} mutants, pollen tubes enter the synergid but fail to
  rupture (continued growth and ``supernumerary'' pollen tube delivery
  --- the polyspermy phenotype).
\item
  \textbf{Sperm cell delivery and double fusion:}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{Sperm 1 + egg cell} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} karyogamy \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{2n zygote} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
    embryo
  \item
    \textbf{Sperm 2 + 2 polar nuclei (central cell)} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} triple fusion \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
    \textbf{3n primary endosperm nucleus} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} endosperm
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\begin{equation}
\text{LURE} \xrightarrow{\text{LRE-FER complex}} \text{tube rupture} \rightarrow 2 \text{ sperm released}
\label{eq:unit_VIII_lre_fer}
\end{equation}

\textbf{Significance of double fertilisation:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Endosperm provides a ``payment on delivery'' mechanism --- primarily
  fertilised ovules develop endosperm, ensuring optimal parental
  investment
\item
  Endosperm in cereals: starch (70-80\%), storage proteins (gluten in
  wheat, zein in maize), oils, vitamins --- source of
  about 60\% of global human caloric intake
\item
  Triploid endosperm (2 maternal : 1 paternal genome dose) provides a
  unique genetic substrate for \textbf{parental conflict}
  (paternally-imprinted genes promote nutrient transfer;
  maternally-imprinted genes restrict it) --- conserved in ratio across
  most flowering plants
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection:} Understanding pollen tube guidance has
implications for crop fertility. In interspecific crosses (e.g., wheat \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x}
rye to produce triticale), pollen tube guidance often fails because LURE
peptides are species-specific. Genetic engineering of LURE receptors
could enable wider crosses for crop improvement.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Endosperm Development and Seed
Biology}\label{endosperm-development-and-seed-biology}

\subsubsection{Endosperm Development: Free-Nuclear, Cellular,
Helobial}\label{endosperm-development-free-nuclear-cellular-helobial}

After triple fusion, the primary endosperm cell (3n; typically 2m:1p
genome ratio) undergoes a stereotyped developmental sequence that
determines the storage architecture of the mature seed. The 2:1
maternal:paternal genome ratio is the canonical angiosperm pattern and
is important for normal seed development, while some lineages show
dosage and developmental variation.

\textbf{Three modes of endosperm development:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Nuclear (free-nuclear) endosperm --- most common:} The primary
  endosperm nucleus undergoes repeated mitosis without cytokinesis,
  producing a \textbf{syncytium} of hundreds to thousands of nuclei in a
  common cytoplasm with a large central vacuole. Examples:
  \emph{Arabidopsis}, maize, rice, wheat, coconut (the ``coconut water''
  of an immature coconut is liquid free-nuclear endosperm). After
  about 6--8 nuclear divisions, \textbf{cellularisation}
  initiates from the periphery inward, with cell walls forming radially
  around each nucleus. The mature cellular endosperm then accumulates
  storage products (starch, protein, oil).
\item
  \textbf{Cellular endosperm:} Cytokinesis accompanies every mitosis
  from the start; the endosperm is cellular throughout. Examples:
  \emph{Petunia}, tobacco, magnoliid lineages.
\item
  \textbf{Helobial endosperm:} The first division separates a small
  chalazal cell from a large micropylar cell; subsequent divisions are
  nuclear in the micropylar half and cellular in the chalazal half.
  Examples: many monocots in Alismatales.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Seed filling:} During the maturation phase (after
cellularisation), endosperm cells accumulate massive amounts of storage
compounds: - \textbf{Starch:} Synthesised from sucrose imported from
maternal phloem; deposited in plastids (amyloplasts). Cereal grain
starch can reach 60--70\% of dry mass. - \textbf{Storage proteins:}
Family-specific (zeins in maize, glutenins/gliadins in wheat, prolamines
in rice, globulins in legumes). Stored in protein bodies derived from
the ER and vacuole. - \textbf{Oils:} Triacylglycerols stored in oil
bodies (oleosomes); dominant in oilseeds (sunflower, canola, soybean).

\textbf{The PEG/MEG pathway and parental conflict:}

The \textbf{FIS-PRC2} (FERTILIZATION INDEPENDENT SEED -- Polycomb
Repressive Complex 2) complex --- comprising MEDEA (MEA), FIS2, FIE, and
MSI1 --- is the master regulator of endosperm initiation and parental
conflict resolution:

\begin{equation}
\text{Maternal MEA-FIE-FIS2-MSI1} \xrightarrow{\text{H3K27me3}} \text{repression of paternally-imprinted genes (PEGs)}
\label{eq:unit_VIII_peg_pathway}
\end{equation}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{PEGs (Paternally Expressed Genes):} Expressed primarily from
  the paternal allele in endosperm (the maternal allele is silenced by
  H3K27me3 deposited by FIS-PRC2). Examples: \emph{PHE1}, \emph{YUC10},
  \emph{AHL10}. PEGs tend to \textbf{promote} endosperm growth and
  nutrient transfer to the embryo.
\item
  \textbf{MEGs (Maternally Expressed Genes):} Expressed primarily from
  the maternal allele. MEGs tend to \textbf{restrict} endosperm growth.
\item
  \textbf{Imbalance in PEG/MEG dosage} (e.g., crosses between species
  with different ploidy) causes seed abortion via the \textbf{endosperm
  balance number (EBN)} mechanism. This is why interploidy crosses fail:
  a 2x \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 4x cross produces triploid embryos with imbalanced PEG/MEG
  expression, triggering seed abortion.
\end{itemize}

The 2m:1p endosperm dosage thus becomes the principal arena for
\textbf{parent-of-origin genetic conflict}, with paternally-imprinted
PEGs evolutionarily favoured to extract more maternal resources for the
offspring, and maternally-imprinted MEGs favoured to ration resources
across multiple offspring.

\subsubsection{Seed Dormancy: Five Classes and
Triggers}\label{seed-dormancy-five-classes-and-triggers}

\textbf{Seed dormancy} delays germination until conditions favour
seedling survival. Baskin and Baskin (2004) classify dormancy into five
types:

\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Physical (PY)} & Water-impermeable seed coat (dense palisade of
macrosclereids; suberin layers) & Scarification: physical abrasion, fire
heat, gut passage, freeze-thaw & Many legumes (clover, \emph{Acacia});
\emph{Convolvulus}; many Malvaceae \\
\textbf{Physiological (PD)} & Hormonal balance (high ABA / low GA)
blocks germination despite imbibition; embryo viable & Stratification
(cold-moist); after-ripening (dry storage at warm); light (Pfr) &
\emph{Arabidopsis}, lettuce, apple, most temperate trees \\
\textbf{Morphological (MD)} & Embryo immature at dispersal; needs time
to develop & Time + warm-moist conditions & \emph{Ginkgo},
\emph{Magnolia}, parsnips, celery \\
\textbf{Morphophysiological (MPD)} & Combined immature embryo + hormonal
block & Warm followed by cold stratification (or vice versa) & Many
woodland herbaceous spring ephemerals; \emph{Trillium},
\emph{Anemone} \\
\textbf{Combinational (PY+PD)} & Both impermeable coat and hormonal
block & Both scarification and stratification & \emph{Tilia} (linden),
some Rosaceae \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Germination triggers (sensory inputs):}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Stratification (cold, moist):} Cold treatment (1--5 °C, weeks
  to months) progressively degrades \textbf{ABA} and induces \textbf{GA
  biosynthesis} genes, shifting the ABA/GA balance toward germination.
  Required by many temperate tree seeds. Mechanism involves cold-induced
  demethylation of GA-biosynthesis gene promoters.
\item
  \textbf{Scarification (mechanical or chemical):} Cracks or thins the
  testa, allowing water and oxygen to enter. Can be achieved naturally
  by passage through animal digestive tracts (where stomach acid +
  abrasion abrade the coat), fire (heat scarification of fire-adapted
  species like \emph{Banksia}), or freeze-thaw cycles. Many savanna
  acacia seeds germinate primarily after passage through elephant or
  ungulate guts.
\item
  \textbf{Light (phytochrome-mediated):} Red light (R, 660 nm) converts
  Pr to active Pfr, promoting germination in light-requiring seeds
  (lettuce, \emph{Arabidopsis}, many small-seeded weeds). Far-red light
  (FR, 730 nm) inhibits germination. The R:FR ratio under a leaf canopy
  is low (chlorophyll absorbs R, transmits FR), so seeds under shade
  remain dormant until canopy opening --- an exquisite mechanism for
  detecting gaps in vegetation. The Borthwick-Hendricks experiments
  (1952) on lettuce seeds first demonstrated the R/FR reversibility that
  defined phytochrome.
\item
  \textbf{Temperature fluctuation:} Diurnal temperature swings (e.g., 40
  °C day / 10 °C night, typical of bare soil under sun without
  insulating vegetation) signal a gap in canopy cover. Many desert and
  weed species require such fluctuations.
\item
  \textbf{Smoke and karrikins:} Karrikin compounds (KAR1--KAR6) in
  plant-derived smoke bind the \textbf{KAI2 receptor} (a
  strigolactone-related \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}/\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} hydrolase). KAR signalling promotes
  germination of fire-adapted species and many weeds (KAR2 promotes
  germination in \emph{Arabidopsis}).
\item
  \textbf{Chemical leaching:} Some desert species require leaching of
  inhibitory compounds (e.g., NaCl in halophytes; phenolic germination
  inhibitors) by sufficient rainfall --- ensuring germination primarily
  after enough rain has fallen to support seedling establishment.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Germination Physiology --- Molecular
Framework}\label{germination-physiology-molecular-framework}

The balance between ABA (dormancy-promoting) and GA
(germination-promoting) signals is the central regulatory axis:

\textbf{ABA pathway (dormancy):}

\textbf{DOG1} (DELAY OF GERMINATION 1): A seed-specific
RNA-binding-domain protein. DOG1 dosage determines dormancy depth by
stabilising ABI3 and ABI5 mRNA --- master transcription factors of the
ABA response. \emph{DOG1} expression peaks at seed maturation,
quantitative trait locus (QTL) responsible for natural variation in
dormancy across \emph{Arabidopsis} accessions (Bentsink \emph{et al.},
\emph{PNAS} 2006).

\begin{equation}
\text{ABA} + \text{PYR/RCAR} \rightleftharpoons \text{ABA-PYR complex} \xrightarrow{} \text{PP2C inhibition (ABI1/ABI2 released)} \rightarrow \text{SnRK2 kinase active}
\label{eq:unit_VIII_aba_germination}
\end{equation}

Active SnRK2 phosphorylates \textbf{ABF/AREB} transcription factors \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
dormancy gene transcription (ABI5 targets: \emph{LEA} proteins, stress
tolerance genes). PP2C inhibition is the key switch: normally PP2C keeps
SnRK2 dephosphorylated (inactive); ABA binding to PYR/RCAR pulls PP2C
off SnRK2.

\textbf{GA pathway (germination):}

\begin{equation}
\text{GA} + \text{GID1} \rightleftharpoons \text{GA-GID1-DELLA complex} \xrightarrow{\text{SCF}^{\text{GID2}}} \text{Ub-DELLA} \xrightarrow{26S} \text{DELLA degradation}
\label{eq:unit_VIII_ga_della}
\end{equation}

DELLA degradation (of RGA, GAI, RGL1-3 in \emph{Arabidopsis}) releases
repression of: - \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-Amylase \hyperref[gl:promoter]{\textbf{promoter}}s
(mobilise endosperm starch \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} maltose \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} glucose) - Lipase genes (mobilise
stored triacylglycerols) - Protease genes (mobilise globulins and
albumins)

\textbf{ABA--GA antagonism:} - ABA stabilises DELLA proteins (by
downregulating GID1 and upregulating PP2C) - GA degrades DELLA and
suppresses ABI5 - Environmental cues (light via Pfr, cold via DOG1
degradation, smoke via KAI2) tip the balance toward GA-dominated
germination competence

\textbf{Concept Check 4:} Some desert annual plant seeds require
specific temperature fluctuations (e.g., 40 °C day / 10 °C night) to
break dormancy. Explain why this diurnal fluctuation --- rather than
constant warm temperature --- is required. Connect your answer to the
molecular ABA/GA balance.

\textbf{Concept Check 5:} A \emph{dog1} loss-of-function mutant of
\emph{Arabidopsis} shows severely reduced primary dormancy: seeds
germinate immediately at maturity. Predict the ecological consequence in
(a) a Mediterranean climate with hot dry summers, and (b) a tropical
evergreen forest understory.

establish auxin gradient \\
2-cell & Asymmetric division: apical cell (embryo) + basal cell
(suspensor) & WOX9 signalling \\
Globular & 8-cell through 32-cell globular stage & WOX2 (apical domain),
WOX9 (basal) pattern embryo \\
Heart & Cotyledon primordia emerge; first visible bilateral symmetry &
YAB/PIN1 separate cotyledons; ARF5/MP establishes vascular axis \\
Torpedo & Elongation; hypocotyl + radicle extend & Protoderm,
procambium, ground meristem differentiate \\
Mature embryo & Desiccation; ABA accumulates; storage proteins deposited
& Two cotyledons + SAM + RAM + hypocotyl + radicle \\
\end{longtable}
}

The \textbf{suspensor} (from the basal cell) anchors the embryo to the
maternal tissue and transfers nutrients. It is programmed for cell death
after the globular stage.

\subsubsection{Shoot Apical Meristem (SAM) -- Stem Cell
Niche}\label{shoot-apical-meristem-sam-stem-cell-niche}

The SAM maintains a pool of pluripotent stem cells throughout the
plant's life:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Central Zone (CZ):} 2-4 slowly dividing stem cells at the
  summit
\item
  \textbf{Peripheral Zone (PZ):} Faster-dividing cells that are
  displaced outward and form lateral organ primordia (leaves, flowers)
\item
  \textbf{Rib Zone:} Beneath the CZ; contributes to stem internodes
\end{itemize}

\textbf{WUS-CLV3 negative feedback loop} (the ``stem cell thermostat''):

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{WUSCHEL (WUS)} -- homeodomain transcription factor expressed
  in the organising centre (below CZ). WUS protein moves to CZ via
  plasmodesmata. Activates \textbf{CLAVATA3 (CLV3)} expression.
\item
  \textbf{CLV3} -- a secreted CLE peptide (12 amino acids). CLV3 binds
  the \textbf{CLV1/CLV2/CRN receptor kinase} complex in underlying
  cells, activating a MAPK cascade that represses \textbf{WUS}
  transcription.
\item
  \textbf{Negative feedback:} WUS activates CLV3; CLV3 represses WUS.
  This maintains a constant stem cell pool size.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{SAM auxin-driven phyllotaxis:} - Each leaf primordium is
initiated where PIN1 (auxin efflux carrier) creates a local auxin
maximum - The established primordium depletes local auxin from
surrounding cells - The next primordium arises at the position of the
next auxin maximum - Mathematical result: primordia arise at
\textbf{137.5 degrees divergence angle} (the ``golden angle'' = 360
degrees \(\times\) (1 \(-\) 1/\(\varphi^2\)) where \(\varphi\) = golden
ratio 1.618) - This produces Fibonacci spirals (1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8,
13\ldots) visible in pine cones, sunflower heads, and succulent leaf
arrangements

\subsubsection{Worked Example: Calculating the Golden Angle in
Phyllotaxis}\label{worked-example-calculating-the-golden-angle-in-phyllotaxis}

\textbf{Problem:} The arrangement of leaves on a stem (phyllotaxis) is
often determined by the golden angle, which minimises shading of lower
leaves by upper leaves. Calculate the exact value of the golden angle in
degrees using the golden ratio \(\varphi \approx 1.618034\). If a plant
produces a new leaf every 5 days, what will be the total angular
divergence between the first leaf and a fourth leaf (leaf 1 and leaf 4)?

\textbf{Solution:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Calculate the golden angle:} Using the formula given: Angle
  \(= 360^\circ \cdot (1 - \frac{1}{\varphi^2})\) First, calculate
  \(\varphi^2\):
  \[ 1.618034^2 \approx 2.618034  \label{eq:unit_VIII_plant_reproduction_item_1}\]

  Calculate the fraction:
  \[ \frac{1}{2.618034} \approx 0.381966  \label{eq:unit_VIII_plant_reproduction_item_2}\]

  Apply to the angle formula:
  \[ \text{Angle} = 360^\circ \cdot (1 - 0.381966) = 360^\circ \cdot 0.618034 \approx 222.49^\circ  \label{eq:unit_VIII_plant_reproduction_item_3}\]

  However, angles are typically measured by the shorter path around the
  circle, so we subtract from \(360^\circ\):
  \[ 360^\circ - 222.49^\circ = 137.51^\circ  \label{eq:unit_VIII_plant_reproduction_item_4}\]

  This is the \textbf{golden angle (about 137.5°)}.
\item
  \textbf{Calculate the total angular divergence:} Between leaf 1 and
  leaf 4, there are 3 developmental intervals (1 to 2, 2 to 3, and 3 to
  4).
  \[ \text{Total Divergence} = 3 \cdot 137.5^\circ = 412.5^\circ  \label{eq:unit_VIII_plant_reproduction_item_5}\]

  To find the apparent angle relative to the first leaf on a single
  \(360^\circ\) circle, take the modulo:
  \[ 412.5^\circ - 360^\circ = 52.5^\circ  \label{eq:unit_VIII_plant_reproduction_item_6}\]

  The fourth leaf will be separated from the first leaf by
  \textbf{\(52.5^\circ\)} on the stem circumference.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Root Apical Meristem
(RAM)}\label{root-apical-meristem-ram}

RAM structure mirrors SAM with distinct anatomy: - \textbf{Quiescent
Centre (QC):} 4-6 slowly dividing cells (divide about  once per
200 h); WOX5 expression maintains surrounding stem cells -
\textbf{Initial (stem) cells} directly surrounding QC produce clonal
cell files for most root tissues - \textbf{Root cap/columella:} Rapidly
replaced (slough off as root grows); amyloplast-containing statocytes
for gravitropism - \textbf{Casparian strip} in endodermal cells seals
apoplastic pathway for selective mineral transport

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Fruit Development, Vegetative Reproduction, and
Apomixis}\label{fruit-development-vegetative-reproduction-and-apomixis}

\subsubsection{Fruit Development: Hormonal Regulation, Parthenocarpy,
and Climacteric
Ripening}\label{fruit-development-hormonal-regulation-parthenocarpy-and-climacteric-ripening}

Fruit development is initiated by fertilisation and proceeds through
cell division, expansion, and ripening --- each phase under distinct
hormonal control.

\textbf{Phase 1: Fruit set (post-fertilisation initiation):} Auxin from
developing seeds and gibberellins from the maternal pericarp suppress
the abscission programme that would otherwise drop unfertilised flowers.
Without seeds, \textbf{parthenocarpy} can be induced --- fruit
development without fertilisation: - Natural parthenocarpy: cultivated
banana (triploid, sterile), pineapple, navel orange, some \emph{Citrus}
and \emph{Vitis} cultivars - Induced parthenocarpy: exogenous auxin
(NAA, 2,4-D) or GA (GA\(_3\)) sprayed at anthesis. Used commercially in
seedless grapes, watermelons, and tomatoes - Genetic parthenocarpy:
\emph{pin} mutants (pinoid; auxin-overproducing) or \emph{fwf} mutants
(FRUIT WITHOUT FERTILIZATION; tomato) develop fruit without seeds

\textbf{Phase 2: Cell division and expansion:} Cytokinins drive early
cell division in the pericarp; auxin and GA drive subsequent cell
expansion. Cucumbers and watermelons reach mature size by predominantly
cell expansion (each cell can balloon 30-fold).

\textbf{Phase 3: Ripening --- climacteric vs non-climacteric fruits}

The most studied transition is in \textbf{climacteric fruits} (banana,
tomato, apple, avocado, peach, mango), characterised by an
\textbf{autocatalytic burst of ethylene production} at the onset of
ripening:

\begin{equation}
\text{Methionine} \xrightarrow{\text{SAM synthetase}} \text{SAM} \xrightarrow{\text{ACC synthase (ACS)}} \text{ACC} \xrightarrow{\text{ACC oxidase (ACO), O}_2} \text{Ethylene}
\label{eq:unit_VIII_ethylene_pathway}
\end{equation}

\textbf{Two systems of ethylene biosynthesis:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{System 1:} Basal, auto-inhibited ethylene production occurring
  in vegetative tissues and pre-climacteric fruit. Low ethylene levels.
  Maintained at low rates throughout development.
\item
  \textbf{System 2:} Auto-catalytic, ripening-associated ethylene burst.
  Activated by transcription factors (RIN/MADS-RIN, NOR, CNR) that turn
  on a ripening-specific ACS isoform (ACS2) and ACO1. Once initiated,
  the ethylene produced positively feeds back on its own biosynthesis
  (auto-catalysis), generating an exponential rise. Ethylene then
  orchestrates ripening.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Ripening events under ethylene control:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Cell wall softening:} Polygalacturonase (PG), pectin
  methylesterase (PME), expansins, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-galactosidase degrade cell wall
  polysaccharides; tissue softens
\item
  \textbf{Sugar accumulation:} Starch \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} soluble sugars via amylases;
  sucrose conversion via invertase. Banana goes from 1\% to 18\% sugar
  content during ripening
\item
  \textbf{Pigment changes:} Chlorophyll degradation (Stay-Green protein,
  chlorophyllase) reveals carotenoids (red/orange) and anthocyanins
  (red/purple)
\item
  \textbf{Volatile production:} Esters (banana: isoamyl acetate),
  lactones, terpenes --- aroma compounds that attract dispersers
\item
  \textbf{Acid metabolism:} Malic and citric acids decline, sometimes
  through respiratory consumption
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Non-climacteric fruits} (strawberry, grape, citrus, pineapple,
cherry) do not show the ethylene burst; ABA and auxin appear to
substitute as the master ripening signals. Strawberries in particular
are ABA-responsive: applying ABA accelerates ripening; inhibiting ABA
biosynthesis (NDGA) blocks ripening.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection:} The commercial fruit industry manipulates
ethylene extensively. Bananas are picked green, shipped under
ethylene-suppressed conditions (using KMnO\(_4\) as an ethylene scrubber
or 1-MCP --- 1-methylcyclopropene --- as an ethylene perception
inhibitor that competitively blocks ETR1), and then ripened on demand by
ethylene gas treatment at distribution centres. The Flavr Savr tomato
(1994) was the first commercial GMO food, with antisense PG suppressing
wall softening; ethylene-resistant tomatoes (silenced ACS or ACO)
preserve fruit quality during long-distance transport.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Fruit Types and
Dispersal}\label{fruit-types-and-dispersal}

\subsubsection{Vegetative Reproduction: Mechanisms and Practical
Applications}\label{vegetative-reproduction-mechanisms-and-practical-applications}

Plants have diverse mechanisms for \textbf{vegetative (asexual)
reproduction}, each with distinct anatomical and ecological
characteristics that have been widely exploited in agriculture and
horticulture:

\textbf{Stolons (runners)} & Horizontal above-ground stems that root and
form daughter plants at nodes & Strawberry (\emph{Fragaria}), spider
plant (\emph{Chlorophytum}) & Commercial strawberry production: each
``mother'' plant produces 5--10 daughter plants per season; entire
fields propagated clonally from elite cultivars \\
\textbf{Rhizomes} & Horizontal underground stems with nodes,
scale-leaves, and adventitious roots & Ginger (\emph{Zingiber}), bamboo,
iris, bracken fern, turmeric & Survives fire, frost, and grazing --- one
rhizome system can persist for centuries (single bracken stand
\textgreater1000 years; \emph{Pando} aspen clone in Utah,
about 80,000 years old). Commercial ginger and turmeric grown
entirely from rhizome divisions \\
\textbf{Bulbs} & Modified shoots with fleshy storage leaves on a short
basal plate; central apical bud & Tulip, garlic, onion, daffodil, lily &
Year-round storage in cold rooms allows seasonal flower forcing (Dutch
tulip industry); garlic propagated entirely by clove (a single bulb
scale) \\
\textbf{Corms} & Solid swollen stem base; superficially bulb-like but no
fleshy storage leaves & Crocus, gladiolus, taro (\emph{Colocasia}) &
Annual replacement: each corm produces ``cormels'' used for the next
planting \\
\textbf{Tubers} & Swollen subterranean stem (stem tubers, e.g., potato)
or root (root tubers, e.g., sweet potato) with axillary buds (eyes) &
Potato (\emph{Solanum tuberosum}), Jerusalem artichoke, sweet potato &
Each ``eye'' can regenerate a complete plant. Global potato cultivation
is essentially clonal --- major cultivars (Russet Burbank, Yukon Gold)
are genetically uniform clones. This uniformity is also their
vulnerability (e.g., the 1845 Irish potato famine, in which a single
\emph{Phytophthora infestans} genotype destroyed a near-monoclonal
crop) \\
\textbf{Adventitious roots} & Roots forming on stem cuttings, leaves, or
other non-root tissue & Willow (\emph{Salix}) cuttings root readily;
many succulents form leaves & Foundation of horticultural cuttings:
roses, grape, citrus, blueberry are commercially propagated by stem
cuttings under mist with rooting hormone (auxin) treatment \\
\textbf{Adventitious plantlets} & Plantlets form spontaneously on leaves
or other organs & \emph{Kalanchoe} (leaf margins), \emph{Bryophyllum} &
Drop from parent and root in soil --- example of natural clonal
propagation \\
\textbf{Fragmentation} & Twig or stem fragments that detach and root &
Willows, many aquatic plants (\emph{Elodea}, \emph{Myriophyllum}) &
Aggressive invasive species often spread by fragmentation (e.g.,
\emph{Elodea canadensis} in European waterways) \\
\textbf{Layering} & Stem touches soil and roots while still attached to
parent & Blackberry, raspberry; horticultural air layering & Common in
commercial production of difficult-to-root species; air layering used
for tropical fruit trees and ornamentals \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Grafting} (not strictly vegetative reproduction but related):
Joining a scion (desired cultivar) onto a rootstock (provides root
system, often with disease/drought resistance). Used almost universally
in apple, pear, citrus, grape, and stone fruit cultivation. The
19th-century \emph{Phylloxera} aphid pandemic destroyed European
vineyards; the rescue was grafting European \emph{Vitis vinifera} scions
onto American \emph{V. labrusca} rootstocks (which carry natural
resistance) --- every European wine grape today is grown on American
roots.

\subsubsection{Apomixis: Sporophytic and Gametophytic
Pathways}\label{apomixis-sporophytic-and-gametophytic-pathways}

\textbf{Apomixis} is seed formation without fertilisation, producing
genetically identical maternal clones in a seed package. Apomixis is a
powerful evolutionary ``frozen'' genotype dispersal mechanism and the
holy grail of crop breeding.

\textbf{Types of apomixis:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Sporophytic (adventitious) apomixis (adventive embryony):}
  Embryos arise directly from sporophytic (somatic) cells of the ovule
  (typically the \textbf{nucellus} or \textbf{integuments}) ---
  bypassing the gametophyte entirely. The embryo is genotypically
  identical to the maternal parent (2n, same as mother). Multiple
  embryos may form per seed (\textbf{polyembryony}). Example: citrus
  (most cultivars produce both zygotic and apomictic embryos in the same
  seed; nucellar embryos eventually outcompete the zygotic embryo,
  preserving the elite genotype). Mango polyembryonic cultivars use the
  same mechanism.
\item
  \textbf{Gametophytic apomixis:} A diploid embryo sac forms without
  meiosis, retaining the maternal genome unreduced. Two sub-types:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{Apospory:} Embryo sac arises from a somatic nucellar cell
    that does not undergo meiosis. The MMC degenerates without producing
    megaspores; instead, an adjacent nucellar cell expands and divides
    mitotically to form an unreduced (2n) embryo sac. Examples:
    \emph{Hieracium} (hawkweed), \emph{Pennisetum} (pearl millet
    relatives), \emph{Hypericum}
  \item
    \textbf{Diplospory:} Megaspore mother cell skips or modifies meiosis
    (replacing meiosis with mitosis; ``MiMe''), producing an unreduced
    megaspore that develops into a 2n embryo sac. Examples: dandelion
    (\emph{Taraxacum}; many dandelion species are obligate apomicts),
    \emph{Tripsacum} (relative of maize), some \emph{Boechera}
  \item
    In both, the egg cell is unreduced (2n) and develops
    parthenogenetically into a 2n embryo (matching the mother)
  \item
    \textbf{Endosperm formation in gametophytic apomicts:}

    \begin{itemize}
    \tightlist
    \item
      \textbf{Pseudogamous:} Central cell still requires fertilisation
      by sperm to form endosperm (typical in apomictic grasses like
      \emph{Poa}, \emph{Pennisetum})
    \item
      \textbf{Autonomous:} Central cell develops into endosperm without
      fertilisation (typical of dandelions and \emph{Hieracium})
    \end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Agricultural significance --- clonal seed and the holy grail of
breeding:}

The dream of apomixis in major crops: capture the \textbf{hybrid vigour
(heterosis)} of an elite F1 hybrid in a self-perpetuating apomictic
seed, eliminating the need to re-create the hybrid each generation.
Currently, F1 hybrid maize, rice, and sorghum require expensive annual
production crosses (typically requiring about 2--3 isolated
hectares of cytoplasmic male sterile mother lines and pollen donor
lines). If apomixis could be engineered into rice or maize, subsistence
farmers could save F1 seed indefinitely and continue to capture hybrid
vigour.

\textbf{Synthetic apomixis breakthrough:} Synthetic apomixis studies in
rice combine apomeiosis with parthenogenesis triggers to produce clonal
seed from hybrid plants. High-frequency systems in hybrid rice reported
many lines with \textgreater80\% clonal seeds and selected lines above
95\%, while subsequent transgenerational work found largely stable
clonal inheritance with rare aneuploid progeny that still require
monitoring
\citep{vernet2022highfrequencyapomixis,liu2023syntheticapomixis}. The
mechanism combines three modifications:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{MiMe} (Mitosis instead of Meiosis): triple knockout of
  \emph{OSD1}, \emph{PAIR1}, \emph{REC8} converts meiosis into mitosis,
  producing unreduced gametes
\item
  \textbf{MTL} (MATRILINEAL): pollen-specific phospholipase knockout
  enabling haploid induction --- sperm cannot complete fusion with the
  egg
\item
  \textbf{BBML} or \textbf{DMP} transgenes inducing parthenogenesis ---
  egg cells initiate embryogenesis without sperm contribution
\end{enumerate}

The combination yields rice plants that produce maternal clones in seed
form across multiple generations --- a foundational step toward
apomictic crops at scale. Field translation remains conditional:
breeders must quantify seed-set frequency, transgene segregation, rare
chromosome loss, fitness under local climates, containment of gene flow
to wild relatives, and whether farmers would gain durable access rather
than new seed-locking arrangements.

\textbf{Risks to wild relatives:} Apomictic hybrids could become
invasive (since each seed is a perfect copy of the elite plant) and
could erode genetic diversity in wild populations through escapes.
Regulatory caution is warranted.

\subsubsection{Plant Biotechnology}\label{plant-biotechnology}

Modern plant biotechnology builds on understanding of plant
reproduction:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Tissue culture and micropropagation:} Totipotent plant cells
  can regenerate whole organisms. The auxin:cytokinin ratio determines
  differentiation: high auxin promotes roots; high cytokinin promotes
  shoots; balanced ratio maintains callus.
\item
  \textbf{Somatic embryogenesis:} Somatic cells (non-reproductive) can
  be induced to form embryo-like structures that develop into complete
  plants. Used commercially for oil palm, conifers, coffee.
\item
  \textbf{Agrobacterium tumefaciens:} Natural genetic engineer. Its Ti
  \hyperref[gl:plasmid]{\textbf{plasmid}} contains T-DNA that integrates
  into the plant \hyperref[gl:genome]{\textbf{genome}}. Modified T-DNA
  (with antibiotic resistance and gene of interest replacing oncogenes)
  is the primary tool for plant transformation.
\item
  \textbf{Applications:} Bt crops (insecticidal crystal protein gene
  from \emph{Bacillus thuringiensis}), golden rice (beta-carotene
  biosynthesis genes), drought-tolerant cultivars (DREB/CBF
  overexpression), herbicide-resistant varieties (modified EPSPS gene).
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection:} The Bt toxin proteins (Cry proteins) are
harmless to mammals because they require alkaline gut
\hyperref[gl:ph]{\textbf{pH}} (found in insect midguts but not mammalian
stomachs) to become active. Bt crops have reduced insecticide use by
37\% globally while increasing yields 22\% in developing countries
(meta-analysis, Klumper \& Qaim, 2014).
\end{quote}

\textbf{Concept Check 6:} A breeder wishes to create a triploid (3n)
seedless watermelon for commercial sale. Outline the crossing scheme
starting from diploid (2n) parents. Why are triploid offspring sterile
(no viable seeds), and which cross --- 2n \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 4n or 4n \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 2n --- yields the
best fruit set?

\textbf{Concept Check 7:} \emph{Pyrus communis} (European pear) requires
a pollinator of a different cultivar to set fruit (pollinizer system)
due to gametophytic SI. A grower plants 100\% `Bartlett' (S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}S\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}) pears in
an orchard. Predict the fruit yield. Then describe the genetic logic of
selecting a pollinizer cultivar --- what S-genotype is required?

\textbf{Concept Check 8:} Argue for or against this proposition:
``Apomixis is evolutionarily dead-end because it eliminates genetic
recombination. Hence apomictic species should be short-lived
geologically.'' Cite specific apomictic lineages in your answer (e.g.,
dandelions are apomictic and remain abundant on multiple continents).

\textbf{Concept Check 9:} A tomato cultivar bred for parthenocarpy
carries a constitutively active PIN1 transgene driving auxin
overproduction in the ovary. Predict fruit set in the absence of
pollination, and predict the dormancy and germination behaviour of any
seeds that do form (assuming some pollination occurs by accident).

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-28}

For \textbf{Plant Reproduction and Development}, frontier biology
belongs inside the evidence logic of the chapter. Plant biology links
molecular regulation to climate stress, water limitation, crop
resilience, phenology, and ecosystem feedbacks. The core reading
question is this: plant reproduction links pollination, development,
genetics, phenology, dispersal, and environmental filtering.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

A strong plant explanation names the tissue, signal, environmental
driver, measurable trait, and tradeoff between growth, reproduction,
defence, and water use.

\textbf{Source practice:} For plant-stress and crop claims, name the
tissue, environmental driver, field context, and growth-reproduction
tradeoff; separate laboratory potential from agronomic adoption.

\subsubsection{Field Translation: Fertility, Phenology, and
Containment}\label{field-translation-fertility-phenology-and-containment}

Plant reproductive claims are especially sensitive to the step being
measured. Heat can reduce seed set by damaging tapetum development,
microspores, pollen viability, pollen-tube growth, or ovule/endosperm
development, and these stages differ in timing and temperature threshold
\citep{malik2022heatstressmale}. Phenology claims need the cue model:
spring ephemeral flowering in \emph{Corydalis ambigua} tracked snowmelt
and surface degree-days, while bumblebee emergence tracked soil warming;
seed set declined when flowers opened before bee emergence in a 19-year
field series and snow-removal experiment
\citep{kudo2019phenologicalmismatch}.

The same logic applies to gene drives and engineered reproductive
systems. A plant gene drive or apomictic trait is not just a molecular
construct; it is a population process shaped by dispersal, seed
dormancy, mating system, hybrid fitness, and governance. Responsible
evaluation uses staged containment, ecological risk assessment,
community engagement, and explicit reversibility or mitigation planning
before open release \citep{nasem2016genedrives}.

\textbf{Alternation of generations} & Diploid sporophyte
