\begin{quote}
\textbf{Opening Vignette --- Darwin's Love Affair with Carnivorous
Plants}

``I care more about Drosera than the origin of species in the world,''
Darwin wrote to his friend Asa Gray in 1860. For fifteen years he
systematically experimented on sundews and Venus flytraps, weighing
morsels of meat to 1/78,000 of a grain, timing trap closure, and testing
with hundreds of chemical solutions --- establishing that carnivorous
plants actively respond to nitrogenous stimuli, not merely mechanical
touch. His 1875 book \emph{Insectivorous Plants} described hormone-like
chemical signals in plants decades before the word ``hormone'' existed.
In those experiments lurked the seed of plant hormone biology: auxin,
gibberellins, abscisic acid, cytokinin, ethylene --- the five classical
plant hormones whose discovery unfolded over the next century. Darwin
rarely found them by name, but his insight that plants sense and respond
to their environment through diffusible chemical signals laid much of
the groundwork that followed.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Plant Hormones Overview}\label{plant-hormones-overview}

Plant hormones (phytohormones) are small organic molecules produced in
low concentrations that regulate virtually every aspect of plant growth,
development, and stress responses. Unlike animal hormones, plant
hormones are often produced at many sites throughout the plant and can
act locally.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0147_94efd40a8d97.png}
\caption{Overview of major plant hormone signalling pathways from biosynthesis through perception to cellular response Each pathway follows a general scheme: stimulus triggers hormone biosynthesis, the hormone is perceived by a specific receptor, and downstream signalling leads to gene expression changes.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Auxin (Indole-3-Acetic Acid,
IAA)}\label{auxin-indole-3-acetic-acid-iaa}

\textbf{Biosynthesis:} Primarily from tryptophan via the TAA1/YUCCA
pathway. Produced in young leaves, shoot apical meristem, and developing
embryos.

\textbf{Transport:} Auxin moves by \textbf{polar auxin transport} (PAT),
unique among plant hormones: - \textbf{PIN efflux carriers} (PIN1-8):
Localised to specific faces of the plasma membrane; their polar
distribution determines the direction of auxin flow. PIN proteins cycle
between plasma membrane and endosomal compartments; their localisation
is regulated by phosphorylation (PID kinase) and vesicle trafficking. -
\textbf{AUX1/LAX influx carriers:} Import auxin into cells; less polar
than PIN proteins - Polar transport rate: about 1 cm/h in stems
(basipetal in shoots, acropetal in roots)

\textbf{Signalling mechanism (TIR1 pathway):} 1. Auxin binds TIR1/AFB
F-box proteins (nuclear receptors) 2. Auxin acts as ``molecular glue''
between TIR1 and Aux/IAA transcriptional repressors 3. Aux/IAA proteins
are ubiquitinated by SCF\(^{TIR1}\) complex and degraded by 26S
proteasome 4. \textbf{ARF (Auxin Response Factor)}
\hyperref[gl:transcription]{\textbf{transcription}} factors are released
from Aux/IAA repression 5. ARF activates auxin-responsive genes

\textbf{Key functions:} - \textbf{Apical dominance:} High auxin from the
apex suppresses lateral bud outgrowth; removal of apex (decapitation)
releases lateral buds - \textbf{Phototropism:} Asymmetric auxin
distribution bends shoots toward light. - \textbf{Gravitropism:}
Asymmetric auxin distribution in response to gravity - \textbf{Root
initiation:} High auxin promotes adventitious and lateral root formation
- \textbf{Fruit development:} Auxin from developing seeds promotes fruit
growth

\subsubsection{Gibberellins (GAs)}\label{gibberellins-gas}

\textbf{Biosynthesis:} From the MEP pathway in plastids; active forms
include GA\(_1\), GA\(_3\), GA\(_4\). Produced in young leaves, root
tips, and developing seeds.

\textbf{Signalling mechanism:} 1. GA binds the soluble receptor
\textbf{GID1} 2. GA-GID1 complex interacts with \textbf{DELLA proteins}
(transcriptional repressors: GAI, RGA, RGL1-3 in \emph{Arabidopsis}) 3.
DELLA proteins are ubiquitinated by SCF\(^{SLY1}\) E3 ligase and
degraded 4. Release of DELLA repression allows growth-promoting
transcription factors to act

\textbf{Key functions:} - \textbf{Stem elongation:} Promotes internodal
elongation; GA-deficient mutants are dwarf plants (basis of ``Green
Revolution'' semi-dwarf wheat: \emph{Rht} gene encodes GA-insensitive
DELLA) - \textbf{Seed germination:} GA induces \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-amylase synthesis in
cereal aleurone layer, mobilising starch reserves - \textbf{Fruit
development:} Can induce parthenocarpy (seedless fruit production
without fertilisation; seedless grapes) - \textbf{Flowering:} In some
long-day plants, GA can substitute for the long-day photoperiod
requirement

\subsubsection{Cytokinins}\label{cytokinins}

\textbf{Biosynthesis:} From adenine derivatives via IPT
(isopentenyltransferase). Primarily synthesised in \textbf{root tips}
and transported to shoots via \hyperref[gl:xylem]{\textbf{xylem}}.

\textbf{Key functions:} - \textbf{Cell division:} Essential for
cytokinesis; cytokinin + auxin together drive cell proliferation -
\textbf{Shoot promotion:} Antagonise auxin's apical dominance; promote
lateral bud outgrowth - \textbf{Delay of senescence:} Maintain
\hyperref[gl:chlorophyll]{\textbf{chlorophyll}} and protein levels in
leaves; SAUR (senescence-associated ubiquitin-related) pathway -
\textbf{Tissue culture:} Auxin:cytokinin ratio determines organogenesis
-- high auxin = roots; high cytokinin = shoots; equal = callus
(undifferentiated cell mass)

\subsubsection{Abscisic Acid (ABA)}\label{abscisic-acid-aba}

\textbf{Biosynthesis:} From carotenoid cleavage (NCED3
\hyperref[gl:enzyme]{\textbf{enzyme}}, 9-\emph{cis}-epoxycarotenoid
dioxygenase). Produced in roots under soil drying and in leaves under
dehydration stress.

\textbf{Key functions:} - \textbf{Stomatal closure:} The primary drought
response hormone, detailed in the abscisic-acid discussion. -
\textbf{Seed dormancy:} Maintains dormancy until conditions favour
germination; antagonised by GA - \textbf{Stress gene expression:}
Activates LEA (Late Embryogenesis Abundant) protein genes; dehydrins;
osmolyte synthesis

\textbf{Signalling:} ABA binds PYR/PYL/RCAR receptors, which inhibit
PP2C phosphatases, activating SnRK2 kinases. SnRK2 phosphorylates SLAC1
(stomatal closure), AREB/ABF transcription factors (stress genes), and
ion channels.

\subsubsection{Ethylene}\label{ethylene}

\textbf{Biosynthesis:} From methionine via SAM (S-adenosylmethionine) to
ACC (1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylic acid) by ACC synthase, then to
ethylene by ACC oxidase. Ethylene is a \textbf{gas} -- it diffuses
freely between cells and even between plants.

\textbf{Key functions:} - \textbf{Fruit ripening:} Climacteric fruits
(banana, tomato, apple, avocado) show a burst of ethylene production
triggering ripening. Non-climacteric fruits (strawberry, grape, citrus)
do not show this burst. - \textbf{Senescence:} Promotes leaf yellowing
and abscission (leaf drop); petal senescence in cut flowers -
\textbf{Triple response:} In dark-grown seedlings, ethylene causes: (1)
shortened, thickened hypocotyl, (2) exaggerated apical hook, (3)
horizontal growth. This protects the seedling apex as it pushes through
soil. - \textbf{Flooding response:} Submerged roots accumulate ACC
(cannot oxidise to ethylene without O\(_2\)); when ACC reaches shoots,
aerenchyma formation is triggered (programmed cell death creates air
channels) - \textbf{Abscission:} Ethylene activates cellulase and
pectinase in the abscission zone at the leaf petiole base

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection:} The commercial fruit industry manipulates
ethylene extensively. Bananas are picked green, shipped under
ethylene-suppressed conditions (using KMnO\(_4\) as an ethylene scrubber
or 1-MCP as an ethylene perception inhibitor), and then ripened on
demand by ethylene gas treatment at distribution centres. This enables
global tropical fruit supply chains.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Jasmonates (JA)}\label{jasmonates-ja}

\textbf{Biosynthesis:} From linolenic acid (membrane lipid) via the LOX
(lipoxygenase) pathway. The active form is \textbf{JA-Ile}
(jasmonyl-isoleucine conjugate, produced by JAR1).

\textbf{Signalling:} JA-Ile binds \textbf{COI1} (F-box protein of the
SCF\textsuperscript{COI1} E3 ubiquitin ligase), which recruits
\textbf{JAZ} (Jasmonate ZIM-domain) repressor proteins into the SCF
complex:

\begin{equation}
\text{JA-Ile} + \text{COI1-JAZ} \xrightarrow{\text{SCF}^{\text{COI1}}} \text{Ub-JAZ} \xrightarrow{\text{26S proteasome}} \text{MYC2/3/4 activation}
\label{eq:plant_responses_1}
\end{equation}

Pre-wounding, JAZ proteins recruit \textbf{TOPLESS} corepressor via the
\textbf{NINJA} adaptor, forming a trimeric JAZ-NINJA-TOPLESS complex
that represses MYC2 through \hyperref[gl:histone]{\textbf{histone}}
deacetylase recruitment. Post-wounding JA-Ile surge displaces this
complex by directing SCF\textsuperscript{COI1} to ubiquitinate JAZ via
the \textbf{SLY degron} motif (Jas domain). 2024 cryo-EM structures
(\hyperref[gl:allosteric]{\textbf{allosteric}} lid closure model) show
COI1 undergoes a conformational switch upon JA-Ile binding, with
ASK1-CUL1-RBX1 forming the catalytic core (Sheard \emph{et al.},
\emph{Nature} 2010; Xu \emph{et al.}, \emph{bioRxiv} 2024). COI1
paralogs (COI1a/b) fine-tune JAZ subtype specificity across
defence/development contexts.

\textbf{Key functions:} - \textbf{Wound/herbivore defence:} Protease
inhibitors, alkaloids (nicotine in tobacco), glucosinolates, terpene
volatiles - \textbf{UV damage response:} Accumulation of UV-absorbing
flavonoids - \textbf{Mycorrhizal signalling:} JA promotes mycorrhizal
colonisation - \textbf{Pollen development:} Required for stamen
maturation and pollen release

\subsubsection{Salicylic Acid (SA)}\label{salicylic-acid-sa}

\textbf{Biosynthesis:} From phenylalanine (PAL pathway) or chorismate
(ICS pathway; \hyperref[gl:dominant]{\textbf{dominant}} in
\emph{Arabidopsis}).

\textbf{Key functions:} - \textbf{Systemic Acquired Resistance (SAR):}
After local pathogen infection, SA signals spread systemically, priming
distant tissues for enhanced defence in the plant-immunity response. -
\textbf{PR protein induction:} Pathogenesis-related proteins (PR-1,
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-1,3-glucanase, thaumatin-like proteins)

\textbf{Concept Check:} Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is derived from
salicylic acid, originally extracted from willow bark (\emph{Salix}).
Why might plants produce SA in response to pathogens, and what does this
tell us about the evolutionary age of this defence pathway?

\subsubsection{Strigolactones}\label{strigolactones}

\textbf{Biosynthesis:} From carotenoid precursors via D27 isomerase and
CCD7/CCD8 cleavage. Produced primarily in roots.

\textbf{Key functions:} - \textbf{Branch suppression:} Inhibit lateral
bud outgrowth; work with auxin in apical dominance - \textbf{Mycorrhizal
recruitment:} Secreted into rhizosphere to attract AM fungi -
\textbf{Root architecture:} Promote lateral root elongation -
\textbf{Parasitic plant germination:} \emph{Striga} (witchweed) seeds
germinate in response to strigolactones from host roots, a devastating
crop \hyperref[gl:parasite]{\textbf{parasite}} in Africa

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Phototropism}\label{phototropism}

The molecular pathway for phototropism in \emph{Arabidopsis thaliana} is
one of the best-characterised plant signalling cascades:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Blue light} (390-500 nm) illuminates the shoot asymmetrically
\item
  \textbf{PHOT1} or \textbf{PHOT2} (LOV1/LOV2-domain photoreceptors; LOV
  = Light Oxygen Voltage) absorbs blue light. Photochemical covalent
  FMN-cysteine adduct forms, causing conformational change and
  autophosphorylation (Ser849 of PHOT1, kinase domain released).
\item
  PHOT1/2 phosphorylate \textbf{NPH3} (Non-Phototropic Hypocotyl 3).
  NPH3 interacts with ARF7/ARF19 and reorganises.
\item
  \textbf{Auxin lateral redistribution} (the Cholodny-Went hypothesis,
  quantified by \citet{went1926} \emph{Avena} coleoptile bioassay):

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    PHOT1/2 triggers \textbf{PIN3} (auxin efflux carrier) relocalisation
    from the bottom to the lateral face of shoot endodermal cells
  \item
    More auxin (IAA) is transported to the shaded side; less to the
    illuminated side
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Acid growth hypothesis} \citep{hager1971}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    High {[}IAA{]} on shaded side activates plasma membrane
    \textbf{H\(^+\)-ATPase} (AHA1/2). Proton extrusion acidifies the
    cell wall (\hyperref[gl:ph]{\textbf{pH}} 5.5 to 4.5).
  \item
    Acidic pH activates \textbf{expansins} (proteins that disrupt
    H-bonding between cellulose microfibrils and hemicellulose) causing
    wall loosening. Turgor-driven elongation follows.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Differential elongation (shaded side elongates more than lit side)
  causes the shoot to bend toward light. Phototropic curvature is
  completed within 30-60 minutes.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}
Historical note: Darwin and Darwin (\emph{Power of Movement in Plants},
1880) first demonstrated that the phototropic signal originates in the
coleoptile tip. \citet{went1926} isolated auxin using agar blocks. The
molecular receptors (PHOTs) were identified in 1997 by Briggs and
colleagues.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Worked Example: Phototropic Curvature from a Lateral
Auxin
Gradient}\label{worked-example-phototropic-curvature-from-a-lateral-auxin-gradient}

\textbf{Problem:} A coleoptile segment is illuminated from one side.
Following Cholodny-Went redistribution, the shaded flank receives more
auxin and, via acid growth, elongates 30\% while the illuminated flank
elongates 10\%. Each flank starts at length \(L_0 = 10\) mm and the
coleoptile diameter (distance between the two flanks) is \(w = 1.5\) mm.
Calculate the phototropic bending angle.

\textbf{Solution:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Elongation of each flank.} Apply the relative growth fractions
  to the initial length:
  \[ \Delta s_{\text{shaded}} = L_0 \times 0.30 = 10 \times 0.30 = 3.0 \text{ mm}, \qquad \Delta s_{\text{lit}} = L_0 \times 0.10 = 10 \times 0.10 = 1.0 \text{ mm} \label{eq:unit_VIII_plant_responses_item_5}\]
\item
  \textbf{Differential elongation.} The bend is driven by the difference
  in arc length between the two flanks:
  \[ \Delta s_{\text{shaded}} - \Delta s_{\text{lit}} = 3.0 - 1.0 = 2.0 \text{ mm} \label{eq:unit_VIII_plant_responses_item_6}\]
\item
  \textbf{Bending angle.} When an organ of width \(w\) bends through
  angle \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\theta}}{theta} (radians), the arc-length difference between its two surfaces
  equals \(w\theta\), so
  \(\theta = (\Delta s_{\text{shaded}} - \Delta s_{\text{lit}})/w\):
  \[ \theta = \frac{2.0 \text{ mm}}{1.5 \text{ mm}} = 1.33 \text{ rad} = 1.33 \times \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} \approx 76.4^\circ \label{eq:unit_VIII_plant_responses_item_7}\]
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Interpretation:} A 3:1 ratio of differential flank elongation
over a 1.5 mm-wide coleoptile produces about a 76 degree bend toward the
light --- quantitatively illustrating how a modest lateral auxin
gradient, amplified by acid-growth wall loosening, generates the large
directional curvature characteristic of phototropism.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Gravitropism}\label{gravitropism}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0148_234141e89d08.png}
\caption{Gravitropism in roots and shoots In both organs, amyloplast settling triggers asymmetric auxin redistribution via PIN protein relocalisation. The critical difference: root cells are INHIBITED by high auxin concentrations (causing the lower side to grow less, bending the root downward), while shoot cells are PROMOTED by high auxin (causing the lower side to grow more, bending the shoot upward).}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Key molecular details --- statoliths and PIN asymmetry:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Statocytes:} Specialised gravity-sensing cells. In roots,
  these are the \textbf{columella cells} of the root cap (a few central
  cells just behind the meristem). In shoots, they are the
  \textbf{endodermal cells} (starch sheath surrounding the vascular
  cylinder).
\item
  \textbf{Amyloplasts (statoliths):} Starch-filled plastids (1--10 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m
  diameter) that sediment under gravity within seconds of reorientation.
  Their settling pulls on the actin cytoskeleton and ER membranes,
  generating mechanical signals that are transduced via \textbf{TOC
  (translocon of outer chloroplast) complex} to the LAZY1/IGT proteins
  on the new lower face of the cell.
\item
  \textbf{PIN auxin transporter asymmetry:}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    In root columella cells, \textbf{PIN3} is initially symmetrically
    localised at the plasma membrane. Within minutes of gravity
    stimulation, PIN3 relocalises to the \textbf{new lower (now
    downward-facing) face} of the cell.
  \item
    In the elongation zone, \textbf{PIN2} is permanently localised on
    the upper face of cortical and epidermal cells; PIN2 is critical for
    transporting auxin from the root tip back along the upper side of
    the elongation zone toward the shoot. Relocalisation of PIN3 in
    columella cells biases auxin export toward the lower side, where
    PIN2 then carries it acropetally, accumulating auxin on the lower
    side of the elongation zone.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Lateral auxin redistribution:} In \emph{Arabidopsis} roots,
  the asymmetry develops within about 5 min of gravity
  stimulation; bending is visible by 20 min and complete within 1--2
  hours.
\item
  \textbf{LAZY1 protein:} Required for normal gravitropism. \emph{lazy1}
  mutants show reversed gravitropic responses (shoots grow down,
  branches grow at unusual angles). LAZY1 relocalises to the lower side
  of the cell after gravity stimulation and facilitates PIN
  relocalisation.
\item
  \textbf{Root vs shoot dose-response difference:} The same auxin
  redistribution (more auxin on the lower side) has opposite effects
  because root cells have a much \textbf{lower optimal auxin
  concentration} (about \(10^{-9}\) M for root elongation)
  than shoot cells (about \(10^{-5}\) M for stem elongation).
  Above the root optimum, auxin \textbf{inhibits} elongation via the
  stabilisation of Aux/IAA repressors and ethylene production; thus the
  lower side of the gravity-stimulated root grows less than the upper,
  and the root bends downward.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Photomorphogenesis: Phytochromes and
Cryptochromes}\label{photomorphogenesis-phytochromes-and-cryptochromes}

Plants integrate diverse light signals --- wavelength, intensity,
direction, duration, timing --- through a constellation of
photoreceptors. The two most studied families are phytochromes
(red/far-red sensors) and cryptochromes (blue/UV-A sensors).

\subsubsection{Phytochrome Biochemistry}\label{phytochrome-biochemistry}

Phytochromes are dimeric about 125 kDa chromoproteins. Each
monomer carries a bilin chromophore (phytochromobilin) covalently
attached to a conserved cysteine in the photosensory module. The
chromophore exists in two photointerconvertible forms:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Pr (red-absorbing form, \(\lambda_{max} = 660\) nm):} Inactive
  form; synthesised in the dark; primarily cytoplasmic
\item
  \textbf{Pfr (far-red-absorbing form, \(\lambda_{max} = 730\) nm):}
  Active form; translocates to the nucleus where it interacts with PIFs
  (Phytochrome Interacting Factors); triggers physiological responses
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Photoconversion:}

\begin{equation}
\text{Pr} \xrightarrow{\text{red 660 nm}} \text{Pfr}
\qquad
\text{Pfr} \xrightarrow{\text{far-red 730 nm or dark reversion}} \text{Pr}
\label{eq:unit_VIII_phytochrome_photoconversion}
\end{equation}

Red light (660 nm) converts Pr to Pfr; far-red light (730 nm) converts
Pfr back to Pr. In darkness, Pfr slowly reverts to Pr (thermal
reversion, half-life about  hours) and is also degraded by the
COP1 ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. The R/FR reversibility of
physiological responses (Borthwick and Hendricks, 1952) is the
diagnostic signature of phytochrome involvement.

\textbf{Phytochrome diversity:}

\emph{Arabidopsis} has five phytochromes (PhyA--PhyE), each with
distinct light-stability and physiological roles:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{PhyA:} Light-labile (degraded rapidly in light). Mediates
  very-low-fluence and far-red-high-irradiance responses (FR-HIR). PhyA
  is the principal sensor for \textbf{shade-avoidance under deep shade}
  (where FR predominates) and for \textbf{de-etiolation in dim light}.
\item
  \textbf{PhyB:} Light-stable. Mediates the classic R/FR reversible
  (low-fluence) responses. PhyB is the \textbf{principal sensor of
  canopy shade} via the \textbf{R:FR ratio} (high R:FR = open sun; low
  R:FR = under leaf canopy because chlorophyll absorbs red and transmits
  far-red). Loss-of-function \emph{phyB} mutants are constitutively
  shade-avoiding (elongated, pale, early-flowering).
\item
  \textbf{PhyC, PhyD, PhyE:} Specialised roles in flowering time, leaf
  angle, and modulating the responses of PhyA/B.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Shade avoidance via R:FR ratio:} Sun-grown plants typically
experience R:FR ratios of about 1.2; under a leaf canopy, the
ratio drops to 0.1--0.4 because chlorophyll preferentially absorbs red.
PhyB Pfr is destabilised under low R:FR (returning to Pr); this releases
PIF4/5/7 from PhyB-mediated degradation, activating YUCCA-driven auxin
synthesis and triggering hypocotyl elongation, petiole elongation, and
accelerated flowering --- the \textbf{shade avoidance syndrome}.

\subsubsection{Cryptochrome Signalling --- Blue Light and
FAD}\label{cryptochrome-signalling-blue-light-and-fad}

\textbf{Cryptochromes (CRY1/CRY2)} are blue/UV-A photoreceptors with two
cofactors: a \textbf{FAD} (flavin adenine dinucleotide) chromophore for
blue light absorption (about 450 nm) and an MTHF antenna
pigment that broadens absorption.

\textbf{Photoactivation mechanism:} 1. Blue light reduces FAD from
oxidised (FAD\(_{ox}\)) to neutral semiquinone (FADH•) 2. Reduction
triggers conformational change in the C-terminal extension of CRY 3.
Activated CRY interacts with multiple downstream targets: - \textbf{COP1
(CONSTITUTIVE PHOTOMORPHOGENIC 1):} an E3 ubiquitin ligase; CRY binding
inhibits COP1, thereby stabilising COP1 substrates (HY5, HFR1, CO, LAF1)
--- bZIP and bHLH transcription factors that drive photomorphogenic gene
expression - \textbf{SPA proteins:} COP1 partners; CRY binding disrupts
COP1-SPA interaction - \textbf{PIFs:} CRY can also directly modulate PIF
activity

\textbf{Key blue-light responses:} - \textbf{Hypocotyl growth
inhibition:} Light-grown seedlings have short hypocotyls; \emph{cry1
cry2} double mutants show etiolated (long-hypocotyl) phenotype in blue
light despite normal red light response - \textbf{Anthocyanin
biosynthesis:} Blue light induces phenylpropanoid pathway genes (PAL,
CHS, CHI) producing UV-protective and pigment compounds -
\textbf{Photoperiodic flowering:} CRY2 stabilises CONSTANS protein in
long days - \textbf{Stomatal opening:} Cooperatively with phototropins
(covered in \cref{sec:unit_VIII_plant_structure_and_water})

\textbf{CRY-COP1-HY5 module:} The COP1/SPA E3 ubiquitin ligase complex
is the master ``darkness'' enforcer. In darkness, COP1-SPA ubiquitinates
HY5 and other photomorphogenic TFs, targeting them for degradation.
Light activates CRYs and PhyB, which physically interact with COP1 and
disrupt the COP1-SPA complex; HY5 accumulates and drives
photomorphogenic gene expression (chlorophyll biosynthesis, anthocyanin
synthesis, hypocotyl growth arrest). Loss-of-function \emph{cop1}
mutants are constitutively photomorphogenic in darkness --- confirming
the central role of this regulator.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{The Plant Circadian Clock --- Molecular
Architecture}\label{the-plant-circadian-clock-molecular-architecture}

Plants maintain an endogenous \textbf{about 24-hour oscillator}
(circadian clock) that anticipates dawn/dusk and gates downstream
processes including photosynthesis, growth, flowering, and stress
responses. The plant clock comprises interlocked transcriptional
feedback loops with morning, evening, and intermediate components.

\subsubsection{Morning Loop: CCA1/LHY Repressors and TOC1
Activator}\label{morning-loop-cca1lhy-repressors-and-toc1-activator}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{CCA1 (Circadian Clock Associated 1) and LHY (Late Elongated
  Hypocotyl):} Single-MYB transcription factors expressed at dawn (peak
  about  ZT0, where ZT0 is dawn). They function as a
  heterodimer and act as \textbf{repressors} of evening-expressed genes
  (TOC1, ELF3, ELF4, LUX, GI).
\item
  \textbf{TOC1 (Timing of CAB expression 1; pseudo-response regulator
  PRR1):} Expressed at dusk (peak about  ZT12). TOC1 binds and
  represses the \emph{CCA1} and \emph{LHY} promoters, closing the
  negative feedback loop. TOC1 also activates morning genes after dusk
  through PIF interactions.
\end{itemize}

The morning loop is the ``central oscillator'': CCA1/LHY repress TOC1 in
the morning; as CCA1/LHY decay through the day, TOC1 rises; TOC1 then
represses CCA1/LHY through the night until they rise again at dawn.

\subsubsection{Evening Loop: PRR9 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PRR7 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PRR5 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
TOC1}\label{evening-loop-prr9-prr7-prr5-toc1}

A cascade of \textbf{pseudo-response regulators (PRRs)} sequentially
repress CCA1/LHY through the day:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{PRR9:} Peaks about 4 h after dawn (ZT4); repressed by
  CCA1/LHY; represses CCA1/LHY transcription
\item
  \textbf{PRR7:} Peaks about 8 h after dawn (ZT8); repressed by
  PRR9 partially; represses CCA1/LHY
\item
  \textbf{PRR5:} Peaks at midday (ZT10--12); activates downstream
  targets including CO
\item
  \textbf{TOC1/PRR1:} Peaks at dusk (ZT12); closes morning loop
\end{itemize}

This PRR cascade creates a wave of repression sweeping across the day,
with each successive PRR repressing the previous one's targets. The
molecular result is a robust about 24 h oscillation despite
individual gene half-lives of primarily hours.

\subsubsection{Evening Complex:
ELF3-ELF4-LUX}\label{evening-complex-elf3-elf4-lux}

The \textbf{Evening Complex (EC)} comprises ELF3, ELF4, and LUX (LUX
ARRHYTHMO; a Myb-domain TF). ELF3 is a scaffold protein; LUX provides
DNA binding. The EC peaks at ZT12--16 and represses morning genes (PRR9,
PIF4, GI) --- gating early-night growth. \emph{elf3} mutants are
arrhythmic.

\subsubsection{Temperature Compensation}\label{temperature-compensation}

A defining property of the circadian clock is \textbf{temperature
compensation}: the period remains about 24 h across a wide
temperature range (10--30 °C) despite the underlying biochemical
reactions accelerating with temperature (Q\(_{10}\) about 
2). Mechanisms include: - \textbf{Alternative splicing of CCA1:} at
lower temperature, an alternative splice form (CCA1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}) acts as a
repressor of CCA1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}, slowing the loop - \textbf{Temperature-dependent
protein stability of PRR proteins:} PRR9/7 are more rapidly degraded at
higher temperatures - \textbf{JMJ30 demethylase:} counters temperature
effects on chromatin marks at clock loci

\subsubsection{Clock Outputs}\label{clock-outputs}

The clock gates numerous physiological processes by regulating
downstream gene expression: - \textbf{Stomatal opening:} Anticipatory
opening before dawn; controlled by clock-gated H\(^+\)-ATPase activity -
\textbf{Photosynthesis genes:} CAB (chlorophyll a/b binding protein),
Rubisco activase peak at dawn - \textbf{Flowering:} GI-CO-FT pathway is
clock-gated through photoperiodic hormone signalling. - \textbf{Growth:}
Hypocotyl elongation peaks in the late night/early morning (gated by
PIF4-driven YUCCA expression) - \textbf{Defence:} Many pathogen
resistance genes (e.g., \emph{PR1}) show circadian regulation,
anticipating bacterial infections that peak at midday

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Photoperiodism, Flowering Time, and
Vernalisation}\label{photoperiodism-flowering-time-and-vernalisation}

\subsubsection{Photoperiodic Categories}\label{photoperiodic-categories}

Plants are classified by their flowering response to day/night length:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Short-day plants} (SDPs): Flower when nights are
  \textbf{longer} than a critical length. Examples: chrysanthemum, rice,
  \emph{Pharbitis} (Japanese morning glory), tobacco (\emph{Nicotiana
  tabacum} Maryland Mammoth), soybean. Despite the name, it is
  \textbf{night length} that matters -- a brief flash of red light
  during the long night breaks the inductive dark period (the
  \textbf{night-break experiment}).
\item
  \textbf{Long-day plants} (LDPs): Flower when nights are
  \textbf{shorter} than a critical length. Examples: spinach,
  \emph{Arabidopsis}, barley, wheat, radish.
\item
  \textbf{Day-neutral plants:} Flower after sufficient vegetative growth
  regardless of photoperiod. Examples: tomato, cucumber, maize.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Night-Length Measurement and Circadian
Gating}\label{night-length-measurement-and-circadian-gating}

\textbf{Phytochrome} is the primary photoreceptor for photoperiodism.
During a long night, Pfr levels decline below a threshold via thermal
reversion and proteolysis. In short-day plants, this decline is required
for flowering. A brief red-light pulse during the night converts Pr back
to Pfr, resetting the clock and preventing flowering. This \textbf{night
break} effect can be reversed by an immediately subsequent far-red light
pulse --- classic evidence for phytochrome involvement.

Photoperiod is measured not by simply timing dark intervals but by
\textbf{circadian gating} --- the clock provides a window during which
light is permissive for flowering. The molecular mechanism (the
``external coincidence model'') is: CO mRNA is rhythmically expressed by
the clock (peaks in late afternoon), but CO protein is stable primarily
in light. Coincidence of light + CO protein \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} FT activation \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} flowering.

\subsubsection{The CONSTANS-FT (Florigen)
Pathway}\label{the-constans-ft-florigen-pathway}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0149_87b101c8c23e.png}
\caption{Molecular pathway of photoperiodic flowering in long-day plants The circadian clock gates CONSTANS (CO) protein stability so that in long days, CO is present in the light (when it is stabilised), activating FLOWERING LOCUS T (FT). FT protein (florigen) moves from leaves to the SAM, triggering flower development.}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Florigen --- FT as the mobile flowering signal:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  In long-day plants, the circadian clock ensures that \textbf{CONSTANS
  (CO)} mRNA peaks in the late afternoon
\item
  CO protein is stabilised by light (blue light via CRY2; far-red light
  via PhyA) but degraded in darkness via COP1 ubiquitin ligase
\item
  In long days: CO mRNA peaks coincide with daylight, CO protein is
  stable, CO binds the \textbf{FT (FLOWERING LOCUS T)}
  \hyperref[gl:promoter]{\textbf{promoter}}, activating transcription
\item
  \textbf{FT protein} --- the long-sought ``florigen'' first
  hypothesised by Chailakhyan in 1937 --- is produced in
  \textbf{companion cells of leaf phloem} and moves systemically via
  sieve tubes to the SAM. FT is a small (about 20 kDa) globular
  protein structurally related to mammalian RAF kinase inhibitors; it is
  loaded into phloem via plasmodesmata and unloaded at the SAM.
\item
  At the SAM, FT interacts with \textbf{FD} (bZIP transcription factor)
  to activate \textbf{AP1} (floral meristem identity) and \textbf{SOC1}
  (flowering pathway integrator). The FT-FD-14-3-3 floral activation
  complex (FAC) was crystallographically resolved in 2011 (Taoka
  \emph{et al.}, \emph{Nature} 2011).
\item
  The vegetative meristem transitions irreversibly to a floral meristem
  --- the moment of ``evocation''
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Diversity of FT homologues:} Most plants have multiple FT
paralogues with distinct functions. Some act as floral activators (FT in
\emph{Arabidopsis}, Hd3a in rice --- the rice florigen); some as floral
repressors (TFL1, BFT). The balance of activator and repressor FT-family
proteins fine-tunes flowering time.

\subsubsection{Vernalisation: Epigenetic Silencing of
FLC}\label{vernalisation-epigenetic-silencing-of-flc}

Prolonged cold exposure (weeks at 4 °C) promotes flowering in winter
annuals (\emph{Arabidopsis} ecotype Ler, accessions from northern
latitudes) and biennials (carrots, foxglove, sugar beet). The molecular
mechanism is a paradigmatic example of \textbf{epigenetic memory}:

\textbf{The FLC repressor (MADS-box):}

\textbf{FLC (FLOWERING LOCUS C)} is a MADS-box transcription factor that
represses \emph{FT} and \emph{SOC1}, blocking the floral transition. In
winter annuals before vernalisation, FLC is highly expressed, preventing
flowering. Vernalisation silences FLC, releasing FT/SOC1 and permitting
flowering.

\textbf{Mechanism of cold-induced FLC silencing --- the VRN2-PRC2
H3K27me3 mark:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Extended cold (\textgreater4 weeks at 4 °C) induces \textbf{VIN3}
  (VERNALISATION INSENSITIVE 3), a PHD-domain protein. VIN3 expression
  depends on a cold-memory element (CME) upstream of the \emph{VIN3}
  promoter; VIN3 transcript accumulates primarily after sustained cold
  (not pulses).
\item
  VIN3 joins \textbf{PRC2} (Polycomb Repressive Complex 2: catalytic
  subunit CLF/SWN, MSI1, FIE, VRN5) at the \textbf{FLC}
  \hyperref[gl:chromatin]{\textbf{chromatin}} via the \textbf{VRN2}
  subunit (a vernalisation-specific PRC2 partner).
\item
  PRC2 catalyses the trimethylation of histone H3 at lysine 27:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{equation}
\text{H3} \xrightarrow{\text{PRC2 (CLF/SWN, VRN2, FIE, MSI1, VIN3)}} \text{H3K27me3 at FLC}
\label{eq:unit_VIII_vernalisation}
\end{equation}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item
  H3K27me3 marks initially appear at a discrete nucleation region within
  the \emph{FLC} locus (a 1.5 kb cold-memory region spanning exon 1 and
  intron 1) during cold exposure; mark spreading across the entire
  \emph{FLC} locus occurs after return to warm.
\item
  \textbf{After return to warm:} VIN3 expression fades, but H3K27me3 is
  \textbf{maintained} by VRN2-PRC2 (which lacks VIN3 in the warm but
  retains the catalytic core), creating a \textbf{mitotically stable
  memory} of cold exposure (Finnegan \& Dennis, \emph{Plant J.} 2007;
  Sheldon \emph{et al.}, 2009).
\item
  \textbf{Mitotic inheritance:} As cells divide during spring growth,
  H3K27me3 is faithfully copied to daughter chromatin, propagating FLC
  silencing throughout the vernalised plant. The memory is gradually
  erased by demethylases in the offspring generation, resetting
  \emph{FLC} for the next winter.
\item
  \textbf{Result:} FLC (MADS-box repressor) can no longer repress
  \textbf{FT} and \textbf{SOC1} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} flowering proceeds in spring
\end{enumerate}

\begin{equation}
\text{Cold} \xrightarrow{\text{VIN3}} \text{PRC2-VRN2} \xrightarrow{\text{H3K27me3 at FLC}} \downarrow \text{FLC} \rightarrow \uparrow \text{FT} \rightarrow \text{Flowering}
\label{eq:unit_VIII_vernalisation_summary}
\end{equation}

\textbf{Concept Check:} Why does vernalisation require weeks rather than
days of cold? What happens if prolonged cold is given in pulses of a few
days each, separated by warm intervals?

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Gravitropism, Touch Responses, and Other
Tropisms}\label{gravitropism-touch-responses-and-other-tropisms}

\subsubsection{Gravitropism --- Statolith and PIN Asymmetry (deep
dive)}\label{gravitropism-statolith-and-pin-asymmetry-deep-dive}

The detailed molecular mechanism of root gravitropism integrates
statolith sedimentation, PIN protein relocalisation, and the
dose-response asymmetry between root and shoot:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Gravity perception} by amyloplast sedimentation in columella
  cells (about 30 s after reorientation)
\item
  \textbf{Mechanical signal transduction} via actin cytoskeleton and ER
  membrane interactions; LAZY1 family proteins relocalise to the new
  lower face
\item
  \textbf{PIN3 asymmetric relocalisation} to the new lower face of
  columella cells (about 3--5 min)
\item
  \textbf{Lateral auxin transport} out the new lower face into the
  cortex below
\item
  \textbf{PIN2 acropetal transport} of auxin in the elongation zone,
  biased toward the lower side
\item
  \textbf{Differential elongation:} auxin inhibits elongation on the
  lower side (root); the upper side grows faster, bending the root
  downward
\item
  \textbf{Bending complete} in 1--2 hours; PIN proteins reset to
  symmetric distribution
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Touch Responses
(Thigmomorphogenesis)}\label{touch-responses-thigmomorphogenesis}

Plants respond to mechanical stimuli --- wind, rain, animal contact ---
through \textbf{thigmomorphogenesis}, often resulting in shorter,
sturdier growth. The molecular pathway:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{TCH (TOUCH) genes} --- first identified in \emph{Arabidopsis}
  by Janet Braam (1990). The four classical TCH genes are:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{TCH1 (CAM2):} calmodulin
  \item
    \textbf{TCH2 (CML24):} calmodulin-like
  \item
    \textbf{TCH3 (CML12):} calmodulin-like
  \item
    \textbf{TCH4 (XTH22):} xyloglucan endotransglucosylase/hydrolase
    (cell-wall modifier)
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Mechanism:} Mechanical perturbation triggers Ca\(^{2+}\)
  influx via mechanosensitive channels (MCA1, MSL2, OSCA1; piezo-like).
  Cytosolic {[}Ca\(^{2+}\){]} rises within seconds.
\item
  \textbf{Calmodulin (TCH1) and CMLs (TCH2/3)} bind Ca\(^{2+}\) and
  translate the calcium signal to downstream targets --- kinases,
  transcription factors, cell-wall enzymes.
\item
  \textbf{Jasmonate production:} Mechanical wounding activates JA
  biosynthesis via the LOX pathway, mobilising defence responses in the
  herbivory and plant-immunity network.
\item
  \textbf{Phenotypic consequences:} Shorter internodes, thicker stems,
  increased lignin, smaller leaves. Brushed \emph{Arabidopsis} plants
  are 30--40\% shorter than unbrushed controls; the response is adaptive
  in windy environments.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Tendril coiling:} Climbing plants like peas, grapes, and
cucumbers produce \textbf{tendrils} that exhibit \textbf{thigmonastic}
coiling on contact with a support. The mechanism involves: -
Differential elongation: cells on the contact side stop elongating;
cells on the opposite side continue - Jasmonate signalling: JA mediates
the coiling response; \emph{Bryonia} tendrils require JA for coiling -
Within minutes of contact, tendril coils a complete 360° around the
support

\subsubsection{Other Tropisms}\label{other-tropisms}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Hydrotropism:} Roots grow toward moisture; mediated by ABA and
  MIZ1 (mizu-kussei 1) protein in root cap. \emph{miz1} mutants lack
  hydrotropism but retain gravitropism.
\item
  \textbf{Thigmotropism in roots:} Roots growing along a substrate
  exhibit obstacle avoidance, mediated by mechanosensitive channels.
\item
  \textbf{Heliotropism (solar tracking):} Sunflowers track the sun
  across the sky (East to West during the day; reverse to East at
  night). Driven by differential growth rates on east vs west sides of
  the stem, gated by the circadian clock.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Abiotic Stress Responses}\label{abiotic-stress-responses}

\subsubsection{Drought -- ABA Signalling
Cascade}\label{drought-aba-signalling-cascade}

ABA is the primary drought stress hormone:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Soil water deficit detected. Root ABA synthesis increases (NCED3
  upregulated). ABA moves via xylem to leaves.
\item
  \hyperref[gl:guard-cell]{\textbf{Guard cell}}: ABA binds
  \textbf{PYR/PYL/RCAR receptors} (14 paralogs in \emph{Arabidopsis})
\item
  ABA-PYR complex inhibits \textbf{PP2C phosphatases} (ABI1, ABI2, HAB1)
\item
  \textbf{SnRK2 kinases} (especially OST1/SnRK2.6) are freed from PP2C
  inhibition and phosphorylate:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{SLAC1} anion channel: Cl\(^-\) efflux depolarises guard cell
    membrane
  \item
    \textbf{GORK} K\(^+\) outward-rectifying channel opens: K\(^+\)
    efflux
  \item
    Water follows osmotically: guard cells shrink,
    \hyperref[gl:stomata]{\textbf{stomata}} close
  \item
    \textbf{AREB/ABF} transcription factors: activate drought-responsive
    genes (dehydrins, LEA proteins, osmolyte synthesis)
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Water use efficiency (WUE):}

\begin{equation}
WUE = \frac{A_{net}}{g_s} = \frac{\text{Net CO}_2 \text{ assimilation}}{\text{stomatal conductance}}
\label{eq:plant_responses_4}
\end{equation}

Plants under water stress maximise WUE by partially closing stomata.

\subsubsection{Worked Example: Calculating Water Use Efficiency
(WUE)}\label{worked-example-calculating-water-use-efficiency-wue}

\textbf{Problem:} An agronomist is evaluating a new drought-tolerant
wheat cultivar. Using a portable photosynthesis system, the researcher
measures a net CO\(_2\) assimilation rate (\(A_{net}\)) of
\(15 \mu\text{mol CO}_2 \text{ m}^{-2} \text{ s}^{-1}\). At the same
time, the stomatal conductance to water vapour (\(g_s\)) is measured at
\(0.15 \text{ mol H}_2\text{O m}^{-2} \text{ s}^{-1}\). 1. Calculate the
intrinsic Water Use Efficiency (WUE). 2. If ABA treatment causes the
stomata to partially close, decreasing \(g_s\) by 50\% but primarily
decreasing \(A_{net}\) by 20\%, what is the new WUE?

\textbf{Solution:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Calculate the initial WUE:} It is standard to express \(g_s\)
  in \(\mu\text{mol}\) or \(A_{net}\) in \(\mu\text{mol}\) so units
  match. First, convert \(g_s\) from mol to \(\mu\text{mol}\):
  \[ g_s = 0.15 \text{ mol} = 150,000 \mu\text{mol H}_2\text{O m}^{-2} \text{ s}^{-1}  \label{eq:unit_VIII_plant_responses_item_1}\]

  Now, apply the WUE formula:
  \[ WUE_{initial} = \frac{A_{net}}{g_s} = \frac{15}{150,000} = 0.0001 \frac{\mu\text{mol CO}_2}{\mu\text{mol H}_2\text{O}}  \label{eq:unit_VIII_plant_responses_item_2}\]

  Alternatively, keeping \(g_s\) in mol:
  \[ WUE = \frac{15 \mu\text{mol CO}_2 \text{ m}^{-2} \text{ s}^{-1}}{0.15 \text{ mol H}_2\text{O m}^{-2} \text{ s}^{-1}} = 100 \frac{\mu\text{mol CO}_2}{\text{mol H}_2\text{O}}  \label{eq:unit_VIII_plant_responses_item_3}\]
\item
  \textbf{Calculate the new rates after ABA treatment:} New \(g_s\):
  \(0.15 \cdot (1 - 0.50) = 0.075 \text{ mol H}_2\text{O m}^{-2} \text{ s}^{-1}\)
  New \(A_{net}\):
  \(15 \cdot (1 - 0.20) = 12 \mu\text{mol CO}_2 \text{ m}^{-2} \text{ s}^{-1}\)
\item
  \textbf{Calculate the new WUE:}
  \[ WUE_{new} = \frac{12}{0.075} = 160 \frac{\mu\text{mol CO}_2}{\text{mol H}_2\text{O}}  \label{eq:unit_VIII_plant_responses_item_4}\]

  The partial stomatal closure significantly improved the water use
  efficiency (from 100 to 160), demonstrating how plants optimize carbon
  gain against water loss during drought conditions.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Root architecture changes under drought:} ABA and auxin promote
deeper root growth. Lateral root emergence is suppressed while primary
root elongation continues, shifting the root system to access deeper
soil water.

\subsubsection{Cold Stress -- CBF-COR
Pathway}\label{cold-stress-cbf-cor-pathway}

\textbf{Cold acclimation} (hardening at 4 degrees C for 1-3 weeks)
increases freezing tolerance:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Temperature drop triggers membrane rigidification (gel-state
  transition) and Ca\(^{2+}\) influx (MCA1/MCA2 mechanosensitive
  channels)
\item
  \textbf{ICE1} (Inducer of CBF Expression 1; bHLH transcription factor)
  activates \textbf{CBF1/CBF2/CBF3} (C-repeat Binding Factors; AP2/ERF
  TFs) within minutes
\item
  CBFs bind CRT/DRE elements in promoters, activating \textbf{COR
  (Cold-Regulated) genes:}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{COR15:} \hyperref[gl:chloroplast]{\textbf{Chloroplast}}
    outer envelope protein; prevents membrane vesiculation
  \item
    \textbf{KIN1/KIN2:} Dehydrins; cryoprotectants that prevent protein
    aggregation
  \item
    \textbf{FAD2/FAD3:} Fatty acid desaturases that increase membrane
    unsaturated fatty acid content, maintaining membrane fluidity
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Extracellular ice management:} Ice nucleates in the apoplast
  (lower solute concentration than
  \hyperref[gl:cytoplasm]{\textbf{cytoplasm}}). Water is drawn
  osmotically from cells, producing controlled dehydration rather than
  lethal intracellular ice formation.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Antifreeze proteins:} Some cold-tolerant plants (rye, carrots)
express proteins that bind ice crystal surfaces and inhibit crystal
growth (thermal hysteresis), protecting membranes.

\subsubsection{Heat Stress -- HSP
Response}\label{heat-stress-hsp-response}

Above 35-42 degrees C, the heat shock response is activated: -
\textbf{HSFA1} transcription factors activate \textbf{HSP70, HSP90,
HSP101} chaperones that prevent protein aggregation and refold misfolded
proteins - \textbf{Small HSPs} (sHSPs, 15-40 kDa): ATP-independent
holdases that accumulate in cytoplasmic aggregates -
\textbf{Thermomemory:} H3K4me3 epigenetic marks at HSP loci persist for
several days, allowing faster response to subsequent heat episodes

\subsubsection{Salt Stress}\label{salt-stress}

High soil salinity (NaCl) causes both osmotic stress and ion toxicity: -
\textbf{SOS pathway} (Salt Overly Sensitive): SOS3 (Ca\(^{2+}\) sensor)
activates SOS2 (kinase), which activates \textbf{SOS1} (Na\(^+\)/H\(^+\)
antiporter) to expel Na\(^+\) from roots - \textbf{Vacuolar
sequestration:} NHX1 antiporter pumps Na\(^+\) into vacuole -
\textbf{Compatible osmolytes:} Proline, glycine betaine, mannitol
accumulate to lower \(\psi_s\) without enzyme inhibition

\subsubsection{Flooding Response}\label{flooding-response}

Submergence deprives roots of O\(_2\): - \textbf{ERFVII transcription
factors} (RAP2.2, RAP2.12): Stabilised under hypoxia (normally degraded
by the N-end rule pathway when O\(_2\) is present -- direct O\(_2\)
sensing) - ERFVIIs activate \textbf{\hyperref[gl:anaerobic]{anaerobic}
genes:} ADH (alcohol dehydrogenase) for
\hyperref[gl:fermentation]{\textbf{fermentation}}, PDC (pyruvate
decarboxylase) - \textbf{Aerenchyma formation:} Ethylene (accumulates
because ACC oxidase requires O\(_2\)) triggers programmed cell death in
cortical cells, creating gas-filled channels for O\(_2\) transport from
aerial parts to submerged roots - \textbf{Escape strategy:} Deepwater
rice varieties elongate internodes rapidly (up to 25 cm/day) via GA and
ethylene signalling to keep leaves above water

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Plant Immunity --- A Two-Layer Defence
System}\label{plant-immunity-a-two-layer-defence-system}

Plants lack circulating immune cells but possess a sophisticated
cell-autonomous immune system organised into two layers. The
Jones--Dangl ``zigzag model'' (2006) is the canonical framework.

\subsubsection{Layer 1: PAMP-Triggered Immunity
(PTI)}\label{layer-1-pamp-triggered-immunity-pti}

Plants recognise broadly conserved molecular signatures of pathogens ---
\textbf{PAMPs} (Pathogen-Associated Molecular Patterns) or
\textbf{MAMPs} (Microbe-Associated Molecular Patterns) --- via
cell-surface \textbf{pattern recognition receptors (PRRs)}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{FLS2} (Flagellin Sensitive 2): A leucine-rich repeat receptor
  kinase (LRR-RK) that binds \textbf{flg22} (a 22 amino acid epitope of
  bacterial flagellin). FLS2-flg22 binding recruits \textbf{BAK1}
  co-receptor, activating intracellular kinase signalling.
\item
  \textbf{EFR}: Recognises bacterial elongation factor Tu (epitope
  \textbf{elf18})
\item
  \textbf{CERK1} and \textbf{LYK} receptors: Recognise fungal chitin
  oligomers (mostly tetra- and pentamers of N-acetylglucosamine)
\item
  \textbf{PEPR1/2}: Recognise plant-derived danger signals (PEPs)
\end{itemize}

\textbf{PTI signalling cascade:} 1. PRR ligand binding \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} BAK1
co-receptor recruitment 2. \textbf{BIK1} receptor-like cytoplasmic
kinase activated 3. \textbf{RBOHD} NADPH oxidase produces apoplastic ROS
burst (reactive oxygen species; H\(_2\)O\(_2\) within minutes) 4.
\textbf{MPK3/MPK6} MAP kinase cascade activated; transcription of
defence genes (PR1, WRKY TFs) 5. \textbf{Stomatal closure} via SLAC1
(preventing bacterial entry through stomata) 6. \textbf{Callose
deposition} at cell wall (papillae) limiting pathogen ingress

PTI provides broad-spectrum, modest resistance to most non-specialist
pathogens.

\subsubsection{Layer 2: Effector-Triggered Immunity
(ETI)}\label{layer-2-effector-triggered-immunity-eti}

Successful pathogens deliver \textbf{effector proteins} into host cells
(via type III secretion systems in bacteria, haustoria in
fungi/oomycetes) to suppress PTI. Plants in turn evolved intracellular
\textbf{NBS-LRR proteins} (also called R proteins or NLRs) that
recognise these effectors:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{NBS-LRR} (Nucleotide-Binding Site, Leucine-Rich Repeat):
  Intracellular immune receptors. \emph{Arabidopsis} has
  about 150 NBS-LRR genes. Two structural classes: TIR-NLRs
  (with N-terminal Toll/Interleukin-1 Receptor domain) and CC-NLRs
  (coiled-coil).
\item
  \textbf{Recognition modes:}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{Direct binding:} R protein binds effector directly (e.g.,
    RPP1 binds \emph{Hyaloperonospora} ATR1)
  \item
    \textbf{Indirect ``guard'' model:} R protein guards a host target of
    effector; effector modification of the target triggers R activation
    (e.g., RPS2 guards RIN4; \emph{Pseudomonas} AvrRpt2 cleaves RIN4,
    activating RPS2)
  \item
    \textbf{Decoy model:} Plant evolves a non-functional mimic of an
    effector target as a ``decoy'' to bait R protein activation
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{ETI signalling and the hypersensitive response (HR):}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  NLR activation \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} oligomerisation (resistosome formation; ZAR1 forms a
  pentameric ``resistosome'' channel; Wang \emph{et al.}, \emph{Science}
  2019)
\item
  Resistosome inserts into plasma membrane and conducts Ca\(^{2+}\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  cytosolic {[}Ca\(^{2+}\){]} surge
\item
  \textbf{EDS1/PAD4 hub} activates downstream signalling
\item
  \textbf{Hypersensitive response (HR):} Programmed cell death at the
  infection site; sacrificial necrotic lesion that prevents pathogen
  spread. HR is morphologically similar to animal apoptosis but
  molecularly distinct (involves vacuolar processing enzymes, autophagy
  components, and ROS).
\item
  \textbf{Salicylic acid (SA) accumulation} locally and systemically
\end{enumerate}

ETI is faster and stronger than PTI --- typically resulting in the
visible \textbf{hypersensitive lesion} within 24--48 hours of infection.

\subsubsection{Systemic Acquired Resistance
(SAR)}\label{systemic-acquired-resistance-sar}

Local infection triggers a long-lasting, systemic defence priming
throughout the plant --- \textbf{systemic acquired resistance (SAR)}.
The mobile signal includes: - \textbf{Methyl salicylate (MeSA)}:
volatile, can travel through phloem and air - \textbf{Pipecolic acid
(Pip)} and N-hydroxy-pipecolic acid (NHP): essential systemic mobile
signals (Bernsdorff \emph{et al.}, \emph{PNAS} 2016) -
\textbf{Glycerol-3-phosphate (G3P)} and azelaic acid

In distal tissues, SA accumulates and activates \textbf{NPR1}
(Non-expressor of PR genes 1):

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  NPR1 in the cytoplasm exists as oligomers (inactive) due to disulfide
  bonds
\item
  SA accumulation alters cellular redox; NPR1 is reduced to monomers
\item
  Monomeric NPR1 enters nucleus and binds \textbf{TGA} transcription
  factors
\item
  NPR1-TGA complex activates \textbf{PR1 (Pathogenesis-Related 1)} and
  other PR genes --- antimicrobial proteins, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-1,3-glucanases,
  chitinases
\item
  SAR provides 1--2 weeks of broad-spectrum resistance to subsequent
  infections
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{JA/SA Antagonism}\label{jasa-antagonism}

The two major immune hormones --- \textbf{salicylic acid (SA)} for
biotrophic pathogens and \textbf{jasmonic acid (JA)} for chewing
herbivores and necrotrophic pathogens --- exhibit pervasive
\textbf{antagonism}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{SA suppresses JA:} SA-induced NPR1 represses \emph{MYC2}
  (master JA TF) and JA-responsive genes; high SA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} low JA defences
\item
  \textbf{JA suppresses SA:} JA-induced \emph{WRKY70} and \emph{MYC2}
  repress SA biosynthesis (ICS1) and PR1; high JA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} low SA defences
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Why antagonism?} Different pathogens require different defence
chemistries: biotrophs (powdery mildew, rust fungi) feed on living
tissue and are best controlled by SA-induced HR; necrotrophs
(\emph{Botrytis}, \emph{Pythium}) and herbivores benefit from cell death
and are best controlled by JA-induced toxins/proteases. Allocating to
both is metabolically expensive; antagonism enables prioritisation.

\textbf{Pathogen exploitation of antagonism:} \emph{Pseudomonas
syringae} pv. \emph{tomato} produces \textbf{coronatine} (COR), a
structural mimic of JA-Ile. COR activates the JA pathway, suppressing
the SA pathway and stomatal-closure-mediated immunity. The bacterium
uses this to enter through normally-closed stomata. \emph{Arabidopsis
coi1} mutants (insensitive to JA) are resistant to COR-mediated stomatal
reopening.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Herbivory and Wound Defence -- Jasmonate
Signalling}\label{herbivory-and-wound-defence-jasmonate-signalling}

Physical insect damage triggers the JA signalling cascade:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Membrane damage releases linolenic acid
\item
  \textbf{13-LOX} (lipoxygenase) pathway in plastids produces 12-OPDA
\item
  Peroxisomal \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-oxidation produces JA
\item
  \textbf{JAR1} conjugates JA with isoleucine to form \textbf{JA-Ile}
\item
  JA-Ile binds \textbf{COI1} (F-box protein), recruiting JAZ repressors
  for ubiquitin-mediated degradation
\item
  \textbf{MYC2/MYC3/MYC4} transcription factors are released,
  activating:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{Protease inhibitors:} Reduce digestibility of plant proteins
    in insect gut
  \item
    \textbf{Alkaloids:} Nicotine in tobacco, glucosinolates in
    Brassicaceae
  \item
    \textbf{Volatile terpenes:} (E)-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-ocimene, linalool attract
    predatory insects and parasitic wasps (indirect defence)
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection:} The wound response in plants is remarkably
fast. Within 30 seconds of \emph{Manduca sexta} (tobacco hornworm)
feeding on \emph{Nicotiana attenuata}, JA-Ile accumulates. Within 1
hour, systemic protease inhibitor expression is detected. Within 24
hours, volatile terpenoids attract predatory \emph{Geocoris} bugs. This
multi-layered defence system has inspired ``push-pull'' agricultural
strategies where companion plants emit volatiles to repel pests and
attract their natural enemies.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Shade Avoidance Syndrome}\label{shade-avoidance-syndrome}

In canopy shade, the R:FR (red:far-red) ratio decreases because
chlorophyll absorbs red light but transmits far-red:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{PhyB} converts from active Pfr to inactive Pr form
\item
  \textbf{PIF4, PIF5, PIF7} (Phytochrome Interacting Factors) freed from
  PhyB repression
\item
  PIF4/5 activate \textbf{YUCCA} genes, increasing auxin synthesis in
  hypocotyls
\item
  Rapid hypocotyl and petiole elongation (shade avoidance)
\item
  Accelerated flowering (via PIF4 activation of FT promoter)
\item
  Reduced branching, leaf area, and root investment
\end{itemize}

This shade avoidance syndrome represents a competitive strategy: grow
taller to overtop neighbours and reproduce before being shaded out.
However, it comes at a cost of reduced root investment and mechanical
stability.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Epigenetic Stress Memory in
Plants}\label{epigenetic-stress-memory-in-plants}

Plants lack a germline-soma separation and can transmit epigenetic marks
trans-generationally:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Somatic priming:} SA treatment deposits H3K4me3 marks at WRKY
  promoters, maintained for weeks. Subsequent pathogen attack triggers
  faster and stronger PR gene induction.
\item
  \textbf{Trans-generational immunity:} Pathogen-stressed parents
  produce offspring with enhanced resistance via DNA methylation changes
  at transposable element loci (RdDM pathway -- RNA-directed DNA
  methylation).
\item
  \textbf{Heat stress memory:} H3K4me3 at HSP genes persists for several
  days after heat episode.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Concept Check:} Why might trans-generational epigenetic stress
memory be particularly advantageous in plants compared to animals?

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Agricultural Applications of Plant Hormone
Biology}\label{agricultural-applications-of-plant-hormone-biology}

Decades of basic research on plant hormones have generated
transformative agricultural technologies:

The strongest applications now combine hormone biology with genotype,
microbiome, water status, and field context. Drought tolerance, heat
tolerance, salinity tolerance, and pathogen resistance often trade off
against growth or yield, so breeders increasingly stack traits and test
them across environments rather than searching for a single
comprehensive ``stress gene.'' Hormone interventions should be evaluated
by phenotype, resource cost, reproductive outcome, and performance under
realistic combined stresses.

\subsubsection{Ethylene Inhibitors --- Postharvest
Storage}\label{ethylene-inhibitors-postharvest-storage}

\textbf{1-MCP (1-methylcyclopropene):} A small gaseous molecule that
competitively binds the ethylene receptor ETR1, blocking ethylene
perception. Commercial product \emph{SmartFresh} applied to apples,
pears, kiwifruit, and avocados: - Apples treated with 1-MCP can be
stored 6--9 months (vs 2--3 months untreated) with retained firmness,
sugar content, and flavour - The North American apple industry is
essentially built on 1-MCP storage - Other ethylene management:
\textbf{AVG} (aminoethoxyvinylglycine; ACS inhibitor) used pre-harvest
in stone fruits to delay ripening; \textbf{silver thiosulfate (STS)} in
cut flowers to preserve vase life

\subsubsection{Gibberellin Biology --- The Green
Revolution}\label{gibberellin-biology-the-green-revolution}

The semi-dwarf wheat varieties that catalysed the Green Revolution carry
mutations in \textbf{gibberellin signalling}: - \textbf{Rht-B1b and
Rht-D1b} in wheat: encode gain-of-function alleles of \emph{DELLA} genes
that produce stable, GA-insensitive DELLA proteins. Plants do not
respond to GA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} reduced internodal elongation \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} semi-dwarf stature \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} no
lodging under heavy grain heads. - \textbf{sd1} in rice (the IR8
``miracle rice'' of 1966): loss-of-function mutation in \emph{GA20ox-2}
(a GA biosynthesis enzyme) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} reduced GA levels \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} semi-dwarf - Both
mutations enable plants to support large grain heads, harvest more
nitrogen-fertiliser into seed, and resist storm damage. Together they
account for \textgreater50\% of global wheat and rice acreage.

\textbf{GA application:} Exogenous GA\(_3\) is sprayed on: - Seedless
table grapes (induces parthenocarpy and elongates clusters) - Sugarcane
(increases stem length and sugar yield) - Hybrid rice seed production
(activates female lines)

\subsubsection{Auxin Herbicides}\label{auxin-herbicides}

\textbf{2,4-D (2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid)} and related compounds
(dicamba, MCPA) are synthetic auxin analogues used as selective
broadleaf herbicides: - Mechanism: synthetic auxins activate the same
TIR1-Aux/IAA-ARF pathway as natural IAA, but at much higher and
sustained concentrations - Sustained activation triggers ethylene
biosynthesis, ABA accumulation, and ultimately growth abnormalities and
death in dicots - Monocots (grasses, including cereal crops) tolerate
2,4-D because they have lower TIR1 binding affinity, faster auxin
metabolism, and morphology that limits leaf retention of spray - 2,4-D
was developed in WWII as part of biological warfare research;
declassified post-war and adopted for agricultural use in 1946. It
became the most-used herbicide globally for decades. -
Glyphosate-resistance now dominates, but 2,4-D and dicamba have
re-emerged in stacked-trait crops (Enlist E3 soybean, Xtend cotton)

\subsubsection{Other Hormone-Based
Technologies}\label{other-hormone-based-technologies}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Cytokinin sprays:} maintain green leaves in cut flowers; delay
  senescence
\item
  \textbf{ABA analogues:} in development for drought-priming of crop
  seedlings
\item
  \textbf{Strigolactone analogues (e.g., GR24):} induce suicidal
  germination of \emph{Striga} parasitic weeds in absence of host,
  reducing field infestation
\item
  \textbf{Plant growth retardants:} uniconazole, paclobutrazol --- GA
  biosynthesis inhibitors used to keep ornamentals compact
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection:} Plant hormone biology supplies an
extraordinary fraction of agricultural innovation. The Green Revolution
(semi-dwarf GA-insensitive wheat and rice), modern fruit storage
(1-MCP), and the largest herbicide markets (2,4-D, dicamba --- synthetic
auxins) most derive directly from understanding hormone signalling
pathways characterised in \emph{Arabidopsis} and other model species.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-29}

For \textbf{Plant Responses to the Environment}, frontier biology
belongs inside the evidence logic of the chapter. Plant biology links
molecular regulation to climate stress, water limitation, crop
resilience, phenology, and ecosystem feedbacks. The core reading
question is this: plant response claims should connect signal
perception, hormone network, gene expression, phenotype, and tradeoff.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

A strong plant explanation names the tissue, signal, environmental
driver, measurable trait, and tradeoff between growth, reproduction,
defence, and water use.

\textbf{Source practice:} For plant-stress and crop claims, name the
tissue, environmental driver, field context, and growth-reproduction
tradeoff; separate laboratory potential from agronomic adoption.

\subsubsection{Current Evidence Map: Plant Stress Response
Decision}\label{current-evidence-map-plant-stress-response-decision}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0150_9c1b03a0028a.png}
\caption{Stress tolerance is not free: the same response that improves survival can reduce growth or reproduction depending on timing and environment.}

\subsubsection{Field Translation: Stress Circuits Are Not Field
Proof}\label{field-translation-stress-circuits-are-not-field-proof}

Synthetic response circuits and hormone interventions should be read as
hypotheses about a controllable decision point, not as proof of
agronomic benefit. A moisture-responsive stomatal circuit must show that
closure occurs before damaging xylem tension but does not depress carbon
gain enough to reduce yield. An inducible defence promoter must show low
leakiness, fast activation under natural herbivory, and minimal cost to
growth or beneficial insects. A flowering-time circuit must be tested
against local chilling, photoperiod, heat, and pollinator windows. The
field claim becomes credible when mechanism, expression stability,
off-target phenotypes, gene flow, management context, and multi-season
yield or fitness data point in the same direction.

\textbf{PIN proteins} & Auxin efflux carriers; polar localisation

\textbf{Acid growth hypothesis} & Auxin activates H\(^+\)-ATPase,

\textbf{DELLA proteins} & Transcriptional repressors degraded by GA-GID1

CO, HFR1 for degradation \\

\textbf{Photoperiodism} & Regulation of developmental events (especially
flowering) by day/night length \\
\textbf{CONSTANS (CO)} & bZIP transcription factor; activator of FT in
long-day flowering \\
\textbf{Florigen (FT)} & Mobile protein produced in leaf companion
cells; travels to SAM via phloem to trigger flowering \\
\textbf{FLC} & MADS-box repressor of flowering; silenced by
vernalisation (H3K27me3 by VRN2-PRC2) \\
\textbf{Vernalisation} & Cold-mediated epigenetic silencing of FLC
enabling flowering \\
\textbf{Circadian clock} & Endogenous about 24 h oscillator;
CCA1/LHY-TOC1-PRR interlocked loops \\
\textbf{CCA1/LHY} & Morning-expressed MYB TFs; repress evening genes \\
\textbf{TOC1/PRR1} & Evening-expressed pseudo-response regulator;
represses CCA1/LHY \\
\textbf{PRR9/7/5} & Sequential daytime PRRs in evening loop \\
\textbf{Evening Complex (ELF3-ELF4-LUX)} & Repressor complex peaking at
ZT12-16; gates early-night growth \\
\textbf{Statolith} & Starch-filled amyloplast in columella cells;

\textbf{LAZY1} & Protein required for normal gravitropism; relocalises

\textbf{TCH genes} & Touch-induced genes (CAM2, CML24, CML12, XTH22);

\textbf{Thigmomorphogenesis} & Mechanical-stimulus-induced morphology

\textbf{ABA} & Abscisic acid; stress hormone; PYR/PYL receptors activate

\textbf{CBF/DREB} & C-repeat Binding Factors; AP2/ERF TFs; cold-induced,

ligand for COI1 receptor \\
\textbf{COI1} & Coronatine Insensitive 1; F-box protein; JA-Ile

\textbf{PTI} & PAMP-Triggered Immunity; first-layer defence via

\textbf{ETI} & Effector-Triggered Immunity; second-layer defence via
intracellular NBS-LRR proteins \\
\textbf{NBS-LRR (NLR)} & Nucleotide-Binding Site, Leucine-Rich Repeat;

\textbf{HR (Hypersensitive Response)} & Programmed cell death at

\textbf{SAR} & Systemic Acquired Resistance; SA-mediated whole-plant

\subsection{Review Questions}\label{review-questions-29}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  An \emph{Arabidopsis phot1 phot2} double mutant is grown under
  asymmetric blue light. Predict the
  \hyperref[gl:phenotype]{\textbf{phenotype}}. Would this mutant show
  any phototropic response under high-intensity white light? (Hint:
  consider cryptochromes.)
\item
  Explain why the same auxin redistribution (accumulation on the lower
  side) causes opposite growth responses in roots vs shoots during
  gravitropism. Include the concepts of optimal auxin concentration,
  dose-response curves, and PIN2 vs PIN3 localisation.
\item
  A farmer notices that long-day wheat varieties flower prematurely when
  grown near street lights that extend the day length. Explain the
  molecular mechanism, starting from phytochrome and proceeding through
  the CO-FT pathway. Include the role of CRY2 in stabilising CO protein.
\item
  Compare the ABA-mediated drought response with the CBF-COR cold
  acclimation pathway. What do they share in common? How do the final
  cellular protective mechanisms differ?
\item
  \emph{Pseudomonas syringae} produces coronatine (COR), a JA-Ile mimic.
  Explain how COR suppresses stomatal immunity (PTI) and promotes
  bacterial entry. Design a crop plant with COR-insensitive COI1 that
  resists this strategy without compromising wound response.
\item
  A researcher discovers that a particular \emph{Arabidopsis} accession
  shows enhanced cold tolerance without prior cold acclimation. The line
  has constitutively high expression of CBF3. What are the likely growth
  penalties of constitutive CBF expression, and why?
\item
  Explain the molecular basis of the ``night break'' experiment in
  short-day plants. Why does a brief pulse of red light in the middle of
  a long night prevent flowering, and why does an immediately subsequent
  far-red pulse restore the flowering response?
\item
  Compare ethylene's role in fruit ripening vs flooding response. How is
  the same hormone adapted for such different functions?
\item
  Sample three points from \breaktt{light\_response\_curve()} and
  identify roughly where the curve saturates for default C3-like
  parameters.
\item
  Explain how \textbf{phyB} thermosensing can decouple flowering time
  from true photoperiod in warming climates.
\item
  Describe the molecular memory of vernalisation in \emph{Arabidopsis}.
  How is the VRN2-PRC2-mediated H3K27me3 mark at \emph{FLC} maintained
  through cell division and erased between generations?
\item
  Distinguish PTI and ETI in the Jones--Dangl zigzag model. What is the
  role of resistosome formation? How does the SA-NPR1 pathway translate
  local infection into systemic acquired resistance?
\item
  Explain why 2,4-D selectively kills broadleaf weeds in cereal crops.
  At the molecular level, how does sustained synthetic auxin signalling
  cause death in dicots but not monocots?
\item
  Trace the \emph{Arabidopsis} circadian clock through one full day
  starting at dawn (ZT0). Identify which genes are expressed at ZT0,
  ZT4, ZT8, ZT12, and ZT16, and explain the negative-feedback
  architecture.
\item
  Tendril coiling in cucumber requires touch and JA. A \emph{coi1}
  loss-of-function mutant cucumber is challenged with a thin string.
  Predict the response, and explain why JA signalling is downstream of
  mechanical perception.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-29}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Plant hormones:} Nine major classes (auxin, GA, cytokinin,
  ABA, ethylene, JA, SA, brassinosteroids, strigolactones) regulate most
  aspects of growth, development, and stress responses through
  receptor-mediated signalling pathways.
\item
  \textbf{Phototropism \citep{went1926}:} PHOT1/2 (LOV-domain kinases)
  trigger asymmetric PIN3 relocalisation, creating a lateral auxin
  gradient. Acid growth (H\(^+\)-ATPase to expansins) drives
  differential elongation \citep{hager1971}.
\item
  \textbf{Photomorphogenesis:} Phytochromes (Pr/Pfr photoconversion at
  660/730 nm) sense R:FR ratio for shade avoidance; cryptochromes
  (CRY1/CRY2 with FAD) sense blue light for photomorphogenesis. PhyA
  mediates FR-HIR; PhyB is the canopy-shade sensor. CRY-COP1-HY5 module
  enforces light/dark choice.
\item
  \textbf{Circadian clock molecular architecture:} Morning loop
  (CCA1/LHY repressors of evening genes; TOC1 activator); evening loop
  (PRR9/7/5/TOC1 cascade repressing CCA1/LHY); evening complex
  (ELF3-ELF4-LUX). Temperature-compensated.
\item
  \textbf{Photoperiodism:} Night length is the true signal. Phytochrome
  (Pr/Pfr) measures dark duration. The CO-FT-AP1 pathway integrates
  circadian clock and light signals. FT protein moves from leaf
  companion cells to SAM as the long-sought florigen.
\item
  \textbf{Vernalisation:} Cold-induced VIN3 joins VRN2-PRC2; H3K27me3
  deposition at \emph{FLC} silences this MADS-box repressor of
  flowering. Memory is mitotically stable but reset between generations.
\item
  \textbf{Gravitropism:} Amyloplast settling in statocytes triggers PIN3
  relocalisation. Same auxin redistribution causes opposite responses in
  roots (PIN2 carries auxin acropetally; high auxin inhibits root cells)
  vs shoots (high auxin promotes shoot cells).
\item
  \textbf{Touch responses:} TCH genes (calmodulins, XTH22) mediate
  Ca\(^{2+}\)-driven thigmomorphogenesis; jasmonate links wound
  perception to defence and tendril coiling.
\item
  \textbf{Drought:} ABA activates PYR-PP2C-SnRK2-SLAC1 cascade for
  stomatal closure plus AREB/ABF for stress gene expression.
\item
  \textbf{Cold:} CBF1/2/3 activated by ICE1 within minutes of cold
  exposure; COR genes produce dehydrins, desaturases, and cryoprotective
  proteins.
\item
  \textbf{Flooding:} ERFVII transcription factors sense O\(_2\) via the
  N-end rule; ethylene promotes aerenchyma formation.
\item
  \textbf{Plant immunity (Jones--Dangl zigzag):} PTI via cell-surface
  PRRs (FLS2/BAK1, CERK1) recognising PAMPs. ETI via intracellular
  NBS-LRR (NLR) proteins recognising effectors; resistosome formation
  triggers HR. NPR1-mediated SAR provides systemic broad-spectrum
  priming via SA. JA-SA antagonism partitions defences;
  \emph{Pseudomonas} coronatine exploits this.
\item
  \textbf{Herbivory:} JA-Ile triggers COI1-JAZ degradation, releasing
  MYC2 to activate protease inhibitors, alkaloids, and volatile-mediated
  indirect defence.
\item
  \textbf{Shade avoidance:} Low R:FR frees PIF4/5 from PhyB repression,
  increasing auxin and accelerating flowering.
\item
  \textbf{Agricultural applications:} Ethylene inhibitors (1-MCP for
  postharvest); GA-insensitive DELLA mutations (\emph{Rht}, \emph{sd1})
  underlie Green Revolution semi-dwarf wheat and rice; synthetic auxin
  herbicides (2,4-D, dicamba) selectively kill broadleaf weeds.
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See \cref{sec:unit_III_photosynthesis} for light
  reactions, \cref{sec:unit_II_cell_signaling} for receptor signalling
  parallels, and Unit X for phenology under climate change.
\end{itemize}

\section*{Unit IX --- Zoology and Systems Physiology:
Introduction}\label{unit-ix-zoology-and-systems-physiology-introduction}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Unit IX --- Zoology and Systems
Physiology: Introduction}

\subsection*{Why This Unit Matters}\label{why-this-unit-matters-9}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Why This Unit Matters}

In 1628, William Harvey published \emph{Exercitatio Anatomica de Motu
Cordis et Sanguinis in Animalibus} (On the Motion of the Heart and Blood
in Animals) and overturned nearly 1,500 years of Galenic medicine.
Harvey demonstrated, through quantitative reasoning alone, that the
heart must be a pump recirculating the same blood --- not a furnace
generating new blood from food. He calculated that the heart pushes
approximately 1.8 litres of blood per minute; if blood flowed outward
and were not returned, the entire blood volume (about 5 litres) would be
exhausted in under 3 minutes. Therefore, it must circulate. This was
physiology as computational biology --- numbers proving mechanism before
any understanding of cellular biology existed.

Modern systems physiology is even more mathematical. The Hodgkin-Huxley
model (1952) describes the action potential as a set of four coupled
nonlinear ordinary differential equations and was solved numerically
before computers capable of doing so efficiently were widely available.
Today, the same mathematical framework underlies cardiac
electrophysiology, pharmacological ion channel modelling, and the design
of neural prosthetics. Homeostasis --- the maintenance of stable
internal conditions --- is formalised as a negative feedback control
system: a detector, comparator, and effector maintaining a set-point,
mathematically identical to engineering control systems.

This unit covers four major physiological systems --- circulatory,
nervous, endocrine, and immune --- with quantitative models throughout.
You will apply the Hodgkin-Huxley equations to the action potential,
calculate Starling forces for capillary filtration, model hormonal
negative feedback with Hill equations, and contrast innate and adaptive
immune responses as computational pattern-recognition systems. Clinical
connections appear in every section: from cardiac arrhythmias to
diabetes mellitus, from anaphylaxis to Parkinson's disease.

\subsection*{Current Evidence Thread}\label{current-evidence-thread-9}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Current Evidence Thread}

Read this unit as physiology that is known because it has been measured:
every claim about action potentials, circulation, hormones, immunity,
and neural circuits rests on a recording, an image, a perturbation, or a
clinical measurement, and the strength of the claim is no better than
the method behind it. Physiology now blends mechanism with allostasis,
immune-endocrine-neural coupling, wearable data, and individualized risk
without reducing bodies to simple machines. As you move through the
chapters, keep a two-column note: \textbf{claim} on the left,
\textbf{evidence that would change my confidence} on the right. By the
end of the unit, each major idea should be tied to a measurement, model,
citation, or paper-based lab decision.
