\textbf{Schwann cells} & PNS & Myelination (one cell per axon segment,
about 1 mm internode); nerve repair via Bands of Bungner \\
\textbf{Microglia} & CNS & Resident macrophages; synaptic pruning
(complement C1q/C3-tagged synapses phagocytosed); neuroinflammation;
activated in Alzheimer's, TBI, MS \\
\textbf{Ependymal cells} & CNS & Line ventricles; ciliated surface moves
CSF; produce CSF (together with choroid plexus; 450-500 mL/day; total
CSF volume about 150 mL, replaced about 3
times/day) \\
\textbf{Radial glia} & Developing CNS & Neural stem cells; scaffold for
neuronal migration (inside-out cortical layering); give rise to both
neurons and glia \\
\textbf{Satellite cells} & PNS & Surround cell bodies in ganglia;
analogous to astrocytes \\
\end{longtable}
}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection:} Microglia-mediated synaptic pruning is
essential during development (eliminating about 50\% of
synapses during adolescence). Dysregulated pruning has been linked to
schizophrenia: the complement component C4A
\hyperref[gl:gene]{\textbf{gene}} is the strongest genetic risk factor
for schizophrenia (Sekar et al., 2016, \emph{Nature}). Individuals with
high C4A expression show excessive synaptic pruning in prefrontal cortex
during adolescence, correlating with symptom onset.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Astrocytes --- More Than
Glue}\label{astrocytes-more-than-glue}

Astrocytes were once considered passive support cells but are now
recognised as active partners in synaptic transmission, brain
metabolism, and homeostasis. A single cortical astrocyte contacts
about 100,000--2,000,000 synapses through its fine processes
(``perisynaptic astrocyte processes'' or PAPs) --- forming the third
element of the \textbf{tripartite synapse} (presynaptic terminal +
postsynaptic spine + astrocyte process).

\textbf{Key astrocyte functions:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{K\(^+\) spatial buffering:} Following synaptic activity,
  extracellular K\(^+\) rises locally. Astrocytes express high densities
  of inwardly-rectifying Kir4.1 channels and aquaporin-4 (AQP4) at
  endfeet on capillaries. K\(^+\) enters astrocytes locally and exits at
  sites of low K\(^+\) via the panastrocytic syncytium (gap junctions
  formed by connexin 43/30) --- preventing extracellular K\(^+\)
  accumulation that would depolarise neurons and disrupt firing.
\item
  \textbf{Glutamate clearance:} EAAT1 and EAAT2 transporters (the
  ``glutamate-aspartate transporters'') on astrocytes clear
  about 90\% of synaptically released glutamate. EAAT2/GLT-1
  dysfunction is implicated in ALS (mutations) and excitotoxicity in
  stroke.
\item
  \textbf{Glutamate-glutamine cycle:} Astrocytes convert glutamate to
  glutamine via glutamine synthetase, then export glutamine to neurons,
  where neurons reconvert it back to glutamate via glutaminase. This
  metabolically traps glutamate within neurons (glutamate is itself a
  metabolic intermediate that cannot be allowed to accumulate in
  extracellular space).
\item
  \textbf{Astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle:} Astrocytes preferentially
  perform glycolysis (express PFK1 and LDH-A) and export lactate. Active
  neurons take up lactate via MCT2 and use it as a major energy
  substrate during sustained activity. This ``ANLS hypothesis''
  (Pellerin and Magistretti, 1994) explains the glucose-lactate
  metabolic coupling underlying fMRI BOLD signals.
\item
  \textbf{Gliotransmission:} Activated astrocytes release glutamate,
  ATP, D-serine (an NMDA receptor co-agonist), and other transmitters
  via Ca\(^{2+}\)-dependent vesicle exocytosis or channel-mediated
  release --- modulating synaptic transmission and plasticity.
\item
  \textbf{Reactive astrogliosis:} After CNS injury, astrocytes
  hypertrophy, upregulate GFAP, and form glial scars. This both contains
  damage and inhibits axonal regeneration (chondroitin sulphate
  proteoglycans). Modulating reactive astrogliosis is a target for
  spinal cord injury therapeutics.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Oligodendrocytes and
Myelin}\label{oligodendrocytes-and-myelin}

Oligodendrocytes wrap layers of plasma membrane around axons in the CNS.
A single oligodendrocyte myelinates segments on up to \textbf{50
different axons} simultaneously (contrast with Schwann cells in PNS: one
cell, one axon). The myelin sheath is up to \textbf{100 layers} thick,
formed by repeated wrapping with extrusion of cytoplasm. The major
proteins are: - \textbf{Myelin basic protein (MBP):} Compaction of
cytoplasmic faces. Major autoantigen in multiple sclerosis. -
\textbf{Proteolipid protein (PLP):} Compaction of extracellular faces.
Mutations cause Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease. - \textbf{Myelin
oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG):} Outer surface; minor protein but
major autoantigen in some demyelinating diseases (e.g., MOG antibody
disease).

Myelin development continues into the third decade of life, particularly
in prefrontal cortex --- coinciding with maturation of executive
function. Adult oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs, NG2+ cells)
maintain a regenerative capacity, but it is incomplete after
demyelinating injury.

\subsubsection{Microglia --- Resident Macrophages of the
CNS}\label{microglia-resident-macrophages-of-the-cns}

Microglia derive from yolk-sac primitive macrophages that colonised the
developing CNS before formation of the blood-brain barrier. They are
\textbf{self-renewing} (independent of blood monocytes) and constitute
about 10\% of CNS cells.

\textbf{States and functions:} - \textbf{Resting (surveillance):} Highly
ramified processes constantly sample the parenchyma; turnover of most
brain volume every few hours. - \textbf{Activated (M1-like,
pro-inflammatory):} Upon detection of pathogens (TLR ligands), tissue
damage (DAMPs: ATP, HMGB1), or aggregated proteins (A\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-synuclein) ---
retract processes, become amoeboid, secrete TNF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}, IL-1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}, IL-6, NO;
phagocytose debris. - \textbf{Alternatively activated (M2-like,
repair):} Secrete IL-10, TGF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}; promote tissue repair. -
\textbf{Synaptic pruning:} Microglia tag underused synapses with
complement (C1q \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} C3) for phagocytic engulfment. Critical during
development; pathological in Alzheimer's (excessive pruning in
hippocampus) and schizophrenia (excessive pruning in prefrontal cortex
during adolescence).

\subsubsection{Blood-Brain Barrier --- Molecular
Architecture}\label{blood-brain-barrier-molecular-architecture}

The \textbf{blood-brain barrier (BBB)} is a selective barrier between
blood and brain parenchyma that excludes most polar molecules, ions,
large molecules, and pathogens, while allowing essential nutrients to
enter. It is formed by:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Tight junctions} between brain capillary endothelial cells,
  sealed by claudin-5, occludin, JAM-1, and zonula occludens (ZO-1,
  ZO-2). Transendothelial electrical resistance is about 1500
  \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Omega}}{Omega}\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.}cm\(^2\) --- orders of magnitude higher than peripheral capillaries
  (about 10 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Omega}}{Omega}\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.}cm\(^2\)).
\item
  \textbf{Pericytes} ensheathing the abluminal endothelial surface ---
  regulate capillary diameter, BBB integrity, and angiogenesis.
\item
  \textbf{Astrocyte endfeet} with AQP4 channels --- form a
  near-continuous covering of capillaries and signal to maintain
  endothelial tight junction integrity.
\item
  \textbf{Basement membrane} between endothelial cells and astrocyte
  endfeet.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Transport mechanisms across the BBB:} - \textbf{Diffusion:}
Small lipophilic molecules (O\(_2\), CO\(_2\), ethanol, anaesthetics)
cross freely. - \textbf{Carrier-mediated transport:} GLUT1 (glucose);
LAT1 (large neutral amino acids --- competition explains why
high-protein meals can affect L-DOPA delivery); MCT1 (lactate, ketone
bodies). - \textbf{Receptor-mediated transcytosis:} Insulin, transferrin
(iron), leptin --- receptors mediate endocytosis on the luminal side and
exocytosis on the abluminal side. This is exploited to deliver
therapeutics: a ``Trojan horse'' strategy fuses drugs to
anti-transferrin-receptor antibodies. - \textbf{Active efflux pumps:}
\textbf{P-glycoprotein (P-gp/ABCB1)} and \textbf{BCRP/ABCG2} on the
luminal surface actively pump substrates back into blood. Many
lipophilic drugs that should enter the brain by passive diffusion are
pumped out --- explaining the limited brain penetration of many
chemotherapies and the role of P-gp polymorphisms in inter-individual
drug response.

\textbf{BBB-bypassing structures (circumventricular organs):}
Subfornical organ, area postrema (chemotrigger zone), median eminence,
neurohypophysis, OVLT, pineal gland --- lack tight junctions and have
fenestrated capillaries to allow hormones and circulating signals to
reach specialised neurons (e.g., AT\(_1\) on subfornical neurons \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
thirst).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection:} BBB breakdown contributes to many CNS
diseases. In multiple sclerosis, autoreactive T cells must first cross
the BBB (via VLA-4/VCAM-1 interaction); the monoclonal antibody
\textbf{natalizumab} blocks VLA-4 and dramatically reduces relapses. In
Alzheimer's, BBB pericyte dysfunction precedes overt neurodegeneration.
In ischaemic stroke, BBB breakdown produces vasogenic oedema and
haemorrhagic transformation. Pharmacologically, the BBB is the major
obstacle to CNS drug delivery --- about 2\% of small molecules and 0\%
of biologics readily cross.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Resting Membrane
Potential}\label{resting-membrane-potential}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth]{../figures/action_potential.png}
\caption{Hodgkin--Huxley action-potential simulation showing membrane voltage over time, resting potential, and threshold.}
\label{fig:unit_IX_action_potential}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Ion Distribution and the Nernst
Equation}\label{ion-distribution-and-the-nernst-equation}

The resting membrane potential (about \(-70\) mV) arises from
unequal ion distributions maintained by the Na\(^+\)/K\(^+\)-ATPase and
selective membrane permeability.

\textbf{Typical neuronal ion concentrations:}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.0492}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3115}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3115}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3279}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Ion
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Intracellular (mM)
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Extracellular (mM)
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Equilibrium Potential
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
K\(^+\) & 140 & 5 & \(-89\) mV \\
Na\(^+\) & 12 & 145 & \(+67\) mV \\
Cl\(^-\) & 7 & 110 & \(-74\) mV \\
Ca\(^{2+}\) & 0.0001 & 2 & \(+132\) mV \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Nernst equation} for a single ion:

\begin{equation}
E_X = \frac{RT}{zF} \ln\frac{[X]_o}{[X]_i} = \frac{61.5 \text{ mV}}{z} \log_{10}\frac{[X]_o}{[X]_i} \quad \text{(at 37°C)}
\label{eq:nervous_system_1}
\end{equation}

\subsubsection{Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz (GHK)
Equation}\label{goldman-hodgkin-katz-ghk-equation}

The \hyperref[gl:resting-potential]{\textbf{resting potential}} is a
weighted average of equilibrium potentials, determined by relative
membrane permeability to each ion:

\begin{equation}
V_m = \frac{RT}{F} \ln\frac{P_K[K^+]_o + P_{Na}[Na^+]_o + P_{Cl}[Cl^-]_i}{P_K[K^+]_i + P_{Na}[Na^+]_i + P_{Cl}[Cl^-]_o}
\label{eq:nervous_system_2}
\end{equation}

At rest, \(P_K : P_{Na} : P_{Cl} \approx 1 : 0.04 : 0.45\), giving
\(V_m \approx -68\) mV.

The resting potential is dominated by \textbf{K\(^+\)} (highest resting
conductance via KCNK leak channels). The Na\(^+\)/K\(^+\)-ATPase (3
Na\(^+\) out, 2 K\(^+\) in per ATP) is electrogenic, contributing
about \(-3\) mV directly, but its main role is maintaining
the concentration gradients.

\textbf{Concept Check:} If you suddenly doubled the extracellular
K\(^+\) concentration from 5 mM to 10 mM, what would happen to E\(_K\)
and the resting membrane potential? Calculate using the Nernst equation.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Cable Properties and Passive Signal
Spread}\label{cable-properties-and-passive-signal-spread}

Before a graded potential can trigger an action potential at the axon
hillock, it must travel electrotonically from the synapse. This passive
spread is governed by the \textbf{cable properties} of the dendrite,
modelled as a leaky electrical cable.

\subsubsection{Length Constant (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda})}\label{length-constant-ux3bb}

The \textbf{space constant} (or length constant) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda} determines how far a
steady-state voltage change spreads along a dendrite or axon:

\begin{equation}
\lambda = \sqrt{\frac{r_m}{r_i}}
\label{eq:nervous_system_3}
\end{equation}

where \(r_m\) = membrane resistance per unit length (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Omega}}{Omega}\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.}cm) and \(r_i\) =
axial (cytoplasmic) resistance per unit length (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Omega}}{Omega}/cm).

\begin{equation}
V(x) = V_0 \, e^{-x/\lambda}
\label{eq:nervous_system_4}
\end{equation}

At distance \(x = \lambda\), the voltage has decayed to
\(V_0/e \approx 37\%\) of its peak value.

\textbf{Typical values:}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1915}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2766}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2979}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2340}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Structure
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Diameter (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m)
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda} (mm)
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Implication
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Thin dendrite & 0.5 & about 0.1--0.2 & Distal synapses
attenuate strongly before reaching soma \\
Large dendrite & 5 & about 0.5--1.0 & Better passive
integration \\
Squid giant axon & 500 & about 5--7 & Enables long-distance
spread in unmyelinated axon \\
Myelinated axon & 10 & about 2--5 & Myelin increases \(r_m\),
dramatically increasing \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda} \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Key determinants of \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda}:} - \textbf{Myelin} increases \(r_m\)
about 100-fold (reduces current leak) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda} increases
about 10-fold - \textbf{Larger diameter} reduces \(r_i\) (more
conducting cross-section) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda} increases - \textbf{GABA\(_A\) receptor
activation} opens Cl\(^-\) channels, reducing \(r_m\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda} decreases ---
a quantitative mechanism for \textbf{shunting inhibition} (nearby
inhibitory synapses drastically reduce the effective length constant,
terminating EPSP integration before reaching the hillock)

\subsubsection{Time Constant (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\tau}}{tau}\_m)}\label{time-constant-ux3c4_m}

The \textbf{membrane time constant} determines how fast the membrane
voltage changes in response to a current:

\begin{equation}
\tau_m = r_m \cdot C_m
\label{eq:nervous_system_5}
\end{equation}

where \(C_m \approx 1\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}F/cm\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2} (specific membrane capacitance --- nearly
constant across cell types). Typical \(\tau_m \approx 10\)--\(20\) ms
for neurons.

\begin{equation}
V(t) = V_\infty \left(1 - e^{-t/\tau_m}\right)\quad \text{(voltage rising in response to a step current)}
\label{eq:nervous_system_6}
\end{equation}

\textbf{Significance:} \(\tau_m\) governs the time window for
\textbf{temporal summation} in neuronal membrane integration. If two
EPSPs arrive within \(\tau_m\) of each other at the same synapse, the
second EPSP begins before the membrane has fully repolarized from the
first, and the \hyperref[gl:depolarisation]{\textbf{depolarisation}}s
summate.

\subsection{Worked Example: Dendritic Length
Constant}\label{worked-example-dendritic-length-constant}

A cortical pyramidal neuron has \(r_m = 40{,}000\;\Omega\text{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.}cm}\) and
\(r_i = 200\;\Omega/\text{cm}\) for a typical basal dendrite (diameter
about 1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m). What is the length constant?

\begin{equation}
\lambda = \sqrt{\frac{40{,}000}{200}} = \sqrt{200} \approx 14.1\;\text{cm?}
\label{eq:nervous_system_7}
\end{equation}

Wait --- the formula uses \emph{specific} membrane resistance per unit
\textbf{length} for a cylinder. For a dendrite of radius \(a\):

\begin{equation}
r_m(\text{per unit length}) = \frac{R_m}{2\pi a}, \quad r_i(\text{per unit length}) = \frac{R_i}{\pi a^2}
\label{eq:nervous_system_8}
\end{equation}

where \(R_m\) = specific membrane resistance (about 20\{,\}000
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Omega}}{Omega}\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.}cm\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}) and \(R_i\) = cytoplasmic resistivity (about 100 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Omega}}{Omega}\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.}cm).
For \(a = 0.5\;\mu\)m \(= 0.5 \times 10^{-4}\) cm:

\begin{equation}
r_m = \frac{20{,}000}{2\pi \times 5 \times 10^{-5}} \approx 6.37 \times 10^7\;\Omega/\text{cm}
\label{eq:nervous_system_9}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
r_i = \frac{100}{\pi \times (5 \times 10^{-5})^2} \approx 1.27 \times 10^{10}\;\Omega/\text{cm}
\label{eq:nervous_system_10}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
\lambda = \sqrt{\frac{r_m}{r_i}} = \sqrt{\frac{6.37 \times 10^7}{1.27 \times 10^{10}}} = \sqrt{0.00501} \approx 0.071\;\text{cm} = 0.71\;\text{mm}
\label{eq:nervous_system_11}
\end{equation}

This means a synapse on a thin distal dendrite 1.4 mm from the soma
delivers primarily \(e^{-2} \approx 13.5\%\) of its peak voltage to the
hillock --- illustrating how \textbf{dendritic location profoundly
affects synaptic efficacy}, and why proximal synapses (closer to the
hillock) have disproportionate influence.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection:} Peripheral neuropathy (e.g., from
diabetes, chemotherapy, or Guillain-Barré syndrome) reduces \(r_m\) in
peripheral axons by disrupting myelin or causing axonal damage. The
resulting decrease in \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda} causes voltage signals to decay faster along the
axon, slowing conduction and reducing EPSP efficacy at nerve-muscle
junctions --- producing the characteristic distal-to-proximal weakness
and sensory loss of a length-dependent neuropathy.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Graded Potentials and Synaptic
Integration}\label{graded-potentials-and-synaptic-integration}

\subsubsection{Graded Potentials}\label{graded-potentials}

\textbf{Excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs):} Depolarising events
(typically caused by Na\(^+\) or mixed cation influx through ionotropic
receptors like AMPA). Amplitude proportional to stimulus strength. Decay
with distance (electrotonic spread governed by the length constant \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda}).

\textbf{Inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (IPSPs):} Hyperpolarising
events (Cl\(^-\) influx through GABA\(_A\) receptors or K\(^+\) efflux
through GABA\(_B\)-activated K\(^+\) channels). Shunting inhibition:
even if IPSP does not change \(V_m\) much, opening Cl\(^-\) channels
increases membrane conductance, reducing the effectiveness of nearby
EPSPs.

\subsubsection{Summation at the Axon
Hillock}\label{summation-at-the-axon-hillock}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0158_e6c1f83cf706.png}
\caption{Neural circuit types and synaptic integration. Convergence allows integration of multiple inputs; divergence allows signal distribution. At the axon hillock, temporal and spatial summation of EPSPs and IPSPs determine whether threshold is reached.}
\end{figure}

If the net depolarisation at the axon hillock exceeds threshold
(about \(-55\) mV), an most-or-none action potential is
generated, with the stereotyped Na\(^+\)- and K\(^+\)-driven waveform of
rise, peak, and hyperpolarisation shown in
\cref{fig:unit_IX_action_potential}. The axon hillock has the highest
density of Nav1.2 and Nav1.6 channels, making it the lowest-threshold
site.

\textbf{Strategic placement of inhibition:} Inhibitory synapses
(GABA\(_A\)) are preferentially located on the soma and proximal
dendrites, positioned to maximally dampen axon hillock depolarisation.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Autonomic Nervous System}\label{autonomic-nervous-system}

The \hyperref[gl:autonomic-nervous-system]{\textbf{autonomic nervous
system (ANS)}} regulates involuntary functions through two antagonistic
divisions:

\subsubsection{Sympathetic Division (``Fight or
Flight'')}\label{sympathetic-division-fight-or-flight}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Preganglionic neurons:} T1-L2 spinal cord (thoracolumbar
  outflow). Short preganglionic fibres to paravertebral (sympathetic
  chain) or prevertebral ganglia.
\item
  \textbf{Preganglionic neurotransmitter:} ACh at nicotinic receptors
\item
  \textbf{Postganglionic neurotransmitter:} Norepinephrine (NE) at \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha} and
  \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} adrenergic receptors on target organs
\item
  \textbf{Exception:} Adrenal medulla -- preganglionic sympathetic
  fibres synapse directly on chromaffin cells (modified postganglionic
  neurons) that release epinephrine (80\%) and NE (20\%) into blood as
  \hyperref[gl:hormone]{\textbf{hormone}}s
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Sympathetic effects:} Increased HR (\(\beta_1\)),
bronchodilation (\(\beta_2\)), pupil dilation (mydriasis), inhibited GI
motility, glycogenolysis in liver (\(\beta_2\)), vasoconstriction
(\(\alpha_1\)) in skin/viscera, vasodilation (\(\beta_2\)) in skeletal
muscle.

\subsubsection{Parasympathetic Division (``Rest and
Digest'')}\label{parasympathetic-division-rest-and-digest}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Preganglionic neurons:} Brainstem (CN III, VII, IX, X) and
  sacral spinal cord (S2-S4; craniosacral outflow). Long preganglionic
  fibres to terminal ganglia near or within target organs.
\item
  \textbf{Both neurotransmitters:} ACh. Preganglionic: nicotinic
  receptors. Postganglionic: muscarinic receptors (M1-M5) on target
  organs.
\item
  \textbf{Vagus nerve (CN X):} Carries about 75\% of
  parasympathetic fibres; innervates heart, lungs, GI tract to splenic
  flexure.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Parasympathetic effects:} Decreased HR (M\(_2\)),
bronchoconstriction (M\(_3\)), pupil constriction (miosis), increased GI
motility and secretion, bladder contraction.

\subsubsection{Enteric Nervous System}\label{enteric-nervous-system}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  about 500 million neurons in the gut wall (more than in the
  spinal cord)
\item
  \textbf{Myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus:} Between longitudinal and
  circular muscle layers; controls motility
\item
  \textbf{Submucosal (Meissner's) plexus:} Controls secretion and blood
  flow
\item
  Uses many neurotransmitters: ACh, NO, serotonin, substance P, VIP
\item
  Can function autonomously but is modulated by sympathetic (generally
  inhibitory) and parasympathetic (generally excitatory) input
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection:} Understanding ANS pharmacology is
fundamental to medicine. Beta-blockers (\(\beta_1\) antagonists:
metoprolol, atenolol) are first-line treatments for hypertension, heart
failure, and arrhythmias. Atropine (muscarinic antagonist) treats
bradycardia. Prazosin (\(\alpha_1\) antagonist) treats hypertension and
PTSD nightmares. Pilocarpine (muscarinic agonist) treats glaucoma by
promoting aqueous humour drainage.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Brain Anatomy and
Function}\label{brain-anatomy-and-function}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0159_7b9f1e7b1bee.png}
\caption{Major brain regions and their functions. The cerebral cortex is divided into four lobes with specialised functions. Subcortical structures handle motor control (basal ganglia), sensory relay (thalamus), homeostasis (hypothalamus), memory (hippocampus), and emotion (amygdala). The cerebellum coordinates movement, and the brainstem controls vital functions.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Cerebral Cortex}\label{cerebral-cortex}

The cortex is about 3 mm thick, contains about 20
billion neurons, and has a surface area of about 2,500 cm\(^2\)
(increased by folding into gyri and sulci).

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Motor homunculus:} Topographic representation of body parts on
  the primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus). Hands and face have
  disproportionately large representations (fine motor control).
\item
  \textbf{Sensory homunculus:} Topographic representation on the primary
  somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus). Hands, lips, and tongue are
  overrepresented (high receptor density).
\item
  \textbf{Broca's area} (left inferior frontal gyrus): Speech
  production. Damage causes non-fluent (expressive) aphasia --
  comprehension intact but speech production impaired.
\item
  \textbf{Wernicke's area} (left posterior superior temporal gyrus):
  Language comprehension. Damage causes fluent (receptive) aphasia --
  speech flows but is nonsensical.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Basal Ganglia}\label{basal-ganglia}

The basal ganglia (caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, subthalamic
nucleus, substantia nigra) modulate cortical motor output:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Direct pathway (Go):} Cortex excites striatum; striatum
  inhibits GPi/SNr (GABAergic); GPi/SNr normally inhibit thalamus. Net
  effect: disinhibition of thalamus, promoting movement.
\item
  \textbf{Indirect pathway (NoGo):} Cortex excites striatum; striatum
  inhibits GPe; GPe normally inhibits STN; STN excites GPi/SNr. Net
  effect: increased GPi/SNr inhibition of thalamus, suppressing
  movement.
\item
  \textbf{Dopamine:} Substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) neurons
  release dopamine onto striatal neurons. D1 receptors excite direct
  pathway neurons; D2 receptors inhibit indirect pathway neurons. Net:
  dopamine facilitates movement.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Parkinson's disease:} Degeneration of SNc dopaminergic neurons
(\textgreater60\% loss before symptoms appear). Loss of dopamine removes
facilitation of movement, causing: bradykinesia (slow movement),
rigidity, resting tremor, postural instability. Treatment: L-DOPA
(dopamine precursor crosses BBB); deep brain stimulation of STN.

\subsubsection{Other Key Structures}\label{other-key-structures}

\textbf{Cerebellum:} Contains more neurons than the rest of the brain
combined (about 70 billion granule cells). Functions: motor
coordination, error correction (compares intended vs actual movement),
timing, motor learning, balance. Damage causes ataxia (uncoordinated
movement) but not paralysis.

\textbf{Hippocampus:} Essential for consolidating declarative (episodic
and semantic) memories from short-term to long-term storage. Contains
place cells (fire at specific locations; O'Keefe, Nobel 2014) and grid
cells (fire in a hexagonal spatial pattern; Moser and Moser, Nobel
2014). One of few brain regions with confirmed adult neurogenesis
(dentate gyrus).

\textbf{Hypothalamus:} Homeostatic control centre with 13+ nuclei
controlling: temperature, hunger/satiety, thirst, circadian rhythms
(suprachiasmatic nucleus, SCN), autonomic output, and endocrine function
(connects to pituitary via the hypothalamo-hypophyseal portal system).

\textbf{Spinal cord:} Grey matter (butterfly-shaped, contains neuronal
cell bodies): dorsal horn (sensory processing), ventral horn (motor
neuron cell bodies), lateral horn (T1-L2: sympathetic preganglionic
neurons). White matter (surrounding, myelinated tracts): ascending
(sensory, e.g., spinothalamic tract for pain/temperature) and descending
(motor, e.g., corticospinal tract for voluntary movement).

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Sensory Systems}\label{sensory-systems}

\subsubsection{Somatosensation}\label{somatosensation}

\textbf{Nociception:} Two fibre types carry pain signals: -
\textbf{A-delta fibres:} Thinly myelinated (5-30 m/s). Sharp,
well-localised ``first pain'' - \textbf{C fibres:} Unmyelinated (0.5-2
m/s). Dull, diffuse ``second pain''

\subsubsection{Visual Pathway}\label{visual-pathway}

Retina (photoreceptors: rods for dim light/peripheral vision; cones for
colour/acuity) to optic nerve to optic chiasm (nasal fibres cross) to
\textbf{lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN)} of thalamus to primary visual
cortex (V1, striate cortex) in occipital lobe.

Beyond V1, visual processing splits into: - \textbf{Dorsal stream}
(``where/how''): V1 to posterior parietal cortex. Motion, spatial
relationships, visually guided action. - \textbf{Ventral stream}
(``what''): V1 to inferotemporal cortex. Object recognition, face
recognition, colour.

\subsubsection{Proprioception}\label{proprioception}

Muscle spindles (detect muscle length and stretch velocity), Golgi
tendon organs (detect muscle tension), and joint receptors provide
unconscious awareness of body position. Information travels via dorsal
column-medial lemniscal pathway (proprioception, fine touch) or
spinocerebellar tracts (to cerebellum for motor coordination).

\subsubsection{Musculoskeletal Control and
Behaviour}\label{musculoskeletal-control-and-behaviour}

Skeletal movement is a loop, not a one-way command. Alpha motor neurons
release acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction; muscle fibres
depolarise, release Ca\(^{2+}\) from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and
contract by the sliding-filament mechanism in which myosin heads
cyclically bind actin, pull, detach, and reset
\citep{huxley1954sliding}. Sensory feedback closes the loop: muscle
spindles report length, Golgi tendon organs report tension, cutaneous
mechanoreceptors report contact, and vestibular inputs report head
acceleration. Reflexes are therefore local control policies embedded in
a larger behavioural system, not primitive leftovers.

Behavioural biology adds four levels of explanation that should not be
collapsed: mechanism (the neural and hormonal circuit), development (how
the behaviour changes across life), function (what fitness problem it
solves), and evolutionary history (how related species differ)
\citep{tinbergen1963aims}. A startle reflex, bird song, courtship
display, or human reaching movement can be read through those four
levels. The organismal habit is to ask which sensory cue, motor
effector, motivational state, developmental window, and ecological
payoff are actually supported by the evidence.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Brain Imaging --- Reading Activity Through Indirect
Signals}\label{brain-imaging-reading-activity-through-indirect-signals}

Modern neuroscience and clinical neurology rely on a portfolio of
imaging modalities, each measuring a different physical correlate of
neural activity.

\subsubsection{fMRI and the BOLD signal}\label{fmri-and-the-bold-signal}

\textbf{Functional MRI (fMRI)} measures the
\textbf{blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD)} signal, which exploits a
magnetic-resonance peculiarity of haemoglobin: oxyhaemoglobin is
\textbf{diamagnetic}, while deoxyhaemoglobin is \textbf{paramagnetic}
and distorts the local T2\emph{-weighted MR signal. Active brain regions
paradoxically }increase* local oxyhaemoglobin (and decrease
deoxyhaemoglobin) within seconds, because the \textbf{neurovascular
coupling} response over-supplies blood relative to the metabolic demand.
The mismatch between blood-flow increase (about 50\%) and
O\(_2\) extraction increase (about 5--20\%) produces the
\textbf{BOLD signal rise}, peaking about 5 s after activity
onset.

The neurovascular coupling that drives BOLD is mediated largely by
astrocytes (recall the astrocyte tripartite synapse): synaptic glutamate
elevates astrocytic Ca\(^{2+}\), which releases vasoactive arachidonic
acid metabolites (PGE\(_2\), EETs) onto local arterioles. The
astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle (ANLS) is the metabolic coupling
underlying fMRI BOLD signals.

BOLD does \emph{not} measure spike rates directly; it measures the
haemodynamic response to recent local-field-potential activity. fMRI
excels at spatial localisation (about 1--3 mm) but trades
temporal resolution (seconds) --- the inverse trade-off compared with
EEG.

\subsubsection{EEG and oscillation
bands}\label{eeg-and-oscillation-bands}

\textbf{Electroencephalography (EEG)} measures the summed extracellular
electrical potentials produced by synchronised cortical pyramidal-neuron
currents. EEG has millisecond temporal resolution but limited spatial
localisation (about 1--2 cm). Brain rhythms occupy distinct
frequency bands tied to behavioural states:

Clinical EEG is the bedside tool for diagnosing \textbf{epilepsy}
(interictal spikes; rhythmic ictal patterns), \textbf{encephalopathy}
(generalised slowing), and \textbf{brain death} (electrocerebral
silence). MEG (magnetoencephalography) measures the same neuronal
currents via tiny magnetic fields with better localisation than EEG.

\subsubsection{Connectivity, MEG, NIRS,
PET}\label{connectivity-meg-nirs-pet}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI):} Maps white-matter tracts by
  measuring water diffusion anisotropy along axons. Used in stroke,
  traumatic axonal injury, neurosurgical planning.
\item
  \textbf{Resting-state fMRI:} Identifies networks of co-fluctuating
  brain regions (default mode network, salience network, frontoparietal
  control). Disturbances correlate with depression, schizophrenia,
  Alzheimer's.
\item
  \textbf{PET (positron emission tomography):} Tracer-based metabolic or
  receptor-binding imaging; FDG-PET shows glucose uptake (epilepsy
  localisation, dementia patterns); amyloid-PET (florbetapir) and
  tau-PET enable Alzheimer's disease characterisation.
\item
  \textbf{NIRS (near-infrared spectroscopy):} Optical analogue of fMRI;
  portable; used in neonatal monitoring and bedside cerebral oximetry.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Neural Prosthetics and Brain-Computer
Interfaces}\label{neural-prosthetics-and-brain-computer-interfaces}

Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) and neural prosthetics convert neural
activity into an external action or stimulation pattern. The strongest
current speech demonstrations are still experimental implants, not
consumer mind-reading devices: 2023 intracortical speech neuroprostheses
decoded attempted speech into text or avatar control at high performance
in single-participant research settings
\citep{willett2023speechneuroprosthesis,metzger2023avatarneuroprosthesis}.
The scientific claim is therefore bounded: motor and speech cortices
contain decodable intention signals, but clinical translation requires
stable implants, calibration, infection and tissue-response management,
privacy safeguards, and evidence that performance generalises beyond
highly supported trials.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Pain Pathways}\label{pain-pathways}

Pain is the body's most clinically important sensory modality and serves
both protective and pathological roles.

\subsubsection{Nociceptors and
transduction}\label{nociceptors-and-transduction}

Free nerve endings of A-delta and C fibres express \textbf{molecular
sensors} that transduce noxious stimuli into membrane depolarisation:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{TRPV1:} Capsaicin- and heat-activated (\textgreater43 °C);
  also activated by acidic pH and inflammatory lipids. Resiniferatoxin
  and lidocaine-soaked TRPV1 agonist patches deplete nociceptors of
  substance P.
\item
  \textbf{TRPM8:} Cold- and menthol-activated (15--25 °C).
\item
  \textbf{TRPA1:} Mustard oil, cinnamaldehyde, environmental irritants;
  cold-activated in some species.
\item
  \textbf{ASICs (acid-sensing ion channels):} Activated by tissue
  acidosis (ischaemia, inflammation).
\item
  \textbf{Nav1.7 (SCN9A):} Voltage-gated Na\(^+\) channel essential for
  nociceptor excitability. \emph{Loss-of-function} mutations cause
  \textbf{congenital insensitivity to pain (CIP)} --- patients fail to
  detect injuries and self-mutilate. \emph{Gain-of-function} mutations
  cause \textbf{inherited erythromelalgia} (severe burning pain).
  Nav1.7-selective inhibitors are in clinical development as non-opioid
  analgesics.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Ascending pathway --- the spinothalamic
tract}\label{ascending-pathway-the-spinothalamic-tract}

A-delta and C fibres release glutamate \textbf{and substance P} into the
dorsal horn of the spinal cord (lamina I, II, V). Second-order neurons
cross the midline (anterior white commissure), ascend in the
contralateral \textbf{spinothalamic tract}, and synapse in the ventral
posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus. Third-order neurons
project to primary somatosensory cortex (S1), insula (interoceptive),
and anterior cingulate (affective dimension of pain). Substance P binds
NK1 receptors on second-order neurons; the combined glutamate-Substance
P transmission distinguishes pain from innocuous somatosensation.

\subsubsection{Descending modulation}\label{descending-modulation}

The brain actively \textbf{suppresses} ongoing pain signalling through
descending circuits:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Periaqueductal grey (PAG)} in the midbrain receives input from
  cortex, hypothalamus, and amygdala
\item
  PAG activates the \textbf{rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM)}
\item
  RVM serotonergic neurons project to the \textbf{dorsal horn (DH)},
  where they release serotonin, noradrenaline, and endogenous opioids
  onto pain-transmission neurons
\end{itemize}

This \textbf{PAG \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} RVM \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} DH} axis is the substrate for
\textbf{stress-induced analgesia} (hand-on-flame reflex without pain in
life-or-death situations) and for the placebo effect. Endogenous opioids
(\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-endorphin, enkephalin, dynorphin) acting on \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}-, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\delta}}{delta}-, and \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}-opioid
receptors are released along this axis. \textbf{Morphine and other
opioid analgesics} exploit the same descending pathway.

\textbf{Gate control theory} (Melzack \& Wall, 1965): A-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} fibres
(mechanoreceptors, ``innocuous touch'') activate inhibitory interneurons
in the dorsal horn that ``gate'' C-fibre transmission --- the basis for
\textbf{rubbing a stubbed toe} to reduce pain, and the rationale for
\textbf{TENS (transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation)} therapy.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection:} Chronic neuropathic pain (post-herpetic
neuralgia, diabetic neuropathy) reflects maladaptive central
sensitisation --- peripheral nerve injury upregulates Nav1.7/1.8 in
nociceptors, expands receptive fields, and reduces descending
inhibition. Treatments include gabapentinoids (target \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}\(_2\delta\)
subunits of voltage-gated Ca\(^{2+}\) channels), SNRIs (boost descending
serotonin/noradrenaline), and topical lidocaine (Nav blocker).
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Sleep --- Two-Process Model}\label{sleep-two-process-model}

Sleep is not the absence of brain activity but a structured succession
of states with distinct functions.

\subsubsection{Architecture}\label{architecture}

Adult sleep cycles between \textbf{NREM} (further divided into N1, N2,
N3) and \textbf{REM} stages, each cycle about 90 minutes:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{N1 (light):} Theta activity; transition from waking
\item
  \textbf{N2:} Sleep spindles (12--14 Hz thalamic bursts) and
  K-complexes; about 50\% of total sleep
\item
  \textbf{N3 (slow-wave / deep):} Delta-dominant; ``homeostatic'' sleep
  restoring tissue and consolidating declarative memory;
  \textbf{glymphatic clearance} of brain metabolites including amyloid-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}
\item
  \textbf{REM (paradoxical):} Low-amplitude desynchronised EEG
  resembling waking; rapid eye movements; \textbf{muscle atonia}
  (mediated by glycinergic inhibition of motor neurons by sublateral
  dorsal nucleus); vivid dreams; consolidation of procedural and
  emotional memory
\end{itemize}

REM proportion is maximal in infancy (about 50\% of sleep) and
declines with age. Sleep deprivation produces a ``REM rebound'' --- REM
disproportionately recovers after deprivation, suggesting it serves a
critical function.

\subsubsection{The two-process model (Borbély,
1982)}\label{the-two-process-model-borbuxe9ly-1982}

Sleep timing is regulated by two interacting processes:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Process C (Circadian):} Sinusoidal drive from the
  suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus, entrained by light
  via the retinohypothalamic tract. Promotes wakefulness during the day
  and sleep at night; mediated by hypothalamic circuits including the
  ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO, sleep-promoting) and
  orexin/hypocretin neurons of the lateral hypothalamus
  (wake-promoting).
\item
  \textbf{Process S (Sleep homeostasis):} Increases monotonically during
  waking and dissipates exponentially during sleep. Its molecular
  substrate is largely \textbf{adenosine}, which accumulates in basal
  forebrain during sustained activity (from local ATP catabolism).
  Adenosine acting on A\(_1\) receptors inhibits wake-promoting neurons;
  acting on A\(_{2A}\) receptors in the ventral striatum, it promotes
  sleep. \textbf{Caffeine} (an adenosine A\(_1\)/A\(_{2A}\) antagonist)
  blocks Process S --- this is its mechanism for reducing sleep
  pressure.
\end{itemize}

Sleep occurs when Process C (low) coincides with Process S (high).
Disruption of either process produces sleep disorders: SCN damage (or
shift work) disrupts Process C, producing irregular sleep timing;
insomnia often reflects elevated arousal that overrides Process S.

\subsubsection{Functions of sleep}\label{functions-of-sleep}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Memory consolidation:} Slow-wave sleep replays hippocampal
  place-cell sequences; REM consolidates emotional and procedural
  memory.
\item
  \textbf{Glymphatic clearance:} During NREM, the brain's glymphatic
  (glial-lymphatic) system expands extracellular space
  about 60\% and accelerates CSF--ISF exchange, clearing
  amyloid-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}, tau, and other metabolites. Chronic sleep deprivation is a
  recognised risk factor for Alzheimer's disease.
\item
  \textbf{Synaptic homeostasis (Tononi-Cirelli hypothesis):} Wake-time
  learning produces net synaptic potentiation; sleep allows broad
  synaptic downscaling, restoring information capacity.
\item
  \textbf{Metabolic and immune restoration:} GH and prolactin peak
  during deep sleep; cytokine cycling supports immune surveillance.
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection:} Narcolepsy type 1 results from loss of
orexin/hypocretin neurons (autoimmune destruction in genetically
susceptible individuals). Without orexin, Process C cannot stably
maintain wakefulness, producing daytime sleepiness, REM intrusion into
wake (cataplexy, sleep paralysis, hallucinations). Treatment includes
modafinil (wake-promoting), sodium oxybate (consolidates sleep), and
emerging orexin receptor agonists.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Neural Plasticity}\label{neural-plasticity}

\textbf{Hebbian learning:} ``Neurons that fire together wire together''
\citep{hebb1949}. Correlated pre- and postsynaptic activity strengthens
synaptic connections.

\textbf{Long-term potentiation (LTP):} Activity-dependent, long-lasting
increase in synaptic efficacy. At Schaffer collateral to CA1 synapses in
hippocampus: 1. High-frequency stimulation depolarises postsynaptic
membrane enough to relieve Mg\(^{2+}\) block of NMDA receptors 2.
Ca\(^{2+}\) influx through NMDA receptors activates CaMKII 3. CaMKII
phosphorylates AMPA receptors (increased conductance) and promotes AMPA
receptor insertion into synapse 4. Structural plasticity: Dendritic
spine enlargement, new spine formation

\textbf{Long-term depression (LTD):} Opposite of LTP. Low-frequency
stimulation activates protein phosphatases (PP1, calcineurin) that
dephosphorylate AMPA receptors and promote their
\hyperref[gl:endocytosis]{\textbf{endocytosis}}. Weakens synaptic
connections.

\textbf{Homeostatic plasticity:} Synaptic scaling adjusts the overall
strength of most synapses on a neuron to maintain a stable firing rate.
If a neuron's activity is chronically reduced, it scales up most
synaptic strengths; if chronically increased, it scales them down. This
prevents runaway excitation or silencing.

\textbf{Critical periods \citep{beggs2003}:} Windows during development
when experience has maximal impact on neural circuit formation.
Monocular deprivation during the visual critical period
(about  birth to age 5 in humans) permanently reduces cortical
responsiveness to the deprived eye (amblyopia). Molecular brakes on
plasticity include perineuronal nets (PNNs), myelin-associated
inhibitors, and GABA maturation.

\textbf{Concept Check:} Explain why the NMDA receptor is called a
``coincidence detector'' and why this property makes it ideal for
Hebbian learning.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Worked Example}\label{worked-example-2}

\textbf{Problem:} Calculate the equilibrium potential for potassium
(\(E_K\)) in a mammalian neuron at \(37^\circ\text{C}\), given an
intracellular potassium concentration \([K^+]_i\) of \(140\text{ mM}\)
and an extracellular concentration \([K^+]_o\) of \(5\text{ mM}\).

The Nernst equation for a monovalent cation at \(37^\circ\text{C}\) is:
\[E_K = 61.5\text{ mV} \times \log_{10}\left(\frac{[K^+]_o}{[K^+]_i}\right) \label{eq:unit_IX_nervous_system_item_1}\]

\textbf{Solution:}

\textbf{Step 1. Identify the given variables.} -
\([K^+]_o = 5\text{ mM}\) - \([K^+]_i = 140\text{ mM}\)

\textbf{Step 2. Substitute the values into the Nernst equation.}
\[E_K = 61.5\text{ mV} \times \log_{10}\left(\frac{5}{140}\right) \label{eq:unit_IX_nervous_system_item_2}\]

\textbf{Step 3. Calculate the logarithm.}
\[\frac{5}{140} \approx 0.0357 \label{eq:unit_IX_nervous_system_item_3}\]

\[\log_{10}(0.0357) \approx -1.447 \label{eq:unit_IX_nervous_system_item_4}\]

\textbf{Step 4. Determine the final potential.}
\[E_K = 61.5\text{ mV} \times (-1.447) \approx -89\text{ mV} \label{eq:unit_IX_nervous_system_item_5}\]

\textbf{Answer:} The equilibrium potential for potassium is
approximately \textbf{\(-89\text{ mV}\)}.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Worked Example: Resting Potential from the
Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz
Equation}\label{worked-example-resting-potential-from-the-goldman-hodgkin-katz-equation}

\textbf{Problem:} Calculate the resting membrane potential of a
mammalian neuron at \(37^\circ\text{C}\) using the Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz
(GHK) equation, given the ion concentrations \([K^+]_o = 5\text{ mM}\),
\([K^+]_i = 140\text{ mM}\), \([Na^+]_o = 145\text{ mM}\),
\([Na^+]_i = 12\text{ mM}\), \([Cl^-]_o = 110\text{ mM}\),
\([Cl^-]_i = 7\text{ mM}\), and the resting permeability ratio
\(P_K : P_{Na} : P_{Cl} = 1 : 0.04 : 0.45\).

The GHK voltage equation, written in base-10 form for a
\(37^\circ\text{C}\) neuron, is:
\[V_m = 61.5\text{ mV} \times \log_{10}\left(\frac{P_K[K^+]_o + P_{Na}[Na^+]_o + P_{Cl}[Cl^-]_i}{P_K[K^+]_i + P_{Na}[Na^+]_i + P_{Cl}[Cl^-]_o}\right)\]

Note that the Cl\(^-\) terms are inverted relative to the cations (a
consequence of the \(z = -1\) charge): the outside-flux numerator
carries \([Cl^-]_i\) and the inside-flux denominator carries
\([Cl^-]_o\).

\textbf{Solution:}

\textbf{Step 1. Form the numerator (outward-driving terms), in mM.}
\[P_K[K^+]_o + P_{Na}[Na^+]_o + P_{Cl}[Cl^-]_i = (1)(5) + (0.04)(145) + (0.45)(7) = 5 + 5.8 + 3.15 = 13.95\]

\textbf{Step 2. Form the denominator (inward-driving terms), in mM.}
\[P_K[K^+]_i + P_{Na}[Na^+]_i + P_{Cl}[Cl^-]_o = (1)(140) + (0.04)(12) + (0.45)(110) = 140 + 0.48 + 49.5 = 189.98\]

\textbf{Step 3. Take the ratio and its base-10 logarithm.}
\[\frac{13.95}{189.98} \approx 0.0734, \qquad \log_{10}(0.0734) \approx -1.134\]

\textbf{Step 4. Scale by the \(37^\circ\text{C}\) Nernst slope.}
\[V_m = 61.5\text{ mV} \times (-1.134) \approx -69.7\text{ mV}\]

\textbf{Answer:} The resting membrane potential is approximately
\textbf{\(-70\text{ mV}\)} --- close to \(E_K\) (\(-89\) mV) but
depolarised relative to it because the finite Na\(^+\) and Cl\(^-\)
permeabilities pull \(V_m\) toward their (more positive) equilibrium
potentials. The K\(^+\) term dominates because \(P_K\) is the largest
permeability.

\textbf{Concept Check:} If \(P_{Na}\) rose tenfold (from 0.04 to 0.40)
while \(P_K\) and \(P_{Cl}\) were unchanged, predict the new sign of the
numerator-vs-denominator imbalance and whether \(V_m\) moves toward
\(E_{Na}\) or \(E_K\).

\textbf{Concept Check:} At rest, which single term in the GHK numerator
and denominator contributes the most to \(V_m\), and predict how \(V_m\)
changes if \(P_K\) is doubled while most concentrations are held fixed.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-31}

For \textbf{Nervous System and Neural Signalling}, frontier biology
belongs inside the evidence logic of the chapter. Physiology now blends
mechanism with allostasis, immune-endocrine-neural coupling, wearable
data, and individualized risk without reducing bodies to simple
machines. The core reading question is this: neural explanations should
separate circuit architecture, glial support, plasticity, behaviour, and
evidence scale.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

Interpret physiological data by separating baseline variation,
perturbation response, compensation, and the threshold where
compensation becomes pathology.

\textbf{Source practice:} For physiology claims, cite the measurement
context and distinguish baseline variation, compensation,
pathophysiology, and treatment evidence.

\endlastfoot
\textbf{Resting membrane potential} & Electrochemical potential across
neuronal membrane at rest; about \(-70\) mV \\
\textbf{Nernst potential} & Voltage at which net flux of a single ion
species = 0 \\
\textbf{GHK equation} & Multi-ion extension of Nernst; weights each ion
by membrane permeability \\
\textbf{EPSP} & Excitatory postsynaptic potential: depolarisation toward
threshold \\
\textbf{IPSP} & Inhibitory postsynaptic potential: hyperpolarisation or
shunting inhibition \\
\textbf{Axon hillock} & Lowest threshold region; highest Nav channel
density; AP initiation site \\
\textbf{Tripartite synapse} & Presynaptic + postsynaptic + astrocyte
glial process \\
\textbf{Sympathetic NS} & Thoracolumbar outflow; fight or flight; NE on
adrenergic receptors \\
\textbf{Parasympathetic NS} & Craniosacral outflow; rest and digest; ACh
on muscarinic receptors \\
\textbf{Basal ganglia} & Subcortical nuclei modulating motor output;
direct (Go) and indirect (NoGo) pathways \\
\textbf{LTP} & Long-term potentiation; Hebbian strengthening of synaptic
connections \\
\textbf{LTD} & Long-term depression; weakening of synaptic
connections \\
\textbf{Broca's area} & Left inferior frontal gyrus; speech
production \\
\textbf{Wernicke's area} & Left superior temporal gyrus; language
comprehension \\
\textbf{Place cells} & Hippocampal neurons firing at specific spatial
locations \\
\textbf{Microglia} & CNS resident macrophages; synaptic pruning;
neuroinflammation \\
\textbf{Myelin} & Lipid-rich insulation produced by oligodendrocytes
(CNS) or Schwann cells (PNS) \\
\textbf{Na\(^+\)/K\(^+\)-ATPase} & Pump maintaining ion gradients; 3
Na\(^+\) out, 2 K\(^+\) in per ATP \\
\end{longtable}
}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Review Questions}\label{review-questions-31}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Calculate E\(_K\) using the Nernst equation for a neuron with
  {[}K\(^+\){]}\(_{in}\) = 150 mM and {[}K\(^+\){]}\(_{out}\) = 4 mM at
  37 degrees C. How does this compare to the resting potential of
  \(-70\) mV, and what accounts for the difference?
\item
  Compare the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions in terms of: (a)
  spinal cord origin, (b) preganglionic fibre length, (c)
  neurotransmitters at ganglia and target organs, (d) receptor types,
  and (e) effects on heart rate.
\item
  A patient presents with non-fluent speech but intact comprehension.
  Which brain region is likely damaged? What would you expect on MRI?
  How does this differ from damage to Wernicke's area?
\item
  Explain the direct and indirect pathways of the basal ganglia. How
  does loss of dopaminergic input from SNc (as in Parkinson's disease)
  shift the balance between these pathways, and why does this cause
  bradykinesia?
\item
  Explain synaptic pruning and its relationship to microglia and
  complement proteins. What evidence links synaptic pruning
  dysregulation to schizophrenia risk? (Sekar et al.~2016,
  \emph{Nature}: C4A).
\item
  A researcher applies a blocker of KCNK leak potassium channels to a
  neuron. Predict the effect on (a) resting membrane potential, (b) the
  relative contribution of Na\(^+\) to the resting potential, and (c)
  neuronal excitability.
\item
  Compare ionotropic and metabotropic receptors in terms of structure,
  speed, ionic selectivity, and role in modulating synaptic gain. Give
  one clinical example for each class.
\item
  Explain why inhibitory synapses are strategically placed on the soma
  and proximal dendrites rather than on distal dendrites. How does the
  concept of shunting inhibition differ from hyperpolarising inhibition?
\item
  A dendrite has specific membrane resistance
  \(R_m = 25{,}000\;\Omega\text{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.}cm}^2\), cytoplasmic resistivity
  \(R_i = 80\;\Omega\text{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.}cm}\), and radius \(a = 1\;\mu\)m. Calculate
  the length constant \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda}. If a synapse is located 2 mm from the soma,
  what fraction of the original EPSP amplitude reaches the soma? How
  would myelination of the dendrite change your answer qualitatively?
\item
  A patient with chronic inflammatory demyelinating
  polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP) has reduced conduction velocity in
  peripheral sensory nerves and complains of ``glove-and-stocking''
  numbness. Using the cable properties framework, explain: (a) why
  demyelination slows conduction velocity, (b) why sensory deficits are
  worse distally (length-dependent), and (c) why IVIG treatment
  (suppressing antibody-mediated myelin attack) can restore sensation.
\item
  Estimate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda} from \breaktt{cable\_voltage\_attenuation} defaults and
  compare to the hand-calculated \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda} in Question 9.
\item
  Why does \textbf{ephaptic coupling} complicate the independence
  assumption of parallel dendritic inputs?
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Optogenetics: Light-Gated Ion Channels as Tools for
Mapping Neural
Circuits}\label{optogenetics-light-gated-ion-channels-as-tools-for-mapping-neural-circuits}

Until 2005, neuroscience had two experimental tools for probing neural
circuits: \textbf{electrical stimulation} (fast, but indiscriminate ---
excites every cell and axon within a about 100 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m radius) and
\textbf{pharmacological inactivation} (specific, but slow and diffuse).
\textbf{Optogenetics} --- introduced by Boyden, Deisseroth, and
colleagues (\emph{Nat. Neurosci.} 2005) --- merged genetic specificity
with millisecond temporal precision by transplanting light-gated ion
channels from microbes into mammalian neurons.

The core tools: \textbf{Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2)}, a blue-light-gated
non-selective cation channel from the green alga \emph{Chlamydomonas
reinhardtii}, opens in about 1 ms on 470 nm illumination and
drives neurons to fire action potentials with up to 40 Hz fidelity.
\textbf{Halorhodopsin (NpHR)} from \emph{Natronomonas pharaonis} is a
yellow-light-driven inward Cl\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-} pump that hyperpolarises neurons and
silences firing. \textbf{Archaerhodopsin (Arch)} is a green-light-driven
outward H\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} pump with similar inhibitory effect. Transgene expression via
AAV with cell-type-specific \hyperref[gl:promoter]{\textbf{promoter}}s
(Thy1 for cortical pyramidal neurons, PV-Cre \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} ChR2 for parvalbumin
interneurons, DAT-Cre for dopamine neurons) delivers the channel
primarily to genetically defined populations. Combined with implanted
optical fibres (for deep structures) or surface-mounted LEDs (for
cortex), the experimenter can turn specific cell types on or off in
milliseconds.

Landmark findings enabled by optogenetics: \textbf{(1) Memory engrams}
--- Tonegawa and colleagues (\emph{Nature} 2012, \emph{Science} 2014)
showed that optogenetic reactivation of the specific hippocampal neurons
active during fear conditioning is sufficient to recall the fear memory
in a neutral context, proving engram cells are \emph{the} physical
substrate of memory. \textbf{(2) Parkinson's disease circuit dissection}
--- Kravitz et al.~(\emph{Nature} 2010) showed that direct-pathway (D1)
striatal neuron optogenetic activation rescues motor deficits in
parkinsonian mice, while indirect-pathway (D2) activation mimics them,
confirming the 1990s pharmacological model. \textbf{(3) Basis of deep
brain stimulation} --- optogenetic DBS mimics in rodents has clarified
which STN cell types produce the therapeutic benefit in Parkinson's
patients. \textbf{Clinical
\hyperref[gl:translation]{\textbf{translation}}}: RST-001 (jSAM for
retinitis pigmentosa, GenSight Biologics) uses ChrimsonR delivered by
AAV to retinal ganglion cells and specialised goggles to convert images
to patterned light. A 2021 \emph{Nature Medicine} report documented
partial restoration of visual function in a blind patient ---
optogenetics' first human therapeutic success.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-31}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{NS organisation:} CNS (brain + spinal cord) + PNS (somatic +
  autonomic + enteric). 86 billion neurons; glia provide myelin, BBB,
  metabolic support, immune surveillance.
\item
  \textbf{Neuron types:} Sensory (afferent, pseudounipolar), motor
  (efferent, multipolar), interneurons (integration). Axon hillock has
  highest Nav channel density.
\item
  \textbf{Resting potential:} E\(_K\) = \(-89\) mV dominates;
  Na\(^+\)/K\(^+\)-ATPase maintains gradients; GHK equation weights by
  permeabilities; \(V_m \approx -70\) mV.
\item
  \textbf{Synaptic integration:} EPSPs (depolarising) and IPSPs
  (hyperpolarising/shunting) summate temporally and spatially at the
  axon hillock. Threshold at about \(-55\) mV triggers
  most-or-none AP.
\item
  \textbf{ANS:} Sympathetic (T1-L2, NE, fight-or-flight) vs
  parasympathetic (craniosacral, ACh, rest-and-digest). Enteric NS:
  semi-autonomous gut control.
\item
  \textbf{Brain:} Cortex (4 lobes, motor/sensory homunculi, language
  areas); basal ganglia (direct/indirect pathways, dopamine); thalamus
  (sensory relay); hippocampus (memory, place cells); hypothalamus
  (homeostasis); cerebellum (coordination); brainstem (vital functions).
\item
  \textbf{Sensory systems:} Mechanoreceptors (Meissner, Pacinian,
  Ruffini, Merkel), nociceptors (A-delta, C fibres), proprioceptors;
  visual pathway (retina to LGN to V1 to dorsal/ventral streams).
\item
  \textbf{Neural plasticity:} LTP (NMDA-Ca\(^{2+}\)-CaMKII-AMPA), LTD,
  homeostatic scaling, critical periods, synaptic pruning.
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See \cref{sec:unit_IX_action_potential_synapses}
  for active propagation, \cref{sec:unit_II_cell_signaling} for second
  messengers, and \cref{sec:unit_0_active_inference} for active
  inference themes.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-32}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Opening Vignette --- The Squid That Explained the Brain}

The squid \emph{Loligo} possesses a giant axon up to 1 mm in diameter
--- large enough for researchers to insert a glass micropipette
electrode into the interior. In 1939, Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley
exploited this remarkable anatomy to make the first intracellular
recordings of an action potential. By 1952, using voltage-clamp
apparatus of their own construction, they had measured the time courses
of sodium and potassium conductances across the membrane with stunning
precision and fitted them to a set of differential equations now known
as the Hodgkin-Huxley model. The equations predicted the shape,
amplitude, threshold, refractory period, and propagation velocity of
action potentials --- most from first principles of ionic movement. The
1963 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine rewarded what remains one of
the most quantitatively rigorous pieces of biological science ever
accomplished. Every antiepileptic, local anaesthetic, cardiac
antiarrhythmic, and membrane biophysics textbook stems ultimately from
that one peculiarly large squid axon.
\end{quote}

\subsection{The Hodgkin-Huxley Model}\label{the-hodgkin-huxley-model}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth]{../figures/nernst_potentials.png}
\caption{Nernst equilibrium potentials for major physiological ions (Na$^+$, K$^+$, Cl$^-$, Ca$^{2+}$) calculated from their inside/outside concentration gradients.}
\label{fig:unit_IX_nernst_potentials}
\end{figure}

Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley recorded action potentials from the
\textbf{squid giant axon} (diameter about 0.5 mm) using voltage
clamp (Hodgkin \& Huxley, 1952, \emph{J Physiol} -- Nobel Prize 1963).
Each ionic current is driven by the difference between \(V\) and that
ion's Nernst equilibrium potential, the gradient-dependent values of
which are plotted in \cref{fig:unit_IX_nernst_potentials}. They
described membrane current as:

\begin{equation}
C_m \frac{dV}{dt} = -I_{Na} - I_K - I_L + I_{ext}
\label{eq:action_potential_synapses_1}
\end{equation}

where: - \(C_m\) = membrane capacitance about 1 uF/cm\(^2\) -
\(I_{Na} = \bar{g}_{Na} m^3 h (V - E_{Na})\); \(\bar{g}_{Na}\) = 120
mS/cm\(^2\); \(E_{Na}\) = +50 mV - \(I_K = \bar{g}_K n^4 (V - E_K)\);
\(\bar{g}_K\) = 36 mS/cm\(^2\); \(E_K\) = \(-77\) mV -
\(I_L = g_L (V - E_L)\); \(g_L\) = 0.3 mS/cm\(^2\); \(E_L\) = \(-54.4\)
mV

\subsubsection{Gating Variables}\label{gating-variables}

Each gating variable (\(m\), \(h\), \(n\)) evolves according to
first-order Markov kinetics:

\begin{equation}
\frac{dx}{dt} = \alpha_x(V)(1-x) - \beta_x(V)x
\label{eq:action_potential_synapses_2}
\end{equation}

At steady state: \(x_\infty(V) = \alpha_x / (\alpha_x + \beta_x)\); time
constant: \(\tau_x(V) = 1/(\alpha_x + \beta_x)\)

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0160_6aa448c0dd72.png}
\caption{Voltage-gated Na\$\textasciicircum{}+\$ channel states. The channel transitions through three states: Closed (resting, ready to open), Open (conducting Na\$\textasciicircum{}+\$, brief about 0.5 ms), and Inactivated (blocked by the inactivation gate, cannot reopen until repolarisation restores the resting state). The inactivated state underlies the absolute refractory period.}
\end{figure}
