\subsubsection{Biophysical Interpretation of the Action
Potential}\label{biophysical-interpretation-of-the-action-potential}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Threshold} (about \(-55\) mV): Point where inward
  Na\(^+\) current exceeds outward K\(^+\) leak. Positive feedback
  begins (more \hyperref[gl:depolarisation]{\textbf{depolarisation}}
  opens more Na\(^+\) channels).
\item
  \textbf{Upstroke (depolarisation):} Rapid m-gate opening
  (\(\tau_m \approx 0.5\) ms). Na\(^+\) rushes in. Membrane potential
  approaches E\(_{Na}\) (+50 mV) but typically peaks at +30 to +40 mV.
\item
  \textbf{Repolarisation:} h-gate closes (Na\(^+\) inactivation,
  \(\tau_h \approx 5\) ms) AND n-gate opens (K\(^+\) delayed rectifier,
  \(\tau_n \approx 5\) ms). Na\(^+\) influx stops; K\(^+\) efflux drives
  membrane back toward E\(_K\).
\item
  \textbf{Afterhyperpolarisation (undershoot):} n-gate slow to close.
  K\(^+\) efflux continues briefly, hyperpolarising membrane below
  \hyperref[gl:resting-potential]{\textbf{resting potential}}
  (about \(-80\) mV). This is the relative refractory period.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Channel Pharmacology}\label{channel-pharmacology}

\textbf{Tetrodotoxin (TTX):} Puffer fish toxin. Blocks Nav channels from
the extracellular side by occluding the selectivity filter pore. Blocks
most AP generation. LD\(_{50}\) in mice: about 10 ug/kg. Used
extensively as a research tool to study Na\(^+\)-dependent processes.

\textbf{4-Aminopyridine (4-AP):} Blocks Kv (voltage-gated K\(^+\))
channels. Prolongs AP duration, enhances neurotransmitter release. Used
clinically as dalfampridine (Ampyra) for multiple sclerosis to improve
conduction in demyelinated axons.

\textbf{Nav channel subtypes:} Nav1.1-Nav1.9 encoded by SCN1A-SCN11A
\hyperref[gl:gene]{\textbf{gene}}s. Different subtypes have distinct
tissue distributions, voltage sensitivities, and pharmacological
profiles: - Nav1.7 (SCN9A): Pain perception. Loss-of-function:
congenital insensitivity to pain. Gain-of-function: erythromelalgia
(burning pain). - Nav1.5 (SCN5A): Cardiac muscle.
\hyperref[gl:mutation]{\textbf{Mutation}}s cause Long QT syndrome,
Brugada syndrome.

\textbf{Concept Check:} TTX blocks Na\(^+\) channels and abolishes
action potentials. Local anaesthetics (lidocaine) also block Na\(^+\)
channels. Why does lidocaine preferentially block pain fibres rather
than motor fibres? (Hint: consider use-dependence and fibre diameter.)

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Refractory Periods}\label{refractory-periods}

\textbf{Absolute refractory period} (about 1-2 ms after spike
peak): Na\(^+\) channels are in the inactivated state (h about 0). They
cannot be re-opened regardless of stimulus strength. This supports: -
Unidirectional AP propagation (the region just behind the AP cannot be
re-excited) - Maximum firing rate (about 500-1000 Hz)

\textbf{Relative refractory period} (about 5-10 ms following
absolute): Na\(^+\) channels are recovering from inactivation (h
recovering), but K\(^+\) channels remain open. The membrane is more
negative than resting potential (afterhyperpolarisation). A
stronger-than-normal stimulus is needed to trigger a second spike. APs
generated during this period have reduced amplitude.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection:} The cardiac refractory period is much
longer than in \hyperref[gl:neuron]{\textbf{neuron}}s
(about 200-300 ms vs about 2 ms) because cardiac AP
duration is prolonged by L-type Ca\(^{2+}\) channels (plateau phase).
This prevents tetanic contraction of the heart (which would be fatal --
the heart must relax to fill). The ``vulnerable period'' near the end of
the T wave (relative refractory period of ventricles) is when a
premature stimulus can trigger ventricular fibrillation.
\end{quote}

\textbf{Concept Check:} During the falling phase of the action potential
the m, h, and n gates are most changing at once. Which single
Hodgkin-Huxley gating variable is the \emph{direct} cause of
repolarisation, and why does Na\(^+\) inactivation (h) alone fail to
repolarise the membrane without it? (Hint: compare what each conductance
does to the driving force toward \(E_K\) versus \(E_{Na}\).)

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Myelination and Conduction
Velocity}\label{myelination-and-conduction-velocity}

\subsubsection{Unmyelinated Conduction}\label{unmyelinated-conduction}

In continuous conduction, the AP generates local circuits along the axon
membrane:

\begin{equation}
\theta \propto \sqrt{a/r_i}
\label{eq:action_potential_synapses_3}
\end{equation}

where a = axon radius and \(r_i\) = axial resistance per unit length.
Increasing diameter reduces axial resistance, increasing velocity. Squid
giant axon (500 um diameter) achieves about 25 m/s by
brute-force gigantism.

\subsubsection{Myelinated Axons -- Saltatory
Conduction}\label{myelinated-axons-saltatory-conduction}

Myelin dramatically increases the \textbf{space constant} (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda}):

\begin{equation}
\lambda = \sqrt{r_m / r_i}
\label{eq:action_potential_synapses_4}
\end{equation}

Myelin increases \(r_m\) (membrane resistance, preventing current leak)
and reduces \(C_m\) (membrane capacitance, reducing charge needed to
change voltage). The result: depolarisation spreads much further without
decay.

APs can primarily arise at \textbf{nodes of Ranvier} (1-2 um gaps
between myelin segments, every about 1 mm). Nodes have
concentrated voltage-gated Na\(^+\) channels
(about 1,000/um\(^2\) at nodes vs about 25/um\(^2\)
under myelin).

\textbf{Saltatory conduction:} The AP appears to ``jump'' between nodes.
In myelinated axons, velocity scales linearly with diameter
(\(\theta \propto d\)), rather than as the square root:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lllll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Fibre type & Diameter (um) & Velocity (m/s) & Myelinated? & Function \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
A-alpha (Ia) & 12-20 & 70-120 & Yes & Muscle spindle afferents \\
A-beta & 6-12 & 30-70 & Yes & Touch, pressure \\
A-delta & 1-5 & 5-30 & Thinly & Sharp pain, temperature \\
B & 1-3 & 3-15 & Yes & Preganglionic autonomic \\
C & 0.2-1.5 & 0.5-2 & No & Slow pain, itch, postganglionic autonomic \\
\end{longtable}
}

\subsubsection{Worked Example: Myelination Gain --- Saltatory vs
Continuous
Conduction}\label{worked-example-myelination-gain-saltatory-vs-continuous-conduction}

Suppose two unmyelinated axons of equal small diameter (\(d = 1\;\mu\)m)
carry the same action potential. Continuous conduction velocity scales
as \(\theta_\text{unmyel} \propto \sqrt{d}\). From empirical data, an
unmyelinated 1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m axon conducts at about 0.5 m/s.

Now myelinate one axon with internodes about 1 mm apart and 100
wraps of myelin. Myelin increases membrane resistance (\(r_m\))
about 100-fold and reduces capacitance (\(C_m\))
about 50-fold:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Length constant \(\lambda = \sqrt{r_m / r_i}\) increases
  about 10-fold
\item
  Time constant at the node \(\tau_m = r_m C_m\) --- although both
  increase, the \emph{time to reach threshold} at the next node depends
  primarily on the rapid charging of node membrane (which has low
  capacitance) by the spreading depolarisation
\item
  Effective conduction velocity in myelinated fibre:
  \(\theta_\text{myel} \propto d\) (linear, not square root)
\end{itemize}

For the same 1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m fibre with myelination, conduction approaches
about 6 m/s (\textgreater10\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} faster). For larger myelinated
fibres (10--20 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m A-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}), the gain is even more striking:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lllll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Fibre & Diameter & Conduction velocity & Myelinated? & Velocity gain \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
C fibre & 1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m & 0.5 m/s & No & (baseline) \\
A-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\delta}}{delta} & 1--5 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m & 5--30 m/s & Thinly & about 10--60\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} \\
A-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha} (Ia) & 12--20 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m & 70--120 m/s & Yes (heavily) &
about 150--250\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{The fundamental insight:} Saltatory conduction provides the
\textbf{same speed at about 50\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} lower diameter} compared to
brute-force gigantism (squid giant axon, 500 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m). The vertebrate
solution to fast conduction --- myelinate small axons rather than grow
giant ones --- is enormously more space-efficient and energetically
cheaper. The about \(10^{12}\) axons in the human white
matter would not fit in the cranium without myelin.

The \textbf{energetic cost} of action potentials is also dramatically
reduced: in unmyelinated axons, Na\(^+\)/K\(^+\)-ATPase must
continuously pump out Na\(^+\) along the entire length. In myelinated
axons, AP-associated ion fluxes occur primarily at nodes
(about 0.1\% of axon surface), reducing the metabolic cost of
spike propagation by a similar factor.

\subsubsection{Multiple Sclerosis}\label{multiple-sclerosis}

\textbf{Multiple sclerosis (MS):} Autoimmune demyelination of CNS white
matter. T cells recognise myelin basic protein (MBP) and proteolipid
protein (PLP) as autoantigens. Inflammatory attack destroys
oligodendrocyte myelin sheaths.

Consequences: Slowed or blocked conduction in demyelinated segments.
Symptoms depend on lesion location: optic neuritis (visual loss),
weakness, sensory loss, fatigue, cognitive impairment.
Relapsing-remitting course in about 85\% of patients.

Treatment: Disease-modifying therapies (interferons, natalizumab,
ocrelizumab) reduce relapse frequency. 4-aminopyridine (blocks exposed
K\(^+\) channels in demyelinated segments) improves conduction.

\textbf{Concept Check:} A 1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m unmyelinated axon conducts at
about 0.5 m/s, yet a 1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m myelinated axon conducts at
about 6 m/s while a 20 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m unmyelinated axon would need a far
larger diameter to match it. Using the velocity scalings
\(\theta \propto \sqrt{d}\) (unmyelinated) versus \(\theta \propto d\)
(myelinated), explain why myelination --- not gigantism --- is the
space- and energy-efficient solution, and predict what happens to
conduction when a node of Ranvier is demyelinated. (Hint: think about
what myelin does to \(r_m\), \(C_m\), and the length constant \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda}.)

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Chemical Synaptic
Transmission}\label{chemical-synaptic-transmission}

\subsubsection{Synapse Types}\label{synapse-types}

\textbf{Electrical synapses} (gap junctions): Connexin/innexin
hemichannels directly connect
\hyperref[gl:cytoplasm]{\textbf{cytoplasm}}s. Bidirectional, nearly
instantaneous (\textless0.1 ms). Found in: cardiac pacemaker cells
(connexin 43), retinal processing (rod-cone coupling), hippocampal
interneuron synchronisation. Connexin 26/30 mutations cause hereditary
deafness.

\textbf{Chemical synapses:} Unidirectional. Modifiable (plasticity).
Synaptic delay: 0.5-2 ms. The \hyperref[gl:dominant]{\textbf{dominant}}
synapse type in the CNS.

\subsubsection{Presynaptic Machinery}\label{presynaptic-machinery}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0161_670c2dedea6d.png}
\caption{Molecular machinery of synaptic vesicle fusion. Depolarisation opens Ca\$\textasciicircum{}\{2+\}\$ channels. Ca\$\textasciicircum{}\{2+\}\$ binds synaptotagmin-1, which displaces the complexin fusion clamp and triggers full SNARE complex zippering, forcing the vesicle membrane to fuse with the plasma membrane and release neurotransmitter into the cleft.}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Key proteins:} - \textbf{SNARE complex:} The minimal fusion
machinery. \textbf{Synaptobrevin} (v-SNARE, on vesicle membrane) +
\textbf{syntaxin} + \textbf{SNAP-25} (both t-SNAREs, on plasma
membrane). The four \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-helices zipper together N-to-C terminally, pulling
membranes into contact. - \textbf{Synaptotagmin-1:} Ca\(^{2+}\) sensor.
Its C2A and C2B domains bind 4-5 Ca\(^{2+}\) ions, triggering membrane
insertion and SNARE complex activation. Cooperativity of Ca\(^{2+}\)
binding gives the steep Ca\(^{2+}\)-release relationship
(about 4th power). - \textbf{Munc18 / Munc13:} Priming factors
that prepare SNARE complexes for fast fusion - \textbf{RIM:} Active zone
scaffold protein. Positions vesicles within nanometres of Ca\(^{2+}\)
channels. - \textbf{Complexin:} ``Fusion clamp.'' Binds partially
zippered SNARE complex and prevents spontaneous fusion.
Ca\(^{2+}\)/synaptotagmin displaces complexin to trigger release. -
\textbf{NSF + alpha-SNAP:} After fusion, these AAA\(^+\) ATPases
disassemble SNARE complexes for recycling.

\textbf{Quantal release (Katz, Nobel 1970):} Neurotransmitter is
released in discrete packets (quanta), each corresponding to the
contents of one vesicle. The end-plate potential (EPP) at the NMJ = n
\(\times\) p \(\times\) q, where n = number of release-ready vesicles, p
= release probability per vesicle, q = quantal size (postsynaptic
response to one vesicle).

Miniature EPPs (mEPPs) represent spontaneous release of single vesicles
and have a constant amplitude (about 0.5 mV at the NMJ). The
evoked EPP is an integer multiple of the mEPP amplitude.

\subsubsection{Synaptic Vesicle Pools}\label{synaptic-vesicle-pools}

A presynaptic terminal does \textbf{not} treat most its vesicles
equivalently. Decades of imaging, electrophysiology, and FM dye
experiments establish three functionally distinct pools that differ in
their release-readiness, location, and mobilisation kinetics:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.0548}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4384}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1096}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2192}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1781}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Pool
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Approximate size per active zone
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Location
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Release kinetics
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Replenishment
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Readily releasable pool (RRP)} & about 10--20 vesicles
(CNS); about 50--100 (NMJ) & Docked at active zone; primed &
Released within about 1 ms of Ca\(^{2+}\) entry; depleted
within first few APs of a high-frequency train & Refilled from recycling
pool over 1--10 s \\
\textbf{Recycling pool} & about 100--200 vesicles & Near active
zone; fused with PM during sustained activity then reformed locally &
Sustains release during moderate-frequency activity & Cycle time
about 30--60 s \\
\textbf{Reserve pool} & about 300--500+ vesicles & Tethered to
actin/synapsin in the cytoplasm & Mobilised primarily during intense or
prolonged activity (typically when synapsin is phosphorylated by
CaMKII/PKA) & Slow refilling (minutes) from synthesis and endocytosis \\
\end{longtable}
}

The three-pool model elegantly explains the kinetics of synaptic
transmission during different activity patterns. \textbf{Brief,
low-frequency stimulation} uses primarily the RRP and the system rapidly
returns to baseline. \textbf{Sustained moderate activity} engages the
recycling pool. \textbf{Tetanic stimulation} mobilises the reserve pool
by phosphorylation of synapsin (which normally clamps reserve vesicles
to the actin cytoskeleton), releasing them to refill the active zone.

\subsubsection{Short-term plasticity --- facilitation and
depression}\label{short-term-plasticity-facilitation-and-depression}

Synaptic strength is dynamic across milliseconds-to-seconds, even before
any LTP/LTD is induced. Two opposing short-term phenomena dominate:

\textbf{Synaptic facilitation} (paired-pulse facilitation; tens to
hundreds of ms): If two APs arrive in close succession, the second
EPSC/IPSC is \emph{larger} than the first. Mechanism: residual
presynaptic Ca\(^{2+}\) from the first AP has not yet been pumped out or
buffered; when the second AP triggers Ca\(^{2+}\) entry, the residual
Ca\(^{2+}\) adds to the new flux, super-linearly increasing release
probability \(p\). Facilitation is most prominent at synapses with low
initial \(p\) (e.g., parallel-fibre to Purkinje cell synapses;
about \(p \approx 0.05\)); high-\(p\) synapses have less room
for further increase.

\textbf{Synaptic depression} (paired-pulse depression; tens of ms to
seconds): If two APs arrive in close succession at a high-\(p\) synapse,
the second EPSC is \emph{smaller} than the first. Mechanism: the RRP is
partially depleted by the first AP and has not had time to refill.
Depression is most prominent at synapses with high initial \(p\) (e.g.,
calyx of Held auditory synapses; \(p \approx 0.4\)).

Whether a given synapse facilitates or depresses depends on its starting
release probability, vesicle pool dynamics, and Ca\(^{2+}\) handling.
Some synapses transition: facilitate at low frequency, then depress as
frequency rises and pools deplete.

\subsubsection{Tsodyks-Markram model}\label{tsodyks-markram-model}

The classical phenomenological model of short-term plasticity (Tsodyks
\& Markram, 1997) treats each synapse as having two state variables:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{\(x\)}: the fraction of available (un-depleted) resources
  (vesicles in the RRP), with \(0 \le x \le 1\)
\item
  \textbf{\(u\)}: the utilisation parameter (effective release
  probability), influenced by residual Ca\(^{2+}\)
\end{itemize}

After each spike, \(x \to x \cdot (1 - u)\) (resources depleted) and
\(u \to u + U \cdot (1 - u)\) (release probability incremented by
Ca\(^{2+}\) accumulation). Between spikes, both variables relax back to
baseline with time constants \(\tau_d\) (recovery, about 500
ms--2 s) and \(\tau_f\) (facilitation, about 100--500 ms):

\[\frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{1 - x}{\tau_d}; \qquad \frac{du}{dt} = -\frac{u - U}{\tau_f} \label{eq:unit_IX_action_potential_synapses_item_1}\]

The post-spike EPSC amplitude is proportional to \(u \cdot x\). This
single model captures the full repertoire of facilitating, depressing,
and mixed synapses --- by varying the parameters \(U\), \(\tau_d\),
\(\tau_f\) --- and is the standard building block for biologically
realistic spiking neural network simulations.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection:} Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS)
is an autoimmune disorder targeting presynaptic P/Q-type Ca\(^{2+}\)
channels at the NMJ, dramatically reducing initial release probability.
The hallmark on bedside testing is \textbf{post-tetanic facilitation}
--- strength briefly improves after sustained voluntary contraction,
reflecting accumulated Ca\(^{2+}\) partially compensating for reduced
channel number. Treatment with \textbf{3,4-diaminopyridine} (a K\(^+\)
channel blocker that prolongs presynaptic AP duration \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} more Ca\(^{2+}\)
entry per spike) increases initial \(p\) and restores neuromuscular
transmission.
\end{quote}

\textbf{NMDA receptor -- ``coincidence detector'':} The NMDA receptor
requires BOTH glutamate binding AND postsynaptic depolarisation (to
relieve Mg\(^{2+}\) block) to conduct. This makes it a detector of
coincident pre- and postsynaptic activity -- exactly the condition Hebb
proposed should strengthen synapses. Ca\(^{2+}\) entry through NMDA
receptors triggers LTP.

\textbf{Concept Check:} At a synapse with \(n = 10\) release-ready
vesicles, release probability \(p = 0.2\), and quantal size \(q = 0.5\)
mV, a single presynaptic spike must drive the postsynaptic membrane from
\(-70\) mV to a \(-55\) mV threshold. Using the \(n \cdot p \cdot q\)
model, decide whether one spike reaches threshold and explain why a drug
that raises \(p\) (e.g., an aminopyridine prolonging the presynaptic AP)
can convert a sub-threshold synapse to a supra-threshold one without
adding any new vesicles. (Hint: compute the expected EPSP amplitude and
compare it to the 15 mV gap.)

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Neurotransmitter Systems}\label{neurotransmitter-systems}

\subsubsection{Glutamate (Excitatory)}\label{glutamate-excitatory}

The major excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS (about 90\% of
excitatory synapses).

\textbf{Receptors:} - \textbf{AMPA} (GluA1-4): Fast Na\(^+\)/K\(^+\)
current. Ca\(^{2+}\)-permeable if lacking GluA2 (GluA2 RNA editing of
Q/R site prevents Ca\(^{2+}\) permeability in most adult neurons). -
\textbf{NMDA} (GluN1/GluN2A-D): Coincidence detector. Requires glutamate
+ glycine/D-serine co-agonist + depolarisation to relieve Mg\(^{2+}\)
block. High Ca\(^{2+}\) permeability. Critical for LTP. -
\textbf{Kainate} (GluK1-5): Similar to AMPA; modulatory roles at some
synapses. - \textbf{mGluR} (mGluR1-8): Metabotropic. Group I (mGluR1/5):
G\(_q\)-coupled, excitatory. Group II/III: G\(_i\)-coupled, inhibitory
(presynaptic autoreceptors).

\textbf{\hyperref[gl:excitotoxicity]{Excitotoxicity}:} Excessive
glutamate release (e.g., during stroke/ischaemia) overactivates NMDA
receptors. Massive Ca\(^{2+}\) influx activates calpains, endonucleases,
and nitric oxide synthase, leading to neuronal death. This is a major
mechanism of ischaemic brain damage.

\subsubsection{GABA (Inhibitory)}\label{gaba-inhibitory}

The major inhibitory neurotransmitter (about 30\% of CNS
synapses). Synthesised from glutamate by glutamic acid decarboxylase
(GAD65/GAD67).

\textbf{Receptors:} - \textbf{GABA\(_A\)} (ionotropic): Cl\(^-\)
channel. Pentameric (typically \(\alpha_1\beta_2\gamma_2\)). Binding
sites for: GABA (agonist), benzodiazepines (positive
\hyperref[gl:allosteric]{\textbf{allosteric}} modulators at \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}/\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma}
interface), barbiturates, neurosteroids, ethanol, anaesthetics
(propofol, isoflurane). - \textbf{GABA\(_B\)} (metabotropic):
G\(_i\)-coupled GPCR. Activates K\(^+\) channels (postsynaptic
hyperpolarisation) and inhibits Ca\(^{2+}\) channels (presynaptic,
reduces NT release). Baclofen is a GABA\(_B\) agonist (used for
spasticity).

\subsubsection{Acetylcholine (ACh)}\label{acetylcholine-ach}

\textbf{Receptors:} - \textbf{Nicotinic (nAChR):} Ionotropic pentamer.
Muscle type (\(\alpha_1^2\beta_1\delta\epsilon\)) at NMJ. Neuronal types
(\(\alpha_4\beta_2\), \(\alpha_7\)) in CNS. Na\(^+\)/K\(^+\) channels. -
\textbf{Muscarinic (mAChR, M1-M5):} GPCRs. M1/M3/M5: G\(_q\)
(excitatory). M2/M4: G\(_i\) (inhibitory, e.g., vagal slowing of heart
rate).

\textbf{CNS cholinergic system:} Basal forebrain (nucleus basalis of
Meynert) projects to cortex. Critical for attention and memory.
Degeneration in Alzheimer's disease.

\subsubsection{Dopamine}\label{dopamine}

\textbf{Receptors:} D1-D5 (most GPCRs). D1-like (D1, D5): G\(_s\),
increase cAMP. D2-like (D2, D3, D4): G\(_i\), decrease cAMP.

\textbf{Major pathways:} - \textbf{Nigrostriatal} (SNc to striatum):
Motor control. Loss causes Parkinson's disease. - \textbf{Mesolimbic}
(VTA to nucleus accumbens): Reward prediction error, motivation.
Hyperactivity linked to positive symptoms of schizophrenia. -
\textbf{Mesocortical} (VTA to prefrontal cortex): Working memory,
executive function. Hypoactivity linked to negative symptoms of
schizophrenia and ADHD. - \textbf{Tuberoinfundibular} (hypothalamus to
pituitary): Inhibits prolactin release.

\subsubsection{Serotonin (5-HT)}\label{serotonin-5-ht}

Synthesised from tryptophan by tryptophan hydroxylase (TPH2 in CNS).
Raphe nuclei in brainstem project widely. 14 receptor subtypes
(5-HT\(_1\)A through 5-HT\(_7\)).

\textbf{Functions:} Mood regulation, sleep/wake cycle, appetite, pain
modulation. about 90\% of body's serotonin is in
enterochromaffin cells of the GI tract.

\subsubsection{Norepinephrine (NE)}\label{norepinephrine-ne}

Synthesised from dopamine by dopamine \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-hydroxylase (DBH). Locus
coeruleus (brainstem) projects to entire cortex. Functions: arousal,
attention, vigilance, stress response.

\textbf{Receptors:} \(\alpha_1\) (G\(_q\)), \(\alpha_2\) (G\(_i\),
presynaptic autoreceptor), \(\beta_1\) (G\(_s\), heart), \(\beta_2\)
(G\(_s\), bronchial smooth muscle, blood vessels).

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{AI and Computational Neuroscience: Modeling the Brain with
Data and
Algorithms}\label{ai-and-computational-neuroscience-modeling-the-brain-with-data-and-algorithms}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0162_36db1762ef16.png}
\caption{The convergence of computational neuroscience and AI. Early neural models (Hodgkin-Huxley, integrate-and-fire) inspired artificial neurons, while modern deep learning architectures are now used to model brain function and analyze neural data.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Computational Neuroscience
Models}\label{computational-neuroscience-models}

\textbf{Biophysical models}:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Hodgkin-Huxley model} (1952): A set of nonlinear differential
  equations that describe how action potentials in neurons are initiated
  and propagated. It remains one of the most important mathematical
  models in neuroscience.
\item
  \textbf{FitzHugh-Nagumo model} (1961): A simplified two-variable model
  that captures the essential dynamics of the Hodgkin-Huxley model while
  being more mathematically tractable.
\item
  \textbf{Izhikevich model} (2003): A hybrid model that combines the
  biological plausibility of Hodgkin-Huxley with the computational
  efficiency of integrate-and-fire models.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Large-scale brain models}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Blue Brain Project} (EPFL): Aims to create a digital
  reconstruction of the rodent brain and ultimately the human brain
  using detailed biophysical models.
\item
  \textbf{Human Brain Project} (EU): A €1 billion initiative to simulate
  the entire human brain using supercomputers.
\item
  \textbf{Spaun} (University of Waterloo): A large-scale functional
  brain model that can perform multiple cognitive tasks.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Machine Learning for Neural Data
Analysis}\label{machine-learning-for-neural-data-analysis}

Modern neuroscience generates massive datasets (e.g., calcium imaging,
EEG, fMRI, intracranial recordings). Machine learning is essential for
extracting meaningful information:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Spike sorting}: Unsupervised learning algorithms (e.g., PCA +
  clustering, deep learning) to separate the activity of individual
  neurons from extracellular recordings.
\item
  \textbf{Calcium imaging analysis}: Deconvolution algorithms (e.g.,
  OASIS, CaImAn) to extract spike trains from fluorescence signals.
\item
  \textbf{Neural decoding}: Supervised learning to predict behavior or
  perception from neural activity (e.g., BMI control, speech decoding).
\item
  \textbf{fMRI pattern analysis}: Multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA)
  and deep learning to identify mental states from brain activity
  patterns.
\item
  \textbf{Connectomics}: Computer vision and graph neural networks to
  map neural connectivity from electron microscopy data.
\end{itemize}

\KeywordTok{class}\NormalTok{ NeuralDecoder(nn.Module):}
    \CommentTok{"""A simple LSTM{-}based decoder for predicting movement from neural spikes."""}
    \KeywordTok{def} \FunctionTok{\_\_init\_\_}\NormalTok{(}\VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{, input\_dim, hidden\_dim, output\_dim, num\_layers}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{):}
        \BuiltInTok{super}\NormalTok{().}\FunctionTok{\_\_init\_\_}\NormalTok{()}
        \VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{.lstm }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ nn.LSTM(input\_dim, hidden\_dim, num\_layers, batch\_first}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
        \VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{.fc }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ nn.Linear(hidden\_dim, output\_dim)}

    \KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ forward(}\VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{, x):}
        \CommentTok{\# x shape: (batch, seq\_len, input\_dim)}
\NormalTok{        lstm\_out, \_ }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{.lstm(x)}
        \CommentTok{\# Take the last time step output}
\NormalTok{        out }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{.fc(lstm\_out[:, }\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, :])}
        \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ out}

\CommentTok{\# Example: Spike sorting with PCA + clustering}
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ spike\_sorting(waveforms):}
    \CommentTok{"""Simple spike sorting using PCA and k{-}means."""}
    \CommentTok{\# Perform PCA}
    \ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ sklearn.decomposition }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ PCA}
\NormalTok{    pca }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ PCA(n\_components}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    pca\_result }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pca.fit\_transform(waveforms)}
    \CommentTok{\# Cluster}
    \ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ sklearn.cluster }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ KMeans}
\NormalTok{    kmeans }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ KMeans(n\_clusters}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{, random\_state}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{).fit(pca\_result)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ kmeans.labels\_}

\CommentTok{\# Example: Calcium imaging deconvolution}
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ oasis\_deconvolution(fluor\_signal, dt}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{, lambda\_}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{):}
    \CommentTok{"""OASIS algorithm for spike inference from calcium imaging."""}
    \ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ oasis }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ oasisAR1N}
    \CommentTok{\# Convert to AR1N model}
\NormalTok{    result }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ oasisAR1N(fluor\_signal, dt}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{dt, lambda\_}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{lambda\_, g}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.95}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ result[}\StringTok{"spikes"}\NormalTok{]  }\CommentTok{\# Estimated spike times}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{AI for Drug Discovery in
Neurology}\label{ai-for-drug-discovery-in-neurology}

Traditional drug discovery takes 10-15 years and billions of dollars. AI
is accelerating the process:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Target identification}: Machine learning models analyze
  genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic data to identify promising drug
  targets.
\item
  \textbf{Compound screening}: Deep learning models predict the activity
  of millions of compounds against specific targets, enabling virtual
  screening.
\item
  \textbf{De novo drug design}: Generative models (GANs, VAEs,
  transformers) can design novel molecules with desired properties.
\item
  \textbf{Clinical trial optimization}: AI helps identify suitable
  patient populations, predict outcomes, and optimize trial design.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Case study}: Insilico Medicine used AI to identify a novel
target for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, design a novel molecule, and
complete preclinical experiments in under 18 months (vs.~typical 4-6
years).

\subsubsection{Brain-Computer Interfaces
(BCIs)}\label{brain-computer-interfaces-bcis}

BCIs translate neural activity into commands for external devices,
offering hope for paralysis, locked-in syndrome, and other neurological
conditions:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Signal acquisition}: Microelectrode arrays (Utah array,
  Blackrock), ECoG, EEG, or optical imaging.
\item
  \textbf{Signal processing}: Filtering, spike detection, feature
  extraction.
\item
  \textbf{Decoding algorithms}: Linear models (Kalman filter, Wiener
  filter), neural networks, and reinforcement learning to map neural
  signals to actions.
\item
  \textbf{Applications}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{Communication}: Typing at 20+ words per minute using
    imagined handwriting.
  \item
    \textbf{Mobility}: Controlling robotic limbs or exoskeletons.
  \item
    \textbf{Sensory restoration}: Cortical visual prostheses for the
    blind.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Neuralink} and other companies are developing high-bandwidth,
minimally invasive BCIs with thousands of channels, aiming to treat
paralysis and eventually enhance human cognition.

\subsubsection{Ethical Considerations}\label{ethical-considerations-1}

As AI becomes more integrated with neuroscience, important ethical
questions arise:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Privacy}: Neural data is the ultimate private information. How
  do we protect brain data from misuse?
\item
  \textbf{Agency and responsibility}: If a BCI-controlled prosthetic
  acts unintentionally, who is responsible?
\item
  \textbf{Cognitive enhancement}: Should AI-assisted cognitive
  enhancement be allowed? What are the societal implications?
\item
  \textbf{Dual-use}: The same technology that helps paralyzed patients
  could be used for military applications or surveillance.
\item
  \textbf{Bias in AI}: If training data lacks diversity, AI systems may
  perform poorly for underrepresented groups, exacerbating health
  disparities.
\end{itemize}

\CommentTok{\# Example: Reinforcement learning for adaptive BCIs}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ gym}
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ stable\_baselines3 }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ PPO}

\CommentTok{\# Create a custom environment for BCI control}
\KeywordTok{class}\NormalTok{ BCIEnv(gym.Env):}
    \KeywordTok{def} \FunctionTok{\_\_init\_\_}\NormalTok{(}\VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{):}
        \BuiltInTok{super}\NormalTok{().}\FunctionTok{\_\_init\_\_}\NormalTok{()}
        \VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{.observation\_space }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gym.spaces.Box(low}\OperatorTok{={-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, high}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, shape}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{100}\NormalTok{,))}
        \VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{.action\_space }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gym.spaces.Box(low}\OperatorTok{={-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, high}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, shape}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{,))}

    \KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ step(}\VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{, action):}
        \CommentTok{\# Simplified: reward based on how close action is to target}
\NormalTok{        reward }\OperatorTok{=} \OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{np.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{((action }\OperatorTok{{-}} \VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{.target) }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}
        \VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{.steps }\OperatorTok{+=} \DecValTok{1}
\NormalTok{        done }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{.steps }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}=} \DecValTok{200} \KeywordTok{or}\NormalTok{ reward }\OperatorTok{\textless{}} \OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{10}
        \ControlFlowTok{return} \VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{.\_get\_observation(), reward, done, \{\}}

    \KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ reset(}\VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{):}
        \VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{.steps }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{0}
        \VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{.target }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.randn(}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}
        \ControlFlowTok{return} \VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{.\_get\_observation()}

    \KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ \_get\_observation(}\VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{):}
        \CommentTok{\# Simulated neural data}
        \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ np.random.randn(}\DecValTok{100}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# Train a policy}
\NormalTok{env }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BCIEnv()}
\NormalTok{model }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ PPO(}\StringTok{"MlpPolicy"}\NormalTok{, env).learn(total\_timesteps}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\subsubsection{Neuropeptides}\label{neuropeptides}

\textbf{Characteristics:} Larger molecules (3-40 amino acids);
synthesised in soma (not terminals); stored in large dense-core
vesicles; released by higher-frequency stimulation; diffuse farther
(volume transmission); slower, longer-lasting effects.

\textbf{Examples:} - \textbf{Substance P:} Pain transmission (dorsal
horn); co-released with glutamate from nociceptors - \textbf{Enkephalins
/ endorphins:} Endogenous opioids; bind mu (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}), delta (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\delta}}{delta}), kappa (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa})
opioid receptors; inhibit pain pathways - \textbf{NPY:} Appetite
stimulation; anxiolysis; one of the most abundant peptides in the brain
- \textbf{Orexin/hypocretin:} Wakefulness promotion; loss causes
narcolepsy type 1

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Synaptic Plasticity and
Memory}\label{synaptic-plasticity-and-memory}

\subsubsection{Long-Term Potentiation
(LTP)}\label{long-term-potentiation-ltp}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0163_fc7d28b2a9c2.png}
\caption{Molecular mechanisms of LTP and neurotransmitter recycling. LTP induction requires NMDA receptor opening (coincidence detection) and Ca\$\textasciicircum{}\{2+\}\$ influx. Early LTP involves CaMKII-mediated AMPA receptor modification. Late LTP requires gene expression (CREB) and structural synaptic changes. Neurotransmitters are cleared by reuptake, enzymatic degradation, or diffusion.}
\end{figure}

\textbf{LTP at Schaffer collateral to CA1 synapse (hippocampus):}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  High-frequency stimulation (100 Hz, 1 s) produces large EPSPs via AMPA
  receptors
\item
  Sufficient depolarisation removes Mg\(^{2+}\) block from NMDA
  receptors
\item
  Ca\(^{2+}\) floods into the postsynaptic spine via NMDA receptors
\item
  Ca\(^{2+}\) activates \textbf{CaMKII} (calcium/calmodulin-dependent
  protein kinase II):

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Autophosphorylation at T286 makes CaMKII constitutively active
    (Ca\(^{2+}\)-independent)
  \item
    Phosphorylates AMPA receptors at Ser831, increasing single-channel
    conductance
  \end{itemize}
\item
  AMPA receptor trafficking: New AMPA receptors inserted into the
  synapse from recycling endosomes
\item
  \textbf{Silent synapses:} Some synapses have NMDA receptors but no
  AMPA receptors. LTP ``unmasks'' these by inserting AMPA receptors,
  converting them to functional synapses.
\item
  \textbf{Late LTP} (\textgreater3 h): Requires new gene expression.
  Ca\(^{2+}\) activates PKA, which phosphorylates CREB. CREB-mediated
  \hyperref[gl:transcription]{\textbf{transcription}} produces Arc,
  BDNF, c-Fos. Structural changes include dendritic spine enlargement
  and formation of new spines.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Long-Term Depression
(LTD)}\label{long-term-depression-ltd}

Low-frequency stimulation (1 Hz, 15 min) produces modest Ca\(^{2+}\)
entry via NMDA receptors: - Lower Ca\(^{2+}\) levels preferentially
activate protein phosphatases (PP1, calcineurin/PP2B) rather than CaMKII
- Phosphatases dephosphorylate AMPA receptors - AMPA receptors are
endocytosed (clathrin-mediated) from the synapse - Synaptic strength
decreases

\textbf{Bidirectional plasticity:} The same synapse can undergo LTP or
LTD depending on the pattern of Ca\(^{2+}\) entry. This is captured by
the \textbf{BCM (Bienenstock-Cooper-Munro) rule:} there exists a
modification threshold (\(\theta_M\)) -- activity above \(\theta_M\)
causes LTP, below causes LTD. The threshold itself slides based on
recent postsynaptic activity (metaplasticity).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 2:} A neuroscientist finds that pharmacologically
blocking the NMDA receptor abolishes LTP at hippocampal
Schaffer-collateral \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} CA1 synapses but does not abolish LTP at
mossy-fibre \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} CA3 synapses. Propose a mechanism that explains why these
two forms of LTP differ. Given that the CA3 form is presynaptic
(cAMP-PKA-dependent), which pharmacological manipulation would
selectively block it without affecting NMDA-receptor-dependent LTP?
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection:} The opioid epidemic has killed over
500,000 Americans since 1999. Understanding the molecular pharmacology
is essential: opioids activate mu receptors on GABAergic interneurons in
the VTA, removing tonic inhibition of dopamine neurons. The resulting
dopamine surge in the nucleus accumbens produces euphoria and
reinforcement. Tolerance develops as mu receptors are desensitised and
downregulated. Withdrawal occurs because the compensatory upregulation
of cAMP signalling is unmasked when the drug is removed. Naloxone
(Narcan) competitively displaces opioids from mu receptors and can
reverse respiratory depression within minutes.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Worked Example}\label{worked-example-3}

\textbf{Problem:} You voltage-clamp a frog neuromuscular junction and
record spontaneous miniature end-plate currents (mEPCs). From 500
events, the mean mEPC amplitude is \(q = 1.2\) nA (quantal size). You
then stimulate the motor nerve with single pulses and measure evoked
EPCs.

Over 200 evoked trials: - 8 trials produce no response (failures) - 72
trials produce a single quantal event (about 1.2 nA) - 68
trials produce two quantal events (about 2.4 nA) - 36 trials
produce three quantal events (about 3.6 nA) - 12 trials produce
four quantal events (about 4.8 nA) - 4 trials produce five
quantal events (about 6.0 nA)

\textbf{(a)} Calculate the mean quantal content \(\bar{m}\) = mean
number of quanta released per stimulus.

\begin{equation}
\bar{m} = \frac{0(8) + 1(72) + 2(68) + 3(36) + 4(12) + 5(4)}{200} = \frac{0 + 72 + 136 + 108 + 48 + 20}{200} = \frac{384}{200} = 1.92
\label{eq:action_potential_synapses_5}
\end{equation}

\textbf{(b)} Use the Poisson approximation to estimate the number of
failures expected if \(\bar{m}\) = 1.92:

For a Poisson process, the fraction of failures
\(P(0) = e^{-\bar{m}} = e^{-1.92} = 0.146\)

Expected failures = \(0.146 \times 200 = 29.3\). Observed failures = 8.
\textbf{The discrepancy} suggests the release is \textbf{not} strictly
Poisson --- there may be heterogeneity in vesicle release probabilities
across active zones, or the preparation has an unusually low failure
rate due to high quantal content.

\textbf{(c)} Use the method of failures to give an alternative estimate
of \(\bar{m}\):

\begin{equation}
\bar{m} = \ln\left(\frac{N}{n_0}\right) = \ln\left(\frac{200}{8}\right) = \ln(25) = 3.22
\label{eq:action_potential_synapses_6}
\end{equation}

The discrepancy between the two estimates (1.92 by direct count vs 3.22
by method of failures) indicates that the \textbf{binomial model} (with
heterogeneous release probabilities) fits better than the simple
Poisson. This is a classic result: real synapses have multiple active
zones with heterogeneous \(p\) values, violating the simple Poisson
assumption (Zucker 1973; Bhumbra \& Bhatt 2022).

\textbf{(d)} Given \(\bar{m} = 1.92\) and the number of release-ready
vesicles \(n = 10\) (estimated by high-osmotic sucrose stimulation),
estimate the mean release probability \(\bar{p}\):

\begin{equation}
\bar{p} = \frac{\bar{m}}{n} = \frac{1.92}{10} = 0.192
\label{eq:action_potential_synapses_7}
\end{equation}

This is a typical resting release probability for a vertebrate
neuromuscular junction (0.1--0.4 at physiological Ca\(^{2+}\)). The
\(n \cdot p \cdot q\) synaptic model predicts that drugs which increase
\(p\) (e.g., by prolonging the AP and increasing Ca\(^{2+}\) influx,
such as aminopyridines) will linearly increase \(\bar{m}\) and thus EPP
amplitude --- a pharmacological basis for treatments in Lambert-Eaton
myasthenic syndrome.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-32}

For \textbf{Action Potentials and Synaptic Transmission}, frontier
biology belongs inside the evidence logic of the chapter. Physiology now
blends mechanism with allostasis, immune-endocrine-neural coupling,
wearable data, and individualized risk without reducing bodies to simple
machines. The core reading question is this: synaptic claims require
ion-channel timing, driving force, transmitter release, receptor
dynamics, and plasticity.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

Interpret physiological data by separating baseline variation,
perturbation response, compensation, and the threshold where
compensation becomes pathology.

\textbf{Source practice:} For physiology claims, cite the measurement
context and distinguish baseline variation, compensation,
pathophysiology, and treatment evidence.

\textbf{Hodgkin-Huxley model} & Mathematical description of AP using
gating variables m, h, n for Na\(^+\) and K\(^+\) conductances \\
\textbf{Threshold} & Membrane potential (about \(-55\) mV) at
which inward Na\(^+\) current exceeds outward K\(^+\) current \\
\textbf{Absolute refractory period} & about 1-2 ms when
Na\(^+\) channels are inactivated; no AP possible regardless of
stimulus \\
\textbf{Relative refractory period} & about 5-10 ms when
Na\(^+\) channels recovering; stronger stimulus needed for AP \\
\textbf{Saltatory conduction} & AP jumps between nodes of Ranvier in
myelinated axons \\
\textbf{SNARE complex} & Synaptobrevin + syntaxin + SNAP-25: core
vesicle fusion machinery \\
\textbf{Synaptotagmin} & Ca\(^{2+}\) sensor that triggers vesicle
fusion; C2 domains bind 4-5 Ca\(^{2+}\) ions \\
\textbf{Quantal release} & Neurotransmitter released in discrete
vesicle-sized packets (Katz, 1950s) \\
\textbf{NMDA receptor} & Coincidence detector: requires glutamate +
depolarisation; Ca\(^{2+}\) permeable \\
\textbf{CaMKII} & Calcium/calmodulin kinase II; autophosphorylation at
T286; key LTP effector \\
\textbf{LTP} & Long-term potentiation: persistent increase in synaptic
strength \\
\textbf{LTD} & Long-term depression: persistent decrease in synaptic
strength \\
\textbf{Excitotoxicity} & Neuronal death from excessive
glutamate/Ca\(^{2+}\) (stroke, epilepsy) \\
\textbf{Tetrodotoxin (TTX)} & Puffer fish toxin blocking Nav channels \\
\textbf{BCM rule} & Sliding modification threshold determining LTP vs
LTD \\
\textbf{Silent synapse} & Synapse with NMDA but no AMPA receptors;
``unmasked'' during LTP \\
\end{longtable}
}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Review Questions}\label{review-questions-32}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Using the Hodgkin-Huxley equations, explain why the peak of the action
  potential does not reach E\(_{Na}\) (+50 mV) but instead peaks at
  approximately +30 to +40 mV. Which gating variable is responsible?
\item
  Explain the molecular basis of the absolute refractory period. Why is
  this essential for unidirectional AP propagation?
\item
  Compare saltatory conduction in myelinated axons with continuous
  conduction in unmyelinated axons. Why does velocity scale as
  \(\sqrt{d}\) in unmyelinated axons but as \(d\) in myelinated axons?
\item
  Describe the roles of the five key presynaptic proteins:
  synaptobrevin, syntaxin, SNAP-25, synaptotagmin-1, and complexin. What
  happens if each is eliminated?
\item
  The NMDA receptor is often called the ``Hebbian synapse detector.''
  Explain this concept, linking the receptor's biophysical properties to
  Hebb's postulate and to LTP induction.
\item
  A patient presents with progressive muscle weakness. Antibodies
  against the nicotinic ACh receptor are detected. Name the disease,
  explain the pathophysiology, and describe two treatment strategies
  based on cholinergic pharmacology.
\item
  Compare the mechanisms of cocaine and amphetamine at dopaminergic
  synapses. Both increase synaptic dopamine, but by different
  mechanisms. Why might their clinical effects and addiction profiles
  differ?
\item
  Explain why benzodiazepines are safer in overdose than barbiturates,
  despite both acting on GABA\(_A\) receptors. (Hint: consider the
  difference between increasing channel open \textbf{frequency} vs open
  \textbf{duration}, and the concept of ceiling effect.)
\item
  Design a hypothetical drug that could enhance memory formation by
  targeting the LTP pathway. Identify the molecular target, predict the
  therapeutic effect, and discuss potential side effects (excitotoxicity
  risk).
\item
  Why does multiple sclerosis cause such diverse neurological symptoms?
  Explain the relationship between lesion location in white matter
  tracts and the specific symptoms produced.
\item
  At a synapse, you observe mEPP amplitude of 0.5 mV and mean EPP
  amplitude of 4.5 mV (low-Ca\(^{2+}\) conditions to allow quantal
  resolution). (a) Estimate the mean quantal content \(\bar{m}\). (b)
  Use the Poisson failure method to calculate the expected probability
  of a failure. (c) If you increase extracellular Ca\(^{2+}\) from 1 mM
  to 2 mM, predict whether \(\bar{m}\) will increase linearly,
  quadratically, or via a 4th-power relationship (based on synaptotagmin
  cooperativity), and explain the molecular basis.
\item
  Clozapine is described as an ``atypical'' antipsychotic with lower
  risk of tardive dyskinesia compared to haloperidol, despite both
  treating positive symptoms of schizophrenia. Using the drug table,
  explain: (a) their differing receptor binding profiles; (b) why high
  D2 occupancy causes tardive dyskinesia; (c) why clozapine's unique
  receptor profile (including 5-HT\(_{2A}\) blockade) may explain its
  superior efficacy in treatment-resistant schizophrenia.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-32}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Hodgkin-Huxley:} \(I_{Na} = \bar{g}_{Na} m^3 h (V - E_{Na})\),
  \(I_K = \bar{g}_K n^4 (V - E_K)\). Gating variables obey first-order
  kinetics. m (fast activation), h (slow inactivation), n (slow
  activation).
\item
  \textbf{Refractory periods:} Absolute (Na\(^+\) inactivated, h about
  0, 1-2 ms): cannot fire. Relative (K\(^+\) channels open, membrane
  hyperpolarised, 5-10 ms): stronger stimulus needed.
\item
  \textbf{Na\(^+\) channel states:} Closed (ready) to Open (conducting,
  about 0.5 ms) to Inactivated (blocked from inside, cannot
  reopen). TTX and local anaesthetics block the pore.
\item
  \textbf{Myelination:} Saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier.
  Velocity proportional to diameter (linear). A-alpha fibres: 70-120
  m/s; C fibres: 0.5-2 m/s. MS: autoimmune demyelination.
\item
  \textbf{Chemical synapse:} AP opens Cav2.1/2.2 channels. Ca\(^{2+}\)
  binds synaptotagmin-1. Complexin displaced. SNARE complex zippers.
  Vesicle fuses. NT released in \textless1 ms. Quantal release (Katz).
\item
  \textbf{Neurotransmitters:} Glutamate (AMPA/NMDA/mGluR, excitatory);
  GABA (GABA\(_A\)/GABA\(_B\), inhibitory); ACh (nicotinic/muscarinic);
  DA (D1-D5, reward/motor); 5-HT (mood/sleep); NE (arousal);
  neuropeptides (volume transmission, pain, reward).
\item
  \textbf{LTP:} NMDA-Ca\(^{2+}\)-CaMKII-AMPA pathway. Early:
  phosphorylation and insertion of AMPA receptors. Late: CREB-dependent
  gene expression, structural spine changes. LTD: opposite; phosphatases
  remove AMPA receptors.
\item
  \textbf{Drug mechanisms:} Cocaine (DAT block), morphine (mu agonist),
  SSRIs (SERT block), benzodiazepines (GABA\(_A\) PAM), ketamine (NMDA
  block), botulinum toxin (SNAP-25 cleavage).
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See \cref{sec:unit_IX_nervous_system} for
  resting potential and integration,
  \cref{sec:unit_VII_infectious_disease} for synaptic pathogens and
  toxins, and \cref{sec:unit_II_membrane_transport} for ion channels.
\end{itemize}

\section{Endocrine and Immune
Systems}\label{endocrine-and-immune-systems}

\label{sec:unit_IX_endocrine_and_immune}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ch 31} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.} Level 2/3 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.} 55 min read \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.} 75 min lecture \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.}
Prerequisites: \cref{sec:unit_IX_circulation_respiration_homeostasis}
\end{quote}

\subsection{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-33}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Compare endocrine and nervous system signalling in terms of speed,
  duration, and specificity.
\item
  Classify \hyperref[gl:hormone]{\textbf{hormone}}s by chemical class
  (peptide, steroid, amine, eicosanoid) and describe their synthesis,
  transport, receptor location, and signalling duration.
\item
  Explain the HPA, HPT, and HPG axes with feedback regulation, including
  detailed steroidogenesis and the circadian profile of cortisol.
\item
  Trace insulin and glucagon signalling in glucose
  \hyperref[gl:homeostasis]{\textbf{homeostasis}}, including
  IR/IRS/PI3K/Akt/GLUT4, crosstalk with leptin and GLP-1, and the
  pathophysiology of diabetes.
\item
  Describe the adrenal gland structure and function (cortex and
  medulla), including cortisol synthesis from cholesterol.
\item
  Describe thyroid hormone synthesis, T4\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}T3 conversion, the nuclear
  receptor mechanism, and the Wolff-Chaikoff effect.
\item
  Describe the growth hormone axis and IGF-1.
\item
  Explain prostaglandin and eicosanoid synthesis from arachidonic acid;
  differentiate non-selective NSAIDs from COX-2 selective inhibitors.
\item
  Describe endocrine disruption by xenoestrogens, BPA, phthalates, and
  PFAS.
\item
  Distinguish innate and adaptive immunity, including PRRs (TLRs, NLRs,
  RLRs) and their downstream signalling pathways (MyD88/NF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}B vs
  TRIF/IRF3 vs cGAS-STING).
\item
  Explain the complement system (classical, lectin, alternative
  pathways), the C3/C5 convertases, the MAC, and amplification dynamics.
\item
  Describe T cell development through the DN1--DN4 stages, positive and
  negative thymic selection, and TCR diversity generation.
\item
  Describe B cell activation, T-dependent vs T-independent responses,
  germinal centre reactions, somatic hypermutation, and class switching.
\item
  Tabulate the cytokine network and key cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF,
  IFN-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma}, IL-10, IL-4, IL-17, etc.).
\item
  Describe immunological memory formation and explain why memory cells
  respond faster.
\item
  Explain mechanisms of central and peripheral tolerance and how their
  failure causes autoimmunity (molecular mimicry, bystander activation,
  epitope spreading).
\item
  Describe the Type I--IV classification of hypersensitivity reactions
  and their treatments.
\item
  Explain immunotherapy: checkpoint inhibitors (PD-1/PD-L1, CTLA-4) and
  CAR-T cell therapy.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Study Blueprint}\label{study-blueprint-33}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Big idea:} Long-range signaling and immune recognition
  coordinate body-wide adaptation and defense.
\item
  \textbf{Core concepts:} hormones, receptors, innate immunity, adaptive
  immunity.
\item
  \textbf{Framework alignment:} Vision \& Change: Structure and
  function, Systems; AP Biology: Systems Interactions, Energetics;
  NGSS-style topics: Structure and Function.
\item
  \textbf{Model or quantitative lens:} Hormone feedback, dose-response,
  and immune-memory reasoning.
\item
  \textbf{Data skill:} Interpret endocrine or immune data from time
  courses, titers, or perturbations.
\item
  \textbf{Practice cadence:} Visual Representations, Statistical Tests
  and Data Analysis, Argumentation.
\item
  \textbf{Common misconception to repair:} Immunity is not just attack;
  recognition, tolerance, memory, and regulation are equally central.
\item
  \textbf{Primary lab:} \cref{sec:lab_unit_IX_endocrine_and_immune}.
\item
  \textbf{Question bank:} \cref{sec:q_unit_IX_endocrine_and_immune}.
\item
  \textbf{Transfer task:} Transfer signaling and immunity reasoning to
  vaccination, autoimmunity, stress, and metabolism.
\item
  \textbf{Bridge to computation:}
  \breaktt{biology.physiology.physiology.homeostasis\_response}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Opening Vignette --- The Hormone That Changed Medicine Forever}

Before 1921, Type 1 diabetes was a death sentence. Children diagnosed
with it were placed on starvation diets --- sometimes eating fewer than
500 calories per day --- which extended their lives by months while
slowly wasting them. Then Frederick Banting, a young Canadian surgeon,
persuaded the University of Toronto to give him laboratory space and a
few dogs. Working with student Charles Best and biochemist J.B. Collip
to purify the extract, they isolated the pancreatic secretion that
controlled blood glucose --- insulin. The first human injection was
given to 14-year-old Leonard Thompson on January 11, 1922. He had been
near death; within days his blood glucose normalised and he survived.
Banting and John Macleod received the Nobel Prize in 1923. Insulin was
the first hormone to be purified, the first to be sequenced (by
Frederick Sanger, 1951), and the first to be produced by recombinant DNA
technology (1982). No single molecule has had a more direct impact on
human survival.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Endocrine System Overview}\label{endocrine-system-overview}

\subsubsection{Endocrine vs Nervous
System}\label{endocrine-vs-nervous-system}

\textbf{Mixed signalling:} Neuroendocrine cells (e.g., hypothalamic
\hyperref[gl:neuron]{\textbf{neuron}}s secreting releasing hormones,
adrenal medulla chromaffin cells) bridge both systems. Sterling and
Eyer's concept of \hyperref[gl:allostasis]{\textbf{allostasis}}
\citep{sterling1988,sterling2015} extends classical homeostasis: the
brain anticipates physiological needs and adjusts setpoints
predictively, integrating endocrine and autonomic outputs.

protein) & VDR (nuclear) & Days & about 15 h \\
\textbf{Epinephrine} & Catecholamine & Adrenal medulla chromaffin cells
& Free & \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}/\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} adrenergic (GPCRs) & Seconds--minutes & about 2
min \\
\textbf{Norepinephrine} & Catecholamine & Adrenal medulla; sympathetic
neurons & Free & \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}/\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} adrenergic (GPCRs) & Seconds--minutes &
about 2 min \\
\textbf{T4 (thyroxine)} & Iodinated tyrosine & Thyroid follicular cells
& 99.97\% TBG/TTR/albumin; 0.03\% free & TR\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}/\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} (nuclear) after D2
conversion to T3 & Days--weeks & about 6--7 d \\
\textbf{T3 (triiodothyronine)} & Iodinated tyrosine & Thyroid
(about 20\%); peripheral D1/D2 (about 80\%) & 99.7\%
bound; 0.3\% free & TR\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}/\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} (nuclear) & Days & about 1 d \\
\textbf{Melatonin} & Indolamine & Pineal gland (from tryptophan via
serotonin) & Albumin & MT\(_1\), MT\(_2\) (G\(_i\) GPCRs) &
Minutes--hours & about 30--50 min \\
\textbf{PGE\(_2\)} & Eicosanoid & Most cells (COX-2 inducible) & Local
(paracrine) & EP\(_1\)--EP\(_4\) (GPCRs) & Seconds & about 30
s \\
\textbf{TXA\(_2\)} & Eicosanoid & Platelets (TXAS) & Local & TP receptor
(G\(_q\)) & Seconds & about 30 s \\
\textbf{Leptin} & Peptide (167 aa) & Adipocytes (proportional to fat
mass) & Free; some bound & LepR (JAK2/STAT3, hypothalamus) & Hours &
about 25 min \\
\textbf{Adiponectin} & Peptide (244 aa) & Adipocytes & Free;
trimers/hexamers/HMW & AdipoR1, AdipoR2 (AMPK pathway) & Hours &
about 14 h \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Key contrasts:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Speed vs duration trade-off.} Membrane receptor signalling
  (peptides, catecholamines) is fast but transient: cAMP, IP\(_3\), and
  Ca\(^{2+}\) signals decay in seconds when ligand washes away. Nuclear
  receptor signalling (steroids, T3) is slow but persistent: transcribed
  mRNAs and translated proteins last hours to days.
\item
  \textbf{Storage vs synthesis.} Peptide hormones are pre-synthesised
  and stored in granules ready for rapid release --- insulin can be
  released within seconds of glucose elevation. Steroids cannot be
  stored (lipid-soluble, would diffuse away); they are synthesised on
  demand, which limits acute response speed.
\item
  \textbf{Carrier proteins as a reservoir.} CBG (cortisol binding
  globulin), SHBG (sex hormone binding globulin), and TBG (thyroxine
  binding globulin) bind 95--99\% of their target hormones. The bound
  fraction is biologically inactive but provides a circulating
  reservoir, buffering plasma levels and extending half-life. Free
  hormone is in equilibrium with bound; pregnancy elevates oestrogen
  which raises CBG, increasing total cortisol while free cortisol
  remains normal.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Quantitative
Endocrinology}\label{quantitative-endocrinology}

\textbf{Hormone--receptor binding.} The dissociation constant \(K_d\)
characterises receptor affinity (lower \(K_d\) = higher affinity):

\begin{equation}
K_d = \frac{[\text{H}][\text{R}]}{[\text{HR}]}; \qquad \text{fractional occupancy} = \frac{[\text{H}]}{[\text{H}] + K_d}
\label{eq:unit_IX_kd}
\end{equation}

Typical \(K_d\) values: \hyperref[gl:insulin-receptor]{\textbf{insulin
receptor}} about 0.1 nM; glucocorticoid receptor
about 5 nM; epinephrine at \(\beta_2\) receptor
about 1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}M. The enormous affinity difference explains why
insulin circulates at picomolar concentrations while catecholamines
require nanomolar--micromolar levels for effect.

\textbf{Hormone half-life and clearance.} Plasma hormone concentration
decays exponentially after secretion ceases:

\begin{equation}
C(t) = C_0 \, e^{-kt}, \qquad k = \frac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}}
\label{eq:unit_IX_halflife}
\end{equation}

Half-lives vary enormously: catecholamines about 1--2 min
(rapid enzymatic degradation by MAO/COMT); cortisol
about 60--90 min (hepatic metabolism); thyroid hormone (T4)
about 6--7 days (protein binding extends clearance).
Protein-bound hormones (e.g., TBG-bound T4, CBG-bound cortisol) are
protected from degradation and renal filtration.

\textbf{Dose--response relationship.} The sigmoidal (Hill)
dose--response curve relates hormone concentration to biological effect:

\begin{equation}
E = E_{\max} \cdot \frac{[\text{H}]^{n}}{EC_{50}^{n} + [\text{H}]^{n}}
\label{eq:unit_IX_doseresponse}
\end{equation}

where \(EC_{50}\) is the concentration producing 50\% of maximal effect
and \(n\) is the Hill coefficient (cooperativity). Spare receptors shift
the \(EC_{50}\) leftward from \(K_d\): insulin requires occupation of
about 5\% of receptors for maximal glucose uptake.

\textbf{\hyperref[gl:herd-immunity]{Herd immunity} threshold.} The
fraction of the population that must be immune to prevent epidemic
spread is:

\begin{equation}
p_c = 1 - \frac{1}{R_0}
\label{eq:unit_IX_herd}
\end{equation}

where \(R_0\) is the basic reproductive number. For measles
(\(R_0 \approx 12\)--18), \(p_c \approx 92\)--95\%, explaining why even
small drops in vaccination coverage trigger outbreaks.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Hypothalamic-Pituitary
Axes}\label{hypothalamic-pituitary-axes}

The hypothalamus serves as the master integrator, linking the nervous
and endocrine systems. It produces releasing and inhibiting hormones
that control the anterior pituitary, which in turn controls target
glands throughout the body.

\textbf{Anterior pituitary hormones:} ACTH (corticotrophs), TSH
(thyrotrophs), GH (somatotrophs), LH and FSH (gonadotrophs), prolactin
(lactotrophs).

\textbf{Posterior pituitary:} Stores and releases ADH (vasopressin) and
oxytocin, which are synthesised in hypothalamic supraoptic and
paraventricular nuclei and transported down axons to the posterior
pituitary for release.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0164_3472280e63b0.png}
\caption{The three major hypothalamic-pituitary axes Each follows the same hierarchical pattern: hypothalamic releasing hormone stimulates anterior pituitary tropic hormone, which stimulates target gland hormone production. Negative feedback at multiple levels prevents overstimulation. The HPG axis uniquely features positive feedback during the mid-cycle LH surge.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{HPA Axis (Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal) --- Detailed
Cortisol
Physiology}\label{hpa-axis-hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal-detailed-cortisol-physiology}

\paragraph{Cortisol synthesis from cholesterol
(steroidogenesis)}\label{cortisol-synthesis-from-cholesterol-steroidogenesis}

Most adrenal steroids derive from cholesterol via a series of cytochrome
P450-mediated hydroxylations and oxidations. The rate-limiting step is
the transport of cholesterol from the outer to the inner mitochondrial
membrane, mediated by \textbf{StAR (steroidogenic acute regulatory
protein)} and stimulated by ACTH via cAMP/PKA.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0165_9ce0bbb6ae5d.png}
\caption{Adrenal steroidogenesis The pathway diverges from common precursor pregnenolone into three parallel routes producing aldosterone (zona glomerulosa), cortisol (zona fasciculata), and androgens (zona reticularis). Each zone expresses zone-specific enzymes; for example, primarily the zona glomerulosa expresses aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2), and primarily the zona fasciculata expresses 11beta-hydroxylase (CYP11B1).}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Glucocorticoid receptor (GR)
mechanism}\label{glucocorticoid-receptor-gr-mechanism}

Cortisol diffuses freely across the plasma membrane (lipid-soluble) and
binds the cytoplasmic GR (NR3C1). In the unliganded state, GR is held in
an inactive complex with HSP90, HSP70, and immunophilins. Cortisol
binding induces a conformational change, releasing the chaperones and
exposing nuclear localisation signals. The activated GR translocates to
the nucleus, dimerises, and binds \textbf{glucocorticoid response
elements (GREs)} in target gene promoters with the consensus sequence
5'-AGAACAnnnTGTTCT-3'.

GR has \textbf{two transcriptional modes:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Transactivation} at positive GREs: directly upregulates
  gluconeogenic enzymes (PEPCK, G6Pase) and anti-inflammatory proteins
  (annexin A1, MKP-1, I\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}B\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}, IL-10).
\item
  \textbf{Transrepression} by tethering to NF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}B or AP-1: GR binds these
  pro-inflammatory transcription factors and prevents their activation
  of cytokine genes (IL-2, IL-6, TNF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}, COX-2). Transrepression mediates
  much of the anti-inflammatory action of glucocorticoid drugs.
\end{itemize}

The dual mechanism is therapeutically central. Most classical
glucocorticoids (prednisone, dexamethasone) drive both modes --- the
unwanted metabolic effects (hyperglycaemia, osteoporosis, muscle
wasting) come predominantly from transactivation, while the
anti-inflammatory benefit comes mostly from transrepression.
Pharmaceutical efforts to design ``selective GR agonists'' (SEGRAs) that
drive transrepression preferentially have been an enduring (but largely
unrealised) goal.

\paragraph{Cortisol effects (anti-inflammatory gene
programme)}\label{cortisol-effects-anti-inflammatory-gene-programme}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Gluconeogenesis} (transactivation of PEPCK, G6Pase via GR;
  mobilises amino acids from muscle protein catabolism)
\item
  \textbf{Immunosuppression} at multiple levels:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Direct: NF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}B inhibition; lymphocyte
    \hyperref[gl:apoptosis]{\textbf{apoptosis}}; suppression of IL-2
    transcription; mast-cell stabilisation
  \item
    Indirect: induction of IL-10, TGF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}, annexin A1; suppression of
    leukocyte trafficking by reducing E-selectin and ICAM-1
  \item
    Net cytokine effect: \textbf{down} TNF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}, IL-1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}, IL-2, IL-6, IFN-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma};
    \textbf{up} IL-10
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Lipolysis} in peripheral adipose tissue (with central fat
  redistribution from chronic excess)
\item
  \textbf{Anti-inflammatory} (inhibits COX-2, phospholipase A\(_2\) via
  annexin A1 induction; reduces histamine, leukotriene production)
\item
  \textbf{Permissive effects} on catecholamine action (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-adrenergic
  receptor expression maintenance)
\item
  \textbf{Bone resorption} (chronic excess: osteoporosis via direct
  osteoblast suppression and indirect calcium handling)
\item
  \textbf{CNS effects} (mood --- chronic excess: depression, psychosis,
  cognitive impairment via hippocampal atrophy)
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Circadian rhythm and
feedback}\label{circadian-rhythm-and-feedback}

Cortisol secretion follows a robust \textbf{circadian rhythm} driven by
the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN): peak at approximately 08:00 (cortisol
awakening response, CAR), nadir at midnight. Superimposed are
\textbf{ultradian pulses} every 60--90 minutes. The pulsatile pattern is
essential for proper GR function --- continuous (non-pulsatile) cortisol
exposure desensitises target tissues.

Schematically, plasma cortisol \(\approx 18\,\mu\text{g/dL}\) at 08:00,
drops through the day to \(\approx 8\,\mu\text{g/dL}\) at 16:00, and is
\(<5\,\mu\text{g/dL}\) at midnight. Disrupted circadian rhythm (shift
work, depression, Cushing's) loses the diurnal variation;
\textbf{midnight salivary cortisol} is one of the most sensitive
screening tests for endogenous Cushing's syndrome.

\textbf{Negative feedback} operates at two levels:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Fast feedback} (minutes): non-genomic; cortisol acts on
  hypothalamic CRH neurons via membrane GRs and presynaptic
  endocannabinoid release to suppress CRH secretion within minutes.
\item
  \textbf{Slow feedback} (hours): genomic; cortisol downregulates POMC
  gene transcription (the ACTH precursor) in pituitary corticotrophs and
  CRH transcription in hypothalamus.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Stress vs basal regulation}\label{stress-vs-basal-regulation}

Under \textbf{basal (non-stress)} conditions, the HPA axis runs on its
circadian/ultradian rhythm with tight negative feedback. The day's
cortisol output is roughly 10--20 mg/24 h.

Under \textbf{acute stress} (trauma, hypoglycaemia, infection, surgery),
hypothalamic PVN neurons receive convergent inputs (limbic, brainstem,
circulating cytokines, baroreceptors) and override basal restraint:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  CRH secretion rises 5--10 fold
\item
  ACTH plasma concentration rises within 5--15 min
\item
  Cortisol peaks about 30 min after stress onset
\item
  Cortisol output can increase 3--10 fold over basal (50--100 mg/24 h in
  major surgery)
\item
  Negative feedback is partially suppressed, allowing sustained
  elevation
\end{itemize}

Chronic psychosocial stress engages the same axis but with
\textbf{glucocorticoid receptor downregulation} and \textbf{flattened
diurnal rhythm} --- features now linked to metabolic syndrome,
depression, hippocampal atrophy, and accelerated cognitive decline.

\textbf{Pathology:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Cushing's syndrome:} Cortisol excess. Causes: pituitary
  adenoma (Cushing's disease, 70\%), ectopic ACTH (lung small cell
  carcinoma), adrenal adenoma, iatrogenic (chronic glucocorticoid
  therapy). Features: central obesity, moon face, purple striae,
  hyperglycaemia, osteoporosis, immunosuppression, hypertension
  (cortisol cross-reacts with mineralocorticoid receptor).
\item
  \textbf{Addison's disease:} Primary adrenal insufficiency (cortisol
  deficiency). Most common cause: autoimmune adrenalitis. Features:
  hypotension, hyperpigmentation (elevated ACTH drives
  melanocyte-stimulating hormone activity, since both are cleaved from
  the same precursor POMC), fatigue, salt craving. Can cause
  life-threatening adrenal crisis.
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection:} The dexamethasone suppression test
exploits negative feedback to diagnose Cushing's syndrome. Dexamethasone
is a synthetic glucocorticoid that normally suppresses CRH and ACTH
secretion. In Cushing's disease (pituitary adenoma), low-dose
dexamethasone fails to suppress cortisol, but high-dose dexamethasone
does. In ectopic ACTH production, neither dose suppresses cortisol. This
distinguishes the source of excess cortisol.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{HPT Axis (Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Thyroid) --- Detailed
Mechanism}\label{hpt-axis-hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid-detailed-mechanism}

\paragraph{Thyroid hormone synthesis}\label{thyroid-hormone-synthesis}

Follicular cells of the thyroid gland surround a colloid-filled follicle
and execute a multi-step iodination process:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Iodide uptake.} The basolateral Na\(^+\)/I\(^-\) symporter
  (NIS) actively concentrates iodide about 25--100-fold above
  plasma. Pertechnetate (\(^{99m}\)TcO\(_4^-\)) is also transported by
  NIS and is used in thyroid scintigraphy.
\item
  \textbf{Thyroglobulin synthesis.} Follicular cells produce
  thyroglobulin (Tg, about 660 kDa glycoprotein with
  about 120 tyrosine residues), packaged into vesicles and
  exocytosed into the colloid lumen.
\item
  \textbf{Iodide oxidation and tyrosine iodination.} At the apical
  membrane, \textbf{thyroid peroxidase (TPO)} oxidises I\(^-\) to a
  reactive iodinating species (I\(_2\) or I\(^+\)) using H\(_2\)O\(_2\)
  as cofactor. Tyrosines on Tg are iodinated to form monoiodotyrosine
  (MIT) and diiodotyrosine (DIT).
\item
  \textbf{Coupling reaction.} Still on the Tg scaffold, TPO catalyses
  oxidative coupling: DIT + DIT \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} T4 (thyroxine, 4 iodines); MIT + DIT \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  T3 (3 iodines).
\item
  \textbf{Endocytosis and proteolysis.} TSH stimulation triggers
  endocytosis of Tg into the follicular cell, where lysosomal proteases
  cleave the iodothyronines from Tg. T4 and T3 are released into the
  bloodstream.
\item
  \textbf{Recycling.} MIT and DIT not coupled into T3/T4 are deiodinated
  by intracellular dehalogenase, recycling iodide.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Wolff-Chaikoff effect}\label{wolff-chaikoff-effect}

Acutely high iodide (e.g., from radiocontrast, amiodarone, or seaweed
binge) paradoxically \textbf{inhibits} thyroid hormone synthesis: excess
iodide downregulates NIS expression and impairs TPO-mediated
organification. Most healthy individuals ``escape'' within 7--10 days as
NIS resets. In patients with autoimmune thyroid disease, escape may fail
--- producing \textbf{iodine-induced hypothyroidism}. Conversely, in
nodular goitres with autonomous follicles, iodine load can drive
\textbf{iodine-induced hyperthyroidism (Jod-Basedow)}. The
Wolff-Chaikoff effect is exploited therapeutically: \textbf{potassium
iodide} (Lugol's solution, SSKI) is given pre-operatively in Graves'
disease to reduce thyroid vascularity and slow hormone release before
thyroidectomy.

\paragraph{T4 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} T3 conversion
(deiodinases)}\label{t4-t3-conversion-deiodinases}

T4 is the predominant secreted form (about 80\%) but is largely
a \textbf{prohormone}. Three iodothyronine deiodinases activate or
inactivate T4 in target tissues:

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2500}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1875}}

\textbf{D1} & T4 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} T3 (5'-deiodination) & Liver, kidney, thyroid & Bulk
plasma T3 production \\
\textbf{D2} & T4 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} T3 (5'-deiodination) & Brain, pituitary, brown
adipose & Local T3 generation; pituitary feedback set-point \\
\textbf{D3} & T4 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} reverse T3 (rT3); T3 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} T2 & Placenta, fetal tissues &
