}

T3 is \textbf{about 4\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} more potent} than T4 at the nuclear
receptor. During fasting, illness, or stress (non-thyroidal illness), D1
activity drops and D3 activity rises, shifting balance toward inactive
rT3 --- adaptive metabolic slowing.

\paragraph{Nuclear thyroid receptor
mechanism}\label{nuclear-thyroid-receptor-mechanism}

T3 enters cells via MCT8/MCT10 transporters and binds nuclear
\textbf{thyroid hormone receptors TR\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha} (cardiac, neural)} and \textbf{TR\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}
(liver, pituitary)}. TRs heterodimerise with \textbf{RXR (retinoid X
receptor)} and bind \textbf{thyroid response elements (TREs)} in target
gene promoters --- even in the absence of T3.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Without T3:} Unliganded TR/RXR recruits corepressors (NCoR,
  SMRT, HDACs) and \textbf{represses} target gene transcription.
\item
  \textbf{With T3:} Conformational change releases corepressors and
  recruits coactivators (SRC-1, p300/CBP, histone acetyltransferases) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  \textbf{active transcription}.
\end{itemize}

This dual mechanism explains why hypothyroidism causes such pronounced
symptoms: target genes are not merely ``not turned on'' but are actively
repressed below baseline.

\paragraph{Effects on metabolism}\label{effects-on-metabolism}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Increased basal metabolic rate (BMR)} through upregulation of
  Na\(^+\)/K\(^+\)-ATPase (each cell uses about 25\% of ATP for
  this pump; T3 increases pump density).
\item
  \textbf{Mitochondrial uncoupling} via UCP-mediated proton leak (heat
  production, calorigenic effect).
\item
  \textbf{Increased cardiac output} (\(\beta_1\)-adrenergic receptor
  upregulation; positive chronotropic and inotropic effects).
\item
  \textbf{Lipolysis and cholesterol degradation} (hyperthyroidism lowers
  LDL; hypothyroidism causes hypercholesterolaemia).
\item
  \textbf{Neurodevelopment:} essential for myelination, synaptogenesis,
  neuronal migration in fetus and infant. Severe untreated congenital
  hypothyroidism produces cretinism (intellectual disability, growth
  retardation) --- preventable by neonatal screening.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pathology:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Hypothyroidism:} Low T3/T4, elevated TSH. Hashimoto's
  thyroiditis (autoimmune; anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies).
  Features: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, bradycardia,
  constipation, myxoedema.
\item
  \textbf{Hyperthyroidism:} High T3/T4, suppressed TSH. Graves' disease
  (autoimmune; TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies ---
  thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins, TSI). Features: weight loss, heat
  intolerance, tachycardia/atrial fibrillation, tremor, exophthalmos
  (due to retro-orbital inflammation), diffuse goitre.
\item
  \textbf{Iodine deficiency:} Most common preventable cause of
  intellectual disability worldwide; affects approximately 1.9 billion
  people. Addressed by salt iodisation programmes.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{HPG Axis and Reproductive
Hormones}\label{hpg-axis-and-reproductive-hormones}

\textbf{GnRH pulsatility is critical:} High-frequency pulses (every
60--90 min) favour LH secretion; low-frequency pulses (every 2--4 h)
favour FSH. Continuous GnRH paradoxically suppresses the axis
(downregulates GnRH receptors), which is the basis of GnRH agonist
therapy for prostate cancer, endometriosis, and precocious puberty.

\textbf{Male reproductive endocrinology:} LH stimulates Leydig cells
(testosterone production). FSH + testosterone stimulate Sertoli cells
(support spermatogenesis; produce inhibin B, which provides negative
feedback on FSH). Testosterone effects: muscle mass, bone density,
secondary sexual characteristics, spermatogenesis, libido.

\textbf{Female menstrual cycle (28-day average):}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Follicular phase} (days 1--14): FSH promotes follicular
  growth. \hyperref[gl:dominant]{\textbf{Dominant}} follicle produces
  rising oestradiol. Oestradiol initially provides negative feedback.
\item
  \textbf{Ovulation} (day approximately 14): \textbf{Positive feedback}
  --- sustained high oestradiol above a threshold for \textgreater36 h
  switches from negative to positive feedback, triggering an LH surge.
  The LH surge induces ovulation (follicular rupture, oocyte release).
\item
  \textbf{Luteal phase} (days 14--28): Corpus luteum (remnant of
  ovulated follicle) produces progesterone + oestradiol. Progesterone
  prepares the endometrium for implantation (secretory phase). If no
  implantation occurs, corpus luteum degenerates (luteolysis),
  progesterone and oestradiol fall, endometrium sheds (menstruation).
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Development and reproduction as endocrine timing problems:}
Fertilisation, implantation, placentation, fetal growth, birth,
lactation, puberty, and reproductive senescence depend on timed
endocrine signals interacting with local tissue cues. Early embryos are
initially regulated by maternal transcripts and local morphogen
gradients; later development adds fetal-placental endocrine exchange,
thyroid-hormone-dependent neurodevelopment, glucocorticoid-driven lung
maturation, and sex-steroid-dependent reproductive tract
differentiation. Clinically, infertility is diagnosed after 12 months of
regular unprotected intercourse without pregnancy (or after 6 months
when the female partner is 35 years or older), because reproductive
physiology depends on ovulation, sperm production, tubal transport,
implantation, uterine receptivity, endocrine timing, and age-dependent
gamete quality \citep{cdc2024reproductivehealth}. The organismal point
is that reproduction is not one organ system; it is a coordinated
life-history transition linking gonads, hypothalamus, pituitary,
placenta, metabolism, immune tolerance, and behaviour.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 1:} Why does continuous GnRH administration
paradoxically suppress the HPG axis rather than stimulate it? How is
this exploited clinically in prostate cancer treatment, where the goal
is to lower testosterone?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Pancreatic Hormones, Glucose Homeostasis, and Energy
Balance}\label{pancreatic-hormones-glucose-homeostasis-and-energy-balance}

\textbf{Normal fasting blood glucose:} 4.0--5.5 mmol/L (72--99 mg/dL).
Post-prandial peak: \textless7.8 mmol/L (\textless140 mg/dL).

\subsubsection{Insulin signalling --- molecular
detail}\label{insulin-signalling-molecular-detail}

\textbf{After a meal (high glucose):}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Glucose enters \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-cells via GLUT2 transporter (high-K\(_m\) ``glucose
  sensor'')
\item
  Glucose metabolism increases the ATP/ADP ratio
\item
  ATP-sensitive K\(^+\) channels (K\(_{ATP}\), SUR1/Kir6.2 subunits)
  close \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} membrane depolarisation
\item
  Voltage-gated L-type Ca\(^{2+}\) channels open \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Ca\(^{2+}\) influx
\item
  Ca\(^{2+}\) triggers \textbf{insulin exocytosis} from dense-core
  granules (mature insulin = A and B chains held by disulphide bonds;
  C-peptide co-released as marker)
\item
  \textbf{Insulin signalling in target cells:}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Insulin binds \textbf{insulin receptor (IR)} --- an
    \(\alpha_2\beta_2\) tetrameric receptor tyrosine kinase. Each
    \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-subunit is extracellular and binds insulin; \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-subunits span the
    membrane and contain intracellular tyrosine kinase domains.
  \item
    Binding causes conformational change \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
    \textbf{trans-autophosphorylation} of \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-subunit tyrosine residues
    (Y1158, Y1162, Y1163 in the activation loop)
  \item
    Phosphotyrosines recruit \textbf{IRS1/IRS2} scaffold proteins \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} IRS
    phosphorylation
  \item
    IRS phosphotyrosines recruit \textbf{PI3K} (p85 regulatory + p110
    catalytic) via SH2 domains
  \item
    PI3K converts PIP\(_2\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{PIP\(_3\)}; PDK1 and mTORC2 dock
    on PIP\(_3\) and activate \textbf{Akt (PKB)} by phosphorylation at
    T308 and S473
  \item
    \textbf{Akt phosphorylates AS160 (TBC1D4)}, releasing Rab-GAP
    inhibition of GLUT4-vesicle exocytosis \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
    \textbf{\hyperref[gl:glut4]{GLUT4} translocation to plasma membrane}
    in muscle and adipose (the dominant mechanism for postprandial
    glucose disposal)
  \item
    \textbf{Akt inhibits GSK3\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} glycogen synthase activation \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
    \textbf{glycogen synthesis}
  \item
    \textbf{Akt activates mTORC1} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} ribosomal S6K1 and 4E-BP1
    phosphorylation \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{protein synthesis}
  \item
    \textbf{Akt phosphorylates FoxO1} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} nuclear export \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} represses
    gluconeogenic gene transcription (PEPCK, G6Pase)
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0166_a076687f9cc5.png}
\caption{Insulin signalling cascade Insulin binding to IR triggers trans-autophosphorylation, recruitment of IRS, activation of PI3K, generation of PIP\$\_3\$, and activation of Akt. Akt then drives four parallel branches: GLUT4 translocation, glycogen synthesis, protein synthesis, and suppression of gluconeogenic gene transcription.}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Glucagon signalling}\label{glucagon-signalling}

\textbf{During fasting (low glucose):}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-cells release \textbf{glucagon} (triggered by low glucose,
  sympathetic activation, amino acids)
\item
  Glucagon binds G\(_s\)-coupled receptor on hepatocytes
\item
  cAMP-PKA pathway: phosphorylase kinase activates \textbf{glycogen
  phosphorylase} for \textbf{glycogenolysis}
\item
  cAMP also activates \textbf{CREB} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PEPCK and G6Pase gene
  transcription \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{gluconeogenesis}
\item
  PKA phosphorylates and inhibits PFK-2/FBPase-2 (PFKFB1), lowering
  F2,6BP \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} favours fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase over PFK-1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  gluconeogenesis dominates
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Crosstalk with leptin, adiponectin, and
GLP-1}\label{crosstalk-with-leptin-adiponectin-and-glp-1}

\textbf{Leptin} is secreted by adipocytes in proportion to fat mass and
acts on hypothalamic neurons (arcuate nucleus POMC and AgRP/NPY neurons)
via the leptin receptor (LepR, JAK2/STAT3 signalling) to suppress
appetite and increase energy expenditure. Leptin enhances central
insulin sensitivity and provides a long-term signal of energy stores.
Most obese individuals have high leptin but show \textbf{leptin
resistance} --- impaired hypothalamic LepR signalling and JAK2/STAT3
attenuation, partly via SOCS3 induction.

\textbf{Adiponectin} is also secreted by adipocytes --- but
\textbf{inversely} with fat mass (higher in lean states). It acts via
AdipoR1 and AdipoR2, activating \textbf{AMPK} (AMP-activated protein
kinase, the cellular ``energy sensor''). AMPK activation:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Increases fatty acid oxidation (phosphorylates ACC, decreasing
  malonyl-CoA, releasing CPT-1 from inhibition)
\item
  Decreases hepatic gluconeogenesis (decreases CREB-regulated
  transcription)
\item
  Increases skeletal muscle glucose uptake (independent of insulin)
\item
  Decreases mTORC1 and protein synthesis (reciprocal to insulin/Akt)
\end{itemize}

Adiponectin therefore acts as an \textbf{insulin sensitiser}. Plasma
adiponectin is reduced in T2DM, obesity, and metabolic syndrome;
pioglitazone (a thiazolidinedione, PPAR\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma} agonist) raises adiponectin and
improves insulin sensitivity.

\textbf{GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide 1)} is an \textbf{incretin}
released from intestinal L-cells in response to nutrient ingestion. It
acts via GLP-1R (G\(_s\)-coupled GPCR) to:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion (primarily when glucose
  elevated \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} low hypoglycaemia risk)
\item
  Suppress glucagon release from \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-cells
\item
  Slow gastric emptying
\item
  Activate hypothalamic anorexigenic circuits \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} reduce food intake
\item
  Promote \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-cell survival and proliferation (animal studies)
\end{itemize}

GLP-1 has a very short half-life (about 2 min) due to
degradation by \textbf{DPP-4} (dipeptidyl peptidase-4). Drug strategies:
GLP-1 analogues with DPP-4--resistant modifications (semaglutide,
liraglutide), or DPP-4 inhibitors (sitagliptin) that prolong endogenous
GLP-1.

\subsubsection{Diabetes Mellitus}\label{diabetes-mellitus}

\textbf{Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM):}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Autoimmune destruction of \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-cells (anti-GAD65, anti-IA-2,
  anti-insulin, anti-ZnT8 antibodies)
\item
  Complete insulin deficiency
\item
  Onset usually in childhood/adolescence (but can occur at any age ---
  ``LADA'' in adults)
\item
  Without insulin: hyperglycaemia, ketoacidosis (lipolysis produces FFA,
  hepatic \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-oxidation produces ketone bodies, metabolic acidosis)
\item
  Treatment: exogenous insulin (basal-bolus regimen), increasingly
  closed-loop insulin pump systems
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM):}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Peripheral insulin resistance: ceramide and pro-inflammatory cytokines
  (TNF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}, IL-6 from visceral adipose tissue) cause serine
  phosphorylation of IRS1, blocking normal tyrosine phosphorylation. ER
  stress and mitochondrial dysfunction also contribute.
\item
  Compensatory \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-cell hyperinsulinaemia initially maintains
  normoglycaemia
\item
  Progressive \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-cell failure (glucotoxicity, lipotoxicity, amyloid
  deposition) leads to overt hyperglycaemia
\item
  Treatment: lifestyle modification + metformin (AMPK activation,
  reduced hepatic glucose production) + GLP-1 receptor agonists
  (semaglutide) + SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin: blocks renal glucose
  reabsorption)
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical Connection:} Semaglutide (Ozempic/Wegovy) has
transformed T2DM and obesity management. Clinical trials show 15--20\%
body weight reduction with semaglutide, plus cardiovascular and renal
benefits, by mimicking natural GLP-1 signalling at hypothalamic appetite
centres and pancreatic \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-cells.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 2:} A type-1 diabetic receives a long-acting
insulin analogue (glargine) once daily. Blood glucose is well controlled
during the day but the patient develops reactive hyperglycaemia every
morning (``dawn phenomenon''). Given that cortisol, GH, and glucagon
most rise in the pre-waking hours, explain \emph{which}
counter-regulatory hormones are responsible for the morning rise and
\emph{why} glargine's 24-hour profile is insufficient to cover it. What
feature of a more modern analogue (e.g.~degludec, with
about 42-h half-life) addresses this?
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Adrenal Gland --- Zonal
Architecture}\label{adrenal-gland-zonal-architecture}

\textbf{Adrenal cortex} (mesodermal origin, steroid hormones):

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Zona glomerulosa:} Aldosterone (mineralocorticoid). Regulated
  by RAAS and K\(^+\). Promotes Na\(^+\) reabsorption, K\(^+\) secretion
  in collecting duct.
\item
  \textbf{Zona fasciculata:} Cortisol (glucocorticoid). Regulated by
  ACTH.
\item
  \textbf{Zona reticularis:} DHEA, androstenedione (adrenal androgens).
  Puberty (adrenarche).
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Adrenal medulla} (neural crest origin, modified sympathetic
ganglion):

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Chromaffin cells release epinephrine (80\%) and norepinephrine (20\%)
  directly into blood
\item
  Epinephrine effects: heart rate increase (\(\beta_1\)),
  bronchodilation (\(\beta_2\)), glycogenolysis (\(\beta_2\) in liver),
  lipolysis (\(\beta_3\) in adipose), vasoconstriction (\(\alpha_1\)) in
  skin/viscera, vasodilation (\(\beta_2\)) in skeletal muscle
\item
  Duration: seconds to minutes (rapid metabolic clearance by MAO and
  COMT)
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Growth Hormone Axis and
IGF-1}\label{growth-hormone-axis-and-igf-1}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0167_3c9c6ef56171.png}
\caption{Growth hormone axis GHRH stimulates and somatostatin inhibits pituitary GH release. GH acts directly on tissues (lipolysis, insulin antagonism - "diabetogenic") and indirectly via hepatic IGF-1, which mediates linear growth and protein synthesis. IGF-1 provides negative feedback at hypothalamus (somatostatin) and pituitary (GH transcription).}
\end{figure}

GH from anterior pituitary somatotrophs: pulsatile release (peaks during
deep sleep and exercise). GH binds the GH receptor (a JAK2-coupled
cytokine receptor) on hepatocytes, activating STAT5, which drives
\textbf{IGF-1 (insulin-like growth factor 1)} transcription and
secretion. Circulating IGF-1 is bound to IGFBP-3 (extends half-life from
minutes to hours).

\textbf{GH/IGF-1 effects:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Linear bone growth (epiphyseal plate chondrogenesis driven by IGF-1)
\item
  Protein synthesis (positive nitrogen balance)
\item
  Lipolysis (direct GH effect; ``diabetogenic'')
\item
  Reduced peripheral glucose uptake (GH antagonises insulin)
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pathology:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Acromegaly:} Excess GH in adults (pituitary adenoma).
  Characteristic features: enlarged hands, feet, jaw; organomegaly;
  impaired glucose tolerance. Diagnosed by failure to suppress GH during
  oral glucose tolerance test.
\item
  \textbf{Gigantism:} Excess GH before epiphyseal plate closure
  (childhood). Tall stature.
\item
  \textbf{GH deficiency in children:} Short stature; treated with
  recombinant human GH (somatropin).
\item
  \textbf{Laron syndrome:} GH receptor mutation; high GH but no IGF-1
  response. Short stature; remarkably, low IGF-1 confers resistance to
  cancer and diabetes.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Prostaglandins and
Eicosanoids}\label{prostaglandins-and-eicosanoids}

\textbf{Eicosanoids} are 20-carbon paracrine signalling lipids derived
from membrane phospholipids. Unlike conventional hormones, they are not
stored, are synthesised on demand, act locally (paracrine/autocrine),
and are rapidly inactivated.

\subsubsection{Synthesis from arachidonic
acid}\label{synthesis-from-arachidonic-acid}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0168_2ed715e1da8a.png}
\caption{Eicosanoid biosynthesis pathways Phospholipase A\$\_2\$ liberates arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids. Three branches generate distinct families: cyclooxygenase (COX) to prostaglandins and thromboxanes; 5-lipoxygenase to leukotrienes; cytochrome P450 to epoxyeicosatrienoic acids. Glucocorticoids inhibit at the PLA\$\_2\$ step; NSAIDs inhibit at COX.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{COX-1 vs COX-2 --- distinct
physiology}\label{cox-1-vs-cox-2-distinct-physiology}

\textbf{Selective COX-2 inhibitors (coxibs)} were developed to spare
COX-1 (preserving gastric prostaglandins and reducing GI bleeding).
Initial successes (Vioxx/rofecoxib, Bextra/valdecoxib) were tempered by
cardiovascular concerns: selective COX-2 inhibition reduces endothelial
PGI\(_2\) (antiplatelet, vasodilator) without reducing platelet
TXA\(_2\) (made by COX-1) --- shifting the haemostatic balance toward
thrombosis. Rofecoxib was withdrawn in 2004; celecoxib remains in use
with cardiovascular labelling.

\textbf{Clinical Connection --- The aspirin paradox:} Low-dose aspirin
(75--100 mg/day) selectively inhibits platelet COX-1 (anucleate
platelets cannot regenerate the enzyme; 7-day duration) but primarily
transiently inhibits endothelial COX-2 (nucleated cells continuously
resynthesise). Result: net antiplatelet effect with preserved
endothelial PGI\(_2\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} reduced thrombotic risk. High-dose aspirin loses
this selectivity.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Endocrine Disruption}\label{endocrine-disruption}

\textbf{Endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs)} are exogenous substances
that interfere with hormone synthesis, secretion, transport, binding, or
elimination. They are particularly concerning for fetal and neonatal
development, when small hormone perturbations can have lifelong
consequences.

\subsubsection{Mechanisms of disruption}\label{mechanisms-of-disruption}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Receptor agonism (mimicry):} Exogenous compound binds and
  activates a hormone receptor, mimicking the endogenous ligand (e.g.,
  xenoestrogens activate ER).
\item
  \textbf{Receptor antagonism:} Block native hormone binding (e.g., DDE
  blocks AR; flutamide-like effect).
\item
  \textbf{Altered hormone synthesis:} Inhibit steroidogenic enzymes
  (e.g., conazole fungicides inhibit aromatase; perchlorate blocks NIS
  at the thyroid).
\item
  \textbf{Altered transport/clearance:} Disrupt carrier protein binding
  or hepatic metabolism (e.g., PCBs displace T4 from transthyretin).
\item
  \textbf{Altered receptor expression:} Epigenetic modification of
  hormone receptor genes.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Bisphenol A (BPA) and other
xenoestrogens}\label{bisphenol-a-bpa-and-other-xenoestrogens}

\textbf{Bisphenol A} is a high-volume industrial monomer used in
polycarbonate plastics, epoxy resins, and thermal receipts. Estimated
production exceeds 6 million tonnes/year. BPA leaches from food
containers, especially when heated or contacting acidic foods.
Detectable BPA is found in \textgreater90\% of US adults' urine.

\textbf{Mechanism:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Weak agonist at classical nuclear oestrogen receptors (ER\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}, ER\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta};
  affinity about 10,000\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} lower than oestradiol)
\item
  High-affinity agonist at the membrane-bound G-protein--coupled
  oestrogen receptor (GPER, formerly GPR30)
\item
  Binds androgen receptor as antagonist
\item
  Binds thyroid hormone receptor as antagonist
\item
  Activates pregnane X receptor (xenobiotic metabolism)
\end{itemize}

The combination of multiple low-affinity but high-prevalence
interactions makes BPA a ``low-dose'' disruptor --- its non-monotonic
dose--response curve (effects at very low doses absent at higher doses)
violates the classical toxicological assumption that ``the dose makes
the poison.''

\textbf{Effects} (animal and observational human studies): altered
pubertal timing, reduced sperm count and quality, increased risk of
breast and prostate cancers, metabolic dysfunction (obesity, diabetes),
neurodevelopmental and behavioural effects in children. Regulatory
responses have lowered BPA exposure limits and led to bans in baby
bottles in the EU, Canada, and US --- though substitutes (BPS, BPF)
appear to share similar disrupting profiles (``regrettable
substitution'').

\subsubsection{Phthalates, PFAS, and other major
EDCs}\label{phthalates-pfas-and-other-major-edcs}

\textbf{Phthalates} (DEHP, DBP, BBzP) are plasticisers added to PVC to
confer flexibility; also used in personal-care products as
solvents/fragrance carriers. Dietary intake is the main route.
Mechanism: act as \textbf{anti-androgens} via reduced testosterone
synthesis (suppression of StAR and CYP17A1) and AR antagonism in the
developing male reproductive tract. Animal exposures during the male
sex-differentiation window produce the \textbf{``phthalate syndrome''}:
cryptorchidism, hypospadias, reduced anogenital distance, decreased
sperm count. Human cohort studies link prenatal phthalate exposure to
similar genitourinary endpoints.

\textbf{PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances)} --- the so-called
``\textbf{forever chemicals}'' (e.g., PFOA, PFOS, GenX) --- are
characterised by C--F bonds that resist environmental and biological
breakdown. Half-lives in humans range from years to decades. Sources:
non-stick cookware (Teflon), water-repellent textiles, firefighting
foams (AFFF), food packaging. Mechanisms include PPAR\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha} activation
(fatty-acid metabolism disruption), thyroid hormone displacement from
carrier proteins, and dose-dependent immunosuppression (reduced antibody
response to childhood vaccines documented in Faroe Islands cohort
studies). The C8 Health Project (West Virginia) linked high-dose
occupational PFOA exposure to elevated risks of testicular cancer,
kidney cancer, ulcerative colitis, thyroid disease,
hypercholesterolaemia, and pregnancy-induced hypertension.

\subsubsection{Vulnerability of
development}\label{vulnerability-of-development}

Fetal and early-life development is uniquely vulnerable to EDCs:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Hormone-dependent organogenesis:} Sex differentiation
  (Wolffian/Müllerian fates), brain dimorphism, and thyroid-driven CNS
  myelination depend on tightly timed hormone windows. A small
  perturbation during these windows can permanently rewire the
  architecture in ways that would not occur in adults.
\item
  \textbf{Limited metabolic clearance:} Fetal liver enzymes (CYPs, UGTs)
  are immature; placenta does not always exclude lipophilic toxicants.
\item
  \textbf{Exponential cell division:} Programming events, including DNA
  methylation and histone modifications, are particularly susceptible to
  epigenetic disruption during rapid cell division.
\item
  \textbf{Critical periods are non-recoverable:} Once a developmental
  window closes, the missing signal cannot be replaced by later
  supplementation.
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check 3:} Why might the developmental period (fetal life
through puberty) be uniquely vulnerable to endocrine disruptors compared
to adult exposures? Consider hormone-dependent organ development and the
absence of redundant pathways during organogenesis.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\newpage

\subsection{Immune System}\label{immune-system}

The immune system protects against pathogens and tumour cells while
preserving tolerance to self. It comprises two integrated arms:
\textbf{innate immunity} (rapid, non-specific, germline-encoded) and
\textbf{adaptive immunity} (slow, antigen-specific, somatically
generated).

\subsubsection{Innate Immunity}\label{innate-immunity-1}

\hyperref[gl:innate-immunity]{\textbf{Innate immunity}} provides
immediate (seconds to hours), non-specific protection:

\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Pattern Recognition Receptors
(PRRs)}\label{pattern-recognition-receptors-prrs-1}

Innate immune cells detect pathogens through germline-encoded
\textbf{PRRs} that recognise conserved molecular signatures unique to
pathogens --- \textbf{pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs)}
--- or signals of cellular damage --- \textbf{damage-associated
molecular patterns (DAMPs)}. PRRs fall into four major families based on
cellular location and ligand class.

\paragraph{Toll-like receptors (TLRs)}\label{toll-like-receptors-tlrs}

Membrane-bound (plasma membrane or endosomal). Humans express 10 TLRs.

Species specificity matters here. Human TLR1--TLR10 are not a
comprehensive mammalian template: mice lack a direct functional
equivalent of human TLR10 but retain TLR11--TLR13, which detect
microbial ligands such as profilin-like proteins and bacterial RNA.
TLR10 itself remains less mechanistically settled than TLR4, TLR7/8, or
TLR9. When comparing innate-immunity experiments across humans, mice,
and cell lines, students should ask whether the receptor repertoire and
ligand preparation actually match the claimed pathogen-sensing pathway.

\paragraph{TLR4 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} MyD88 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} NF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}B pathway (bacterial LPS
response)}\label{tlr4-myd88-nf-ux3bab-pathway-bacterial-lps-response}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0170_f94978e2386b.png}
\caption{TLR4/MyD88/NF-kappaB pathway. LBP and CD14 deliver bacterial LPS to TLR4/MD-2, TLR4 dimerization recruits TIRAP and MyD88, IRAK kinases and TRAF6 activate TAK1 and IKK, and IkappaBalpha degradation releases NF-kappaB to induce inflammatory genes.}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{TLR3/TRIF \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} IRF3 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} IFN-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} pathway (antiviral
response)}\label{tlr3trif-irf3-ifn-ux3b2-pathway-antiviral-response}

A parallel branch is engaged by TLR3 (endosomal dsRNA) and the
late-endosome pool of TLR4. The adaptor \textbf{TRIF} recruits TBK1,
which phosphorylates \textbf{IRF3}. Phospho-IRF3 dimerises, enters the
nucleus, and drives transcription of \textbf{type I interferons
(IFN-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}/\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta})}. IFN-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} released into the extracellular space binds IFNAR on
neighbouring cells, activating JAK1/TYK2 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} STAT1/STAT2 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} ISGF3 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
induction of hundreds of \textbf{interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs)}
that establish an antiviral state. The MyD88/NF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}B vs TRIF/IRF3
dichotomy explains why bacterial LPS produces fever and inflammation
while viral dsRNA produces an interferon-driven antiviral state.

\paragraph{NOD-like receptors (NLRs) and the NLRP3
inflammasome}\label{nod-like-receptors-nlrs-and-the-nlrp3-inflammasome}

Cytosolic. Detect intracellular bacterial components (peptidoglycan
derivatives) and danger signals.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{NOD1} detects iE-DAP (Gram\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}); \textbf{NOD2} detects MDP
  (comprehensive). Both activate NF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}B. NOD2 mutations cause Crohn's
  disease (impaired mucosal immunity \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} dysbiosis \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} inflammation).
\end{itemize}

The \textbf{NLRP3 inflammasome} illustrates the \textbf{two-signal}
model:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Signal 1 (priming):} TLR or cytokine engagement \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} NF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}B \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  upregulates NLRP3 and pro-IL-1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} transcription. Without this, no
  inflammasome assembly.
\item
  \textbf{Signal 2 (activation):} Diverse triggers --- extracellular ATP
  (P2X7), K\(^+\) efflux, lysosomal rupture (urate crystals, cholesterol
  crystals, silica, alum), mitochondrial ROS, mitochondrial DNA in
  cytosol --- activate NLRP3.
\item
  \textbf{Assembly:} NLRP3 oligomerises via its NACHT domain; recruits
  ASC adaptor via PYD--PYD interactions; ASC nucleates pro-caspase-1 via
  CARD--CARD; pro-caspase-1 self-cleaves to active caspase-1.
\item
  \textbf{Output:} Caspase-1 cleaves pro-IL-1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} IL-1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} (released via
  gasdermin D pores) and pro-IL-18 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} IL-18; cleaves gasdermin D, whose
  N-terminal fragment forms 10--20 nm pores in the plasma membrane
  causing \textbf{pyroptosis} (lytic cell death with massive cytokine
  release).
\end{itemize}

NLRP3 mutations cause cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS);
chronic NLRP3 activity drives gout (urate crystals), atherosclerosis
(cholesterol crystals), Alzheimer's-related neuroinflammation, and type
2 diabetes. \textbf{Anakinra} (recombinant IL-1Ra) and
\textbf{canakinumab} (anti-IL-1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}) target the inflammasome output.

\paragraph{RIG-I-like receptors (RLRs)}\label{rig-i-like-receptors-rlrs}

Cytosolic RNA sensors detecting viral replication.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{RIG-I:} detects 5'-triphosphate RNA (host RNA is capped; viral
  RNA is not).
\item
  \textbf{MDA5:} detects long dsRNA.
\item
  Signal via \textbf{MAVS} (mitochondrial antiviral signalling protein)
  \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} IRF3/IRF7 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} type I interferons.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{cGAS--STING pathway (cytosolic DNA
sensing)}\label{cgassting-pathway-cytosolic-dna-sensing}

The \textbf{cGAS--STING} axis is the principal sensor for cytosolic DNA
--- a hallmark of intracellular bacterial or viral infection (and,
problematically, mislocalised mitochondrial or self DNA).

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{cGAS (cyclic GMP--AMP synthase)} binds dsDNA
  non-sequence-specifically through a phase-separation-like
  condensation. Activated cGAS catalyses synthesis of the cyclic
  dinucleotide \textbf{2'3'-cGAMP} from ATP and GTP.
\item
  \textbf{STING (stimulator of interferon genes)}, an ER-resident
  transmembrane protein, binds 2'3'-cGAMP, undergoes a major
  conformational change, traffics from ER to ERGIC/Golgi, and recruits
  \textbf{TBK1}, which phosphorylates \textbf{IRF3} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} type I interferon
  transcription. STING also activates NF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}B via a parallel branch.
\end{itemize}

The cGAS--STING pathway is essential for control of HSV-1, vaccinia, and
many cytosolic bacteria. \textbf{Dysregulation drives autoimmunity:}
mutations causing constitutive STING activation produce \textbf{SAVI
(STING-associated vasculopathy with onset in infancy)}, an
interferonopathy. Aicardi-Goutières syndrome arises when defective
DNases (TREX1, RNASEH2) cannot clear cytoplasmic nucleic acids,
chronically engaging cGAS-STING. Pharmacologically, STING agonists
(ADU-S100) are being trialled as cancer adjuvants because tumour-induced
type I IFN can boost antitumour immunity.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0171_1e90bd6d08e2.png}
\caption{PRR signalling pathways TLRs, NLRs, RLRs, and cGAS converge on transcription factors NF-kappaB (inflammation), IRF3/7 (interferons), and the inflammasome (IL-1beta, pyroptosis). Different pathogen classes preferentially engage different sensors.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Complement System --- Comprehensive
Overview}\label{complement-system-comprehensive-overview}

The complement system comprises about 30 plasma proteins that
amplify innate responses through enzymatic cascades. There are three
pathways of activation, most converging on a common terminal pathway.

\paragraph{Three activation pathways}\label{three-activation-pathways}

\paragraph{C3 convertase, C5 convertase,
MAC}\label{c3-convertase-c5-convertase-mac}

Most three pathways generate a \textbf{C3 convertase} (C4b2a or C3bBb)
that cleaves \textbf{C3 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} C3a + C3b}. C3b is deposited on the pathogen
surface; binding of an additional C3b to the existing C3 convertase
yields the \textbf{C5 convertase} (C4b2aC3b or C3bBbC3b) that cleaves
\textbf{C5 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} C5a + C5b}.

C5b initiates the \textbf{terminal pathway}: C5b \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} C5b-C6 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} C5b-C6-C7
(membrane-inserting) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} C5b-C6-C7-C8 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} addition of multiple C9 monomers
polymerising into the \textbf{membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b-9)}. The
MAC forms a 10 nm transmembrane pore that lyses the target cell.
Gram-negative bacteria are particularly vulnerable; encapsulated
bacteria (\emph{Neisseria}) require complement for clearance, which is
why C5--C9 deficiencies present with recurrent meningococcal infection.

\paragraph{Effector functions}\label{effector-functions}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Opsonisation:} C3b coats pathogen \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} recognised by phagocyte
  receptors \textbf{CR1} (C3b/C4b), \textbf{CR3} (iC3b), \textbf{CR4}.
  Opsonised particles are 1000-fold more efficiently phagocytosed.
\item
  \textbf{Membrane attack complex (MAC):} C5b-9 polymerises in target
  membrane, forming a 10 nm pore.
\item
  \textbf{Anaphylatoxins (chemotaxis and inflammation):} C3a and
  \textbf{C5a} (the most potent) recruit neutrophils, activate mast
  cells, increase vascular permeability, and amplify local inflammation.
\item
  \textbf{Immune complex clearance:} CR1 on erythrocytes binds
  C3b-coated immune complexes and ferries them to liver/spleen for
  disposal.
\item
  \textbf{B cell co-stimulation:} C3d coupled to antigen lowers the BCR
  signalling threshold about 10,000 fold via CR2 (CD21).
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Amplification dynamics and
regulation}\label{amplification-dynamics-and-regulation}

The cascade is intrinsically amplifying because each enzyme cleaves many
substrates. If one C3 convertase cleaves N copies of C3 per second, with
decay rate \(k_d\), the steady-state C3b concentration scales as

\begin{equation}
[\text{C3b}] = \frac{[\text{C3conv}] \cdot N}{k_d}
\label{eq:unit_IX_amplification}
\end{equation}

The \textbf{alternative pathway amplification loop} is positive: each
new C3b binds factor B \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} C3 convertase \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} cleaves more C3 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} more C3b.
Without regulators, this loop would consume most plasma C3 within
minutes.

Regulators confine the cascade to pathogen surfaces:

Patients with \textbf{paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)} lack
the GPI anchor that tethers DAF and CD59 to RBCs \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} uncontrolled
complement activation \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} haemolysis. Treated with \textbf{eculizumab}
(anti-C5 monoclonal antibody; blocks C5 cleavage and MAC formation).
\textbf{C1-INH deficiency} causes \textbf{hereditary angioedema}
(uncontrolled C1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} bradykinin generation via the kinin--kallikrein
system \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} sudden tissue swelling).

\subsubsection{Adaptive Immunity
Overview}\label{adaptive-immunity-overview-1}

\hyperref[gl:adaptive-immunity]{\textbf{Adaptive immunity}} is slower
(7--10 days for primary response) but provides \textbf{specificity}
(each lymphocyte recognises a unique antigen) and \textbf{memory}
(faster, stronger response on re-exposure --- basis of vaccination).

\textbf{Two arms:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Cell-mediated:} T cells (CD8+ cytotoxic kill infected cells;
  CD4+ helper coordinate response)
\item
  \textbf{Humoral:} B cells produce antibodies that neutralise
  pathogens, opsonise, activate complement
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Antigen presentation via MHC:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{MHC class I} (on most nucleated cells): presents endogenous
  peptides (8--10 aa) from cytosolic proteins. Pathway: cytosolic
  protein \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} proteasome \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} TAP transporter \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} ER \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} loaded onto MHC I \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  surface. Presented to \textbf{CD8+ T cells}.
\item
  \textbf{MHC class II} (on professional APCs: dendritic cells,
  macrophages, B cells): presents exogenous peptides (12--25 aa) from
  internalised pathogens. Pathway: phagocytosis \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} endolysosome \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  cathepsin cleavage \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} loaded onto MHC II (after CLIP removal by HLA-DM)
  \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} surface. Presented to \textbf{CD4+ T cells}.
\item
  \textbf{Cross-presentation:} Dendritic cells can also load exogenous
  antigens onto MHC I, important for activating CD8+ responses against
  viruses that don't directly infect APCs.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{T Cell Development and
Selection}\label{t-cell-development-and-selection}

T cell precursors leave the bone marrow as immature CD4\(^-\)CD8\(^-\)
``double-negative'' thymocytes and migrate to the thymus, where they
undergo somatic recombination and selection.

\paragraph{Double-negative (DN1--DN4)
staging}\label{double-negative-dn1dn4-staging}

Within the thymic cortex, double-negative thymocytes pass through four
sequential stages defined by surface CD44 and CD25 expression:

\textbf{DN1} & + & \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-} & Early thymic progenitor; multipotent

\textbf{DN3} & \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-} & + & TCR \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} rearrangement complete; \textbf{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-selection
checkpoint} (primarily cells with productive TCR \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} survive, via

Cells then become \textbf{double-positive (CD4+CD8+)} and rearrange TCR
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}. With both TCR chains expressed, they undergo \textbf{positive} then
\textbf{negative} selection.

\paragraph{TCR diversity generation}\label{tcr-diversity-generation}

Like immunoglobulin loci, the T cell receptor (TCR) loci undergo
\textbf{V(D)J recombination} mediated by RAG1/RAG2 endonucleases:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  TCR \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} chain: V--D--J recombination (about 52 V \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 2 D \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 13 J
  segments \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} about 1,400 combinations)
\item
  TCR \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha} chain: V--J recombination (about 70 V \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x}
  about 61 J segments \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} about 4,300 combinations)
\item
  \textbf{Junctional diversity:} TdT (terminal deoxynucleotidyl
  transferase) adds non-templated N-nucleotides at junctions
\item
  \textbf{Combinatorial diversity:} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} pairing creates about 6
  \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 10\(^6\) unique receptors before junctional diversity
\item
  \textbf{With junctional diversity:} the theoretical TCR repertoire
  exceeds 10\(^{18}\), far larger than the about 10\(^{11}\) T
  cells in the human body --- most TCRs are rarely realised.
\end{itemize}

Rough calculation: \(1{,}400 \times 4{,}300 \approx 6 \times 10^6\)
V(D)J combinations \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} about 10\(^{12}\) junctional possibilities
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 10\(^{18}\) theoretical receptors.

Defects in this recombination machinery cause severe combined
immunodeficiencies (RAG1/RAG2 SCID --- ``bubble boy'' disease);
ataxia-telangiectasia (ATM mutation) causes radiosensitivity and
lymphoid malignancy.

\paragraph{Positive selection (cortex)}\label{positive-selection-cortex}

In the thymic cortex, double-positive (CD4+CD8+) thymocytes encounter
\textbf{cortical thymic epithelial cells (cTECs)} displaying
self-peptide--MHC complexes. T cells whose TCR engages MHC with
sufficient (but not excessive) affinity receive a survival signal. T
cells with no MHC affinity die by neglect (about 95\% of
thymocytes).

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  TCR engagement of MHC I \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} CD8+ single-positive T cell
\item
  TCR engagement of MHC II \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} CD4+ single-positive T cell
\end{itemize}

Positive selection ensures the surviving repertoire is
\textbf{MHC-restricted} --- primarily recognises antigen presented in
the context of self MHC.

\paragraph{Negative selection (medulla) --- AIRE and Treg
generation}\label{negative-selection-medulla-aire-and-treg-generation}

Surviving thymocytes migrate to the medulla and encounter
\textbf{medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs)} and dendritic cells.
mTECs express the autoimmune regulator \textbf{AIRE} transcription
factor, which drives ectopic expression of thousands of tissue-specific
antigens (insulin, thyroglobulin, myelin proteins) normally restricted
to peripheral tissues. T cells whose TCR binds self-peptide--MHC
complexes with \textbf{high affinity} undergo apoptosis (clonal
deletion). A small fraction with intermediate self-reactivity become
\textbf{regulatory T cells (Tregs)} --- CD4+CD25+FoxP3+ cells that
police self-tolerance in the periphery.

\textbf{AIRE mutations} cause autoimmune polyendocrinopathy syndrome
type 1 (APS-1, APECED) --- patients fail to delete autoreactive T cells
against multiple endocrine organs, developing chronic mucocutaneous
candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and adrenal insufficiency.
\textbf{FoxP3 mutations} cause IPEX syndrome --- fatal multi-organ
autoimmunity in infancy from absent Tregs.

\subsubsection{B Cell Activation and Antibody
Diversification}\label{b-cell-activation-and-antibody-diversification}

\paragraph{Stepwise B cell activation}\label{stepwise-b-cell-activation}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Antigen encounter.} Naïve B cell in lymphoid follicle
  encounters cognate antigen (in soluble form, or displayed on
  subcapsular sinus macrophages and follicular dendritic cells).
\item
  \textbf{BCR cross-linking.} Multivalent antigen cross-links several
  BCRs \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} tyrosine phosphorylation of Ig\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}/Ig\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} ITAMs by Lyn/Fyn \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  recruitment of Syk \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} activation of PI3K, PLC\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma}2, Ras/MAPK cascades.
\item
  \textbf{Antigen internalisation.} B cell internalises antigen via BCR,
  processes peptides in MHC class II compartment.
\item
  \textbf{Migration to T-B border.} Activated B cell upregulates CCR7,
  migrates to T-cell zone of lymph node.
\item
  \textbf{T cell help.} Cognate Tfh (follicular helper T cell)
  recognises B cell-presented peptide on MHC II. Engagement of
  \textbf{CD40L (Tfh) -- CD40 (B cell)} plus cytokines (IL-4, IL-21)
  provides ``second signal.''
\item
  \textbf{Outcome:} B cells either differentiate into
  \textbf{short-lived extrafollicular plasmablasts} (rapid IgM, low
  affinity) or enter the germinal centre.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{B cell activation modes}\label{b-cell-activation-modes}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{T-independent (TI) responses:} Polysaccharide and repetitive
  antigens cross-link many BCRs simultaneously. Produces predominantly
  IgM, no germinal centre, no affinity maturation, weak memory.
  Important for encapsulated bacteria (\emph{Streptococcus pneumoniae},
  \emph{Haemophilus influenzae}); explains why polysaccharide vaccines
  work poorly in children \textless2 years.
\item
  \textbf{T-dependent (TD) responses:} Protein antigens. B cell
  internalises antigen via BCR, processes it, presents peptide on MHC
  II, is recognised by cognate CD4+ T helper cell (specifically Tfh ---
  follicular helper T cell). T:B interaction at the T-B border activates
  the B cell to enter the \textbf{germinal centre reaction}. Produces
  high-affinity, class-switched antibodies and long-lived memory.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Germinal centre reaction --- somatic hypermutation and
affinity
maturation}\label{germinal-centre-reaction-somatic-hypermutation-and-affinity-maturation}

In secondary lymphoid organs (lymph nodes, spleen, Peyer's patches),
activated B cells form \textbf{germinal centres} with two zones:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Dark zone (centroblasts):} Rapid proliferation.
  \textbf{Activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID)} introduces
  somatic point mutations into the variable regions of immunoglobulin
  genes --- \textbf{somatic hypermutation (SHM)},
  about 10\(^{-3}\) mutations per base per generation
  (about 10\(^6\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} normal mutation rate).
\item
  \textbf{Light zone (centrocytes):} B cells re-encounter antigen
  displayed on follicular dendritic cells (FDCs). Cells whose mutated
  BCR has improved antigen affinity capture more antigen, internalise
  it, present more peptide on MHC II, and receive stronger Tfh help \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  survival and re-cycling. Cells with reduced affinity die by apoptosis.
  This is \textbf{affinity maturation} --- Darwinian selection at the
  cellular level, driving 1000-fold increases in antibody affinity over
  weeks.
\end{itemize}

Light-zone cells differentiate into:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Plasma cells} (long-lived in bone marrow, secrete antibodies
  for years/decades)
\item
  \textbf{Memory B cells} (rapidly mobilised on antigen re-encounter)
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Class switch recombination
(CSR)}\label{class-switch-recombination-csr}

Initially B cells produce IgM (default isotype). Cytokines from Tfh
cells direct \textbf{class switching} to IgG, IgA, or IgE by recombining
the heavy chain constant region (the variable region --- and thus
antigen specificity --- is preserved). At the molecular level,
\textbf{AID} deaminates cytidines in switch (S) regions upstream of each
constant-region gene; subsequent base-excision repair generates
double-strand breaks that are joined by NHEJ to produce switch
recombination, deleting intervening DNA.

\subsubsection{Cytokine Network --- Comprehensive
Reference}\label{cytokine-network-comprehensive-reference}

Cytokines are small (about 15--25 kDa) signalling proteins that
coordinate immune cell function. They act locally (paracrine/autocrine)
at very low concentrations (pM--nM) via JAK/STAT or other receptor
families.

\textbf{Th polarisation:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Th1} (driven by IL-12; produces IFN-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma}): intracellular
  pathogens, viruses, autoimmunity (MS, T1DM)
\item
  \textbf{Th2} (driven by IL-4; produces IL-4/5/13): helminths, allergy,
  asthma
\item
  \textbf{Th17} (driven by IL-6 + TGF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}; produces IL-17): extracellular
  bacteria, fungi; psoriasis, IBD
\item
  \textbf{Treg} (driven by TGF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}; FoxP3+): peripheral tolerance,
  suppression
\item
  \textbf{Tfh} (in germinal centres; produces IL-21): B cell help
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Immunological Memory --- Why Memory Cells Respond
Faster}\label{immunological-memory-why-memory-cells-respond-faster}

After antigen clearance, about 95\% of effector T and B cells
die by apoptosis (contraction phase). The remaining 5\% become
long-lived memory cells. Memory cells respond to re-exposure 100--1000\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x}
faster and stronger than naïve cells:

The signalling determinants of effector vs memory differentiation
include:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Strong, prolonged TCR signalling + IL-2} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} effector
  (terminally differentiated, short-lived, KLRG1\(^{hi}\))
\item
  \textbf{Brief TCR signalling + IL-7, IL-15} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} memory precursors
  (CD127\(^{hi}\), CD62L\(^+\))
\item
  \textbf{Memory subsets:}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \textbf{Central memory (T\(_{CM}\)):} CCR7\(^+\), CD62L\(^+\);
    recirculate through lymph nodes; high proliferative potential
  \item
    \textbf{Effector memory (T\(_{EM}\)):} CCR7\(^-\); patrol peripheral
    tissues; immediate effector function
  \item
    \textbf{Tissue-resident memory (T\(_{RM}\)):} CD69\(^+\),
    CD103\(^+\); reside in barrier tissues (skin, gut, lung); first to
    detect re-infection
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

Memory persistence depends on tonic IL-7 and IL-15 cytokine signalling
and homeostatic proliferation, not antigen re-stimulation. This is why
vaccine immunity can last decades despite no reinfection --- and why
immunosuppressive therapies that cripple homeostatic cytokines (e.g.,
IL-7 axis blockade) reduce memory.

\subsubsection{Tolerance and
Autoimmunity}\label{tolerance-and-autoimmunity}

Self-tolerance is maintained at two levels:

Autoimmunity is rarely explained by a single broken checkpoint.
Susceptibility alleles, sex-biased immune regulation, molecular mimicry,
epitope spreading, tissue damage, microbiome state, and timing of
infection can most shift the threshold between protective immunity and
self-damage. A precise answer should therefore distinguish the
initiating trigger, the self-antigen or tissue compartment, the effector
mechanism, and the evidence that tolerance failed rather than merely
inflammation increased.

\paragraph{Central tolerance (thymus and bone
marrow)}\label{central-tolerance-thymus-and-bone-marrow}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  T cells: Negative selection in thymic medulla (AIRE-driven
  self-antigen expression)
\item
  B cells: Receptor editing and clonal deletion in bone marrow upon BCR
  engagement of self-antigen
\end{itemize}

Failure modes: AIRE mutations (APS-1); central tolerance is incomplete
because not most self-antigens can be expressed in primary lymphoid
organs.

\paragraph{Peripheral tolerance}\label{peripheral-tolerance}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Anergy:} TCR engagement without co-stimulation (CD28 by B7)
  inactivates rather than activates the T cell.
\item
  \textbf{Treg suppression:} FoxP3+ regulatory T cells suppress
  conventional T cell activation by IL-2 consumption, IL-10/TGF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}
  secretion, CTLA-4 outcompeting CD28, and granzyme killing.
\item
  \textbf{Inhibitory checkpoints:} \textbf{CTLA-4} and \textbf{PD-1}
  restrain T cell responses (see immunotherapy below).
\item
  \textbf{Activation-induced cell death (AICD):} Repeatedly activated T
  cells upregulate Fas \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} undergo apoptosis on Fas ligation.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Mechanisms of autoimmunity}\label{mechanisms-of-autoimmunity}

Failures of tolerance produce autoimmunity through several archetypal
mechanisms:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Molecular mimicry:} A pathogen antigen shares structural
  similarity with self-antigen. Memory cells generated to fight the
  pathogen cross-react with self.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \emph{Example:} Group A \emph{Streptococcus} M protein mimics
    cardiac myosin \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{rheumatic heart disease} after
    streptococcal pharyngitis.
  \item
    \emph{Example:} \emph{Campylobacter jejuni} lipo-oligosaccharide
    mimics peripheral nerve gangliosides \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{Guillain-Barré
    syndrome}.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Bystander activation:} Local infection/inflammation drives
  massive cytokine release, MHC upregulation, and APC maturation.
  Autoreactive T cells that escaped thymic deletion are activated by
  their cognate self-antigen now presented in a strongly stimulatory
  context.
\item
  \textbf{Epitope spreading:} Initial response to one self-antigen
  broadens over time as tissue damage releases additional self-antigens
  that are taken up by APCs and presented to new autoreactive T cell
  clones.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \emph{Example:} In \textbf{Type 1 diabetes}, autoantibodies often
    appear in stereotyped sequence (insulin \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} GAD65 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} IA-2 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} ZnT8) over
    months to years before clinical onset, reflecting progressive
    epitope spreading within the islet.
  \item
    \emph{Example:} In \textbf{multiple sclerosis}, initial myelin basic
    protein (MBP) response can spread to PLP, MOG, and other myelin
    antigens.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Loss of regulatory T cells:} FoxP3 mutations cause IPEX
  syndrome (Immunodysregulation Polyendocrinopathy Enteropathy X-linked)
  --- fatal multi-organ autoimmunity in infancy.
\item
  \textbf{Defective apoptosis:} Fas / FasL mutations (autoimmune
  lymphoproliferative syndrome, ALPS) prevent AICD \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} accumulation of
  self-reactive lymphocytes.
\end{itemize}

asthma, food allergy, hay fever & Epinephrine (anaphylaxis),
antihistamines (H1 blockers --- diphenhydramine, cetirizine), inhaled
corticosteroids, cromolyn (mast cell stabiliser), allergen immunotherapy
(gradual desensitisation), anti-IgE (omalizumab) \\
\textbf{Type II (cytotoxic)} & IgG/IgM antibody against cell-surface
antigen \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} complement, ADCC & Hours & Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia,
transfusion reaction, Goodpasture's, Graves' (stimulating) &
Plasmapheresis, IVIG, immunosuppression (rituximab anti-CD20 for
ITP/AIHA) \\
\textbf{Type III (immune complex)} & Soluble antigen-antibody complexes
deposit in tissues \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} complement, neutrophils & Hours to days & SLE,
serum sickness, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, hypersensitivity
pneumonitis & Corticosteroids, cyclophosphamide, removal of antigen
source, plasmapheresis \\
\textbf{Type IV (delayed/cell-mediated)} & T cell-mediated; no antibody
& 24--72 h & Contact dermatitis (poison ivy, nickel), tuberculin/PPD
test, Type 1 diabetes onset, MS, contact allergy to nickel &
Topical/systemic corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus),
allergen avoidance \\
\end{longtable}
}

\paragraph{Type I --- molecular detail}\label{type-i-molecular-detail}

Sensitisation: First encounter with allergen \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} APCs prime Th2 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} IL-4
drives B cells to class-switch to \textbf{IgE}. IgE binds \textbf{Fc\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}}{epsilon}RI}
on mast cells and basophils with extraordinarily high affinity (K\(_d\)
about 10\(^{-10}\) M) and remains bound for weeks.

Effector: Re-encounter with allergen cross-links mast cell-bound IgE \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
degranulation within seconds: \textbf{histamine} (vasodilation, vascular
leak, smooth muscle contraction, pruritus), \textbf{tryptase} (tissue
damage), \textbf{leukotrienes (C4, D4, E4)} (delayed
bronchoconstriction), \textbf{prostaglandins}, \textbf{TNF},
\textbf{IL-4/IL-5/IL-13} (late phase, 4--8 h: eosinophil and Th2
recruitment).

Clinical spectrum: localised (allergic rhinitis, urticaria) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} systemic
(anaphylaxis with hypotension, bronchospasm, laryngeal oedema).
Treatment of anaphylaxis: \textbf{intramuscular epinephrine} (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}\(_1\)
vasoconstriction reverses hypotension; \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}\(_2\) bronchodilates; \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}\(_2\)
stabilises mast cells), oxygen, fluids, antihistamines, corticosteroids,
possible airway management. \textbf{Allergen immunotherapy (AIT)}
gradually shifts the response from Th2/IgE toward Th1/IgG4 (``blocking
antibodies'') and induces Tregs --- the primary disease-modifying
therapy for allergy.

\subsubsection{Immunotherapy}\label{immunotherapy}

Modern oncology has been transformed by therapies that release brakes on
antitumour immunity (\textbf{checkpoint inhibitors}) or redirect T cells
(\textbf{CAR-T}). Because the product roster and safety language change,
treatment tables below should be read with current FDA product pages and
labels, not as a permanent formulary
\citep{fda2026cellulargeneproducts,fda2024cartwarning}.

\paragraph{Immune checkpoint inhibitors --- PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4
biology}\label{immune-checkpoint-inhibitors-pd-1pd-l1-and-ctla-4-biology}

\textbf{PD-1 (programmed death 1)} is an inhibitory receptor expressed
on activated T cells (and B cells, NK cells, Tregs). Its ligand
\textbf{PD-L1} is widely expressed under inflammatory conditions and
constitutively on many tumours; \textbf{PD-L2} is more restricted to
APCs. PD-1 engagement recruits the SHP-2 phosphatase to the immune
synapse, dephosphorylating proximal TCR-signalling components (CD3\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\zeta}}{zeta},
ZAP70) --- this functionally ``exhausts'' chronically activated T cells
and limits collateral damage. Tumours hijack this brake by upregulating
PD-L1 (often in response to local IFN-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma} from infiltrating T cells --- a
paradoxical ``adaptive resistance''), tonically inhibiting
tumour-infiltrating T cells. Current drug examples and approved-use
language should be checked against NCI or regulatory pages before
publication because checkpoint indications change by tumour type,
biomarker, and line of therapy \citep{nci2026checkpointinhibitors}.

\textbf{CTLA-4 (cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated 4, CD152)} is also
inhibitory but acts at the priming stage in lymph nodes. Resting T cells
receive co-stimulation when CD28 binds B7-1/B7-2 (CD80/CD86) on APCs.
Upon activation, CTLA-4 is upregulated and translocates to the immune
synapse, where it binds B7 with much higher affinity than CD28 and
trans-endocytoses B7 from the APC --- depriving CD28 of its co-stimulus.
CTLA-4 is also constitutively expressed on Tregs, contributing to their
suppressive function. CTLA-4 blockade therefore acts earlier and more
broadly than PD-1 blockade, with stronger autoimmune toxicity.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0172_2aed8e7e5564.png}
\caption{Immune checkpoint blockade Normal T cells use CTLA-4 and PD-1 as brakes to prevent over-activation. Tumours exploit PD-L1 to suppress local T cells. Anti-PD-1 antibodies (pembrolizumab) and anti-CTLA-4 antibodies (ipilimumab) block these interactions, releasing the immune brake on antitumour T cells.}
\end{figure}

The 2018 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to James
Allison (CTLA-4) and Tasuku Honjo (PD-1) for the discoveries underlying
this field. Response rates vary widely by tumour type, biomarker status,
line of therapy, and combination regimen; the table's approximate ranges
are orientation values, not patient-level predictions. A key qualitative
pattern remains \textbf{durable remissions} in some responders (the
``tail of the curve''). Side effects: \textbf{immune-related adverse
events (irAEs)} --- colitis, pneumonitis, hypophysitis, thyroiditis,
hepatitis, dermatitis --- reflecting the breaking of self-tolerance.
Management: corticosteroids; if severe, infliximab (anti-TNF) for
colitis.

\paragraph{CAR-T cell therapy --- design and clinical
outcomes}\label{car-t-cell-therapy-design-and-clinical-outcomes}

\textbf{Chimeric antigen receptor T cells:} Patient T cells are removed
by leukapheresis, genetically engineered ex vivo (lentiviral or
retroviral vector) to express a synthetic receptor combining:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Extracellular antigen-binding domain:} Single-chain variable
  fragment (scFv) derived from a tumour-specific monoclonal antibody
  (e.g., anti-CD19 scFv from FMC63 antibody).
\item
  \textbf{Hinge and transmembrane:} From CD8\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha} or IgG.
\item
  \textbf{Co-stimulatory domain:} CD28 (rapid effector function, shorter
  persistence) or 4-1BB/CD137 (slower expansion, longer persistence).
\item
  \textbf{Activation domain:} CD3\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\zeta}}{zeta} (TCR-derived ITAMs).
\end{itemize}

Modified T cells are expanded in vitro and infused back into the
patient. The CAR-T cells recognise the surface antigen (e.g., CD19 on
B-cell malignancies) \textbf{without MHC restriction}, which enables
recognition of MHC-low tumours that escape conventional T cells.

\textbf{Toxicity:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Cytokine release syndrome (CRS):} fever, hypotension, hypoxia
  within hours-to-days from massive cytokine release (esp.~IL-6, IFN-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma},
  TNF) --- graded 1--4. Treatment: \textbf{tocilizumab} (anti-IL-6R),
  corticosteroids if severe.
\item
  \textbf{Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome
  (ICANS):} confusion, aphasia, seizures, cerebral oedema; treated with
  corticosteroids.
\item
  \textbf{B cell aplasia:} Anti-CD19 CAR-T kills normal B cells too;
  long-term IVIG replacement may be needed.
\item
  \textbf{Second-malignancy surveillance:} FDA required boxed-warning
  language for T-cell malignancies after BCMA-directed or CD19-directed
  autologous CAR-T products in 2024, making long-term follow-up part of
  the source-governance burden for any current CAR-T table
  \citep{fda2024cartwarning}.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Worked Example}\label{worked-example-4}

\textbf{Problem:} A 35-year-old woman is found to have an elevated total
cortisol level of 28 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}g/dL on a morning blood draw. CBG
(cortisol-binding globulin) is also elevated at 60 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}g/mL (normal:
about 30 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}g/mL). She is six months pregnant. Estimate her
\textbf{free (bioactive) cortisol} assuming free cortisol normally
accounts for about 5\% of total at baseline CBG. Should she be
diagnosed with Cushing's syndrome?

\textbf{Solution:}

\textbf{Step 1.} Recognise that pregnancy elevates oestrogen, which
increases hepatic CBG synthesis about 2-fold. Total cortisol
rises in parallel with CBG, but \textbf{free cortisol} --- the
biologically active fraction --- remains in the normal range.

\textbf{Step 2.} Estimate baseline free cortisol fraction. With normal
CBG, 5\% of total cortisol is free. With doubled CBG, the free fraction
drops because more cortisol is sequestered:

\[\text{free fraction} \propto \frac{1}{1 + [\text{CBG}]/K_d^{\text{CBG}}} \label{eq:unit_IX_endocrine_and_immune_item_1}\]

\[\text{free fraction (pregnancy)} \approx \frac{5\%}{2} = 2.5\% \label{eq:unit_IX_endocrine_and_immune_item_2}\]

\textbf{Step 3.} Calculate free cortisol:

\[[\text{cortisol}]_{\text{free}} = 0.025 \times 28\;\mu\text{g/dL} = 0.7\;\mu\text{g/dL} \label{eq:unit_IX_endocrine_and_immune_item_3}\]

This is within the normal range (free cortisol about 0.5--1.0
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}g/dL).

\textbf{Answer:} The elevated total cortisol reflects increased CBG, not
pathological cortisol excess. \textbf{Free cortisol} is normal. The
patient should not be diagnosed with Cushing's syndrome based on total
cortisol alone. The appropriate test in pregnancy is \textbf{24-h
urinary free cortisol} (which measures the unbound fraction excreted by
the kidney) or salivary cortisol (free cortisol equilibrates with
saliva).

This illustrates a fundamental principle: \textbf{for protein-bound
hormones, total plasma concentration is misleading; primarily the free
fraction is biologically active.} The same applies to thyroid hormones
(TBG changes during pregnancy), testosterone (SHBG), and many others.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Worked Example: Clonal
Expansion}\label{worked-example-clonal-expansion}

\textbf{Problem:} During a T-dependent germinal-centre response, an
antigen-specific B-cell clone proliferates in the dark zone with a
doubling time of \(t_d = 6\) h. Starting from \(N_0 = 100\)
antigen-specific cells, calculate the fold expansion and the absolute
clone size after \(t = 72\) h (3 days). Compare the result with the
100--1000-fold higher precursor frequency that defines an established
memory pool.

\textbf{Solution:}

\textbf{Step 1.} State the exponential-growth relation for a clone
dividing with a fixed doubling time. Each doubling multiplies cell
number by 2, and the number of doublings in time \(t\) is \(t/t_d\):

\[N = N_0 \cdot 2^{\,t/t_d} \label{eq:unit_IX_endocrine_and_immune_clonal_1}\]

\textbf{Step 2.} Substitute the measured values. With \(t = 72\) h and
\(t_d = 6\) h, the number of doublings is \(t/t_d = 72/6 = 12\). The
fold expansion is therefore \(2^{12}\):

\[\frac{N}{N_0} = 2^{72/6} = 2^{12} = 4096 \label{eq:unit_IX_endocrine_and_immune_clonal_2}\]

\textbf{Step 3.} Compute the absolute clone size:
\(N = 100 \times 4096 = 4.10 \times 10^{5}\) cells --- a roughly
4000-fold expansion in three days.

\textbf{Answer:} A 6-hour doubling time yields 12 doublings in 72 h,
expanding the clone about 4096-fold (from 100 to
about 4.1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 10\(^5\) cells). This magnitude matches the
chapter's account of dark-zone proliferation and explains how a naive
precursor frequency of about 1 in 10\(^6\) can be driven up to
the 100--1000-fold higher frequency that characterises an established
memory pool. The same \(N = N_0 \cdot 2^{\,t/t_d}\) relation predicts
that even a one-hour increase in doubling time markedly slows the
response --- which is why memory cells, with their lower activation
threshold and shorter effective doubling time, clear a re-challenge far
faster than naive cells.

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(h.corrective\_response, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{), h.is\_within\_tolerance)}

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-33}

For \textbf{Endocrine and Immune Systems}, frontier biology belongs
inside the evidence logic of the chapter. Physiology now blends
mechanism with allostasis, immune-endocrine-neural coupling, wearable
data, and individualized risk without reducing bodies to simple
machines. The core reading question is this: endocrine-immune claims
should include feedback, timing, receptor sensitivity, inflammation, and
allostatic load.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

Interpret physiological data by separating baseline variation,
perturbation response, compensation, and the threshold where
compensation becomes pathology.

\textbf{Source practice:} For physiology claims, cite the measurement
context and distinguish baseline variation, compensation,
pathophysiology, and treatment evidence.

\subsubsection{Current Evidence Map: Allostasis and Immune-Endocrine
Coupling}\label{current-evidence-map-allostasis-and-immune-endocrine-coupling}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0173_32b78aac9da5.png}
\caption{Physiology is often adaptive over short time scales and costly over long time scales, so baseline, perturbation, compensation, and pathology must be distinguished.}

\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-33}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Endocrine system:} Hierarchical hypothalamic-pituitary-target
  gland axes with negative feedback. Three hormone classes: peptide
  (surface receptors, second messengers), steroid (nuclear receptors,
  transcription), amino acid derivatives (variable). Carrier proteins
  (CBG, SHBG, TBG) buffer plasma levels of lipid-soluble hormones.
\item
  \textbf{HPA axis:} Stress \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} CRH \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} ACTH \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} cortisol. Cortisol
  synthesised from cholesterol via StAR-mediated transport and CYP
  enzymes. GR acts via transactivation (gluconeogenic genes) and
  transrepression (NF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}B). Circadian (peak 08:00) and pulsatile.
  Cushing's (excess) vs Addison's (deficiency).
\item
  \textbf{HPT axis:} TRH \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} TSH \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} T4/T3. T4 synthesised on iodinated
  thyroglobulin scaffold by TPO. T4 is prohormone; D1/D2 deiodinases
  convert to active T3. T3 binds nuclear TR/RXR heterodimers at TREs
  (active repression in absence of T3). Increases BMR via
  Na\(^+\)/K\(^+\)-ATPase, mitochondrial uncoupling. Hashimoto's (hypo)
  vs Graves' (hyper). Wolff-Chaikoff effect on iodine load.
\item
  \textbf{HPG axis:} Pulsatile GnRH \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} LH/FSH \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} sex steroids. Continuous
  GnRH suppresses (basis of agonist therapy). Menstrual cycle:
  follicular (oestrogen), ovulation (positive feedback LH surge), luteal
  (progesterone).
\item
  \textbf{Glucose homeostasis:} Insulin (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-cells) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} IR (RTK) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} IRS \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  PI3K \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Akt \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} GLUT4 translocation, glycogen synthesis, FoxO
  inactivation. Glucagon (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-cells) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} cAMP/PKA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis. Crosstalk with leptin (long-term
  energy stores), adiponectin (AMPK insulin sensitiser), and GLP-1
  (postprandial incretin). T1DM: autoimmune. T2DM: insulin resistance
  then \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-cell failure. GLP-1 agonists (semaglutide) and SGLT2 inhibitors
  transforming treatment.
\item
  \textbf{Adrenal medulla:} Chromaffin cells release epinephrine/NE on
  sympathetic stimulation; brief, fight-or-flight effects.
\item
  \textbf{GH axis:} Pulsatile GH \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} JAK2/STAT5 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} hepatic IGF-1. Linear
  bone growth, protein synthesis, lipolysis. Acromegaly (excess),
  gigantism, GH deficiency.
\item
  \textbf{Eicosanoids:} PLA\(_2\) liberates arachidonic acid from
  membrane phospholipids. COX \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} prostaglandins/thromboxanes. 5-LOX \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  leukotrienes. Glucocorticoids inhibit at PLA\(_2\); aspirin
  irreversibly acetylates COX-1. COX-2 selective inhibitors (celecoxib)
  reduce GI toxicity but raise thrombotic risk.
\item
  \textbf{Endocrine disruption:} BPA, phthalates, PFAS interact with
  hormone receptors and enzymes. Most concerning during fetal/neonatal
  development. Non-monotonic dose-responses violate classical toxicology
  assumptions.
\item
  \textbf{Innate immunity:} Immediate, non-specific. Physical barriers,
  complement (opsonisation, MAC, chemotaxis with positive amplification
  feedback), phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages, DCs), NK cells
  (missing self), inflammation, interferons, fever. PRRs: TLRs
  (membrane; TLR4\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}MyD88\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}NF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}B or TLR3\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}TRIF\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}IRF3\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}IFN-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}); NLRs (cytosolic;
  NLRP3 inflammasome \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} caspase-1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} IL-1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} + pyroptosis); RLRs (viral
  RNA); cGAS-STING (cytosolic DNA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} IFN-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}).
\item
  \textbf{Complement:} Three pathways converge on C3 convertase \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} C5
  convertase \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} MAC. Effector functions: opsonisation (C3b), MAC (C5b-9),
  anaphylatoxins (C3a, C5a). Regulators (DAF, CD59, factor H, C1-INH)
  confine to pathogen surfaces. PNH, hereditary angioedema, eculizumab.
\item
  \textbf{Adaptive immunity:} Specific, slow (7--10 days), memory. MHC I
  (endogenous) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} CD8+ CTL. MHC II (exogenous) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} CD4+ Th. T cell
  development DN1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}DN4\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}DP\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}positive selection (cTECs)\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}negative selection
  (mTECs/AIRE/Tregs). Th polarisation: Th1, Th2, Th17, Treg, Tfh.
\item
  \textbf{B cells:} T-dependent vs T-independent activation. Germinal
  centre reaction: SHM (AID) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} affinity maturation; CSR \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} IgG/IgA/IgE.
  Antibody isotypes: IgM (primary), IgG (secondary, opsonisation,
  placenta), IgA (mucosal), IgE (allergy).
\item
  \textbf{Cytokine network:} IL-1/IL-6/TNF (inflammation), IL-2 (T cell
  expansion), IL-4 (Th2/IgE), IL-17 (Th17/barrier), IFN-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma}
  (Th1/macrophage activation), IL-10/TGF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} (anti-inflammatory).
\item
  \textbf{Memory:} T\(_{CM}\) (recirculating), T\(_{EM}\) (peripheral),
  T\(_{RM}\) (tissue-resident); maintained by IL-7/IL-15. Pre-existing
  antigen-specific cells, lower activation threshold, pre-armed effector
  machinery explain the rapid recall response.
\item
  \textbf{Tolerance and autoimmunity:} Central (thymic/BM deletion,
  AIRE) and peripheral (Treg, anergy, PD-1, CTLA-4). Mechanisms of
  failure: molecular mimicry, bystander activation, epitope spreading,
  defective Tregs/apoptosis. Diseases: SLE, RA, T1DM, MS.
  Hypersensitivity I--IV.
\item
  \textbf{Immunotherapy:} Checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1, anti-CTLA-4,
  anti-LAG-3) --- 2018 Nobel Prize; response rates vary by tumour,
  biomarker, line of therapy, and combination strategy, with durable
  ``tail of the curve'' remissions in some responders. CAR-T for
  haematological malignancies (anti-CD19 for B-cell acute lymphoblastic
  leukaemia and DLBCL; anti-BCMA for myeloma); CRS managed by
  tocilizumab.
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See \cref{sec:unit_III_metabolic_integration}
  for insulin/glucagon integration,
  \cref{sec:unit_VII_infectious_disease} for PAMP recognition, and
  \cref{sec:unit_IX_circulation_respiration_homeostasis} for stress
  axes.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{GLP-1} & Incretin from intestinal L-cells; potentiates
