complement (C4b2a or C3bBb / C4b2aC3b) \\
\textbf{MAC} & Membrane attack complex (C5b-9); 10 nm pore lyses target
cell \\
\textbf{MHC I/II} & Antigen-presenting molecules to CD8+/CD4+ T cells \\
\textbf{AIRE} & Thymic transcription factor enabling expression of
tissue-specific antigens for negative selection \\
\textbf{AID} & Activation-induced cytidine deaminase; somatic
hypermutation and class switching \\
\textbf{Germinal centre} & Lymphoid microenvironment for affinity
maturation and class switching \\
\textbf{Treg} & FoxP3+ regulatory T cell; peripheral tolerance \\
\textbf{PD-1 / PD-L1} & Inhibitory checkpoint exploited by tumours;
target of pembrolizumab \\
\textbf{CTLA-4} & Inhibitory checkpoint on activated T cells; target of
ipilimumab \\
\textbf{CAR-T cell} & Engineered T cell with synthetic antigen receptor
for tumour killing \\
\textbf{Hypersensitivity I--IV} & Allergy/anaphylaxis (IgE), cytotoxic,
immune complex, delayed cell-mediated \\
\textbf{Molecular mimicry} & Pathogen antigen resembles self; triggers
cross-reactive autoimmunity \\
\textbf{Epitope spreading} & Autoimmune response broadens from one
self-antigen to many over time \\

\subsection{Review Questions}\label{review-questions-33}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Compare peptide and steroid hormone signalling in terms of synthesis,
  transport, receptor location, signalling speed, and duration. Why do
  steroid hormones have longer-lasting effects despite similar
  half-lives?
\item
  Explain cortisol synthesis from cholesterol, including the role of
  StAR. Which enzyme deficiency causes the most common form of
  congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and why does it produce both
  glucocorticoid deficiency and androgen excess?
\item
  Compare the two transcriptional modes of the glucocorticoid receptor
  (transactivation vs transrepression). Which mediates the
  anti-inflammatory effect of glucocorticoid drugs, and why does this
  dual mechanism complicate the development of ``dissociated''
  glucocorticoids with anti-inflammatory action but no metabolic side
  effects?
\item
  Explain why T4 is called a prohormone. Describe the role of D1, D2,
  and D3 deiodinases. Why is rT3 elevated during severe illness (``low
  T3 syndrome'')?
\item
  A patient has elevated TSH but normal free T4 (``subclinical
  hypothyroidism''). Explain the mechanism (think about the slope of the
  TSH--T4 feedback curve) and the clinical decision about treatment.
\item
  Trace the molecular pathway from insulin binding to GLUT4
  translocation in muscle. Identify three nodes where Type 2
  diabetes-associated defects occur.
\item
  Explain how leptin signals body energy stores to the brain and why
  most obese individuals have leptin resistance. How does adiponectin
  act as a complementary signal? Why doesn't exogenous leptin work for
  obesity?
\item
  Describe TLR4 signalling in response to bacterial LPS. Compare with
  the TRIF-IRF3 branch and the cGAS-STING pathway. Why does septic shock
  result from massive cytokine release, and what is the mechanism of
  action of ``anti-TNF'' therapeutics like infliximab?
\item
  Explain how the alternative complement pathway amplifies its own
  activation. Describe the formation of C3 convertase, C5 convertase,
  and the MAC. Why is complement activity restricted to pathogen
  surfaces and not host cells? What goes wrong in PNH, and how does
  eculizumab work?
\item
  Describe the DN1--DN4 stages of T cell development. What is
  \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-selection? Then describe positive and negative T cell selection in
  the thymus. What is the role of AIRE, and what disease results from
  its mutation?
\item
  Compare T-dependent and T-independent B cell responses. Why are
  conjugate vaccines (PCV13, Hib) more effective in young children than
  pure polysaccharide vaccines? Trace the steps from naïve B cell
  antigen encounter to long-lived plasma cell.
\item
  Explain the molecular basis of affinity maturation in the germinal
  centre. How does AID-mediated somatic hypermutation combined with
  antigen-driven selection produce 1000-fold increases in antibody
  affinity?
\item
  Compare the four types of hypersensitivity reactions. Identify a
  clinical example and treatment for each. Explain the difference in
  time course between Type I and Type IV.
\item
  Explain the difference between molecular mimicry, bystander
  activation, and epitope spreading as mechanisms of autoimmunity. Give
  a specific clinical example for each.
\item
  A patient on pembrolizumab develops new-onset hypothyroidism,
  vitiligo, and colitis. Explain mechanistically why anti-PD-1 therapy
  causes these immune-related adverse events. What does this reveal
  about the normal role of PD-1?
\item
  Describe the design of an anti-CD19 CAR-T cell --- antigen recognition
  domain, hinge, transmembrane, co-stimulatory, and activation domains.
  Why does CAR-T therapy frequently cause cytokine release syndrome, and
  how does anti-IL-6R tocilizumab treat CRS without compromising tumour
  killing?
\item
  Bisphenol A binds oestrogen receptors with much lower affinity than
  oestradiol. Explain the concept of non-monotonic dose-response curves
  and why low-dose endocrine disruption can have greater developmental
  impact than high-dose adult exposure.
\item
  Aspirin and ibuprofen both inhibit cyclooxygenase, but primarily
  aspirin permanently inhibits platelet COX-1. Explain the molecular and
  cellular basis of this difference and its therapeutic significance.
  Why did selective COX-2 inhibitors like rofecoxib increase
  cardiovascular risk?
\item
  Explain why memory T and B cells respond more rapidly and strongly to
  re-exposure than naïve cells. Identify at least four mechanistic
  differences.
\item
  A patient develops anaphylaxis after a wasp sting. Trace the cellular
  and molecular events from prior sensitisation through the acute
  reaction. Explain why intramuscular epinephrine is the first-line
  treatment and how each of its receptor effects (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}\(_1\), \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}\(_1\),
  \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}\(_2\)) addresses different components of anaphylaxis.
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Unit X --- Ecology:
Introduction}\label{unit-x-ecology-introduction}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Unit X --- Ecology: Introduction}

\subsection*{Why This Unit Matters}\label{why-this-unit-matters-10}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Why This Unit Matters}

In 1966, ecologist Robert Paine removed most sea stars (\emph{Pisaster
ochraceus}) from a stretch of rocky intertidal shore in Washington State
and waited. Within 18 months, the mussel population exploded, crowding
out barnacles, limpets, chitons, and anemones. What had been a
15-species community collapsed to a near-monoculture of \emph{Mytilus
californianus}. The sea star was a \textbf{keystone species}: a species
whose removal from the community caused a change in biodiversity
disproportionate to its own abundance. Paine's experiment created the
concept and the measurement --- the ratio of effect to biomass --- and
it changed how biologists think about the architecture of ecosystems
(Paine, 1966, \emph{American Naturalist}).

Ecology is the study of how organisms interact with each other and with
their physical environment. It operates across scales spanning six
orders of magnitude: from the foraging decision of a single aphid on a
single leaf, to the population dynamics of wolves in Yellowstone, to the
cycling of carbon through the entire Earth system. Its models --- the
logistic growth equation, the Lotka-Volterra predator-prey system, the
species-area relationship --- are among the most mathematically
tractable in biology, yet they govern phenomena as urgent as climate
change, mass extinction, and pandemic emergence.

The 21st century has made ecology a discipline under crisis and urgent
relevance. The current mass extinction event --- the sixth in Earth's
history --- is driven by habitat loss, overexploitation, invasive
species, pollution, and climate change. Biodiversity is losing the
equivalent of tens of thousands of species per year. Understanding
population dynamics, community structure, and ecosystem function is no
longer merely academic: it is an existential scientific priority for the
conservation of life on Earth. This unit will give you the quantitative
tools to understand why, and to participate in the solutions.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection*{Current Evidence Thread}\label{current-evidence-thread-10}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Current Evidence Thread}

Read this unit as a chain of ecological evidence rather than a list of
topics: population, community, ecosystem, and conservation claims are
each backed by a characteristic kind of measurement --- field sampling
and mark-recapture, manipulative and observational experiments, remote
sensing and flux networks, dynamical and statistical models, and
long-term monitoring programs. Ecology and conservation decisions
increasingly combine field data, remote sensing, community knowledge,
model uncertainty, and explicit values. As you move through the
chapters, keep a two-column note: \textbf{claim} on the left,
\textbf{evidence that would change my confidence} on the right. By the
end of the unit, each major idea should be tied to a measurement, model,
citation, or paper-based lab decision.

\subsection*{Connections Across the
Textbook}\label{connections-across-the-textbook-10}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Connections Across the Textbook}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Population models} (logistic growth, age structure) use the
  same differential equation framework as Unit VII (SIR epidemiological
  models) --- ecology and epidemiology are mathematically unified.
\item
  \textbf{Species diversity indices} (Shannon \(H'\), Simpson \(D\)) are
  computed using tools from Unit VII (microbial communities) and help
  evaluate ecosystem health.
\item
  \textbf{Nutrient cycling} (nitrogen, carbon, phosphorus) directly ties
  to Unit III (carbon fixation by photosynthesis) and Unit VII
  (microbial decomposers, nitrogen fixation by bacteria).
\item
  \textbf{Climate change impacts} on biomes connect to Unit VIII (plant
  responses to drought, CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} enrichment) and Unit VI (evolution of
  species under selection by climate).
\item
  \textbf{Conservation biology} uses evolutionary genetics (Unit VI:
  effective population size, genetic rescue) and macroecology (island
  biogeography, keystone species).
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Key vocabulary introduced here:} intrinsic rate of increase
(\(r\)), carrying capacity (\(K\)), logistic growth, density dependence,
keystone species, trophic cascade, competitive exclusion, fundamental
vs.~realised niche, coevolution, mutualism, parasitism, primary
productivity (GPP, NPP), trophic efficiency, biogeochemical cycle,
biome, species-area relationship, island biogeography, minimum viable
population (MVP), extinction debt.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Opening Vignette --- The Equation That Explains Why Populations
Don't Grow Forever}

In 1838, Belgian mathematician Pierre François Verhulst looked at census
data and asked: why don't populations simply grow exponentially forever?
His answer was the logistic equation --- dN/dt = rN(1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-} N/K) --- where
K, the carrying capacity, captures the idea that resources limit growth.
For nearly a century, the logistic model was theoretical. Then in 1934,
Russian ecologist Georgy Gause grew two \emph{Paramecium} species in
test tubes and observed the sigmoid growth curve Verhulst had predicted:
slow growth, rapid growth, leveling off at carrying capacity. His
experiments also showed
\hyperref[gl:competitive-exclusion]{\textbf{competitive exclusion}} ---
two species competing for the same \hyperref[gl:niche]{\textbf{niche}}
cannot coexist indefinitely. Gause published this in \emph{The Struggle
for Existence} at age 23. The logistic model now underlies fisheries
management, epidemiology (the SIR model is a direct descendant),
conservation minimum viable population estimates, and pandemic
projections. Verhulst's equation, written in a 4-page paper with no
data, may have saved more lives than any equation since Newton's second
law.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Chapter Roadmap}\label{chapter-roadmap-12}

The chapter spans the full pipeline from individuals to metapopulations.
Read it as three nested scales:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{The individual scale.} Population attributes, life tables,
  survivorship. What you need before any growth equation makes sense.
\item
  \textbf{The population scale.} Exponential growth, logistic growth,
  Allee effects, Lotka-Volterra interactions --- the canonical equations
  and their named modifications.
\item
  \textbf{The spatial, structured, and human scale.} r/K life histories,
  age-structured matrix models, individual-based simulation, population
  viability analysis, metapopulation dynamics, field-estimation
  techniques, and human demographic transitions.
\end{itemize}

For a brief treatment, focus on the core growth mathematics and the
applied field-estimation and demographic-transition material. For a full
quantitative course, work through most sections including the
matrix-model and PVA toolkit, which underlie modern conservation
practice.

\subsection{What Is a Population?}\label{what-is-a-population}

A \textbf{population} consists of individuals of a single species
(conspecifics) inhabiting a defined area at a given time. Population
ecology investigates the factors that regulate population size, density,
distribution, and growth over time. Understanding population dynamics is
fundamental to wildlife management, conservation biology, epidemiology,
and sustainable resource harvest.

\subsubsection{Population Attributes}\label{population-attributes}

Populations are characterised by several measurable attributes:

Attribute
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Symbol
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Definition
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Units
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Census size & \(N\) & Total number of individuals & Individuals \\
Population density & \(D\) & Individuals per unit area or volume &
ind/km\(^2\) or ind/L \\
Per capita birth rate & \(b\) & Births per individual per time unit &
births/ind/time \\
Per capita death rate & \(d\) & Deaths per individual per time unit &
deaths/ind/time \\
Intrinsic rate of increase & \(r\) & \(r = b - d\) (can be negative) &
time\(^{-1}\) \\
Finite rate of increase & \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda} & \(\lambda = e^r\); \(\lambda > 1\)
growing; \(\lambda < 1\) declining & dimensionless \\
Net reproductive rate & \(R_0\) & \(R_0 = \sum l_x m_x\); female
offspring per female per lifetime & offspring/female \\
Generation time & \(T\) & \(T = \sum x \cdot l_x \cdot m_x / R_0\) &
time units \\
\end{longtable}
}

The fundamental relationship between \(R_0\), \(T\), and \(r\) is the
\textbf{Euler-Lotka equation}:

\begin{equation}
\sum_{x=0}^{\omega} e^{-rx} l_x m_x = 1
\label{eq:population_ecology_1}
\end{equation}

For approximate computation: \(r \approx \ln(R_0) / T\)

\subsubsection{Dispersion Patterns}\label{dispersion-patterns}

Individuals within a population are distributed in one of three spatial
patterns:

\textbf{Clumped} & Aggregated in patches & Resource heterogeneity,

fungi near rotting logs \\
\textbf{Uniform} & Evenly spaced & Territoriality, allelopathy,

The \textbf{variance-to-mean ratio} (\(\sigma^2 / \mu\)) of quadrat
counts distinguishes these patterns: ratio = 1 (random, Poisson),
\textgreater1 (clumped, negative binomial), \textless1 (uniform).

From this table:

\begin{equation}
R_0 = \sum l_x m_x = 0 + 0.400 + 0.720 + 0.200 + 0 = 1.320
\label{eq:population_ecology_2}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
T = \frac{\sum x \cdot l_x m_x}{R_0} = \frac{2.440}{1.320} = 1.848 \text{ generations}
\label{eq:population_ecology_3}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
r \approx \frac{\ln(R_0)}{T} = \frac{\ln(1.320)}{1.848} = \frac{0.278}{1.848} = 0.150 \text{ per time unit}
\label{eq:population_ecology_4}
\end{equation}

Since \(R_0 > 1\), this population is \textbf{growing}.

A \textbf{static life table} (vertical life table) uses age structure
data from a single time point --- useful when tracking cohorts is
impractical (e.g., long-lived species like elephants or trees). It
assumes stable age distribution.

\subsubsection{Survivorship Curves}\label{survivorship-curves}

Three canonical survivorship curve types (Pearl 1928; Deevey 1947):

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0175_d4c12273ba7b.png}
\caption{Flowchart for Survivorship Curves: Convex curve on log plot, Straight line on log plot, Concave curve on log plot, and High parental investment, few offspring, K-selected traits"] form the diagram's primary path or branches.}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Mathematical representation of survivorship:}

For Type I: \(l_x \approx e^{-bx^n}\) where \(n > 1\) (Gompertz-Makeham
law for human mortality)

For Type II: \(l_x = e^{-\mu x}\) (constant hazard rate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu})

For Type III: \(l_x \approx e^{-bx^n}\) where \(n < 1\)

\begin{quote}
\texorpdfstring{}{} \textbf{Clinical Connection --- Actuarial Science and Human
Survivorship:} Human survivorship curves have shifted dramatically over
the past 200 years. In 1800, human survivorship resembled a Type II
curve due to high infant and childhood mortality from infectious
disease. Modern medicine, sanitation, and nutrition have transformed the
human curve to an extreme Type I, with about 99\% survival to
age 50 in high-income countries. The \textbf{Gompertz law of mortality}
states that human death rate doubles approximately every 8 years after
age 30: \(\mu(x) = \alpha e^{\beta x}\). This principle underlies life
insurance actuarial tables and pension fund projections.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check:} Sea turtles lay 50-200 eggs per nesting event
but about 1 in 1,000 hatchlings survives to reproductive age. Which
survivorship curve type does this represent, and what would a
conservation program need to achieve (in terms of stage-specific
survival rates) to increase population growth?
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Reproductive Value}\label{reproductive-value}

Fisher's \textbf{reproductive value} (\(v_x\)) quantifies the expected
future contribution of an individual of age \(x\) to population growth:

\begin{equation}
v_x = \frac{e^{rx}}{l_x} \sum_{y=x}^{\omega} e^{-ry} l_y m_y
\label{eq:population_ecology_5}
\end{equation}

Reproductive value peaks at the age of first reproduction in growing
populations and declines thereafter. This concept is critical for
conservation: protecting age classes with highest \(v_x\) yields the
greatest impact on population recovery. For sea turtles, subadult and
adult females have the highest reproductive value --- hence
\textbf{Turtle Excluder Devices (TEDs)} in fishing nets target this life
stage.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Exponential Growth}\label{exponential-growth}

When resources are unlimited and the environment exerts no
\hyperref[gl:density-dependent-regulation]{\textbf{density-dependent
regulation}}, population growth is \textbf{exponential} (or geometric in
discrete-time models):

\textbf{Continuous-time model:}

\begin{equation}
\frac{dN}{dt} = rN \quad \Rightarrow \quad N(t) = N_0 e^{rt}
\label{eq:population_ecology_6}
\end{equation}

\textbf{Discrete-time model (non-overlapping generations):}

\begin{equation}
N_{t+1} = \lambda N_t \quad \Rightarrow \quad N_t = N_0 \lambda^t
\label{eq:population_ecology_7}
\end{equation}

where \(\lambda = e^r\) is the \textbf{finite rate of increase}.

\textbf{Doubling time:}
\(t_2 = \frac{\ln 2}{r} \approx \frac{0.693}{r}\)

The St.~Matthew Island reindeer population illustrates the
\textbf{catastrophic crash} that follows unsustainable exponential
growth: 29 reindeer introduced in 1944 grew to 6,000 by 1963, then
crashed to 42 by 1966 due to overgrazing of lichen habitat. This case
study is a classic illustration of \textbf{ecological overshoot}.

\subsection{Logistic Growth and Density
Dependence}\label{logistic-growth-and-density-dependence}

As \(N\) approaches the \textbf{carrying capacity} (\(K\)),
intraspecific competition for resources reduces the per capita growth
rate. The \textbf{logistic growth equation} \citep{verhulst1838}
incorporates this density dependence:

\begin{equation}
\frac{dN}{dt} = rN\left(1 - \frac{N}{K}\right)
\label{eq:population_ecology_8}
\end{equation}

The term \((1 - N/K)\) is the \textbf{density-dependence factor} (or
unused portion of carrying capacity), and it bends exponential growth
into the S-shaped trajectory of \cref{fig:unit_X_logistic_growth} with
the following key properties:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  When \(N \ll K\): growth is approximately exponential
  (\(dN/dt \approx rN\))
\item
  When \(N = K/2\): \(dN/dt\) is \textbf{maximised} (inflection point of
  the sigmoid curve)
\item
  When \(N = K\): \(dN/dt = 0\) (population is at equilibrium)
\item
  When \(N > K\): \(dN/dt < 0\) (population declines toward \(K\))
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Analytical solution:}

\begin{equation}
N(t) = \frac{K}{1 + \left(\frac{K - N_0}{N_0}\right)e^{-rt}}
\label{eq:population_ecology_9}
\end{equation}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0176_f42f98ef3168.png}
\caption{State diagram for Logistic Growth and Density Dependence showing transitions among N0 << K, Growth accelerates, N approaches K/2, and N = K/2, max dN/dt.}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Density-Independent
Factors}\label{density-independent-factors}

Some factors affect populations regardless of density:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Weather extremes} (frost, drought, hurricanes)
\item
  \textbf{Volcanic eruptions}, wildfires, floods
\item
  \textbf{Pesticide application}
\end{itemize}

In practice, most populations are regulated by a combination of
density-dependent and density-independent factors.

\subsubsection{Maximum Sustainable Yield
(MSY)}\label{maximum-sustainable-yield-msy}

From the logistic equation, the maximum absolute growth rate occurs at
\(N = K/2\):

\begin{equation}
\text{MSY} = \frac{rK}{4}
\label{eq:population_ecology_10}
\end{equation}

Fisheries and wildlife management use MSY to set harvest quotas.
However, MSY has significant limitations:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Assumes logistic growth} --- real populations often show
  non-logistic dynamics
\item
  \textbf{K and r are difficult to estimate} --- environmental
  stochasticity changes both
\item
  \textbf{Ignores age/size structure} --- harvesting large,
  reproductively valuable individuals disproportionately impacts growth
\item
  \textbf{No safety margin} --- harvesting exactly at MSY leaves no
  \hyperref[gl:buffer]{\textbf{buffer}} for environmental variation
\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}
\texorpdfstring{}{} \textbf{Clinical Connection --- Pacific Sardine Collapse:} The
Pacific sardine (\emph{Sardinops sagax}) fishery collapsed in the
1940s-1950s, with the population crashing from 3 million tonnes to
near-zero. The collapse resulted from harvesting above MSY during a
period when ocean conditions (Pacific Decadal Oscillation) shifted
unfavorably, reducing \(K\). The combined effect of over-exploitation
and environmental change was catastrophic. This case led to the
development of \textbf{precautionary reference points} in modern
fisheries management, where harvest targets are set below MSY (typically
at 0.5-0.8 MSY) to provide a buffer.
\end{quote}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ biology.ecology }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ logistic\_growth}

\NormalTok{result }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ logistic\_growth(}
\NormalTok{    initial\_population}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{,}
\NormalTok{    growth\_rate}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.8}\NormalTok{,}
\NormalTok{    carrying\_capacity}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{,}
\NormalTok{    time\_steps}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{30}
\NormalTok{)}
\CommentTok{\# Find maximum per{-}capita growth (should be near K/2 = 500)}
\NormalTok{growth\_rates }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [result.trajectory[i}\OperatorTok{+}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ result.trajectory[i]}
                \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(result.trajectory)}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)]}
\NormalTok{peak\_N }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ result.trajectory[growth\_rates.index(}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(growth\_rates))]}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"Peak growth at N ≈ }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{peak\_N}\SpecialCharTok{:.0f\}}\SpecialStringTok{ (expect K/2 = 500)"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{Extensions of the Logistic
Model}\label{extensions-of-the-logistic-model}

\textbf{Theta-logistic model} --- allows flexible density dependence:

\begin{equation}
\frac{dN}{dt} = rN\left[1 - \left(\frac{N}{K}\right)^\theta\right]
\label{eq:population_ecology_11}
\end{equation}

When \(\theta = 1\): standard logistic. When \(\theta > 1\): density
effects are weak until \(N\) is close to \(K\) (concave per-capita
growth). When \(\theta < 1\): density effects are strong even at low
\(N\) (convex). Empirical estimates for large mammals typically give
\(\theta \approx 2-7\) (Sibly et al.~2005, \emph{Science}), meaning
density dependence is weaker than the standard logistic assumes.

\textbf{Time-lagged logistic model:}

\begin{equation}
\frac{dN}{dt} = rN\left(1 - \frac{N(t-\tau)}{K}\right)
\label{eq:population_ecology_12}
\end{equation}

When the time lag \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\tau}}{tau} is large relative to \(1/r\), the population can
\textbf{overshoot} \(K\) and exhibit damped oscillations, limit cycles,
or even chaos (May 1976, \emph{Nature}).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check:} A population of deer has \(r = 0.3\)/yr and
\(K = 5000\). Calculate MSY and the population size at which it occurs.
If the current population is 4000, how many deer can be sustainably
harvested per year?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{The Allee Effect}\label{the-allee-effect}

The \textbf{Allee effect} \citep{allee1931} occurs when per capita
fitness \emph{decreases} at low population density --- the opposite of
standard logistic density-dependence. This creates a positive feedback
loop where small populations become increasingly vulnerable.

\subsubsection{Strong vs.~Weak Allee
Effects}\label{strong-vs.-weak-allee-effects}

\textbf{Strong Allee effect} --- per capita growth rate becomes negative
below a threshold:

\begin{equation}
\frac{dN}{dt} = rN\left(\frac{N}{A} - 1\right)\left(1 - \frac{N}{K}\right)
\label{eq:population_ecology_13}
\end{equation}

where \(A\) = \textbf{Allee threshold}. Below \(A\), the population
declines deterministically to extinction. There are three equilibria:
\(N = 0\) (stable), \(N = A\) (unstable), and \(N = K\) (stable).

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth]{../figures/allee_threshold_dynamics.png}
\caption{Strong Allee-effect threshold dynamics. Initial population sizes below, at, and above the Allee threshold show extinction, unstable threshold persistence, and recovery toward carrying capacity.}
\label{fig:unit_X_allee_threshold_dynamics}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Weak Allee effect} --- per capita growth rate decreases at low
density but remains positive. No threshold exists; the population can
recover from any positive size, but growth is slower than expected at
low \(N\).

\subsubsection{Mechanisms of Allee
Effects}\label{mechanisms-of-allee-effects}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2727}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2121}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5152}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Mechanism
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Example
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Effect on fitness
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Mate finding} & Ivory-billed woodpecker; many marine
invertebrates & Low density \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} failed mate encounter \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} reduced
reproduction \\
\textbf{Predator satiation} & Mast-seeding trees (oaks, beeches) & Below
threshold seed output \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} disproportionate predation loss \\
\textbf{Cooperative breeding/hunting} & African wild dogs (pack size \texorpdfstring{\textgreater{}=}{>=} 5
for efficient hunting) & Small packs \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} insufficient prey capture \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
starvation \\
\textbf{Cooperative defence} & Muskoxen forming defensive circles & Too
few adults \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} predators penetrate defence \\
\textbf{Genetic diversity} & Florida panther (pre-1995,
\(N_e \approx 25\)) & Small \(N\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} inbreeding depression \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} reduced
fitness \\
\textbf{Pollination failure} & Rare plants in fragmented meadows & Low
density \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} pollinators don't visit \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} seed set fails \\
\textbf{Environmental conditioning} & Soil
\hyperref[gl:microbiome]{\textbf{microbiome}} enrichment by plant roots
& Few plants \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} soil biota depauperate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} poor seedling establishment \\
\end{longtable}
}

Stephens et al.~(1999, \emph{Trends Ecol. Evol.}) distinguished the
\textbf{component Allee effect} (reduction in any fitness component at
low density) from the \textbf{demographic Allee effect} (reduction in
per capita population growth rate). A species may experience component
Allee effects in reproduction without a demographic Allee effect if
compensating survival increases at low density offset the reproductive
reduction.

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"Above A: N\_final ≈ }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{above}\SpecialCharTok{.}\NormalTok{populations[}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}\SpecialCharTok{:.1f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}

\begin{quote}
\texorpdfstring{}{} \textbf{Clinical Connection --- Northern White Rhinoceros:} The
northern white rhinoceros (\emph{Ceratotherium simum cottoni})
represents a tragic Allee effect in action. As of 2024, two females
remain (Najin and Fatu at Ol Pejeta Conservancy, Kenya). Even with
preserved sperm and IVF technology, the population has fallen below
plausible demographic and genetic recovery thresholds for conventional
breeding. Stem cell-derived \hyperref[gl:gamete]{\textbf{gamete}}s from
banked fibroblasts represent a highly experimental rescue pathway rather
than a routine conservation tool. This case illustrates that for species
with strong Allee effects, conservation intervention must occur while
demographic options and genetic variation are still large enough to
matter.
\end{quote}

\textbf{Concept Check:} A whale population has an Allee threshold of

intrinsic growth rate (in the absence of Allee effects) is
\(r = 0.04\)/yr. What will happen to this population without
intervention? What minimum number of individuals would need to be
translocated to push the population above the threshold?
\end{quote}

\subsection{Lotka-Volterra Competition and
Predator-Prey}\label{lotka-volterra-competition-and-predator-prey}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth]{../figures/lotka_volterra.png}
\caption{Lotka--Volterra predator--prey dynamics: oscillating population cycles of prey and predator plotted over time and as a phase-plane portrait.}
\label{fig:unit_X_lotka_volterra}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Interspecific
Competition}\label{interspecific-competition}

Two species sharing a limiting resource compete. The Lotka-Volterra
competition model:

\begin{equation}
\frac{dN_1}{dt} = r_1 N_1 \left(1 - \frac{N_1 + \alpha_{12} N_2}{K_1}\right)
\label{eq:population_ecology_14}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
\frac{dN_2}{dt} = r_2 N_2 \left(1 - \frac{N_2 + \alpha_{21} N_1}{K_2}\right)
\label{eq:population_ecology_15}
\end{equation}

The \textbf{competition coefficient} \(\alpha_{12}\) represents the
per-capita effect of species 2 on species 1, expressed in units of
species-1 equivalents. If \(\alpha_{12} = 0.5\), each individual of
species 2 has half the competitive impact of one individual of species
1.

\textbf{Zero-growth isoclines} (setting \(dN/dt = 0\)): - Species 1
isocline: \(N_1 = K_1 - \alpha_{12}N_2\) (line from \(K_1\) on
\(N_1\)-axis to \(K_1/\alpha_{12}\) on \(N_2\)-axis) - Species 2
isocline: \(N_2 = K_2 - \alpha_{21}N_1\) (line from \(K_2\) on
\(N_2\)-axis to \(K_2/\alpha_{21}\) on \(N_1\)-axis)

\textbf{Phase-plane outcomes:}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2195}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1707}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.6098}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Condition
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Outcome
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Biological interpretation
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\(K_1 > K_2/\alpha_{12}\) and \(K_2 < K_1/\alpha_{21}\) & Species 1
wins; species 2 excluded & Species 1 tolerates competition better \\
\(K_2 > K_1/\alpha_{21}\) and \(K_1 < K_2/\alpha_{12}\) & Species 2
wins; species 1 excluded & Species 2 tolerates competition better \\
\(K_1 < K_2/\alpha_{12}\) and \(K_2 < K_1/\alpha_{21}\) & \textbf{Stable
coexistence} & Intraspecific \textgreater{} interspecific competition
(niche differentiation) \\
\(K_1 > K_2/\alpha_{12}\) and \(K_2 > K_1/\alpha_{21}\) &
\textbf{Unstable equilibrium} (priority effect) & Interspecific
\textgreater{} intraspecific; winner depends on initial \(N\) \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Chesson's modern coexistence theory} (Chesson 2000, \emph{Annu.
Rev.~Ecol. Syst.}): Stable coexistence requires that intraspecific
competition exceed interspecific competition:
\(\alpha_{11}\alpha_{22} > \alpha_{12}\alpha_{21}\), or equivalently,
niche overlap \(< 1\). Two mechanisms enable this:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Stabilising mechanisms} --- increase niche differentiation
  (negative frequency dependence; rare species advantage)
\item
  \textbf{Equalising mechanisms} --- reduce fitness differences between
  species (similar competitive abilities)
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Lotka-Volterra
Predator-Prey}\label{lotka-volterra-predator-prey}

\begin{equation}
\frac{dV}{dt} = \alpha V - \beta VP \quad \text{(prey: grow in absence of predator; decline with encounters)}
\label{eq:population_ecology_16}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
\frac{dP}{dt} = \delta VP - \gamma P \quad \text{(predator: grow via prey; decline without prey)}
\label{eq:population_ecology_17}
\end{equation}

This system produces \textbf{neutrally stable oscillations} with period
\(\approx 2\pi/\sqrt{\alpha\gamma}\) and amplitude that depends on
initial conditions, tracing the offset prey--predator cycles and closed
phase-plane orbit shown in \cref{fig:unit_X_lotka_volterra}.

\textbf{Functional responses} \citep{holling1959} describe the per
capita predation rate as a function of prey density:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1667}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2083}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2917}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Type
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Equation
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Shape
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Example
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Type I} & \(f(V) = aV\) & Linear & Filter feeders (whale sharks,
baleen whales) \\
\textbf{Type II} & \(f(V) = \frac{aV}{1 + ahV}\) & Decelerating
(hyperbolic) & Most predators; handling time \(h\) limits intake \\
\textbf{Type III} & \(f(V) = \frac{aV^2}{1 + ahV^2}\) & Sigmoidal &
Predators that switch prey; search image formation \\
\end{longtable}
}

The Type II functional response is also known as the
\textbf{Michaelis-Menten} or \textbf{disc equation}. The parameter \(a\)
= attack rate and \(h\) = handling time per prey item. Maximum
consumption rate = \(1/h\).

Type III responses are stabilising because at low prey density,
per-capita predation risk is low (predator switching to alternative
prey), creating a \textbf{low-density refuge}.

\textbf{Numerical response:} predator population growth rate as a
function of prey density --- driven by the functional response but with
a time lag (gestation, maturation).

\subsubsection{Lynx-Hare Cycle: A Case
Study}\label{lynx-hare-cycle-a-case-study}

The snowshoe hare (\emph{Lepus americanus}) and Canada lynx (\emph{Lynx
canadensis}) display coupled about 10-year population cycles
across boreal Canada, documented from Hudson's Bay Company fur trading
records (1845-1935; Keith 1963). Modern analysis reveals the cycle is
more complex than simple Lotka-Volterra:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Predation} accounts for about 60\% of the cycle
  driver (Krebs et al.~2001, \emph{Science})
\item
  \textbf{Food quality} --- at high hare density, overgrazing induces
  plant chemical defences (phenolic compounds in willow/birch browse),
  reducing hare food quality (about 20\% of cycle)
\item
  \textbf{Stress physiology} --- high density and predation risk elevate
  \hyperref[gl:cortisol]{\textbf{cortisol}}, suppressing reproduction
  (about 20\% of cycle)
\item
  The \textbf{tri-trophic interaction} (vegetation-hare-lynx) is
  necessary to explain the observed amplitude and period
\end{enumerate}

the oscillations are neutrally stable. What modification to the model
would produce damped oscillations converging to a stable equilibrium?
(Hint: consider what happens when you add density dependence to the prey
equation.)
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Beyond r-K: Modern Life History
Theory}\label{beyond-r-k-modern-life-history-theory}

The r-K framework has been largely superseded by more nuanced models:

\textbf{Stearns' (1992) demographic classification} uses age-specific
mortality patterns rather than a single r-K axis, predicting that: -
High juvenile mortality \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} early maturation, high fecundity - High adult
mortality \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} delayed maturation, high reproductive effort per event -
Variable mortality \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} bet-hedging strategies

\textbf{Bet-hedging} (Philippi \& Seger 1989, \emph{Trends Ecol.
Evol.}): In variable environments, intermediate-risk reproductive
strategies outperform extreme approaches by reducing \textbf{variance}
in fitness rather than maximising mean fitness: - \textbf{Conservative
bet-hedging:} Low-variance strategy (e.g., typically produce moderate
number of offspring) - \textbf{Diversified bet-hedging:} Produce
variable \hyperref[gl:phenotype]{\textbf{phenotype}}s (e.g., desert
annual plants with variable seed dormancy --- don't germinate most seeds
in a single good year)

\textbf{Grime's CSR triangle} (plants): Competitors (large, slow),
Stress-tolerators (tough, slow), Ruderals (fast, weedy) --- a three-way
classification rather than binary r-K.

\begin{quote}
\texorpdfstring{}{} \textbf{Clinical Connection --- Human Life History and Demographic
Transition:} Human populations have undergone a dramatic
\textbf{demographic transition} as societies industrialise: from high
birth rates and high death rates (Stage 1) through declining death rates
(Stage 2, rapid population growth), declining birth rates (Stage 3), to
low birth/death rates (Stage 4). Some developed nations are now in Stage
5 with birth rates below replacement (\(R_0 < 1\)). Japan's population
declined by about 800,000 in 2023 alone
(\(r \approx -0.006\)/yr). The demographic transition illustrates a
shift from r-selected to K-selected reproductive strategy within a
single species as environmental conditions change.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{7B Age-Structured Models and the Leslie
Matrix}\label{b-age-structured-models-and-the-leslie-matrix}

The scalar growth models treat most individuals as demographically
identical. Real populations are structured by age (or stage), and
demographic rates are highly age-specific: a one-year-old salmon and a
four-year-old salmon contribute very differently to population growth.
\textbf{Matrix population models} \citep{lotka1925} make this structure
explicit and underlie virtually every modern population viability
analysis, \hyperref[gl:fisheries]{\textbf{fisheries}} stock assessment,
and conservation triage exercise.

\subsubsection{Leslie Matrix
Construction}\label{leslie-matrix-construction}

A \textbf{Leslie matrix} \(\mathbf{L}\) is a square non-negative matrix
that projects an age-classified population vector
\(\mathbf{n}(t) = (n_0, n_1, \ldots, n_\omega)^T\) from time \(t\) to
\(t+1\):

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{n}(t+1) = \mathbf{L}\,\mathbf{n}(t)
\label{eq:unit_X_leslie_projection}
\end{equation}

For a population with maximum age \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\omega}}{omega}, the Leslie matrix has age-specific
fecundities \(F_x = l_x m_x / l_{x-1}\) on the top row and survival
probabilities \(P_x = l_{x+1}/l_x\) on the sub-diagonal:

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{L} = \begin{pmatrix}
F_0 & F_1 & F_2 & \cdots & F_{\omega-1} & F_\omega \\
P_0 & 0   & 0   & \cdots & 0           & 0 \\
0   & P_1 & 0   & \cdots & 0           & 0 \\
0   & 0   & P_2 & \cdots & 0           & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\
0   & 0   & 0   & \cdots & P_{\omega-1} & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\label{eq:unit_X_leslie_matrix}
\end{equation}

By the \textbf{Perron--Frobenius theorem}, \(\mathbf{L}\) has a unique
positive dominant eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\) --- this is the
\textbf{asymptotic finite rate of increase}. The associated right
eigenvector \(\mathbf{w}\) gives the \textbf{stable age distribution}
(the proportions \(n_x/N\) to which the population converges) and the
left eigenvector \(\mathbf{v}\) gives the \textbf{age-specific
reproductive value} \(v_x\) (\cref{eq:population_ecology_5}, but now
read off the matrix directly).

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{L}\mathbf{w} = \lambda_1 \mathbf{w}, \qquad \mathbf{v}^T \mathbf{L} = \lambda_1 \mathbf{v}^T
\label{eq:unit_X_leslie_eigen}
\end{equation}

The Euler-Lotka equation (\cref{eq:population_ecology_1}) is the
characteristic polynomial of \(\mathbf{L}\) --- every demographic
statement made in the life-table and survivorship discussion is
recoverable from the matrix.

\subsubsection{Sensitivity and Elasticity
Analysis}\label{sensitivity-and-elasticity-analysis}

Conservation managers rarely have the luxury of changing every
demographic rate. Which rate, if perturbed by 1\%, would change
\(\lambda_1\) the most? \textbf{Sensitivity} \(s_{ij}\) and
\textbf{elasticity} \(e_{ij}\) answer this:

\begin{equation}
s_{ij} = \frac{\partial \lambda_1}{\partial a_{ij}} = \frac{v_i w_j}{\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w} \rangle}, \qquad e_{ij} = \frac{a_{ij}}{\lambda_1}\,s_{ij}
\label{eq:unit_X_sensitivity_elasticity}
\end{equation}

where \(a_{ij}\) is the matrix entry,
\(\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}\rangle = \sum_x v_x w_x\), and
elasticities sum to one (\(\sum_{ij} e_{ij} = 1\)), making them directly
interpretable as proportional contributions.

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3200}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5600}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1200}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Quantity
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Interpretation
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Use
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Sensitivity \(s_{ij}\) & Absolute change in \(\lambda_1\) per unit
change in \(a_{ij}\) & Rates measured on different scales (survival
0--1, fecundity 0--\(\infty\)) --- direct comparison misleading \\
Elasticity \(e_{ij}\) & Proportional change in \(\lambda_1\) per
proportional change in \(a_{ij}\) & Comparing across rates; identifying
highest-leverage management target \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Worked Example --- Loggerhead sea turtle.} Crouse, Crowder \&
Caswell (1987, \emph{Ecology}) built a 7-stage Leslie-style matrix for
\emph{Caretta caretta} in the southeastern USA. Hatchling protection
(the dominant 1980s strategy) had elasticity \(\approx 0.04\), whereas
adult survival had elasticity \(\approx 0.20-0.30\). A 1 \% increase in
adult survival raised \(\lambda_1\) five to seven times more than a 1 \%
increase in egg-stage survival. This elasticity result drove the
regulatory adoption of \textbf{Turtle Excluder Devices} in shrimp trawls
--- a direct policy outcome of matrix sensitivity analysis. The same
logic explains why protecting reproductive-aged females beats protecting
eggs, echoing the reproductive-value argument developed earlier.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check:} A 3-stage matrix has elasticities
\(e_{\text{juvenile survival}} = 0.05\),
\(e_{\text{subadult survival}} = 0.35\),
\(e_{\text{adult survival}} = 0.50\),
\(e_{\text{adult fecundity}} = 0.10\). Which life-stage transition
should a recovery plan target first, and why is ``save the babies''
intuition misleading here?
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Stage-Structured
Generalisations}\label{stage-structured-generalisations}

Many organisms are better classified by \textbf{stage} (size, instar,
reproductive status) than by age --- trees, corals, and
indeterminate-growth fish are obvious examples. The \textbf{Lefkovitch
matrix} generalises Leslie by allowing positive entries on the diagonal
(probability of remaining in the same stage) and on multiple
sub-diagonals (skipping stages, regression). The eigen-analysis
machinery is shared with Leslie models, while the biological
interpretation of each entry changes.

\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\CommentTok{\# Loggerhead{-}style 5{-}stage matrix (illustrative)}
\NormalTok{L }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.00}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.00}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.00}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{4.66}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{61.9}\NormalTok{],   }\CommentTok{\# fecundities (eggs, hatchlings)}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.68}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.74}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.00}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.00}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.00}\NormalTok{],   }\CommentTok{\# juvenile survival}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.00}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.66}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.00}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.00}\NormalTok{],   }\CommentTok{\# subadult transition}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.00}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.00}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.02}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.68}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.00}\NormalTok{],   }\CommentTok{\# novice breeder}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.00}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.00}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.00}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.06}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.81}\NormalTok{],   }\CommentTok{\# mature breeder}
\NormalTok{])}

\subsection{7C Individual-Based Models and Stochastic
Simulation}\label{c-individual-based-models-and-stochastic-simulation}

Matrix models are deterministic and assume infinite, well-mixed
populations. Two regimes break those assumptions and demand a different
tool:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Small populations} (conservation contexts) where demographic
  stochasticity dominates --- a population of 30 condors with mean
  \(\lambda_1 = 1.05\) can still go extinct from an unlucky run of
  male-heavy chicks.
\item
  \textbf{Heterogeneous individuals} --- variation in body size,
  behaviour, territory quality, or local conditions that cannot be
  averaged into a mean rate without losing the dynamics.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Individual-based models (IBMs)}, also called agent-based models,
simulate each organism explicitly. Births, deaths, dispersal, and
interactions are drawn as random events from probability distributions
parameterised by individual attributes. Across many replicate runs, IBMs
produce \emph{distributions} of outcomes (extinction probability, time
to recovery) rather than single trajectories.

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3214}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.6786}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Advantage
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Why IBMs deliver it
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Demographic stochasticity & Discrete birth/death events --- no
fractional individuals \\
Individual heterogeneity & Each agent carries its own age, size,
genotype, location \\
Spatial structure & Landscape grids, dispersal kernels, local
interactions \\
Emergent dynamics & Allee effects,
\hyperref[gl:self-organization]{\textbf{self-organization}}, threshold
behaviours arise naturally \\
Complex behaviours & Mate choice, learning, territoriality without
analytical closed form \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Limitations:} IBMs trade analytical clarity for realism. They
are computationally expensive (millions of replicates needed for
tail-probability estimates), parameter-hungry, and validation is harder
than for closed-form models. Best practice: build the simplest model
that captures the focal mechanism, then add complexity primarily when
justified by data (the \textbf{Pattern-Oriented Modelling} philosophy of
Grimm \& Railsback 2005).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check:} Two black-footed ferret populations both have
mean \(\lambda_1 = 1.02\). Population A has \(N = 500\); population B
has \(N = 25\). Why does the IBM extinction probability differ vastly
between them despite identical mean growth rates? What would a
deterministic model predict?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{7D Population Viability Analysis
(PVA)}\label{d-population-viability-analysis-pva}

\textbf{Population viability analysis} integrates matrix models and
stochastic simulation into a quantitative extinction-risk forecast. PVA
is the formal answer to ``How long does this species have, and what
intervention buys the most time?'' --- required by the U.S. Endangered
Species Act, the IUCN Red List Criterion E, and most national recovery
plans.

\subsubsection{Inputs to a PVA}\label{inputs-to-a-pva}

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2400}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5600}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Input
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Source
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Why it matters
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Stage- or age-specific vital rates & Mark-recapture, life table & Mean
dynamics \\
Variance in vital rates & Long-term monitoring & Environmental
stochasticity \\
Catastrophe frequency and severity & Disturbance history & Tail risk
(fire, disease, storm) \\
Density dependence (often theta-logistic,
\cref{eq:population_ecology_11}) & Time-series fits & Carrying-capacity
feedback \\
Initial age/stage distribution & Field census & Starting condition \\
Habitat capacity \(K\) & Resource estimates & Ceiling on population \\
Inbreeding cost on vital rates & Pedigree or ROH & Genetic stochasticity
(link to \cref{sec:unit_X_biomes_and_conservation}) \\
\end{longtable}
}

\subsubsection{Outputs and Decision
Rules}\label{outputs-and-decision-rules}

The two headline outputs are \textbf{extinction probability}
\(P_{ext}(T)\) over a horizon \(T\) (commonly 100 years or 100
generations) and \textbf{mean time to extinction} \(\bar{T}_{ext}\).

\begin{equation}
P_{ext}(T) = \Pr\bigl(\,N(t) < N_{\text{crit}}\ \text{for some } t \le T\bigr)
\label{eq:unit_X_extinction_probability}
\end{equation}

The threshold \(N_{\text{crit}}\) (often called the
\textbf{quasi-extinction threshold}) is set above zero --- typically the
Allee threshold \(A\) (\cref{eq:population_ecology_13}) or a number
below which the population is ``functionally extinct.'' Hitting
\(N_{\text{crit}}\) counts as failure even if the simulation has not
bottomed out.

The \textbf{minimum viable population (MVP)} in standard usage is the
smallest \(N_0\) such that \(P_{ext}(100\,\text{yr}) \le 0.05\). Reed et
al.~(2003, \emph{Biol. Conserv.}) reviewed PVAs across 102 vertebrates
and found MVPs clustering at 5,000--7,000 adults --- far above the
classical \(N_e = 500\) rule of thumb (which ignores demographic and
environmental stochasticity) and a key empirical result that pushed
conservation toward the \textbf{100/1000 rule} discussed in
\cref{sec:unit_X_biomes_and_conservation}.

\subsubsection{Worked Example --- California Condor
PVA}\label{worked-example-california-condor-pva}

In 1982 the known California condor (\emph{Gymnogyps californianus})
population had fallen to 22 birds. A PVA built around captive-breeding
fecundity, juvenile mortality from lead poisoning, and stochastic
catastrophe (wildfire) gave \(P_{ext}(50\,\text{yr}) > 0.99\) for the
no-intervention scenario. The same model showed
\(P_{ext}(50\,\text{yr}) < 0.10\) if (i) the remaining birds were
captured for breeding, and (ii) released birds were protected from lead
ammunition. The captive-breeding decision, controversial at the time,
was justified directly by PVA elasticities --- adult survival and
juvenile lead mortality had the largest leverage on \(\lambda_1\). The
wild population is now \textgreater{} 250 (see
\cref{sec:unit_X_biomes_and_conservation}).

\subsubsection{Limitations and Honest
Use}\label{limitations-and-honest-use}

PVA outputs depend on the model structure, input data, and uncertainty
assumptions; small-population data are often sparse and biased toward
observed survivors. Best practice (Beissinger \& Westphal 1998, \emph{J.
Wildl. Manage.}):

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Treat absolute \(P_{ext}\) values with skepticism; use \emph{relative}
  comparisons across management scenarios
\item
  Report sensitivity to parameter uncertainty (Monte Carlo over input
  distributions)
\item
  Update PVAs as monitoring data accumulate --- they are living tools,
  not one-off reports
\item
  Avoid the temptation to over-parameterise; structural uncertainty
  often exceeds parameter uncertainty
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check:} A PVA gives \(P_{ext}(100\,\text{yr}) = 0.30\)
under current management and 0.05 under a proposed habitat-corridor
intervention. Should you trust the absolute numbers, the difference, or
both? What three sources of uncertainty would you investigate before
recommending the corridor?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Metapopulation Dynamics}\label{metapopulation-dynamics}

A \textbf{metapopulation} (Levins 1969; Hanski 1994) is a ``population
of populations'' --- a set of spatially separated subpopulations
(patches) connected by dispersal. Local extinctions are balanced by
recolonisation from other patches.

In conservation practice, the important question is usually whether
dispersal is functional, not whether habitat patches are merely drawn on
a map. Roads, dams, fences, heat waves, disease, and behavioural
avoidance can lower effective colonisation even when patches appear
close. Corridor design therefore needs demographic monitoring, genetic
connectivity, mortality-risk mapping, and sensitivity analysis for \(c\)
and \(e\), because a corridor that increases movement can still fail if
it also increases mortality or spreads disease.

\subsubsection{The Levins Model}\label{the-levins-model}

\begin{equation}
\frac{dp}{dt} = cp(1-p) - ep
\label{eq:population_ecology_18}
\end{equation}

where: - \(p\) = proportion of occupied patches - \(c\) = colonisation
rate - \(e\) = extinction rate per patch

At equilibrium: \(\hat{p} = 1 - e/c\)

The metapopulation persists if \(e/c < 1\) (colonisation rate exceeds
extinction rate). If habitat patches are destroyed (reducing total
patches available), the effective \(c\) decreases, potentially pushing
\(e/c > 1\) and causing \textbf{metapopulation collapse}.

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Source-Sink Dynamics
\citep{pulliam1988}}{Source-Sink Dynamics}}\label{source-sink-dynamics}

Patches differ in leverage:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4000}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4400}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1600}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Patch type
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Growth rate
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Role
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Source} & \(\lambda > 1\) & Produces surplus individuals; net
emigration \\
\textbf{Sink} & \(\lambda < 1\) & Cannot sustain itself; relies on
immigration from sources \\
\end{longtable}
}

A population can persist in sink habitats indefinitely if immigration
from sources is sufficient. This has profound conservation implications:
protecting source habitats is critical, while sink habitats may appear
to support populations but are ``ecological traps'' without the source.

\subsubsection{Rescue Effect and
Connectivity}\label{rescue-effect-and-connectivity}

The \textbf{rescue effect} (Brown \& Kodric-Brown 1977): immigration
from nearby patches prevents or delays local extinction. This means: -
Closely spaced patches have lower extinction rates - Habitat corridors
increase connectivity and reduce local extinction - Isolation increases
both extinction probability and time to recolonisation

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check:} A metapopulation has 100 habitat patches with
\(c = 0.3\) and \(e = 0.1\). Calculate the equilibrium proportion of
occupied patches. If 40\% of patches are destroyed (reducing total to 60
patches), what happens to the metapopulation? (Consider how reduced
patch number affects colonisation rate.)
\end{quote}

\subsection{Estimating Population
Size}\label{estimating-population-size}

\subsubsection{Mark-Recapture Methods}\label{mark-recapture-methods}

The \textbf{Lincoln-Petersen method} (simplest mark-recapture) estimates
population size from two sampling events:

\begin{equation}
\hat{N} = \frac{M \cdot C}{R}
\label{eq:population_ecology_19}
\end{equation}

where: - \(M\) = number marked and released in first sample - \(C\) =
total captured in second sample - \(R\) = number of marked individuals
recaptured

\textbf{Assumptions:} (1) Closed population (no births, deaths,
immigration, emigration between samples), (2) marks are not lost, (3)
marked and unmarked individuals have equal capture probability, (4)
marks do not affect survival.

\textbf{Chapman's correction} for small samples:

\begin{equation}
\hat{N} = \frac{(M+1)(C+1)}{R+1} - 1
\label{eq:population_ecology_20}
\end{equation}

\textbf{Jolly-Seber method} --- for open populations with multiple
sampling occasions. Estimates \(N\), survival rate (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\varphi}}{phi}), and recruitment
(\(B\)) at each time point. Computationally intensive; requires at least
3 capture occasions.

\subsubsection{Distance Sampling}\label{distance-sampling}

\textbf{Line transect distance sampling} estimates density from the
perpendicular distances of detected objects from the transect line:

\begin{equation}
\hat{D} = \frac{n \cdot \hat{f}(0)}{2L}
\label{eq:population_ecology_21}
\end{equation}

where \(n\) = number detected, \(L\) = total transect length,
\(\hat{f}(0)\) = estimated probability density function of detection
distances evaluated at zero distance. The key assumption is that most
objects on the line are detected (\(g(0) = 1\)).

\begin{quote}
\texorpdfstring{}{} \textbf{Clinical Connection --- Epidemiological Surveillance:}
Mark-recapture methodology has been adapted for human epidemiology as
\textbf{capture-recapture estimation} to estimate the completeness of
disease registries. For example, comparing hospital records with death
certificates as two independent ``captures'' allows estimation of the
true number of opioid overdose deaths, accounting for under-reporting.
The WHO uses this approach for HIV prevalence estimation in populations
where direct surveys are impractical.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Human Population
Demographics}\label{human-population-demographics}

The global human population reached 8 billion in November 2022. The UN
World Population Prospects 2024 projects continued growth to about 10.3
billion in the mid-2080s, followed by a slight decline toward about 10.2
billion by 2100 \citep{un2024population}. Treat this as a scenario-based
projection rather than a fixed destiny: fertility, mortality, migration,
policy, and environmental stress can shift regional trajectories.

\subsubsection{Age Structure and Population
Pyramids}\label{age-structure-and-population-pyramids}

The \textbf{age structure} of a population determines its future growth
trajectory:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Expansive pyramid} (broad base): high proportion of
  pre-reproductive individuals; rapid growth (e.g., Nigeria,
  \(r \approx 0.025\)/yr)
\item
  \textbf{Stationary pyramid} (column shape): roughly equal proportions
  across age classes; near-zero growth (e.g., USA,
  \(r \approx 0.002\)/yr)
\item
  \textbf{Constrictive pyramid} (narrow base): higher proportion of
  older individuals; declining population (e.g., Japan,
  \(r \approx -0.006\)/yr)
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Population momentum:} Even after fertility drops to replacement
level (\(R_0 = 1\)), a population with an expansive age structure
continues growing for decades because the large cohort of young people
has not yet reproduced. This explains why the world population will
continue growing despite declining global fertility rates (from 5.3 in
1963 to 2.3 in 2023).

\subsubsection{Total Fertility Rate (TFR) and Replacement
Level}\label{total-fertility-rate-tfr-and-replacement-level}

The \textbf{total fertility rate} is the average number of children born
to a woman over her lifetime. \textbf{Replacement-level fertility} is
TFR \(\approx 2.1\) in developed nations (slightly above 2 to account
for child mortality). In 2023, global TFR was 2.3 --- barely above
replacement.

\textbf{Demographic dividend:} Countries in mid-transition (declining
fertility, large working-age cohort, low dependency ratio) experience
accelerated economic growth. East Asia (1965-1990) and sub-Saharan
Africa (projected 2030-2060) demonstrate this phenomenon.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Worked Examples}\label{worked-examples-3}

\subsubsection{Worked Example 1: Leslie Matrix
Projection}\label{worked-example-1-leslie-matrix-projection}

\textbf{Problem:} A 3-age-class population (juvenile, subadult, adult)
has Leslie matrix
\[\mathbf{L} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1.2 & 3.0 \\ 0.4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.6 & 0.7 \end{pmatrix} \label{eq:unit_X_population_ecology_item_1}\]

with initial vector \(\mathbf{n}(0) = (40, 20, 10)^T\). (a) Project the
population one time step. (b) Compute \(\lambda_1\) and decide whether
the population is growing, stable, or declining.

\textbf{Solution:}

\textbf{Step 1. One-step projection.}
\(\mathbf{n}(1) = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{n}(0)\) -
\(n_0(1) = 0 \cdot 40 + 1.2 \cdot 20 + 3.0 \cdot 10 = 54\) -
\(n_1(1) = 0.4 \cdot 40 + 0 + 0 = 16\) -
\(n_2(1) = 0 + 0.6 \cdot 20 + 0.7 \cdot 10 = 19\) - Total: \(N(1) = 89\)
vs.~\(N(0) = 70\) --- apparent growth, but transient.

\textbf{Step 2. Characteristic polynomial.} The asymptotic rate
\(\lambda_1\) solves
\(\det(\mathbf{L} - \lambda \mathbf{I}) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; -\lambda^3 + 0.7\lambda^2 + 0.48\lambda + 0.72 = 0\)

Numerical root-finding gives \(\lambda_1 \approx 1.094\).

\textbf{Step 3. Interpretation.} Because \(\lambda_1 > 1\), the
population grows asymptotically at \(\sim 9.4\%\) per time step once it
converges to its stable age distribution. The transient ratio
\(89/70 = 1.27\) overstates long-run growth because the initial vector
is juvenile-heavy.

\textbf{Answer:} \(\lambda_1 \approx 1.09\); the population is
\textbf{growing} in the long run.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsubsection{Worked Example 2 --- Mark-Recapture
Estimation}\label{worked-example-2-mark-recapture-estimation}

\textbf{Problem:} A population ecologist uses the mark-recapture method
to estimate the size of a grasshopper population in a meadow. On the
first day, she captures, marks, and releases 120 grasshoppers (\(M\)).
On the second day, she captures a total of 150 grasshoppers (\(C\)), of
which 30 are marked (\(R\)). Calculate the estimated population size
(\(N\)).

\textbf{Solution:}

\textbf{Step 1. Identify the given variables.} - Number marked in first
sample (\(M\)) = 120 - Total number in second sample (\(C\)) = 150 -
Number of marked recaptures (\(R\)) = 30

\textbf{Step 2. Use the Lincoln-Petersen estimator.} The formula for the
total population size (\(N\)) is:
\[N = \frac{M \times C}{R} \label{eq:unit_X_population_ecology_item_2}\]

\textbf{Step 3. Calculate \(N\).}
\[N = \frac{120 \times 150}{30} \label{eq:unit_X_population_ecology_item_3}\]

\[N = \frac{18,000}{30} \label{eq:unit_X_population_ecology_item_4}\]

\[N = 600 \label{eq:unit_X_population_ecology_item_5}\]

\textbf{Answer:} The estimated size of the grasshopper population is
\textbf{600 individuals}.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-34}

For \textbf{Population Ecology and Growth Models}, frontier biology
belongs inside the evidence logic of the chapter. Ecology and
conservation decisions increasingly combine field data, remote sensing,
community knowledge, model uncertainty, and explicit values. The core
reading question is this: population claims require density dependence,
demographic stochasticity, dispersal, age structure, and management
objective.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

Use biodiversity metrics carefully: population indices, extinction risk
categories, ecosystem services, and management targets answer different
questions
\citep{ipbes2019global,ipbes2024transformative,wwf2024livingplanet,iucn2025redlist,fao2024sofia}.

\textbf{Source practice:} For conservation claims, cite assessment
sources and state whether the evidence is a population index,
extinction-risk assessment, ecosystem-service valuation, satellite
product, or policy synthesis
\citep{ipbes2024transformative,noaa2025coralbleaching,fao2025sofi}.

\subsection{Key Terms}\label{key-terms-34}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2857}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.7143}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Term
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Definition
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Carrying capacity (\(K\))} & Maximum population size supported
by a given environment \\
\textbf{Intrinsic rate of increase (\(r\))} & Per capita growth rate in
ideal conditions (\(= b - d\)) \\
\textbf{Net reproductive rate (\(R_0\))} & Mean lifetime offspring per
individual; \(R_0 > 1\) means growing \\
\textbf{Allee effect} & Positive density-dependence; fitness decreases
at low \(N\) \\
\textbf{Allee threshold (\(A\))} & \(N\) below which population declines
deterministically (strong Allee effect) \\
\textbf{Competition coefficient (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha})} & Per-capita interspecific
competition effect \\
\textbf{Competitive exclusion} & One species eliminates another when
niches overlap completely \\
\textbf{Maximum sustainable yield (MSY)} & \(rK/4\); optimal harvest at
\(N = K/2\) \\
\textbf{\hyperref[gl:lotka-volterra-equations]{Lotka-Volterra
equations}} & ODEs describing competition and predator-prey dynamics \\
\textbf{Bet-hedging} & Variable reproductive strategy reducing variance
in fitness \\
\textbf{Functional response} & Per-capita predation rate as a function
of prey density (Types I, II, III) \\
\textbf{Metapopulation} & Network of subpopulations connected by
dispersal; local extinction balanced by recolonisation \\
\textbf{Source-sink dynamics} & Source patches (\(\lambda > 1\)) sustain
sink patches (\(\lambda < 1\)) via emigration \\
\textbf{Mark-recapture} & Method for estimating population size using
marked individuals \\
\textbf{Reproductive value (\(v_x\))} & Expected future contribution of
age-\(x\) individual to population growth \\
\textbf{Demographic transition} & Shift from high birth/death rates to
low birth/death rates during development \\
\textbf{Theta-logistic model} & Extension of logistic growth with
flexible density-dependence exponent \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\theta}}{theta} \\
\textbf{Survivorship curve} & Plot of proportion surviving (\(l_x\))
vs.~age; Types I (late loss), II (constant), III (early loss) \\
\textbf{Leslie matrix} & Age-structured projection matrix; dominant
eigenvalue \(= \lambda_1\) \\
\textbf{Sensitivity / Elasticity} &
\(\partial \lambda_1/\partial a_{ij}\) (absolute) and proportional
analogue; identify highest-leverage rate \\
\textbf{Stable age distribution} & Right eigenvector of Leslie matrix;
long-run age proportions \\
\textbf{Individual-based model (IBM)} & Stochastic simulation tracking
each organism; captures demographic stochasticity and heterogeneity \\
\textbf{Population viability analysis (PVA)} & Stochastic projection of
extinction probability over a fixed horizon \\
\textbf{Quasi-extinction threshold} & \(N_{\text{crit}}\) below which a
population is treated as functionally extinct in PVA \\
\end{longtable}
}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Review Questions}\label{review-questions-34}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  A whale population has \(R_0 = 0.95\) and \(T = 20\) years. Estimate
  \(r\). Is this population growing or declining? Calculate how many
  years until the population halves. What conservation interventions
  could change the trajectory?
\item
  Explain why maximum sustainable yield \(\text{MSY} = rK/4\). A
  fisheries manager observes that the current catch equals MSY but the
  population continues to decline. Identify at least three reasons why
  this might occur despite apparently sustainable harvest levels.
\item
  A large predator population is reintroduced into a prey-depleted
  ecosystem with 40 prey individuals remaining. The predator's Allee
  threshold is \(A = 100\). Quantitatively predict whether the predator
  population will recover. What two conditions must simultaneously be
  met for recovery?
\item
  Two grass species compete: \(\alpha_{12} = 0.8\),
  \(\alpha_{21} = 0.7\), \(K_1 = 1000\), \(K_2 = 900\). Use phase-plane
  analysis to determine whether stable coexistence, competitive
  exclusion, or priority effect is predicted. Show your work by
  comparing isocline intercepts.
\item
  Compare the lynx-hare cycle with a simple Lotka-Volterra prediction.
  What additional factors (beyond \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\delta}}{delta}, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma} parameters) are needed to
  explain the observed 10-year periodicity? Cite at least one primary
  study.
\item
  A metapopulation of a rare butterfly occupies 25 of 100 available
  habitat patches. The colonisation rate is \(c = 0.15\) and extinction
  rate is \(e = 0.05\). (a) Calculate the expected equilibrium
  occupancy. (b) A highway project will destroy 30 patches. Will the
  metapopulation persist? (c) What colonisation rate would be needed to
  maintain the same equilibrium occupancy after the loss, with 70
  patches remaining?
\item
  You capture 200 salamanders from a pond, mark them, and release them.
  Two weeks later, you capture 250 salamanders and find that 40 are
  marked. (a) Estimate the population size using the Lincoln-Petersen
  method. (b) List three assumptions of this method and describe how
  violating each would bias your estimate.
\item
  Using the concept of reproductive value, explain why protecting adult
  female sea turtles (through Turtle Excluder Devices in fishing nets)
  is more effective for population recovery than protecting eggs on
  nesting beaches.
\item
  Japan has a current population of 125 million and
  \(r \approx -0.006\)/yr. Assuming constant \(r\), project the
  population in 2050, 2075, and 2100. What demographic, economic, and
  social challenges does population decline create?
\item
  The St.~Matthew Island reindeer population grew from 29 to 6,000 in 19
  years, then crashed to 42. (a) Calculate \(r\) during the growth
  phase. (b) What caused the crash in ecological terms? (c) How does
  this case study illustrate the limitations of exponential growth
  models?
\item
  From \texttt{logistic\_growth}, read off \(N(t)\) near \(K/2\) and
  relate to MSY management targets.
\item
  When does the Levins metapopulation model \(\hat p = 1 - e/c\) predict
  \textbf{rescue} vs.~extinction?
\item
  A 4-stage Leslie matrix yields elasticities \(e_{F_3} = 0.08\) (adult
  fecundity), \(e_{P_1} = 0.32\) (juvenile\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}subadult survival),
  \(e_{P_2} = 0.34\) (subadult\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}adult survival), \(e_{P_3} = 0.26\)
  (adult survival). A wildlife agency proposes (i) doubling clutch size
  via supplemental feeding or (ii) a 5\% absolute increase in subadult
  survival. Which delivers more growth, and what does the elasticity
  comparison imply about the limits of headcount-centered conservation?
\item
  Explain why an individual-based model and a deterministic Leslie
  matrix model can give the same \(\lambda_1\) yet completely different
  extinction predictions for a small population. Under what conditions
  do the two approaches converge?
\item
  Sketch the workflow of a PVA for a critically endangered amphibian:
  (a) what data must be collected, (b) how is the quasi-extinction
  threshold \(N_{\text{crit}}\) chosen, (c) why are \emph{relative}
  comparisons across management scenarios more defensible than absolute
  extinction probabilities?
\end{enumerate}
