\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-34}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Demographics:} \(r = b - d\); \(R_0 = \sum l_x m_x\); doubling
  time \(= \ln 2/r\); generation time
  \(T = \sum x \cdot l_x m_x / R_0\). Euler-Lotka equation provides
  exact relationship.
\item
  \textbf{Dispersion patterns:} clumped (most common), uniform, random
  --- detected by variance-to-mean ratio.
\item
  \textbf{Survivorship curves:} Type I (late loss, K-selected), Type II
  (constant), Type III (early loss, r-selected). Gompertz law for human
  mortality.
\item
  \textbf{Logistic growth:} \(dN/dt = rN(1 - N/K)\); inflection at
  \(K/2\); MSY \(= rK/4\). Extensions: theta-logistic, time-lagged
  logistic.
\item
  \textbf{Allee effect:} \(dN/dt < 0\) below threshold \(A\); threatens
  small surviving populations. Component vs.~demographic Allee effects.
\item
  \textbf{LV competition:} stable coexistence requires niche
  differentiation (\(\alpha_{12}\alpha_{21} < 1\)); otherwise exclusion
  or priority effects. Chesson's theory: stabilising + equalising
  mechanisms.
\item
  \textbf{LV predator-prey:} neutral oscillations; period
  \(\approx 2\pi/\sqrt{\alpha\gamma}\); lynx-hare 10-yr cycle requires
  tri-trophic explanation.
\item
  \textbf{Functional responses:} Type I (linear), Type II (decelerating,
  Holling disc equation), Type III (sigmoidal, stabilising).
\item
  \textbf{Age-structured models:} Leslie matrix \(\mathbf{L}\) with
  fecundities on top row and survivorships on sub-diagonal; dominant
  eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\) = asymptotic growth rate; right and left
  eigenvectors give stable age distribution and reproductive value.
  \textbf{Sensitivity} \(s_{ij} = \partial \lambda_1/\partial a_{ij}\)
  and \textbf{elasticity} \(e_{ij}\) identify highest-leverage
  demographic rates (loggerhead turtle adult survival \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} TEDs).
\item
  \textbf{Individual-based models (IBMs):} stochastic agent-based
  simulations capture demographic stochasticity, individual
  heterogeneity, and emergent dynamics that mean-field models miss.
\item
  \textbf{Population viability analysis (PVA):} integrates matrix and
  stochastic machinery into extinction-probability forecasts;
  quasi-extinction threshold \(N_{\text{crit}}\); empirical MVPs cluster
  at 5,000--7,000 adults (Reed et al.~2003), well above the classical
  \(N_e = 500\) rule.
\item
  \textbf{r vs.~K continuum:} life-history trade-offs shaped by habitat
  stability; superseded by Stearns' and Grime's frameworks; bet-hedging
  in variable environments.
\item
  \textbf{Metapopulations:} Levins model (\(\hat{p} = 1 - e/c\));
  source-sink dynamics; rescue effect. Habitat corridors increase
  connectivity.
\item
  \textbf{Population estimation:} mark-recapture (Lincoln-Petersen,
  Jolly-Seber), distance sampling.
\item
  \textbf{Human demographics:} 8 billion (2022); demographic transition;
  population momentum; TFR declining globally.
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See \cref{sec:unit_X_community_ecology} for
  species interactions, \cref{sec:unit_V_population_genetics} for
  \hyperref[gl:allele]{\textbf{allele}} frequencies in subdivided
  populations, and Unit VI for life-history evolution.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-35}

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Define a community and categorise the six types of biotic interactions
  with examples.
\item
  Apply Lotka-Volterra competition equations to predict competitive
  outcomes and explain the
  \hyperref[gl:competitive-exclusion]{\textbf{competitive exclusion}}
  principle and \hyperref[gl:niche]{\textbf{niche}} theory.
\item
  Explain \hyperref[gl:trophic-cascade]{\textbf{trophic cascade}}s and
  keystone \citep{paine1966} species with quantitative examples.
\item
  Compare primary and
  \hyperref[gl:secondary-succession]{\textbf{secondary succession}} and
  explain the intermediate disturbance \citep{connell1978} hypothesis.
\item
  Calculate Shannon diversity (H'), Simpson index, and species evenness
  and explain what each measures.
\item
  Apply \hyperref[gl:island-biogeography]{\textbf{island biogeography}}
  theory, the
  \hyperref[gl:species-area-relationship]{\textbf{species-area
  relationship}}, and SLOSS debate to conservation design.
\item
  Describe the role of disturbance, facilitation, and alternative stable
  states in shaping communities.
\item
  Explain food web topology, connectance, network robustness, and the
  relationship between complexity and stability.
\item
  Compare niche-based and neutral theories of biodiversity, and explain
  when each null model is appropriate.
\item
  Use functional traits (CSR strategies, leaf economics spectrum) to
  predict community assembly and ecosystem function beyond species
  lists.
\item
  Distinguish classical, augmentative, and conservation biological
  control, and evaluate their risk profiles using community ecology
  principles.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Opening Vignette --- How Wolves Changed Rivers}

In 1995, 14 gray wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park
after a 70-year absence. What happened next has become one of ecology's
most vivid demonstrations of a trophic cascade. With predators back, elk
avoided grazing in valleys and riverside areas where they were
vulnerable. Vegetation in those areas --- willows, aspens, cottonwoods
--- rebounded within years. With trees stabilising river banks, erosion
slowed. Beaver colonies, dependent on willows, increased sixfold. Beaver
dams created wetlands that supported fish, otters, ducks, and
amphibians. River channels narrowed and meandered, becoming more
complex. The wolves, through fear alone --- the ``landscape of fear''
effect documented by William Ripple --- had changed the physical
geography of the park. The Yellowstone study has been cited thousands of
times, popularised by a viral YouTube video with 40 million views, and
debated (some effects took decades to show). But it remains the
canonical example that removing or restoring apex predators cascades
through every \hyperref[gl:trophic-level]{\textbf{trophic level}} of a
community.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{Chapter Roadmap}\label{chapter-roadmap-13}

This is a long chapter that covers eight closely-related but
distinguishable topics. Read it as \emph{two halves}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Part A --- Local interactions between species:} what happens
  when two or a few species meet. The chapter begins with community
  definitions, then develops competition, predation and trophic
  cascades, \hyperref[gl:mutualism]{\textbf{mutualism}}, and parasitism.
\item
  \textbf{Part B --- Community-scale patterns and assembly:} what
  emerges when you scale up. Succession, diversity measurement, island
  biogeography, and food-web network structure become the organising
  themes.
\item
  \textbf{Part C --- Process-level theory and applications:} neutral
  theory supplies a null model for biodiversity; trait-based ecology
  (CSR, leaf economics) predicts ecosystem function; biological control
  applies the entire chapter to pests and disease vectors.
\end{itemize}

If you are reading for a one-semester survey, Part A supplies the
mechanistic vocabulary and Part B supplies the integrative patterns.
Part C provides the modern frameworks and applied translations.
Instructors wanting to split the chapter over two lectures can use the
Part-A/Part-B boundary; a third lecture can cover Part C.

\subsection{Community Ecology
Fundamentals}\label{community-ecology-fundamentals}

An \textbf{ecological community} is an assemblage of populations of
different species occupying the same region and time, interacting with
each other and their \hyperref[gl:abiotic]{\textbf{abiotic}}
environment. Community ecology analyses the \textbf{biotic interactions}
among species and their effects on community structure --- species
composition and relative abundance --- as well as the processes driving
community assembly and succession.

\subsubsection{Emergent Properties of
Communities}\label{emergent-properties-of-communities}

Communities possess properties that cannot be predicted from studying
individual species in isolation:

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}

\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Property
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Definition

Measurement
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Species richness (\(S\))} & Number of species present & Count of
unique species \\
\textbf{Species evenness} & How equal are species abundances? & Pielou's
\(J'\) \\
\textbf{Diversity} & Combined richness and evenness & Shannon \(H'\),
Simpson \(1-D\) \\
\textbf{Community structure} & Food web topology, trophic levels,
functional groups & Network analysis, connectance \\
\textbf{Resistance} & Ability to withstand perturbation without change &
Deviation from baseline after disturbance \\
\textbf{Resilience} & Speed of return to baseline after perturbation &
Recovery time \\
\textbf{Rank-abundance distribution} & Pattern of relative abundance
across species & Log-normal, geometric series, broken stick \\
\end{longtable}

\subsubsection{Rank-Abundance Models}\label{rank-abundance-models}

The distribution of individuals among species in a community follows
predictable patterns:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1163}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1628}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3256}}

\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Model
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Pattern
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Interpretation
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Typical community
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Geometric series} & Steep, convex & Strong dominance; niche
pre-emption & Species-poor, harsh environments \\
\textbf{Log-series} & Moderate slope & Many rare species, few common &
Island faunas, successional communities \\
\textbf{Log-normal} & Moderate, symmetric bell curve on log scale & Most
natural communities & Large, undisturbed communities \\
\textbf{Broken stick} & Shallow, even & Resources divided equally &
Species-poor, saturated communities \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Preston's canonical log-normal} (1962): In most large
communities, when species are binned by abundance in octaves
(doublings), the distribution is approximately log-normal. This has deep
connections to the species-area relationship.

\subsubsection{Types of Biotic
Interactions}\label{types-of-biotic-interactions}

\subsection{Competition Theory}\label{competition-theory}

\subsubsection{Lotka-Volterra Interspecific
Competition}\label{lotka-volterra-interspecific-competition}

Two competing species \(N_1\) and \(N_2\) with shared resources are
modelled by:

\begin{equation}
\frac{dN_1}{dt} = r_1 N_1 \left(1 - \frac{N_1 + \alpha_{12} N_2}{K_1}\right)
\label{eq:community_ecology_1}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
\frac{dN_2}{dt} = r_2 N_2 \left(1 - \frac{N_2 + \alpha_{21} N_1}{K_2}\right)
\label{eq:community_ecology_2}
\end{equation}

where: - \(\alpha_{12}\) = competitive effect of species 2 on species 1
(per individual) - \(\alpha_{21}\) = competitive effect of species 1 on
species 2 - \(K_1\), \(K_2\) = carrying capacities of each species

\textbf{Isocline analysis:} Four outcomes depending on isocline
intersections: 1. \textbf{Species 1 wins:} \(K_1 > K_2/\alpha_{12}\) AND
\(K_1/\alpha_{21} > K_2\) 2. \textbf{Species 2 wins:}
\(K_2 > K_1/\alpha_{21}\) AND \(K_2/\alpha_{12} > K_1\) (symmetric case)
3. \textbf{Unstable equilibrium (priority effect):}
\(K_1 > K_2/\alpha_{12}\) AND \(K_2 > K_1/\alpha_{21}\) --- whoever
starts higher wins 4. \textbf{Stable coexistence:}
\(K_1 < K_2/\alpha_{12}\) AND \(K_2 < K_1/\alpha_{21}\) ---
interspecific competition weaker than intraspecific

\subsubsection{Competitive Exclusion Principle (Gause's
Law)}\label{competitive-exclusion-principle-gauses-law}

\textbf{\citet{gause1934}:} Two species competing for the same limiting
resource cannot stably coexist; the superior competitor excludes the
other. Demonstrated with \emph{Paramecium aurelia} vs.~\emph{P.
caudatum} grown together on a single bacterial food source --- \emph{P.
aurelia} consistently drove \emph{P. caudatum} to extinction within 20
days.

\textbf{Important qualifications:} Competitive exclusion requires (1)
complete niche overlap, (2) constant environment, (3) no spatial
refugia, and (4) sufficient time. In nature, these conditions are rarely
fully met.

\subsubsection{Hutchinson's Niche
Concept}\label{hutchinsons-niche-concept}

\textbf{Fundamental niche} \citep{hutchinson1957}: the n-dimensional
hypervolume of environmental conditions and resources permitting a
species to maintain \(r \geq 0\).

\textbf{Realised niche:} the subset of the fundamental niche actually
occupied after accounting for interspecific competition, predation, and
other biotic interactions. Typically smaller than or equal to the
fundamental niche.

\begin{equation}
\text{Realised niche} = \text{Fundamental niche} - \text{Competitive exclusion zone}
\label{eq:community_ecology_3}
\end{equation}

\textbf{Hutchinson's paradox of the plankton} (1961): Why do hundreds of
phytoplankton species coexist in the apparently homogeneous water
column, most competing for the same light and nutrients? Violates
competitive exclusion. Solutions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Temporal niche partitioning} --- seasonal turnover,
  disturbance prevents equilibrium
\item
  \textbf{Spatial heterogeneity} --- microscale gradients in light,
  nutrients, turbulence
\item
  \textbf{Predation (selective grazing)} --- zooplankton preferentially
  graze \hyperref[gl:dominant]{\textbf{dominant}} species
\item
  \textbf{Allelopathy} --- chemical warfare among phytoplankton
\item
  \textbf{Non-equilibrium dynamics} --- the system rarely reaches
  competitive exclusion
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Modern Coexistence Theory
\citep{chesson2000}}{Modern Coexistence Theory}}\label{modern-coexistence-theory}

Coexistence requires that \textbf{intraspecific competition
\textgreater{} interspecific competition} for both species. This is
enabled by two classes of mechanisms:

\textbf{Stabilising mechanisms} (niche differences): - \textbf{Resource
partitioning:} different foods, microhabitats, activity times -
\textbf{Janzen-Connell effect:} species-specific enemies concentrate
near conspecifics, giving heterospecifics an advantage - \textbf{Storage
effect:} temporal environmental variation favours different species at
different times; long-lived adults ``store'' good years -
\textbf{Relative nonlinearity:} species respond differently to resource
fluctuations

\textbf{Equalising mechanisms} (fitness similarity): - Trade-offs
between competitive ability and other traits (dispersal, stress
tolerance) - Similar per-capita growth rates at low density

The mathematical condition for coexistence is:

\begin{equation}
\rho < \frac{\kappa_j}{\kappa_i} < \frac{1}{\rho}
\label{eq:community_ecology_4}
\end{equation}

where \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\rho}}{rho} = niche overlap (0 to 1) and \(\kappa_i/\kappa_j\) = fitness
ratio. Lower \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\rho}}{rho} (more niche differentiation) allows greater fitness
inequality.

\begin{quote}
\texorpdfstring{}{} \textbf{Clinical Connection --- Competitive Exclusion in the
\hyperref[gl:microbiome]{\textbf{Microbiome}}:} The competitive
exclusion principle operates within the human gut microbiome.
\textbf{Clostridium difficile} infection (CDI) typically occurs after
antibiotic treatment eliminates normal gut flora, removing competitive
exclusion and allowing \emph{C. difficile} to proliferate unopposed.
\textbf{Fecal \hyperref[gl:microbiota]{\textbf{microbiota}}
transplantation (FMT)} restores competitive exclusion by reintroducing a
diverse microbial community, achieving about 90\% cure rates
for recurrent CDI. This is Gause's principle applied to clinical
medicine.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Predation, Keystone Species, and Trophic

\subsubsection{Predator-Prey Arms Races}\label{predator-prey-arms-races}

\hyperref[gl:coevolution]{\textbf{Coevolution}} \citep{ehrlich1964}
between predators and prey drives a Red Queen dynamic of escalating
adaptations:

\textbf{Anti-predator defences:}

\textbf{Counter-adaptations in predators:} - \textbf{Kingsnakes}
(\emph{Lampropeltis}) evolved resistance to rattlesnake venom -
\textbf{Rough-skinned newt} (\emph{Taricha granulosa})
vs.~\textbf{garter snake} (\emph{Thamnophis sirtalis}): escalating toxin
(tetrodotoxin) and resistance --- one of the best-documented
coevolutionary arms races \citep{brodie1999} - \textbf{Cuckoo}
(\emph{Cuculus canorus}) egg mimicry vs.~host egg discrimination ---
classic parasitic arms race

\subsubsection{Hare-Lynx Cycle}\label{hare-lynx-cycle}

\emph{Lepus americanus} (snowshoe hare) and \emph{Lynx canadensis} show
coupled about 10-year population cycles in boreal Canada.
Hudson's Bay Company fur trading records from 1736-1940 reveal the
cycle. Modern analysis:

\begin{equation}
\frac{dH}{dt} = r_{max}H - aPH \qquad \frac{dP}{dt} = b \cdot a \cdot P \cdot H - dP
\label{eq:community_ecology_5}
\end{equation}

The cycle is driven by multiple feedback loops: 1. \textbf{Predation}
(about 60\% of cycle) --- lynx consumption drives hare decline
2. \textbf{Food quality} (about 20\%) --- hare overgrazing
induces phenolic toughening of willow/birch browse 3. \textbf{Stress
physiology} (about 20\%) --- predation risk elevates
\hyperref[gl:cortisol]{\textbf{cortisol}}, suppressing reproduction 4.
True cycles require \textbf{tri-trophic} feedbacks; purely
Lotka-Volterra predation alone is insufficient (Krebs et al.~2001,
\emph{Science})

\subsubsection{Keystone Species}\label{keystone-species}

A \textbf{\hyperref[gl:keystone-species]{keystone species}} (Paine 1966,
1969) has disproportionately large effects on community structure
relative to its abundance. Removal of the keystone causes dramatic
community reorganisation.

\textbf{Types of keystone effects:}

create wetland habitat for diverse communities \\

\subsubsection{Trophic Cascades}\label{trophic-cascades}

A \textbf{trophic cascade} occurs when changes at one trophic level
ripple through the food web to affect non-adjacent levels:

\textbf{Top-down cascade} (predator-driven): - Sea otter \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} sea urchin \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
kelp cascade \citep{estes1974} - Wolf \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} elk \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} willow cascade in
Yellowstone \citep{ripple2012}

\textbf{Bottom-up cascade} (resource-driven): - Nutrient enrichment \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
phytoplankton \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} zooplankton \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} fish

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0180_18b43723222a.png}
\caption{Sequence diagram for Trophic Cascades showing ordered interaction among Wolves (reintroduced 1995), Elk, Willows/Cottonwoods, and Beavers.}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Quantitative trophic cascade --- Sea Otter example:} - 1 sea
otter consumes about 10 kg sea urchin/day - Each urchin removed
protects about 1 m\(^2\) of kelp - Kelp productivity:
about 300 g C/m\(^2\)/yr - Therefore: 1 otter \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
about 3,650 m\(^2\) kelp protected \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} about 1,095 kg
C/yr sequestered - Kelp forests also attenuate wave energy by 60-70\%,
providing coastal protection valued at about \$10,000/km/yr

\textbf{Mesopredator release:} removal of apex predators \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} explosion of
medium-sized predators \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} disproportionate prey decline. Example: coyote
increase after wolf removal \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} ground-nesting bird decline in North
America.

\begin{quote}
\texorpdfstring{}{} \textbf{Clinical Connection --- Trophic Cascades and Lyme Disease:}
The decline of apex predators in eastern North America has contributed
to a trophic cascade affecting human health. Wolf and cougar removal \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
deer population explosion \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} increased tick-deer encounters \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} increased
\emph{Borrelia burgdorferi} transmission \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Lyme disease incidence
increased 25-fold from 1990 to 2020 in the northeastern USA. Deer also
browse forest understory, reducing small mammal habitat diversity, which
concentrates ticks on the most competent reservoir hosts (white-footed
mice), further amplifying transmission. Predator restoration could
reduce disease burden --- a health-relevant trophic cascade.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Mutualism, Parasitism, and
Facilitation}\label{mutualism-parasitism-and-facilitation}

\subsubsection{Mutualism}\label{mutualism}

\textbf{Obligate mutualism:} neither partner can survive without the
other (e.g., fig-wasp pollination; lichens = fungus +
alga/cyanobacterium).

\textbf{Facultative mutualism:} both benefit but can survive
independently (e.g., seed-dispersing birds and fruiting trees).

\textbf{Mycorrhizal networks:} - \textbf{Arbuscular mycorrhizae (AM,
Glomeromycota):} obligate symbionts; hyphae form arbuscules inside root
cortex cells; deliver P and micronutrients; receive up to 30\% of plant
photosynthate; present in about 80\% of land plant species -
\textbf{Ectomycorrhizae (EM, Basidiomycota + Ascomycota):} hyphae form
Hartig net around root cells; dominant in temperate/boreal forests
(\emph{Pinus}, \emph{Betula}, \emph{Fagus}); provide N via proteolytic
\hyperref[gl:enzyme]{\textbf{enzyme}}s - \textbf{Common mycorrhizal
networks (CMNs) --- ``Wood Wide Web'':} CMNs transfer carbon, water, and
nutrient signals between plants of same and different species; large
``mother trees'' supply carbon to understory seedlings (Simard et
al.~1997, \emph{Nature}). Contested: whether transfer is truly adaptive
signalling or passive diffusion remains debated (Karst et al.~2023,
\emph{Nature Ecology \& Evolution})

\subsubsection{Parasitism and Disease
Ecology}\label{parasitism-and-disease-ecology}

Parasites regulate host populations and can function as keystone
species:

\textbf{The parasite-mediated competition hypothesis:} parasites can
determine competitive outcomes between host species, effectively
functioning as ``hidden'' keystone species.

\subsubsection{Facilitation}\label{facilitation}

\textbf{Facilitation} occurs when one species improves the survival or
reproduction of another. Unlike mutualism, facilitation can be
unidirectional:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Nurse plants} in deserts: cacti establish under the shade of
  nurse shrubs (\emph{Larrea}, \emph{Ambrosia})
\item
  \textbf{Foundation species:} create habitat structure (e.g., corals,
  kelp, \emph{Spartina} grass in salt marshes)
\item
  \textbf{Nitrogen fixers:} \emph{Lupinus} colonises volcanic
  substrates, enriching soil N for later successional species (Mount
  St.~Helens \hyperref[gl:primary-succession]{\textbf{primary
  succession}})
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check:} The relationship between clownfish and sea
anemones is often described as mutualism. The clownfish gains protection
from predators; the anemone may benefit from clownfish defending against
butterfly fish that eat anemone tentacles. How would you design an
experiment to determine whether this interaction is truly mutualism
(+/+) or commensalism (+/0)?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Ecological Succession}\label{ecological-succession}

\textbf{Succession} = directional, generally predictable change in
community composition over time after disturbance or on newly available
substrate.

Contemporary succession ecology is less deterministic than the classical
``march to climax'' story. Recovery trajectories depend on surviving
legacies, seed banks, dispersal corridors, disturbance severity,
herbivory, invasive species, soil microbes, and climate conditions
during recovery. The practical question is not only which stage comes
next, but which intervention would change the trajectory: protecting
refuges, adding propagules, removing barriers, or accepting a novel
stable state.

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Example
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Facilitation} & Early species modify environment to favour later
species & Nitrogen-fixing \emph{Alnus} (alder) enriches soil, enabling
spruce colonisation (Glacier Bay, Alaska) \\
\textbf{Tolerance} & Later species can establish regardless of early
species but grow more slowly & Shade-tolerant species slowly replace
shade-intolerant pioneers \\
\textbf{Inhibition} & Early colonists resist replacement; succession
proceeds primarily when pioneers die & \emph{Cladonia} lichen crusts
inhibit vascular plant establishment on sand dunes \\
\end{longtable}
}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth,height=4.2in,keepaspectratio]{../figures/mermaid_inline/inline_mermaid_0181_5b60733bc96e.png}
\caption{Ecological succession pathways. Primary succession begins on bare substrate and takes centuries; secondary succession begins with intact soil and proceeds in decades. Three mechanisms (facilitation, tolerance, inhibition) operate at transition points. Modern ecology views the endpoint as a dynamic equilibrium rather than a fixed climax state.}
\end{figure}

In reality, most successional sequences involve most three mechanisms
operating simultaneously at different stages and spatial scales.

\subsubsection{Climax Community Concept}\label{climax-community-concept}

\textbf{Classical view \citep{clements1916}:} Succession proceeds toward
a single, deterministic climax community determined by regional climate
(the ``organismal'' model --- community as superorganism).

\textbf{Modern view (Gleason 1926; Whittaker 1953):} Communities are
assemblages of individually distributed species (the ``individualistic''
model). Multiple stable endpoints possible; disturbance history,
stochastic colonisation, and priority effects most influence trajectory.
The concept of a single climax is largely abandoned.

\subsubsection{Intermediate Disturbance Hypothesis
(IDH)}\label{intermediate-disturbance-hypothesis-idh}

\textbf{Connell (1978):} Communities at intermediate levels of
disturbance frequency and intensity show maximum species diversity:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Low disturbance} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} competitive exclusion \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} low diversity
  (dominant competitor wins)
\item
  \textbf{High disturbance} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} primarily r-selected pioneers survive \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  low diversity
\item
  \textbf{Intermediate} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} prevents competitive dominance while enabling
  diverse colonisation
\end{itemize}

\begin{equation}
H' = f(\text{disturbance frequency, intensity})
\label{eq:community_ecology_6}
\end{equation}

\textbf{Evidence:} Coral reefs, tropical forests, stream invertebrate
communities --- moderate disturbance (hurricanes, floods, fires)
increases diversity.

\textbf{Criticisms:} The IDH has been challenged as overly simplistic
(Fox 2013, \emph{Ecology}). Some communities show monotonic
diversity-disturbance relationships. The hypothesis also assumes a
competition-colonisation trade-off that is not comprehensive.

\subsubsection{Alternative Stable States and Regime
Shifts}\label{alternative-stable-states-and-regime-shifts}

\textbf{Alternative stable states} (Lewontin 1969; Scheffer et
al.~2001): Some ecosystems can exist in multiple stable configurations
under the same environmental conditions. Transitions between states
(\textbf{regime shifts}) can be triggered by small perturbations near
\textbf{tipping points}:

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1892}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4595}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
System
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
State 1
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
State 2
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} \\

Shallow lake & Clear water (macrophytes dominant) & Turbid (algal bloom)
& Nutrient loading exceeds P threshold \\
Coral reef & Coral dominated & Macroalgae dominated & Overfishing of
herbivorous fish \\
Savanna & Grassland with scattered trees & Closed-canopy forest & Fire
suppression \\
Arctic & Perennial sea ice & Seasonal/ice-free & Ocean warming
threshold \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Early warning signals} of approaching tipping points: -
Increased temporal variance (flickering) - \textbf{Critical slowing
down} --- recovery from perturbation becomes slower - Increased spatial
correlation - Skewed distribution of system state

These early warning indicators are being applied to monitor reef, lake,
and climate system stability.

\begin{quote}
\texorpdfstring{}{} \textbf{Clinical Connection --- Microbiome Regime Shifts:} The human
gut microbiome exhibits alternative stable states analogous to
ecological regime shifts. A healthy, diverse microbiome represents one
stable state. Antibiotic treatment or \emph{C. difficile} infection can
trigger a regime shift to an impoverished, pathogenic state. Once
established, the unhealthy state resists return to the diverse state
(hysteresis) --- explaining why probiotics alone are often insufficient
and why fecal microbiota transplantation (which provides a complete
microbial community) is more effective.
\end{quote}

predicted. Surviving pocket gophers, ants, and lupine plants in patches
of surviving soil created nuclei of rapid recovery. Which successional
mechanism(s) does this illustrate, and why does it challenge Clements'
classical model?
\end{quote}

\subsection{Measuring Biodiversity}\label{measuring-biodiversity}

\subsubsection{Alpha, Beta, and Gamma
Diversity}\label{alpha-beta-and-gamma-diversity}

\textbf{\citet{whittaker1960}} distinguished three scales of diversity:

These scales also clarify what modern biodiversity tools can and cannot
show. Environmental DNA, acoustic monitoring, camera traps, remote
sensing, and citizen-science records can reveal turnover across space
faster than classical plots alone, but each method has detection bias,
taxonomic gaps, and scale limits. A credible diversity comparison states
the sampling unit, detection method, taxonomic resolution, and whether
the result is richness, evenness, composition, or functional change.

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2857}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Scale
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Definition
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Metric
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Alpha (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}) diversity} & Species richness within a single
community/habitat & \(H'\), Simpson's, species count \\
\textbf{Beta (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}) diversity} & Turnover in species composition between
communities & Jaccard index, Bray-Curtis dissimilarity \\
\textbf{Gamma (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\gamma}}{gamma}) diversity} & Total diversity across most communities
in a landscape & \(\gamma = \bar{\alpha} \times \beta\)
(multiplicative) \\
\end{longtable}
}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Shannon-Wiener Diversity Index
(\(H'\))}{Shannon-Wiener Diversity Index (Htextquotesingle)}}\label{shannon-wiener-diversity-index-h}

\begin{equation}
H' = -\sum_{i=1}^{S} p_i \ln p_i
\label{eq:community_ecology_7}
\end{equation}

where \(p_i\) = proportion of individuals belonging to species \(i\).

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Range: \(H' = 0\) (monoculture) to \(H' = \ln(S)\) (perfectly even)
\item
  Sensitive to rare species
\item
  Typical values: 1.5-3.5 for most communities; \textgreater4.0 for
  extremely diverse tropical communities
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Simpson Diversity Index
(\(1-D\))}{Simpson Diversity Index (1-D)}}\label{simpson-diversity-index-1-d}

\begin{equation}
D = \sum_{i=1}^{S} p_i^2 \qquad \text{Simpson's diversity} = 1 - D
\label{eq:community_ecology_8}
\end{equation}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Range: 0-1; probability that two randomly selected individuals are
  from \textbf{different} species
\item
  Weighted toward dominant species (less affected by rare species than
  \(H'\))
\item
  Also expressed as reciprocal: Simpson's reciprocal \(= 1/D\)
  (effective number of species)
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Pielou's Evenness
(\(J'\))}{Pielou's Evenness (Jtextquotesingle)}}\label{pielous-evenness-j}

\begin{equation}
J' = \frac{H'}{\ln S} \in [0, 1]
\label{eq:community_ecology_9}
\end{equation}

\(J' = 1\) means most species equally abundant; \(J' \to 0\) means
dominated by one species.

\subsubsection{Worked Example}\label{worked-example-5}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lllll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Species & Abundance & \(p_i\) & \(p_i \ln p_i\) & \(p_i^2\) \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
A & 50 & 0.500 & -0.347 & 0.250 \\
B & 30 & 0.300 & -0.361 & 0.090 \\
C & 15 & 0.150 & -0.285 & 0.023 \\
D & 4 & 0.040 & -0.129 & 0.002 \\
E & 1 & 0.010 & -0.046 & 0.000 \\
\textbf{Total} & \textbf{100} & \textbf{1.000} & \textbf{-1.167} &
\textbf{0.364} \\
\end{longtable}
}

\(H' = 1.167\); \(H'_{max} = \ln 5 = 1.609\);
\(J' = 1.167/1.609 = 0.725\)

Simpson's \(D = 0.364\); Simpson's diversity \(= 1 - 0.364 = 0.636\)

\subsubsection{Beta Diversity: Measuring
Turnover}\label{beta-diversity-measuring-turnover}

\textbf{Jaccard similarity index:}

\begin{equation}
J = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|}
\label{eq:community_ecology_10}
\end{equation}

where \(A\) and \(B\) are species sets from two communities. \(J = 1\)
means identical composition; \(J = 0\) means no shared species.

\textbf{Bray-Curtis dissimilarity} (incorporates abundance):

\begin{equation}
BC = 1 - \frac{2 \sum_i \min(a_i, b_i)}{\sum_i (a_i + b_i)}
\label{eq:community_ecology_11}
\end{equation}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]

\CommentTok{\# Community counts (array of species abundances)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"Species richness: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{result}\SpecialCharTok{.}\NormalTok{species\_richness}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"Shannon H\textquotesingle{}: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{result}\SpecialCharTok{.}\NormalTok{shannon\_index}\SpecialCharTok{:.3f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"Simpson 1{-}D: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{result}\SpecialCharTok{.}\NormalTok{simpson\_index}\SpecialCharTok{:.3f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"Evenness J\textquotesingle{}: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{result}\SpecialCharTok{.}\NormalTok{evenness}\SpecialCharTok{:.3f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}

\subsection{Island Biogeography
Theory}\label{island-biogeography-theory}

\subsubsection{MacArthur-Wilson Equilibrium
Model}\label{macarthur-wilson-equilibrium-model}

\textbf{\citet{macarthur1967}:} \emph{The Theory of Island Biogeography}
--- equilibrium species richness on islands balances immigration
(colonisation) rate and extinction rate:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Immigration rate} decreases as \(S\) increases (fewer
  uncolonised species remain in the mainland pool)
\item
  \textbf{Extinction rate} increases as \(S\) increases (more species
  present means more potential extinctions)
\item
  At \textbf{equilibrium} (\(\hat{S}\)): immigration rate = extinction
  rate
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Effects of island characteristics:}

\subsubsection{Empirical Tests}\label{empirical-tests}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Post-Krakatoa recolonisation} (1883-1983): After complete
  sterilisation by eruption, species accumulated toward equilibrium;
  initial overshoot then relaxation \citep{whittaker1975}
\item
  \textbf{Florida Keys experiment} \citep{simberloff1969}: Fumigated
  small mangrove islands \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} recolonisation to predicted equilibrium
  within 2 years; confirmed immigration-extinction dynamics
\item
  \textbf{Habitat fragments as islands:} Biological Dynamics of Forest
  Fragments Project (BDFFP, Amazonia; Laurance et al.~2011) --- 40 years
  of data on isolated 1-100 ha fragments showing predictable species
  loss following species-area relationship
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{SLOSS Debate}\label{sloss-debate}

\textbf{Single Large Or Several Small} --- for conservation, which
reserve design maximises biodiversity?

\textbf{Single large} & Lower edge-to-interior ratio; larger MVPs;

\(S\) per patch; connectivity problems \\

\textbf{Modern consensus: Core-corridor-matrix design:} - Large core
reserves (the ``single large'' benefit) - Habitat corridors or stepping
stones connecting reserves - Matrix land uses compatible with wildlife
movement (agroforestry, wildlife-friendly farming) - Example
initiatives: Yellowstone-to-Yukon (Y2Y, 3,200 km); Florida Wildlife
Corridor (1,000+ miles)

\subsubsection{Extinction Debt}\label{extinction-debt}

\textbf{Extinction debt} (Tilman et al.~1994, \emph{Nature}): Species
currently present in degraded/fragmented habitats may be committed to
future extinction --- but the extinction is \textbf{delayed} by decades
to centuries as existing individuals slowly die without replacement.

\begin{equation}
\text{Species committed to extinction} = S_{\text{pre-fragmentation}} - c \cdot A_{\text{remaining}}^z
\label{eq:community_ecology_13}
\end{equation}

\textbf{Implications:} - Present-day species richness
\textbf{overestimates} long-term viability - Conservation assessments
based on current presence may be dangerously optimistic - European
calcareous grasslands: 20-50\% of plant species face committed
extinction due to historical fragmentation \citep{lindborg2004} - Amazon
deforestation: 25-year extinction debt means current biodiversity
surveys underestimate eventual losses

\subsubsection{Metapopulation Dynamics (Levins, 1969; Hanski,
1994)}\label{metapopulation-dynamics-levins-1969-hanski-1994}

A patchwork of habitat fragments connected by dispersal --- local
extinctions offset by recolonisation. Metapopulation persistence
requires fraction of occupied patches to exceed extinction threshold:

\begin{equation}
\hat{p} = 1 - \frac{e}{c}
\label{eq:community_ecology_14}
\end{equation}

where \(e\) = extinction rate per patch, \(c\) = colonisation rate;
metapopulation persists if \(e/c < 1\).

\textbf{Hanski's incidence function model} extends this by incorporating
patch area (affects extinction rate) and isolation (affects colonisation
rate):

\begin{equation}
J_i = \frac{1}{1 + (e_i/c_i)^2}
\label{eq:community_ecology_15}
\end{equation}

where \(J_i\) = probability that patch \(i\) is occupied,
\(e_i \propto A_i^{-x}\), and \(c_i\) depends on distance to occupied
patches.

\begin{quote}
\texorpdfstring{}{} \textbf{Clinical Connection --- Habitat Fragmentation and Zoonotic
Disease:} As forests are fragmented into small patches, edge effects
increase human-wildlife contact, facilitating zoonotic pathogen
spillover. The emergence of Nipah virus in Malaysia (1998-99) was linked
to bat habitat loss: displaced fruit bats (\emph{Pteropus} spp.) moved
to pig farms near forest fragments, facilitating transmission to
livestock and then humans. Similarly, Ebola outbreaks correlate
spatially with deforestation frontiers. Island biogeography theory
predicts that small fragments lose apex predators first (mesopredator
release), increasing populations of rodents and bats that serve as
pathogen reservoirs.
\end{quote}

\textbf{Concept Check:} A national park of 10,000 km\(^2\) is split by a
highway into two fragments of 6,000 km\(^2\) and 4,000 km\(^2\). Using
\(S = 50A^{0.25}\), calculate species richness for: (a) the intact park,
(b) each fragment separately, (c) both fragments combined assuming no
species overlap. How does a wildlife corridor change your prediction?
\end{quote}

\subsection{Food Web Structure and Network
Ecology}\label{food-web-structure-and-network-ecology}

\subsubsection{Food Web Topology}\label{food-web-topology}

Food webs are network representations of feeding relationships in
communities --- a graph where nodes are species (or trophic units) and
directed edges encode ``\(i\) eats \(j\).'' Treating the community as a
graph unlocks the entire toolbox of network science (degree
distributions, clustering, modularity, motif analysis), which has
reshaped community ecology over the past two decades. Key metrics:

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2069}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3448}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4483}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Metric
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

Typical value
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Connectance (\(C\))} & \(C = L/S^2\) (or \(L/[S(S-1)/2]\));
fraction of possible links realised & 0.05-0.30 \\
\textbf{Links per species (\(L/S\))} & Average number of trophic links
per species & about 2 for most food webs \\
\textbf{Chain length} & Number of links from base to top & 3-5
typically \\
\textbf{Omnivory} & Fraction of species feeding at \textgreater1 trophic
level & about 50\% in many webs \\
\textbf{Mean trophic level} & Average path length from primary producers
& 2.5--3.5 typical \\
\textbf{Generality} & Mean number of resources per consumer & Skewed:
most consumers specialised \\
\textbf{Vulnerability} & Mean number of consumers per resource & Skewed:
most prey have few predators \\
\textbf{Nestedness} & Specialists' diets are subsets of generalists'
diets & High in mutualistic networks \\
\end{longtable}
}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Minimal food{-}web statistics from an adjacency dictionary}
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ web\_stats(web):}
\NormalTok{    species }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{set}\NormalTok{(web).union(\{p }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ prey }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ web.values() }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ p }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ prey\})}
\NormalTok{    S }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(species)}
\NormalTok{    L }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(v) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ v }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ web.values())}
\NormalTok{    C }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ L }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (S }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ S)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ \{}\StringTok{"S"}\NormalTok{: S, }\StringTok{"L"}\NormalTok{: L, }\StringTok{"L/S"}\NormalTok{: L }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ S, }\StringTok{"connectance"}\NormalTok{: C\}}

\NormalTok{example }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{}
    \StringTok{"phyto"}\NormalTok{: [], }\StringTok{"zoo"}\NormalTok{: [}\StringTok{"phyto"}\NormalTok{], }\StringTok{"shrimp"}\NormalTok{: [}\StringTok{"phyto"}\NormalTok{],}
    \StringTok{"minnow"}\NormalTok{: [}\StringTok{"zoo"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"shrimp"}\NormalTok{], }\StringTok{"bass"}\NormalTok{: [}\StringTok{"minnow"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"shrimp"}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{\}}

\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{Cascade Effects and
Robustness}\label{cascade-effects-and-robustness}

Food webs are not just descriptive: their topology predicts how
perturbations propagate. Removal experiments (real or simulated) reveal
three classes of network response:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2105}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2368}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5526}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Response
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Mechanism
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Topological signature
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Bottom-up cascade} & Loss of a producer ripples upward through
consumers & Few generalist consumers; long chains \\
\textbf{Top-down cascade} (\cref{eq:community_ecology_5} system) & Loss
of a top predator releases mesopredators or herbivores & Strong vertical
interaction strengths \\
\textbf{Horizontal cascade} & Loss of one prey shifts predator to
alternative prey, harming it indirectly & Apparent competition; shared
predators \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Robustness analysis} (Dunne et al.~2002, \emph{Ecol. Lett.})
sequentially removes species (random order, most-connected first, or
rarest first) and tracks the fraction of secondary extinctions. Results
across 16 well-resolved food webs:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Random removal: about 50\% of species can disappear before
  web collapse
\item
  \textbf{Most-connected-first removal: collapse after about 20\% of
  species removed} --- hubs (highly connected generalists) are
  disproportionately important
\item
  Rarest-first: minimal cascade --- rare species are weakly embedded
\end{itemize}

This is a striking parallel to the \textbf{scale-free network}
robustness literature (Barabási \& Albert 1999): tolerance to random
failure but vulnerability to targeted attack. For conservation, hub
species are ecological-network analogues of keystone species,
identifiable from topology alone.

\subsubsection{Complexity-Stability
Debate}\label{complexity-stability-debate}

\textbf{May (1972, \emph{Nature}):} Mathematical analysis of random
community matrices showed that complexity (high \(S\), high \(C\),
strong interaction strengths) \textbf{destabilises} communities ---
contradicting the intuitive ``diversity begets stability'' hypothesis.
The May criterion: a random Jacobian is locally stable primarily if
\(\sigma\sqrt{SC} < 1\) (with \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\sigma}}{sigma} = standard deviation of interaction
strengths).

\textbf{Resolution (McCann 2000, \emph{Nature}; Allesina \& Tang 2012,
\emph{Nature}):} - Weak interactions stabilise food webs (dampen
oscillations) - Non-random interaction structure (modularity,
nestedness) promotes stability - Real food webs are not random --- they
have specific architectures that enhance stability -
\textbf{Weak-interaction dominance:} most interactions are weak; few are
strong. The many weak links act as stabilisers.

\textbf{Modularity:} food webs are organised into modules (compartments)
with strong within-module interactions and weak between-module
interactions. This structure limits the spread of perturbations --- a
forest pathogen outbreak in one module rarely cascades into the aquatic
module of the same landscape food web.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Neutral Theory of
Biodiversity}\label{neutral-theory-of-biodiversity}

The competition-coexistence theory developed earlier explains community
structure through \textbf{niches} --- species coexist because they
differ. \textbf{Hubbell's unified neutral theory of biodiversity and
biogeography (UNTB; Hubbell 2001)} proposes the radical alternative: at
the scale of trophically similar species (e.g., canopy trees in a
tropical forest), \textbf{most individuals are demographically
equivalent} regardless of species, and observed community patterns
emerge from random birth--death--dispersal--speciation alone.

\subsubsection{The Neutral Assumption}\label{the-neutral-assumption}

Each individual, regardless of species, has the same per-capita
probabilities of: - Birth (replacement of a vacancy by an offspring) -
Death (creation of a vacancy) - Immigration \(m\) from a regional
\textbf{metacommunity} (replaces local community via dispersal) -
Speciation (rate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\nu}}{nu} in the metacommunity)

The local community has fixed size \(J\) (zero-sum constraint --- every
death is replaced); dynamics are pure ecological drift, mathematically
isomorphic to neutral \hyperref[gl:genetic-drift]{\textbf{genetic
drift}} (\cref{sec:unit_V_population_genetics}). Two parameters do most
of the work:

\begin{equation}
\theta = 2 J_M \nu \qquad \text{(fundamental biodiversity number)}
\label{eq:unit_X_neutral_theta}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
m = \text{immigration probability per local death}
\label{eq:unit_X_neutral_m}
\end{equation}

The metacommunity size is \(J_M\). Together, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\theta}}{theta} and \(m\) predict species
abundance distributions, species--area curves, and beta diversity ---
without invoking niche differences at most.

\subsubsection{Predictions and Empirical
Successes}\label{predictions-and-empirical-successes}

UNTB predicts: - \textbf{Species abundance distribution} follows a
zero-sum multinomial (very close to the rank-abundance pattern
introduced earlier, but with a heavier tail of rare species) -
\textbf{Species--area relationships} with \(z \approx 0.20\)--0.30
(matching empirical island values, \cref{eq:community_ecology_12}) -
\textbf{Beta diversity} declines with geographic distance even in
homogeneous habitat (purely from limited dispersal)

Hubbell's analysis of the Barro Colorado Island 50-ha forest plot
(Panama, \textgreater{} 200 tree species) showed UNTB fit the species
abundance distribution as well as niche-based models. Volkov et
al.~(2003, \emph{Nature}) confirmed neutral fits across forests in
Panama, Ecuador, India, and Malaysia.

\subsubsection{Limits and Synthesis}\label{limits-and-synthesis}

UNTB has been heavily criticised: real species are \emph{not} equivalent
(massive trait variation; clear niche differences in measured
demographic rates), and dynamic predictions (e.g., extinction times)
often fail. The modern view, following Adler, HilleRisLambers \& Levine
(2007, \emph{Ecol. Lett.}), is that \textbf{niche and neutral processes
co-occur}: Chesson-style niche differences stabilise coexistence, while
neutral drift adds stochastic variation in relative abundance. UNTB is
the null model --- if your data look neutral, you have not yet found the
ecology that distinguishes species.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check:} Two tropical forest plots have nearly identical
species-abundance distributions. The first sits in a homogeneous lowland
habitat; the second spans a steep elevation gradient. Why is the
\emph{neutral} explanation of the species-abundance pattern more
plausible for the first plot than the second, and what additional data
would discriminate the two hypotheses?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Trait-Based Community
Ecology}\label{trait-based-community-ecology}

Counting species ignores that a 1 mm aphid and a 10 m oak both add
``+1'' to richness. \textbf{Trait-based ecology} replaces (or
complements) species lists with measured \textbf{functional traits} ---
morphological, physiological, or phenological attributes that influence
performance. This shifts community ecology from a taxonomic enterprise
to a quantitative, predictive one.

\subsubsection{Grime's CSR Triangle}\label{grimes-csr-triangle}

Grime's CSR scheme (1977, 2001) classifies plant strategies along two
stress axes --- disturbance and stress (resource limitation) ---
yielding three primary strategies and the gradients between them:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2000}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2500}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3500}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2000}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Strategy
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Conditions
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Trait syndrome
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Examples
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{C --- Competitor} & Low stress, low disturbance & Tall,
fast-growing, high biomass, deep roots; leaves long-lived but expensive
& Mature forest dominants (oak, beech, \emph{Eucalyptus}) \\
\textbf{S --- Stress-tolerator} & High stress, low disturbance & Slow
growth, evergreen, sclerophyllous leaves, conservative resource use &
Desert succulents, alpine cushion plants, lichens, conifers in
nutrient-poor soils \\
\textbf{R --- Ruderal} & Low stress, high disturbance & Short-lived,
high seed output, rapid maturation, weak competitors & Annual weeds
(\emph{Senecio}, \emph{Capsella}); pioneer trees \\
\end{longtable}
}

Most species fall along intermediates (CR, CS, SR, CSR). Crucially, the
CSR axes capture independent gradients to the
\hyperref[gl:r-strategist]{\textbf{r-strategist}}/\hyperref[gl:k-strategist]{\textbf{K-strategist}}
axis of population ecology --- a stress-tolerator is K-like in longevity
but slow-growing, not high-fecundity.

\subsubsection{The Leaf Economics
Spectrum}\label{the-leaf-economics-spectrum}

Wright et al.~(2004, \emph{Nature}) analysed \textgreater{} 2,500 plant
species globally and uncovered a stunningly tight axis along which leaf
traits co-vary --- the \textbf{leaf economics spectrum (LES)}:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4889}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5111}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Acquisitive (fast) end
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Conservative (slow) end
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
High specific leaf area (SLA, m\(^2\) kg\(^{-1}\)) & Low SLA (thick,
dense leaves) \\
High mass-based photosynthetic rate (\(A_{\text{mass}}\)) & Low
\(A_{\text{mass}}\) \\
High leaf N concentration (Rubisco-rich) & Low leaf N \\
Short leaf lifespan (months) & Long leaf lifespan (years; evergreen) \\
Low construction cost per unit area & High construction cost;
defended \\
\end{longtable}
}

The LES is widely observed across biomes --- tropical pioneer trees and
desert annuals can occupy the same acquisitive end of the axis despite
very different evolutionary histories. The axis captures a major
trade-off between rapid resource capture and resource conservation, but
local exceptions occur because water stress, herbivory, nutrient
limitation, and phylogeny can bend the relationship. Analogous spectra
exist for roots (Bergmann et al.~2020, \emph{Sci. Adv.}) and for
whole-plant strategy axes (Diaz et al.~2016, \emph{Nature}).

\subsubsection{Functional Diversity and Community
Assembly}\label{functional-diversity-and-community-assembly}

Trait data enable \textbf{functional diversity} indices (functional
richness, evenness, divergence; Villéger, Mason \& Mouillot 2008,
\emph{Ecology}) that detect community assembly mechanisms invisible to
species lists:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Functional clustering} (traits more similar than expected by
  chance) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \emph{environmental filtering} (primarily some strategies
  tolerate the local abiotic conditions)
\item
  \textbf{Functional overdispersion} (traits more different than
  expected) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \emph{competitive exclusion} via limiting similarity and
  Chesson-style stabilising mechanisms.
\end{itemize}

A community of 30 alpine cushion plants and a community of 30 tropical
canopy trees both have \(S = 30\), but their trait spreads on the LES
are wildly different --- and that difference predicts ecosystem function
(productivity, decomposition, drought response) far better than richness
alone.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check:} Two grassland plots have identical Shannon
diversity \(H' = 2.5\). Plot A's plants cluster tightly on the
conservative end of the LES; plot B's plants span the entire LES. Which
plot is more productive on average, which is more drought-resilient, and
which would you predict has stronger competitive interactions?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Biological Control}\label{biological-control}

The competition, predation, and parasitism theory developed above has
direct translational application: \textbf{biological control} uses
natural enemies to suppress pest populations, replacing or reducing
chemical pesticides. It is community ecology deployed for agriculture,
public health, and invasive-species management.

\subsubsection{Three Classical
Strategies}\label{three-classical-strategies}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2105}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2105}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2632}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3158}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Strategy
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Approach
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Time scale
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Risk profile
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Classical (importation)} & Import a specialist natural enemy
from the pest's native range; expect it to establish and self-perpetuate
& Years to decades; one-shot release & High --- non-target effects if
enemy is not specialist enough \\
\textbf{Augmentative} & Mass-rear and release natural enemies repeatedly
to suppress current outbreak & Weeks to months; greenhouse, glasshouse &
Low --- released organisms typically fail to overwinter \\
\textbf{Conservation} & Modify habitat to favour resident natural
enemies (hedgerows, beetle banks, insectary plants, reduced pesticide
use) & Continuous & Lowest --- uses native species \\
\end{longtable}
}

\subsubsection{Classical Successes and
Failures}\label{classical-successes-and-failures}

\textbf{Cottony cushion scale (\emph{Icerya purchasi}) and the vedalia
beetle (\emph{Rodolia cardinalis}).} Imported in 1888 from Australia to
California citrus groves --- within two years the citrus industry was
saved. This is the textbook success and the prototype for most
subsequent classical biocontrol programs.

\textbf{Prickly pear (\emph{Opuntia stricta}) and \emph{Cactoblastis
cactorum}.} Released in 1925 in Australia, the moth larvae cleared 25
million ha of invasive cactus by 1940 --- one of the largest-scale
ecological interventions in history.

\textbf{Cane toad (\emph{Rhinella marina}).} Released in 1935 in
Queensland to control sugarcane beetles; the toads ignored the beetles,
ate everything else, and are now an invasive plague across northern
Australia. Classical biocontrol's most-cited cautionary tale: a
generalist natural enemy will eat non-target species, and the lesson
cost ecologists decades of credibility.

\subsubsection{Risk Assessment and Modern
Practice}\label{risk-assessment-and-modern-practice}

After the cane-toad era, regulatory frameworks (e.g., the FAO
\textbf{Code of Conduct for the Import and Release of Exotic Biological
Control Agents}, 1996) require:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Host-specificity testing} --- quarantine trials against native
  non-target species
\item
  \textbf{Climate matching} --- does the agent's native climate predict
  its spread in the target range?
\item
  \textbf{Population modelling} --- Lotka--Volterra or matrix projection
  of agent and target dynamics; predicted suppression vs.~escape
\item
  \textbf{Reversibility analysis} --- can the agent be eradicated if it
  causes damage? (Almost typically: no.)
\end{enumerate}

Modern programs increasingly favour \textbf{conservation biological
control}, which avoids introducing non-native species entirely. Field
margins of insectary plants (e.g., \emph{Phacelia}, \emph{Fagopyrum})
increase syrphid and parasitoid wasp populations that suppress aphids in
adjacent crops by 30--50 \% (Tscharntke et al.~2007, \emph{Biol.
Control}). This connects directly to ecosystem-services valuation
(\cref{sec:unit_X_ecosystem_ecology}).

\begin{quote}
\texorpdfstring{}{} \textbf{Clinical Connection --- \emph{Wolbachia} and Mosquito-Borne
Disease.} Conservation biological control extends to public health.
\emph{Wolbachia} is an intracellular bacterium that, when introduced
into \emph{Aedes aegypti} mosquitoes, blocks dengue, Zika, and
chikungunya virus transmission. Field trials in Yogyakarta (Indonesia)
and Niterói (Brazil) released \emph{Wolbachia}-carrying mosquitoes that
spread the bacterium through the wild population via cytoplasmic
incompatibility. Within 27 months of release in Yogyakarta, dengue
incidence dropped 77\% in treated neighbourhoods (Utarini et al.~2021,
\emph{N. Engl. J. Med.}). This is biological control of disease vectors
via a manipulative endosymbiont --- community ecology in service of
pandemic prevention.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check:} A regulator must approve or reject a proposed
classical biocontrol release of a parasitoid wasp against an invasive
moth pest. (a) What three host-specificity tests would you require? (b)
Why is ``the agent attacks the target moth in the lab'' insufficient
evidence for safety? (c) How does a sound elasticity analysis
(\cref{eq:unit_X_sensitivity_elasticity}) of the \emph{target's} matrix
model help you predict whether the release will succeed?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Worked Example}\label{worked-example-6}

\textbf{Problem:} An ecologist surveys a small forest patch and
identifies three species of trees: - Species A: 50 individuals - Species
B: 30 individuals - Species C: 20 individuals

Calculate the Shannon Diversity Index (\(H\)) for this tree community.
The formula is:
\[H = -\sum (p_i \ln p_i) \label{eq:unit_X_community_ecology_item_1}\]

where \(p_i\) is the proportion of total individuals belonging to the
\(i\)-th species.

\textbf{Solution:}

\textbf{Step 1. Calculate the total number of individuals (\(N\)).}
\[N = 50 + 30 + 20 = 100 \label{eq:unit_X_community_ecology_item_2}\]

\textbf{Step 2. Calculate the proportion (\(p_i\)) for each species.} -
\(p_A = 50 / 100 = 0.50\) - \(p_B = 30 / 100 = 0.30\) -
\(p_C = 20 / 100 = 0.20\)

\textbf{Step 3. Calculate \(p_i \ln p_i\) for each species.} - Species
A: \(0.50 \times \ln(0.50) \approx 0.50 \times (-0.693) \approx -0.347\)
- Species B:
\(0.30 \times \ln(0.30) \approx 0.30 \times (-1.204) \approx -0.361\) -
Species C:
\(0.20 \times \ln(0.20) \approx 0.20 \times (-1.609) \approx -0.322\)

\textbf{Step 4. Sum the values and multiply by \(-1\).}
\[H = - (-0.347 + -0.361 + -0.322) = - (-1.030) = 1.030 \label{eq:unit_X_community_ecology_item_3}\]

\textbf{Answer:} The Shannon Diversity Index for this tree community is
approximately \textbf{1.03}.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-35}

For \textbf{Community Ecology and Species Interactions}, frontier
biology belongs inside the evidence logic of the chapter. Ecology and
conservation decisions increasingly combine field data, remote sensing,
community knowledge, model uncertainty, and explicit values. The core
reading question is this: community claims should identify interaction
type, network position, disturbance regime, and observational limits.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

Use biodiversity metrics carefully: population indices, extinction risk
categories, ecosystem services, and management targets answer different
questions
\citep{ipbes2019global,ipbes2024transformative,wwf2024livingplanet,iucn2025redlist,fao2024sofia}.

\textbf{Source practice:} For conservation claims, cite assessment
sources and state whether the evidence is a population index,
extinction-risk assessment, ecosystem-service valuation, satellite
product, or policy synthesis
\citep{ipbes2024transformative,noaa2025coralbleaching,fao2025sofi}.

\subsection{Key Terms}\label{key-terms-35}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2857}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.7143}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Term
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Definition
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Competitive exclusion principle} & Two species cannot stably
coexist if they occupy the exact same niche; the superior competitor
excludes the other \\
\textbf{Keystone species} & Species with disproportionately large
effects on community structure relative to its abundance \\
\textbf{Trophic cascade} & Indirect effect of apex predator on plant
biomass via suppressing herbivores; top-down regulation \\
\textbf{Succession} & Directional change in community composition over
time; primary (bare substrate) or secondary (after disturbance) \\
\textbf{Intermediate Disturbance Hypothesis} & Moderate disturbance
frequency/intensity maximises species diversity by preventing
competitive exclusion \\
\textbf{Shannon diversity (\(H'\))} & \(H' = -\sum p_i \ln p_i\);
quantifies species richness and evenness simultaneously \\
\textbf{Simpson index (\(1-D\))} & Probability that two random
individuals are from different species; weighted toward dominant
species \\
\textbf{Species-area relationship} & \(S = cA^z\); species richness
increases with area; \(z \approx 0.25\) for habitat islands \\
\textbf{SLOSS} & Single Large Or Several Small reserves debate in
conservation biology \\
\textbf{Extinction debt} & Species present today but predicted to go
extinct based on current habitat loss; time-delayed response \\
\textbf{Metapopulation} & Network of semi-isolated subpopulations
connected by dispersal; local extinctions offset by recolonisation \\
\textbf{Alternative stable states} & Multiple stable community
configurations under the same environmental conditions; regime shifts
between states \\
\textbf{Niche differentiation} & Process by which competing species
evolve to use different resources, reducing niche overlap \\
\textbf{Fundamental niche} & Full range of environmental conditions
where a species can maintain \(r \geq 0\) (Hutchinson) \\
\textbf{Realised niche} & Subset of fundamental niche actually occupied
after biotic interactions \\
\textbf{Connectance} & Proportion of possible trophic links that are
realised in a food web \\
\textbf{Facilitation} & One species improves survival or reproduction of
another; mechanism of succession \\
\textbf{Beta diversity} & Species turnover between communities; measured
by Jaccard or Bray-Curtis indices \\
\textbf{Neutral theory (UNTB)} & Hubbell's framework: per-capita
demographic equivalence; biodiversity arises from drift, dispersal, and
speciation \\
\textbf{Fundamental biodiversity number (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\theta}}{theta})} & \(\theta = 2J_M\nu\);
controls species richness in the metacommunity under UNTB \\
\textbf{CSR strategies} & Grime's competitor / stress-tolerator /
ruderal classification of plant strategies \\
\textbf{Leaf economics spectrum (LES)} & Comprehensive axis from
acquisitive (high SLA, short-lived leaves) to conservative (thick,
long-lived) leaves \\
\textbf{Functional diversity} & Trait-based diversity metric; clustering
vs.~overdispersion diagnoses assembly mechanism \\
\textbf{Classical biological control} & Importation of a specialist
natural enemy from a pest's native range \\
\textbf{Conservation biological control} & Habitat modification to
favour resident natural enemies; lowest-risk strategy \\
\textbf{Network robustness} & Resilience of a food web to species
removal; collapses fastest under most-connected-first deletion \\
\end{longtable}
}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Review Questions}\label{review-questions-35}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Two warbler species (\emph{Dendroica castanea} and \emph{D. fusca})
  share a boreal spruce tree habitat. MacArthur (1958) showed they
  coexist by partitioning the tree into feeding zones. Using Chesson's
  modern coexistence theory: (a) Which of Chesson's two mechanisms
  (equalising vs.~stabilising) enables their coexistence? (b) Write
  \hyperref[gl:lotka-volterra-equations]{\textbf{Lotka-Volterra
  equations}} and specify the condition for stable coexistence in terms
  of \(\alpha_{12}\) and \(\alpha_{21}\).
\item
  A trophic cascade operates in Yellowstone: wolves \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} elk \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} willows \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  beavers \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} altered stream morphology. (a) Is this a bottom-up or
  top-down cascade? (b) Predict what happens to each level if chronic
  wasting disease eliminates 90\% of the elk population. (c) How does
  the ``landscape of fear'' concept modify purely density-mediated
  cascade predictions?
\item
  A tropical rainforest island (area = 500 km\(^2\)) currently has
  \(S = 200\) bird species. Deforestation reduces area to 125 km\(^2\)
  (25\% of original). (a) Using the species-area relationship with
  \(z = 0.25\) and appropriate \(c\), predict the final equilibrium
  species richness. (b) If the extinction debt takes 50 years to fully
  manifest, what is the expected species number at year 10 assuming
  linear debt decay?
\item
  Compare the Shannon diversity index (\(H'\)) for three communities:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Community A: 4 species, abundances = {[}25, 25, 25, 25{]}
  \item
    Community B: 4 species, abundances = {[}97, 1, 1, 1{]}
  \item
    Community C: 8 species, abundances = {[}50, 20, 10, 8, 5, 4, 2, 1{]}
    Calculate \(H'\) and \(J'\) for each. Which community shows: highest
    richness? highest evenness? highest \(H'\)?
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Explain Hutchinson's ``paradox of the plankton.'' Why does the
  coexistence of hundreds of phytoplankton species apparently violate
  competitive exclusion, and what are three mechanisms that resolve the
  paradox?
\item
  The Biological Dynamics of Forest Fragments Project (BDFFP) in
  Amazonia found that 1-ha fragments lost 50\% of their bird species
  within 15 years, while 100-ha fragments lost 10\%. (a) Calculate \(z\)
  from these two data points. (b) Predict the species richness of a
  10-ha fragment relative to a 100-ha fragment. (c) What role do edge
  effects play beyond the simple species-area prediction?
\item
  A shallow lake in the Netherlands exists in a clear-water state with
  abundant macrophytes. Nutrient loading from agriculture gradually
  increases. Describe the regime shift to the turbid, algal-dominated
  state using the framework of alternative stable states. Why is
  reducing nutrients back to the original level insufficient to restore
  the clear-water state (hysteresis)?
\item
  Design a reserve system for a large mammal species (home range = 100
  km\(^2\), \(N_e\) requirement = 500) in a landscape of forest
  fragments. Use island biogeography principles to specify: (a) minimum
  total reserve area, (b) number and size of core reserves, (c) corridor
  design, (d) matrix management. Justify each design element.
\item
  The rough-skinned newt and common garter snake represent one of the
  best-documented coevolutionary arms races. Describe the escalation:
  what toxin does the newt produce, what resistance mechanism has the
  snake evolved, and what geographic mosaic pattern is observed? How
  does this relate to Red Queen dynamics?
\item
  Explain how the competitive exclusion principle applies to
  \emph{Clostridium difficile} infection and its treatment by fecal
  microbiota transplantation. What ecological principles make FMT more
  effective than antibiotic treatment for recurrent CDI?
\item
  Using \texttt{lotka\_volterra}, estimate whether predator peak
  \textbf{lags} prey peak for default parameters (inspect time series
  qualitatively).
\item
  How does \textbf{connectance} \(C=L/S^2\) relate to stability
  arguments in diverse food webs?
\item
  Hubbell's neutral theory predicts a species-abundance distribution
  from drift and dispersal alone. (a) Why is UNTB best regarded as a
  \emph{null model} rather than a competitor to niche theory? (b) If a
  community fits UNTB perfectly, what does that \emph{not} prove about
  the underlying ecology? Cite the Adler, HilleRisLambers \& Levine
  (2007) synthesis.
\item
  Two oak forests share identical species lists (\(S = 30\),
  \(H' = 2.8\)) but differ markedly in leaf economics: forest A's
  species cluster on the conservative end of the LES; forest B's species
  span the entire spectrum. (a) Which forest is more functionally
  diverse? (b) Predict relative productivity, decomposition rate, and
  drought-resilience for each. (c) Why do two communities with identical
  Shannon diversity behave differently?
\item
  A food-web robustness analysis simulates extinctions in random
  vs.~most-connected-first orders. The web collapses after 50\% removal
  under random deletion but after 18\% removal under
  most-connected-first deletion. (a) Explain the asymmetry using network
  topology. (b) Translate the result into a conservation prioritisation
  rule for hub species (analogous to keystone identification but
  topological).
\item
  A government agency proposes releasing a parasitoid wasp from East
  Asia to control an invasive aphid species in California. (a) Outline
  the host-specificity testing required before approval. (b) Why is the
  cane toad disaster relevant precedent? (c) Sketch how the agent and
  aphid populations would interact in a coupled Lotka-Volterra model ---
  and what condition supports long-term aphid suppression rather than
  coexistence?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-35}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Biotic interactions:} mutualism (+/+), commensalism (+/0),
  parasitism (+/-), predation (+/-), competition (-/-), amensalism (0/-)
  --- shape community composition and evolution.
\item
  \textbf{Competition:} Lotka-Volterra equations; competitive exclusion
  if niches overlap completely; stable coexistence if intraspecific
  \textgreater{} interspecific effects. Modern coexistence theory
  \citep{chesson2000}: stabilising + equalising mechanisms.
\item
  \textbf{Niche theory:} Hutchinson's n-dimensional hypervolume;
  fundamental vs.~realised niche; paradox of the plankton resolved by
  non-equilibrium dynamics and niche partitioning.
\item
  \textbf{Trophic cascades:} keystone predators suppress herbivores \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  plant biomass increases (wolves\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}elk\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}willows; sea otters\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}urchins\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}kelp).
  Behavioural cascades via ``landscape of fear.''
\item
  \textbf{Succession:} primary (bare substrate, slow) vs.~secondary
  (disturbed community, faster); facilitation/tolerance/inhibition
  mechanisms; IDH: intermediate disturbance maximises diversity;
  alternative stable states and regime shifts with hysteresis.
\item
  \textbf{Diversity indices:} \(H'\) (Shannon) combines richness +
  evenness; Simpson \(1-D\) = probability of inter-specific encounter;
  \(J'\) (evenness) = \(H'/\ln S\). Alpha, beta, gamma diversity at
  different spatial scales.
\item
  \textbf{Island biogeography:} \(S = cA^z\); equilibrium balances
  colonisation and extinction; SLOSS debate resolved toward
  core-corridor-matrix design; extinction debt warns of delayed species
  loss.
\item
  \textbf{Food web structure:} connectance, modularity, weak-interaction
  dominance stabilise complex communities. \textbf{Network robustness}
  under targeted (most-connected-first) deletion collapses faster than
  under random deletion --- hub species are topological keystones.
\item
  \textbf{Neutral theory (UNTB):} Hubbell's per-capita-equivalence
  framework; two parameters \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\theta}}{theta} and \(m\) predict species-abundance
  distributions and species--area relationships from drift, dispersal,
  and speciation alone. Best treated as a null model that niche-based
  theory must beat.
\item
  \textbf{Trait-based ecology:} Grime's CSR triangle; the leaf economics
  spectrum (LES) is a widely observed acquisitive\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\leftrightarrow}}{<->}conservative axis with
  local exceptions. Functional diversity diagnoses assembly mechanisms
  (clustering = environmental filtering; overdispersion = limiting
  similarity) that species lists miss.
\item
  \textbf{Biological control:} classical importation (vedalia beetle
  success; cane toad disaster), augmentative releases, and conservation
  biological control. \emph{Wolbachia}-loaded \emph{Aedes aegypti}
  extends the framework to vector-borne disease.
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See \cref{sec:unit_X_population_ecology} for
  consumer-resource oscillations, \cref{sec:unit_X_ecosystem_ecology}
  for energy flux, and \cref{sec:unit_VII_microbial_ecology} for
  microbial communities.
\end{itemize}
