\subsection{Population Viability and the 50/500
Rule}\label{population-viability-and-the-50500-rule}

\subsubsection{Minimum Viable Population
(MVP)}\label{minimum-viable-population-mvp}

The \textbf{minimum viable population} is the smallest population with
at least 95\% probability of persistence for at least 100 generations,
accounting for four types of stochasticity:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3396}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1698}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4906}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Stochasticity type
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Mechanism
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Effect on small populations
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Demographic} & Random variation in births/deaths & Even when
\(r > 0\), small \(N\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} high extinction probability \\
\textbf{Environmental} & Weather, food fluctuations & Entire population
experiences same bad conditions \\
\textbf{Genetic} & Inbreeding depression, drift & \(F\) per generation
\(= 1/(2N_e)\); \(F > 0.10\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} fitness costs \\
\textbf{Catastrophes} & Fire, disease epidemic, storm & Sudden
\textgreater50\% mortality events; frequency matters \\
\end{longtable}
}

\subsubsection{Franklin's 50/500 Rule}\label{franklins-50500-rule}

\textbf{Franklin (1980) and \citet{franklinsoule1980}:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{\(N_e \geq 50\):} Short-term viability --- prevents rapid
  inbreeding depression

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Inbreeding rate: \(\Delta F = \frac{1}{2N_e} \leq 1\%\) per
    generation
  \item
    At \(F > 0.10\): measurable inbreeding depression (reduced litter
    size, increased juvenile mortality)
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{\(N_e \geq 500\):} Long-term viability --- maintains additive
  genetic variance for adaptive evolution

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Genetic variance lost per generation: \(\frac{1}{2N_e} = 0.1\%\)
  \item
    Balanced by new \hyperref[gl:mutation]{\textbf{mutation}} if
    \(N_e > 500\) \citep{frankham1995}
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Revised 100/1000 rule} (Frankham et al.~2014, \emph{Biol.
Conserv.}): More conservative; accounts for reduced purging
effectiveness and updated genomic data.

\textbf{\(N_e\) vs.~census \(N\):} Effective population size is
typically much smaller than census size:

\begin{equation}
N_e = \frac{4N_m N_f}{N_m + N_f}
\label{eq:biomes_and_conservation_3}
\end{equation}

Typical \(N_e/N\) ratio: 0.10-0.25 for vertebrates. Therefore, to
achieve \(N_e = 500\), census population needs to be
\(N = 2,000-5,000\).

\subsubsection{Population Viability Analysis
(PVA)}\label{population-viability-analysis-pva}

\textbf{PVA} uses species-specific demographic data and stochastic
simulation models (VORTEX, RAMAS) to project extinction probability:

\textbf{Inputs:} age/sex-specific survival, fecundity, variance in vital
rates, carrying capacity, catastrophe frequency, inbreeding
coefficients, habitat area.

\textbf{Outputs:} extinction probability over specified time horizon,
mean time to extinction, quasi-extinction threshold probability.

\textbf{Case study --- Florida panther} (\emph{Puma concolor coryi}): -
1994 PVA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} predicted extinction within 25 years without intervention -
\(N \approx 30\), \(N_e \approx 10\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} severe inbreeding (kinked tails,
cryptorchidism, heart defects) - 1995: 8 female Texas cougars introduced
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \textbf{genetic rescue} - 2023: population \textgreater200
individuals; heterozygosity increased, inbreeding depression reversed -
One of conservation biology's greatest success stories

\begin{quote}
\texorpdfstring{}{} \textbf{Clinical Connection --- Conservation Genetics and Inbreeding
Depression in Human Populations:} The principles of MVP and inbreeding
depression apply to human populations. Small, isolated populations
(e.g., the Amish community of Lancaster County, Pennsylvania) show
elevated frequencies of rare autosomal recessive disorders including
Ellis-van Creveld syndrome (6-fingered dwarfism; about 5\%
carrier frequency vs.~about 0.001\% in general population),
maple syrup urine disease, and glutaric aciduria. The
\textbf{\hyperref[gl:founder-effect]{founder effect}} --- establishment
of a population by a small number of individuals carrying a
non-representative sample of the gene pool --- mirrors the
\hyperref[gl:genetic-drift]{\textbf{genetic drift}} effects that reduce
\(N_e\) in endangered wildlife. Genomic screening programs in such
communities follow the same logic as conservation genomics: identifying
deleterious \hyperref[gl:allele]{\textbf{allele}}s and managing their
frequency.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Extinction Debt and Its Conservation
Implications}\label{extinction-debt-and-its-conservation-implications}

\textbf{Extinction debt} (Tilman et al.~1994, \emph{Nature}): Species
present in degraded/fragmented habitats are committed to future
extinction because habitat can no longer support viable populations ---
but extinction is \textbf{delayed} (50-500 years) by existing long-lived
individuals.

\subsubsection{Mathematical Framework}\label{mathematical-framework}

\begin{equation}
\text{Species committed to extinction} = S_{\text{pre-fragmentation}} - c \cdot A_{\text{remaining}}^z
\label{eq:biomes_and_conservation_4}
\end{equation}

where \(S_{\text{pre-fragmentation}}\) is species richness before
habitat loss, \(A_{\text{remaining}}\) is remaining habitat area, and
\(c\) and \(z\) are the species-area parameters whose log--log slope
steepens from contiguous continental biomes toward isolated oceanic
islands (\cref{fig:unit_X_species_area}).

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering

\subsubsection{Relaxation Time}\label{relaxation-time}

\textbf{Relaxation time} = the period between habitat loss and final
extinction of committed species. Determined by: - Longevity of
individuals (trees: centuries; insects: months) - Generation time
(longer generation = longer debt) - Habitat quality of remaining
fragments - Connectivity between patches (rescue effect)

\textbf{Conservation implication:} Present-day species richness
\textbf{overestimates} long-term viability. Conservation assessments
based on current presence may be dangerously optimistic. Extinction debt
means that the full consequences of today's deforestation will not be
realised for decades to centuries.

\subsubsection{Edge Effects}\label{edge-effects}

Habitat edges create microclimatic gradients that penetrate 100-300 m
into forest fragments:

predation increase \\
Invasive species & 100-500 m & Exotic plants establish in disturbed
edges \\
\end{longtable}
}

For a circular reserve:

\begin{equation}
\text{Interior area} = \pi(r - d)^2
\label{eq:biomes_and_conservation_5}
\end{equation}

where \(r\) = reserve radius and \(d\) = edge penetration distance. For
a 10-ha circular reserve (\(r = 178\) m) with 200-m edge effects:
\textbf{zero interior habitat.} This illustrates why small fragments are
ecological traps for interior-dependent species.

\subsubsection{Habitat Corridors}\label{habitat-corridors}

\textbf{Evidence for corridor effectiveness:} - Tewksbury et al.~(2002,
\emph{PNAS}): Connected patches had 25-100\% more pollinator movement
than unconnected - Gilbert-Norton et al.~(2010, meta-analysis): Movement
between patches 50\% higher with corridors - \textbf{Florida Wildlife
Corridor} (legislated 2021): 1,000+ mile protected corridor from
Everglades to Okefenokee Swamp

\textbf{Stepping stones:} For species that can cross moderate distances
(birds, bats, strong-flying insects), stepping stone patches may be as
effective as continuous corridors at lower cost.

\begin{quote}
\texorpdfstring{}{} \textbf{Clinical Connection --- Urban Green Corridors and Human
Health:} The principles of habitat corridors extend to urban planning
and human health. Studies in Philadelphia, Chicago, and Singapore
demonstrate that connected urban greenways (tree-lined corridors
connecting parks) reduce urban heat island effects by 2-5\(^\circ\)C,
decrease particulate matter (PM\(_{2.5}\)) by 15-25\%, and increase
physical activity by 30-40\% in nearby residents. Green corridors also
reduce stress biomarkers (salivary
\hyperref[gl:cortisol]{\textbf{cortisol}} decreased 20\% after 30-minute
walks in urban green corridors vs.~streets; Roe et al.~2013).
Conservation biology's core-corridor-matrix design principles thus have
direct applications to One Health approaches integrating biodiversity
conservation, climate adaptation, and human wellbeing.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check:} A conservation planner has a budget to protect
1,000 ha of tropical forest. Option A: one 1,000-ha reserve. Option B:
ten 100-ha reserves spread across different habitat types. Option C:
five 100-ha reserves connected by 100-m-wide corridors (total 500 ha
reserves + 500 ha corridors). Which design best protects: (a) a
large-bodied apex predator? (b) maximum regional species richness? (c)
genetic connectivity? Justify each answer using island biogeography
theory.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Emerging Conservation
Strategies}\label{emerging-conservation-strategies}

\subsubsection{Rewilding}\label{rewilding}

\textbf{Rewilding} (Soule \& Noss 1998; updated Jorgensen 2024,
\emph{Nat. Ecol. Evol.}): Restore ecological processes --- especially
trophic interactions --- by reintroducing lost species, particularly
apex predators and megaherbivores.

\textbf{Three types of rewilding:}

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2105}}

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3684}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Trophic rewilding} & Reintroduce apex predators/herbivores to
restore cascades & Wolves in Yellowstone (1995); lynx in UK
(proposed) \\
\textbf{Pleistocene rewilding} & Use ecological proxies for extinct
megafauna & Pleistocene Park, Siberia (bison, horses to create mammoth
steppe) \\
\textbf{Passive rewilding} & Remove human disturbance; allow natural
regeneration & European farmland abandonment \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} forest recovery \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Quantitative outcomes of wolf reintroduction in Yellowstone:} -
Elk: population reduced about 50\% (12,000 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} 6,000); behaviour
change (avoid riverbanks) - Willows: height increased 5-fold in riparian
areas within 15 years - Beavers: 0 colonies in 1995 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} 12 colonies by
2012 - Songbirds: 5 species returned to recovering riparian habitat -
Stream morphology: channels narrowed and deepened as bank vegetation
stabilised soil - Berry production: increased \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} grizzly bear diet
shifted (consuming 10x more berries)

\textbf{Pleistocene Park hypothesis:} Zimov et al.~(2012,
\emph{Science}): Reintroducing large herbivores to Arctic tundra
compacts snow in winter, allowing cold air to freeze soil deeper,
\textbf{slowing permafrost thaw} by about 80\% compared to
snow-insulated control plots.

\subsubsection{Conservation Genomics}\label{conservation-genomics}

\textbf{Whole-\hyperref[gl:genome]{\textbf{genome}} sequencing} of
threatened populations enables:

Conservation genomics is strongest when sequencing is tied to a
management decision rather than treated as an expensive description.
Runs of homozygosity estimate recent inbreeding, allele-frequency
outliers can nominate local adaptation, pangenome or long-read
approaches can reveal structural variation, and pedigree-aware sampling
can separate ancestry from recent bottlenecks. The ethical layer is
inseparable: sampling permits, Indigenous data sovereignty,
benefit-sharing, and the risk of over-prioritising ``genetically
interesting'' populations most affect whether the genomic evidence
should guide action.

\subsubsection{Assisted Gene Flow and Assisted
Migration}\label{assisted-gene-flow-and-assisted-migration}

\textbf{Assisted gene flow:} Intentionally moving alleles from adapted
to non-adapted populations of the same species: - Coral: transplanting
heat-tolerant \emph{Acropora} genotypes to vulnerable reefs (Palumbi et
al.~2014, \emph{Science}) - Trees: moving southern seed sources to
northern planting sites to pre-adapt to warming (assisted migration of
\emph{Pinus contorta} in British Columbia)

\textbf{Assisted migration (managed relocation):} Moving entire species
to new locations outside their historical range where future climate is
suitable. Controversial due to invasion risk.

\textbf{De-extinction:} Using genomic engineering to resurrect
functional analogues of extinct species: - \textbf{Woolly mammoth
project} (Colossal Biosciences): Editing Asian elephant genome with
mammoth cold-adaptation genes (TRPV3, haemoglobin variants, fat
deposition); goal: produce cold-adapted elephants for Arctic rewilding -
\textbf{Thylacine project} (Colossal): Reconstructing thylacine genome
from museum specimens - \textbf{Ethical debates:} Should resources be
spent on de-extinction rather than preventing current extinctions?

\subsubsection{Climate-Adaptive
Management}\label{climate-adaptive-management}

Traditional conservation aims to preserve historical baselines.
\textbf{Climate-adaptive management} accepts that ecosystems are
changing and manages for future conditions:

The hard part is deciding when to resist change, when to help a system
transition, and when to redirect effort toward ecosystem function rather
than historical composition. Coral reefs illustrate the tradeoff:
assisted gene flow, symbiont management, shading, and local
water-quality improvement can raise local resilience, but they do not
remove the external heat and acidification drivers. Climate-adaptive
management is therefore a portfolio problem, pairing local stress
reduction with monitoring, emissions context, social feasibility, and
explicit thresholds for changing strategy
\citep{noaa2025coralbleaching,ipbes2024transformative}.

\subsection{7B Climate Velocity, Refugia, and Range
Shifts}\label{b-climate-velocity-refugia-and-range-shifts}

\citet{ripple2012} and Loarie et al.~(2009, \emph{Nature}) established
\textbf{climate velocity} as the central organising metric for
climate-adaptive conservation. The velocity is the speed at which a
given thermal envelope moves across the landscape, and species must
disperse at least this fast to track their climatic niche.

\begin{equation}
v_{\text{climate}} = \frac{\partial T/\partial t}{|\nabla T|}
\label{eq:unit_X_climate_velocity}
\end{equation}

The numerator is the rate of climate change at a point (°C/yr); the
denominator is the local spatial temperature gradient (°C/km).
Rearranging gives velocity in km/yr.

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4792}}@{}}

Mountain (e.g., Andes) & 5 °C/km vertically & 0.006 km/yr (6 m/yr ---

Temperate plains & 0.05 °C/km & 0.6 km/yr \\

Subtropical plains & 0.003 °C/km & 10 km/yr \\
\end{longtable}
}

The flattest landscapes generate the fastest velocities --- exactly
where species cannot escape upslope. \textbf{Migration lags} therefore
cluster in lowland tropical and temperate plains: trees often disperse
at roughly 0.1--0.5 km/yr, which can be 10--100\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} too slow for tropical
lowlands but adequate for some mountain settings.

\subsubsection{Refugia and Their
Identification}\label{refugia-and-their-identification}

\textbf{Climate refugia} are locations where the local climate changes
more slowly than the regional average, providing temporary or permanent
havens for species unable to track climate velocity. Recognised refugia
types:

\endlastfoot
\textbf{Topographic} & Cold-air pooling, north-facing slopes, deep
canyons buffer temperature & Klamath-Siskiyou (NW USA); Mediterranean
canyons \\
\textbf{Hydrological} & Groundwater-fed streams, springs, lakes maintain
cool temperatures & Spring-fed cold-water salmonid habitat \\
\textbf{Microclimatic} & Forest interior buffering (--2 to --5 °C
vs.~open canopy) & Cathedral-grove old growth; tropical understory \\
\textbf{Elevational} & Mountains hold residual cool habitat above
warming lowlands & Alpine ecosystems globally \\
\textbf{Coastal upwelling} & Cold-water upwelling buffers warming
surface oceans & California Current; Benguela; Peru \\
\textbf{Cryptic / paleo} & Sites that remained inhabitable through
Pleistocene glaciations & Many high-biodiversity hotspots map onto past
refugia \\
\end{longtable}
}

Refugia identification is a major effort of climate-adaptive
conservation planning: high-resolution climate downscaling (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\leq}}{<=} 1 km
grids) plus species distribution modelling reveals locations where
target species can persist longest, prioritising them for protection.
The \textbf{Adapt West} initiative (Conservation Biology Institute) maps
climate refugia for North American species; analogous tools exist in
Australia, Europe, and parts of South America.

\subsection{7C Ecosystem-Based Adaptation: Using Nature for Climate
Resilience}\label{c-ecosystem-based-adaptation-using-nature-for-climate-resilience}

\textbf{Ecosystem-Based Adaptation (EbA)} uses biodiversity and
ecosystem services as part of an overall adaptation strategy to help
people adapt to climate change. The framework --- formalised by the CBD
and IUCN in 2009 --- sits at the intersection of conservation and human
resilience: protecting and restoring ecosystems to buffer communities
against floods, storms, droughts, heat waves, and rising seas, while
simultaneously sequestering carbon and conserving biodiversity.

tropical forest density); fisheries nursery \\
\textbf{Coral reef restoration} & Wave dissipation (reefs reduce wave
energy 70--95 \%); coastal protection valued at
about \$10,000/km/yr & Tourism; fisheries; biodiversity \\
\textbf{Urban green infrastructure} & Tree canopy reduces urban heat
island by 2--5 °C; permeable surfaces reduce flooding & Air quality;
mental health; physical activity \\
\textbf{Wetland conservation} & Floodplain water storage; nutrient
filtration & Wildlife habitat; recreation \\
\textbf{Reforestation / agroforestry} & Soil retention; rainfall
recycling; microclimate stabilisation & Carbon storage; smallholder
livelihoods \\
\textbf{Drought-tolerant agroecosystems} & Diverse cropping, perennial
roots, soil organic matter & Food security; reduced N\(_2\)O \\
\textbf{Living shorelines} & Marsh and oyster reef construction
replacing seawalls & Habitat; better long-term storm performance than
hard infrastructure \\
\end{longtable}
}

\subsubsection{Quantified Performance}\label{quantified-performance}

EbA projects often outperform engineered alternatives on cost and
resilience:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Mangroves vs.~seawalls.} Coastal protection from mangroves in
  the Philippines averages \$94/m of coastline; equivalent seawall
  construction averages \$2,000/m, with no co-benefits and high
  maintenance (Beck et al.~2018, \emph{Nat. Commun.}).
\item
  \textbf{Hurricane Katrina (2005).} Wetland loss in the Mississippi
  Delta increased storm surge by about 25\%; restoring 100
  km\(^2\) of marsh would reduce surge damage in vulnerable parishes by
  about 10--15 \% (Day et al.~2007, \emph{Science}).
\item
  \textbf{2003 European heat wave.} Cities with dense urban green
  infrastructure (e.g., Vienna) experienced about 30 \% fewer
  heat-related deaths than comparable cities with less greening
  (Smargiassi et al.~2009).
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Limits of EbA}\label{limits-of-eba}

EbA is not a panacea. Limitations:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Cannot substitute for emissions reduction.} No amount of
  coastal restoration prevents the catastrophic outcomes of 4 °C
  warming.
\item
  \textbf{Climate change itself is undermining the adapters.} Coral
  bleaching kills the reefs we want to use for coastal protection;
  mangroves face sea-level rise faster than they can build sediment.
\item
  \textbf{Equity and tenure issues.} EbA projects fail when they ignore
  Indigenous land rights or displace communities.
\end{itemize}

EbA is best understood as one component of a multi-layered adaptation
portfolio that also includes hard infrastructure, social systems, and
aggressive emissions cuts.

\begin{quote}
\texorpdfstring{}{} \textbf{Clinical Connection --- Heat Action Plans and Public Health.}
Following the 2003 European heat wave (about 70,000 excess
deaths) and the 2010 Russian heat wave (about 55,000 excess
deaths), cities increasingly couple ecological strategies (urban tree
planting, cool roofs, restored wetlands and parks) with public health
interventions (heat warning systems, cooling shelters,
vulnerable-population outreach). Ahmedabad, India implemented South
Asia's first Heat Action Plan in 2013 after a 2010 heat wave killed
\textgreater{} 1,300 residents; subsequent years saw about 30\%
reductions in heat-related mortality despite continued warming. Mexico
City, Phoenix, and Chicago have similar plans. These One Health
interventions integrate biodiversity conservation, urban ecology, and
human health --- operationalising the EbA framework.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check:} A coastal municipality must spend its limited
adaptation budget on protecting 20 km of shoreline from increasing storm
surge. (a) Compare the cost-benefit profile of seawall construction
vs.~mangrove restoration. (b) Why is EbA not always the best choice ---
what conditions favour hard infrastructure? (c) How does coral bleaching
complicate the math?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsubsection{The 30x30 Target}\label{the-30x30-target}

The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF, 2022) set a
target to protect 30\% of land and 30\% of ocean by 2030
\citep{cbd2022kunmingmontreal}. Current status:

\begin{equation}
\text{Terrestrial: } 16.7\% \xrightarrow{\text{need}} 30\% \text{ (add 20 million km}^2\text{)}
\label{eq:biomes_and_conservation_6}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
\text{Marine: } 8.3\% \xrightarrow{\text{need}} 30\% \text{ (add 78 million km}^2\text{)}
\label{eq:biomes_and_conservation_7}
\end{equation}

\textbf{Challenges:} - Quality vs.~quantity (many protected areas are
``paper parks'' with no enforcement) - Indigenous and local community
rights (30x30 must not displace indigenous peoples) - Representativeness
(current protected areas biased toward ``rock and ice'' ---
high-altitude, low-productivity areas) - Financial gap: estimated \$700
billion/yr needed; current spending about \$100 billion/yr

\subsubsection{Payments for Ecosystem
Services}\label{payments-for-ecosystem-services}

\textbf{REDD+} (Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest
Degradation): International carbon market payments incentivise
forest-rich developing nations to avoid deforestation. \$5 billion in
pledges as of 2024, but implementation faces challenges of
additionality, leakage, permanence, and measurement.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Concept Check:} The Aichi Targets (2010-2020) were largely
unmet. What factors contributed to their failure, and how does the
Kunming-Montreal Framework attempt to address these shortcomings?
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Worked Example}\label{worked-example-8}

\textbf{Problem:} An ecologist studies bird species on an archipelago.
The species-area relationship for this region follows the equation
\(S = cA^z\), where \(c = 10\) and \(z = 0.3\). Island X has an area
(\(A\)) of \(1,000\text{ km}^2\). Calculate the expected number of bird
species (\(S\)) on Island X.

\textbf{Solution:}

\textbf{Step 1. Identify the given variables.} - Area (\(A\)) =
\(1,000\text{ km}^2\) - Constant (\(c\)) = 10 - Exponent (\(z\)) = 0.3

\textbf{Step 2. Substitute the values into the species-area equation.}
\[S = cA^z \label{eq:unit_X_biomes_and_conservation_item_1}\]

\[S = 10 \times (1000)^{0.3} \label{eq:unit_X_biomes_and_conservation_item_2}\]

\textbf{Step 3. Calculate the exponent.} Notice that \(1000 = 10^3\).
Therefore:
\[(10^3)^{0.3} = 10^{(3 \times 0.3)} = 10^{0.9} \label{eq:unit_X_biomes_and_conservation_item_3}\]

Let's approximate \(10^{0.9}\). Since \(10^1 = 10\) and
\(10^{0.5} \approx 3.16\), \(10^{0.9} \approx 7.94\). (Exact value:
\(10^{0.9} \approx 7.943\))

\textbf{Step 4. Solve for \(S\).}
\[S = 10 \times 7.943 \label{eq:unit_X_biomes_and_conservation_item_4}\]

\[S \approx 79.43 \label{eq:unit_X_biomes_and_conservation_item_5}\]

\textbf{Answer:} Island X is expected to support approximately
\textbf{79 bird species}.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Worked Example: Effective Population Size and the 50/500
Rule}\label{worked-example-effective-population-size-and-the-50500-rule}

\textbf{Problem:} A captive recovery herd of an endangered ungulate has
a census size of \(N = 120\) individuals, but primarily \(N_m = 20\)
males and \(N_f = 100\) females actually breed. Calculate the effective
population size \(N_e\), the per-generation inbreeding rate
\(\Delta F\), and evaluate the herd against the 50/500 rule for
short-term and long-term viability.

\textbf{Solution:}

\textbf{Step 1. Identify the given variables.} - Breeding males
(\(N_m\)) = 20 - Breeding females (\(N_f\)) = 100 - Census size (\(N\))
= 120

\textbf{Step 2. Substitute into the unequal-sex-ratio effective-size
equation.}
\[N_e = \frac{4 N_m N_f}{N_m + N_f} \label{eq:unit_X_biomes_and_conservation_item_6}\]

\[N_e = \frac{4 \times 20 \times 100}{20 + 100} = \frac{8{,}000}{120} \approx 66.7 \label{eq:unit_X_biomes_and_conservation_item_7}\]

\textbf{Step 3. Compute the per-generation inbreeding rate.}
\[\Delta F = \frac{1}{2 N_e} = \frac{1}{2 \times 66.7} \approx 0.0075 = 0.75\%\text{ per generation} \label{eq:unit_X_biomes_and_conservation_item_8}\]

\textbf{Step 4. Evaluate against the 50/500 rule.} With
\(N_e \approx 67\), the herd clears the short-term threshold
(\(N_e \geq 50\)) that guards against rapid inbreeding depression, but
it falls far short of the long-term threshold (\(N_e \geq 500\)) needed
to retain additive genetic variance for future adaptation. The skewed
sex ratio is the cause: the effective size is barely over half the
census size, even though 120 animals are present.

\textbf{Answer:} \(N_e \approx 67\) and \(\Delta F \approx 0.75\%\) per
generation. The herd is demographically defensible in the short term but
is genetically committed to losing roughly 0.75\% of its heterozygosity
each generation; without managed gene flow or population growth it
remains at elevated long-term extinction risk because it cannot meet the
\(N_e \geq 500\) adaptive-potential standard.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsubsection{Minimum Viable Population and Genetic Rescue: Case
Studies from Conservation
Biology}\label{minimum-viable-population-and-genetic-rescue-case-studies-from-conservation-biology}

\textbf{Minimum viable population (MVP)} is defined as the smallest
population size with \(\geq 95\ \%\) probability of persistence over 100
generations, incorporating demographic stochasticity, environmental
variance, and genetic deterioration from inbreeding depression and loss
of adaptive variation. The classical rule-of-thumb is the \textbf{``50 /
500 rule''} (Franklin 1980): \(N_e \geq 50\) to avoid short-term
inbreeding depression, \(N_e \geq 500\) to retain long-term adaptive
potential against mutation-drift balance. Modern refinements (Frankham,
Brook \& Bradshaw 2014) revise these upward --- \(N_e \geq 100\) and
\(N_e \geq 1000\) --- as the more defensible thresholds given empirical
estimates of mutational-variance and inbreeding-load effects.

\textbf{Case 1 --- The Arabian Oryx (\emph{Oryx leucoryx})}. Extinct in
the wild by 1972 after hunting reduced the Arabian population to zero,
the species survived primarily in a 9-founder ``World Herd'' assembled
at Phoenix Zoo. Careful pedigree management and reintroduction programs
(Oman 1982, Saudi Arabia 1989, Jordan 1997) have grown the wild
population to about 1250 (IUCN 2017, Vulnerable). The genetic
cost: current population heterozygosity is about 70 \% of the
pre-bottleneck estimate, and most 6 microsatellite loci have at most 2
alleles --- a cautionary example that demographic recovery does not
erase the genetic signature of a bottleneck.

\textbf{Case 2 --- The California Condor (\emph{Gymnogyps
californianus})}. From a 1982 low of 22 individuals (the entire species
in captivity by 1987), a captive-breeding / release program has grown
the population to \textgreater{} 500 (half wild, half captive). Genomic
sequencing (Ralls et al.~2020) detected \textbf{23 known deleterious
alleles} in the founders, two fixed during the bottleneck. The ongoing
challenge is not census size but \textbf{lead toxicosis} from ingestion
of lead ammunition in carcasses --- a clear example of \emph{why}
habitat and regulatory intervention remain necessary even when
demographic targets are met.

\textbf{Genetic rescue} is the deliberate introduction of unrelated
individuals into a small, inbred population to restore heterozygosity.
The textbook case is the \textbf{Florida panther (\emph{Puma concolor
coryi})}: by the 1990s, about 30 individuals remained, with striking
inbreeding-depression \hyperref[gl:phenotype]{\textbf{phenotype}}s
(cryptorchidism, cardiac defects). Introducing 8 female Texas cougars in
1995 doubled heterozygosity within one generation; population is now
about 200 with reduced deformities and increased reproductive
success (Johnson et al., \emph{Science} 2010). The Isle Royale wolves
(introduction of 19 wolves 2018--2021) represent the latest live
experiment. Genetic rescue is \emph{not} a comprehensive solution --- it
can disrupt locally adapted gene complexes, introduce maladapted
alleles, and dilute evolutionary uniqueness (the Florida panther now
bears about 5 \% Texas-cougar ancestry). The decision is
typically a balance of short-term demographic benefit against long-term
evolutionary coherence.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Current Evidence and Frontier
Biology}\label{current-evidence-and-frontier-biology-37}

For \textbf{Biomes and Conservation Biology}, frontier biology belongs
inside the evidence logic of the chapter. Ecology and conservation
decisions increasingly combine field data, remote sensing, community
knowledge, model uncertainty, and explicit values. The core reading
question is this: conservation claims must separate ecological evidence,
social values, feasibility, and uncertainty in tradeoffs.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{What to verify:} identify the observation, model, assay, or
  dataset that would make the claim stronger or weaker.
\item
  \textbf{What to qualify:} state the scale, organism, cell type,
  environmental condition, or population where the claim is expected to
  hold.
\item
  \textbf{What to compare:} test at least one alternative explanation,
  baseline, or null model before treating the pattern as causal.
\item
  \textbf{What to cite:} distinguish primary evidence, review synthesis,
  public dataset, and institutional guidance; for recent or numeric
  claims, prefer the source closest to the measurement and state what
  has changed since it was published.
\end{itemize}

Use biodiversity metrics carefully: population indices, extinction risk
categories, ecosystem services, and management targets answer different
questions
\citep{ipbes2019global,ipbes2024transformative,wwf2024livingplanet,iucn2025redlist,fao2024sofia}.

\textbf{Source practice:} For conservation claims, cite assessment
sources and state whether the evidence is a population index,
extinction-risk assessment, ecosystem-service valuation, satellite
product, or policy synthesis
\citep{ipbes2024transformative,noaa2025coralbleaching,fao2025sofi}.

Definition

\endlastfoot
\textbf{Biome} & Large-scale ecological zone defined by climate and
\hyperref[gl:dominant]{\textbf{dominant}} vegetation type \\
\textbf{Net primary productivity (NPP)} & Carbon fixed by plants minus
autotrophic respiration; g C/m\(^2\)/yr \\
\textbf{IUCN Red List} & Global system for evaluating extinction risk
using quantitative criteria \\
\textbf{Minimum viable population (MVP)} & Smallest population with at
least 95\% persistence probability for at least 100 generations \\
\textbf{50/500 rule} & \(N_e \geq 50\) short-term; \(N_e \geq 500\)
long-term viability (Franklin/Soule) \\
\textbf{Effective population size (\(N_e\))} & Genetically effective
number of breeding individuals; typically \(0.1-0.25 \times N\) \\
\textbf{Extinction debt} & Delayed extinction of species committed to
disappear due to past habitat loss \\
\textbf{SLOSS debate} & Trade-off between single large vs.~several small
reserves \\
\textbf{Rewilding} & Restoration of ecological processes via
reintroduction of lost species \\
\textbf{Population Viability Analysis (PVA)} & Stochastic simulation of
extinction probability \\
\textbf{Conservation genomics} & Application of whole-genome analysis to
conservation management \\
\textbf{Assisted gene flow} & Intentional translocation of alleles from
adapted to non-adapted populations \\
\textbf{Genetic rescue} & Introduction of unrelated individuals to
reverse inbreeding depression \\
\textbf{Climate velocity} & Speed at which climate conditions shift
geographically (km/yr) \\
\textbf{Edge effect} & Microclimatic and biotic changes at habitat
fragment boundaries \\
\textbf{Coral bleaching} & Thermal stress-induced expulsion of
zooxanthellae; loss of coral energy supply \\
\textbf{30x30} & Target to protect 30\% of land and ocean by 2030
(Kunming-Montreal GBF) \\
\textbf{De-extinction} & Using genomic engineering to resurrect
functional analogues of extinct species \\
\textbf{Novel biome} & Ecosystem with no historical analog, arising from
climate change \\
\textbf{IPBES} & Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on
Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services; ``IPCC for biodiversity'' \\
\textbf{Climate refugia} & Locations where local climate changes more
slowly than the regional average; havens for slow-dispersing species \\
\textbf{Ecosystem-based adaptation (EbA)} & Use of biodiversity and
ecosystem services to help people adapt to climate change \\
\textbf{Living shorelines} & Marsh, oyster reef, and mangrove
infrastructure replacing seawalls for coastal protection \\
\textbf{Living Planet Index} & WWF metric of mean change in monitored
vertebrate populations since 1970 \\
\textbf{Heat Action Plan} & Coupled public-health and ecological
response to extreme heat events \\
\textbf{Genetic load} & Accumulated deleterious alleles; heightened in
bottlenecked populations; affects translocation strategies \\
\textbf{Runs of homozygosity (ROH)} & Long stretches of homozygous DNA
indicating recent inbreeding; key conservation-genomic metric \\
\end{longtable}
}

\subsection{Review Questions}\label{review-questions-37}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Using the species-area relationship \(S = cA^z\) with \(c = 6\) and
  \(z = 0.28\), calculate species richness for a 50,000 ha intact forest
  and after fragmentation into 5 patches of 1,000 ha each. What fraction
  of species are committed to extinction via the fragmentation-driven
  extinction debt? How long might this debt take to be ``paid'' for
  long-lived tree species?
\item
  A population of sea turtles has \(N_e = 35\) and current
  heterozygosity \(H = 0.60\). (a) Apply the 50/500 rule to evaluate its
  short-term and long-term viability. (b) Calculate how many generations
  until \(H < 0.40\) using \(H_t = H_0(1 - 1/2N_e)^t\). (c) What genetic
  rescue strategy could improve the prognosis?
\item
  The Amazon has currently lost about 17\% of its original
  forest cover. Lovejoy and Nobre's tipping point threshold is
  about 20-25\%. (a) Explain the tipping mechanism (why is it
  non-linear?). (b) What conservation interventions are needed in terms
  of scale, urgency, and geographic targeting? (c) How does the
  transpiration recycling mechanism create a positive feedback loop
  during deforestation?
\item
  Explain the difference between demographic, environmental, genetic,
  and catastrophic stochasticity in an MVP context. Which was most
  important in the Florida panther case, and how was it mitigated?
  Calculate the inbreeding rate (\(\Delta F\)) for the panther
  population at \(N_e = 10\) vs.~after genetic rescue at \(N_e = 50\).
\item
  Compare rewilding and assisted gene flow as conservation strategies
  for climate change adaptation. For each, give one specific
  quantitative example (species, location, outcome metric, timescale).
\item
  A conservation biologist must design a reserve system for a large
  carnivore with home range = 200 km\(^2\) and an MVP of \(N_e = 500\)
  (\(N/N_e\) ratio = 4). Calculate: (a) minimum total census population
  needed, (b) minimum reserve area assuming 50\% habitat overlap between
  individuals, (c) whether a single reserve or corridor-connected system
  is more feasible. Design the reserve system.
\item
  The Great Barrier Reef has experienced 6 mass bleaching events in 10
  years. Using the degree heating weeks (DHW) metric, explain the
  mechanism of bleaching. At what level of global warming does coral
  reef survival become highly improbable? What is the economic value at
  stake (cite Deloitte or similar valuation studies)?
\item
  Evaluate the 30x30 target (Kunming-Montreal Framework). Calculate the
  additional area of land and ocean that must be protected to reach 30\%
  from current levels. What are the three most significant
  implementation challenges, and how might they be addressed?
\item
  The woolly mammoth de-extinction project aims to create cold-adapted
  elephants for Arctic tundra. (a) What ecological function would they
  serve? (b) How would they slow permafrost thaw? (c) What are the
  strongest ecological and ethical arguments for and against this
  approach?
\item
  Using the concept of climate velocity, explain why montane species are
  at lower risk of range contraction than lowland species. Calculate
  climate velocity for a flat landscape with temperature change =
  0.03\(^\circ\)C/yr and spatial gradient = 0.005\(^\circ\)C/km, vs.~a
  mountain with spatial gradient = 5\(^\circ\)C/km. What are the
  implications for conservation prioritisation?
\item
  Compute \breaktt{species\_area\_relationship} for
  \(A \in \{1, 10, 100\}\) km\(^2\) with \(c=2\), \(z=0.25\); discuss
  reserve sizing.
\item
  Contrast \textbf{inbreeding depression} vs.~\textbf{outbreeding
  depression} in translocation programs.
\item
  The IPBES 2019 Global Assessment ranked land-use change as the
  dominant terrestrial driver of biodiversity loss (about 30
  \%), with climate change at about 14 \% but rising. (a) Why
  is this \emph{current} ranking expected to invert by 2050? (b) How
  should conservation priority-setting respond to this projected shift?
  (c) The Transformative Change Assessment (IPBES 2024) argues that
  incremental conservation cannot meet biodiversity targets. What three
  systemic reforms does it recommend, and why are they outside
  traditional conservation biology?
\item
  Compare two endangered birds: species A in the high Andes (5 °C/km
  gradient) and species B on the Brazilian cerrado (0.005 °C/km
  gradient), with both facing 0.03 °C/yr warming. (a) Calculate climate
  velocity for each. (b) Predict their relative extinction risks. (c)
  How does this calculation re-prioritise conservation funding between
  the two regions?
\item
  A coastal municipality is choosing between (a) a 20-km concrete
  seawall (\$2,000/m, 50-yr lifetime, no co-benefits, requires periodic
  rebuilding) and (b) a 20-km mangrove restoration project (\$94/m
  initial, low maintenance, multiple co-benefits, but vulnerable to
  sea-level rise faster than mangrove sediment accretion). Calculate
  total costs over 50 years for each, and identify under what
  climate-change scenario each option is preferred.
\item
  Explain how the 50/500 rule, conservation genomics (runs of
  homozygosity, genetic load), and population viability analysis
  converge to inform genetic rescue decisions for the Florida panther.
  Why was the 1995 Texas-cougar introduction successful, and what risks
  (e.g., outbreeding depression) had to be balanced?
\item
  Define a climate refugium and list four types (topographic,
  hydrological, microclimatic, elevational). Why is identifying refugia
  critical for 21st-century reserve design? What datasets (climate
  models, species distribution models, paleoecology) does refugium
  identification require?
\item
  Critically evaluate the 30x30 target. (a) Calculate the additional
  area of land and ocean needed to reach 30 \% from current levels. (b)
  Why is \emph{quality} of protection (effective management, no ``paper
  parks'') at least as important as quantity? (c) How can 30x30 be
  implemented without violating Indigenous land rights, given that
  about 80 \% of remaining biodiversity is on
  Indigenous-managed lands?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Computational Bridge}\label{computational-bridge-34}

The power-law S--A curve is a one-liner:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]

\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ a }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ (}\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{10.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{100.0}\NormalTok{):}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Clinical / systems note:} Habitat fragmentation in zoonotic
emergence maps onto the same area-dependent extinction risk curves used
in terrestrial conservation.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Summary}\label{summary-37}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Nine terrestrial biomes:} tropical rainforest highest NPP
  (about 1,750 g C/m\(^2\)/yr); desert lowest
  (about 45-125); boreal forest largest land biome by area.
  Five aquatic biome types including coral reefs (most biodiverse marine
  ecosystem, threatened by bleaching).
\item
  \textbf{Climate change:} biome boundaries shifting 5-10 km/decade
  poleward; Amazon at about 17\% deforestation approaching
  20-25\% tipping point; permafrost thaw adds 2-5 Gt C/yr; novel biomes
  emerging on about 20\% of Earth's surface by 2100.
\item
  \textbf{Sixth Mass Extinction:} 100-1,000x background extinction rate;
  73\% vertebrate population decline since 1970; 1 million species
  threatened.
\item
  \textbf{IPBES findings:} about 1 million species threatened
  (12.5\%); 85\% of wetlands lost since 1700; 50\% coral reef loss since
  1870. Drivers ranked: land-use change \textgreater{} exploitation
  \textgreater{} climate change (rising fast) \textgreater{} pollution
  \textgreater{} invasives. Transformative Change Assessment (2024)
  argues incremental conservation insufficient.
\item
  \textbf{Climate velocity} \(v = (\partial T/\partial t)/|\nabla T|\):
  fast in flat tropical and temperate plains (6--10 km/yr), slow in
  mountains (6 m/yr); refugia (topographic, hydrological, microclimatic,
  elevational) are the key targets for climate-adaptive reserve design.
\item
  \textbf{Ecosystem-based adaptation (EbA):} mangroves, coral reefs,
  urban green infrastructure, wetlands, agroforestry. Often outperforms
  hard infrastructure on cost (\$94/m vs.~\$2,000/m for coastal
  protection) and provides co-benefits, but cannot substitute for
  emissions reduction.
\item
  \textbf{IUCN Red List:} CR = at least 80\% population decline under
  Criterion A; version 2025-1 listed 47,187 threatened species among
  169,420 assessed, and totals change as assessments expand
  \citep{iucn2025redlist}.
\item
  \textbf{MVP:} 50/500 rule (Franklin); revised 100/1000
  \citep{frankham2014}; PVA accounts for most stochasticity types.
  \(N_e/N\) ratio typically 0.10-0.25.
\item
  \textbf{Extinction debt:} fragmented species committed to extinction
  with 50-500 yr lags; current surveys overestimate long-term viability.
\item
  \textbf{Reserve design:} core-corridor-matrix; edge effects penetrate
  100-300 m; corridors increase movement 50\%; 30x30 target.
\item
  \textbf{Emerging strategies:} rewilding
  (\hyperref[gl:trophic-cascade]{\textbf{trophic cascade}}s),
  conservation genomics (ROH, adaptive variation), assisted gene flow
  (coral heat tolerance), de-extinction (mammoth project),
  climate-adaptive management.
\item
  \textbf{International frameworks:} CBD, CITES, 30x30 target; \$700
  billion/yr funding gap; quality and representativeness challenges.
\item
  \textbf{Connections:} See \cref{sec:unit_VI_phylogenetics} for
  phylogenetic diversity, \cref{sec:unit_X_community_ecology} for
  trophic rewilding, and \cref{sec:unit_V_population_genetics} for
  small-\hyperref[gl:population-genetics]{\textbf{population genetics}}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\section*{Lab A --- Systems Science and the Logic of
Emergence}\label{lab-a-systems-science-and-the-logic-of-emergence}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Lab A --- Systems Science and the Logic
of Emergence}

\label{sec:lab_unit_0_systems_science}

\emph{This activity accompanies \cref{sec:unit_0_systems_science} of the
textbook --- review that chapter before attempting the exercises below.}

\textbf{Unit 0 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.} Lab A}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection*{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-38}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Learning Objectives}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Identify the three canonical elements of a system (components,
  interactions, boundary) in concrete biological examples.
\item
  Diagram negative- and positive-feedback loops for real physiological
  systems and predict their stabilising or amplifying behaviour.
\item
  Compute response curves from the Hill equation and relate the Hill
  coefficient \(n\) to cooperativity and switch-like behaviour.
\item
  Reason about the difference between a complicated machine and a
  complex system using a worked example.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsubsection*{Alignment and Rubric
Map}\label{alignment-and-rubric-map}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Alignment and Rubric Map}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 1 (LO1):} Interpret the supplied evidence or model
  output for Systems Science and the Logic of Emergence.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 2 (LO2):} Identify controls and comparison groups that
  make the claim testable.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 3 (LO3):} Quantify uncertainty, boundary conditions,
  or alternative explanations before concluding.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 4 (LO4):} Transfer the mechanism to a new biological
  case or public-facing decision.
\item
  \textbf{Chapter LO coverage:} LO1, LO2, LO3, LO4
\item
  \textbf{Rubric dimensions:} evidence; controls; uncertainty;
  mechanism; transfer. \#\# Background \{.unnumbered\}
\end{itemize}

A \textbf{system} is a set of interacting components, bounded against
its surroundings, whose behaviour depends on the interactions as much as
on the parts. The central mathematical tool for stability is the
\textbf{Hill equation}:

\begin{equation}
\theta \;=\; \frac{[L]^n}{K_d^n + [L]^n}
\label{eq:lab_a_hill}
\end{equation}

where \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\theta}}{theta} is the fraction of receptors bound, \([L]\) the ligand
concentration, \(K_d\) the dissociation constant, and \(n\) the Hill
coefficient. For \(n = 1\) the curve is hyperbolic (graded response);
for \(n = 4\) it is steep and switch-like (as in haemoglobin's O\(_2\)
binding).

Today's lab trains three intuitions: what counts as ``the system'', how
feedback loops behave, and how cooperativity converts graded chemistry
into binary biology.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

  \(n = 1, 2, 4\) at \([L] = K_d\), \(2K_d\), \(5K_d\). Tabulate.
\item

\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection*{Part 1 --- Identifying
Systems}\label{part-1-identifying-systems}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Part 1 --- Identifying Systems}

For each of the following, identify: (a) the components, (b) the key
interactions, (c) the boundary separating system from environment, and
(d) one input and one output crossing the boundary.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  A single mitochondrion.
\item
  The glucose-insulin-glucagon regulatory axis.
\item
  A coral reef.
\item
  A bacterial biofilm on a medical catheter.
\item
  A neuron's axon hillock.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection*{Part 2 --- Feedback Loop
Diagrams}\label{part-2-feedback-loop-diagrams}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Part 2 --- Feedback Loop Diagrams}

For each system below, diagram the feedback loop and classify it as
positive or negative. Predict the steady-state behaviour (stable fixed
point, oscillation, or runaway).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Blood pressure \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} baroreceptor firing \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} vagal tone \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} heart rate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} blood
  pressure.
\item
  Oxytocin \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} uterine contraction \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} stretch receptor \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} oxytocin (during
  labour).
\item
  Luteinising hormone \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} ovarian oestradiol \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} hypothalamic GnRH
  (follicular phase).
\item
  Luteinising hormone \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} ovarian oestradiol \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} hypothalamic GnRH
  (ovulatory phase).
\item
  Depolarising Na\(^+\) current \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} more open Na\(^+\) channels \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  depolarisation (action potential upstroke).
\end{enumerate}

Why do loops 3 and 4 have different signs, and what does the switch
imply for the dynamics of the menstrual cycle?

\subsubsection*{Part 3 --- Hill Curve by
Hand}\label{part-3-hill-curve-by-hand}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Part 3 --- Hill Curve by Hand}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Using \(K_d = 10\,\mu\mathrm{M}\), compute \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\theta}}{theta} at
  \([L] = 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100\,\mu\mathrm{M}\) for three values of
  \(n\): 1, 2.8 (physiological Hb), and 4.
\item

  where small changes in \([L]\) produce large changes in \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\theta}}{theta}.
\item
  For which \(n\) is the transition sharpest? How does this
  cooperativity benefit an oxygen-carrying pigment?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}

\item
  For haemoglobin (\(n \approx 2.8\)), compute the difference in O\(_2\)

  capillaries (\([\mathrm{O}_2] = 20\,\mathrm{mmHg}\)). Why is the

\item
  In Part 2, the ovarian-pituitary loop reverses sign across the

  can be added without breaking old ones). Give one counter-example ---
  a domain where modularity \emph{constrains} evolution rather than
  freeing it.
\item
  The textbook notes that biological delays destabilise feedback. A
  surgical patient on a mechanical ventilator has a CO\(_2\)-sensing
  feedback loop with a built-in 10-second measurement lag. Predict what
  happens as you increase the loop gain; suggest one design fix.
\item
  Design a paper-based experiment to test whether a bacterial-population
  model exhibits emergent collective behaviour distinct from
  isolated-cell behaviour. What is the null hypothesis and what
  observation card would refute it?
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Lab B --- Complex Adaptive
Systems}\label{lab-b-complex-adaptive-systems}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Lab B --- Complex Adaptive Systems}

\label{sec:lab_unit_0_complex_adaptive_systems}

\emph{This activity accompanies
\cref{sec:unit_0_complex_adaptive_systems} of the textbook --- review
that chapter before attempting the exercises below.}

\textbf{Unit 0 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.} Lab B}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection*{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-39}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Learning Objectives}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Simulate a simple agent-based system on paper and observe emergent
  global behaviour.
\item
  Compute the period of a logistic map for selected reproductive rates
  and identify the onset of chaos.
\item
  Sketch a phase diagram for a two-basin attractor landscape and reason
  about tipping points.
\item
  Distinguish \emph{robustness} from \emph{redundancy} using a worked
  biological example.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsubsection*{Alignment and Rubric
Map}\label{alignment-and-rubric-map-1}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Alignment and Rubric Map}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 1 (LO1):} Interpret the supplied evidence or model
  output for Complex Adaptive Systems.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 2 (LO2):} Identify controls and comparison groups that
  make the claim testable.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 3 (LO3):} Quantify uncertainty, boundary conditions,
  or alternative explanations before concluding.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 4 (LO4):} Transfer the mechanism to a new biological
  case or public-facing decision.
\item
  \textbf{Chapter LO coverage:} LO1, LO2, LO3, LO4
\item
  \textbf{Rubric dimensions:} evidence; controls; uncertainty;
  mechanism; transfer. \#\# Background \{.unnumbered\}
\end{itemize}

A \textbf{complex adaptive system (CAS)} is a population of agents whose
collective behaviour emerges from local rules rather than central
control. Examples run from neurons in a cortical circuit to ants in a
colony to species in an ecosystem. Two mathematical tools recur across
scales:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{The logistic map} --- a discrete-time model
  \(x_{n+1} = r x_n (1 - x_n)\) that passes from stable fixed point \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  period-2 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} period-4 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} chaos as the parameter \(r\) increases. It
  captures the essence of bifurcation theory in a single line of
  algebra.
\item
  \textbf{Phase-space attractor landscapes} --- a potential-well picture
  that shows how systems can occupy alternative stable states with a
  ``tipping point'' between them, and how hysteresis delays recovery.
\end{enumerate}

This lab is paper-based; a calculator and graph paper are the only tools
needed.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsubsection*{Part 1 --- The Logistic Map by
Hand}\label{part-1-the-logistic-map-by-hand}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Part 1 --- The Logistic Map by
Hand}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Starting from \(x_0 = 0.2\), compute 20 iterations of the logistic map
  for each of these \(r\) values: \(r = 2.5,\; 3.2,\; 3.5,\; 3.8\).
\item
  For each \(r\), plot \(x_n\) against iteration number \(n\) on the
  same axes (use a different colour for each \(r\)).
\item
  Identify the long-term behaviour: fixed point, period-2, period-4, or
  chaotic.
\item
  Bonus: compute \(x_{100}\) for \(r = 3.8\) with \(x_0 = 0.2\) and
  \(x_0 = 0.20001\). How different are they? Relate to ``sensitive
  dependence on initial conditions.''
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection*{Part 2 --- Attractor Landscape and Tipping
Points}\label{part-2-attractor-landscape-and-tipping-points}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Part 2 --- Attractor Landscape and
Tipping Points}

A shallow lake has two alternative stable states: \textbf{clear} (low
algae, clear water) and \textbf{turbid} (high algae, murky). Phosphorus
loading \(P\) shifts which state is stable.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Sketch the potential landscape \(U(A)\) (where \(A\) = algal biomass)
  for three values of \(P\): low (primarily clear is stable),
  intermediate (both states stable), and high (primarily turbid is
  stable).
\item
  Mark the \textbf{tipping point} (\(P_1\)) where the clear state loses
  stability as \(P\) increases.
\item
  Mark the \textbf{restoration point} (\(P_2\)) where the turbid state
  loses stability as \(P\) decreases.
\item
  Compare \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) --- which is smaller? This gap is the
  hysteresis loop and explains why eutrophication is hard to reverse.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection*{Part 3 --- Robustness Versus
Redundancy}\label{part-3-robustness-versus-redundancy}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Part 3 --- Robustness Versus
Redundancy}

Consider the mammalian immune system as a CAS. It has five categories of
robustness:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Redundancy} --- multiple B-cell clones specific to the same
  antigen.
\item
  \textbf{Degeneracy} --- T- and B-cells with overlapping but distinct
  function.
\item
  \textbf{Modularity} --- innate vs.~adaptive compartments.
\item
  \textbf{Negative feedback} --- regulatory T cells suppress overactive
  responders.
\item
  \textbf{Diversity} --- V(D)J recombination generates
  about \(10^{11}\) receptor sequences.
\end{itemize}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  For each category, give one concrete example from the immune system.
\item
  Then list one \emph{fragility} that the same architectural feature
  introduces. (E.g., immune redundancy also means multiple places
  autoimmunity can arise.)
\item
  Discuss in your group: would a maximally robust system also be
  maximally evolvable?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-1}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The logistic map transitions from periodic to chaotic behaviour as
  \(r\) passes through the Feigenbaum point (about 3.57). Why
  does this transition occur even though the underlying equation is
  completely deterministic?
\item
  In Part 2, you drew a hysteresis loop. Why can reducing \(P\) to the
  level \emph{at which} eutrophication occurred fail to restore the
  clear-water state? What mechanism sustains the turbid attractor?
\item
  Power-law distributions appear in earthquake magnitudes, neural
  avalanches, and extinction events. What common CAS mechanism could
  explain most three?
\item
  Cancer has been described as a ``failed CAS'' where normal tissue
  homeostasis breaks down. Identify two CAS features that go wrong in
  malignancy.
\item
  Propose a paper simulation or card-based experiment using a
  bacterial-biofilm model to demonstrate one CAS principle (e.g.,
  stigmergic self-organisation, threshold transitions, or robustness to
  perturbation). Describe the set-up, observable, and expected result.
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Lab C --- Active Inference and the Free Energy
Principle}\label{lab-c-active-inference-and-the-free-energy-principle}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Lab C --- Active Inference and the Free
Energy Principle}

\label{sec:lab_unit_0_active_inference}

\emph{This activity accompanies \cref{sec:unit_0_active_inference} of

\textbf{Unit 0 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.} Lab C}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection*{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-40}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Learning Objectives}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Apply core principles of active inference to concrete biological
  observations.
\item
  Compute a Bayesian posterior by hand for a one-dimensional inference
  problem and interpret the result in terms of prior, likelihood, and
  evidence.
\item
  Distinguish \emph{perceptual} inference (updating beliefs) from
  \emph{active} inference (acting to satisfy beliefs) using everyday
  examples.
\item
  Quantify how sensor precision changes the trade-off between updating a
  belief and acting to make a belief true.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsubsection*{Alignment and Rubric
Map}\label{alignment-and-rubric-map-2}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Alignment and Rubric Map}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 1 (LO1):} Interpret the supplied evidence or model
  output for Active Inference and the Free Energy Principle.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 2 (LO2):} Identify controls and comparison groups that
  make the claim testable.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 3 (LO3):} Quantify uncertainty, boundary conditions,
  or alternative explanations before concluding.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 4 (LO4):} Transfer the mechanism to a new biological
  case or public-facing decision.
\item
  \textbf{Chapter LO coverage:} LO1, LO2, LO3, LO4
\item
  \textbf{Rubric dimensions:} evidence; controls; uncertainty;
  mechanism; transfer. \#\# Background \{.unnumbered\}
\end{itemize}

Active inference proposes that living agents minimise a quantity called
\textbf{variational free energy} --- an upper bound on the ``surprise''
of observed sensory data given the agent's internal generative model.
The core equation (simplified):

\begin{equation}
F \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{Q}[\,\log Q(\mathbf{z}) - \log P(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{z})\,]
\label{eq:lab_ai_fe}
\end{equation}

where \(Q(\mathbf{z})\) is the agent's current belief about hidden
causes \(\mathbf{z}\), and \(P(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{z})\) is the agent's
model of how those causes generate observations \(\mathbf{o}\).
Minimising \(F\) is achieved either by \textbf{updating beliefs}
(perceptual inference) or \textbf{changing the world through action}
(active inference).

Today's lab is paper-based: you will work through two hand-computed
examples and one behaviour-card classification exercise. No computer is
required, though a calculator (or phone app) is useful for the Gaussian
arithmetic.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsubsection*{Part 1 --- Hand-computed Bayesian
Update}\label{part-1-hand-computed-bayesian-update}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Part 1 --- Hand-computed Bayesian
Update}

A bird forages for seeds hidden under two snow patches. Its prior belief
about the location of food is a Gaussian centred at position
\(\mu_0 = 10\) m (where food was yesterday) with variance
\(\sigma_0^2 = 4\,\mathrm{m}^2\). A partial snow melt gives a noisy
visual cue that food is at position \(o = 16\) m with likelihood
variance \(\sigma_o^2 = 12\,\mathrm{m}^2\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Compute the \textbf{prediction error}: \(\varepsilon = o - \mu_0\).
\item
  Compute the \textbf{Kalman gain}:
  \(K = \sigma_0^2 / (\sigma_0^2 + \sigma_o^2)\).
\item
  Compute the \textbf{posterior mean}:
  \(\mu_1 = \mu_0 + K \, \varepsilon\).
\item
  Compute the \textbf{posterior variance}:
  \(\sigma_1^2 = (1 - K) \, \sigma_0^2\).
\item
  Re-compute \(\mu_1\) under the assumption that the cue is \emph{very}
  noisy (\(\sigma_o^2 = 100\)) and \emph{very} precise
  (\(\sigma_o^2 = 0.5\)). Explain in words how the bird's final belief
  depends on sensor precision.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection*{Part 2 --- Perceptual vs.~Active
Inference}\label{part-2-perceptual-vs.-active-inference}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Part 2 --- Perceptual vs.~Active
Inference}

A person wakes up cold. Their generative model has a tight prior on body
temperature (\(\mu = 37\) °C, \(\sigma = 0.5\)). Their interoceptive
sensor reports 34.5 °C with \(\sigma = 1.0\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Compute the posterior belief about their body temperature (same
  formulae as Part 1).
\item
  The posterior free energy is reduced but still positive. List
  \textbf{three actions} the person could take that would drive free
  energy further toward zero by \emph{changing the observation} rather
  than the belief.
\item
  Argue in one paragraph why active inference is more effective than
  perceptual inference when the prior precision is tight (small
  \(\sigma_0\)) --- i.e., when the organism is ``committed'' to a
  particular internal state.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection*{Part 3 --- Behaviour Scenario
Classification}\label{part-3-behaviour-scenario-classification}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Part 3 --- Behaviour Scenario
Classification}

annotate whether it is perceptual (sampling information) or active
(imposing prediction on the environment). Record the evidence phrase

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-2}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Explain in one paragraph how the Kalman gain can be read as
  ``precision-weighted uncertainty reduction'' --- why \(K\) depends on
  the ratio of prior variance to total variance.
\item
  The generative model in Part 2 uses a \emph{tight} prior (low
  variance) on body temperature. How would the calculation change if the
  prior were loose (\(\sigma = 5\) °C)? Which regime corresponds to a
  pre-homeostatic organism; which to a strictly regulated endotherm?
\item
  In humans, chronic anxiety is sometimes described as a ``tight prior
  on safety.'' Using your computation from Part 2, explain why normal
  day-to-day sensory noise becomes persistently surprising to an anxious
  agent and what ``widening the prior'' (via exposure therapy or
  pharmacology) is doing mathematically.
\item
  Scientists have attempted to build artificial life --- robots that
  minimise free energy with respect to a battery-level sensor. Describe
  what the agent's \textbf{prior} on battery state and \textbf{action
  repertoire} would need to be so that the robot ``feels hungry'' at low
  charge and seeks a charging pad.
\item
  The textbook chapter notes that evolution itself can be cast as
  free-energy minimisation at the population scale: organisms whose
  generative models fail are eliminated. Argue for or against this
  framing by contrasting it with the Modern Synthesis's emphasis on
  fitness differentials.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection*{Discussion Questions}\label{discussion-questions-7}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Discussion Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Is ``surprise'' a purely mathematical quantity, or does it have
  phenomenal correlates? Consider how a newborn infant's surprise
  differs from an adult's when encountering the same stimulus.
\item
  Could two agents with identical sensory input hold different beliefs
  and both be rational under active inference? If yes, what determines
  each?
\item
  Does the free-energy principle predict that living things should seek
  complexity or simplicity in their environments? Justify using the
  trade-off between epistemic and instrumental value.
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Lab 1 --- Atoms, Molecules, and Chemical
Bonds}\label{lab-1-atoms-molecules-and-chemical-bonds}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Lab 1 --- Atoms, Molecules, and Chemical
Bonds}

\label{sec:lab_unit_I_atoms_molecules}

\subsection*{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-41}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Learning Objectives}

\emph{This activity accompanies \cref{sec:unit_I_atoms_molecules} of the
textbook --- review that chapter before attempting the exercises below.}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Identify polar and non-polar molecular regions using electronegativity
  reasoning
\item
  Interpret hydrogen bonding properties using printed observations and
  molecular cards
\item
  Distinguish ionic, covalent, and hydrogen bonds from structural and
  data evidence
\item
  Apply molecular polarity concepts to explain biological solubility
  patterns
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Alignment and Rubric
Map}\label{alignment-and-rubric-map-3}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Alignment and Rubric Map}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 1 (LO1):} Interpret the supplied evidence or model
  output for Atoms, Molecules, and Chemical Bonds.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 2 (LO2):} Identify controls and comparison groups that
  make the claim testable.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 3 (LO3):} Quantify uncertainty, boundary conditions,
  or alternative explanations before concluding.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 4 (LO4):} Transfer the mechanism to a new biological
  case or public-facing decision.
\item
  \textbf{Chapter LO coverage:} LO1, LO2, LO3, LO4
\item
  \textbf{Rubric dimensions:} evidence; controls; uncertainty;
  mechanism; transfer. \#\# Background \{.unnumbered\}
\end{itemize}

Chemistry underpins every biological process. Atoms bond through
electronegativity differences: when atoms share electrons unequally,
they form polar covalent bonds (as in O--H), creating partial charges
(\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\delta}}{delta}+ and \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\delta}}{delta}\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}). These partial charges enable hydrogen bonding --- the weak
but pervasive force that gives water its remarkable properties and
stabilises the three-dimensional shapes of proteins and DNA.

In this lab, you will use a paper dataset of solubility and
surface-tension observations as proxies for molecular polarity and
hydrogen bonding capacity: ``like dissolves like'' --- polar solutes
dissolve in polar solvents (water), while non-polar solutes dissolve
primarily in non-polar solvents (oil). You will also visualise electron
sharing differences using electronegativity tables and molecule cards.

\item

  Note whether the change improved consistency with the evidence.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-3}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Which solutes dissolved in water but not oil? Which dissolved in oil
  but not water? Explain in terms of bond polarity.
\item
  Why did NaCl dissolve in water but not in vegetable oil? What type of
  bond holds NaCl together, and how does water break it apart?

  systems?

  a large non-polar body) would dissolve in blood plasma (aqueous) or in
  a membrane (lipid). Justify your answer using polarity principles.
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Lab 2 --- Water --- The Molecule of
Life}\label{lab-2-water-the-molecule-of-life}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Lab 2 --- Water --- The Molecule of Life}

\label{sec:lab_unit_I_water_and_life}

\subsection*{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-42}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Learning Objectives}

\emph{This activity accompanies \cref{sec:unit_I_water_and_life} of the
textbook --- review that chapter before attempting the exercises below.}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Compare specific heat capacity patterns for water and oil using a
  printed dataset
\item
  Explain cohesion, adhesion, and capillarity from diagrams and model
  observations
\item
  Use solute concentration data to reason about water potential and
  osmosis
\item
  Relate water's physical properties to biological functions
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Alignment and Rubric
Map}\label{alignment-and-rubric-map-4}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Alignment and Rubric Map}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 1 (LO1):} Interpret the supplied evidence or model
  output for Water --- The Molecule of Life.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 2 (LO2):} Identify controls and comparison groups that
  make the claim testable.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 3 (LO3):} Quantify uncertainty, boundary conditions,
  or alternative explanations before concluding.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 4 (LO4):} Transfer the mechanism to a new biological
  case or public-facing decision.
\item
  \textbf{Chapter LO coverage:} LO1, LO2, LO3, LO4
\item
  \textbf{Rubric dimensions:} evidence; controls; uncertainty;
  mechanism; transfer. \#\# Background \{.unnumbered\}
\end{itemize}

Water's extraordinary properties arise from its bent molecular geometry
(104.5° H--O--H bond angle) and the resulting network of hydrogen bonds.
Each water molecule can form up to four hydrogen bonds --- two through
lone pairs (O as H-bond acceptor) and two through O--H groups (H-bond
donor). This network gives water its high specific heat (4.18 J/g\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.}°C),
high surface tension (72 mN/m), strong cohesion/adhesion, and the
ability to dissolve ionic and polar solutes. Most of these properties
are exploited by living organisms.

In this lab you will analyse heat-absorption data for water and oil,
interpret capillary-rise diagrams, and track osmotic movement in a model
membrane dataset. The required work is paper-based so the scientific
reasoning is centred on controls, units, gradients, and reproducible
interpretation.

\textbf{Part A --- Specific Heat}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Graph the provided temperature data for equal masses of water and oil
  under the same heat input.
\item

  buffered temperature change more strongly.
\item
  Mark the baseline, the controlled variables, and one possible
  measurement uncertainty on the graph.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Part B --- Capillarity}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item
  Use the capillary-rise diagrams to measure the height of model water
  and oil columns in millimetres.
\item
  Compare the xylem diagram with the capillary tube model. Identify
  where adhesion, cohesion, and tube diameter enter the explanation.
\item
  Write one prediction for how capillary height would change if tube
  radius doubled, then check it against the model card.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Part C --- Osmosis}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{6}
\tightlist
\item
  Use the membrane-bag dataset to calculate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Delta}}{Delta}mass over time for
  hypotonic, isotonic, and hypertonic surroundings.
\item
  Draw the water-potential gradient for each condition and identify
  which case functions as the best negative control for net water
  movement.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-4}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}

\item

  reflect differences in specific heat, and what is the ecological
  significance for oceans moderating coastal climates?
\item
  Why did water rise higher than oil in the capillary tube? Name the two
  adhesive forces responsible and identify the molecules involved.

\item

  direction of movement.
\item

  saline) rather than pure water. Predict what would happen if red blood
  cells were placed in pure water vs 3\% NaCl solution. Explain using
  water potential (\(\Psi = \Psi_s + \Psi_p\)).
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Lab 3 --- Biological
Macromolecules}\label{lab-3-biological-macromolecules}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Lab 3 --- Biological Macromolecules}

\label{sec:lab_unit_I_macromolecules}

\subsection*{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-43}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Learning Objectives}

\emph{This activity accompanies \cref{sec:unit_I_macromolecules} of the
textbook --- review that chapter before attempting the exercises below.}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Apply simulated colorimetric-test evidence to identify carbohydrates,
  proteins, and lipids
\item
  Distinguish reducing sugars from non-reducing sugars using structural
  logic
\item
  Identify proteins and lipids from reaction cards, labels, and model
  results
\item
  Interpret qualitative colour evidence with controls, uncertainty, and
  reproducibility checks
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Background}\label{background}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Background}

Macromolecules --- carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids
--- form the molecular architecture of cells. Each class has distinctive
chemical groups that produce diagnostic patterns in classic colorimetric
tests. Reducing sugars (glucose, fructose, maltose) donate electrons to
Cu\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} in classic reducing-sugar assay, producing a colour change from
blue to yellow/orange/red; sucrose (non-reducing) does not react unless
hydrolysed. The classic peptide-bond assay reaction turns purple in the
presence of peptide bonds (\texorpdfstring{\textgreater{}=}{>=}2). classic lipid-partition assay, an
oil-soluble dye, partitions into lipids and stains them red-orange.

In this lab you will interpret a blinded paper dataset for five unknown
samples (A--E), compare it with positive and negative controls, and
identify the macromolecules present in each. The chemistry is treated as
evidence to reason from, not as a required wet procedure.
