\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-5}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Which samples tested positive for reducing sugars? Were any positive
  for sucrose (hint: sucrose does NOT turn classic reducing-sugar assay
  red without hydrolysis)? How would you distinguish glucose from
  sucrose using primarily classic reducing-sugar assay test?
\item
  A sample of milk tested positive for both classic reducing-sugar assay
  (weakly) and classic peptide-bond assay (strongly) and showed a grease
  spot. Name the three macromolecule classes present in milk.
\item
  Why does classic reducing-sugar assay require heating to detect
  reducing sugars, while classic peptide-bond assay works at room
  temperature? What does this reveal about the reaction mechanisms?
\item
  Dietary fibre (cellulose) is a polysaccharide. Predict whether it
  would give a positive classic reducing-sugar assay test. Explain in
  terms of glycosidic bond type (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha} vs \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} linkage) and digestibility.
\item
  A patient has phenylketonuria (PKU) --- inability to metabolise
  phenylalanine. Which macromolecule class and which specific monomer is
  relevant? How does dietary management (low-phenylalanine diet) relate
  to the biochemistry of this lab?
\item
  An AlphaFold-derived packet predicts a ligand contact in a
  low-confidence loop. What additional evidence would move the claim
  from ``hypothesis'' to ``supported mechanism''? Name at least one
  sequence, structural, and biochemical check.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Extension Analysis
Questions}\label{extension-analysis-questions}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Extension Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{6}
\tightlist
\item
  Galactosaemia patients cannot metabolise galactose (a component of
  lactose). Using your understanding of glycosidic bonds, explain why
  such a patient must avoid milk but can safely consume glucose or
  fructose sweetened foods.
\item
  The Keto diet shifts metabolism to fat oxidation. Predict which
  macromolecule category would dominate your test results on a piece of
  bacon vs a slice of bread. Discuss why each is energy-dense but in
  biochemically different ways (immediate vs sustained release).
\item
  Protein-losing enteropathy causes albumin leakage into the gut. Given
  classic peptide-bond assay's sensitivity (about 0.1 mg/mL),
  would you expect a positive classic peptide-bond assay reaction on a
  faecal sample from such a patient? Why might faecal protein
  quantification via classic peptide-bond assay be unreliable (hint:
  digestive proteolysis)?
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Lab 4 --- Enzymes and the Kinetics of
Catalysis}\label{lab-4-enzymes-and-the-kinetics-of-catalysis}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Lab 4 --- Enzymes and the Kinetics of
Catalysis}

\label{sec:lab_unit_I_enzymes_and_kinetics}

\subsection*{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-44}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Learning Objectives}

\emph{This activity accompanies \cref{sec:unit_I_enzymes_and_kinetics}
of the textbook --- review that chapter before attempting the exercises
below.}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Interpret enzyme activity data by tracking O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} production as a proxy
  for reaction rate
\item
  Determine how temperature, pH, and substrate concentration affect
  enzyme rate (Vmax approximation)
\item
  Construct a rate vs \hyperref[s]{S} curve and identify qualitative Km
\item
  Interpret enzyme inhibition from a competitive inhibitor treatment
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Alignment and Rubric
Map}\label{alignment-and-rubric-map-6}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Alignment and Rubric Map}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 1 (LO1):} Interpret the supplied evidence or model
  output for Enzymes and the Kinetics of Catalysis.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 2 (LO2):} Identify controls and comparison groups that
  make the claim testable.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 3 (LO3):} Quantify uncertainty, boundary conditions,
  or alternative explanations before concluding.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 4 (LO4):} Transfer the mechanism to a new biological
  case or public-facing decision.
\item
  \textbf{Chapter LO coverage:} LO1, LO2, LO3, LO4
\item
  \textbf{Rubric dimensions:} evidence; controls; uncertainty;
  mechanism; transfer. \#\# Background \{.unnumbered\}
\end{itemize}

Enzymes are biological catalysts that lower activation energy. The
enzyme catalase converts hydrogen peroxide (H\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}) to water and oxygen:
\textbf{2 H\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} 2 H\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}O + O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}}. This reaction is often monitored by
counting O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} bubbles per minute or by measuring the height of foam
produced. Catalase is one of the fastest known enzymes (k\_cat
about 40,000,000 s\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}) and is found in nearly most aerobic
organisms.

In this lab you will analyse a paper dataset showing how temperature,
pH, substrate concentration, and inhibition affect catalase activity.
The goal is to infer mechanism from controlled comparisons rather than
to run a wet reaction.

\subsection*{Paper-Based
Investigation}\label{paper-based-investigation-6}

\textbf{Part A --- Temperature Effect}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Plot the provided catalase-rate data for 0°C, 22°C, 37°C, 50°C, and
  denatured enzyme conditions.
\item
  Calculate the mean and range for each condition. Identify the
  denatured enzyme as a negative control and the 37°C condition as a
  reference comparison.
\item
  Use the active-site cards to explain why low temperature and
  denaturation reduce activity for different reasons.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Part B --- pH Effect}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item
  Graph catalase rate across pH 2.5, 5, 7, 8.5, and 11. Mark the pH
  optimum and one condition where enzyme structure is likely disrupted.
\item
  Decide whether pH changes primarily affect enzyme shape, substrate
  charge, or both. Support the claim with one pattern in the dataset.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Part C --- Substrate Concentration Effect}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{5}
\tightlist
\item
  Plot rate versus {[}H\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}{]} for 0\%, 1\%, 3\%, and 6\% substrate.
\item
  Estimate the concentration where the curve begins to plateau and label
  it as a qualitative Vmax region. Use the inhibitor cards to predict
  how a competitive inhibitor would change apparent Km and Vmax.
\end{enumerate}

version belongs only in an optional extension.

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-6}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Plot the simulated O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} proxy vs temperature. Identify the approximate
  optimal temperature. Explain the molecular basis for activity loss at
  0°C and above 50°C.
\item
  Explain why the denatured-enzyme condition showed no activity using
  the concept of protein denaturation and active site geometry.
\item
  Plot the simulated O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} proxy vs {[}H\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}{]}. Describe the shape of the
  curve. At what concentration does activity appear to plateau? How does
  this relate to the concept of Vmax and enzyme saturation?
\item
  If you added a competitive inhibitor (e.g., a molecule structurally
  similar to H\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}), predict how the rate vs \hyperref[s]{S} curve would
  change in apparent Km and Vmax relative to uninhibited enzyme.
\item
  Catalase deficiency is a human genetic condition (acatalasia)
  associated with recurrent oral infections. Using your experimental
  results, explain why catalase is biologically important in protecting
  cells from H\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} produced during oxidative metabolism.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}

  \textbf{magnification}, \textbf{field of view (FOV)}. Note which

\item

  4.5 mm \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 40/400 = 0.45 mm = 450 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m.)
\item

  sentences, explain who saw what first and why both contributed to cell
  theory.
\item

  subtilis} cells (2 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m long) would fit end-to-end across the diameter
  of the FOV? (Answer: 450 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m / 2 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 225 cells.)
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Background}\label{background-1}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Background}

Cell theory, formalised by Schleiden, Schwann, and Virchow (1838--1855),
states that: (1) most living things are composed of cells; (2) the cell
is the basic unit of life; and (3) most cells arise from pre-existing
cells. Two fundamental cell types exist: \textbf{prokaryotes} (Bacteria,
Archaea --- no nucleus, typically 0.5--5 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m) and \textbf{eukaryotes}
(Eukarya --- membrane-bounded nucleus, 10--100 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m). Light microscopy can
resolve features above about 200 nm, allowing clear
visualisation of cell walls, chloroplasts, and the nucleus, though the
electron microscope is needed for ribosomes and membranes.

\subsubsection*{Part E --- Scale Bar
Arithmetic}\label{part-e-scale-bar-arithmetic}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Part E --- Scale Bar Arithmetic}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{7}
\item
  The instructor will distribute a printed micrograph of a eukaryotic
  cell with a labelled scale bar of 10 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m. Measure the longest cell
  diameter with a ruler (mm); convert to true \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m using the scale-bar
  ratio. This is the core arithmetic for every published micrograph:
  \emph{true size = (measured distance \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\div}}{/} scale bar length) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} scale bar
  value}.
\item
  Using the same formula, estimate the total surface area of a spherical
  epithelial-cell image (diameter \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 60 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m):
  \(A = 4\pi r^2 = 4\pi(30)^2 \approx 1.13 \times 10^4\) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}. Compare
  with a spherical \emph{Bacillus} (diameter 2 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m, \(A \approx 12.6\)
  \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}). Note the about 1000\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} difference --- which cell has a
  larger surface-to-volume ratio, and why is that biologically
  important?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-7}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  How does the size of \emph{Bacillus} compare to the onion epidermal
  cell? Express as a ratio. What structural feature allows eukaryotic
  cells to be so much larger (hint: internal compartmentalisation)?
\item
  The onion image packet includes a starch-localisation annotation. What
  molecule was detected? Which organelle does this implicate, and why is
  this unexpected in onion cells that are not green?
\item
  Both onion and leaf mesophyll cells are plant cells, but mesophyll
  cells have abundant chloroplasts and onion epidermal cells typically
  do not. Explain using cell theory and differential gene expression.
\item
  A printed pond-water image shows cells with a nucleus but without a
  cell wall. Is this organism a plant, animal, or fungus? What
  additional image feature or molecular marker would narrow the
  identification?
\item
  Devise a paper-based study using time-series image cards to test
  whether temperature affects the rate of cytoplasmic streaming.
  Identify your independent, dependent, and controlled variables.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Extension Analysis
Questions}\label{extension-analysis-questions-1}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Extension Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{5}
\tightlist
\item
  Hooke's 1665 \emph{Micrographia} described ``cells'' in cork --- but
  what he saw were primarily the \textbf{walls} of dead plant cells, not
  living matter. Why does this still count as the founding observation
  of cell theory? How does it illustrate the difference between
  \textbf{observing} a cell and \textbf{understanding} it?
\item
  Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own DNA, 70S ribosomes (like
  bacteria, not the 80S eukaryotic ribosomes in cytoplasm), and divide
  independently. Connect these facts to the \textbf{endosymbiotic
  theory} (Margulis, 1967) --- why is maternal inheritance of
  mitochondrial DNA in humans a direct prediction of this theory?
\item
  A single mammalian cell contains about 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{7}}{7} proteins. Given a cell
  volume of 1000 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}m\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{3}}{3}, compute the approximate bulk protein concentration
  (mass/volume). Discuss why ``macromolecular crowding''
  (about 30\% by volume) changes effective reaction kinetics
  relative to dilute test-tube conditions.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Background}\label{background-2}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Background}

Eukaryotic cells are organised into membrane-bounded compartments
(organelles) that divide labour: the nucleus stores and expresses DNA;
the rough ER synthesises membrane and secretory proteins; the Golgi
receives, modifies, and sorts vesicle cargo; mitochondria generate ATP
via oxidative phosphorylation. The type and abundance of organelles
reflects a cell's function --- liver hepatocytes are rich in rough ER
(secretory proteins) and smooth ER (lipid metabolism); muscle cells are
packed with mitochondria; leaf mesophyll cells contain hundreds of
chloroplasts.

\section*{Lab 7 --- Membrane Structure and
Transport}\label{lab-7-membrane-structure-and-transport}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Lab 7 --- Membrane Structure and
Transport}

\label{sec:lab_unit_II_membrane_transport}

\subsection*{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-47}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Learning Objectives}

\emph{This activity accompanies \cref{sec:unit_II_membrane_transport} of
the textbook --- review that chapter before attempting the exercises
below.}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Interpret osmosis data and estimate osmotic potential from model
  tissues
\item
  Quantify plasmolysis using annotated image packets across NaCl
  concentrations
\item
  Relate membrane lipid bilayer fluidity to temperature through
  simulated colour-leakage data
\item
  Apply the fluid-mosaic model to explain observed transport phenomena
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Alignment and Rubric
Map}\label{alignment-and-rubric-map-9}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Alignment and Rubric Map}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 1 (LO1):} Interpret the supplied evidence or model
  output for Membrane Structure and Transport.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 2 (LO2):} Identify controls and comparison groups that
  make the claim testable.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 3 (LO3):} Quantify uncertainty, boundary conditions,
  or alternative explanations before concluding.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 4 (LO4):} Transfer the mechanism to a new biological
  case or public-facing decision.
\item
  \textbf{Chapter LO coverage:} LO1, LO2, LO3, LO4
\item
  \textbf{Rubric dimensions:} evidence; controls; uncertainty;
  mechanism; transfer. \#\# Background \{.unnumbered\}
\end{itemize}

The plasma membrane is a selectively permeable phospholipid bilayer with
embedded proteins. Water moves by osmosis across membranes from regions
of high water potential (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Psi}}{Psi}) to low \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Psi}}{Psi} (high solute concentration). In
plant cells, plasmolysis occurs when the cell is placed in hypertonic
solution --- the cytoplasm shrinks away from the rigid cell wall. In
animal cells, a hypertonic solution causes crenation (cell shrinking).
Membrane fluidity depends on phospholipid composition (unsaturated fatty
acids \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} more fluid) and temperature (higher temperature \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} more fluid).

In this lab you will use printed datasets to investigate how temperature
damages membranes (simulated betacyanin leakage) and how plasmolysis
changes across a NaCl concentration gradient. The required work is
paper-based and emphasises controls, graphing, and model interpretation.

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-9}

  (shrink away from the cell wall) instead of simply shrinking like
  animal cells?

\section*{Lab 8 --- Cell Signalling and
Communication}\label{lab-8-cell-signalling-and-communication}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Lab 8 --- Cell Signalling and
Communication}

\label{sec:lab_unit_II_cell_signaling}

\subsection*{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-48}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Learning Objectives}

\emph{This activity accompanies \cref{sec:unit_II_cell_signaling} of the
textbook --- review that chapter before attempting the exercises below.}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Model the three-stage cell signalling cascade (reception \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  transduction \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} response) through a physical simulation
\item
  Analyse how signal amplification occurs through enzymatic cascades
\item
  Evaluate the role of second messengers using a classroom analogy and
  data interpretation
\item
  Design an experiment to test how a signalling inhibitor disrupts a
  cellular response
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Alignment and Rubric
Map}\label{alignment-and-rubric-map-10}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Alignment and Rubric Map}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 1 (LO1):} Interpret the supplied evidence or model
  output for Cell Signalling and Communication.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 2 (LO2):} Identify controls and comparison groups that
  make the claim testable.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 3 (LO3):} Quantify uncertainty, boundary conditions,
  or alternative explanations before concluding.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 4 (LO4):} Transfer the mechanism to a new biological
  case or public-facing decision.
\item
  \textbf{Chapter LO coverage:} LO1, LO2, LO3, LO4
\item
  \textbf{Rubric dimensions:} evidence; controls; uncertainty;
  mechanism; transfer. \#\# Background \{.unnumbered\}
\end{itemize}

Cell signalling enables cells to detect and respond to extracellular
information. The three stages are: (1) \textbf{Reception} --- a ligand
binds its receptor (GPCR, RTK, nuclear receptor); (2)
\textbf{Transduction} --- signal is converted and amplified through a
cascade of molecular switches; (3) \textbf{Response} --- altered gene
expression, enzyme activity, or cytoskeletal change. Amplification is a
key feature: one activated receptor can activate hundreds of G proteins,
each activating dozens of adenylate cyclase molecules, each producing
thousands of cAMP molecules --- giving a cascade amplification of
\textgreater10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{6}}{6}.

In this lab you will simulate and calculate signal amplification through
a cascade model, analyse a published cell signalling dose-response
dataset, and design an inhibitor experiment.

\subsection*{Paper-Based
Investigation}\label{paper-based-investigation-10}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Paper-Based Investigation}

\textbf{Part A --- Signal Amplification Simulation}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  One student is the ``ligand'': activate one ``receptor'' card. Each
  activated receptor activates 10 G protein cards. Each G protein
  activates 10 ``adenylate cyclase'' steps (represented by producing 10
  cAMP tokens). Each cAMP activates 5 PKA tokens.
\item
  Count total active tokens at each level. Record in the amplification
  table.
\item
  Calculate total fold amplification from ligand to PKA response.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Part B --- Dose-Response Curve Analysis}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item
  Using the provided dataset of heart rate (bpm) vs {[}adrenaline{]}
  (nM), plot a dose-response curve on semilog paper (log
  {[}adrenaline{]} on x-axis, heart rate on y).
\item
  Identify the EC\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{5}}{5}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0} (concentration producing 50\% of maximal response)
  from your curve.
\item
  A second curve shows the same response in the presence of propranolol
  (a \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-blocker). Plot both curves; compare EC\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{5}}{5}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0} values and maximum
  responses.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Part C --- Inhibitor Experiment Design}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{6}
\tightlist
\item
  Design a controlled paper experiment to test whether blocking
  adenylate cyclase with SQ 22536 would prevent an adrenaline-mediated
  response. Use provided pathway cards and a simulated response dataset
  rather than cells or tissue.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-10}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Calculate the fold amplification your cascade produced. How does this
  compare to the theoretical amplification cited in the chapter
  (about 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{6}}{6})? What real-world factors account for the
  difference?
\item
  Propranolol is a competitive antagonist of the \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-adrenergic receptor.
  Based on your dose-response curves, does it shift the EC\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{5}}{5}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0}, reduce
  Emax, or both? What does this pattern indicate about mechanism?
\item
  Steroid hormones such as oestrogen can enter cells and bind nuclear
  receptors directly. Why is this signalling pathway typically slower
  (minutes to hours) than GPCR cascades (seconds)? What is the cellular
  destination of the hormone-receptor complex?
\item
  Tamoxifen is a selective oestrogen receptor modulator (SERM) that acts
  as an antagonist in breast tissue but a partial agonist in bone.
  Explain how the same molecule can produce opposite effects in
  different tissues.
\item
  A mutation makes the Gs protein GTPase-inactive (cannot hydrolyse GTP
  to GDP). Predict the effect on adenylate cyclase activity, cAMP
  levels, and PKA activity in the affected cell. What disease would this
  phenotype resemble?
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Lab 9 --- Bioenergetics and Cellular
Respiration}\label{lab-9-bioenergetics-and-cellular-respiration}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Lab 9 --- Bioenergetics and Cellular
Respiration}

\label{sec:lab_unit_III_bioenergetics_and_respiration}

\subsection*{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-49}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Learning Objectives}

\emph{This activity accompanies
\cref{sec:unit_III_bioenergetics_and_respiration} of the textbook ---
review that chapter before attempting the exercises below.}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Interpret CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} and O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} datasets as indicators of cellular respiration
  rate
\item
  Compare aerobic respiration, fermentation, and the effect of substrate
  type on respiration rate
\item
  Calculate respiration rate (mL CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} per minute per gram of tissue)
\item
  Distinguish the contributions of glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, and
  the Krebs cycle to overall ATP yield
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Alignment and Rubric
Map}\label{alignment-and-rubric-map-11}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Alignment and Rubric Map}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 1 (LO1):} Interpret the supplied evidence or model
  output for Bioenergetics and Cellular Respiration.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 2 (LO2):} Identify controls and comparison groups that
  make the claim testable.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 3 (LO3):} Quantify uncertainty, boundary conditions,
  or alternative explanations before concluding.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 4 (LO4):} Transfer the mechanism to a new biological
  case or public-facing decision.
\item
  \textbf{Chapter LO coverage:} LO1, LO2, LO3, LO4
\item
  \textbf{Rubric dimensions:} evidence; controls; uncertainty;
  mechanism; transfer. \#\# Background \{.unnumbered\}
\end{itemize}

Cellular respiration converts the chemical energy in organic molecules
to ATP. The complete aerobic pathway --- glycolysis \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} pyruvate oxidation
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Krebs cycle \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} oxidative phosphorylation --- yields a theoretical
maximum of about 30 ATP per glucose. The overall equation is:
\textbf{C\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{6}}{6}H\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{6}}{6} + 6 O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} 6 CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} + 6 H\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}O + about 30 ATP}. CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}
production rate and O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} consumption rate can serve as proxies for
metabolic rate. In this lab, printed datasets provide model evidence for
comparing aerobic respiration, fermentation, and substrate effects.

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-11}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Which substrate model produced the fastest CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} increase --- sucrose or
  glucose? Explain using the concept of hydrolysis and substrate entry
  into glycolysis.
\item
  Why did the starch treatment model produce less CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} than sucrose? How
  does this relate to enzyme availability for substrate breakdown?
\item
  The active-tissue model showed higher O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} consumption than the
  dormant-tissue model. Explain at which stage of respiration this O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} is
  consumed and write the half-reaction involved.
\item
  Facultative anaerobe models can continue producing CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} with little O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}
  available. Predict whether CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} production would stop, slow, or
  continue in a no-O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} scenario. Explain using fermentation pathways and
  the role of NAD\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} regeneration.
\item
  A marathon runner transitions from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism
  past about 80\% VO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}max. Explain what metabolic shift occurs
  in muscle cells, what molecule accumulates (not lactic acid --- what
  is the actual molecule?), and why fatigue results.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Hypothesis Formation}: Based on the absorption spectra of
  chlorophyll a and b, predict which color of light (red, blue, green,
  or clear) will result in the fastest photosynthesis rate. Write a
  clear, testable hypothesis statement.
\item
  \textbf{Experimental Design}: What is the independent variable in this
  experiment? What is the dependent variable? List at least 5 variables
  that should be controlled to ensure a fair test.
\item
  \textbf{Scientific Context}: The Ruben \& Kamen (1941) experiment used
  \(^{18}\)O-labeled water to prove that oxygen released during
  photosynthesis comes from water, not carbon dioxide. Why was this
  experiment groundbreaking? How did it change our understanding of
  photosynthesis?
\item
  \textbf{Quantitative Reasoning}: Calculate the energy per photon for
  red light (\(\lambda = 700\) nm) and blue light (\(\lambda = 450\)
  nm). Which has more energy? How might this affect photosynthesis
  efficiency?
\item
  \textbf{Real-World Application}: Commercial greenhouses often use LED
  grow lights. Based on your knowledge of photosynthesis, what light
  spectrum would you recommend for maximizing plant growth? Consider
  both energy efficiency and photosynthetic efficiency.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Background}\label{background-3}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Background}

Photosynthesis converts light energy to chemical energy: \textbf{6 CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} +
6 H\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}O + light \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} C\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{6}}{6}H\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{6}}{6} + 6 O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}}. The light-dependent reactions in the
thylakoid membrane split water (photolysis) and generate NADPH and ATP;
the Calvin cycle in the stroma uses NADPH and ATP to fix CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} into G3P
and ultimately glucose. A floating leaf-disc assay can estimate
photosynthesis because O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} accumulation increases buoyancy; here, an
image-and-data packet provides the same ET\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{5}}{5}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0} evidence without requiring
plant material, bicarbonate solution, lamps, or cutting tools.

\subsubsection*{Part 1: Experimental Design and Hypothesis
Testing}\label{part-1-experimental-design-and-hypothesis-testing}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Part 1: Experimental Design and
Hypothesis Testing}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Formulate Your Hypothesis}: Based on your pre-lab research,
  write a clear hypothesis about how light color will affect
  photosynthesis rate. Example: ``If photosynthesis is driven by
  chlorophyll absorption, then red light will result in a faster
  photosynthesis rate (lower ET\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{5}}{5}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0}) than green light because chlorophyll
  absorbs red wavelengths more efficiently.''
\item
  \textbf{Identify Variables}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Independent variable: Light color (red, blue, green, clear)
  \item
    Dependent variable: ET\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{5}}{5}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0} (time for 50\% of discs to float)
  \item
    Controlled variables: Temperature, CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} proxy concentration, disc
    size in the model, initial disc status, light-source distance, etc.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Set Up Controls}: Why is it important to have a clear filter
  (white light) control? What other controls could you include?
\item
  \textbf{Audit the Simulated Assay}: Use the method card to check
  whether disc size, starting status, CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} availability, temperature, and
  light distance are controlled across most conditions.
\item
  \textbf{Data Collection}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Read the number of floating discs at 1-minute intervals for 20
    minutes from the dataset
  \item
    Use the three provided replicate runs for each condition
  \item
    Calculate ET\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{5}}{5}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0} for each replicate using linear interpolation or the
    formula: ET\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{5}}{5}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0} = (t\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} - t\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} (5 - n\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}) / (n\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} - n\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}) + t\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-12}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Which wavelength produced the fastest disc floating (lowest ET\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{5}}{5}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0})?
  Which produced the slowest? How does this correlate with the
  absorption spectrum of chlorophyll a and b? Was your hypothesis
  supported?
\item
  Why were discs first made to sink? What gas was removed during vacuum
  infiltration, and why does replacing it with CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}-solution cause
  sinking?
\item
  As light intensity increases, photosynthesis rate increases to a
  plateau (light saturation point). Identify the limiting factor at each
  side of this curve and explain at the biochemical level.
\item
  The Calvin cycle does not directly require light. Why would removing
  light quickly halt the Calvin cycle reactions? (Hint: consider the
  fate of NADPH and ATP between the two stages.)
\item
  A crop scientist wants to maximise yield using artificial grow lights.
  Using your results, recommend the optimal light wavelength(s) and
  explain. What other environmental factors (CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}, temperature, water)
  should she simultaneously optimise, and what law of limiting factors
  applies?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Extension Analysis
Questions}\label{extension-analysis-questions-3}

\begin{enumerate}

\item
  Rising atmospheric CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} (from about 280 ppm pre-industrial to
  \textgreater420 ppm today) is predicted to increase C3 photosynthesis

\item

  isolated chloroplasts can reduce artificial electron acceptors (e.g.,

  proved about the separability of the light and dark reactions --- and

\subsection*{Real-World Problem Solving: Climate Change and
Photosynthesis}\label{real-world-problem-solving-climate-change-and-photosynthesis}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Real-World Problem Solving: Climate
Change and Photosynthesis}

\textbf{Case Study: Rising CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} and Plant Productivity}

Very high-emissions scenarios can push atmospheric CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} toward roughly
800-1000 ppm by 2100, while lower-emissions pathways remain far below
that range \citep{ipcc2021ar6wg1}. While C3 plants may benefit from CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}
fertilization under controlled conditions, temperature, water
availability, nutrient limitation, ozone exposure, pests, and sink
demand often constrain the effect in real ecosystems and farms.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Research Task}: Investigate the concept of CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} fertilization.
  Which plant types (C3 vs C4) benefit more? What are the limitations of
  this effect in natural ecosystems?
\item
  \textbf{Ethical Consideration}: Should we rely on enhanced plant
  growth to offset carbon emissions? What are the potential ecological
  consequences of artificially increasing CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} levels in forests or
  agricultural systems?
\item
  \textbf{Policy Proposal}: Design a policy that balances the need for
  carbon sequestration through plant growth with the preservation of
  biodiversity and ecosystem function.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Background}\label{background-4}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Background}

Metabolic integration means that pathways (glycolysis, gluconeogenesis,
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-oxidation, glycogen synthesis) are coordinated by hormonal signals and
allosteric regulators, not running independently. Insulin (released
postprandially) activates GLUT4 translocation, glycogen synthase, and
fatty acid synthesis; it inhibits gluconeogenesis and lipolysis.
Glucagon (released during fasting) does the reverse. PFK-1 is the key
allosteric valve of glycolysis: activated by AMP, ADP, and
fructose-2,6-bisphosphate; inhibited by ATP and citrate.

In this data-analysis lab you will interpret simulated glucose tolerance
test data from three subjects (normal, pre-diabetic, type 2 diabetic)
and model the allosteric regulation of PFK-1.

    Independent variable: Subject group (normal, pre-diabetic, type 2
    diabetic)
  \item
    Dependent variable: Blood glucose concentration (mM) over time
  \item
    Controlled variables: Glucose dose, timing of measurements, subject
    age/fasting status, etc.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Set Up Controls}: Why is it important to have a normal control
  group? What other controls could you include in a clinical GTT study?
\item
  \textbf{Data Analysis}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Plot blood glucose (mM) vs time (min, 0--120 min) for most three
    subjects on the same graph
  \item
    Annotate key events: glucose ingestion (t = 0), peak blood glucose,
    return to baseline
  \item
    Calculate AUC for each subject using the trapezoid rule at 30-minute
    intervals
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-13}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Based on the GTT data, which AUC threshold might a clinician use to
  diagnose type 2 diabetes? How does the shape of Subject C's curve
  differ from Subject A's, and what does this indicate about \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-cell
  insulin secretion capacity?
\item
  Subject B is pre-diabetic. Suggest two lifestyle interventions that
  would shift Subject B's GTT curve toward Subject A's profile. For
  each, identify the specific metabolic pathway or hormone axis
  restored.
\item
  In the post-meal state (high insulin), what happens to hepatic
  fructose-2,6-bisphosphate levels? Trace: insulin \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PFK-2
  phosphorylation state \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} {[}fructose-2,6-BP{]} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} PFK-1 activity \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  glycolysis rate.
\item
  During intense exercise, AMP levels spike. Using the allosteric model,
  predict and explain the combined effect of elevated AMP and elevated
  fructose-2,6-BP on glycolytic flux in exercising muscle.
\item
  Metformin, the first-line drug for type 2 diabetes, inhibits Complex I
  of the mitochondrial electron transport chain, increasing the AMP:ATP
  ratio. Using your metabolic knowledge, predict at least three
  downstream effects of elevated AMP: (a) on PFK-1; (b) on glycogen
  synthase; (c) on gluconeogenesis. Does this make metabolic sense as a
  diabetes treatment?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Background}\label{background-5}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Background}

DNA replication is semiconservative (Meselson--Stahl, 1958): each
daughter double helix retains one original strand and one newly
synthesised strand. Replication proceeds bidirectionally from origins of
replication; DNA polymerase extends DNA in the 5'\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}3' direction,
requiring the lagging strand to be synthesised discontinuously as
Okazaki fragments. The cell cycle (G\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} S \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} G\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} M) is driven by
cyclin-CDK complexes and monitored by checkpoints (G\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}/S, G\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}/M, spindle
assembly checkpoint). The mitotic index (fraction of cells in mitosis)
reflects proliferative activity and is elevated in tumours.

\subsubsection*{Part 1: Mitotic Index Determination from Image
Cards}\label{part-1-mitotic-index-determination-from-image-cards}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Part 1: Mitotic Index Determination
from Image Cards}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Formulate Your Hypothesis}: Based on your pre-lab research,
  write a hypothesis about how the mitotic index might differ among root
  tip, embryo, and tumour image datasets.
\item
  \textbf{Identify Variables}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Independent variable: Tissue dataset type
  \item
    Dependent variable: Mitotic index (\% cells in mitosis)
  \item
    Controlled variables: image source, magnification label, counting
    frame size, staging key, scorer training, and exclusion rules.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Set Up Controls}: Use the instructor-provided answer-key
  subset as a positive control for each mitotic stage and a non-dividing
  tissue card as a negative control. Before scoring the unknown cards,
  each group must reach at least 80\% agreement on the control cards.
\item
  \textbf{Apply the Staging Key}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Place the transparent grid over each printed image card.
  \item
    Classify exactly 100 consecutive visible cells per card as
    interphase, prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, or
    ``uncertain.''
  \item
    Record uncertain cells separately; do not force a stage call unless
    the chromosome features match the decision key.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Data Collection}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Score three cards per tissue dataset, with two students
    independently scoring one shared card to estimate inter-rater
    reliability.
  \item
    Calculate mitotic index = (cells in mitosis \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\div}}{/} total cells counted) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x}
    100\%.
  \item
    Report the mean, range, and standard error across replicate cards;
    flag any card whose uncertain-cell count exceeds 10\%.
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-14}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Which stage of mitosis took the longest (highest proportion)? Which
  was shortest? Explain in terms of the molecular events occurring in
  each stage.
\item
  Your mitotic index suggests what fraction of cells are actively
  dividing. Would you expect a higher or lower mitotic index in: (a) a
  tumour; (b) a mature neuron; (c) a healing wound? Explain for each.
\item
  In the Meselson-Stahl simulation, after two rounds of replication in
  light medium: (a) what fraction of DNA molecules are hybrid (\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{5}}{5}N/\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{4}}{4}N)?
  (b) What fraction are light-light? How do these proportions
  distinguish semiconservative from conservative replication?
\item
  DNA polymerase requires a primer and extends DNA in the 5'\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}3'
  direction. Explain why the lagging strand is initiated multiple times
  as Okazaki fragments, and name the enzyme that seals these fragments.
\item
  A drug (e.g., taxol) stabilises microtubules and prevents spindle
  disassembly. At which checkpoint would cells arrest, and what specific
  checkpoint protein detects unattached kinetochores? Why is this drug
  effective against rapidly dividing cancer cells?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Extension Analysis
Questions}\label{extension-analysis-questions-5}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Extension Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{5}
\item
  \textbf{Statistical Analysis}: Calculate the standard error of the
  mean (SEM) for your mitotic index across replicate cards. Construct a
  95\% confidence interval. How precise is your estimate?
\item
  \textbf{Experimental Error Analysis}: What are three potential sources
  of error in image-based mitotic staging? How could you modify the
  scoring rules or dataset design to reduce each source of error?
\item
  \textbf{Experimental Design}: If you wanted to test the effect of a
  new chemotherapy drug on cell cycle progression, what would you
  measure? How would you distinguish between drugs that affect DNA
  synthesis vs.~those that affect mitosis?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Group Project Extension
(Multi-Session)}\label{group-project-extension-multi-session-2}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Group Project Extension
(Multi-Session)}

\textbf{Design a Cancer Cell Detection Tool Using Machine Learning}

This project will span 2-3 lab sessions:

\textbf{Session 1}: Research Question and Hypothesis - Can we
distinguish cancer cells from normal cells based on cell cycle
abnormalities? - What features (size, shape, staining intensity, mitotic
index) are most predictive? - Write a reproducible sampling plan for
choosing public image datasets and metadata fields

\textbf{Session 2}: Data Collection and Analysis - Use public image
datasets of normal and cancer cells - Extract features using image
analysis software - Train a simple machine learning classifier (e.g.,
logistic regression)

\textbf{Session 3}: Tool Development and Testing - Test your classifier
on unseen data - Calculate sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy -
Create a scientific poster or presentation

\subsection*{Real-World Problem Solving: Cancer
Diagnostics}\label{real-world-problem-solving-cancer-diagnostics}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Real-World Problem Solving: Cancer
Diagnostics}

\textbf{Case Study: Liquid Biopsy for Cancer Detection}

Liquid biopsies detect circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) or circulating
tumor cells (CTCs) in blood samples.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Research Task}: Investigate the advantages and limitations of
  liquid biopsies compared to traditional tissue biopsies.
\item
  \textbf{Ethical Consideration}: Should liquid biopsy screening be
  offered to asymptomatic individuals? What are the potential benefits
  and risks of early detection?
\item
  \textbf{Policy Proposal}: Design a screening program for a specific
  cancer type using liquid biopsy technology. Consider
  cost-effectiveness, accessibility, and follow-up procedures.
\end{enumerate}

\item

\subsubsection*{Alignment and Rubric
Map}\label{alignment-and-rubric-map-15}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Alignment and Rubric Map}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 1 (LO1):} Interpret the supplied evidence or model
  output for Gene Expression --- Transcription and Translation.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 2 (LO2):} Identify controls and comparison groups that
  make the claim testable.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 3 (LO3):} Quantify uncertainty, boundary conditions,
  or alternative explanations before concluding.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 4 (LO4):} Transfer the mechanism to a new biological
  case or public-facing decision.
\item
  \textbf{Chapter LO coverage:} LO1, LO2, LO3, LO4
\item
  \textbf{Rubric dimensions:} evidence; controls; uncertainty;
  mechanism; transfer. \#\# Background \{.unnumbered\}
\end{itemize}

Gene expression flows from DNA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} mRNA (transcription, in the nucleus) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
protein (translation, by ribosomes in the cytoplasm). The genetic code
is triplet (3 nucleotides = 1 codon), non-overlapping, comprehensive,
and degenerate (multiple codons = one amino acid). A \textbf{polysome}
(polyribosome) consists of multiple ribosomes simultaneously translating
the same mRNA; the number of ribosomes per mRNA is proportional to
protein production demand and mRNA length.

In this lab you will perform manual transcription/translation using
codon tables, predict the effect of mutations, and interpret blot data
to determine whether gene expression changes are occurring at the
transcriptional or translational level.

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-15}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Card B (missense mutation): the amino acid sequence changed but the
  protein was still functional. Explain how this is possible using the
  concept of functionally conservative amino acid substitutions (e.g.,
  Leu \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Ile).
\item
  Card C introduced a premature stop codon. How does the cell detect and
  degrade mRNAs with premature stop codons? Name this quality-control
  pathway.
\item
  If Northern blot shows no change in mRNA level, but Western blot shows
  dramatically reduced protein, at what level is gene expression being
  regulated? Name two possible regulatory mechanisms.
\item
  A gene has 8 ribosomes per mRNA; a second gene's mRNA has 40 ribosomes
  present. Which gene is being translated more actively? What are two
  reasons a cell might load one mRNA with more ribosomes than another?
\item
  The antibiotic streptomycin causes misreading of the A-site codon by
  destabilising the decoding centre of the 30S ribosomal subunit.
  Predict the effect on translation fidelity and which kingdom of
  organisms would be most affected (hint: consider that streptomycin
  targets 30S vs 60S subunits).
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Background}\label{background-6}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Background}

Mutations --- heritable changes in DNA sequence --- can be neutral
(synonymous), harmful (loss-of-function missense or nonsense), or
beneficial (gain-of-function). CRISPR-Cas9 (Clustered Regularly
Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) is a programmable nuclease: the
guide RNA (gRNA; about 20 nt complementary to the target)
directs Cas9 to create a blunt-ended double-strand break 3 bp upstream
of the PAM sequence (5'-NGG-3'). Repair by NHEJ creates indel mutations
(disruptive); HDR with a template creates precise edits.

\subsubsection*{Part 2: Computational Biology Exercise - CRISPR gRNA
Design and Efficiency
Analysis}\label{part-2-computational-biology-exercise---crispr-grna-design-and-efficiency-analysis}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Part 2: Computational Biology
Exercise - CRISPR gRNA Design and Efficiency Analysis}

\emph{Optional computational check: run this self-contained Python
snippet from the project root. It uses tested \texttt{src/biology}
modules and requires no external notebook or CSV file.}

Quantify sequence change with the same distance functions used in the
chapter.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ biology.genetics }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ gc\_content, hamming\_distance, jukes\_cantor\_distance}

\NormalTok{reference }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"ATGCGTAC"}
\NormalTok{variant }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"ATGAGTTC"}
\NormalTok{p\_distance }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ hamming\_distance(reference, variant) }\OperatorTok{/} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(reference)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"GC reference:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(gc\_content(reference), }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Hamming distance:"}\NormalTok{, hamming\_distance(reference, variant))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Jukes{-}Cantor distance:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(jukes\_cantor\_distance(p\_distance), }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-16}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Why does a frameshift mutation typically have a more severe effect on
  protein function than a missense mutation? Under what circumstance
  could a frameshift mutation be silent (no effect on protein)?
\item
  A gRNA with sequence mismatches at positions 1--4 from the PAM distal
  end is less likely to cause cutting than mismatches at the seed region
  (positions 1--12 from PAM-proximal end). Why? What does this imply
  about gRNA design strategy to minimise off-target effects?
\item
  The T7E1 enzyme cleaves primarily at mismatched positions in
  heteroduplex DNA. Explain why NHEJ-induced indels would create
  mismatches and thus be detectable by T7E1, whereas HDR edits with
  perfect template would not be.
\item
  In 2018, He Jiankui used CRISPR to edit the CCR5 gene in human
  embryos, which were then implanted and brought to term. The stated
  goal was to confer HIV resistance. Using your ethical framework from
  Part D: name two distinct ethical objections to this experiment beyond
  the scientific accuracy concerns.
\item
  A patient with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) has a frameshift in
  exon 51 causing a premature stop codon. Propose a CRISPR-based
  strategy (exon skipping via splice site disruption) to restore the
  reading frame. What are the limitations of this approach?
\item
  A short-read sample maps poorly to a disease locus because one
  haplotype contains a 3-kb insertion absent from the linear reference.
  Explain how a pangenome graph could represent the evidence more
  fairly, and name one validation step before using the call clinically.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Extension Analysis
Questions}\label{extension-analysis-questions-6}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Extension Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{6}
\item

  replicate editing-efficiency estimates for each gRNA, how would you
  analyze the variation? What statistical test would you use to

\item

\item

  specific mutation on protein function, how would you design a

  phenotype readouts, and off-target checks would be required?
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Design a CRISPR-based Diagnostic Tool for Infectious Disease}

This project will span 2-3 lab sessions:

\textbf{Session 1}: Research Question and Hypothesis - Can CRISPR-Cas12a
(Cpf1) be used to detect viral DNA (e.g., SARS-CoV-2) with high
specificity? - What are the advantages of CRISPR diagnostics over PCR? -
Write a detailed decision workflow for a CRISPR-based diagnostic assay
using provided sequences and fluorescence traces

\textbf{Session 2}: Data Collection and Analysis - Design gRNAs specific
for a viral target from printed sequence alignments - Simulate detection
by classifying provided fluorescence-output traces - Analyze detection
thresholds, false positives, and false negatives over time

\textbf{Session 3}: Tool Development and Testing - Optimize assay
conditions in a decision matrix (gRNA concentration, reaction time,
detection threshold) - Test specificity against related viral strains -
Create a scientific poster or presentation

\subsection*{Background}\label{background-7}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Background}

Epigenetic regulation controls gene expression without altering DNA
sequence: DNA methylation (CpG islands; methylation = gene silencing,
generally), histone modification (H3K4me3 = activation; H3K27me3 =
silencing; H3K9ac = activation), and non-coding RNA (miRNA, siRNA). The
lac operon is the classical model for prokaryotic transcription
regulation: the lac repressor blocks transcription in the absence of
lactose; allolactose (a lactose isomer) binds the repressor and releases
it from the operator.

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-17}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  The lac repressor is an allosteric protein. How does allolactose
  binding change the shape of the repressor so that it can no longer
  bind the operator? Relate this to the induced fit model.
\item
  In catabolite repression, high glucose causes low cAMP because glucose
  inhibits adenylate cyclase. Trace: high glucose \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} {[}cAMP{]} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  CAP-cAMP binding \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} lac promoter activity. Why does the cell
  preferentially use glucose over lactose?
\item
  A cancer cell has methylation of a tumour suppressor gene promoter but
  no mutation in the coding sequence. Is this a genetic or epigenetic
  mutation? Why is this clinically important for therapy selection
  (hint: methyltransferase inhibitors vs traditional chemotherapy)?
\item
  The agouti mouse model showed that maternal diet (methyl-group-rich
  foods) changes offspring coat colour and obesity risk through
  epigenetic marks. Name the methyl donors involved (from diet) and the
  epigenetic writing enzyme that places the mark on CpG islands.
\item
  Design an experiment using induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)
  technology to test whether erasing epigenetic marks (global
  demethylation) is sufficient to reprogram a differentiated skin
  fibroblast. What control groups would you include?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Extension Analysis
Questions}\label{extension-analysis-questions-7}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Extension Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{5}
\item
  Methylation-sensitive restriction enzymes (e.g., HpaII) and
  methyl-insensitive isoschizomers (e.g., MspI) cut the same sequence
  but primarily MspI cuts methylated DNA. Describe one experimental use
  of this enzyme pair for mapping genome-wide methylation without
  bisulphite conversion.
\item
  Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance in humans remains
  controversial. What \emph{specific} molecular evidence would convince
  you it is real? (Address confounding: shared environment, germline
  reprogramming.)
\item
  The textbook introduces CRISPR-dCas9 epigenome editing. Design a
  dCas9-based experiment to re-activate the silenced tumour-suppressor
  gene you identified in the ChIP-seq analysis, and predict one
  off-target risk.
\item
  \textbf{Statistical Analysis}: If you performed three replicates of an
  MS-PCR experiment, how would you analyze the variation in methylation
  status? What statistical test would you use to determine if
  differences between groups are significant?
\item
  \textbf{Experimental Error Analysis}: What are three potential sources
  of error in epigenetic data analysis? How could you modify the
  procedure to reduce each source of error?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Safety and Ethics Notes}\label{safety-and-ethics-notes-17}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Safety and Ethics Notes}

Data-analysis primarily lab --- no reagents, no risk. Discussions of
patient cancer data should respect privacy principles
(de-identification; aggregate reporting). Agouti mouse studies involve
animal experimentation --- students should briefly discuss the 3Rs
framework (Replacement, Reduction, Refinement) and when mouse models are
(and are not) scientifically justified. Epigenetic age clocks have
attracted commercial wellness-industry interest; discuss the limits of
current evidence before drawing lifestyle conclusions from a single
patient's clock.

  different from the expected 3:1 ratio at p = 0.05?

\subsection*{Background}\label{background-8}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Background}

Gregor Mendel's experiments with pea plants (1856--1863) established the
laws of segregation (allele pairs separate during gamete formation) and
independent assortment (non-linked genes assort independently).
Monohybrid crosses between heterozygotes (Aa \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} Aa) produce 3:1 phenotype
ratios; dihybrid crosses produce 9:3:3:1 ratios. Deviations from these
ratios suggest linkage, incomplete dominance, codominance, or epistasis.

\begin{enumerate}

  \textbf{Formulate Your Hypothesis}: Based on your pre-lab research,
  write a hypothesis about how the inheritance pattern of a specific
  trait (e.g., pea seed shape) follows Mendelian ratios.
\item
  \textbf{Identify Variables}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Independent variable: Parental genotypes
  \item
    Dependent variable: Offspring genotype/phenotype ratios
  \item
    Controlled variables: Cross design, counting method, environmental
    conditions, etc.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Set Up Controls}: Why is it important to use true-breeding
  parental lines? What other controls could you include in a Mendelian
  inheritance experiment?
\item
  \textbf{Data Collection}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Complete monohybrid crosses: Aa \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} Aa; AA \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} Aa; Aa \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} aa. Record
    genotype and phenotype ratios.
  \item
    Complete a dihybrid cross: AaBb \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} AaBb. Record the 9:3:3:1 phenotype
    ratio.
  \item
    Complete an incomplete dominance cross: R\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}R\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1} (red) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} R\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}R\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} (white).

\subsubsection*{Part 2: Computational Biology Exercise - Statistical
Analysis with
Python}\label{part-2-computational-biology-exercise---statistical-analysis-with-python-1}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Part 2: Computational Biology
Exercise - Statistical Analysis with Python}

\emph{Optional computational check: run this self-contained Python
snippet from the project root. It uses tested \texttt{src/biology}
modules and requires no external notebook or CSV file.}

Validate the paper Punnett-square and chi-square calculations.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ biology.genetics }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ chi\_squared\_test, punnett\_square}

\NormalTok{cross }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ punnett\_square(}\StringTok{"Aa"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Aa"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{observed }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\FloatTok{450.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{130.0}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{expected }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\FloatTok{0.75} \OperatorTok{*} \BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(observed), }\FloatTok{0.25} \OperatorTok{*} \BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(observed)]}
\NormalTok{chi }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ chi\_squared\_test(observed, expected)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"genotype ratios:"}\NormalTok{, cross.genotype\_ratios)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"phenotype ratios:"}\NormalTok{, cross.phenotype\_ratios)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"χ²:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(chi.chi\_squared, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{), }\StringTok{"reject?"}\NormalTok{, chi.reject\_null)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

  does this illustrate the concept of a lethal allele modifying a

\textbf{Design a Population Genetics Study of a Human Trait}

This project will span 2-3 lab sessions:

\textbf{Session 1}: Research Question and Hypothesis - Choose a human
Mendelian trait (e.g., attached earlobes, tongue rolling, hitchhiker's
thumb) - Formulate a hypothesis about its inheritance pattern in your

\subsection*{Background}\label{background-9}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Background}

Genes on the same chromosome are linked and tend to be inherited
together (violating independent assortment). The \textbf{recombination
frequency} between linked genes --- measured as the percentage of
recombinant offspring among total --- is proportional to map distance
(1\% recombination = 1 centimorgan, cM). X-linked traits are carried on
the X chromosome; since males are hemizygous (XY), a single recessive
allele is expressed. Nondisjunction during meiosis (failure of
chromosomes to separate) produces aneuploid gametes, leading to
conditions such as trisomy 21 (Down syndrome).

\subsubsection*{Part 1: Genetic Linkage
Mapping}\label{part-1-genetic-linkage-mapping}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Part 1: Genetic Linkage Mapping}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Formulate Your Hypothesis}: Based on your pre-lab research,
  write a hypothesis about the order of three genes given their pairwise
  recombination frequencies.
\item
  \textbf{Identify Variables}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Independent variable: Gene order (which gene is in the middle)
  \item
    Dependent variable: Recombination frequencies between gene pairs
  \item
    Controlled variables: Population size, crossover detection method,
    etc.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Set Up Controls}: Why is it important to have a large sample
  size in linkage mapping? What other controls could you include to
  ensure accurate recombination frequency measurements?
\item
  \textbf{Data Collection}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Given pairwise recombination frequencies: genes A--B = 12 cM, B--C =
    8 cM, A--C = 20 cM.
  \item
    Draw the linear linkage map. Which gene is in the middle? Indicate
    the distances between each adjacent pair.
  \item
    Calculate the expected coefficient of coincidence (observed double
    crossovers / expected double crossovers) and interference (1 -
    coefficient of coincidence).
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection*{Part 2: Computational Biology Exercise - Linkage
Analysis with
Python}\label{part-2-computational-biology-exercise---linkage-analysis-with-python}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Part 2: Computational Biology
Exercise - Linkage Analysis with Python}

\emph{Optional computational check: run this self-contained Python
snippet from the project root. It uses tested \texttt{src/biology}
modules and requires no external notebook or CSV file.}

Infer a simple three-point map from pairwise recombination distances.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ biology.genetics }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ genetic\_distance, infer\_three\_point\_order}

\NormalTok{distances }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{(}\StringTok{"A"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"B"}\NormalTok{): }\FloatTok{12.0}\NormalTok{, (}\StringTok{"B"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"C"}\NormalTok{): }\FloatTok{8.0}\NormalTok{, (}\StringTok{"A"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"C"}\NormalTok{): }\FloatTok{20.0}\NormalTok{\}}
\NormalTok{order }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ infer\_three\_point\_order(distances)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"gene order:"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{" {-} "}\NormalTok{.join(order.order))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"adjacent distances:"}\NormalTok{, order.adjacent\_distances\_cM)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"24 recombinants among 200 progeny:"}\NormalTok{, genetic\_distance(}\DecValTok{24}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{200}\NormalTok{), }\StringTok{"cM"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-19}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  In linkage mapping, why does the A--C recombination frequency (20 cM)
  not simply equal A--B + B--C (12 + 8 = 20 cM) in real experiments?
  Explain the concept of double crossovers and interference.
\item
  A woman is a carrier of haemophilia A (X\^{}H X\^{}h) and is also
  heterozygous for an autosomal trait (Aa). She marries a normal man
  (X\^{}H Y; AA). Calculate the probability their first-born son is
  affected with haemophilia. Show most steps using the product rule.
\item
  Karyotype Case 3 showed trisomy 21. During which meiotic division is
  nondisjunction most commonly occurring in cases of Down syndrome, and
  what is the evidence supporting this conclusion (hint: consider
  maternal age effects and the stage vulnerable to cohesin loss)?
\item
  An individual with Turner syndrome (45,X) is phenotypically female.
  Explain why the presence of a single X chromosome leads to infertility
  and why males (46,XY) with a single X chromosome are not similarly
  affected.
\item
  Philadelphia chromosome (a translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22,
  creating BCR-ABL fusion oncogene) causes chronic myeloid leukaemia
  (CML). Explain: (a) why a translocation creates a fusion gene; (b)
  what the BCR-ABL kinase does biochemically; (c) why imatinib (a
  tyrosine kinase inhibitor) is effective.
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Lab 18 --- Population Genetics and Hardy-Weinberg
Equilibrium}\label{lab-18-population-genetics-and-hardy-weinberg-equilibrium}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Lab 18 --- Population Genetics and
Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium}

\label{sec:lab_unit_V_population_genetics}

\subsection*{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-58}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Learning Objectives}

\emph{This activity accompanies \cref{sec:unit_V_population_genetics} of

\subsubsection*{Alignment and Rubric
Map}\label{alignment-and-rubric-map-20}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Alignment and Rubric Map}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 1 (LO1):} Interpret the supplied evidence or model
  output for Population Genetics and Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 2 (LO2):} Identify controls and comparison groups that
  make the claim testable.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 3 (LO3):} Quantify uncertainty, boundary conditions,
  or alternative explanations before concluding.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 4 (LO4):} Transfer the mechanism to a new biological
  case or public-facing decision.
\item
  \textbf{Chapter LO coverage:} LO1, LO2, LO3, LO4
\item
  \textbf{Rubric dimensions:} evidence; controls; uncertainty;
  mechanism; transfer. \#\# Background \{.unnumbered\}
\end{itemize}

The Hardy-Weinberg principle states that in a large, randomly mating
population with no selection, mutation, migration, or drift, allele
frequencies (p, q) and genotype frequencies (p\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}, 2pq, q\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}) remain
constant across generations. Deviations from HWE indicate one or more of
these forces is acting. Genetic drift --- random changes in allele
frequency --- is most powerful in small populations, causing loss of
variation and potentially fixing or eliminating alleles by chance alone.

\textbf{Part A --- Hardy-Weinberg Calculation}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Using the provided MN blood group data (genotype counts \textbf{MM =
  298, MN = 489, NN = 213}, from a sample of \emph{n} = 1000; classic
  combined US-Caucasian MN blood-group survey, as reproduced in standard
  population-genetics texts): calculate allele frequencies \emph{p} (M)
  and \emph{q} (N). \emph{(Check: p(M) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 0.5425, q(N) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 0.4575.)}
\item
  Calculate expected genotype frequencies under HWE (p\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}, 2pq, q\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}) and
  expected counts.
\item
  Perform chi-square test to determine whether the population is in HWE.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Part B --- Genetic Drift Simulation}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item
  Place 50 red (A) and 50 blue (a) beads in the bag: this represents a
  population of 100 with p = q = 0.5.
\item
  Without looking, draw 10 beads (simulating a bottleneck to N=10).
  Record the frequency of red (A) beads drawn. Then \textbf{discard the
  old bag and rebuild a fresh 100-bead pool at the drawn allele ratio}:
  multiply the observed red fraction by 100, round to the nearest whole
  bead, and use that many red beads with the remainder blue (e.g.~6/10
  red \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} 60 red + 40 blue). Repeat the draw--rebuild cycle for 5
  generations, recording \emph{p} (red fraction) each generation.
\item
  A second group runs the same simulation with N=50 (draw 50 beads, then
  rebuild a 100-bead pool at the drawn allele ratio by the same rounding
  rule) for 5 generations.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Part C --- Selection Simulation (Optional)}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{6}
\tightlist
\item
  In generation 1 of the drift simulation, designate aa (2 blue drawn)
  as lethal --- remove any drawn aa pairs and resample. Track p over 3
  generations.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-20}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Was the MN blood group population in HWE? Which of the HWE assumptions
  might be violated in a real human population, and how would each
  violation shift allele frequencies over generations?
\item
  Was there more variation in allele frequency across generations in the
  N=10 or N=50 group? Define genetic drift in terms of sampling error
  and explain why population size affects drift magnitude.
\item
  Founder effect: a group of 20 individuals colonises a new island. By
  chance, the founding group contains no aa individuals. Even without
  selection against aa, will this condition persist? Explain using HWE
  and the concept that mutation-selection equilibrium is absent if
  frequency starts at zero.
\item
  Heterozygote advantage: sickle-cell anaemia (aa) is lethal, but
  carriers (Aa) are more resistant to malaria than AA homozygotes. With
  the heterozygote Aa as the fittest genotype, let \emph{s} be the
  selection coefficient against AA and \emph{t} the selection
  coefficient against aa (relative fitnesses 1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}\emph{s} : 1 :
  1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}\emph{t}). The stable equilibrium allele frequency of \emph{a} is
  \textbf{q̂ = s / (s + t)}. For a malarious region with \emph{s} = 0.2
  (AA disadvantage) and \emph{t} = 1 (aa lethal), compute q̂ and
  interpret why the \emph{a} allele persists in the population despite
  being lethal in homozygotes.
\item
  A conservation biologist studying a population of 25 cheetahs finds
  they are almost completely genetically homogeneous (very low
  heterozygosity). Explain two consequences of this for: (a) short-term
  disease resistance; (b) long-term adaptive capacity. What management
  intervention would restore genetic variation?
\end{enumerate}

  of 0.8, what is its selection coefficient? If the initial frequency of

\item

  example of natural selection. How does the overuse of antibiotics
  create selection pressure for resistant bacteria? What can be done to
  slow this process?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Background}\label{background-10}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Background}

Natural selection operates when three conditions are met: (1) heritable
variation exists; (2) variation affects survival/reproduction (fitness);
(3) traits are inherited. Over generations, favourable alleles increase
in frequency (directional selection), multiple phenotypes are maintained
(balancing/disruptive selection), or variation is reduced around an
optimum (stabilising selection). The selection coefficient \emph{s}
quantifies fitness cost: a lethal allele has s = 1.0; a neutral allele
has s = 0.

\subsubsection*{Part 1: Predator-Prey Selection
Simulation}\label{part-1-predator-prey-selection-simulation}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Part 1: Predator-Prey Selection
Simulation}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Formulate Your Hypothesis}: Based on your pre-lab research,
  write a hypothesis about how different colored prey will survive on
  different colored backgrounds.
\item
  \textbf{Identify Variables}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Independent variable: Prey color and background color
  \item
    Dependent variable: Survival rate (\% of prey consumed or surviving)
  \item
    Controlled variables: Foraging time, number of prey, predator type,
    etc.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Set Up Controls}: Why is it important to have a control
  background (e.g., green prey on green background)? What other controls
  could you include in a predation simulation?
\item
  \textbf{Data Collection}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Scatter 90 coloured squares randomly across a green (grassy)
    background table.
  \item
    Students ``forage'' for 30 seconds using forceps, prioritising
    whatever they can pick up fastest (competitive foraging).
  \item
    Count survivors in each colour category. Calculate \% survival per
    colour on the green background.
  \item
    Repeat on a brown paper background.
  \item
    Perform at least 3 replicates for each background type.
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection*{Part 2: Computational Biology Exercise - Selection
Coefficient Analysis with

\emph{Optional computational check: run this self-contained Python
snippet from the project root. It uses tested \texttt{src/biology}
modules and requires no external notebook or CSV file.}

Compare a hand-calculated allele-frequency change with the selection
simulator.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ biology.evolution }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ Population, simulate\_selection}

\NormalTok{start }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Population(name}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{"demo"}\NormalTok{, p}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, q}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.7}\NormalTok{, fitness\_AA}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, fitness\_Aa}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.9}\NormalTok{, fitness\_aa}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.6}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{history }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ simulate\_selection(start, generations}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-21}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  On the green background, which colour survived best? Explain in terms
  of camouflage and predator visual system. How does this simulate
  directional selection in a real habitat?
\item
  If the green background was then ``burned'' and replaced with brown
  substrate (environmental change), predict how allele frequencies for
  ``green colour'' would change over generations. Which type of
  selection would now operate?
\item
  The finch beak data showed that species with deep beaks eat harder
  seeds. Explain how this pattern could arise through: (a) individual
  phenotypic plasticity within one generation; (b) natural selection
  across many generations. How would you distinguish these mechanisms
  with an experimental test?
\item
  Antibiotics are not ``mutagens'' --- they do not create resistant
  mutants. They primarily \emph{select for} pre-existing resistant
  mutants. Explain why this distinction matters for how we should use
  antibiotics clinically, and how the selection coefficient for
  resistance changes with antibiotic presence vs absence.
\item
