\subsection*{Background}\label{background-11}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Background}

Even without natural selection, populations evolve through random
genetic drift, gene flow, and mutation. The \textbf{founder effect} (a
special case of bottleneck) occurs when a small number of individuals
colonise a new area, carrying primarily a subset of the original gene
pool's variation. \textbf{Speciation} --- the formation of new species
--- occurs when reproductive isolation evolves between populations,
typically after geographic (allopatric) or ecological (sympatric)
separation. The Fixation Index \textbf{Fst = (H\_T \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-} H\_S) / H\_T}
quantifies genetic differentiation between populations (0 = no
differentiation; 1 = complete differentiation).

\subsubsection*{Part 1: Founder Effect
Simulation}\label{part-1-founder-effect-simulation}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Part 1: Founder Effect Simulation}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Formulate Your Hypothesis}: Based on your pre-lab research,
  write a hypothesis about how the size of a founding population affects
  the rate of genetic drift.
\item
  \textbf{Identify Variables}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Independent variable: Founder population size (6 vs 20 individuals)
  \item
    Dependent variable: Change in allele frequency from source
    population
  \item
    Controlled variables: Source population allele frequency, number of
    generations, etc.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Set Up Controls}: Why is it important to start with a known
  source population allele frequency? What other controls could you
  include in a genetic drift simulation?
\item
  \textbf{Data Collection}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Start: 100 beads at p = 0.5. Draw 6 beads randomly (founder
    population) --- do not replace.
  \item
    Record allele frequencies in the founder group; use these to
    repopulate to 100 (multiply founder frequencies \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 100).
  \item
    Repeat sampling: draw 20 from the new population to simulate a
    moderate founding event.
  \item
    Compare p values: original, 6-founder, 20-founder.
  \item
    Perform at least 3 replicates for each founder size.
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

Run deterministic drift simulations by fixing the random seed.

\NormalTok{small }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ simulate\_drift(p}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{, N}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{20}\NormalTok{, generations}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{, rng\_seed}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{7}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{large }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ simulate\_drift(p}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{, N}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{500}\NormalTok{, generations}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{, rng\_seed}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{7}\NormalTok{)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"large{-}population final p:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(large[}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{], }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"isolation example:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(isolation\_index(gene\_flow\_rate}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.01}\NormalTok{, mutation\_rate}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.001}\NormalTok{), }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-22}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  How did the allele frequencies in the 6-founder event compare to the
  original population? What does this demonstrate about why small
  colonising populations often show low genetic diversity compared to
  mainland populations?
\item
  The mockingbird populations on different Galapagos islands show
  morphological divergence. What mechanism prevented gene flow between
  islands, and what type of speciation does this represent? What
  reproductive isolation mechanisms would need to evolve for them to
  become separate species?
\item
  Fst = 0 indicates populations are identical (freely exchanging genes).
  Fst = 1 indicates complete isolation. How would you interpret Fst =
  0.15 --- is there gene flow? Use your calculated Fst to describe the
  degree of isolation between cichlid populations A, B, and C.
\item
  Lake Victoria cichlids underwent adaptive radiation in
  about 15,000 years, producing \textgreater500 species. What
  does this rapid speciation suggest about the speed at which
  reproductive isolation can evolve? What kind of speciation
  (allopatric, parapatric, or sympatric) is most consistent with this
  pattern?
\item
  Ring species (like Larus gulls circling the Arctic) demonstrate
  speciation in action: adjacent populations can interbreed, but the two
  ends of the ring cannot. Explain what this demonstrates about the
  continuity of the speciation process and why ring species challenge a
  strict definition of ``species.''
\end{enumerate}

\item
  \textbf{Rubric dimensions:} evidence; controls; uncertainty;
  mechanism; transfer. \#\# Background \{.unnumbered\}
\end{itemize}

Phylogenetics reconstructs evolutionary history by identifying shared
derived characters (\textbf{synapomorphies}) that define clades. Maximum
parsimony selects the tree requiring the fewest evolutionary changes.
Molecular phylogenies use DNA/protein sequence differences, calibrated
with fossil dates, to construct ultrametric trees with branch lengths
proportional to substitution rate or time. Bootstrap values (percentage
of resampled datasets recovering the same clade) indicate support for
individual nodes.

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-23}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  In your character matrix, which character (vertebrae, four limbs,
  feathers, etc.) defines the broadest clade (most inclusive group)?
  Which is the most restricted synapomorphy (smallest clade)? Explain
  the concept of nested hierarchy.
\item
  Crocodiles share a more recent common ancestor with birds than with
  lizards, despite looking more like lizards. What does this illustrate
  about the limits of morphological similarity as an indicator of
  evolutionary relationship?
\item
  A bootstrap value of 95\% means that 95\% of resampled datasets
  recover that node. How would you interpret a node with 42\% bootstrap
  support? Should it be included in the published tree?
\item
  Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in bacteria allows genes to jump
  between unrelated lineages --- violating the vertical
  (parent-to-offspring) assumption of phylogenetics. Explain how HGT
  would appear as a misleading signal in a molecular phylogeny, and
  describe one method used to detect it.
\item
  The ``Tree of Life'' analogy implies a bifurcating, hierarchical
  structure. However, hybridisation (interspecies mating, e.g., in
  plants) produces reticulate evolution --- a network rather than a
  tree. Name two plant genera where reticulate evolution occurs and
  describe how allopolyploidy contributes to speciation.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Background}\label{background-12}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Background}

Prokaryotes --- Bacteria and Archaea --- are the most abundant life
forms on Earth (about 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{3}}{3}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1} cells). Gram staining differentiates
bacteria based on cell wall composition: Gram-positive (thick
peptidoglycan layer retains crystal violet --- purple) vs Gram-negative
(thin peptidoglycan + outer membrane --- loses crystal violet, appears
pink after safranin counterstain). Viruses are acellular entities that
replicate primarily inside host cells; bacteriophages infect bacteria
and follow either lytic (immediate replication and lysis) or lysogenic
(DNA integration, dormancy) cycles.

\subsubsection*{Part 1: Gram-Stain Image
Classification}\label{part-1-gram-stain-image-classification}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Part 1: Gram-Stain Image
Classification}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Formulate Your Hypothesis}: Based on your pre-lab research,
  write a hypothesis about how the Gram stain results will differ
  between \emph{E. coli} and \emph{Bacillus} species.
\item
  \textbf{Identify Variables}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Independent variable: Bacterial species
  \item
    Dependent variable: Gram stain result (purple vs pink) and cell
    morphology
  \item
    Controlled variables: image source, colour-calibration note, scale
    label, scoring key, scorer training, and blind-card order.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Set Up Controls}: Score the known Gram-positive and
  Gram-negative control cards first. What other controls could you
  include to ensure accurate identification, such as a mixed-species
  image, a low-quality image, or a blinded duplicate?
\item
  \textbf{Data Collection}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Classify each blinded image card as Gram-positive, Gram-negative,
    mixed, or uninterpretable.
  \item
    Record: colour (purple = Gram+, pink = Gram-), cell shape (coccus,
    bacillus, spirillum), arrangement (single, pairs, chains, clusters),
    and confidence score (1-5).
  \item
    Compare independent scorers. Resolve disagreements primarily after
    recording the original calls.
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

material-handling or equipment version belongs only in an optional
extension.

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-24}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Why does \emph{E. coli} stain Gram-negative? Describe the structural
  difference between the cell walls of Gram-positive and Gram-negative
  bacteria, and explain why ethanol decolourises Gram-negative but not
  Gram-positive cells.
\item
  Calculate the CFU/mL from your best printed plate count. Assuming
  exponential growth at a doubling time of 20 minutes, estimate how many
  cells would be present after 4 hours if starting from 100 CFU/mL.
\item
  Penicillin inhibits transpeptidase (cross-links peptidoglycan). Based
  on cell wall structure, predict whether penicillin is more effective
  against \emph{E. coli} or \emph{Bacillus subtilis}, and why
  Gram-negative bacteria often require higher doses.
\item
  A bacteriophage follows a lysogenic cycle for 200 generations, then
  enters the lytic cycle. What molecular signal might trigger the switch
  from lysogeny to lysis? Name the specific protease involved and the CI
  repressor it degrades.
\item
  SARS-CoV-2 is a single-stranded, positive-sense RNA virus with an
  envelope. Compare its replication cycle to a lytic bacteriophage:
  identify two key differences in where replication occurs, the host
  enzyme used, and the method of exiting the host cell.
\item
  A carbapenemase gene appears in related \emph{Klebsiella} isolates on
  two hospital wards and in a wastewater sample. Use plasmid, integron,
  and clonal-spread evidence to decide what additional data would
  distinguish horizontal transfer from one expanding clone.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Extension Analysis
Questions}\label{extension-analysis-questions-12}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Extension Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{6}
\item
  \textbf{Statistical Analysis}: If the dataset includes three replicate
  plate images, how would you analyze the variation in CFU/mL estimates?
  What statistical test would you use to determine if differences
  between species are significant?
\item
  \textbf{Experimental Error Analysis}: What are three potential sources
  of error in bacterial colony counting from images? How could you
  modify the scoring rules or image set to reduce each source of error?
\item
  \textbf{Experimental Design}: If you wanted to test the effectiveness
  of different antibiotics on bacterial growth without culturing, how
  would you design the dataset? What controls would you include? How
  would you measure the effect from growth curves, MIC tables, or
  inhibition-zone images?
\end{enumerate}

(Multi-Session)}

\textbf{Design a Study of Antibiotic Resistance Evolution}

This project will span 2-3 lab sessions:

\textbf{Session 1}: Research Question and Hypothesis - How does
sub-lethal antibiotic concentration affect the rate of resistance
evolution in bacteria? - Formulate a hypothesis about the relationship
between antibiotic concentration and resistance development - Design a
simulation using provided \emph{E. coli} growth curves and different
antibiotic concentrations

\textbf{Session 2}: Data Collection and Analysis - Analyze printed
growth curves collected under antibiotic gradients - Measure resistance
levels from minimum inhibitory concentration tables - Analyze
allele-frequency changes using provided PCR or sequencing summaries

\textbf{Session 3}: Data Interpretation and Presentation - Compare
resistance evolution across different antibiotic concentrations -
Calculate selection coefficients for resistant vs sensitive bacteria -
Create a scientific poster or presentation

  diversity, and what are the potential health consequences of this

\subsection*{Background}\label{background-13}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Background}

The human gut microbiome contains about 3.8 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{3}}{3} bacteria
from hundreds of species; the ratio of microbial to human cells is
approximately 1:1 (revised from earlier overestimates). Culture-based
methods recover about 1\% of environmental microbes (the ``great plate
count anomaly''). Metagenomics and 16S rRNA gene sequencing (amplifying
the hypervariable V3--V4 region) now allow culture-independent
assessment of community composition. The \textbf{Shannon diversity index
H' = \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Sigma}}{Sigma}(p\_i \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} ln p\_i)} integrates species richness and evenness.

\subsubsection*{Part 1: Community Diversity from Case
Packets}\label{part-1-community-diversity-from-case-packets}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Part 1: Community Diversity from
Case Packets}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Formulate Your Hypothesis}: Based on your pre-lab research,
  write a hypothesis about how the provided community datasets will
  differ in microbial diversity.
\item
  \textbf{Identify Variables}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Independent variable: Community source represented in the case
    packet
  \item
    Dependent variable: Taxon richness, Shannon diversity index, and
    network connectance
  \item
    Controlled variables: sequencing depth, primer region, read-quality
    threshold, rarefaction rule, metadata completeness, and replicate
    count.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Set Up Controls}: Why is it important to use the same
  sequencing-depth rule for most samples? What other controls could you
  include, such as a mock community, a blank extraction control, or a
  duplicate sample?
\item
  \textbf{Data Collection}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Use the printed OTU table to calculate total reads, relative
    abundance, richness, Shannon diversity, and evenness for each
    sample.
  \item
    Use the archived colony-image panel primarily as a comparison for
    why morphology underestimates molecular diversity.
  \item
    Check whether each sample has enough reads for fair comparison; if
    not, apply the rarefaction rule provided in the case packet.
  \item
    Compare at least three replicate rows per sample type before drawing
    conclusions.
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection*{Part 2: Computational Biology Exercise - Diversity
Analysis with
Python}\label{part-2-computational-biology-exercise---diversity-analysis-with-python}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Part 2: Computational Biology
Exercise - Diversity Analysis with Python}

\emph{Optional computational check: run this self-contained Python
snippet from the project root. It uses tested \texttt{src/biology}
modules and requires no external notebook or CSV file.}

Calculate diversity from table counts and compare named reference
organisms.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ biology.ecology }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ biodiversity\_indices}
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ biology.microbiology }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ REFERENCE\_ORGANISMS}

\NormalTok{counts }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\DecValTok{42}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{18}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{15}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{9}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{diversity }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ biodiversity\_indices(counts)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Shannon:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(diversity.shannon\_index, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"evenness:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(diversity.evenness, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"reference domains:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{sorted}\NormalTok{(\{organism.domain }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ organism }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ REFERENCE\_ORGANISMS\}))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-25}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  The soil dataset likely shows higher richness than the skin or
  tap-water dataset. Why are soils among the most microbially diverse
  environments on Earth? What physical and chemical habitat
  heterogeneity drives this?
\item
  Antibiotic treatment usually reduces H'. What does low H' indicate
  about community stability? Name one specific clinical consequence of
  reduced microbiome diversity following broad-spectrum antibiotic use.
\item
  The ``great plate count anomaly'' refers to the fact that about 1\% of
  environmental microbes form colonies on standard media. Propose three
  reasons why the remaining 99\% are ``unculturable'' and describe one
  molecular technique that can characterise them without culturing.
\item
  \emph{Akkermansia muciniphila} (a gut commensal) degrades mucin and
  produces acetate and propionate consumed by other bacteria. If
  \emph{Akkermansia} is lost, predict the cascade effects on adjacent
  taxa in your interaction network.
\item
  A patient receives a faecal microbiota transplant (FMT) to treat
  recurrent \emph{C. difficile} infection. Using the concept of
  competitive exclusion and microbiome diversity, explain the mechanism
  by which FMT suppresses \emph{C. difficile} and describe what the
  ideal donor microbiome looks like.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Background}\label{background-14}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Background}

Epidemiology uses epidemic curves (cases vs time), attack rates,
secondary attack rates, and reproductive numbers (R\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0}) to characterise
outbreaks. R\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0} is the average number of secondary cases generated by one
infected individual in a fully susceptible population; herd immunity is
achieved when the fraction vaccinated exceeds the threshold \textbf{p\_c
= 1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-} (1/R\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0})}. Antimicrobial susceptibility datasets often report
disc-diffusion zones of inhibition from Kirby-Bauer assays --- larger
zone = more susceptible pathogen --- but this lab interprets printed
data primarily.

\subsubsection*{Part 1: Epidemic Curve
Analysis}\label{part-1-epidemic-curve-analysis}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Part 1: Epidemic Curve Analysis}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Formulate Your Hypothesis}: Based on your pre-lab research,
  write a hypothesis about the transmission dynamics of the norovirus
  outbreak.
\item
  \textbf{Identify Variables}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Independent variable: Time (hours since exposure)
  \item
    Dependent variable: Number of new cases
  \item
    Controlled variables: Population size, exposure source, reporting
    methods, etc.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Set Up Controls}: Why is it important to have accurate case
  reporting? What other controls could you include in an epidemic
  investigation to ensure valid conclusions?
\item
  \textbf{Data Collection}:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Plot the epidemic curve (cases per 2-hour interval).
  \item
    Identify the single peak (suggesting point-source exposure) or
    multiple waves (suggesting person-to-person spread).
  \item
    Calculate: (a) attack rate = (cases / total exposed) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 100\%; (b)
    approximate incubation period from the peak; (c) R\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0} from the growth
    rate during exponential phase using the provided formula.
  \item
    Compare two blinded disc-diffusion image replicates, measure zone
    diameters from the printed scale, and classify each antibiotic as
    susceptible, intermediate, or resistant using the provided
    breakpoint table.
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-26}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  If the epidemic curve shows a single sharp peak within a window
  shorter than the incubation period, what type of source does this
  suggest? How would a propagated (person-to-person) epidemic curve look
  different?
\item
  \emph{E. coli} showed resistance to ampicillin but susceptibility to
  kanamycin. Explain the likely molecular mechanism of ampicillin
  resistance (naming the specific enzyme) and why one \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactamase can
  create cross-resistance to several related \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactams while still
  leaving some \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactam/\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactamase-inhibitor combinations, carbapenems,
  or non-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-lactam drugs active depending on the enzyme and permeability
  context.
\item
  Measles has an R\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0} of about 15, requiring about 93\%
  vaccination for herd immunity. Your calculation shows that even high
  measles vaccination coverage is needed. What happens to herd immunity
  when 5\% of a vaccinated population declines vaccination? Relate this
  to observed measles outbreaks in Europe (2019).
\item
  An immunocompromised patient (CD4 T cell count \textless{} 200/\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}L,
  HIV+ AIDS) contracts measles despite prior vaccination. Explain: (a)
  why the vaccine may be insufficient; (b) which branch of adaptive
  immunity (humoral or cellular) is most deficient; (c) what specific
  viral clearance mechanism is impaired.
\item
  The O'Neill Review's 10-million-deaths-per-year by 2050 AMR estimate
  is a historical warning scenario, not a current burden count
  \citep{oneill2016amr}. Describe three specific mechanisms by which
  bacteria acquire resistance genes, and evaluate two distinct policy
  interventions that would slow the spread of AMR at a population level.
\item
  A malaria programme already distributes insecticide-treated nets, but
  household surveys show substantial indoor activity before bedtime. Use
  the vector-control matrix to decide whether spatial emanators could be
  an added tool, and state two evidence gaps that would still require
  local monitoring.
\end{enumerate}

demonstrations must use approved BSL-1 organisms under instructor

\subsection*{Background}\label{background-15}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Background}

Vascular plants have three tissue systems: dermal (epidermis, cuticle,
guard cells), ground (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma), and
vascular (xylem for water/mineral transport upward; phloem for
sugar/assimilate transport, bidirectional). Transpiration ---
evaporation of water from stomata --- drives the cohesion-tension
mechanism that pulls water from root to leaf. Environmental factors
(light, humidity, temperature, wind) modulate transpiration rate by
affecting stomatal aperture.

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-27}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  The diagram packet traces water movement through xylem rather than
  phloem. Why does bulk water transport follow xylem pathways, and what
  would you predict for sugar movement in phloem under the pressure-flow
  hypothesis?
\item
  Which condition produced the highest transpiration rate --- bright
  light or fan? Explain why wind increases transpiration using the
  concept of the diffusion boundary layer.
\item
  Stomata open when guard cells swell (K\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} influx followed by water via
  osmosis). Explain how light triggers stomatal opening via the proton
  pump (H\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+}-ATPase) and K\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} channels, and why abscisic acid (ABA) causes
  stomatal closure during drought.
\item
  The Casparian strip forces water from the cortex to enter the
  endodermis symplastically (through cells), not apoplastically (through
  cell walls). Why is this selectivity important for plant mineral
  uptake?
\item
  A plant biologist clips the tip of a phloem sieve tube using a laser
  scalpel. Predict what happens to sugar transport above and below the
  cut within 30 seconds, using your knowledge of the pressure-flow
  hypothesis for phloem loading and unloading.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Group Project Extension
(Multi-Session)}\label{group-project-extension-multi-session-12}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Group Project Extension
(Multi-Session)}

\textbf{Design a Study of Plant Water Use Efficiency}

This project will span 2-3 lab sessions:

\textbf{Session 1}: Research Question and Hypothesis - How does water
use efficiency (WUE) vary among plant species from different
environments? - Formulate a hypothesis about the relationship between
WUE and drought tolerance - Design an experiment measuring transpiration
and photosynthesis rates

\textbf{Session 2}: Data Extraction and Analysis - Extract transpiration
rates from printed potometer or gravimetric datasets - Compare
photosynthesis rates from CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} exchange or O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} evolution data tables -
Calculate intrinsic water use efficiency (photosynthesis/transpiration)

\textbf{Session 3}: Data Interpretation and Presentation - Compare WUE
across species - Correlate WUE with environmental adaptations (e.g.,
leaf thickness, stomatal density) - Create a scientific poster or
presentation

\subsection*{Background}\label{background-16}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Background}

Angiosperms (flowering plants) undergo \textbf{double fertilisation}:
one sperm nucleus (n) fuses with the egg (n) to form the zygote (2n); a
second sperm fuses with the two polar nuclei (2\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x}n = 2n) to form the
primary endosperm nucleus (3n), which nourishes the developing embryo.
Pollen grains (male gametophytes, n) germinate on the stigma and grow a
pollen tube through the style to deliver sperm to the embryo sac (female
gametophyte) in the ovule.

  \textbf{Reproducibility Check}: For the printed pollen-tube dataset,
  calculate mean growth rate and standard deviation for each treatment.
  Decide whether the temperature effect is larger than within-treatment
  variation.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-28}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Pollen tube growth is driven by cytoplasmic streaming and tip-directed
  vesicle fusion. What is the role of Ca\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} ions (specifically the
  tip-focused Ca\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} gradient) in regulating pollen tube polarity and
  growth direction?
\item
  Describe double fertilisation: where does each sperm go, what does
  each produce, and what are the ploidy levels of the zygote and
  endosperm?
\item
  A bee visits a fragrant, brightly coloured flower with sticky pollen.
  A grass flower has no petals, no fragrance, and produces vast
  quantities of dry pollen. Explain the evolutionary logic behind each
  strategy using cost-benefit trade-offs.
\item
  Self-incompatibility (SI) systems prevent self-fertilisation in many
  plant species. The S-RNase system in \emph{Petunia} involves the
  pistil secreting an RNase that degrades pollen tube RNA if the pollen
  S-allele matches the pistil S-allele. How does this mechanism
  selectively destroy ``self'' pollen without harming ``foreign''
  pollen?
\item
  Seedless watermelons are triploid (3n). Explain the steps used to
  produce them (starting from a colchicine treatment of diploid cells),
  and why triploid plants are sterile --- using the concept of
  homologous chromosome pairing during meiosis.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Extension Analysis
Questions}\label{extension-analysis-questions-16}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Extension Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{5}
\item
  \textbf{Statistical Analysis}: If the pollen germination dataset
  includes three replicates per treatment, how would you analyze
  variation in growth rates? What statistical test would you use to
  determine if differences between temperatures are significant?
\item
  \textbf{Experimental Error Analysis}: What are three potential sources
  of error in pollen tube growth measurements? How could you modify the
  procedure to reduce each source of error?
\item
  \textbf{Experimental Design}: If you wanted to test the effect of a
  specific hormone (e.g., auxin) on pollen tube growth using archived
  image measurements, what concentrations would you test, how would the
  images be blinded, and how would you measure the effect?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Group Project Extension
(Multi-Session)}\label{group-project-extension-multi-session-13}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Group Project Extension
(Multi-Session)}

\textbf{Design a Study of Plant Reproductive Strategies}

This project will span 2-3 lab sessions:

\textbf{Session 1}: Research Question and Hypothesis - How do flower
traits correlate with pollination syndrome? - Formulate a hypothesis
about the relationship between specific traits (e.g., petal colour,
nectar production) and pollinator type - Design a study comparing
multiple plant species

\textbf{Session 2}: Data Extraction and Analysis - Extract flower
morphology data from species cards, image databases, or published
datasets - Score pollinator visits from provided video stills or
summarized observation tables - Analyze correlations between traits and
pollinator type

\textbf{Session 3}: Data Interpretation and Presentation - Perform
statistical analysis (e.g., principal component analysis) - Discuss the
evolutionary implications of your findings - Create a scientific poster
or presentation

\subsection*{Real-World Problem Solving: Plant Reproduction and
Agriculture}\label{real-world-problem-solving-plant-reproduction-and-agriculture}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Real-World Problem Solving: Plant
Reproduction and Agriculture}

\textbf{Case Study: Pollinator Decline}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Research Task}: Investigate the causes and consequences of
  pollinator decline (bees, butterflies, etc.). What crop groups depend
  on animal pollination, and how do dependence estimates differ between
  staple calories, fruits, nuts, and specialty crops?
\item
  \textbf{Field-Translation Consideration}: A warming treatment advances
  flowering in a chamber experiment, but a field dataset shows variable
  pollinator emergence. What evidence would let you decide whether the
  crop faces pollen heat failure, pollinator mismatch, or both?
\item
  \textbf{Policy Proposal}: Design a policy to protect pollinator
  populations while supporting agricultural productivity. Consider:
  incentives for habitat restoration, pesticide timing, heat-wave
  monitoring during flowering, and seed-set surveillance.
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Lab 27 --- Plant Responses to the
Environment}\label{lab-27-plant-responses-to-the-environment}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Lab 27 --- Plant Responses to the
Environment}

\label{sec:lab_unit_VIII_plant_responses}

\subsection*{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-67}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Learning Objectives}

\emph{This activity accompanies \cref{sec:unit_VIII_plant_responses} of
the textbook --- review that chapter before attempting the exercises
below.}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Interpret phototropism and gravitropism from time-series images and
  angle data
\item
  Measure the effect of exogenous auxin concentration from a printed
  dose-response dataset
\item

  replicated growth tables
\item

  red/far-red treatment data
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Alignment and Rubric
Map}\label{alignment-and-rubric-map-29}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Alignment and Rubric Map}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 1 (LO1):} Interpret the supplied evidence or model
  output for Plant Responses to the Environment.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 2 (LO2):} Identify controls and comparison groups that
  make the claim testable.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 3 (LO3):} Quantify uncertainty, boundary conditions,
  or alternative explanations before concluding.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 4 (LO4):} Transfer the mechanism to a new biological
  case or public-facing decision.
\item
  \textbf{Chapter LO coverage:} LO1, LO2, LO3, LO4
\item
  \textbf{Rubric dimensions:} evidence; controls; uncertainty;
  mechanism; transfer. \#\# Background \{.unnumbered\}
\end{itemize}

Plants integrate environmental signals and respond through
photoreceptors and hormone signalling. Auxin (IAA) is produced in the
shoot apex and promotes elongation at low concentrations but inhibits at
high concentrations (biphasic response). Gibberellins (GAs) promote stem
elongation and seed germination by targeting DELLA protein degradation.
Phototropism (bending toward light) results from asymmetric auxin
distribution driven by the PIN auxin efflux carriers. Phytochrome Pr
(inactive, absorbs red 660 nm) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\leftrightarrow}}{<->} Pfr (active, absorbs far-red 730 nm)
provides a light quality sensor --- Pfr promotes seed germination and
flowering.

\textbf{Part A --- Phototropism Demonstration}

  Use the image sequence to compare unilateral light, darkness, and
  rotated-orientation treatments. Measure the angle of curvature from

\textbf{Part B --- Auxin Dose-Response}

\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}

\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Part C --- Gibberellin Effect on Dwarfism}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\tightlist
\item

  relative to control.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Part D --- Phytochrome and Seed Germination}

  -\textgreater{} red -\textgreater{} dark.
\item

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-29}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  In the phototropism experiment, which side of the shoot had longer
  cells? Explain how asymmetric auxin distribution (mediated by PIN
  proteins) creates differential elongation, and name the specific plant
  hormone involved.
\item
  Your auxin dose-response curve should show a bell shape. At what
  concentration did you see maximum curvature? Explain why very high
  auxin concentrations actually inhibit shoot elongation (relate to the
  acidic growth hypothesis and receptor downregulation).
\item
  GA-treated dwarf peas grew taller than controls. Explain the molecular
  mechanism: how does GA binding its receptor (GID1) lead to degradation
  of DELLA proteins and activate cell elongation genes?
\item
  Interpret your phytochrome germination results: which treatment(s)
  promoted germination? Which inhibited it? Explain why the red/far-red
  ratio in natural shade (under a canopy) would suppress germination of
  shade-intolerant species.
\item
  Long-day plants flower when nights are shorter than a critical length
  (they actually measure night length via phytochrome). Explain why a
  brief red light pulse in the middle of an otherwise long night would
  prevent flowering in a short-day plant, but a subsequent far-red pulse
  would restore it --- and what this tells us about the form of
  phytochrome that promotes flowering inhibition.
\item
  Choose one environmental cue card (drought, canopy shade, salinity, or
  warming). What field measurement would you need before turning the
  hormone-response result into a crop-management recommendation?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-68}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Learning Objectives}

\emph{This activity accompanies
\cref{sec:unit_IX_circulation_respiration_homeostasis} of the textbook
--- review that chapter before attempting the exercises below.}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Analyze resting and post-exercise heart rate and blood pressure
  datasets and apply the Frank-Starling law
\item
  Calculate cardiac output and stroke volume from anonymized case data
  using CO = HR \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} SV
\item
  Apply Fick's principle to estimate oxygen consumption from heart rate
  data
\item
  Analyse spirometry data to determine tidal volume, IRV, ERV, and FVC
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Alignment and Rubric
Map}\label{alignment-and-rubric-map-30}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Alignment and Rubric Map}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 1 (LO1):} Interpret the supplied evidence or model
  output for Circulation, Respiration, and Homeostasis.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 2 (LO2):} Identify controls and comparison groups that
  make the claim testable.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 3 (LO3):} Quantify uncertainty, boundary conditions,
  or alternative explanations before concluding.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 4 (LO4):} Transfer the mechanism to a new biological
  case or public-facing decision.
\item
  \textbf{Chapter LO coverage:} LO1, LO2, LO3, LO4
\item
  \textbf{Rubric dimensions:} evidence; controls; uncertainty;
  mechanism; transfer. \#\# Background \{.unnumbered\}
\end{itemize}

The cardiovascular system delivers oxygen and removes CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} at a rate
matched to tissue demand. Cardiac output (CO) = stroke volume (SV) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x}
heart rate (HR). The Frank-Starling law states that greater ventricular
filling (preload) stretches sarcomeres to a more optimal myosin--actin
overlap, increasing stroke volume. Spirometry measures lung volumes:
tidal volume (TV about 500 mL), inspiratory reserve (IRV
about 3,000 mL), expiratory reserve (ERV about 1,200
mL), and FVC = (TV + IRV + ERV) for healthy adults.

\subsection*{Paper-Based
Investigation}\label{paper-based-investigation-30}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Paper-Based Investigation}

\textbf{Part A --- Cardiovascular Measurements}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Use the cardiovascular response dataset to compare resting HR,
  estimated stroke volume, and recovery time across cases.
\item
  Plot HR at rest, 0, 1, 2, 5, and 10 minutes post-exercise for the
  printed subjects. Identify the baseline control and the slowest
  recovery profile.
\item
  Calculate CO = HR \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} SV at rest and immediately post-exercise. Check
  whether the data are consistent with the Frank-Starling mechanism and
  autonomic regulation.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Part B --- Spirometry Analysis}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item
  Use the printed spirometry dataset to calculate TV, FVC, FEV1, and
  FEV1/FVC where available.
\item
  Compare FVC and FEV1/FVC ratios for normal, asthmatic, and COPD
  subjects.
\item
  Use the altitude case card to connect PaO2 changes to ventilation,
  erythropoietin, hematocrit, and acclimatization.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Part C --- Digestive-Renal Homeostasis}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{6}
\tightlist
\item
  Use the digestive-renal cards to trace how a high-protein salty meal
  changes gut absorption, hepatic urea production, plasma osmolality,
  ADH release, and urine concentration.
\item
  Compare a freshwater fish, a desert mammal, and a bird/reptile
  excretory strategy. Identify whether ammonia, urea, or uric acid is
  the dominant nitrogen-waste solution and what water trade-off that
  solution implies.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-30}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Why did HR increase during exercise, and why did it remain elevated
  for several minutes post-exercise? Name the autonomic branch primarily
  responsible for the exercise-induced HR increase.
\item
  A reduced FEV\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}/FVC ratio below the age-dependent lower limit of normal
  supports an obstructive pattern; a fixed 70\% cutoff is a screening
  shortcut, not a comprehensive diagnostic boundary. The asthmatic shows
  reduced FEV\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1} but relatively preserved FVC. Explain the structural
  difference in the airways that causes obstructive vs restrictive
  spirometry patterns.
\item
  Calculate the difference in cardiac output between rest and peak
  exercise in your data. Using Fick's principle (VO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} = CO \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} (CaO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}
  CvO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2})), estimate oxygen consumption if the arterio-venous O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}
  difference increases from 50 mL/L at rest to 150 mL/L during maximal
  exercise.
\item
  A patient with congestive heart failure has chronically elevated
  ventricular end-diastolic pressure. Explain how this shifts the
  Frank-Starling curve and contributes to pulmonary oedema (connect to
  Starling capillary forces).
\item
  At high altitude (3,500 m), PaO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} drops from 100 to about 60
  mmHg. Identify three physiological acclimatisation responses (acute
  and chronic) and for each, specify the sensing mechanism and the
  effector system involved.
\item
  A dehydrated student eats a salty, high-protein meal. Predict the
  direction of change for plasma osmolality, ADH, urea production, and
  urine concentration. Which measurements would distinguish ``not enough
  water intake'' from impaired kidney concentrating ability?
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Lab 29 --- Nervous System and Neural
Signalling}\label{lab-29-nervous-system-and-neural-signalling}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Lab 29 --- Nervous System and Neural
Signalling}

\label{sec:lab_unit_IX_nervous_system}

\subsection*{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-69}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Learning Objectives}

\emph{This activity accompanies \cref{sec:unit_IX_nervous_system} of the
textbook --- review that chapter before attempting the exercises below.}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Interpret reflex arc function using a clinical timing dataset and map
  receptive fields from paper data
\item
  Analyze two-point discrimination thresholds from anonymized class
  datasets
\item
  Analyse an action potential recording and identify threshold, peak,
  undershoot, and refractory periods
\item
  Apply the length constant equation to predict how signal decay differs
  in myelinated vs unmyelinated axons
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Alignment and Rubric
Map}\label{alignment-and-rubric-map-31}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Alignment and Rubric Map}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 1 (LO1):} Interpret the supplied evidence or model
  output for Nervous System and Neural Signalling.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 2 (LO2):} Identify controls and comparison groups that
  make the claim testable.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 3 (LO3):} Quantify uncertainty, boundary conditions,
  or alternative explanations before concluding.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 4 (LO4):} Transfer the mechanism to a new biological
  case or public-facing decision.
\item
  \textbf{Chapter LO coverage:} LO1, LO2, LO3, LO4
\item
  \textbf{Rubric dimensions:} evidence; controls; uncertainty;
  mechanism; transfer. \#\# Background \{.unnumbered\}
\end{itemize}

Neural signalling depends on the passive spread of graded potentials
and, for long-distance signalling, the most-or-nothing action potential
(AP). The \textbf{two-point discrimination threshold} (Weber's two-point
test) reveals the density of somatosensory receptors in the skin:
fingertips (2--3 mm threshold) vs upper back (40--70 mm). The patellar
reflex is monosynaptic: stretching the patellar tendon activates Ia
afferents in the quadriceps \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} synapse on \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha} motor neurons in the spinal
cord \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} quadriceps contraction. The entire arc takes \textless50 ms.

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-31}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The fingertip had a much shorter two-point discrimination threshold
  than the upper back. Relate this to somatotopic mapping in the
  somatosensory cortex --- which area of the sensory homunculus
  represents fingers vs trunk, and what is the neural basis for this
  high-density representation?
\item
  The Jendrassik manoeuvre increased the patellar reflex. Explain this
  using the concept of motor neuron excitability and descending
  facilitation from the cortex/brainstem.
\item
  The action potential's absolute refractory period prevents reversed
  signal propagation (backward re-excitation). Explain how sodium
  channel inactivation (h-gate closed) creates this period and why this
  is essential for unidirectional propagation.
\item
  Your cable property calculation showed much higher \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda} in the myelinated
  axon. Relate this to saltatory conduction: why does an action
  potential jump between nodes of Ranvier rather than regenerate
  continuously along the axon?
\item
  In multiple sclerosis, the myelin sheath is destroyed. Using your \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda}
  calculations, predict what happens to action potential propagation in
  demyelinated axons, and explain why patients might experience
  increased sensitivity to heat (Uhthoff's phenomenon).
\item
  A speech BCI card reports high decoding accuracy from one participant
  during attempted speech. Which conclusion is directly supported, and
  which conclusions would require additional controls or longitudinal
  data?
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Lab 30 --- Action Potentials and Synaptic
Transmission}\label{lab-30-action-potentials-and-synaptic-transmission}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Lab 30 --- Action Potentials and Synaptic
Transmission}

\label{sec:lab_unit_IX_action_potential_synapses}

\subsection*{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-70}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Learning Objectives}

\emph{This activity accompanies
\cref{sec:unit_IX_action_potential_synapses} of the textbook --- review
that chapter before attempting the exercises below.}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Analyse a compound action potential (CAP) recording from a nerve
  preparation to distinguish A, B, and C fibre types
\item
  Simulate quantal neurotransmitter release and calculate mean quantal
  content
\item
  Model the effect of GABA-A receptor modulation by benzodiazepines vs
  barbiturates
\item
  Evaluate synaptic plasticity mechanisms using an LTP induction
  protocol dataset
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Alignment and Rubric
Map}\label{alignment-and-rubric-map-32}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Alignment and Rubric Map}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 1 (LO1):} Interpret the supplied evidence or model
  output for Action Potentials and Synaptic Transmission.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 2 (LO2):} Identify controls and comparison groups that
  make the claim testable.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 3 (LO3):} Quantify uncertainty, boundary conditions,
  or alternative explanations before concluding.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 4 (LO4):} Transfer the mechanism to a new biological
  case or public-facing decision.
\item
  \textbf{Chapter LO coverage:} LO1, LO2, LO3, LO4
\item
  \textbf{Rubric dimensions:} evidence; controls; uncertainty;
  mechanism; transfer. \#\# Background \{.unnumbered\}
\end{itemize}

Synaptic transmission involves vesicle fusion (Ca\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+}-triggered SNARE
complex assembly), neurotransmitter diffusion across the synaptic cleft,
and receptor binding on the postsynaptic membrane. Release is quantal:
the minimum unit is the vesicle (one quantum, about 5,000
molecules). The mean quantal content (m̄) can be estimated by the Poisson
failure method: m̄ = ln(N/F\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0}) where N = total trials and F\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0} = failures.
Long-term potentiation (LTP) at Schaffer collateral \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} CA1 synapses
requires NMDA receptor-mediated Ca\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} influx and CaMKII
autophosphorylation.

\subsection*{Paper-Based
Investigation}\label{paper-based-investigation-32}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Paper-Based Investigation}

\textbf{Part A --- Compound Action Potential Analysis}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  From the CAP trace, identify the three peaks (A\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}, A\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\delta}}{delta}, C fibre).
  Measure the latency of each peak from the stimulus artefact.
\item
  Given the distance from electrode to nerve (30 mm), calculate
  conduction velocity for each peak (velocity = distance/time).
\item
  Compare your calculated values to known conduction velocities (A\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}:
  70--120 m/s; A\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\delta}}{delta}: 5--30 m/s; C: 0.5--2 m/s).
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Part B --- Quantal Analysis Simulation}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item
  From the dataset (100 trials, F\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0} = 8 failures): calculate m̄ by Poisson
  failure method (m̄ = ln(100/8) = ln(12.5)).
\item
  Also calculate m̄ by direct count method (m̄ = total quanta released /
  100 trials).
\item
  Estimate release probability: p̄ = m̄/n (where n = total available
  release sites, given as 15).
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Part C --- GABA-A Pharmacology}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{6}
\tightlist
\item
  From the worksheet, benzodiazepines increase the \textbf{frequency} of
  Cl\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-} channel opening; barbiturates increase \textbf{duration} of Cl\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}
  channel opening (at low concentration) and open channels directly (at
  high concentration). On the I-V plot provided, annotate the effect of
  each drug class on Cl\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-} current.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Part D --- LTP Dataset}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{7}
\tightlist
\item
  Plot EPSP slope (\% baseline) vs time (minutes) for control and
  AP5-treated groups before and after high-frequency stimulation (HFS at
  t=0).
\item
  Calculate the LTP magnitude: (mean EPSP slope 30--60 min post-HFS /
  mean EPSP slope 10 min pre-HFS) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 100\%.
\item
  Reproducibility check: record the baseline window, post-HFS window,
  and any outlier rule before calculating LTP magnitude.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-32}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  C fibres (unmyelinated) have much slower conduction velocities than A\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}
  fibres (myelinated). Using your cable property knowledge from Lab 29,
  explain the molecular basis for this difference.
\item
  The two methods for calculating m̄ gave similar but not identical
  answers. Which method is more reliable when there is heterogeneity in
  release probabilities across synapses? Explain the statistical
  assumption violated by each method.
\item
  A patient given a benzodiazepine (e.g., diazepam) overdose can be
  treated with flumazenil (a competitive benzodiazepine antagonist).
  Explain why flumazenil doesn't cause seizures on its own even though
  it fully blocks GABA-A modulation, while complete GABA-A inhibition by
  bicuculline does cause seizures.
\item
  AP5 (an NMDA receptor antagonist) blocked LTP induction. Explain the
  molecular events from NMDA receptor opening to CaMKII
  autophosphorylation to AMPA receptor insertion (at least 5 steps).
\item
  Ketamine is an NMDA receptor open-channel blocker used as an
  anaesthetic and, at sub-anaesthetic doses, as a rapid antidepressant.
  Propose a mechanism by which blocking NMDA receptors could relieve
  depression --- consider what happens to synaptic strength in GABAergic
  interneurons when their NMDA receptors are blocked.
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Lab 31 --- Endocrine and Immune
Systems}\label{lab-31-endocrine-and-immune-systems}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Lab 31 --- Endocrine and Immune Systems}

\label{sec:lab_unit_IX_endocrine_and_immune}

\subsection*{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-71}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Learning Objectives}

\emph{This activity accompanies \cref{sec:unit_IX_endocrine_and_immune}
of the textbook --- review that chapter before attempting the exercises
below.}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Interpret blood hormone panels to diagnose endocrine disorders (hypo-
  vs hyperthyroidism, diabetes, Cushing's)
\item
  Analyse a cytokine profile to determine the type and severity of an
  inflammatory response
\item
  Model the HPT axis feedback loop using a paper-based regulatory
  diagram
\item
  Evaluate innate immune pattern recognition using TLR ligand-response
  data
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Alignment and Rubric
Map}\label{alignment-and-rubric-map-33}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Alignment and Rubric Map}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 1 (LO1):} Interpret the supplied evidence or model
  output for Endocrine and Immune Systems.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 2 (LO2):} Identify controls and comparison groups that
  make the claim testable.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 3 (LO3):} Quantify uncertainty, boundary conditions,
  or alternative explanations before concluding.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 4 (LO4):} Transfer the mechanism to a new biological
  case or public-facing decision.
\item
  \textbf{Chapter LO coverage:} LO1, LO2, LO3, LO4
\item
  \textbf{Rubric dimensions:} evidence; controls; uncertainty;
  mechanism; transfer. \#\# Background \{.unnumbered\}
\end{itemize}

The endocrine system uses hormones (chemical messengers released into
the bloodstream) to coordinate physiology across long timescales.
Negative feedback loops maintain homeostasis: in the HPT axis, TRH
(hypothalamus) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} TSH (pituitary) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} T3/T4 (thyroid) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} inhibit TRH and
TSH. In the innate immune system, Toll-like receptors (TLRs) detect
conserved pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs; e.g., LPS,
flagellin) and activate NF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}B, triggering pro-inflammatory cytokine
production (IL-6, TNF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}, IL-1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}).

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-33}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  In Case A (primary hypothyroidism), TSH is elevated but T4 is low.
  Trace the negative feedback loop to explain why TSH is high despite
  low thyroid function. What drug would you prescribe, and which axis
  level does it target?
\item
  Graves' disease (Case B) involves thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins
  (TSI) that mimic TSH. Why does the pituitary produce less TSH even
  though T4 is high? Can negative feedback suppress TSI production?
\item
  The cytokine data showed PCT was elevated 360-fold in sepsis while
  TNF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha} was elevated 38-fold. Why is PCT particularly specific for
  bacterial infection over viral infection, and why does this make it a
  better guide for antibiotic prescribing?
\item
  NF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}B is activated during sepsis and produces the cytokine storm that
  contributes to multi-organ failure. A drug (TAK-242) blocks TLR4
  signalling. Predict the effect on: (a) cytokine levels; (b) pathogen
  clearance. What is the risk of fully blocking TLR4 signalling?
\item
  An athlete uses anabolic steroids (supraphysiological testosterone
  dose). Predict the effect on LH and FSH levels via the HPG axis
  feedback. After stopping steroids, how long does hormonal recovery
  take, and which cells in the testes are most affected during prolonged
  suppression?
\item
  A couple has not conceived after 12 months of regular unprotected
  intercourse. Build a first-pass evidence map that separates ovulation,
  sperm production, tubal transport, implantation, uterine receptivity,
  endocrine feedback, and age-dependent gamete quality.
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Lab 32 --- Population Ecology and Growth
Models}\label{lab-32-population-ecology-and-growth-models}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Lab 32 --- Population Ecology and Growth
Models}

\label{sec:lab_unit_X_population_ecology}

\subsection*{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-72}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Learning Objectives}

\emph{This activity accompanies \cref{sec:unit_X_population_ecology} of
the textbook --- review that chapter before attempting the exercises
below.}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Fit logistic and exponential growth equations to real or simulated
  population data
\item
  Calculate intrinsic rate of increase (r) and carrying capacity (K)
  from population time series
\item
  Apply the mark-recapture method (Lincoln-Petersen) to estimate
  population size
\item
  Evaluate density-dependent vs density-independent limiting factors
  from case study data
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Alignment and Rubric
Map}\label{alignment-and-rubric-map-34}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Alignment and Rubric Map}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 1 (LO1):} Interpret the supplied evidence or model
  output for Population Ecology and Growth Models.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 2 (LO2):} Identify controls and comparison groups that
  make the claim testable.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 3 (LO3):} Quantify uncertainty, boundary conditions,
  or alternative explanations before concluding.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 4 (LO4):} Transfer the mechanism to a new biological
  case or public-facing decision.
\item
  \textbf{Chapter LO coverage:} LO1, LO2, LO3, LO4
\item
  \textbf{Rubric dimensions:} evidence; controls; uncertainty;
  mechanism; transfer. \#\# Background \{.unnumbered\}
\end{itemize}

Population growth follows exponential growth (dN/dt = rN) when resources
are unlimited, and logistic growth (dN/dt = rN(1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-} N/K)) as populations
approach the carrying capacity K. Real populations fluctuate around K
due to density-dependent factors (competition, predation, disease ---
intensify as N increases) or may crash due to density-independent
factors (storms, droughts --- unrelated to N). The Lincoln-Petersen
mark-recapture estimate: N̂ = (M \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} C) / R, where M = initial marked
individuals, C = recapture sample size, R = recaptured marked
individuals.

\subsection*{Paper-Based
Investigation}\label{paper-based-investigation-34}

\textbf{Part A --- Growth Curve Fitting}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Plot most three population time series on graph paper. For the yeast
  data, identify: lag phase, exponential phase, plateau (K).
\item
  Estimate K from the plateau of the logistic curve.
\item
  Estimate r from the exponential phase: r \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} (ln N\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-} ln N\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}) / (t\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-} t\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1})
  during the period of fastest growth.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Part B --- Mark-Recapture}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item
  Use the printed capture-history table: M = 50 initially marked
  individuals and C = 30 individuals in the recapture sample. Count the
  marked recaptures (R) in the table and calculate Nhat = (50 x 30) / R.
\item
  Repeat the calculation for the second printed sampling event. Compare
  both estimates with the known simulated population size and calculate
  percent error.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Part C --- Density Dependence Analysis}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{5}
\tightlist
\item
  Given data on white-tailed deer population growth rate (r) vs density
  in 4 regions: plot r vs N/K (relative density). Identify whether r
  decreases with increasing density (density-dependent regulation) ---
  this confirms a logistic pattern.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-34}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Why does the yeast population growth slow as it approaches K? Use the
  term ``intraspecific competition'' and identify two specific
  density-dependent resources that become limiting.
\item
  Snowshoe hare populations cycle with about 10-year
  periodicity (tied to lynx cycles). Is this best explained as: (a)
  density-dependent predation; (b) density-independent weather events;
  or (c) a two-species coupled oscillator? Describe the evidence.
\item
  Your two mark-recapture estimates probably differed slightly. List
  three assumptions of the Lincoln-Petersen method and explain which
  assumption is most likely violated in the printed capture-history
  simulation.
\item
  Invasive species often exhibit exponential growth in new habitats.
  Name a specific invasive species, identify what density-dependent
  factor is absent in the new habitat, and predict when/how logistic
  behaviour will eventually emerge.
\item
  Apply a fisheries management scenario: a cod population has K =
  500,000 tonnes and r = 0.2/year. Using the maximum sustainable yield
  formula (MSY = rK/4), calculate the MSY and the population size at MSY
  (N = K/2). If fishing reduces the population below K/4, explain why
  the population will continue to decline even if fishing stops.
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Lab 33 --- Community Ecology and Species
Interactions}\label{lab-33-community-ecology-and-species-interactions}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Lab 33 --- Community Ecology and Species
Interactions}

\label{sec:lab_unit_X_community_ecology}

\subsection*{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-73}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Learning Objectives}

\emph{This activity accompanies \cref{sec:unit_X_community_ecology} of
the textbook --- review that chapter before attempting the exercises
below.}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Interpret a paper-based competition dataset between two species using
  Lotka-Volterra predictions
\item
  Analyse food web data to determine trophic levels and calculate energy
  transfer efficiency
\item
  Evaluate keystone predator effects using a removal/addition case study
\item
  Apply successional theory to interpret vegetation data from different
  chronosequences
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Alignment and Rubric
Map}\label{alignment-and-rubric-map-35}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Alignment and Rubric Map}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 1 (LO1):} Interpret the supplied evidence or model
  output for Community Ecology and Species Interactions.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 2 (LO2):} Identify controls and comparison groups that
  make the claim testable.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 3 (LO3):} Quantify uncertainty, boundary conditions,
  or alternative explanations before concluding.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 4 (LO4):} Transfer the mechanism to a new biological
  case or public-facing decision.
\item
  \textbf{Chapter LO coverage:} LO1, LO2, LO3, LO4
\item
  \textbf{Rubric dimensions:} evidence; controls; uncertainty;
  mechanism; transfer. \#\# Background \{.unnumbered\}
\end{itemize}

Community ecology studies how species interact (competition, predation,
mutualism, commensalism, parasitism) and how those interactions shape
community composition. The Lotka-Volterra competition model predicts
stable coexistence primarily when intraspecific competition
\textgreater{} interspecific competition for both species (Gause's
principle: competitive exclusion eliminates one species if niches
overlap completely). Energy flows through trophic levels with
about 10\% efficiency: about 10\% of energy at level N reaches
level N+1 (ecological pyramid).

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-35}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  In the Lotka-Volterra framework, stable coexistence requires \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}
  \textless{} K\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}/K\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} and \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1} \textless{} K\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}/K\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}. What do these
  inequalities mean biologically in terms of intra- vs interspecific
  competition strength?
\item
  The pyramid of energy shows that far more humans can be supported by
  eating at lower trophic levels. Calculate the maximum number of humans
  at each trophic level from your energy data. What are three reasons
  why human food systems often involve higher trophic level consumption?
\item
  When \emph{Pisaster} (sea star) was removed, mussel populations
  exploded and crowded out other species, reducing diversity. Define
  keystone species and explain why removing an apex predator can reduce
  community diversity (trophic cascade).
\item
  Primary succession begins on bare rock (no soil) while secondary
  succession follows disturbance on existing soil. Explain how pioneer
  species (lichens, mosses) facilitate succession on bare rock --- which
  physical and chemical properties of soil do they create? Name Connell
  and Slatyer's facilitation model.
\item
  A student claims ``climax forests are the most stable and should
  generally be our conservation goal.'' Critique this statement using
  the concept of intermediate disturbance hypothesis (Connell 1978) and
  give an example of an ecosystem that requires periodic disturbance to
  maintain high diversity.
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Lab 34 --- Ecosystem Ecology and Biogeochemical
Cycles}\label{lab-34-ecosystem-ecology-and-biogeochemical-cycles}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Lab 34 --- Ecosystem Ecology and
Biogeochemical Cycles}

\label{sec:lab_unit_X_ecosystem_ecology}

\subsection*{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-74}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Learning Objectives}

\emph{This activity accompanies \cref{sec:unit_X_ecosystem_ecology} of
the textbook --- review that chapter before attempting the exercises
below.}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Calculate primary productivity of an aquatic ecosystem from light-dark
  bottle datasets
\item
  Model nitrogen cycle transformations using an annotated diagram
\item
  Calculate carbon flux between reservoirs using published global carbon
  budget data
\item
  Evaluate the impact of nutrient loading on eutrophication using
  scenario data
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Alignment and Rubric
Map}\label{alignment-and-rubric-map-36}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Alignment and Rubric Map}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 1 (LO1):} Interpret the supplied evidence or model
  output for Ecosystem Ecology and Biogeochemical Cycles.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 2 (LO2):} Identify controls and comparison groups that
  make the claim testable.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 3 (LO3):} Quantify uncertainty, boundary conditions,
  or alternative explanations before concluding.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 4 (LO4):} Transfer the mechanism to a new biological
  case or public-facing decision.
\item
  \textbf{Chapter LO coverage:} LO1, LO2, LO3, LO4
\item
  \textbf{Rubric dimensions:} evidence; controls; uncertainty;
  mechanism; transfer. \#\# Background \{.unnumbered\}
\end{itemize}

Ecosystems are characterised by flows of energy (one-way, lost as heat
at each step) and cycles of matter (recycled through biogeochemical
pathways). \textbf{Gross primary productivity (GPP)} is total
photosynthesis; \textbf{net primary productivity (NPP) = GPP \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}
respiration}. The nitrogen cycle includes fixation (N\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} NH\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{3}}{3} by
nitrogenase), nitrification (NH\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{3}}{3} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} NO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} NO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{3}}{3}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-} by \emph{Nitrosomonas},
\emph{Nitrobacter}), denitrification (NO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{3}}{3}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} N\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} by anaerobic bacteria),
and assimilation (NH\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{4}}{4}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+}/NO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{3}}{3}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} amino acids by plants).

\subsection*{Paper-Based
Investigation}\label{paper-based-investigation-36}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Paper-Based Investigation}

\textbf{Part A --- Primary Productivity (Light-Dark Bottle)}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Use the provided initial, light-bottle, and dark-bottle dissolved
  oxygen data. Confirm that each treatment has three replicates and the
  same incubation time.
\item
  Calculate mean DO and range for each bottle type.
\item
  Compare the light and dark treatments to the initial baseline, then
  flag any replicate that strongly changes the mean.
\item
  Calculate: NPP = DO\_light \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-} DO\_initial; Respiration = DO\_initial \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}
  DO\_dark; GPP = NPP + Respiration.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Part B --- Nitrogen Cycle Annotation}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{4}
\tightlist
\item
  Complete the blank nitrogen cycle diagram: label most 5 processes
  (fixation, nitrification, denitrification, assimilation,
  decomposition/ammonification). Name one key organism for each process.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Part C --- Carbon Budget Calculation}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{5}
\tightlist
\item
  Using IPCC data (approximate 2022 values): GPP (terrestrial) = \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}120 Gt
  C/yr (uptake); plant respiration = +60 Gt C/yr; FF emissions = +10 Gt
  C/yr; ocean uptake = \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}3 Gt C/yr; land use change = +2 Gt C/yr.
  Calculate net atmospheric accumulation of CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} per year. Compare to
  measured atmospheric growth rate (about 5 Gt C/yr).
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Part D --- Eutrophication Experiment}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{6}
\tightlist
\item
  Use the eutrophication case packet to compare control and
  nutrient-addition scenarios over 5 days. Interpret turbidity,
  chlorophyll-a, dissolved oxygen, and fish-kill observations as
  indicators of algal bloom risk.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Analysis Questions}\label{analysis-questions-36}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Analysis Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The dark bottle showed decreased DO while the light bottle showed
  increased DO. Explain why: which process dominates in the light
  bottle, and which process in the dark bottle? Why is O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} a useful proxy
  for carbon fixation here?
\item
  Your carbon budget calculation: does the simple sum of sources and
  sinks balance with the measured atmospheric accumulation
  (about 5 Gt C/yr)? What are the largest sources of
  uncertainty in the global carbon budget?
\item
  Nitrogen fixation by \emph{Rhizobium} in legume root nodules requires
  enormous amounts of ATP and anaerobic conditions (nitrogenase is
  inactivated by O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}). Explain why this process is energetically costly
  and how the leghaemoglobin protein maintains low O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} in the nodule
  while supporting aerobic bacterial respiration.
\item
  In the eutrophication case packet, the nutrient-addition scenario
  shows increased chlorophyll-a followed by bottom-water hypoxia. Trace
  the ecological mechanism from nutrient addition -\textgreater{} algal
  bloom -\textgreater{} bacterial decomposition -\textgreater{} hypoxia
  -\textgreater{} fish kill.
\item
  Wetlands are sometimes called ``kidneys of the landscape.'' Explain
  their role in nitrogen cycling (using specific N-cycle steps),
  phosphorus immobilisation, and carbon sequestration. Why is wetland
  drainage for agriculture a double ecological concern?
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Lab 35 --- Biomes and Conservation
Biology}\label{lab-35-biomes-and-conservation-biology}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Lab 35 --- Biomes and Conservation
Biology}

\label{sec:lab_unit_X_biomes_and_conservation}

\subsection*{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-75}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Learning Objectives}

\emph{This activity accompanies
\cref{sec:unit_X_biomes_and_conservation} of the textbook --- review
that chapter before attempting the exercises below.}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Classify biomes from climate data (mean annual temperature,
  precipitation, Whittaker diagram)
\item
  Calculate species-area relationship parameters and predict extinction
  risk from habitat loss
\item
  Evaluate minimum viable population (MVP) and reserve design principles
  for a case species
\item
  Apply IUCN Red List criteria to classify conservation status of a
  provided species profile
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Alignment and Rubric
Map}\label{alignment-and-rubric-map-37}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Alignment and Rubric Map}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 1 (LO1):} Interpret the supplied evidence or model
  output for Biomes and Conservation Biology.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 2 (LO2):} Identify controls and comparison groups that
  make the claim testable.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 3 (LO3):} Quantify uncertainty, boundary conditions,
  or alternative explanations before concluding.
\item
  \textbf{Outcome 4 (LO4):} Transfer the mechanism to a new biological
  case or public-facing decision.
\item
  \textbf{Chapter LO coverage:} LO1, LO2, LO3, LO4
\item
  \textbf{Rubric dimensions:} evidence; controls; uncertainty;
  mechanism; transfer. \#\# Background \{.unnumbered\}
\end{itemize}

Biomes are large-scale communities determined primarily by climate
(temperature and precipitation). The species-area relationship
\textbf{\(S = cA^z\)} (log-linear: log S = log c + z\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.}log A) predicts
that decreasing habitat area reduces species richness; the exponent z
(typically 0.2--0.35 for oceanic islands) can be used to predict
extinction rates from deforestation. Minimum viable population (MVP)
analyses determine the population size needed for a defined probability
of persistence over a defined time frame. IUCN Red List criteria assign
species to categories (LC, NT, VU, EN, CR, EW, EX) based on population
decline rates, geographic range, and quantitative extinction risk.
