\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Questions 11--20: Application and
Analysis}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{10}
\tightlist
\item
  Using the Nernst equation (E = (RT/zF)
  ln({[}ion{]}\_out/{[}ion{]}\_in)), calculate the equilibrium potential
  for K\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} given {[}K\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+}{]}\_out = 5 mM and {[}K\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+}{]}\_in = 150 mM at 37°C.
  Then calculate E\_Na with {[}Na\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+}{]}\_out = 145 mM and {[}Na\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+}{]}\_in =
  15 mM. Which equilibrium potential is closest to the resting membrane
  potential?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{11}
\tightlist
\item
  Tetrodotoxin (TTX, from pufferfish) blocks voltage-gated Na\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} channels.
  Tetraethylammonium (TEA) blocks voltage-gated K\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} channels. Predict the
  effects on the action potential waveform when: (a) TTX alone is
  applied; (b) TEA alone; (c) both together.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{12}
\tightlist
\item
  Quantal analysis of neurotransmitter release: at the neuromuscular
  junction, each synaptic vesicle contains about 10,000 ACh
  molecules (one ``quantum''). The miniature end-plate potential (mEPP)
  = 0.4 mV. A normal EPSP = 40 mV. Estimate the quantal content (m =
  EPSP/mEPP). What parameter does the quantal content depend on (n =
  number of release sites, p = release probability)?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{13}
\tightlist
\item
  NMDA receptors are both ligand-gated (glutamate) AND voltage-gated
  (Mg\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} block removed at depolarised potentials). Explain: (a) why NMDA
  receptors function as ``coincidence detectors'' (both presynaptic
  glutamate and postsynaptic depolarisation are required); (b) why this
  property is considered the molecular basis for Hebbian learning
  (``neurons that fire together, wire together''); (c) the Ca\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} signal
  that enters via NMDA receptors and triggers LTP.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{14}
\tightlist
\item
  Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disease where antibodies
  target nicotinic ACh receptors at the NMJ. Predict: (a) whether the
  EPSP amplitude at the NMJ is increased or decreased; (b) the clinical
  manifestation (fatigable muscle weakness); (c) why
  acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (pyridostigmine) temporarily improve
  symptoms.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{15}
\tightlist
\item
  GABAergic inhibition: GABA\_A receptors are Cl\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-} channels. In adult
  neurons E\_Cl \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}70 mV (inhibitory). In neonatal neurons E\_Cl \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}40
  mV (excitatory because resting potential is about \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}55 mV).
  Explain: (a) why GABA is excitatory in neonatal neurons; (b) the
  developmental switch (upregulation of KCC2 Cl\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-} transporter); (c) why
  this has implications for neonatal seizure treatment.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{16}
\tightlist
\item
  Short-term plasticity: paired-pulse facilitation (PPF) occurs when the
  second of two closely-spaced stimuli evokes a larger EPSP. Explain the
  residual calcium hypothesis: Ca\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} from the first stimulus remains and
  adds to Ca\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} from the second stimulus, producing greater vesicle
  release. Predict: would PPF be increased or decreased by a Ca\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+}
  chelator (BAPTA)?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{17}
\tightlist
\item
  Excitotoxicity: excessive glutamate release (e.g., during stroke)
  causes neuronal death via NMDA receptor overactivation \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} excessive
  Ca\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} influx \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} mitochondrial dysfunction \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} ROS production \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} cell death.
  Explain: (a) why NMDA-blocking drugs (memantine, at low doses) are
  neuroprotective in clinical trials; (b) why high-dose NMDA block
  causes psychotic symptoms (dissociative anaesthetics --- ketamine);
  (c) what the narrow therapeutic window implies for stroke
  intervention.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{18}
\tightlist
\item
  Synaptic vesicle recycling occurs via three modes: kiss-and-run
  (transient fusion pore, rapid), full collapse/clathrin-mediated
  endocytosis (5--20 s), and bulk endocytosis (during intense
  stimulation). Explain: (a) how each mode is suited to different firing
  rates; (b) what happens when recycling capacity is exceeded (synaptic
  depression); (c) the role of dynamin GTPase in clathrin-mediated
  endocytosis.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{19}
\tightlist
\item
  Long-term depression (LTD) at cerebellar parallel fibre-Purkinje cell
  synapses is triggered by climbing fibre co-activation \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Ca\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} + PKC \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  AMPAR internalisation. Explain: (a) how LTD differs from LTP
  mechanistically (removal vs insertion of receptors); (b) the role of
  LTD in motor learning (error correction signals from climbing fibres);
  (c) how cerebellar LTD produces adaptation in the vestibulo-ocular
  reflex.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Questions 21--30: Synthesis and
Evaluation}\label{questions-2130-synthesis-and-evaluation-29}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Questions 21--30: Synthesis and
Evaluation}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{20}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the Hodgkin-Huxley (HH) model of the action potential (1952,
  Nobel Prize): using voltage-clamp data, they described Na\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} and K\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+}
  conductances as m\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{3}}{3}h and n\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{4}}{4} gating variables. Assess: (a) the key
  insight (ion-specific conductances with distinct kinetics); (b) the
  predictive power of the model (propagation velocity, frequency
  coding); (c) the limitations (no molecular detail, does not account
  for ion channel diversity, subthreshold oscillations).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{21}
\tightlist
\item
  Design an experiment to determine whether a specific synapse exhibits
  Hebbian LTP, anti-Hebbian LTP, or homeostatic plasticity. Describe:
  the stimulation protocols (high-frequency \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} Hebbian, low-frequency \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  homeostatic), the electrophysiological measurements (field EPSP
  slope), and the pharmacological tools (NMDA antagonist, AMPAR
  antagonist) needed to distinguish these forms.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{22}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the ``synaptic tagging and capture'' hypothesis (Frey and
  Morris, 1997): early LTP is protein synthesis-independent (lasts
  about 1--2 h), while late LTP requires new protein synthesis.
  A weak stimulus sets a ``tag'' at activated synapses; the tag captures
  plasticity-related proteins (PRPs) synthesised in response to a strong
  stimulus at another input. Evaluate: (a) the evidence for this model;
  (b) how it explains input-specificity of LTP; (c) implications for
  memory consolidation.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{23}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the role of astrocytic gliotransmission (release of
  glutamate, D-serine, ATP from astrocytes) in modulating synaptic
  plasticity. What evidence supports the ``tripartite synapse'' model,
  and what criticisms have been raised about the specificity of
  astrocytic Ca\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} signals and the difficulty of distinguishing neuronal
  from glial glutamate release?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{24}
\tightlist
\item
  Channelopathies: mutations in ion channels cause neurological
  diseases. Evaluate three examples: (a) SCN1A (Nav1.1) mutations \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  Dravet syndrome (severe childhood epilepsy); (b) KCNQ2/3 mutations \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  benign familial neonatal seizures; (c) CACNA1A mutations \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} familial
  hemiplegic migraine. For each, describe the channel, the mutation's
  effect on neuronal excitability, and the therapeutic approach.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{25}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia: (a) traditional
  version (excess D\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} receptor signalling in mesolimbic pathway); (b)
  revised version (hypo-dopaminergia in prefrontal cortex,
  hyper-dopaminergia in striatum); (c) the glutamate hypothesis (NMDA
  receptor hypofunction). How do these hypotheses explain the positive
  symptoms (hallucinations, delusions) and negative symptoms (flat
  affect, cognitive deficits) of schizophrenia?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{26}
\tightlist
\item
  Spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP): if the presynaptic neuron
  fires before the postsynaptic neuron (within about 20 ms),
  the synapse is strengthened (LTP). If after, the synapse is weakened
  (LTD). Evaluate: (a) the molecular mechanism (STDP timing depends on
  NMDA receptor/Ca\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} dynamics); (b) the computational significance (STDP
  allows precise temporal learning of sequences); (c) how STDP differs
  in inhibitory vs excitatory synapses.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{27}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the molecular mechanism of presynaptic neurotransmitter
  release: Ca\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} entry \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} synaptotagmin-1 (Ca\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} sensor) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} conformational
  change \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} interaction with SNARE complex \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} fusion pore opening \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  transmitter release. Specifically: why is synaptotagmin-1 the timing
  sensor (low Ca\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} affinity, fast kinetics, about 200 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}s from
  Ca\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} binding to fusion), and what does the about 4th power
  Ca\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} dependence of release tell us about the number of Ca\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} ions
  needed to trigger a single vesicle fusion event?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{28}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the clinical utility of transcranial magnetic stimulation
  (TMS) for modulating neural circuits non-invasively. How does TMS
  induce action potentials in cortical neurons, what stimulation
  patterns produce LTP-like (theta-burst) vs LTD-like (continuous
  low-frequency) effects, and what is the evidence for therapeutic
  efficacy in treatment-resistant depression?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{29}
\tightlist
\item
  Critically evaluate the concept of the ``synaptome'' --- the catalogue
  of synapse types and their molecular composition across the brain.
  Using proteomics of isolated synaptosomes, researchers have identified
  \textgreater1,000 proteins at excitatory synapses. Evaluate: (a) what
  the molecular diversity of synapses implies for circuit function; (b)
  whether the synaptome concept is more informative than the connectome
  for understanding brain computation; (c) how synaptome-level mutations
  (SHANK3, PSD-95) cause neurodevelopmental disorders.
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Questions --- Ch 31: Endocrine and Immune
Systems}\label{questions-ch-31-endocrine-and-immune-systems}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Questions --- Ch 31: Endocrine and Immune
Systems}

\label{sec:q_unit_IX_endocrine_and_immune}

\subsection*{Instructor Use and Coverage
Notes}\label{instructor-use-and-coverage-notes-33}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Instructor Use and Coverage Notes}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Coverage target:} Predict the consequence of changing a
  hormone, receptor, antigen, or immune-cell population.
\item
  \textbf{Model/data emphasis:} Hormone feedback, dose-response, and
  immune-memory reasoning.
\item
  \textbf{Assessment alignment:} Visual Representations, Statistical
  Tests and Data Analysis, Argumentation.
\item
  \textbf{Misconception probe:} Immunity is not just attack;
  recognition, tolerance, memory, and regulation are equally central.
\item
  \textbf{Transfer product:} Transfer signaling and immunity reasoning
  to vaccination, autoimmunity, stress, and metabolism.
\item
  \textbf{Grading focus:} award full credit for mechanism, evidence,
  boundary conditions, and units when a calculation is required.
\item
  \textbf{Suggested use:} draw one recall item, one application item,
  and one synthesis item when building a short quiz from this bank.
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Questions 1--10: Recall and
Comprehension}\label{questions-110-recall-and-comprehension-30}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Questions 1--10: Recall and
Comprehension}

\emph{This activity accompanies \cref{sec:unit_IX_endocrine_and_immune}
of the textbook --- review that chapter before attempting the exercises
below.}

\begin{enumerate}

  What is the endocrine system? How does it differ from the nervous

\subsection*{Questions 11--20: Application and
Analysis}\label{questions-1120-application-and-analysis-30}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Questions 11--20: Application and
Analysis}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{10}
\tightlist
\item
  The HPA axis: CRH (hypothalamus) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} ACTH (anterior pituitary) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  cortisol (adrenal cortex). Cortisol feeds back negatively on CRH and
  ACTH secretion. If a patient has an adrenal tumour autonomously
  producing cortisol, predict: (a) ACTH levels; (b) CRH levels; (c)
  contralateral adrenal gland size; (d) response to the dexamethasone
  suppression test.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{11}
\tightlist
\item
  Insulin (from pancreatic \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-cells) and glucagon (from \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-cells) have
  opposing metabolic effects. Compare: (a) the stimulus for secretion of
  each; (b) the target tissue responses (liver, muscle, adipose); (c)
  the blood glucose level at which each dominates. What happens in Type
  1 Diabetes (complete \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}-cell destruction)?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{12}
\tightlist
\item
  Thyroid hormones (T\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{3}}{3}/T\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{4}}{4}) are unusual peptide-derived hormones that act
  like steroids (entering cells, binding nuclear receptors). Explain:
  (a) why T\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{3}}{3}/T\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{4}}{4} can cross membranes (lipophilic due to iodination); (b)
  how T\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{3}}{3} binds thyroid hormone receptors (TR\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}/TR\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}) to regulate gene
  transcription; (c) why hypothyroidism causes bradycardia, fatigue, and
  weight gain.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{13}
\tightlist
\item
  The inflammasome (NLRP3) is activated by diverse danger signals (K\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+}
  efflux, ROS, crystal particles). Trace: (a) NLRP3 oligomerisation; (b)
  ASC adaptor recruitment; (c) caspase-1 activation; (d) IL-1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} and IL-18
  maturation and release; (e) pyroptosis (inflammatory cell death). Name
  two diseases where NLRP3 is inappropriately activated.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{14}
\tightlist
\item
  Neutrophils are the first responders to bacterial infection. Describe
  their killing mechanisms: (a) phagocytosis and phagolysosome fusion;
  (b) respiratory burst (NADPH oxidase \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} superoxide \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} HOCl via
  myeloperoxidase); (c) NETosis (neutrophil extracellular trap
  formation). What disease results from NADPH oxidase deficiency (CGD)?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{15}
\tightlist
\item
  Adrenal medulla catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine) are
  released in response to sympathetic stimulation. Compare: (a) the
  receptor subtypes activated by each (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}); (b) the effects
  on heart rate, blood vessels, and bronchioles; (c) why
  phaeochromocytoma (adrenal medullary tumour) causes paroxysmal
  hypertension.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{16}
\tightlist
\item
  Growth hormone (GH) from the anterior pituitary has both direct and
  indirect (via IGF-1 from the liver) effects. Explain: (a) the GH pulse
  pattern (nocturnal secretion regulated by GHRH and somatostatin); (b)
  the metabolic effects of GH (lipolysis, anti-insulin, protein
  synthesis); (c) why acromegaly (GH excess in adults) causes the
  symptoms it does.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{17}
\tightlist
\item
  Dendritic cells (DCs) bridge innate and adaptive immunity. Explain:
  (a) how immature DCs in tissues sample antigens via macropinocytosis
  and TLR activation; (b) how DC maturation involves upregulation of MHC
  class II and co-stimulatory molecules (CD80/86); (c) how mature DCs
  migrate to lymph nodes to activate naïve T cells (antigen
  presentation). Why are DCs the most potent professional
  antigen-presenting cells?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{18}
\tightlist
\item
  Parathyroid hormone (PTH) and calcitonin regulate blood calcium. PTH
  increases Ca\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} by: (a) stimulating osteoclasts (bone resorption); (b)
  increasing renal Ca\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} reabsorption; (c) activating 1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}-hydroxylase
  (vitamin D activation \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} intestinal Ca\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} absorption). Calcitonin
  decreases Ca\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} by inhibiting osteoclasts. What disease results from
  PTH excess (hyperparathyroidism)?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{19}
\tightlist
\item
  Natural killer (NK) cells use the ``missing self'' mechanism:
  inhibitory KIR receptors bind MHC class I on normal cells and suppress
  killing. Virus-infected cells and tumour cells often downregulate MHC
  I, releasing the NK cell from inhibition. Explain: (a) the activating
  receptors (NKG2D, recognising stress ligands MICA/MICB); (b) how the
  balance of activating vs inhibiting signals determines the NK cell
  response; (c) how cancer immunotherapy exploits NK cells (bispecific
  engagers).
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Questions 21--30: Synthesis and
Evaluation}\label{questions-2130-synthesis-and-evaluation-30}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Questions 21--30: Synthesis and
Evaluation}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{20}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the integration of endocrine and immune systems: cortisol (a
  glucocorticoid) suppresses inflammation by: (a) inhibiting NF-\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\kappa}}{kappa}B
  transcription factor; (b) reducing prostaglandin synthesis (inhibiting
  PLA\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} and COX-2); (c) inducing lymphocyte apoptosis. Why do critically
  ill ICU patients sometimes develop adrenal insufficiency, and why does
  physiological stress-dose hydrocortisone improve sepsis survival?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{21}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the molecular mechanisms of endocrine disruptors (BPA,
  phthalates, pesticides): how do these chemicals interfere with hormone
  signalling (estrogenic, anti-androgenic, thyroid-disrupting), at what
  environmental concentrations are effects seen (non-monotonic
  dose-response), and what evidence from wildlife populations
  (feminisation of male fish, reproductive abnormalities in alligators)
  supports endocrine disruption in the environment?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{22}
\tightlist
\item
  Design an experiment to determine whether a newly discovered peptide
  is a hormone: (a) demonstrate that it is secreted into the bloodstream
  in response to a physiological stimulus; (b) show that it has a target
  tissue with specific receptors; (c) prove that removing the source
  gland eliminates the response and that hormone replacement restores
  it; (d) show that the response is dose-dependent.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{23}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the concept of ``trained immunity'' --- epigenetic
  reprogramming of innate immune cells (monocytes/macrophages) by prior
  pathogen exposure, resulting in enhanced responses to subsequent
  unrelated infections. How does BCG vaccination induce trained immunity
  (H3K4me3 at inflammatory gene promoters, mTOR-dependent metabolic
  shift from OXPHOS to glycolysis), and what are the implications for
  broad-spectrum vaccine development?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{24}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the evolutionary conservation and divergence of the HPA axis:
  fish have an HPI axis (hypothalamic-pituitary-interrenal), amphibians
  have an HPA axis with cortisol, and birds have corticosterone. What
  does this conservation tell us about the fundamental biological
  requirement for glucocorticoid stress response across vertebrates?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{25}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the therapeutic potential of checkpoint immunotherapy
  combined with endocrine modulation: tumour-associated macrophages
  (TAMs) are often immunosuppressive (M2-polarised). Propose a strategy
  combining: (a) CSF1R inhibitor to repolarise TAMs; (b) anti-PD-1 to
  release T cell checkpoint brakes; (c) low-dose dexamethasone to reduce
  treatment-related inflammation without suppressing anti-tumour
  immunity. What preclinical evidence supports this combination?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{26}
\tightlist
\item
  The pineal gland produces melatonin in response to darkness (via the
  suprachiasmatic nucleus \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} sympathetic \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} pinealocyte). Evaluate: (a)
  the circadian rhythm of melatonin secretion; (b) the evidence for
  melatonin's role in sleep-wake regulation vs a ``darkness signal'';
  (c) the efficacy of exogenous melatonin for jet lag and shift work
  disorder; (d) the immunomodulatory effects of melatonin
  (anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, NK cell activation).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{27}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate autoinflammatory diseases (distinct from autoimmune):
  conditions caused by inappropriate innate immune activation without
  autoantibodies. Using familial Mediterranean fever (FMF, pyrin
  mutations) as a case study: (a) how does mutant pyrin activate the
  inflammasome; (b) why does colchicine (inhibiting neutrophil
  migration) work as treatment; (c) how does IL-1 blockade (anakinra,
  canakinumab) provide definitive treatment?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{28}
\tightlist
\item
  The gut-brain-immune axis: enteroendocrine cells in the gut produce
  \textgreater30 hormones (GLP-1, PYY, CCK, serotonin) that signal to
  the brain and immune system. Evaluate: (a) how gut serotonin
  (\textgreater90\% of body's serotonin) modulates gut motility and
  immune cell function; (b) the evidence linking gut endocrine
  dysfunction to IBS (irritable bowel syndrome); (c) how GLP-1 receptor
  agonists (semaglutide) affect not just glucose metabolism but also
  neuroinflammation.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{29}
\tightlist
\item
  Critically evaluate the concept of ``immunometabolism'' --- the idea
  that metabolic reprogramming of immune cells determines their
  functional polarisation. Using the M1 (pro-inflammatory, glycolytic)
  vs M2 (anti-inflammatory, OXPHOS) macrophage paradigm: (a) how does
  TCA cycle disruption in M1 macrophages lead to itaconate and succinate
  accumulation; (b) how does succinate stabilise HIF-1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha} and promote
  IL-1\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\beta}}{beta} production; (c) why targeting immunometabolism (e.g., dimethyl
  fumarate activating Nrf2) is a therapeutic frontier? Then apply the
  chapter's evidence-map habit to reproductive physiology: what evidence
  separates ovulation timing, sperm production, tubal transport, uterine
  receptivity, endocrine feedback, implantation, and age-dependent
  gamete quality after 12 months without conception?
\end{enumerate}

below.}

\begin{enumerate}

\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}

  What is the logistic growth model? Write its equation and define K

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item

\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}

\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}

\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}

\tightlist

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}

  What is the difference between density-dependent and
  density-independent limiting factors?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Questions 11--20: Application and
Analysis}\label{questions-1120-application-and-analysis-31}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Questions 11--20: Application and
Analysis}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{10}
\tightlist
\item
  An E. coli population starts with N\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0} = 100 cells. The intrinsic rate
  of increase r = 0.693 h\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1} (doubling time = 1 hour). Calculate N\_t at
  t = 5 hours using N\_t = N\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0}e\^{}(rt). At what time would the
  population reach 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{6}}{6} cells?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{11}
\tightlist
\item
  A deer population (K = 1,000) starts at N = 50 and grows logistically
  with r = 0.3/year. Calculate dN/dt at N = 50, N = 500, and N = 900. At
  which population size is growth rate highest? What happens to growth
  rate as N approaches K?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{12}
\tightlist
\item
  In a mark-recapture study: 200 butterflies are captured, marked, and
  released. A week later, 250 butterflies are captured, of which 40 are
  marked. Estimate population size using the Lincoln-Petersen formula.
  What assumptions must hold for this estimate to be valid?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{13}
\tightlist
\item
  A population crash occurs when a population overshoots K (exceeds
  carrying capacity) and resources are depleted, causing K to decline.
  Using the logistic model, explain: (a) why the population exceeds K
  (time lag in density-dependent response); (b) the population
  trajectory after overshooting (damped oscillations vs extinction); (c)
  a real-world example (reindeer on St.~Matthew Island).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{14}
\tightlist
\item
  Compare r-selected (small, many offspring, high mortality, short
  lifespan) and K-selected (large, few offspring, low mortality, long
  lifespan) strategies. Place the following organisms on the r-K
  continuum: elephant, dandelion, oak tree, mosquito, whale, annual
  grass. Explain why the r/K model is now considered an
  oversimplification.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{15}
\tightlist
\item
  A Type I survivorship curve (e.g., humans) shows high survival until
  old age. A Type III curve (e.g., sea turtles) shows high juvenile
  mortality with high adult survival. Calculate: if a sea turtle lays
  100 eggs per year and 2\% survive to adulthood, what is the expected
  number of adult recruits per year? How many years of reproduction are
  needed to replace a dying adult (assume one-for-one replacement)?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{16}
\tightlist
\item
  The Allee effect describes a positive relationship between population
  density and per capita growth rate at low densities (below a
  threshold, the population cannot recover). Explain: (a) three
  mechanisms (mate finding difficulty, loss of cooperative defense,
  genetic problems from inbreeding); (b) how the Allee effect creates an
  extinction vortex for small populations; (c) what conservation
  strategies address the Allee effect.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{17}
\tightlist
\item
  Age-structured population models (Leslie matrix): a population with
  two age classes (juvenile and adult) has the following transition
  rates: juvenile survival = 0.5, adult survival = 0.8, adult fecundity
  = 3 juveniles/adult. Write the Leslie matrix and project the
  population for two time steps from an initial vector of {[}100
  juveniles, 50 adults{]}.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{18}
\tightlist
\item
  Source-sink metapopulation dynamics: a ``source'' habitat (birth rate
  \textgreater{} death rate) produces emigrants that maintain a ``sink''
  population (death rate \textgreater{} birth rate). Using a specific
  example (e.g., wetland birds using good-quality vs poor-quality
  wetlands), explain: (a) why the sink population would go extinct
  without immigration from the source; (b) what happens if the source
  habitat is destroyed; (c) implications for habitat conservation
  priority.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{19}
\tightlist
\item
  Climate change is shifting species' ranges poleward and upslope.
  Evaluate: (a) the evidence from range shift data (butterflies, birds,
  trees); (b) why some species cannot keep pace (dispersal limitation,
  habitat fragmentation); (c) how population viability analysis (PVA) is
  used to predict extinction risk under different warming scenarios.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Questions 21--30: Synthesis and
Evaluation}\label{questions-2130-synthesis-and-evaluation-31}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Questions 21--30: Synthesis and
Evaluation}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{20}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the applicability of the logistic growth model to real
  populations: where does it succeed (general S-shaped growth curves in
  laboratory conditions) and where does it fail (time lags,
  environmental stochasticity, age structure, Allee effects)? Propose a
  more realistic model that incorporates at least two of these omitted
  features.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{21}
\tightlist
\item
  Design a long-term population monitoring programme for a threatened
  species (e.g., African wild dog, \emph{Lycaon pictus}). Describe: (a)
  the sampling methodology (camera traps, aerialsurveys, genetic
  mark-recapture using faecal DNA); (b) the demographic parameters to
  estimate (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda} = finite rate of increase, survival by age class,
  reproductive output); (c) how you would build a PVA model and define
  minimum viable population (MVP) size.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{22}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate invasive species population dynamics: the brown tree snake
  (\emph{Boiga irregularis}) invaded Guam after WWII and caused the
  extinction of most native forest birds. Using population ecology
  theory: (a) what growth model best describes the initial invasion
  (exponential growth in the absence of natural enemies); (b) what new
  carrying capacity was reached; (c) what control strategies (traps,
  acetaminophen-laced dead mice) have been attempted, and why are they
  insufficient?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{23}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the concept of ``ecological traps'' --- habitats that appear
  attractive to organisms but result in reduced fitness (e.g., sea
  turtles attracted to coastal lights, birds nesting in mowed
  agricultural fields). How do ecological traps arise (evolutionary
  mismatch between environmental cues and habitat quality), and how
  might they contribute to population decline in rapidly changing
  environments?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{24}
\tightlist
\item
  The maximum sustainable yield (MSY) of a fishery occurs at N = K/2 in
  the logistic model. Evaluate: (a) why harvesting at MSY maximises
  catch; (b) why MSY is inherently unstable (small perturbations can
  push the population toward collapse); (c) why modern fisheries
  management uses precautionary approaches (reference points below MSY,
  no-take zones) rather than attempting to maintain stocks at MSY.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{25}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the role of demographic stochasticity vs environmental
  stochasticity in small population extinction risk. Using Monte Carlo
  simulations: (a) at what population size does demographic
  stochasticity dominate (N \textless{} 50); (b) how does environmental
  stochasticity affect populations of any size (droughts, disease
  outbreaks); (c) what does the combination of both stochastic forces
  imply for the ``50/500 rule'' in conservation genetics (Ne
  \textgreater{} 50 to avoid inbreeding, \textgreater{} 500 to maintain
  evolutionary potential)?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{26}
\tightlist
\item
  Human population grew exponentially from about 1 billion
  (1800) to about 8 billion (2024). Evaluate: (a) which
  technological advances removed carrying capacity limits (agriculture,
  medicine, energy); (b) the demographic transition model (stages I--IV)
  and where different countries are; (c) whether global population will
  stabilise (UN WPP 2024 median projection: peak near 10.3 billion in
  the mid-2080s, then about 10.2 billion by 2100) or decline,
  and the assumptions underlying different projections.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{27}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the ``landscape of fear'' concept: predator presence alters
  prey behaviour (reduced foraging time, habitat avoidance), which
  reduces prey population growth rate even without direct predation.
  Using the wolf-elk-aspen trophic cascade in Yellowstone as a case
  study, evaluate the evidence that wolf reintroduction changed elk
  behaviour enough to allow aspen regeneration, and whether this
  qualifies as a ``landscape of fear'' effect or simply reduced elk
  density.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{28}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the mathematical basis for chaos in ecological populations:
  discrete-time logistic models (N\_\{t+1\} = rN\_t(1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-} N\_t/K)) with
  high r (r \textgreater{} 2.57) produce chaotic dynamics where
  population size is deterministic but unpredictable. What does chaos
  imply for long-term population prediction, and how can evidence of
  chaos be detected in real population time series (e.g., flour beetles,
  \emph{Tribolium})?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{29}
\tightlist
\item
  Critically evaluate the concept of ``planetary boundaries'' (Stockholm
  Resilience Centre, 2009) in relation to human population ecology. Of
  the nine identified boundaries (climate change, biodiversity loss,
  nitrogen cycling, etc.), which have been transgressed, and how do
  population density, consumption patterns, and technology interact to
  determine whether human civilisation is operating within sustainable
  limits?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Questions 1--10: Recall and
Comprehension}\label{questions-110-recall-and-comprehension-32}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Questions 1--10: Recall and
Comprehension}

\emph{This activity accompanies \cref{sec:unit_X_community_ecology} of
the textbook --- review that chapter before attempting the exercises
below.}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Define a biological community. How does it differ from a population?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  Name five types of species interactions. Give one example of each.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\tightlist
\item
  What is interspecific competition? State the competitive exclusion
  principle (Gause's law).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item
  What is a niche? Distinguish fundamental niche from realised niche.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{4}
\tightlist
\item
  What is predation? Name two anti-predator adaptations.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{5}
\tightlist
\item
  Define mutualism. Give one obligate and one facultative example.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{6}
\tightlist
\item
  What is a food web? How does it differ from a food chain?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{7}
\tightlist
\item
  What is a keystone species? Give one classic example.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{8}
\tightlist
\item
  Define ecological succession. Distinguish primary from secondary
  succession.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{9}
\tightlist
\item
  What is species richness? How does it differ from species diversity
  (Shannon index)?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Questions 11--20: Application and
Analysis}\label{questions-1120-application-and-analysis-32}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Questions 11--20: Application and
Analysis}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{10}
\tightlist
\item
  The Lotka-Volterra competition model uses two equations: dN\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}/dt =
  r\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}N\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}(K\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-} N\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}N\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2})/K\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1} and dN\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}/dt = r\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}N\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}(K\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-} N\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}N\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1})/K\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}. If K\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}
  = 1,000, K\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} = 800, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} = 0.5, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1} = 1.2, predict the outcome of
  competition. Under what conditions do two species coexist (K\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}/\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}
  \textgreater{} K\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} AND K\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}/\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{alpha}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1} \textgreater{} K\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1})?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{11}
\tightlist
\item
  Paine's classic experiment (1966) removed the sea star \emph{Pisaster
  ochraceus} from intertidal rocks. The result was dominance by the
  mussel \emph{Mytilus californianus}, which outcompeted most other
  sessile species. Explain: (a) why \emph{Pisaster} is a keystone
  predator; (b) how its removal reduced species diversity; (c) the
  concept of ``keystone species'' and why biomass alone does not predict
  ecological importance.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{12}
\tightlist
\item
  Character displacement: Darwin's finches on islands where two species
  coexist show greater beak size divergence than on islands where they
  occur alone. Explain: (a) the mechanism (sympatric competition selects
  for niche divergence); (b) the evidence from \emph{Geospiza fortis}
  and \emph{G. fuliginosa} beak depth distributions; (c) how this
  relates to niche partitioning.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{13}
\tightlist
\item
  Trophic cascades: when wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone, elk
  herbivory decreased, allowing aspen and willow regeneration, which
  stabilised stream banks and increased beaver populations. Trace this
  top-down trophic cascade: wolves \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} elk behaviour change \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} vegetation
  recovery \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} stream geomorphology change \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} beaver habitat expansion. Is
  this primarily a density-mediated or trait-mediated cascade?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{14}
\tightlist
\item
  Mycorrhizal networks (``wood-wide web'') connect trees underground,
  potentially allowing nutrient and carbon transfer between individuals.
  Evaluate the evidence: (a) \texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{3}}{3}C/\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{5}}{5}N labelling experiments showing
  carbon transfer between Douglas fir and paper birch; (b) whether
  transfer is mutualistic (mother trees provisioning seedlings) or
  incidental (fungal self-interest); (c) the evidence from Simard's
  studies and the controversy around the ``mother tree'' narrative.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{15}
\tightlist
\item
  Island biogeography theory (MacArthur and Wilson, 1967): species
  richness on an island results from a balance between immigration
  (decreasing with distance from mainland) and extinction (increasing
  with island size decrease). Apply this to habitat islands: predict
  species richness on forest fragments of 1 ha, 10 ha, and 1,000 ha that
  are 5 km from a large continuous forest. What does the ``species-area
  relationship'' (\(S = cA^z\)) predict?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{16}
\tightlist
\item
  Herbivore-plant coevolution has produced elaborate chemical defence
  systems. The milkweed (\emph{Asclepias}) -- monarch butterfly
  (\emph{Danaus plexippus}) system illustrates escalation: (a) milkweed
  produces cardenolides (toxic Na\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+}/K\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+}-ATPase inhibitors); (b) monarch
  larvae sequester cardenolides for their own defence; (c) monarch
  Na\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+}/K\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+}-ATPase has evolved resistance mutations. Trace this
  coevolutionary arms race.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{17}
\tightlist
\item
  Primary succession on volcanic islands (e.g., Surtsey, Iceland, formed
  1963): pioneer species (lichens, mosses) \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} grasses \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} shrubs \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  woodland. Explain the facilitation model: how do early colonisers
  modify the environment (soil formation, nitrogen fixation) to enable
  later successional stages?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{18}
\tightlist
\item
  Calculate the Shannon diversity index (H' = \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Sigma}}{Sigma}p\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{i}}{i} ln p\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{i}}{i}) for a
  community with 4 species at proportions: 0.50, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10. Then
  calculate for a community with 4 species at equal proportions (0.25
  each). Which community is more diverse? What does evenness contribute
  to diversity?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{19}
\tightlist
\item
  Parasitoids (e.g., parasitoid wasps) lay eggs inside or on host
  insects; the larva consumes the host from inside. Compare
  parasitoid-host dynamics to classical predator-prey dynamics: (a) why
  parasitoid search efficiency matters (Nicholson-Bailey model); (b) why
  parasitoid-host systems tend toward unstable oscillations in simple
  models; (c) what stabilising mechanisms exist in nature (spatial
  refugia, host immunity).
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Questions 21--30: Synthesis and
Evaluation}\label{questions-2130-synthesis-and-evaluation-32}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Questions 21--30: Synthesis and
Evaluation}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{20}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the intermediate disturbance hypothesis (IDH, Connell 1978):
  species diversity is maximised at intermediate disturbance
  frequency/intensity. Evaluate: (a) the mechanism (low disturbance \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  competitive exclusion; high disturbance \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} primarily ruderals survive);
  (b) empirical support from coral reef and tropical forest studies; (c)
  criticisms (meta-analyses showing weak or inconsistent support for
  IDH).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{21}
\tightlist
\item
  Design an experiment to test whether a suspected keystone species is
  truly a keystone (disproportionate effect on community structure
  relative to its biomass). Describe: (a) the removal experiment design;
  (b) what community metrics (species richness, evenness, biomass
  distribution) you would measure before and after removal; (c) how you
  would distinguish keystone effects from dominant species effects.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{22}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the ``biodiversity-ecosystem function'' (BEF) debate: does
  higher species diversity lead to greater ecosystem productivity? Cite:
  (a) the Cedar Creek grassland experiments (Tilman); (b) the ``sampling
  effect'' (more species \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} more likely to include a highly productive
  species) vs ``complementarity effect'' (niche partitioning \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} more
  complete resource use); (c) implications for conservation (``every
  species matters'' vs ``some species are redundant'').
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{23}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the role of facilitation (positive interactions) vs
  competition in structuring communities under environmental stress. The
  stress gradient hypothesis (SGH) predicts facilitation dominates in
  harsh environments and competition in benign ones. Evaluate the
  evidence from: (a) alpine cushion plants facilitating other species;
  (b) coral reef structure facilitating fish diversity; (c) exceptions
  where competition dominates even under stress.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{24}
\tightlist
\item
  Biological invasions: invasive species can restructure entire
  communities. Evaluate three hypotheses for why invasive species
  succeed: (a) enemy release hypothesis (no predators/parasites in new
  range); (b) novel weapons hypothesis (allelochemicals that native
  species cannot tolerate); (c) empty niche hypothesis (exploiting
  unused resources). For each, cite one case study.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{25}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the concept of ``ecological networks'' beyond food webs:
  mutualistic networks (plant-pollinator, plant-seed disperser) show a
  nested structure where specialist species interact with a subset of
  the partners of generalist species. What does nestedness imply for:
  (a) network stability (resilience to species loss); (b) the order of
  species extinction under habitat loss; (c) the importance of highly
  connected ``hub'' species for network integrity?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{26}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate Hubbell's Neutral Theory of Biodiversity (2001): species are
  ecologically equivalent, and community composition is determined by
  stochastic birth, death, and migration rather than niche differences.
  Compare neutral theory predictions with niche-based models: (a) what
  patterns can neutral theory explain (species-abundance distributions,
  species-area relationships); (b) what it cannot (functional trait
  differences, competitive exclusion); (c) is neutral theory ``wrong but
  useful''?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{27}
\tightlist
\item
  Climate change is causing phenological mismatches between interacting
  species (e.g., caterpillar peak occurring before oak leaf-out, but
  after great tit breeding initiation). Evaluate: (a) the evidence from
  long-term phenological datasets; (b) whether species can adapt quickly
  enough (evolutionary rescue vs extinction); (c) what community-level
  consequences emerge from cascading mismatches across multiple trophic
  levels.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{28}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the concept of ``alternative stable states'' in ecological
  communities: an ecosystem can exist in multiple stable configurations
  (e.g., clear-water lake vs turbid-water lake), and transitions between
  states (regime shifts) are driven by perturbations that push the
  system past a tipping point. Using the shallow lake eutrophication
  example: (a) what drives the regime shift; (b) why is the shift often
  irreversible (hysteresis); (c) what early warning signals predict an
  approaching tipping point?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{29}
\tightlist
\item
  Critically evaluate the use of ecological network analysis for
  predicting the cascading effects of species extinction. Using
  simulated extinction sequences (removing species from most to least
  connected): (a) how do co-extinction cascades propagate through food
  webs; (b) why do mutualistic networks (plant-pollinator) collapse more
  rapidly than antagonistic networks (predator-prey) under targeted
  extinction; (c) what does this imply for setting conservation
  priorities in species-rich ecosystems?
\end{enumerate}
