\section*{Questions --- Ch 34: Ecosystem Ecology and Biogeochemical
Cycles}\label{questions-ch-34-ecosystem-ecology-and-biogeochemical-cycles}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Questions --- Ch 34: Ecosystem Ecology
and Biogeochemical Cycles}

\label{sec:q_unit_X_ecosystem_ecology}

\subsection*{Instructor Use and Coverage
Notes}\label{instructor-use-and-coverage-notes-36}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Instructor Use and Coverage Notes}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Coverage target:} Calculate a flux or efficiency and explain
  which pool or process limits the system.
\item
  \textbf{Model/data emphasis:} Energy-flow, productivity, and
  nutrient-budget calculations.
\item
  \textbf{Assessment alignment:} Representing and Describing Data,
  Statistical Tests and Data Analysis, Argumentation.
\item
  \textbf{Misconception probe:} Energy flows through ecosystems, but
  matter cycles; confusing the two breaks many explanations.
\item
  \textbf{Transfer product:} Transfer ecosystem reasoning to
  eutrophication, carbon budgets, agriculture, and climate feedback.
\item
  \textbf{Grading focus:} award full credit for mechanism, evidence,
  boundary conditions, and units when a calculation is required.
\item
  \textbf{Suggested use:} draw one recall item, one application item,
  and one synthesis item when building a short quiz from this bank.
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Questions 1--10: Recall and
Comprehension}\label{questions-110-recall-and-comprehension-33}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Questions 1--10: Recall and
Comprehension}

\emph{This activity accompanies \cref{sec:unit_X_ecosystem_ecology} of
the textbook --- review that chapter before attempting the exercises
below.}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Define an ecosystem. What are its biotic and abiotic components?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  What is primary productivity? Distinguish GPP, NPP, and NEP.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\tightlist
\item
  What is a trophic level? Name four trophic levels in a food chain.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item
  What is ecological efficiency? What is the typical transfer efficiency
  between trophic levels?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{4}
\tightlist
\item
  Define the carbon cycle. Name the major carbon reservoirs on Earth.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{5}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the nitrogen cycle? Name the four major transformations.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{6}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the phosphorus cycle? How does it differ from the nitrogen and
  carbon cycles?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{7}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the water cycle (hydrological cycle)? Name the major fluxes.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{8}
\tightlist
\item
  What is eutrophication? What nutrients cause it and why?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{9}
\tightlist
\item
  Define decomposition. What organisms are primary decomposers?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Questions 11--20: Application and
Analysis}\label{questions-1120-application-and-analysis-33}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Questions 11--20: Application and
Analysis}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{10}
\tightlist
\item
  In a grassland ecosystem, GPP = 5,000 kcal/m\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}/yr and plant respiration
  = 3,000 kcal/m\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}/yr. Calculate NPP. If herbivores consume 20\% of NPP
  and their assimilation efficiency is 40\%, calculate secondary
  production at the herbivore level. How much energy reaches the top
  predator (3rd consumer) assuming 10\% transfer efficiency?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{11}
\tightlist
\item
  The inverted biomass pyramid of the open ocean: phytoplankton biomass
  is much lower than zooplankton biomass at any instant, yet
  phytoplankton NPP exceeds zooplankton production. Explain this paradox
  using turnover rate (phytoplankton divide daily; zooplankton live
  weeks to months).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{12}
\tightlist
\item
  Nitrogen fixation by \emph{Rhizobium} in legume root nodules adds
  about 200 kg N/ha/yr to agricultural soils. Haber-Bosch
  industrial fixation produces about 150 Tg N/yr globally.
  Compare: (a) the energy cost of each; (b) the environmental
  consequences of excess reactive nitrogen (N\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}O greenhouse gas, aquatic
  eutrophication, acid rain); (c) why reducing fertiliser overuse is
  critical for planetary health.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{13}
\tightlist
\item
  The biological pump in the ocean: surface phytoplankton fix CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
  organic particles sink \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} deep ocean decomposition releases CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}
  is sequestered for centuries. Calculate: if the biological pump
  sequesters about 11 Gt C/yr and anthropogenic emissions are
  about 10 Gt C/yr, what fraction of emissions is the
  biological pump offsetting? What would happen to atmospheric CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} if
  the biological pump weakened by 20\%?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{14}
\tightlist
\item
  A mesocosm experiment measures primary productivity using the
  light-dark bottle method. The light bottle shows dissolved O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} increase
  of 3 mg/L over 24 hours. The dark bottle shows O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} decrease of 1.5
  mg/L. Calculate: (a) NPP (net change in light bottle); (b) respiration
  (O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} loss in dark bottle); (c) GPP (NPP + R). Convert to carbon units
  assuming 1 mg O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} = 0.375 mg C.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{15}
\tightlist
\item
  Phosphorus is the limiting nutrient in most freshwater ecosystems
  (unlike marine systems where nitrogen often limits). Explain: (a) why
  P availability limits productivity (no atmospheric reservoir; P cycles
  primarily through rock weathering); (b) how agricultural runoff causes
  lake eutrophication (Schindler's whole-lake experiments); (c) why
  banning phosphate detergents was effective in lake recovery.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{16}
\tightlist
\item
  Decomposition rates vary with temperature and moisture. Using the ``k
  constant'' for leaf litter decomposition (mass remaining =
  M\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0}e\^{}(\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}kt)): if k = 0.5/yr in a temperate forest and k = 2.0/yr in a
  tropical forest, calculate the time for 90\% decomposition in each
  ecosystem. What does this imply for nutrient cycling rates?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{17}
\tightlist
\item
  The sulfur cycle includes atmospheric SO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} (from volcanic eruptions and
  fossil fuel combustion), which forms sulfuric acid (H\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}SO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{4}}{4}) in clouds.
  Trace: SO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} sulfate aerosol \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} acid rain \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} soil and lake acidification
  \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} biological damage. Name the specific impacts on: (a) fish
  populations; (b) forest soil chemistry (Al\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{3}}{3}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} toxicity); (c) building
  materials (limestone dissolution).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{18}
\tightlist
\item
  Carbon budget: the global carbon budget (2024) estimates: fossil fuel
  emissions = 9.9 Gt C/yr; land-use change emissions = 1.0 Gt C/yr;
  ocean sink = 2.8 Gt C/yr; land sink = 3.3 Gt C/yr; atmospheric growth
  = 4.8 Gt C/yr. Verify: do sources = sinks + atmospheric growth? What
  is the ``residual'' and what does it reveal about our understanding of
  the carbon cycle?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{19}
\tightlist
\item
  Wetlands serve as both carbon sinks and methane (CH\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{4}}{4}) sources.
  Evaluate: (a) how waterlogged, anoxic conditions promote
  methanogenesis (aceticlastic vs hydrogenotrophic pathways); (b) the
  100-year global warming potential of CH\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{4}}{4} (about 27--30\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} depending
  on fossil vs biogenic accounting in IPCC AR6); (c) the net climate
  effect of wetlands --- do they cool or warm the planet considering
  both C sequestration and CH\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{4}}{4} emission?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Questions 21--30: Synthesis and
Evaluation}\label{questions-2130-synthesis-and-evaluation-33}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Questions 21--30: Synthesis and
Evaluation}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{20}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the concept of ``planetary boundaries'' for biogeochemical
  cycles (Rockström et al., 2009). Which cycles have transgressed safe
  operating spaces (nitrogen, phosphorus, climate change), and what does
  this mean for Earth system stability? Propose specific policy
  interventions for the nitrogen cycle that would bring humanity back
  within the safe boundary.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{21}
\tightlist
\item
  Design an ecosystem-scale experiment (like Biosphere 2) to test
  whether a simplified ecosystem (5 trophic levels, 50 species) can
  maintain biogeochemical cycling in a sealed environment. What are the
  critical species you would include, what cycling processes must be
  maintained (C, N, P, H\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}O), and what failure modes would you predict?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{22}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the ``metabolic theory of ecology'' (MTE, Brown et al.,
  2004): body mass and temperature determine metabolic rate, which
  scales ecosystem processes (productivity, decomposition, nutrient
  flux). What does MTE predict about the response of tropical vs boreal
  ecosystem productivity to climate warming, and where does MTE break
  down (nutrient limitation, biodiversity effects)?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{23}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the role of fire as an ecosystem process: (a) how fire
  releases nutrients (P, K) from biomass; (b) how fire-adapted
  ecosystems (savanna, chaparral, boreal forest) depend on periodic fire
  for regeneration; (c) how fire suppression in fire-dependent
  ecosystems leads to fuel accumulation and catastrophic megafires; (d)
  how indigenous fire management (``cool burns'') can be integrated into
  modern land management.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{24}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the evidence that ocean acidification (decreasing pH from CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}
  absorption, currently pH 8.1 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} projected 7.8 by 2100) threatens marine
  ecosystems: (a) what organisms are most affected (calcifiers ---
  corals, pteropods, coccolithophores); (b) how does reduced aragonite
  saturation state (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Omega}}{Omega}\_ar \textless{} 1) dissolve CaCO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{3}}{3} shells; (c) what
  cascading ecosystem effects are predicted; (d) is there evidence of
  evolutionary adaptation to lower pH in any marine organisms?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{25}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the concept of ``natural capital'' --- valuing ecosystem
  services (pollination, water purification, carbon storage) in monetary
  terms. Using Costanza et al.~(1997, updated 2014) estimates of global
  ecosystem services at \$125 trillion/yr: (a) is monetary valuation of
  nature scientifically valid; (b) does it effectively change policy;
  (c) what ethical concerns arise from commodifying nature?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{26}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the role of permafrost thaw in the global carbon cycle:
  about 1,500 Gt C is stored in permafrost (twice atmospheric
  carbon). As Arctic warming thaws permafrost: (a) what forms of carbon
  are released (CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} from aerobic decomposition, CH\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{4}}{4} from anaerobic
  decomposition); (b) what is the ``permafrost carbon feedback'' and how
  much warming does it add to existing projections; (c) is permafrost
  thaw a tipping point (irreversible once initiated)?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{27}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the concept of ``novel ecosystems'' --- ecosystems with no
  historical analogue, arising from human activity (urban ecosystems,
  post-mining landscapes, invasive-dominated habitats). Should
  conservation efforts attempt to restore historical ecosystems or
  manage novel ecosystems for desired functions? Use a specific example
  to argue both sides.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{28}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate geoengineering approaches targeting biogeochemical cycles:
  (a) ocean iron fertilisation (stimulating phytoplankton growth to
  increase biological pump CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} sequestration); (b) enhanced weathering
  (grinding silicate rocks to accelerate CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} consumption); (c) bioenergy
  with carbon capture and storage (BECCS). For each, evaluate the scale
  of CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} removal, the ecological risks, and the technological readiness.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{29}
\tightlist
\item
  Critically evaluate whether Earth's biogeochemical cycles constitute a
  self-regulating system (Gaia hypothesis, Lovelock 1979). Specifically:
  (a) what evidence supports biological regulation of atmospheric O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} at
  about 21\%; (b) what evidence supports biological regulation
  of ocean salinity; (c) what is the difference between ``strong Gaia''
  (Earth as a superorganism) and ``weak Gaia'' (life influences but does
  not control the environment); (d) which version, if either, is
  scientifically defensible?
\end{enumerate}

\newpage

\section*{Questions --- Ch 35: Biomes and Conservation
Biology}\label{questions-ch-35-biomes-and-conservation-biology}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Questions --- Ch 35: Biomes and
Conservation Biology}

\label{sec:q_unit_X_biomes_and_conservation}

\subsection*{Instructor Use and Coverage
Notes}\label{instructor-use-and-coverage-notes-37}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Instructor Use and Coverage Notes}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Coverage target:} Evaluate a conservation scenario using
  evidence, tradeoffs, and uncertainty.
\item
  \textbf{Model/data emphasis:} Species-area, risk, and prioritization
  calculations.
\item
  \textbf{Assessment alignment:} Representing and Describing Data,
  Statistical Tests and Data Analysis, Argumentation.
\item
  \textbf{Misconception probe:} Conservation is decision-making under
  constraints and uncertainty, not only preserving untouched nature.
\item
  \textbf{Transfer product:} Transfer conservation reasoning to land
  use, climate corridors, restoration, and environmental justice.
\item
  \textbf{Grading focus:} award full credit for mechanism, evidence,
  boundary conditions, and units when a calculation is required.
\item
  \textbf{Suggested use:} draw one recall item, one application item,
  and one synthesis item when building a short quiz from this bank.
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Questions 1--10: Recall and
Comprehension}\label{questions-110-recall-and-comprehension-34}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Questions 1--10: Recall and
Comprehension}

\emph{This activity accompanies
\cref{sec:unit_X_biomes_and_conservation} of the textbook --- review
that chapter before attempting the exercises below.}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Define a biome. What two abiotic factors primarily determine biome
  distribution?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  Name six major terrestrial biomes and list their characteristic
  temperature and precipitation ranges.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the difference between weather and climate?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item
  What is biodiversity? Distinguish genetic, species, and ecosystem
  diversity.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{4}
\tightlist
\item
  Define an endangered species. What organisation maintains the Red
  List?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{5}
\tightlist
\item
  What is habitat fragmentation? Why does it threaten biodiversity?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{6}
\tightlist
\item
  Name three causes of the current biodiversity crisis.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{7}
\tightlist
\item
  What is a biodiversity hotspot? Name two examples.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{8}
\tightlist
\item
  What is an in situ conservation strategy? What is an ex situ strategy?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{9}
\tightlist
\item
  Define sustainability. What are the three pillars of sustainability?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Questions 11--20: Application and
Analysis}\label{questions-1120-application-and-analysis-34}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Questions 11--20: Application and
Analysis}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{10}
\tightlist
\item
  The species-area relationship (\(S = cA^z\), where z \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 0.25 for
  oceanic islands) predicts that reducing habitat area by 90\% reduces
  species number by about 50\%. Calculate: if a 10,000 km\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}
  forest is reduced to 1,000 km\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}, and the original forest had 200 bird
  species, how many bird species are expected in the remaining fragment?
  What assumptions does this model make?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{11}
\tightlist
\item
  EDGE scores (Evolutionarily Distinct and Globally Endangered) are used
  to prioritise species for conservation investment. The aye-aye
  (\emph{Daubentonia madagascariensis}) --- the sole living member of
  its family --- has a very high EDGE score. Explain: (a) what
  evolutionary distinctiveness means; (b) why losing an ``edge species''
  results in greater phylogenetic diversity loss than losing a species
  in a species-rich clade; (c) how EDGE scoring changes conservation
  priorities compared to a focus on charisma.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{12}
\tightlist
\item
  Minimum viable population (MVP) analysis: a PVA model estimates that a
  population of 500 individuals has a 95\% probability of persisting for
  100 years, but a population of 50 has a 20\% chance. Identify three
  factors incorporated in the model (demographic stochasticity,
  environmental stochasticity, inbreeding depression) and explain how
  each reduces persistence probability.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{13}
\tightlist
\item
  Climate change is shifting biome boundaries: the boreal-temperate
  boundary is moving northward, and the Sahel-Sahara boundary is
  fluctuating. Predict the consequences for: (a) species that cannot
  migrate fast enough (boreal specialists trapped in shrinking habitat);
  (b) agricultural zones (expansion of growing season in formerly cold
  regions); (c) novel community assemblages (no-analogue communities
  formed by differential range shifts).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{14}
\tightlist
\item
  Coral reef bleaching occurs when accumulated heat stress disrupts the
  coral-Symbiodiniaceae partnership. Explain: (a) how
  degree-heating-week evidence links heat exposure to symbiont
  photosystem stress, reactive oxygen species, and symbiont loss; (b)
  why recovery depends on repeated heat exposure, water quality,
  recruitment, and symbiont community composition rather than a fixed
  clock; (c) how assisted evolution or symbiont turnover could improve
  local resilience while still failing as a substitute for climate
  mitigation.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{15}
\tightlist
\item
  Protected areas currently cover about 17\% of land and
  about 8\% of ocean. The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity
  Framework (2022) targets 30\% by 2030 (``30 by 30''). Evaluate: (a)
  whether area alone is sufficient (effective management, connectivity,
  representativeness); (b) the concept of ``half-Earth'' (Wilson, 2016
  --- protecting 50\% of Earth's surface); (c) the social justice
  concerns (indigenous displacement, land rights).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{16}
\tightlist
\item
  Invasive species economic damage: the global estimated cost of
  invasive species is \textgreater\$423 billion/yr (2019). Using the
  example of the invasive cane toad (\emph{Rhinella marina}) in
  Australia: (a) what was the original purpose of introduction; (b) what
  ecological impacts have occurred (native predator mortality from toad
  toxin); (c) what control strategies have been attempted (biological
  control, trapping, gene drive research).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{17}
\tightlist
\item
  Payment for ecosystem services (PES): Costa Rica's PES programme pays
  landowners to conserve forest (carbon storage, water regulation).
  Evaluate: (a) how PES monetises ecosystem services; (b) evidence of
  effectiveness (Costa Rica reversed deforestation); (c) criticisms
  (additionality --- would forests have been conserved anyway? Equity
  --- do poor landowners benefit or are payments captured by wealthy
  elites?).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{18}
\tightlist
\item
  The IPBES Global Assessment estimates that about one million species
  are threatened, while the IPBES Transformative Change Assessment
  argues that biodiversity loss is driven by economic, governance, and
  social systems as well as local habitat conversion. Evaluate: (a) how
  threatened-species estimates combine assessed taxa, extrapolation, and
  habitat trends; (b) why food systems, healthy diets, agroecology,
  fisheries, and commodity supply chains belong inside conservation
  biology; (c) how to distinguish evidence-based transformative change
  from vague sustainability branding.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{19}
\tightlist
\item
  Rewilding involves reintroducing apex predators and megafauna to
  restore ecosystem function. Evaluate the Eurasian rewilding movement
  (European bison in Romania, wolves in Germany, lynx in UK): (a) what
  ecological functions are restored; (b) what human-wildlife conflict
  arises; (c) the evidence from existing rewilding projects
  (Oostvaardersplassen, Netherlands) --- successes and failures.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Questions 21--30: Synthesis and
Evaluation}\label{questions-2130-synthesis-and-evaluation-34}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Questions 21--30: Synthesis and
Evaluation}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{20}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the ``extinction debt'' concept: habitat destruction in the
  past has committed species to future extinction even if no further
  habitat is lost, because small fragments cannot sustain viable
  populations over decades. Using the example of tropical forest
  fragmentation (Ferraz et al., 2003): (a) how is extinction debt
  estimated; (b) how long is the time lag (about 20--100
  years); (c) what does this imply for current biodiversity assessments
  (we are underestimating the true impact of past deforestation)?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{21}
\tightlist
\item
  Design a conservation genetics programme for a critically endangered
  species (e.g., California condor, about 500 individuals):
  describe (a) the genetic assessment (genomic sequencing of sampled
  individuals, measurement of heterozygosity and inbreeding
  coefficient); (b) the breeding management strategy (maximising N\_e,
  using mean kinship to minimise inbreeding); (c) the genetic rescue
  strategy (introducing individuals from a genetically distinct
  population to restore lost alleles). What are the risks of genetic
  rescue (outbreeding depression)?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{22}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate climate-smart conservation: traditional conservation aims to
  protect current biodiversity in current locations. Climate change
  requires protecting future habitats and enabling species movement.
  Evaluate three climate-smart strategies: (a) connectivity corridors
  between protected areas; (b) assisted migration (moving species to
  suitable future habitat); (c) protecting climate refugia (areas
  predicted to remain climatically stable). What are the risks of each?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{23}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the role of indigenous and traditional ecological knowledge
  (ITEK) in conservation: (a) the evidence that indigenous-managed lands
  have higher biodiversity than conventional protected areas; (b) the UN
  IPBES recognition of ITEK as an evidence base equal to scientific
  knowledge; (c) the challenges of integrating ITEK with Western science
  (different epistemologies, power dynamics, intellectual property).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{24}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the concept of ``de-extinction'' in the context of
  conservation biology: if woolly mammoths could be de-extincted (via
  CRISPR editing of Asian elephant genome), would this be a conservation
  priority? Discuss: (a) the opportunity cost (diverting funds from
  existing species); (b) the ecological benefit (restoring mammoth
  steppe ecosystem, permafrost preservation); (c) the ethical questions
  (welfare of first-generation animals, ecological risk).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{25}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the impact of plastic pollution on marine biomes: (a)
  microplastic ingestion by marine organisms across trophic levels; (b)
  bioaccumulation and biomagnification of associated chemical pollutants
  (phthalates, BPA); (c) the ``plastisphere'' --- microbial communities
  colonising marine plastic that can include pathogens; (d) policy
  interventions (single-use plastic bans, Extended Producer
  Responsibility).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{26}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate Nature-based Solutions (NbS) to climate change: (a)
  reforestation and afforestation (potential about 10 Gt
  CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}/yr); (b) peatland and mangrove restoration; (c) regenerative
  agriculture (soil carbon sequestration). For each, evaluate the
  permanence of carbon storage, the biodiversity co-benefits, and the
  risk of ``greenwashing'' (using NbS to justify continued fossil fuel
  use).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{27}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the role of zoos and botanical gardens (ex situ conservation)
  in preventing extinction: (a) the success stories (Arabian oryx,
  black-footed ferret, California condor --- saved from extinction by
  captive breeding); (b) the limitations (genetic bottlenecks,
  behavioural domestication, space constraints); (c) the shift from
  ``Noah's Ark'' (saving species) to ``conservation hubs'' (research,
  education, advocacy).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{28}
\tightlist
\item
  Evaluate the ``triage'' approach to conservation: given limited
  resources, should we focus on: (a) species most likely to be saved
  (pragmatic triage); (b) species with highest evolutionary
  distinctiveness (phylogenetic triage); (c) species with greatest
  functional importance (ecosystem triage)? Compare these approaches
  using a specific threatened community (e.g., coral reef, tropical
  forest), and discuss the ethical implications of explicitly choosing
  to let some species go extinct.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{29}
\tightlist
\item
  Critically evaluate whether the concept of ``ecological footprint''
  (measuring human demand on Earth's biocapacity in global hectares) is
  a scientifically rigorous and policy-useful metric. Compare ecological
  footprint to alternative sustainability metrics (planetary boundaries,
  natural capital accounting, genuine progress indicator). What does
  each capture that others miss, and which is most actionable for policy
  change?
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Appendix A --- Curriculum
Map}\label{appendix-a-curriculum-map}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Appendix A --- Curriculum Map}

\label{sec:appendix_curriculum_map}

This appendix is generated from \breaktt{src/biology/curriculum.py} and
\breaktt{src/biology/alignment.py}. It links each chapter to its
companion lab, question bank, model/data skill, misconception probe,
transfer task, and standards/skills alignment so the textbook can be
composed into different course formats without losing pedagogical
coherence.

\subsection*{Unit 0}\label{unit-0}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Unit 0}

\subsubsection*{Systems Science and the Logic of
Emergence}\label{systems-science-and-the-logic-of-emergence-1}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Systems Science and the Logic of
Emergence}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Chapter:} \cref{sec:unit_0_systems_science}.
\item
  \textbf{Lab:} \cref{sec:lab_unit_0_systems_science}.
\item
  \textbf{Question bank:} \cref{sec:q_unit_0_systems_science}.
\item
  \textbf{Big idea:} Biological explanation improves when parts,
  interactions, feedback, and scale are kept in view together.
\item
  \textbf{Core concepts:} systems boundaries, feedback, emergence, state
  variables.
\item
  \textbf{Framework alignment:} Vision \& Change: Systems, Structure and
  function; AP Biology: Systems Interactions; NGSS-style topics:
  Structure and Function, Interdependent Relationships in Ecosystems.
\item
  \textbf{Practice cadence:} Questions and Methods, Representing and
  Describing Data, Argumentation.
\item
  \textbf{Model/data skill:} Box-and-arrow causal models with explicit
  inputs, outputs, and feedback signs. Translate a verbal biological
  system into variables, links, and testable predictions.
\item
  \textbf{Misconception probe:} A system is not just a list of parts;
  the interactions are part of the explanation.
\item
  \textbf{Transfer task:} Apply the same feedback map to a cell,
  organism, and ecosystem, then name what changes at each scale.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Complex Adaptive
Systems}\label{complex-adaptive-systems-1}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Complex Adaptive Systems}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Chapter:} \cref{sec:unit_0_complex_adaptive_systems}.
\item
  \textbf{Lab:} \cref{sec:lab_unit_0_complex_adaptive_systems}.
\item
  \textbf{Question bank:} \cref{sec:q_unit_0_complex_adaptive_systems}.
\item
  \textbf{Big idea:} Local rules can generate population-level patterns
  without a central controller.
\item
  \textbf{Core concepts:} nonlinearity, self-organization, attractors,
  power laws.
\item
  \textbf{Framework alignment:} Vision \& Change: Systems, Structure and
  function; AP Biology: Systems Interactions; NGSS-style topics:
  Structure and Function, Interdependent Relationships in Ecosystems.
\item
  \textbf{Practice cadence:} Questions and Methods, Representing and
  Describing Data, Argumentation.
\item
  \textbf{Model/data skill:} Agent-rule and scaling arguments for
  emergent biological patterns. Distinguish deterministic trends from
  stochastic variation in repeated simulations.
\item
  \textbf{Misconception probe:} Emergence is not mysterious; it is a
  reproducible consequence of interactions plus constraints.
\item
  \textbf{Transfer task:} Compare flocking, immune activation, and
  microbial biofilms as adaptive systems.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Active Inference and the Free Energy
Principle}\label{active-inference-and-the-free-energy-principle-1}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Active Inference and the Free
Energy Principle}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Chapter:} \cref{sec:unit_0_active_inference}.
\item
  \textbf{Lab:} \cref{sec:lab_unit_0_active_inference}.
\item
  \textbf{Question bank:} \cref{sec:q_unit_0_active_inference}.
\item
  \textbf{Big idea:} Living systems reduce uncertainty by acting on the
  world as well as by updating internal models.
\item
  \textbf{Core concepts:} prediction error, Bayesian updating, policy
  selection, homeostasis.
\item
  \textbf{Framework alignment:} Vision \& Change: Systems, Structure and
  function; AP Biology: Systems Interactions; NGSS-style topics:
  Structure and Function, Interdependent Relationships in Ecosystems.
\item
  \textbf{Practice cadence:} Questions and Methods, Representing and
  Describing Data, Argumentation.
\item
  \textbf{Model/data skill:} Bayesian belief updating and
  expected-free-energy-style policy comparison. Read a small probability
  table and update a prediction after new evidence.
\item
  \textbf{Misconception probe:} Active inference is not passive
  prediction; action changes the sensory data that arrive next.
\item
  \textbf{Transfer task:} Map prediction-error reasoning onto
  chemotaxis, thermoregulation, and attention.
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Unit I}\label{unit-i}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Unit I}

\subsubsection*{Atoms, Molecules, and Chemical
Bonds}\label{atoms-molecules-and-chemical-bonds-1}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Atoms, Molecules, and Chemical
Bonds}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Chapter:} \cref{sec:unit_I_atoms_molecules}.
\item
  \textbf{Lab:} \cref{sec:lab_unit_I_atoms_molecules}.
\item
  \textbf{Question bank:} \cref{sec:q_unit_I_atoms_molecules}.
\item
  \textbf{Big idea:} Atomic structure constrains the bonds, charges, and
  geometries that make biological molecules possible.
\item
  \textbf{Core concepts:} valence, electronegativity, formal charge,
  isotopes.
\item
  \textbf{Framework alignment:} Vision \& Change: Structure and
  function, Pathways and transformations of energy and matter; AP
  Biology: Energetics, Systems Interactions; NGSS-style topics: Matter
  and Energy in Organisms and Ecosystems, Structure and Function.
\item
  \textbf{Practice cadence:} Concept Explanation, Statistical Tests and
  Data Analysis, Argumentation.
\item
  \textbf{Model/data skill:} Formal charge and
  electronegativity-difference reasoning. Use tabular atomic data to
  predict polarity, solubility, and biological reactivity.
\item
  \textbf{Misconception probe:} Weak interactions are not unimportant;
  many weak interactions together dominate structure and specificity.
\item
  \textbf{Transfer task:} Use atomic reasoning to explain a medical
  tracer, enzyme cofactor, or membrane-solubility problem.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Water --- The Molecule of
Life}\label{water-the-molecule-of-life-1}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Water --- The Molecule of Life}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Chapter:} \cref{sec:unit_I_water_and_life}.
\item
  \textbf{Lab:} \cref{sec:lab_unit_I_water_and_life}.
\item
  \textbf{Question bank:} \cref{sec:q_unit_I_water_and_life}.
\item
  \textbf{Big idea:} Water's polarity, hydrogen bonding, and ionization
  make cells physically possible.
\item
  \textbf{Core concepts:} hydrogen bonding, cohesion, pH, buffers.
\item
  \textbf{Framework alignment:} Vision \& Change: Structure and
  function, Pathways and transformations of energy and matter; AP
  Biology: Energetics, Systems Interactions; NGSS-style topics: Matter
  and Energy in Organisms and Ecosystems, Structure and Function.
\item
  \textbf{Practice cadence:} Concept Explanation, Statistical Tests and
  Data Analysis, Argumentation.
\item
  \textbf{Model/data skill:} Henderson-Hasselbalch and pH-scale
  calculations. Convert between pH, hydrogen ion concentration, and
  buffer ratios.
\item
  \textbf{Misconception probe:} Water is not an inert background; it is
  an active participant in structure and reaction chemistry.
\item
  \textbf{Transfer task:} Transfer water-property reasoning to blood
  buffering, plant transport, or protein folding.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Biological
Macromolecules}\label{biological-macromolecules-1}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Biological Macromolecules}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Chapter:} \cref{sec:unit_I_macromolecules}.
\item
  \textbf{Lab:} \cref{sec:lab_unit_I_macromolecules}.
\item
  \textbf{Question bank:} \cref{sec:q_unit_I_macromolecules}.
\item
  \textbf{Big idea:} Macromolecule structure links monomer chemistry to
  biological function and information storage.
\item
  \textbf{Core concepts:} polymers, dehydration synthesis, protein
  structure, nucleic acids.
\item
  \textbf{Framework alignment:} Vision \& Change: Structure and
  function, Pathways and transformations of energy and matter; AP
  Biology: Energetics, Systems Interactions; NGSS-style topics: Matter
  and Energy in Organisms and Ecosystems, Structure and Function.
\item
  \textbf{Practice cadence:} Concept Explanation, Statistical Tests and
  Data Analysis, Argumentation.
\item
  \textbf{Model/data skill:} Polymerization energetics and
  sequence-to-structure reasoning. Classify molecules from structural
  evidence rather than names alone.
\item
  \textbf{Misconception probe:} Structure is not decoration; small
  chemical changes can redirect function and recognition.
\item
  \textbf{Transfer task:} Explain how a mutation, lipid substitution, or
  glycosylation change propagates to phenotype.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Enzymes and the Kinetics of
Catalysis}\label{enzymes-and-the-kinetics-of-catalysis-1}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Enzymes and the Kinetics of
Catalysis}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Chapter:} \cref{sec:unit_I_enzymes_and_kinetics}.
\item
  \textbf{Lab:} \cref{sec:lab_unit_I_enzymes_and_kinetics}.
\item
  \textbf{Question bank:} \cref{sec:q_unit_I_enzymes_and_kinetics}.
\item
  \textbf{Big idea:} Enzymes accelerate reactions by stabilizing
  transition states without changing thermodynamic endpoints.
\item
  \textbf{Core concepts:} activation energy, Michaelis-Menten kinetics,
  inhibition, allostery.
\item
  \textbf{Framework alignment:} Vision \& Change: Structure and
  function, Pathways and transformations of energy and matter; AP
  Biology: Energetics, Systems Interactions; NGSS-style topics: Matter
  and Energy in Organisms and Ecosystems, Structure and Function.
\item
  \textbf{Practice cadence:} Concept Explanation, Statistical Tests and
  Data Analysis, Argumentation.
\item
  \textbf{Model/data skill:} Michaelis-Menten, Lineweaver-Burk, and
  inhibition-pattern calculations. Fit or interpret enzyme-rate data and
  identify which parameter changed.
\item
  \textbf{Misconception probe:} A catalyst changes rate, not the
  equilibrium constant or the sign of delta G.
\item
  \textbf{Transfer task:} Apply enzyme-kinetic reasoning to drug dosing,
  metabolic control, or diagnostic assays.
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Unit II}\label{unit-ii}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Unit II}

\subsubsection*{Cell Theory and Cell
Types}\label{cell-theory-and-cell-types-1}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Cell Theory and Cell Types}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Chapter:} \cref{sec:unit_II_cell_theory}.

  \textbf{Lab:} \cref{sec:lab_unit_II_cell_theory}.

  \textbf{Question bank:} \cref{sec:q_unit_II_cell_theory}.

  \textbf{Core concepts:} microbiomes, symbiosis, diversity,
  biogeochemical cycling.
\item
  \textbf{Framework alignment:} Vision \& Change: Evolution, Systems,
  Structure and function; AP Biology: Evolution, Systems Interactions;
  NGSS-style topics: Structure and Function, Interdependent
  Relationships in Ecosystems.
\item
  \textbf{Practice cadence:} Questions and Methods, Representing and
  Describing Data, Argumentation.
\item
  \textbf{Model/data skill:} Diversity indices, richness estimates, and
  interaction-network reasoning. Compute or interpret community metrics
  from abundance data.
\item
  \textbf{Misconception probe:} A microbiome is not automatically
  beneficial; context determines the effect.
\item
  \textbf{Transfer task:} Transfer microbial ecology to soils, oceans,
  digestion, disease, and climate feedbacks.
\end{itemize}

\section*{Appendix B --- Instructor Orchestration
Guide}\label{appendix-b-instructor-orchestration-guide}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Appendix B --- Instructor Orchestration
Guide}

\label{sec:appendix_instructor_orchestration}

This appendix is generated from the same curriculum and alignment
records that populate chapter Study Blueprints. It gives instructors a
compact sequence for turning the textbook into lectures, labs, quizzes,
and transfer tasks without hand-rebuilding a course map.

\subsection*{Reusable Teaching Loop}\label{reusable-teaching-loop}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Reusable Teaching Loop}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Launch from a phenomenon.} Begin with a case, dataset, model
  failure, or observed pattern that makes the chapter question
  necessary.
\item
  \textbf{Model the mechanism.} Ask students to draw, compute, simulate,
  or annotate the causal structure before reading the full explanation.
\item
  \textbf{Gather evidence.} Use the companion lab as the measurement and
  reproducibility surface for the chapter.
\item
  \textbf{Check transfer.} Use the question bank to sample recall,
  application, data interpretation, and argumentation.
\item
  \textbf{Close the loop.} Return to the transfer task and require a
  claim, evidence, reasoning, and uncertainty statement.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Chapter Orchestration
Matrix}\label{chapter-orchestration-matrix}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Chapter Orchestration Matrix}

\subsubsection*{Unit 0}\label{unit-0-1}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Unit 0}

\paragraph*{Systems Science and the Logic of
Emergence}\label{systems-science-and-the-logic-of-emergence-2}
\addcontentsline{toc}{paragraph}{Systems Science and the Logic of
Emergence}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Core thread:} Use systems diagrams, uncertainty, and feedback
  as recurring sense-making tools.
\item
  \textbf{Instructor move:} Launch from a phenomenon, have students
  model it with Box-and-arrow causal models with explicit inputs,
  outputs, and feedback signs, then test the model through data.
\item
  \textbf{Formative check:} Ask students to translate a verbal
  biological system into variables, links, and testable predictions and
  then answer: given a biological scenario, identify the system
  boundary, feedback loop, and missing measurement.
\item
  \textbf{Summative product:} Apply the same feedback map to a cell,
  organism, and ecosystem, then name what changes at each scale.
\item
  \textbf{Lab/question pair:} \cref{sec:lab_unit_0_systems_science};
  \cref{sec:q_unit_0_systems_science}.
\item
  \textbf{External alignment:} Vision \& Change: Systems, Structure and
  function; AP Biology: Systems Interactions; NGSS-style topics:
  Structure and Function, Interdependent Relationships in Ecosystems.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph*{Complex Adaptive Systems}\label{complex-adaptive-systems-2}
\addcontentsline{toc}{paragraph}{Complex Adaptive Systems}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Core thread:} Use systems diagrams, uncertainty, and feedback
  as recurring sense-making tools.
\item
  \textbf{Instructor move:} Launch from a phenomenon, have students
  model it with Agent-rule and scaling arguments for emergent biological
  patterns, then test the model through data.
\item
  \textbf{Formative check:} Ask students to distinguish deterministic
  trends from stochastic variation in repeated simulations and then
  answer: explain an observed population pattern from individual-level
  rules and identify one falsifiable prediction.
\item
  \textbf{Summative product:} Compare flocking, immune activation, and
  microbial biofilms as adaptive systems.
\item
  \textbf{Lab/question pair:}
  \cref{sec:lab_unit_0_complex_adaptive_systems};
  \cref{sec:q_unit_0_complex_adaptive_systems}.
\item
  \textbf{External alignment:} Vision \& Change: Systems, Structure and
  function; AP Biology: Systems Interactions; NGSS-style topics:
  Structure and Function, Interdependent Relationships in Ecosystems.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph*{Active Inference and the Free Energy
Principle}\label{active-inference-and-the-free-energy-principle-2}
\addcontentsline{toc}{paragraph}{Active Inference and the Free Energy
Principle}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Core thread:} Use systems diagrams, uncertainty, and feedback
  as recurring sense-making tools.
\item
  \textbf{Instructor move:} Launch from a phenomenon, have students
  model it with Bayesian belief updating and expected-free-energy-style
  policy comparison, then test the model through data.
\item
  \textbf{Formative check:} Ask students to read a small probability
  table and update a prediction after new evidence and then answer:
  calculate a posterior belief and explain what action would reduce
  uncertainty or restore a set point.
\item
  \textbf{Summative product:} Map prediction-error reasoning onto
  chemotaxis, thermoregulation, and attention.
\item
  \textbf{Lab/question pair:} \cref{sec:lab_unit_0_active_inference};
  \cref{sec:q_unit_0_active_inference}.
\item
  \textbf{External alignment:} Vision \& Change: Systems, Structure and
  function; AP Biology: Systems Interactions; NGSS-style topics:
  Structure and Function, Interdependent Relationships in Ecosystems.
\end{itemize}

  predict polarity, solubility, and biological reactivity and then
  answer: predict bond polarity, formal charge, or isotope behaviour and
  connect it to a biological consequence.
\item
  \textbf{Summative product:} Use atomic reasoning to explain a medical
  tracer, enzyme cofactor, or membrane-solubility problem.
\item
  \textbf{Lab/question pair:} \cref{sec:lab_unit_I_atoms_molecules};
  \cref{sec:q_unit_I_atoms_molecules}.
\item
  \textbf{External alignment:} Vision \& Change: Structure and function,
  Pathways and transformations of energy and matter; AP Biology:
  Energetics, Systems Interactions; NGSS-style topics: Matter and Energy
  in Organisms and Ecosystems, Structure and Function.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph*{Water --- The Molecule of
Life}\label{water-the-molecule-of-life-2}
\addcontentsline{toc}{paragraph}{Water --- The Molecule of Life}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Core thread:} Connect chemical structure, water, polymers, and
  catalysis to biological mechanism.
\item
  \textbf{Instructor move:} Launch from a phenomenon, have students
  model it with Henderson-Hasselbalch and pH-scale calculations, then
  test the model through data.
\item
  \textbf{Formative check:} Ask students to convert between pH, hydrogen
  ion concentration, and buffer ratios and then answer: calculate a pH
  or buffer ratio and interpret what it means for a biological system.
\item
  \textbf{Summative product:} Transfer water-property reasoning to blood
  buffering, plant transport, or protein folding.
\item
  \textbf{Lab/question pair:} \cref{sec:lab_unit_I_water_and_life};
  \cref{sec:q_unit_I_water_and_life}.

\section*{Appendix C --- Mathematical Review for
Biology}\label{appendix-c-mathematical-review-for-biology}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Appendix C --- Mathematical Review for
Biology}

\label{sec:appendix_math_review}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Appendix C} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.} Level 1/3 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.} 45 min read \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.} Prerequisites: none \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.}
Use as reference
\end{quote}

This appendix collects the mathematics a reader needs to work through
the quantitative chapters of this textbook. It is not a course in
mathematics --- it is a compact reference for the specific tools used in
the chapters. Each section is self-contained; dip in as needed.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection*{C.1 Logarithms and the Natural
Log}\label{c.1-logarithms-and-the-natural-log}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{C.1 Logarithms and the Natural Log}

\subsubsection*{Definition}\label{definition-1}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Definition}

\[ \log_b(x) = y \iff b^y = x  \label{eq:appendices_appendix_math_review_item_1}\]

Biology uses two bases heavily:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Base 10} (\(\log_{10}\)) --- pH, sound intensity, earthquake
  magnitude, powers-of-ten units (nM, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\mu}}{mu}M, mM).
\item
  \textbf{Base \(e\)} (\(\ln\), natural log) --- most first-order
  kinetics (exponential growth, decay, enzyme kinetics), where
  \(e \approx 2.71828\).
\end{itemize}

Conversion: \(\log_{10}(x) = \ln(x) / \ln(10) \approx \ln(x) / 2.303\).

\subsubsection*{Key identities}\label{key-identities}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Key identities}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2667}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.7333}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Identity
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Biological application
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\(\log(ab) = \log a + \log b\) & Combining probabilities across linked
loci \\
\(\log(a/b) = \log a - \log b\) & Henderson-Hasselbalch
\(\text{pH} = \text{p}K_a + \log([\text{A}^-]/[\text{HA}])\) \\
\(\log(a^n) = n \log a\) & Hill equation --- slope in log-log plot \\
\(\log_b(b^x) = x\) & Inverting exponential growth:
\(t = \ln(N/N_0)/r\) \\
\end{longtable}
}

\subsubsection*{Worked example --- doubling
time}\label{worked-example-doubling-time}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Worked example --- doubling time}

A bacterial culture grows at \(r = 0.5\) h\(^{-1}\). When does the
population double?

\[ N(t) = N_0 e^{rt} = 2 N_0 \implies e^{rt} = 2 \implies t = \frac{\ln 2}{r} = \frac{0.693}{0.5} \approx 1.39 \text{ h}  \label{eq:appendices_appendix_math_review_item_2}\]

The \textbf{``ln 2 trick''} recurs throughout biology: half-life
\(t_{1/2} = \ln 2 / k\) (decay); doubling time \(t_d = \ln 2 / r\)
(growth). Memorise \(\ln 2 \approx 0.693\).

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection*{C.2 Differential and Integral
Calculus}\label{c.2-differential-and-integral-calculus}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{C.2 Differential and Integral
Calculus}

Biology rarely requires advanced calculus, but the reader must be
comfortable with:

\subsubsection*{Derivatives as rates}\label{derivatives-as-rates}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Derivatives as rates}

\[ \frac{dN}{dt} = \text{rate of change of } N \text{ over time}  \label{eq:appendices_appendix_math_review_item_3}\]

In population ecology, \(dN/dt > 0\) means the population is growing;
\(dN/dt = 0\) is equilibrium; \(dN/dt < 0\) is decline. In enzyme
kinetics, \(d[P]/dt\) = reaction velocity \(v\).

\subsubsection*{Integration as
accumulation}\label{integration-as-accumulation}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Integration as accumulation}

\[ \int_0^T \frac{dN}{dt} dt = N(T) - N(0)  \label{eq:appendices_appendix_math_review_item_4}\]

The integral sums up infinitesimal contributions. Examples:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Total drug dose delivered by an infusion:
  \(\text{Dose} = \int_0^T (\text{infusion rate}) dt\).
\item
  Net photosynthesis over a day: \(\int_0^{24\text{h}} P(t) dt\).
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{First-order ODE: exponential growth and
decay}\label{first-order-ode-exponential-growth-and-decay}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{First-order ODE: exponential growth
and decay}

\[ \frac{dN}{dt} = kN \implies N(t) = N_0 e^{kt}  \label{eq:appendices_appendix_math_review_item_5}\]

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(k > 0\): growth with doubling time \(t_d = \ln 2 / k\).
\item
  \(k < 0\): decay with half-life \(t_{1/2} = \ln 2 / |k|\).
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection*{Logistic growth
(nonlinear)}\label{logistic-growth-nonlinear}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Logistic growth (nonlinear)}

\[ \frac{dN}{dt} = rN\left(1 - \frac{N}{K}\right)  \label{eq:appendices_appendix_math_review_item_6}\]

The closed-form solution is:

\[ N(t) = \frac{K}{1 + \left(\frac{K-N_0}{N_0}\right) e^{-rt}}  \label{eq:appendices_appendix_math_review_item_7}\]

Inflection (maximum rate) at \(N = K/2\), giving the sigmoid shape.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection*{C.3 Basic Probability}\label{c.3-basic-probability}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{C.3 Basic Probability}

\subsubsection*{Independent events}\label{independent-events}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Independent events}

\(P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)\) when events are independent. Example:
the probability that both parents transmit the recessive allele at a
locus (\(Aa \times Aa\)) is \((1/2)(1/2) = 1/4\).

\subsubsection*{Conditional probability and Bayes'
theorem}\label{conditional-probability-and-bayes-theorem}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Conditional probability and Bayes'
theorem}

\[ P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}  \label{eq:appendices_appendix_math_review_item_8}\]

Bayes' theorem --- central to \cref{sec:unit_0_active_inference} and to
medical testing:

\[ P(\text{disease} \mid +) = \frac{P(+ \mid \text{disease}) \cdot P(\text{disease})}{P(+)}  \label{eq:appendices_appendix_math_review_item_9}\]

A highly sensitive test can still have a low positive predictive value
if the disease is rare --- a counterintuitive result with major clinical
consequences.

\subsubsection*{Binomial distribution}\label{binomial-distribution}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Binomial distribution}

Number of successes in \(n\) independent trials, each with probability
\(p\):

\[ P(k \text{ successes}) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}  \label{eq:appendices_appendix_math_review_item_10}\]

Used for Punnett-square ratios, mark-recapture statistics, and
Hardy-Weinberg proportion testing.

\subsubsection*{Poisson distribution}\label{poisson-distribution}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Poisson distribution}

For rare events at mean rate \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\lambda}}{lambda} per interval:

\[ P(k) = \frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!}  \label{eq:appendices_appendix_math_review_item_11}\]

Used for spontaneous mutation counts per locus, bacterial cell counts in
Petri dishes (when plates are not overgrown), rare-disease incidence.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection*{C.4 Dimensional Analysis}\label{c.4-dimensional-analysis}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{C.4 Dimensional Analysis}

Every physical quantity carries \textbf{units}. Units must balance on
both sides of every equation --- if they don't, the equation is wrong.

\subsubsection*{Example --- diffusion
distance}\label{example-diffusion-distance}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Example --- diffusion distance}

Fick's rule for mean diffusion distance:

\[ x = \sqrt{2Dt}  \label{eq:appendices_appendix_math_review_item_12}\]

Check units: \(D\) has units of m\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2} s\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}; \(t\) has units of s; so
\(\sqrt{2Dt}\) has units of \(\sqrt{\text{m}^2} = \text{m}\). \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\checkmark}}{[ok]}

If a student wrote \(x = Dt\), units would be m\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2} s\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1} \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\cdot}}{.} s = m\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2} ---
dimensionally wrong.

\subsubsection*{Standard SI units used in this
book}\label{standard-si-units-used-in-this-book}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Standard SI units used in this
book}

Time & \(t\) & s & AP: 1 ms; cell cycle: 24 h \\
Amount & \(n\) & mol & ATP in a cell: 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{5}}{5} mol \\
Concentration & \([X]\) & mol L\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1} = M & cytoplasmic ATP: 5 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{3}}{3} M \\
Energy & \(E\) & J & ATP hydrolysis: 5 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{0}}{0} J per molecule, \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~}30.5 kJ
mol\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1} \\
Force & \(F\) & N & myosin step force: 5 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x} 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2} N = 5 pN \\
Electric potential & \(V\) & V & resting membrane: \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}0.07 V = \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}70 mV \\
\end{longtable}
}

\subsection*{C.5 Linear Algebra
Miniature}\label{c.5-linear-algebra-miniature}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{C.5 Linear Algebra Miniature}

Primarily trace knowledge is required for this book, but the two ideas
below recur.

\subsubsection*{Matrices as transitions}\label{matrices-as-transitions}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Matrices as transitions}

Allele-frequency change under migration between two populations is a 2 \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\times}}{x}
2 matrix multiplication. Markov transition matrices describe stochastic
gene expression (lac operon), state transitions in ion channels, and
Wright-Fisher drift.

\subsubsection*{Eigenvalues and
equilibrium}\label{eigenvalues-and-equilibrium}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Eigenvalues and equilibrium}

The dominant eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\) of a Leslie matrix equals the
long-term finite rate of increase. Eigenvectors give the stable age
distribution. This is the formal underpinning of
\cref{sec:unit_X_population_ecology}'s demographic analysis.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection*{C.6 Common Pitfalls in Biological
Math}\label{c.6-common-pitfalls-in-biological-math}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{C.6 Common Pitfalls in Biological
Math}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Confusing concentration and amount.} 1 nM is a concentration;
  1 nmol is an amount. A picomole of hormone in 5 L of blood is 0.2 pM.
\item
  \textbf{Units of rate constants.} First-order: s\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}. Second-order: M\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}
  s\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}. Third-order: M\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2} s\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}. Dimensional analysis typically exposes an
  order-of-magnitude error.
\item
  \textbf{Exponents and prefixes.} Milli- (10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{3}}{3}), micro- (10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{6}}{6}), nano-
  (10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{9}}{9}), pico- (10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{2}}{2}), femto- (10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{5}}{5}), atto- (10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{8}}{8}). Shifting by
  three orders of magnitude is common in biology; single errors are
  catastrophic.
\item
  \textbf{Logarithmic vs linear differences.} A tenfold change in
  {[}H\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+}{]} is a one-pH-unit change. ``Twice the acidity'' means \(0.3\)
  pH unit down, not \(2\) pH units.
\item
  \textbf{Error propagation.} Small errors in input variables compound
  through multi-step calculations. The textbook flags this at
  thermodynamics, kinetics, and evolutionary rate estimation in
  particular.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

The rule ``\(k_B T \approx \tfrac{1}{40}\) eV
\(\approx \tfrac{2.5}{1000}\) kJ mol\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1} at room temperature'' is useful:
hydrogen bonds (about 20 kJ mol\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}) are about 8
\(k_B T\), so they survive thermal fluctuations; van der Waals contacts
(about 1 kJ mol\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}) are about 0.4 \(k_B T\), so each
one is barely stable but collectively numerous contacts summate.

\item
  Standard \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Delta}}{Delta}G°\texorpdfstring{'}{'} for ATP \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} ADP + P\(_i\): \textbf{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}30.5 kJ mol\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}}.
\item
  Cellular \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\Delta}}{Delta}G (physiological {[}ATP{]}/{[}ADP{]}): \textbf{\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}57 kJ
  mol\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}}, roughly 22 \(k_B T\).
\item
  Number of ATP hydrolyses required to lift a 1 kg mass 1 m:
  about 300,000 --- illustrating why muscle needs 10\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{8}}{8} ATP
  molecules consumed per second.

C--C covalent bond & about 350 kJ mol\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1} \\
ATP hydrolysis (standard) & \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}30.5 kJ mol\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1} \\
ATP hydrolysis (cellular) & \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}57 kJ mol\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1} \\
Glucose complete oxidation & \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}2870 kJ mol\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1} \\
Photosynthesis per photon (680 nm) & 176 kJ mol\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1} \\
Daily human basal energy & 7000 kJ d\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1} (\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~}1700 kcal d\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}) \\
\end{longtable}
}

\subsection*{E.4 Ultra-Trace and Context-Dependent
Elements}\label{e.4-ultra-trace-and-context-dependent-elements}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{E.4 Ultra-Trace and Context-Dependent
Elements}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Nickel (Ni)} --- cofactor in urease (bacterial, plant) and
  hydrogenase; suspected but not proven essential in mammals.
\item
  \textbf{Silicon (Si)} --- structural in diatoms, horsetails, grasses
  (silica phytoliths); supports collagen cross-linking in vertebrates.
\item
  \textbf{Boron (B)} --- essential in plants (cell-wall cross-linking
  via borate--rhamnogalacturonan); possibly beneficial in vertebrates.
\item
  \textbf{Vanadium (V)} --- sea-squirt blood pigment (vanadocytes);
  pharmacology for insulin-mimetic effects.
\item
  \textbf{Tungsten (W)} --- used instead of molybdenum by
  hyperthermophilic archaea.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection*{E.5 Life Without an Expected
Element}\label{e.5-life-without-an-expected-element}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{E.5 Life Without an Expected Element}

Biology has bent the rules. Examples of organisms that substitute or
replace commonly ``essential'' elements:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Iron-free bacteria in deep-sea hydrothermal vents} --- use
  manganese peroxidases instead.
\item
  \textbf{Selenocysteine} (the ``21st amino acid'') --- expands the
  amino-acid alphabet using the rare element Se.
\item
  \textbf{Pyrrolysine} (the ``22nd amino acid'') --- found in
  methanogenic archaea; does not require a rare element, but is an
  unusual 22-atom residue.
\item
  \textbf{Arsenic-based life controversy (GFAJ-1, 2010)} --- claim of As
  replacing P in DNA of a \emph{Halomonas} strain; later retracted.
\end{itemize}

The periodic table remains under-explored for biological innovations.
Astrobiological life may use different element sets entirely.

\section*{Appendix F --- Master Glossary of Biological
Terms}\label{appendix-f-master-glossary-of-biological-terms}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Appendix F --- Master Glossary of
Biological Terms}

\label{sec:glossary}

\emph{Etymology notation: {[}Gk{]} = Greek; \hyperref[l]{L} = Latin;
{[}OFr{]} = Old French; {[}Ar{]} = Arabic.} \emph{Cross-references use
semantic \texttt{\textbackslash{}cref\{...\}} links generated from the
canonical table of contents.}

\emph{Maintenance note: glossary terms must use a Pandoc bracketed span,
\texttt{{[}**Term**{]}\{\#gl:\textless{}slug\textgreater{}\}} (with
\breaktt{markdown+bracketed\_spans}, Pandoc emits a real LaTeX
\texttt{\textbackslash{}label\{gl:...\}} in PDF). Chapters link with
\texttt{{[}**term**{]}(\#gl:\textless{}slug\textgreater{})}. After
editing terms, run
\breaktt{uv\ run\ python\ scripts/link\_glossary.py\ -\/-check} from the
project root and verify \breaktt{tests/test\_build\_invariants.py} plus
markdown validation.}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection*{A}\label{a}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{A}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:abiotic}{\textbf{Abiotic}} {[}Gk
\emph{a} = without + \emph{bios} = life + \emph{-ic} = pertaining to{]}
--- Non-living physical and chemical components of an environment
(light, temperature, water, minerals). Contrast with \textbf{biotic}. \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
\cref{sec:unit_X_biomes_and_conservation}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:actin}{\textbf{Actin}} {[}Gk
\emph{aktis} = ray or beam{]} --- A 42 kDa globular protein (G-actin)
that polymerises into filaments (F-actin); a major component of the
cytoskeleton, sarcomeres, and lamellipodia. \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
\cref{sec:unit_II_cell_structure}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:action-potential}{\textbf{Action
potential}} {[}L \emph{actio} = a doing + \emph{potentia} = power{]} ---
A transient, all-or-none reversal of membrane potential
(about \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}70 mV to +40 mV) propagated along neuronal axons; gated
by voltage-dependent Na\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} and K\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} channels. Described mathematically by
the Hodgkin-Huxley equations (1952). \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \cref{sec:unit_IX_nervous_system}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:adaptive-immunity}{\textbf{Adaptive
immunity}} {[}L \emph{adaptare} = to fit + \emph{immunis} = exempt{]}
--- Antigen-specific defence mediated by B and T lymphocytes. It is
slower than innate immunity during a first exposure but generates
immunological memory, enabling faster and stronger secondary responses.
\texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \cref{sec:unit_IX_endocrine_and_immune}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:adenosine-triphosphate}{\textbf{Adenosine
triphosphate (ATP)}} {[}Gk \emph{aden} = gland (as in adenine,
identified in gland tissue) + \emph{tri} = three + \emph{phosphorus} =
light-bearer{]} --- A central phosphoryl-group donor and short-term
energy carrier in cells. Hydrolysis to ADP + P\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{i}}{i} releases
about 30.5 kJ/mol under biochemical standard conditions, while
the effective cellular free energy is often larger in magnitude because
ATP, ADP, and P\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{i}}{i} concentrations are far from equilibrium. \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
\cref{sec:unit_III_bioenergetics_and_respiration}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:aerobic}{\textbf{Aerobic}} {[}Gk
\emph{aer} = air + \emph{bios} = life{]} --- Requiring molecular oxygen
(O\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2}) as the terminal electron acceptor in cellular respiration.
Opposite: \textbf{anaerobic}. \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
\cref{sec:unit_III_bioenergetics_and_respiration}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:allele}{\textbf{Allele}} {[}Gk
\emph{allelon} = of each other; shortened from \emph{allelemorph}{]} ---
One of two or more alternative forms of a gene at the same chromosomal
locus. Defined by a distinct nucleotide sequence. \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
\cref{sec:unit_V_mendelian_genetics}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:allostasis}{\textbf{Allostasis}} {[}Gk
\emph{allos} = other + \emph{stasis} = standing{]} --- Predictive
physiological regulation in which the brain adjusts setpoints and
resource allocation in anticipation of demand, rather than merely
correcting error after disturbance. \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
\cref{sec:unit_IX_endocrine_and_immune}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:allosteric}{\textbf{Allosteric}} {[}Gk
\emph{allos} = other + \emph{stereos} = solid/space{]} --- Describing a
regulatory site on an enzyme or receptor that is spatially distinct from
the active site; ligand binding there changes the macromolecule's
conformation and activity. \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \cref{sec:unit_I_enzymes_and_kinetics}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:anaerobic}{\textbf{Anaerobic}} {[}Gk
\emph{an} = without + \emph{aer} = air + \emph{bios} = life{]} ---
Occurring without oxygen. Anaerobic respiration uses alternative
electron acceptors (nitrate, sulphate); fermentation regenerates NAD\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+}
without any external acceptor. \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
\cref{sec:unit_III_bioenergetics_and_respiration}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:anaphase}{\textbf{Anaphase}} {[}Gk
\emph{ana} = up/apart + \emph{phasis} = appearance{]} --- The stage of
mitosis/meiosis in which sister chromatids (mitosis, meiosis II) or
homologous chromosomes (meiosis I) are pulled to opposite poles by
spindle fibres. \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \cref{sec:unit_IV_dna_replication_and_cell_cycle}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:angiosperm}{\textbf{Angiosperm}} {[}Gk
\emph{angeion} = vessel/container + \emph{sperma} = seed{]} --- A
flowering plant whose seeds are enclosed within a fruit derived from the
ovary wall; the dominant plant group (about 300,000 species).
Contrast: \textbf{gymnosperm}. \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
\cref{sec:unit_VIII_plant_structure_and_water}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:anticodon}{\textbf{Anticodon}} {[}Gk
\emph{anti} = against or opposite + L \emph{codex} = writing block{]}
--- The three-nucleotide sequence on a tRNA molecule that base-pairs
with the complementary codon on mRNA during translation. \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
\cref{sec:unit_IV_gene_expression}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:apoptosis}{\textbf{Apoptosis}} {[}Gk
\emph{apo} = away + \emph{ptōsis} = a falling{]} --- Programmed,
caspase-mediated cell death characterised by chromatin condensation, DNA
fragmentation, and membrane blebbing, without inflammatory response.
Contrast: \textbf{necrosis}. \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \cref{sec:unit_II_cell_signaling}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:archaea}{\textbf{Archaea}} {[}Gk
\emph{archaios} = ancient{]} --- One of three domains of life;
prokaryotes with ether-linked isoprenoid membrane lipids, histone-like
proteins, and replication/transcription machinery closer to eukaryotes
than to bacteria. Discovered by Woese \& Fox (1977). \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
\cref{sec:unit_II_cell_theory,sec:unit_VI_phylogenetics}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:atp-synthase}{\textbf{ATP synthase}}
{[}see ATP + Gk \emph{syn} = together + \emph{thesis} = a placing{]} ---
Also Complex V; a rotary F\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{0}}{0}F\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{1}}{1} molecular motor driven by the
proton-motive force to phosphorylate ADP to ATP. The c-ring rotation of
120° per ATP was directly visualised by Noji et al.~(1997). \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
\cref{sec:unit_III_bioenergetics_and_respiration}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:autotroph}{\textbf{Autotroph}} {[}Gk
\emph{autos} = self + \emph{trophe} = nourishment{]} --- An organism
that produces its own organic molecules from inorganic carbon (CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2});
either \textbf{photoautotroph} (energy from light) or
\textbf{chemoautotroph} (energy from inorganic chemicals). \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
\cref{sec:unit_II_cell_theory,sec:unit_X_community_ecology}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:autonomic-nervous-system}{\textbf{Autonomic
nervous system (ANS)}} {[}Gk \emph{autonomos} = self-governing{]} ---
The visceral motor division of the peripheral nervous system; divided
into \textbf{sympathetic} (thoracolumbar; noradrenaline/adrenaline;
``fight-or-flight'') and \textbf{parasympathetic} (craniosacral;
acetylcholine; ``rest-and-digest'') branches. ANS innervates smooth
muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands. \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \cref{sec:unit_IX_nervous_system}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:axon-hillock}{\textbf{Axon hillock}}
{[}Gk \emph{axon} = axis + OE \emph{hyll} = small hill{]} --- The region
of the neuron where the axon originates from the cell body (soma); the
site of action potential initiation due to the high density of
voltage-gated Na\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} channels. EPSPs must summate here to reach threshold
(about \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{-}}{-}55 mV). \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \cref{sec:unit_IX_nervous_system}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection*{B}\label{b}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{B}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:base-pair}{\textbf{Base pair (bp)}}
{[}Gk \emph{basis} = step, foundation{]} --- A complementary nucleotide
pair held by hydrogen bonds in double-stranded nucleic acids: A--T (2
H-bonds in DNA) and G--C (3 H-bonds). One bp \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\approx}}{~} 0.34 nm along the DNA
helix. \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \cref{sec:unit_IV_dna_replication_and_cell_cycle}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:biofilm}{\textbf{Biofilm}} {[}Gk
\emph{bios} = life + L \emph{filum} = thread{]} --- A structured
community of microorganisms attached to a surface and enclosed in a
self-produced extracellular polysaccharide matrix; regulated by quorum
sensing; often up to 1,000-fold more antibiotic tolerant than planktonic
cells because matrix diffusion limits, slow growth, stress responses,
and persister cells overlap. \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
\cref{sec:unit_VII_bacteria_archaea_viruses}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:biome}{\textbf{Biome}} {[}Gk
\emph{bios} = life + \emph{-ome} = mass/body{]} --- A large-scale
terrestrial or aquatic ecosystem characterised by a distinctive climate,
vegetation, and fauna. Classified by Whittaker (1975) primarily by mean
annual precipitation (MAP) and mean annual temperature (MAT). \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
\cref{sec:unit_X_biomes_and_conservation}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:buffer}{\textbf{Buffer}} {[}OFr
\emph{bufer} = to protect from a blow{]} --- A solution containing a
weak acid and its conjugate base that resists changes in pH by absorbing
added H\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{+}}{+} or OH\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{-}}{-}. Effective within \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\pm}}{+/-}1 pH unit of pK\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{a}}{a}
(Henderson-Hasselbalch). \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \cref{sec:unit_I_atoms_molecules}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection*{C}\label{c}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{C}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:calvin-cycle}{\textbf{Calvin cycle}}
{[}named for Melvin Calvin, who elucidated it using \texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{1}}{1}\texorpdfstring{\textsuperscript{4}}{4}C radioisotopes,
1950{]} --- The light-independent carbon-fixation reactions of
photosynthesis in the chloroplast stroma; not literally dark, because
they depend on ATP and NADPH produced by the light reactions. Also
called the Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle. Net: 3 CO\texorpdfstring{\textsubscript{2}}{2} + 9 ATP + 6 NADPH \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->}
G3P. \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \cref{sec:unit_III_photosynthesis}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:caspase}{\textbf{Caspase}} {[}L
\emph{caspase} = cysteine-containing aspartate protease{]} --- A family
of cysteine proteases that execute apoptosis; exists as inactive
zymogens; activated by cleavage at specific aspartate residues in a
proteolytic cascade. \texorpdfstring{\ensuremath{\to}}{->} \cref{sec:unit_II_cell_signaling}

\protect\phantomsection\label{gl:cell-cycle}{\textbf{Cell cycle}} {[}L
